The Yogavāsiṣṭha of...
The *Vālmīki-Śrīvāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, together with its commentary titled *Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The *Vāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*, edited by Vāsudeva Śarman, son of Paṇaśīkara Upāhv Lakṣmaṇa Śarman.
Edited by Vāsudeva Laxmaṇa Śāstrī Paṇśīkar. The Third Chapter: On Origination.
First Chapter.
The knower of Brahman shines as Brahman within himself through the splendors of speech, like a dream;
whatever one knows through the words arising from his own [inner voice], that he truly knows.
Truth, knowledge, infinite, one, undecaying, eternal, all-pervasive, perpetual, the inner Brahman, the elixir, a mass of bliss, full, supreme, and purifying;
the light of one's own Self, without beginning, middle, or end, [repeatedly] by the play of Māyā—
I pay homage to the pure state, which possesses every form, from which all illusion has been cast away, and which is free from fear. || 1 ||
Liberation of the self comes from knowledge alone, and not through ritual actions or meditative concentrations;
it is proclaimed that when this [self] is unknown, it creates its own manifestation (or "its own object of perception," according to the variant reading).

Now, for the qualified seeker who is endowed with the aforementioned means of accomplishment— [the reading being "svayaṃ dṛśyam"]— the wise one should investigate until he attains rest within the Self, that peace called the fourth state (*turyapada*), which is beyond further destruction.

Now, the sequence of knowledge is correctly taught to Śrī Rāma— the foremost among qualified aspirants who is endowed with all the means described in the two preceding chapters— as follows: "The method of inquiry, which must be performed until the direct realization of reality is attained, is now [to be explained]."

Having first made a formal proposition, the venerable Śrī Vasiṣṭha proceeds to describe it in detail through the subsequent text; he now briefly states the essential purport of the "Chapter on Origination" (Utpatti-prakaraṇa), which was begun for the sake of easily awakening [the disciple] to the non-duality of Brahman by means of describing the manner of creation.
Desiring to demonstrate that very point,

[the author] intends to show here as well— just as in the case of the comprehension of the meaning of great sayings (mahāvākya) such as "I am Brahman"— the scriptural passage beginning with "In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated" which demonstrates the process of creation, [reading the text as] "of the nature of an existent entity."

When the awakening of understanding regarding the object to be known arises through even a single part of the illustration, the determination of the meaning of the Great Sentence (mahāvākya) should be grasped as something to be adopted; thus, he shows that the conclusion follows the manner previously stated with the words "By the rays of speech," etc., [establishing] Brahman alone.

The knower of Brahman, having directly realized his own true nature through the light of the Self ignited by the non-dual mental modification (*akhaṇḍākāra-vṛtti*) produced by the great sayings (*mahāvākya*), shines forth as his ultimate, eternally liberated, and perfect essence. The sense is that for his own liberation, he requires nothing other than the mental modification generated by the [great] sayings. Why is that?

The meaning is this: since this visible world, consisting of the body, senses, and so forth, as well as space and the rest—which is of the nature of bondage—appears within the Self, which is the innermost self that is Brahman itself, like a dream; for the cessation of a dream-bondage does not require any means other than awakening. And thus:

In the Śruti, having raised the objection—"What indeed was that Brahman, unknown, by knowing which humans imagine they shall become [Brahman], from which all this has come into being?"—the answer is stated: "Verily, in the beginning, this was Brahman;
it knew only itself: 'I am Brahman. Therefore, it became all this. All this...

"Full" means having the single nature of the bliss of the non-transmigrating state (*asaṃsāribhūmānanda*). In this scriptural passage, it is stated that Brahman itself, through the awakening to its own true nature, became liberated from bondage and full; therefore, prior to that awakening to its own true nature, it was characterized by the perception of duality—consisting of the pleasant and the unpleasant—as well as limitation, just like a dream.
The fact that bondage is experienced as if it were real makes it clear that bondage is false and that the inner self (pratīc) alone is Brahman.

In this regard, just as there are explanatory passages (arthavāda) that establish this truth—such as "By name and form alone is That differentiated; He has entered here even unto the tips of the fingernails"—it is understood with even greater clarity.

By thus establishing that the world and the state of being the individual soul— which have ignorance as their sole material cause (upādāna) consisting of Brahman alone— possess no existence apart from Brahman even during the three periods of time such as origination, and so forth, as indicated by the scriptural passages concerning the entry into the previous creation and so on, their falsity (mithyātva) alone is proven.

The sense is that, just as [the Upaniṣads] culminate in the non-duality of Brahman—which is the subject matter of the purport of their own principal great sentences—so too should it be understood here. To the question, "Let it be so; what does that matter to us?", he replies with the words beginning with "That" (tad):
"That Brahman, even now, by one who is qualified such as ourselves, through those [means] arising from the word 'self'..."

Through the means of hearing and so forth, he who knows reality exactly as it is— that "I am indeed Brahman"— and directly realizes it, knows even that previously described fruit of liberation, which is Brahman, full, eternal, free, and of the nature of light (or, according to another reading, of existence), while still living.

One experiences it directly. And thus says the Śruti: "Whosoever among the gods awakened to this, he indeed became that; as it was for the seers, so it was for human beings. Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva realized: "I was Manu and I was the Sun. Or else, [this applies] to this section as well.

[The reading: That which is desired to be known by those seeking liberation because it is unknown to them—this world, which appears as the manifestation of the signified (*bhā*) and the manifestation of the objects revealed by that signified (*bhās*), consisting of the word "Brahman" and the verbal proliferation of expressive sounds (*vāk*); and these three—the name, form, and action—are indeed this [world].

The knower of Brahman, seeing his own self as non-distinct from the states of the manifold world of duality shown by the scriptures—just as one sees a dream within one's own self—[perceives] "this is action" (karma). (p. 126)
That which appears as having the nature of suffering— such as slaughter, bondage, grief, and delusion— is indeed Brahman appearing in that way; yet,

only that qualified seeker who knows what remains when all duality is negated by such statements as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) arising from their own words— which leave only the pure Self— is truly [Brahman].

The meaning is that he knows that Brahman in its true essence (*tattvataḥ*), and not as one who perceives it as conjoined with superimposed name, form, and so forth. Alternatively, "vāk" (speech) indicates the organs of action (*karmendriya*), which are primarily characterized by the power of activities such as speaking;
"bhā" (light) indicates the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), which are primarily characterized by illumination. He is the knower of Brahman who, through these gateways, [perceives] reality.

Even Brahmā, though being Brahman, perceives himself as if he were not Brahman, appearing otherwise like a dream; for one whose face is turned outward cannot achieve the vision of reality. As the scripture declares: "The Self-existent pierced the openings [of the senses] outward; therefore one looks outward, and not at the inner self," and so forth.
But that qualified person who knows— even though this world-appearance is well-known— that even this entire universe is Brahman alone,
and "all this is the Self alone," through cognitions produced by supreme statements concerning ultimate reality such as these, [knows] that which is pure Being, the substratum of all.

With the outward movement of the external senses withdrawn and turned inward, one knows that Brahman. Thus, by an external perspective even Brahman, when seen, is indeed a source of misfortune; however, by the authoritative inward perspective, even the world, when seen, leads to the supreme goal. This is stated under the guise of elaborating upon the process of creation.
The meaning is that the purpose (*tātparya*) of this treatise is the cultivation of the inward vision (*pratyagdṛṣṭi*). Alternatively, the ellipsis is to be supplied as follows:

"This is being stated by means of the rays of the words of instruction (*upadeśavāk*) that are about to be spoken, and by the illuminations of examples, narratives, and logical arguments (*dṛṣṭāntākhyānopapatti*). That which is Brahman is, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), indeed the Knower of Brahman (*brahmavit*).

One should not be deluded into thinking that there exists some other distinct entity called "Brahman," separate from one's own self, located in a distant or remote place. Furthermore, this visible phenomenal world (dṛśyaprapañca) appears as something superimposed upon the Self alone, like a dream;
one should not be deluded into thinking that even this is a separate ultimate reality. In that regard:

Regarding the two states— the state of Brahman and the state of the world— whether one is discriminating or non-discriminating, that which is well-known in common worldly usage as "I am a Brāhmaṇa," "I am a Kṣatriya," or "I am Devadatta," arising from words belonging to oneself, or even that which is produced by one's own words and is inherently false, [is sublated by the realization] "I am indeed Brahman."

If one knows one's own true nature—be it of such-and-such a kind—as produced by cognitions arising from words denoting the reality taught in scriptures such as "I am indeed consciousness" (cidevāham), then one knows that very thing and experiences it again and again. For one who perceives the self as a transmigrating being, only transmigration bears fruit; but for one who perceives the self as Brahman, only the state of Brahman bears fruit. Therefore, it is only by such a perceiver [that this is known].
The term *bhāva* means "that which is to be cultivated. Alternatively: [5] But has not Brahman already been taught previously?

The true nature of Brahman as it exists is called the "determination of existence" (*sattāniyati*), by such passages as: "There exists the Self of infinite manifestations, all-pervading, the refuge of all," and so forth. Since there is an absence of tranquility and other qualities regarding that Brahman thus taught, the mind remains unstable.
Once [the truth] has been attained, the means such as tranquility (*śama*) and the like, as well as human effort for its firm consolidation, have been taught;

thus, no further instruction remains to be given. If Brahman does not shine forth through the illumination of the meaning of the sentence taught even once, then it will be exactly the same even if it is taught a hundred times—what can be done about this?
Fearing that repeated instruction might amount to the mere grinding of what is already ground, he says: "By the splendors of speech.

That knower of Brahman—the seeker of Brahman or the listener—by means of the splendors of speech, that is, by the reasons consisting of the illuminations of the meaning of the words of instruction given once, that Brahman shines forth and manifests as being itself.

The meaning is that it is as if a dream: it is mostly faded and does not become very firm; or rather, like a whispered awakening statement composed of one's own name and so forth while under the influence of sleep—where the names of the constellations and such are not clearly fixed—one does not perceive it correctly. "He himself, O Devadatta, O... [he says].
Just as one recognizes someone by means of an address using a name long established through constant usage— such as "Yajñadatta"—

so too, by means of the cognitions arising from the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) which have been firmly familiarized through long-term practice of hearing and so forth, he who knows [the Self] knows that very [Self]. The meaning is that such an indubitable self-awareness alone is the cause for the destruction of ignorance.

And thus, for the sake of such firm certainty and immediate experience (*aparokṣānubhava*), the instruction through repeated logical arguments must be practiced until the fruit arises; this is the sense in which the subsequent text is justified. And so says the Sūtra:
"Repetition [is required] because of the repeated instruction.

Alternatively, just as one who does not know Brahman— being permeated by long-standing latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such as fear arising from the waking state— is, through ignorance (*avidyā*), [afflicted] in a dream by words of contempt, rebuke, and intimidation, and by appearances of trembling with fear, fleeing, falling into pits, and so forth;

Or, as characterized by suffering, one appears like a lay devotee (*upāsaka*) who, being permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of his waking state as a god, appears in a dream like a deity or a king through such verbal expressions as praise and eulogy, and through appearances such as laughing, playing, ascending a celestial chariot (*vimāna*), and roaming through the sky.

Just as that which is characterized by the [reading "vāgbhā"] appears [as such], so too the knower of Brahman, permeated by long-practiced hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other means, perceives in a dream: "All this is indeed Brahman; all this is indeed the Self;
I alone am all this; I am everything."

It shines through words that establish the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and through the manifestations of the true nature of Brahman (*vāstavabrahmabhāva*). Likewise, even in the state of the fruit (*phalāvasthā*), the results pertaining to the next world are like a dream;
for it will be demonstrated in the *Līlopākhyāna* and other passages that these results follow from the force of deeply cultivated latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Now, what is the proof for this? To that he says: "That which... That very fact—that even the next world follows from latent impressions (vāsanā) just like a dream—is expressed by the words themselves; it is not dependent on an external source.
Thus, the Śruti texts, being "self-expressive" (sva-śabda), are determined by the cognitions arising from them, which are intrinsically valid (svataḥ-pramāṇa).

Now, when it seems as though they are killing him, or conquering him, or an elephant is frightening him, or he falls as if into a pit—whatever fear he perceives while awake, that he imagines there through ignorance. Furthermore, when he thinks, "I am like a god," or "I am like a king," or "I am indeed all this"—that is his supreme world. Thus, whether he is a tiger here or a lion...

Whatever they become, that they become; whatever the mind is, one becomes absorbed in that. This is an eternal secret, according to such scriptural passages as: "By the action of the mind, one enters this body," and so forth. Furthermore: "Whichever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end, to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, being constantly permeated by that thought."
The meaning is that this is also supported by such Smṛti passages as, "Therefore, at all times remember Me.

Thus, just as one who knows the transmigrating self or the nature of Brahman during the stage of practice (abhyāsa) knows and experiences that very same thing in the state of fruition, there is only the latent impression (vāsanā) of the continuous experience of Brahman.

The sense is that the intended meaning of the section on origination is that [Brahman] is to be made firm. Alternatively, through words— that is, the means of valid cognition consisting of the Śruti, Smṛti, and so forth— and through lights— that is, the illuminations of the experience of the wise—
the knower of Brahman is indeed Brahman itself.

That which is known as its state of non-Brahmanhood during the condition of ignorance, as well as the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], appear within the Self like a dream; for the Śruti says, "It has three abodes and three dreams.
Therefore, transmigratory existence is merely a matter of imagination within the innermost Self. This is the meaning stated.
"And doubt—let these be examined with the vision turned inward.

This is established by such statements in the *Vārttika* and the experiential testimony of the learned. Thus, the qualified person who possesses these two aforementioned qualities—one who has directly realized the truth of the Self as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand and is skilled in instruction—[is the fit recipient].
The teacher, through methods such as reasoning and refutation that arise from the words of his instruction and are conducive to personal experience, knows whatever is of a certain nature;

he knows that very thing through his own experience as well. "A person who has a teacher knows. "From the teacher alone does knowledge, once understood, reach its most excellent state. The teacher is the knower, one who is skilled in instruction.

This is the meaning of such scriptural passages as these. Alternatively, Brahman—which is established through the experience of those who know Brahman—appears in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) as being identical with speech and light; just as words such as "pot" manifest their objects as colored by themselves through convention, so too Brahman, having attained that state, manifests itself.

Just as light manifests itself as illumination, so too Brahman manifests as colored by the objects of manifestation, its own self-luminosity being inseparable from them; this is the meaning. Now, one might ask: how can that which is unattached and non-dual manifest through the coloring of another? To this, he says: "That which..."

For this reason—namely, because through superimposition upon the Self it extends this [universe] like a dream—it is called "idam-tat" (this-that); the meaning is that it is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*). And thus, there is a coloring of the cause by the effect.
This is indeed appropriate; the sense is that because the effect is illusory, there is no contradiction with the state of being unattached and non-dual.

That Brahman, being of such a nature, is [grasped] by words such as "Self" (ātman) and so forth—words which, arising from its own [etymological] roots, refer exclusively to its own pervasive form through a cognition refined [of all else].

He knows that [Brahman], whose nature is pure consciousness, self-luminous, unattached, and indifferent; the meaning is that he does not perceive it as being conjoined with specific names and forms. Alternatively, because Brahman is self-luminous, even though the knower of Brahman is independent of anything else in his own manifestation, [the scripture says] "by means of speech," for speech alone is his [instrument].

"Light exists; indeed, the sun itself becomes his light," according to the statement of the Śruti. Due to delusion caused by other lights, [the Self] shines forth in its isolated state—unmixed with other lights—only during states such as *samādhi*, like in a dream, and not during the waking state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). To that very effect, the Śruti says: "The Self alone becomes his light; by the light of the Self alone does he sit."

"He ages" and "he performs action"—this is stated to demonstrate the manifestation of his self-luminosity (*svayaṃjyotiṣṭva*). Thus, he states the means for experiencing the self-luminous Self (*svayaṃjyotirātman*), which has been explained in the context of dream, even during the waking state:
"That which," "this," "that," and "self."

That collection of objects which approaches—that is, comes toward—the enjoyer by means of sounds arising from the notions of objects pertaining to the physical, the divine, and the personal (ādhibhautika, ādhidaivika, and adhyātmika)—he who knows that [collection] knows it as being Brahman itself, and not as a self characterized by imagined limiting adjuncts (upādhi). This is because a dull-witted self lacks the power of cognition; therefore, there is no other seer than this.

The sense is that there is no other hearer than this [Self], because of the negation of any other seer or hearer. Thus, while in the manifestation of external objects there may be a commingling with another light, there is no such commingling in the presentation of internal objects; therefore, even in the waking state, the Self as its own light is easily understood by the discerning at all times.

The intention is that one should remain intent upon the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that. Alternatively, [verse 10]: That which appears through the cognitions arising from the words of the *karmakāṇḍa*—which set forth this triad: this world as the locus of action (*karmasthāna*), heaven and so forth as the locus of its fruit (*tatphalasthāna*), and oneself as the enjoyer of that fruit—is [the object of this contemplation].

And whatever appears through the words of the Upanishads and the illuminations of reflection and so forth—such as "I am the knower of Brahman" or "I am Brahman"—all that shines within the Self only so long as one is unawakened, like a dream, and not in the *bhūman* (the Infinite) Self. For the Shruti declares: "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the *bhūman*. And all the scriptures [teach this].

And from the Bhāṣya: "Injunctions, prohibitions, and those concerning liberation do not transcend having as their object one who is possessed of ignorance. Thus, imitating the Vedic revelation that "Yoga knows this secret," he says: "He who knows what [knows it].
The meaning is that this is established solely by the experience of the wise. Regarding this difficult verse, even for the intelligent...
Difficult to traverse; these ten topics have been fully elucidated through the grace of the Guru. || 1 ||
By this reasoning, while this world exists within the creation in the expanse of Brahman, the objection—"What is this? Whose is it? Where is it?"—has been refuted.

Having thus demonstrated the intermediate subject matter by way of showing a summary of the treatise's meaning, he says "by means of reasoning" (*nyāyena*), because the resolution of the previous objection— which follows as a necessary consequence of the intermediate purpose characterized by the knowledge of the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva-jñāna*)— is also established by implication. By this [statement], in brief...

By means of the principle that what is superimposed has no existence apart from its substratum— as indicated by what has been shown and will be explained in detail, or by the method of superimposition and negation (*adhyāropāpavāda*)—
within this visible creation consisting of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which exists through a process of superimposition upon the ether of Brahman.

Or, if creation exists and the process of negation (apavāda) is observed in the world, while only the Brahma-ether—the mere space of Brahman—remains, then, O Blessed One, tell me this: what is it that perishes? What is it that is born again? What is it that increases? By such means as these, you previously raised the objection regarding the impossibility of the destruction and so forth of that which is existent; [now explain] that by its own nature...

It was already refuted [in the previous verse]. The meaning is that since the destruction of an existing thing is not admitted, and the existence of a perishable thing is not admitted, there is no basis for the objection. || 2 ||
O wise one, listen as I speak all of this according to my knowledge, according to the facts, in their proper order, and according to their true nature. (3)
Having thus demonstrated the intermediate subject matter and its results, he promises an extensive exposition with the words "I [shall speak].

The meaning is: "I shall state in detail this collection of topics which has been shown here in brief. This is done respectively according to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and experience (*anubhava*), according to the investigation of knowledge as it truly is (*yathājñāna*), and according to the determination of the logical justification for the proofs (*sādhana-upapatti*) as they actually exist (*yathāvastu*).

And according to the maturation of the intellects of the listeners, it is in accordance with their own nature. Since the meaning of the word applies everywhere without deviation, there is an *avyayībhāva* compound. Alternatively, "yathāvastu" refers to the state prior to creation;
since at that time the entire world consists of pure existence (*sanmātra*), "yathājñāna" refers to the state of being oriented toward the reckoning of the commencement of creation.

"Respectively" refers to the statement of the sequence of emanation through the process of becoming gross. "According to its own nature" refers to the statement that its nature remains unmodified even during the state of superimposition upon the world. "All" refers to the statement of the fullness to be attained through knowledge. This is based on the Vedic scripture: "Therefore, it became all," which refers to the state of fullness.
Because all sounds are seen [as such]. The address "O wise one" (*budha*) is a reminder of the status of the highest qualification, intended to generate reverence for the hearing [of this teaching].
One sees the world as if in a dream, being oneself the knower whose body is the space of consciousness (or, according to another reading, *cinmaya*, consisting of consciousness).
The very analogy of the dream and the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) includes both "I-ness" and "you-ness. (4)

He clarifies the intended meaning of what was stated—that the world is like a dream within the Self—with the words "like a dream. Whatever world one perceives as having assumed the state of the body and the individual soul (*jīva*) within the space of consciousness (*cin-nabhas*), one perceives that just like a dream.
Just as the perception of a dream is not sublated even when its objects are sublated, so too is the perception of the world. This is because of the nature of the seer (*dṛśi*).

The sense is that the purport [of the scripture] lies in its being real. Likewise, even the form of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which appears as "I" through identity with the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and as "thou" through the state of externality (*parāgbhāva*), is properly connected—that is, correctly correlated—as the illustrated case (*dārṣṭāntika*) to the example of the dream-world. The purport regarding it is its falsity (*mithyātva*).

[This is] the state of being. Or rather, one might object: "How can a dream-vision, which is not born of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), serve as an illustration for that which is born of the means of valid cognition? To this he says: "The knower of the body" (*dehavit*). Although one perceives the external world through the means of valid cognition, nevertheless, [the Self] is the illuminator of the individual and collective bodies, which consist of the aggregate of causes and effects.

[The reading is *kāraṇasaṃghātāḥ*] means that it is not itself dependent upon external means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, one might object: "Since the body also possesses color and other qualities, it too should appear through the eyes and other senses. To this he says: "I-ness" (*ahaṃtva*). If that [body] were to appear through the eyes and so forth, then it would appear as "this" (*idam*) alone. Regarding its object:

Because "this-ness" (idaṃtva) is observed everywhere [in the waking state], whereas "I-ness" (ahaṃtva) and "you-ness" (tvaṃtva) appearing therein are only consistent and logical when viewed through the analogy of the dream-world; this is the meaning. Alternatively, even if the body shares the same nature as a dream, how can the entire external world, consisting of name and form, be likewise?

To this, he says: "endowed with 'I' and 'you'. It is not merely the external form and so forth that appears as something extracted; rather, it is the form of the object as integrated with the meaning of "I" (the *ahamartha*), appearing as a triadic structure (*tripuṭī*) such as "I see the form. And that...

Because it is accessible solely through direct perception (*sākṣimātragamyatvāt*), the illustrative example of dreaming and the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) necessarily applies to the case being illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*); this is the remainder [of the argument]. For when there is a cognition whose object is superimposed (*adhyasta*), a real entity does not become its object. Indeed, only that which is superimposed manifests itself in delusions (*bhrama*); nothing else whatsoever manifests in delusions.

The meaning is that for those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that fall outside the established tenets (*siddhānta*), their status as conventionally valid (*vyāvahārikaprāmāṇya*) is not obstructed even by their mere non-contradiction with objects in worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*). || 4 ||
(128) Following this treatise,
which consists of the discourse on the conduct of those seeking liberation,
I shall now fully expound this subsequent treatise concerning origination. || 5 ||
The word "atha" (now/then) indicates an immediate sequence and a causal connection. || 5 ||

This bondage arises from the existence of the visible; [the reading is "sadbhāvo dṛśyābhāvena" (existence by means of the absence of the visible)]. Bondage is not possible when the visible does not exist; listen now to how this visible [world] comes to be, in due order.

To the objection, "But for me, who seeks the means for the removal of bondage, what is the use of hearing this section on the falsity of the visible world and its subsequent production?", he says: "Bondage... (verse 6).
Whatever arises in the world, that indeed grows;
that very same thing attains liberation, or heaven, or even hell. (7)
Now, it may be objected that the cessation of bondage does not occur merely through the impossibility of the visible [world],
because bondage— consisting of birth, growth, destruction, heaven, hell, and so forth—
is perceived as a quality of the seer; thus, even when the visible world ceases, [bondage would remain] due to its inclusion within the self.

Anticipating the objection that [the self] would not cease [to exist], he says in two verses beginning with "it arises": It is true that that which arises experiences growth, decay, heaven, hell, and so forth, as well as bondage and liberation; however, the Self does not have arising and so on as its inherent nature. This is solely due to the non-comprehension of its own true nature.
The meaning is: because of the thorough investigation of the delusion regarding its arising and so forth. || 7 ||
Therefore, for the sake of your own understanding, I shall first explain how and by whom this creation originated within the cycle of worldly existence.

Since bondage arises solely from one's own lack of realization, I shall now explain—in the manner that follows—the impossibility of that which is seen (*dṛśya*), for the sake of self-realization. Just as the connection with birth and so forth occurs within the cycle of existence (*saṃsṛti*) at the extreme limit of the phenomenal world (*dṛśya-saṃsāra-koṭi*), and not at the extreme limit of the Self (*ātma-koṭi*); for the Self is, prior to the arising of the phenomenal world, just as it is.

The meaning is that it does not undergo even the slightest modification in that very same way. And so says the Śruti: "There is no cessation and no origination; no one bound and no seeker; no one desiring liberation and no liberation—this is the ultimate reality" (the reading is *ity eṣā paramārthatā*). || 8 ||
O Raghava, listen briefly to this meaning of the section;
thereafter, I shall relate it to you in detail according to your desire.

He says "this" (*idam*) to show briefly in this canto that "this alone is the meaning of this treatise," serving as an introduction to the detailed exposition that is about to be given. The compound *ayaṃ cāsau prakaraṇārthaśca* is a *karmadhāraya*. [This is stated] for the purpose of introducing the meaning of the treatise by way of an introduction to the section on its origin.
Or rather, this is to be understood as "this is that" (idam etat). || 9 ||
All this that is seen—the entire world, both stationary and moving—is like a dream in deep sleep; it perishes at the end of the kalpa.
Indeed, in order to provide a justification for the meaning already stated— that "whatever was [in the past] was exactly as it is"—

and to describe the nature of the Self remaining during the state of dissolution, he speaks by means of an illustration regarding the manner of dissolution into the cause of the previous creation, beginning with the words "yad idam" (that which this...).

The statement of the illustrative example is for the purpose of showing the dissimilarity with the dissolution that consists in the survival of the *pradhāna*, atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth, as maintained by the Sāṃkhyas, Naiyāyikas, and others. || 10 ||
Then, neither light nor pervasive darkness remains; there persists a certain reality that is unnameable, unmanifested, tranquil, and profound.
It is motionless and inactive because it is formless; it is profound because it is indivisible. It is not light because it lacks material form;
it is not darkness because its nature is pure light. It is inexpressible because it is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*);
it is unmanifest because it is veiled by ignorance (*ajñāna*), or else because it is the substratum for the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*).
"Ṛta," "Ātman," "Paraṃ Brahma," "Satya," and so forth—these names of that Great Soul have been conceived by the wise for the sake of conventional usage. (12)

The *ātman* is so called according to the teaching of Vyāsa: "Because it is the supreme measure and is accessible through revelation; because it attains, because it takes up, and because it consumes objects here in this world; and because its existence is continuous—therefore it is designated as 'ātman'. Furthermore, it is *para* (the Supreme) because it is the ultimate limit of excellence in truth, or because of its vastness (*bṛhattva*), or because it expands (*bṛṃhaka*) into the form of the universe.
Brahmā said: That which is experienced by the wise according to the scriptures is the truth; worldly convention exists for the purpose of instruction between the teacher and the taught. (12)

That very Self, though being such, shining forth as if it were another, enters, as it were, into the state of a living being— a state rendered insignificant by its future name— at the beginning of creation. He describes its false collective state of being a living being at the start of creation with the verse beginning "sa" (He).

Remaining as such in the very nature of consciousness, through delusion it appears as another— a dull, insentient entity consisting of the aggregate of subtle bodies (liṅga) produced in the sequence of ether and so forth; by entering into that and identifying with it, it shines as if it were that [consciousness] itself, due to the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the vital breath (prāṇa) contained within it.

Because it is dependent upon the manifestation of speech that occurs subsequent to the completion of the body, one goes—as it were—into a state called "living" (jīvatām), which is rendered contemptible (kadarthitām) by its base meaning; this is due to delusion (bhrāntyā).
In reality, however, the meaning is that he does not go there at all. || 13 ||
Then, having fallen into the agitation of conceptualizing the meaning of the term "jīva," it becomes the mind (manas), the self of the elements, becoming sluggish through the act of thinking.

Having thus described creation as accomplished by the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) alone, he speaks of that which is accomplished by it when assisted by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), beginning with the word "tataḥ" (thence). The meaning of the term *jīva* is the maintenance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is dominated by the power of action;

through its differentiation (*kalanena*), there arises agitation, that is, instability. The "self of the elements" (*bhūtātmā*) is the self consisting of the subtle body (*liṅga*) composed of the material elements.
Becoming sluggish through conceptualization, discursive thought, and reflection, and becoming dull through inertia. || 14 ||
By that [mind], the mind arises from the Great Supreme Self, possessing an unstable form despite its source being perfectly stable, like a wave from the ocean. (15)
"By that state of mind": the two ablative cases (*mahataḥ* and *paramātmanaḥ*) are used here with the elision of the suffix *-lyap* (meaning "having forgotten").
The sense is: having forgotten such a state of the Supreme Self, he thinks, "The mind becomes [the self]," identifying the self with the mind and its functions such as volition and the like. || 15 ||
He himself constantly and spontaneously conceives this [world] at his own will;
by that means, this vast splendor of a magical illusion is thus spread out.

Thus, the meaning is this: Brahman, known as Hiraṇyagarbha, having attained the state of the collective mind (samaṣṭimanobhāva), even though not awakened by another, constantly and spontaneously conceives—by virtue of its own prior latent impressions—the state of Virāj, the state of the worlds and so forth, and therein the state of the fourfold aggregate of living beings. By that [means]:
By means of one whose resolve is true. || 16 ||
Just as the referent of the word "bracelet" is not distinct from the gold,
nor is the gold distinct from the bracelet, so too the referent of the word "world" is not distinct from the Supreme.

Thus, in order to demonstrate that even by means of a thousand superimpositions (*adhyāropa*) the ultimate status (*pāramārthika-sthiti*) of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not destroyed, he provides an illustration with the word "just as" (*yathā*).
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: just as the referent of the word "bracelet" (*kaṭaka-śabdārtha*) is not separable from the gold that constitutes the form of the bracelet.
The meaning is that even the status of being the referent of the word "world," which appears within the Supreme Brahman, is not capable of being separate from it.
(17) This world exists as it is within Brahman alone, whose nature is infinite;
the referent of the word "world" does not exist [apart from it], just as the nature of a bracelet does not exist apart from gold. (18)

The fact that the two possess a single existence is established by their inability to exist as separate entities; and while this [unity] is intrinsic in the case of the adventitious nature of Brahman, it is not intrinsic but dependent upon Him in the case of the world-nature—thus he says: "In Brahman alone. This world exists as the very nature of Brahman, whose essence is devoid of all limitation abandoned by the infinite Self.

But in the case of the world, which is the object denoted by the word "world," there is no nature of the self that has an end; just as the nature of gold exists [in a bracelet] but the nature of the bracelet does not exist [in the gold], so it is here. || 18 ||
Whether real or unreal, like the shimmering waves of the river of heat,
this worldly splendor is spread out by the mind as a magical illusion (*indrajāla*). (19)

If it does not exist by itself, how is it that it appears as if it were real? To this he says: "as if real" (satī). The connection of the words is as follows: just as a wave in a river imagined within the heat of a mirage in the desert, so too the splendor of the world—an illusion like a magician's trick—is spread out as if real, even though it is unreal. || 19 ||
Ignorance, cyclic existence, bondage, illusion, delusion, and the great darkness—these are the names by which she is designated by those who know all things. (20)

Intending to show that this [universe] is non-existent because it consists of ignorance (avidyā) by virtue of being produced by ignorance, he points to ignorance through names corresponding to its nature, beginning with "ignorance" (avidyā). It is called "ignorance" because it is to be removed by knowledge (vidyā).

It is called "transmigration" (saṃsṛti) because it is the cause of wandering through the upper, lower, and horizontal realms. It is called "bondage" (bandha) because it brings about a lack of independence.

It is called *māyā* because of its falsity; *moha* because it is the cause of delusion; *mahat* because it is difficult to cross; and *tamas* because it conceals one's true nature—such are its names. (20)
First, listen to this description of the nature of bondage as it is being told;
thereafter, O moon-faced one, you will understand the true nature of liberation.
The existence of the seer and the seen is called bondage;
the seer is bound by the power of the seen [the reading "by the power" (vaśāt) is preferred], and in the absence of the seen, he is liberated. (22)

He states the true nature of bondage and liberation, which are respectively to be sublated and attained through knowledge—beginning with the words "of the seer" (draṣṭuḥ). The word "aṅga" is used as an affectionate address. || 22 ||
The world, the self, the "I," and so forth—the false nature of the seen—is called the object of perception;
as long as this persists, liberation is not found. (23)

The disease of the visible world is not pacified by useless chatter such as "this is not it" or "that is not it"; on the contrary, it increases through those very thoughts that give rise to mental constructs.

Now, one might object: "If liberation is simply the impossibility of the visible world, then whenever the visible world appears, liberation will be achieved merely by its rejection through the thought 'this is not it, this is not it,' just as health is restored by the removal of disease; what then is the need for the exertion of knowing reality? To this, he says: "Not this. For the mere prattle of "not this" occurs only while the visible world exists.

Because its object is sublated, that which contradicts it must be described as something that, by the intention (or by the act) of producing another perceptible object, eliminates the previous perceptible object through that production. This being so, the meaning is that it "grows" because two perceptible objects are generated for the sake of eliminating one perceptible object. || 24 ||
For those who investigate, the world— which is real and perceptible— does not pass away through the crushing of logical arguments nor through pilgrimages, religious observances, and the like.

For those who investigate, as long as the visible world exists, the disease of the visible world does not subside merely through superior reasoning and the like; rather, another [disease] also arrives—that is, it comes. The genitive case here is used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*), according to the rule for the genitive denoting a characteristic state (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*). Thus, the existence of the visible world is not to be disregarded or ignored, but must instead be examined through inquiry.
The meaning is "is to be suppressed. || 25 ||
If the world-appearance were real, it would never cease for anyone;
for there is no coming into being of the non-existent, nor the passing away of the existent. (26)

Furthermore, if one were to admit the intrinsic existence of the perceptible world, liberation would be impossible because that which exists cannot be sublated; thus he says: "The world... (verse 26).
Wherever the Self, whose nature is neither consciousness nor unconsciousness, abides,
there the splendor of its object of vision arises for the observer— even within the interior of an atom.

Now, one might argue: "This seer, by the power of austerity, meditation, and so forth, having gone to a place such as the interior of an atom—which is devoid of objects of sight and incapable of being permeated by them—will remain there free from objects of sight;
how then can there be no liberation? To this he replies: "acetya" (unthinkable). By means of austerity and the like, it becomes unthinkable.

The meaning is as follows: since the seer is one whose self (ātman) is impossible to comprehend—an "unknowing" self whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*)—and because such a self alone is the seed of the visible world, the bondage of the visible is unavoidable even within the interior of an atom; for there is no contradiction in the appearance of vastness through delusion even in that [minute space]. || 27 ||
Therefore, this world-appearance exists; it was emitted by me and then abandoned through asceticism, meditation, and recitation, like one who is satisfied with sour gruel. (28)

He concludes what has been stated with the words "therefore" (tasmāt). The meaning is that it has been wiped away in its own place and abandoned by reaching another location. *Kāñjika* refers either to the water of stale boiled rice or to a specific type of liquor. || 28 ||
O Rāma, if this visible world exists,
it is reflected in this mirror of consciousness (cid-ādarśa) in exactly the same way, even within the interior of a single atom.
The word "in a mirror" is used for the purpose of illustrating the possibility of the cosmic egg entering into the Self, even within the interior of an atom;
the meaning is that it occurs exactly as it does in a vast space, without any contraction. || 29 ||
Just as whatever stands here or there is reflected in a mirror, so indeed are the sky, the ocean, the earth, and the waters of the rivers reflected in the mirror of consciousness.
Then, there again arises suffering—old age, death, and birth;
the grasping and abandoning of existence and non-existence; and that which is gross and subtle, moving and unmoving. (31)
In the waking state it is gross, in the dreaming state it is subtle, and in deep sleep it is the relinquishing of the grasping at existence and non-existence;
thus it is moving, unsteady, and unstable. || 31 ||
"This visible world has been wiped away by me, and yet I remain established herein;
this very thing is the inexhaustible seed for the recollection of cyclic existence within meditative absorption. (32)
Anticipating the objection that the visible world might be wiped away by a conceptual meditative absorption (*savikalpaka-samādhi*) independent of knowledge, he says "this" [the reading is:
"he states the impossibility of wiping away"]. The sense is that it is impossible to wipe away what has not been remembered, yet if one remembers it, the meditative absorption is broken. || 32 ||
But while this visible world exists, how can there be non-conceptual absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*)?
However, within that absorption, both consciousness and the fourth state (*turya*) are indeed possible. (33)
For this very reason, he says "when [it exists]" (*sati*) to show that even by means of non-conceptual concentration (*nirvikalpaka-samādhi*), there is no cleansing of that [impurity].

For when non-conceptual concentration exists, the existence of the mind (*citta-sattva*) implies its state as consciousness (*cetana-tva*); and when that is sublated, its state as the Fourth (*turya-tva*) is established.

However, while the object of perception (*dṛśya*) exists, how can there even be non-conceptual concentration? This is the logical connection (*anvaya*). Nor is there the state of an inexhaustible deep sleep (*akṣaya-suṣupti-tva*).
But in the reading "turyaṃ cāpi," it is clear. || 33 ||
For upon emerging from meditative absorption, just as at the end of deep sleep, this entire world-appearance shines forth in its true state, unbroken and with all its suffering. (34)
Or, even if such a state of meditative absorption (samādhi) were to exist, saṃsāra remains difficult to ward off; thus he says: "In the case of emergence" (vyutthāne).
The connection with what follows is: "it becomes attained" when the inner self (pratīci) is shining forth (bhāti), that is, being perceived. || 34 ||
O Rāma, what indeed is gained by meditative absorptions (samādhis)? For when one falls again into misfortune, what happiness is there in a momentary state of equanimity? (35)
Furthermore, when the occurrence of misfortune is anticipated, what happiness can there be in a momentary composure?
The particle *kimiti* is used here as an interrogative particle implying negation; the meaning is that there is no happiness at all. || 35 ||
Or if one should attain stability in non-conceptual meditative absorption (samādhi),
that should be considered the stainless state, resembling inexhaustible deep sleep.

"If one were to reach a state of non-conceptualization from which there is never again emergence, then one might think that imperishable bliss has been attained even without [supreme] knowledge"—this is a restatement of the opponent's intention. By the phrase "resembling an imperishable deep sleep," it is indicated that because delusion has not been eradicated, this state lacks the quality of being the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). || 36 ||
(130) While this visible world exists, nothing whatsoever is attained by anyone;
for wherever the mind goes, there indeed arises the delusion of this world. || 37 ||

He states the reply: "It is attained. When this object of perception characterized by the mind exists, what object indeed cannot be attained even by someone exerting effort in meditative concentration?
The meaning is that since the state of this [mind] follows after whichever object it approaches, the delusion of the world attached to it is difficult to ward off. || 37 ||

If, however, the observer forcibly dwells upon the state of being a stone while contemplating, then even at the conclusion of that [contemplation], the state of being an object of perception arises once again for him. (38)

Furthermore, if one, out of ignorance, were to cultivate a non-self such as a stone and so forth in meditative absorption (samādhi), then at the conclusion of that practice, even at the time of the fruit, that very object would appear; thus, the perfection of the samādhi in which only pure vision remains would not be achieved. To this he says: "The seer... (Verse 38).
Nor do non-conceptual meditative absorptions, which are like a state of stone-like insensibility, remain for anyone as they are experienced by all. (39)

He says "not even" to indicate that there is no stability—or rather, according to another reading, no hope for stability—even when one has attained the state of a stone free from suffering through the power of samādhi. This meaning is experienced by all those established in samādhi. || 39 ||
And yet, these meditative absorptions (samādhis) have not reached a state of firm establishment—[the reading is "have not reached growth"]—equal to that of stone;
rather, they become the supreme state, which is peaceful, of the nature of consciousness, unborn, and undecaying. || 40 ||
Let it not be that there is stability for those [samādhis] that have not taken root; however, there may be stability for those samādhis that have taken root to the extent of attaining that state.

To this, he says: "And not... Even if they have reached firm rooting, samādhis that are insentient—comparable to eternal stone and the like—do not constitute the supreme state characterized by the cessation of all saṃsāra.
They do not possess the nature of liberation. || 40 ||
Therefore, if this visible world were real, it could never cease;
that the visible world might cease through austerity, recitation, and meditation is merely the imagination of the ignorant. (41)
Therefore, he says "tasmāt" (therefore) to show that what was stated previously is established. || 41 ||
Just as the seed of a lotus dwells within the hollow of a lotus-stamen in the form of a clinging creeper, so does the cognition of the visible reside within the seer.

He establishes the existence of the visible object within the seer who possesses ignorance through four examples, beginning with "ālīna" (merged). Just as the seed of a future lotus-creeper, which has become merged—that is, subtle—within the hollow of a lotus-stamen, exists in the form of a lotus-vine though it is [currently] non-existent; so too does the world exist within the Seer.
The meaning is that, because arising is impossible [otherwise], the intellect exists together with the object of perception even in the case of the seer. || 42 ||
Just as flavor exists in substances, as oil exists in sesame seeds and the like,
and as fragrance exists in flowers, so does the perception of the visible exist within the seer.
Just as the fragrance of camphor and other such substances arises wherever they are situated, so too does the world arise within the belly of the element of consciousness (ciddhātu). 44.
Since even the arising of what already exists is difficult to prevent, he provides an illustration for this as well, beginning with "where. || 44 ||
Just as here your dream, volition, and the intellect’s sovereignty over the mind are seen through your own experience, so too does the ground of the visible world exist within the heart.

Regarding what was said—that [the world exists] even within the interior of an atom—he explains that as well with the word "yathā" (just as): "Just as in your heart the cognition of internal mental kingship is seen by your own experience; 'dream and conceptualization are seen'—this is the grammatical modification. (45)
Therefore, just as a piśāca dwelling within the mental constructions of a child utterly destroys that child, so too does this [grasping] which takes the form of the visible destroy the observer.
Just as in the example thus stated, this *rūpikā* also destroys the seer by means of the characteristics of the visible.
Female spirits (*piśācīs*) who delude men with female attire and then kill them are called *rūpikās*. || 46 ||
Just as the sprout, established within the seed according to place and time,
produces and extends a radiant body, so indeed does the intellect perceive the visible world.

If everything visible exists within the heart, then why is it not experienced by everyone right now? To this he replies with the word "yathā" (just as). The meaning is that the ripening of place, time, and action are also auxiliary factors for its manifestation.
Just as there is a sense of wonder regarding a substance only within the heart... [47]
Just as the interior of a substance that is eternally risen and free from setting remains its inherent nature,
so too does the existence of the world reside within the interior of that whose body is pure consciousness alone.

That wonder is the power of inconceivable and diverse effects; just as it exists within the interior, the hollow, the heart, and the essential core of a substance such as a seed, so too does it exist within the interior of the substance of the Self— which, though its nature is pure consciousness and whose body is knowledge— as that which consists of the nature of the intermingling of consciousness and unconsciousness.
The persistence of the world is the conclusion of the stated meaning: that the existence of the past and future worlds is real. || 48 ||

Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Description of the Cause of Bondage," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* (Section on Origination) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (Sage) tradition.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Cause of Bondage," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Second Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen to this narrative called "The Birth from Space," which is an ornament for the ears.
By this, O Raghava, you understand the chapter known as "Origination. (Alternatively, according to another reading, "you are made to understand. || 1 ||
One who is ignorant, whose self is the elemental body, and who is devoured by death, does not know reality;
he is proclaimed to be the self that is pure consciousness alone, like a twice-born man born from space. || 1 ||
The Self itself, conditioned by ignorance and nourished by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire and action, is the seed of the world and the seed of death.

However, when the power of that seed is burnt by knowledge (*vidyā*), one no longer falls under the sway of death; thus, in order to demonstrate this specific point regarding the meaning previously stated, [the text proceeds] with the purification of the reality that is the creator of the world and so forth.
Intending to describe a narrative that serves as an introductory context (*upoddhāta*) for the meaning to be explained hereafter, the venerable Vasiṣṭha said:

"This... [referring to the verse]. "Born from space" (*ākāśaja*) refers to the collective subtle body (*liṅgasamaṣṭyātmā*), which arises from Brahman—which is similar to space because it is the substrate of the superimposed ignorance (*avidyā*) and possesses a slight luminosity due to being veiled by ignorance.
The narrative concerning Hiraṇyagarbha. || 1 ||
For there is a twice-born man named Ākāśaja, who is supremely righteous, constantly devoted solely to meditation, and ever intent on the welfare of all creatures. (2)

Just as, according to the Vedic text beginning with "When the principal has been won, the others are thereby won," it is described that all duties performed by all people are included within such dharmas as the Saṃvarga-vidyā which lead to the attainment of the station of Hiraṇyagarbha; therefore, he is supremely righteous.
Meditation is the contemplation of the Self; he is solely devoted to that. || 2 ||
When he lived for so long, Death thought to himself:
"I am indeed inexhaustible; I devour all beings one after another in due order. (3)
The meaning is: when he lives long, he does not fall under the power of death. || 3 ||
"Why do I not devour this Brahmin born of space?
Against him my power is blunted, like the edge of a sword upon a stone. (4)
Having reflected thus, he then went to that city to slay him;
for no one who is diligent abandons their own exertion in their own tasks.
That city is renowned as being in the center of Meru; for death does not enter Satyaloka. "Exerted" means endowed with effort and capable. || 5 ||
Then, before Death himself enters that abode,
the fire— resembling the conflagration at the end of an aeon— burns him.
Agni was previously conceived by Brahmā as a rampart to ward off and obstruct those who would hinder his concentration; he is this very Death. 6.
Having split open the great garland of fire-flames, he entered within;
seeing the twice-born man, he strove diligently, wishing to seize him with his hand.
Having torn through a great circle and garland of blazing flames. || 7 ||
And though he was powerful, he was unable to seize the twice-born man— even one seen right before him— despite his hundred hands, just as one cannot grasp a person created by mere thought.
To seize or to touch. || 8 ||
Then Death, having approached Yama, the dispeller of doubts, asked:
"O Lord, why am I unable to consume that which is born of space?"
Yama said:
"O Death, you alone are not capable of killing anyone by force;
it is the deeds of the one to be killed that bring about their death, and nothing else."
"Single" means without assistance. "Performing that" means performing the act of killing. Thus, from this [statement], the remainder is that there is no other cause for your incapacity. || 10 ||
Therefore, having diligently investigated the deeds of this Brahmin who is to be slain, you shall devour him with their assistance.
"Having searched, perform a thorough investigation. Here, *śyan* is the suffix for the root *gam* (to go) in the imperative (*loṭ*) with the augment *hi*. "With assistance" means with favor. || 11 ||
Then that Death wandered about, intent on searching for that deed,
through regions, the ends of the quarters, lakes, rivers, and all directions.

The statement that [the soul] "wanders" refers to the process of reflection with focused concentration on such questions as "In which country did this person previously perform such an action?", for this takes a long time to accomplish; it does not refer to physical movement from one place to another.
This is because it is impossible to search externally for those unseen forces (adṛṣṭas) which are inherent in the agent and his characteristics. || 12 ||
Forests, thickets, and groves; mountains and the shores of the ocean;
other islands, wild tracts, cities, and towns. || 13 ||
Ancient towns in the vicinity of great cities are branch cities. ||13||
Having thus wandered over the entire circle of the earth— including principalities, all kingdoms, and the dense forests within the various regions— he did not find anything whatsoever from anywhere.
Death exerted himself to obtain those actions born of space, just as a wise man [seeks] the son of a barren woman, or another [seeks] a mountain of volition. || 15 ||
He has obtained and he has not obtained; he is another person, distinct from the one who forms volitions. || 15 ||
Then, having approached, he questioned Yama, who is skilled in all matters;
for he is the ultimate refuge and the source of authority for his subjects in times of doubt.
Of the dependents and servants. || 16 ||
Death said:
"O Lord, tell me where the deeds of one born of space reside.
Then Dharmarāja, having reflected for a very long time, spoke this: ||| 17 ||
The King of Dharma said:
"O Death, there are no actions whatsoever belonging to one born from space.
This brahmin, Ākāśaja, was born solely from the sky. (18)

Since those karmas whose fruits have already begun their operation are destroyed by the very commencement of those fruits, those accumulated [karmas] are sublated by knowledge, and those yet to come lack seeds; therefore, it is said that they simply do not exist. || 18 ||
He who is born from space alone must be as pure as the sky itself;
he has no auxiliary causes, nor does he possess any actions whatsoever. (19)
The pride, passion, and so forth associated with the co-operators, or the actions performed today that act as co-operatives in the killing by Death—that is the remainder [of the meaning]. || 19 ||
There is not even the slightest connection between this [present life] and past karma, just as there is none for the son of a barren woman or for one who has never been born. (20)
Regarding the term "connection": thus says the Sūtra—"Upon the attainment of that [Self], there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins.
It is like one whose form has not arisen—that is, one whose appearance has not been produced. || 20 ||
Due to the absence of causes, he is therefore nothing but space;
he possesses no prior karma, just as a great tree does not exist in the sky.
Because the causes, such as ignorance and the rest, are the causes of modification for that which is itself unchanging; therefore, modification is impossible for it.
This mind of his is not subject to its own will because of the absence of prior karma;
for today, he has not accumulated even the slightest karma. (22)
"Let there be no physical [suffering], but might there be mental [suffering]? To this he says: "Not so.

For the vibration of the mind is indeed under the influence of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from the movements of the previous body; due to the absence of those, even the present physical [state] is not subject to the first sexual urge, and thus no karma leading to death has been accumulated. || 22 ||

Thus, the self whose nature is the treasury of space, eternally abiding in its own cause which consists of the clear ether, is eternal; for it has no actions whatsoever, nor does it have any causes whatsoever. (23)
And this being so, he says "evam" (thus) [in verse 23], meaning that this [Self] remains as the very nature of the Supreme Brahman and not as the nature of the visible world.
He has no past actions, nor does he perform any today;
thus, in this world, he consists of nothing but the space of pure consciousness.
But since that [state] exists, there is no possibility whatsoever of past karma and so forth; thus he says: "The past... (verse 24).
The movement of his vital breath, which is perceived as action by people such as ourselves,
is seen by us in this way; however, he possesses no conscious thought regarding that action here.

[Objection: "In that case, how is it that we perceive this [Self] as possessing activities such as vital breath (*prāṇa*), body, and so forth? To this he says: "Vital breath... The meaning is that this is perceived by us through our own ignorance and delusion; there is no conviction regarding its reality therein. || 25 ||

Established as if contemplating from the supreme state, she is indeed of the nature of consciousness; like a statue carved upon a pillar of consciousness, she appears to have a form distinct from herself.

How, then, does he explain his notion of a body and so forth? He says: "Established... In the pillar of consciousness (*cit-stambha*), there exists a statue (*śālabhañjikā*) consisting of consciousness itself, which remains as if imagining its own distinct form, different from consciousness.
Thus, the meaning is that this notion of his is merely a product of imagination and is not real. || 26 ||
In that very same way, O twice-born one, he remains established as his own self from the perspective of ultimate reality. (Note: The reading "paramārthantaḥ svātmabhūtaḥ" is also found.)
Just as liquidity exists in water and emptiness in the sky, so it is here.
In some places, however, for the sake of providing an illustration, the phrase "like a carved figure (śālabhañjikā) situated on a pillar" is read as an additional half-verse. || 27 ||
And just as there is vibration in the wind, so too is this [vibration] in the supreme state;
for he has no actions performed today, nor any accumulated [karmas]. (28)
Because these [causes] are not prior, he does not here fall under the power of saṃsāra;
for that which arises when the auxiliary causes are absent [does not continue]. (29)

The statement of the result of the restatement of the impossibility of action—in the manner already established—is that "he has not fallen under the sway of *saṃsāra*. Just as with the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, which is not produced by the causes of [real] silver well-known in the world, once the falsity of his body and so forth is determined, there is no possibility of being overcome by death, because the agency and other attributes caused by that [body] are sublated; thus he says:
[This is explained] by the passage beginning with "sahakārī" and ending with "vada. || 29 ||
It is experienced that this [Self] does not become different from its own cause;
therefore, due to the absence of causes, it is self-existent.
Tell me, how can he be overcome, since he was not a creator in the past nor is he one today, yet he will bring about the mental construction known as death? (31)
Now, one might ask: since other individual souls (*jīva*) are also distinct entities, why are they not seized by death? To this, he says:

"When this... When a soul possesses the conviction that its body, composed of earth and other elements, is indeed the "I," that deluded one remains merely a physical being; for him, when this Brahmā, through a mind of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*), [acts].
The meaning is that when he forms the conceptualization named "death," then he can be seized by you. || 31 ||
And he who possesses the conviction, "I am this earth and so forth," quickly becomes one with the earth; and he can be grasped. (32)
Due to the absence of any conceptualization of earth and the other elements, this Brahmin possesses no form;
it is as impossible for him to grasp the sky as it is with a sturdy rope. (33)
Because there is an absence of the conceptualization of a body composed of earth and the other elements, he possesses neither form nor shape.
Death said: "O Blessed One, tell me how indeed it is that [the world] is born from the void;
and how do earth and the other elements exist, or how is it that they do not exist? (34)

Not conceiving how there could be modification for that which is changeless, birth for that which is unborn, or non-existence for the existent elements such as earth, Death said: "O Blessed One... (34).
Yama said:
He was never born, nor is he ever non-existent;
the twice-born one is merely the light of pure consciousness, and thus he remains.
The statement that the other [the Self] is space-like and the statement that earth and the other elements are non-existent do not intend to convey emptiness (śūnyatva) in an absolute sense;

rather, they intend to convey that the effect is devoid of an existence separate from its cause. Similarly, the statement regarding the birth of the Unborn intends to convey the doctrine of illusory manifestation (vivarta), not the doctrine of transformation (pariṇāma). Thus, [the author] indicates this underlying intention.

He said: "Never. For this twice-born one is, in the ultimate sense, nothing but pure light of consciousness; therefore, for that reason, he remains always exactly as he is, meaning he is never subject to transformation. || 35 ||
Upon the occurrence of the great dissolution, nothing whatsoever remains;
only Brahman exists—peaceful, undecaying, infinite, and absolute.

With the intention that, because at the beginning and the end only those subtle elements remain, that alone is its natural, true form, he says [the following] with the verse beginning "mahāpralaya" (36).
Then, following that, there arose near him a mountain-like radiance—void, eternally manifest, subtle, free from limiting adjuncts, supreme, and established. || 37 ||

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the world] existed during that dissolution (*pralaya*). He establishes what was stated—that "it is seen by us in this way"—with the passage beginning with "tadanu" and so forth.

Subsequently, at the time of the commencement of creation, by that cause which consists of the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), nourished by latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), [the world appears] in proximity to this [soul], because its essential nature is pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*).

When one perceives— that is, slightly manifests— the gross form of light, which is like a mountain (adri-nibha) in its nature as an object before one, which is like a mountain (parvata-vat) in being unimpeded, which is the Virāj-form or the four-faced [Brahmā], and which is worthy of being designated as "I am the body," then,
by that very cause of such ignorance, it appears as something delusive and false, like a dream, occurring suddenly and unexpectedly, as in the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit (kākatālīya).
He perceives that form; the meaning is: people such as ourselves. || 37 ||
Because its essential nature is pure consciousness alone, it conceives "I am the body";
thus, it perceives a deluded form as if by chance, like the "crow and the palm fruit" coincidence.
That very Brahman, at the beginning of that creation, remained within the belly of the sky,
established in the form of the thought-free space of consciousness.

And thus, with the intention that the previously stated point—that there is no impairment of his state of non-conceptuality (nirvikalpatā) and so forth by means of the body and other things superimposed from the perspective of another—is uncontradicted, he says: "He, this very one," and so forth. || 39 ||
He has no body, no actions, no agency, and no latent impressions;
he is the pure space of consciousness, a pervasive mass of pure awareness.
No web of past latent impressions exists for him at all,
for he is of the nature of pure space, like a light of the nature of radiance.
Even such [distinctions] are not seen when there is the complete pacification of mere sensation;
therefore, as is the space of consciousness, so too are the means of its realization.
Feeling (*vedanā*) is the outward-turning activity of consciousness; when that [activity] alone is stilled, it is of such a nature as a mere appearance (*prātibhāsika*).

If so, how is there the cessation of feeling? To this he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Through the realization of the reality of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-tattva*), when the object is sublated, even those feelings which were cognitions of it become just like the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*).
The meaning is that they abide because of the existence of that [state]. || 42 ||
"From where indeed does the earth and the rest originate here, what is their nature, and how do they come to be?
Therefore, O Death, do not be so intent on assailing this. (43)

Since even sensations whose nature is mere consciousness cannot be endured there, let alone the possibility of enduring earth and other elements; with the intention that you have no hope of advancing, he says:
"From where? (43).
"It is never possible for anyone to grasp the sky.
Having heard this, Death was struck with wonder and departed for his own abode.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Grandfather, this god whom you have described to me as Brahmā is,
in my opinion, the self-born, unborn, singular Self, whose nature is pure consciousness."

Gladdening his guru by indicating that he had realized both the essential meaning of the narrative—that Brahman alone is indicated by the alternative name "the twice-born born of space"—and that the world is illusory, Śrī Rāma said:
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"It is even so, O Rāma; this Brahman has been described by me to you.
Long ago, on account of this very matter, Death engaged in a dispute with Yama."
Dispute and agreement. || 46 ||
During that Manvantara, when Mṛtyu, devouring all beings, was carrying away the subjects,
he attained great strength and himself began an assault upon the Lotus-born One.
During the period of transition between the two Manvantaras; at the onset of the lotus-born Brahmā's [reign], for the purpose of slaying; the undertaking, the exertion. || 47 ||
At that very time, he was instructed by Dharmarāja:
"In whatever is done constantly, in that alone does delight arise. (48)
If it is asked how one can exert effort again and again against death when it is impossible, he says [the answer is] "out of madness": "That very [Brahmā]...
It is said that Brahmā is approached as having the form of the supreme ether; yet how can he be approached?
For he is merely mind, consisting of volition, and his form is devoid of earth and the other elements. (49)
Even while stating verbally the meaning already expressed at the beginning of the narrative, he declares that the body and so forth are nothing but mind, saying: "Brahman... (verse 49).
Whatever wonder of consciousness appears as the experience of forms, that is indeed consciousness-space itself; it possesses neither causality nor the state of being an effect.
Just as a person created by imagination appears with a form shimmering in space, though devoid of earth and other elements, so does the Self-born One manifest. (51)
The meaning is: just as in the sky there appears the form of a great inverted sapphire bowl, devoid of earth and other elements, so it is. || 51 ||
Just as a city in a dream or a mental construction of a string of pearls appears in the stainless sky, though it lacks earth and other elements, so too does the Self-existent One manifest.
In the absolute, solitary Supreme Self, there is neither the visible object nor the seer;
nevertheless, this self-born one shines forth as the very mind itself.
The very nature of one's own mind is indeed nothing but pure consciousness. || 53 ||
This mind, which is nothing but mere volition (saṃkalpa), is called Brahman;
it is the person of the ether of volition, and for it, no earth or other elements exist.
The meaning is that he whose form is mind consists of mere volition alone, not composed of earth and other elements; he is Brahmā, the lotus-born. || 54 ||
Just as a bodiless figurine situated within a painting appears,
even so does Brahmā appear from the ether of consciousness, which is pure and stainless.

To the question of how a formless volition can take on a human form, he says: "Just as... For a painter, having first conceived within his mind the form of a figure to be painted and then drawing it externally exactly as it was, the doll within him appears in that very form even though it is bodiless; in the same way, the pure [consciousness] of the space of the Intellect...
That mind which is transparent and capable of receiving reflections shines as Brahmā, taking on the form of the body of Prajāpati.
The self-existent one shines forth as Brahman— the solitary space of consciousness, infinite, without beginning or middle— by the power of its own mind;
yet in reality, it is like a form or like a person.
But for him, there is no body, like the son of a barren woman. || 56 ||

In this regard, he states that the transformation of the mind into those forms through conceptualization is not real, but rather that pure Brahman itself appears as such through ignorance—expressed by the words "the ether of consciousness" (cidvyoma). The grammatical connection is: "Brahmā, the Self-existent One, appears as if possessing such a form. (56)
Thus ends the second canto, titled "Description of the First Creator," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Creator of the First Creation," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Third Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said:
"In this very way, the mind is purified by you, being devoid of earth and the other elements."
"The mind is Brahman"—this has been declared as the truth, devoid of earth and the other elements. || 1 ||
Since Brahmā is of the nature of mind, this world consists of his volition;
therefore, it is proclaimed here that this world is unreal, just like a kingdom of the mind.

Thinking that if Brahman is accepted as being of the nature of the mind— according to the previously stated principle that "volition consists of mind alone and has no form apart from earth and the other elements"—

then since the mind is of the nature of a web of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the statement that "no prior web of latent impressions exists for it" would be incorrect, Śrī Rāma said: "It is exactly so."

By two [verses]. The mind is pure, being devoid of earth and the other elements; it is well-known to be exactly thus. Since the word "that" (*tat*) is used later in the sense of "then," its antecedent must be supplied here as "if" (*yadi*). || 1 ||
