Therefore, O Brahmin, tell me this: why is past memory not the cause here for me, for you, for others, and for all living beings? (2)

In this body of Brahmā, why is it that there is no memory—just as there is a memory from a previous time arising at the moment of abandoning a former body, whether for you, me, or any other person, or even in the bodies of beings such as animals—for what reason is there not such a memory? As it is said: "Remembering whatever state... [and so forth].

This is because of such Smṛti passages as these. The point is that if a prior memory exists, then the impressions (*saṃskāra*) which serve as the basis for its arising, as well as the body and so forth, must also necessarily have existed previously; this cannot be avoided. || 2 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For one who possesses a previous body today, accompanied by past karma, memory arises; that is the cause for the persistence of worldly existence.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "If it were true that the attainment of a previous body and so forth were established, then memory whose object was experienced therein would be the cause; however, that very thing is unestablished. He says this in two verses beginning with "pūrvam" (previously).

Now, [one might argue] that by such Śruti passages as "This indeed is the conqueror of worlds," and by the principle of "the sacrifice according to one's resolve" (*tatkratu-nyāya*), the status of the station of Hiraṇyagarbha...

Since it is well known that the fruit [of liberation] results from the combination of ritual action (*karman*) and meditative worship (*upāsana*), how can there be a statement regarding the non-existence of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the previous body?

Or how can there be a statement that this mind-made body (*manomaya-deha*) is not composed of earth and the other elements, given that "the mind, my dear, is made of food" (*anna-mayaṃ hi saumya manaḥ*)?

If you argue that this contradicts other Vedic texts which state that [the body] is a modification of food, and contradicts the established doctrine that it is an effect of the unevolved elements (*apañcīkṛta-bhūta*), then [we reply]:

True. However, from the perspective of one who lacks knowledge—who thinks, "Since there is nothing other than Me, why should I fear?"—it is indeed so; yet, from the perspective of His true nature as established by Śruti and Smṛti, such as the fourfold group [of elements] being co-existent with Him, even the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) throughout the three periods of time [is seen as non-different from Him].

Because there is sublation throughout the three periods of time—[in the sense that] "it did not exist, it does not exist, and it will not exist"—there is no reality to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of a previous body; thus it is so stated.

However, regarding the persistence of what has been sublated, just as a burnt cloth still possesses the nature of a web of threads, the mind and that body do not possess the nature of earth and the other elements as they did before; therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Intending to show that if even a city created by the mental resolve of Brahmā— whose command is unimpeded— is neither real nor material,

then what need be said regarding the nature of this universe, which persists even after being sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and is born from the mental resolve of the Enemy of Vṛtra (Indra)?

Because it is necessary for the falsity of the world that is about to be explained, one must rely solely on the vision of reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*) to negate the impressions of previous bodies and so forth; this is not done by prioritizing the scriptural statements regarding the fruits of meditation as understood through the perspective of the ignorant (*ajñadṛṣṭi*).
When no prior karma whatsoever exists for Brahmā, how and from where could his recollection of the past arise? (4)
Therefore, it appears either without a cause or with its own mind as the sole cause;
being non-different from its own cause, it is self-existent and possesses its own nature.
One's own mind is the mind that perceives the body; since that alone is the cause, it is stated that for him there is no mind of its own. || 5 ||
This body of the Self-born is indeed subtle (ātivāhika);
O Rāma, a material (ādhibhautika) body is not possible for the Unborn.
The *ātāvahana* (conveying vehicle) is that which carries one to another world via the path of light, smoke, and so forth; it is "excellent" (*sādhu*) in that regard.
It is called *ativāhika*, like the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) of people such as ourselves. That is to say, it is subtle. The *ādhibhautika* (material) body is born from the gross elements. || 6 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Is there one subtle body (ātivāhika) and another material body (ādhibhautika)? Is there only one [body] for all classes of beings, or is there one for Brahmā alone? (7)
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
For all beings whose nature is causal, there are indeed two bodies;
for the Unborn (Ātman), however, because of the absence of a cause, there is only one, the subtle transportive body (ativāhika).

Because of the absence of a cause for those things whose nature is that of a cause— namely, those whose nature is the unquintuplicated elements, which serve as the causes for the forms of the quintuplicated elements, just like the empirical means of knowledge such as the eye.

The meaning is that because ignorance (avidyā) and the unquintuplicated elements (apañcīkṛtabhūta) are not perceivable by the eyes and other senses through the authority of the Vedas—being instead perceivable only by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin)—they possess only an apparent reality (prātibhāsikatva) and lack empirical truth (vyāvahārikasatyatva); or, as stated previously, they do not exist due to the absence of their cause. || 8 ||
The one Unborn (Aja) is the supreme cause of all classes of beings;
there is no cause for the Unborn, and therefore He possesses a single body.
He has also stated this by another method: "Of all [the mantras]," etc. (9).
The body of the first Prajāpati is not composed of the elements at all;
consisting of the nature of space, he shines forth possessing a subtle, transportable body (ātivāhika-deha).
The Self is of the nature of space, having the form of the void of consciousness alone; for that which is superimposed has no essential nature apart from its substratum.
Having a body consisting of mind alone, he does not consist of the sequence of earth and the other elements;
the primordial Lord Prajāpati, whose form is space, extends forth all creatures.
And thus, intending to show that even the world fashioned by its own conceptualization is realized as being nothing but the pure consciousness that is its substratum, he says: "Know...
And those [cognitions] have the nature of space (vidyā-ākāśa), even without other causes;
for it is experienced by everyone that whatever is [produced] from something, that is indeed of the same nature as that.

By other causes—that is, by different causal factors distinct from that [Brahman’s] volition—from whatever material source (*upādāna*) it is produced, such is the ellipsis; this is experienced in the case of golden earrings and the like. Thus, the sense is that the world is established as being nothing but Brahman. || 12 ||
Nirvāṇa alone is the Supreme Person, and that very thing is supreme awakening;
it remains as mind-only and does not undergo the state of being earth and so forth.
By this, it is established that the individual soul (jīva) is also nothing but that [pure consciousness]; thus he says: "merely liberation" (nirvāṇamātra).

Since that adjunct of the mind (cittopādhi), though appearing as mind alone due to the delusion of the mind, in ultimate reality remains as the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) itself and does not undergo the state of being a material person or the like—this is the meaning. || 13 ||
For all classes of beings engaged in the worldly course of saṃsāra,
this first vibration is the mind-body, which arises from itself.
The state of "self-ness" (svatā) is the sense of "I" (ahambhāva); its arising [is what is meant]. || 14 ||
Non-different from this preceding vibration and having its very nature identical to it, this creation has issued forth like the creation of movement from the wind. (15)
Because the gross [world] derived from this [subtle cause] is nothing but this, it has no other nature and is of the same essence as it. || 15 ||
From this [reality] whose form is creative intuition (pratibhā), this creation—which possesses the nature of mere intuition—shines forth as if it were established with real experience. || 16 ||
He states that the world, which is a superimposition of mental modifications, is itself established as a mere superimposition: "pratibhāna... etc.
"Pratibhāna" means appearance; the meaning is "from a form established as mere appearance," that is, from a phenomenal form.
Alternatively, [the meaning is] that even though it assumes the nature of pure consciousness, creation is thus [mere appearance] from the perspective of the form of ultimate pure consciousness.
The meaning is that it appears as something being perceived in the form of insentient matter (acid-ākāra). || 16 ||
An illustration for this is the sexual union with a woman in one's dream-city— as it appears in the printed edition, "the woman in a dream-dream"—
which, though non-existent, shines with the experience of reality through the fulfillment of its object. (17)
The phrase "another dream within a dream" refers to sexual union with a woman therein;

this is intended to establish the validity of using it as an illustration for gross conceptualization occurring within subtle conceptualization. "By the fulfillment of the object" means by the accomplishment of the purpose of worldly activity. || 17 ||
Not composed of earth or other elements, he shines with the form of space, bodiless;
yet the Lord of Beings, whose own self is the ground of all, appears as if embodied, taking the form of a person.
And so, he states that what was previously mentioned is not impossible: "Not earth, etc. (18).
Because its nature consists of consciousness and volition, it neither arises nor emerges;
because its own-being is self-dependent, it neither arises nor subsides. (19)

It does not arise from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); it arises through delusion (*bhrānti*). Regarding these, he establishes the first [point] with the words "because it is dependent on itself" (*svāyattatvāt*).
The sense is that, unlike the existence of the world, it is not dependent on ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like. This refers to the abiding of its own nature (*svarūpa-sthiti*).
Brahmā is the personification of volition, whose form is devoid of earth and other elements;
consisting solely of the nature of consciousness, he is the cause of the existence of the three worlds. (20)
Just as this very volition of the Self-born One shines forth,
so too does this space-nature appear like the mountain of your own volition.
In whatever manner and by whichever means it shines and unfolds in accordance with the karma of various living beings, in that very manner [it appears]. || 21 ||
Due to a firm forgetfulness of its own subtle, transportive nature,
it falsely appears like a ghost through the perception of the material world.

If that is so, how is it that everyone experiences the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) and other properties, which are material in nature and distinct from the mountain of mental constructs? To this, he says:
This is the first awakening of the exertion of the Great Consciousness;
because of its pure nature of awareness, no forgetfulness of the subtle body arises.
In that case, one might ask: why should Viriñci (Brahmā) not also suffer the loss of memory regarding his subtle body (*ātivāhika-bhāva*), just like those of us?

To this, he says: "This... This form of Vairiñca is the first manifestation of the Great Consciousness—the Brahman variegated by *māyā*—meaning it consists of the subtle elements which serve as the cause in relation to the entire gross phenomenal world (*sthūla-prapañca*). In that regard:

The meaning is that, because of his exertion and resolve—due to his nature of having true resolve (satyasaṃkalpatva)—it manifests in that very way as fully awakened and perceptible; therefore, since Viriñci’s consciousness is pure and not shrouded by darkness, no memory of the subtle body (ativāhika) arises. || 23 ||
For him, no fever born of material existence arises;
it is unreal, like a mirage, falsely bestowing the delusion of dullness. (24)

When Brahmā is merely mind—as the reading "as Brahmā" suggests—and not composed of earth and the other elements, then the entire universe is likewise merely mind; for whatever has arisen is indeed that very mind. (25)
The meaning is either "in which kalpa" or "from which"; that which is born from [the source] is "yad-ja-tam. || 25 ||
Since there are no cooperative causes for the unproduced, there are likewise none at all for that which is produced from it; therefore, some [causes] do not exist.

And thus, according to the principle shown by the Śruti passage, "In this way, my dear, seek the root of water through this sprout of food," the non-duality of Brahman is established as the result: that the world is merely mind, and the mind is merely Brahman.
He states this with the three verses beginning with "of the unborn" (ajasya). || 26 ||
The diversity of effects arises from the cause; therefore, there is nothing here that is otherwise.
It is established that whatever the nature of the pure cause, such is the nature of the effect.
For here, the relationship of cause and effect is not at all tenable;
for exactly as the Supreme Brahman is, so too are the three worlds. (28)
And thus, because there is no differentiator and because the relationship of cause and effect is untenable, the world has become Brahman itself; so he says: "The effect," etc. (28).
The world is stretched out by Brahman, which has, as it were, attained the state of mind;
it is non-different from the pure Self, just as fluidity is non-different from water. (29)
All this that is stretched out is woven by the mind; it is entirely unreal, like a city of the imagination or a city of the Gandharvas. (30)
There is no state of being material, just as there is no state of being a snake in a rope;
how then could those who are awakened, such as Brahmā and the others, remain therein? (31)

And thus, since the entire world is sublated for those who possess knowledge of reality, the notion of materiality regarding the body and so forth cannot possibly arise; this is what he states in the verse beginning with "ādhibhautikatā" (31).
Indeed, for one whose mind is awakened, there exists only the subtle body (*ātivāhika*);
how and from where could there be any talk of a material body (*ādhibhautika-deha*) here? [The reading here is *vācaś caracaiva*]. 32.
He strengthens the stated point by means of the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so"): "The subtle body (*ātivāhika*)...

etc. Even that which is merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*), such as the subtle body, does not exist there; for what reason and in what manner could there be anything material (*ādhibhautika*), such as speech? || 32 ||
For the person named Manu, who assumes the form of Viriñci, the kingdom of the mind known as the world stands as if it were of the nature of reality. 33.
The phrase "of a human being" is stated by way of recalling his previous state as a practitioner. || 33 ||
The mind alone is the state of Viriñci, for it consists essentially of volition;
having brought its own form to expansion, this world is spread out by the mind.

The state of being Viriñci is the state of being the creator of all; for that state of being Viriñci consists of the volition of Viriñci and is not dependent upon external instruments. [He attains] expansion—that is, vastness—this entire universe. || 34 ||
Viriñca is the form of the mind, and the mind is the body of Viriñca;
earth and the other elements do not exist here [independently], and therefore earth and the rest are merely imagined.
In this context, it refers to the mind (*manasi*). By that cause, or by the mind, it is imagined or superimposed upon the Self; this is the ellipsis. || 35 ||
Just as within a lotus there is the lotus-plant, so within the mind there is the object of sight;
the mind and the vision of the object of sight have never been distinct from one another by anyone at any time. (36)

The mind is in the heart; by the term "mind," the entire range of the visible world is indicated through metaphorical usage (*lakṣaṇā*). Now, one might ask: how can this be said, for it seems contradictory? If it is argued, "Earth and the other elements do not exist here [in the heart], yet the mind exists in the heart and perceives them," to that he says: "by the mind and the visible" (*manodṛśya*). This is because it is a compound of both "mind" (*manaḥ*) and "the visible" (*dṛśyam*).

The mind is the seer of the visible, and the witnessing Self is the witness of both; these two are never at any time separate or distinguished from one another by anyone. The sense is that as long as they are not distinguished, [the world] truly exists because ignorance has not been eradicated. Alternatively, the mind is the seer of the visible, and the visible is the object of sight; thus, by means of that [mind], they appear distinct. And so, regarding the mind...
The meaning is that annihilation itself is the annihilation of the seen and the seeing. || 36 ||
Just as here your dream, your volition, and the intellect that rules the mind are evident through your own experience, so too the realm of the visible exists within the heart.
In this regard, he concludes by stating examples established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), beginning with "Just as" (yathā). || 37 ||
Therefore, just as a demon residing in the mental construction of a child destroys that child,
so too does this [demon] appearing in the form of the visible destroy the internal observer.
Just as the sprout situated within the seed manifests a radiant body according to place and time, so indeed does the intellect of the visible expand.
The mind is the cognition of the visible. || 39 ||
If the suffering of the visible world does not ever subside,
then while the visible persists, there can be no isolation for the knower.
Furthermore, when the visible is impossible, the state of being a knower cannot exist in the knower.
For even while remaining [in that state], he becomes tranquil; indeed, they call this his liberation.

Now, one might ask: for what purpose is the falsity of the perceptible world established with such great effort? What harm is there if it were real? To this he says: "If it were real... (verse 40). The meaning is: even if it were established [as real], it would be extinguished; how much more so when it is false!
They say that liberation is indeed its absolute isolation (*kaivalya*).
Thus ends the third canto, titled "Description of the Cause of Bondage," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition.
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Description of the Cause of Bondage," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
(p. 136) The Fourth Canto.
4 Śrī Vālmīki said:
While the leader of sages was speaking these unrestrained words, the assembly became single-minded in its desire to hear, and silence ensued.
Having heard the instruction, the sequence of the night beginning with rising and so forth,
and the arrival in the morning, as well as the wondrous nature [or, according to another reading, the nature of the mind], are described here. (1)
In that which has a single flavor, with one-pointed focus. || 1 ||
The tinkling of the networks of small bells had become silent, and even the hārīta birds and parrots within their cages had ceased their play, no longer fluttering about.
He demonstrates this very state of single flavor through its characteristic signs, beginning with the words "In those that are peaceful," and so forth. *Hārītas* are a particular species of birds.
Even while the women remained with their graceful charms completely forgotten,
the entire royal assembly was fixed as if upon a painted wall.

In the phrase "in the royal palace," by means of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), it refers to the multitude of living beings residing in the royal palace; the connection [of the verb] is to be supplied by changing the case ending to "standing like a painting" (citra iva sthite) upon the painted wall. || 3 ||
The day, with its sweet sunlight, had but a single *muhūrta* remaining;
all worldly activities, along with the rays of the sun, began to diminish.
[He made] them small. || 4 ||
Fragrant with the rich scent of clusters of blooming lotuses, gentle breezes blew with sweet vibrations, as if they had come to hear [the teachings]. || 5 ||
"Āmodena māṃsalāḥ" means nourished and robust by fragrance. "Madhuraḥ" refers to those whose movement is pleasant due to its slowness.
All these adjectives apply universally [to all the bees]. This is either a simile (upamāna) or a poetic fancy (utprekṣā). || 5 ||
As if to contemplate what he had heard, the Sun abandoned his confusion regarding the arrangement of the day and went alone to the solitary slope of the sunset mountain.
The sun, as if to contemplate—that is, to strengthen through reflection—the sacred learning (śruta) which had been grasped by his ears, [seemed to enter]; "empty" means devoid of people. || 6 ||
In the forest lands, coolnesses arose like the onset of mist,
becoming inwardly cooled through the hearing of the consciousness, as if they were states of peace.
"By the onset of mihikās, that is, frost, they are equal, meaning non-different; 'cool within' is the common attribute. (7)
People in all ten directions became motionless,
as if they had abandoned all activity in order to listen with full attention.
Those by whom all activities and other occupations have been completely abandoned.
The shadows grew long, as if all things with elongated necks had stretched their heads forward to hear the sequence of Vasiṣṭha’s words.
The shadows of all objects and the long necks of all listeners attained lengthiness, as if to hear the sequence of his words; the absence of a compound (asamāsa) is a Vedic usage (chāndasa). || 9 ||
The doorkeeper, bowing low before him, said to the lord of the earth:
"O Lord, a great deal of time has passed since the bathing and the worship of the brahmins."
The *pratīhāra* is the doorkeeper; having become *prahva*, that is, bowed down. || 10 ||
Then the venerable Vasiṣṭha, having withdrawn his sweet speech, said:
"O Great King, let this much suffice for you to hear for now."
Having repeatedly withdrawn [them]. || 11 ||
"I shall say something else tomorrow morning," having said this, he observed silence.
Upon hearing this, the king said, "So be it," for the sake of increasing his prosperity. (12)
Having said, "So be it," [he departed]. || 12 ||
With flowers, water for the feet, the arghya offering, respectful honors, and the giving of sacrificial fees,
he reverently worshipped the gods, celestial rishis, sages, and brahmins.
Then the entire assembly rose, including the circle of kings and sages,
their faces surrounded by the halo of the mass of jewels strewn across the circle.

The word *sabhā* refers to a crowd of people. Because the sages, free from desire, disregarded the jewels bestowed by the king, their faces were obscured by the halo of light emanating from the masses of gems scattered there in a circular pattern.
The armlets and bracelets jingled as their limbs brushed against one another;
the space between their broad breasts was filled with golden bands drawn down by the weight of their necklaces.
In which [city] the spaces between the thighs and breasts possessed a luster like that of silken garments inlaid with gold, as if they had been stolen away. || 15 ||
With the sounds of awakened bees resting upon the lap of their crests,
they seemed to speak through their hair, which was heavy with a humming drone.
On the broad surface of the crest—the top of the head—the word "ghuṃghuma" is an imitation of an indistinct sound. || 16 ||
The quarters of the sky were turned golden by the radiance of their golden ornaments;
their sensory functions were completely stilled by the meaning of the Sage’s words held within their intellects. || 17 ||
The sky-dwellers went to the heavens and the earth-dwellers to the terrestrial sphere;
they all performed their daily routines in their respective homes.
In the meantime, the dark night appeared,
freed from the crowd of people, like a young woman in her home released from the company of men. (19)

Śyāmā means dark-complexioned; a young woman—alternatively, one who has reached the prime of youth. By the very possibility [of the comparison], it is understood that the observation of the object of comparison also pertains to that same time. || 19 ||
The lord of the day departed to illuminate another region;
for it is the very vow of the virtuous to act as a bringer of light everywhere.
The True Brahman is that Self, and the Person is Brahman; one who is established in That—this is the vow of both. (20)
The twilight arose on all sides, bearing a multitude of stars,
like the beauty of spring arisen with forests of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees.
The birds settled within the mango, nīpa, and kadamba trees, at the village shrines, and inside the houses, just as pure mental activities settle within the mind.
"Pure" means stainless; it is understood that this refers to the mind being shrouded by sleep. (22)
With fragments of clouds adorned by the light of the sun,
as if with the hue of saffron,
the western mountain appears like one clad in yellow garments amidst the clouds.
The one whose food is the stars, endowed with glory, has joined with the void of space. || 23 ||

Adorned by clouds variegated with the sun’s light, which possesses a hue like that of saffron in various degrees, and endowed with the beauty of a necklace characterized by stars— that aforementioned western mountain of sunset [appears] as if it were the sun itself, distinguished by fragments of clouds adorned by the sun’s light, and thus possessing a necklace of stars.

And being "endowed with Śrī," he has entered together with his own space (ākāśa), which possesses identical attributes. Just as Viṣṇu, clad in yellow garments and possessing the aforementioned qualities, being endowed with Śrī, enters the unobstructed heart-space of those who meditate in a manner corresponding to himself; likewise [is this]. For meditation upon the Lord during the junctions of the day (saṃdhyā) is indeed highly praised.
It is understood through elliptical expression (samāsokti). || 23 ||
Having taken the offerings at twilight, when [the time] had passed,
the darknesses arose like vetālas in bodily form as they had come. (24)
When the goddess had departed after receiving her worship at twilight, her attendants, the Vetālas, rose up from their bodies just as they were. || 24 ||
The cool breeze blew, causing the droplets of dew to quiver, with playful flashes of lightning as its sprouts; it was tender, promising the lilies, and refreshing. (25)
He is one whose nature it is to proclaim—that is, to cause one to infer—the lilies on all sides by the blooming of their buds.
Following the three qualifying adjectives, the mention of "extremely cool" is also indicative of slowness and fragrance.
The quarters of the sky, with their stars no longer distinct, fell into utter darkness.
With their hair extremely long and hanging down, they were like widowed women. || 26 ||
Because they were veiled by a mantle of frost, their stars—the constellations and the pupils of their eyes—were indistinct;
thus they were like widows due to the setting of their husband, the sun.
The lunar ocean of milk, whose form consisted of elixir, arrived at the world, filling the sky with a flood of milk and its own brilliance. (27)
Filling [the world] with a stream of milk characterized by brilliance, he whose form was composed of that [light] became the elixir of immortality.
The masses of darkness fled and vanished somewhere beyond sight,
just as ignorance departs from the minds of kings upon hearing the words of wisdom.
By whom such words of wisdom have been heard from the minds of kings of that sort.
The sages, the protectors of the earth, the ascetics, and the brahmins, finding their various purposes as if within their own minds, took rest in their respective abodes. (29)
The various matters instructed by Vasiṣṭha found rest and became settled within their own hearts, as if in their very abodes. || 29 ||
Thick darkness, dark as a mass of collyrium, departed;
there, at dawn, a vast mist slowly approached them.
Śyāmā means night; uṣas and pratyūṣa mean dawn. || 30 ||
The radiant stars in the sky vanished,
like showers of blossoms swept away by the morning breeze.
"Carried away" means removed. The intended meaning here is that the showers of flowers were like rainfalls of falling blossoms.
32. Behold, the sun has arrived with its rays causing the eyes to open, like the newly arisen faculty of discernment in the minds of great souls.
By whom the eyes of people were opened wide by his radiance.
With fragments of clouds adorned by the light of the sun,
as if with the hue of saffron,
the eastern mountain appeared as if wearing yellow garments, accompanied by clouds that dispel the darkness.
The one who consumes the stars, endowed with glory, joined with the sky. || 33 ||
In the reading "tamoghnaiḥ," the meaning is "by those which destroy darkness," that is, by those with golden horns. || 33 ||
The sky-dwellers and earth-dwellers returned once more to the assembly hall,
having performed their morning rites in the same sequence as the previous day.
By that of yesterday and by that of the day before yesterday. || 34 ||
The entire assembly entered with their former arrangement;
it became motionless in appearance, like a lotus pond when the wind has ceased.
She was like a lotus-filled lake that had been freed from the wind and was now devoid of agitation. || 35 ||
Then, seizing the opportunity, Rāma spoke with a sweet voice to Vasiṣṭha, the tiger among sages and the best of speakers.
Prasaṅga means an occasion or a context. || 36 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, tell me clearly what the nature of the mind is,
by which this entire cluster of worlds is expanded.

Form is the true essential nature. Since the mind will declare that whatever is the form of the mind is also the very form of the world, the falsity characterized by a lack of reality cannot be established; such is Rāma’s intention. || 37 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, no form whatsoever is seen of this mind, except for its mere name, like the void and inert appearance of space. 38.

"From name alone" (nāmamātrāt). Therefore, the meaning is that the falsity (mithyātva) established by the scriptural statement, "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name," is logically consistent with respect to its effects. The phrase "of the void-like inert form" (śūnyajaḍākṛteḥ) applies commonly to both the elemental ether (bhūtavyoman) and the mind (manas). || 38 ||
The mind does not exist as a real entity either externally or within the heart;
know, O Rāma, that it is situated everywhere, just like space. (39)
He establishes the very similarity with space [with the words] "not," [verse 39].
This form has arisen from this [consciousness] and is like the water of a mirage; it is a momentary conceptualization, comparable to the delusion of a second moon. (40)
This world is an illusion of our mind; that is to say, it is superimposed upon its [underlying] object. It is like that [illusion]. || 40 ||
Know that this manifestation of an object which has attained prominence in the midst [of consciousness], whether it be existent or non-existent, is the mind and nothing else. (41)

Although that which is called "mind" (*manas*) does not exist at all from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), nevertheless, he describes its imagined form as it is employed in scriptural convention, saying: "in the middle. That manifestation which has attained prominence in the middle—between an object present before one's eyes through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and an object absent from memory and so forth through indirect cognition (*parokṣa*)—is this very appearance in the form of that [object].
The meaning is that it is the mind of all people. || 41 ||
That which is the manifestation of objects is designated as "mind" (manas);
other than this, there never exists anything whatsoever called "mind. (42)
He states that same point in brief with the words "that which": the meaning is that the superimposition of the form of an object upon the formless consciousness is the mind (manas). || 42 ||
Know that the mind is volition; therein it is differentiated from volition, just as water [is differentiated] from fluidity and movement from the wind. (43)
Having thus described its definition by means of common functions, he also states it by means of its unique function:
"volition" (saṃkalpanam). || 43 ||
Where there is volition, O dear one, there the mind likewise resides;
volition and the mind are never, for anyone, distinct.
He confirms this very point by demonstrating the established distinction between the objects [of cognition], beginning with the words "yatra" (where). || 44 ||
Whether the appearance of objects be real or unreal, know that it is merely the mind; that mind, O Grandfather, is indeed Brahman itself. (45)

[Objection: Is it not the case that it is precisely the mental modification (vṛtti) conjoined with consciousness (cit) that is said to be the manifestation of the object? In that case, since consciousness is real, how can the mind—which is composed of it—be unreal? To this, he says: "True. Whether [the cognition] be unreal due to its having the form of an unreal object, or real due to its conjunction with real consciousness, let it be as intended; it does not matter.

Regarding that lack of grasping: he states that it is not contradictory to say that whatever the nature of the individual mind may be, its collective totality (saṃghāta) is likewise of the same essential nature (tanmātra-svabhāva), and that very [totality] is Viriñci—expressing this with the words "asatya" and so forth. || 45 ||
The self consisting of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) is designated as the mind (manas); through its long duration, it indeed imparts the material intellect (ādhibhautika-buddhi). (46)
If this mental body (*manodeha*) possesses all forms, then what else remains for it to create? To this he replies: "The subtle body" (*ātivāhika*).

Because the subtle elements alone remain joined together for a long time, through their mutual blending in the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), that very [mental body] sustains the notion of gross earth and so forth; this is its nature as a creator—this is the meaning. || 46 ||
Ignorance, transmigratory existence, the mind, the intellect, bondage, impurity, and darkness—these, the most excellent knowers understand, are synonyms for the visible world. (47)

Since the entire proliferation beginning with the mind is merely the play of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is indeed ignorance itself; he states that these are simply successive names for that very same ignorance in the verse: "Ignorance" (verse 47).
Indeed, there is no form of the mind whatsoever apart from the object of perception;
furthermore, I shall explain again that this object of perception has indeed arisen and does not [ultimately] exist.

If it is argued that the manifested object (dṛśya) is either ignorance (avidyā) or the mind (manas), then how can their beginninglessness be established? To this, he says: "And the object... (verse 48).
Just as a lotus stalk exists within the seed of a lotus, so the visible world exists within the atom of the Great Consciousness. 49.
And thus, with the intention that it follows that the very persistence of the ignorance of the Intellect (citi) is the persistence of the world, he says: "Just as... (verse 49).
Just as light belongs to illumination, as mobility belongs to the wind, and as fluidity belongs to water, so is visibility perceived in the Seer. 50.
Because the visible object does not deviate from consciousness accompanied by ignorance, it follows that the nature of the visible is that [consciousness];
thus he says: "of the light" (*prakāśasya*). "Of such a kind" (*īdṛśam*) means of this very sort; that is to say, its very nature (*svabhāva*). || 50 ||
Just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, just as water exists in a mirage,
and just as a wall exists in a dream-city, so too does the perception of the visible object exist within the seer.
Since its being of that same nature results in its non-separate existence from it, he says: "the state of being a bracelet" (aṅgadatvam). || 51 ||
In this way, even that quality of being an object of sight which resides in the seer as if it were non-different from him—
I quickly wipe away that impurity from the mirror of your mind.

Know that state to be absolute isolation (kevalībhāva), wherein the seer’s status as a seer necessarily ceases upon the absence of the seen; it is from this very [realization] that the non-existent becomes existent.

Regarding the word "yat" (that which): since the existence of the object of perception (*dṛśya*) apart from the perceiver (*draṣṭṛ*) is untenable—because one thing cannot possess existence through the existence of another—when the object of perception is absent, that very absence results in this pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), the perceiver, being non-perceiving.
Precisely because of that, from the unreal and sublated object of perception, [the Self] exists as the real, by way of its nature as pure consciousness (*sanmātracidrūpa*).
The meaning is: "Know that to be the state of absolute isolation (kaivalya) of the remaining Self. || 53 ||
When the state of reality has been attained, the latent impressions of passion, hatred, and the like subside,
just as the turbulence of movement ceases when the wind is stilled.
"Let it be so; nevertheless, how is the cleansing of the impurities visible in the mirror of my mind accomplished?
To this he says: "That state," etc. When the mind (*citta*) is in its true state (*tattā*), through the realization of absolute liberation (*kaivalya-bodha*), it attains that very nature.
[The impurities are] the agitations of forest ponds and the like, caused by the movement of the wind. (54)
When everything—consisting of the directions, the earth, and space—is incapable of being manifested, the form of the light remains as it is, pure and stainless. (55)
He causes [the student] to experience the abiding in objectless knowledge through an illustration, by means of the words beginning with "it is impossible" (asaṃbhavati). || 55 ||
When the visible world—including the three worlds, you, and I—has attained non-existence, such a state of absolute isolation belongs to the seer, the pure-souled one. (56)
The word division is *asattām iti*. || 56 ||
For just as the nature of a mirror remains solely its own essential form when it reflects mountains and other objects that are not inherently part of it, so too is the case here.
She whose essential nature is like a pure mirror. || 57 ||

When the agitation of the visible world—such as "I," "you," and "the universe"—has subsided, there arises that state of absolute oneness (kevalatā) when the seer remains in a state of non-seeing. (58)
The state of being oriented toward the visible is "seeing" (vīkṣaṇa) within that void. || 58 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
If this world were truly existent, it would never cease to be; for there is no non-existence of that which is real.
Yet we do not perceive non-existence in this visible world, which bestows such manifold defects.

If the visible world were non-existent, then the "state of isolation" (kevalībhāva) spoken of by you would follow; however, that very point contradicts experience, because the visible world is experienced as "existent, existent. With this in mind, regarding the doctrine of transformation (pariṇāmavāda), Śrī Rāma raises an objection in two verses beginning with "If it [the world] exists... (59).
Therefore, O Brahmin, how can this cholera-like affliction of the visible world be pacified—it which causes the mind to wander in delusion and bestows a continuous succession of sufferings? (60)
Existence, beginning with birth, is produced by the mind; it is that which causes delusion.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen to this mantra for the pacification of this demon of the visible world, by which, O Rāma, it shall utterly perish and meet its end. 61.

The hidden intention is this: although the unreal object of perception appears to have existence due to the false cognition of it as real through ignorance (*avidyā*), this delusion does not arise once ignorance is destroyed by the direct realization of the state of absolute oneness (*kevalībhāva*). First, [the opponent] raises an objection regarding the possibility of non-liberation, based on the observation of the signs of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
And warding off the conviction of reality regarding that which is perceived, Śrī Vasiṣṭha spoke by resorting to the doctrine of illusory transformation (vivartavāda):
"It will perish"—thus sublation (bādha) has been described in two ways. || 61 ||
O Rāghava, that which exists can never perish;
therefore, even when it has seemingly perished, it remains within the heart as a seed (or, according to another reading, "in the form of a seed").

He states the defect in the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) with the words "yad" (that which). This is the intended meaning: in the theory of transformation, indeed, there is merely the concealment (*tirobhāva*) of each preceding state by each succeeding state, not its destruction, because it is impossible for that which exists to become non-existent; and thus, even by means of the sixth modification characterized as destruction, duality remains concealed within the mind.

Alternatively, for one who remains in the state of primordial nature (prakṛti), rebirth from the seed of the latent impressions of desire and action is unavoidable; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of no liberation at all. || 62 ||
From the seed of memory, the perception of the visible world arises once more in the space of consciousness and spreads its vast defect in the form of the worlds, mountains, and sky.
The mention of "recollection" (smṛti) is an indicative mark for the entire world, beginning with the modifications of the internal organ that have been employed for experience.
Thus, there would be the fault of non-liberation, yet that is not possible here,
because gods, sages, and seers are seen to be recipients of liberation.
Those who are liberated while living are the vessels of liberation. || 64 ||
If this world were beginningless, then liberation would not belong to anyone;
whether it resides outside or within the heart, the visible world exists solely for the sake of destruction.

Now, it may be argued that this conscious self perceives the visible world—which actually resides outside itself within primordial matter (pradhāna)—as residing within its own heart due to a lack of discrimination; this is what constitutes saṃsāra.
Upon the arising of discriminative knowledge, when the conceit of non-discrimination ceases, liberation occurs from that [bondage], even though the world remains externally as before.
Anticipating the Sāṃkhya position that "it might be so," he says: "If... (verse 65).
(139) Therefore, listen to this most terrifying proposition from me, O Rāma, which you will surely comprehend through the subsequent text. (66)
Therefore, with the intention that the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*) alone remains as the final conclusion, he says "therefore," and so forth.
It is terrifying for those who are attached to sense objects and for those who maintain the doctrine of creation (*ārambhavāda*). As the teacher Gauḍapāda has said:
"This is called the Yoga of Non-contact; it is difficult to perceive for all yogis. Yogis are afraid of it."
"Because they see fear in that which is fearless. (66)
"This is space, this is the primary element (earth), and this is I"—thus characterized is the referent of the word "world" (jagat); indeed, there is no such thing at all. (67)
Whatever collection of visible objects is seen here before one, all that is indeed the Supreme Brahman—undecaying, immortal, and immutable. (68)
In the full, the full expands; in the tranquil, the tranquil remains firmly established (the reading *paraṃ sthitam* is found).
Just as space arises within space, so Brahman abides within Brahman. (69)
That unity of Brahman which is inward expands as fullness within the Full;

for therein, in its state of peace, the duality of space and so forth remains quiescent. And since, even within the void itself, it arises as the very void upon the removal of limiting adjuncts such as the jar, therefore Brahman abides in Brahman alone.

The meaning is that it is not altered even in the slightest degree. For when something is superimposed upon another, the latter is not connected even in the slightest degree with any quality or defect produced by the former. || 69 ||
There is no visible object possessing the nature of existence, nor is there a seer, nor an act of seeing;
it is neither empty, nor inert, nor is it consciousness—this all-pervading reality is simply peace.
Citi is the consciousness that is the reflection in the intellect. || 70 ||
Śrī Rāma said: A mountain is ground to powder by the son of a barren woman; a hare’s horn sings aloud;
and a stone, stretching out its mass of arms, performs the tāṇḍava dance.

Having stated the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*), Śrī Rāma spoke—beginning with the words "by the son of a barren woman"—to dispel the incredulity of the common folk; here, such examples are generally employed to demonstrate the impossibility of both the meaning of the individual words and the meaning of the sentence [in the opponent's view]. (71)
"Sands flow oil, stone statues recite, and painted clouds thunder"—such, O Lord, is this very saying. (72)
The ellipsis is that these appear as if they were words. || 72 ||
The world consists of the mountain-like void of the sufferings of old age, death, and so forth;
why do you say even to me that "this does not exist"? (73)

"Even by you, the preeminent among the authoritative, [it is said] 'even of me, who possess discernment and am not to be deceived'—this is a statement that reveals the very essence of the mindset of the vulgar. (73)
O Brahman, tell me how this universe is neither established, nor produced, nor existent, so that this may become certain for me. (74)
Now he speaks according to his own inclination, beginning with "yathā" (as). || 74 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, listen as I speak; my words are not inconsistent.
Hear how this world appears as unreal, like the son of a barren woman or a city in the sky.

Having set aside the aforementioned objection, Śrī Vasiṣṭha, wishing to demonstrate that even what is non-existent can appear as if real by means of the example of a dream, said: "No," and so forth. [The word] *āravī* means possessing sound. || 75 ||
This was unarisen at the beginning; therefore, it does not truly exist.
For this appears to the mind like a city in a dream or similar state. (76)
And at the beginning of creation, the mind alone was unarisen and of non-existent form;
listen as I shall explain how this very thing is experienced in such a manner. (77)
The mind spreads this defect consisting of what is seen, which is by nature subject to decay;
though unreal, it takes on the form of the real, just as one dream follows another.
That [consciousness] itself spontaneously and swiftly conceives a body;
by that means, this splendor of a magical illusion is spread out by what has been spread out. (79)
By means of that which is extensive, long-lasting, and vast through cultivation. || 79 ||
It throbs, leaps, moves, begs,
wanders, sinks, and withdraws by itself;
it even assumes the state of another, yet remains solely [the Self].
And the mind moves due to its flickering power. || 80 ||

The sense is that there is merely the perception of an illusion, such as [thinking] that it is the mind alone which, due to its flickering power, moves and vibrates only where it does so. It attains both the state of otherness—
the degradation caused by the worldly condition— and the excellence characterized by absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).

Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Conceptualization of the Meaning of the Section on Origination," in the Utapatti-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (sage-authored) tradition. || 4 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Conceptualization of the Meaning of the Chapter on Origination," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Fifth Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, tiger among sages, what indeed is this mental delusion here?
How can that which has arisen exist? From where does the mind consisting of illusion come? || 1 ||
For the mind is indeed the root of the universe; it is said here to be its very root.
That same essence of the mind is described as the essence of the universe. (1)

Having thus established the subject matter of the discourse by describing the falsity of the mind, Śrī Rāma, desiring to know in detail its underlying reality, the manner of its superimposition, and the cause of its falsity, said: "O Blessed One, what truly exists? Is the mind the ultimate root of delusion?"
What is the meaning? || 1 ||
"O Lord, tell me in brief about origination at the beginning;
thereafter, O best among speakers, you shall explain the remainder that is yet to be told."
Having set aside the root of the origin of the entire world, he states the seed for the question concerning the mind alone as the root: "In the beginning" (ādau).
The intention is that by thoroughly understanding the first [root], the thorough understanding of all roots is established in brief.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the great dissolution has arrived and all that is non-existent has come forth, at the beginning of the entire visible creation, only the tranquil remains.

Regarding that, because it is the primary one, Vasiṣṭha spoke at length until the end of the chapter as the answer to the first question, beginning with "mahāpralaye": [The state] in the world (implied by the context); "asattām" means the incapacity for causal efficiency due to becoming subtle; "ādau" means at the beginning of the entire future visible creation; "śāntam" means tranquil and free from agitation. || 3 ||
The unborn, faultless Lord, the radiant one who never sets, the Supreme Self, the Great Lord—He who is everything, the doer of all, and eternal, remains ever-present. || 4 ||
He is the doer of all, endowed with the power for every action. || 4 ||
From which words turn back, who is realized by the liberated, and for whom designations such as "self" and so forth are merely conceptual constructs and not born of intrinsic nature. (5)

It is realized and directly experienced by the liberated ones who are free while living; it is one's own nature, which is unimposed, whereas those [other states] are not born from that, but rather arise from imposed attributes. || 5 ||
He who [is the Self] for those with the Sāṃkhya view, for the Vedāntins who proclaim Brahman,
and for the knowers of consciousness as mere consciousness (vijñāna), which is absolutely pure.
There is no dispute among any proponents that this very [reality], through various distinctions imagined by their respective intellects, is the object of their established tenets;
he says "yaḥ" (that which) with reference to that which is the substrate of all. It is "vijñānamātraṃ," meaning mere momentary consciousness. || 6 ||
He who is the emptiness of the proponents of emptiness, and the illuminator of the splendors of the sun;
he is always the speaker, the thinker, the knower of truth, the enjoyer, the seer, and the agent.
He states that the inner self (pratyagātman) of all is indeed that very same one: "The Speaker" (vaktā). *Ṛtam* means truth (*satyam*). || 7 ||
Though present, it is as if non-existent in this world; though residing within the body, it is far away—this radiance of consciousness, for it is like the light of the sun.
Because it is veiled by ignorance that renders it non-existent, it is "non-existent" from the perspective of the common person; for this very reason, it is "far-reaching. (8)
From whom the gods, Viṣṇu and the others, emerge like rays from the sun;
from whom the infinite worlds arise like bubbles from the ocean.
The gods are like rays of light due to their predominance of luminosity; however, because they lack consciousness, the worlds arise like bubbles—this is the implied meaning. || 9 ||
Into whom all visible multitudes dissolve like waters into the great ocean, and who illuminates both the self and objective phenomena like a lamp; (10)
They go forth and they dissolve even through dissolution. Because that very [Self] is self-luminous, it brings about the manifestation of both itself and others; thus he says:
"He who is established in space and in the body, in stones, in waters, and in creepers; in dust, in mountains, in winds, and in the netherworlds. (11)
He states its omnipresence by virtue of being the innermost of all with the words "He who... (verse 11).
He who washes away the agitated group of eight cities here and there;
by whom the deluded have been rendered mute, remaining as if fixed in meditation like stones.

It drenches with its own consciousness—both internally and externally—the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*), which consists of the organs of action, the organs of knowledge, the subtle elements, the vital breaths, ignorance, desire, karma, and the internal organ; this [city] is agitated and engaged in its respective functions. It is the source of consciousness for all conscious beings.
The meaning is "that by which it is impelled. Thus, he states with the words beginning "by which" that this very same [cause] is the cause for the diversity even of insentient things. || 12 ||
By whom the sky was made empty, by whom the mountains were made solid, by whom the waters were made fluid, and under whose control the sun is a lamp. (13)
He whose will is the sun-lamp, which has light as its very nature—that is to say, that which illuminates—according to the Vedic revelation: "By whom the sun blazes, kindled with splendor. || 13 ||
From this flow forth the various rains of the essenceless cycle of existence,
just as rains fall from a cloud filled with inexhaustible nectar. (14)

The showers of *āsāra* (outflows) are indeed the views of worthlessness, which are the characteristics of *saṃsāra*. The two qualifiers apply respectively: [the mountain] is "filled with the water of immortality" and "filled with the water of bliss," which is inexhaustible, eternal, and abundant. || 14 ||
In which [Brahman], which is of infinite extent, the waves of the three worlds— consisting of manifestation and disappearance—
quiver like mirages in a desert.
The suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in the sense of abundance. "Atitate" means extremely extensive. "Marīcayaḥ" refers to those waters. || 15 ||

He whose nature is imperishable, whose essence is indestructible, who dwells within all living beings; who, though hidden, yet transcends them, and who is established within all states of existence. || 16 ||

In the form of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*), it is of the nature of destruction; but in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is of the nature of non-destruction. Because it is most subtle, it is hidden within; because it is most great, it transcends everything.
Being free from phenomenal manifestation, it alone remains. And so says the Śruti: "All beings are but one foot of Him."
"Three-quarters of it are the immortal in heaven. || 16 ||
By which wind does that creeper of primordial nature dance—produced in the sky, bearing the cosmic egg as its excellent fruit, with the mind as its root and the senses as its leaves? 17.
Nature is Māyā; she herself is the creeper or vine. In the sky—that is, in pure consciousness—by which Lord... [17]
That jewel which shines within the casket of every body, in which moon these rays of the web of worlds flicker. (18)
In a small box or a casket. || 18 ||
In that tranquil mass of consciousness, which rains down nectar, living beings are like falling drops of water, and creations are like vivid flashes of lightning. (19)

The elements (bhūtas) are like streams of water due to the predominance of inertia (jāḍya); the manifest creations (sṛṣṭis) are like flashes of lightning due to the predominance of the light of consciousness (citprakāśa). || 19 ||
When objects marvel at one another through the light of that [consciousness],
by which the unreal has become born as unreal and by which the real has attained its state of being real.
They perform wonders; they carry out diverse deeds.
The body of one who does not desire [worldly things] trembles in the presence of whomever it may be;
yet for the one who is supremely detached and abides in peace within the Self, it remains inert.

That which is well-known as the body of gods, humans, animals, and so forth—this visible world, which is for that very reason utterly insentient, moves in the presence of Him who is unattached, unbound, and desireless.
[The neuter gender is used in the sense of a general category, following the rule of grammatical refinement. 21.
By him, who transcends all existence, destiny, place, time, movement, vibration, and action were brought into being. (22)

*Niyati* (the principle of necessity) is the fixed rule that at the time of creation there must necessarily be creation, and at the time of dissolution there must necessarily be dissolution; *deśa* (space) and *kāla* (time) are its delimiters. Within that [process], there is first the *calana* (movement) of the effect contained within the seed, by way of the swelling of the seed; then the *spandana* (vibration), by way of the breaking of the seed's husk and the emergence of the sprout and so forth; and after that—

Action (*kriyā*) is an operation that culminates in a fruit, proceeding through stages such as the stalk, the leaf, and the branch. It is by means of this very sequence that all entities attain existence—that is, the capacity for conventional usage and causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
By saying "transcending all existence," its ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-sattā*), which is distinct from the world, is expressed. (22)
Because it consists of pure consciousness, that which is space becomes [manifest] through the contemplation of the void;
yet, being presided over, it remains as the state of objectivity through the contemplation of objects, just as [the void appears as] substantiality. (23)

Alternatively, it is said that he himself, through the contemplation of illusory states such as space and so forth, becomes endowed with the nature of space and the like, and that there exists no other entity apart from him that possesses the designation "space" and so on; thus [the author] says: "Pure," etc. And so the Śruti declares: "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and made their names, sits calling them by those names."
With these four verses beginning with "camatkurvanti" and ending with "ityādi," the answer to the question regarding the manner in which the world is superimposed has also been stated. || 23 ||
Even while performing here the infinite multitude of great deeds for the worlds, he does nothing at all, nor does he do anything whatsoever,
remaining within his own self which is changeless and possesses consciousness that never sets.
Having abandoned arising, abiding, and dissolution, he remains as the one alone.
Now he states the reason for His being beyond falsehood: "Even while acting," and so forth.

Because He remains in that which is changeless—and therefore devoid of the arising and so on of its own kind—He performs no action whatsoever, even while manifesting a multitude of worlds, that is, multitudes of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*), along with their various divine sports (*līlā*) therein.
The meaning is that the fact that certain actions are performed is itself the reason for the falsity of the effect, because its material cause is changeless.
Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "Description of the Nature of the Divine Root Cause," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the sage Vālmīki. || 5 ||
Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "Description of the Nature of the Deity who is the Root Cause," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Sixth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Of this supreme God of gods, the Supreme Self—
Supreme perfection arises from knowledge alone, and not from the suffering of ritual performance.
Having thus described the divine nature of the primordial cause of the world, Śrī Vasiṣṭha, desiring to instruct upon the means for attaining that knowledge, said: "Of this," and so forth.
Because Hiraṇyagarbha is the primordial cause, [the following refers] to his presiding deity.
Or rather, because they are illuminators, they are the presiding deities (adhidevatā) of the senses and the mind as well, since they manifest them by acting as witnesses. || 1 ||
In this matter, neither knowledge nor ritual practice is of any use;
this has been established in order to pacify the delusion of water in a mirage. (2)

Since knowledge is to be accomplished through effort as will be described hereafter, it is also called "practice" (anuṣṭhāna) in a figurative sense. To provide an appropriate illustration for the cessation [of ignorance] by knowledge alone—something that cannot be pierced even by millions of ritual acts—he says: "like a mirage. This has been explained and observed.
This is neither far away nor near, neither unattainable nor in an inaccessible place;
having the nature of the manifestation of one’s own bliss, it is obtained from one’s very own body.
Action bears fruit when the result is neither too distant nor too near, and is obtainable through effort, as in the case of a fruit located on uneven ground;
however, since the Self is not like that, it cannot be obtained through action. Thus he says: "Not indeed...
On the other hand, its obtainability through knowledge is easily accessible, like a golden necklace forgotten around one's own neck; thus he says: "...one's own bliss..."
In this regard, asceticism, charity, vows, and the like do not provide any assistance;
there is no means here other than resting in the ultimate nature alone.
In this regard, [it refers] to the attainment of the aforementioned deity. || 4 ||
Devotion to the company of the virtuous and to the true scriptures is the cause here;
it is the genuine means for subduing the net of delusion.
Regarding this, he explains why there is absolute independence from action even with respect to the knowledge that is the means to attain That:

"The means," etc. The meaning is that since Brahman alone—which is non-artificial and eternally established—is the sublater of the web of delusion when it has ascended onto the final direct-perception modification (*vṛtti*), and thus serves as the cause of sublation, nothing else does so.
Merely through the thorough realization that "this is indeed the Real," suffering does not arise for a person, and he attains the state of liberation while living.
If it were merely through the cessation of suffering or liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), then there would be another means required; to that he says: "This... (Verse 6).
Śrī Rāma said:
"Indeed, by this Self alone, through the mere complete recognition of the Self [the reading *ātmanaḥ* is also found]..."
Furthermore, defects such as death and the like will never, under any circumstances, cause him affliction. (Note: The reading "kathaṃcana" is preferred over "kadācana.")

Thinking that the statement, "This very [Self] by the study of the Vedas..."—which directly hears of sacrifice, charity, and austerity as means to knowledge—suggests that these do not contribute anything at all, and that such an assertion refers to ordinary austerities and the like with the intent of prescribing more intense austerities and so forth, Śrī Rāma said: "Saṃpari... (verse 7).
"From how far away can this great God of gods be reached?
By what intense austerity, or by how much hardship? (8)
It is attained quickly from not far away; it is reached through knowledge. The meaning is: by what means is that knowledge swiftly accomplished? || 8 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, that Divine One is known through the effort of one's own human exertion and through blossoming discernment; He is not known by means of austerities, ritual baths, or external rites.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha spoke, considering that since the desireless actions prescribed for the purpose of seeking knowledge— which are common to those performed in other lifetimes— are exhausted at the very moment the desire to know arises, once that intense desire to know has been established, it is only the effort toward hearing [the scriptures] and so forth that is useful, not austerity and the like: Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
By the verse beginning with "svapauruṣa" (one's own prowess), etc., [it is explained]. 9.
O Rāma, without the abandonment of passion, hatred, delusion, anger, pride, and envy, austerity and charity are nothing but suffering; they are not real.
The ellipsis is "it is not a real means of proof. || 10 ||
When the mind is overcome by passion and the like, one deceives others to acquire wealth;
whatever is acquired in that state, the fruit thereof belongs to the one to whom that wealth was given. (11)

To explain why that is so, he says: "Because of passion and so forth. When passion and the like exist, since deception of others and such are inevitable in the pursuit of wealth, purity of mind is extremely difficult to attain; consequently, even the desired fruit of giving and other meritorious acts is hard to obtain, let alone knowledge and liberation (the reading *mokṣapratyā* is noted).
With the intention of providing a rebuttal, he says the two verses beginning with "rāgādi" (passion, etc.). 11.
When vows and other such practices are performed with a mind afflicted by passion and the like, that is called hypocrisy; its fruit is indeed meager. (12)
Therefore, by human effort, one should acquire the primary medicine:
association with sacred scriptures and virtuous people, which destroy the disease of worldly existence. (13)
He first shows the primary medicine itself in two ways, beginning with "sacchāstra" (the true scripture). || 13 ||
In this matter, apart from a single human effort, no other way whatsoever is found for attaining the destruction of all suffering. (14)
The other course is an alternative means. || 14 ||
Listen to what that human effort is like for the sake of attaining self-knowledge, by which the cholera-like plague of passion and hatred is entirely pacified. (15)
With a mind satisfied by contentment, one should abandon even the mere scent of worldly enjoyment, acting according to one's capacity in a manner that does not contradict the world or the scriptures.

By "livelihood" (vṛtti) is meant the acquisition of the means for living; "the scent of enjoyment" (bhogagandha) refers to the latent impression of enjoyment—that is to say, attachment to it. || 16 ||
One should first, according to one's capacity, through diligent effort and with an undisturbed mind, resort to the company of the virtuous and devotion to the true scriptures. (17)

By being undisturbed—that is, by avoiding the agitation that constitutes despondency over thinking "this is impossible"—one should act with one's own [effort], meaning with what is beneficial to oneself. || 17 ||
He who is content with whatever he has obtained, who disregards what is censurable, and who is devoted to the company of the virtuous and the study of the true scriptures, is swiftly liberated. (18)
It is censured among those instructed in the scriptures and is condemned. || 18 ||
To the great-minded one who has fully realized the nature of reality through discernment, even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara become objects of compassion. (19)
Of him by whom the nature of the self-tattva has been fully understood. || 19 ||
In whatever region people who are for the most part virtuous designate someone as "good," that person is distinguished; he is a true saint, and one should resort to him with diligent effort. (20)

He characterizes a *sādhu* with the word "place" (*deśa*). The meaning is as follows: if that place which people call a region where virtuous persons—who are devoted to the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and established custom—predominate and abound, should also be endowed with distinguished qualities such as knowledge and dispassion, then it would be a *sādhu*.
Among all branches of knowledge, the science of the inner self (adhyātmavidyā) is the foremost;
they call that treatise which relies upon its discourse a "true scripture," and through its investigation, one is liberated. (21)
Knowledge concerning the self is *adhyātmavidyā* (the science of the inner self);
the treatise that serves as the basis for discourse consisting of inquiry conducive to the arising of that knowledge is the *Upaniṣads*, the *Sūtras*, the *Bhāṣya*, this very work, and so forth. 21.

Just as impurities in water are destroyed by contact with *kataka* nuts, so too are ignorance and its effects forcibly destroyed by the discernment born from true scriptures and the company of the virtuous.
Just as the cognitions of people [and indeed the cognitions themselves] arise from conjunction. || 22 ||
Now, since there are many means [to liberation], why are only the company of the virtuous (sādhusaṃgama) and the true scripture (sacchāstra) praised? To this he says:

"The true scripture... Ignorance (avidyā), delusions (moha), and the passions such as attachment (rāga) and so forth, which are opposed to knowledge (vidyā)—the word "of waters" implies "of the mud"—these are destroyed through the practice of yoga; that is, the mental fluctuations (matayaḥ) of the external mind perish. || 22 ||

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Effort of the Seeker of Liberation," in the section on Origination within the *Mokṣopāya* of the holy *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Effort of the Seeker of Liberation," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Seventh Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said:
"This deity who has been described—the knowledge of whom brings about liberation—"
"Tell me, O Brahmin, where does he reside, and how may I obtain him?
That God who was previously described as the root of the world, beginning with Viriñci,
whose true nature is now spoken of as being free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi)."

When the proof for what was sought through this incidental inquiry had been fully understood, Śrī Rāma, desiring to know the true nature of the cause of the world under discussion, said: "He who... [referring to] that very God previously described, who is the cause of Viriñci and the others, and who is the inner self (pratyagātman)—where is he?

"In dependence upon what limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is [the Self] manifested through non-obscuration? Or in what kind of reality (*tattva*) does it abide? How may I obtain it?"—this is an expression of longing; or, since the means (*sādhana*) have already been mentioned previously, it is a question regarding another internal means (*antaraṅga-upāya*). || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This God who has been described does not abide at a distance;
he is eternally established within the body, renowned as pure consciousness alone (cinmātra).

In this regard, he first states the answer to the initial question with the word "He" (yaḥ). The statement "He does not abide at a distance" is spoken for the purpose of removing [the disciple's] anxiety. He is well-manifested in general throughout the body, but specifically and perfectly manifested within the lotus of the heart; such is the meaning of "abides. || 2 ||
This [Self] is this entire universe, yet it is not the universe; it is all-pervading.
Indeed, only this one exists, for there is no perception of anything designated as "the universe."

If it be asked, "Is he then limited solely by the body? he says, "No"—namely, "This one. If it be asked, "Is he then of the very form of the visible universe? he says, "No. The intention is that the statement regarding his being the self of the universe is made in order to establish his omnipresence by virtue of being the substratum of all. || 3 ||
This moon-bearer is pure consciousness alone; Garuḍeśvara is pure consciousness alone;
the sun is indeed pure consciousness alone; and the lotus-born Brahmā is pure consciousness alone.

With the intention of showing that not only is the entire universe consisting of effects non-existent apart from Him, but even its cause—Māyā—together with the deities who identify with its qualities (guṇas)—is likewise so, he says: "This is pure Consciousness alone. Viṣṇu is the Lord, the controller of Garuḍa. Since it is well known that the Sun is one of the three forms of the Trinity (Trimūrti), he is mentioned in that series. || 4 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
If even children say that this world is merely consciousness alone, then what indeed would remain here for instruction?

In the term *cinmātram*, by adding the suffix *mātra* to the root *cit* ending in the *kvip* suffix (denoting the agent), the meaning "the universe is mere consciousness" is obtained. Rāma raises an objection—beginning with the words "Even children"—to reveal the underlying intention of those who think that this [realization] is not fit for instruction because it is well-known even among the ignorant and cowherds in the world, and because it does not result in the ultimate human goal (*puruṣārtha*). || 5 ||
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
"That you have realized that the universe is nothing but pure consciousness and sentience— "
You have not understood even a little of that which destroys worldly existence.

Vasiṣṭha, considering that the suffix *kvip* here does not denote the agent (*kartṛ*) but rather the abstract state (*bhāva*), and thus the aforementioned fault does not apply, censures the previously mentioned view with the words "mere consciousness" (*cinmātra*). The sense is that nothing at all, however slight, has been realized; for even a trace of ignorance—the cause of delusion—has not been removed. (6)
O Rāma, consciousness is the cycle of existence; this living soul is known as a bound beast.
From this very source emerge the fears of old age and death. (7)

To the question "Why is it not understood there?", he says: "Because it is consciousness" (*cetana*). If the suffix *kvip* were applied in the sense of the agent, the words *cit* and *cetana* would have identical meanings; for since the suffix *lyu* (in *citi*) is also prescribed in the sense of the agent, its meaning would be "the agent of consciousness" (*citikartṛ*). And this is not the case for eternal consciousness.

Regarding the possibility of agency: when consciousness (cit) is reflected in the fluctuations of the impermanent mind and thus embraced by them, one who grasps the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—which serves as its substrate—as the Self is called the "individual soul" (jīva). And because he perceives only external objects as essential due to his outward orientation, he is a "bound beast" (paśu). Precisely for this reason—

The meaning is that, in accordance with the latent impressions (vāsanā) of bodies, senses, and objects, old age, death, and so forth—which reside within—seem to emerge or manifest upon the assumption of this or that body. || 7 ||
For the ignorant person, though formless, is indeed a vessel for suffering;
because it possesses consciousness, the mind—being itself an object of consciousness—remains as its own calamity.
One might object: "Is it not established by the very knowledge of that [Self] as distinct from the gross, embodied body that there is no notion of old age, death, and so forth?
For the Śruti says, 'Verily, pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless'? Anticipating this, he says:
"The beast. Even though he is devoid of a gross, unembodied body, he has not achieved his purpose because he is ignorant—that is, possessed of nescience (ajñāna).
That mind which is characterized by volition (*cetanīya*) becomes that very form of misfortune and remains as such; therefore, it is itself a vessel for suffering.

According to the Vedic scripture beginning with "the bodiless," the meaning is that the three bodies—known as the gross, the subtle, and the causal—are devoid [of agency], and thus pleasure and pain do not touch them, not merely that they are devoid of the gross body alone. Even so, in the dream state...
The meaning is: "from the sight of what is pleasant and unpleasant. || 8 ||
That which is freedom from objects of thought, or rather, the state of being turned toward the non-objective—
that is its "full" state (or, according to another reading, its "become" state); having known that,
one does not grieve.
To the question of what kind of knowledge of that [Self] leads to the state of having accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatā*), he says: "cetya... etc.

It is well known that freedom from the object of thought (*cetya*) pertains to liberation, whereas being oriented toward the non-object of thought (*acetyonmukhatā*) pertains to meditative absorption (*samādhi*). || 9 ||
The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.
In this regard, he cites scripture as authority with the words "it is split.

Due to the destruction of the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), the "knot of the heart"—characterized by the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of identity with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is its effect—is split, that is, it perishes; and by that very destruction, the doubts and so forth rooted in it also cease to exist. This is the meaning.
Even the supreme cause becomes inferior when [the object] is of such a nature.
Moreover, its tendency toward the object of thought cannot be restrained without the non-occurrence of that object; for how indeed can the visible object of thought be stilled? (11)

[Objection: But then, since the tendency toward objects of thought (*cetyonmukhatva*) can be restrained simply by means of the yoga characterized by the cessation of the mind (*cittanirodha*), what is the use of the effort for knowledge? To this he replies with the words "of that" (*tasya*). The impossibility of the object of thought—the visible world—is its sublation at the root through knowledge. [The ellipsis is: "How indeed would it be stilled without knowledge? And thus, without...
The meaning is that such knowledge, which is indeed samādhi in its very nature, does not even come to fruition. || 11 ||
