That which is of the nature of neither object nor subject cannot, without the absence of manifestation, turn toward its own essential nature;
for how could there be such a turning toward one's own nature solely through the cessation of objects? (12)
Thus, he says "acetya" (without an object of thought) to show that liberation, too, is difficult to attain without knowledge:

that which is called liberation is the nature of non-objectifying consciousness (*acetya-cit-svarūpa*); and where could that exist without the previously mentioned impossibility of an object of thought (*cetya*)? For, in *samādhi*, it is solely...

The state of being oriented toward one's own true nature (*svarūponmukhatva*) also occurs only through the obstruction of the object of cognition and the sublation of the visible world (*dṛśyabādha*); therefore, the sense is that its necessity for liberation is self-evident. || 12 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, when which living being is realized does transmigratory existence not perish? Where and of what nature is that ignorant beast who is of the form of space? (13)

Regarding the phrase "in which": [the opponent objects] that these two verses of Rāma’s inquiry are inconsistent; for since the nature of the *jīva*, its substratum, and the root cause based on the mind—namely, that "O conscious Rāma, this transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is remembered as the beast (*paśu*)"—have already been stated previously, the first verse would not arise [as a new inquiry]. [The term *prāktanatvena* means "by virtue of having been stated previously."]

[The reading: "And because the nature of Brahman was already addressed as the subject of the first verse concerning creation, it is not fit to be questioned again. If this is argued, then the question as heard in the literal text was not what Rāma intended;

rather, it is an objection (*ākṣepa*). For instance: "But surely it has been stated that the transmigrating being (*jīva*) alone is the world; [how then can there be liberation] when he attains Brahman?"

Otherwise, it would follow that even Brahman is subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*). If that [transmigratory state] were not attained [by Brahman], then the scriptures concerning the knowledge of its means and so forth would be rendered useless. Therefore, the nature belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*) must be stated as something entirely different.
Likewise, is its substratum (*ādhāra*) also Brahman itself, or something else? In the first case, by means of knowledge...

Thinking that if all duality were sublated along with Brahman, it would result in the "logic of killing the bridegroom" (varaghātanyāya), and that in the second case it would contradict the non-duality of Brahman, Śrī Rāma asks: "In which...
[He is] like the sky, yet possessing a form, meaning he has an imagined form. On what substratum does he abide? Of what nature is he? What...?
"At the limit of saṃsāra" means at the limit of the self; [there is also a reading: "or at another limit"]. || 13 ||

O Brahmin, tell me: what is that Supreme Self like, which is seen through the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures, and which enables one to cross the ocean of saṃsāra? (Note: The reading *bhavitāvasthā* is found in the text.)

Furthermore, if the individual soul (jīva) were indeed within the realm of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), then what would be the nature of that which is taught in the scriptures as the one who enables its crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra? For no one can enable one to cross the very ocean of water by means of that same ocean.
Therefore, the statement that the soul is subject to transmigratory existence is contradictory. || 14 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Those who desire this consciousness—the individual soul (jīva)—which has perished in the wilderness of births, are ignorant even though they are considered learned. (15)

This might be so if the individual soul (*jīva*) alone were to transmigrate, if the individual soul alone were liberated through its own knowledge, or if the individual soul alone were the ultimate reality (*tattvika ātmā*). But it is not so. For the Śruti states: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself, thinking 'I am Brahman,' and therefore it became all. Thus, transmigration arises from the ignorance of Brahman itself.

This is because it would contradict the teaching that liberation arises from one’s own knowledge, and it would also contradict the negation of any other conscious principle, such as in the passage "There is no other seer but this," and so forth; for [the individual self] is not the Self, being an object of the notion of "this" (idamkāra) and being merely imagined, according to the scriptural text: "Brahman itself, by means of this living self... and so on.

Intending to show that— since the individual soul (jīva), which is erroneously grasped as the self due to being included within the limits of saṃsāra, transmigrates while thinking "I am the jīva" by means of its [illusory] attributes— it follows that the state of being a transmigrator belongs to the jīva alone; therefore, even when that [illusory identification] is sublated, there is no fault such as the "fallacy of slaying the bridegroom" (varaghātanyāya).
Strengthening his own statement, Śrī Vasiṣṭha said with the words beginning "yadetad" (this which...): the taking of birth is an indicative mark for the acquisition of a physical body. || 15 ||
The individual soul (*jīva*) alone is indeed transmigratory existence—the continuity of consciousness and the succession of suffering.
When this is known, nothing remains unknown anywhere. (16)
O Rāma, if the Supreme Self is known, the continuity of suffering comes to an end,
just as cholera ceases when the influence of poison has subsided.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, describe to me truly the form of the Supreme Self, by seeing which the mind will completely cross over all delusions. (18)

Thus composed, Rāma asks again clearly about the very matter concerning the commencement of creation—which had been previously mentioned but was interrupted by incidental discourse—using the words "rūpam" (form). The plural number in "mohāt" (from delusions) is used because of the multiplicity of effects.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The form that exists in the interval when consciousness has traveled from one distant place to another in the very twinkling of an eye— that is its true nature.
Of the Supreme Self. || 19 ||
In this world, since a cognition devoid of an object is not established, and because the nature of immediate consciousness— which is unobscured and objectless—

does not enter the path of experience even when it is described as "That," he says "from the place" (*deśāt*) so that it may ascend to that [realization]. This is like the perception of the moon at the tip of a branch through the gateway of the eyes.
For one whose immediate, non-mediated consciousness has emerged and been manifested within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),

the region of the moon is reached from the region of the branch in a mere moment; since the simultaneous perception of both the branch and the moon would otherwise be inexplicable, [the visual ray] begins from the location of the branch.

The state of being continuously interwoven up to the moon must necessarily be asserted; for in the interval, there is an absence of both a cause and the experience [of such a break]. In that case, although that [continuity] has as its objects the branch and the location of the moon, it is well known that its very nature—which exists in the middle—is the nature of immediate consciousness (*cidrūpa*) devoid of an external object.
The meaning is that even the Supreme Self should be known as having that same form. || 19 ||
The absolute non-existence of saṃsāra as it appears [or, according to another reading,
"of the world's existence"] exists within that great ocean of awakening which is the very nature of the Supreme Self. (20)

The meaning is that it has fallen into falsity in its own place (or, according to another reading, in its own substratum), without undergoing any modification such as destruction, while the world remains as it is— or, even with the reading "in a mere moment" (*nimeṣeṇaiva*), the meaning remains the same, based on the etymology *jagat* = that which goes toward sublation (*bādha*). 20
That in which the sequence of seer and seen, though present, has reached its setting;
that which is space yet not of space—that is the nature of the Supreme Self. (21)
He states that very point clearly: "The Seer," etc. Even though space is sublated [by higher knowledge], it is called "space" because of its vastness due to being unlimited. || 21 ||
That which is empty yet as if not empty, wherein the world remains empty;
that which is empty despite the flood of creation—that is the form of the Supreme Self.

The meaning is that although the world is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), because it is full by virtue of its true reality as the essential nature of all things, it is as if not empty even in the slightest degree; thus, the world—which is empty and non-existent—is established within Him and attains the state of existence. This occurs while ignorance, characterized by the flood of creation, persists.
That which, though existent, is as if empty because it is useless, is indeed empty. || 22 ||
That which, though consisting of pure consciousness, remains like a massive stone—insentient within and indeed insentient in form—is the nature of the Supreme Self. (23)

Because of the abundance of the Great Consciousness (mahācit), although it possesses attributes such as being non-material (*asthūla*), it appears to the vision of the ignorant as something massive and gross like a stone, or indeed as insentient—*iva* being used in the sense of *vā*. The meaning is that it exists as if it were insentient. || 23 ||
That by which everything, both external and internal, having attained union,
reaches the state of its own true nature— that is the form of the Supreme Self.

The meaning is that the entire world— including the external (consisting of the objective elements and their presiding deities) and the internal (the spiritual self)— having attained an illusory identity through conjunction with Him, acquires its own essential existence, characterized by the fitness for the empirical usage "existent, existent. || 24 ||
Just as light is to illumination, and as emptiness is to the sky, so is this established in that which is the nature of the Supreme Self. 25.

"Just as light and so forth exist as the very self of luminosity and so forth"—this statement of an illustration is made from the perspective of worldly perception. In reality, however, it is Brahman alone that, persisting through to the final effect, is the self of all entities; it is not intermediate states such as light and the like. || 25 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
How indeed is it understood that the Supreme Self is of the nature of pure existence?
And how is it that this visible world, known as the "universe," is impossible [within that reality]? (26)

Indeed, whatever is apprehended by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as it is, that exists exactly in that way and not in another form. Since Brahman is not so apprehended, how can it be determined to have the nature of existence? And how can the world, being apprehended in such a manner, be unreal? Rāma raises this doubt with the words, "The nature of existence," referring to this much [of] the means of valid cognition.
The meaning is: "of the vast," that is, of that which is established as having great measure. || 26 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: If there should arise a firm realization of the absolute non-existence of this worldly delusion, which has arisen like the color of the sky; || 27 ||

It is unproven that Brahman cannot be known through means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for when there is no obstacle, It is understood through the Great Sentences (*mahāvākya*). The removal of obstacles occurs precisely through the realization of the falsity of the duality superimposed upon That. Indeed, the reality of the rope cannot be realized without first setting aside [the appearance of] the snake and so forth.
Intending to show that it is possible to awaken [the mind], the venerable Vasiṣṭha said, beginning with the words "of delusion" (bhramasya), etc. (verse 27).
That is known to be the true form of Brahman, which cannot be attained by any other action;
for there is no other auspicious path except through the absolute non-existence of the perceptible world. (28)
When this visible world has reached the state of absolute non-existence, that which remains as it truly is—
the ultimate reality— is then realized and born from that.
The meaning is this: that which remains is awakened; he who is awakened becomes, through that awakening, the very Self of the knower.
There is no reflection of consciousness anywhere except where there is an object of perception;
indeed, a mirror never exists without a reflection.
He states the reasoning for the point already mentioned with the word "no. The meaning is that there is no reflection of the Knower, who is Brahman, in the intellect (*buddhi*).

For Brahman, when reflected in the intellect, would burn away the ignorance that obscures it and would thus be perceived in its true nature. However, Brahman does not reflect in an intellect in which the superimposed [world] is regarded as real.

The meaning is that when the intellect is occupied by opposing duality, the reflection of non-duality cannot arise. Now, [the author] says "in some cases" (kvacit) regarding the state where the intellect is devoid of the reflection of duality, so that Brahman may be reflected there:
just as a mirror does not remain in any state whatsoever without the grasping of some reflection.
In the same way, the intellect (*buddhi*) also [does not perceive] without the grasping of the reflection of duality; such is the meaning. || 30 ||
Without the possibility of its own existence, this visible world called "jagat" can never, by anyone, be understood as the supreme reality. (31)

He states that by this reasoning as well, what was previously mentioned is established—namely, "the world" (jagat). This refers to falsity (*mithyātva*), which is the impossibility of its own existence; in other words, the ascertainment thereof. || 31 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O sage, how can there be non-existence for this entire range of visible things, for the cosmic egg and the stability of the world? Where is Mount Meru within the interior of a mustard seed?
Rāma, intending a further distinction, raises a second question with the words "iyata" (of this much):

"This might be so if the world were superimposed upon Brahman; however, that itself is impossible, because in Brahman—which is of the nature of pure consciousness and supremely subtle—of this much [the world cannot exist]."
Since it is impossible for the gross phenomenal world, as vast as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), to be superimposed [upon the Self], he says this: "Where is Meru? (verse 32).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, if you remain for a few days with an undisturbed mind, intent upon the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures, then in an instant— || 33 ||

"This would indeed be so if grossness were capable of withstanding investigation in this world, but it is not so. When we have, over time, weakened your very conviction regarding grossness through logical arguments, then you will comprehend what we have said. With this intention, the venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
By the words "for days" and so forth; one whose intellect is untiring is one whose mind is undisturbed. || 33 ||
I cleanse your perception of the visible world as one would [wash away] a mirage in the desert;
when the visible object ceases to exist, the state of being a perceiver also subsides, and pure awareness alone remains.

The state of being a seer exists when there is an object to be seen; the state of being an object to be seen exists when there is a seer. Indeed, duality exists when there is unity, and unity exists through the application of duality.

He demonstrates that in the absence of the duality of the visible object, there is not only the absence of the seer alone, but also the absence of both duality and unity—stating: "The state of being a seer... The meaning is: "when there is a seer," i.e., when the observer exists.
For unity is postulated as a negation of duality and so forth only when those [categories] are well-established elsewhere; it is not [postulated] otherwise.
The meaning is: "when that which is to be excluded is not established. || 35 ||
For when one is absent, the establishment of both does not indeed occur here;
when duality, unity, the seer, and the seen have ceased, that which is eternal remains.
Thus, he says that only pure Being (sanmātra), devoid of both duality and unity, remains: "dvitvaikya... (verse 36).
I cleanse from the mirror of the mind all the impurities— the entire world of perception such as the sense of "I" and so forth— by means of the realization of their absolute non-existence.
He also declares the cleansing of the visible through another method: "Ahamtādi... (verse 37).
The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being.
Since that which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature cannot be found, what defilement is there to be cleansed? (38)

For an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) cannot be called either the existence of what is non-existent, its own nature, or both—since none of these three are observed in the case of a sky-flower and the like. Likewise, the non-existence of even that which exists is impossible because it would contradict its own nature;
thus, once the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*) is established, there is no difficulty in clearing away that [objection].
This is the meaning. || 38 ||
That which is seen spread out here, though unproduced at the beginning of the world,
is expanded within its own pure self by virtue of the Brahman-consciousness.

Thus, origination, even if it were real, would be purposeless; however, [origination] of that which is non-existent is impossible. Therefore, he says in two verses beginning with "jagat" (the world), that the state of being a bracelet imagined in gold is easily established by the very perception of the gold itself. || 39 ||
That which is called the world has not arisen, does not exist, and is not perceived; just as the state of being a bracelet and so forth exists in gold, why this effort to polish it? (40)
Thus, I shall explain this in detail through many logical arguments, so that the uncontradicted reality may be experienced by oneself. (41)
He also promises, by way of digression, to state other modes that will be explained further on, beginning with the word "likewise" (tathā). || 41 ||
For how could there be existence here for that which has never arisen from the very beginning?
How could there be a river of water in a desert, or a planet in a second moon? (42)
He states that even the apprehension of a non-arisen thing as if it were existent is itself non-existent, by saying "in the beginning" (ādau). || 42 ||
Just as the son of a barren woman does not exist, just as there is no water in a desert,
and just as there is no yakṣa in the sky, so too the delusion of the world does not exist. (43)
And thus, since the non-existence of both the error and its object is established, he states this with an illustration: "Just as... (verse 43).
O Rāma, that which is seen here is indeed the stainless Brahman;
this I shall explain further on through reasoning, and not merely by words.

What then? He says "this which" (yadidam) to show that [the object] exists in reality within the appearances of perception, by way of reasoning—that is, by way of logical consistency such as narrative and so forth. || 44 ||
O noble-minded one, it is improper to show contempt for that which those who know the truth proclaim here through reason;
for they know that one who, being of deluded intellect, disregards what is consistent with reason and persists in a stubborn grasp, is indeed ignorant.

Fearing that there might be contempt—thinking, "What is the use of even a thousand arguments when one has missed the mark, like an archer whose arrow has gone astray?"—since [the truth] does not enter the path of experience—he says: "That which...

Those who know it are the knowers of reality (*tattvajñāḥ*). "Having disregarded" means having shown no respect for. One whose stubborn insistence (*abhiniveśa*) is fixed upon something difficult and irrational is so described.
Those who are wise know such a person to be truly ignorant; this is the implied meaning. || 45 ||

Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Declaration of the Non-existence of the Worldly Manifestation from the Beginning," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (sage-authored) tradition.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Declaration on the Non-Existence of the World and Other Objects of Perception," in the Utapatti-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Eighth Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said: By what reasoning is this known, and how is this accomplished?
When this has been realized through logic, nothing remains to be known. || 1 ||
The knowledge of reality previously described is obtained from authentic scriptures and not from elsewhere;
even among authentic scriptures, this treatise is said to yield immediate results.
Śrī Rāma asks about that which was promised by the Guru, namely, "I shall explain it through reasoning":
"By what means is this so?"—referring to what was stated, "O Rāma, that which is seen here is indeed the stainless Brahman.
By the word "in this" (*etasmin*), there is a reference back to this very same point. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For a long time, this cholera of false knowledge has been deeply rooted.
That which is called "the world" (jagat), known as the result of non-investigation, does not cease without knowledge. || 2 ||
O Rāma, I shall tell you these narratives for the sake of attaining awakening;
if you listen to them, O virtuous one, you will indeed be liberated and wise. (3)
"I speak" means "I shall say"; these [arguments] present before you are primarily composed of reasoning. || 3 ||
If, out of a habit of agitation, you rise from the midst [of your task] and depart,
then nothing at all will be accomplished today for you who possess the nature of an animal.

If not—that is, if you do not hear—it is because of the cause stated as "distress" (udvega) and so forth. Therefore, that [inability] is the nature of animals such as beasts, namely the unfitness for hearing the true scriptures; and you possess that [nature]. || 4 ||
Whoever desires an object and strives for it accordingly will certainly attain it, provided he does not turn back out of exhaustion.

Anticipating the doubt of one of dull intellect—who might think, "Surely this is difficult even for the great; how could it be obtained by someone like me?"—he says: "He who... (verse 5). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "turns back from half-effort."
O Rāma, if you become devoted to the company of the virtuous and to the true scriptures,
then within days, or at most months, you shall attain the supreme state.
Śrī Rāma said:
O best among those who know the scriptures, for the awakening of self-knowledge, what indeed would be that principal scripture by knowing which one no longer grieves? (7)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O high-minded one, for those whose primary concern is the knowledge of the Self, this auspicious Great Rāmāyaṇa is the supreme scripture among all scriptures.
From hearing this supreme history, awakening arises;
this is declared to be the essence of all histories.
To the question "Whence does its superiority come?", he says: "Of all... (verse 9).
Since the state of liberation while living arises spontaneously upon hearing this verbal composition, it is therefore exceedingly purifying.
In the realm of speech, that is, in a book consisting of a composition of sentences. || 10 ||
Through inquiry, the world of appearances, though seemingly established, comes to an end—
just as when a dream is fully recognized, the mental impression of that dream and so forth vanishes right there.
Just as when one is in a dream and realizes "this is a dream," the perception of the reality of the dream comes to an end, so it is in this case. || 11 ||
"What exists here exists elsewhere; what does not exist here exists nowhere else.
The wise know this to be the treasury of all sciences and treatises. (12)
Elsewhere, in another treatise: "The collection of reasonings employed for awakening is the treasury-house of those who possess the wealth of the science of consciousness. (12)
Whoever should hear this constantly, the intellect of that person of noble wonder will undoubtedly attain the supreme awakening even beyond awakening itself. (13)
"Of awareness" (bodhasya) means even of an awareness produced by other texts; "supreme" (param) means most excellent. The genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative (pañcamyarthe). || 13 ||
For one who does not find pleasure in this due to the arising of evil deeds, let him examine whatever true scripture exists within the body of knowledge. (14)
The meaning is: if this does not please someone, let him investigate another true scripture; we have no animosity toward that. || 14 ||
Upon hearing this, liberation while living (jīvanmuktatva) is experienced by oneself, just as freedom from disease is felt when an excellent medicine has been drunk. || 15 ||
What, then, is the cause of its superiority? He states it: "the state of being liberated while living" (jīvanmuktatva). || 15 ||
For when this scripture is being heard, the listener understands it within himself:
"This was indeed spoken by us exactly as it is, like a boon or a curse. (16)

This state of liberation while living (jīvanmuktatva) he himself knows and experiences by his own self; the meaning is that what has been stated by us here is exactly as it is, whether like a boon or like a curse—it is precisely according to reality and not otherwise. || 16 ||
This suffering of saṃsāra perishes for you through the very discourse of self-investigation;
it does not [perish] by wealth, charity, austerity, sacred learning, or the Vedas.
By means of hundreds of efforts arising from that narration. || 17 ||
It perishes through the very discourse of this present work, which consists of inquiry into one's own self;
and it does not perish through wealth, gifts, austerities, sacred learning, the hearing of dualistic scriptures, the Vedas consisting of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa),
or through the verbal compositions characterized by dualistic Vedic and scriptural teachings.
And by hundreds of efforts such as performing sacrifices and offering oblations at sunrise, the suffering of saṃsāra is not destroyed for you; this is the meaning. || 17 ||
Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "The Exposition of the True Scripture," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the True Scripture," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Ninth Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
With their minds fixed on that and their lives absorbed in it, they were awakening one another.
And constantly speaking of that, they are satisfied and they rejoice. || 1 ||
The characteristics of one liberated while living, as well as his state of being the self of all, and the nature of the Self remaining after the dissolution of the world, are here proclaimed. (1)

Even self-inquiry must be characterized by a one-pointedness that persists until final ascertainment; it is not sufficient if it is merely occasional, interrupted by other activities, or obscured by them. This is with the intention of [citing] such scriptural passages as: "He who sports in the Self, rejoices in the Self, and is active [in this way], he is the best among the knowers of Brahman," and "Established in Brahman, he attains immortality."

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "With their minds fixed on That" means those whose consciousness (citta) is centered solely upon that Self. "Whose vital breaths are directed toward That" means those whose life-functions (prāṇas) are exerted exclusively for the attainment of That. || 1 ||
For those who are solely devoted to knowledge and who investigate self-knowledge,
that state of liberation while living arises, which is indeed the very same as liberation after death.

Those whose single-pointed devotion (*ekaniṣṭhā*)—characterized by being free from all other activities—is directed toward knowledge and the means of attaining it, such as hearing [the scriptures], for them there is only pure liberation following the departure from the body; it is nothing else. || 2 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, [tell me] the characteristics of one who is liberated while living and of one who is liberated after the body has fallen away.
Speak so that I may likewise strive with an intellect guided by the vision of the scriptures.

When the description of the fruits of hearing [the teachings] and so forth led to the mention of the characteristics of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and one liberated after death (videhamukta), the seeker Śrī Rāma said, "O Brahman," with an intellect produced by the vision characterized by the scriptures. || 3 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He for whom this world remains exactly as it is, even while engaged in worldly activity—remaining like the sky that has set—is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 4 ||

Since liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is the prerequisite for disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*), and according to the maxim that "the order of meaning (*arthakrama*) is stronger than the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*"),

Śrī Vasiṣṭha, bypassing the sequence of the questions, first spoke regarding the characteristics of one liberated while living, beginning with the word "yathā" (just as): "For one who, even while engaged in worldly activities not forbidden by the scriptures, [perceives] the universe through the vision of ultimate reality..."
The meaning is that once the sun has set, the sky remains like the void—empty—and like a city in a mirror, it appears even though it does not exist at all. || 4 ||

One who has attained exclusive devotion to pure awareness, who remains as if in deep sleep even while awake, and who conducts worldly affairs—such a person is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 5 ||

He who, though engaged in worldly activity, considers himself disciplined in the thought "I do nothing at all"—according to the direction taught by the Blessed One as being a knower of reality—remains free from modification even while awake, like one who is asleep. || 5 ||
He whose facial radiance neither rises nor sets in the face of pleasure or pain,
remaining steadfast in whatever circumstances arise— he is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
He who remains awake while in the state of deep sleep, for whom no waking state exists,
and whose consciousness is free from latent impressions— he is called liberated while living.

He remains as if in deep sleep within his own changeless self; thus, although he is in such a state, he awakens within himself through the destruction of the sleep of ignorance (*avidyā*). For him, there exists no waking state characterized by the perception of objects through the senses, which arises from the identification with the body, senses, and so forth. For him—
The meaning is that for one whose awakening is free from latent impressions (nirvāsana), even a dream—which has as its cause the arising of the impressions of the waking state—does not exist. || 7 ||
Even while acting in accordance with passion, hatred, fear, and the like,
he who remains as pure as the inner sky is called liberated while living.

"Anurūpam" means appropriate or as is fitting; or it refers to an imitation and dramatic representation like that of an actor. "Acchasthaḥ" means one who abides in the clear, unobstructed Self; according to the rule *supi sthaḥ*, the suffix *ka* is applied. || 8 ||
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not defiled—
whether he is acting or not acting— he is called liberated while living.
The meaning is that one is not smeared by the notions of agency or non-agency. || 9 ||
He who, within half a blink of an eye, perceives the dissolution and creation of the three worlds as being equal to himself, is called one liberated while living.

The meaning is that he who would perceive the dissolution of the three worlds from the opening (*unmeṣa*)—that is, the removal of the veil—of his own conscious self (*ātman*), and their prior origination from its closing (*nimeṣa*)—that is, from the presence of the veil. This expression "half [a day]" is used because in the state of disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*) there is the complete opening of the self, while in the Lord (*Īśvara*) there is the absence of any veil; thus it applies to both cases. || 10 ||
He from whom the world does not shrink away, and who does not shrink away from the world, being liberated from joy, envy, and fear—he is called one liberated while living. 11.
He is neither agitated nor afraid; "the world" refers to the people, because he is liberated from ignorance, pride, and the causes of joy, resentment, and fear. || 11 ||
He whose mental agitation regarding saṃsāra has been stilled, who, though possessing parts, is partless;
who, though possessing a mind, is mindless—he is called one liberated while living.

For although he possesses mind and consciousness, he is without mind and without mental faculty; he is one for whom the conceptualization of saṃsāra has been stilled and whose intellect perceives reality. From the perspective of others, though he possesses parts as limbs of the body, he is partless and without divisions.

He who, though engaged in the practical dealings of all kinds of objects, remains cool and whose self is complete even amidst material things—he is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 13 ||

He is cool, for he is not scorched by passion and the like; because this Self is complete even within objects such as those of passion, since He is the very essence of them. The meaning is that passion and the like cannot arise toward one's own Self—which is neither to be rejected nor acquired—nor toward an object superimposed upon it, once that object has been determined to be false. || 13 ||
Having abandoned the state of liberation while living when the body has come under the power of time, he enters into disembodied liberation, just as the wind enters a state of motionlessness.

Now he begins to describe the characteristics of liberation while in the disembodied state (*videhamukta*), which was asked about first—starting with the words "jīvanmukta" (liberated while living). This means when [the body] has been brought under control or swallowed by time; that is to say, when the *prārabdha* karma has been exhausted. || 14 ||
The one liberated while in the body (videhamukta) neither rises nor sets, nor does he cease;
he is neither existent nor non-existent, neither far away, nor am I, nor anything other than that.
First, he states the definition of its essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*), which is established through the experience of the wise: "He is the one liberated while in the body" (*videhamukta*).
Rising and setting refer to growth and decay. "Being" (*sat*) is the manifest; "non-being" (*asat*) is the unmanifest. Nor am I "I," nor am I "not-I. Nor am I anything else. || 15 ||
Becoming the sun, he blazes; as Viṣṇu, he protects the three worlds;
as Rudra, he withdraws all things; and as the lotus-born Brahmā, he creates the emanations.

Regarding that [Self], he states its "incidental definition" (taṭasthalakṣaṇa), characterized by being the universal self from the perspective of the world, beginning with the words "the sun," and so forth. || 16 ||
Having become space, he supports the mass of wind along with the serpents, gods, and demons;
and having become situated upon the principal mountain ranges, he serves as the abode for the cities of the world-protectors.
The Kulācala mountains are Meru and Mānasottara; for it is these two alone that are renowned as the cities of the world-protectors. || 17 ||
Having become the earth, she sustains this unbroken stability of the world;
having become grass, shrubs, and creepers, she yields a continuous succession of fruits.
The stability of the world and the social conventions of people. || 18 ||
Bearing the forms of both water and fire, it blazes and flows swiftly;
the moon produces nectar, yet it also produces the deadly poison Hālāhala.
"Having become the poison known as *hālāhala*, it produces death—that is, it causes dying"—here there is a Vedic substitution of verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇavyatyaya*). || 19 ||
Fire manifests as light, darkness becomes blindness,
the void attains the state of space, and the mountain, being present, effectively obstructs.
The light manifests the quarters of the sky. || 20 ||
The mind makes the moving immobile and the immobile takes on a stationary form;
having become the ocean, it encircles the woman Earth like a bracelet.

"Citta" refers to one whose consciousness is clearly manifested through the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); "sthāvarākṛtiḥ" means having a form that is mostly insentient due to the lack of clear consciousness. [He approached] her, who was actually the Earth in the form of a woman. || 21 ||
Having become the embodiment of the supreme sun, spreading light to its furthest limit,
it remains in a state of absolute tranquility, extending even to the mass of motes of dust within the three worlds. (22)

The Supreme Sun, whose body is the unconditioned conscious self, though it radiates and expands the multitude of objects— from the light itself down to the entire three worlds, from the first principles to the smallest mote of dust— remains itself eternally tranquil and changeless. || 22 ||
Whatever appears here— whether it has appeared,
is appearing, or will appear— that entire visible world throughout the three periods of time is indeed this [Self]. (23)
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, why do you speak thus? For this vision of mine has indeed become difficult; it is my firm conviction that it is hard to attain and difficult to master. (24)

Considering that liberation is difficult to attain because an even vision [of reality] is rare due to the abundance of obstacles, and longing for the means to achieve it, Śrī Rāma said: "How so? For indeed, this uneven vision makes liberation difficult to reach; yet, even if it should somehow be attained, therein—
The grammatical connection is as follows: "It is my conviction that [this path] is difficult to ascend because of the difficulty of stabilizing the mind. || 24 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, this is called liberation; this is declared to be Brahman; this is described as Nirvāṇa. Listen now: how is it attained? (25)
Thus, consoling the longing Rāma by instructing him on the means to attain that [state], Vasiṣṭha said:
"This visible world which is perceived, joined with 'I-ness,' 'this-ness,' and so forth [in some versions: 'you-ness,' 'that-ness,' etc.],"
Even though this exists, it is attained through the intellect by means of its non-arising. || 26 ||

The nature of "I" (ahantva) is the superimposition of subjectivity upon that which is not the self; the nature of "thou" (tvam) is object-consciousness. Although this appears as "existent" (sat), like the son of a barren woman, it is absolutely unproduced—[the reading is "anutpanna," meaning "unborn"].

Śrī Rāma said: "O best among those who know what is to be known, when those liberated while in the body (videhamukta) attain the three worlds, do they consider themselves as having merely entered into creation?"

Rāma raises an objection, wondering whether, because the scriptures declare that Brahman is the self of all, the attainment of the state of Brahman might not actually result in the attainment of saṃsāra through its very nature; he says: "Those who are liberated while in the body..."—I believe those liberated while in the body have merely gone to the state of creation, that is, to the condition of saṃsāra. || 27 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: If the three worlds exist, then let them all go to that place where not even the slightest meaning of the word "the three worlds" can possibly occur.

Vasiṣṭha refutes this by relying precisely on the previously mentioned absolute non-arising (*atyantānutpatti*), stating: "If [it] exists... and so forth. The connection with the subsequent verse is as follows: "If that [world]—in the form of this or that creation—exists, then how can there be the cognition of the aforementioned meaning (non-existence) in a place where those liberated ones do not exist? || 28 ||
Since this has attained the state of being the three worlds, how can there be an understanding of the meaning of the word "Brahman" as previously stated?
Therefore, this conceptualization of the referent of the word "world" is not possible for us.
The cognition of the stated meaning is the understanding of the intended meaning; "therefore" is the conclusion. || 29 ||
Through the awakening of true being, all this is realized as Brahman alone—the non-dual, peaceful, mere appearance, as stainless as space. (30)
It is non-dual and not other than itself; it is mere appearance, mere consciousness. Being is the state of pure existence through the realization of that. 30.
For even after searching throughout the golden bracelet, I did not perceive anywhere that which is called "bracelet-ness" apart from the pure gold itself. (31)
When examining through the inward vision, he demonstrates by means of examples the unreality of that which is superimposed upon it:
"Without water, I do not perceive anything at all in a wave of milk;
for such a thing as 'waveness' is seen only where it does not exist at all. (32)
Vibration is never, at any time or place, anything other than wind;
wind is always vibration itself, and therefore the world is not distinct from it. (33)
Just as emptiness is in the sky, heat alone is water in the desert, and light alone is always in the world, so too is Brahman the three worlds. (34)
Śrī Rāma said: O sage, instruct me in that supreme method by which liberation arises through the realization of the absolute non-existence of the visible world.

Having thus reflected upon the examples shown and synthesizing the meaning of the Guru’s teaching in two verses, one should not remain unsettled due to the arising of conceptual doubts regarding impossibility, caused by distractions from contrary mental impressions.

As if unable to comprehend it with the mind alone, he asks for the means of such comprehension, beginning with the words "atyanta" (absolute) and so forth. [The meaning is: by that sublation (*bādha*), which consists in the attainment of the absolute non-existence of the world as an object of perception. || 35 ||
When the seer and the seen, which have mutually coalesced and are of a single number, reach a state where duality has ceased to exist, only nirvāṇa remains. (36)

"Of the two [factors] that have become one" (muthaḥ ekasaṃkhyayoḥ) means that they have attained the state of being sublated and remaining, respectively, as the self-luminous nature (svaprakāśātmabhāva). || 36 ||
Therefore, just as the visible world is absolutely non-existent, so too does Brahman alone, abiding in its own nature, perceive it; explain this to me. (37)
How is this known through reasoning, and how is it established? O Sage, if this were established, nothing further would remain to be proven. (38)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This cholera of false knowledge has been firmly rooted for a long time;
it is surely pacified, uprooted, by the mantra of inquiry. 39.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said that when conviction regarding the meaning heard arises even once, repeated and long-term non-practice is itself the means for its stabilization and ascertainment—beginning with the words "for a long time" (bahukālam) and so forth. (39)
It is not possible to destroy this suddenly in an instant,
for it involves ascending and descending equally upon a mountain.

Just as for a man standing on a mountain peak, falling straight down from all sides onto such a mountain—where ascent and descent are equal—it is impossible to perform them both simultaneously and with such speed; so it is here. || 40 ||
Therefore, so that the delusion of the world may be stilled through the yoga of practice, by means of reasoning and logical arguments, this is being told; listen. (41)
O Rāma, I shall relate this narrative for the sake of attaining awakening;
if you listen to it, O virtuous one, you will indeed be liberated and awakened. (42)
The narrative concerning the dissolution of the world, which is about to be told.
Now, this section on origination is being told by me to you;
for, O Rāma, that which indeed originates becomes liberated thereby.

Now, following the narrative of dissolution (*pralaya*), there is the section on origination (*utpatti-prakaraṇa*), which is the process of the world’s arising. Since that process culminates in a mere illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) based upon an unchanging material cause (*upādāna*), liberation is established by its very nature once bondage is proven to be false; such is the intended meaning of the description [of this section]. He states this with the words beginning "whatever is produced" (*yad-yad-utpadyate*). Whatever is produced... [is merely an illusory transformation of the unchanging Brahman].
By each means [of realization], one who is liberated remains—that is, abides—in that very state which is devoid of those respective bonds; this is the meaning.
"This delusion of the world appears as something unborn, having the nature of space"—this is what is now being stated by me in this chapter on origination. (44)
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving— everything, enriched with all its various forms, including gods, asuras, and kinnaras— [is perceived]. (45)

He begins to support the point already stated—that "even while unborn, it appears as having the nature of space"—by means of the narrative called *Pralaya*: "That which is this... The connection with what follows is that "this world which is seen becomes non-existent at the time of dissolution. (45)
When that great dissolution arrives, which brings about the transformation of Rudra and the other deities, it becomes non-existent and invisible in nature; it goes somewhere or perishes.

In the primary dissolution (prākṛta-mahāpralaya), [the world] undergoes transformation and is made to disappear by Rudra and the others; the explanation of the term "perishes" (vinaśyati) is that its nature becomes non-existent and invisible. 46.
Then, neither light nor pervasive darkness remains; there persists a certain reality that is unnameable, unmanifest, tranquil, and profound.
Does that which ends in emptiness perish? He says "no," with the word "tataḥ" (from that). "Inexpressible" and "unmanifested" constitute the negation of name and form. || 47 ||
It is neither empty nor devoid of form; it is neither the object seen nor the act of seeing;
nor is it a multitude of real entities, for it abides as that which is infinite.

Since a substance that is empty of name and form is absolutely unknown in the world, one might suspect it to be a void; therefore, he says "no. If that is so, then by process of elimination, its state as a non-void possessing forms, objects of sight, and the act of seeing would follow; to this he replies:
"Not even," and so forth. The word "ākāram" is either a Vedic form (chāndasa) or it ends in the suffix -matup (-vant) in the sense of possession. || 48 ||
It is something whose nature is indefinable, a form more full than the full;
it is neither being nor non-being, neither being-and-non-being, neither an entity nor a becoming.

Precisely because it is inexpressible, its nature is indefinable. He elaborates upon this very indefinability with the words "not existent," and so forth. Existence (*bhavana*) is the connection with time or origination; that which possesses this is an entity (*bhāva*). || 49 ||
It is pure consciousness alone, devoid of objects of thought, infinite, undecaying, and auspicious;
it is without beginning, middle, or end—beginningless and free from all affliction.
That which has no beginning—that is, no cause—is "beginningless" (anādi).
In whom the world vibrates like a visible pearl upon a swan;
he who is both this and not this—the God whose nature is both being and non-being. (51)

Or it is like a swan made of pearls, which is perceived through a variegated illusion as being first of the nature of liberated souls and subsequently of the nature of swans, because it is a transformation of those [pearls], just like a substance that has been seen to follow both states.

And this [reality] is seen through the perspective of superimposition, not through the perspective of negation; it consists of both the existent and the non-existent, and follows the two states of the manifest and the unmanifest. (51)
Devoid of ears, tongue, nose, skin, and eyes, he who hears, tastes, smells, touches, and sees everywhere and at all times; (52)
Even in the absence of ears, nose, and so forth, hearing and other such functions are directly perceived by this [self] in a dream. Thus says the Śruti:
"Without hands or feet, it is swift and a grasper; it sees without eyes and hears without ears. (52)

That very [consciousness], by which light, perceives the form of existence and non-existence—the beginningless and endless variegated painting of creation, as well as its own nature, free from coloring—is [the Self]. (53)

That light by which the previously mentioned nature of existence and non-existence is perceived is that very same light of consciousness (*cidāloka*). Likewise, while ignorance exists, the variegated picture of creation appears; but upon the cessation of ignorance, having attained its own beginningless and endless essential nature, that very same [consciousness] is what remains—this is the meaning of "the manifestation of coloring" (*rañjana-prathana*). || 53 ||
He who perceives the world as like a star within the space between his eyebrows—half-closed and barely visible—as being always a mere appearance whose true nature is the void itself; || 54 ||

Thus, he says "half" (ardha) to indicate that even the perception of the appearance of the world, though sublated, is that very same [consciousness] during the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukta). Just as for a yogi, when the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows in the khecarīmudrā, the half-opened eyes perceive the space fixed between the eyebrows.

Just as people see the world as always appearing [as such] because the black pupil is not clearly perceived, so too he who sees his own nature—which is like the sky—as always appearing [in that way], he too is that very same [Self]; this is the meaning. Furthermore, the definition of the Khecarīmudrā is stated in the Yogaśāstra: "The tongue, turned backwards, enters the hollow of the skull."
"The gaze directed between the eyebrows is the Khecarī Mudrā. He is not afflicted by disease, nor is he tainted by karma; he who knows the Khecarī Mudrā is not constrained by time. (54)
For that Lord, there is no other cause, as it would be like the horn of a hare;
yet this world is his effect, like a mass of waves arising from water. (55)
By the light of that lamp of pure consciousness, which blazes incessantly on all sides and abides within the seats of the mind, the three worlds are illumined.

Having thus demonstrated that which has the nature of the reality of the "That" (tatpadārtha), which is the substratum of all dissolution, he begins to demonstrate it also in the form of the reality of the "Thou" (tvaṃpadārtha) with the words "jvalataḥ" and so forth. [He describes it] as that which shines or blazes everywhere in a general sense, because it is not obstructed in various locations, and because of its constant manifestation through specific forms.
"Stay burning! || 56 ||
Without whom even these luminaries such as the sun would be like darkness; and in whose presence the three worlds proceed like a mirage. (57)
Just as for a blind man even a day that has dawned is of the nature of darkness, so too, without Him, all things are like a cataract to one whose form is vision. 57.

In that [consciousness] in which this splendor of the world arises as if throbbing when it is active, yet does not arise when it has entered a state of non-throbbing—just as the appearance of a wheel occurs in a whirling firebrand—[that consciousness is the Self]. 58.

In that [Self], when there is vibration through the state of the mind, the Fortune of the world seems to arise; but when it has become motionless within, having attained the reality of the Inner Self (pratyaktattva), it does not arise at all. The word "ca" is used for emphasis. It is well known that when a burning brand (alāta)—a flaming torch—is whirled about at night, it takes on the form of a circle. || 58 ||
The pervasive and great one, whose nature is both motion and stillness, is stainless and imperishable; his play consists in the creation and dissolution of the universe. (59)
He states clearly what has already been said: "The world... [verse 59]. The nature of which, its ultimate form, is stainless and imperishable.
The existence of that [Self], which consists of both vibration and non-vibration, is all-pervading like the wind;
it appears as if divided merely by name for the sake of conventional usage, but not in reality.

The meaning is that since the previously mentioned states of vibration (*spanda*) and non-vibration (*aspanda*) are essentially real and full, they do not undergo any change; therefore, any apparent change distinct from them results ultimately in being a mere illusory manifestation (*vivarta*). Thus, they are different only in name, but not in reality. || 60 ||
He who is always awakened, he who is always asleep,
and he who is neither asleep nor awakened, being everywhere and at all times.
He states that the threefold nature of his vision, which is established as being released from the state of non-perception upon awakening, is "always indeed" [as follows]: || 61 ||
That which is motionless is Śiva, the peaceful; that which is its movement is the existence of the three worlds.
He who is the single one, whose nature is the play of both movement and stillness, is of a full form [the land of Bharata, according to another reading].

With the intention that even for one desiring liberation (mumukṣu), the two aforementioned forms alone serve as the basis for what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, he says: "That which... (verse 62).
Like fragrance in flowers that are subject to decay, it does not perish;
though present before the eyes, it is nevertheless ungraspable, just like the whiteness in a white cloth. (63)

The word "essence" (*sāra*) is to be understood as "like fragrance" (*āmoda*). Although it exists in the form of manifestation within all perceptual functions of objects, it is ungraspable—[according to the reading *asaṃnikarṣagrāhya*] because it cannot be apprehended through the extraction of the specific objects of those functions. || 63 ||
Though like a mute, he is not mute; though like a stone, he is a thinker;
though an enjoyer, he is eternally satisfied; and though a doer, he possesses nothing.

Due to the absence of the organ of speech, he is like a mute; yet, because he is the cause for the operation of all speech, he is not mute. In the same way, it should be understood that although he is like a stone due to being devoid of the modification of thinking, he is a thinker, and so forth. He is "possessing nothing" (*akiñcana*) because he has no basis whatsoever for action and the like.
He who, though bodiless, possesses all limbs, and has a thousand hands and eyes;
by whom, even while remaining as nothing at all, this entire world is pervaded. (65)
He whose very limbs are all [the constituent parts], and for that very reason, he who possesses thousands—infinite—hands, eyes, and so forth. || 65 ||
Even though he is devoid of the power of the senses, all sensory activities belong to him; even though he is without thought, these modes of mental creation belong to him.
These are the well-known forms of the world. || 66 ||
Because it is not seen, there is fear of the serpent of delusory saṃsāra;
when it is seen, all hopes and all fears flee away. (67)
Or, "āśāḥ" means desires and the directions. || 67 ||
In that witness, which is a vast and steady manifestation like a lamp, all activities proceed;
it is in its presence that the impulses of the mind, preceded by movement, arise.

Just as the performance of dance and other arts occurs when there is a lamp, so too, when there is the pervasive, undivided, and luminous manifestation—which is for that very reason the Witness—it is in its presence that the activities and impulses of the mind proceed. || 68 ||
For from it arise hundreds of rows of objects in the form of jars, cloths, and so forth, just as the multitude of waves, surges, and ripples arise from the ocean. (69)
"They proceed like [the waves] of the ocean"—this is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. || 69 ||
That very same [reality] arises as something else through the delusions of hundreds of objects,
just as gold appears as bracelets, armlets, neck-ornaments, and anklets.

That very conscious Self (cidātman) appears as something else, in the form of the insentient phenomenal world (jaḍaprapañca); and those well-known hundreds of delusions regarding objects are thus [described], where the third case ending is used in the sense of "being such" (itthaṃbhāva) following a *karmadhāraya* compound. 70.
That which is the one luminous self— you, I, and these people;
and that which is not you, whose nature is unawakened, nor I, nor these people (the reading "janāśca ye" is preferred)— that is [the Self].

That which appears—that manifestation which has been directly realized by you—is the Self, and you alone are that one. Likewise, that which has been directly realized by me or by other people is each their own respective Self, and that alone is the one. But the "unawakened self" (abuddhātman) is the opposite of that;
such is the meaning. || 71 ||
The world of the visible flashes forth like a row of waves upon the water—neither different nor non-different, neither existent nor non-existent, and yet fragile. (72)
She is non-different, yet as if different; non-excessive, yet as if excessive. Here, "excess" (atireka) means "separateness" (pṛthaktva)—this reading avoids tautology.
She is established from the very beginning, yet she appears as if established through birth. || 72 ||
From whom comes the reckoning of time, from whom comes the visibility of the visible world,
by whom mental construction is made, and by whose light all things shine.

The reckoning of time consists of the six modifications of existence; the visibility of the visible is the pervasion by the fruit of perception; and mental reckoning refers to the conceptualizations of desire and aversion regarding the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired, by which means [the world] is sustained. This means that it is ultimately sustained by the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda) belonging to Him. And all these three [time, space, and causality] exist by whose light.
It is indeed the illumination of the world and nothing else. Being (*sattā*) is the universal pervasiveness common to all that is unknown.
Perception (*darśana*) is the pervasiveness of that which is merely unobscured.

Therein, bliss (*ānandatā*) is the pervasiveness of that which is merely experienced as agreeable; thus, although there is a distinction based on intermediate limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), [the essence remains the same].
The meaning is that this is because of the oneness resulting from the pervasion of the nature of light. || 73 ||
Action, form, taste, smell, sound, touch, and consciousness—whatever you perceive, that is this God; and that by which you perceive, that too is He. (74)

That which, being your own essential nature, perceives action within the adjunct of the body and the organs of action, form and so forth within the adjunct of the organs of knowledge, and consciousness as well as the knower within the adjunct of the internal organ— that is the pure conscious nature extracted from the knower; by means of that pure conscious nature extracted from the mental modification pervaded by objects, you perceive.
The meaning is that he too is a god. || 74 ||
O virtuous one, through focused attention, you shall realize your own self as that vision which abides among the seer, the seeing, and the seen. 75.

And thus it follows that he is the witness of the triad; so he says: "The seer," etc. "Observation" (darśana) is the act of perceiving by means of a one-pointed mind, having extracted [the self] from its limiting adjuncts (upādhi). || 75 ||
The unborn, undecaying, beginningless, eternal, constant, auspicious, stainless, unfailing, highly venerable, irreproachable, devoid of all mental constructs, and the cause of all causes— Brahman.
The experience within is the experience of the entire universe, which is not an object of cognition.
Having thus pointed out the meanings of the words *tat* and *tvam*, he shows the meaning of the sentence at the end with the word "unborn" (*ajam*).

"The cause of causes" is the indication of the referent of the word *tat* (according to the reading *vākyārthasya*). "Empty" (*śūnyam*) indicates the ultimate referent (*lakṣyārtha*) of the word *tat*. "The entire universe" (*viśvam kṛtsnam*).

"Feeling" refers to the state of being the witness of the three states of the referent (*vācya*) of the term "that" (*tat*); "feeling that is not an object of knowledge" refers to the state of being free from the three states of the object of knowledge for the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) of the term "that.
And through this co-utterance, there is the instruction on the meaning of the sentence as an indivisible whole (*akhaṇḍavākyārtha*). || 76 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Supreme Cause," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Supreme Cause," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
(p. 151) The Tenth Canto. 10.
Śrī Rāma said:
When the great dissolution has occurred, that which remains here becomes formless;
of this there is no doubt. (1)
Anticipating an apparent contradiction regarding the previously stated definition of Brahman,
the intended meaning is here described by means of its successive refutation.
At the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), whatever remains cannot be conceived as possessing contradictory forms such as "neither light nor darkness";

thus, Śrī Rāma— desiring to know the intended meaning of that statement and intending to establish the context for his inquiry by proposing one possible interpretation— frames his question as follows:

Regarding the term *mahāpralaya*: the particle *nāma* is used to indicate that this [term] is a mere designation, for it is conceivable [only] because formlessness (*anākāratā*) is established upon the dissolution of forms (*ākāra*). || 1 ||
How could this not be empty? How could it not be luminous? Or how could it not be of the nature of darkness? And how could it not indeed be radiant? (2)
Now he shows the point to be questioned with the words beginning with "no" (*na*). The meaning is that the non-voidness of that which has perished is difficult to establish;
for even when one of two things—light or darkness—is destroyed, the non-remainder of the other is not proven.
This is because, due to the dissolution of the object to be illumined, at that time there is an absence of the nature of supreme illumination.
The meaning is: why should it not be luminous by illuminating itself alone, like a firefly? || 2 ||

Or how could it not be of the nature of consciousness? Or how could it not be the individual soul (jīva)? How could it not be the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva)? Or how could it not be the mind (manas)? || 3 ||
Anticipating the objection that such a statement contradicts common experience— since it is well known that the act of seeing is distinct from the object seen— the author asks, "Or how? If, however,

it is argued that the seer alone is established as distinct from the object and the act of seeing, then [the opponent might reply] that the individual soul (*jīva*), the intellect-principle (*buddhitattva*), or the mind (*manas*) [is that seer].

Or else, how could there not be such a difference of opinion among them, given that the seer is established in this way? Furthermore, since for those very people the multitude of elemental objects is designated by words denoting living beings in common worldly usage, there would be a contradiction in their statement that "it is not [the case] because of being denotable by words" (the reading is *śabdābhidheyatvāt*). This is the intended meaning. || 3 ||
Or how could there be nothing at all, or how could there be everything?
By this very turn of phrase, a kind of delusion has arisen within me.

Regarding what was said—"You who are the one whose nature is light, and I, and these people; and that which you are not, being of the nature of the unawakened, nor am I, nor are these people"—the author says "Or how? intending to show that this too is contradicted by its own statement. For [in that case], there would be something such as "you," "I," and so forth. (4)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This very difficult question has been posed by you;
I shall dispel it with ease, as the sun dispels the darkness of night.

A question that transcends my intention is an "excessive question" (atipraśna). He is the piercer and cutter of the seed of that question—the doubt—by revealing his own intention; this is the implied meaning. Aṃśumān refers to the Sun. || 5 ||
O Rāma, listen as this is told: that which remains at the conclusion of the great kalpa is not, in fact, empty. || 6 ||
Just as a carved figure remains on a pillar even though it has not been carved out [as a separate entity], so too does the universe exist therein; therefore, that state is not empty.

The meaning is that because the image carved upon a pillar lacks an existence distinct from the existence of the pillar itself, its persistence through that [pillar's] existence remains undiminished even in its uncarved state. || 7 ||
This world, known as the universe, appears here with such great abundance;
whether it be real or unreal, wherever it exists, there is non-emptiness.

Whether this conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) be true from the standpoint of conventional usage or false from the standpoint of ultimate reality, it cannot be non-empty (*śūnyatā*) with respect to that substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) upon which it appears; for the meaning is that what is empty cannot serve as the locus for superimposition. || 8 ||
Just as a pillar that has not been carved with figures is not empty of those figures,
so too the world appears as Brahman; therefore, that state is not empty of it.
He supports the meaning established by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) also by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), beginning with the word "yathā" (just as).
The connection is: "likewise, that term 'jagat' (the world) is not empty. The meaning is: because the world appeared previously as Brahman itself, for that reason [it is not empty]. || 9 ||
Just as a wave in gentle water neither exists nor does not exist,
so this world in Brahman has reached a state that is both void and non-void.

Now, if the world exists at that time, then dissolution (pralaya) would be impossible; if it does not exist, then its emptiness is already established—thus there is a contradiction regarding its existence or non-existence. He wards off this [objection] by means of an illustration, saying "O gentle one" (*saumya*). The words "dissolved like a wave" (*vīcilīna*) are to be supplied. The phrase "the state of being empty or not empty" refers to its indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*).
Or rather, it is the attainment of the ultimate reality, which is the basis for the conceptualizations of emptiness, non-emptiness, and both. || 10 ||
Because place, time, and so forth are quiescent, the fashioning of a doll upon a tree is impossible; therefore, one is indeed deluded regarding the Infinite.

If the world exists at the time of dissolution just like a statue carved from a pillar, then why do disputants become deluded regarding it? He explains that it is not so in the case of the statue by saying "place" (*deśa*), etc.
[This refers to] the place which serves as the substratum for the agent and the action suitable for the creation of the statue, as well as the time such as day and so forth.

The meaning is that, because of the peacefulness and lack of expectancy regarding the agent, instrument, auxiliary means, and so forth— indicated by the word "ādi" (and the rest)— all the necessary conditions are fulfilled. Just as the carving of a figurine is possible upon a pillar made of wood, which is a modification of a tree, so too can its existence there be conceived.

The meaning is that it is possible. However, regarding the infinite Brahman—which is devoid of the three kinds of limitations—the meaning is that there is no observation of the causal complex as previously described. "Vai" signifies certainty. Therefore, by that well-known class of disputants, one is deluded; the meaning is that confusion is attained. || 11 ||

Therefore, this comparison— such as that of the statues on a pillar— is similar only in a partial respect regarding the existence of the world in ultimate reality, and not in every way [or "in all respects," according to the reading *sarvataḥ*].
If there is disparity according to the reasoning stated, how then is the example of the pillar-doll (stambhaputrikā) applicable? To this, he says:

"That" (tat). This aforementioned pillar-doll and so forth exist within the ultimate reality, Brahman, by way of a single part—that is, by way of the aspect in which its existence is not sublated [the reading is *tatsattānucchedāṃśena*, meaning "by way of the aspect in which the existence of that [pillar-doll] is not sublated"].
This never arises from another, nor does it cease;
thus established as the absolute, existent Brahman, it abides within its own self. 13.
Now, one might object: "Granted that the existence of the world is as stated; however, since its arising and passing away are contradictory, how can both exist there simultaneously?

Anticipating this doubt, [the author] replies: since it is not admitted that these two possess an existence distinct from their own substrata, once the existence of the properties apart from the substratum is refuted, the very possibility [of such simultaneous existence] is eliminated.
With the intention that "it does not exist," he says: "never. || 13 ||
The conceptualization of the meaning of the word "empty" depends upon the non-empty;
since the non-empty does not exist, how can there be emptiness or non-emptiness? (14)

[Objection: But surely, since it arises and does not cease by virtue of non-emptiness (*aśūnyatva*), how can there be a mention of "emptiness" (*śūnya*) by means of the negative particle (*nañ*)—for the reading is *aśūnyārthakanañaḥ*? To this he says: "Non-empty," etc. Having taken for granted the non-emptiness of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), one postulates its emptiness with respect to another entity; and that [emptiness] is merely conceptualized (*kalpitā*).

The meaning is: if one conceives of emptiness and non-emptiness as being mutually dependent—wherein non-emptiness exists in dependence upon emptiness as its counter-correlative—then how could emptiness and non-emptiness possibly exist? || 14 ||
Indeed, this light born of the elements is not possible in Brahman; for how could it exist there in that imperishable [reality], where the sun, fire, moon, stars, and so forth are absent? (15)

Having thus established the first point of the question (the reading *praśne padaṃ* is found in the text), he resolves the second as well, beginning with the words "In Brahman" (*brahmaṇi*). For the existence of the sun, fire, and so forth occurs through the non-destruction (*avyaya*) of either water or earthly fuel; but since Brahman is indestructible (*avyaya*), how could that [fuel] exist there? Thus, [their] manifestation does not occur.
Such is the meaning of the statement "thus it is said. By this, the answer to the question "How is it not luminous? has also already been stated. || 15 ||
The absence of the manifestations of the great elements is called darkness;
however, since that [darkness] arises from the absence of the great elements, there is no darkness whatsoever here.
Or how is it that darkness is not of the nature of *tamas*? He provides this resolution with the words "the great elements" (*mahābhūta*).

But as for the darkness born from the absence of the light of the sun and so forth—that darkness, being the absence of the luminosity of the great elements such as earth and the rest, acts as an opponent to things illuminated by another.

Darkness is said to exist only in earth and the other elements, not in that which is self-luminous; therefore, the meaning here is that there is no darkness in this [Self]. The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of excluding the darkness of *māyā*. || 16 ||
Self-experience alone is the illumination of this [reality], which is of the nature of pure space;
that which exists within is experienced by that very self, and not by anything else. (17)

He establishes self-luminosity through experience: "One's own experience," etc. Although cognitions and the like are experienced by another, nevertheless that which exists as their inner essence is experienced by that [inner essence] alone; it does not require an experience distinct from itself. Otherwise, there would be the consequence of infinite regress (anavasthā); such is the meaning. || 17 ||
This undecaying state is liberated from both darkness and light;
know this very treasury of space to be the treasury for the existence of the world. 18.

He concludes the explanation of the answers to the second and third questions with the word "muktam" (released). The ellipsis "iti" implies that it should be understood in the manner described. The meaning is: know that Brahman, which is like a treasury for the world's existence—which is like wealth—is as clear as the interior of space. || 18 ||
Just as there is no distinction whatsoever between the wood-apple tree and the interior of the wood-apple fruit, so too there is not even the slightest difference between Brahman and the world. 19.
He states the answer to the final and penultimate questions with the words "of the *bilva*": [it refers to] the middle, that is, the belly. || 19 ||
Just as a wave exists within water, or as a jar exists within clay,
so too, since the existence of the world resides therein, how could that [reality] be of the nature of space? (20)
A small jar is a *ghaṭaka*. He speaks according to the maxim of the lion’s backward glance: "How so? [The answer is: it consists of space, which is emptiness. || 20 ||
The splendor of the earth, water, and so forth, ending with the formed (sākāra), is equal-minded;
but Brahman is as pure as space, and it likewise resides within that.

[Objection: But since the earth situated within water, or the water and so forth contained within a jar, are not observed to have the nature of a support [for themselves], how can the world contained within Brahman have the nature of Brahman at that time? To this he says: "Earth, water, etc. The beauty of the analogies of earth, water, and so forth mentioned by you is not equal [to the case at hand], because:

That which has form, limit, end, and a boundary of perception—such is the world; yet that world resides within that formless Brahman, and because it has dissolved [into Him], it is indeed formless. This is the meaning of "in that very same way. || 21 ||
Therefore, just as the space of consciousness is even purer than physical space,
so too is that which exists within it— the referent of the word "world"— of the very same nature.
He states the very same point clearly: "Therefore," etc. (22).
Just as the pungency within a pepper is not perceived by one who does not eat it,
so too is the state of pure consciousness in the space of consciousness not perceived without the element of the object of thought.
For this very reason, he states "Marīci" to show that the fourth question has also been refuted.

The meaning is this: while it is true that what is well-known as "seeing" is indeed distinct from the "seen," yet in the absence of anything seen, it is merely fit for the conventional designation of "seeing. || 23 ||
Therefore, even consciousness, when devoid of objects within itself, takes on an insentient form;
this world-appearance is likewise of that very nature, by virtue of being identical to that alone. (24)

"Therefore" means: for this very reason, words such as "consciousness" (cit) and so forth apply to the inner self (pratīc) only through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), not through primary denotation; this is the sense. Just as at the dissolution of the world, the state of being an object of consciousness—which is the defining characteristic of the mind (citta)—ceases, so too does the state of being a world—which is the defining characteristic of the world—cease when it becomes an object of consciousness; thus he says, "the state of being a world."

The connection with what follows is as follows: by virtue of having that [object] alone as their essence, both the external forms of light and the internal mental attentions consist of that very [object]. || 24 ||
Form, light, and mental attention are themselves identical with that [Reality] and nothing else;
therefore, the universe as it exists is either deep sleep or indeed the Fourth State (turya). || 25 ||
Among the seven stages to be described, deep sleep belongs to those situated in the fifth stage, while the fourth state (turya) pertains to the two subsequent ones.
Therefore, the yogi, though engaged in worldly activity, remains with a tranquil mind like one in deep sleep;
he abides as the non-manifest Brahman, which is the casket containing all manifestations.

He clarifies the very meaning already stated through the preceding and following halves [of the verse], beginning with "by that": "The casket (*samudraka*)—that is, the container (*sampuṭaka*)—of all appearances and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). (26)
Just as great waves abide within calm water that possesses form,
so does the universe abide within the Supreme, which is formless and similar to them.

Having raised the doubt as to how the existence of the world with its manifold forms can be [possible] from the perspective of Brahman, which is formless and of the nature of the Self, he says "ākāriṇī" (possessing forms), intending that there is no contradiction because various forms such as waves exist within the single-natured water.
