It is "saumye" (serene) because of its immobility and clarity. 27.
From the Full, the Full flows forth; that which is the Full is formless.
The universe has appeared from Brahman, for that manifestation of the universe is indeed intended for its own sake. (28)

Having thus stated that the world, which serves as an adjunct (*upādhi*), is non-different from its cause, he now states the same for the individual soul (*jīva*) who is conditioned by that adjunct, beginning with the words "From the Full" (*pūrṇāt*). That which flows forth in the form of a living being through the distinction of adjuncts from the Full Brahman is, in ultimate reality, itself entirely full. In this context, since it is impossible for that which possesses a formal shape (*sākāra*) to be full, that which is full—
Refutation of that [objection]: If [the Self] is complete, then for what purpose has it appeared as the universal self and as the individual soul (jīva)?

To this he says: "That which... That which has appeared as the universal self was indeed "intended" (*vicakṣita*)—that is, desired to be seen—for its own sake, for the accomplishment of the purpose of attaining its own true nature.

The meaning is that, by gradually attaining a body suitable for the office [of a teacher] and through the direct realization of its own true nature (*svatattva*), it expands out in the form of the world and living beings (*jagajjīvabhāva*) for the sake of recovering its own self which had been obscured by ignorance. And thus says the Śruti: "He became the counterpart of every form; such is his form."
"For the sake of clear perception," so [it is said]. || 28 ||
From the Full, the Full emanates; that which is established remains the Full itself. Therefore, the universe is unarisen; and whatever has arisen, that is indeed the Full.
He explains how that [reality] is desired to be seen: "From the Full" (pūrṇāt). This has already been explained. || 29 ||

Since the object of thought is impossible within that [consciousness], how could there be any single purpose for the world? Since the enjoyer is impossible, O mirage, what indeed could its pungency be? (30)

The meaning is that for this reason, the referent of the word "world" has become one, of a single flavor (*ekarasa*). In the reading *pade*, the word *kā* is used in the sense of concealment (*apahnava*). || 30 ||
(153) This state of being mind and object, etc., exists only as unreal for the Supreme;
since that [reality] is absent, how could there be the capacity to be a reflection for a reflection? (31)
The meaning is that because there is only a single flavor (ekarasa), the manifold flavors such as the mind (citta) and its objects (cetya) appear as if real even though they are unreal.

Thus, the underlying intention is that once the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) are absent, the doubt—namely, "how could the state of being a reflected soul (pratibimba-jīva) not exist for the Worthy One (arhat), or how could he not be a living being (jīva)?"—is also dispelled. || 31 ||
It is subtler than even the atom, for it is more minute than the minute;
it is pure, subtle, supreme, and more tranquil than even the interior of space.
Because its nature is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, it is exceedingly vast;
it is without beginning or end, a manifestation devoid of anything to be manifested. || 33 ||

For the individual soul (jīva) is well known to be either atomic or of intermediate size, impure due to being defiled by merit, demerit, and so forth, and the enjoyer of objects manifested by its own light; but that [Supreme Self] is the opposite of that— thus he says in two verses beginning with "Even smaller than an atom" (32–33).
Wherein even the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) is not found, how could there be the state of being a living soul (*jīvatā*),
or a latent impression (*vāsanā*) characterized by the form of mentation (*cittatākārā*) which is eternal in nature [the reading *anilarūpiṇī* is also found]?
That which is characterized by the manifestation of objects [the reading *viṣayapratyāyyatvalakṣaṇaṃ* is also found].

It cannot tolerate its very nature as consciousness, let alone its state as a *jīva*, which is characterized by being an enjoyer of objects that are favorable or unfavorable to it; thus he says, "of the nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpam*). By this, the doubt as to how it could not be the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*) or how it could not be the mind (*manas*) is also refuted; thus he says, "how? (verse 34).
Precisely because the nature of consciousness does not arise there, there is no state of being a living soul (jīvatā);
nor is there the state of intellect (buddhitā), nor the state of mind (cittatā), nor the state of the senses, nor any latent impression (vāsanā).
He clarifies exactly what was stated [in the previous verse]: "In the form of consciousness," etc. (35).
Thus, although this state is full of great undertakings, it is undecaying;
from our perspective, it remains peaceful, empty, and more vast than space. (36)
He concludes the result of the resolution of all questions with the words "evam" (thus). || 36 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
What is the nature of the supreme reality, which has the form of infinite consciousness?
Explain this to me again skillfully for the increase of my understanding. (37)
When the mind is thus concentrated, desiring to discern that unique form by which that [object] can be experienced directly, he asks again: "of the ultimate reality" (paramārthasya).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the great dissolution has occurred, that which remains is the Supreme Brahman, the cause of all causes; this very thing is now described—listen.
This very [reality] is immediate. || 38 ||
Having destroyed one's own self through the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, that which is of the nature of existence and inexpressible is the true form of that reality. (39)

The meaning is as follows: just as in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), when the cessation of mental fluctuations occurs through restraint, the mind—like a fire without fuel—destroys even its own nature, the very form of the mind itself; that which remains is the indescribable, self-luminous reality of Being. || 39 ||
There is no visible world, and the seer, due to the absence of the visible, is as if dissolved; that which appears as "it shines" is the very nature of that reality. (40)

Thus, at the commencement of non-conceptual samādhi, because the object of perception (dṛśya) has ceased to exist, the perceiver—the subject (pramātā)—also appears as if dissolved; the meaning is that this is the manifestation of the dissolution of the triad (tripuṭī), which is the nature of the witness (sākṣin). || 40 ||

That form of the individual soul (jīva), which by its very nature is turned away from the objectless [state], is pure consciousness—stainless and peaceful; that is the nature of the Supreme Self (paramātman). (41)

This means that it is the very nature or form of consciousness—which possesses the nature of the future living being—that is directed toward the non-objective at the time prior to emerging from samādhi. Although even during the middle of samādhi there is only the shining form of the Supreme Self, nevertheless, that too [is so because of its extreme subtlety]. (Note: the reading is *tadatisūkṣmatvāt*).
Because of its subtlety, it cannot be perceived by one who merely desires to ascend during the stage of practice; thus, the beginning and end are shown. || 41 ||
Even when wind and other elements touch the limbs, that which is the nature of the mind of one who is living, even without the experience of touch and so forth, is indeed the Supreme Self.
Now, he shows that [the Self] is also established as the manifest form within that [state], which has been ascended to through experience, by means of the word "limb" (aṅga).

Because the mind possesses an uninterrupted, immediate mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of Brahman, while the individual soul is still living, the mind has become one with Brahman—like milk and water—and has thus disappeared; the meaning is that one should disregard the mind.

The genitive case here is used in the sense of "disregard" (anādare), according to the rule for the genitive denoting a characteristic state (bhāvalakṣaṇe). The meaning is that even when the wind or other elements touch a limb, that very form which flashes forth without the experience of that touch and so on is "that form. However, in some manuscripts, instead of this first half-verse, there is the reading: "when the wind and so on do not touch the thumb or a finger."

It is recited there that when the winds and so forth belonging to the thumb and the finger do not touch—that is, when there is no contact or joining of the touch—the [sensation] does not arise. The root *vā* means "to go" or "to move"; the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). || 42 ||
O sinless one, that which remains is the very nature of that long-lasting sleep—the state of the mind which is dreamless, infinite, and non-inert. (43)
Now, he explains how [this state] comes within the range of experience even for those devoid of the practice of yoga:

"asvapnāyā" (of that which is dreamless). That very deep sleep (*suṣupti*), which is free from dreaming, uninterrupted by mosquitoes, bedbugs, and the like, and which serves as the cause for the mind's rest—that alone, when devoid of mental inertia (*jāḍya*), should be cultivated for a long time.
The meaning is that such a form remains at the time of dissolution. || 43 ||
That which is the heart of space, or that of stone and wind—
that is the form of the Supreme Self, the inconceivable sky of consciousness.

The meaning is this: whatever may be the nature of that which exists as the sky of consciousness (cidvyoman)—which is the heart and secret of the sky, the emptiness of the wind, the fullness within and without of the stone, and the density of the stone itself—it is that very thing, being non-conceptual, undifferentiated from the conceptual, and devoid of the conceptual. 44
The state that exists by its own nature for one who is without thought-constructs and without mind while living—this is the supreme, tranquil existence of that primordial reality. (45)

What need is there for much [explanation]? He says that the state which remains when all objects of thought have been abandoned by every living being is that very nature itself: "of that which is beyond thought" (acetyasya). || 45 ||
That which is the center of the light of consciousness, or of light itself, or of space, and that which is the center of vision—that they know to be the form of Brahman. (46)

That which, within the range of the seer— from the *annamaya* up to the end— is the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*) that has extended forth as the Self; when analyzed through the discernment of each successive sheath (*kośa*), it is found to be even more internal than the *ānandamaya* sheath, and thus constitutes the "middle" relative to the range of the seen.

That which is the middle—meaning the interior—of the light consisting of the Sun, which is the essence of the manifested (mūrta) world; of the ether (kha or ākāśa), which is the essence of the unmanifested (amūrta) world; or of the unevolved ether (avyākṛtākāśa), which consists of the aggregate of subtle bodies (liṅgasamaṣṭi); and of vision, which consists of the functions of the eyes and other senses.

The meaning is this: because it has the nature of internal vibration, that which is the center is well-known as being, in sequence, bliss (*ānanda*), existence (*sat*), and consciousness (*cit*). And so, in the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad*, after demonstrating the innermost sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*) among the sheaths beginning with that of food (*annamaya*), it is shown that "joy (*priya*) alone is its head; delight (*moda*)," and so forth.

"The right side is the wing; joy (*pramoda*) is the left wing; bliss (*ānanda*) is the self (*ātman*); Brahman is the tail, the support"—thus the inner Brahman is shown even there. And in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, having introduced the two forms of Brahman as "the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*"), it says: "Of this formed [Brahman], this is the essence (*rasa*), namely—"
"This one who shines—of that formless one, this is the essence: namely, this person who is in this orb.

Having thus demonstrated the essence of both [the formed and the formless], it is then said, "Now, therefore, the instruction: 'Not this, not this'"; by the negation of that [duality] which is the substrate for the superimposition of the formed and the formless, the inner Brahman is shown. It is known as that which is realized through awakening.
In the Upaniṣad of the seekers of knowledge (Talavakāriṇām), it is stated that Brahman is internal to all modifications of the intellect. || 46 ||
The experience of sensation, of light, of the visible, and likewise of darkness—
that experience which is without beginning or end is the nature of the Supreme Self. (47)

The meaning is that the awareness which is the witness of the mental modification, the manifestation of the object, the object itself, and ignorance is without beginning or end, because it is the primordial and final manifestation of all those things. || 47 ||
That nature which, though eternally unarisen, appears as if the world arises from it;
and which, though non-different, appears as if different—that is the ultimate reality. (48)
That state of remaining like a stone even while engaged in worldly activity,
which is the very nature of space though not space itself— that is the form of the Supreme Self.
The meaning is: "that" refers to the one whose seat is as immovable as a stone, even though he is the Knower or the Lord devoted to illusory worldly activity;
and who possesses the nature of space (*vyomatva*) because, being without fissure, he provides space for the entire universe—this is the implied sense.
This triad consisting of the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower stands before us.
Whatever arises and passes away therein is exceedingly difficult to attain.
He states that the very nature of the Saccidātman, which is the cause of the triad beginning with the object of knowledge (vedya) and of birth and so forth, is indeed that [Supreme Reality]:

"That form in which this state of being the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower is reflected in the great mirror of the non-intellect (abuddhi) and so on—that is remembered as the Supreme. (51)
He states that even its state as a causal sign (*nimitta*) is not through transformation (*pariṇāma*), but rather by way of illusory appearance (*vivarta*): "The object of cognition," etc. (51).
That form of the Great Consciousness which remains when liberated from the mind, dreams, and the senses—
whether in the moving or the stationary— is all that remains at the end of everything.

That mind which is liberated from dreams and from waking states characterized by the senses, and which takes the form of the self in deep sleep—that alone remains at the time of the dissolution of the visible world, whether in the stationary or the moving. || 52 ||
If the nature of immobile beings were to consist of pure consciousness, being free from mind, intellect, and the like, it would be comparable to the Supreme. || 53 ||
The form of stationary beings has the nature of immovability; [it is] by means of the Supreme, the Supreme Self. 53.
Brahmā, Arka, Viṣṇu, Hara, Śakra, Sadāśiva, and the rest— when all is stilled, this one supreme Śiva alone remains here;
through the cessation of all limiting adjuncts, he exists in a form free from conceptual construction.
Consisting solely of pure consciousness and abandoned by all worldly attachments.
He concludes the discussion on the state of the reality of the self as dissolution with the word "Brahman.

This [Brahman] is the inner self established through the experience of all. "In this" means in this world. "The cessation of all adjuncts" means the dissolution of all limiting conditions (*upādhi*). The suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in the sense of abundance because of its connection with *māyā*. 54.

Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "The Description of the Supreme State Remaining at the End of the Great Kalpa," in the section on Origination within the *Mokṣopāya* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage. 10.
Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "The Description of the Supreme State Remaining at the End of the Great Kalpa," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Eleventh Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said:
This visible world, which appears in this form, does not exist.
It is radiant.
O Brahmin, when the great dissolution has arrived, where indeed does it abide—or, according to another reading, where does it go?
Existence is not precluded even in dissolution by virtue of its constant substratum;
however, the inherent existence of the world is here precluded even at the time of creation. (1)

Granted that at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), because nothing remains but Brahman—which is the universal essence of the world’s existence—the world ceases to exist through its individual existence (*prātisvikasattā*); nevertheless, since the difference between the state of creation (*sarga*) and dissolution is established by the experience of all, another independent existence must be asserted for the world during creation. And thus, endowed with that [existence], [the world...]

It is only conceivable that the world, while ceasing within Brahman, remains elsewhere; for you yourself have refuted the non-existence of that which exists, stating, "There is no non-existence of the existent. Therefore, thinking that one should point out exactly where it remains—that very thing being the ultimate refuge of the world—Śrī Rāma said: "This... [idam].

Where indeed does this world—of such a nature, consisting of an infinite expansion of fourteen worlds including gods, humans, asuras, animals, and so forth, appearing thus radiant and most manifest, and confirmed by perception and other means—remain when the great dissolution arrives? This is the sense; for even if the reading were "gacchati" (it goes), the meaning remains the same.
The meaning of the root *gam*, which signifies "attaining," has already been stated. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
From where does the son of a barren woman come, or what is he like, and where does he go?
Tell me, where does the forest of the sky go, and from where does it come?
If, at the time of the origination of all things, there were an arrival from somewhere with a separate existence,

then at the time of their dissolution there would have to be a departure elsewhere; and if there were a stay there with that same existence, then such a thing would be as impossible as the son of a barren woman.
With the intention that [it] does not exist, Vasiṣṭha said: "From where? (2)
Śrī Rāma said: The son of a barren woman and the forest of the sky neither exist nor will they ever exist.
What kind of visibility could he have, and what kind of non-existence?
Rāma raises an objection regarding the disparity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "vandhyā" (barren woman).
The disparity lies in the fact that neither [the barren woman nor her son] possesses existence at the present time, nor can their future existence be known through perception;
thus, since the existence of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is unestablished, their non-existence (*nāstitā*) is likewise difficult to assert. || 3 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as the son of a barren woman and the forest in the sky never exist at any time,
so too this entire visible world, beginning with the universe itself, never exists at any time.
If this is so, then the world as well does not exist by its own being, will not come to be, and is not even visible; thus it is identical to that [dream].
To this Vasiṣṭha says: "Like a barren woman's son... (verse 4).
That which did not exist at the beginning is neither produced nor destroyed. What kind of production can there be for it? What talk can there be of the word "destruction"? (5)
He states that even the origination and so forth of the world are not established in the absence of existence, saying: "And not... (verse 5).
Śrī Rāma said:
Indeed, there exists the conceptualization of the son of a barren woman and a tree in the sky;
just as that [conceptualization] is characterized by birth and destruction, why should this [world] not be the same?

Rāma raises an objection: "Surely the world, which possesses origination and so forth established by perception, cannot have the son of a barren woman as its point of comparison (*upamāna*), for an absolutely non-existent thing is never seen to serve as a point of comparison. Therefore, by process of elimination, the very cognition of that [world]—which is of the nature of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—is the point of comparison, since it is possible for it to share the common characteristics (*sādharmya*) with the world by virtue of possessing birth, destruction, and so forth."
"Barren," thus [it is said]. || 6 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Indeed, the weighing of that which is equal yet incomparably situated by means of mental conceptions is like a statement devoid of logical connection; for such indeed is the existence of the world.

It could serve as a point of comparison only if it were not included within the world that is being compared; however, since it is included therein, its status as a point of comparison is impossible. With the intention that, for this world which is not ultimately real, only the example I have stated remains, Vasiṣṭha said: "Of that which is equal," meaning of that which is intended to be compared.

When the object of comparison (*upameya*)—being difficult to establish because it lacks an external standard for comparison and thus impossible to compare—is weighed by means of qualities that have entered the very category of the object of comparison itself, and this verbal expression constitutes a comparison, that is the *niranvaya* (non-analogous) ornament, which serves as an illustration of The statement, "The sky has the form of the sky; the ocean is like the ocean," culminates in the sense of being beyond comparison (*anupamatva*);

likewise, [the claim] "it would be so" is not an example based on conceptual construction (*vikalpakalpanā*). Therefore, the meaning is that the separate existence of the world is exactly like the existence of a barren woman’s son and so forth, as stated by me—[namely,] of that which is non-existent (*asat*).

Even when a valid example is not observed, the absence of a valid example is not contradictory; the sense is that the statement "a sky-flower is non-existent, like the son of a barren woman" is made because it is observed [to be so]. || 7 ||
Just as this bracelet-ness clearly seen in a golden bracelet does not exist at all [as something other than gold], so too world-ness does not exist in the Supreme. (8)

Now, raising the objection, "How can that which is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) be non-existent?", he replies with the five verses beginning with "The state of being a bracelet" (*kaṭakatvam*), stating that even for such things, non-existence is well-established through numerous examples because they are sublated upon the attainment of right vision (*samyagdarśana*). || 8 ||
Just as emptiness does not exist in space as something distinct from it,
so too the state of being the world does not exist at all in Brahman, even though it is perceived there.
Exclusion (*vyatireka*) is likewise a distinction; it applies both to that which possesses perception and to that which is being perceived. (9)
Just as blackness does not exist apart from collyrium, nor coldness apart from snow, so too the world is not perceived as separate from the Supreme State. 10.
Just as coolness is not distinct from the moon or from snow, so too creation does not exist as something separate from Brahman. (11)

Just as water does not exist in a mirage-river, and just as the nature of the moon does not exist in a second moon, so too this thing called "the world" does not exist at all here, even though it is perceived within the stainless Self.
Even that which is being experienced is seen.
For that which does not exist at the very beginning due to the impossibility of its own cause, does not exist even in the present; what kind of destruction could there be for it? (13)

How could an insentient entity such as earth, which possesses an inherent dullness that cannot possibly arise [from anything else], be capable of being the cause [of consciousness], just as sunlight cannot be the cause of shadow? (14)

He states how there is an impossibility of a cause with the words "Where? (kvā). For an insentient object such as earth and so forth can only have an insentient cause; Brahman, however, possesses an inherent sentience that is impossible for such things to possess. The point is that nowhere is a transformation into something contrary to its own nature ever observed. || 14 ||
Due to the absence of a cause, this effect has not arisen as anything at all;
that which exists is the cause itself, and it is simply abiding in this manner.

From the perspective of transformation (*pariṇāma-dṛṣṭi*), nothing at all has arisen here; however, from the perspective of illusory appearance (*vivarta-dṛṣṭi*), although even a contradictory superimposition is possible, the meaning is nevertheless this: it is that very cause which exists in the form of the world, and there is no separate existence of an effect. || 15 ||
That which appears as ignorance is indeed nothing but the manifestation of consciousness;
that which is seen as the world in a dream is nothing but the radiance of consciousness.
"In that case, ignorance itself must be the transformative cause (pariṇāmikāraṇa); so how can there be an absence of a cause?

To this he replies: "Ignorance itself. That which is said to appear as having transformed into the form of the world—[in some places it is read as "that which, through knowledge," etc.]—is called "the manifestation of consciousness" (saṃvidābhāsa), because it causes consciousness to appear in the form of the world.

The meaning is that consciousness itself undergoes a transformation (*vivarta*) into the form of the world. He states—beginning with "That which"—that it is well known in the case of dreams that a transformation of ignorance is indeed a transformation of consciousness. || 16 ||
Just as the world-delusion in a dream is merely the manifestation of consciousness within,
so too at the beginning of creation, the expansion of the world is the manifestation of Brahman.
He states that very point clearly: "Consciousness," etc. (verse 17).
Whatever is seen here always abides within the Self;
no world ever sets nor does it ever rise. (18)
And thus, he says "yad idam" (this which... to show that the proposition—that the world is nothing but Brahman—is established:
[it exists] in the Self, whose nature is ultimate reality. || 18 ||
Just as liquidity is water, as movement is wind,
and as radiance is light, so too the three worlds are Brahman alone.
Just as the city of a dream-appearance exists within consciousness alone,
so too one's own self alone appears as the world within the Supreme Self. 20.
The consciousness of the dreamer, existing within the dream-consciousness, abides as pure consciousness itself, like a city. || 20 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
If this is so, O Brahman, then tell me how there can be such a firm conviction?
This poison of the visible world has arisen as something unreal, like the experience of a dream.

Rāma raises the doubt that liberation is impossible because of the disparity between the world-cognition, which is extremely solid, and the dream, which is entirely unmanifest and thus fragile, and because the relationship between the seer and the seen is natural and therefore unavoidable— thus: "In this way..."

By the words "If" (*cet*) and so forth: the meaning is this— if this object of perception were non-existent in the manner described above, like a dream-experience, then how did it come to be such that there arises the conviction that it is "very dense" and "firm," capable of withstanding non-contradiction in worldly transaction until the end of the kalpa?
Even if the reading is *svapnānubhūtimat*, the meaning is simply that it is like the experience of a dream by virtue of being one's own illustration (*svadṛṣṭāntatayā*). || 21 ||
Indeed, when there is an object of perception, there is a perceiver; when there is a perceiver, there is the state of being an object of perception.
When both exist together, there is bondage for the single being; when one of the two ceases, there is liberation from both.

"He has been seen" is the ellipsis, meaning he is difficult to ward off. The same applies to the two subsequent sentences as well. The sense is that liberation would indeed occur upon the destruction of one of the two, but that very thing is difficult to accomplish. || 22 ||

(156) As long as there is no absolute impossibility—that is, as long as the disappearance of the perceivable has not been realized—so long is the state of being perceivable not possible in the perceiver; thus, the knowledge of liberation does not arise. 23.

He explains why this is difficult to establish with the words "atyanta" (absolute). That which makes absolute the impossibility of leaving even a trace of a root [cause]—the meaning is that it is absolute because of the sublation of root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*). The ellipsis is "the state of being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*) is unavoidable.
Therefore, the meaning is that liberation-cognition (*mokṣadhī*) is not possible. || 23 ||
If the visible world were to first come into existence and later undergo destruction, then bondage—in the form of the uselessness of remembering that which was seen—would never cease. (24)

"Let there not be the realization of its absolute non-existence; rather, let there be the destruction of that which has already arisen through knowledge. To this he says: "The visible object" (dṛśyam). Then, like a memory, it is a recollection—the re-emergence of that which persists in the form of a latent impression (saṃskāra); that itself is the evil. || 24 ||
Wherever consciousness may be situated, just as in the case of one's own mirror,
a reflection consisting of all memories indeed adheres to it completely.

He says "where... [verse 25], meaning that the very removal of the visible region constitutes the refutation of the doubt regarding the impossibility of the visible, as you yourself have already stated previously.
If the visible world has never arisen from the very beginning and does not exist by itself,
then liberation occurs because the seer is of the same nature as the seen.

If it were unarisen, then liberation would be possible for the seer, because consciousness would possess the nature of the seen; however, since it is not experienced as unarisen, the sense is that there is no liberation from the seer's own nature. Therefore, having dispelled my [objection] regarding the impossibility of liberation through these arguments—
O best among the knowers of the Self, there is an absolute impossibility as long as one speaks [of such a thing]. (27)
Therefore, [tell me] until my doubt regarding the impossibility of liberation for one like me—[that is,] the doubt that liberation is impossible—is completely suppressed. (27)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Rāma, listen as I relate to you through this long narrative how the entire world, though non-existent, always appears as if it were real."

Vasiṣṭha promises to resolve the doubt regarding the discrepancy with dreams by means of the narrative of creation to be described hereafter— beginning with the words "It is unreal": "Although [the world] has a very dense conviction because it is expanded through long narratives such as the story of the pavilion, it is nevertheless unreal."

The sense is that there is indeed a similarity to a dream in the respect that [the object] appears as having the nature of reality; however, its status as a dense cognition is due to its long-term persistence. || 28 ||
As long as that place is not described there by means of accounts and words concerning your resolve,
so long will it find no rest in your heart, just as dust does not settle upon a lake.
The resolve of the ancestors was their worldly conduct, expressed through the sentences of their discourses. || 29 ||
Having realized the absolute non-existence of this delusion regarding the creation of the world,
you shall carry out your worldly affairs with a self established in the single-pointed meditation of battle.

He says that by this very means, your second doubt will be dispelled, and your repose in reality as well as worldly activity will be established: "Perceptions—whether grasping or rejecting existence and non-existence, gross or subtle, moving or unmoving—will not pierce you, just as arrows do not pierce a great mountain. (31)
They are called *grahas* (seizers) because they are grasped when there is a purpose (*prayojana*), and they are called *utsargas* (releases) because they are released when there is no purpose.
Regarding objects such as the gross and the subtle, the shifting and unshifting perceptions—which correspond to those objects—are the perspectives of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-dṛṣṭayaḥ*);
they will not pierce [the self], meaning they will not afflict it through the arising of passion (*rāga*) and so forth. Or, the meaning has been explained previously.
It is to be grasped. || 31 ||
This very Self is one alone; there is no second conceptualization.
O Rāghava, I shall explain to you how the world has arisen within this.
In this case, even though the self is devoid of a second conceptualization (dvitīya-kalpanā), || 32 ||
Therefore, O dear one, all these manifestations are his; that Great-Souled One is also this "entirely-and-not-entirely" (sakalāsakala) state,
consisting of the modes of beholding forms and mental reflection.
The locus of action arises by itself and dissolves by itself. || 33 ||

Indeed, these worlds have unfolded and manifested from that Self. Is it as if from a detached Lord (taṭastheśvara) through a sense of difference? No; he says "He" to show this is not so. That Great Soul, though one, is both the totality and the individual—the aggregate and the distinct—this which is perceived by the external senses.

The mind, having become the locus for the modes of perceiving forms within, and likewise the locus for the modes of the act of thinking, arises and dissolves by itself; the meaning is that it is perceived through delusion as having the nature of arising and dissolution. || 33 ||
Thus ends the eleventh canto, titled "The Description of the Ultimate Reality," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki. 11.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Ultimate Reality," in the section on Origination within the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa.
The Twelfth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: From this supreme, tranquil state, which is the most purifying, [arises...]
Listen with the highest intelligence to how this universe arose.

In order to declare the absolute impossibility [of duality] by means of negation (apavāda) in its entirety, the superimposition (adhyāropa) of creation corresponding to that [negation] is demonstrated in this [treatise]. (1)
Commencing to state the matter he had promised, the venerable Vasiṣṭha said: "From this... (1).
Deep sleep appears like a dream, and Brahman alone appears like a creation;
that state is the self of all—now hear the sequence regarding it. || 2 ||

The meaning is that this conceptualization follows empirical observation: just as for each individual the very nature of the self in deep sleep manifests as a dream, so too does Brahman manifest. In that regard, because a dream is the effect of the impressions (vāsanā) of a single person, it is not a solid conviction; whereas the phenomenal world (prapañca), being the effect of all impressions, is a solid conviction.

Anticipating the removal of a prior doubt, he says: "And [it is] the soul of all. Its being the soul of all follows from its grammatical coordination with the word *idam* (this), which denotes everything, in the Vedic text: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" (*ātmā vā idameka evāgre āsīt*).
Its locus is Brahman, which exists in the state of the collective deep sleep of all and the state of cosmic dissolution. || 2 ||
Of that infinite jewel of consciousness, whose nature is infinite light, the universe—which by its very essence consists of mere existence—arises perpetually from its own inherent nature. (3)

Because, for this reason, the universe is the consciousness-jewel whose self is pure existence alone—that is, whose nature is the ultimate reality—therefore it appears as if it were an object of cognition; such is the connection with what follows. || 3 ||
Then, within that very self, consciousness itself undergoes, as it were, a slight state of being an object of cognition,
preceded by the reflective awareness of "I," even though its own nature remains ungrasped. (4)

He shows that the state of reflection (*īkṣaṇa*), established by the scripture, "In the beginning, he reflected: 'May I create the worlds,'" through the three verses beginning with "That" (*tat*). By "consciousness" (*saṃvidā*) is meant: without the superimposition of the ego (*ahaṃkāra-adhyāsa*), which is not grasped as the Self and is preceded by the awareness of "I."

The grammatical connection is as follows: that which is the subtle and pure awakening from space—which possesses within it certain manifested forms produced by the contemplation of future names and forms regarding the entire range of objects to be created—becomes, as it were, the object of cognition (*saccetyatā*). || 4 ||
With its forms slightly inferred through the mental constructions of future objects,
this pure consciousness, subtler than space, shines as the awakening within everything.
Then that supreme being, becoming conscious and oriented toward sentience,
becomes fit for the name "Citi" (Consciousness) by virtue of being somewhat attainable.

He shows that the states of being the Lord (Īśvara) and the individual soul (jīva) arise from the function of that [intellect] and its limiting adjuncts (upādhi), respectively, by the words "thence" (tataḥ).

The intellect is the function consisting of perception; when accompanied by that, it is consciousness—the consciousness manifested therein. Being directed toward that and having that as its primary focus, it perceives; thus, it is "Cit," meaning the omniscient Lord, and is fit for that name.
Or [it is so] because it possesses the property of being an object of the activity of speech, and thus is obtainable through verbal usage. || 6 ||
Subsequently, dense perception—known as the "living soul" (jīva) and so forth—arises once it has assumed calculation;
this occurs when it abandons the supreme state.
When the perception of the eyes has become dense and solidified through long-standing habituation, such being the case, the grasping of a mental construction—
the construction of limitation characterized by the nature of the subtle phenomenal expansion (prapañca) which is its object— occurs; and for this very reason, it is supreme.

The meaning is that when that state— which is the self-nature of the undivided ground— [the reading is *sadaiva kāla*] is forgotten, then there arises what is named "jīva," "Hiraṇyagarbha," and so forth, conditioned by the future maintenance of vital breaths. || 7 ||
Existence alone, whose essence consists merely of mental cultivation, is oriented toward transmigration;
yet at that time, by virtue of the true nature of reality, it does not arise for those [who have realized it].

Likewise, even when there is manifestation, there is no impairment of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the existence of Brahman; thus he says: "Existence" (*sattā*). At that time, the very existence of Brahman becomes oriented toward transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), having as its essence mere mental ideation (*bhāvanāmātra*), and not as its essence actions such as modification (*vikāra*); this is the meaning. Why is that? To this he says: "By the very nature of reality" (*vastusvabhāvena*). How then [is it]?

The sense of being a living soul (jīvabhāva) arises there as "I am [this]. The meaning is that, following after this very Being (sat), the sense of being a living soul emerges, like the appearance of a snake in a rope. || 8 ||
Immediately upon its destruction, emptiness arises from its own existence;
it is the seed of the qualities such as sound, and it bestows the objects that will be designated in the future.

Now, desiring to describe the creation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), he first speaks of the creation of space with the words "immediately after" (*samanantaram*). Immediately after this existence of the individual soul (*jīva-sattā*), its own existence arises—being predominantly emptiness because it provides space for the other elements. This occurs after the creation of the sun and so forth.
When words such as "space" (ākāśa) and so forth—which refer to things yet to come—attain their own state, they signify meanings such as "it shines forth" and so on.
Thereafter, it arises together with the existence of time as its true nature;
by means of the meaning expressed as "the future," it is the seed for the primary abiding of the world. (10)

In that regard, he describes the emergence of the ego-identification (*ahaṃtābhimāna*) of the previously mentioned living being (*jīva*), as well as his acquisition of a lifespan lasting two *parārthas* from that time onward, with the words "Ego-identification" (*ahaṃtā*). The phrase "will come to be," etc., is to be understood as before. || 10 ||
Of that supreme power (parā-śakti), this net—which is essentially unreal—arises as a mere self-awareness; though unreal in nature, it emerges as something real, throbbing with vitality.

This creation, which produces the half of space, does not arise from Hiraṇyagarbha alone, but rather from the very existence of the Supreme Self (paramātman) as conditioned by that [Hiraṇyagarbha]; for it is that [Supreme Self] alone which is the cause of all.
Thus he says: "of that" (tasyāḥ). By the word *śakti*, the supreme function (*paravṛtti*) is intended; this is used to indicate its unmodified state.
It is merely self-cognition. || 11 ||
Consciousness of this nature is the seed of the tree of volition;
from that arises the spark of ego, which, through its vibrancy, becomes the vital breath.

Thus, that whose nature consists of such [ego], in which the self (*ātman*) exists as a state of modification through the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), is the seed of the tree of volition whose sphere of activity is the effects of consciousness. For this very reason,
it is like a single grain or a portion of that ego-sense.
The meaning is that it manifests. || 12 ||
I, as consciousness, through the contemplation of the subtle element of sound within the ether, gradually solidify by myself and become fully my own subtle element.

The meaning is this: from that very [state]—which is the supreme existence (parasattā) conditioned by the non-egoity of space (viyadahantā)—there arises the state of sound (śabdatā), which is the seed of all things.

Due to its extremely subtle nature as the essence of space (ākāśabhāva), it becomes dense and thus becomes its own subtle element, the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra). Although [this is stated] in the Sāṃkhya system, the Purāṇas, and other such texts regarding the subtle elements (tanmātra)...

The origination of the elements is well-established; for in such scriptural passages as "From the Self, space was produced" and "That [Self] produced fire," the direct causality of space and the other elements is heard. This is just as in the passage beginning with "As of a beaten drum," where [the cause of] the general category of sound is [indicated].

Because it is heard that there is no difference [between them] and because they are non-existent, from space alone—which is the universal form of sound—the mere manifestation of the future objects arises;
that seed of the tree of the stream of words has caused the multitude of Vedas, known as words, sentences, and means of valid cognition, to blossom. (14)
He states that the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*) is the material cause of all specific manifestations, such as the Vedas and so forth,
in the verse beginning with "bhāvi" (14).
Therefore, the entire glory of the world will emerge from the Supreme Self, which spreads forth through the transformation of the multitude of objects produced by the multitude of sounds. 15.

Therefore, from the existence of the Veda, [it follows that] the world [proceeds] from the Supreme Self; for the meaning of such scriptural passages as "Prajāpati created the gods," "the humans as drops," and "the ancestors," and so forth, is this. || 15 ||
That very consciousness, accompanied by such a retinue, is designated by the word "jīva" (living being);
it is the seed of the tree of forms, through the web of future words and objects.
Regarding what was stated, "as in the case of future living beings and so forth," that [is explained as follows]: it is the cause of all material forms for her; he states this with the word "seed.
Here, "form" (rūpa) refers to the shape of the head. || 16 ||
Then, indeed, the fourteen-fold web of living beings, with its interior filled and the flood of the world’s belly-pit, will spread forth.

He states that [the breath] is the cause of action by virtue of its nature as the vital force (*prāṇa*)—namely, "fourteenfold. Because of the fourteen divisions of the worlds, the multitude of living beings is of fourteen kinds; therefore, by means of the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*), [it serves as] the instrumental cause (*nimitta*).
This pit will expand and it will spread in five directions.
With her body quivering from intense speed, as if she had not yet attained her proper conduct,
she becomes in an instant, through meditative cultivation, the subtle element of touch.

He further explains how that very consciousness, conditioned by egoity (*abhimāna*), becomes the cause of the movement and activity of all objects through its division into the forty-nine groups of winds— such as the *pravaḥa* and others— which bring about the state of the *sparśatanmātra*, the substrate for all specific types of touch: *...* [text fragment] *...he states that it serves as the cause for the vibration and activity of all objective entities by means of the division into the forty-nine classes of wind, beginning with the *pravaha*, which brings about the state of the *sparśatanmātra* that is the material cause of all specific sensations of touch.*
"Not yet attained" refers to two [stages]. Even before attaining the conduct designated as such, her body quivers due to the impulse born from the conceit of being in the state of wind. (18)
The seed of the tree of the flood of contact has the expanse of the mass of wind as its root;
from it, the vibration of the activity of all beings will spread forth. (19)
In that very place, through the play of consciousness (cidvilāsa), light arises from experience;
that is the subtle element of fire (tejas-tanmātra), which serves as the designation for what is yet to come.

Then he speaks of the arising of fire (tejas) with the word "therein" (tatra). The play of consciousness (cidvilāsa) is the contemplation of having the nature of light. The rest is as before. Fire-tanmātra is the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra). || 20 ||
From that seed of the sun and fire, which is the expansion [of consciousness] and the root of the tree of light,
the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) will spread forth through the differentiation of forms.
That is fire; lightning is like a flash during a momentary opening of the mouth; and by the word "etcetera," the moon, stars, and so forth are included. || 21 ||
As it is being cultivated, becoming increasingly subtle like the water-element within the aggregate of taste,
that relish of the assembly is called the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra).

Next, he describes the origin of water with the words "bhāvayan" (contemplating). That self, having become fire, while contemplating its own attenuation—that is, its state of being that body or its limitedness—thinking "I am [this]," enters into that state; this is the ellipsis. Of that aggregate consisting of water, which is a material substance...

The meaning is that the tasting which occurs when something is tasted with the tongue, such as "this is sweet," is called *rasatanmātra* because it consists of the general form that underlies the specific qualities of taste. || 22 ||
The essence of the future play of the world is the seed of that tree of aesthetic flavor (rasa);
from their mutual devouring, the cycle of worldly existence will expand.

The meaning is that when that very *rasa* is tasted by one another through the state of being sense-objects for the senses, the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*)—which consists in the repeated engagement in acquiring objects due to the arising of passion and other afflictions toward those objects—will expand. This is also the case in the preceding [verse]. || 23 ||
This [element], consisting of conceptualization and named after its future form,
perceives the state of the subtle element of smell through the qualities inherent in its nature of volition.

Next, he describes the creation of the earth with the words "bhaviṣyat" (it shall be). That Supreme Self, having entered the state of water and being of the nature of the volition "I am indeed the earth," becomes [according to the reading *bhaviṣyadrūpa*] the volition of its future form; then, by means of the qualities consisting of the volition of smell, of itself—
The meaning is that he perceives the state of being the subtle element of smell. || 24 ||
From that seed, which is the soul of all supports and the future earth-globe, the world-tree will expand forth.

He states its application with the word "bhāvi" (future): as a terrestrial globe, as a cosmic egg, or as the terrestrial globe well-known in astronomy; "form" refers to the human and other shapes. || 25 ||
The subtle elements (tanmātras), being clearly perceived as they mutually transform themselves, are like waters that flow continuously and without interval.
Thus, he describes the transformation of the arisen elements into the form of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) through their intermingling,

beginning with the word "consciousness" (*citā*). By consciousness— which has assumed the state of the aforementioned elements and ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*)— the elements are conceptualized in the form of the cosmic egg,
like bubbles within the waters of the successive internal coverings, each ten times greater than the preceding one.
The meaning is that they have evolved into the form of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 26 ||
In this way, these elements, whether mixed or separate, are no longer perceived as pure until their total destruction. 27.

He states for how long their state of being mixed persists: "In that manner. These elements remain thus mixed such that they are not perceived as distinct or pure again until the point of universal dissolution. || 27 ||
Existing within the belly of the sky as forms consisting of pure consciousness,
they become like networks of banyan trees from within the interior of a tiny seed.

He states, with an illustration, that through the existence of Brahman, there is first existence itself, which then manifests in a gross form: "Consciousness... and so forth. Here, "gagana" refers to the unmanifested space (avyākṛtākāśa). || 28 ||
They behold an emanation that branches out into a hundred shoots and quivers;
they shine within a single atom and in an instant become an entire aeon.
[Objection: But surely, because they are most subtle, a gross state of existence is contradictory within the *tanmātras*, which allow no space; to this he replies:

"It is merely the perception of a creation consisting of *māyā*, and that is possible even within atoms and the like. The sense is that in a dream, one perceives an immensely vast world even within the extremely subtle apertures of the channels (*nāḍī*). || 29 ||
They rush toward manifestation alone, yet they remain without manifestation;
pierced by consciousness, all things coalesce into a mass in an instant.

He states that even though these [elements] exist in a gross state, there is no loss of their subtle essential nature, because a phenomenal manifestation (*vivarta*) is non-transformative (*avikāraka*):

"For this very reason, there is no delay," he says, using the word "in an instant" (*kṣaṇāt*). For in the case of the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*), there would indeed be a delay, as in the case of the growth of a gourd. || 30 ||
This group of subtle elements (tanmātras) would be that consciousness whose nature is volition (saṃkalpa);
appearing like a mote of light within sensation, it perceives while remaining formless.
He concludes by reminding of what has been stated: "tanmātra" (that alone). This refers to the manner already described. The neuter gender is used according to Vedic usage. || 31 ||
Indeed, the seed within the worlds is merely the pentad;
the primordial power is the seed whose state remains unseparated from Parā.
It is perpetually experienced that the seed is indeed that very [power].
Thus, the glory of the world is nothing but pure consciousness, unborn and primordial.

And thus, he states that what was said—that Brahman itself becomes the form of the world—is established, by saying "the seed": the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are the seed, that is, the cause of the world; and the seed of that [fivefold group] is none other than the power of *māyā*, which is the immediate and direct cause of the world's existence, being inseparable from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). And so it is.

The meaning is that the very reality of the Supreme Self becomes the seed through the power of *māyā*, and upon the disappearance of *māyā*, it becomes that [Supreme Self] once again; thus, the matter proposed is established. || 32 ||
Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The Description of the Origin of the World," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 12.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the World," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, within the supreme Brahman—vast, equanimous, and all-pervasive;
the self-nature of consciousness wherein there is no existence of space, light, or darkness, and which is unarisen.
By the description of creation, the prior unreal state of the world as Brahman was described;
now his state as a living being (jīva) and his acquisition of a body and so forth are described.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha spoke in five verses beginning with "parama" regarding the sequence of the re-manifestation of the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) of the individual souls (jīvas), which had attained the state of Brahman mixed with Māyā through dissolution— as in deep sleep or at the time of cosmic dissolution— along with its underlying cause: "In that which is both equal and unequal, due to being mixed with Māyā yet devoid of the inequality created by modifications..."

And when the substratum is present, that which is the existence of unarisen things—such as space, fire, darkness, and so forth—in the form of their causal nature, resides within the conscious self (cidātman) in that very form. || 1 ||
First, the conceptualization of "the object of consciousness" arises from the consciousness of the objective portion within that which exists;
then, the conceptualization of "mind" (citta) arises from the consciousness of the nature of the power of consciousness (cit-śakti). || 2 ||

Since the state of being a living soul, characterized by the nature of a conscious cognizer (*cetayitṛ*), is preceded by the establishment of objects and the sense organs, he first demonstrates the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of that [soul-nature) with the word "first" (*pūrvam*). *Kalana* means conceptualization (*kalpana*). The reason for this is that the manifestation of the real entity (*sad-vastu*) is its very nature. The same applies to what follows. That which is superimposed is as follows:
Since the nature of that manifestation is already established in consciousness, it serves as the cause everywhere. || 2 ||
Then, from the consciousness that is conjoined with the object of thought, there arises the perception of the living skin (the subtle body);
then, by virtue of being solely intent upon the object of thought, there occurs for him the perception of Māyā and the perception of the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva). || 3 ||
Illusion is the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva). However, if the reading is *ahaṃbhāvakalanam* ("the conceptualization of I-ness"), it is clear.
For that [illusion] is the firmly established state of the individual soul (jīva), a state of single-minded focus, the conceit that "I am only this much. || 3 ||

Then, from the transformation of the intellect (buddhi), ego-sense (ahaṃtā), and the subtle element of touch (tvak), there arises this very [mind] which possesses the nature of the mind (manas) and so forth, as well as the subtle elements of sound and the rest. (4)

Through transformation and through accumulation—in this way, when the nature of phenomena is established, because one contemplates the mere objects such as sound and so forth, which exist within oneself in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), just as in a dream, this very thing results in the form of the mind (*manas*) composed of them; such is the meaning. || 4 ||
From the swelling of that other subtle element (*tanmātra*), which has become a gross material form— [the reading "bhāvanodbhūtaḥ" is also found]—
this great thicket of the world and its origins is perceived in this manner. (5)
He describes the attainment of the state of the gross body by that [subtle body] with the words "from the swelling" (*ucchūnāt*).

Due to the blending (*melanāt*) of the sound-tanmātras— which exist as latent impressions (*vāsanā*)— with the other tanmātras such as touch and so forth, through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkṛta-bhāvena*), there arises from the swelling the internal [body].
"Of those who have not yet attained a physical form"—that is to say, of the mind that has assumed the state of a gross body. || 5 ||
In this manner, either instantaneously or through a gradual process, it arises again and again and perishes like a city created in a dream within the great forest of the vast sky.
He concludes what has been said with the words beginning "instantly" (jhaṭiti) and so forth: "unperformed" means not accomplished through desire. || 6 ||
This seed, born from its own sowing, produces the groves of the world’s karañja trees;
it requires nothing at all, such as earth, water, fire, or other elements.
This [consciousness], which is of the nature of pure awareness, will subsequently create the earth and other elements,
just as one who has awakened from a dream perceives a city that was nothing more than pure consciousness alone.

"Later," meaning at a subsequent time; "one who knows the dream" means a dreamer. "His own" refers to that which is being experienced by himself. But in reality, that is indeed non-attachment itself; thus he says: "consisting of pure consciousness alone. The connection with what follows is this: that which consists of pure consciousness, even while situated here or there, certainly emits the sprout of the world and so forth. || 8 ||
Wherever it may be situated, it releases the sprout of the world;
the imperishable Consciousness is the seed of the fivefold world, and of those five, it is the immutable Consciousness itself.
The pentad consists of the subtle elements.
Know that whatever is the seed, that is the fruit; therefore, the world is composed of Brahman.
Thus, at the beginning of creation, this group of five [elements] exists within the great space.
The word "evam" (thus) and all that follows are connected with what comes after. || 10 ||
The self, which has become its own limb, is imagined by the power of consciousness (cicchakti) and is not real;
it is by means of this [imagined self] that this [universe], having attained a state of swelling, is projected forth.

By the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) and the power of the manifestation of the object of consciousness (*cetyaprathanaśakti*), he whose self has become his own limb—having attained a form as if it were his own body—[is realized] through this group of five. This is the gross (*sthūla*). || 11 ||
Even that [space] is essentially composed of existence when conceived within the self;
for indeed, nothing is ever established by means of what is itself unestablished. (12)
The meaning is that, like the form of space, it consists of existence (*sanmaya*) because it resides within the self which is the locus of one's own conceptualization, but not by its own nature.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "In some places" (*kvacid*). || 12 ||
How can that which is essentially of the nature of conceptual construction attain reality?
Or, if the pentad [of elements] is Brahman through the cognition that it has Brahman as its essence— || 13 ||

Now, it may be argued: "Granted that the group of five, being superimposed upon Brahman, may consist of Brahman alone; but how can its effect [consist of Brahman alone]? To this he says: "Now (atha)," etc. (Verse 13).
Know that quintet to be the mature Brahman itself, the sequence of the three worlds;
for in this way, at the beginning of creation, this arises as the manifestation of the quintet.

That pentad—that group of five gross elements which constitute its effects—is also nothing but the Consciousness-Brahman. The word "hi" (for/indeed) signifies the reason for this: the well-known identity between cause and effect. Thus, it is established that Brahman alone is the mature, fully manifested order of the world; such is the meaning. How then [is it] in the non-different [state]?
Regarding the conventional usage of "cause and effect" therein, he says: "Just as... (the word *kārya* is not found in some versions). || 14 ||
In the very same way, here in this present state of being, it itself becomes the cause;
thus, nothing at all is born, nor is the world perceived as having been born.
"In its reality" means in its state of belonging to a prior time. "By itself" implies "only with respect to itself," which is the ellipsis for the subsequent time.
He concludes with the word "thus. || 15 ||
Like a city in a dream or a mental construction, that which is unreal is experienced as real;
within the supreme space of Brahman, the state of being the space of the individual soul (jīvākāśa) is perceived in the Self.

Showing that even the state of being a living soul (jīva) conditioned by those [attributes] is indeed non-existent, he dispels the possibility of experiencing the existence of what is non-existent through an illustration: "In a dream... etc. Within the Self, which is the supreme ether—the ether of Brahman and the supreme light—the state of being the ether of the individual soul (jīvākāśatva) is experienced as if it were real, though it is unreal. || 16 ||
Thus, because earth and the other elements do not exist, the self is pure like the funeral pyre;
this is described as the living being (jīva), arisen in the void like the nature of space itself. || 17 ||

The syntactical connection is to be understood by supplying the words "the pure-souled one perceives. In reality, since limiting adjuncts such as earth and so forth are impossible [in the case of space],
it is merely through mental construction that space itself appears as if divided by things like cities of Gandharvas, houses, or jars within the sky.
The meaning is that this very Self is called the individual soul (jīva). || 17 ||
(160) Listen now to how the living space (jīvākāśa) enters this body:
that very living space exists within that Supreme Lord. (18)

Having thus described the state of Brahman as the collective individual soul (*samaṣṭijīva*) through the conceit of universality (*sāmānyābhimāna*), [the author] begins to elaborate upon the process of superimposing identity with the gross body through the conceit of particularity (*viśeṣābhimāna*) by means of its state as the individual soul (*vyaṣṭi*). He begins with the words "The space of the individual soul" (*jīvākāśa*), etc. Therein, first, by means of contemplation alone (*bhāvanayaiva*):

He shows the commencement of the sprout of the individual internal organ (*vyaṣṭyantahkaraṇa*) from the adjunct of the collective totality (*samaṣṭyupādhi*) with the words "the space of the individual" (*jīvākāśa*),

etc.: within that Supreme Lord, the imagined space of the collective individual (*samaṣṭijīvākāśa*), though vast, [thinks] "I am a minute, even smaller spark, a particle of light like a firefly," and by such contemplation, conceives itself as exactly so.

The connection with the subsequent clause is that "it perceives" and "it experiences. Intending this very point, the Śruti says: "Just as tiny sparks fly forth from a fire, even so all these selves fly forth from this Self. (18)
When it perceives through thought, "I am a minute particle of light," that very thing,
as if swelling, imagines itself within the void of space. (19)
He states its increase through the intensification of its cultivation with the words beginning "that which," etc.: "Whatever one perceives, that very thing one cultivates as if it were swollen. (19)
Just as the moon, when conceptualized as being real though it is unreal, does not truly exist, so too the mind,
while contemplating that very [unreal] object, remains established in the form of both the seer and the seen.
Whatever one contemplates, that becomes difficult to distinguish from reality, as if it were real; the meaning is that it is indeed unreal.
He states the fruit of that contemplation: "That very [Self]... (verse 20).
Though it is truly one, it becomes twofold, like the perception of one's own death in a dream;
it assumes, as it were, a slight degree of grossness, and thereafter attains the state of the *tāraka*.
He demonstrates its growth within the conjunction of the seer and the seen with the words "something" (kiñcit).
Having abandoned the state of being a minute particle of light, perceiving a resemblance to a star, it seems to assume a certain degree of grossness.
This very state is its condition as the *liṅga-ātman* (subtle body) conjoined with the subtle elements (*bhūta-mātrā*). || 21 ||
Because he has cultivated the state of being all forms through the cultivation of the object as it truly is— [the reading is *bhāvitvādyatsvarūpataḥ*]—
he himself, though eternally that very Self, realizes "I am He" by himself.
Then, from that such-like experience, this living soul (jīva) became its own self in the very form of the star.
He states two reasons for this: "yathābhāvita" (as it was meditated upon) and "so'ham" (that am I), which is the manifestation of identification with that state. || 22 ||
From the mind it assumes a condition like that of a traveler in a dream,
likewise taking on a star-like form designated as the future body.

He states that this perception of the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) and the perception of the future gross body (*sthūladeha*) arise solely through the power of mental construction, beginning with the words "from the mind" (*cittāt*). [The phrase] "having the form of a star" refers to the previously mentioned form of the subtle body. || 23 ||

"Meditating" means that the mind, as it were, having abandoned the state of being an object— that is, the state of being perceived— along with its external aspects, then [remains] within the hollow of the *tāraka*. (24)
In this regard, the analogy is that the mind appears as if it were the object— that is, as if it possessed the form of the object.

Demonstrating through an analogy how even the reality that is free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) appears to be included within those adjuncts due to delusion— by abandoning its true nature— he describes the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of dreams and so forth:
By the words "having abandoned" and so forth; in the hollow of the *tāraka*, that is, in the space imagined within the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). || 24 ||
Just as a mountain, though situated outside, appears within a mirror;
just as the body [appears] within a well; and just as speech is contained within a casket. (25)
Just as a body capable of all worldly transactions appears to engage only in those limited when situated in a well;
or just as a word such as an insult, though fit to be heard from afar, remains confined within a casket and does not spread outside when placed inside a sealed box. (25)
The individual soul (jīvaka) knows this consciousness within both dreams and mental constructs;
situated within the star of its own essential nature, this very soul perceives by itself. (26)

Or, just as in dreams and mental constructs one perceives the dream and so forth within another body of consciousness, so too, within the subtle atom (*aṇuka*)—which possesses the aforementioned limiting adjuncts similar to sparks—the consciousness, situated within the imagined star-like [point of light], perceives the empirical functioning of the body and other things composed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). This is the meaning. "The mind, as it were, becomes the object of cognition."
Even in the case of the illustrative examples, only the two and a half verses beginning with "parityajya" (having abandoned) should be applied.
Just as an object situated outside both dreams and mental constructs appears internally even while remaining external—
like a body reflected in the water of a well, or like an echo of speech contained within a cave or similar enclosure— so it is here.
Jīvaka knows this object of cognition (vedya) as consisting of latent impressions (vāsanāmaya). The rest is as before. || 26 ||
This very [Self], which takes the form of the existence of knowledge such as the intellect and the mind,
is the space of the individual soul (jīvākāśa); it exists there by its own nature, contained within the casket of the sky of the stars.

Thus, from the perspective of the empirical dealings involving the body and so forth—which are composed of latent impressions (vāsanā)—it appears in those various forms because it is a modification of the intellect, mind, and other faculties; yet, when analyzed from the perspective of ultimate reality, it consists solely of consciousness, existence, and bliss. For one who has become identified with those respective gross bodies through the constant contemplation of them as such—
Through the conceptualization of the eye and so forth, he elaborates upon the worldly cycle of waking experience with the passage beginning "the space of the individual soul" (jīvākāśa). || 27 ||
With the thought "I shall look," it seems to spread through the void in order to see;
then, by means of the two apertures, it again [perceives] that which is called the external.
That by which one sees shall be known by the name "the pair of eyes";
that by which one touches is indeed the skin; and that by which one hears is the sense of hearing.
That by which one smells is the sense of smell; he perceives it within himself. That is his own tasting, and thereafter the tongue shall manifest.
Tasting is the gustatory faculty. || 30 ||
That which vibrates is the wind; contemplate it as the activity of the group of action-faculties, and likewise as the collection born of form, light, and mental attention. (31)
That which vibrates is the wind, whose functions are prāṇa and the rest. || 31 ||
The self consisting of the subtle body (ātivāhikadeha) remains in the ether within the ether;
in this way, contemplate its swelling within that spark of fire (or, according to another reading, "within the fire of being").
Meditating and superimposing, he abides as Brahman.
Though non-existent, it appears as if real, like the word "living being" (jīva) applied to Brahman;
thus, the meaning of the term "living being" has fallen into a state of conceptual confusion.
The self whose nature is the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), having the form of the sky of the mental body (citta-deha),
perceives the entire cosmic egg (ākāra-maṇḍa) situated within the limits of its own imagination.

The meaning is that he perceives the Brahmāṇḍa— the cosmic egg consisting of the covering and other structures— situated within that Brahman which, though its very nature is the sky of the mind's body, assumes the form of a gross body through its density, and which takes on the forms of its own mental constructions ranging from the external objects such as sparks and shapes to their inner essence. || 34 ||
Someone perceives him as being within the water; someone else perceives him as having the form of a sovereign emperor; and some even behold and experience his manifestation as the future cosmic egg.

He states that there is a twofold nature to this: the experience of the sense of "I" as the body of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) situated within the water, and the experience of the sense of "I" as the body of the four-faced Brahmā within that [egg]—expressed by the words "some... and so forth.
The womb-chamber of the self is the mind, which is according to the self's own volition; it is that which perceives the conceptualization of place, time, action, and substance. (36)
From the very mind— which is conceived as the self by the self— as a cause, according to its own volition,

the Lord who fashions names and so forth, while contemplating the womb-house as the cause for the self’s dwelling in a womb, creates those various objects and the self itself through those respective words, consisting of the perception of the conceptualization of place and so on.
The connection is with the subsequent [verse], "he binds. || 36 ||
Constructing words while meditating, he binds himself with imagined sounds;
this is the delusion of an unreal world, wherein one possesses a subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*). (37)
Just as in a dream, that which is unreal appears as if one were flying;
so too, this Self-born One, though unarisen, has arisen by himself. (38)
He states the application of the illustrative narrative concerning origination that has been established: "Thus, [the Self] is unarisen" (verse 38).

"The primordial Lord Prajāpati, whose self is the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), [remains so] even when this delusion, which takes the form of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), has come into being" (verse 39).
Nothing at all has been accomplished, nor has anything been born, nor is anything seen;
that Brahman is the infinite space, remaining as space alone. 40.
This world has the form of a city of imagination; though it exists, it is not real at all.
It is uncreated and free from passion; indeed, this is a marvelous painting arisen in the sky. (41)
It is free from passion and devoid of the substances of color. || 41 ||
That which was uncreated yet experienced is not [merely] truth, though it stands as if it were truth;
for, without doubt, even Brahmā and the others are liberated within the Great Kalpa. 42.
The distinction is that [the world] is not produced by external causal conditions (*bāhyasāmagrī*), but is rather uncreated by internal effort (*āntaraprayatna*). Now, one might ask:
"In that case, why could the world not be produced solely by a collection of causes such as unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)?
To this he replies: "At the time of the great dissolution (*mahākalpa*). The intended meaning is as follows: "When the period of reabsorption has arrived, all those [beings] together with Brahmā..."
Having perfected themselves at the end of their time, they enter the supreme state.
According to the principle demonstrated by such Smṛti and Sūtra passages as "The abiding of those who hold office lasts as long as their office" (*yāvad-adhikāram-avasthitir-ādhikārikāṇām*),

since it is determined that the former [beings] such as Brahmā and others are liberated at the end of a great aeon (*mahākalpa*), the creation of the subsequent world does not occur through the residual impressions of their unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*). However, as for the practitioner (*upāsaka*) at the beginning of the aeon...
One may attain such states as that of Hiraṇyagarbha, yet by that alone the world was never previously created;
since there is an absence of experience [of such a prior creation], the latent impressions (saṃskāra) thereof are impossible, and thus the world cannot be born from impressions.
Therefore, like a dream or a magical illusion, it has arisen suddenly through ignorance (avidyā) alone, and is therefore nothing but false (mithyā). || 42 ||
There is no prior memory nor any cause for the Self-born;
therefore, whatever the Self-born may be, this world born of him is remembered as being exactly like that.
But this beginningless experience which exists here—
in trees and so forth—
is like the earth and other elements experienced in a dream, as they would appear upon waking. (44)

[Objection: "In that case, let the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that [world] arise from the very beginningless experience of the Witness (*sākṣin*), and let the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) born therefrom also exist.

To this, he says: "anādi... [etc.]. Regarding the creation of earth and so forth, such as the egg of Brahmā (*aṇḍaka*); the ellipsis is "it would be of whatever kind [it might be]. [The answer is: because we observe the falsity of dreams and the like which are cognizable by the Witness, [the world] born from a latent impression produced by those [dreams] must likewise be false.
The sense is that it would simply be falsehood. || 44 ||

He is remembered as being of the nature of pure space alone, and the entire world is always remembered as such; wherever and in whatever way fluidity appears to be divided within water, [so too is this world perceived]. (45)
He explains what was stated—that "as is the Self-born (Svayambhū), so is that which is born from Him"—in the verse beginning with "smṛta" (remembered).

The meaning is that this Self-born One is "as if remembered"; like a past object being recalled, He is of the nature of pure space, having the essential character of mere emptiness, and the world is likewise. In whatever place and at whatever time, just as in water...
The term "is not divided" (*na bhidyate*) from the subsequent *nañ* (negative particle) is also connected here. The word "namely" (*nāma*) indicates well-known status. || 45 ||
In each and every instance, there is no other creation within the Supreme Self;
this creation is thus matured, yet He remains exactly the same.
He appears mature; yet, in ultimate reality, he remains equal and entirely devoid of the world's inequalities. || 46 ||
Thus indeed does this universe shine, as pure as the very nature of space;
this visible world is thus tranquil, a delusion created by one's own self. (47)
