He explains what has already been stated with the words beginning "bhāti" (it shines), etc. || 47 ||
Without support and without that which is supported, non-dual and devoid of unity—nothing at all has arisen within consciousness, even when the world appears to have arisen. 48.
In the absence of dualistic transaction, because there is nothing to be excluded, consciousness is even devoid of the number one; this refers to the case of error. || 48 ||
The supreme space is established as immediately empty and utterly transparent;
that which is so established is devoid of all the nature of saṃsāra. (49)
In that [state], the entire cycle of existence does not exist. || 49 ||
Therein there is nothing to be placed, no locus, no object of sight, and no state of being a seer;
there is neither the cosmic egg nor Brahmā, nor are there any cavilers anywhere.

The multitude of elephants that are people blinded by the intoxication of delusion—those disputants who, in their investigation of the world, find no position to be established—are liable to be regarded as mere cavillers (*vaitaṇḍika*). (50)
Neither the world nor the earth exists; rather, everything remains in a state of absolute peace.
It is Brahman alone that shines forth, pure, in this manner—by itself, through itself, within itself.

Due to its nature as consciousness, like water through its fluidity, this world—though non-existent—appears within the Self in the form of a whirlpool; though unreal, it is experienced here as if it were real.
In the end, that which is unreal perishes, just like one's own death in a dream;
or rather, because it is its own true nature, this [reality] is indeed existent,
free from affliction, undivided, without beginning or end, and having the interior of the sky of pure consciousness as its belly.

Having thus stated the emptiness of the world from its own side by way of the view of negation (apavāda-dṛṣṭi), he speaks, however, by way of the view of the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna-dṛṣṭi): "Or else" (athavā). || 53 ||
In the supreme space itself, the first Lord of Creatures shines eternally by himself, equal to emptiness;
for he possesses a subtle, transportable body and not a form composed of the gross elements.
Therefore, earth and the other elements do not exist as real; they have not been produced. (54)
Concluding by way of the "lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokana*)—that is, by referring back to everything previously stated—he summarizes with the words "in space alone" (*ākāśa eva*).

In the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of Creatures (*prajeśa*), the Self-born (*svayaṃbhū*), is space itself, which is emptiness (*śūnya*). That which is the Equal One, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), shines forth and manifests as the very nature of emptiness, the Lord of Creatures, and so on; for he is that Lord of Creatures.

The subtle body (*ātivāhika-vapuḥ*) consists of a mind-made form (*manomaya-śarīra*) and is not composed of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*). Therefore, because it consists of mere volition (*saṃkalpa-mātra*), the earth and other elements are not real (*sat*) or true (*satya*). The meaning is that they do not exist, just as things such as a rabbit's horn—which are unborn (*ajāta*) and unproduced (*anutpanna*)—do not exist. It has been described how, just as that which is unborn does not exist, so too [the elements] are [unreal].
Or the remainder. || 54 ||

Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Self-Arisen Origin," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (sage-authored) tradition. || 13 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Self-Arisen Origin," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
In this way, the entire collection of perceived phenomena, such as the world and the sense of "I," is nothing at all.
Because it is unarisen, that which exists does not exist at all; rather, it is the Supreme alone.

Having refuted, through reasoning, the doubts concerning limitation and other attributes regarding the nature of the individual soul (jīva) described previously, its identity with Brahman is here further elaborated as the remaining conclusion. || 1 ||

Therein, first, in order to dispel the notion of limitation regarding the universal collective (samaṣṭi), the cosmic Virāj, and the individual soul (jīva), he prepares the introductory stage by restating what has preceded, beginning with the words "In this manner" (ittham) and so forth. || 1 ||
In the beginning, the supreme space itself becomes conscious of its own living state,
like water beginning to stir within the hollow of a motionless ocean.

Desiring to explain the conceptualization of the body as the Virāṭ (the cosmic form), which conforms to that [creation], he states the establishment of the state of being the collective individual soul for that purpose: "The Supreme... (verse 2).
Without ever abandoning its ethereal nature, consciousness thus experiences a state of internal loveliness,
like an inner mental modification occurring within dreams, volitions, or the body of a statue.

"Not abandoning its ethereal form"—this phrase connects with what precedes. The internal mental modification (*cid-vṛtti*), consisting of volition (*saṃkalpa*), as will be described, perceives—as it were—the loveliness of the Virāṭ, which has the aforementioned universe as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), through the error of identifying it with the Self, thereby making it an object of love. || 3 ||
The great body consisting of Virāj, which is devoid of earth and the other elements,
is indeed the subtle body (ātivāhika), composed of pure consciousness like the clear sky.
He shows the result of the statement regarding their being born of volition (saṃkalpa) with the words "earth, etc. (pṛthvyādi). || 4 ||

It is imperishable, resembling a mountain in a dream, like a city seen in a steady dream; it has the appearance of an army depicted in a painting, situated within a mind that is itself as stable as a painting. || 5 ||

Destruction is its dwelling place, and it is devoid of that. If a dream-city were to be stable and long-lasting, then it would be comparable to that. If a painting created by an artist were to be stable and motionless, then it would have the same appearance as an army composed of painted figures. || 5 ||
He is like a multitude of statues on great pillars that have not been fixed in the ground;
his self is unfixed in the space of Brahman, like a carved figure on a sturdy pillar.

The multitude of great pillars and statues that are neither fixed in the ground nor carved out, as well as all others like them—all these serve as metaphors for her. This is a metaphorical representation (*rūpaka*): she is a statue (*śālabhañjikā*) whose nature is uncarved, standing upon a firm pillar whose characteristic is the space of Brahman (*brahmākāśa*), while her own self remains unfixed. || 6 ||
In the beginning, the first Lord of Creatures was renowned as Svayambhū;
he was without cause, even due to the absence of his own prior effects.
Having stated that the material form (*ādhibhautika*) is illusory, he says with the verse beginning "In the first," etc., that its divine form (*adhidaivika*) is likewise so.
Therein, he recalls the very reasons previously described with the half-verse beginning "Of the former," etc. [The phrase] "of their own effects" refers to their own actions (*svakarma*). || 7 ||
At the conclusion of the great dissolution, all the primordial Grandfathers (Pitāmahas) are indeed liberated; therefore, what prior karma could there be for them?
He is indeed without a wall, yet has the nature of a wall; visible and invisible, he abides in himself.
He is neither the object seen, nor the seer, nor the creator, and yet he is everything.
Although it appears like the nature of the wall itself in a mirror or the like upon a wall, it is not fit for perception because of its non-existence.

To demonstrate this non-existence, he states that in the unattached and changeless consciousness (*cit*), the triad of triads—the seer, the seen, and the seeing; the creator, the creation, and the act of creating; and the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the enjoyment—is impossible: "No."
And "all" includes the group of six that has not been explicitly mentioned. || 9 ||
This very [Self] is the source of all things, including words and their meanings; from it arises the multitude of living beings, just as a row of lamps arises from a single lamp.

Thus, even when everything is negated, the meanings of the words "prati" (each/individual) do not become void; for this very inner self (pratyagātman) is established as the essence of the referents of the words "prati. || 10 ||
It is indeed from volition alone— devoid of earth and the other elements— that it arises from volition,
as if from the beginning, utterly empty, just as one enters another dream from a dream.

Because the Virāṭ is an effect consisting of dense volition (*saṃkalpa*), even individual embodied beings consist of mere volition and are not composed of real earth and so forth; thus he says: "Volition. Just as the Virāṭ was produced from the primordial Hiraṇyagarbha—who is utterly void due to his own falsity—in the same way, from the Virāṭ...
The meaning is that it is also the individual self (vyaṣṭy-ātman) [the reading "dṛśyātmāpi" is also found]. || 11 ||
Those individual souls who emanate from this single vibration are,
due to the absence of auxiliary causes, that very same [vibration] itself.

Having established the identity of the individual and the collective through their very nature as a single essence, he states— beginning with "asmāt"— that by this means the remaining conclusion of the oneness of Brahman is proven: those individual souls who,
due to the absence of auxiliary causes, move about alone and without assistance.
From such a Virāj, those [beings] emanate; they are that very [Virāj] and nothing else.

The sense is that, just as branches and so forth that have issued from a tree of such a kind are not seen to be distinct from it, so too is the relationship of cause and effect when auxiliary causes are absent.
Therefore, this delusion of creation is one with that [Supreme], and not different from it. || 13 ||
The speaker of Brahman is the Virāj-self; like the Virāj-self, he is the state of emanation.
He alone exists as the space of the individual soul (jīvākāśa), from which the unreal earth and other elements arise.
Śrī Rāma said:
Is the individual soul (jīva) limited, or is it an infinite multitude? Or rather, is there an infinite self that constitutes a mass of souls as vast as a mountain?

If the individual (vyaṣṭi), the collective (samaṣṭi), and their root were one, then how could it be that the individual and the collective are unreal while only their root is real? Why should the unreality of the root and the collective not apply, while the reality of the division into individuals—
established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception— is maintained, as in the case of an army or an assembly?

Thinking that its reality might be established by the persistence of the individual (vyaṣṭi) even upon the disappearance of the collective (samaṣṭi), Śrī Rāma said: "What would happen? [He meant: if only the individual were real, then the individual soul alone [would remain], because it is limited by a single cognition or because it occupies only one location.
The sense is that, due to their mutual cohesion, they attain the state of a single mass, and thus a conceptualized collective whole (kalpitasamaṣṭyātmā) is conceivable. || 15 ||
Why do the Jīvakas emerge like streams from a rain-cloud, like spray from the ocean, or like sparks from heated iron? (16)

And this must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, if [the world] were to arise from the universal aggregate (*samaṣṭi*) like raindrops from the ocean or like sparks [from fire], it would follow that [the world] is impermanent, resulting in the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāni*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*).
With this intention, he says: "The streams. Why? Because they emerge from there.
The meaning is that it is capable of being honored. || 16 ||
"O Blessed One, tell me this definitive teaching on the net of living beings (jīvajāla).
This has been mostly understood by me; please make that very thing manifest. (17)

He says—"It is known"—to show that the production of a contrary state [in the opponent] was due to a desire for further distinction, and not because of dull-wittedness or a failure to understand your intention. || 17 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
There is not even a single individual soul; how then can there be the arising of multitudes? Indeed, your words are like saying that the horn of a hare has flown away.

For the sake of establishing the purposeful oneness of Brahman and the Self, it is simpler to postulate a single locus for multiple conceptualizations; thus, having postulated the universal soul (*samaṣṭi-jīva*), I have described the postulation of individual souls (*vyāṣṭi*) as being conditioned by that [universal soul]. This was not intended to establish the reality of either the individual or the universal, nor to propound the origination of individual souls, and therein—
With the intention of dispelling your apprehension, Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "One," etc. The particle *eva* is used in the sense of "even" or "indeed. (18)
There is no individual soul, O Raghava, nor are there multitudes of souls;
nor does there exist any single mass of soul resembling a mountain. (19)
Let your firm conviction be this: that here there are no conceptualizations whatsoever—neither the conceptualization of the meaning of the word "jīva" nor any other conceptualizations at all. (20)
The appearances are conceptual constructions. || 20 ||
Indeed, there exists here the pure, stainless, and all-pervading Brahman, which,
by virtue of its omnipotence, assumes whatever powers (kalās) it chooses of its own accord.
He finds or obtains the *kalās*, which are the skills of conceptualization; that is to say, he connects them together. || 21 ||
Indeed, by means of the very sequence of pure consciousness, one quickly beholds that [reality] alone— whether embodied or unembodied— like a creeper in full bloom.
By means of the entry of the measures (*mātrā*) and manifestations (*ābhāsa*) of consciousness— which follow the sequence of various volitional activities—
one perceives that very *kalā* appearing in both embodied (*mūrta*) and unembodied (*amūrta*) forms, just as one [perceives] oneself through the process of a creeper.
Then he perceives her as being both delighted and fully blossomed, just like that. || 22 ||
The individual soul, the intellect, the vibration of action, and even the duality or unity of the mind—all these direct that self-luminous existence toward cognition. (23)

He clarifies this very point regarding the stage of perception through an elaboration of the subject matter: "The individual soul (jīva). That Brahman itself impels one toward knowledge; that is to say, it makes it its own object. || 23 ||
Thus, while remaining unawakened, it becomes Brahman itself through awakening (or "being awakened," according to another reading).
Ignorance perishes through discernment, yet it does not truly awaken.

Thus, its manifestation occurs through ignorance alone; however, upon the removal of that [ignorance], it remains only in its own nature free from distraction. To this he says: "That" (seti). It is "unawakened," meaning veiled by ignorance, and thus exists in the manner described. By "contemplation" (prekṣayā), [he means] by self-awakening; awakening itself [is what is meant].
He says that it is difficult to obtain: "But not," etc. (24).
Just as darkness perishes when observed by means of a lamp,
yet its true nature is not known [by the lamp itself], so indeed is it with non-awakening.

If, then, ignorance has been removed, what remains of it? It cannot remain as the nature of consciousness (*bodha*), because consciousness does not produce that [ignorance] and because the two are contradictory. Nor can it remain as something else, for that would imply the persistence of something other [than itself]. Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Just as... (verse 25).
Thus, Brahman alone is the individual soul (jīvātman), undivided and continuous;
it possesses all powers, is without beginning or end, and has the nature of the essence of great consciousness.
He concludes what has been established with the word "evam" (thus): "If that alone is the essence, the unsublated portion, then by that very form of ultimate reality, it possesses form. (26)
Because it is entirely without atomicity, no conceptualization of difference exists in it anywhere;
for whatever conceptualization occurs, that is itself [the reality] through direct experience.

Because it is not minute in any respect and is therefore undivided, when the distinction of objects has vanished, even the differentiation of its own manifestations [the word "api" is sometimes not read] disappears—just as the distinction between forest and sunlight vanishes when the forest is cut down—and thus only Brahman remains; so he says: "it exists. || 27 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brahman, how is it that all the living beings of the world do not become one with the Great Soul (Mahājīva) by virtue of the will of that single soul? This does not seem logical. (28)

Having accepted what was stated, Śrī Rāma raises an objection regarding the lack of distinction between enjoyment and liberation; for if the individual (vyaṣṭi) and universal (samaṣṭi) souls are non-different as previously argued, then even the desires and so forth of the individual soul would possess the attributes of the universal soul, resulting in their being unfailing, which would lead to a lack of systematic order in enjoyment and liberation. He introduces this with the words "evam" (thus).
The acceptance that "this is exactly as previously described" refers to all other living beings in the world. || 28 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That Great Soul, which is Brahman, consisting of all powers, remains here exactly as it wills, undivided and continuous. (29)
Brahman, having first attained the state of the collective individual soul (*satya-saṃkalpa-samaṣṭi-jīva-bhāva*),
subsequently assumes the state of the individual souls (*vyaṣṭi-jīva-bhāva*) whose functions are dependent on their own [limited] volitions. In this regard,

he [the author] refutes the objection that the individual souls cannot achieve the status of "those whose volitions are true" (*satya-saṃkalpatā*) with respect to objects contrary to the prior [collective] volition.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "Mahājīva" means: just as the order of the world is established, so too is there the desire—"May I myself always be one whose resolve is true with respect to all things"—meaning that such is his will. "Nirvibhāgam" (undivided) refers to the state prior to the division into individual manifestations (*vyaṣṭi*); it is "void of that" [distinction]. "Nirantaram" (uninterrupted) is to be connected with what follows. || 29 ||
Whatever that Great-Souled One desires, that very thing comes to him quickly;
first, he desires what was previously wished for, and from that, duality arises.

His will is true; by the word "etcetera" (ādi), it is implied that other [individual] desires are obstructed by Him. Duality is the division into individual manifestations, which is subsequently fashioned from His own powers once they have been divided by duality.
By this [will], in this manner, indeed, the sequence of action is brought about.

"Of its own powers" means of the living beings who are its own parts. By this it is meant that the sequence of action—such as "a jar or the like comes into being through this external apparatus of staff, wheel, and so forth, and by such processes as rotation"—is not from mere volition alone. || 31 ||
In the absence of that [external object], when these [cognitions] do not arise, it is the primary desire alone that grows;
for this restriction has been established by the unborn power of Brahmā. (32)

[Objection: "In that case, how is it that for other great sages (*maharṣi*) as well, an effect is seen to arise from mere intention even without a sequence of action? To this, he says: "That" (*tam*). Thus, since it is a settled rule that an effect does not arise without a sequence of action, [the author explains] that in some cases there is a desire on the part of these individual powers of the great sages and others, even without a sequence of action.

It grows; indeed, the will of the Pradhāna as a collective whole (samaṣṭi) grows. The meaning is that the intention "may this resolve of his be accomplished" is attributed to the Pradhāna itself. || 32 ||

That [power] called the individual soul (jīva), which bears fruit in dependence upon [the Supreme] Power, does not do so, however, without the performance of the regulation of the primary power (pradhāna-śakti). || 33 ||
He clarifies the very meaning already stated with the words "yasyā" (of whom): "that one bears fruit. || 33 ||
If the regulation of the power of Pradhāna were not well-established, it might [not exist]. (Note: The reading "bhavet" is preferred over "na bhavet".)
Because that fruit is dependent upon [one's] capacity, it may not occur in some cases for those who have made efforts. || 34 ||
He states that even the accomplishment of the fruit of a ritual procedure (*kriyākrama*) is dependent solely upon the primary resolve (*pradhānasaṃkalpa*), by saying "the primary" (*pradhāna*).

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: if [the resolve] were well-established—that is, conducive to the proper accomplishment of the fruit—then there would be no fruit even for the desired activities such as ritual acts and so forth. || 34 ||
Thus, Brahman exists as the Great Life (Mahājīva), devoid of end, beginning, and middle;
it becomes millions and billions of individual lives, yet is nothing at all.

And thus, as a conclusion, he summarizes that when the essential point is drawn out, Brahman alone is the Great Jīva, and it is that very same [Brahman] which becomes the two poles of the individual (vyaṣṭi) and the collective (samaṣṭi): "Thus," etc. (35).
Through the perception of the object of thought, the individual soul comes into being and enters the cycle of transmigration;
through the non-perception of that, it returns once again to its state of equilibrium as the Form.
To facilitate understanding, he presents what was explained at length in a condensed form: "cetya" etc. "Equal" means non-differentiated, the very nature of Brahman. || 36 ||
In this way, through the sequential and non-sequential processes of the younger and elder vitalities (jīvas),
the state of being the Self-vitality (ātmajīvatva) arises, just as the nature of gold emerges from copper.

He says "Thus" to explain that the state of Brahman for individual souls arises either through meditation by means of attaining the state of the cosmic totality (*samaṣṭi*), or directly in this very life through knowledge. "The nature of the Self as a soul" refers to the great state of being a soul as the aforementioned Brahman. It is just as the state of gold is produced in copper by means of mercurial elixirs.
Just as it occurs either through a sequence of cooking or without sequence upon contact with fire, so it is in this case. || 37 ||
In this interval, within the great void, even this non-existent multitude arises as if real, being nothing other than one's own self, consisting of the wondrous play of consciousness.

He states that within this inquiry, the states of the individual soul and the world are merely the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*) and not separate entities—referring to "here" as the inner, immediate Great Space (*mahākāśa*). (38)
That which is the spontaneous wonder arising from consciousness itself—
the future notion of "I" regarding the body, name, and so forth— is known as *ahaṃbhāvanā* (the sense of egoity).
Because consciousness is the substrate of consciousness, it is infinite due to its identity with that [consciousness];
this very expanse of the worlds is reflected within it.
What is this "wonder of consciousness" (ciccamatkāra)? He explains it with the words "of consciousness" (citaḥ).

Through the reflection of Māyā, which is conditioned by the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of the world, and through its identity with that [world], one's own Self becomes the relish of the experience of consciousness; that [Self] is reflected—that is, it flashes forth—within that very consciousness of the Self. || 40 ||

By means of such words as "transformation" (pariṇāma) and "modification" (vikāra), that very same immutable consciousness, though inseparable from its own nature, becomes awakened through its own power alone. (41)

Although that consciousness, being of the nature of pure reality, cannot be divided even when embraced by consciousness, it is nevertheless perceived as if divided by such terms as "transformation" (pariṇāma) and the like. || 41 ||

That which is the self-experience of consciousness (cit), whose nature is uninterrupted play, and which consists of both the object of cognition and its illumination—that alone exists as the world. (42)

The meaning is that the world exists as an error, consisting of the very act of tasting—which is inherently and naturally of the nature of uninterrupted play and characterized by non-discrimination—belonging both to the cognizer, whose manifestation depends upon that [tasting], and to the object of cognition. || 42 ||
This pervasive power of consciousness, subtler even than space, perceives this sense of "I" by its very nature. (43)

In that regard as well, he says with two verses beginning with "From space" (ākāśāt) [verses 43–44], that first there is the perception of the ego, and then the perception of the limited form of the world produced by it.
When that which vibrates within herself by her own self like water— extending from the self to the world— then she perceives it as the subtle atom of egoity (ahaṃtā).
At the end of a succession of increasingly gross external objects, there is the world-egg;
within that is such a subtle atom of the ego (ahaṃtā).
Because consciousness itself produces wonder within its own self, that which is beautiful and wondrous, it is for that very reason given the name "the world" (jagat). || 45 ||
And thus, since the world is merely the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkṛti*), it follows that there is no world existing apart [from it]; so he says: "The wonder... (verse 45).
O Raghava, the ego (ahaṃkāra) is the perceiver of the perceived; that itself is mere conceptual construction (kalpanā).
Since even the subtle elements (tanmātra) and so forth are nothing but consciousness, where can duality or unity reside? 46.

Since the conceptualization of the ego (ahaṃkāra) is dependent on consciousness (cit), and the conceptualization of the world beginning with the subtle elements (tanmātra) is dependent on that [ego], it is established that whatever is dependent for the conceptualization of another is itself what remains as the ultimate reality; thus he says: "of consciousness" (citaḥ). || 46 ||
Upon abandoning the notion of a living soul, its causes, and so forth, abandon both "you" and "I. That which remains between existence and non-existence becomes the true essence of reality.

Between the two conceptualizations of existence and non-existence, or truth and falsehood—the conceptualization that "you" and "I" are distinct conscious entities—is indeed difficult to abandon. He says, "jīva," etc., to show that when this [duality] is relinquished, what remains is, by its very nature, of the form of pure Being (sanmātra), due to the absence of any further conceptualization. [The word "jīva"] is used with the abstract sense as the primary meaning.
Explanation: The cause or the instrumental condition (*nimitta*) for the state of being a living being (*jīvabhāva*) consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), karma, and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the appropriation of the material cause (*upādāna*) is included. The meaning of the root *bhū* is existence (*sattā*); [the living being] is of that nature. (47)
Just as that self-existence was first conceived by consciousness, so it has arisen;
it is seen as non-different from space. We do not know existence or non-existence.

He says "citā" (by consciousness): when, through knowledge (*jñāna*), the existence that is conjoined with the object of perception (*dṛśya*) ceases, the previously established existence of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) remains exactly as it was, just like the existence of the stainless sky when the clouds have vanished. || 48 ||
The sky called the world-activity is the entire universe; it is the void that is the abode of the wise.
Because its nature is the wonder of consciousness, it possesses form; indeed, nothing else exists.
He further confirms this state of non-proliferation (*niṣprapañcatva*) through inference as well—beginning with the word "the universe" (*viśvam*).

The subtle world, consisting of the activity of the mind known as *īhā* (volitional effort), is indeed the void (*kha*). Likewise, the abode of the wise—the sense organs and their presiding deities—is that which possesses form and is gross.

The meaning is that both types of the universe—namely, as the form of Viśva and Virāj—are indeed the void (kha), which is emptiness, because their nature is the wonder of consciousness (ciccamatkāra). || 49 ||
Whatever is a manifestation of something is never distinct from it;
since this is so even in the case of that which has parts, what need be said regarding that which is partless? (50)

In that regard, he shows the example and so forth for the sake of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other logical requirements with the words "yo yad" (whatever which...). The meaning is: if it is observed to be so even in the case of effects such as water with parts, like waves and the like, what need is there to mention the case of the effect of partless consciousness? || 50 ||
The form of the world is the very form of that which is eternal, inconceivable, nameless, and of infinite form—the form of that whose nature is pure radiance. (51)

And thus, it is established that the true nature of the world is indeed the form of consciousness alone, which is undivided and distinct from name-and-form (nāmarūpa); so he says: "Of consciousness... (verse 51).

The mind, the intellect, the ego, the elements, the mountains, and the directions—whatever such arrangements exist for the persistence of the world, they all arise from the reality of consciousness. (52)

Even when viewing things from the opposite perspective, the conclusion remains that the construction of the world is nothing but the construction of consciousness; thus he says: "The mind... (verse 52).
Know that the world is the consciousness of Cit; for there is no such thing as a world that is not consciousness.
Since it is not a non-world, it would be non-consciousness if it were not consciousness; how then could there be a distinction between them through mere appearance? (53)
Thus, since the world consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*), it follows that the very nature of consciousness itself has borne fruit; so he says: "Of consciousness" (*citaḥ*).

Since both consciousness (*cit*) and the object of consciousness (*cetya*)—or as the reading goes, *cit* and *cittva*—appear in the form of mental construction, there is no difference between them in reality;
therefore, from where could the world arise? (53)
The innate wonder residing within the seed of a mirage is this very thing:
it exists as the world, which is nothing more than the subtle element of the living soul (jīva). (54)

He begins to firmly establish the previously described fact that the world is nothing but consciousness (*cinmātra*) through various modes of liberation, starting with the verse beginning "Of consciousness" (*citeḥ*).

The meaning is that the very power of consciousness to manifest objects exists in the specific form of the individual soul (*jīva*), its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) which constitute the world. (54)

The manifestation of its own power from consciousness—which is the consciousness’s sense of "I"—is the individual soul (jīva); for it is that which has the nature of the activity of vibration and will indeed be designated by such a name. (55)

Then he says—starting with "from the mind"—that it is precisely the vibration of the power of egoity within the mind that, when conjoined with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and its functions of movement, will become what is designated by the term "living being" (*jīva*). || 55 ||

That which manifests as consciousness by its very nature, consisting of its own self-established designations, is differentiated from its own modifications; yet it is neither divided nor non-existent.

He says "yat" (that) to show that even when [the world] exists in such a way, there is no difference in the nature of consciousness (citsvabhāva): although the manifestation of consciousness as consciousness—being differentiated by its own modifications such as egoism and the like—becomes that which is designated as the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, which is not produced by itself; nevertheless...

Because that delimited form does not exist due to the falsity of the limiting adjunct (upādhi), it is not differentiated; the meaning is that there is no possibility of differentiation at all. || 56 ||
There is no difference between the agent and the action, for both consist of the vibration of consciousness;
the action is merely vibration, and that alone is known as the Puruṣa.

Anticipating the objection that there might be a distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) as conditioned by egoity (*ahaṃkāra*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) due to the difference between the powers of consciousness (*cit*) and vibration (*spanda*), he says:

"Consciousness... Egoity, in which consciousness predominates, is the agent; the vital breath, in which vibration predominates, is the action. For an agent is not differentiated by his own action; therefore, the meaning is that the person, the *jīva*, is precisely consciousness conjoined with vibration. (57)

The life-force (*jīva*) is the vibration of the mind (*citta*), and for men, the mind is that very same thing; the internal organ (*manas*), being of the nature of the senses, attains as it were a manifold existence within its own reality. (58)

Thus, even though there are distinctions such as mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and the sense organs (*indriya*), there is no difference in the individual soul (*jīva*). He states this—namely, that the *jīva* [is one]—because it is the mind, which is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the *jīva*, that exists in the form of the sense organs through the distinction of their physical locations (*golaka*). || 58 ||
For the world is indeed a flash of the light of consciousness in which all particularity has been stilled;
therefore, nothing other than that exists, such as the states of cause, effect, and so forth. (59)
Thus, he concludes the result of the refutation of the distinction between the world and the individual soul with the word "śānta" (peaceful).

For, because the world—whose nature consists of extremely insubstantial cause-and-effect relations and so forth—is, according to the previously stated method, like the fringe of a flash of consciousness, possessing an appearance of existence that is non-different from it; for that reason, elsewhere...
"It exists" means that it has become the very nature of the inner self (pratyagātman), in which all particularities have been stilled. || 59 ||
"I am indestructible, I am unburnable, I am indeed unmoistenable and un-dryable;
I am eternal, all-pervading, fixed, and immovable"—thus it is established.
In that regard, he shows the cessation of all misfortunes with the words: "indestructible" (acchedya). || 60 ||
For here they dispute just as those who dispute do through delusions; yet we, while causing them to wander in error, have ourselves become free from delusion. (61)
He says, "They dispute," meaning that it is precisely due to the lack of full comprehension of this [reality] that there is a diversity of disputes among the proponents of duality, but not for us;
just as those who, by their own delusions, cause others to be deluded, so it is in this case. (61)

When the visible, embodied form is firmly established in the Knower, modifications and the like appear as distinct; but they do not exist in the formless, which is the consciousness-reflected in the Knower, the space of consciousness whose nature is both being and non-being.

He states that for both the ignorant and the knower of reality, the distinction between duality and non-duality—arising from the attribution of truth or falsity—is caused solely by the conceptualization of the visible as either having form or being formless: "In the visible," etc. (62).
The splendor of the honey of consciousness, through the essence of the sap of the tree of the mind, extends its own blossom—pure as the sky—the power known as Time and the rest. (63)

Attachment to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) within the object of consciousness is like the sprinkling of water; from that, the power (*śakti*)—whose nature is the glory of the spring of consciousness—extends its own blossom, known by names such as *māyā* and *kāla*, which is pure in the ether, the first element, and in the upper region. (63)
The unstruck staff of consciousness vibrates by itself in manifold ways;
the wind of consciousness, whose nature is born from the egg, itself possesses a movement of diverse characteristics. (64)

Just as Brahman attained the state of the world and of individual souls through its own independent sequences of conceptualization, so too does it abide in its own essential nature through its own independent sequences of awakening; thus he says in the four and a half verses beginning with "svayam" (itself).
Consciousness itself, being unstruck (*anāhata*) and possessing an uninterrupted core, first [engages] in the conceptualization of space.
Because it possesses openings, it manifests as having the form of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), resembling a hollow egg or a water-pot;
from that, the wind consisting of the egg, or the *sūtrātman* in the form of a mass of air, manifests—this is to be supplied everywhere. || 64 ||
The water of consciousness itself possesses a manifold shimmering, yet it does not reside within that which is excavated;
it itself has fashioned the state of diverse elements, even the most excellent of limbs.

Then, immediately after the birth of the fire-element which is about to be described, it manifests as water, the water-element (*aptattva*). And that [water] is not situated in excavated places such as ponds, because prior to the creation of the earth, such [locations] are impossible. That consciousness itself is the state of that earth in which there are various minerals such as gold and silver; this is the nature of the excellent ones.
Through his creative power (nirmāṇa), he brought about the limbs and even the bodily forms of gods, asuras, and humans. || 65 ||
The moonlight of consciousness, ever-risen and radiant with its own manifold aesthetic flavors, is consciousness itself; it is the manifest, great-souled illumination of consciousness.
He says "himself" (svayam) to show that he himself became the moon, who nourishes the world.

It is described as "his own manifold" because even the various juices of earthly herbs are dependent upon the moon. Here, the sequence of creation of light (tejas) should be understood as occurring after the previously mentioned creation of air (vāyu), since the sequential order of meaning (arthakrama) is more authoritative than the sequential order of the text (pāṭhakrama).
The entire compound beginning with "cidaṇḍakam" should be understood everywhere as a metaphor (rūpaka). || 66 ||
When the external has subsided of its own accord, consciousness (citi) arises from its own knowledge;
it itself enters the state of deep sleep through its own inertia within the insentient.

When the external object of perception has set through one’s own knowledge alone, she remains with her full being manifested; this is the ellipsis. [This applies] to insentient things such as stationary objects and the like. || 67 ||
Because the unmoving consciousness is itself the vibration [of all], it is the great sky of consciousness;
for the world exists and does not exist as the radiance of the light of consciousness.

He states the same point in brief with half a verse: "By oneself" (*svayam*). The meaning is that when there is no inquiry, by imagining the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth—which are of the nature of vibration (*spanda*)—as one's own self, one becomes a mere vibrating transmigrator (*saṃsārin*).
However, through the manifestation of consciousness (*cittva*) arising from self-inquiry, one abides in consciousness itself, which is one's own true nature. For one in that state...

Anticipating the doubt—whether the world exists or does not exist; for if it exists, there would be the consequence of falling into *saṃsāra*, and if it does not exist, there would be the consequence of the pervasion of non-existence—he states that the world always exists solely by the existence of Brahman, but does not exist by its own existence, in the six and a half verses beginning with "The light of consciousness" (*citprakāśa*). This applies everywhere.
The description of [the Lord] as possessing various attributes, such as light and so forth, is for the purpose of demonstrating that He subsists through the existence of consciousness (*cit-sattā*).
The "light" of light—that is, of fire—is its radiant form. (68)
The world both exists and does not exist as the singular void of the sky of consciousness;
the world both exists and does not exist as the great form of the light of consciousness. (69)
The world exists and does not exist through the vibration of the wind of consciousness;
the world exists and does not exist as the blackness of the darkness of the mass of consciousness. (70)
The world exists and does not exist on the day of the light of the sun of consciousness (*cidarka*).
The sequence of the world is like a particle of soot in the oil of consciousness; [the reading *jagadbhramaḥ* is also found].

Just as when the oil is burned, the soot remains, so too when the world is sublated, consciousness alone remains; thus it is called "soot" because of its residual nature, not with the intention of implying it is an effect.

The heat of the fire is consciousness; the world-line is consciousness; the whiteness of the conch-shell of the world is consciousness; the interior of the mountain of the world is consciousness; and the liquidity of the water of the world is consciousness.
The world is the sweetness of the sugar-cane of consciousness; the world is the oiliness of the milk of consciousness.
The world is the coolness of the snow of consciousness; the world is the blazing of the flame of consciousness.
The world is the oil within the mustard seed of consciousness; the world is a wave in the river of consciousness;
the world is the subtle sweetness of consciousness; the world is a golden armlet of consciousness.

The world is the fragrance of the flower of consciousness; the world is the fruit at the tip of the creeper of consciousness. The very existence of consciousness is the existence of the world; the very existence of the world is the body of consciousness.
He clearly states that because the world exists as non-different from consciousness (*cit*) in every respect, its nature is that of consciousness itself:
"Here, difference, modification, and so forth, reside like dirt on a fingernail;
thus, these three worlds, whether existent or non-existent, consist of *Cit*. (76)

Just as the impurity perceived in the sky is not actually present there—namely, its blueness—the three worlds, though non-existent, are said to be "existent" in the sense that they consist of Being (sanmaya), according to the manner previously described. || 76 ||
Because it is non-conceptual and of that very nature, existence and non-existence are indeed one;
the relationship of part and whole, as well as word and meaning, are like the horn of a hare.
"In that case, the non-existence of the world would be a separate entity"; to this he replies: "non-conceptual" (*avikalpa*).
The meaning is that no existence or non-existence, whether imagined or determined, is observed to transcend its substratum.
[An objection: "How can there be non-separate existence between that which has parts and that which is partless?"
The statement "the members," etc., rebukes the logicians who deny the experience of the wise. || 77 ||
Fie upon those by whom [this world] was imagined for the sake of denying direct experience—that world wherein neither mountains, oceans, earth, rivers, nor lords exist! (78)
In this regard, he states the contradiction with reason: "It does not exist.
The world, together with the mountains, oceans, the earth, and so forth, along with their respective lords. (78)
Since consciousness is one, such a consequence would follow; what room then is there for the delusion of "otherness"?
Though as solid as the heart of a stone, consciousness is indeed transparent within its own space.

"Prasaṅga" means that which follows as a consequence (*prasajyate*). It is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). The meaning there is: what kind of error regarding the other [element], such as the parts and so forth, would be entailed? "Viśadā" means clear or transparent. || 79 ||
Just as a stone contains within it its entire tranquil configuration, so too this impurity born of space exists within the space of the collection of objects. (80)

Everything is entirely quiescent because it is unreal, just like the arrangement of a city reflected in a crystal slab; it bears that appearance in the same way. To the question "How is everything quiescent?", he says: "In the substrate of all objects..."—in the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), which is the substratum of all things, this [universe] born of the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*)...

The impurity consists of the elements such as air and so forth, which form a manifold of parts. If there are no attachments to their effects even in the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), whose nature is unattached, then it follows that in the ether of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), attachments such as existence and non-existence are all the more non-existent;
this is the meaning. || 80 ||
For you, there are no attachments to existence, non-existence, selfhood, otherness, or possession;
[all] is spread out like the arrangement of a multitude of lines within a leaf. 81.

To the question, "In that case, how does the appearance of the world-structure—which is non-existent within consciousness—occur?", he replies with the verse beginning "pallava" (the leaf). Just as a leaf bears the arrangement of a multitude of veins and lines which, because they cannot be established as separate from the leaf, are non-existent [independently], yet exist as being neither different nor non-different from it; so too does Consciousness bear the world. This is the meaning. || 81 ||
By its very nature as consciousness, this [Self] holds within itself all the multitudes of causes, both distinct and non-distinct, beginning with the primary cause, the Grandfather (Brahmā). 82.

The falsity of the world as a modification has been stated on the grounds that it has the unchanging space (*nirvikārākāśa*) as its material cause; now, he states that the world is also false because it has Hiraṇyagarbha—as consisting of the aggregate of all minds, which are themselves composed of thousands of false conceptualizations—as its source: "samasta... (verse 82).

By its very nature, the mind is of the essence of the cause because it is experienced as consciousness; nor can the non-existence of consciousness—which is beyond the reach of thought—be established even by words. (83)

The meaning is that because mental activities, desires, and conceptual constructions (*manorathika-vikalpa*) are non-existent, the mind itself is without cause; thus, it is the Grandfather (*pitāmaha*). If the object of cognition (*cetya*) is non-existent, then consciousness (*cit*) is also non-existent, because its existence is seen to be invariably concomitant with that [object]. However, even so, the non-existence of consciousness is not established by mere words; for consciousness is established through experience (*anubhūti*), and what is contrary to experience cannot be proven.
The meaning is that the authority belongs to the word. || 83 ||
It is observed that whatever exists arises, just as a sprout [arises] from a seed and so forth. (84)

If the world were real by its own nature, then it would be impossible to destroy even by thousands of means such as knowledge; for since the absolute destruction of what is real is impossible, its reappearance would be unavoidable, leading to the consequence of no liberation.
With this intention, he says: "That which... (verse 84).
O dear one, within this great consciousness there exists the three worlds, which, though appearing as a manifold division, are like the utterly empty sky; indeed,
the entire visible universe is composed of the supreme state.
For you possess the certainty that "this is indeed so," based on experience. || 85 ||

If there is such great insistence on the existence of the visible world, then, having dispelled its difference through direct experience, one must accept it as being that very existence consisting of pure consciousness (cinmaya), which is the supreme state; thus he says: "In the sky... (verse 85).
When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed;
the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites.
Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe.
And at the end of the night, she returned together with the rays of the sun. || 86 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "The Exposition of Brahman," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition. 14.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Brahman," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The third day.
(p. 167) The fifteenth canto. 15
This world is indeed the very sky of the universe; for just as a pearl shines within the pure firmament, so too does one's own self shine as the world within the sky of consciousness.
Constantly demonstrating the meaning stated by the wise through examples and logical reasoning,
the Sage here begins the detailed narrative of Maṇḍapa.
The proposition is that the world is indeed the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). To the question, "How then does it appear as something separate?", he says: "Just as...

Just as a cluster of pearls appears as a string of pearls through delusion in a pure sky, so too the space of consciousness—which is one's own self—appears as the world; this is the illustration, and the word "be heard" is to be supplied. || 1 ||
The Shalabhanjika statue of the three worlds appears as if carved, yet it is not actually carved;
it is carved by the pillar of consciousness alone, and no carver exists here.
"And it does not cut [itself].
The sense is that this is because no other conscious agent capable of cutting it is established, and because cutting is impossible for that which is changeless and unattached. || 2 ||
Just as the surges of waves in the ocean, though never falling from their inherent nature,
appear to move within the water, so too do others who perceive external objects appear to exist.
Those who perceive the visible world are the cognitions of the universe. || 3 ||

The light of the sun passing through a lattice, as well as the particles of dust in the form of the lattice itself, appear gross in relation to the perception of the world, yet they are as motionless as atoms in comparison to a minute particle. || 4 ||

He says "jāla" (the net) to show that although the world is perceived by the ignorant as being of immense magnitude, it is in reality, from the perspective of the wise, even more subtle than the motes of dust within the sunbeams passing through a lattice opening. These are the particles of dust contained within those rays of the sun which, due to a lattice opening, take on the appearance of staffs, clubs, and so forth.

The intention is that, by the use of the word "api" (also/even), it goes without saying that other things possess an even greater degree of grossness. Alternatively, he states that the light of the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), which illuminates the universe, is subtler than the light of the sun and so forth, and even subtler than the atoms and other elements contained therein: [He says: "Furthermore... [and so on].
He kindles [it]. || 4 ||
This appearance of the world does not manifest as something separate from Brahman;
yet, like the web of rays from the sun through a lattice, it provides the experience of apparent separation.
To establish that very point, he demonstrates the difference between a mirage and the atoms in consciousness with the verse beginning "The world" (jagat) || 5 ||
Even these worlds, consisting of earth and the other elements, though experienced, do not exist at all within that which has the nature of space, just like those in dreams or mental constructs.

He removes the contradiction with experience resulting from the statement that [the objects] do not appear through exclusion (vyatirekataḥ), by saying: "Even though they have been experienced" (anubhūtāny api). || 6 ||
In this world, which has the nature of the space of consciousness, the grasping of a solid mass does not exist anywhere, just like water in a mirage-river.
To the question of how that which is differentiated by states persisting over many days can be similar to a dream or a mental construction, he says: "piṇḍa," etc.
"Piṇḍagraha" means the acceptance of material form. || 7 ||
In this world, which consists of grasping at a solid mass and is comparable to a city of one’s imagination,
the appearance of visible objects shines forth like a river in a desert, taking the form of an illusion.
By what measure could the splendor of the visible world, which is like a dream and free from conceptual construction, ever be weighed? It expands as the infinite void.

If the visible splendor of the worlds is projected as a dream upon the Witness-consciousness alone within the vision, and is weighed with equanimity by means of that faculty of discernment which distinguishes essence from non-essence— like the central prong of a scale— then that very splendor, being free from conceptualization in the waking state just as it was in the dream, becomes the void of space.
Or rather, Brahman itself yawns—that is, it expands. || 9 ||
Excluding the knowledge of the Knower, there is no difference whatsoever in the meaning of the words "world," "object," "receptacle," "world," "Brahman," and "one's own. (10)

Thus, he states that the distinction between the referent of the word "Brahman" and the referent of the word "world" exists only from the perspective of one who lacks discrimination, and not from the perspective of one who knows reality, by saying: "having excluded... (verse 10).
This pure consciousness, devoid of objects, shines toward the sky like the light of the sun;
it is as subtle as the cloud of volition is toward a physical cloud.
If it is asked, "How then is there a perception of the world by those who see according to reality, as if it were a witness?
he says "this" (idam), comparing it to the perception of light as illumination with respect to the void-like sky.
Then, as to how there can be a perception of the world with respect to the witnessing consciousness, he says "likewise" (tathā). || 11 ||
Just as a dream-city appears clear in relation to an excellent waking city,
so too does this world appear clear in relation to a world created by mere volition.

Anticipating the objection— how can that which is seen be of the nature of pure consciousness, which is utterly stainless?— he says "Just as" (yathā), explaining that the impurity of the external and mental objects exists only at the time of perception; however, at the time of their disappearance, what remains is their state of being most transparent in relation to one another.
The world is the waking manifestation; the mention of "grasping through conceptualization" (sāṃkalpikagrahaṇa) is also an elliptical expression for the dream state.
Therefore, the world, being of the nature of consciousness and devoid of objects of thought, is nothing but the absolute void;
know that the words "void" and "world" are synonyms, both consisting of pure consciousness.
He concludes with the words "Therefore," and so forth: [the two] are empty, meaning they have the sense of emptiness, or they are devoid of objects. || 13 ||
Therefore, nothing whatsoever has arisen here in this world that is perceived;
it remains as it is, unnameable and unmanifested. (14)
Thus the world exists in the great space of consciousness, which is without a supporting wall;
it does not fill even an atom’s worth of that space, nor does it equal a fraction of its measure.

In the manner thus described, the world situated within the great space—the illusory space—is nothing but the unobstructed space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), which is without a foundation. To preclude the possibility that consciousness itself might be limited to the same extent as the delimited world—given their non-difference—he says: "of that region. This refers to even the smallest or most minute portion of that region, the part of consciousness.

The sense is this: even in that portion of consciousness which is extremely minute, being delimited by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and its latent impressions (vāsanā), the entire universe appears as a limitation; since the universe contained therein does not fill that [consciousness], the idea that the Brahman-consciousness is merely that much is far from the truth. || 15 ||
It is transparent, having the very nature of space, devoid of any grasping at solid form;
it is a wondrous expanse within the void, composed of space itself, existing like a city of one's imagination.

To explain how the vast existence of the world, which is included within the mental states and their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that are nearly as empty as space, resides therein, he says: "ākāśa... (Space...). "Piṇḍagraha" means the assumption of a physical form.
To bring this into the range of experience, he provides an illustration: "saṃkalpa... (Volition... || 16 ||
In this regard, listen to this narrative of the pavilion, which is an ornament for the ears, so that this matter may find rest within your mind without any doubt. (17)

Having observed through various signs that Rāma experienced doubt, delusion, and a lack of certainty regarding the matter just explained, Śrī Vasiṣṭha pledges to narrate the extensive *Maṇḍapopākhyāna* (The Tale of the Pavilion), which is accompanied by thousands of illustrative stories designed to delight and resolve those very doubts, saying: "In this regard... (verse 17).
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahmin, for the increase of true awakening, please tell me briefly and quickly.
The entire narrative of the pavilion, by which awakening increases. || 18 ||
"In brief" means in a concise manner regarding a matter that has not yet been fully utilized.
Anticipating the objection that there might be a delay in speech—as occurred in the previous proposition—he says: "Immediately. (18)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: On this surface of the earth, there was a radiant lotus of a lineage,
a glorious king named Padma, who possessed many sons and was endowed with discernment.
He is Padma because, like a lotus, he is the cause of the fragrance of the fame of his family and lineage. || 19 ||
He is an ocean for the preservation of moral boundaries, a sun to the darkness of his enemies, a moon to the night-lotus of his beloved, and a fire that consumes the weeds of vice. (20)
The boundaries of the castes and stages of life, and the boundary of the continents. || 20 ||
He is the Meru mountain for the hosts of gods, the moon of glory in the ocean of worldly existence,
a lake for the swans of virtuous qualities, and the stainless sun for the lotuses.
The wise ones, the learned, and the gods—of those multitudes, he is the sun to the lotuses, which are their riches characterized by such lotuses. (21)
A wind for the creepers of battle, a lion for the elephants of the mind, beloved of all branches of knowledge, and a mine of all wondrous qualities. || 22 ||

In battle, he is like the wind that causes even the enemy forces—who are as fragile as mere creepers—to tremble; for this very reason, he is a lion to the elephants characterized by the pride of the arrogant, one who bends his enemies by shattering their pride rather than killing them—this is the intended meaning. He is beloved and dear. (22)
He is the Mandara mountain shimmering during the agitation of the ocean of the enemies of the gods;
he is the honey from the clusters of flowers of his own playfulness, and his flower-weapon is his own good fortune.
He states his status as the conqueror of Indra’s enemies with the words "surāri" (enemy of the gods). "Madhu" refers to the spring season. || 23 ||

Keśava is the wind that impetuously excites the dance of the *līlā-lata* (the vine of divine play); he is the moon for the white lotuses of goodness and the fire for the creepers of wicked conduct. || 24 ||
The exertion toward accomplishing the lifting up of the entire earth—which is otherwise impossible to achieve—is *sāhasa* (recklessness).
It is like fire to the poisonous creepers of evil conduct; the suffix *-kan* is used here in the sense of contempt. (24)
He has a fortunate wife named Līlā,
a playful woman endowed with all auspicious charms, who appeared upon the earth like a lotus risen from the ground.
*Valitā* means enveloped or surrounded. *Kamalā* is Lakṣmī. || 25 ||
Her graceful movements were followed by all, her speech was sweet,
she moved slowly with joy, and her smile was like the rising of a second moon.
Lalitā was skilled in all forms of service to her husband and in all manner of agreeable conduct toward every member of the retinue.
Possessing a lotus-face as enchanting as a swarm of bees, with a white body and fair as the pericarp of a lotus, she was like a moving lotus-pond. (27)
The *alayas* are indeed the *alakās*, the bees; she is *sitāṅgī*, one with pure limbs; and like the *karṇikā*, she is *gaurī*.
Thus, in what follows as well, the qualifying attributes common to the objects of comparison (*upamāna*) should be applied. || 27 ||
Shining with a profusion of jasmine-like playful gestures, full of aesthetic essence,
with hands like young sprouts and possessing the luster of flowers, she was like the embodied splendor of spring.
Rasa is love and nectar. || 28 ||
With a pure white body, auspicious and bringing delight through her touch, she was like the Ganges descended to earth in embodied form, graceful as a swan. (29)
She has a pure white body and a translucent form. || 29 ||
To perform for a long time the service of that god whose arrows are flowers of the earth and who bestows all delight, another woman appeared like Rati herself. (30)
When he is anxious, she is deeply anxious;
when he is joyful, she is joyful; when he is agitated, she is agitated.
Like a reflection, the beloved is identical to him.
They were merely terrified when he became enraged. || 31 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "The Description of the King," within the "Story of the Pavilion" in the "Section on Origination" of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 15.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the King," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixteenth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Together with the celestial nymph Bhūtalā, whose husband had no other beloved wife...
He took delight with that beloved wife in the essence of unfeigned love.
The insatiability regarding the enjoyment of desires and their ultimate result in further suffering—how even the gods cannot alter this—is proclaimed here. (1)
"A husband who is beloved by no other" is the reason for the unartificiality of the essence of love. || 1 ||
In the groves of garden forests and in the thickets of *tamāla* trees,
in the delightful flower-pavilions and in the dwellings formed by circles of creepers.
The connection of the phrases beginning with "in the groves of the garden forest" (udyānavanagulmeṣu) extends only as far as the word "he enjoyed" (reme). || 2 ||
Upon flower-beds in the inner apartments, on pathways strewn with heaps of blossoms,
on swings in the spring gardens, and in the pleasure-pools.
Upon mountains of sandalwood trees and beneath *saṃtānaka* groves, in the dwellings of *kadamba* and *nīpa* trees, and within the hollows of *pāribhadra* trees; || 4 ||
The *saṃtānaka* trees are a specific kind of wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*); they were obtained either through their own power or by the grace of Indra, and [he dwelt] at their bases. || 4 ||
In the clusters of spring forests, fragrant with the nectar of blossoming kunda and mandāra flowers,
where birds and cuckoos warbled, || 5 ||
And upon the soft-glittering patches of various forest grasses,
and at the waterfalls where dense showers of rising, bright droplets were falling.
The "tarasīkarāsāra" is a downpour, a falling stream of spray from those crossing or floating. || 6 ||
And upon the surfaces of mountains made of gems and rubies, in the dwellings of divine sages and seers, and in hermitages of remote sanctity; || 7 ||
In the dwellings of divine sages and seers, there was delight in the form of traveling together. || 7 ||
(169) When the night-lotuses have blossomed and the day-lotuses are smiling,
and when the dark forest grounds are covered with flowering and fruit-bearing trees; (8)
In the night, among the night-lotuses; by day, among the day-lotuses.

They were beautiful with their amorous dalliances and the rosy glow of passion; they were lovely through their mutual desires, which were enriched by the essence of intense and tender love for one another.
With youthful vigor resembling that of the gods, and with the desired pursuits of beautiful sense-objects—here, "pursuits" (īhita) refers to playful gestures and amorous activities. || 9 ||
With riddles, narratives, and likewise with "fistfuls" of syllables, with chess-like grids, many kinds of gambling, and likewise with those where the fourth [line] is hidden; || 10 ||
Riddles (*prahelikā*) are worldly humorous tales; narratives (*ākhyāna*) are those belonging to the Purāṇas; and *akṣaramuṣṭi* and so forth are specific types of gambling. || 10 ||
By means of dramas and narratives, by verses following the *vindumatī* meter, by divisions of place and time, and by the activities of cities and villages; || 11 ||
Dramatic compositions whose subject matter is intended for performance are *nāṭikās*.

Narrative works composed as poetry to be savored through hearing alone are *ākhyāyikās*. "By means of the progressions of the intellects of the discerning" (*vindumatikramaiḥ*) refers to verses of hidden intent that are traversed—that is, understood—by the minds of the wise (*vindūnām*).
That is to say, by means of imitated activities of cities and villages. || 11 ||
Adorned with garlands of flower-strings and various arrangements of ornaments, with playful and restless movements, and partaking of diverse flavorful foods. || 12 ||
By means of folds and wrappings. || 12 ||
By chewing fresh saffron, camphor, and betel leaves;
and by the nail-marks on her body hidden by blossoming flower-vines and *guñjā* berries. (13)
By means of nail-marks—wounds inflicted by the nails—which serve as a covering or concealment for the body, resembling blossoming flowers, creepers, or guñjā berries. || 13 ||

By means of the pastimes of mutual anointing, by the sequence of striking one another with garlands, by flower-swinging in the house, and by the manner of swinging one another back and forth; || 14 ||
Touching occurs through pursuing [the object], and that is the full embrace through His primary pastimes. || 14 ||
By means of the coming and going of pairs of boats, elephants, horses, tamed camels, and other vehicles, and through the playful sport of water-sports consisting of mutual splashing; || 15 ||

Traveling by water by means of boats; and by the coming and going, the walking back and forth, and the turning around of pairs of elephants, horses, camels, and other animals that have been tamed and trained. || 15 ||
With dances, songs, artistic gestures, rhythmic clapping, and the *tāṇḍava* dance; with ornaments, musical performances, conversations, and the playing of the *mṛdaṅga* drum. (16)
Songs, stories, conversations, and discourses. || 16 ||
In gardens, by the trees on riverbanks, along excellent streets,
in inner apartments, and in palatial mansions, they sported by swinging upon flowering swings.
Having been thus brought up in happiness, that beloved and affectionate wife of his, the fair-browed one endowed with resolute will, once reflected: || 18 ||
"This husband of mine, the lord of the world, is dearer to me than my very life;
how might he, full of youthful splendor and glorious, become free from old age and death? (19)
"With this husband, may I, possessed of lofty breasts, sport at will for a hundred yugas with my beloved in houses made of flowers. (20)
Therefore, one should exert effort through austerity, recitation, and self-restraint, so that the king may become like the moon-faced [Soma], free from old age and death. (21)
By means of the observances consisting of the performance of restraints (yama) and rules (niyama). || 21 ||
I shall ask those twice-born ones who are advanced in knowledge, advanced in austerity, and advanced in learning: "How may death not occur for men? (22)
Having thus brought them and honored the twice-born ones, she bowed and asked them again and again, "O Brahmins, how may immortality be attained? (23)
The phrase "he thought thus" connects with what precedes it; the ellipsis is "the immortality of her husband and of herself. || 23 ||
The Brahmins said:
"O Goddess, all the perfections (siddhis) and accomplishments (siddhayas) are attained through austerity, recitation, and self-restraint;
however, immortality is never obtained. (24)
Having heard this from the mouth of the twice-born, she, terrified of separation from her beloved, reflected once more with her own intelligence: (25)
By his own wisdom alone, he reflected upon this which is about to be stated. || 25 ||
If, by fate, my death should occur before that of my husband, then, liberated from all suffering, I shall abide happily in the Self. (26)

The sense is that she is liberated from all suffering in this life, and because there is no recollection of this birth in the next world, the suffering of separation from her husband does not arise. || 26 ||
"Then, even if my husband should die at the beginning of a thousand years,
I shall act in such a way that his life-force does not depart from this house."
While my husband’s life-breath wanders here in this inner apartment of my own, I shall dwell at ease, constantly beheld by my lord. (28)
In the pavilion of the inner apartments of the harem. || 28 ||
"Starting this very day, for the sake of this purpose, I shall worship the goddess Jñapti Sarasvatī with recitations, fasts, and observances until she is fully gratified. (29)
The act of informing is the nature of consciousness. || 29 ||
Having thus resolved, that excellent woman, without even informing her husband,
undertook a severe vow according to the scriptures and remained established in it.

Regarding the phrase "without having addressed her lord": one might object, "But this is censured by the text: 'If a woman, without being permitted by her husband, should observe a fast or a vow, she takes away the longevity of her husband and, upon death, falls into hell. How then can this [practice] be said to be in accordance with the scriptures? To this we reply:
"She should always act for the welfare of her husband, whether it be witnessed by him or not."

"By means of vows, fasts, observances, and worldly services"—since this censure of the scriptures refers to such things as voluntary fasts for one's own desires that exceed what is beneficial to the husband, there is no fault. || 30 ||
At the conclusion of every three-night period, she broke her fast, being devoted to the worship of gods, brahmins, gurus, the wise, and the learned. (31)
Her body is constantly engaged in bathing, giving, austerity, and meditation;
she practices all forms of faith and right conduct, and she is the remover of suffering.
The conviction that there is necessarily a fruit for every meaning taught in the scriptures is "universal faith" (sarvāstikya). || 32 ||
Without her husband being aware of her presence, she gratified him at the proper time, with appropriate effort, according to the scriptures, and in due order.
In this manner, that young woman, steadfast in her observances, remained for three hundred nights without ceasing,
devoted to asceticism through arduous exertion.
She remained, having performed [her duty]. || 34 ||
Then, after a hundred three-night fasts, having been worshipped and honored,
the blessed Goddess Gaurī, the Mistress of Speech, being pleased, spoke to her. (35)
She was worshipped with external offerings and honored with offerings of devotion. || 35 ||
Śrī Sarasvatī said:
"O child, I am well-pleased with you because of your uninterrupted austerity and your exceptional devotion to your husband; accept the boon you desire."
The Queen said:
Victory to you, O moonlight that dispels the defect of the burning heat of the flames of birth and old age! Victory to you, O sunlight that wards off the mass of darkness within the heart! 37.
By divine providence, the queen uttered a praise that was entirely consistent with her fortune—the attainment of the knowledge of Brahman and the life of her future husband—saying, "Victory! (37).
"O Mother, O Mother of the World, protect this wretched woman!
O Auspicious One, grant these two boons that I request. (38)
The word "me" (mām) is to be supplied as the object of "this" (imām). || 38 ||
First of all, O Mother, let the life-force of my husband, the King of Videha, not depart from this very pavilion in his own inner apartments. (39)
O Great Goddess, I entreat you for a second boon: whenever I desire to see you for the sake of a blessing, then grant me your vision. (40)
The syntactical connection is: whenever I pray for the sake of a boon or for the sake of a vision, then grant me that vision. || 40 ||
Having heard this, the Mother of the World herself said,
"Let it be so," and then vanished, rising up like a wave in the ocean.
Then that queen, her desired deity being well-pleased,
became filled with joy like a doe hearing a song.
Then, the Kālacakra, consisting of moments and pulsations, flows through the fortnights, months, seasons, days, nights, years, and the staffs of time.

The fortnights are its rim and felloes; the months are the middle felloes; and the seasons are the hub-felloes, according to the Vedic scripture: "The wheel with three hubs is undecaying. The days interwoven through the three [seasons] are its spokes;
the transverse pegs are its filaments; and the year is its axle-shaft.
A *kṣaṇa* consists of thirty *kalās*; [the term refers to] that which has the navel as its central aperture, being thus composed of the vibrations of the sun and other [planets]. || 43 ||
That consciousness of her husband vanished from his body while it was still visible,
like the sap of a withered leaf.

"Of the body mangled in battle"—this is understood from the subsequent [verse]. [This word *dehasya* is a genitive singular form; it appears as if it were intended as the locative singular *raṇakhaṇḍitadehe* found in the forty-fifth verse.
Consciousness, which is almost perceptible through signs such as the husband's breathing and so forth, resides in the body—that is, in the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*).
He vanished and underwent disappearance through his illusory power.
When he, whose body was mangled in battle, died within the inner apartments,
she became like a waterless lotus and fell into extreme witheredness.
Nalinī means a lotus pond. || 45 ||
With all her lower lip-sprouts withered by the hot, poisonous breaths,
she reached the state of death, like a doe pierced by an arrow.

"Destroyed and turned pale by a hot sigh like poison"—this is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). "Like a doe"—this is a simile (*upamā*). There is no tautology of the word *yathā*, for *saśalyā* (pierced by an arrow) is an epithet qualifying the doe as well. || 46 ||
When he had reached death, she fell into the blinding darkness of grief, like the beauty of a decorated house when the flicker of its lamp-flame has been extinguished. (47)
The splendor of the dwelling is the beauty of the house; it was adorned, meaning previously decorated with a lamp. || 47 ||
In an instant, that young woman became emaciated and fell into a state of despondency,
like a river whose current has failed, grey with alkaline silt.
Upon the exhaustion and drying up of the stream's flow, it becomes greyish-white with alkaline heat.
The proud woman, on the verge of death, quickly became one who wailed aloud and then suddenly became silent and mute like a female ruddy goose separated from her mate.
The proud woman, previously possessed by pride toward her husband, was on the verge of death due to its destruction. || 49 ||
Then Sarasvatī, whose abode is the sky, out of compassion [spoke] to her who was exceedingly overwhelmed,
like a small fish distressed by the drying up of a lake.
She trembled like the first rain from a cloud that has just begun to shake.
"Compassionate" (sakṛpā) means she whose compassion culminates in the bestowal of the knowledge of reality because she had been propitiated by him in many previous births.
"Born of the sky" (ākāśabhavā) means, that is to say, bodiless (aśarīriṇī). "She took pity" (anvakampata) indicates the result of her compassion, which was the granting of consolation. || 50 ||

Thus ends the sixteenth canto, titled "The Lamentation of the Queen," within the "Episode of the Pavilion" in the "Section on Origination" of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (sage-authored) tradition. 16.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Lamentation of the Queen," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventeenth canto.
Śrī Sarasvatī said:
"O child, place this husband of yours, who has become a corpse, upon a heap of flowers."
Having covered him, place him there; you shall obtain a husband once again. || 1 ||
Through positive and negative concomitance regarding the new and former creations,
it is understood here that they are identical because both are mere manifestations of the mind.
Compassionately consoling him by means of both a voice from the sky and the granting of a boon, the illustrious Sarasvatī said:
