"It has become a corpse," [referring to] the heap of flowers (*puṣparāśi*). || 1 ||
The flowers will wither, but he shall not perish;
moreover, he will soon restore you to the status of a wife.
The particle *na*, having the sense of negation, is a *nipāta* (indeclinable) that connects with what precedes. || 2 ||
And this life-force of yours, as clear as the sky, shall not quickly depart from this inner-chamber pavilion. (3)
He dispels the suspicion that the previous lover might be unfaithful with the words "belonging to him" (etadīya). || 3 ||
Having heard this from her kinsmen, she whose eyes were like rows of bees was comforted by their arrival, as a lotus is refreshed by waters.
Just as a lotus pond that has withered due to the drying up of its water is revived by the arrival of water, so it is in this case. || 4 ||
Having established her husband right there and concealed him with a profusion of flowers,
she remained somewhat consoled, like a poor woman who has found a hidden treasure.
On that very day, at midnight, in that very inner apartment pavilion, while the entire retinue had been carried away by sleep— (6)
The inner apartments are called the *śuddhānta* or *avarodha*.
With a mind fixed on pure meditation, he summoned the blessed goddess Jñapti from the realm of suffering; she approached him and spoke to her.

The figure of speech (utprekṣā) is that she was "summoned" (*āhūta*) as if she had arrived by herself through the great intellect accompanied by pure meditation (*śuddhadhyāna*). [The form *āhūtā*] is correct according to the rule *śācchāsāhvā-* etc., which is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *artihrī-*. She is Sarasvatī. (7)
"Why do you remember me, my child? Why do you bear such grief? The delusions of saṃsāra appear as vainly as water in a mirage."
Therein, first, in order to remove sorrow, he states the falsity of its causes: "In saṃsāra... (verse 8).
Līlā said: "Where is my husband staying? What is he doing, and what is he like?
Lead me to him; I am unable to live alone."
The Śrī Devī said:
"The space of the mind, the space of consciousness, and the third, the [outer] space—know, O fair-faced one, that the space of consciousness is more void than the other two. (10)

In order to demonstrate that the conception of the next world, just like this world, has pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) as its substratum, he analyzes and reveals the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) with the verse beginning "citta": the space of the mind (*cittākāśa*) consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which is well-established and empirical;
the third [space], which is conventional; and the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), which is empty of both and situated at the junction between the two.
The meaning is that it is easily perceived. || 10 ||

Through the contemplation of the singular nature of the space of consciousness, that which is essentially the sheath of the space of consciousness appears and is experienced instantly, even though it does not exist [as a separate entity]. || 11 ||

He says "that" (tat) to explain that the very sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), when undifferentiated from its own obscuring ignorance (*ajñāna*), suddenly appears in the form of the unreal world and is thereby experienced as suffering and so forth:
"That," though non-existent as something separate, is seen immediately from this very state through one-pointed contemplation of the sky of consciousness; and then—
The meaning is that, having gone there, it is experienced. || 11 ||

O lady of excellent complexion, know that which is the very interval between consciousnesses when one reaches another place from one's own place in a mere moment—that is the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). 12.
For that purpose, he introduces the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) with the words "from place" and so on.
The meaning is that at the junction between the appearances of two successive objects, the space of consciousness, which is empty of both, is easily perceived.
If you attain a state in that [space] wherein all volitions have been entirely cast out—
You will undoubtedly attain that state, which is the reality consisting of all things.

Therefore, with the intention that for you, the attainment of that [state] is itself the attainment of being near your husband who remains in that state—since the husband's transition to the next world is conceived as occurring right there—he says: "In that... (verse 13).
This is attained by the complete cessation of the world, and not otherwise; yet, O beautiful one, you shall attain it quickly through my boon.

How, then, is that attained? He states the means for it: "absolutely" (*atyanta*). When ignorance is destroyed through the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*), the non-arising of duality itself constitutes the attainment of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). Intending to show that the scriptural authority for this is the Śruti passage, "There is no other path," he says: "not otherwise. How, then, is it for me?
Regarding the attainment of knowledge therein, he says: "By my boon. (14)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess departed for her own divine abode;
Līlā, however, remained effortlessly absorbed in unwavering samādhi.
By the power of the boon, effortlessly and without the toil of practice. || 15 ||
In an instant,
she abandoned her own body along with the cage of the internal organs, like a bird that has fled its nest soaring into the sky.

The gross body, together with the internal organ that is as difficult to pierce as an iron cage, is to be [penetrated] by one whose mind is made steady; what is intended here is the relinquishing of identification with it, and not its exit from the outside like death. || 16 ||
Remaining in the sky, she beheld her husband,
the protector of the earth, seated in that very celestial abode within an assembly hall filled with many kings.

"Kha" here refers to the space of consciousness (cidākāśa); "satī" residing therein means that which is established within the sky of the substrate-consciousness (ālaya-ambare) through the attainment of bodies, houses, and so forth, in accordance with its own manifested latent impressions (vāsanā) and karma. || 17 ||
Seated upon the lion-throne, he was hailed with cries of "Victory! Live long!", and was intent upon undertaking the task of the army's mandala.
To undertake and accomplish the task that has been introduced and presented. || 18 ||
Situated within the royal capital, which was strewn with clusters of banners,
he saw a circle of countless sages, brahmins, and seers stationed at the eastern gate.
He was staying in the principal palace of the capital city, which was covered with banners and circular canopies; from this point onward, all [compounds] are multi-word *bahuvrīhi*s. (19)
The circle of countless kings and lords of kings situated at the southern gate;
the circle of countless assemblies of women situated at the western gate. (20)
The "worlds of Lalanā" refers to women. || 20 ||
The northern gate was crowded with countless chariots, elephants, and horses,
while the conflict in the southern region was decided by a single servant.
By whose word alone was the conflict—the state of war—decided upon in the southern region. || 21 ||
The eastern regions followed the ritual procedures established by Karṇāṭanātha,
while all the Mleccha territories of the northern path were determined by the Lord of Surāṣṭra.

He demonstrates the subjugation of all regional kings with the words "Karṇāṭa," etc. *Kriyākrama* refers to the establishment of the boundaries of legal procedure; *nirṇītāḥ* means they were captured and brought under control. || 22 ||
All the western tribes were overrun by the Mālava country,
while Laṅkā was entertained by messengers arriving from the shores of the southern ocean.
The Taṅgaṇa regions were completely overrun by the king, the lord of the Mālavas. || 23 ||
[He saw] the Mahendra mountain on the shore of the eastern ocean, where the Siddhas speak of the celestial river (Ganges);
and the Guhyakas described by messengers who had arrived from the shore of the northern ocean.

Bhava is Mahendra because he dwells on Mount Mahendra; as a perfected ascetic, he described and praised to him the celestial river Gaṅgā, which is wondrous with its thousandfold expansion of mouths and other features. || 24 ||
Its entire courtyard was filled with the splendor of countless bound kings, and it bore the description of the sequence of sunset as seen from the shores of the western ocean.
The messenger described the ocean shore as having been beheld by him; it was [beheld] through the arts—that is, the splendors—of innumerable kings arranged in rows. (25)
The sound of the foremost musical instruments played by the Brahmins reciting within the sacrificial enclosure resounded there,
while the forest elephants echoed the joyous clamor of the bards.
He whose forest elephants produce echoes for the joyous clamor of his panegyrists, [and who possesses] the *turyāgra*, the best of musical instruments. 26.
(172) Amidst the sounds of singing accompanied by the resonance of lutes, flutes, and drums, the sky was thick with clouds of dust from the rows of horses, elephants, and chariots. 27.
The middle of whose sky resounded with the sounds of songs and musical instruments played by those intent on performance,
and where rows of horses and other animals extended on all sides.
Rich with flowers, camphor, and incense, its mountains fragrant with perfumes,
it contained many edicts fashioned from the materials of every maṇḍala.

By the word "mountain" (parvata), palaces resembling mountains are meant. To those ministers who, having gathered offerings and the like from all the provinces, filled his residence, he issued many edicts. (28)
He was a mountain of exceedingly white garments like clouds of fame-sandalwood;
he alone served as a pillar for heaven and earth, having surpassed the sun with his own majesty.
For whom the clouds—white as heaps of camphor from his own fame—are like mountains arisen in the sky. || 29 ||

The lord of the earth was busily occupied with grand undertakings that proceeded slowly at their commencement; he was the sovereign master of architects diligently engaged in the construction of various cities.

The kings and vassals were busily occupied with his noble undertakings, which involved heavy efforts and slow progress; likewise, the architects and masters of the guilds of artisans were engaged in them. || 30 ||
Then that [illusion], with its great onset, fell upon the assembly hall of the king—she who is of the nature of space, like mist falling upon the forest of the sky. (31)
She fell and entered; that was Līlā. Because both consist of mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they possess the nature of space. *Mihikā* is a mass of frost or mist. (31)
No men there beheld her wandering before them,
for she was like a woman of desire created by mere imagination.
"Created by mere volition" applies to both [the dream and the waking state]. (32)
Thus they did not see her as she moved before them,
just as one does not see a city fashioned by another's imagination when it is conceived by someone else.
He saw all those very same people from his past gathered in the assembly hall,
just as one who has traveled from one city to another sees the mountains he previously encountered.
"His own" means his relatives; the words "along with the king" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 34 ||
Those regions, those customs, as well as those very children, those same young women, and those very ministers; (35)
Those whose conduct is the same as that of the inhabitants of their own country.
Those very same rulers of the earth, those very same learned men,
those very same ministers of pleasure, and those very same servants of such a kind— || 36 ||
[He appointed] the ministers of the sky as companions for deliberating on secrets. || 36 ||
Then he [addressed] other wise men and friends who were likewise unprecedented, as well as other legal proceedings, and other citizens as well. (37)
He states that, as in a dream consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is no necessity of similarity with what preceded: "Now," etc. (37).
At midday, during that day, the quarters were agitated by dense forest fires;
the atmosphere, along with the moon and sun, was filled with the roar of clouds and the wind.
By dense and thick forests and wildernesses. || 38 ||
Adorned with trees, rivers, mountains, cities, and towns,
it was crowded with various arrangements of cities, jungles, and villages.
The king was twice eight years of age and free from his former old age;
he [beheld] all the people of former times and all the inhabitants of the village. (40)
Beholding them, that woman became overcome with anxiety, wondering:
"Have all those inhabitants of the city died? (or, according to another reading: "Are they even dead? || 41 ||
Having perceived that city of latent impressions (vāsanā), the inhabitants of the former city who resided there [realized their true nature]. || 41 ||
Again, through her awakening to conventional designations, she went to her former inner apartments;
and in an instant, at midnight, she saw them there exactly as they were before.

The designation is Sarasvatī; by means of the awakening born from her grace, there is the emergence from meditative absorption (*samādhi*). "Remaining just as they were before" is the remainder [of the sentence], just as previously stated. || 42 ||
Then she awakened her circle of female friends who were overcome by sleep, and said, "I am in extreme distress; please grant me an audience. (43)
"Āsthāna" means presence in an assembly. || 43 ||
If I stand by the side of this lion-throne of my husband, and I behold the assembly of my own kinsmen, then I shall live;
not otherwise. (44)
Then, when she had said "So be it," that entire royal retinue, according to their respective orders, became wakeful and alert in every one of their own duties. (45)
Respectively and appropriately, in every action suitable to each [individual]. || 45 ||
Rows of staff-bearers went forth to assemble the citizens and members of the assembly— [the reading "all the members of the assembly" is also found]—
just as the rays of the sun spread across the earth to oversee worldly affairs.
And the servants, acting with great care, swept the grounds of the assembly hall,
just as autumn days cleanse the sky soiled by the rains.
Multitudes of lamps stood in the courtyard, having drunk up the waters of darkness,
like rows of stars arrived as if to behold this wonder.
The rows of bears are the clusters of constellations. || 48 ||
They filled the courtyards with floods of people,
just as in the beginning of creation the oceans— formerly dried up at the time of dissolution— are filled with water.
By "pūraiḥ" (with floods), it is meant with multitudes proceeding like floods; "purāsargaḥ" (the creation of the city) refers to the period prior to the creation of people. || 49 ||
The blameless ministers and vassal lords returned to their respective places,
like the world-protectors returning to their quarters when the three worlds have been restored.
Winds blew, cooled by dense frost infused with camphor,
and made fragrant by the thick scent exhaled by blossoming flowers.

*Avaśyāya* means frost. The phrase *ākīrṇakarpūra-* is used to establish a similarity [between the breath and frost] by virtue of their whiteness and coolness. Those [lotuses] from which a thick (*māsala*) fragrance has arisen due to the nectar (*makaranda*) exuding from the flowers; the suffix *-ita* is applied here according to the rule for the *tārakādi* group. (51)
At the perimeter stood doorkeepers dressed in white garments,
like rows of clouds on mountains distressed by the heat of the sun atop Mount Ṛṣyamūka.

In the remote borderlands and outlying regions; at Ṛṣyamūka, the abode of Sugrīva, where those distressed by the heat [of the sun] gather due to the special presence of the sun there for the sake of favoring Sugrīva; and on the mountains such as Himavat and others.
Masses of flowers, their brilliance surpassing the darkness, fell upon the earth like clusters of stars scattered by a fierce wind. (53)
The fierce wind here is the wind of universal dissolution.
The followers of the king filled the assembly hall,
just as swans fill a lake strewn with blossoming lotuses. (54)
She, Līlā—who was like the very playfulness within the mind of the God of Love—sat down upon a new, golden, and variegated seat situated near the lion-throne. || 55 ||
Līlā is like Rati in the mind of Smara, or like a graceful amorous gesture in a mind transformed by love. || 55 ||
He beheld all those kings, as well as his elders, noble ladies, friends, courtiers, allies, kinsmen, and relatives, exactly as they had been before.
To the noble ones who are worthy of honor. || 56 ||
Indeed, beholding everything exactly as before, she attained supreme joy;
for the king and the people of the kingdom were truly restored to life.
And she shone with a splendor that had arisen [within her], like the moon.
Indeed, life is certain life through that which has arisen from it. || 57 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth canto, titled "The Description of the Kingdom of Sandeha," within the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 17.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kingdom of Doubt," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighteenth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"In this way, I shall sufficiently divert this sorrowful mind."
Having awakened the kings by means of gestures, she then rose from her seat.

Since the creation perceived in meditative absorption and the previous creation are now seen to be equally unreal because they are both objects of perception, the state of pure consciousness alone is declared [to remain].
"Thus, by means of visiting the assembly hall and other such activities,

I shall divert and console [the king]," [she thought]. Then, having entered the inner apartments, she stood near her husband in the pavilion of the harem, observing his gestures— those physical movements that reveal one's inner intentions.
He entered [the house] of Puṣpagupta and reflected in his mind.
"Having sat down by the side of her husband, who was hidden and covered with flowers"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 2 ||
"Aha! How wondrous is this illusion! These people of our city are situated both there and here, as if in a space that possesses both an exterior and an interior. (3)
In that regard, in a place with an interior and open space visible through meditative concentration, and here in our city—(3).
Even these mountains, garlanded with *tālī*, *tamāla*, and *hiṅgula* trees, appear exactly as they did there; alas, this illusion is spread far and wide! (4)
Likewise here too, the phrase "are established" is to be supplied. || 4 ||
Just as a mountain is perceived both inside and outside in a mirror,
so too is creation perceived within and without the mirror of consciousness.
He confirms its very nature as an illusion through an analogy: "In a mirror," etc. (verse 5).
In this regard, I ask the Goddess of Speech, having worshipped her: "Which creation is composed of delusion, and which is ultimate reality? She spoke without any doubt: (6)

In that case, since it is possible that, just like the example, falsity belongs to only one of the two and not to both, he shows this doubt with the word "therein" (*tatra*). Having worshipped the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati), I ask him about the doubt expressed by me before him, so that it may become free from uncertainty. (6)
Having thus resolved, she then worshipped that goddess,
and beheld her arrived before her, assuming the form of a young maiden.
Seated before the Goddess who was upon her auspicious throne,
Līlā, remaining on the ground, questioned that Great Power of the Ultimate Reality.
The grammatical connection is that Līlā, standing on the ground, having come forward and sat down, asked thus. || 8 ||
Līlā said:
O Goddess, even the most exalted beings feel great agitation for one who is worthy of compassion;
indeed, this supreme order was established by you alone at the beginning of creation.
The phrase "in the case of one who is to be pitied" implies "one who is worthy of compassion. "Stability" means the established limit or boundary. || 9 ||
O Supreme Goddess, please tell me that which I ask you with such humility before you; let your grace toward me surely bear fruit. (10)
Therefore, for that reason, I ask this; tell me that. || 10 ||
This mirror named "the world" is even more stainless than the sky;
its minute fraction consists of tens of millions upon tens of millions of yojanas.

By way of an introduction (*upodghāta*) for the purpose of uprooting the seed of doubt, he first restates the nature of the Self experienced through meditative absorption (*samādhi*) with the three verses beginning with "of this" (*asya*). [The word] *manāk* means "slight" or "small. || 11 ||
A mass of light consisting of words free from seams, soft and very cool,
known by the name "the inconceivable consciousness," it stands before [all] as the foundationless.

It is that in which words—meaning those that are free from syntactical connection (*niḥsandhi*), beyond the sphere of relational association (*saṃsarga*), and thus possessing an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*)—are found;
such is the mass of the light of wisdom (*prajñānajyotirghana*). Because it is formless, it is soft and not hard;
because it has extinguished all suffering, it is cool; and it is without walls, without obstruction, or without division.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "shining forth at the forefront in all worldly transactions. || 12 ||
Space, time, the divisions of space, light, necessity, and succession—these, having reached their supreme transformation, are reflected within it. (13)

In that mirror of the Self, space and time exist, as do the mental constructions of all effects; therein occurs their arising, the finding of room for those already arisen within space, and the illumination of those illuminated by light, the eyes, and so forth.
And by this [consciousness], these [objects] have been established in such a way for the sake of purposeful action (arthakriyā) as to be suitable for such worldly transaction;
thus, having reached a supreme transformation—a diversity of modifications—that extends through space and time in a fixed sequence, they flash forth within [consciousness] like reflections. || 13 ||
The splendor of the reflection of the three worlds is situated both outside and within;
therein, what indeed could be artificial, and what could be non-artificial?

He asks about the subject at hand, which was introduced as a preliminary digression: "The three worlds," etc. Therein, between those two, it is artificial—that is, conceptual; in other words, false. || 14 ||
The Goddess said:
"O beautiful one, tell me what the lack of artificiality in creation is like;
and what its artificiality might be—explain this to me exactly as it is. (15)

With the intention that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛśā*), there is no such thing as "uncreated-ness" (*akṛtrimatva*) in the world, the Goddess asks—thereby intending to dispel the seed of doubt—"Uncreated-ness? (verse 15).
Līlā said:
"O Goddess, O Mother, just as I stand here, so do you stand."
O Goddess of gods, I know that this creation is not artificial. || 16 ||

Līlā, perceiving the difference—that the delimitation by space and time which is insufficient for that which is measured by its vastness is pervaded by falsity, as seen in the case of mountain reflections and the like, and that such [delimitation] is seen in Bhartṛprapañca alone and not in this [Lord]—spoke with two verses beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*), saying, "I know; I conceive. (16)
That creation wherein my husband now resides is artificial, for I consider it to be empty, lacking the fulfillment of space, time, and other such factors. (17)

The meaning is that because it is empty and false, it does not fulfill even a small portion of its own persistence— such as the conventional usage of space and time— and is thus seen to be like a reflection, a dream, or a mountain [in a dream]. || 17 ||
The Goddess said:
A created thing can never arise from that which is uncreated;
for an effect that is dissimilar to its cause never arises anywhere.

Is the creation by the Lord (bhartṛsarga) without a cause or with a cause? Not the first, because it would entail the consequence of non-origination. In the second case, is it caused by something artificial (kṛtrima) or by something non-artificial (akṛtrima)? If so, in the first of these two, is it caused by this very creation or by another cause?
Since another [cause] is unestablished, when only the first alternative remains, even for this creation caused by something artificial—
[Otherwise] there would be the consequence of [the world] being artificial, because the relationship of cause and effect is not observed between two things existing at different times.
With the intention that there is thus no dissimilarity between the two creations, the Goddess speaks the reply beginning with "artificial" (kṛtrima). || 18 ||
Līlā said:
O Mother, the effect is seen to be quite distinct from its cause;
clay is unable to hold water, yet the jar born from it is its receptacle.

Suspecting that the previously stated rule might be contradicted by the case of *līlā* (divine play), he says: "It is seen. Clay in its solid form (*piṇḍabhūtā mṛt*) is unable to take up or hold water; however, the jar produced from it is seen to be the receptacle for that water and capable of holding it. Thus, the rule of equal capacity does not hold in this case.
The intention is that even the rule of equal existence is possible. || 19 ||
The Goddess said:
"Indeed, whatever effect is produced by means of auxiliary causes, some diversity in the primary cause is observed therein. (20)

Let there be a difference between a lump of clay and a jar due to a diversity of material causes (*upādāna*) or a diversity of auxiliary instrumental causes (*sahakāri-nimitta*); however, in that which has identical material and instrumental causes—such as one lamp from another lamp—no difference is observed.
With the intention that the same applies to the two creations under discussion, the Goddess replies: "It comes about" (*saṃpadyate*).
The primary [cause] is the uncommon [cause], such as the rod, the wheel, and so forth. || 20 ||
Tell me, O fair-faced one, what is the cause of that husband’s creation within the earth and other elements? From which portion of that terrestrial sphere was his birth produced there? (21)

However, with the intention that there can be no uniqueness in the causal variety of your husband’s creation—since it is no different from yours in being rooted solely in *māyā*, desire, and the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of karma—he says:
"He speaks. Among the earth and other elements contained within this creation, what [is unique] of your husband’s creation?

The cause by which there would be diversity [is as follows]: even among material things, just as the production or birth of beings arises from this earth-sphere, so too it arises from that earth-sphere; thus, there is no inequality—this is the meaning. || 21 ||
If it is argued that it has gone from memory, then from where could it have flown here to this ground? And what would be the auxiliary causes for this cause? (22)
If it is argued that the production of the earth and so forth in that [other] place may simply arise from the earth and so forth located here, he says in response: "It has gone" (gatam).
The meaning is that it is impossible for something that has not gone there to produce an effect in that location. || 22 ||
Even in the absence of [primary] causes, that which arises as a cooperative condition is experienced by everyone as nothing other than a result of those preceding causes. (23)

Therefore, even in the absence of the auxiliary causes pertaining to this [present] state, that cooperation characterized as a causal totality (*sāmagrī*) which arises and is postulated because the effect would otherwise be inexplicable,
is not something other than the causes of the preceding creation— namely, those consisting of desire, action, latent impressions, and ignorance. This is the Vedic [view].
This is impotence; thus, the meaning is that no distinction [between the two cases] is established. || 23 ||
Līlā said:
"O Goddess, that memory of my husband has thus expanded;
I know that memory is its cause, for this is the certainty: 'This is creation.'"

"This is true; let the creation of my husband be like a dream—arising from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of a prior creation, resembling a memory whose objective reality has been lost. In this manner, she raises the objection regarding the difference in nature (*vaidharmya*) as a playful alternative (*līlā*). [The verse begins with: "Memory... (*smṛtiḥ*).
The Goddess said:
"Memory is of the nature of space, and that which is born from it is likewise for you;
O gentle lady, even though the creation of your husband was experienced, it is just like space."
In that case, that creation born from him—which arises from the previous creation seen before by means of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—is like a memory;

it is "of the nature of space" (*ākāśarūpa*), just as a memory is of the nature of space because it is devoid of an object present before one. Likewise, the previous creation, which was the object of the experience that caused the latent impression, is also merely empty space (*vyoma*). For that [previous creation] was also just like that.
The meaning is that it arises from the residual impressions (saṃskāra) of that previous creation. || 25 ||
Līlā said: Just as the creation consisting of the ether of memory was described by my husband, so do I consider this [present] creation; that [previous] creation is the illustration here.
Having reflected upon the matter thus stated, Queen Līlā accepted it and spoke in accordance with the Goddess’s intention:
"Smṛti... (verse 26).
The Goddess said: "It is even so; this creation of my Lord appears radiant through them. In that very way, it appears here; I see this, O daughter. (27)

Approving of these playful words, the Goddess said, "So it is. In every respect, the Self alone—which is free from all association—shines forth for the Lord through those various states of manifestation.
Līlā said: "Tell me how this illusory creation arose from my formless husband, so that the delusion regarding the world may cease. (28)
The Goddess said: Listen as this is told: just as this creation, which consists of nothing but delusion prior to memory, appears as being composed of the error of a dream, so it is described. (29)

In order to establish the point already stated— that this creation, too, is nothing but an illusion produced by the latent impressions (saṃskāra) derived from the objects of previous creations— he announces the commencement of the narrative of the pavilion (maṇḍapopākhyāna) with the words "prāk" (formerly). || 29 ||
Somewhere in the space of consciousness, there exists a pavilion of saṃsāra;
its form is covered by a structure resembling a pane of glass made of ether. (30)
For the sake of its utility, he describes *saṃsāra* as a dilapidated pavilion, beginning with the words "There exists" (*asti*) and so forth.

"In a certain place" refers to a portion covered by ignorance; even there, "in a certain part" refers to a section of the creative internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). This is clear if the reading is "someone" (*kaścit*). That which has the nature of space (*ākāśa*), like a fragment of glass, is blue and situated in its upper parts.
His form was thus concealed by that.
With Mount Meru as its central pillar, the consorts of the World-Lords as its statues, the fourteen worlds as its inner chambers, and the three hells as its pits, the sun serves as its lamp. (31)

In which [palace] there were statues possessing the characteristics of the world-protectors and their consorts; in which there were inner chambers having the form of the fourteen worlds; and in which there were pits representing the intermediate spaces between the three worlds. || 31 ||
Its corners were filled with termite mounds and earth from mountains,
and it was the dwelling place of an aged Brahmin who was the lord of many sons and subjects.
In this [place], there are fragments of mountain clay pervaded by anthills and cities of living ants;
the Lord of Creatures (Prajeśa) is Brahmā, who is himself the Brāhmaṇa.
It is rich with the silkworms that are the multitudes of living beings; it possesses the blackness of the upper surface of the sky;
and it resounds with the humming of the swarms of mosquitoes that are the hosts of Siddhas dwelling in the firmament.
"Cosmakers" refers to a specific kind of insect that produces its own binding cocoon; "ghuṃghuma" is an imitation of a sound. (33)
Its corners were enveloped by a fierce mass of smoke from houses of clouds;
it was a great bamboo pole upon the path of the wind, with celestial chariots clinging to it like insects. || 34 ||
That very flood of the path of the wind is the great bamboo frame; for it is stated in the Madhu-vidyā that the sky itself is the cross-beam. (34)
It was filled with the tumultuous clamor of the playful antics of foolish gods, asuras, and others;
it was overflowing with the houses, villages, vessels, and utensils of other worlds.
The towns and villages within the worlds, beginning with Bhūr, are like the abundance of vessels and utensils contained within a pavilion. || 35 ||
The surface of the earth was sprinkled with water from lakes, streams, oceans, and ponds;
its hollows shone with portions of the netherworld (pātāla), the earth, and heaven.
There, in one particular corner within the hollow of the sky,
upon the surface of a rock or a clod of earth, there was a certain pit belonging to a mountain village.

There, in that pavilion; the plural number used for "corner" (koṇa) and "lump of earth" (loṣṭatala) is not intended to be significant, just as it is not intended in the case of the plural "nooses" (pāśa). A small village is a *grāmaka*, and that very same thing is a *gartaka* (a pit). || 37 ||
In that place, sheltered by rivers, mountains, and forests, he—
possessing his fire, his wife, and his sons, free from disease,
and possessing cows and milk— was released from the fear of the king.
He was a twice-born man devoted to dharma and hospitable to all guests. || 38 ||

Although the state of possessing milk is already implied by the fact of being a cow, the expression "possessing milk" (kṣīravān) is used specifically to indicate that he does not obtain the essence from other animals.
All castes and stages of life are his guests, worthy of worship and to be nourished by him. || 38 ||

Thus ends the eighteenth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Delusion of the World," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* within the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the work of the Sage. 18.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Illusion of the World," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The nineteenth canto.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"By means of wealth, dress, age, actions, learning, power, and behavior..."
He was indeed similar to Vasiṣṭha himself, yet he did not possess the conduct of a descendant of Vasiṣṭha.
The birth of this Padma-sarga is described here by recounting his previous life, arising from his firm resolve to see the King and to desire the kingdom.
Wealth is of two kinds: divine and human.
The activities of Vasiṣṭha—such as his service as priest to the Ikṣvāku dynasty and his instruction of Rāma—are examples of the former; he was devoid of the latter. || 1 ||
He had a wife named Arundhatī, who was as beautiful as the moon; by name she was Vasiṣṭhā, yet she was Arundhatī in both the earth and the sky. || 2 ||
The well-known Arundhatī is in the celestial sky, whereas this one is in the earthly sky; such is the distinction. || 2 ||
She was equal even to Arundhatī in terms of wealth, dress, age, action, learning, power, and conduct, but not in the quality of her inner consciousness.

The meaning is as follows: "conscious" refers to the *jīva* (individual soul) by virtue of its existence—that is, by its abiding in its own nature. This is because Arundhatī and Vasiṣṭha are well-known for their realization of reality and their state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukta*); yet, since they possess knowledge that will arise in a future birth, they are at that time ignorant and thus bound. || 3 ||
She, who possessed the flavor of unfeigned love, whose gait was languid with grace,
and who smiled like a white water-lily, was his entire essence within this worldly existence.
Once, while seated upon the grassy plateau of that mountain covered with *sarala* trees, that brahmin beheld the lord of the earth from below.
On the ridge, that is, on the plateau region; it is one where the *sarala* [grass] is level and the *śādvala*, meaning the grounds are covered with green grass. || 5 ||
He was proceeding with his entire retinue, out of a desire for the hunt,
accompanied by the great roar of the army as if wishing to split Mount Meru.

*Ākheṭaka* means hunting. [The suffix] *san* is applied in the sense of "desire to split," that is, the apprehension of tearing [something apart]; for it is said that *san* is to be used in the sense of apprehension (*āśaṅkā*). || 6 ||
With yak-tail fans that resembled banners of moonlight, it made the grove of creepers appear like a forest;
with its circles of white umbrellas, it made the sky appear like a floor of silver mosaic.
The grove of creepers, with its chowries and banners, made the sky appear as if filled with moonbeams;
likewise, the circle of white umbrellas made the sky appear like a palace of silver—meaning it was similar in both cases.
The sky was covered by a flood of dust rising from the earth, kicked up by the sound of horses' hooves.
It was protected by watchtowers whose battlements were hidden by the wind from the trunks of elephants raised aloft.

The sky was filled with dust raised by the hooves of horses—those iron-shod feet which, because the earth was soft, became favorable to their digging; the present participle *khanantyām* is used here with the sense of agency (*kartṛtva*) because the earth acted in accordance with the action, just as one says "the elephant mounts" (*ārohati hastī*). If that is so, then...
Is the king also covered with dust? No; so he says: "hāstika... etc. A multitude of elephants is *hāstikam*;

[the suffix] *ṭhak* is applied here according to the rule *acittahastidhenoṣṭhak*. By means of such watchtowers (*aṭṭālakaiḥ*) situated upon those [elephants], whose trunks (*karāḥ*)—meaning the rays of the sun and the winds—are raised up and obstructed.
It was concealed and protected by pavilions made of gold, silver, pearls, and jewels. || 8 ||
(176) A circle of the elements of the quarters flowing like a great whirlpool of tumultuous noise;
a circle of shimmering golden necklaces, rubies, strings of pearls, and armlets. 9.
He from whom circles of beings, such as deer and others, flee toward the ten directions like whirlpools due to their confusion of the quarters caused by those clamorous outcries. || 9 ||
Beholding that protector of the earth, he thought this:
"Oh, how delightful is sovereignty, illumined by every form of prosperity! (10)
He reflected; that is, he formed a resolution preceded by reflection. || 10 ||
"When shall I become a lord of the earth, filling the groves of the ten directions with foot-soldiers, chariots, elephants, horses, banners, umbrellas, and yak-tail whisks? (11)
When will the breezes, fragrant with the nectar of kunda flowers, drink the perspiration droplets from the women of my inner apartments caused by the fatigue of love-making? (12)
"When shall I make the faces of noble women as bright as the rising moon with camphor, and the quarters of the sky with my full glory? (13)

When shall I make the faces of the city matrons— and by extension, the very quarters of the sky— bright and radiant through their instruction in the practice of virtuous conduct, as if whitened by the rising of the moon, using sandalwood mixed with camphor and their own fame respectively? (13)
Thus, from that time forward, this brahmin remained resolved,
constantly devoted to his own duty, untiring throughout his entire life.
Having thus described the desire regarding the desired object, he states the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "In this way," etc. (14).
Then, intent on shattering him like a frost-bolt upon a lotus,
old age approached the twice-born man as if she herself were shattered by the water.
The meaning is that the thunderbolt, consisting of ice, is like a lotus in the water of a lake; it is shattered, just as a bridge is weakened. || 15 ||
Then, as death drew near, his wife fell into a state of withering,
like a creeper whose flowering season has ended due to the fear of summer heat.
In the spring season, when the flowers are in bloom. || 16 ||
Having propitiated me just as you have, that woman then chose this boon—immortality so difficult to attain—having realized its rarity. (17)
"O Queen, because the life-breath of my deceased husband did not depart from his own pavilion, that very [pavilion] was accepted by me as hers. (18)

The phrase "outside his own pavilion" is to be understood as the ellipsis. The construction is "she became Māyā herself. Therefore, by virtue of that prayer, the requested object was accepted—that is to say, it was granted. || 18 ||
Then, by the power of time, that brahmin passed away;
yet he remained within that very space of the house in the form of the vital breath (jīvākāśa).
Pañcatva is death. Brahman, delimited by the impressions (vāsanā) of the internal organ, is the space of the individual soul (jīvākāśa); he exists in that state. || 19 ||
By the power of his own numerous past resolves,
this Lord, possessed of supreme power, has himself become one whose very body is space.
The king is "accomplished"—this is the syntactical connection with what follows. He is supremely powerful, distinguished by both divine and human powers. || 20 ||
The king was the conqueror of the three worlds: he had triumphed over the surface of the earth by his splendor, pervaded the heavens by his majesty, and protected the netherworld by his compassion.
These two powers are expressed by the terms *prabhāva* and *pratāpa*. Here, "Viṣṭapa" refers to heaven (*triviṣṭapa*), since earth and the netherworld (*pātāla*) have been mentioned separately. (21)

He was like the fire at the end of an eon to the trees that were his enemies; like the god of love to women; like Mount Meru to the winds of sensual objects; and like the sun to the lotuses that were the virtuous. || 22 ||

Furthermore, while there may still be the possibility of regrowth in a forest fire, there is none in the fire at the end of an aeon (kalpāgni). The sense objects themselves are like winds because they cause instability; [the yogi] is unshakable and a firm support for them, like Mount Meru. || 22 ||
It is a mirror for all scriptures, a wish-fulfilling tree for seekers, a footstool for the foremost of the twice-born, and the moonlight of the nectar of the full-moon dharma. (23)
She is the full-moon night of the moon that possesses the immortal radiance of the true nature of phenomena. || 23 ||

When that twice-born one, whose body was composed of the elemental ether, had become a corpse within the space inside his own house— the space which is the self consisting of the space of consciousness— (24)

When [the body] has become a corpse—that is, when it is dead—within that Self which consists predominantly of the space of Brahman delimited by mental formations (cittasaṃskāra), and which is for that very reason "space-bodied" (ākāśaśarīrin). || 24 ||
His Brahmin wife, utterly emaciated by grief, was split in two at her heart like a parched bean pod. (25)
Having become a corpse along with her husband and casting off her body far away, she approached her husband by means of her subtle, transportive body (ātivāhika-deha). || 26 ||
By means of a mental body capable of traversing to the other world. || 26 ||
Following that husband like a riverbed that has been excavated,
she attained freedom from sorrow, just as a vāsantī flower-cluster reaches its full bloom.
"Nikhāta" means a low-lying place. "Sā" refers to that which is well-known. "Vāsantī" means that which has grown during the spring season. || 27 ||
There, this brahmin possesses houses, lands, immovable property, and other such wealth;
today the eighth day since his death has arrived.
The living soul resides in the caves of the mountain village. || 28 ||
In that village on the mountain, the day was passing—this is the ellipsis. By the word "cavern" (kaṃdara), the house-pavilion is spoken of figuratively. || 28 ||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Death of the Brāhmaṇa," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 19.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Death of the Brahmin," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Twentieth Chapter.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"He who was your husband has now become a twice-born man who has attained the status of a king."
She who was the Brahmin woman named Sāvaruṇḍatī, you are she, O lady. || 1 ||
Even though she had heard of her previous births, Līlā remained hesitant due to a lack of conviction; therefore, here the Goddess instructs her through examples and logical arguments. (1)
That twice-born man, having attained the status of a king today, has become your husband.
May you two, a noble husband and wife, rule this kingdom here like a pair of young cakravāka birds, or like Śiva and Pārvatī born upon this earth.
Śiva and Śivā are the two Śivas.
(177) Thus has been described to you the entire sequence of prior transmigrations;
it is mere delusion, like the sky itself, assuming the form of the individual soul (jīva).
Concluding the narrative told, he states that even the previous creation, like the two preceding ones, was merely an illusion—using the words "This" (eṣa).
In that regard, he says "Through delusion" (bhrānti) to show that the root cause of the Brahma-space’s delusion of being a living soul (jīva) is indeed delusion itself.
From this delusion, this [worldly] delusion is reflected within the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
Or perhaps that which is truly unreal becomes real for you both, bringing about the destruction of worldly existence.
He shows that in a series of successive delusions, each preceding delusion is the cause of each succeeding one—by the words "from delusion" (bhramāt).
From its own perspective, it is indeed unreal; yet from the perspective of the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), it is real. || 4 ||
Therefore, who could consist of delusion, or who could be free from delusion? No creation other than this unfolds, arising from the unobstructed cognition of what is not real.
And thus, because all creations are equal in being false cognitions of non-existent objects, he says: "Therefore... (verse 5).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard this, her eyes blossomed wide with wonder for a long time at its beauty.
Having become so, Līlā spoke words whose syllables were languid with playfulness.
And having remained for a long time with eyes wide open in wonder due to her disbelief, || 6 ||
Līlā said: O Goddess, how has your word become so false?
Where is the life of the brahmin in his own home, and where are we standing here? (7)
The meaning is: "Is your word false or untrue? How has such a contradiction come to pass?"—in this vast region here. || 7 ||
How do such other worlds, that earth, those mountains, and those ten directions shine within my house, where my husband resides? (8)
He says "tādṛk" (such) [in verse 8], meaning that even the creation of a husband seen in meditative concentration is impossible within one's own home.
The intoxicated Airāvata was bound within the hollow of a mustard seed;
a battle was waged by a mosquito against a pride of lions within the hollow of an atom.
To strengthen the lack of conviction regarding the meaning stated by the Goddess, he establishes its inconsistency through three examples beginning with "From me" (mattaḥ). || 9 ||
Mount Meru, established upon a lotus-stalk, was swallowed by the son of Bhṛṅga;
hearing the roar of the dream-ocean, the peacocks dance in wonder. (10)
This is indeed inconsistent, O Sovereign of all sovereigns;
likewise, it is inconsistent that the earth and mountains exist within the house. (11)
O Queen of the Gods, relate this exactly as it is with a pure mind;
for those of great majesty, when favored by your grace, do not tremble.
"Yathāvat" means "in such a way that this is logically established. || 12 ||
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"I do not speak this falsely; listen exactly as it is, O beautiful one.
Indeed, the subversion of the laws of destiny is not performed by those such as us."

Avoiding the charge of falsehood that might arise from the demonstration of inconsistency, the Goddess says "I am not... in two verses. [She refers to] the scriptural injunctions such as "One should not speak untruth under any circumstances. (13)
I alone establish that very boundary which, when being divided by another, is then breached by me; who else will maintain it? (14)
The soul of the twice-born who had been in battle, while in that very same abode of his own,
perceives this Mahārāṣṭra as being in the sky itself, for he is of the nature of space.
It is the very Self, the space of consciousness, conditioned by the latent impressions of royalty. || 15 ||

That former memory has been lost—[the reading "smṛtir naṣṭā" is found instead]—and thus what arose for you two was otherwise; O lady, this is like the memory of waking that occurs in a dream; such is death. (16)
If we two are indeed those very same persons, why do we not recognize one another? Or what is the nature of death? To this, he says:
"The former... (verse 16).

Just as the three worlds appear in a dream, just as the triple universe appears in a mental construction, just as a battle of heroes appears in a story, and just as water appears in a desert land. (17)
This earth, together with its mountains, forests, and cities, stands within that brahmin’s house like a mental construction or a reflection in a mirror.
This dense manifestation indeed appears as if it were real;
therefore, within the hollow of the sheath of the sky of consciousness, there is the appearance of reality.
He states the cause for the appearance of even that which is unreal as if it were real: "Therefore" (tasmāt).
This means: due to the cause of the true, conscious space (satyacidvyoman) contained within the five sheaths (pañcakośa). || 19 ||
That which has arisen from the unreal, such as memory, is itself unreal;
for even a wave does not truly exist in the river of the craving for the dead. (20)
If the previous creation is unreal, what [is the status] of this present creation? To that he says: "From the unreal" (asatyāt) || 20 ||
Know this dwelling of yours to be situated within the space-receptacle of that [Supreme] Abode; know me, you, and everything else to be nothing but that singular sky of consciousness.
Dreams, delusions, mental constructs, and successions of one's own experiences are the primary means of valid cognition here for the sake of awakening, like lamps.

He states the means of valid cognition (anumāna-pramāṇa) by way of examples established through experience, regarding the falsity of all conceptual proliferation (prapañca) and the fact that only pure consciousness (cinmātra) remains, with the words "In a dream... (svapne...). || 22 ||
The soul of the twice-born remained within the house of the brahmin in that sky,
while the earth with its oceans and forests stood like a bee upon a lotus.

By this creation, not only is the space of the house not filled, but even a portion of the space occupied by the living being situated within one part of it [is not filled]. Therefore, he states its falsity with two verses beginning with "sthitaḥ" (situated). || 23 ||
Within some single, delicate corner-cavity of that [space], this city-body and so forth appear like a tuft of hair in the sky. (24)
A *keśoṇḍraka* is the illusion of the form of matted hair in a cloudless sky. || 24 ||
O slender one, that very same abode remains within this city;
therefore, is it not as if a multitude of worlds resides within a single mote of dust? (25)

And thus, because it has taken root within the expansive creation of the Brahmin’s residence—just as a fetus does not cause the destruction of a she-mule’s womb—he says, "In that [residence]... The particle *eva* (only/just) is to be understood as displaced in its order.
The sense is: even though this creation and this city have become established within that residence, that Brahmin’s residence remains just as it was.

The meaning is that it was not rent asunder. And thus, what wonder is there that from that aforementioned abode of Brahmā, the entire multitude of worlds remains even within a single mote of dust? The particle *iva* is intended to indicate that any apparent inconsistency is resolved by [the fact that the world] is illusory (*mithyātvena*). || 25 ||
"O child, within every single atom of the conscious self there exist worlds within worlds; yet, this is merely what is suspected. (26)

He says "in the atom" (paramāṇau) to show that even though such a possibility exists within the conscious Self—which is not limited by the creation of the world beginning with space—the doubt regarding its impossibility is entirely groundless. || 26 ||
Līlā said:
O Supreme Goddess, on the eighth day that Brahmin died.
"O Mother, many years have passed for us; how could this be? (27)

The illustrious Goddess said: "O lady, just as there is no such thing as the length of space, so too there is no such thing as the length of time. Listen as I explain this according to the proper reasoning. (28)
Just as this manifestation of the creation of the world is mere appearance, so too is this manifestation of moments and eons mere appearance. (29)
In a mere moment, the entire world appears as "you" and "I" to those born from the Self;
I shall explain the sequence of this manifestation exactly as it is—listen to it. (30)

To the question "Whence [arises] its status as mere appearance?", he says: "In a moment," etc. The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: because the entire world—from a moment to an eon—is manifested only to those who possess the delusion of the birth of a self, which depends upon the superimposition (adhyāsa) of "thou-ness" and "I-ness.
He promises to describe the sequence of that manifestation with the words: "as it truly is. || 30 ||
O virtuous lady, having experienced for a moment the swoon of a false death, the living soul forgets its former state and perceives another.
By that very act of unfolding, although he is of the nature of space within space itself, he perceives in his mind:
"I am situated here as the object to be supported within this support. (The reading "cetasi" occurs everywhere.)

Like the sky, though devoid of a supporting body and so forth, it perceives—[the reading "cetati" is found everywhere; however, "smarati" (remembers) is intended], meaning that a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) arises. || 32 ||
He perceives this body, beginning with the hands and feet, as "this is my own";
whatever he conceives in his mind, that very thing he perceives as the body.
"I am the son of this father; these years have passed for me.
These are my lovely kinsmen, and this is my delightful abode. (34)
The abode is the house. || 34 ||
"I was born as a child, and I have grown to be such as I am;
all these kinsmen of mine likewise conduct themselves in this same manner. (35)
Because of the oneness of the mind, the sky, and the cloud, those [states] exist both within oneself and in others;
likewise, even when this fragment of saṃsāra arises in his mind, it is so.
Now, one might object: "Since relatives are merely conceptualized as such due to their connection with the body, even if they belong to him [the practitioner], how can they be his own?

To this he says: "By the mind" (*cittena*). Because of the very firm superimposition of identity between the space of the Self (*ātma-ākāśa*) and the mind that has assumed the state of the body, even though they are in reality different, they become his own; this is the meaning. Thus...
This being so, it is merely a name applied to that which has attained the state of a body. || 36 ||
Nothing at all has arisen; it remains as the stainless sky alone.
Just as consciousness exists in the dreamer, so too in the object of perception, that is consciousness itself. 37.
Because that [consciousness], through its all-pervading unity, perceives what was seen in a dream, it arises in the same way through the perception of the next world and so forth. (38)

Since, in a dream, throughout all things, the mind—following upon non-perception amidst the imagined distinctions of the seer and the seen—is observed again as a single unity when both [subject and object] are sublated; therefore, nothing at all has arisen. This is the connection with what precedes. || 38 ||
Just as it arises in the other world, so does it arise here;
therefore, those [distinctions] between the dream-world, the other world, and this world—whether they be non-existent or existent—[are all alike]. 39.
Of things that are non-existent, yet [perceived] as existent through delusion. || 39 ||
There is not even the slightest difference [between them], just as there is none between waves and water.
Therefore, this universe has arisen [from that which is] unborn, and because it is unborn, it is indestructible.

But because it is one's own essential nature, that which appears does not exist at all; it is consciousness itself, just as it is—devoid of any object of thought (cetya) and having the form of the supreme ether. 41.

Because its own self alone is the ultimate reality, it does not exist at all in the form of the world. What then appears through means of valid cognition such as perception? To this he says: "And that which... It is the foundational consciousness (*adhiṣṭhāna-caitanya*) itself that appears through all means of valid cognition; for it alone, by virtue of being unknown and being unsublated, is fit to be the object of valid cognition, and not [the world].

The meaning is that the insentient [object] lacks the function of obscuration there, because of the absence of the fruit of the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (41) Even when accompanied by the object of cognition (*sacetya*), this [consciousness] remains likewise as having the nature of the supreme ether (*paramavyoma*);
therefore, the object of cognition is not other than that, just as a wave is not distinct from the water. (42)
"Because it is with an object" (sacetya) means that the sense is that it is due to being presided over by and corrupted by a superimposed object; therefore, of this consciousness (citi). || 42 ||

The state of being a wave does not exist in the taste, for it is just like the horn of a hare; yet that very [taste], though never falling from its own nature, appears as if it has become the object of cognition. (43)

For the essence of water is indeed the subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*) alone, and it does not possess the nature of a wave therein, because it is not perceived by the sense of taste. As for the perception of it as such by the eye, the point is that this is conditioned by the association with other elements. || 43 ||
Therefore, the visible object does not exist at all; how then could there be the cognition of a seer and a seen?
This occurs for the living being in an instant, immediately following the delusion of death. (44)
The splendor of the creation visible in the three worlds manifests according to its location,
according to its time, according to its commencement, and according to its sequence.

Since latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have specific objects such as particular places and times, the manifestation produced by them is likewise; thus he says: "According to [the father's] origin, according to the mother, according to the father, according to the [child's own] nature, according to age, according to consciousness, according to place, and according to activity. (46)
Like a kinsman, like a servant, and according to its setting and rising here, the one whose body is consciousness perceives in the mind: "I am born," though indeed unborn. (47)
Place, time, action, substance, mind, intellect, the senses, and so forth—
[all these] he perceives in his body as if it were in its youth, even at the very end of life, instantaneously.

The connection with the subsequent [verse] is as follows: although she first attained youth by reaching an age equal to that of her mother due to Śambhu’s boon while in the womb of a Rākṣasa, the sequence consisting of the recollection of [her previous] childhood and so forth arose later.

"This is my mother, this is my father, and I myself was once a child"—whether such a sequence consists of actual experience or is merely composed of memory, it remains a succession of mental impressions. (49)
Afterwards, that [result] arises for him like the emergence of fruit from a flower; it is experienced by him as if an eon had passed in a mere moment. (50)
Thus, for Hariścandra, the night lasted twelve years;
for those separated from their beloveds, even a single day stretches out like a year.
And this is well known in the Mārkaṇḍeya and other Purāṇas, as well as in the world; thus he says: "The night," etc. (51).

Just as in dreams, one thinks, "I am dead," "I am born," or "This is another father of mine"; so too, the notion that an experience has been enjoyed arises even for an enjoyment that has not been experienced. (52)
Even when one has eaten, the perception remains that one has not; thus it is said among those who speak with embellishment:
"The empty becomes crowded, and calamities are equal to festivals."
Even deception and gain occur within the consciousness of intoxication, sleep, and so forth.

Regarding the characteristics of men: they say that which is adorned by means of proofs is "unmarked" (*alakṣita*) among those simple folk who speak of virtues as being "unadorned" (*alaṅkita-vādiṣu*).

Thus, all this previously mentioned has been observed. Not only is there the appearance of the non-existent through ignorance, but the appearance of what is contrary to the real is also well-known; thus he says: "empty" (*śūnyam*). [He describes] its state of being crowded...
The pervasiveness of the assembly of people. || 53 ||
Just as pungency resides within the tiny seed of a pepper, and a network of carved figures exists within a pillar,
so too does this peaceful, non-differentiated world exist within the Unborn.
For one who perceives the bondage and liberation of that [mind], from where could there be any [bondage] and what [liberation] could there be? // 54 //
Just as pungency exists inherently in a grain of the *marica* plant, and a multitude of uncarved statues exists within a block of wood,

so too does this visible world exist non-different from that Unborn (*aja*) by virtue of His very being (*sattā*). Of that Self, who perceives the bondage and liberation of existence— where "exists" (*asti*) is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) functioning like a verbal form— the [bondage and liberation are but appearances].
The meaning is: views regarding the bondage and liberation of truth. From what cause would they arise, and what would their form be?
The meaning is that they are in every way impossible. || 54 ||

Thus ends the twentieth canto, titled "The Description of the Ultimate Reality," in the *Līlopākhyāna* (The Narrative of Līlā) within the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* (Book on Origination) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Rishis.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of Ultimate Reality," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Twenty-first Chapter.
The Illustrious Goddess said: Immediately after the delusion of death, the worlds appear once again.
Just as all forms [become visible] through the opening of the eyes of a living being, so too [is everything revealed]. || 1 ||
The gross is [perceived] through investigation, and the subtle through the investigation of that ignorance;
even that [ignorance] is nothing but pure consciousness—thus is the divine play of the Goddess understood here. (1)
In order to state a specific detail regarding the very meaning already mentioned, [the author] speaks again, elaborating upon it, saying: "They appear" (pratibhānti) || 1 ||
And [these worlds], composed of space, time, ether, dharma, and karma,
manifest infinitely and possess stability until the end of the aeon.
Those consisting of dharma are heaven and so forth; those consisting of karma are houses and so forth; those possessing stability until the end of the kalpa are the earth and so forth. || 2 ||
Even that which was neither experienced nor seen arises at that very moment as a memory, thinking "this was done by me," just like one's own death in a dream.
He states the difference between illusory memory and perception and ordinary memory and perception:
"Thus, this infinite delusion shines within the void of the sky of consciousness;
it is an imaginary city called 'the world,' devoid of walls. (4)
In the sky of consciousness, within the space of illusion. || 4 ||
This world and this creation expand as nothing but memory, whose singular nature consists in the reversal produced by the habitual association of the distant past and the present moment. (5)
Among the sixfold modifications, *sarga* (creation) occurs through the predominance of the first three, while *jagat* (the world) occurs through the predominance of the last three.

"Memory" (*smṛti*) refers to its cause, namely *vāsanā* (latent impression). For that [impression], even when present and immediate, exists as something distant and remote due to the nature of spatial and temporal distance, and thus pertains to that which is eternal and inactive.
And she is of a single nature with that delusion—the error consisting of moments, their repetitions, and the forms of ghaṭikās, muhūrtas, days, fortnights, and so forth. || 5 ||
Thus, cognition is of two forms: that which has experienced [an object] and that which has not;
yet, being devoid of any prior cause, it proceeds as nothing other than the very nature of consciousness.
He concludes what has been said: "Not experienced," etc. (6).

Even in the case of something experienced, no further consciousness of its having been experienced arises; just as in a dream-delusion or the like, there is no memory of a father within that very experience, as there might be for a father [of a son]. (7)
Now, one might ask: "Where has the delusion of having experienced something that was not actually experienced ever been seen? To this, he says: "Not [previously] experienced," etc. (Verse 7).
At times, having abandoned the state of being a memory, it appears as mere intuition alone;
through that sequence, it shines forth in its form during the first creations.

[Objection: "But surely, since everything has been experienced in beginningless *saṃsāra*, memory [of it] would establish identity; however, that memory is one whose true nature is obscured, so it is not an error. To this he says: "Sometimes" (*kadācit*). "Appearance" (*pratibhā*) means experience. "Of Prajāpati" means in the first creations. "By form" means by way of the form of memory. (8)
O slender one, this visible world, beginning with the three worlds, which has been experienced, remains in the memory of some; for others, that which was never experienced remains in their memory.
And thus, he states that there is no rule that only what has been previously experienced appears [in cognition], by saying: "the visible" (dṛśyam) || 9 ||
This lordship over the subjects appears to some atoms of consciousness even without prior recollection, occurring by mere chance, like the "crow and the palm fruit" coincidence. (10)

The status of being a lord of subjects was certainly not experienced before. The point is that since the four [perfections] are attained simultaneously, according to the traditional teaching (smṛti), knowledge necessarily arises therein; therefore, a rebirth is impossible. || 10 ||
The total forgetting of the universe is designated as liberation;
therein, neither the desired nor the undesired exists for anyone whatsoever.

Since saṃsāra consists of the mind whose nature is a mass of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), therefore, through its eradication, liberation (*mokṣa*) results as precisely that forgetfulness which is by nature entirely devoid of impressions;
thus he says: "absolute," etc. "Desirable and undesirable" means pleasant and unpleasant. "Verily, for one who is bodiless, there is neither pleasant nor unpleasant."

This is because of the scriptural text: "They touch [one another]. To the question "Why do they not exist there?", he says: "kācana" (any whatsoever). The meaning is: whatever consciousness remains in liberation, for what object or what enjoyer could there be that pleasure and pain would be caused by?
Thus says the scripture: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see? and so forth.
But if the reading is "kecana," it is clear. || 11 ||
Without the attainment of absolute non-existence of the persistence of "I" and the world, this liberation consisting of non-arising certainly does not arise. (12)
The persistence and foundation of the world and the sense of "I" is ignorance; its sublation is the attainment of the absolute non-existence of that [ignorance]. || 12 ||
The delusion of a snake in a rope persists because the referent of the word "snake" is impossible;
for even though it is composed of non-arising and is quiescent, it does not truly subside. (13)
Having abandoned—that is, having disregarded—the impossibility and non-existence of the snake and its object, which exists in the form of the rope;
that is to say, not perceiving them [as real]. || 13 ||
(180) This is not "half-quiescent," for it is quiescent again by virtue of being a composite entity;
indeed, upon the cessation of one demon, another arises for the one lacking wisdom. (14)

[Objection: Surely that [mind] may be stilled simply through yoga by the cessation of mental fluctuations; what is the use of knowledge? To this he replies with the word "ardha" (half). By that [yoga], through the cessation of the portion consisting of distraction, it is only half-stilled and not fully stilled, because upon emerging from meditation it arises again for the sake of distraction. [Furthermore,] there is dejection and delusion for one who possesses that [state]. || 14 ||
And this expansive cycle of existence is indeed supreme; such is the certainty.
Due to the absence of a cause, that which appears here is nothing but what has already appeared.

And thus, he says "saṃsāre" (in saṃsāra) to show that liberation occurs through knowledge alone: because of the absence of its cause, whatever appears once ignorance has been sublated, that indeed remains as a mere appearance; the meaning is that there is no longer any suspicion of obscuration or the like. || 15 ||
Līlā said:
How did the recollection of the cause arise within this creation regarding the forms of the Brahmin and the Brahmin woman, since there was nothing here to be remembered? (16)

Regarding what was previously stated—that this creation is the effect of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) derived from the previous creation of Brahmins and Brāhmaṇīs—the author raises the objection that this is untenable, stating "brāhmaṇa... and so forth. In this context, the "recollection" (*saṃsmṛti*) which serves as the cause for this creation refers everywhere to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*). That which is to be remembered is "the object fit for recollection."

The meaning is as follows: "previously experienced" refers to that which was perceived at an earlier time. Without this [present object] being visible at that time, since the present object did not exist previously, there could have been no experience of it; therefore, the latent impression (vāsanā) characterized by a mental trace (saṃskāra) cannot possibly exist at that time. || 16 ||
The Goddess said:
"O Grandfather, the cause of that is memory; it is not memory itself.
It is simply not possible for him to have a prior [existence], because he is liberated from a previous birth. (referring to the Lotus-born One)
[The reading: || 17 ||

Latent impression (*vāsanā*) is not merely a mental formation (*saṃskāra*), because a second [type] will also be mentioned later. However, if you consider that even a mental formation is necessarily required there, then since the Grandfather (Brahmā) is omniscient and thus possesses experience even regarding future objects, his own mental formation alone would be the cause for that [creation]. Regarding the production of that body and so forth—

But even for him, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is not the cause; nor is the latent impression of his grandfather the cause, because he was liberated at the end of the previous aeon (*kalpa*). This is the meaning. || 17 ||
Since it was previously impossible for anything to be remembered,
consciousness itself comes to possess the state of being born from a lotus and so forth, because it exists in such a manner.
He states that even the impossibility of memory there is caused by the absence of something to be remembered—namely, "previously.

Therefore, because the consciousness conditioned by Māyā remains in such a state due to the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the previous body of Brahmā and so forth, that very [consciousness] manifests as "this" in the form of the unprecedented Brahmā; this is the meaning of its transformation (vivarta). || 18 ||
Another knower of creatures, distinct from Prajāpati, thinks "I existed"; such a one arises by chance, consisting of mere mental representation. (19)

Regarding the observation that ignorance, which is augmented by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the previously arisen lotus, is sublated by the knowledge of its true nature (*tattvajñāna*), he says:
"I existed" (verse 19).
Thus, when the world has risen, there is nothing whatsoever that has ever arisen anywhere;
what is called "arisen" is merely the established sky of consciousness.
With the intention that sublation is indeed possible for both that [dream] and its creation precisely because they consist of creative intuition (*pratibhā*), he says:
"In this way" (verse 20).
The supreme state is the cause of this twofold mindfulness;
this relationship of cause and effect exists as one alone within the sky of consciousness.

The two types [of knowledge] are: that which arises from impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by previous experience, and that which arises from other latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) in the form of the power of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), whether belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha or to someone else.
Here, the "supreme state" (*paramaṃ padam*) is Brahman variegated by *māyā*; however, it is not so in the case of the pure [Brahman].
He states that there is not even a scent of any distinction such as the relation of cause and effect, etc., in the words: "kārya... (verse 21).
The effect and the cause, together with the auxiliary causes—because of the identity of cause and effect, it does not cease upon their absence. (22)

To demonstrate that the conceptualization of cause and effect, produced by Māyā whose nature is non-reflection (*avimarśa*), is sublated within reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), he reflects: "The effect... [and so on]. [He asks: "How could it be that the cloth is the effect and the threads are the cause, through causes such as the shuttle, loom, and other auxiliaries, when [those auxiliaries] do not provide any assistance therein?"

The meaning is as follows: because cooperation is impossible, even an effect in the form of an auxiliary benefit must be described by those very same [factors] as being of that same nature; thus, there results an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Since that auxiliary benefit does not exist, the causal relationship is subverted, and consequently, the unity of the threads and so forth—which serve as the substratum for that conceptualization—does not cease, because there is no cause for their distinction. || 22 ||
Know that you are indeed the very form of the Great Consciousness; [know] recollection as perception.
Therefore, the relation of cause and effect exists, yet that terminology is not ultimately real.

Granted that this may be so through reasoning, how can it be established as being rooted in direct experience? To address this, he explains the vision of the inner self (pratyagdṛṣṭi) with the words "the great form of consciousness" (mahācidrūpa). That by which something is remembered is the memory;
it is the individual and collective internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) permeated by consciousness, and that alone is the act of knowing. For...

The effect belongs to the Lord who is variegated by *māyā*. In that regard, when the distinction between the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *māyā* and the limiting adjunct in the form of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is perceived, a conceptualization of difference arises even with respect to the pure Being (*sanmātra*) which is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) conditioned by those two. Thus, through delusion, one conceives that the existence of the effect has its birth dependent upon the existence of the cause, [regarding it] as being in a prior state.
If you think that the cause exists as the prior state and the effect exists as the subsequent state, know that it is not so;

rather, setting aside the forms of *māyā* and its effects, recognize remembrance (*smaraṇa*) as being essentially the Great Consciousness (*mahācit*), which consists of pure Being (*sanmātra*) pervading both. By that aforementioned realization of the inner self (*pratyagdarśana*), [the world] is sublated.

That very relationship of cause and effect will be examined through the words "cause" and "effect" themselves; even that, when viewed from this perspective, is seen not to be real. This inward vision has been most clearly established by us in the *Svārājyasiddhi*: "When one perceives in the mind the state of a lump of clay as being a jar, there arises the notion of cause and effect."
"Just as for one who clearly perceives that which is merely clay, there is neither cause nor effect;

likewise, for one who suddenly realizes that Brahman alone is the cause of the universe and is of the nature of pure Being (*sanmātra*), being single in form, there is neither the illusory power (*māyā*) nor the universe. Thus it is stated in the *Vārttika*.

Therefore, transmigratory existence is merely a mental construct within the inner self. If there should be doubt regarding the matter thus stated, let it be examined through the vision of the inner self. Thus [ends verse 23].
