Thus, nothing whatsoever has arisen, not even the visible world or the universe of consciousness;
in the space of consciousness, only the space of consciousness itself abides within its own self.

And thus, he concludes that the state of being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcatva*) is firmly established, saying "evam" (thus). Regarding the phrase "the space of consciousness" (*cidākāśa*), the intended meaning is based on the Vedic scripture: "He is established in his own glory" (*sve mahimni pratiṣṭhitaḥ*). || 24 ||
Līlā said:
"Aha! O Goddess, a supreme vision has indeed been shown to me by you;
the beauty of form in the world is like the radiance of the sun at dawn. (25)
Awakened by that vision, Līlā said, "Aho! [The term] *īkṣaṇadyutiḥ* means that which is illuminated or made manifest by the gaze; that is to say, it is clearly revealed. || 25 ||
"Now that I have reached such a state of perfection in this vision, O Goddess, pierce through this wonder without further practice. (26)
Maturity is the firmness of understanding. Break, that is, destroy, this curiosity and longing which is about to be described. 26.
"Lead me to that mountain village, that very creation, where that Brāhmaṇa dwelt in his home together with his Brāhmaṇī; I wish to behold it. (27)
The Goddess said: "O stainless one, having taken recourse to that supreme, purifying vision which consists of the nature of consciousness beyond the object of thought, abandon this form."
He states that, upon beholding That, it is necessary—as before—to forget this body by means of samādhi, saying "acetya":

[one should forget] that which consists of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa-mayīm*). The suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in the sense of abundance; that is to say, the state of being the causal Brahman (*kāraṇa-brahma-rūpatām*). || 28 ||
Then, you will undoubtedly attain the one whose self is space, abiding in the sky—
just as the mental conception of a man standing on the ground [perceives] a city within the expanse of the heavens.
That creation, whose nature is the illusory void, remained situated within the heart of consciousness.
This being the case, let us behold that [Self] along with its creation without obstruction;
for this body is indeed the supreme bolt upon the door to seeing it.
"Let us see together" means we shall see. "Argala" means a bolt; that is to say, an obstacle. || 30 ||
Līlā said:
"O Goddess, by means of this body another world is attained; why is it not so here? Out of your gracious favor, please tell me the reasoning for this. (31)
From attachment, which is characterized by a persistent clinging resulting from the application of favor, [arises] dogmatic adherence. || 31 ||
The Goddess said: "These worlds, which are formless, have been perceived by you as having form through a vain obsession, just as one might perceive gold as being a ring."
Because they are mere illusions, they are formless; [they appear so] due to false knowledge arising from vain grasping. "Ūrmikā" refers to a ring for the finger.
Just as the nature of a ring does not exist even in that which assumes the form of a golden ring,
so too the world does not exist within Brahman, even though it appears in the form of the world.
The meaning is that the state of being a ring is the very form of gold. || 33 ||
This world is indeed the sky of consciousness; here, it is Brahman alone that is perceived.
Yet, something resembling a visible object is seen here, like a speck of dust in the ocean.
It is a certain illusion, like dust reflected in the ocean that contradicts the presence of actual dust.
This phenomenal world is indeed false; I am the non-dual Brahman, which is Truth.
Regarding this, the Vedāntas, the teachers, and personal experience are the authorities. (35)

To eliminate the very root of the doubt regarding the impossibility of proof for the stated subject matter, he shows more firm proofs with the words "This [is... etc. The primary proof is the Vedāntas;
the teachers are for the purpose of instilling the experience of their respective intended meanings; and one's own experience is the resulting fruit.
The meaning is "a means of valid cognition. || 35 ||
Brahman alone perceives Brahman; that which is not Brahman does not perceive Brahman.
Such is the very nature of this [Reality], which is celebrated by names such as "creation" and so forth. (36)
The intrinsic nature is an existence that is obscured. || 36 ||
There is no arising of the relationship between cause and effect for Brahman and the worlds,
because of the absence of all auxiliary causes.
As long as your cognition of duality has not been stilled through the practice of yoga, you certainly do not perceive Brahman, which is of a nature other than that [duality]. 38.

Because it is a cognition of a self consisting of a non-Brahma-body and so forth, which are not of that [true] nature, it is "of that nature" [in appearance]. The word "nūnam" (surely) is used in the sense of conjecture. || 38 ||
In this regard, those such as ourselves who have attained proficiency through the practice of the realization of Brahman indeed perceive that supreme reality. (39)
Those who [possess] conventional usage and firm proficiency—these very ones we observe. (39)
The body of this city of my own conceptualization is composed of space;
within it, I perceive Brahman alone—that supreme state—by means of this very body.
Consisting of space, it consists of the space of the pure mind. || 40 ||
Likewise, these [deities] such as Padmajā and others are worthy of the body of pure gnosis;
O Aṅganā, they are established as portions of Brahmā, Ātman, Jagat, and so forth. (41)

"Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is that by which something is known; it is the mind (*citta*). By means of that purified [mind], they are "worthy" (*arhāḥ*), always fit for the vision of Brahman. In reality, having transformed the sense [of the verb], it is connected as follows: they see the "abiding" (*saṃsthānam*), the persistence, of the world and its conventional activities within a "fraction" (*aṃśe*), a mere trace, of those whose nature is Brahman. "A foot of this is all... (*pādo'sya viśvā*...).
The meaning is that this is according to such scriptural passages as, "The beings are one-third of Him; His immortal part is in heaven. || 41 ||
O child, without practice, your form has not attained the state of Brahman; it remains as the nature of conceptualization, and for that reason you do not perceive it.
The reflection of consciousness within the internal organ (antakaraṇa) is of that nature; that is Brahman, which was previously mentioned as Girigrāmaka. || 42 ||
Where one's own city of volition cannot be attained even by one's own body, how could another's city of volition be attained by another body there? (43)

He confirms, by means of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic, that the very fact of being produced by mere volition (*sāṃkalpikatva*) is the reason for the non-perception [of the body] with this [present] body, in the verse beginning with "where" (*yatra*). || 43 ||
Therefore, having abandoned this body, you who are of the nature of the space of consciousness—
O best among those who know what must be done, perform immediately whatever it is that you perceive (or, according to another reading, whatever penance you practice).
"You see" means "you will see"; this is an expression in the present tense used because of its proximity to the present. || 44 ||
A city of one’s imagination is real with respect to that which was imagined;
it is neither a doubt nor a disembodied state, nor anything else whatsoever.

Whether with a body—that which is accomplished by a body—or without a body, that imagined experience of the city's activities and enjoyments is real insofar as it is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). As for other worldly transactions, however, it is nothing at all; it is, in short, insubstantial.
Just as this delusion of the world came to exist at the beginning of creation, so it remains.
Thus, from that time onwards, destiny has attained such maturity.

If it is asked, "Since there is no difference in the fact that both this world of Dhātṛ-sāṃkalpika and our own world of asmad-sāṃkalpika are products of volition (saṃkalpa), from where does their internal distinction arise?", he replies: "It is solely due to the power of Māyā, characterized by the will of the Lord in the form of beginningless necessity," as stated in the verse beginning with *ādisarge*.
Līlā said:
"O Goddess, you have said, 'Let us go to the world of the Brahmin and his wife'; I am able to do this, but tell me, O Mother, how we are to go? (47)
"Having left this body here, with a mind following pure beings, I am going to that supreme world; how will you go there? (48)
"How do you go with your own body? is the implied question. || 48 ||
The Goddess said:
Just as that tree of the sky of volition, though existing, is of the nature of its own self, it is not of the nature of a wall, nor is it obstructed by a wall, nor does it destroy a wall. (49)
Though existing by way of conceptual existence, it is of the nature of space by way of real existence; it is not material like a wall, yet it destroys the wall, being the breaker of the wall. (49)
The manifestation as a single pure being is indeed [the manifestation] of that which has consciousness as its very form; therefore, it differs only slightly from that supreme [consciousness]. (50)

That which is the manifestation—the effect—of the pure quality of *sattva*, such as our own bodies and so forth, is indeed said to be the appearance of that very same form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*); for this reason, it differs only slightly from the supreme Brahman.
The sense is that just as the form of a cloth in a burnt cloth is in reality nothing but its ashes, so it is here. || 50 ||
Such as this body is, I shall not depart leaving it behind;
by means of this very body, I shall reach that region, just as the wind reaches its fragrance.
Just as water mingles with water, fire with fire, and wind with wind,
so too does this body merge with other bodies composed of mind.
To the question, "How then can there be a union with this [world] created by the volitional power (*saṃkalpa*) of our Lord? he replies with the word "yathā" (just as).
The meaning is: "by means of other bodies consisting of mind (*manomaya*) and other objects. || 52 ||
For the cognition of "earthen-ness" does not attain identity with the cognition of "an earthen object";
where, then, could there be a mutual impact between a mountain of conceptual construction and a [real] mountain? (53)

In that case, since my body also is in reality nothing but mind, it shares the same nature as your body; therefore, having merged with your body through either identity or conjunction, let it go there. To this, he replies: "No," because it is perceived as being of the nature of earth, a modification (*vikāra*) of the earth element.

Because your body possesses the consciousness of being composed of earth, it does not attain oneness with, nor union with, my body which is the consciousness of pure spirit—the opposite of that [earthly nature]. *Āhati* means impact or striking. 53.
This mental body of yours and those like you is indeed purely *ātivāhika*;
it has been grasped as a material (*ādhibhautika*) entity due to long-standing habitual conditioning.
Now, one might ask: "If this [body] is also mental, how can it be composed of earth? To this he says: "It is *ātivāhika* (subtle/transcendental). || 54 ||
Just as in a dream, just as in long-term meditation, just as in a delusion,
just as when a mental resolve has arisen, and just as in a city of the Gandharvas.
When the attenuation of your latent impressions (vāsanā) has indeed reached stability,
then the subtle body (ativāhika-bhāva) will once again enter this physical frame.
When, then, does the cessation of this state of being earthly occur? To that he says: "Vāsanā...
The state of the body (*tanu*) is its becoming thin, which is to say, its diminution; this will come about through the practice of *samādhi*. This is the sense. || 56 ||
Līlā said: When the conviction that this is a subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) becomes solidified, does this [gross] body attain that same state, or rather, does it perish? (57)

Līlā, suspecting that because the destruction of the gross body is observed in others, the destruction of the body of a yogi who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) must likewise occur and that it cannot possess a subtle (ātivāhika) nature, asks: "Is it subtle?
[The answer is: "It has attained density," meaning solidity; the phrase "by the practice of samādhi" is to be supplied. || 57 ||

The Goddess said: "If that which exists were indeed subject to the process of destruction and non-destruction, then what kind of destruction could there be for that which, in reality, does not exist at all? (58)

The body of one who knows reality does not exist at all, because it has been sublated by knowledge, like a burnt cloth; yet, due to residual impressions (*vāsanā*) from the past, it continues to appear like the reflection of a cloth. However, as those impressions diminish and become increasingly subtle, it attains the state of the *ātivāhika* (subtle) body rather than undergoing total destruction. With this intention, the Goddess gives the following reply.
—By the words beginning with "yad," etc. || 58 ||
When the delusion of a snake in a rope has vanished through the power of realizing the truth, O son (this is an address to Līlā),
what talk can there be of whether the snake was destroyed or not destroyed? 59.
Or even so. || 59 ||
Just as a snake is no longer seen in a rope through the full comprehension of the truth, so too the material body is no longer seen through the knowledge of the subtle body. 60.
Knowledge of Brahman, which has as its cause the state of being *ātivāhika*, is *ātivāhika-jñāna*. || 60 ||
Even conceptual construction would cease if it were imagined by someone; for that which never exists here [in reality] has already been cast aside like a stone. (51)

The conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) existed previously as something imagined, but it has been eradicated along with its root by knowledge; thus, even the conceptualization of such conventional usage exists only from the perspective of superficial vision. From the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*), however, there is not even the possibility of that [conventional usage], as he says: "conceptualization" (*kalpanā*). It is "imagined," meaning established. Thus it was said by Gauḍapāda:
"Conceptual proliferation would cease if it were imagined by someone; this discourse exists for the sake of instruction, but once [reality] is known, duality does not exist. (61)
"O blessed lady, we perceive this truth—that this body and so forth exist as the supreme within the supreme, filled with the beyond—but you do not perceive it. (62)

How then do you perceive your own body and so forth? To that he says: "By the Supreme. This pentad of sheaths, beginning with the body, is filled by the Supreme Brahman; since it exists through the entry of each [sheath] into the interior of the next, we perceive—truly and without contradiction—that it is indeed the Supreme Brahman itself, abiding in its own supreme glory. You...
Because your awakening has not yet fully blossomed, you do not perceive it.
When, at the beginning of creation, the state of being a mind arises as something fashioned by conceptualization,
from that time onward, it perceives the visible world as a single sentient being.
Indeed, how can consciousness (*cit*), which is invisible, attain the nature of the visible? To this, he says: "From the beginning" (*ādau*).

At the creation of the subtle body (*liṅga-ātman*) from the beginning, there arises a property of consciousness called "cittva" (the state of being the mind), which takes that [subtle body] as its object.
But when, through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), a gross form is imagined by conceptualization, then—

From that time forward, due to the influence of the perceivable, one perceives even oneself as having become an object of perception—a single, underlying reality—through delusion; this is the meaning. || 63 ||
Līlā said: When the supreme reality alone exists— tranquil, devoid of distinctions such as direction and time— whence can there be an occasion for conceptualization?

Regarding what was stated previously—that all conceptualization is dependent upon mental construction—an objection is raised concerning the impossibility of divine play (*līlā*) in the verse beginning with "In one" (*ekasmin*). Milk, which exists at an earlier time, undergoes transformation into the form of curds and so forth at a later time; and in the state of being curds, the milk ceases to exist. [This objection applies] to that which is eternal and devoid of connection with time.
The meaning is that while Brahman exists, there is no occasion for even the first modification, known as conceptualization (kalanā). || 64 ||

The Goddess said: Just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, just as the state of being a wave exists in water, and just as reality exists in dreams, mental constructs, cities [of the mind], and the like; || 65 ||

The Goddess refutes [the objection] by stating that the fault mentioned by you would apply only if a real modification were admitted, but not if it is illusory: "In the case of a real experience, such [a fault] indeed exists; but in Brahman, it does not exist at all, because its true nature is free from affliction and distinct from conceptual construction. (66)
Just as there is no dust in the sky, so there is no part in the Supreme;
this one, unborn, and pervasive reality is tranquil, being the perception of that which has no parts.
The apprehension of parts is the object. || 67 ||
Whatever appears here is, in its very essence, free from all affliction—
like the luminosity of a flawless crystal or a radiant, supreme gem. (68)
Gold is the appearance at first sight; an *atimaṇi* is a jewel that excels [others], like that very [gold]. 68.
Līlā said:
O Goddess, tell us, by whom have we been thus deluded for so long a time with the conceptual constructions of duality and non-duality? (69)
Līlā asks for the cause of the aforementioned delusion: "For so long... (verse 69).
The Goddess said:
O fickle one, you have long been deluded and distressed by lack of inquiry.
This lack of inquiry arises from one's own nature; it perishes through inquiry. 70.

The Goddess stated that "by non-investigation" (avicāreṇa) means that delusion (*moha*) itself—designated as "non-investigation"—is the cause of that [bondage], because it is sublated by investigation (*vicāra*).
Non-investigation perishes through investigation in the mere twinkling of an eye; therefore, this very existence is internal ignorance, and it does not truly exist.
This ignorance, characterized by a lack of inquiry, when sublated by inquiry, becomes the very existence of Brahman; this is the implied meaning.
Therefore, there is no lack of inquiry, no ignorance, and no bondage;
there is no liberation either—this world is unimpeded, pure consciousness. (72)

He states that the sublation of that [bondage] occurs throughout the three periods of time: "Therefore," etc. Since there is no bondage, there is also no liberation. 72. For as long as this was not investigated by you, during that time you were not fully awakened; you remained merely deluded, like one tossed about in a turbulent ocean.
[The reading is: "confused. || 73 ||
From this day forward, you are awakened; you are liberated and discerning.
The seed of latent impressions has fallen away from your mind.
When the latent impression of duality is sublated by knowledge, the residual impression of reality is the very attenuation of impressions; that alone is the seed of liberation.
For if the visible world called "saṃsāra" has never arisen from the very beginning, then how could it be perfumed by it, and what impression could there even be? (75)
Anticipating the possibility that the sprout of dualistic tendencies might arise once again, he says, beginning with "In the beginning," etc. (verse 75).

When the absolute non-existence [of all things] has been attained, and when the mind is firmly established in supreme one-pointed meditation within the non-conceptual samādhi, [the state of the seer, the seen, and the seeing is realized]. (76)
When it has taken root and ascended in the mind. || 76 ||
When this seed for the destruction of latent impressions has sprouted even slightly within the heart,
the perceptions of attachment, aversion, and the like will gradually cease to arise.
This arising of saṃsāra will reach a state of rootlessness;
it will attain a firm foundation in non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi). || 78 ||
Free from the stain of temporal impurity,
by means of the stainless support of the intermediate space of the sky,
[he dwells] within the entirety of the causal and effected processes of manifestation.
"In the course of some time, you shall become [so]. || 79 ||

Thus, by means of such establishment in non-conceptual samādhi, through the support (*ālambana*) of the stainless Self— which is the inner substratum of the sky, the illusory space (*māyākāśa*), its constituent parts, and their effects— the darkness characterized by the movement of delusion (*bhrānti-kalana*) is dispelled after some time.

Because of this very reason, she is stainless— being free from the stain of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) [of duality]— and you alone are that supreme goal of human life called liberation (*mokṣa*), which is the ultimate limit of the sublation of all the conceptualizations (*kalanā*) of living beings, their resulting latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), and their cause, ignorance (*avidyā*).
The meaning is "you shall become. || 79 ||

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "Instruction on Rest," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (sage-authored) tradition. || 21 ||

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "Instruction on Rest," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* (Section on Origination) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the *Tātparya-prakāśa* (The Illumination of the Essential Meaning).
The Twenty-second Chapter.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
Just as the dream-body is not real due to the full comprehension of the dream, [so too is this world].
Even though this has been experienced, it is likewise devoid of existence due to the attenuation of latent impressions (vāsanā).

The characteristics of the fourth state (turiya) are described here, as well as the condition of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), the means for the attenuation of latent impressions (vāsanā), and the practice thereof. || 1 ||

The Goddess begins with the words "Just as" (*yathā*) in order to illustrate, through examples, the cessation of the perception of the gross body and the attainment of the subtle body (*ātivāhika-bhāva*), which were previously mentioned as resulting from the firmness of knowledge. This refers to the gross body. || 1 ||
Just as the dream-body subsides through the thorough understanding of the dream,
so too the waking body subsides through the attenuation of latent impressions (vāsanā).
Just as this body is perceived at the end of a dream or a mental construction,
so too does the subtle body (ativāhika) arise at the end of the waking state's mental projection.
The "waking-state ideation" is the sense of "I-ness" regarding the gross body; "at its end" means when it has been destroyed by cutting off its root. || 3 ||
Just as the state of deep sleep arises in a dream when the seed of latent impressions has ceased, so too does liberation arise in the waking state when the seed of latent impressions has ceased. (4)

The meaning is: "in the seed of latent impressions that have ceased" (*nirvāsanābīje*) means in the seed of latent impressions that has not arisen (*anudbhūtavāsanābīje*), or in the seed of latent impressions that is not interrupted (*anucchinnavāsanābīje*); for otherwise, dreams would recur. "In the seed of latent impressions that has vanished" (*avāsanābīje*) means in the seed of all latent impressions that has been sublated (*bādhitasarvavāsanābīje*). "Liberation" (*vimuktatā*) refers to liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). || 4 ||
However, that which is the latent impression (vāsanā) of those liberated while living is not truly a latent impression;
it is called "pure being" (śuddhasattva), and is said to be the universal essence of existence (sattāsāmānya). || 5 ||
[Objection: But surely even for those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), there is indeed residual impression (vāsanā), since otherwise worldly activity would be impossible; to this he says:

"This which... It is not a [true] residual impression, but rather the designation "pure residual impression" refers to the very existence of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) which serves as the limit for the sublation of all residual impressions—just as the term "burnt cloth" is a designation for the ashes alone.
The meaning is that what was previously described as the universal existence (sattāsāmānya) accompanied by all latent impressions (vāsanā) is what is referred to in that manner. || 5 ||
That sleep in which latent impressions remain is known as *suṣupti* (deep sleep);
that waking state in which latent impressions remain is called delusion (*moha*). (6)

He shows the internal distinction between fainting (*mūrchā*) and deep sleep (*suṣupti*) with the word "yet" (*yā*). The deep sleep of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is their non-manifestation and suppression. Thus, the meaning is: deep sleep is the sleep-state of those impressions that have not yet arisen; while fainting is the delusion of the waking state in which the impressions are suppressed.

For those whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have become extremely dense, there occurs at that time a transformation into the state of delusion (*moha*) without abandoning their density, due to being forcibly overwhelmed by an intense suffering suddenly arisen while they are awake; it is to indicate this that "dense" (*ghana*) is used as an epithet for delusion. || 6 ||
Sleep in which all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been destroyed is designated by the term "the Fourth" (*turya*).
This indeed occurs even while awake, when the supreme state has been realized.
Since the word "sleep" is not intended here in its literal sense, the Fourth state arises through knowledge even during waking, once the latent impressions have been destroyed along with their roots.
The meaning is that it indeed exists. || 7 ||
The state of existence of those living here whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been exhausted,
yet which remains unrecognized by those who are not liberated, is called "liberation while living" (*jīvanmukti*).
He states that this very state for one who is living is liberation while living (jīvanmukti) in the verse beginning with "prakṣīṇa" (verse 8).
The mind, fallen into pure being and possessing attenuated latent impressions,
attains the state of a subtle body, just as snow becomes water through heat.
It has fallen into the pure *sattva* previously explained, and through the proficiency of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it remains firmly established for a long time. || 9 ||
The mind, having attained the state of a subtle, transportive body (ātivāhika), meets with other minds—
those of perfected beings (siddhas) who have entered into other creations and births— but not with anything else.

Even at the time of the conventional activity of arising, the mind of the Buddha— possessing self-awareness— merges into a state of oneness with other minds belonging to different creations and different births, as well as with perfected beings (siddhas) and those possessing bodies such as the *devayogya*. || 10 ||
When this sense of "I" comes to rest through your own practice,
then the expansive awareness of the end of the visible world will arise for you.
Awakening by itself. || 11 ||
The limit of the phenomenal world of the visible is awareness itself, which is the ultimate boundary and the innate nature of consciousness. || 11 ||
When the knowledge of the subtle body (ātivāhikatā) attains a permanent state,
then indeed you shall behold the purifying worlds through the absence of volitional thought.
Those which are free from volitional construction (asaṃkalpa), yet purified precisely because they have been defiled by such construction.
Therefore, O blameless one, exert yourself toward the attenuation of latent impressions;
when that [attenuation] reaches full maturity, you will become liberated while living.
"As long as this cool moon of enlightenment has not been fulfilled, let the body be maintained and the other world be observed. (14)

With the intention that neither the fulfillment of awakening nor the practice of attenuating latent impressions (vāsanā) is possible for one whose mind is obstructed by the desire to see Girigrāmaka, he says: "As long as... (verse 14).
A body of flesh will unite only with another body of flesh, and not with a mental body during worldly activities and actions. (15)

Now, one might ask: for what purpose is my body being retained? And why, through union with your body, would this [body] not also possess the power of movement? To that, he says: "The body of flesh" (māṃsadeha). || 15 ||
This has been illustrated exactly as it exists and according to experience;
it is established among everyone from children to the perfected ones, and is not like a boon or a curse.
"Will he come to union with you merely by your word, like the excellent Vatsāpa? To this he says "no," beginning with "yathā" (just as).

The meaning is that I have merely restated a matter established by the experience of all people, even among the most ignorant and unlearned children—taking the perfected ones (siddhas) as the limit—and have not forcibly produced some unprecedented object. || 16 ||
Through the intense practice of awakening, as the latent impressions of worldly existence wane within this very body, the state of being a "mind-body" (citta-śarīratā) truly arises.

If the nature of things established by worldly consensus does not undergo subversion, then one might suspect that even when latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are attenuated, the state of this body as a subtle, transportable vehicle (*ātivāhika*) cannot be possible; anticipating this objection, he says: "avabodha... [and so on].
The state of having the mind as its body is the state of having a subtle, transportable body (*ātivāhika-śarīratā*). || 17 ||
And that very [self] which is about to arise here is not perceived by anyone;
rather, only the body is seen by people as it dies. (18)

Now, one might object: "The departure of living beings to the next world is well known to occur by means of the *ātivāhika* body, whereas the gross body (*sthūladeha*) is seen to remain right here after death; how then can there be both life through the state of the *ātivāhika* and death through the state of the gross body for a single entity at the same time? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And as she is about to rise," etc. That [consciousness].
Furthermore, this state of being *ātivāhika* (subtle/transitional), which is about to arise in this very body at the time of death,

is not perceived by anyone— whether dying or living. This is according to such scriptural passages as, "Just as a weaver [weaves a new cloth]," and so forth, regarding the one who is dying for the purpose of constructing a body for the next world.

Since it is only that which is conjoined with the portions of the elemental constituents (*bhūtamātra*) imagined through one's own ignorance (*svājñāna*) that goes to the other world, there is no contradiction in those constituents being in a subtle, transportive state (*ātivāhika*), even if they are not perceived by him; whereas the body of ignorance (*ajñānadeha*) consists of the portions of elemental constituents imagined through the ignorance of another.
The meaning is that he is seen by other people as he is dying. || 18 ||
This body neither dies nor lives;
what then to you are death and life, which are indeed but errors of dream and mental construction?

Furthermore, this body is unreal; it neither dies nor does it live. Since both life and death are not any real entity at all, it is not reasonable to suspect a contradiction here—this is the meaning. || 19 ||
Just as life and death appear in a person created by imagination,
so too, O daughter, do they appear— though they are unreal— within this body.
Līlā said:
"O Goddess, this stainless knowledge has been taught to me by you;
once it has entered my hearing, the cholera of the perceptible world attains peace. (21)
The two verses regarding Līlā’s questions are clear. || 21 ||
In this regard, help me by telling me: what is practice, or of what nature is it?
How does it attain nourishment, and what occurs when it has been nourished? (22)
The Goddess said:
Whatever is performed by whomever, whenever, and in whatever manner—if it is done without practice, it never attains perfection in this world. (23)
The wise know that practice to consist of reflecting upon That, speaking of That, mutually awakening one another to That, and being solely intent upon That. (24)

Therein, he first states the nature of practice: "That reflection" (*taccintanam*). By means of these methods—reflection for the sake of bringing [the truth] onto one's own intellect without doubt, narration for the sake of corroboration with the intellects of other experts, and mutual instruction for the sake of awakening each other to parts unknown to one another—one overcomes improbabilities (*asambhāvanā*).
The fruits are: conduct characterized by single-minded devotion to this [practice], and the cessation of contrary mental impressions. || 24 ||

Those noble souls who, being detached, cultivate the attenuation of the inclination toward enjoyments within themselves for the sake of non-becoming— they, the fortunate ones, are victorious upon this earth.
He shows, by way of praising those who are dispassionate, that firm detachment and so forth are indeed the characteristics of such persons—starting with the words "ye" (those who).

They cultivate, that is, they produce through effort, the attenuation—the diminution—of the inclinations toward enjoyment, which are the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding sense objects. || 25 ||

Those practitioners who possess a mind colored by the essence of dispassion toward the exalted beauty of the Sublime (Uditaudārya), and which vibrates with bliss— these are the supreme ones. (26) [The reading "rasagarbhiṇī" is also found.]
Magnanimity consists in the renunciation of all possessions; it is colored by the beauty of its defining characteristics and by the essence of dispassion.
Others are those who are superior. 26.
Those who strive through reasoning and the scriptures for the attainment of the absolute non-existence of the knower and the object of knowledge are established as practitioners of Brahman. (27)

He states that even the state of being intent on hearing and so forth is characterized by the repeated practice of that [meditation], saying "absolutely" (atyanta). By means of reasoning (yukti)—that which is conducive to the ascertainment of the reality of the means of knowledge and conducive to the ascertainment of the reality of the object of knowledge—and by means of the scriptures (śāstra), that is, the treatises on the inner self (adhyātma-śāstra). || 27 ||
From the very beginning of creation, the visible world was never produced; it does not exist at all, always.
"This world" and "I"—the practice of realizing this is what others call the cultivation of awakening (bodhābhyāsa). || 28 ||

He states that even the non-recurrence of the perception of sublation regarding objects seen throughout the three periods of time constitutes that very practice: "At the beginning of creation," and so forth.

When passion, hatred, and the like have been thinned through the realization of the impossibility of the perceptible world, that delight which arises from strength is declared to be the practice of Brahman. (29)
Strength is the firmness of the latent impressions of knowledge born from reflection; the delight arising from that is "delight in the Self" (ātmarati). || 29 ||

Without the realization of the impossibility of the perceptible [object], there can be no attenuation of hatred and the like; therefore, that is called austerity (tapas), not knowledge, and it is of the nature of suffering.

He states that [meditation] characterized by the practice of that [knowledge] at that time is not of another kind, because it is precisely useful for prior knowledge when passion and the like have been severed through the firm conviction in the unreality of the visible world—beginning with the words "dṛśya" (the visible).
That austerity is "duḥkhataḥ" (consisting of suffering), as it extends or expands the suffering caused by the suppression of false hatred and so forth. || 30 ||
For the realization of the impossibility of the visible world is called both knowledge and the object of knowledge;
through its practice comes nirvāṇa—thus, this practice is of great benefit.
Having stated the reason there, he concludes by showing the fruit of practice with two verses beginning with "dṛśya":

for (hi) because knowledge consisting of the final direct realization and its object, Brahman, are such that the non-existence of the visible (dṛśya) is said to occur therein—or rather, such an awakening is described as occurring therein—this is the meaning. || 31 ||

The intense sleep of the long night of worldly existence completely melts away through the constant sprinkling of the water of discernment, which is as cool as ice. (In some recensions, the reading is *aśeṣā*.)
Like a great mist in autumn within the mind. || 32 ||

In the mind and heart, through the constant sprinkling of the water of discernment and awakening— which are cooled by frost because they are practiced as the cause for the subsiding of all afflictions— the intense sleep characterized by delusion has set in during this long night of existence, that is, within the cycle of saṃsāra, which is like the night of the dark fortnight.
Even without leaving behind any trace of its conditioned nature (*saṃskāra*), it flows away and dissolves; it is like a great mist, a mass of frost. || 32 ||
When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the performance of the evening rites,
and the assembly, having offered salutations, departed to bathe.
And at the waning of the night, he arrived together with the rays of the sun. || 33 ||

Thus ends the twenty-second canto, titled "The Description of the Practice of Higher Knowledge," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (sage-authored) tradition.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Practice of Higher Knowledge," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Fourth Day.
The Twenty-third Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus conversed that night with that beautiful woman,
while the attendants were indeed asleep in the pavilion of the inner apartments, [he departed].
Through yoga, having abandoned the gross body with the desire to behold the mountain village,
the movement within the vast sky of the house is described as the play of knowledge and bliss.

When the attendants and the excellent women were fast asleep, without exception or remainder, Jñapti and Līlā went to a place of meditative concentration and remained there; this is the connection with the fourth verse. || 1 ||
In that mind which was clever, whose doors and windows were secured by all manner of firm bolts,
and which was languid with the thick fragrance emitted by heaps of flowers— [the reading "puṣpaprākāra" also occurs]. || 2 ||

"Dakṣacetasī" is either an epithet of the former attendants (meaning it is used figuratively) or, as the intended sense is that it is an epithet of the pavilion itself; "dṛḍhāḥ" means all or entire; "bahuvidhāḥ" means of many kinds;
and "argalāḥ" refers to the bolts or crossbars for the door-panels—such were the doors and windows in which.
It was filled—that is, packed—with heaps of flowers that had been spat out and cast aside, and with thick, abundant fragrances that were heavy with scent. || 2 ||
Seated beside a corpse adorned with unfading garlands and garments,
her abode illuminated by a face like the entire, stainless, full moon.

The analysis of the compound is: "those whose faces are like the full moon, being *sakala* (entire), *samagra* (whole), *amala* (stainless), and *akalaṅka* (spotless). It is not, however, "like the full moon accompanied by its digits (*kalā*)," for that would result in the fallacy of superfluous qualifiers. || 3 ||
Having gone to the place of meditation, they stood with motionless limbs,
like figures carved from jeweled pillars or as if depicted in a painting upon a wall.
The word "putrikā" (dolls) is to be supplied after "utkīrṇe" (carved); "citre" means painted images. || 4 ||
They both abandoned all their anxieties when their contraction had ceased,
like two lotus plants at the end of the day whose rows of fragrance have spread abroad.
"Contraction," characterized by the withdrawal of all the senses; "those two [lotuses] from which streaks of fragrance—portions of perfume—have spread forth on all sides. (5)
The two of them became intensely tranquil, pure, and devoid of movement,
like a mountain in autumn when the wind has ceased and the garlands of clouds have fallen away.

Just as on a windless autumn mountain, when the clouds have dispersed and the garlands of mist have descended, it is pure, auspicious, tranquil, cool, and devoid of movement—so too [is that state]. || 6 ||
Through non-conceptual meditative absorption, the two of them abandoned external consciousness,
just as the lovely wish-fulfilling vine previously gave up its sap at the end of the season. (7)

It refers to the reconnection of consciousness with external objects that are not the self, such as the body and so forth; the meaning is that it is like one who, when another season such as spring has arrived, abandons the previous [flavor], as seen from the withering of old leaves and the like. || 7 ||

When it is understood by both [the teacher and the disciple] that the illusory appearance of "I" and "the world" has no origination from the very beginning, and is essentially characterized by absolute non-existence; (8)

He states— through the verse beginning with "I am" (aham) and its half— that the cause for the final establishment in non-conceptual samādhi by means of the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*), which consists in the absolute cessation of all that is visible (*dṛśya*), is precisely the sublation of the visible along with its root throughout the three periods of time. || 8 ||
Then, O sinless one, this visible demon has completely set for both of us, because of its very non-existence, like the horn of a hare.

Vasiṣṭha, addressing Rāma, says with the half-verse beginning "asattvāt" (due to non-existence) that for us, the sublation of the visible world throughout the three periods of time is established by experience, just as it is in samādhi: "In our view, the world appears like the water of a mirage, yet it does not appear [as real] like the horn of a hare. For...
The positive concomitance (anvaya) is that whatever does not exist at the very beginning likewise does not exist in the present. || 9 ||
For that which does not exist at the very beginning likewise does not exist in the present;
whether it has appeared or not appeared, the world is therefore like the water of a mirage. (10)
Those two women became solely their own true nature, tranquil,
like the sky utterly free from the masses of objects such as the moon and the sun.

He explains how those two appeared at the disappearance of the visible world with the words "svabhāva... and so forth. Just as the sky is known to be far removed from all masses of objects such as the moon and sun—at the beginning of creation, prior to the arising of air, and at the dissolution of the air—it was likewise [at that time]. || 11 ||

By that very body of knowledge, the goddess of cognition moved; but by the other, which was quickly conformed to human form and to her meditative knowledge [or: conformed to both knowledge and ignorance], she moved as a mortal woman.
He describes the difference in their bodies regarding the flight through the sky that is about to be described, with the words "by that" (tena). || 12 ||
Having ascended by their consciousness to the height of a span within the house itself,
they became two beings whose form was the sky of consciousness, possessing the appearance of birds in the air.

And he says— “within the house” (gehāntaḥ)— to show that this conceptualization of traveling through distant space occurs only within the portion of space inside one’s own home pavilion, and not outside; for in the reading “within the body” (dehāntaḥ),
the meaning is that one ascends the path of the channels (nāḍī) measuring a span (prādeśa) from the heart up to the throat.
By means of consciousness—that is, by means of consciousness consisting of the awakened latent impressions (saṃskāra) of previously formed volitions (saṃkalpa). || 13 ||
Then those two women, playful in their dalliance and lovely-eyed, by the very nature of their perception of objects, departed far from here into the sky. (14)

The objects are the cognizable things; their nature is the conceptualization of practical activity corresponding to those objects, which arises through the cognition of them—this is the meaning. || 14 ||
Remaining there, they then soared through the sky by means of their mental faculties,
spanning ten million yojanas, reaching from one distant point to another even more remote.

"Tatrasthe" means situated there or at home; the word "vā" (or) is used for emphasis. "Cidvṛttyā" means by a mental function consisting primarily of consciousness, in the form of the thought, "We two shall fly through the sky. || 15 ||
Even here, within the body of space, those two— whose intrinsic nature is the continuous pursuit of the visible—
are mutually [united] by beholding each other’s form.
The two became companions devoted to affection. || 16 ||

In reality, even though their bodies are the ether of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), they have attained the nature of the mind through the pursuit of previously conceptualized objects of perception; [the term] *vayasye* means "two female friends. || 16 ||

Thus ends the twenty-third canto, titled "The Flight of Līlā and Prajñā through the Space of the Body of Knowledge," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus [ends] the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-third canto, titled "The Travel through the Sky in the Body of Knowledge by the Goddesses Līlā and Prajñā."
The twenty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having leaped from afar to even further distances, he gradually ascended to the highest state.
Holding hand in hand, as they were walking along, they beheld the sky.
Here, the sky—its interior filled with the playful manifestations of infinite universal variety—is described as the path upon which the two, Knowledge and Play, proceed. (1)
"Uccaiḥ pada" means a high position or an elevated station. || 1 ||
It was like a single vast ocean, swollen yet deep, with a pure interior;
it was exceedingly soft, bestowing the blissful enjoyment of contact with a gentle breeze.

It was swollen, that is, fully expanded; it was deep, like a single vast ocean; it was soft, as if tender and smooth; and through the contact—that is, the union—with the gentle breezes of the soft winds, it provided a pleasant experience. || 2 ||
It is delightful and serene because it is immersed in the waters of emptiness;
it is utterly pure and profound, yet clear even because of its association with the virtuous. (3)

It is exceedingly refreshing because of its immersion—that is, its plunging—into the water characterized by emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Alternatively, it is a lotus that serves as a cause of delight for the bees that are living beings, due to their first emerging after having plunged into the Brahma-water characterized by the emptiness of the world. In this regard:
The term "profound" (*gambhīram*) is an explicit qualifier [for the teaching], whereas previously it was a qualifier for the simile; thus, there is no tautology.
It is more serene even than that which comes from a virtuous person (*sajjana*). (3)
They rested upon the peaks where the pure waters of the clouds gathered like a swelling breast of nectar, within the stainless interior of the full moon that pervades all directions.

In the various directions, upon the peaks of Mount Meru and other mountains, or within a palace—a celestial abode of nectar—characterized by a belly as vast as a mass of pure clouds, situated deep within that expansive interior; || 4 ||
They took delight in the sweet breeze, which had issued from the lunar orb and was enchanting with the fragrance of the Mandāra garlands of the Siddhas and Gandharvas.

In some places, near the lunar disc, [the breezes] emerge from the lunar disc; since coolness and fragrance have already been conveyed by the two preceding adjectives, the word "sweet" (madhura) refers here to softness and pleasant touch. || 5 ||
At the end of the intense heat, they swam within the mass of clouds, which was thick with water and filled with red lotuses like flashes of lightning,
resembling a lake sluggish with an abundance of water.
At the end of the summer heat—that is, at its conclusion—in the case of the lake, the lightning flashes are like red lotuses;
in the case of the mass of clouds, the lightning flashes are like red lotuses. || 6 ||
p.

187) Like two female bees wandering at will among lotus ponds, they roamed freely through the quarters of the world, upon the great mountain ranges of the earth's surface, and upon the tips of lotus stalks and sprouts. (7)
The great mountains such as Himavat and Kailāsa, situated upon the vast expanse of those respective grounds, appear like the tips of sprouts from the lotus-roots (mṛṇāla) within them. || 7 ||
Perceiving the cascade-bearing Gaṅgā as a shower-house, the two wise ones wandered within the pavilion of the circle of clouds agitated by the wind.
By the word "sound of the mountain stream," its spray is indicated.
Then, moving gracefully and resting according to their strength,
they beheld in the void a sky that was exceedingly sluggish due to its great exertion.
It is exceedingly sluggish and afflicted by great undertakings and the creation of the worlds and their inhabitants. || 9 ||
Never before seen, one another’s [faces], a hollow of total distress,
it was not filled even by hundreds of millions of worlds, yet it remained utterly empty.

Although it was indeed seen before by way of conventional designation (*prajñapti*), nevertheless, through their mutual association—that is, by being together with one another—it was not seen previously. It is that which possesses all parts, such as narrow crevices and internal cavities;
or rather, the meaning is that it is a cavity serving as the locus for the sufferings of existence for all living beings.
The state of not being filled is the cause of non-emptiness. || 10 ||
Higher and higher, ever more lofty, it was filled with various distinct levels and excellent celestial palaces, adorned with diverse ornaments and forms.
By those [mountains] which possess beautiful celestial palaces, characterized by their surfaces that resemble various ornaments, [and thus] by their world-regions. || 11 ||
Its interior was like the conflagration at the end of an aeon, filled on all sides by the radiance from the ruby slopes of the principal mountains such as Meru, which completely fill the sky.
By the radiance and illumination of the banks and sides made of ruby gems. || 12 ||
Beautiful with the peaks of the Himavat mountain filled with masses of pearls,
it shone like the golden plateau with the radiance of the ground of the Golden Mountain.
The plateau of the Himalayas was likewise radiant with the floods of light— the streams of splendor— from those very mountains whose peaks were composed of pearls.
The greenness of the grassy grounds was intensified by the luster of great emeralds,
while a blackness arose from the darkness produced by the attachment to the destruction of both the observer and the observed.

Likewise, its blueness was such that it was as if the very blueness of the green meadows had been produced by the luster of those very mountains— which were like great emeralds, those most precious green gems— and which, in certain places,
became intent upon and devoted to the destruction of the various forms perceived by those with eyes. Thus it arose, having come into being.
That which possesses such blackness arising from darkness.
With its multitude of celestial chariots swaying like *pārijāta* creepers serving as banners,
the ground of lapis lazuli appeared from there like a cluster of flower blossoms.
In some places, however, because it is situated above the groves of *pārijātaka* and *kalpalatā* trees which serve as the abode for swarms of hovering celestial chariots,
the meaning is that when viewed from nearby it appears like a cluster of forest blossoms, whereas when viewed from afar it stands like a ground made of lapis lazuli. || 15 ||
[He saw] the coming and going of the great siddhas, swift as thought, who had conquered the winds;
it resounded with the humming of celestial chariots, palaces, and the songs and instrumental music of divine women.
In that [state], the coming and going of the wind—the force of the movement of the vital air—has been conquered by the great adepts (mahāsiddhas) through the swiftness of the mind;
"ghuṃghumam" is an imitation of a sound. 16.
With the dense intervals between them filled by the movement of the multitudes of beings, the most excellent in the three worlds,
it was crowded with hosts of gods and asuras whose movements were not seen by one another. (17)
The circle of Kūṣmāṇḍas, Rākṣasas, and Paiśācas stationed at the periphery;
and the multitude of celestial chariots (vaimānika) borne along with great speed by the mass of wind.
The "winds" (vātaskandha) are the various divisions of wind, such as Āvaha, Pravaha, and so forth. || 18 ||
It produced a whistling sound from its moving celestial chariots, possessed deep thundering roars that could be grasped by the fist,
and had its wind-machines set in motion by the movement of planets, stars, and clouds.
In which [chariot], the sounds of clouds were captured by its fist—the seizing, overpowering, and crushing of the whistling of the celestial palaces (*vimāna*) and the roar of their velocity;
and which was a wheel of light in the form of a mechanical device (*vātayantraka*) consisting of a restraint of the wind. || 19 ||
The abodes of the minor Siddhas, scorched by the nearby heat, have been abandoned;
their charming celestial chariots have been consumed by the winds from the mouths of the Sun’s horses.

In some places, the site was abandoned by a class of divine beings known as *siddhas*, who, having attained only minor perfections through the practice of austerity, yoga, and elixirs (*rasāyana*), were scorched and tormented by the heat of the sun in its proximity; furthermore, their small celestial chariots (*vimānas*) had been driven away, cast off, or burnt by the sun and by the breath from the mouths of its horses, as the case may be.
In which there are celestial palaces. || 20 ||
The sky was restless with the movements of throngs of world-protecting deities and celestial nymphs, while its clouds were formed by the incense smoke burning within the queens' inner apartments.
With its feet, it was as if moving about; with its other limbs, it was as if performing various appropriate actions—thus it was "as if restless" through those activities.

With the smoke of incense, it stood as if the sky were covered by clouds. Because of the constructed distinction [of the simile], Viṣṇu is the object of comparison (upameya) on the grounds that [the king] is equal to Viṣṇu in prowess, just like Rāma.
The ornaments fallen from the limbs of the celestial women summoned by the gods to their respective heavens;
the mass of darkness that possesses the power of the fierce splendor of the assembly of common *siddhas*.

Because it was such that the ornaments had fallen from their own bodies due to the celestial women, the apsarases— who, having been summoned to their respective worlds designated as "heaven" by Indra, Candra, and others, were therefore running in a scramble for precedence while disregarding one another— [it was there that they fell]. Therefore, those [women...]

Of that mass of fierce splendor belonging to the assembly of those other celestial beings— who, though striving and possessing common attainments, were devoid of specific powers such as *aṇimā* and the like, like Indra and others— [there arose] through anger, envy, and so forth.
The meaning is that the power of darkness (tamobala), which causes concealment, stands there as if it were the quality of darkness (tamas) intensified, appearing blue. || 22 ||
By the dense clouds, shaken by the coming and going of powerful throngs of *siddhas*,
the Himavat, Meru, and Mandara mountains stood as if clothed in white raiment at their sides.

Likewise, by the collisions and crushings of powerful Siddhas belonging to specific divine classes, the clouds were shattered and pulverized by their passage; and as if out of fear of that, [the mountains] remained still.

In that [place], Himavat, Meru, and Mandara became as if possessed of sisters, having become "clothed in white" by taking refuge on the plateaus of the Himalayas and other mountains situated at their sides.
It was surrounded by swarms of crows, owls, vultures, and hawks gathered together and moving about,
and by throngs of dancing ḍākinīs, like waves surrounding the ocean.
Owls and other such species of birds. || 24 ||
It was filled with throngs of active yoginīs whose faces had the voices of dogs, crows, and camels,
who were traveling back and forth for no purpose across a hundred yojanas.

The meaning is that although the desired object is obtained right at their own place because the yoginīs possess supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* (the power of becoming minute), it is nevertheless useless for them to go far away and then return. || 25 ||
In the cloud-palace, smoky-grey with the smoke of the darkness that precedes the world-protectors; [the reading *dhūmrābhramandiram* is also found].
Where pairs of Siddhas and Gandharvas had commenced the festival of amorous dalliance.

In that temple, which was smoke-grey in form like a cloud, obstructing the spread of vision as if it were darkness, and which stood as if right before the eyes of the world-protectors presiding over their respective directions because it extended to the very ends of the horizon.
Its path was traversed by Madana, who was intoxicated by the songs of praise from heaven;
its wings were marked by the circles of constellations moving without ceasing.

In which [world], the sky-going beings are intoxicated and overcome by passion by means of divine songs and divine hymns of praise being sung in heaven that kindle their desire; and in which, within the wheel of light (jyotiścakra) consisting of the abodes of the stars that flows incessantly,
the divisions of time such as the bright and dark fortnights are marked by the movement of the sun and other luminaries.
The water of the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā) flowed within the hollows dug out by the mass of winds,
while the children of the gods moved about, preoccupied with gazing at the wonders.

In that very wheel, which takes the form of a division of the wind-column (vātaskandha), a hollowed-out depression has been fashioned; within it flows the water of the triple-pathed river (tripathagā). || 28 ||

In some places, there were palaces moving through the air with their physical forms, equipped with vajras, discs, tridents, swords, and spears; in others, there were buildings without walls, where Nārada and Tumburu sang.
By terms such as "Vajracakra" and so forth, the deities who preside over them are expressed; therefore, their possession of a body is logically established. || 29 ||
In some places, it was agitated by the great onset of clouds upon the path of the sky;
in others, it resembled a painted cloud at the end of an eon, motionless and fixed in form.

In the region of the path of the clouds, it was agitated by the onset of a great cataclysmic rain from the great clouds such as Puṣkarāvartaka and others; yet in some places, like figures in a painting, the clouds at the end of the aeon were motionless, mute, and silent.
In some places it had clouds as beautiful as a rising mountain of black collyrium; in other places it had clouds lovely like molten gold at the end of the summer heat.
The heat of asceticism is like the beautiful liquefaction of gold; that very heat is the summer, and the onset of the rainy season occurs within it. || 31 ||
In some places, it was rich with the heat of forest fires, like the cloud-garments of Mount Ṛṣyamūka; in other places, it possessed the turbulence of a windless ocean, like the waters of emptiness.
On Mount Ṛṣyamūka, his garments were as if being rained upon by clouds in the manner described in the earlier Rāmāyaṇa; "viṣpavana" means motionless. || 32 ||
In some places, it had the young grass-blades of aerial chariots tossed by the powerful rivers of wind;
in other places, it was stainless with the luster of the skin on the backs of swarms of moving bees.
In which [place], the river of wind—that is, the current of air—is such that even great celestial chariots are situated in the place of grass and sprouts being carried away by it. || 33 ||
In some places it was grey with dust stirred up by winds resembling those that blow over the rivers of Mount Meru;
in other places its surface was variegated by the radiance of celestial chariots and gods.
The mountain rivers of Meru,

by figurative usage referring to the rivers of the rainy season mountains, have their currents agitated by winds carrying dust of similar color; thus, his body is variegated with a diverse and powerful mottled hue.

In some places it was garlanded by circles of Mothers dancing without clothes [the reading *nirantaronnṛtta* is also found]; in other places there were groups of Yoginīs perpetually agitated by fresh intoxication. || 35 ||
In some places, it was garlanded by sages resting in peaceful meditative absorption;
it was equally captivating to the minds of the virtuous, as all agitation had been cast far away.
By that virtuous mind, all agitations such as anger and the like have been cast far away.
In some places there were circles of singing kinnaras, gandharvas, and celestial women;
in other places it was filled with motionless cities, and in yet others it carried magnificent cities in transit.
It was filled with cities that were rigid and motionless; within it flowed and wandered the foremost of cities, such as Tripura and others.
In some places it was filled with the city of Rudra; in some places the great city of Brahmā;
in some places a city created by Māyā; and in some places a city yet to come.
In some places there were lakes with wandering moons, in others lakes consisting of stillness;
in some places there were throngs of moving Siddhas, and in others the rising of the moon.

In which [place] there is a lake of illusion (*māyāsara*) that is like the moon because it is filled with nectar, or rather, it is the revolving moon itself; in which there is a lake consisting of water that has become solidified by the power of the Lord (*devaśakti*), being composed of the syllable *sta* (from *stabdha*). The absence of the case-ending (*vibhaktyaluk*) is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). || 39 ||
In some places it consisted of the rising sun; in others, of the darkness of night;
in some, tawny with the silken garment of twilight; and in others, grey with mist.
In some places white with snow-clouds, in others with rain-bearing clouds;
in some places the world-protector rested even in the sky as if on dry land.

"Ākāśa eva viśrāntalokapaḥ" (the protector of the world who has found rest in space alone): because the action of resting (*viśrānti*) requires a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and because [the compound] is eternal and a relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*), it does not become "incapable" (*asamartha*) due to its dependence; thus, there is no fault of being an "incapable compound" (*asamarthasamāsa*). And so it has been said: "A relative term is eternally dependent..."
"Everything is compounded; for that mutual expectancy which exists in a sentence is not lost even in a compound. (3.1.41)
In some places, the hosts of gods and asuras were busily engaged in ascending and descending;
in other places, they were agitated by their movements toward the east, west, north, and south.

The word *aparā* refers to the western direction by process of elimination. In the compound *uttarāyāmyā*, the absence of the masculine form (*apumbadbhāva*) for the pronoun in its usage is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). It is "disturbed" (*ākula*) by those who wander through the directions (*diksaṃcāra*).
In some places there are mountains difficult to reach, extending for hundreds of thousands of yojanas;
in other places they are filled with indestructible darkness, resembling mere heaps of stones.
In some places, beyond the Lokāloka mountain.
He is indestructible and vast splendor, resembling the sun or fire in some places, yet as cold as the interior of a mass of snow or like the moon and other such bodies in others.
A mass of snow is a *himānī*; it is as cold as the interior of that [snow-mass]. || 44 ||
In some places there were forests of kalpa-tree creepers appearing before one as they flowed along;
in other places, there were cities of the gods falling from their lofty heights after being struck by the daityas.

In some places, the groves of *kalpa*-trees and creepers were being uprooted and carried away by the attendants of the gods out of fear of the Daityas, yet they remained positioned in front and held as a vanguard in that place.
In some places it was marked by streaks of fire from the falling of celestial chariots; in other places it was scarred by the mutual clashing of hundreds of rising comets.

In some places it was marked and distinguished by the falling of celestial beings from the heavenly realms, as if by a line of fire from a shooting star with its brilliance elongated; it was "paṭṭita," meaning tightly woven or covered like a silk cloth. || 46 ||
In some places the foremost mandala was seized by a host of auspicious planets;
in some places it was pervaded by the darkness of night, and in some places it was radiant with daylight.
That which has a supreme, most excellent, and upward-turning mandala. || 47 ||
In some places there were thundering clouds, in others clear and silent clouds;
in some places it was strewn with white cloud-fragments like scattered flowers by the wind.
For him, fragments of clouds themselves were the "flower-surpassing" or "flower-strewn" [beds].
In some places it is utterly empty, pure, and without interval;
like the heart of a wise man, it is spread forth as blissful, soft, peaceful, and transparent. (49)
It is utterly devoid of any object of perception; it is pure and translucent; it is immediate, being free from the obstruction of the clouds of ignorance; it is clear and free from dust. || 49 ||
In some places, the field of the sky-dwellers resounded with the croaking of swarms of frogs riding on semen, while elsewhere it was submerged in the waters of emptiness.

The multitude of frogs are indeed the mounts of all the sky-dwellers (gods) characterized by semen; by them, the field—the cultivated plot—is filled, being enveloped by the water of emptiness (śūnyatā).
In some places it was covered by birds such as peacocks with golden crests,
and in others by the mounts of Vidyādharīs and goddesses that had taken up their positions there.
In one place, there was a circle of peacocks dancing amidst the clouds; in another, it was dark with fire-parrots, like a patch of land covered in young grass.

Guha is Skanda. Regarding "by the parrots that are the vehicles of Agni": although it is well known that Agni has a ram as his vehicle, nevertheless, because of what is stated here, it should also be understood that he has parrots as his vehicle. || 52 ||
In some places, due to the majesty of the buffalo of the Lord of the Dead (Yama), the clouds appeared small;
in other places, dark clouds were swallowed by horses out of a mistaken fear that they were a village of grass.
(53) [Note: An alternative reading is *grastāmitāmbudaṃ* ("the immeasurable clouds were swallowed").]

Yama, the lord of the departed, due to the greatness—that is, the massive body—of that buffalo, experienced the suspicion that it was a mere clump of grass, a delusion that it was a heap of straw. (53)
In some places it was pervaded by the cities of the gods, and in others it was filled with the cities of the Daityas;
their cities were unable to reach one another, while the wind blew through the gaps between them.
In that city which was inaccessible and impossible for others to reach, the reason is this:
it was a place where the exceedingly powerful wind, capable of creating gaps even among the mountains (naga), blew. || 54 ||
In some places it was radiant with Bhairavas dancing like the Kulācala mountains;
in other places, Vināyakas were dancing along with the winged lords of mountains.
In some places, mountains were being tossed up by the wings of a torrent of gurgling winds;
in other places, it was made beautiful by throngs of celestial women from the city of the Gandharvas.
In which [place] mountains flew up on their wings in such a way that there was a torrent of gurgling wind. 56.
In some places, clouds rose high, having destroyed hundreds of thousands of trees with their torrents;
in other places, it was as cool as the water of a celestial lotus-pond created by illusion.

In which [ocean], clouds raised like umbrellas were shattered and pulverized by mountains that flew upward and moved along, carrying with them hundreds of thousands of trees; even if the reading is *ambudhim*, by the etymology "those in which waters (*ambu*) are held (*dhīyante*)," it refers precisely to those who hold water, namely the clouds (*ambuda*). || 57 ||
In some places there was a breeze, cool and refreshing, drawn by the rays of the moon; in other places there were trees, mountains, and clouds scorched by a scorching wind.
In some places it was utterly silent due to the complete stillness of the wind;
in other places, hundreds of peaks of cloud-tops arose, resembling mountains.
Utterly solitary and completely silent. || 59 ||
In some places it resounded with the gurgling roar of clouds intoxicated by the onset of the rainy season;
in other places it was difficult to traverse due to battles waged by hosts of gods and asuras.
In one place, he saw the lotus-vehicled god (Brahmā) summoned by the cries of the female swans in the celestial lotus-pool;
in another, the wind plundering the lotuses on the banks of the Mandākinī.
In the word *abjavāhana*, there is the elision of the vowel *a* according to the rules of prosody (*chandasa*). He is the plunderer of lotuses, the stealer of their fragrance. || 61 ||
By means of his own body, through the proximity of rivers such as the Gaṅgā,
he [beheld] schools of leaping fish, crocodiles, crabs, lotuses, and tortoises.
"With her own body" means with the body of the deity. The expression beginning with "proḍḍīna" (having flown up) is a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*). || 62 ||
In various regions, the orbs of the moon and sun were eclipsed by the flickering shadows of the earth cast down from the sun situated in the netherworld (pātāla).

Relying on the astronomical method, he says: "In Pātāla," etc. When the sun revolves around the terrestrial globe, the shadow of the earth also revolves around it; when the sun is in Pātāla, that very shadow extends upwards.
Because it is dark, it is like a crow (*kāka*), and by its "approaches" (*upanaiḥ*)—the root *cup* meaning slow movement—it means by its advances. This is that [shadow].
This logical proof applies to a lunar eclipse; however, this proof does not apply to a solar eclipse. Therefore, another meaning is stated through a pun (*śleṣa*).

By the word "Pātāla" (the netherworld), the distant rear portion of the moon is indicated by metaphorical extension (*lakṣaṇā*); when the sun is situated behind that [portion], the shadow of the earth produced upon the lunar disc causes it to become dark, like a crow (*kāka*).
The moon is perfected by those very offerings. || 63 ||
In some places, there was a forest of illusory flowers shaken by the winds of creation,
where the celestial women trembled at the falling frost-like pollen of the petals.

The meaning is: in which [place] there is a grove of illusory flowers, shaken by the winds produced by the gods of the celestial mansions (*vaimānika*) for the purpose of causing wonder at their own women. || 64 ||
O excellent lady, having leaped high into the sky above that mass of living beings contained within the three worlds— which were whirling like gnats inside the hollow of a fig tree— [he departed].
He is now prepared to go once again to the surface of the earth. || 65 ||
Thus, lest there should arise passion for those celestial beings whose majesty has been described in the sky, he says "udumbara... in order to treat them as insignificant;
that is to say, their status is like the progression of a mosquito. 65.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the Departure of the Goddesses Līlā and Prajñā," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* (Section on Origination) of the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, a work of the Ṛṣis. || 24 ||

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Departure of the Goddesses Līlā and Prajñā," in the *Tātparyaprakāśa* (Illumination of the Essential Meaning) of the glorious *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the section on Origination (*Utpatti-prakaraṇa*).
The twenty-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: As you two were traveling from the sky toward a mountain village, you encountered someone.
The two women saw the surface of the ground occupied by the mind of the formal motion (jñapticitta). || 1 ||
An unprecedented world, surrounded by the seven oceans and continents and endowed with the enclosures of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), was seen by those two; it is described here.
It means that she intended to show to Līlā a certain unprecedented state of mind established through an announcement—that is, one she had previously kept hidden. || 1 ||
The great heart-lotus of the man within the cosmic egg has the eight directions as its petals;
it is densely packed with the filaments of the mountains and is beautiful with the abundance of its own fragrance. (2)
He describes that very surface of the earth as the heart-lotus of the Cosmic Person (Brahmāṇḍapuruṣa) with the words beginning "brahmāṇḍa... and so forth. || 2 ||
In the midst of the stalks of the lotuses of the rivers was a dewdrop,
frequented by the female bees of the night and swarming with the mosquitoes of the multitudes of living beings.
Because they originate from the *girikesaras* (mountain-crests), the rivers are called *kesarikās*; these are the intermediate branches of the *kesaras*.
In this [place], the drops of frost are themselves the drops of nectar. || 3 ||
It was filled with a multitude of internal qualities, possessed of beautiful apertures and hollows,
carrying floods of water, and possessing the splendor of the light of day.

The internal fibers within the stalks are the qualities of the objects of enjoyment; and by means of the hollows of the netherworld (pātāla) and other regions, which act like beautiful openings in the stalks, the floods of water are drawn upward—this is the qualification of the hollows. It is radiant with the light, that is, the illumination, of the day. (4)

Moist with nectar, it was a lotus stalk with a swan wandering in the sky, a vessel for the contraction of night, and its root submerged in the mud of the underworld where the lord of serpents dwells. (5)
By "flavors" (rasa) is meant the nectars and the erotic sentiments (śṛṅgāra) and so forth; by "swans" (haṃsa) is meant the sun and the well-known swans. || 5 ||
At times, its base caused the entire expanse of the directions to tremble with the shaking of the ocean,
while its roots reached downward, where the Daityas and Dānavas were like thorns.

According to the Vedic revelation, "That which was the foam of the waters solidified and became the earth," and because it is well-known in the Purāṇas that the Earth was lifted up by the Boar and established upon the waters,
when that great ocean— the very foundation of the Earth— trembled, the quarters of the sky shook due to the earthquake. || 6 ||
Having reached the heart of the great seed of the mountain king by means of the creeper of the Asura women— tender with the enjoyment of love and possessing the seed of all beings.

Having reached, by means of a creeper characterized by the seeds of beings below— namely, the seeds of beings and living creatures within her own lineage— the hearts of the mountains such as Meru, which serve as the locus for great seeds, that host of Asura women (straiṇa) is capable of attaining what is to be attained.
That for which the root is not the navel, but rather the heart is the cause of its life.
Therein, he fashioned a vast pericarp known as Jambudvīpa,
with rivers as its filaments and cities and villages as its stamens.
In that regard, it is understood that they both beheld the pericarp of the earth-lotus. || 8 ||
She is beautiful with the seven lofty seed-syllables of the lords of the principal mountain ranges;
the expanse of her sky is occupied by the seed-syllable of the great Meru situated at her center.
It was like a drop of frost upon a lake, or the pollen of forest-born lotuses;
upon the dry lands, it formed circles within which swarms of people gathered like bees. (10) [The reading "maṇḍalām" is preferred for "maṇḍalānta-"].
In which [the lotuses] the drops of frost are like lakes; the dust is like pollen;
and in the areas extending to the pericarp, the swarms of bees are like circles of people situated all around within the mandala. 10.
It was pervaded by oceans that appeared like bees, extending for hundreds of yojanas, awakening [the world] every night, and possessing the four directions.
She rests upon the eight petals of the directions, with the oceans and gods as her bees,
and is fashioned in nine ways by the nine royal brothers.
