In this [city], the six oceans together with the eight gods who guard the directions (dikpālas) are like bees; whereas previously there was the conception of four oceans as bees based on the four directions of a single ocean, here the distinction is that there is a conception of eight oceans as bees upon the petals based on the eight guardians of the directions.
[He was accompanied] by nine [kings], Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, and the others. || 12 ||
It was a hundred thousand yojanas in extent, filled with particles of dust,
and thick with the spray from the hoarfrost of the various arrays of inhabited lands.
Twice the size of the continent, it is encircled on the outside by the line of the salt ocean,
which resembles the outer whorl of a conch shell.

It should be understood that there is no fault [in this statement], because it refers to another cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) due to its being a statement contrary to the Puranic system which holds that each continent is twice the size of the preceding one, and because its intent lies in its illusory nature (*māyikatva*). "Prakoṣṭha" means the base of the forearm.
"Kambu" means a conch-shell bracelet. || 14 ||
Beyond that, she bears a body twice as large, circular in shape,
which is pervaded by the world-surface vine known as the island-strip of Śāka.
It was encompassed by the ring-shaped landmass known as Śāka-dvīpa, which, assuming a circular form, appeared like a lotus-creeper that has become the very essence of the world. || 15 ||
Beyond that, she was encircled by a double-folded garment,
like a band of the ocean of fresh milk, sweet and cool.
Beyond that, it was encircled by the coastal range of the island named Kuśa, which was twice as large in form and adorned with various kinds of people.
Beyond that, it was encircled by a ring of the Ocean of Curds, twice its size, which eternally satiates the hosts of gods.
Then, by that very strip of land called the Krauñca island, which was of such dimensions,
it was encircled like a new royal city surrounded by a moat.
With a moat (*khāta*) of such measure—as previously described, but with double the dimensions—the construction of the excavation is performed;
that which is a moat is called a *parikhā*. The suffix *aṅ* is applied here according to the rule for words beginning with *bhid*. (19)
Beyond that, it was encircled by a strip of the ocean of ghee of the same extent,
and beyond that, by a strip of Śālmalī-dvīpa filled with impurities.
Because it is surrounded by the ocean of wine, which is full of impurity, it is [therefore] full of sin.
Then, with a streak of the great ocean of wine, white as flowers,
she was like the form of Hari enveloped by the coiled body of Śeṣa.
Then, by a line of the Gomedaka island of such measurement, and likewise by a line of the sugarcane ocean, pure as the slopes of the Himalayas; || 22 ||
The ocean of sugarcane juice is the ocean of sugarcane sap. Gomedaka is a specific kind of gem;
the island (dvīpa) characterized primarily by that is [Gomeda], while the remainder is Plakṣadvīpa. || 22 ||
Beyond that, it is surrounded by a ring of Puṣkaradvīpa, twice its size,
and finally by a ring of the Sweet-water Ocean (Svādūdakāmbhodhi) of equal extent.
Then, ten times greater than that, there was a high circular trench reaching down to the depths of the netherworld (pātāla), appearing like a vast accumulation of abysses.

"Nikhāta" means a low-lying place; by its force, there is a "śvabhra," which is a pit. Its "saṃbhāra" is a collection, and it is of that nature. Regarding the statement in the Purāṇas that the golden ground has a width double that of the preceding [layer], the resolution of that contradiction should be understood according to the method previously stated. Thus it was said by Śrīdharācārya:
"If a contradiction is observed here and there in the Purāṇas and other texts, the wise maintain that it is resolved through differences in *kalpas* and similar factors. (24)
(191) It is coiled by way of the path leading to the netherworld (pātāla), being of a terrifying nature;
indeed, it is ten times greater in its accumulation than all of this.
In all four directions as far as the sky, she was terrifying with her mass of caverns,
and she wore a garland of blue lotuses clinging to her form, which was like the dark gloom half-fading away.

Frightening with a mass of abysses mentioned as being present within the boundaries of the sky, reaching upward to the very limits of space; on one side, it is withered, while on the other side, in its upper portion,
it is almost faded due to the loss of its dark nature through contact with the light of the sun.
By her who was adorned with a garland of blue lotuses that clung to her in the form of a dark-colored circle. || 26 ||
With its lofty and vast garland of mountains reaching from the Lokāloka range, adorned with peaks of various jewels and white, night-lotus, and day-lotus flowers; (27)

The connection with the following verse is as follows: she is as if encircled by a garland that is "lofty" (uttālayā) in its height—characterized by the Lokāloka mountain—because it possesses various kinds of rubies on its peaks; "vast" (vipulayā) in its circumference, because it has white and blue water-lilies growing upon its lakes; and "excellent" (uddāmayā) in its qualities, because its lotuses are indeed kahlāras and kumudas. || 27 ||
It was like the gathered tresses of the hair-ornament of the Fortune of the Three Worlds;
and from all this [glory], it was tenfold greater.
*Dhammillāḥ* refers to hair that is bound or tied up. || 28 ||
It was garlanded by a forest named Ajñātabhūtasaṃcāra,
which was ten times greater than all of this [previously mentioned].

In accordance with all the Purāṇas, and because the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) is stronger than the sequence of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), it should be understood that the pervasion of the wall of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍakuḍya*), which will be described later in the verse beginning "Then, of millions of *yojanas*," occurs right here.
He describes the coverings of water and so forth outside of that, starting with the words "From this very [egg]," etc. (verse 29).
It pervades the four directions like the sky with incomparable water [the reading "amalamāriṇā" is also found];
and from all of this, it is ten times greater in nature.
Adorned with a mass of flames eager to liquefy Mount Meru and other such peaks,
[it is] ten times greater than all this.

The "melting" (*dravaṇa*) of Meru and other mountains means their liquefaction; that is to say, their dissolution (*pralaya*). In this context, the substantive "the cosmic egg" (*brahmāṇḍa*)—as if it were being churned by the wind [of destruction] as if with longing (*utkaṇṭhita*)—is to be supplied here and in what follows as well. || 31 ||
It carried away the mass of mountains beginning with Meru like blades of grass or dust;
it bore along the bursting of great mountain peaks and robbed one of their speed.
The statement beginning with "lead" expresses the capacity [of the vehicle]; it refers to other beings who deprive one of speed. || 32 ||
Because it is devoid of emptiness, it is surrounded on all sides by the soundless wind;
then, from all this, it [arises] with a nature ten times greater.
Because it is utterly devoid of corporeality and resistance, it is without sound. // 33 //
The sky was completely enveloped by that which is of a single form and devoid of emptiness;
then, it was pervaded for a hundred crores of yojanas by the golden wall of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which is solid in form and consists of two layers.
Thus, having beheld the interior of the world— encircled by the ocean, great mountains, the guardians of the quarters, the city of the gods, the sky, and the earth—
the human woman suddenly saw her own house-cavity upon the ground.
Human play; his own mountain-cave dwelling as the support for his temple, situated within the space of the mountain village. || 35 ||

Thus ends the twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Earth," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. || 25 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth canto, titled "Description of the World of Beings," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Twenty-sixth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, O fair-complexioned lady, those two [daughters] then [departed] from the sphere of the cosmic egg.
Having departed and reached another place, he arrived at that abode of the brahmin.
Having seen her own kinsmen in their home and having heard their lamentations, the grace of Līlā and the true nature of the world are described here. || 1 ||
He restates what has been said in order to establish the connection with the narrative that is about to be told: "iti" (thus).
"When another Brahmāṇḍa-maṇḍala had been reached"—that is, in the manner described—other than the Brahmāṇḍa-maṇḍala which has King Padma as its support. || 1 ||
Then those two perfected women beheld their own abode,
an invisible pavilion— the dwelling place of Brahmā— unseen by the world.
One's own abode is one's home. || 2 ||
With its female servants overwhelmed by anxiety, the faces of the women drenched with tears, and its countenance mostly ruined, it resembled a lotus with withered petals. || 3 ||
Where the female servants were distressed and overwhelmed by anxiety;
where the faces of the people were almost ruined by the dirt of tears, dust, and grime, and from which ornaments and forehead marks had been removed. || 3 ||
It was like a city whose festivals had vanished, resembling the ocean swallowed by Agastya;
like a garden scorched by summer heat, or like a tree consumed by lightning.
It was taken up and drunk by Agastya; it was scorched and dried up by the summer heat. || 4 ||
Like a cloud severed by the wind, like a lotus withered by frost, or like a lamp in a state of low oil whose light is fading; || 5 ||

Oil and the like constitute the *sneha* (lubricant), and the wick is the *daśā*. That by which one sees is *ālokana*, namely the eye; its piercing is what is meant by "difficult to behold" (*durdarśam*). || 5 ||
With the luster of his face clouded by compassion for those whose death was near, resembling a forest of withered and decaying tree leaves,
and as parched as a region turned grey by the cessation of rain—
That household, once born, is now ruined by separation from its master.
[The one] who is agitated by that [state], which is either a specific emotion (*rasa*) or a particular state of being that inflames compassion and grief—meaning, she is overwhelmed.

Whose beauty is crooked? Precisely for that reason, he remains in a state where death is imminent. That forest in which withered leaves of aged trees have fallen is the simile for him. "The cessation of rain" refers to drought. (6)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, by means of the long-practiced cultivation of pure knowledge, that beautiful woman—
She was perfected, possessing the power of true resolve and true desires, like a goddess.
That is *līlā*. || 7 ||
He thought: "Let my kinsmen see me and this goddess for a moment as bearing the form of an ordinary woman."
Then, his household members saw there two women who illuminated the palace like a pair of Lakṣmī and Gaurī.
Beautiful with various garlands and garments that had faded since the month of Āṣāḍha, it was like the pair of Vasantalakṣmī and her consort, making the forest fragrant.

With the eight verses beginning with "āpāda," he describes two women. The mention of "from the feet" (āpāda) is also indicative of [the description] up to the head. By means of the "valanas"—that is, the spreading—of various unfading garlands. || 10 ||
Filling the entire grove of medicinal herbs with elixirs, they were like two risen moons, bestowing coolness, refreshment, and happiness. (11)

Herbs end with the ripening of their fruit; [the word] *pūrayanti* (they fill) [is used for] *pūrayat* (filling), because the neuter singular is employed as the single substantive, resulting in a Vedic deviation of gender and number.
With elixirs that are like the nectar of moonlight... 11.
With glances from eyes as restless as long, creeper-like locks of hair,
she scatters heaps of *mālatī* flowers mingled with blue water-lilies.
The meaning is that, because of their restlessness in the presence of the *alaka* (curling locks of hair), her eyes were transformed into bees;
thus, due to the dark-white luster of her side-glances (*kaṭākṣa*), they are imagined as clusters of jasmine flowers interspersed with blue water-lilies (*kuvalaya*). || 12 ||

With a stream of bodily radiance that was captivating like the swift flow of a river filled with the essence of molten gold, he turned the forest into gold—[the reading "prabhavina" is noted as an alternative].
It was as enchanting as the current of a river whose waters consist of a flowing torrent of liquefied golden mercury. (13)
These [limbs] of his, who sports upon the playful swing of the innate beauty of his body,
are like the waves of the ocean of his own loveliness.
Like swings fashioned for the play of Lakṣmī, whose characteristic is the beauty of her form,
these playful ones— whose nature is to sport— are like the finest waves of the ocean of their own splendor, which is inherently beautiful as the Brahman, or of their own physical loveliness.
The ellipsis is: "They are recognized as being these very same ones, O lady, by means of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) [that they are so]. || 14 ||
With her pair of tremulous creeper-like arms and her reddish hands,
she was scattering a forest of golden kalpa-vṛkṣa creepers, ever-new in every way.

By qualifying each of the creeper-like arms and the reddish hands with the attribute of "tremulousness," and by means of their changing positions at every moment, she scatters— that is, spreads out— a forest of ever-new celestial *kalpa* trees and creepers within the whole [of her form], as if creating a distinct arrangement of a forest. (15)
With feet that were tender like soft petals and flowers, never crushed and unfading, they appeared like garlands of land-lotus petals, yet did not touch the ground. (16)

"By feet that are like flowers or tender sprouts which are neither crushed nor withered"—if the reading were *pallavakomalaiḥ*, it would be self-evident. Since the resemblance to a lotus is already obtained through the metaphor (*rūpaka*) of the feet being flowers, the phrase "resembling a garland of petals" (*dalamālābhaiḥ*) is stated to avoid redundancy. || 16 ||
By the nectar-like sprinklings of their gaze, they caused young sprouts to emerge from the dry trunks of the palmyra and tamāla trees, which possessed pure luster. || 17 ||
Of those with pure radiance and white color. || 17 ||
Having said, "Homage be to the two forest goddesses," Jyeṣṭhaśarman then offered a handful of flowers along with his household.
The eldest son was named Jyeṣṭhaśarman. || 18 ||
A handful of flowers fell at their feet within the house,
like a shower of frost-drops upon the two lotuses of a lotus-pond.
A shower of frost-spray is a rain of droplets of ice; [this refers to] the lotus-plant, the creeper of lotuses. || 19 ||
"Jayatam" is the second person dual of the imperative mood. || 20 ||
Jyeṣṭhaśarman and the others said:
"Victory to you two forest goddesses, who have come for the sake of destroying our suffering!
For the protection of others is generally the innate duty of the virtuous. (20)
At the conclusion of those words, the two goddesses spoke with reverence: "Tell us the cause of this suffering, by which this person is seen to be so distressed. (21)
Jyeṣṭhaśarman and the others related their own suffering, consisting of the calamity that had befallen the couple, to the two goddesses in due order.
The vice and misfortune of a husband and wife consist of that very nature. || 22 ||

Jyeṣṭhaśarman and the others said: "O Goddesses, may you both become affectionate Brahmin couples here, the founders of a lineage who welcome all guests and serve as pillars for the stability of the twice-born. (23)
The two goddesses are the lineage and the progeny of the twice-born; they are the pillars that serve as the support for the stability of the world's moral order.
Since our parents have abandoned their home—including their sons, cattle, and kinsmen—and departed for heaven, the three worlds are empty because of them.
The word "today" (*adya*) signifies a state of not being long [since]. It is empty, as if it were empty. || 24 ||
Perching upon his house and scattering [their cries] at every moment, the birds mournfully lament with sweet voices for his body, which lies dead in the empty dwelling out of devotion. || 25 ||

"According to the maxim: 'The full man sees the world as full; the lustful man sees the world as lustful; the afflicted man sees the universe as consisting of affliction; and the greedy man sees it as greedy, just like his own mind'—they say this with the words beginning 'the birds,' etc., tossing their own bodies into the empty sky. (25)
Distraught by the wailing and lamentation of the deep, heavy roar from within its caves,
the mountain weeps profusely with streams of tears as thick as rivers.
It was filled and overwhelmed by those mouths, which were like caves and whose speech consisted of the loud cries and lamentations of the preceptor and his disciples. || 26 ||
The quarters of the sky, raising cries of lamentation, with their garments of clouds stripped away and their breasts of clouds exposed,
were reduced to extreme emaciation, shattered by the heat of sighs.
Those whose clouds—acting as breasts—are "muktāmbara" (having abandoned the sky) and "tyaktavastra" (having cast off their garments);
in the case of the celestial side, the winds, being similar to sighs due to their dustiness from tears, are the "niḥśvāsāḥ" (sighs).
"Kārśyam" means lack of nourishment or emaciation. || 27 ||
With all his limbs wounded and mangled, making piteous and harsh cries, the wretched village remained intent on fasting, devoted to death. || 28 ||
With all his limbs wounded and mangled by rolling on the ground, striking himself, and so forth; the word "village" (grāma) here refers to people;
"intent on death" means desiring to die. || 28 ||
Day after day, from the clusters that serve as the sockets of their eyes, the trees shed warm teardrops of dew falling downward. (29)

"Day by day," [meaning] having made it the object of observation; the accusative case is used because of the rule "lakṣaṇetthaṃbhūtākhyāna... when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*. "Heat" (*tāpa*) refers both to sunlight and the fire of grief. || 29 ||
The street, where the movement of people had ceased, was grey with dust;
it stood empty-hearted, like a widow bereft of joy. (30)
The road, grey with alkaline salt-earth, stood like a widow, devoid of joy.
The creepers, whose chatter consists of the cries of cuckoos and bees, have had their tears of rain washed away;
sighing most fervently with heat, they strike their bodies with hands of tender shoots. (31)
They were made to chatter by cuckoos and bees. || 31 ||
To divide themselves into a hundred forms upon the surface of the great rock in this vast chasm,
these waterfalls fall down with bodies tormented by heat.

"To cut into a hundred pieces" means, that is to say, to pulverize. "In a chasm" refers to a pit; on the stone surface therein. If the reading is *śubhre*, it means on a crystal stone surface. || 32 ||
Deprived of their splendor, they became fearless, mute, and agitated in heart;
filled with blinding darkness, the houses fell into a state of profound desolation.
Mute and distressed by news of their joy, with their inner hopes shattered like household utensils and furnishings scattered within them— since they were of such a nature,
they, having become devoid of fortune beyond all doubt, entered the density of the forest. 33.
From the garden flower-beds, as they seem to weep with the humming of bees, a foul stench issues forth, which is another name for one's own fragrance. (34)
Even a sweet fragrance is censured as a "stench" by those afflicted with grief because it causes pain to their sense of smell. || 34 ||
Day by day, the vines that once sported upon the trees of Caitra become tasteless and withered;
they dissolve away, their eyes—clusters of blossoms—closing up. (35)
Those of such a nature cause the Caitra trees to flourish; if the reading is *caitya*, it is clear [that they cause the shrines to flourish]. They dissolve and fall apart.
Agitated, they set out to cast their bodies into the ocean; the small streams, tossing their forms upon the ground with a tumultuous clamor, began to flow away.
The mention of "canals" (kulyā) is an indicative mark for [the inclusion of] mere rivers. || 36 ||
The ponds remained within themselves in a state of motionless bliss, perceiving even their own extreme restlessness— the movement caused by the landing of mosquitoes— as free from fear.
Even though they were once exceedingly restless, even before the worldly activities of people began, these ponds now remain— without fear—

in a state of motionless bliss within their own essential nature, as if established in meditative absorption (samādhi), such that not even the slightest ripple caused by the landing of a mosquito can be imagined there. || 37 ||
"Surely today the sky has become adorned by our father with singing kinnaras, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and celestial nymphs. (38)
The mention of "father" (tāta) is also an elliptical expression for "mother. || 38 ||
Therefore, O two goddesses, please perform for us now the destruction of our grief;
for the sight of the great is never in vain. (39)
Having thus described grief, they state the intended meaning with the word "tat" (that): "tattasmāddhetoḥ" (for that reason). || 39 ||
When her son had spoken thus, she touched him on the head with her hand,
as a lotus plant, bending low with its leaf, touches its own supple root-knot.
By means of its sprout, it is as if [it loosens] the root-knot of its own continuum; by implication, this is understood to occur "when the water has receded. || 40 ||
By her touch, he abandoned that distress of suffering and misfortune, just as a mountain sheds the heat of summer through contact with the clouds of the rainy season.
Then, by the sight of those two goddesses, all the members of that household became possessed of fortune and liberated from suffering, like those who drink nectar.
Śrī Rāma said:
Why was the sight of his mother not granted to her son Jyeṣṭhaśarman by that playful power? Dispel my delusion for now.

Rāma raises a doubt, wondering why Līlā did not manifest herself in her former mother’s body to comfort her son, given her power of true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpatva*); he does so with the words "tayā" (by her). "Mātrā" means by means of the mother's body.
Regarding the word "moha" (delusion): the intention is that once delusion has vanished, the resulting doubt will disappear of its own accord. || 43 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
He by whom the collection of earth and the other elements is understood through the realization of them as such, for him they possess the nature of a physical body;
for another, however, they are merely empty space.

Since Līlā’s coming to her son’s house was for the purpose of examining the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca) and was not motivated by affection for her son, and since there is an absence of affection for the son once the falsity of the phenomenal world— including the son— is ascertained, the sublation of the root [cause] occurs through the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna).

Vasiṣṭha begins his reasoned reply with the words "By one who has awakened," etc., to show that the assumption of a previous body is untenable because it is impossible for one to maintain a material body distinct from the present one.
For one who is ignorant, the body is a collection of false earth and other elements; but for one who has awakened through the realization of true earth and so forth, [that body] is in reality...
The meaning is this: through delusion, the non-dual, absolute sky of consciousness alone assumes the nature of a physical body;
however, for another who knows the reality, because of the absence of that cause—ignorance—it remains as nothing but the non-dual, absolute sky of consciousness. || 44 ||
O dear one, that which is purely non-existent appears as if it were existent because of the perception of earth and so forth;
just as a ghost does not appear to a child when it is not perceived. (45)
Due to the delusion of a fool, or because of not perceiving it as such, a man appears as a ghost.

Just as that which appears as earth and so forth may in an instant become non-earth and so forth through the recognition of it as a dream within a dream, so too is it clearly evident even in the waking state. (46)
Through the thorough knowledge of the dream, that is, through the thorough knowledge of its nature as a dream. || 46 ||
Earth and the other elements are perceived as space when they are dissolved;
thus, indeed, for those whose constituent elements are agitated, there is an effort [of perception] toward space even within walls. (47)

This refers to those whose bodily constituents, such as bile, have been disturbed— that is, to those who are deranged. In dreams, one perceives cities or the earth, or empty excavations, against walls made of glass-like substances or similar materials that appear like openings.
And a woman seen in a dream, though empty of reality, performs a causal function for men. || 48 ||
An empty city is understood as a level expanse of ground that has been excavated; it performs purposeful functions such as massaging the feet and so forth. (48)
When space is perceived as earth and so forth, earth and the other elements arise in an instant;
even the next world is directly experienced during a state of fainting. (49)

He states with the words beginning "one's own" (*svam*) that it is established by the experience of all [beings] that the ultimate reality manifests according to its realization; the ellipsis to be supplied is "it is experienced by some. (49)
One fool perceives a Vetāla in the sky, while another, as he dies, sees a forest in the atmosphere; one perceives a mass of hair in the sky, and another perceives pearls in the sky.
Those who are terrified, intoxicated, half-asleep, or traveling by boat always see and experience things such as Vetālas, forests, and trees in the sky. (51)
The meaning is that—being terrified, frightened, agitated, intoxicated, half-asleep, and half-awake—they experience the activities resulting from that, such as fleeing and so forth. || 51 ||
(194) Therefore, the form of these categories appears as it has been cultivated through practice; it does not exist as a single [unit] from the perspective of ultimate reality. (52)
One is fixed. || 52 ||
But through effortless play, having realized as it truly is the non-existence of earth and the other elements, space alone shines forth in consciousness, though it has arisen as an error. (53)
How did the Buddha then say it was "just space"? Because it is an illusion and a false proliferation.
(53) For the sage who possesses the realization that the Self is Brahman, the mere space of pure consciousness—how, what, when, and from where could there be sons, friends, or wives? (54)
By means of four interrogative pronouns (*kiṃvṛtta*), the manner, the thing characterized by that manner, time, and cause are implied. || 54 ||
The visible world is unarisen from the very beginning, and that which appears is indeed the unborn itself;
for those possessing such perfect knowledge, how could there be perceptions of attachment and aversion? (55)
That the hand was placed playfully upon the head of Jyeṣṭhaśarman was the fruit of the consciousness that had awakened to the undertaking established by its power. (56)
One might ask: "In the absence of affection for his son and the like, why was the hand placed on his head as a mere play? To this he says:

"The hand... The fact that the hand was placed on the head was not the result of affection for his son; rather, it was for the sake of the power of that Jyeṣṭhaśarman, for the purpose of future welfare, and for the awakening of his resolve regarding his steadfastness.

The meaning is that in such [cognition], which consists of the commencement of past merit and the awareness of the Lord who bestows its fruit, the result is merely an illusory manifestation (vivarta) of the very consciousness that is the substratum of all. || 56 ||
For consciousness perceives exactly as it does; yet the subtle is even more pure than space.
O Rāghava, that very [consciousness] is everywhere the entire web of objects.
This has been experienced within imagined cities in dreams. || 57 ||
Restating the essential meaning of the creation, he concludes with the words "bodha" (awakening): "Just as [the Self] previously perceived and reflected."

Thus ends the twenty-sixth canto, titled "The Narration of the Cause for the Siddha’s Vision," within the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* in the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. || 26 ||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Explanation of the Causes for the Vision of the Siddhas," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
On that mountain slope, in that village, within the hollow of his pavilion—
Then those two women, who were accomplished yoginīs, vanished from sight while remaining right there. (Note: The reading "antardhim āpatur dṛṅmārgāt" is also found.)
Līlā, further amazed and longing to see her husband, was awakened by Jñapti; remembering her own births, she spoke at length. (1)

In the interior of that pavilion belonging to the brahmin’s residence—that is, within the open space of the pavilion—while they were situated there in front of Jyeṣṭhaśarman and the others, the two attained disappearance, that is, they vanished. || 1 ||
Then, while his household members remained with their suffering pacified and were occupied with their own duties, he thought, "A favor has been bestowed upon us by the two forest goddesses. (2)
They were intent upon their own duties and the tasks of their own homes.

Sarasvatī spoke of Līlā, who was merged in the space of the pavilion— she who is of the nature of the void, standing as if silent (or, according to another reading, "standing silently") out of a smile toward her who is likewise of the nature of the void. || 3 ||

"Reclined" means hidden from the sight of other people. To the question, "In that case, do you truly possess a body? he replies: "Of the nature of space. That is to say, she has a body consisting of empty volition (*saṃkalpa*). Such is the meaning. "From wonder" means from amazement;
it refers to those for whom there is a mutual conversation regarding volition and dreams.
Just as it performs causal efficiency here, so too is the discussion regarding those two.

"Surely, since those who exist through mutual volition cannot see one another, how can their agreement be possible? Having perceived this doubt of Rāma through his physical signs, Vasiṣṭha himself resolves it with the verse beginning "saṃkalpa-": "In the world, for those [beings] who, through the grace of a deity or other causes, possess exactly the same... as in the case of Uṣā and Aniruddha.

The meaning is this: just as a dream or a mutual consensus arises among them, and their subsequent conversation there brings about future causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), so too does the conversation—the mutual agreement—between those two acts of cognition (*jñapti*) function in the same way. || 4 ||
Even without the earth, the channels, the vital breaths, and so forth,
that consciousness of conversation arises between those two, just as it does in dreams and mental constructs.
The venerable Sarasvatī said: "The external elements, such as earth and so forth, and the internal body, characterized by the channels, vital breaths, and so on— even without these,
the object of knowledge has been known in its entirety through the consciousness of both seen and unseen objects."
[The reading is *draṣṭavyasaṃvidaḥ*]. Such is this reality of Brahman; tell me, what else do you ask? || 6 ||
Having thus resolved the doubt expressed, she follows the narrative at hand: Śrīsarasvatī said;
Līlā said: "This is the soul of my deceased husband, where he rules his kingdom."
"In that place, why was I not seen by them? And here, have I been seen by my son?"
For what reason? The meaning is that she was not seen. || 7 ||
Śrī Sarasvatī said: "O child, O lady of excellent complexion, without practice, your conviction regarding duality at that time certainly did not set completely."
"Without practice" means due to the absence of practice. "Certainty regarding duality" is the certainty that the phenomenal world (prapañca) is real. || 8 ||
How can one who has not attained non-duality (advaita) be joined with the practices of non-duality? For one established in asceticism, how could there be the experience of a shadow-body?

It has not gone away because it has not been reached through the destruction of the ignorance that causes differentiation. It is attained through non-dual actions, such as the purposeful activities of having true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*) and so forth. "A limb of the shadow" refers to its quality, coolness, or the experience thereof;
or it is the experience of the person whose limbs are seated in the shade. (9)
Without practice, the thought "I am Līlā" did not become established in you;
when that state of being arose, your power of true resolve (satyasaṃkalpatva) did not yet belong to you.
The firm latent impression (saṃskāra) is the state of mind that "I am indeed the body of divine play (līlādeha). || 10 ||
"Today you have become one whose resolve is true; therefore, O beautiful one, your cherished wish that 'my son may behold me' has borne fruit."
Today your true resolve has been fulfilled; your cherished desire, "May my son see me," has been attained.
(195) Now, if you go into the presence of that husband of yours, then your dealings with him will proceed just as before. (12)
Līlā said: "Right here, in the space of this temple, my husband was a Brahmin;
right here he died and became a lord of the earth. (13)

Thus, through both direct perception and instruction, her doubt regarding the impossibility of the meaning spoken by Prajñā having been removed, Līlā once again affirmed the existence of the two worlds of her husband and of thousands of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*), just as one might describe the presence of a palace within the space of a pavilion.
He requests the vision of his own circle of lords with the words beginning "here" (iha), etc. || 13 ||
Right here in this very cycle of existence, within that same circle of the earth,
in that royal capital city, I am stationed before him as his consort— this is the reading. (14)
The word *purandhrī* means the queen, the chief consort of the lord of the earth; this is to be supplied as the subject for the following. (14)
Right here in this very inner apartment, my lord of the earth has died;
right here in the space of the inner apartments, in that very city, is the king.
Endowed with sovereignty over various provinces upon the surface of the earth, he remains established right here in this very state, possessing the nature of speed through complete uprightness.

The straightness and lack of deceit in all things is the immutable, ultimate Brahman; the state of mobility imagined within it is merely a transformation such as illusory movement. Thus, that which is characterized by what has been described, seen, and heard, is established right here in the space of this pavilion. || 16 ||
I consider all the lands of the universe to be situated within this very space of the house, like heaps of mustard seeds inside a small water-jar.
In a small vessel, in a casket. || 17 ||
"I always consider that orb of my husband to be not far away;
act in such a way that I may see it as if situated right here at my side. (18)
"Not distant" means very near. || 18 ||
The illustrious Goddess said: "O daughter of Arundhatī on this earth, do you have three husbands at present, or were there many, numbering as many as a hundred? (19)
This is not only the case with what is present here in the space of the pavilion; rather, everything past and future is also there.

With the intention of asking which of the three mandalas situated nearby should be shown—since it is impossible for them all to see the various bodies denoted by the word "husband" belonging to their many past lives—he said: [He spoke with the thought: "Among these three [mandalas] present here, which one shall be revealed?"
But among those three who were nearest, O twice-born one, he was reduced to ashes;
the king remained as a corpse within the inner apartments, hidden inside a garland.
Among those that are most proximate; in the domain of the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*, the suffix *īyasun* is Vedic. || 20 ||
For in this mandala of saṃsāra, the third lord of the earth has fallen into the great ocean of saṃsāra and come to wander within it. (21)
Having fallen, he entered. || 21 ||
Devoid of the play of the waves of enjoyment, his consciousness is defiled;
with the functions of his mind shattered by dullness, he is a tortoise in the ocean of saṃsāra. 22.

He is distressed and distracted by the mental constructions of the waves characterized by worldly enjoyments; for this very reason, his consciousness—his intellect—is joined with impurity. Consequently, even the activity of the conscious principle reflected within him is shattered and rendered almost inert by that very dullness. 22.
Even while performing various and tumultuous royal duties, he remains as if asleep or standing in a state of dullness; he does not awaken from the delusion of worldly existence.
"I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, powerful, and happy"—bound by this great rope of misfortune, he has fallen under its control. (24)
Lack of mastery means lack of independence. || 24 ||
Tell me, O woman of excellent complexion, for which husband do I bring you from the forest to his presence, like a whiff of fragrance carried by the wind from one forest to another? (25)
A collection of winds is a *vātyā*. [The suffix] *ya* is applied after words such as *pāśa*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.2.49).
For this cycle of existence is indeed one thing, and that pavilion of the cosmic egg is another;
O child, the successions of worldly activities are likewise entirely different. (26)
They are extended and broad. || 26 ||
Even though those circles of cyclic existence (saṃsāramaṇḍala) stand here at one's side,
the distance between them here is many millions of millions of yojanas.
"Here" means in this space of the pavilion. "Internally," by the perspective of the foundational consciousness (*adhiṣṭhāna-cit*), means in the vicinity—so to speak.
"Even though" (*api*) means even if that is so; nevertheless (*tathāpi*), in this worldly perspective (*sāṃsārika-dṛṣṭi*), there is a great distance, meaning a separation. || 27 ||
Behold again and again how their bodies are merely empty space;
yet within them reside millions upon millions of Merus and Mandaras. (28)
But from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), it says: "merely space.
This is the ultimate body, the true nature, of these circles of saṃsāra—namely, merely the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) situated within the pavilion. Within all of these... || 28 ||
In every single atom, all categories flash forth without obstruction from the Great Consciousness, like motes of dust shimmering in the rays of the sun. (29)
Within the rays situated amidst the mass of light of the sun. || 29 ||
For even though the cosmic eggs are thus heavy with great undertakings,
they do not equal even a single grain of rice on a scale.
In this way, just like the manifested universe, those seeds—

though heavy and vast due to the commencement of great continents, oceans, worlds, and so forth— are seen by the balance of the vision of consciousness as mere grains, like the seeds of a banyan tree. (The reading "dhānakā" refers to the seeds.)
The meaning is that they do not exist even to that extent. || 30 ||
Just as a forest shines in the sky with the stainless radiance of various jewels,
so the world shines as consciousness when devoid of the elements such as earth, through meditative reflection.

In reality, consciousness alone, devoid of distinctions such as earth and so forth, shines as the world; it appears so only through thought—that is, through the firm latent impressions born of ignorance.

"This world is nothing but pure consciousness (jñapti) alone"—such [a realization] shines forth within the Self, but not as something consisting of earth and other elements that was produced at the beginning of creation. 32.
He says that even though the world appears through delusion, nothing whatsoever has ever actually come into being in reality:
"Just as a wave in a lake, having arisen again and again, may appear to possess various forms, times, limbs, and locations, so too is this [world] merely a manifestation of the Command (ājñā). (33)

The meaning is that times of various forms, the limbs of time such as days and nights, and the worlds such as the cosmic eggs and regions, having come into being again and again within the Great Consciousness (mahāciti) which is pure awareness, they continue to exist. || 33 ||
Līlā said: "O Mother of the World, it is exactly as I have now remembered here;
this birth of mine is characterized by passion (rājasa), neither of darkness (tāmasa) nor of goodness (sāttvika). (34)

This birth as Līlā is characterized by *rajas*, being an effect of *rajas* due to the abundance of suffering and torment; for it is said that "those of a *rājasa* nature remain in the middle," and because of the traditional teaching that human births possess a *rājasa* quality—this is the meaning. || 34 ||
"O Brahmā, as I have descended [into this world], I now see again, as it were, the eight hundred births through which I have passed in various wombs. (35)

This refers to her who has descended there as a reflection at the beginning of this kalpa, due to the arising of the internal organ (antahkarana) as an adjunct from Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha; "I see clearly" means, in effect, "I remember. || 35 ||
O Goddess, in a certain part of the circle of saṃsāra in the past, I was a Vidyādhara woman, a bee among the lotuses of other worlds. (36)
One should know that the world of the Vidyādharas is another world; that itself is the lotus.
Then, defiled by evil latent impressions (vāsanā), I became a human woman;
in another cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra), I was the beloved of the Lord of Serpents.
Having become a human woman, she remained there; then, the connection is that she became the beloved of the lord of the serpents. || 37 ||
Dwelling in groves of kadamba, kunda, jambīra, and karañja trees, clad in leaves for garments, I then became a dark-skinned Śabarī. (38)
Deluded by my dwelling in the forest, I then became arrogant;
with eyes like flower-clusters and hands like leaves, I was a playful maiden of the woods.

In the reading *vāsanayā*, the meaning is clear. However, in the reading *vāsatayā*, it means "by virtue of dwelling in the forest" (*vana-vāsa*); she is "deluded" (*mugdhā*), that is, ignorant, insofar as she is unaware of the boundaries of dharma (*dharma-maryādā*). For this very reason, she is "arrogant" (*uddhatā*) due to the accumulation of evil deeds. The word *guluccha* refers here to a cluster of its flowers; [the creeper] has become a forest-dwelling vine (*vanavilāsinī latā*).
By implication, it is understood that she is like a cluster of blossoms. || 39 ||
I, that very same creeper from the meritorious hermitage, purified by association with sages, became the daughter of that very great sage after being consumed by the forest fire. (40)
Through the ripening of those karmas that yield the fruit of non-femininity,
I became a glorious king in the Surāṣṭra lands for a hundred years.

The state of being male, rather than female, [is attained] for as many years as there were [instants] of the previously accumulated karmas that bestow the fruits of enjoyment such as sovereignty upon one so engaged. || 41 ||
Due to the fault of the king's evil deeds, I became a female mongoose with limbs ruined by leprosy for nine years on the marshy banks of the Tālī trees. (42)
*Kaccha* refers to regions consisting mostly of water. *Rājaduṣkṛtadoṣaḥ* refers to the king's fault of committing evil deeds, such as the seizure of others' property and so forth. (42)
O Goddess, for eight years in the lands of Surāṣṭra, I assumed the form of a cow out of delusion, through the playful behavior of wicked, ignorant, and foolish cowherd boys. (43)

Surāṣṭra refers to specific regions. "Cowhood was made" means that the state of being born as a cow was experienced. [This was brought about] by the play of beating, chasing, and so forth, on the part of those cowherds who were wicked, evil, ignorant, and childish. || 43 ||
The snare set by Vaira for the bird in the forest expanse was severed with great effort,
just like the base latent tendencies (vāsanā).
By me, having attained birth as a female bird through a female bird, snares were set by hunters due to groundless enmity;
these are base latent impressions, namely the latent impressions of duality. 44.
She rested together with her soiled companion, who lay within the heart of the lotus's pericarp,
having enjoyed the filaments in private within the hollows of the lotus buds.
The centers of the pericarps, the middles of the filaments—these indeed are the beds. "Buds" means closed blossoms.
"Together with the bees"—by implication, it is understood that [the bees] have attained birth as female bees. || 45 ||
She wandered through the delightful forest glades on her lofty-horned antelope, whose eyes were captivating, while her vital organs were being struck by Kirātas.
I shall seize her who is to be sought by me, she whose eyes captivate and whose glances are delightful. 46.

As she was being carried away by the waves of the ocean when all directions had vanished from her sight, she saw that her striking of her face against the leaping of fish, water, and turtles was in vain. (47)

Carried away by the waves of the ocean, I was [caught] like a fish—there is the elision of the *ya* of the suffix *yat* according to the rule "sūryatiṣyāgastyamatsyānāṃ ya upadhāyāḥ. When the directions had vanished due to a confusion of the quarters (*digbhrama*), I arrived near a fisherman; that is to say, I reached the vicinity of a fisherman. There, a beating was inflicted upon the region of my face by the fishermen with sticks and other implements, brought about as if by fate.
The meaning is that it was seen to have become futile and useless due to falling into the water of great waves, into the tossing about of turtles, and onto the bones of a turtle's shell. || 47 ||

On the banks of the Carmaṇvatī, he drank the coconut-juice liquor after lovemaking with a Pulinda woman who was singing in a sweet voice. (48) [In the reading *pulindasuratānteṣu*, the meaning is "with a Pulinda woman" (*pulindyā*) at the conclusion of sexual unions.]
"It was drunk by me, the Pulindī"—this is the ellipsis. || 48 ||
The crane, delighted by amorous play with his mate who was languid with passion— she who uttered sweet,
sighing sounds— was as charmed as a vassal king by his pleasures.
Just as a passionate female bee remains motionless upon a lotus pond full of nectar,
so too was the lord— the sovereign, that is, my husband— delighted and gratified by me with sweet-sounding *sītkāra* (the sighing sounds of sexual union). || 49 ||
In the groves of *tālī* and *māla* trees, she whose face and eyes were tremulous cast glances at her lover with the agitation of intoxicated looks. (50)

I cast glances like those of one intoxicated—looks full of passion—and gazed upon my beloved with the agitations of love caused thereby; by this, a birth in a future life worthy of such [passion] has been indicated.
In heaven, the celestial bees were quickly gratified by the lotus-like Apsaras with their bodily frames as beautiful as a mass of flowing gold.
*Syanda* means flowing. By means of the lotus-pond characterized as an *apsaras*, the gods themselves—acting as bees—were gratified by drinking the honey of her lower lip and so forth. || 51 ||
On the ground strewn with heaps of jewels, gold, rubies, and pearls,
amidst groves of wish-fulfilling trees on Mount Meru, he took his pleasure with the youth.
In that very same birth, [he was] Devayūnā. || 52 ||
I have long remained in the form of a tortoise upon the shores agitated by great waves, amidst the shimmering clusters of creepers, and within the forest caves on the ocean's edge.
In the form of a tortoise, that is, as a female tortoise. || 53 ||
In the waves that rose and fell, I sported with the female royal swans as they dangled among the moving clusters of their wings. 54.

In the lakes whose waves were trembling, upon my own moving lotus leaves which were like white cloths, I made the rows of bees— sitting there under the delusion that they were lotuses— perform the role of royal female swans (*rājahaṃsī*) by means of their swaying.
That is to say, "experienced. In the reading *nalinīnāladolāsu*, the meaning is clear. || 54 ||
Having observed the wretched state of the mosquito, who was being worn out by the swaying of the *śālmalī* leaf, I remained as still as a mosquito myself. (55)

While a single śālmalī leaf was swaying amidst many restless mosquitoes, seeing that a certain mosquito who had fallen from it was unable to settle there and was thus deprived of the motion, [the others]— by the very impression of that [state]— ...
The meaning is that, according to the Smṛti passage, "Whatever state one remembers at the time of death," I too, having become a mosquito, remained in a miserable condition when she died. || 55 ||
And he wandered among the mountain torrents, where the waves were rising higher and higher, kissing the tips of the dancing ripples, and mimicking the playful movements of water-fowls. (56)
By his playful movement, the *vetasa* reeds along with the water in the mountain streams and mountain rivers [were stirred]; "by his birth" means by his coming into existence. || 56 ||
Formerly, young Vidyādhara princes, afflicted by passion, fell at her feet in the Mandāra palace on Mount Gandhamādana. (57)
Having described births in the lowest wombs ending with those of immobile beings, he also speaks of superior births, beginning with "Gandhamādana... and so forth.
Afflicted by my passion, I have long wallowed upon couches strewn with heaps of camphor, like the radiance of the moon upon the lunar orbs.
There too, he shows the abundance of suffering with the word "strewn": afflicted by calamity, which is the pain of separation from that [beloved]. (58)
I have wandered through wombs filled with hundreds of various kinds of suffering, my limbs agitated by rising and falling,
like a shifting wave upon the long river of saṃsāra.
In the manner of the flight of a doe pursued by an irresistible wind. || 59 ||

He summarizes what has been said concisely with the words "among wombs" (*yoniṣu*). Like the tip of a balance scale, rising is upward movement and bowing is downward movement; she whose limbs were agitated by these two was one whose mind was distraught. A *vātahariṇī* is a "wind-deer.
For it is well known that by its very nature, it follows the flow of the wind and wanders through high and low places. (59)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh canto, titled "The Description of Previous Births," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, a work of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Previous Births," in the Utthāna-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-eighth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
From the wall of the cosmic egg, which is a dense sphere with a core as solid as adamant, [he emerged].
How did you two, being so weak, emerge from that place which was ten million yojanas thick?
Because the manifold of appearances has been seen to be false, the reality of the space of consciousness [is established];
here, the mountain and the mountain village are described in detail. (1)

"Like a limb of a diamond, [it is] firm due to its essence; from that which is thus characterized—being perfectly nourished and solid internally for many millions of *yojanas* according to the manner previously described—the intention of the objector is that exit is impossible because even a wall or similar object, though illusory, is observed to obstruct movement in a dream. (1)
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
Where is the cosmic egg, where its wall, and where in this context is that adamantine hardness,
when the two goddesses are surely situated within the space of the excellent inner apartments?

With the intention that "let there be a sublater in an uncontradicted state, for it is not seen even in a dream to be itself contradicted," Vasiṣṭha replies with the verse beginning "Where is the cosmic egg? and so forth. [The word] "necessarily" (avaśyam) refers to the actual reality.

Regarding the term "the two goddesses" (devyau), it is a *ekaśeṣa* compound formed by retaining both the word *devī*, derived from the king's title *deva*, and another [instance of the same word]. || 2 ||
In that very mountain village, in that same celestial abode,
that Brāhmaṇa named Vasiṣṭha enjoys sovereignty.
Being far removed, he relishes and experiences [it]. || 3 ||
That very corner of the pavilion's space, which was mere emptiness,
he experienced as the surface of the earth extending to the limits of the four oceans.
Padmabhūpāla experienced this while being alive.
Upon the surface of the earth within the self of space is that royal city;
there he experiences the royal palace, and she too experiences it as Arundhatī.

A *pattana* is a city; in that [city] is the royal palace. And as for the phrase "she experiences," this is an indication in the present tense used for the immediate future (*vartamānasāmīpye*). Alternatively, having attained a state of being essentially identical with the other *līlās* (pastimes) to be described—which were produced by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of Vidūratha—Arundhatī experiences them; thus, the primary sense of the present tense is established. || 5 ||
She was born with the name Līlā, and by her Jñapti was worshipped;
together with Jñapti, she leaped across the sky, which was wondrous and enchanting.
In a space of only a span within that very interior of the house,
she reached another universe within the temple of the mountain village.
Having emerged from the cosmic egg, he returned to his own abode,
just as a man lying on a bed passes from one dream to another.
All this is merely a mental flash, nothing but empty space;
there is no cosmic egg, no cycle of existence, no walls and such, and no distance.
Inspiration is merely that [mental] error. 9.

Their own mind alone shines forth as such a captivating thing, with its delineation arising from mere latent impressions (vāsanā); where is the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and where is worldly existence (saṃsṛti)? 10.
By means of mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it shines forth together with the manifestation of the conventional usage of various objects;
thus, their own mind alone shines and expands in that manner. (10)
This infinite space of pure consciousness is indeed without obstruction;
it is merely stirred by one's own mind, just as the wind is set in motion by the principle of vibration.

The space of cognition is indeed the space of consciousness; by those two, nothing in the form of a cosmic egg has been projected or imagined within one's own mind. Just as space itself is conceived as "wind" through its association with vibration, so it is here. 11.
The unborn and tranquil sky of consciousness indeed exists everywhere and at all times;
yet, by virtue of its nature as consciousness, it appears of its own accord as the world within itself, by means of itself.
The world appears as if it were real; that by which it is not perceived—that is the vision—such is the remainder [of the verse]. || 12 ||
For one by whom the Buddha is not perceived, this [world] is even more empty than space;
for one by whom the Buddha is perceived, this [world] is like a mountain of solid essence.

He says "by which" (*yena*) to show that for one who has seen the Buddha, [the world] does not exist at all. Then, as to how others likewise do not emerge outside the wall of the universe, he says "not the Buddha" (*na buddham*). || 13 ||
Just as a brilliant city appears within a house in a dream,
so too does this unreal world appear luminously within the element of consciousness.
Just as water is perceived in a mirage and the state of being a bracelet in gold,
so too does this objectivity appear as if real within the Self, though it is unreal. (15)
"Being an object of vision" means having the nature of the manifest world of objects. || 15 ||
Thus conversing, those two women of graceful form emerged from the house and went outside with beautiful, measured steps.
An external location; walking is the act of moving. || 16 ||
While being watched by the villagers from a visible distance,
he [the mountain] stood before them, kissing the hollow of the sky and touching the orb of the sun.
The "hollow of the sky" refers to its central cavity; this is a conceptual distinction made for the sake of description, similar to the expression "the head of Rāhu.
The phrase "having touched the solar disc" is a hyperbole (atiśayokti). || 17 ||
It was pure with various multicolored and fully blossomed, diverse groves;
it resounded with the noise of many waterfalls and the warbling of forest birds.
The circle of clouds was tawny with masses of variegated flower-clusters,
and the cranes and sarasa birds rested upon the tips of their own swaying tufts of blossoms.

This describes the height of the tree: it possesses circles of clouds that are tawny with clusters of flower-buds and are therefore variegated; for this very reason, its own sky is endowed with beautiful clouds. "Gulucchā" refers to specific types of creepers. || 19 ||
Its entire riverbank was concealed by a dense thicket of *vañjula* trees laden with fruit;
there, the wind was occupied with carving out stone cavities and winding through the creepers.

Where the riverbanks are protected from falling by the strong trunks of *vañjula* trees, or by the extensive root-systems of *atimuktaka* and water-reeds (*ambuvetasa*), and where there is the winding movement of creepers grown in rock fissures that have not properly reached or secured a support upon the trees.
In which [the syllable] Māruta [is located]. || 20 ||
The sky was its inner chamber, covered by the tips of flowers as its walls;
it was a cloud from which fell the long streams of rivers like shimmering clusters of pearls.
Its walls of the sky-receptacle—the clouds—are concealed by mountain-trees whose tips are laden with flowers;
its waterfalls are like shimmering strings of pearls.
Its riverbanks were stirred by winds blowing through groves of swaying trees,
and its outskirts were perpetually cooled by the shade of various forests.
In which [forests] the arrays of groves consist of swaying trees; for that very reason, the riverbanks therein are characterized by being enveloped by the wind. || 22 ||
Then those two young women themselves beheld that mountain village there, appearing like a fragment of heaven fallen from the sky. (23)
Having praised the mountain, he speaks in order to describe Girigrāma, beginning with "atha" (now). || 23 ||
It possessed a multitude of water-channels resounding with noise and clusters of full lotus-pools;
its marshy banks were filled with the playful warbling of birds and the soft cooing of cuckoos.

By the qualifying term "raṭat" (resounding), systems such as water-wheels (ghaṭī-yantra) are to be understood. Through the imitation of sound in the word "kucakucaiḥ," there is an expression of superimposition (āropa) based on similarity to that sound.
In that [place], there were ravines and hollows intended for the sport of his village, which resounded with birds (dvijaiḥ) of that kind. 24.
The entire grove was made formidable by the "hum" sounds of herds of cows passing through; it was rich with bowers, thickets, and clusters of trees, and possessed shady, lush grassy meadows.
In that regard, he describes the abundance of cattle with the word "gacchat" (going); he describes the prosperity of the cows' fodder, shade, and so forth with the word "kuñja" (bush). || 25 ||
The interior of the street was difficult for the rays of the sun to enter, grey with lingering mist,
and tangled with dense clusters of lofty blossoms.
Grey with stones, rocks, and mists as if smeared with ashes,
it was a mountain whose few peaks had matted locks hanging down from the intervals between them in the form of clusters of upright flower-buds.
With waterfalls released by the splashing of the waters within the rocky caverns,
it recalled the beauty of the milk-ocean waters churned by the mountains.

In that place, the splendor of the waters of the Ocean of Milk churned by Mount Mandara is recalled by waterfalls from which drops resembling pearls fly upward upon the impact of the water against the crevices in the rocks.
The courtyard was crowded with trees that seemed to stand there having brought a mass of flowers, shining with the great weight of their fruits and blossoms.
The courtyard is a place of no decay. || 28 ||
It was showered with scattered flowers by trees agitated by emotion, which were themselves shaken by winds producing the "jhāṃkāra" sound from the rippling waves.

The meaning is: since even the trees, agitated by *rasa*—both nectar and the excess of love—have showered [their bounty] perfectly upon supplicants, how much more so must it be for human beings? || 29 ||
The birds, though hidden, let out slight cries as they were startled by the sounds of water droplets trickling from the unsuspected peaks of the rocks; thus, those who were unafraid became fearful.

By those who were unsuspecting— though they were actually worthy of suspicion— and who remained hidden and concealed precisely because they had become suspicious due to the *ṭakṛt* sounds caused by water droplets falling and trickling from the mountain peak; these sounds being similar to the twang of a pellet-bow.
By birds. || 30 ||
It was surrounded by birds that, weary from leaping upon the waves, tasted the spray,
and moved with the circling motion of the moon’s reflection in the river.
Fatigue is the cause for tasting the spray [of water]. By those birds—swans—whose movement is like the revolution or turning around of the *uḍu* stars, the constellations. || 31 ||
The children, fearing the gaze of crows resting on the tall palm trees,
had hidden away the pieces of sugarcane molasses that they themselves had previously eaten.
The mention of "crows" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) that includes cats and other such creatures.

It refers to a place where pieces of *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) have been hidden and protected in a secluded spot with the thought, "We shall eat these when they are old and from our own morning meal. *Āmikṣā* is milk that has been thickened. 32.
It was cooled by the thickets of date palms, neem trees, and citron trees at its edge, and filled with village boys wearing flower garlands, festive ornaments, and fine garments.
Where village boys were present, who had flowers alone as their collection of garlands, and whose head-ornaments and so forth, as well as their garments, were likewise made of flowers. || 33 ||
With hands and garments of fine linen, her ears filled with flower-clusters, emaciated by hunger, that beloved of a village wretch traversed the highway. (34)

In that context, he describes the poor wife of a Bhilla and others with the verse beginning "kṣauma": she whose garments (*ambara*)—the tips of the flax plants (*atasī*), which are their branches (*śākhā*)—are so long they can be grasped by the hand; she who is like an insect in the village, neglected by the wives of those who are poor, low-born, and indolent. (34)
The clamor of the collision of the waves was drowned out by conversation;
there, the people remained in solitary retreat, desiring to escape the dense fear born of the dullness of karma. (35)

Where conversations and dialogues are not heard due to being overwhelmed by clamor and loud noises; where solitude is desired by those who are charmingly languid, their fear of wealth arising from clumsiness and dullness in performing tasks. (35)
The courtyard was crowded with naked children whose faces, hands, and shoulders were smeared with curd, who wore fresh flower-garlands, and who were marked with streaks of cow-dung mud.
(199) With its sandy banks marked by lines [of footprints], it was being swept by waves that caused the grass, creepers, and vines on the shore to sway like swings. (37)
If "tīraśādvala" and so forth are taken as qualifiers of the previously mentioned young women (*bālā*), they mean those who cause them to sway upon swings;

if, however, they are qualifiers of the waves, they mean those that cause the water being carried along to sway like a swing, and thus the sandy bank is marked by the streaks or lines of that water. 37.
The bees were sluggish and intoxicated by the fragrance of the thick curd and milk;
the children were broken with tears arising from the exhaustion of having consumed as much as they desired.

Wherein there are women who are weak, emaciated, and dependent, their voices broken by tears from weeping for the sake of enjoying sensual pleasures—that is, for eating according to their desires—and wherein there are children. 38.
Women in the courtyards, having sprinkled cow dung, were feigning anger; while other women, terrified, were laughing as they busied themselves arranging their braided hair. 39.

In that place, people laugh upon seeing those women who, having loosened their braided hair, are busily occupied with it, while they appear as if enraged toward other women because they have smeared their hands with cow-dung around their wrists.
Where crows were swooping down upon the abundant petals of *dānta* flowers,
and where cruel *kuraṇṭaka* shrubs were scattered across the house-alleys, courtyards, and gateways.

Where the ravens, falling upon the mountain peaks (*kakuda*) to consume the offerings of *balikarma* such as unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), have been driven away by sages who have subdued their anger and are self-controlled— not with wood or clods of earth, lest there ever be injury— [the place] is overgrown with flowers, canopies, or leaves; [the place] is cruel because of its thorns.
*Kuraṇṭakas* are well-known varieties of shrubs where [they grow]. || 40 ||
Every morning, the courtyard was strewn with flowers up to the ankles by ravines and hollows situated at the side of the house, which possessed the luster of blossoming flowers.
It contained patches of forest thick with nets of *cāra*, *camara*, and *sāraṅga* deer;
there, fawns of wild animals slept upon the young grass growing within the thickets of *guñjā* shrubs. (42)
The *camara* deer, the *sāraṅga* deer, and birds are wandering about, feeding on the young grass (*śaṣpa*) that has grown in the bower—
the vine-cottage. Regarding the word "village" (*grāma*),
its usage includes not only the boundary stones (*sīmā*) but also the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), as seen in the *Mahābhāṣya* and other texts.
Because it is well-known, there is no contradiction even when describing the jungles, groves, and other features within it. || 42 ||
Like those who have fallen into a deep sleep, they were stirred by the twitching of a single ear;
like curd left over by a cowherd, they were visited by flies and the flickering of gnats.
[He was seen] on the curved sides of the cowherds' mouths, which were smeared with curd from leftover food. || 43 ||
Honey was scattered by bees whose homes were destroyed throughout the entire dwelling;
the house was made crimson with lac from the garden of blossoming aśoka trees. 44.
In all the houses, the honey had been gathered and collected in such a way that the bees were completely exhausted; and in that place, there were play-palaces made of wood and dyed with lac.
The trees were perpetually moist and in full bloom due to winds carrying showers of spray;
all the grass covering the ground was pierced by the buds of the *kadamba* tree.
Because they are eternally moist, they are *vikaca*, meaning fully blossomed. The adjective *samasta* (all) is used for the sake of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
[The forest] is white with clusters of blooming *ketaka* flowers from every creeper, and it carries the deep, heavy humming sound of swarms of bees moving through the network of living channels.
Precisely because they were adverse, there was no obstruction from the creepers that had been cut and severed, nor from those in full bloom. || 46 ||
Clouds rested upon the palaces emerging from the windows of the caves;
it was filled with rows of full lotus-pools and abounded in vast royal elephants.
In the rows of lotus ponds, the full moons are the fully blossomed lotuses;
by means of these, it is "pṛthūttaram," meaning exceedingly vast or most excellent. Alternatively, it is called "pṛthūttaram" because it is crossed over by those who are broad and tall. || 47 ||
The cool, pure grassy meadow was shaded by dense foliage,
and the stars were reflected in the dewdrops upon the tips of every blade of young grass.
Its dwellings were white with an incessant, falling rain of blossoming snow;
its trees bore wonderful clusters of blossoms, leaves, and excellent fruits.
They were white and brilliant with blossoms and showers of snow. || 49 ||
The young women were asleep within the inner chambers of the house because the clouds had settled there,
and the lightning from the clouds over the mansions rendered the lamps useless.
Where young women and married ladies are asleep; "not to be taken" means not to be accepted because the accomplishment of the task can be achieved by other means.
Its pavilions resounded with the deep, humming gurgling of winds from the mountain caves;
its delightful dwellings were graced by wandering cakoras, hārītas, and female deer.
Wherein there were pavilions thickened by echoes, making them resonant with a deep humming sound;
or, like clouds, they were resonant and thundering, or [the pavilions] were beautiful like the *cakora* and *hārīta* birds. They were lovely (*hārīṇi*).
With breezes moving slowly toward it, languid with the thick fragrance exhaled by blossoming kandalī flowers, the tree’s tender leaves were set in motion.
With *kandalas*, that is, *kandalī* flowers; filled with slow-moving fragrances as if they were being vomited forth or issued out. || 52 ||
It was filled with throngs of women absorbed in the playful conversation of quails,
and it was tumultuous with the clamor of ruddy geese, cuckoos, and crows.
The mention of quails (*lāvaka*) is also indicative of parrots, starlings, and the like; *kākolāḥ* refers to *droṇa*-crows. || 53 ||
It was garlanded with the blue fruits of *śāla*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, and *abja* trees,
and its trees were entwined with the graceful arrangements of encircling creepers.
Of those pavilions formed by the dancing leaves of *tālī* and *tamāla* trees,
whose windows were entwined with creepers of swaying shoots, and which were fragrant with blooming *kandalas* and *śilīndhras*;
Of those [places] cooled by trees with blossoming flowers that dispel the heat of Māra. || 55 ||

"Ālolapallavalatānām" refers to the circles, coils, or rows of trembling leafy creepers; "tāyanānām" refers to those which serve as the substratum for their continuity. Alternatively, it means those whose paths or passages on all sides are entwined or obstructed by creepers.
All these are adjectives for the phrase "girimandirāṇām" (mountain-dwellings) found at the end of the verse in the section on creation. 55.
Of the herds of cows agitated by the movement of the boat's rudder, beautified by dark crops and flowering grounds,
and whose river-crossings were concealed by rows of trees on the banks—
Of those [trees] whose canopies of flowering creepers were densely interwoven. || 56 ||
Those [forests] whose cow-pens were agitated while crossing the waters during the movement of the rains—[the forests] where the currents of the rivers were hidden and covered. || 56 ||
[The lakes] whose lotuses were concealed by swarms of bees blinded by the fragrance, which was as sweet as the nectar of the jasmine flowers in the gardens;
Whose temples surpassed the abode of Indra in beauty, and whose garments were reddened by the pollen from rows of lotuses; || 57 ||
The lotuses in which were hidden or obscured by swarms of bees attracted by the fragrance; the implication is that this was due to pollen carried up by the wind. 57.
Of those [palaces] resounding with the gurgling roar of mountain rivers swiftly borne along,
radiant with the splendor of clouds as white as kunda flowers,
and where flowering creeper-cottages shimmered atop the mansions;
Of the birds with sweet voices, playful and restless. || 58 ||

Flowing with speed and force; radiant with the splendor of clouds, beautiful and as white as jasmine flowers; "kalakaṇṭhas" refers to those with sweet throats—the word "kaṇṭha" here indicates their song. || 58 ||
Where young men reclined upon carpets of blooming flower petals, and playful women moved about with garlands draped down to their feet;
a place bristling everywhere with beautiful, fresh sprouts.
The path of the arrows was filled with beautiful, shimmering, excellent creepers. || 59 ||
In which [forests] there were playful women wearing garlands that hung down to their feet;
and in which the paths were crowded with, or filled by, excellent creepers—or, alternatively, by supplicants who were like clusters of reeds.
Of those places crowded with soft, newly sprouted lotuses,
whose dwellings are veiled by lingering clouds,
and whose grounds are renowned for being green with necklaces of frost;
Of the women on the palace rooftops, whose limbs were agitated by the clouds and lightning.
By the word "nīhāra" (mist), rows of those water droplets are indicated; by means of such green grounds which possess "hāras"—that is, pearl necklaces—those [forests] are renowned. || 60 ||
Of those [forests] beautiful with the wafting fragrance of blooming blue lotuses, where herds of cows look upward toward the green pastures with lowing sounds,
and where the courtyards of the houses are filled with trusting and innocent deer;
Of the mountain torrents consisting of dense sprays of water dancing forth from the mouth. || 61 ||

In these [mountains], there are herds of cattle (*gokula*) that are captivating with their lowing sounds (*huṃkāra*), enchanting, and directed toward the green pastures—that is, toward the green grass. Because of the abundance of deer wandering here in confidence and trust, the suffix *ghan* is applied in the sense of a locus according to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*). Due to the thick spray from the waterfalls, they mistake them for rain.
It is the cause for the dancing of peacocks. || 61 ||
Of those whose distress was fanned by winds intoxicated by fragrance, who had forgotten their lamps due to the light of medicinal herbs blazing upon the ramparts,
and whose dwellings were filled with the clamor of agitated flocks of birds;
Of those whose conversations consist of the clamor of noble lineages and the unrefined.

Struck and driven away by the wind, which was reeling as if intoxicated by fragrance; the word *viklava* refers to a state of distress. On the ridges (*vapra*), the medicinal herbs are themselves the blazing creepers of light. Here, "clamor" (*kolāhala*) refers to the cries of birds.
A "nest" (*kulāya*) is a bird's dwelling. By the word "rivulet" (*kulyā*), mountain torrents are meant.
The conversations—the dialogues—in which [the sounds] were not heard, being overwhelmed, that is to say, eclipsed on all sides by the clamorous noises of those belonging to that family. || 62 ||

The beauty of all the trees, creepers, grasses, and tender shoots— whose drops of dew were as lovely as a scattering of pearls and whose flowers remained in full bloom without ever fading— was restored.
Who is able to calculate the number of mountain-dwellings? || 63 ||
To measure—that is, to calculate—the splendor or beauty of the mountain-dwellings, meaning those of the mountain village.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mountain Village," within the *Līlopākhyāna* (The Story of Līlā) of the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* (Book on Origination) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, a work of the Seers (*ārṣa*). || 28 ||
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Mountain Village," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
There, those two goddesses wandered within the village, which was cool in its inner nature.
The splendors of both enjoyment and liberation reside in one who is peaceful, just as they do in a man who has realized the Self.
Here, the recognition of Līlā’s former deeds is described,
as well as her return journey through the sky adorned by the multitude of worlds.
In the peaceful one, who is endowed with the means for achieving peace and so forth. || 1 ||
In that much time, through that practice, she became Līlā;
because her sole body was pure knowledge, she possessed stainless vision of the three periods of time.
Then she herself, by her own natural inclination, recollected all those previous states of existence from former births, including birth, death, and so forth.
"By its own force" means by effortlessness alone. || 3 ||
Līlā said:
"O Goddess, having seen this place through your grace, I remember everything that occurred here in the past, as well as all other subsequent deeds."
The other activity is the activity performed throughout the succession of his previous births. || 4 ||
In this world, I was once an old woman, with limbs covered in veins, emaciated and white-haired;
a Brahmin woman whose hands and belly were as rough as the tips of dry *darbha* grass.
"Jīrṇā" means aged. She is one whose hands and belly are rough with the tips of dry *darbha* grass—specifically their sharp parts, the points, and the splinters or fragments. || 5 ||
The wife is the perpetuator of her husband’s lineage, skilled in milking and churning;
she is the mother of all sons and the one who brings pleasure to guests. (6)
The churning-stick is the staff for churning curds.
Devoted to the gods, the twice-born, and virtuous men, her limbs were moistened with ghee and cow's milk;
she was the cleanser of frying pans, sacrificial pots, jars, and all other household utensils.

She is one whose nature is to purify through cleaning and other means the frying pan, the cooking pot, the sacrificial vessel, the cauldron for boiling offerings, and all other utensils and implements. (7)
(201) Her forearms were constantly smeared with fragments of food;
she was devoted to the worship of her son-in-law, daughter, brother, father, and mother. (8)
