A single glass conch or glass bracelet; for if many are worn, they are liable to break due to impact from haste in activity. || 8 ||
From the very moment she entered the house until her body perished, she spoke incessantly with agitation, saying "Wait, wait! for a long time.
By the word *deha* (body), its fall is indicated. *Sadmabhṛtiḥ* means the maintenance of the household.

She was habitually saying such things as, "You have bathed for a long time," "You have delayed for a long time," or "Why do you linger? regarding her sons, daughters-in-law, and circle of servants, for the sake of urging them to their tasks; she was thus agitated and distracted. || 9 ||
"What am I? What indeed is this saṃsāra?"—even such a conversation as this does not occur even in a dream for the wife of such a dull-witted, ignorant Vedic scholar. 10.
"Of such a one" means of one like me who is excessively attached to domestic duties; "of dull intellect" means of impure understanding. || 10 ||
She was intent on a single goal: the gathering of cow-dung fuel for cooking;
her head was wrapped in a faded blanket, and her limbs were emaciated. (11)
Regarding the collection of sacrificial fuel and other materials, she is single-minded—that is, one-pointed in mind; in other words, she is attentive. || 11 ||
She was intent on extracting the caterpillars from the ears of the calves; she was in a hurry to water the vegetables in the house-garden; and she had called for a broken potsherd.

*Tarṇakī* refers to a young calf; *karṇajāha* means the root of the ear; those who are situated at the root of her ears are the worms (*kṛmi*), and she is intent upon their extraction (*niṣkāsa*). In this compound, the suffix *jāhac* is applied according to the rule *pākan-mūla-pīlv-ādi-karṇādibhyaḥ kuṇap-jāhac-au*. In the house, *śākāyana* refers to a field of vegetables (*śāka-kedāra*); they were summoned there for the purpose of watering it.

By the word *karpara* (skull-cup), her hands—which hold the skull-cups used for the ritual of consecration (*sekasādhana*)—are indicated through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), meaning they are her servants.
The young calves were satisfied by the grass at the edge of the waves of the deep blue water;
every moment, the doors of the house were smeared with fresh plaster and color.

She by whom the cows with their young calves were nourished out of affection with grasses brought from there— the dark-blue limit, the boundary, and the bank of the water-waves— and by whom the door of the house was smeared with ointments and where decorative patterns of colored powders were fashioned.
For the sake of policy, she never transgressed the bounds of speech toward her household servants,
remaining as constant as the shore of the ocean due to its regulation by the law of the tides.

"Policy" (*nīti*) refers to instruction in discipline, conduct, and so forth; for that purpose, "blame" (*vācyatā*)—meaning public censure—is brought about or manifested in such a way as to be accompanied by extreme wretchedness (*ādīna*), such that people will say, "How can such ill-behaved and undisciplined servants remain in the house of these [people]? and so forth. This is the nature of such blame.
He states that [the Lord] is also a teacher of those boundaries by means of His own conduct: "The boundary," etc. (verse 14).
With one ear mounted upon a swing made of withered leaves,
she was marked as if by the very livelihood of living beings who, terrified of old age, strike themselves with wood.

Thus, she describes that state of life which belongs to her who has remained thus for so long, when—due to the extreme progress of old age—there is deafness in the left ear, trembling of the head, hunchbackedness, and movement dependent upon leaning on a staff:
"Withered," etc. Of the body, whose color is like a withered leaf, it is only the single right ear...

Because it was shaken by the trembling of the head, the ear— like a swing mounted upon it— was dependent on that very movement for its function of hearing; thus, when the supporting staff was raised, it was as if the sense of hearing were afraid of old age, which deserved to be struck by that very staff, and had consequently retreated from its final mode of existence.
The meaning is that one should remain unafraid here, as if marked by a sign. || 15 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, she wandered within the hollows of the mountain villages and,
with a smile, showed them to Sarasvatī as she was wandering along.
"Moving about" means wandering; "smaya" here signifies wonder. || 16 ||
This is my flower garden, adorned with clusters of *pāṭala* trees;
this is my grove of *aśoka* trees, a pavilion within a blossoming park. (Note: the reading *śokapeṭikā* is also found.)
It was adorned with clusters of trumpet-flower trees that were unbroken and uninterrupted.
This is the lotus pond where the young calves are unbound at the edge of the trees;
this is that cow named Karṇikā, who has cast off her withered leaves.

"Unknotted" means those that were slightly bound with knots have become loose; "muktaparṇikā" (one whose leaves have fallen) is understood here to mean [the creeper] due to the sorrow of separation from me. || 18 ||
This is that wretched water-carrier of mine, overcome by lethargy;
today, for the eighth day, she weeps with eyes drenched in tears. (19)
"Alasā" means incapable of performing her own duties due to distress; "strewn with dust" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 19 ||
"O Goddess, here I have eaten, here I have fasted, here I have stayed; here I have slept, here I have drunk, here I have given, and here I have taken. (20)
"Āhṛta" means brought or fetched; [it refers to] fruits, grain, and so forth. || 20 ||
"This son of mine, named Jyeṣṭhaśarman, is weeping in the house;
this milch-cow of mine grazes on the lush grass in the forest. (21)
May we behold this porch of mine, grey with dry salt and dust, which, like my own five-sensed body, exists only to burn down the house.
The ellipsis is "prepared for the burning of the Holi at the onset of spring. "Dusty with ash" means covered with alkaline ash.
"As dear to me as my own body"—the ellipsis is "my beloved. In the case of the body, "pañcākṣa" refers to the five windows (gavākṣas);
in the case of the [other] side, "akṣas" refers to the organs of perception. "Prapaṇam" refers to the outer porch of the doorway. || 22 ||
This kitchen area, surrounded by formidable and lush gourd vines,
is like a second body of mine.

It was encircled by bitter, pungent, and robust *tumbī* creepers and *alābu* vines—as if they had been planted and nurtured by her own hand—appropriately covering the area of the roof; "mahānasa-sthāna" means the kitchen. || 23 ||
These kinsmen, their eyes copper-red from weeping, have become a bond for the earth;
with rudrākṣa beads placed upon their armlets, they carry fuel for the fire.
Bondage consists of kinsmen who have become manifest bonds. || 24 ||
In the rocky clefts,
its form was constantly veiled by waves that snapped at clusters of flowers and touched the leaves of the creepers on the shore.
In the marshy region abounding in rocks, there is the clashing and striking [of waves].
By means of the waves— specifically characterized by the term "with sprays of blue lotuses"—
the mass of rays from the midday sun has been turned into frost, such that its true nature is veiled and its form obscured.
The connection with the subsequent verses is as follows: "This house-pavilion appears surrounded by a village canal that is filled with such trees on its banks. (25)
With its marshy banks and creepers on the edges drenched by spray, and with the spray from blue lotuses frothing as they strike against the surfaces of stone slabs; || 26 ||
The tips of which were covered with spray as they stood on grassy grounds; those [trees] had *phalahakas*, which are planks, and the striking against them was the "striking" (*āsphāla*);
by that, they became frothy, their spray being scented by blue lotuses. || 26 ||
(202) With the masses of rays from the midday sun turned into frost,
and with the trees on the banks resounding intensely due to the downpour of clusters of blooming flowers; || 27 ||
The bees, with showers of falling full-blown flowers, approached; by their loud humming, the trees on the bank stood as if filled with longing.
It was filled with heaps of flowers that caused great brilliance, appearing like coral through the reflected splendor of the blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees.

[The region] was filled with trees that produced the splendor and adornment of heaps of blossoms— like coral sprouts— by means of the beauty of the blooming *kiṃśuka* (palāśa) flowers that had been transferred and settled within [the water] by their reflections. 28.
By the village stream, intoxicated by its great tumultuous whirlpools, with its village children busily occupied by the abundance of fruit being carried along; (29)

In that [river], the village children were utterly distracted by thirst and fear as the flood of mangoes and other fruits was carried away by the currents; it seemed intoxicated, as it were, by its great clamor, its many tumults, and its whirlpools. (29)
Its rocky floor was washed by the waters tossed by the waves,
and it was perpetually cooled by the shade cast by dense-leaved trees.
This house-pavilion is now visible, beautiful with its swaying blossoming creepers, its windows covered by clusters of falling petals. (31)
It is beautiful because of its winding enclosures; its windows are covered by clusters of fruits and flowers that are falling and dispersing. || 31 ||
"Here resides my husband in the form of the space of life;
he was the lord of the earth, whose girdle extends as far as the four oceans. (32)
By virtue of being the living space (jīvākāśa), although he is formless and inactive, he remains established as the Lord of the Earth. || 32 ||
He remembered that previously he had indeed desired this:
"May I quickly become a king," by him whose nature was characterized by intense spiritual urgency.

The particle *ā* is not used for salutation, because it lacks the *ṅit* designation when expressing remembrance. O Supreme Goddess, with intense spiritual fervor and firm resolve, he obtained within eight days alone that prosperous kingdom which provides confidence for a long time.
O King, that lord of mine, my husband’s soul, remains here in the house in the sky, invisible like the wind in the atmosphere or like fragrance in the breeze. (35)
Right here, at the end of the space the size of a thumb, that very station is situated; my husband’s kingdom, extending for millions of yojanas, has been fully realized within that very void.
The meaning is that the state which abides as the ultimate reality, reaching the pinnacle of all connection with things, has been attained through delusion.
(36) "O Mistress, both we two and my husband’s kingdom are but the void, situated within the void;
it is filled with thousands of mountains—this is the expansion of Great Māyā. (37)
Kha here refers to the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). || 37 ||
Therefore, O Queen, it is my desire to go back to my husband’s city;
come, let us go there—for what distance is too great for those who are resolute? (38)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, she bowed to the Goddess and quickly entered the pavilion;
together with her, she flew through the sky, which was as white as a crane.
He flew up and soared into the great space conceived as the interior of the pavilion of the sky. || 39 ||
Resembling a mass of crushed collyrium, beautiful as a single tranquil ocean,
like the body of Nārāyaṇa, and possessing the pure luster of a bumblebee’s back.
"Saumyena" means with one that is unagitated; that is to say, motionless. "Ekārṇavasaṃnibham" means resembling or equal to a single ocean. || 40 ||
Having transcended the path of the clouds and likewise the region of the winds,
he then ascended the path of the sun and passed beyond the path of the moon.
The word "avani" refers to a specific location. || 41 ||

Having gone beyond the path of the fixed stars (Dhruva), having reached the path of the Sādhyas, and having completely traversed the earth and leaped over the realm of heaven (Svarga), [he proceeded]. 42.
The word "path" (mārga) refers to the world, because there is no path for the Pole Star (dhruva). The same applies to the word "earth" (urvī).
Having gone beyond the world of Brahmā to the realm of the Tuṣitas, and having transcended Goloka, Śivaloka, and the world of the ancestors; || 43 ||

The Vaikuṇṭha is the realm of the Tuṣitas, who are eternally content. It is called Pitṛloka because the two parents, Śiva and Śivā, are beheld there, or because it is beheld by the parents; thus, it is indeed the world of Śiva.
This is because the world presided over by the ancestral deities such as Kavyavāḍ and others is situated far below, and therefore is not applicable here.
Having crossed over the worlds of the disembodied and the embodied— [the reading "lokam uttīrya" is also found]—
and having gone further and further into the distance, she became somewhat awakened.

Because the Purāṇas state that those who have attained liberation in the form of Śiva (śivasārūpya-mukti) exist in two states—both with bodies and without bodies by their own will—their world [is as follows]:
due to forgetting their own unlimited nature, they perceive it as something limited. (44)
Afterwards, he gazed at the expanse of the sky that had passed above; for as far as he looked down, not even a trace of the moon, sun, stars, or anything else could be perceived.
The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: "For as long as and for as far as nothing was perceived and darkness remained, for that long he looked back. (45)
It stood motionless and profound with darkness,
filling the hollows of the quarters like the interior of a single ocean, as solid as the heart of a rock.
Hope is the filler of the cavities—the openings—of those ten directions.
Līlā said: "O Goddess, tell me, where has the splendor of the Sun and others gone?
How can darkness be so solid within the belly of a stone, motionless, and graspable by the fist?"
In that regard: because of its density, it is as if graspable by the fist; "from where has it been obtained? is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 47 ||
The Goddess said: O Lord, you have come to such a height in the sky that even the splendors of the sun and other luminaries are no longer visible from here. 48.
Just as a firefly is not seen from below within a great dark well, so here the sun is not seen from below by one who stands behind it. || 49 ||

A firefly (*khadyota*) is so called because it illuminates the sky (*kham dyotayati*) or because it shines in the sky (*khe dyotate*); the meaning is that it is not seen by one who is behind it and situated at a great distance above. || 49 ||
Līlā said:
"Aha! We have indeed traveled a long distance along this path;
even the sun is not perceived in the least, appearing like a mere atom."
The path is the track. A *kaṇa* is a particle; like that is the *paramāṇu*, the triad of atoms (*tryaṇuka*). || 50 ||
"O Goddess, beyond this, what other path might there be, and of what nature is it? And how, O Mother, is it to be traversed? Please tell me. (51)
It is to be traversed; it is to be gone to. || 51 ||
The illustrious Goddess said:
Beyond this, ahead of you, is the shell-like crust of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
from which the moon and other celestial bodies have arisen as mere specks of dust.
The hollow of a casket or a box, the upper shell, the skull; like particles of dust. || 52 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
While they were conversing in this manner, they reached the shell of the cosmic egg,
like two bees reaching the dense interior of a mountain cave.
"Densely covered pavilion" means, that is to say, one whose interior is without gaps. || 53 ||
Therefore, you have emerged from that state without any affliction, as if from the sky;
for that which is established in certainty is the Vajra Master, and nothing else. 54.
Certainty (*niścaya*) is the determination of truth; that which resides therein is an imagined object such as a wall and so forth. The other is sublated by the cognition of falsity. || 54 ||
Then, her consciousness being free from all veils, she beheld that vast expanse extending beyond the cosmic egg,
intensely radiant, yet obscured by the veil of water and other elements.
Water ten times the size of the cosmic egg is situated there,
enveloping it like the skin covering the surface of a walnut.
She rests upon the surface of a walnut seed-shell.
Therefore, fire is ten times [greater] than that; from that, wind is ten times greater;
from that, space is ten times greater; and beyond that is the supreme ether.
Supremely pure is the "garment," which is the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), because with the destruction of ignorance, only the unmanifested space (avyākṛtākāśa) remains. || 57 ||
In that supreme void, no conceptualizations of middle, beginning,
or end arise at all, just like talk of the son of a barren woman.
He states its indefiniteness with the words: "In that... (58).
Purely expansive, peaceful, beginningless, and free from delusion, it remains within the Great Self, devoid of beginning, middle, or end. (59)
The meaning is that [the Lord] abides in the Great Self, for the Śruti says, "He is established in His own majesty. || 59 ||
Even if a stone were to fall from the sky with supreme force for an entire kalpa, and even if the king of birds were to fly upward with all his might,
he would not reach the end of that yojana in the stainless sky.
Even the wind, though possessing the speed of a single impulse, would require an eon to traverse it.

In that stainless sky, if a stone were to fall from the upper region with supreme strength and extreme velocity until the end of the kalpa, and if the king of birds, Garuḍa, were to fly upward from the lower region until the end of the kalpa— if there were to be a measurement of the space between those two such that it would be capable of being traversed by both moving with equal speed from either side.
The wind cannot find a space of even one yojana for the meeting of those two, let alone their end on all sides; the meaning is that it is thus unlimited in every respect. || 60 ||
Thus ends the twenty-ninth canto, titled "The Description of the Supreme Space," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 29.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Supreme Space," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Thirtieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Therein, [one perceives] the earth, water, and fire, as well as air and space.
Having transcended the obscurations by tenfold increments in each successive moment. || 1 ||
Such diverse and infinite millions of cosmic eggs are seen like motes of dust within the space of consciousness; this is described here as being for the sake of divine play (līlā). || 1 ||
Nabhasvat and nabhas refer to air and space, respectively. || 1 ||
He beheld that supreme ether, devoid of all measurement;
this entire world was spread out therein as if it were merely a single cosmic egg.

The meaning is that he saw all that consists of the cosmic egg— the entire multitude of universes— just as this world, characterized by the aforementioned cosmic egg, was spread out and expanded within that previously mentioned space of cognition (pramākāśa), which is the sky of consciousness (cidākāśa) variegated by ignorance (avidyā). || 2 ||
She beheld such creations, veiled within the cosmic eggs,
flashing by the millions in the sky like motes of dust in a sunbeam.
He clarifies that very point with the words "tādṛśa" (of such a kind): "sphuritān" means those manifested by the consciousness that is their own self-luminous substratum. || 3 ||
In the great ocean of space, within the waters of great emptiness,
there arise bubbles of the nature of the great flow of consciousness, possessing the radiance of a hundred million.
Ignorance is the state of great emptiness; it is the very water in which [the embryo] resides. The mention of the *arbuda* stage implies its immeasurable duration. (4)
Some he saw falling downward, some ascending upward,
others moving horizontally, and still others standing motionless in their own consciousness.

"Thus, millions upon thousands of such cosmic eggs (aṇḍas) are to be known, situated horizontally, above, and below, because the Pradhāna is all-pervasive. Following this statement from the Purāṇas, he says "some" (kāṃścit).
The meaning is: "by one's own consciousness," that is, in accordance with the consciousness of the individual soul (jīva) who identifies with each respective cosmic egg. || 5 ||
Wherever this consciousness has arisen for whomever,
and in whatever manner, there and for them, the form has arisen in that very same way.

He states—in the verse beginning with "yatra"—that even the arising [of diversity] through the diversity of form, due to the variety of present actions, occurs precisely in accordance with the consciousness of prior worship (upāsanā). || 6 ||
There is no "here" in this world, nor indeed "there," neither above nor below, nor any coming and going; that which is called the body is merely some other state distinct from that [reality].

And this was stated subsequently from the perspective of one who perceives a creator; however, in ultimate reality, there is nothing at all even here in this region of the cosmic egg within that space of consciousness (cidākāśa), let alone "above"—this is for the purpose of absolute negation.
Furthermore, there is no coming or going of those cosmic eggs, but rather something entirely different.
There exists a reality that is the state beyond the sphere of speech and mind, devoid of all duality such as the divisions of space;
therefore, the description of the birth of the universe and its attainment of a body is stated as such with reference to the perspective of the ignorant. This is the meaning. || 7 ||
There, consciousness arises spontaneously again and again by its very nature;
it comes to rest through one's own volitions, like the web of a child's imaginings.

If it is asked, "If the substratum itself (the *dharmin*) does not exist, then where is the conceptualization of arising and so forth? he replies with the word "utpadya" (arising): "It arises as if by its own volitions produced from its own ignorance (*svāvidyā*);
it goes as if to peace. This is the meaning. || 8 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
What would be below, what would be above, and what would be horizontal there, O Bhūsure?
"Speak thus to me, O Brahmin, if indeed I am not already established here. (9)

Now, one might object: "If there is no division of directions in the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), then it cannot exist in the superimposed (*adhyasta*) either; for there is a rule that what is superimposed must reside solely within the directions of its substrate. With this intention, Rāma raises the doubt: "Is it below? Here, if [the object] was not previously situated in the east within the substrate itself, then how could it be so through mental construction (*kalpanā*)?
The meaning is: what could possibly be inferior in this radiant world? || 9 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: All these cosmic eggs, together with their coverings, shine within the great, limitless void due to faulty vision, like a mass of hair floating in the sky.

With the intention that such a deviation from the rule does not constitute a fault within this illusory phenomenal world (*māyika-prapañca*), Vasiṣṭha states the first response: "sasarva... [and so on]. [The term] *durdṛṣṭeḥ* means of one whose vision is impaired by the cataract of false perception (*timira*).
Since all categories of things indeed run toward it because they lack independence,
the earthly portion within the cosmic egg is below that [central point], while the other is above.
With the intention that there is no fault in the transgression of [spatial] restriction because all things are dependent upon the will of the Lord (Īśvara), he says:

"Because of lack of independence" (*asvātantryāt*). Just as the determination of the root-location of the filaments of a *kadamba* flower is conceived only in relation to the globular pericarp which serves as their support, so too [is it] with respect to all entities within the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*).

The conception of "down" is relative to the earth. Nor should it be argued that, in the absence of an objective "downward direction," there would be a lack of a determining factor for the downward fall of a fruit released from its stalk due to its weight; for weight indeed [belongs] to objects.

Just as the power to attract its own respective sense organs is not a distinct quality [other than the organs themselves], so too the power to attract parts of the earth and other elements connected to what it is capable of attracting is not a separate quality. For this very reason,
since there is no division of space in the external direction, even the most massive cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍas*) do not face the possibility of falling or similar occurrences.

Or else, there would be the consequence of the separation of that [consciousness] from its covering, such as water and so forth; thus, with the intention that the foundational consciousness (*adhiṣṭhāna-cit*) does not depend on spatial divisions, he states another solution: "In the cosmic egg" (*brahmāṇḍe*).
A portion of the cosmic egg consisting of earth—that is, the form of the great earth—is "below" that object composed of all elements.
Otherwise, the conceptualization would be that "the other part of space above" is [the object]; such is the meaning. || 11 ||
When large ants move upon a round clod of earth in the sky,
their feet are said to be directed toward the ten directions and below, while their backs are directed upward.

With the intention of showing that this model is also accepted by the authors of the *Jyotiḥśāstra*, who maintain that the terrestrial globe is surrounded on all sides by the celestial sphere— the support of the circle of luminaries—
he provides the following illustrative example: "Of ants," etc., meaning on a clod of earth, a lump of clay.

The meaning is that it is well-known in the established astronomical treatises (siddhānta) that for the great luminaries such as the sun and others, their feet are directed downwards and their backs upwards throughout the ten directions in every direction. || 12 ||
To some, the ground appeared as a mass of trees and anthills;
to others, the pure sky was surrounded by gods, humans, and demons.

Having thus resolved this doubt, he begins to describe the diversity of the present Brahmāṇḍas with the verse beginning "vṛkṣa... and so forth. In the heart (interior) of some Brahmāṇḍas, the subterranean realm is enveloped by a network of trees and anthills, and is not accessible to humans; however, the sky—
The meaning is that it was surrounded by those various worlds consisting of gods, non-humans, humans, beings resembling humans, kimpuruṣas, and daityas. || 13 ||
This world, together with its villages, cities, and mountains, has arisen along with that which is born; it is like a ripe walnut covered by its shell, produced through conceptual construction.

However, some portion of the created universe was produced simultaneously with the fourfold classes of living beings— consisting of that which is born of the elements and that which is immediately of the nature of mental construction— such as the *ākṣoṭa*,
the fruit of the *kaṃdarāla* tree. || 14 ||
Just as female elephants roam about in the expanse of the Vindhya forest,
so do the atoms of the cosmic egg within its vast interior.

In the expanse (*ābhoga*) characterized by the forest of the Vindhya mountain, which has assumed a particular configuration (*kalpita-saṃsthāna*), there are female elephants (*kareṇavaḥ*, i.e., *kariṇyaḥ*). [Similarly,] in the expanse of the Supreme Being (*paraḥ paramātman*), which is a configuration variegated by *māyā*, there are "elephants" (*gajāḥ*). While "elephants" (*gajāḥ*) could have been used, the term "female elephants" (*kareṇavaḥ*) is employed for the sake of the *yamaka* (rhyme). || 15 ||
In that [Brahman] everything is contained; from it everything arises; it is everything and exists everywhere.
It is eternally composed of all things, and likewise, it exists even within each atom.

Now, one might object: "Just as the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) are atoms in relation to the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), why could the space of consciousness itself not be an atom in relation to some other entity? To this he replies with the words "In that" (tasmin). In its persistence, everything is in it;
in its arising, everything comes from it; in its dissolution, everything is it. Since this is so, therefore [it exists] everywhere, in all directions.

At all times and in all things, it is that very same thing; and that is this very Self (ātman), as established by the Śruti, which consists of this, consists of that, and consists of everything. And how could that, being of such a nature, belong to anyone else, even to a single atom? It belongs to no one other than Him—the ocean of supreme light, consisting of pure consciousness.
The waves known as cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa) come and go incessantly.
In "śuddhabodhamaye," the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in its own sense (denoting identity). || 17 ||
Some remain empty within, their nights of conceptual construction having come to an end;
like waves in the ocean, they are carried along in the ocean of emptiness.
Regarding this, he says "within" (antar) to show that some cosmic eggs remain unmanifest within.

This refers to the nights, which consist of darkness, occurring when the limiting adjuncts of the subtle body (*liṅga*)—which contain the seeds of all volitions belonging to the previous kalpa—are dissolved; it is just like deep sleep.
This is as expressed in the Śruti passage, "In the beginning, this was non-existent," where the word "non-existent" (*asat*) is used.

By the word "emptiness" (śūnyatā), the indeterminate (avyākṛta) is expressed. In that ocean characterized by such [emptiness], they are "carried forth" (ūhyante)—that is, they are inferred. The meaning is that, according to the reasoning stated in the Śruti, "How could the existent be born from the non-existent?", they are inferred to exist. || 18 ||
For some, the gurgling roar of the end of the intermediate aeon had begun;
it was neither heard nor perceived by others, whose senses were overwhelmed by their own inherent nature.

By their own nature, through their innate delusion, they were not even aware that the "taste"—meaning passion for sense objects—was being experienced by others who were agitated by it; indeed, they did not know it at all. || 19 ||
In others, at the very beginning of its commencement, creation unfolds within the pure stages, like the sprout within the husk of moistened seeds. (20)

The meaning is that at the initial commencement of other cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), during the beginning of the first kalpa and yuga, creation proceeds within pure worlds upon pure lands, because they have not been defiled by beings produced previously. In the sheath—that is, the seed-pod—the sprout itself is the "kalā" (digit/part) due to its whiteness. || 20 ||
When the great dissolution occurs, the sun’s rays, lightnings,
and mountains begin to melt away, like particles of frost under the heat.
In certain cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), when the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) has occurred— that is to say, at the time of its full manifestation—
the meaning is that the sun and other celestial bodies, having first burned the world-system, themselves began to dissolve. || 21 ||
Some who have not yet attained the [spiritual] stages fall indeed until the end of the kalpa;
they remain thus until, having dissolved, they are born again as consisting of pure consciousness. 22.

Some cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) have not reached the earth as their support. [Objection: But was it not previously stated that falling is impossible for them? To what end, then, would they go there? He says: "In that way" (tathā). The meaning is that in those [worlds] consisting of the consciousness of falling, falling is not contradictory. || 22 ||
Some remain as if paralyzed, like tufts of hair in the sky;
likewise, those in whom consciousness has arisen shine forth like the vibrations of the wind. (23)

Others are rigid and motionless; likewise, those in whom consciousness has arisen [are so] because they originate from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the consciousness of the vibrating Self (*spandātman*). This is the meaning. 23.

When the very first [teacher] has taught the Veda and the Śāstras otherwise than according to established practice (ācāra), the undertaking of others likewise remains unstable; such is the nature of the sequence. (24)
[Objection: But surely the Vedic scripture, "As the Creator fashioned [the world] in the past," establishes a uniformity among creations;

how then can this diversity be asserted as being contrary to that? To this, he says: "From custom" (*ācārāt*). By that scripture, it is established that just as the Creator's creation was of such a nature in the previous kalpa, so too is it in the second and subsequent ones. In that regard:

When, in the very first creation, there arose a mode of being characterized by conduct consisting of the knowledge and performance of the rites pertaining to the Vedic scriptures from a previous birth—
being distinct from the creations of other creators— for others...

The meaning is that although the commencement of the creations belonging to subsequent kalpas may indeed be like that—just as before—nevertheless, in comparison with the creation of other creators, its sequence remains non-eternal and indeed unrestricted; thus, the establishment of diversity is proven. || 24 ||
Some are beings such as Brahmā and others, some are creators and protectors such as Viṣṇu and others,
some are lords of other creatures, and some are beings without a protector.

"Having gratified their father, the Supreme Lord, through austerity, they are born from one another, each desiring victory over the other. Since it is thus stated in the Purāṇas that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra arise from one another according to the distinction of kalpas, when the progenitor is primary, the creation [proceeds] due to the difference in their respective qualities.
With the intention that the diversity resulting from the predominance of qualities such as *sattva* and the rest is likewise unavoidable, he says "some" (*kecit*) and so forth.
Some [world-systems] have Brahmā—the four-faced one—as their *ādi-puruṣa* (primordial person); others have Viṣṇu alone as their *ādi-sarga-pa* (lord of creation), the sovereign of creation. Others...

In those [worlds], there are lords of creatures such as Rudra, Bhairava, Durgā, Vināyaka, and others, for it is heard in the Purāṇas and other texts that explain their respective majesties that they too exercise control over Brahmā and the rest.
In those [other worlds], however, there are creatures such as beasts and birds that are "without a lord," meaning they are devoid of a controller. 25.
Some are lords of diverse creations, some are of the nature of animals,
some are filled with the single ocean, and others are devoid of birth.
If Brahmā and the others were of equal preeminence, they would be the lords of diverse creations.

Thus, with the intention that the diversity of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is easily accounted for by the variety of the latent impressions of the karma of living beings, as well as by the variety of the will, cognition, and other faculties of the creators, he says: "Among those consisting of animals," and so forth.
Some were solid masses of stone; some had worms within them;
some were entirely composed of deities; and some had humans within them. || 27 ||
"Niṣpiṇḍā" means thoroughly condensed, that is to say, dense. || 27 ||
Some are filled with eternal darkness, and likewise inhabited by creatures; others are filled with eternal light, and likewise inhabited by creatures. || 28 ||
Likewise, there are those beings and living creatures in whom vision has been cultivated through habit; the meaning is that bats and others possess sight even in darkness. || 28 ||
Some are filled with mosquitoes, possessing the beauty of udumbara fruits;
some are eternally hollow within, while others are beings whose very nature is the vibration of emptiness.

Other worlds, filled with such creations, exist here within the inner consciousness that they do not even enter the range of conceptual thought, just as mountains filling the sky [do not obstruct it]. (30)

Those creations which are filled with such a [supreme] creation belong to certain yogis who possess internal vision; they do not fall within the range of conceptualized activity—that is, they do not become objects of determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*). Even if the reading is *asmāddhiyām*, the meaning remains the same: those yogis whose intellects are like our own [ordinary] intellects. || 30 ||
Their sky-like expanse is the vast great space that remains spread out,
which cannot be measured by those traveling until the end of their lives, even as they travel with all their speed.

The word "tādṛk" (such) is connected both with what precedes and what follows, according to the maxim of the lamp on the threshold (*dehalī-dīpaka-nyāya*). Thus, just as the sky-filling mountain (*vyomapūrṇācala*) is of such a nature, so too is the *ambara*—that is, the *ākāśa* (space)—of that same nature; in other words, its essential nature is non-empty (*aśūnya-svabhāva*). Furthermore, the Great Space (*mahākāśa*), which is the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*), is likewise spread out and expanded in that manner.

Even by Viṣṇu and the other gods, who travel and run throughout the duration of their own lives until the end of existence, that [reality] is not measured; the meaning is that it cannot be delimited as being "this much. || 31 ||
Situated like a jeweled girdle upon each individual cosmic egg,
the elemental nature of earth, by its own inherent character, acts as an attractor of all beings.

Granted that there may be an infinity of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) and their diversity; nevertheless, one might raise the objection: "In the absence of a supporting agent, how is it that the external coverings of water and so forth do not disintegrate?
Anticipating this, he provides a solution by relying on the power of attraction mentioned by us previously: "Of each... [and so on].
The "drawing-in" (ākṛṣṭi) of beings is attraction; the state that effects this is a particular power (śaktiviśeṣa) which exists pervading all around, like a bracelet set with jewels. || 32 ||

O one of great intelligence, since that which is our all-encompassing glory does not fall within the scope of our intellects, I have no power to describe that world. (The reading "śaktirmama nāsti" is preferred.)

He concludes the description of the expansion of the universe under the pretext of revealing his own incapacity [to describe it further], beginning with the word "ya" (which). The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: "That which is the full majesty of our intellects regarding the subject of describing the universe has been shown. Beyond that, whatever is not the object of the intellects—that is, not within their range—is the subject [of this conclusion]. The neuter gender of the word *viṣaya* is archaic (*chāndasī*). Regarding its description:
The meaning is that I have no power. || 33 ||
In a vast forest dense with terrifying darkness,
intoxicated yakṣas dance without even seeing one another, just as they do in the far-stretching, supreme sky.
In this way, very many great worlds manifest.
One should not think that there are only this many worlds due to the limitation of my descriptive power;

rather, there are infinite others unperceived by others as well, because of the infinity of the creative power (*sarga-śakti*) within *māyā*. He states this with an illustration: "Just as [the forms] were not shown to one another... and so forth.
Just as the hosts of yakṣas and bhūtas dance, so too do very many worlds flash forth within Brahman when it is veiled by ignorance; this is the meaning. || 34 ||

Thus ends the thirtieth canto, titled "The Description of Tens of Millions of Variegated Cosmic Eggs," in the *Līlopākhyāna* within the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Multitude of Variegated Cosmic Eggs," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Thirty-First Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Reflecting thus, the two of them departed from their own world and, having emerged,
immediately beheld the inner apartments.

Furthermore, the inspection of the inner apartments, the vision of the interior of the universe, and the observation of the army equipped with the insignia of heroes and the like are described here. (1)

Having emerged from their own world of a previous birth and perceiving in this manner the manifold variety of infinite millions of universes, they both beheld them; then, suddenly entering one particular universe among those, they saw an inner palace, and within that— nothing else.
"But they dwelt there for a long time; however, they departed instantly"—this is a restatement of what is about to be described. || 1 ||
The great corpse of Mahārāja was filled with flowers standing upon it;
by the side of the corpse sat the body of Cittalīlā.

The bahuvrīhi compounds beginning with "sthitā" (stationed) are adjectives qualifying the inner apartment (*antaḥpura*). It refers to that [place] in which the mind is established in internal meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and which possesses such a body of divine play (*līlā-śarīra*). || 2 ||
Crowded with people in deep sleep due to the dense darkness of night,
it was languid with the fragrance of incense, sandalwood, camphor, and saffron.
By the word "dense" (ghana), the protracted duration caused by grief is indicated; it was crowded with people overcome by a deep, heavy sleep—that is, profound slumber. || 3 ||
Beholding that other world of her husband,
Līlā, intent on departing for that state of existence, fell from that very sky right here with her body of mere resolve.
Right here, within the inner apartments themselves, is that sky—the space of the previously mentioned pavilion.
Having pierced through the shell of the cosmic egg and having shattered the veil of worldly existence, she entered the slightly expanded cycle of her husband’s creative will.
Together with that goddess, he reached once more the vast pavilion of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which was surrounded by protective enclosures; having entered it, he proceeded with great speed.
Sphāram means extensive. || 6 ||

She beheld her husband’s world, which was like a puddle in the mire of his own mental constructs— dark and muddy with clouds, just as a lioness might gaze upon a mountain cave shrouded in darkness and mud.
It stood like a small pool or a pond of mud and mire, rendered turbid as if with silt by the two clouds of darkness.
O Goddesses, you two entered that void which is the self of the void of the universe;
just as an ant enters a ripe bilva fruit within the shell of the earth.
There, having passed beyond other worlds, mountains, and the intermediate space,
they reached the surface of the earth, which was crowded with mountain ranges and oceans.
Jambudvīpa is adorned by Meru like the interior of a nine-petaled lotus;
and within Bhārata-varṣa is the realm of the Lord of Līlā, [surrounded] by cows.
The nine petals are the nine regions; the construction of the sentence is: "He beheld the kingdom, the mandala of Līlānātha.
(10) In the meantime, in that mandala on the adorned earth, a certain king, empowered by his vassals, launched a sudden assault. (11)

*Avaskandana* is an assault by means of an army. The lord of the earth, Sindhu-rāja, was augmented—that is, increased—by his neighbors, the lords of the surrounding regions (*maṇḍaleśvara*), who were his allies. || 11 ||
Because of those beings of the three worlds who had gathered for the sake of witnessing the fury of the battle, that sky became exceedingly crowded.
When the fury of battle with him had commenced—this is the ellipsis—the three worlds became crowded and congested with living beings. || 12 ||
While they were thus unawares, those two goddesses beheld the sky filled with hosts of celestial beings, like a canopy garlanded by clouds.

He had come in such a way as to be free from apprehension—that is, devoid of any fear or suspicion—due to his certainty regarding [the truth] and his skill in making himself invisible and so forth. The words beginning with "moving through the sky" (*nabhaścara*) are adjectives qualifying the sky, [introduced] after the question concerning the grove (*ārāma*).
It was accompanied by hosts of Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and Vidyādharas,
and surrounded by Apsarases from the heavenly world who were eager to seize the heroes.
It was filled with blood-thirsty, flesh-eating, and intoxicated bhūtas, rākṣasas, and piśācas,
while the hands of the vidyādhara women were laden with showers of flowers.
From this point onward, many bahuvrīhi compounds will appear as appropriate. 15.
It was surrounded by vetālas, yakṣas, and kuśmāṇḍas who, out of curiosity to witness the duel,
had seized mountain slopes to protect themselves from the falling of weapons.
Vetālas and others are specific classes of spirits (*bhūta*). By the word "pair" (*dvandva*), their activity—namely, combat—is indicated.
[The mountain] whose rocky slopes were resorted to and taken as a refuge by them for the sake of protecting themselves from the falling of weapons on all sides. 16.
The circle of spirits fled from the region of the sky along the path of the missiles,
while the spectators, agitated by their own vanity, were filled with intense excitement.
From the portion of space immediately adjacent to the path of the missiles, there arose the conceit "Oh, I am a man!"—this is *āhopuruṣikā*. (17)
There, amidst rumors of an imminent and terrifying battle,
beautiful women, eager for playful laughter and amorous dalliance, held chowries.
"Kiṃvadantī" means popular rumor; [the women were] longing and filled with yearning for his playful gestures and the charm of his smiles. (18)
[He recited] the hymn of auspiciousness for the Supreme Sage, which is applied through the contemplation of the Dharma;
[and he recited] the hymn on the occasion of the many perfected goddesses of the world-lords.

In which [place] there exist many hymns of praise to the deities recited by the foremost and most excellent sages— whose power of yoga, through its preeminent qualities, enables them to behold those things that cannot be seen or even imagined by others— for the sake of the world’s well-being; and in which they have been perfected for the sake of the many world-protectors, such as the Gandharvas and others.

In that place, there are hymns concerning women, appropriate for those occasions, such that even the celestial nymphs (apsarases), disregarding their own husbands, would not approach their new lovers; thus, the lords of the world praise them—this is the meaning. (Note: The reading is *svān upekṣya abhinavān*.)
It was radiant with Indra’s soldiers, who were busily engaged in bringing back heroes worthy of heaven;
and it possessed the lofty elephants known as the world-protectors, adorned for the sake of those heroes.
"Worthy of heaven" means fit for heaven because they serve as its ornaments; "the elephants known as world-protectors" refers to Airāvata and the others. || 20 ||
The Gandharvas and Cāraṇas were intent on honoring the arriving heroes,
while the noble warriors were gazed upon by the side-long glances of the celestial women who were eager for the brave.
By the *straiṇa*, that is, by the multitude of women (*strī-samūha*) of the immortals. || 21 ||
It was a source of women eager for the embrace of the staff-like arms of heroes,
and it made the sun appear like the moon through the white glory of its warriors.
Because his heat was overcome by the coolness of his fame, he was turned into the moon. || 22 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, what kind of warrior is designated by the word 'hero' (śūra)?"
Who could be the ornament of heaven, or who might be a child-warrior? || 23 ||
In this context, Rāma, desiring to know the characteristics of the brave and others, asks out of curiosity: "O Blessed One.

Although the battle of the children (ḍimbhāhava) was not explicitly mentioned but merely indicated, the inquiry here regarding its characteristics should be understood as incidental, because it consists of the nature of being an ornament to heaven for the brave and its opposite. || 23 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He who, for the sake of his lord engaged in conduct prescribed by the scriptures, dies or becomes victorious in battle, is a hero and a partaker of the world of heroes.
The ellipsis is "fought in battle. || 24 ||
Otherwise, a man who meets his death in battle with his limbs severed by living beings is said to have been slain in a tumultuous fray; such a person becomes an inhabitant of hell. (25)
That man who fights for wealth by acting contrary to the conduct prescribed in the scriptures shall dwell in an inexhaustible hell when he dies in battle. || 26 ||
Clarifying exactly what was stated previously, he says: "Not according to the scriptures," and so forth. || 26 ||
One who fights while conforming to the meaning of the scriptures as far as possible and to worldly custom,
and who is likewise devoted— such a person is called a hero.
O noble-minded one, for the sake of a cow, for the sake of a Brahmin, and for the sake of a friend, he died through his effort to protect one who had sought refuge; he is now an ornament of heaven.
For the sake of protecting one who has come for refuge, through the exertion of battle. || 28 ||
Those kings who were always intent on protecting their own country alone, and those who died for that purpose, are heroes who dwell in the world of heroes. (29)
Established—that is, intent—in the primary duty of protecting, that is, guarding his own country, which must necessarily be protected and is worthy of protection; || 29 ||
Those who die in battle for the sake of a king who is intent on harming his subjects, or even for a master who is not a king, surely go to hell.
For those who, whether belonging to kings or non-kings, die in battle with their limbs severed while acting contrary to the scriptures, they indeed go to hell. || 31 ||

With the intention that even taking refuge with one who acts contrary to the scriptures leads to hell, let alone taking refuge with one who causes harm to living beings, he says again: "Those who... The words "for the sake of those who act contrary to the scriptures" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 31 ||
If the battle were conducted according to the law (dharma), then order would prevail;
however, being intoxicated and devoid of fear for the next world, they would utterly destroy me.
He says that even for one who has taken refuge in righteousness, if he fights unrighteously and is slain, there is no heaven—this is expressed by the word "dharmyam.

That which does not deviate from dharma is "dharmyam. "Saṃsthitiḥ" means abiding in heaven (the reading is *svargasthitiḥ*). If heaven were attained even by one slain in an unrighteous battle, then what would remain of the next world?
The meaning is that, being fearless and excessively intoxicated by unrighteous warfare, they might utterly destroy their enemies. || 32 ||
"Wherever a hero is slain, he goes to heaven"—such are the common sayings; however, the definitive conclusion of the scriptures is that a hero is one who fights in accordance with dharma. (33)

"If a hero, raising his weapons, stakes his own life against the lives of others, wherever he is slain, heaven is there at every step"—what then is the status of such general sayings? To this, he says: "Wherever... (verse 33).
Those who endure the edge of a sword for the sake of those who possess virtuous conduct are called heroes; all others are merely children slain in battle.
For their sake, celestial nymphs stand in the sky during battle with longing hearts, uttering words of endearment to those great beings who have become heroes.
They remain in such a manner that it is as if they are saying, "We are beloved" to those heroic great beings of great strength; that is to say, they wait expectantly. || 35 ||
Containing the sweet and languid songs of the Vidyādharīs, with amorous women busy arranging garlands of Mandāra flowers,
and where rows of celestial chariots belonging to the Suras and Siddhas have come to rest.
It shone forth as if possessing the splendor of the sky's festival being proclaimed. || 36 ||

In which [city] the passionate women were distracted and agitated by the weaving of *mandāra* garlands to offer as gifts upon the chests of heroes, or by the braiding of their own hair; it was as if its splendor had risen upward, uttered for the sake of a festival—such is the poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*). 36.

Thus ends the thirty-first canto, titled "The Description of the Sky-Faring Beings Beholding the Battle," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, a work of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Sky-Dwellers Beholding the Battle," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the *Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Thirty-second Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, while the Apsarases were dancing with longing for Vīravara [the reading "varātkaṇṭhā" is also found].
Standing there,
she beheld with playful glances the earth endowed with knowledge in the sky.
The two armies, equipped for battle and stationed in celestial chariots that appeared by mere resolve, are now described as they gaze upon one another with playful curiosity, eager for combat.
The connection [of the verses] is as follows: Sarasvatī, who is Vidyā, together with Līlā, beheld the two armies upon the earth.
(1) In a certain vast forest within the circle of his own kingdom—which was protected by her husband and adorned with military force—the second army, terrifying as the sky, spread out. (2)
It was garlanded—that is, surrounded—by a fourfold army;
and because it served as the abode for lions, scorpions, rākṣasas, and piśācas, it was as terrifying as a second sky.
The two armies stood undisturbed, resembling two calm oceans; they were filled with great elephants and intoxicated with pride, accompanied by their respective kings.
By means of great undertakings and efforts toward their duties. || 3 ||
Ready for battle and well-armored, he was as wonderful as a blazing fire;
his eyes were marked by agitation as they watched for the impact of the first blow.
It carried people along by means of a downpour from the edge of uplifted, stainless swords;
it was filled with glittering battle-axes, spears, slings, lances, and mallets.
Where people carry the very edges of *nistriṃśa* swords—that is, blades—as showers of water;
where *paraśvadhas* (battle-axes) are used; and where *bhindipālas* and other such specialized weapons are employed. || 5 ||
(208) It was shaken by the falling of forests agitated by the flapping of Garuḍa’s wings; its golden armor shimmered with the light of the rising sun.
Kaṅkaṭa means armor. || 6 ||
With weapons raised in fury as they gazed at one another’s faces,
they were fixed in mutual stares, appearing like figures painted upon a wall.
They were raised up and brandished out of anger. || 7 ||
Its established order was fixed by long-standing written conventions,
while the clamor of its irresistible great armies rendered conversation impossible to hear.
By a boundary marked by a line drawn between the two armies— resembling the lines traced by a mantra-expert for the purpose of warding off snakes and other dangers—
in which conversations and mutual discourses were unheard because they were overwhelmed by the sounds of the syllable "jhām. || 8 ||
The drum had long since fallen silent from the pride of the first blow,
and the entire army was sluggish, with its ranks occupied by soldiers who remained fixed in their positions.
Thinking, "Let there be no blow before the king's command," and fearing that [the enemy] might be arrogant on account of that [command],
he advanced slowly with his entire army— whose battle arrays were already largely formed by the warriors themselves— possessing such a configuration of its principal constituent parts.
It was divided by a single bridge in its center, which was empty for a distance of two bow-lengths,
like a single ocean agitated by the winds at the end of an aeon.
The middle portion, measuring two bow-lengths and devoid of people, was characterized by a single bridge.
In the body— [the reading is *kāryasaṃkara*]—
where the Lord is subject to the anxieties of distress and agitation;
where the cave of the heart is distressed and fragile due to the skin of the croaking frog’s throat.
The two lords are kings; there, the cave-like hearts of the afflicted and the timid tremble and quiver like the croaking skin of a frog out of fear. || 11 ||
[He saw] one whose countless soldiers were ready to sacrifice their very lives and all their possessions,
and whose bow was drawn back by Karna with a multitude of arrows aimed for release.
Of the flood characterized by a torrent of arrows, that is, of the stream. || 12 ||
Countless soldiers stood motionless, watching the falling blows;
the scene was crowded with the frowns of those whose brows were knit by the weight of mutual intensity and hardness.
The hardness resulting from the longing for battle is mercilessness—that is to say, anger.
Due to the frowns produced by the weight of that [anger], it is "constricted," meaning difficult to behold. || 13 ||
The armor [of the battlefield] resounded with the harsh clashing of weapons as they struck one another;
it was a hollow space sought by cowards who were scorched by the presence of heroic warriors.
Where, due to intense collisions and impacts, there were harsh clanging sounds from armor and breastplates;
where mountain caves were sought out as hiding places by cowards whose faces had turned dark as if scorched by the fire from the mouths of heroic warriors.
Its life was uncertain, lasting only as long as its mutual configuration and light;
it possessed tall, aged elephants with their human riders clinging to every hair on their bodies.
That battle was a formal contest, lasting until the very sight of it, for those whose lives were beyond doubt;
it was a place where both elephants and men were closely embraced by their well-erected, bristling body-hairs, and were thus elevated on high and increased in bulk in every direction. 15.
Because of that state in which all living beings were preoccupied with anticipating the first blow,
the sound of the waves was completely stilled, and it resembled a city sealed in sleep.
By the word "prāṇa," the mind under its control is indicated. || 16 ||
The clamor of conch shells, musical ensembles, and kettledrums was completely stilled, and all the clouds of dust settled upon the earth and in the sky. (17)
The connection between the dust and the breasts is respectively [as follows]. || 17 ||
The circle of auspicious marks (*maṅgalamaṇḍala*) was left behind by those intent on flight;
it shone like an ocean filled with countless fish in the form of spreading arrays of sea-monsters (*makara*). || 18 ||
The brave warriors were like auspicious ornaments adorning the army; it was a battle like that between crocodile-formations and fish, resembling the radiant ocean itself.
The clusters of flower-bunches on its banners surpassed the stars in the sky,
while the forest-like trunks of elephants raised aloft filled the expanse of the atmosphere.
In which [procession] the open space of the sky was made to resemble a forest by the trunks of the elephant-riders' elephants, which were raised high and extended upward. 19.
The entire array of weapons was on his side, shimmering with a flood of trembling light;
and the space between his lips was blown by the sounds "dham-dham" arising from his breath.

In that [battle], all the weapons became as if winged by the surging, floating, and flickering floods of arrows; it was made to resound with the "dham-dham" sounds of blowing drums and other instruments arising from their breath, as well as the sounds of conchs, kāhalas, and the like. || 20 ||
It was radiant with gods whose wicked conduct had been trampled by the formation of the discus,
and it caused the multitudes of nāgas to flee in terror through the fury of the formation of Garuḍa.

Now, describing the difference in the arrangement of battle arrays (*vyūha*) due to the distinction between the two armies, he qualifies [the army] with the word "cakra": "It was radiant like the gods, by whom the wicked Dānavas had been overcome by the hands— the agents— of the *cakravyūha*."

By means of a superimposition of non-difference based on the punning application of the word *nāga*, elephants are referred to as being of the nature of serpents. [The reading is "based on the cause of *śleṣa*"]. || 21 ||
With its vanguard shattered by the falcon-formation (śyenavyūha) and its excellent ranks broken by the sound of their cries,
the vast multitude fell in heaps as they struck one another down without exception.

In some places, however, it was characterized by a supreme, most intense clamor caused by the various arrays of hawks (*śyenavyūha*) that were broken and dispersed as they encountered the formations of the opposing armies; in other places, however, there were vast multitudes (*bhūrivṛndaka*) falling down entirely and in their totality due to the forceful slapping of arms against one another in their fury.
It resounded with the fierce cries of excellent heroes emerging from the arrangement of various arrays,
and it was filled with circles of intoxicated mallets brandished aloft by hands.
In which [battle] there was a supreme clamor from the heroes who had emerged from their ranks and advanced to the front;
and in which circles of mallets (mudgara-maṇḍala) whirled about as if intoxicated by the exhilaration caused by lifting them up with the hand.
The sun was darkened by the clouds formed by the rays of Kṛṣṇa’s weapons,
while the sound of his arrows resembled the whistling of dry leaves shaken by the wind.
It was darkened—that is, obscured—by clouds that had arisen like the rays of black and dark weapons. *Palyūla* refers to a specific kind of grass;
*sūtkṛtam* is an onomatopoeic imitation of the sound produced by the friction of air against those blades. (24)
It stood like a multitude of many kalpas and the highest kalpas;
it rose up like a single ocean agitated by the winds of universal dissolution. || 25 ||

The *kalpakalpas* are the clouds such as the Puṣkarāvartaka and others, so called because they are capable (*kalpante*) of bringing about the dissolution (*pralaya*) of an eon (*kalpa*). With many of these, it was as if the vanguard had become a massed multitude. 25.
It quivered like the two wings of Mount Mahāmeru recently severed,
resembling a mountain of collyrium shaken by a turbulent wind.
"Kajjalaparvata" means the "Mountain of Collyrium. This comparison is made because of the abundance of extremely dark elephants and other such creatures there. || 26 ||
It was like the agitated darkness rising from the caverns of Pātāla,
with its banks swaying and tossing like the Lokāloka mountain during a wild dance.
Having pierced through the mass of the great hell, he rose up like the earth itself. || 27 ||
Whose banks and embankments were shimmering and agitated by the frantic dancing [of the gods].
With the floods of water that were the sunlight of the day turning dark with the rays of their swaying spears, maces, swords, and axes,
he will in no long time turn the vessel of the world into a single ocean.
He prepared to fill [it] with infinite, bottomless floods. || 28 ||

Or, [the world] is filled by clouds that are "floods of water" (vāripūra)—that is, clouds which fill the universe with endless floods or currents—by means of waters that are darkening the sunlight of the day with rays (aṃśu) characterized by spears and other weapons; or rather, [it is filled] by those waters which fill the world with such [weapons].
Thus, through these infinite floods and flows, the vessel of the world becomes a bottomless single ocean.
The meaning is that it was as if prepared to act. || 28 ||

Thus ends the thirty-second canto, titled "The Commencement of the Battle," in the *Līlopākhyāna* (The Story of Līlā) within the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* (Book on Origination) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (Sage) tradition. || 32 ||
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Commencement of the Battle," in the Utapatti-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, within the Tātparya-prakāśa commentary.
The thirty-third canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, tell me briefly this battle in its essence."
For by these utterances, the hearing of the listener is brought to delight. || 1 ||
Observed with ease by the wisdom of those seated in chariots created by mere resolve,
the battle that then commenced between the two armies is now described.
The meaning is that the faculty of hearing (*śruti*) is gladdened by the removal of the defect of weariness (*jāmitā*), which obstructs the reception of the instruction on reality (*tattva*). || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, right there, those two goddesses ascended a beautiful, stable, and enclosed celestial chariot that had been prepared, in order to witness that battle.
They ascended a celestial chariot that had been fashioned by one of true resolve, which was lovely, situated in the sky, rendered motionless, and for that very reason made stable. || 2 ||
In the meantime, Līleśa, being unable to withstand him in that face-to-face encounter in battle, [withdrew] from the opposing side.
There, when the clash of the two armies— the mutual collision of their vanguards—

had commenced, and while a certain fearless warrior, rising up like a wave from the ocean of dissolution, emerged from the enemy host with the desire to strike at a rival, Līleśa Vidūratha sought to withstand him.
Unable to endure it, he hurled a mallet at the chest of that soldier; "he struck," is the connection with the subsequent verse. || 3 ||
Like a wave in the ocean of dissolution rising at the moment of creation,
he hurled the mallet upon the chest of the warrior, as if casting a stone down a mountain slope.
Then the clash of weapons between the two armies began violently, with the speed of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution, scattering sparks like flashes of fire and lightning.
Now, immediately after the king's departure; by the word "fire," weapons similar to it are indicated, and by the word "lightning," its splendors are indicated. || 5 ||
The surface of the sky was marked by lines at the tips of the shimmering, trembling streams,
while the sound of "ṭāṃ" was perceived amidst the humming "kaṇa-kaṇa" noise.

From this point forward, all the adjectives ending with "raṇa-saṃbhrama" (the tumult of battle) are located at the end of the verses describing the creation. The phrase "marked by lines" (*rekhāṅkitam*) is a poetic conceit (*autprekṣika*), suggesting that the surface was inscribed by the tips of the flickering edges of weapons as they were being brandished. || 6 ||
He is the devourer of the world with his fierce, gurgling roar mingled with the sound of "dhīṃ" and "huṃ";
he is the canopy of solar rays at the onset of the torrential downpour of arrows.

Because of its varying intensity mixed with the sound *huṃ*, it is the devourer—that is, the eclipser—of the deep, gurgling roars at the end of summer; it is that which has a canopy formed by the very rays of the sun reflected in the streams of autumnal rain. || 7 ||
The fire of sparks flew up from the clanging of armor as they roared;
the sky was filled with fragments of weapons severed by mutual blows and scattered by the flight of arrows.

In which [battle] sparks of fire flew up with a *ṭaṅkāra* sound from the armored coats of mail as they roared while struck by arrows, swords, and other weapons; and where the sky was filled with fragments of weapons— namely pieces of swords— which, because they were flying upward, acted like birds.
The sky-terrain became a forest where the movement of the heroes' tree-like arms caused a wind,
and where the whirring of bows and wheels sent the celestial women fleeing in terror.
In that place, the expanse of the sky was such that its forests were being carried along by the movements of the arms of those marching forth.
The deep roar of the clouds was turned into the great humming of bees by him,
who, through the power of his singular density, remained as if established in a state of non-conceptual meditative absorption.
By the word *bhṛṅga*, sound is indicated.

It is where the thunder of the clouds is rendered insignificant, like the humming of bees, due to being overwhelmed by tumultuous cries (*halahalārāva*). As it is said: "Just as a solid mass of salt has no interior or exterior but is entirely a single mass of flavor, even so, my dear, is this Self."

The meaning is as follows: the Supreme Self, shown in the scripture as "a mass of consciousness alone" (*vijñānaghana eva*), being a single undifferentiated mass, does not experience external objects such as sound and so forth by virtue of that state, just as one established in non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) does not. Thus it has been said: "Thereafter, there may be the non-conceptual [state]. (10)
The heads of heroes were severed by the foremost torrents of iron arrows,
while the air was crowded with armor clashing and rattling against one another's shoulders.
The harsh clanging of the impact of fierce weapons was struck down by the sound of "Hūṃ";
the faces of all directions were jagged with clouds that were like surging waves of flowing torrents.
Where the faces of the quarters were made jagged by the waves of sword-blades, as if they possessed protruding tusks. || 12 ||
With the clashing and agitation of weapons, it resounded with the *jhaṇajjhaṇa* noise as they were grasped in fists;
for a long time there was the sound of *caṭacaṭa* from the striking, clashing, and rolling [of the arms]. || 13 ||

Where, upon the enemy being thrown into confusion by a sword-stroke, the hand of one who had set out to seize his head—failing to find it—became as if graspable by the fist in the form of the very *jhana-jhana* sound itself;
and where, amidst the slapping of the arms of heroic warriors, there were crackling sounds that seemed to roll about. (13)
(210) With the whistling sound of brandishing swords and the clanging noise of flaming sparks;
with the roar of autumnal thunderbolts amidst the darkness thickened by autumnal arrows. || 14 ||

Where there was the sound of "saṇasaṇa" from the sparks of blazing iron produced by the friction of swords being drawn swiftly from their scabbards and emerging; and where there was the path of the multitudes of arrows as they sped toward the end of the road— that is, toward the target.
Where there is the harsh, grating sound of things prone to crumbling.
With blood from his life-force gushing from his throat with a "dhagaddhagi" sound, and with the gaps in the sky filled by the fragments of severed arms, heads, and swords, [he lay there]. (15)
Where the vital breaths and the blood rose up from the severed throat with a "dhagaddhag" sound.
His hair was touched by the flickering flames arising from his armor,
while he made a deep "jhaṇajjhaṇa" sound as he fiercely drank in the multitude of clashing swords falling upon him in battle.

Where the hair on the heads [of the warriors] was touched by the flames of the fire, which resembled matted locks; where the swarms of swords caused the heroes to become intoxicated—their minds overcome with joy, their bodies swelling with martial zeal—and thus produced a clanging *jhaṇajjhaṇa* sound. 16.
The blood was as crimson as the high-arching waves of elephants struck by spears, and it was harsh with the piercing whistling sounds produced by the crushing of tusks against tusks. || 17 ||
Where there was a wave-high torrent of blood from elephants blunted by various types of weapons such as spears. || 17 ||
The air resounded with the piteous cries of those crushed by the impact of great clubs,
while the sky was covered by a profusion of lotus-like heads of tigers and heroes.
With the lord of serpents held in his arms against the sky, he was like a cloud filled with thick dust; he had severed the head of the man who had begun the hair-to-hair combat with Keśin.
The battle that proceeded by seizing each other by the hair is called *keśākeśi*; it is that very [battle] wherein there is retaliation for the offense of cutting off weapons.
His eyes, ears, nose, lips, and neck were sliced by the claws of those who were clawless;
he gained the ground by effortlessly tossing aside great wrestlers whose weapons had been severed.

Where many wrestling grounds were obtained through the effortless, disdainful tossing up and down of great wrestlers whose weapons had been severed, by means of their superior sport of arm-wrestling. || 20 ||

The earth trembled from the falling elephants in rut, the rivers flowed as the mountains rolled down, and paths of streaming blood were formed by the blood gushing from the rattling chariots. || 21 ||
Where the speed [of the army] was such that the earth, shaken by the Mātaṅgas and unable to run because of it, rolled along;
where a mist was created by the dust, the weapons gleamed as they were brandished, and there was the roar of the ocean-like army with its dense agitation all unified. || 21-22 ||

He was devoured by Death through the playful sport of his intoxicated laughter; his thundering roar, once like that of the clouds, was now dwarfed by the proud king of mountains and the lord of serpents.

*Carvitaḥ* means chewed or eaten; if the reading is *carcitaḥ*, it means harmed or reviled. It refers to that place where the clouds and their thunders have been diminished—in both height and roar—by the lords of elephants, the best of tuskers. 23.
The mountain range was covered with trees, chasms, and slopes, where discuses, spears, double-edged swords, and mallets lay hidden;
it was a mountain girdled by warriors who, like dense woolen threads, were ground down by the friction of battle.

Where discuses and other weapons, hurled for the purpose of slaying those who struck by taking refuge behind trees, chasms, and the like, became concealed therein; where the mountain slopes, characterized by warriors of various colors, were densely covered and interwoven with wool-like threads in the form of arrows; and where the mountain ridges were thickly strewn.
The banners, cloths, and chowries were broken and scattered like clouds;
the sky-dwellers were driven far away by the flood of mechanical stones and wheels. || 25 ||

Wherein the sky-dwellers, such as birds and other creatures, have fled far away— driven off by stones discharged from machines called *kṣepaṇa* and by volleys of discs, which are either intercepted by the resting attacks of clouds or by lightning and other phenomena resting within the clouds. || 25 ||
It was exceedingly hoarse with the wailing of warriors whose limbs were hacked by those frantic with death,
and it resounded with the mass of heads being split open by the blows of axes.
The sky was starred with fragments of swords flashing as they soared far aloft, while the earth was covered by hosts of elephants pierced by the streams of spears hurled from spears.
Where the sky became as if starred with the fragments of swords, appearing like a firmament filled with stars, due to the multitudes of spear-weapon missiles discharged by force and power.
The mallets were released by the female vetālas who were agitated by the army; [an alternate reading is *dhūtamudgaraḥ* (the mallets were shaken)].
High, heroic *tomara*-lances served as triumphal arches, propped up toward the sky. || 28 ||
Where the lofty, raised spears of heroes in the sky were like a garland upon an archway.

The sky was like a mass of hair with its multitude of broken swords from *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons, while the luster of the garments of the sky took on the appearance of tresses scorched by the forest of spears. || 29 ||
Where the sky has for its tresses the very rows of sword-blades;

where, in the bamboo forest characterized by a multitude of spears, the heat—like a forest fire—is cast and released into the atmosphere, and where the luster—the brilliance of the spears—shines forth.
His army was nourished by a rain of swords and spears and honored by kings;
it endeavored to capture the Apsarases by means of excellent heroes raised aloft on pikes.
By those lords and kings who were well-nourished and satisfied.

The quarters of the sky were illuminated by his armlets shimmering as they were washed by the sweat of exertion; he was fierce in his intense struggle, having violently crushed his adversaries with his spear.
Where the faces of the warriors, whose armlets quiver as they face all directions, wither like lotuses by frosty snows marked by maces.
Horses, men, and elephants were cut down by the movement of wheels and saws;
intoxicated elephants fell, struck by the falling mass of axes.
The fierce warriors leaped up, struck down by clubs, as they were being tossed about;
the trees that were chariots and the banners were crushed by the falling of stones from the siege-engines.
*Taṭāka* and *taḍāga* are synonyms; likewise, *mañcaka* and *mañjaka*; *maṇḍapa* and *maṇṭapa*;

and *lakuṭa* and *laguṭa*—as stated in the *Dvirūpakosha*. By means of these *lakuṭas*, which are large staffs, there was a stirring up like the agitating of cows; by that [stirring], they became as if flown away, having gone out of sight, being utterly formidable (*proḍḍāmarāḥ*).
And where the soldiers, having the habit of leaping up and shouting, cover themselves with trees, walls, skins, and so forth—that covering is called *caṭa*. || 33 ||
White as a lotus from a royal parasol severed at its tip by a sword, he was free from any ill omen, even though the agitation of his army had been diminished by the turbulence of his projectiles.
Pale with lotuses used as ear-ornaments, he is "unobserved" (alakṣaṇa), meaning that he does not take notice of, or rather, does not even reckon with, the agitation of the army. || 34 ||
The elephant, its flanks crushed by the falling of the leader who was binding the headless trunks (kabandha),
had its advancing force checked by great heroes standing with their goads ready.
Leaping up, those who sought to seize the charioteers alive were intercepted; headless trunks with severed heads were locked in embraces by their own bonds;
and those moving along the flanks were crushed by the falling of living chariot-commanders whose drivers had lost control, as well as by chariots and other vehicles that had veered onto wrong paths.
