Where, even by the blows of the goads from grooms wielding them, the elephants—though marked by those wounds—were either held back or repelled in battle by heroic strikers who remained steadfast in the count of their blows. || 35 ||
(211) Where the furious elephants fell under the impact of a multitude of falling axes;
where the heroes, experts in the various uses of nooses and weapons, uttered their cries of lamentation. || 36 ||
It was a game of dice involving life itself, where the gods played on all sides with extraordinary intensity against the heroes. || 36 ||
The lotuses falling from the throats of those whose bellies were split open by the *kṣurikā* blade, and the dancing of the throngs of heroes maddened by the brandishing of tridents; || 37 ||
The "lotus" is the lotus of the heart. The "heroes' assembly" refers to warriors abounding in heroism; they are dancing due to the tossing of their limbs. || 37 ||
It resounded with the shrill cries of flocks of fleeing archers, and it was a theater for the martial dance of the *bhindipāla* weapons, whose swelling bristles let out roars of defiance. (38)
Those whose weapon is the bow are archers (*dhānuṣka*). *Kākali* is a sweet yet indistinct sound;
*saṭāṭopa* is the grand display of the mane, and *ārabhaṭī* is the roar of arrogant pride. Wherein the warriors are like actors in the role of Narasiṃha by means of these two [qualities]. (38)
He was surrounded by a multitude of excellent warriors crushed like flour by his adamantine fists; his sharp battle-axes flew swiftly through the path of the sky like hawks.

The "vajramuṣṭi" (diamond-fist) is well known among wrestlers; [the battle] was crowded with other excellent warriors who were crushed by those [fists]. The compound "protpatatpaṭupaṭṭiśa" is an irregular (asamartha) compound used in the Vedic style (chāndasa). || 39 ||
The heroes, elephants, chariots, horses, and banners were dragged away by his hook; the great mountain ranges, agitated by his effortless play, were severed by his plowshare as it struck them.

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing the *dvandva* "śūra-ādi" (heroes and so forth). *Ketanāni* means banners or flags. *Halāhalam* refers to a battle where the weapon is the plow; therein, there is the "hatā-lūnānām helā-vahelanam"—the sportive disregard for those who have been slain or cut down. In that [battle], the heroes are agitated, yet they remain as immovable as the great mountain ranges (*kulācala*), or they are unshakable within the host of enemies. || 40 ||
The forest floor was dug up by sharp-pointed hoes, and the rows of stones were reduced by people using axes with a range twice that of a bow. || 41 ||

By means of instruments consisting of men who were as tall as palm trees, with high-lifting spades and raised pickaxes, [the ground] was dug up, uprooted, and leveled. By the word "bow" (*dhanuḥ*), the place for discharging arrows is indicated;
at a distance twice that measure, stakes were cast down, cut, and severed to facilitate the movement of troops during battle.
Wherein the worlds, the people, and the circles of stones [are found]. || 41 ||
On both sides were elephants as formidable as thunderbolts that had shattered rutting tuskers;
it was a battle where the pestle-like maces ground the grain of living beings in a mortar.

The term *mausalī* refers to that [battle] which contains a club-fight (*musalyuddha*)—whereby the clubs are metaphorically identified with pestles through a pun (*śleṣa*)—as brought about by the form of the pestle, mortar, and so forth. Thus it is called *mausalī*. (42)

The birds of his army were bound by a net of chains shining like missiles; the courtyards of the enemy's houses were brought under his control by the flickering swords and fierce daggers of the heroes.
Those heroes who were eager for battle were [slain] by his particular swords, *nistriṃśas*.

Here, "Vādi" refers to one whose name begins with the letter *va*, namely Vaivasvata; by implication, he is conceived of as the lord of hunters (*vyādha*) and others. Otherwise, it would be impossible for the birds of the bound army to have been led into his courtyard. (43)
Filled with the roars of the foremost beasts of prey being led away in herds, and with the clanging sounds of arrows whose nocks were struck by their claws and thumbs; (44)
The foremost [elephants], being led away,

were being dug up and extracted by those beasts of prey— tigers, wolves, and the like— with their thumb-like claws, which are characterized by their nails; this is expressed through the aspect of the object's activity, as in the expression "the elephant ascends" (*ārohati hastī*).

The suffix *śatṛ* is used here because of the intention to express autonomy (*svātantrya*). The "swinging" (*preṅkhā*) refers to the velocity of those arrows characterized by their feathered shafts (*puṅkha*). || 44 ||
Coloring all the quarters with his rays like condiments,
he raised up weapons from the warriors consumed by the fire of the jars cast among the troops (or, as another reading has it, from the soldiers cast away).

The army was one where the jars were cast down, the warriors were consumed by fire, and the weapons had been abandoned [or, according to alternative readings: the warriors were killed by fire, the weapons were seized, or the weapons were taken from the slain]. || 45 ||
"Rañjayan" means pleasing by means of mixing; "kumbhāgni" is well known [as a specific type of fire]. || 45 ||
With his frontal globes struck by the army, his eyes scorched by glowing embers,
and his face withered by the poisonous water discharged from the jars set upon him by the troops.
They were shattered, being struck by the spray of poisonous waters. || 46 ||

Like the end of the eon, he was like a mass of clouds intoxicated by a flood of heroes— a rain of excellent iron arrows— and with headless trunks dancing in agitation like peacocks; he whirled about with great speed.
Enveloped by the Mātaṅga mountain, there arose a tumultuous commotion of battle.
Where the clouds, intoxicated by the appearance of a flood of heroes, bestow excellent water characterized by showers of iron arrows;
where peacocks in the form of headless trunks dance with agitation and sport; and which is encircled by mountains in the form of elephants whirling and roaming about with great speed. || 47 ||
Thus ends the thirty-third canto, titled "The Description of the First Clash of the Two Armies," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the First Flight," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, among the kings eager for battle, as well as their soldiers and ministers—
Then these words arose from the sky and from the spectators there: || 1 ||
Here, the wonder of battle itself is described in detail by the face of the spectator of the fray, through compositions of diverse subjects. (1)
From the sky, they appeared—manifested themselves—before the spectators, such as the gods, gandharvas, and others. || 1 ||
Like a lake with swaying lotuses and like the sky filled with birds,
the firmament, strewn with the heads of heroes, shines with the appearance of being studded with stars.
"Carrying birds" is an attribute common to both the sky and the lake.

Because of the distinction between the attributes—namely, that [the sky] has a form like that of one "studded with stars"—it is conceived as the object of comparison through the attribution of difference. (2)
Behold, at midday, these clouds and sunbeams appear as if they were twilight, reddened by the winds carrying a flood of vermilion mixed with crimson droplets.
By means of the masses— that is, the collections— of red specks, which are droplets of blood,
appearing as if they were vermilion due to the winds, the evening clouds and the rays of the sun [became reddened]. (3)
(212) "O Blessed One, what is this? Is the sky filled with straw?
This is not straw; these are clouds of arrows from the heroes. (4)
From a distance, amidst a shower of chaff, someone, mistaking it for straw, asks his own master, "What is this?
He replies, "This is not it. || 4 ||
As many thousands of years as there are particles of dust on the earth moistened by blood, for that long do warriors find their abode in heaven.
"Do not fear; these are not swords possessing the luster of blue lotus petals.
These are the playful glances from the eyes of Lakṣmī as she gazes upon the heroes."
Of Lakṣmī—whether of the Fortune of Heaven or of the Fortune of Victory. || 6 ||
The flower-armed god began to loosen the girdles upon the hips of the celestial women, who were eager for the embrace of their heroes.
The term "heroism" (vīra) refers to the description of those who move through the sky. || 7 ||
With their trembling vine-like arms, their hands like red sprouts, their eyes intoxicated by the clusters of blossoms, and fragrant with the scent of honey; (8)
The reply of one hero to another hero, characterized by radiant splendor, is expressed in two verses. || 8 ||
The deities of the Nandana grove, singing with sweet voices,
have begun to dance in anticipation of your arrival.
This army breaks its own opposition from within with harsh axes, just as a village woman breaks her lover's heart with her glances and gestures.
By means of their glances, gestures, and playful movements of the eyes. || 10 ||
Alas! My father’s head, adorned with blazing earrings, has been carried by my broad-headed arrow to the vicinity of the sun, like the eighth planet [Rāhu] drawn near the sun by Time. (11)
At the proper time, as at the time of a solar eclipse; Rāhu is the eighth planet. || 11 ||
With his arms raised high, he whirled with speed a wheel called Citradaṇḍa, upon which two massive stones were mounted on chains attached to his feet and rotated rapidly.
The response to the timid person's fear is given by two verses.
A wheel-machine (cakropalayantra) is a wheel fixed upon a mechanical chain that hangs down from the feet. || 12 ||
This warrior shines like Yama; he comes from the region of the South.
As he withdraws the army from all sides, come, let us go back the way we came. (13)
"From the southern direction, from Yama"—the word "withdrawing" (*saṃharan*) is an epithet for both Yama and Yodhaya. || 13 ||
With their heads suddenly severed, the battlefields are crowded with flocks of herons swooping down from the hollows of the corpses;
headless trunks dance about, leaping as high as palm trees upon the arena of war.
Agitated by flocks of herons plunging into their gaping throats like abysses,
they surged upward with great force, struck by the rhythmic beats of the *tāla* drums used as musical instruments for battle.
In the assemblies of the hosts of gods, conversations were held among themselves:
"When will these wise ones go to the other world? How will they go? Who will go? From where? (15)
By means of four interrogative pronouns (kiṃvṛtta), the time, manner, person, and cause are questioned. || 15 ||
He swallows the approaching armies as the ocean swallows flowing rivers;
alas, what an extraordinary warrior he is, with his battle-arrays of fish and sea-monsters! 16.
"Flowing rivers" and "abounding in fish and crocodiles" are adjectives qualifying the rivers and the armies respectively. (16)
Rows of sharp iron arrows were scattered upon the temples of the elephants,
like full-fledged showers of rain fallen upon the peaks of mountains.
The ellipsis implies that they shine like full showers of rain fallen upon the masses of mountain peaks. || 17 ||
As he was about to say, "Alas! My head has been taken away by the spear," a voice from the sky cried out, "I live through my head! like the cry of a bird.

The remainder of the sentence is as follows: because he perceived the severing of his head as a source of suffering, he intended to speak accordingly; however, when his severed head flew away and he beheld the festival of his ascent to heaven, he cried out in the sky with joy, "I am alive, I have not died!"—this was heard by the people like the warbling of a bird (*khaga*) or a winged creature (*pakṣin*). This is the warbling of animals.
It has been uttered. || 18 ||
"Let this army, which drenches us with a rain of mechanical stones, be forcibly restrained by means of a network of iron chains. (19)
"This army is being drenched; it is entangled and enveloped by a net of chains—act [to free it]!"—such are the words of the soldiers.
Having recognized that her husband had been slain in battle, his former wife, now an Apsaras, who was previously free from wrinkles and grey hair, accepts him as her lord once more. (20)

The gods declared: "His former wife, who had died long ago, exists as an Apsaras; having recognized her husband—now deceased in battle, freed from wrinkles and grey hair, and become a god—she accepts him. || 20 ||
The splendors of the forest of spears, fashioned from the very beginning, appeared like rows of steps for the heroes to ascend to heaven. (21)
The splendors of that forest of spear-weapons have spread as far as heaven, the celestial realm; they are imagined as if they were rows of steps constructed [to ascend to the sky]. || 21 ||
On the chest of the warrior, whose body was as beautiful as lovely gold, that beloved woman was seen—a celestial nymph intent on searching for her husband. (22)

This woman, who was seen dead upon the chest of a warrior whose limbs—hands, feet, and so forth—were naturally beautiful with gold ornaments, is now seen to have become a celestial nymph (devapurandhrī) and is searching for her husband; this is the implied meaning. || 22 ||
"Alas! Our army has been destroyed by warriors with uplifted fists, just as the plateau of the divine mountain is overwhelmed by the great waves of the final dissolution. (23)
"Alas, it is destroyed!"—this is the utterance of one who is cowardly. || 23 ||
"Fight at the front, you fools! Carry away the half-dead men; do not strike down your own kin with kicks, you base ones! (24)
One's own, that is, belonging to oneself. || 24 ||
While the host of Apsarases is preoccupied with braiding their hair and filled with intense longing, let this soldier, having attained a divine body, be observed as he approaches their side. 25.
*Dhammilla-valanā* means the braiding of the hair. || 25 ||
On the banks of the celestial river, where golden lotuses are in bloom, gladden him who has come from afar with shade, cool water, and breezes. (26)
"Divert yourself, take rest by the heavenly river Gaṅgā"—this is the speech of the Apsaras friend. || 26 ||
With the tips of their fierce bones shattered by the clash of various weapons,
they fell through the sky with their thorny limbs outstretched like stars.
The word *koṭi* refers to the innumerable; *kaṇatkāraiḥ* means jingling or resonating. || 27 ||
In the sky, which is like a life-giving river flowing with the water of arrows and whirling with circles of fire,
even mountains are reduced to the state of minute silt.
The wheels cause it to whirl and possess eddies; the mud is characterized by its atoms (aṇu) and dust (reṇu).
The mud is indeed imagined, corresponding to the previously imagined flood. || 28 ||
The heads of the heroic kings, whirling in their orbital paths,
were caught upon the stalks of the creepers that were the rays of their weapons, with sword-blades serving as thorns.

The connection with the subsequent clause is: "The sky was turned into a lotus-pond by the heads of heroic kings wandering through the paths of the planets. To justify this, he qualifies [the heads] with the words beginning with "āyudhāṃśu" (rays of weapons):
the rays of the weapons are themselves the stalks of the lotus-creeper, and the swords attached to them are the petals.
And those whose thorns are spears, lances, and so forth, which are instruments for rending. || 29 ||
With the banners as its lotus stalks and petals, and with the bees acquired [in the form of] the flags,
the sky was turned into a lotus pond, where the lotuses swayed in the wind. (30)

Those [trees] which have banners as their flag-cloths—that is, leaves that constitute parts of their lotus-stalks—and by whom bees, characterized as arrows, were obtained through wordplay (śleṣa). || 30 ||

Like ants on a mountain covered with a heap of dead elephants, the timid women shrink away; and he used the word "ca" (and) for the purpose of combining the two similes, as if [the women] were clinging to the chests of men. || 31 ||
Winds blow that stir the tresses of the Vidyādhara women, heralding their union with beloveds of unprecedented and supreme beauty.

The sense is that, as they emerge from their homes with their curls tossed upward, these [women] take on the form of auspicious omens due to their favorable nature, thereby foretelling the fulfillment of their heart's desires. || 32 ||
As the parasols were raised aloft and remained suspended in the sky, they attained the state of moons;
indeed, by means of his fame incarnate, the moon itself was made into a white parasol.

The particle *iva* is connected to what precedes as well. Consequently, two metaphors (*utprekṣā*) are obtained: that the moon-hood was as if produced by the umbrellas situated in the sky, and that the state of being a white parasol on earth was as if produced by the moon in the form of his fame. || 33 ||
At the end of his death-faint, the soldier, in the blink of an eye, attained an immortal body fashioned by the artisan of his own karma, like a city in a dream.
Showers of spears, javelins, double-edged swords, and discuses were released with joy;
their fragments remained in the ocean of the sky, crowded with fish and sea-monsters.

Free from contentment, yet appearing as if characterized by discontent, they remain agitated; their limbs are crowded together like those of fish and sea-monsters (or, according to another reading, *śepha*).
The notion that fish and other creatures dwelling in the ocean constitute limbs of the ocean is merely figurative. || 35 ||
The expanse of the sky, filled with white umbrellas severed by arrows like swans,
shone as if covered by hundreds of thousands of gathered full moon discs.
It is rendered beautiful by chowries flying in the sky with lovely gurgling sounds,
possessing the luster of a mass of waves whose flow is obstructed and shaken by the wind.
The stability of those waves which was shaken by the wind [was restored]. || 37 ||
Umbrellas, chowries, and banners, shattered by weapons, are seen scattered across the field of the sky like stalks of the rice-plant of fame. (38)
Behold, as they are carried through the sky in safety, they are being brought to destruction by my arrows, like the beauty of the crops when a shower of locusts approaches. (39)
"Sakṣemā" is an address to the listener; "upāyantī" means approaching, drawing near, and having its fruit imminent. || 39 ||
This clashing sound of the swords of soldiers with outstretched staff-like arms,
produced from their hard armor, is like the fierce roar of Death itself.
"Chaṭātkṛti" is an imitation of the sound produced by the falling of a sword; it is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā) that this very sound is the "huṃ" roar of Death. || 40 ||
Shattered by the wind of false reasoning, with the streams of their tusks blocked,
the elephants of this age of universal decay lie broken like mountains.
The weapons, such as swords and other arms, are like the winds at the end of an aeon (*kalpānila*), by which [the mountains] were shattered.
Their tusks are like the waters of waterfalls, due to the similarity between them in being white and flowing outward; these elephants are like mountains (*naga*). 41.
The chariot-city, with its horses yoked to the wheels of the Lord of the Discus, is tossed about in the great lake of blood; its movement overwhelmed by cries of "Alas! Alas!", it struggles on. (42)
Arrayed and armored; overcome in the great lake of blood, its movement vanished due to the obstruction of the discus, yet it still exerts itself and quivers with cries of "Alas! Alas!
in distress, amidst the clanging sounds produced by the striking together of swords against the walls of leather armor.
As Kālarātri dances, she plays like a lute of battle. || 43 ||

With their hands bearing heroic elephants and other [implements], and with armor and wall-like shields marked by the impressions of bowstrings, they produced the sounds of musical performance through the clashing of swords. || 43 ||
Behold how the quarters of the sky are reddened by the wind sprinkled with drops from the streams of blood shed by men, elephants, donkeys, and horses.
In the sky, which was like a cloud of the rays of weapons and dark as Kālī’s hair, she appeared like lightning rising amidst clouds heavy with a mass of arrow-buds. (45)
The *cikuras* are like my dark, glossy locks of hair; the *korakas* are the arrows themselves, which are the buds—their "burden" (*bhāraḥ*) is a mass, and that constitutes the garland (*srak*).

The word *jalade* is a generic term for a cloud; it is further qualified by the word *meghe* (cloud), derived from the root *miha* meaning "to sprinkle," signifying that which is primarily characterized by such moisture. || 45 ||
With weapons whose blades were smeared with fresh blood clinging to them,
the world shone like the agitated realm of fire, as if ablaze.

The world, filled with infinite weapons that were smeared with blood, exhausted, shattered, and fallen upon the ground, shone like the realm of Agni—this is the sense. In the reading *agniśoka iva*, it should be explained as "like [the world] distressed by the sorrow caused by fire, such as the burning of a city. || 46 ||
Showers of *bhuśuṇḍīs*, spears, tridents, swords, clubs,
and javelins fell from their hands in great numbers, mutually cutting and piercing one another.
The battle, in which the Yātudhānas struck with unshakable singular blows and whose wisdom was clouded by the sight of one another's fury, stood like a dream.

[This refers to] the heroic exploits of many [demons], who were incapable of moving Akṣobhya (the Immovable One) because of the extreme lightness of a single most valiant [hero’s] strike; where the heroic conduct is to be inferred (*unneya*) by means of *yātudhānī*—the illusory power (*māyā*) of the *yātudhānas*, the Rākṣasas. [The form] *nayateṣṭilopa* is a Vedic irregularity (*chāndasa*). [It occurs] through fury (*saṃrambheṇa*).

That by which one looks with anger is "looking with agitation" (*saṃrambhāvekṣaṇi*); such is the wisdom (*prajñā*) in which there is the thought of a combatant. In the context of dreams, it refers to a single [combatant] amidst dream-objects that are "unshakable"—that is, devoid of movement such as cutting or piercing conducive to destruction.
By mere vigilance, through the striking down [of enemies], the false activity of the Yātudhānas—comparable to illusions—is overcome by affliction and the like.

Where there is the self-luminous wisdom of the Self, which observes with intensity and absorption, one perceives the battle standing before one as if it were a dream; the sense is that "I see the battle standing before me as if it were a dream. || 48 ||
With the incessant clashing of weapons whose sounds do not cease,
the terrifying roar of battle, arising from the agitation of wounds, seems to sing aloud.
By the continuous and incessant clanging sounds arising from the blows and counter-blows—the mutual striking—of weapons. || 49 ||
The ocean of battle, filled with the fierce dust raised by the weapons of mutual combat,
became as if composed entirely of sand, with severed umbrellas for its waves.
It consists of sand and abounds in sandy soil. || 50 ||

This mountain of battle, filling the world of the world-protectors with the echoes of musical instruments spread abroad with impetuous and passionate force, is fierce in its skillful wings. (The reading "ravamugra" is preferred.)
Like the revolving sphere at the end of an eon in the sky. || 51 ||

This visible sign of battle is one by which the worlds of the world-protectors, the lords of the quarters, have been filled with the impetuous, flavorful, sweet, spreading, and far-reaching echoes and reverberations of musical instruments (*tūrya*); that is to say, it seems to roar as if through the effort of ascending caused by the sounds of those instruments.

Or rather, the mountain—standing near the battlefield—is perceived as if it has begun to fly into the sky at the end of the eon, due to the mutual opposing movements of the two capable wings characterized by the two armies, both fierce and harsh in combat. This is the meaning. || 51 ||
Alas, alas! Woe to those scorched by the manifest flashes of lightning leaping forth from the mouths of the vast, armored [serpents]!
Resounding with the twang of their vibrating strings, the iron arrows, as they strike, carry away heaps of mountain rocks.
Lamenting that their own arrows were rendered futile against the thick armor, even though they were capable, the heroes cried out, "Alas! Alas!

Yet those mountain-like iron shafts (ārāca), having struck the formidable and exceedingly hard armor, pierced right through it; then, as if flying up from the impact, they emitted flames resembling flashes of manifest lightning, thereby heating the armor.

They carry away the mass of stones from the nearby mountain. "Hā hā! expresses grief. The sense is that even one who, having been urged toward a desired task, fails to do it and instead performs a great task that was undesired, is simply to be censured.
In the reading *araṇītaḥ*, [it refers to] the bow characterized by its vibrating string, which was drawn (*īritāyāḥ*).
It should be explained that "nārācas" refers to arrows which are like fires produced from the friction of the *araṇi* wood that has been pulled out and churned from the forest (*araṇya*). || 52 ||
Before these arrows, blazing like a flaming fire, can sever our limbs with a sharp *cham* sound and bring about our destruction,
come here quickly, my friend, driven by passion; let us depart!
This watch passes; it is the fourth day.

Now, a certain reply to one who is weary from battle: "O you whose desire is severed"—that is, O friend, you whose desire for combat has been cut off by fatigue—"listen to this beneficial advice which is *acchaṃ*, meaning clear, pure, and faultless," as will be stated hereafter. [The arrows] are like blazing fire, radiant with their shafts.
Before they cause the breaking— that is, the severing— of our limbs, such as our hands and feet, we shall go away, depart quickly, swiftly, and with haste, so that it may be so;
for this is the fourth watch, the hour belonging to Yama.
It flows on for the destruction of people, like a day of fixed fasting; the meaning is that it revolves.
However, if the reading is *chinneccācchṛṃ*, it should be construed as: "those who do not cause the breaking of limbs with the sound *chācchṛṃ* when armor and such have been severed. || 53 ||

Thus ends the thirty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the Words of the Spectators at the Battle," in the *Līlopākhyāna* (The Story of Līlā) within the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* (Book on Origination) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. || 34 ||
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Words of the Spectators of the Battle," in the Utpttiprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirty-fifth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Now, the waves of horses were intent upon flying upward.
That ocean of battle became like one intoxicated, as if possessed by a frantic dance.
In this work, the battle of the fourfold army is described at length through extensive descriptions of various forms resembling oceans, forests, and the dissolution of the world. (1)
Therein, first intending to describe [the reality] by way of the ocean through thirteen verses, he says, beginning with "atha" (now), etc. || 1 ||
With the white spears resting upon the foam of the parasols,
it was filled with the cavities agitated by the surging, restless waves of the cavalry.
The white arrows resting upon the masses of foam are like *śaphara* fish—a specific species of small fish—and the cavalry troops, due to their habit of leaping up, are like waves. || 2 ||
It possessed the swirling eddies of armies led by rivers of various weapons, and its moving great mountains were the massive, shifting temples of rutting elephant herds.

"Vivṛtti" means revolving; "tadvān" refers to that which possesses such motion. A "ghaṭā" is a multitude; characterized by this, the "kulācalāḥ"—the great mountain ranges such as Mandara and others—were "āpīṭham," from their bases to their very roots, "calācalāḥ," or exceedingly unsteady and trembling, in that place. In the reading "balābala," it must be construed with some difficulty: "they were like the Kulācalas fighting for the sake of testing strength and weakness. || 3 ||
With his head whirling from the circular motion of hundreds of whirling discuses, he was like one whose hair is caught in the wind;
the water-like luster of his brandishing sword was swallowed by the clouds of dust.
Where the movement of whirlpools is a circling motion, by which the severed-head grasses are made to spin;
there, the covering of sword-blade dust is conceived as their drink. (4)
The two ships, which had shattered the masses of unbroken soldiers within the vast array of crocodiles,
caused the mountain caves to resound with the great gurgling roar of their whirlpools.

In the context of the army, it refers to the arrangement of the troops in a formation shaped like a sea-monster (*makara*). It is where the thick mountain caves—the hollows or crevices of the clouds that resound as echoes—resonate. (5)
The mustard seeds were the flood of arrows emerging from the array of fish; the circles of waves were the banners torn away by the surging billows of weapons.
The dead men, like fish (mīna), having emerged from their arrays,
were like mustard seeds (sarṣapa) that had borne fruit in the field, possessing heads like pods filled with a mass of seeds; in the case of the ocean,
they were like the white masses of *kāśa* seeds born from the schools of fish (*mīna*).
Where mustard seeds [float] like eggs, amidst the garments of waves—that is, by means of powerful billows.
His earrings were like whirlpools in an ocean formed by weapons and water;
his army, with its dense movement of fury, was like the great timi and timingila fish.

He whose [hair] has curls like whirlpools, unstable like clouds resembling the ocean; by means of his fury (saṃrambha), which is anger, there is a dense movement of troops like a sea where there are *timi* and *timiṅgila*—varieties of great fish. (7)
The army was terrifying like a body of water with its black iron armor acting as its dark ripples;
it was adorned by the soldiers and others caught within the swirling lines of headless trunks that served as its eddies.

With an army that was like a revolving body of water, whose essence consisted of black iron and which was clad in armor made of that same material; wherein ornaments belonging to the soldiers and others were fixed and settled within the lines of the whirlpools— whirlpools being both water and headless trunks.
In the sense of the ocean, "sainyādīni" refers to the *rākṣasas* who devour (*adanti*) the armies; he is one whose ornaments are those very beings. || 8 ||
(215) The quarters of the sky were thick with the spray of arrows like mist and darkness;
all sound was silenced by the roar, leaving only a single, dense, and tumultuous *bhuṃbhuma* resonance. || 9 ||
By its resonance, all sounds have been rendered imperceptible, as if completely dried up; for this very reason, it is a single, solid *ghuṃghuma* sound. || 9 ||
With droplets from fragments of heads scattered by the frantic falling and rising [of warriors], and with pieces of men as timber whirling within the arrays of whirlpools and circles; || 10 ||
Fierce in its agitation as it churned the coils of the bow that emitted a harsh *ṭāṅkāra* sound,
it rose up from the netherworld itself, as if with waves of soldiers surging forth without hesitation.
The bows themselves were earrings; [the phrase refers to] the crushing and cutting of those serpent-bodies.
It was foamy with the parasols and banners that flew back and forth in endless succession; the rushing force of the flowing rivers of blood carried away the trees that were the chariots.
It was filled with great bubbles of blood resembling elephants,
and its aquatic creatures were the horses and elephants moving within the current of the army.
In that place, horses and elephants themselves became aquatic creatures moving in the water. || 13 ||
That battle was as wondrous to men as the village of Ambara;
it was as restless as mountains shaken by the earthquake at the time of universal dissolution.
Ambaragrāma is a city of the Gandharvas. Now, he describes that very battle as being like the end of an aeon (kalpānta), beginning with the words "abhūt" and so forth. 14.
With birds [in the form of] leaping waves, with the flanks [of the river] struck by falling herds of elephants, and with the loud "ghuru-ghuru" roar of the throngs of terrified deer; || 15 ||
Wherein the birds are like shimmering waves. || 15 ||
His army was as fragile as hundreds of locusts amidst rows of autumn reeds;
his leaping horses were like śarabhas, and the earth was covered with a forest of arrows. || 16 ||
Where the horses themselves were śarabhas; where the forest ground was such that the loads of arrows (śarabhārāḥ) bore arrows (śarān). 16.

With the humming of moving bees [the reading "jaladvirepha" is also found], with the sound of trumpets deep within its caves, that cloud-like army, after a long time, had lions among its warriors rolling on the ground. || 17 ||

The phrase "after a long time" (cirāt) connects with what follows later—that is, with what occurs in the twentieth verse. Where the elephants and other troops, accompanied by their armies, were like clouds;
where the spreading dust was like a cloud and the retreating army was like a mountain range. [Verse 17]
His body was adorned with excellent falling chariots, and he brandished a circle of blazing swords. || 18 ||
There, the limbs of great chariot-warriors mounted on excellent chariots fell down; likewise, there were swords, specific types of deer, and scimitars. 18.
With a mass of flowers falling from their feet, with banners and parasols serving as clouds, and with elephants falling along with the rushing current of rivers of blood; || 19 ||
The footprints themselves are the very footsteps; they are indeed floods of flowers. || 19 ||
That battle became like the end of an aeon, agitated by the devouring of the world,
with its standards, umbrellas, banners, chariots, and cities overturned.
He was like a sun intensely radiant with a multitude of falling streams of pure weapons,
scorching the minds of all with the heat of his fierce vital force.
By means of severe hardship and the torment of life. || 21 ||
It was incessantly filled with showers of arrows from bows like Puṣkarāvarta clouds,
while the sky was encircled by the lightning-like streaks of the whirling sword-blades.
The bows are the rainbows of those clouds known as Puṣkarāvarta—the clouds of universal dissolution;
and the swords are the streaks of lightning, appearing as the polished edges upon the stone. || 22 ||
The mountain-like herds of elephants fell into the ocean of blood that had been severed;
the stars, like falling drops of light, were scattered across the sky.
Scattered and spread throughout the sky, they fall and mingle with one another; thus, the large drops of blood become like stars where they gather. 23.
The sky was filled with clouds resembling whirlpools in the waters of the Cakrakulyā river;
the world of the enemy host was reduced to the state of the end of an aeon by the fire of his weapons.

Where the celestial veins (*vyoma-śirā*) and the clouds are filled with river-like successions of wheels (*cakra-paramparā-saridbhiḥ*)—resembling whirlpools—as they revolve in the region of the waters;
and where there is the transition to other worlds, that is, the crossing over to the world beyond (*paraloka*). || 24 ||
The pure mountain [of the world] had its surface covered by the rain of thunderbolts from the clouds of causes;
the multitudes of people were crushed by the falling mass of the king of elephants and the mountains. || 25 ||
The earth and sky were covered by clouds in the form of dense masses of arrow-showers;
the ground became soft from the impact of the agitation caused by the great ocean-like army. || 26 ||
With dense and thick clouds of armies, like showers of arrows. || 26 ||
It was pervaded by [beings] tossed about by fierce winds like a mountain by aquatic monsters,
appearing like a sudden eruption of weapons as they busied themselves with crushing one another.

[The ocean] was [filled] with aquatic predators and *laḍuṇḍubha* crocodiles; by implication, it is understood that it was "immovable" because it was within the ocean. The phrase "intent on crushing one another" implies "with weapons. There is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) suggesting that it was as if rising up during the cataclysmic dissolution (*saṃvarta*) when a rain of weapons falls. 27. [It was filled with] spears, swords, discuses, arrows, javelins, maces, and *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles...
Palaces and other structures, crashing against one another and resounding with noise,
blazed as they whirled about by the hundreds,
displaying the likeness of objects tossed about by the winds at the end of an aeon.

Blazing tridents and other weapons, clashing against one another and resounding as they whirled through the quarters, displayed the playful grace of objects such as rocks, trees, and missiles tossed about by the winds at the end of a kalpa. The meaning is that they bore [that appearance]. || 28 ||

Thus ends the thirty-fifth canto, titled "Description of the Battle," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. || 35 ||
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Battle," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-sixth canto.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, while the heaps of arrows stood like mountain peaks,
all those who were timid were broken and fled in the ten directions.
In this [chapter], duels with equal weapons and the allies are described,
as well as the lords of the various regions together with their respective territories, such as the Easterners and others.
The connection with the following verse is as follows: "While heaps of arrows, resembling mountain peaks, remained upon the bodies of the Mātaṅgas. (1)
Upon mountains of elephant carcasses where rows of clouds rest, and amidst Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas sporting in an ocean of blood; (2)
Of the great ones established in dharma, endowed with virtue, vigor, and courage; pure lotuses of their lineage, heroes who never retreat. (3)
Virtue is good conduct; strength is power. "Of the lotuses of noble families" means of those who, like lotuses, perfume their own family with the fragrances of their own glory. || 3 ||
Duels broke out like the thundering of clouds;
eager to swallow one another, they clashed like the surging floods of rivers.
"Mutual combat" refers to devouring or swallowing one another; "as if longing for it" is an adjective qualifying the duel. The ellipsis is "the heroes meet. (4)
A cage met with a cage, a multitude of elephants with a mass of elephants,
a forest with a forest, and a mountain with a mountain, as they clashed by force.
The mountain, accompanied by the forest, was like that [other] mountain which was likewise accompanied by such a forest.
The flood of horses, with its multitude of horses meeting together in a roar and great speed,
was like a surge of waves upon the ocean, possessing the sound of a mass of billows.
One division of men fought against another division of men with equal weapons,
just as a gust of wind driven by the breeze strikes against another gust of wind.
He is Marudvala because he turns and moves with the Maruts. || 7 ||
And one flood of chariots crushed the entire body of the other flood of chariots,
just as a city, driven by fate, might crush another city belonging to the Asuras.
The body is the mutual arrangement [of its parts]. || 8 ||
The army of archers, with its banners covering the sky, fought like an unprecedented rain-cloud formed by the autumnal downpour of arrows.
In which action a previously unseen and novel rain-cloud was created or produced, [and] how he fought;
[the sky was] "sthagitākāśā," meaning the sky was covered or obscured.
When warriors of feeble resolve flee by some stratagem during battles with uneven weapons in that fire of the world-destruction at the end of the age, then—
They are of tender disposition and timid hearts. || 10 ||

Wielders of the discus clashed with wielders of the discus, archers with archers, swordsmen with sword-fighters, and those armed with *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles with those armed with *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles. (11)
In this context, throughout the work, those who carry weapons are indicated by the names of the weapons in the instrumental case;
by the word *bhuśuṇḍī*, those who carry the *bhuśuṇḍī* are expressed through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). || 11 ||
The great wielders of maces fought with maces, the Kuntis with their spears,
those armed with double-edged swords with sword-bearers, and those with darts in hand with other dart-wielders.

Those with mallets fought with mallet-wielders; those with gleaming clubs fought with those possessing clubs; those skilled with spears fought with spear-fighters; and those expert with pikes fought with pike-bearers. || 13 ||
Those skilled with spears fought with spears, those praised for their axes with battle-axes,
the mace-wielders with raised clubs, and those armed with stones with stones.

Those who know [the art] describe the throwing of darts as *āsana* (seizing) and *kṣepaṇa* (casting); these are what is meant by "axes" (*paraśu*), that is to say, they are renowned [for such skills].
Those who have raised clubs—that is, bamboo staves—are called *lakuṭodya*; [the action is performed] by them. || 14 ||
With nooses they were bearers of nooses; with spikes, bearers of spikes; with daggers they were bearers of daggers, and with slings they were equipped with them. (15)
The armies are those bearing nooses; *śaṅku* and *kṣurikā* are specific types of minor weapons;
"those belonging to them" means those joined with them. || 15 ||
They hold vajra-fists and are raised up by vajras and hooks; they are skilled at scratching with plows and possess tridents as those who bear tridents.

"With vajras held in their fists" means with vajra-fists (*vajramuṣṭi*). By the term "vajra-fist," the clenched fists of wrestlers bound with iron pins are meant. "Nikāṣa" means rubbing or grinding. || 16 ||
With nets of chains and with chains as delicate as bees,
they were like masses of waves from the agitated ocean, tossed about by the disturbances of the end of the eon.
"Śṛṅkhalājāla" refers to a specific type of chain-mail armor; those cavalrymen possessing it are called "śṛṅkhalājālinaḥ.
The word "komala" denotes a glossy, dark-blue hue. The term "militāḥ" (joined together) is to be supplied everywhere [in the verse]. The simile, moreover, is common to all that has preceded. || 17 ||
The single ocean of the sky appeared with the whirling fragments of the shattered discus as its eddies, the spray of arrows as its wind, and the revolving weapons as its sea-monsters. || 18 ||
In which [ocean] there were whirlpools consisting of those wheels and wheel-spokes that, being agitated, revolved like petals.
With its aquatic creatures consisting of the heads of waves that were blooming weapons,
this ocean within the cavity of heaven and earth became impossible for even the gods to cross.

The blossoming marks of weapons are the crests of its waves, and the channels are the ripples; that very ocean is the cavity—the intermediate space—between the two worlds, heaven and earth, which is difficult for the living gods to cross. 19.
The army of the eight divine classes, divided into those two factions,
stood thus enraged against the two kings, half on one side and half on the other.

His battle-array was such that it possessed the well-known eightfold divine and unimpeded equipment— knowledge, intellect, strength, heroism, missiles, horses, chariots, and the bow— and with that aforementioned force, joined in pairs on both sides, the two armies stood enraged, each side facing the other.

Why is that? Because it was situated in such a way as to be favorable to the two kings, Sindhurāja and Vidūratha; or else, because of that army consisting of the eight classes of divine beings—yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and asuras on one side, and gods, gandharvas, kinnaras, and vidyādharas on the other.
The meaning is that the army stood divided into two wings, each consisting of half the force, according to whether victory or defeat was destined for them;
for even the two kings remained thus, owing to their being possessed of such corresponding unseen merit (adṛṣṭa).
These [kings] had arrived from the eastern directions and other regions, as calculated in the enumeration of the Middle Country and so forth.
Hear now of the districts belonging to Padma, the Lord of Līlā. || 21 ||

Now, Vasiṣṭha makes a formal declaration to describe in sequence the people who serve as allies to Padma and Sindhurāja, categorized by their respective regions according to the divisions of the directions, such as the East and so forth:
In the east are the Kosalas, Kāśis, Māgadhas, Mithilas, and Utkalas;
as well as the Mekhalas, Karkaras, Mudras, and those who are skilled in battle.

The names of the regions are clear. Although some differences and discrepancies are observed between the names of the regions mentioned here and those stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya-purāṇa* and other Purāṇas, there is no fault, as they belong to different cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*). In the eastern direction, there are 24 regions and 7 mountains. (22)
The Mukhyas, the Himas, those headed by Rudra, the Tāmraliptas, as well as the Prāgjyotiṣas, the Vājimukhas, the Ambaṣṭhas, and the cannibals; || 23 ||
The Varṇakoṣṭhas, the Saviśvotras, the Āmamīnāśanas, as well as the Vyāghravakras, the Kirātas, the Sauvīras, and the Ekapādakas. || 24 ||
There is a mountain here named Mālyavat, as well as Śibirāñjana;
likewise, there are Vṛṣala, Dhvaja, Padma, and others, as well as the mountain Udayakara.
Now, to the southeast, these inhabitants of the Vindhya and other regions reside:
the Cedis, the Vatsas, the Daśārṇas, and the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, and Upavaṅgas. (26)

The eastern and the southern directions; the intermediate direction between these two is the southeast (*prāgdakṣiṇā*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the rule "the names of directions [are compounded] when referring to an intermediate direction. Here too, there are twenty-seven regions. 27. 26.
The Kaliṅgas, Puṇḍras, Jaṭharas, Vidarbhas, and Mekhalas;
those with the complexion of Śabara faces, and the Karṇātris who fill the city. (27)
The Kaṇṭakasthala people, the Pṛthagdīpaka-soft ones, the Karṇāndhra, the Caulika, and likewise the Ārmaṇvata; || 28 ||
The Kākakas, Hemakuḍyas, and likewise those with beards;
the Baligrīvas, Mahāgrīvas, Kiṣkindhas, and Nālikerins.
Now, these kings belong to the southern side of this Lord of Līlā:
Vindhya, Kusumāpīḍa, Mahendra, and likewise Dardura. (30)
In the south, there are 6 mountains and 63 countries. || 30 ||
Malaya and Sūryavān, as well as the Gaṇas known as Rājyasamṛddhaka,
along with those celebrated as Avantī and Śāmbavatī.
The Daśapūraka, Kathācakra, Āreṣika, Āturaka, and Kacchapa; the Vanavāsa, Upagiri, and likewise the Bhadragiri mountains.
The Nāgaras, the Daṇḍakas, the Gaṇarāṣṭras, the Nṛrāṣṭrakas, the Sāhas, the Śaivārṣyamūkas, the Karkoṭas, and the Vanabimbalas. || 33 ||
The Pampānivāsins, the Kairakas, the Karkavīrakas, the Sverikas, the Yāsikas, and the Dharmapattanapañjikās; || 34 ||
The Kāśikas, Tṛṣṇakhallūlas, Yādās, Tāmraparṇakas, Gonardas, Kanakas, and those belonging to Dīnapattana; || 35 ||
Tāmrīkā, those filled with *dambharākī*,
as well as *sahakāraiṇaka*,
*vaituṇḍaka*, *tumbavanāla*, *ajinadvīpa*, and *karṇikā*. (36)
The Śivayas, the Kauṅkaṇas, the Citrakūṭakas, the Karṇāṭas, the Maṇṭavaṭakas, and likewise the Mahākaṭakikas; (37)
The Āndhras, the Kolagiris, the Avantikas, the Vicerikas, the Caṇḍāyattas, the Devanakas, the Krauñcas, and likewise the Vāhas; || 38 ||
Śilākṣārodabha, Nanda, and Mardana— those known as the Malayas—
are remembered as the peaks of Citrakūṭa, which are the hosts of Rākṣasas in Laṅkā.
Then, in the south-western direction, there are the Mahārājya and Surāṣṭra peoples,
as well as those known as Sindhu, Sauvīra, and Śūdra, along with the Ābhīras and Draviḍas.
In the south-eastern direction, there are four mountains and nineteen regions. 40.
The Kīkaṭas are known as Siddhakhaṇḍa, as well as the Kāliruhās;
here is the Hemagiri mountain, as well as the Raivataka mountain.
Jayakaccha, Mayavara, the Yavanas, and the Jantus there;
the Bāhlīkas, Mārgaṇas, Āvantas, Dhūmras, and those named Tumbakas. || 42 ||
Likewise, the hosts of Lājagaṇas and those who dwell upon the mountains, as well as millions of people from the coastal regions— these are the subjects of the Lord of Līlā.
Now, hear of these districts situated as its antidote; first, these great mountains are prominent in the western direction. (44)
In the west, there are nine mountains and eighteen regions. || 44 ||
The lord of mountains named Maṇimān, as well as Kurārpaṇagiri;
the forest Arkaha, Meghabhava, Cakravān, and Astaparvata. || 45 ||
The people known as Pañcajanas were those who brought an end to the Kāśa-Brahmacaryas; likewise there were the Bhārakṣatas, the Pārakas, and the Śāntikas. || 46 ||
"End-makers of the Kāśas and the Brahmaṇacas"—this is an epithet for the Pañcajanas. || 46 ||
The Śaibyās, Āramarakas, Chāchās, Karachāyās, Mahulās, and likewise the Niyamās; the Haihayas, Suhmagas, Tājikas, and likewise the Hūṇakas. || 47 ||
In Pārśva and Kataka, there are the Karkas, Giriparṇāvas, and others;
these castes, having abandoned the boundaries of dharma, are Mleccha tribes.
The Karkas are on the flanks of the southern and northern parts of the hexagon. || 48 ||
Beyond that is a land devoid of human settlements for two hundred yojanas;
beyond that is the peak of Mahendra, whose ground is composed of pearls and gems.
The word division is *ajanapade*. || 49 ||
Beyond the hundreds of mountains is the mountain named Aśva;
beyond that is the fearsome great ocean on the slope of Mount Pāriyātra.
"On the shore" means, by implication, on the shore of the great ocean. || 50 ||
In the northwestern direction lies the region of Girimati;
likewise Veṇupati, and beyond that, the great earth ruled by Narapati.
In the north-western direction, there are nineteen countries; the country known as Veṇupati is situated there, as is Narapati, and Mahī, which is ever-celebrated with festivals.
Likewise, there were the Phalguṇas, the Māṇḍavyas, and the Ekanetrakas;
the Purukundas, the Pārās, and those who meditate upon the orb of the sun.
Vanmilās, Nalinās, Dīrghās, and those with long hair, limbs, and arms; as well as Raṅgās, Stanikās, Guruhās, and Clahās (according to the reading). || 53 ||
Since their hair, limbs, and arms are long, they are therefore called "Long" (Dīrgha); this is the meaning. || 53 ||
p.
218) Beyond that is the incomparable kingdom of women, where cows, bulls, and offspring are their food.
Then, in the north, there is the Himavat, then the Krauñca, and then the Madhumān mountain. 54.
In the north, there are six mountains; in their foothills and bordering mountains, there are forty-four regions. || 54 ||
Kailāsa, Vasumān, and Meru; in their foothills dwell people, both Madrās and Ārevayas, Audheyas, Mālavas, and Śūrasenikas. || 55 ||
The Rājanyas are to be known as such, as well as the son of Arjuna; likewise the Trigartas, the Ekapāts, the Kṣudrās, the Abalās, and those dwelling in Asvastava.
The Abalas, Prakhalas, Śākas, and Kṣemadhūrtis;
likewise the Daśadānas, Āgāvās, Anyadaṇḍas, and Anyasanās. (57)
The Dhānadās, the Sarakas, and likewise the Vāṭadhānas; the Gāndhāras of Antaradvīpa, as well as the Avantyas and the Suras. || 58 ||
Then there was the city named Takṣaśilā; after that, Vīlavagodhanī;
then the land of Puṣkarāvarta; and beyond that, Yaśovatimahī.
Then there are Nābhimati, Bhūmi, Tikṣā, and likewise Kālavarā;
also the city of Kāhaka and the city of Surabhūti. || 60 ||
Likewise, there were Ratikādarśas and Antarādarśas;
then the Piṅgalapāṇḍavyas and the Yātudhānakas of the Yamunā.
The Mānavas, the Aṅgas, the Hematālas, and likewise the Svasvamukhas;
as well as Himavat, Vasumān, Krauñca, and Kailāsa—these were the mountains. (62)
Beyond that is a land devoid of human settlements, measuring one hundred and eighty yojanas.
Now, listen to the names of the inhabited regions in order, starting from the northeast.
In the north-eastern direction, there are twenty-four regions and one mountain. 63.
The Kālutas, the Brahmaputras, the Kuṇidas, and likewise the Khadinas;
the Mālavas, the Randhrarājyas, and similarly the Vanas and the Rāṣṭras. || 64 ||
The Keḍavastās, the Siṃhaputrās, as well as those who have become dwarfs (vāmanatāṃ gatāḥ), the Sāvākāḥ, the Cāpalavahas, the Kāmiras, and likewise the Daradas; 65.
Then there were the Abhisāsadas, Jārvākās, Palolas, Kuvikas, and Kautukas;
and the Kirātas who were seized in Ayodhyā, as well as the wretched Svarṇas and Mahīs. 66.
Then there was the ground of the divine groves, followed by the splendor of Viśvāvasu’s excellent palace,
and then Mount Kailāsa with its beautiful forests.
Its ground is equal to the celestial chariots of the Vidyādharas and the immortals. || 67 ||
Thus ends the thirty-sixth canto, titled "Description of the Provinces," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Provinces," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In that battle, which was terrible with men and elephants violently torn asunder,
"Me first! Me first!"—thus did they follow in the crowd.

The people of the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa) are celebrated by the name of their respective regions (janapada), as well as the victories and defeats in dual combats among those of the various districts. || 1 ||
In groups within groups, or following after that which has the nature of falling in succession. || 1 ||
These and many others there were reduced to ashes as they entered with great effort, like moths into a fire. || 2 ||
In this regard, other people from the Middle Country have not been cited by me;
listen to these as I shall describe the various positions of King Līlā. (3)
The peoples of the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa). 29 || 3 ||
The Taddehikas, Śūrasenas, Guḍas, Aśvaghanāyakas, Uttamajyotis, Bhadrāṇis, Madamadhyamikas, and others [are there]. (4)
The Sālūkākodyamālāsya, the Daurjñeyas,
the Pippalāyanas, the Māṇḍavyas, the Pāṇḍunagaras, and the Saugrīvādyas are the Gurugrahas. (5)
The Pāriyātras, Kurāṣṭras, and also the Yāmunas and Udumbaras;
the Rājyāhvās, Ujjihānas, Kālakoṭikas, and Māthuras.
The Pāñcālas and those from Dharmāraṇya, likewise those from the north and the south;
the people of Pāñcālaka, Kurukṣetra, and the Sārasvatas.
Driven by the forces of Avantī, Syandana, Śreṇī, Kunti, and Pañcanada, the army,
quivering and fleeing, fell into a great abyss.

Regarding what was stated—that these and others were reduced to ashes in battle—he explains that very manner of occurrence by dividing it according to the names of the regions, from the verse beginning with "Avantī" until the end of the chapter. "Avantī" refers to Ujjayinī, which is famous among the Mālavas; the "array of chariots" (*syandana-śreṇī*) belonging to those there, as well as those from the land of Kunti—

And by the impetuous thrusts— meaning the urges for battle, or alternatively, the weapons hurled— of the people of the Five Rivers, she, trembling with fear and fleeing, fell into a vast abyss, a mountain precipice. Thus, in the subsequent passages as well, [the meaning applies] to those words denoting locations expressed in the nominative case.
Defeat is to be understood as being expressed by words denoting a location in the locative case (third case). || 8 ||
Their armor and their hair-crests were torn away by the women of Vastravatī as if by weapons;
falling to the ground, they were trampled and crushed by rutting elephants. || 9 ||
"Militāḥ" means gathered together; that is to say, crushed. || 9 ||
The heroes of Daśapura, their bellies and necks severed by weapons,
were attacked by the arrows of Kṣiti and cast into the Yojana lake.
Having attacked—that is, having conquered and pursued—their compatriots who were stationed on the ground of Bāṇa (the land of Bāṇa), they fled for a *yojana*;
by chance, when they reached a lake, they were driven into it and submerged. || 10 ||
(219) Bound by the strings of their own entrails emerging from their split bellies,
these peaceful beings, whose movements have ceased, were devoured at night by *piśācas*.
Being restrained and suppressed, their movement is therefore stilled. || 11 ||
By the Udravas and Bhadragiris, who were consecrated for the sacrifice of battle, the Maras were cast into the pits of the earth like tortoises. 12.
By those [arrows] possessing an exceedingly excellent flow, impetus, roar, or resonance, [the enemies were driven] into the hollows of the earth, such as ponds and the like.
(12) Chased away, their blood flowing, and their great speed shattered, they were scattered by the Haihayas like deer driven by the wind from the stalks of *daṇḍikā* grass. (13)
Daṇḍikā is the city; those residing there [are meant]. "Driven by the wind" (*aniloddhūtāḥ*) is an epithet of the deer (*hariṇa*); the sandhi here is archaic (*ārṣa*).
By implication, it is understood that they were put to flight by the Haihayas. The "deer" (*hariṇa*) refers to the Vātapramyas. || 13 ||
Shattered by the tusks of elephants and having crushed their enemies,
they were carried away like the sprouts of trees by the great river of blood.
Devoured by iron arrows, the Chinese, their lives worn out and shattered,
cast off their bodies in the ocean as if they were mere burdens.
With their necks pierced by spears hurled by the brave warriors of Karṇāṭa, the heroic Naladas were shattered like clusters of stars. || 16 ||
With their necks severed by upward-flying spears,
and with their weapons shattered and destroyed by the force of the arrays of lordly elephants and sea-monsters,
the Śakas and Dāśakas, engaged in a hair-to-hair struggle, cried out in agony.

The Dāśakas and Śakas, fighting by chance against lordly elephants as if against a makara-array with great speed, had their weapons shattered; seizing one another by the hair, a battle of "hair-to-hair" ensued, and those who had undertaken that struggle roared aloud. || 17 ||
The people of Daśārṇa, like timi fish among reeds, were freed from their fetters and chains yet remained terrified of the net;
they hid themselves in the blood-slime like the reeds themselves.

The timid ones, having been freed from the nets of chains by those from the region of Pāśa; *jambāle* means in the mud; *vaitasāḥ* refers to timi fish that take refuge at the roots of reeds (*vetasa*). || 18 ||
By destroying the Gurjara army, the plucking out of the hair of the Gurjara women was accomplished in battle by hundreds of the tall, spear-like noses of the lofty Taṅgaṇas.
By those [warriors] whose swords and hundreds of spears possessed a high, surging upward thrust, it was performed or brought about. || 19 ||
The clouds of the heroes’ weapons, consisting of the spray from the torrent of their arms, drenched the mountain caves with drops [of blood],
like clouds of rain showers drenching forests.
Like the Karṇas among those who bear weapons— so named because they held their weapons aloft—

the local people, renowned for their prowess, emerged from the ranks of the army like clouds flashing with the lightning of heroic missiles; they showered down streams of arrows upon the mountain caves and the local inhabitants, just as follows:
Just as clouds, possessing a radiance like the weapons of heroes, drench the forests with their own drops as the cause, so too [did the arrows fall]. 20.
Frightened by the portents of the sun turning dark due to the glare of the *bhuśuṇḍī* discs, the enemies fell upon the cowherds (*ābhīra*) like herds of cattle falling upon green pastures. 21.

By the radiance of the *bhuśuṇḍī* circles, the sun—the solar orb—was turned dark blue; or rather, by the omen characterized by that sun which had become dark through the radiance of the *bhuśuṇḍī* circles.
As it has been said: "If the sun, like the moon, possesses a central hole within its circle of rays..."
"Having black and red edges signifies the destruction of those people. Thus [ends verse 21].
The army of Tāmra, though beautiful with its lovely golden ornaments, was devoured by the Gauḍa warrior, O dear one, through his clutching of their nails and hair in battle.
The Tāmras are a division of the Yavanas; their army, prepared for battle, was that very heroine who was enjoyed—that is, consumed—by the hero Gaudabhaṭa. "Aṅga" is an address to Rāma. || 22 ||
In the battle, by means of the slicing of thousands of mountain-like [elephants] with his discus,
the Taṅgaṇas were scattered in fragments, becoming prey for herons, vultures, arrows, and hawks.
With such endless, roaring wheels— saws, cutters, and cleavers— they lead away and strip away even mountains, trees, and rocks, along with the local people who are shouting.
Hearing the "guḍuguḍa" sound of the Gaudas flying up as they were being churned by clubs, the Gandhara cows fled before them like Dravidas.

The indistinct sound of muffled speech (*guḍuguḍā-rava*) belonging to the Gauḍa warriors, characterized by their whirling as they were stirred about with clubs, rose up like the lowing of Gāndhāra cows;
this is a compound of comparison (*upamita-samāsa*). The absence of the suffix *ṭac* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). || 24 ||
Resembling the ocean of the sky and carrying a multitude of thunderbolts, it created the illusion of thick nocturnal darkness among the Pārasīkas. (25)

The multitude—that is, the host—of Śakas was descending from the mountains like rivers flowing down; it is understood that the Śakas generally wear blue garments, whereas the Pārasīkas wear white garments. || 25 ||
Within the interior of the pure Ocean of Milk, which surged at the blow of Mount Mandara,
his weapons appeared like forests upon the snowy peaks of his enemies.

Therefore he says: "Mandara... and so forth. In that context, it should be understood that for those fighting, the weapons were like the forests of Mount Mandara within the depths of the Ocean of Milk; but for the spectators, they were like those same forests upon the peaks of the Snowy Mountain (Himālaya). || 26 ||
That multitude of weapons, which had flown into the courtyard of the sky like clouds,
was seen as if it were surging upon the ocean with the rolling of its waves.

The word *uḍḍīnam* is formed with the suffix *kta* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). The substitution of *na* for *ta* occurs according to the rule *lvādibhyaḥ*. By "turnings" (*valanaiḥ*), one means "by mergings" (*saṃvalanaiḥ*), that is to say, by waves merged with other waves.
Although it was seen as if a cloud were flying up from the ground when viewed from the earth, to those moving through the sky, it appeared like leaping upon the waves.
The meaning is that it has been seen. || 27 ||
The forest of the sky was seen filled with hundreds of moons by means of white umbrellas, dense with locust-like arrows, and indeed packed tight with spears.
It was densely and intensely pervaded by locusts and moths; it was without gaps and left no space.
(28) The Kekayas were made to utter cries like the intoxication of heroes;
their heads were covered in dust as they were overtaken in the sky by flocks of herons. (29)
The phrase "made into enemies" is to be understood as applying to both [cases], according to the maxim of the lamp on the threshold (dehalīdīpanyāya). || 29 ||

The daughters of the Kirāta army, having reduced their limbs to the state of being bodiless by means of their impassioned clamor, seemed to roar as if with terrifying thunderclaps. (Or, according to another reading: "as if with terrifying roars.

The Kirāta armies themselves were those maidens; by means of their limbs (*aṅgaiḥ*), which are [parts of] the countryside (*jānapadaiḥ*), they attained bodilessness (*anaṅgatām*)—that is, the state of being without a body (*videhatām*)—and the intensification of passion (*manmathodreka*). || 30 ||
Their bodies were overwhelmed by invisible birds of illusion that moved like grass,
as if by winds agitated and stripped of their wings, like particles of dust.
With the Kāśas, the Sāmudras, and the Narabhedas; with the Māyās and the Khagas who have become birds. || 31 ||
Maddened, thoroughly shaken loose, and having cast aside their weapons,
armor, and garments, the Narmadās, creators of sport, danced, laughed, and sang.
"Unmattāḥ" means those intoxicated by battle; "narma-līlā-tannirmātṛ" (the creator of that playful sport) is an adverbial modifier [of the action]. || 32 ||
The mass of tinkling bells, having become a shower of spears,
rose up from the wind of Śālva’s arrows and took on the appearance of a spray of water droplets. (33)
"Having the form of a speckled drop" means having the shape of a dot; that is to say, its state of being shattered. || 33 ||
The Śaibyas, mangled by the Kauntas and struck down by their whirling spears, became corpses and were seen being led to heaven like Vidyādharas. (34)
By the Kauntas, those born in the Kunti country. || 34 ||
By the steadfast army, whose nature was to support the earth,
the cities of the Pāṇḍus were plundered by the mere thrill of their movement.
By the army of those provincial people who were not deficient in their mastery of the terrain—that is, the occupation or seizing of the battlefield, the earth—and who possessed that quality. || 35 ||
Those soldiers were crushed by the men of Pañcanada, who were as intoxicated as the people of Kāśī,
just as trees with their formidable trunks and branches are crushed by rutting elephants.
With spears, elephant tusks, trees, and weapons, they were fierce and skilled in combat; "nagāḥ" means trees.
The Brahmāvatsanaka trees, cut down by the discuses, fell to the earth;
along with their horses, they were hewn asunder by the saw-like blades like flowering trees.
The Brahmāvatsanaka people were conquered by the Nīpa people. || 37 ||
The grove of white crows was cut down by axes impelled from bellies;
standing at its side, Bhadreśa consumed it with the fire of his arrows.
The face, mouth, or head—meaning the countenance—of the Śvetakākas, who are people of the countryside; by the bellies, meaning by the people of the countryside.
This is the strength of the belly. 38.
Against the wooden warriors, the aged elephants, deprived of their tethering posts, sank down and met their destruction in the battle, like fuel in a blazing fire. (39)

Having sunk into the mud characterized by wooden weapons and shields without any support or binding pillar, those born in the land of Mataṅga have perished through exhaustion, clinging [to life] like elephants. || 39 ||
Having wandered upwards from Trigarta as far as Mitragarta like blades of grass, they entered the depths of Pātāla with their heads cast down in order to flee. 40.
"Seized" means captured by the Trigartas. || 40 ||
Amidst the Magadhan forces, which shone like an ocean stirred by a gentle breeze,
the Mandas were submerged, sluggish as aged elephants sunk in the mud.
The Vanilās are country-dwellers. || 41 ||
On the field of battle, the Cedis abandoned their resolve, just as heat causes the delicacy of fallen flowers on a path to wither away. (42)
Volition, the intellect of discernment, or the individual soul. || 42 ||
The people of Kausala, unable to endure the clamor of the Pauravas, became like the God of Death himself;
they unleashed a torrential rain of maces, spears, arrows, and javelins.

The Kausalas, born in the Kosala country—meaning they were like Yamas (the Ender) in their slaughter—the showers of maces and other weapons released by those Pauravas fell upon them; such was the state they became, as the verse implies. || 43 ||
With their limbs mangled by arrows, the deer became motionless like coral trees on a mountain; then, with forms as bright as the sun due to their thick, flowing blood, they fled in panic.

Among them, those whose limbs were mangled by arrows remained unperturbed and devoid of any sense of wonder at the prowess of their enemies; for this reason, with their forms resembling the rising sun due to the fresh, thick blood [flowing from them], they appeared as if they were coral trees (*vidrumadruma*) on the mountain, running or fleeing away. || 44 ||
With their forms shaken by the wind of the great weapons— the showers of iron arrows— they wandered about, radiant like swarms of bees, resembling clouds.

The clouds were like water-bearing rain-clouds, the rams were filled with wool as thick as arrows, and the trees were covered with arrow-leaves; the elephants roamed about, driven by the roar of that [battle].
The elephants of those Kosalas, characterized by their trumpeting and covered with the tips of arrows,
are successively imagined— due to being strewn with shafts resembling stalks, feathers, and barbs— to take on the nature of clouds, rams, and trees respectively. || 46 ||
The creatures dwelling on the ground of thorns— worn out by old age in the forest kingdom—
snapped when violently pulled, like delicate threads. (47)

The creatures born from the soil of bulbous roots— such as humans, elephants, and others— and those born from the forest-kingdom— the inhabitants of the countryside— becoming worn out and deprived of strength by that characteristic decay, were utterly drawn away and snapped like fragile threads. || 47 ||
When the wheels of the chariots were shattered and their axles sank into the heads [of the enemies],
throngs of people fell like clouds upon forested mountains.
As the wheels of the chariots were shattered by being forced into deep pits and brought to a halt, the throngs of enemy warriors fell upon those very chariot-heads, intent on striking them down.
Having reached the forest of *śāla* and *tāla* trees, which agitates the masses of people,
there occurred the severing of his arms in that lofty grove of *sthāṇu* trees.

Having reached that battlefield— which, due to the mingling of the two masses of people in combat, became like a forest (*vana*) because of the clashing (*valana*) of the *śālavana* (mango grove) and *tālavana* (palmyra grove)— and having encountered there the severing of arms and, by the force of the word "ca" (and), the severing of heads;
In due order, there was a forest of stumps where the palm trees had mostly become uprooted and stood upright;

and around the *śāla* trees, by the cutting of their branches, they became like palms, while for the palms, by the severing of their tops, only the state of being stumps remained—thus the intended meaning is that what occurred was entirely appropriate. || 49 ||
Beautiful women, intoxicated by youth, from the Nandana and other celestial gardens,
resided upon the excellent peaks of Mount Meru within its forested and grove-filled regions.
The excellent forest of the army shone with the sound of "tāra" cries for as long as it had not been reached by the enemy side, which was like the flame of the fire at the end of an aeon.
In which [army] there was loud shouting; the army itself was the forest. 51.
Severed and joined with piśācas, their weapons snatched away by bhūtas,
the Daśārṇas fell upon Karṇa like young calves.

Engaged in battle with the Piśācas—led by Piśācas and consisting of the local inhabitants of Kāmarūpa and other regions—the Daśārṇas had their weapons snatched away by supernatural beings (bhūtas). Fleeing like young calves, they dropped their *karṇas* along the way as they went; in the case of the calves, the word *karṇa* refers to ears, while here it refers to sprouts that have emerged like ears, namely two or three leaves.
The gulmas are now being described. || 52 ||

Desirous of conquering that splendor by their own vigor, those whose lords were broken abandoned it, just as the *kāśa* reeds abandon their lotuses through the force of a river whose current has dried up.

With their lords broken and their masters slain, they were [the subjects] of the various rural folk who desired to conquer that [city]. By means of such summer heat, the streams, the fillers of the lakes, and the mountain torrents had all gone dry. 53.
Strewn with husks, with girdles [or "encircled" according to another reading], and with arrows, spears, swords, and mallets;
even the deceptive ornaments on their bracelets were cast away as they fled from the hells.
Scattered and driven out by the local inhabitants, even the deceptive bands of warriors were routed and fled. || 54 ||
The Kauntakṣetra people, having remained surrounded by warriors stationed at Prasthava,
clearly fell into a state of powerlessness, like virtues overcome by the wicked. (55)

Remaining in their very positions, they were surrounded by brave warriors whose nature was that of fighters; having seized the heads of the Bāhudhānas in an instant with broad-headed arrows (bhallas), the elephants quickly fled like lotus plants whose stalks have been severed. 56.
Those by whom the lotuses have been plucked are like men who have had their wealth confiscated. || 56 ||
Having led one another through the beginning to the end of the Sarasvatī [grammar], they achieved victory;
like scholars in debates, they were neither agitated nor defeated. (57)

The Sārasvatas, born on the banks of the Sarasvatī, having engaged in mutual combat and fought with one another, brought their conflict to its conclusion at the end of the day; yet they remained unperturbed until the very end of the day.
Dwarfish, mangled, and insignificant, they were turned back by the Yātudhānas;
yet they attained supreme splendor, like fires that have been extinguished being rekindled by fuel.
They were devoured and put to flight by the Yātudhānas residing in Laṅkā, and having been turned back, they were driven away along with their companions. || 58 ||
How much can even Vāsuki describe this, he who is indeed overwhelmed by his mass of tongues as if by flowing venom?
O Rāma, he is not capable of facing the best of battles.
He concludes the description of the battle that has been underway with the verse beginning "kiyat":
even Vāsuki, the serpent Śeṣa, would be utterly overwhelmed and distracted by the task of describing it fully with his multitude of tongues—that is, with his two thousand tongues. || 59 ||
Thus ends the thirty-seventh sarga, titled "Description of the Country," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmīki. (Mohanlal Lachhmanlal) 37.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Provinces," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, while the battle was extremely tumultuous and crowded with the terrifying sound of slapping arms,
When the sun was shrouded in darkness, its hard armor crackling.
At the end of the day, when both armies had withdrawn from battle, the battlefield—terrible, fearsome, and loathsome like a Piśāca—is described here in detail. (1)

In that tumultuous scene, where those who had achieved victory were slapping their arms and the defeated were overcome with fear, the water—meaning the liquid moisture born from the wetting of blood—flows and streams forth upon that hard armor; such is the connection with the following verse. || 1 ||
The waters flow as showers of stones fall,
while the rivers are choked by the casting of nets and the rows of lotuses.
While showers of white stones were rising up in one place and falling in another from the hands of those throwing pebbles,
and while the rows of lotuses in the rivers, as well as the *vara* and *saṃvara* flowers, were closing up—
the change in gender [of the nouns] is Vedic. (2)
And as the autumnal rivers approached and receded far away, emitting sprays of fire arising from the friction of their colliding banks; || 3 ||
In the autumn rivers, which were misty with sparks of fire arising from the mutual friction of the tips of reeds; || 3 ||

The ocean of the sky was filled with the whirlpools of the lotus-like heads of those being carried away, surging with waves, while the multitude of weapons became like the clusters of the celestial Gaṅgā.

When the ocean of the sky was filled with multitudes of weapons— which were like groups of celestial Gaṅgās— whose whirlpools were the discs [of chariots] containing lotuses whose stalks had been severed as they flowed and surged along. || 4 ||
The thick clouds were filled with weapons that rattled like the wind;
when they reached the ends of the doubts, they became perfected, causing the pain of *kapikacchu* (itching nettle).
Because the weapons resound like the wind and are so dense and thick as to be like clouds,

the monkeys suspect the onset of the rainy season; thus, due to the increase in redness on their foreheads— which provokes the pain of desire— they are uncertain whether the Siddhas have been hidden by the clouds.
When such beings exist, who possess internal dissolution characterized by doubt.
With his majestic form sweetened by the remaining splendor of his eightfold portions,
he attained a state of emaciation through the force of wounds from weapons, like a hero [at the end of his life].
With the vigor exerted by the stroke of the weapon and with the luster of his blood, the hero was like a [bloodthirsty] beast. || 6 ||
With their horses and elephants exhausted, their ranks broken, and the brilliance of their masses of weapons blunted,
the armies, along with the day itself, lost their former splendor.
Then, after deliberating with their ministers, the two generals dispatched messengers to one another, saying, "Let the battle be called off."
They have been performed; they have been set in motion. || 8 ||
There, due to exhaustion, all of them agreed at that time to cease the battle, as the power of their machines and weapons had been dulled.
By those whose power of machines and weapons has been rendered dull and weakened; or it may be analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
"Saṃharaṇa" means withdrawal or retraction. || 9 ||
Then, one warrior from each of the two armies climbed onto the tip of the lofty banner of a great chariot, like the Pole Star [Dhruva].

[It refers to] two long bamboo pillars, which have taken their place and found their support at the high tip of the banner of the great chariot—this is the sense. Now, as for the reduplication "eka eka" (one one), it occurs if there is an intention to express distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
