If, however, the status of a *bahuvrīhi* is applied according to the rule "ekaṃ bahuvrīhivat," the form would be "ekaika."

If it is argued that, in the absence of the intention to express that [repetition], there would be a *sarūpaikaśeṣa* (retention of a single form), we say no; for here there is no *vīpsā* (repetition for distributive purpose), because there is no intention to express multiple pervaded objects. Nor is there an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one out of many), because there is no intention to express them together.
Since the word "one" (*eka*) expresses a number, it is unfit for the dual case-ending; therefore, by means of the singular, [the term applies] to both armies (*senayoḥ*).

Furthermore, because it is impossible to convey a distinction between two persons [simultaneously], there is no fault whatsoever; for one intends to express the connection of the two persons with the act of ascending by means of a *tantra* (a single common action), while the two persons remain mutually independent. || 10 ||
He whirled his white silk garment throughout the circle of all directions,
as if making the long, pure rays dark, saying, "Let the battle be withdrawn!"
The dark night [embraced] the moon, which possesses long and pure rays, with its own beams.
Then the kettledrums resounded, their echoes filling the quarters of the sky,
like the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds at the conclusion of the great dissolution.
While the vast sky was filled with rivers of arrows and other weapons,
he proceeded easily, like water flowing from a lake into a river.
It is easy to come and to fall [into this state] without obstruction, just as from lakes such as Mānasa or from rivers such as the Sarayū. || 13 ||
The movement of the soldiers' arms gradually became thin,
like the trembling of trees at the end of an earthquake, or like an ocean that has ceased its agitation. (14)
In the autumn, when there is no delusion. || 14 ||
Then the two armies began to withdraw from the battlefield,
like a flood of water flowing in the four directions from the single ocean at the time of universal dissolution.
Regarding the phrase "full of water": by implication, it is understood as "at the end of the dissolution. || 15 ||
With its faces agitated like the churned ocean of milk on Mount Mandara,
the army gradually attained calmness as its whirlpools subsided.
Because Mount Mandara was lifted up and cast out [from the churning], it was like that very ocean of milk;
"sāmya" refers to a state of composure and lack of agitation. || 16 ||
Gradually, in a mere moment, the battlefield became terrifying with its hideous corpses; it was utterly empty, like the ocean after it had been swallowed by Agastya.
In the sequence of her birth and departure, Vikaṭā Pūtaneśvarī has an abdomen as terrifying as that [of the demoness]. (17)
It was filled with a continuous succession of corpses and agitated by flowing rivers of blood, resembling a forest of crickets (*jhillī*) filled with the humming and chirping of their cries. (18)
Jhillikas are a species of forest-dwelling insects. || 18 ||

Resounding with the gurgling roar of waves from the currents of many great rivers of blood, it was filled with men who were agitated— some calling out in lamentation, some half-dead, and others still clinging to life.
A torrential waterfall of blood flowed from the masses of corpses, some dead and others half-dead;
it caused the delusion that the lifeless bodies lying upon the backs of living men were still moving.
By the throbbing of corpses, it produces the illusion of being alive.
It was like a great forest torn apart by the wind, where fragments of clouds rested upon the peaks of mountain-like heaps of lordly elephants, and masses of chariots lay shattered.
Where masses of clouds rest upon the peaks at the forefront of the Śavara ranges—this is a poetic hyperbole (atiśayokti).
The ellipsis to be supplied is "like a great forest torn asunder by the wind. || 21 ||
The force of the flowing rivers of blood carried away horses and elephants,
while the field was crowded with arrows, spears, double-edged swords, maces, clubs, and darts.
The ground was covered with saddles, wooden frames, armor, and breastplates;
the corpse lay there, shielded by a multitude of banners, yak-tail whisks, and silk streamers. (23)

Where the surface of the earth was covered with saddles, pack-saddles, elephant-armor, body-guards, leather gear, and other armaments such as coats of mail; where the ground was protected and concealed by the bodies of the dead. || 23 ||
Where the wind whistled through the groves of quivers with their hoods unfastened,
and where the piśācas slept upon beds made of heaps of corpses and masses of straw.
Where the wind, whistling through quivering reed-thickets like hollowed quivers with their tips raised high like hoods and pierced with holes, was blowing. 24.
It was covered by the rainbow-like luster of crowns,
necklaces, and armlets, while long ropes of thick entrails were being dragged away by the hands of dogs and jackals.

It was covered—that is, pervaded—as if by a forest (vanena), meaning a multitude, of rainbows (śakracāpānām) produced by the luster of the crest-jewels (mauli-hārāḥ)—those which are taken away by the head (maulinā hriyante)—and of their armlets (aṅgadāni). || 25 ||
It was bristling with the teeth of men whose lives were barely remaining, jingling slightly in the field of blood;
it resounded with living men, like frogs, submerged in the mire of gore.

In that field filled with blood, men—groaning with gurgling voices, crying out in agony, gnashing their teeth, and baring their fangs—are there; indeed, living men themselves are there as frogs and toads. (26)
It bore a hundred rivers of terrible blood flowing from the mass of wooden logs that were its arms and thighs, with hundreds of protruding eyes resembling the armor of the finest elephants.
The armor of excellent limbs and the variegated tunic. || 27 ||
It was crowded with wailing kinsmen, with men who were half-dead or dead, and with no space remaining between the arrows,
weapons, chariots, horses, and elephants.
That which has its interior—the middle part—covered by a saddle-cloth and other such items until the very bridle.
The sky was bent low by the circles of the staff-like arms of dancing headless trunks,
while the cavities of the nostrils were parched by the oppressive stench of rutting ichor, fat, and marrow.
"Ānamitam" means lowered by its height; that is to say, surpassed. || 29 ||
The lives of those being warded off by elephants, horses, and men were cut short; the drums were struck by the blows of the waves of rivers flowing with blood. (30)
With their palates upturned by those who were eager [to lick them]. || 30 ||
It was a hundred rivers of blood from slain elephants, horses,
and crocodiles, with channels of blood hissed forth by the hosts of dying men.
[That] wherein blood-channels, being blown forth by a hissing sound (*phutkāra*), were expelled and extended from the region of the mouth. || 31 ||
It had a face filled with arrows and small living creatures, its eyes and voice were lovely,
it was reddened by the wind from the scent of the final remains of its body and wife, and it was crushed by the pressure of the atmosphere.

Where cries of lamentation were bound together by men whose mouths and eyes were filled with arrows and whose lives were nearly spent—the root *bandh* meaning "to bind. A specific knot of flesh situated in the left side of the abdomen is called *piṇḍabhāryā*.
It was marked by the smell of its fat and, by the touch of the wind at its end, became like a swelling (*utpīṭha*).
Where the blood has become thickened. || 32 ||

It was filled with headless trunks (kabandhas) trampled by the trunks of lordly elephants whose noses were half-snorted, and where high headless trunks had been cast down by elephants and horses that were no longer under control. || 33 ||
From the beginning until death, by those who are neither established nor restrained. || 33 ||
[He saw] one weeping and crying out, another fallen down, one agitated, one vomiting blood,
one with his husband dead upon his neck, and noble women who had abandoned their lives along with their weapons.
Where the ground was agitated by weeping, wailing, and by corpses fallen and tumbling about,

where there was a surging of blood and a splashing of gore; where noble women, having embraced the necks of their deceased husbands— implied— and having surrendered their lives through a stroke of a weapon brought by fate, did so intentionally.
However, following one's husband in death by means of a weapon-wound is not the intended meaning of the scripture. || 34 ||
It was crowded with many travelers who had emerged from their tents to observe [the scene],
and it was filled with the living attendants being dragged away by the hands of corpse-carriers.

The examination of their own respective kinsmen’s corpses was carried out by many travelers who had departed from the army encamped at the campsite— having been dispatched by the king’s command to bring back the corpse of the one to be consecrated— and who, having each fled individually due to a dread of entering the battlefield, were now moving swiftly and continuously along the path.

Where it was crowded with attendants and servants who carried corpses—the "corpse-bearers"—who, in their haste to search for the corpses they desired, were agitated by their followers and subordinates who had seized living men by the hands. || 35 ||
It was a hundred rivers with hair for moss, curved lotuses for whirlpools,
and high waves for its abundant currents, carrying along a great river of flowing blood.
In that place, there was a hundred rivers of blood, wherein the hair was the moss, the faces were the lotuses, and the wheels were the whirlpools.
[He saw a city] where half-dead men were frantic in their efforts to extract weapons stuck in their limbs;
where there was the wailing of those who had died abroad; and where elephants and horses had their bodies offered as oblations [to the flames].

In that [sacrifice], the ornaments and other belongings of those who had died abroad were offered as oblations along with elephants and horses, accompanied by wailing out of grief; the elision of the case-ending (subluk) after the word *klība* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). || 37 ||

(223) It is known by the names "Life-Ending," "Recollection of Sons," "Desired," "Mother," "Deity," and "Supreme"; it is described as the piercing pain that cuts through the vital organs, uttered as "Hā! Hā! and "Hī! Hī! (38).
"Another" means someone else or the Supreme Lord; "their" refers to their designations or names. || 38 ||
Then he beheld one who was dying, whose accumulation of prārabdha karma had been exhausted,
who was incapable of fighting elephants, and for whom his own body was the desired deity at the moment of death.
Where the enemy— possessing greater strength and more intense power— is hated and censured by those who, failing to exert their prowess, die while being crushed by elephants;
where, at the front of the elephants, there are those incapable in elephant-duels, yet whose own accumulated store of commenced actions remains there.
There, the deities were implored and entreated by those with bodies nearly dead out of fear of being crushed.
It was the flight of those who had taken refuge with the great hero Mahāvajrāśūra as he was dying;
it was the departure of those eager for a dwelling place, terrifying with whirlpools of unexpected blood.

Where, while others were dying, the cowardly took refuge in flight out of great contempt and offense, such as kicking with their feet; and for that very reason, they became fearless and eager to go, even toward places terrifying with whirlpools of blood, being intent on departing. 40.
Aware of its own misdeeds through the agony of being struck by arrows that pierce its vital organs,
it began to be overwhelmed by the mouths of vetālas emerging from the mass of headless trunks.
There, the suffering from the piercing of vital spots by the strike of arrows made known and inferred the evil deeds committed in previous lives; there,
the succession of Vetāla mouths began to devour blood by seizing the headless trunks as they fled.
It bore aloft beautiful banners, umbrellas, and chowries, as well as lotuses;
it scattered a crimson glow like the twilight in all directions, possessing the splendor of a red lotus.
In those blood-lakes, banners, parasols, and chowries were carried along like white lotuses;
there, the red water— characterized as a mass of fiery energy— became crimson from the reflection of the twilight glow,
and it scattered and dispersed red lotuses, *kokanadas*, throughout the quarters.
The eighth [ocean] was like a sea of blood, with the revolving rims of chariot wheels for its whirlpools,
rich with clusters of foam from the banners, and beautiful chowries for its bubbles.

Where the chariots and their wheels are successively the earths, the mountains, and the whirlpools—such is that [ocean], which, by having seven well-known oceans plus one more, stands like an eighth ocean of blood. (43)
With its chariots overturned, resembling a city submerged in the mud of the earth,
it was like a vast forest where the trees have been blown down by a cataclysmic wind.
It resembled a world consumed by the fire at the end of an eon, or like the ocean drunk up by a sage; it was like a region devastated by excessive rain, abandoned by all its people.
The reading "hato deśaḥ" with the nominative case ending is Vedic (archaic). || 45 ||
It was crowded with bundles of spears and whirled with circles of *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons;
it possessed corpses resembling hundreds of rutting elephants, along with *tomara* lances and mallets.
It was enveloped and pervaded by sets of ornaments, weapons, and arrows; where there were corpses in the form of elephants (nāgas), and tomara-spears and mallets in the form of serpents (nāgas). 46.
It was like an extensive grove of palmyra trees growing on a rocky peak;
it had spears rising like tall trees along the banks of flowing rivers of blood.
The meaning expressed in the second half [of the verse] is the reason for the meaning expressed in the first half. || 47 ||
It was filled with trees of weapons sewn together with elephant hide and strewn with flowers;
its sky was covered by a web-like mass of the tongue-like entrails dragged out by herons.

The flood of weapons, pierced and fixed into the limbs of the elephants and serpents, were like trees; it was crowded with their rays as if they were flowers, and thus it became "latticed," as if a lattice-work had been produced. || 48 ||
The raised forest trees were the spears growing on the banks of the rivers of blood;
the clusters of lotuses were the banners standing high upon the lakes of blood. (49)
It was a place where friends were summoned by men submerged in blood-red mud;
it was watched by the survivors as the carcasses of lordly elephants fell, crushing those who had been turned aside.
It was observed by the elephants emerging slightly from their broken temples and other parts as they issued forth from the corpses— the carcasses— of lordly elephants.
With trees stripped of their branches by elephants' tusks, it appeared as if half-severed headless trunks were suspended from them;
with blood flowing like rivers, it was filled with crowds of elephant-hide garments serving as rafts.
There, the temples of elephants floating upon rivers of blood served as rafts, while their housings and saddle-cloths formed a multitude of boats. 51.
It was a mass of foam consisting of white garments shimmering within the stream of blood,
where men were incessantly driven about by swift servants under strict command.
Foam is *ḍiṇḍīra*. They were separated and cleared away by servants who were appointed for the purpose of moving about—servants who were swift, prompt in action, and disciplined. || 52 ||
Here and there fell headless trunks and Dānavas;
with the multitudes of upward-rolling, massive wheel-axles, the fleeing soldiers of the army were being cut down.
With masses of wheels having large apertures and thick axles turned upwards. || 53 ||
It resounded with the cries of blood-drinking jackals, the *bhāṅkāra* and *phetkāra* howls of those half-dead,
and the birds were driven away by the dust stirred up by the streams of blood trickling from the stone slabs.
Where there are the cries of half-dead creatures accompanied by blood-sounds, in the form of *bhāṅkāra* and *phetkāra*; where,
for the sake of drinking the streams of blood flowing from the mouths of rocks as they sport, birds such as herons raise up dust with their unsupported flapping of wings.
It was a scene of perilous *tāṇḍava* dancing by Vetālas, swift as the wind, amidst the clatter of chariots;
where noble warriors were hidden within the gaps between the shattered timbers of overturned vehicles.
Good warriors are living warriors. || 55 ||
It strikes terror with the throbbing movements of the living warriors stationed within;
its mouth is filled with the mire of blood, and it is a corpse toward whom even a little life shows compassion.
Where even corpses, by virtue of possessing some slight life-force, ultimately attain compassion.
In some places, dogs and crows were seen with their necks raised in suffering;
in others, it was tumultuous with the clamor of carnivorous beasts fighting over a single piece of meat;
and in yet others, it was crowded with flesh-eaters who had died while contending for that same morsel.
By means of battles and martial endeavors. || 57 ||
With its overflowing rivers of blood gushing from the necks of horses, elephants, men, lords of chariots, camels, and oxen that had been overturned,
that battlefield became the garden of Death, where the creepers of weapons remained unwithered.
Like the entire world with its mountains overturned at the end of an aeon. || 58 ||

Where rivers were beautiful with gushing streams of blood flowing from the severed necks of countless horses, elephants, and other creatures that had been slaughtered, killed, and overturned; where the creepers of weapons remained unfaded, as if put forth anew by the sprinkling of blood. Such was that place.
The characteristics of the battlefield were like a garden or grove for Death. || 58 ||
Thus ends the thirty-eighth canto, titled "The Description of the Battle," in the section on Origination within the *Mokṣopāya* of the holy *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Seers. 38.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle," in the Utthāna-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, like a hero turned away from battle, the sun set in due time, its redness faded.
His majesty withered by the splendor of the weapon, he was cast into the ocean. || 1 ||
The sunset, the twilight crowded with Rākṣasas and Vetālas, and the battlefield at night, loathsome and thick with darkness, are described. || 1 ||
On the solar side, when the brilliance of the weapon has faded in the clear sky, it becomes weak in its rays; "abandoned" means cast off or, in other words, fallen. || 1 ||
Gleaming with the blood of battle and reflected in the mirror of the sky,
the streak of twilight vanished for a moment at the severing of the Sun’s head.

When the head of the rider, who bore the marks of the sun, was severed and cast down, the crimson luster reflected previously in the mirror of the sky abandoned the heavens for a moment—that is, for a brief duration. || 2 ||
From the earth, the netherworld, the sky, and the cardinal directions, the Vetālas arrived like the surging waters of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution,
beating their hand-claps as if they were bracelets.

Because they circle all directions, they are ring-shaped; they are "stanantaḥ" (roaring) and "dhvanantaḥ" (resounding), and their "tālāḥ" (hand-claps) are like long "vetālāḥ" (vampires) that roar and resound. || 3 ||
Upon the head of the lordly elephant of the day, which was smeared with the sword-like darkness that had been polished away,
there lay scattered the pearls of the star-cluster, reddened by the glow of twilight.

When the head of the lord of elephants, the best of tuskers, was struck and split by the sword of darkness—polished and sharpened on a whetstone—the elephant’s pearls, characterized by their clusters of stars, were scattered; they appeared red with the blood [of the wound], thus forming a poetic conceit (utprekṣā). || 4 ||
In those beings who were devoid of essence, blinded by darkness, and possessed of the flavor of passion,
the lotuses of nectar-like hearts contracted as if they were closing.

In lakes abounding in water (*rasa-śāli*), which were once full of life and love, and now devoid of living beings— bereft of swans and other creatures, breathless, blinded by the darkness of gloom and delusion— the tongues [of the bees] previously resounded with the humming of bees and other living beings. (5)
With their wings closed, sleeping for a moment with their necks painfully upraised,
the birds in their nests were like arrows lodged in the limbs of corpses.
Those by whom the necks (kandharāḥ) were raised up (procchritāḥ), that is, lifted upward, with difficulty due to the suffering of death, in the state of [holding] a weapon (hetipakṣe). || 6 ||
The worlds, made beautiful by the approaching moon, became like rows of flowers with throbbing hearts, like the goddesses of fortune among the factions of heroes.
The moon, approaching with its auspiciously radiant appearance, and the rows of water-lily and other flowers resembling it; || 7 ||
The lotus pond became like a battlefield: filled with water as red as blood, with bees hidden within its parts, and its lotuses closing their faces.

In the case of the lotus-lake (abjinī), it is abundant with water resembling blood due to the reflection of the twilight glow; "śilīmukhas" refers both to arrows and to bees; and "vakrāṇi" refers both to crooked [arrows] and to the lotuses themselves. || 8 ||
Above was the lake of the sky, adorned with the lilies of the stars; below was the lake of water, with shimmering lilies in the form of stars.
The beings, freed from fear in the darkness, gathered together in great numbers and spread out in every direction like waters breaking through their banks.

The meaning is that the battlefield was crowded with throngs of singing *vetālas*—creatures who were previously separated and now reunited, yet remained afraid of one another due to their lack of familiarity;
it was filled with the sport of *kaṅkas* and *kākolakas* perched upon the laps of rattling skeletons. (11)
Upon the lap, that is, the bosom, of skeletons—that is, of corpses. || 11 ||

Then [he saw] a fire consisting of fat and flesh, blazing with the light of the stars from the flames of the wood-pile, resounding with the sound "paca paca paca," and glowing like the sky filled with stars.
Now, the description of the battlefield, characterized by the attributes about to be mentioned, continues until the end of the chapter. 12.
With the entire mass of bones in its limbs cracking and bursting open, it was about to manifest as a heap of skulls;
yet it was obscured by the water-sports commenced by the female Vetālas.

Where the funeral pyres themselves, bursting with the clearly visible cracks of bones on all sides, appear prominently like heroes facing upward; where, as if in a water-sport commenced by female *vetāla* spirits, there is a disappearance within the funeral fires.
It was intense with the clamor of dogs, crows, yakṣas, vetālas, and tālas; it resembled a forest where birds were taking flight due to the coming and going of spirits.
The ḍākinīs were busily engaged in extracting blood, flesh, fat, and marrow;
the piśācas had their lips dripping with chewed blood, fat, and flesh. (15)
Where there are such Piśācas whose corners of the mouth and lips are dripping. || 15 ||
The middle-of-the-middle cremation ground was filled with clearly visible heaps of blood and corpses;
there, Virūpikā was being led away, carrying a great corpse placed upon her own shoulder.
In those middling-of-the-middling cremation grounds, there were lights observed by piśācas, where multitudes of corpses displayed their raw blood, and there were the deformed pūtanās. || 16 ||
Its interior was made terrifying by a circle of fierce Kumbhāṇḍas dancing wildly;
it ended with the "chamicchami" cries [of the spirits] and had fat, blood, and tears for its clouds.

There, the kumbhāṇḍas— those pot-bellied varieties of piśācas— uttered cries like "chamicchami" resembling the sounds of flames from the mouths of corpses; with the vapors of fat and blood rising as moist smoke, the place seemed as if filled with clouds.
It was filled with land-dwelling creatures carried away by the surging currents of rivers of flowing blood,
and it resounded with the confused cries of hosts of *vetālas* as they dragged along skeletons.
Where the *rūpikā* plants, having grown with their roots firmly planted in the current of the river of blood, appear as if they were walking upon the ground;
where there are the shrill cries appropriate to the lineage of the *vetāla* hordes, their joyful and discordant shrieks during the dragging away of skeletons and corpses. 18.
A young vetāla sleeping within the belly of a dead elephant like a casket;
a rākṣasa engaged in the sport of drinking at a secluded spot where the senses are solitary. || 19 ||
It was illuminated by the flaming funeral torches from the quarrels of intoxicated Vetālas,
and its winds were made fragrant by the scent of flowing blood and fat.
That battle was radiant and blazing with funeral pyres made of firebrands and flaming torches. || 20 ||
(225) It resounds with the clamor of *vāntaraṇa* and *ḍraṭaraṭa* cries from baskets of cooked meat;
it is filled with strife as yakṣas, greedy for the taste of half-cooked corpses, frolic there. 21.
The *peṭikās* and *karaṇḍas* are well-known containers for *rūpikās*, which are types of *pūtanās*.
[This place] is where the clamor of the Yakṣas is ever-present. || 21 ||
It was filled with birds perched on the peaks of Tuṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Aṅga, Taṅgaṇa, and Aṅgala;
it bore the appearance of flames blazing directly toward one another, resembling the falling of stars.
Where night-roaming birds alight upon the lofty limbs of those born in the lands of Vaṅga and other regions;
where [the women] laugh with teeth resembling falling stars, making the flames before them appear like their own countenances.
It was disfigured by blood in the midst of the joyful frolics of falling vetālas,
and its vicinity was filled with the sound of yoginīs being summoned by piśācas.
Where blood-smeared Vetālas fall down with exuberant laughter and the like, and where the Virūpikās abound in blood.
There,

men had become like female Piśācīs, their human nature departed due to the latent impressions of Piśācas, as they played musical instruments consisting mostly of great lutes made from protruding entrails.
Where musical instruments are generally provided with large strings made of intestines.
In some places, good warriors were half-dead from the terror caused by the sight of the Rūpikā; in others, the Madra army was incomplete due to being devoured by Vetālas and Rākṣasas.
From the sight of the *rūpikās*, there was a prior terror, that is, a sudden fear; therefore, the *madraka* is a festival of auspiciousness. || 25 ||
The night-stalkers were terrified by the garments falling from the shoulders of those who had assumed their true forms,
while the sky became congested with throngs of unprecedented hosts of spirits.
The sky was crowded and without interval by unprecedented and extraordinary collections of spirits that had collided together. || 26 ||
It was like a heap of corpses scattered among birds that look only for their own food— a feast of dying men snatched away with extreme effort.
Toward their own, personal factions that were desirous of food. || 27 ||
With its red-colored rays, which appeared like fragments produced from the flame-tips of the fire from Śiva’s mouth,
it was as if it were surrounded on all sides by clusters of newly blossomed Aśoka flowers flying upward.
The jackals,

with their mouths emitting flames of fire, were [drowned out] by the incessant, unceasing howling of those men who had regained consciousness after fainting and were covered in blood as it flowed from their wounds. || 28 ||
It had young vetālas with necks bound by the trunks of headless corpses,
and it scattered sparks like firebrands through the sky with its yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and other spirits.
There, young *vetāla* spirits were busily engaged in the sport of binding severed heads to the necks of headless trunks;
there, the flaming torches of the *yakṣas* and others, glowing and moving through the sky, shone like blazing firebrands.
The sky was filled with a mass of pitch-black clouds, like a single boulder filling the hollows and caves within mountain thickets;
meanwhile, the winds of the end of the aeon were agitated by the frantic rush of trembling spirits.
It is like a basket filled with the scattered husks of the world's people. || 30 ||
In the sky-mountains, within the thickets and the interiors of their caves,
it was adorned with a mass of darkness so dense as to be like a solid lump;
therein lay a multitude of clouds established like pedestals upon cloud-pedestals, amidst which were restless spirits.

The meaning is that the interior of the cosmic egg (the *aṇḍaka-peṭa*), which was agitated by the impetuous force [of the battle] and shaken by the winds of the kalpa— wherein the worlds, people, and the collections of his thunderbolts and other weapons were tossed about— became like a *kalpa* (an aeon) upon the field of battle. || 30 ||
Thus ends the thirty-ninth sarga, titled "The Description of the Battlefield at Night, Filled with Night-Rangers," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battlefield at Night amidst the Host of Night-Rangers," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Fortieth Sarga.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, on the field of battle that had become long-terrible through the conduct of the night-stalkers, [the conflict continued].
Just as day and night abide in the conduct of people, so too do the watches of the night pass away.
While Vidūratha was asleep, [the Lord’s] entry into his house occurred as a playful manifestation of His knowledge;
herein, the true nature of the *ātivāhika* body is also described. (1)

The meaning is: while the night-stalkers were engaged for a long time in their conduct upon the terrible and fearsome battlefield, and while the activities of the Yama-related messengers (yāmas), the inferior and base ones such as the Piśācas and others, were being carried out; that is to say, while things remained in the manner described, just like the appropriate conduct of people during the day.
In the house at night, where the walls were clearly visible even in the gloom that could be grasped by hand,
the host of spirits leaped about, their garments fluttering in their greed for gain.

In that house characterized by night, where the walls were clearly manifested as if by dense masses of darkness capable of being grasped by the hand; and which, upon the acquisition of an abundance of food,
was such that it possessed an "ucchada"— meaning clothed or covered— and was "uccala," meaning rising up or fleeing away, due to the wretchedness of the beggar.

While the host of spirits was leaping and playing, [the word] *cat* means "to beg. The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the abstract noun (*bhāva*) according to the rule "the application of *ka* in the sense of the *ghañ* suffix. || 2 ||
In the silence of the spreading darkness, when the quarters of the sky were blocked by sleep,
the noble-souled husband of Līlā appeared as if somewhat dejected in mind.

Having set aside his presence on the field of battle, he describes his stay in the city with the words "silent" (*niḥśabda*). By the term *kakubgaṇa*, the living beings situated within the collection of directions are indicated. (3)
Having quickly deliberated upon the morning duties with his ministers who were skilled in counsel,
[he lay] upon a bed as cool as snow and shaped like a long crescent moon.
In that beautiful house resembling the interior of the moon, within a cool cave,
he fell asleep for a moment with his lotus-like eyes closed.
"Agamat" means he reached or attained. || 5 ||
Then those two playful women, leaving that sky, entered that house through its openings like two streaks of wind entering a lotus bud.
Those two are the playful manifestations of cognition. || 6 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O best among those who know speech, how large is this gross body, and how, O Lord, did it quickly enter through an opening as thin as a thread?

Regarding the exit from the aperture of the most subtle cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), Rāma asks again with a desire for further knowledge in order to confirm the meaning previously stated: "How much? (verse 7). This means: of what measure? That is to say, how long is it, measuring four cubits (*hasta*) in length?
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
For one who possesses the deluded notion, "I am this physical body composed of the elements," [there is no liberation].
O sinless one, he is not able to pass through its minute aperture.
This refers to the gross body; "through the minute aperture" means through a subtle opening. || 8 ||
"He has obstructed me," "I am not sinking here"—such is the thought of one who experiences what has been experienced; thus it is experienced. || 9 ||

To explain why that is so, he says: "obstructed" (*rodhita*). One whose mind previously experienced the nature of the gross body hundreds of times thinks, "I am obstructed and confined here in this cavity; because of my human bodily nature, I am unable to measure [the infinite]. Thus it becomes.

The absence of the *num* augment after the roots *śap* and *śyan* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*) due to the rule stating they are always [conjugated with *ātmanepada*]. Therefore, the meaning is that in this manner, only non-attainment is experienced. || 9 ||
How can that which has experienced the first half [of its existence] with the thought "I am going" become, in the second half, a consciousness intent on departing? (10)
However, for one who— due to the absence of the notion of identity with the gross human body and due to the certainty that it is merely the *ātivāhika* (subtle) body—
has experienced hundreds of times, even in the slightest opening, "I am going" and "I am capable of going," being enriched by firm latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from previous occasions, he...

How can the person (puruṣa), whose nature consists of a portion of self-consciousness directed toward such a movement, subsequently possess that same action—characterized by activities such as cessation in accordance with the gross body?
The sense is that it is impossible for that which has previously manifested as having the nature of power (śakti) to undergo any change [into something else]. || 10 ||
For fire does not rise upward when obstructed, nor does it go downward;
in whatever manner consciousness has proceeded, in that very manner it remains established.

He says "not indeed" because even externally, the nature of the power of things is observed to be equally restricted; [the power] has already proceeded, its capacity having previously manifested. || 11 ||
For one seated in the shade, how can there be experiences of heat?
For no other object is experienced within his own consciousness by anyone else.

With the intention of stating that there is no need to say that such suffering does not exist for those who possess knowledge of reality—who are free from the superimposition of mere duality and for whom even yogis and piśācas, who lack the notion of the gross body as the self, are devoid of the suffering of cessation—he says: "In the shadow," etc. [This refers to] the perfect realization of that Supreme Self.
When there is direct realization. || 12 ||
As is consciousness, so is the mind; it has come to abide in that very state. Yet, through supreme effort, it may again be led to another condition. (13)

Now, one might ask: even though the powers of grossness, subtlety, and so forth manifest within consciousness—the substratum—how is it that the mind conforms to them? To this he says: "Just as... (yathā). Then, how does its transformation occur otherwise?
To this he says: "By the supreme... (parameṇa); the meaning is: by effort such as the practice of yoga and knowledge. || 13 ||
The cognition of a snake regarding a rope is forcibly sublated by the cognition of "no snake";
otherwise, however, it remains exactly as it was. || 14 ||

In that regard, he illustrates transformation through the effort of knowledge with the words "snake," etc. When there is the determination of the true nature of the rope, the cognition of it as a snake ceases. || 14 ||
As is consciousness, so is the mind; as is the mind, so is one's striving.
This is well-established even for a child; who has not experienced it? (15)
Since it is even more well-known that activity follows the mind just as the power of cognition follows the mind, he says "just as" (yathā) [in verse 15].
Furthermore, as for that person who is a mere mental construction of a dream, whose form is like a reflected image and whose nature is nothing but space—how and by whom could he be obstructed? (16)
Now, one might ask: why is the subtle body (ātivāhika), like the gross body, not restrained? To this he says: "He who... [referring to the verse beginning with *yaḥ*].
For indeed, the body of everyone consists entirely of mind alone;
because it is experienced as such, it seems to go somewhere from within the heart. (17)
Now, one might ask: how can this material body attain the state of being a mental body through the power of knowledge? To this he says:
"And thus, the elements do not exist apart from the mind"—this is the sense. (17)
Just as he desires, so indeed occurs his setting and rising;
in the original creation it arises from inherent nature, and subsequently it becomes the cause for both duality and unity.

He establishes that the existence of beings is not separate from the mind with the words "according to its will" (*yathābhimatam*). "According to its will" means that which does not transcend the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) intended by this Supreme Self.

"Of this collection of beings" refers to *asya bhūtajātasya*. "Setting and rising" (*astamayodayam*) is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*). This is their inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
The meaning is as follows: innate ignorance or the karma arising from it [produces] the gross elements and their derivatives;

duality consists of these, and their unification through their combination into a single body occurs subsequently by means of the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), which serves as the cause therein. || 18 ||
Know that these three—the space of consciousness (*cittākāśa*), the space of awareness (*cidākāśa*), and the third, [the physical] space (*ākāśa*)—are one, by virtue of their inseparable nature. (19)
Thus, he states that for the mind and the unmanifest as well, there is no separate existence apart from pure consciousness—namely, "the space of the mind" (cittākāśa).
"Inseparability" (avinābhāvanā) means not appearing apart from the existence of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), by virtue of which [they appear]. || 19 ||

Know this state of being the body of consciousness to be the arising of the all-pervading, which arises according to the nature of one's perception and desire, just as it arises according to the nature of one's perception.

Thus, although there is equality in terms of having existence dependent on the existence of its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), he says "this" to indicate that there is a distinction whereby the subtle is not subject to cessation as compared to the gross. Know it to be such—that whose power of manifestation arises spontaneously and has reached all things. Why is that? Because:

"Arising in accordance with perception" means that its nature is such that its emergence does not transcend the manifestation of objects which follow from prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and karma;
it is not a nature that follows the power of external objects. Why is that so?

Because there is a desire for experience as it is perceived. For one desires even mother-of-pearl when it is perceived in the form of silver, and does not remain indifferent by following the actual power of the mother-of-pearl. Thus, since the gross [citta] follows external objects, the cessation of the body of the mind—which follows merely the desire for experience—does not occur upon the cessation [of those objects]; this is the sense. || 20 ||
It dwells within a mote of dust, it is withdrawn into the belly of the sky;
it dissolves within the sheaths of sprouts and becomes sap within the leaf.
He elaborates upon the state of being omnipresent and arising by means of the passage beginning with "he dwells," and so forth. || 21 ||
It exults in the state of water-waves, it dances within the heart of a stone;
having become a rain-cloud, it pours forth, and having become solidified as a rock, it remains still.
He travels through the sky at will, and even within the bellies of mountains; possessing a body of infinite space, he then assumes the state of an atom.
There exists no end; that which has the nature of space, having the form of vacuity, assumes the state of an atom. || 23 ||
The mountain becomes the support of the earth, its base firmly fixed and its peak reaching to the sky;
it bears forests as its body hair both within and without its form.
Possessing hair characterized by forest-like qualities, it truly becomes a mountain; it has a firmly established seat and deep roots.
The state of being a mountain and so forth within the body is well known in dreams, while externally it is seen in illusions such as those of Indra. 24.
Space becomes the support for millions of lotus-born abodes,
which are non-different from its own self, just as the formations of whirlpools are non-different from the ocean. (25)
Not different from and non-distinct from the nature of his own mind, he bears throughout all directions millions of Brahmāṇḍas, the abodes of those born from the lotus. || 25 ||
At the beginning of creation, this one, whose body is the mind, awakens without agitation;
having become the great Self of space, it then perceives its state as primordial nature (prakṛti).

"Unperturbed" means one who is not deluded by agitation; "whose awakening follows karma" refers to one whose realization conforms to the sequence of actions. Having become the "space-self"—that is, having become the Great Soul (Mahat) and the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa) through the sequence beginning with space—he [perceives] the state of being under discussion, the state of being introduced, namely, the activity that follows the impulse of commenced karma. || 26 ||
In that same way, non-existence itself arises as if it were existence through the intellect,
just as a man in a dream experiences the delusion that "this is the son of a barren woman."

The ellipsis is to be supplied as "just as in the case of a dead person, heat, and so forth. The syntactical connection is: "Just as the delusion arises in a dream that 'this man is the son of a barren woman. (27)
Śrī Rāma said: What is this mind? How does it come to be, or how does it not come to be?
Why is it that, upon observation, it is neither of the nature of existence nor anything else? (28)

The mind alone is the most subtle, possessing all power throughout the entire world; that very same [mind], when its true nature is not fully known, becomes as if gross and dependent on others. However, when its true nature is fully known, it is said to be independent and unimpeded in all worldly activity. In this regard, what is this mind?

Does each [moment of consciousness] possess such power individually, or not? In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence that every moment of consciousness would manifest all the various distinct types of sentient beings. In the second case, however, the world-form would be something other than the mind and not produced by the mind; and since it is perceived as such by everyone, even when the mind is destroyed by knowledge, [the world would remain].

With the intention that there should indeed be conformity with the world, Śrī Rāma asks: "What?"—that is, does this mind belonging to ourselves and others possess the aforementioned power, or not? In the first case, why would there not be a separate world corresponding to each individual mind? In the second case, however, why would it not be otherwise?
How is there a separate connection for each of the two words "katham"? || 28 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Each individual mind possesses such power; thus, for every single mind, the delusion of the world arises separately.
Accepting the very first alternative there, Vasiṣṭha gives the reply: "Each individually," [verse 29].
The multitudes of worlds, though lasting for a moment or an eon, arise and dissolve;
for some it is in a mere blink of an eye, for others it is after an eon—listen now to the sequence.
O wise one, know that this fainting which is experienced by each individual at the time of death and other such occasions is the night of the great dissolution. (31)

How then is the doctrine of creation following the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) explained? To this he says: "maraṇa... etc. The meaning is that in the case of an individual creation (vyaṣṭi-kṛta-sarga), the preceding death itself constitutes the great dissolution. || 31 ||
At the end of that [state], everyone individually unfolds creation—consisting of innate dreams and mental constructs—like the frantic dancing of those on a moving mountain. (32)

The three states arising from innate, intrinsic ignorance—dreams and mental constructs—are its three abodes, for the scripture says, "There are three dream-states. Confusion is the delusion of the mind. || 32 ||
Just as at the end of the night of the great dissolution, the body of the Self and the mind gradually unfolds this [universe],
so too does it unfold for each individual immediately after death.
Hiraṇyagarbha, whose body is the collective mind (*samaṣṭimanovapuḥ*) of the Self that is the Supreme Brahman, expands [the world] through his will of truth (*satyasaṃkalpa*);

likewise, he does not overstep that [will]. Thus, there is no contingency of the diversity of the waking world occurring for every individual mind. As for the diversity in dreams and so forth, it is indeed accepted because it is observed; this is the sense. Alternatively, this is an illustrative example:

Just as Hiraṇyagarbha, whose body is the collective mind, projects the collective phenomenal world as its object of experience, so too does the individual soul (jīva), whose nature consists of the individual mind, project its own respective objects of experience—the individual phenomenal world of dreams and the like. || 33 ||
Śrī Rāma said: Just as the creation after death is experienced through memory, so too does one experience it after a long time; therefore, the universe is not without a cause.

Now, since the scripture states, "What one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech, and that one performs with action," and because this is confirmed by universal experience, it is certain— just as in the case of memory— that actions have a single object. Furthermore,
memory is accurate when its causal experience is true, but inaccurate when its causal experience is untrue.

In that regard, because we are subject to manifold delusions and lack the power of true resolve, our memory may be non-conformable with reality; consequently, let the unreality of the limited expansion of dreams and the like produced by it be granted. However, since Hiraṇyagarbha is omniscient and thus free from delusion, and possesses true resolve, it is impossible for his memory to be non-conformable with reality.

With the intention that there is no consequence of falsity for the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) created by Him, Rāma raises an objection with the words "from death" (*mṛteḥ*). Just as individual souls (*vyaṣṭijīva*) experience their own created worlds through memory at the time immediately following death, so too does the universal soul (*samaṣṭi*) [experience its creation] after a long period following the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).

One experiences the manifested universe as created by one's own true memory (*yathārthasmṛti*); therefore, since it is possible for those very real objects of the past, established through that memory, to be the cause of the real universe of this present cycle, it follows that the previously asserted proposition— that the universe is without a cause, being devoid of any real cause other than Brahman— is established.
The meaning is that there is a contradiction of that [proposed] view. || 34 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, during the great dissolution, all beings beginning with Hari and Hara attain the state of disembodied liberation; what possibility then remains for memory? (35)

This might be so if, at the initial creation, there could exist for him a memory that serves as the cause of creation and is produced by a veridical experience; however, such [memory] is not possible for the practitioner who has first attained the state of Hiraṇyagarbha, because his memory is produced by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) brought forth through meditative cultivation (*upāsanā*), and not by a veridical experience. Meditative cultivation...

Furthermore, the contemplation of the collective whole (*samaṣṭi*) as being identical with the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) is not a perception of reality, because it is produced by memory born from the impressions of unreal meditation; thus, there is no possibility of the reality of the primordial creation.
Indeed, there are no other omniscient beings existing at that time, since all have already attained liberation prior to it.

However, since the memory that serves as the cause for the creation at the beginning of the second kalpa has as its object only the false things experienced during the previous creation, there is no possibility whatsoever of the reality of creation; with this intention, Vasiṣṭha replies with the verse beginning "mahatī" (great).
Since even those like us, once awakened to the Self, are surely liberated, how could the lotus-born Brahmā and others not have become liberated and bodiless? (36)
The awakened self is the knower of reality. || 36 ||
But others, however—those living beings like you and those within you—for them, memory becomes the cause here in matters of death and birth due to the absence of liberation. (37)

The intention is that in deaths and births—that is, in the creations that cause death and birth—memory is produced solely by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) arising from the prior experience of false objects. (37)
For that which exists within the living being, as if emerging at the end of death or fainting,
yet remains unemerged, is designated as Pradhāna. (38)

Now, one might object: "The creation of Hiranyagarbha is heard of in the Purāṇas and other texts as proceeding from Pradhāna through the sequence of Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, and so forth; however, that of the individual soul (jīva) arises all at once. How, then, can there be a similarity between the creation of the individual soul and that [creation]? Anticipating this doubt, he establishes that even in the latter case, the sequence of Pradhāna, Mahat, and so forth exists—beginning with the word "jīvaḥ."

By the words "hi" and so forth; the ellipsis is "not yet manifested externally. The meaning is that this state of being is designated as *pradhāna* or *mūlaprakṛti* (the root-nature) in the Purāṇas and other such texts. || 38 ||
That is declared to be the nature of space (vyoma); it is the unmanifest (avyakta), both insentient and sentient.
This is the sequence in the arising of existence, occurring through both recollection and non-recollection.

He states that even words such as "space" (vyoman) are well-known to refer to that [Brahman], based on such scriptural passages as, "In that, [all] is woven lengthwise and crosswise like space. It is both insentient and sentient because it receives the reflection of consciousness. The meaning is that this sequence—from the remembrance of creation to the non-remembrance of dissolution—constitutes its beginning and its end. || 39 ||

For when that [intellect] becomes oriented toward awakening and is fully awakened, then from the void (ākāśa) arise the subtle elements, space, time, and action, as well as the gross elements and so forth.
The syntactical connection is as follows: when that very same principle, being oriented toward awakening, becomes fully awakened and is called the "I-maker" (ahaṃkāra), then from that state of space—
specifically from the previously mentioned subtle element of space— it arises, extending through the subtle elements (tanmātras) up to the gross elements and their physical derivatives.
That very [subtle body] becomes swollen and awakened as the pentad of sense organs;
that alone is what perceives in the body, and this is its subtle, transportable form (ātivāhika).
"Ā-ucchūnam" means slightly swollen, that is to say, in a subtle state; it is perceived during both sleep and waking.
Through long-standing habituation, this [mind], thickened by conceptual construction, brings about the perception of materiality, just like a child. (42)
The realization of the elemental nature [is the removal] of the ego-identification with the gross physical body composed of elements. || 42 ||
Then, the divisions of space and time, existing as its substratum, arise—though they have not yet arisen—just like the activity of vibration in the wind. (43)
By the term "space and time," the categories of objects dependent upon them are indicated.

The meaning is that the cognitions of various objects existing in those respective places and times—which exist by virtue of being supported by the gross body and depend upon the eyes and other senses—arise, that is, they manifest. || 43 ||
Thus has this wandering through the world increased in vain;
though experienced, it is composed of unreality, like union with a woman in a dream. (44)
Wherever a living being dies, he immediately perceives that very place; right there, he sees this entire expanse of the world situated in such a manner. (45)
The sky alone experiences the delusion that "I am the clear world";
having the nature of space, the living being (jīva), though possessing a self, appears as if born from that very form of space.
The meaning is that, as if having become possessed of a self through the nature of adventitious things such as the body, one experiences the delusion of "I" and "the world. || 46 ||
[The meaning is that in the forty-sixth verse it was stated that one experiences only the void.
Beautiful with the city of the gods, mountains, the sun, and clusters of stars,
yet hollow with the perils of old age, death, distress, and disease— 47.
He elaborates upon the very delusion of the world through specific attributes, beginning with "sure" and so forth. The gods are Indra and the others; their cities are Amarāvatī and the rest;

the mountains supporting them are Meru and the others. It is beautiful with the clusters of suns and stars revolving around those [mountains]. Here, "koṭara" refers to the cavity or opening of the mortal world and so forth. || 47 ||

The intense activity of the absence of intrinsic nature, comprising the gross and the subtle, the moving and the unmoving, along with the oceans, mountains, earth, rivers, the directions, day and night, and the destruction of kalpas and moments; || 48 ||

Wherein there are gross and subtle beings, both mobile and immobile— mobile beings being those endowed with exertion and zeal toward the presence of favorable conditions and the absence, prevention, or removal of unfavorable ones;
and even among the immobile, such as creepers, there is the spreading [of growth] in a location that provides support.
And because it is seen that even regions devoid of support are avoided [by those seeking refuge], there is the statement regarding the commonality of its movement.
"The oceans, mountains, earth, rivers, and their respective lords"—it is where these, together with day and night and so forth, reside. 48.
"I was born here by this father"—thus with firmly established conviction;
"this is my mother, this is my wealth"—thus with arisen latent impressions (vāsanā). (49)
"This is my good deed and this is my evil deed"—such is the constructed imagination;
"I was a child, but today I am a youth"—thus it sports within the heart. (50)
The connection with the preceding [verse] is: "He perceives the world-delusion shining and flickering within the heart.
The neuter gender of the masculine qualifier is due to resorting to the view that word-formation (*padasaṃskāra*) takes precedence [over sentence-meaning]. || 50 ||
Thus has each individual forest-thicket of saṃsāra been described:
blossoming with stars and possessing leaves as flickering as dark clouds. (51)

Now he describes that very individual cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) as a forest grove, beginning with the words "each one" (*pratyekam*): it is "flowered by the stars," meaning blossoms have come forth. (51)
Moving about with herds of deer as its game, with gods and asuras as its birds, with the light of the sun as its pollen, and with dark forest thickets as its groves; (52)
Where human beings themselves were the herds of deer; where the days, dominated by light, consisted of the pollen of flowers;
and where the nights, dark and dense, were the thickets and bower-houses difficult to enter. 52.
It is like a pond in the ocean filled with clouds and the like, or a clod of earth from a mountain;
it is the sprout of experience hidden within the seed of the lotus of the mind. (53)
In this [state], the sprouts—the mental fluctuations which are experiences—remain latent, existing in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). || 53 ||
Wherever this living being dies, there he sees [the same] in an instant; thus it occurs repeatedly in each of the many fragments of the world that have arisen. (54)
"He beholds [it]," the remainder of the sentence being "as a described forest grove. || 54 ||
Tens of millions of Brahmās, Rudras, Indras, Maruts, Viṣṇus, and Vivasvats have passed away, their vision extending to mountains, oceans, circles, islands, and other worlds.
The Maruts are the gods; those who see the intermediate spaces at the ends of the worlds situated within the womb of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) possess that vision.
Tens of millions of such beings, beginning with Brahmā, have passed away. || 55 ||
Those views which have passed away, those that will pass, and those that are passing—these are forms that have perished.
But as for those views which are richly augmented by Brahman, who is capable of counting them? (56)

"Naṣṭarūpiṇīḥ" means those whose nature is non-existent; this is a Vedic anomaly (chāndasa) regarding the case ending. "Upabṛhaṇam" means expansion or manifestation; they are rich in that [expansion]. The suffix *ka* is used here in the sense of the suffix *ghañ*. || 56 ||
Thus, this universe composed of walls does not exist at all apart from mental construction;
it is merely moving within the mind—consider this now.

Having thus described the process of superimposition (*samāropa*) regarding phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*), he explains the process of negation (*apavāda*) in sequence, beginning with the words "In this way" (*evam*).

Apart from the subtle mind characterized by volition (*saṃkalpa*), which consists of mentalization (*manana*), the universe—which is gross like a wall or a plastered surface—does not exist at all as something distinct from it. These three...

"Forms alone are real," according to such scriptural passages. Now, an objection may be raised: the external world is gross and stable in nature, whereas the mind is mobile by nature; how then can this [world] be merely the mind? To this he says: "In the act of thinking. Although the external universe appears stable, nevertheless, when it is conceptualized at will by the mind through the process of thinking (*manana*), [it is seen to be nothing but the mind].

Only a nature that is calamitous and unstable is experienced. It is experienced by everyone as if wandering in the mind when it is wandering, as if clear when it is clear, as if turbid when it is turbid—within the realm of desires and the like—as if produced in one place and then superimposed upon another.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Now, you should investigate this through your own direct experience. || 57 ||
That which is the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) is itself known as the act of reflection (manana);
and that which is the space of consciousness is itself the supreme state (paramaṃ pada). || 58 ||

And regarding the investigation of the mind, he says "That which alone... to show that the mind's nature is that of being a mere witness, and that the witness is nothing but Brahman—thus, there remains only the one full, pure consciousness. The connection is: "That which is the act of thinking is the very same as the space of consciousness. (58)
That which is the water is itself the whirlpool; the whirlpool does not exist as a separate substance.
Likewise, it is the seer who remains as if it were the object of sight; the object of sight does not exist as a real entity.
He establishes the stated point by means of an illustration with the words "yadeva" (that very thing). The elision of the case-ending in the word "āvarta" is a Vedic archaism. || 59 ||
That which is the manifestation of the sky of consciousness within the elemental ether, like the luster of a gem,
is this world— a manifold reality yet to come— like a cavity in the atmosphere.

In that which is unreal, untrue, or beginningless— like a magical illusion in the sky, or like the manifestation within the subtle elemental effects and the sky of the mind— that very shimmering vibration which occurs as the state of the individual soul (*jīva*), and which is destined to become name and form, having the nature of manifesting as various worlds, is called the "existent world" (*saj-jagat*). It is just like the shimmering of a magician’s gem in the sky.
It becomes like a void within a city of Gandharvas of many kinds; that very space of consciousness (cidvyoma) is the reality, the ultimate truth—this is the meaning. || 60 ||

The word "world" (jagat) exists as the supreme nectar when understood through my intellect; however, when understood through your intellect, it does not exist at all—even from the words "you" and "I. [The portion "tvamahaṃśabdau kāyatīti" should be investigated. || 61 ||
The object of my cognition is pure existence (*sanmātra*) as the substratum; the object of your cognition has a superimposed existence (*āropitasattā*).

Thus, that cognizer of the world who expresses—i.e., denotes—the words "you" and "I" (the *tvamahaṃśabdakāt*), he too is merely my cognition, whose nature is pure witnessing-consciousness (*sākṣicinmātrasvabhāva*); he does not have the nature of a living soul (*jīvasvabhāva*) as perceived by you. This is the meaning.
Therefore, Līlā and Sarasvatī abide as the very embodiment of space within the all-pervading Supreme Self, which is pure, omnipresent, unobstructed, and stainless.

Having concluded what was said, he applies it to the subject at hand with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). "Possessing the form of space" means having bodies consisting solely of the space of the mind whose volitions are true. "Impenetrable" means free from any obstruction to entry, even through an extremely subtle aperture. || 62 ||
Wherever they always manifest in the great void— according to their desire and according to their wish— their movement is within that very house.
The distinction is that *īpsā* is the desire to obtain what has not yet been obtained, while *kāma* is the desire for the enjoyment of what has already been obtained. *Udayam* means manifestation;
by that cause, [she was seen] in his house, that is, in the house of Vidūratha. || 63 ||
The sky of consciousness exists everywhere; therein, true perception, conceptualization, reflection, and expansion [“turning” (*valana*) is read in some manuscripts] spread forth.
And they say that this body here is merely a subtle, transportable one (ativāhika) and not made of walls; tell me, how, like what, and what could possibly obstruct it? 64.

The sky of consciousness (*cidgagana*) exists everywhere; that is to say, it is not obstructed. That very same [consciousness], when it is in the state of mental construction (*kalana*), becomes the act of reflection (*āmanana*)—extending as far as the ascertainment of the objects of the mind—and being expansive, having the nature of outward diffusion, it becomes the experience of existence (*sadvedana*), which is knowledge according to reality. They say it is without walls, not gross, but indeed subtle. Who...?
"For what reason does it obstruct, and in what manner or by what means? The meaning is that there is no possibility whatsoever of its being obstructed. || 64 ||

Thus ends the fortieth sarga, titled "The Description of the Experience Following the Recollection of the Battle," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
This concludes the [section] in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The fortieth canto, titled "The Description of the Experience of Recollecting the Battle Immediately Following It."
The Forty-first Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When those two goddesses had entered, that lotus-palace became [filled with light].
Beautiful in its interior, white with the radiance arising from the appearance of two moons. || 1 ||
Once the two had entered, King Suptabuddha performed worship for them;
then the lineage of the king, his recollection, and the instruction on the nature of consciousness are described. (1)
It was beautiful and radiant, with an interior as bright and white as the rising of two moons. || 1 ||
By its power, the gentle breeze from the soft and pure-scented mandāra trees lulled the king and the other men and women to sleep.

Where there are soft, pleasant-to-the-touch, and pure-scented breezes, gentle and carrying the fragrance of wish-fulfilling mandāra flowers—by the power (prabhāva) of those two goddesses, that is, by them as the cause;
for since a relative term is inherently dependent [on its correlate], the compound is valid as it does not violate the requirement of semantic connection (sāmarthya). || 2 ||
It was like a grove of Saubhāgyanandana, with the pains of disease dispelled;
it was like a forest in springtime, or like a lotus blooming at dawn.
In its splendor, it was like the Nandana garden. || 3 ||
Refreshed by the floods of light emanating from their bodies, which were as cool as the flow of moonlight,
he woke up as if sprinkled with nectar.
"Ukṣitaḥ" means as if sprinkled. || 4 ||
He beheld two celestial nymphs resting upon two seats,
like two lunar orbs risen upon the two peaks of Mount Meru.
He was seated, resting upon two imagined seats; [he beheld] a pair of Apsarases, a pair of celestial women. || 5 ||
Having reflected for a mere moment, the king, his mind filled with wonder,
rose from his bed like Śeṣa, the bearer of the discus and mace.

"Having reflected for a moment" means having contemplated within for a very short time; for if one were to reflect for a long duration, an offense would occur due to the delay in performing the worship and other rites. Therefore, the particle *eva* is used to indicate that even this slight reflection is to be concealed. (6)
With his garlands, necklaces, and lower garments hanging down and properly restrained,
he took up a handful of flowers, like a cluster of blossoms upon a flowering tree.

At the time of sleep, his garlands and other ornaments—which had been disarrayed—were gathered from all sides, restored to their respective proper places, and consequently hung from his neck and other parts; thus, like a servant who gathers flowers, he was one whose [ornaments] were such as those. || 7 ||

(230) Having emerged from the hollow of his own chest, which served as the place for his pillow, he sat upon the ground in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) and spoke these words with humility: || 8 ||
The chapter on the flower-basket is the eighth.

Victory to you two goddesses, who possess the luster of the moon that cools the defect of the burning distress of worldly existence, and who possess the luster of the sun that dispels the darkness of both the external and the internal!
Instability is a life of suffering; burning refers to the threefold affliction. || 9 ||
Having spoken thus to them, he offered a handful of flowers at their feet,
like a blossoming tree on the bank [offering itself] to two lotuses.
Having spoken thus, he cast a handful of flowers at their feet; this is the syntactical connection. || 10 ||
Then, in order to explain Līlā’s birth as a king, the Sovereign Goddess Sarasvatī awakened the minister standing at her side through a mere mental resolve.
Seeing that the two celestial nymphs had awakened, he prostrated himself, offered a handful of flowers at their feet, and entered before them with humility.
The queen said, "O King, who are you? Whose son are you? When were you born here? Having heard this, the minister spoke these words: || 13 ||
Having heard this question, that minister— || 13 ||
O Goddesses, by your grace, I am able to speak even before you; therefore, O Goddesses, let this birth of my Lord be heard. (Note: The reading "tadidam" is also found.)
There was a lotus-eyed king born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, the illustrious one named Kunda-ratha, whose shadow from his arms covered the earth. || 15 ||
He by whom the earth was protected—shielded as it were from the shadow of faults and preserved by warding off the torments of enemies, poverty, and the like.
He had a son named Bhadraratha, whose face was like the moon;
his son was Viśvaratha, and his son was Bṛhadratha.
His son was Sindhuratha; his son was Śailaratha;
his son was Kāmaratha; and his son was Mahāratha.
Viṣṇuratha was his son, and Nabhoratha was his son;
this lord here, whose form is full and pure, is his son.
He was born from the store of merits of that celestial chariot. || 18 ||
Filling people with nectar like the moon from the Ocean of Milk, he was known as Vidūratha on account of his great accumulation of merit. (19)
By whom people were filled with qualities such as affection, sweetness, and magnanimity that were like nectar;

the phrase "by accumulations of merit" (puṇyasaṃbhāraiḥ) is connected to this [word "filled"] according to the maxim of the lamp on the threshold (dehalīdīpakanyāya), and thus applies to the mother as well. 19.
Born of his mother Sumitrā like a second Guha born of Gaurī,
his father, when he was ten years old, gave him the kingdom and departed for the forest.

Regarding the phrase "of this ten-year-old," the genitive case is used according to the rule *anādare* (Pāṇini 2.3.38); it is a genitive denoting a characteristic state (*bhāvalakṣaṇe*), intended to indicate his disregard for both the kingdom and his son due to the excellence of his dispassion. || 20 ||
From that time forth, he has protected the surface of the earth according to righteousness,
now that the tree of his good deeds has borne fruit upon reaching this present age.
Today, when our tree of merit has borne fruit, it has been attained. || 21 ||
"O two goddesses, whose sight is difficult to obtain even through hundreds of hardships from long asceticism—this lord of the earth known as Vidūratha [seeks you]. (22)
"Today, by your grace, I have attained supreme purification.
Having spoken thus, the minister and the king likewise remained silent.
O King, as he stood on the ground with palms joined, face bowed, and seated in the lotus posture,
remember by yourself through discernment your former birth.
The connection with the subsequent clause is: "Sarasvatī, speaking thus, touched [him] on the head. || 24 ||
As she was speaking, Sarasvatī touched him on the head with her hand;
then the darkness of the heart, which is the lotus of Māyā, came to its destruction.
The "hārda" is that which covers the individual soul (jīva) residing within the space of the heart. || 25 ||
And at the arising of the touch of the request, his heart became fully blossomed;
he remembered his former history as if it were pulsating within him. (26)
The heart is the mind, characterized by excellent expansion and internal luminosity. || 26 ||

Having understood that the state of having renounced both body and sole sovereignty was accompanied by the playful manifestations of Līlā, one realizes that this is indeed the unfolding of Līlā’s own power of creative intelligence.

He alone is the king of this world; that state of being its sole ruler is "monarchy" (*aikarājyam*). The body is also "monarchy," and thus there are the two: the body and monarchy. When both the body and monarchy are abandoned, one is "one by whom the body and monarchy have been abandoned";

the state of such a person is "the condition of having abandoned the body and monarchy. Even that which has not been previously experienced [arises] through the power of the grace of pure consciousness.
He says that he "knew" by the words "having known. || 27 ||
He felt like one being swept away in a sea;
he said to himself: "Alas! This illusion has spread throughout the cycle of worldly existence."
"Ātmodantam" means his own previous history; "ātmani" means in his own mind. || 28 ||
"By my grace, the two goddesses have now been fully recognized by me here.
The king said:
"O two goddesses, what is this? For me, who am as if dead, even a single day [seems like an eternity]. (29)
Seventy years have passed since I was born here;
I remember many deeds, and I remember my great-grandfather.
"I remember my childhood, my youth, my friends, kinsmen, and retinue.
Jñapti said:
"O King, immediately after the swoon of the great delusion of death," (31)
"Paricchadaṃ parīvāram" means retinue and attendants. "What is this that I remember?"—this is a question arising from a desire to know the reality (tattva) of that very thing.

In order to teach the truth—that the nature of all things is the underlying pure consciousness alone, while everything else is merely illusion (māyāmātra)—[the text first mentions] that which exists at a distant place and time.
Preventing the delusion of having traveled to another world, Jñapti said, beginning with the words "O King," and so forth.
When that other world had passed away, in that very moment,
in this very house, and even in this very dwelling within the sky.
Indeed, within this very abode of yours, in that sky of consciousness which is its substratum— though transcendent, veiled by *māyā*, and hidden— there exists,
situated within the house of a Brahmin in a mountain village, that other world (*loka*) of Padma; and within that very royal palace,
even further inside the space of the principal chamber, there is said to be this pavilion of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
The sequence follows the order of the previous narrative. || 32 ||
O King, this pavilion is indeed situated within the inner space of that house,
inside the dwelling of the Brahmin from Girigrāma.
Within that [space], this world-house shines forth individually;
indeed, the living soul within the house of Brahmā has come to me for refuge.
Within that pavilion of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍamaṇḍapa), this [universe] consisting of your birth and so forth appears; it manifests at first sight.
If one asks, "Does that very world of Brahmā appear in this way?
he says "no"—"each one," meaning distinct and separate. He explains this very state of being individual by saying:
By the words "kila" and so forth: "madupāsthitaḥ" means one who has approached me, that is to say, my devotee. || 34 ||
Right there is his ground, and indeed within that very pavilion,
inside that very house, is this entire circle of worldly existence (saṃsāra). (35)
This is the proximate maṇḍala of the lotus-like cycle of existence.
Right there this house of yours stands, though slow to begin;
right there, within your mind, which is as pure as the clear sky.

In that very lotus-palace pavilion, with the intention that even the threefold phenomenal world (prapañca) is merely a modification of the mind, he says: "in that very mind. The mention of its purity is for the purpose of establishing the possibility of the reflection of consciousness. || 36 ||
This [world], which is spread out by the delusion of worldly activity, has come into my vision; just as this is my name and my birth, so too is the lineage of Ikṣvāku mine.
Having delineated the experience of the pervasive delusion of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), he elaborates upon it with the words "Just as... and so forth;
the particle *nāma* is used in the sense of "indeed" (*kila*). || 37 ||
"These were my grandfathers, who bore such names;
I was born as a child, and when I was ten years old, my father passed away. (38)
"Having consecrated me here in this kingdom, the wandering mendicant has gone to the forest;
then, having conquered the quarters and made the kingdom free of thorns," (39)
With these ministers and citizens, I protect the earth,
performing the sequence of sacrificial rites while upholding the dharma and protecting my subjects.
"With the ministers and the citizens"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 40 ||
Seventy years of my life have passed away;
now this enemy force has arrived, and for me there is a terrible conflict. (41)
The phrase "a terrible conflict, a battle, has arrived" is to be supplied by way of ellipsis. || 41 ||
"Having fought this battle, I have returned home as it was before;
these two goddesses have arrived at my house, and I shall worship them. (42)
The ellipsis is: "as before, I remained in this house. || 42 ||
For when worshipped, the deities grant their own desired objects;
of these two, this one of mine bestows knowledge and the recollection of past births. (43)
Between these two goddesses is one. 43.
"Here the Goddess has bestowed [upon me] the blossoming of my lotus-like heart;
now I have accomplished my purpose and am freed from all doubt. (44)
"I am at peace, I am fully extinguished, and I abide in absolute bliss"—this is the pervasive delusion of yours, fraught with great agitation. (45)

Through the cessation of all suffering, I am stilled; through the abundance of unsurpassed bliss, I attain final nirvāṇa. Having become nothing but pure, single-flavored bliss, I remain and abide. || 45 ||
Rich in various modes of conduct and dwellings, and wandering through other worlds, it was at that very moment when you previously met your death. (46)
We and others like us are Siddhas who travel between worlds, accompanied by them. || 46 ||
At that very moment, this intuition arose spontaneously within your heart;
it is like how, having abandoned one movement of a whirlpool, another is given [as before].
Just as the flow of a river and its current,
