mingled within the midst of whirlpools, proceeds according to the turning of the eddies— knowing this, it is called "viccita," and that is its "pravāha" (current). || 48 ||
Sometimes the splendor of creation thus increases, both mixed and unmixed;
at that very moment of dissolution, your intuitive insight has arrived. (49)

The mixed [states] are awake, conjoined with the creation of other living beings; the unmixed [state] is in dream. The connection is: "the manifestation of that sun of consciousness has arrived. || 49 ||
This unreal net has appeared before the sun of consciousness,
just as within a moment of a dream there occurs the delusion of a hundred years.
Just as life and death again occur within a creation of one's own imagination, and just as there is the perception of walls and ornaments in a city of the Gandharvas. (51)
The perception and sight of walls and their decorations, such as paintings and the like. || 51 ||
Just as trees and mountains tremble during the agitation of a ship's voyage,
so do the eastern mountains dance when one's own elements are disturbed.
Trembling is shaking; it is like an unprecedented dancing of the mountains caused by the agitation and derangement of one's own constituent elements—wind, bile, and phlegm. || 52 ||
Just as the severing of one's own head in a dream is entirely unreal, so too is this matured delusion, which has assumed an expansive form, purely illusory. (53)
"Inconsistent" means unsuitable for worldly conduct; "only by churning [it] is it so," is the remainder of the sense. || 53 ||
In reality, you have never been born, nor have you ever died;
you are of the nature of pure consciousness and abide as peace within the Self.
In that case, what is the ultimate truth? To this he says: "But in reality... (verse 54).
You see all this, yet you do not see anything at all;
by virtue of being the self of all, you eternally shine forth by yourself within yourself.

With the intention that, since the visible world is false, the perception of it—characterized by the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) conjoined with that [world]—is also necessarily false, and thus only pure consciousness remains as the residue devoid of objects, he says: "As if you see. You shine forth; you blaze.
Noble like a great jewel and radiant like light, in reality this is neither the surface of the earth nor are you this [ordinary person]. (56)
Light is the sun and so forth; you are this very body of Vidūratha. (56)
"Neither these mountains nor these villages, nor indeed we ourselves, belong to this Brahmin of the mountain village within the small pavilion in the open air. (57)

These are both your attendants and your enemies. With the intention that for one of great stature, being treated with disrespect by those who are much inferior is indeed a cause for spiritual delusion (*mithyātva*), he says: "In a mountain village," and so forth. (57)
The world shines brilliantly, enriched by the wives of the Lord of Līlā;
therein lies the royal capital of Līlā, its form adorned with pavilions. (58)
Its form—that is, its configuration—is adorned on all sides with pavilions and halls. || 58 ||
In the sky that is His belly, this world is thus perceived;
and within that world, in a house therein, we are situated here. (59)
The meaning is that the house in which we are currently staying here shines forth. || 59 ||
Thus, for those pavilions, the sky was as stainless as the sky itself;
likewise, within those pavilions there was neither earth nor a city.
That which is the space of those pavilions is non-space; it is Brahman alone, empty like the sky and the quarters.
Neither forests, nor mountain ranges, nor clouds, rivers, and oceans exist;
people dwell there in their homes entirely alone in that void. (61)
The meaning is that within that Brahman—which is devoid of all else and filled with pure consciousness—false people wander about in a false house. || 61 ||
Neither people, nor kings, nor even the mountains see [them].
Vidūratha said:
"If this is so, O Goddess, then how is it that these are my attendants here?"

When it was said, "The people do not see [it]," the ministers, servants, and others attained a status equal to the members of the assembly seen in a dream; finding this impossible, the king asks with the words beginning "If it were so," etc. (62).
Are they complete within themselves, or are they not? To him, the world appears like the objects of a dream, and for him, dream-people and the like [are real]. (63)
They are endowed with and joined to the *ātman*, that is, the living soul (*jīva*), as I am joined to the *ātman* which is the true nature (*satsvabhāva*).
He states the seed of his own doubt: "the world" (*jagat*); the meaning is "of that [world], mine" (*mama*). || 63 ||
"Tell me, how could they be real or unreal when the Self exists?
Śrī Sarasvatī said:
"O King, among those who have known what is to be known and whose nature is solely pure awakening..."

The meaning is: "How could they be real according to the system you have described? If you ask about their reality from the perspective of an ignorant person (*ajña-dṛśā*) by way of their status as individual souls (*jīva-bhāvena*), then that reality does not exist for you either. However, with the intention that from the perspective of ultimate truth (*tattva-dṛśā*) by way of their nature as the underlying pure consciousness (*adhiṣṭhāna-cinmātra-bhāvena*), they indeed possess that reality, the Goddess gives the following reply:
By the words "O King," and so forth. (64)

This world does not possess even the slightest degree of real existence within the self-nature of the sky-like consciousness; it appears only to the one whose nature is pure awakening—so how can there be such a thing as the delusion of a "world"? (65)
When the delusion of a snake in a rope has subsided, how can the delusion of a snake arise again?
When the non-existence [of the world] is fully realized, how can there be existence in the delusion of the world?
Once a mirage is fully understood as such, how can there again be the notion that it is water?

When one's own dream is recognized as a dream, how can there be fear of death within that dream? For one who has died in their own dream, the terror of dying in a dream arises only for one who is already dead.
When one's own nature as the individual soul (*jīva*) is fully realized through awakening at the time of dreaming, how and why could dream-death be real? This is the meaning. || 67 ||
For the Buddha, who is pure like the glory of the autumn sky and whose intention is transparent, bright, and vast,
the distinction between "I" and "the world" is a mere false word.
For in reality, my dear, that is not verbal [action]. // 68 //

Through awakening, when the veil of ignorance and mental dullness has vanished, the Buddha—the knower of reality—is like the splendor of the autumnal sky: clear, stainless, and purified by the radiance of his own shining self-nature. Having attained a state of uniformity with that [reality], his disposition has become pervasive, reaching an extreme vastness characterized by fullness; such is he, as perceived by the vision of the ignorant.
The well-known notions of "I" and "the world" do not have any objective reality whatsoever as the referents of those contemptible and trivial words.
The word "aṅga" is used here as a gentle address. For indeed, that which is expressed by speech is a mere modification originating from speech;
as the Śruti declares: "Modification is a mere name arising from speech; 'clay' alone is the truth," and so forth.
The state of being. || 68 ||
When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites;
and the assembly, having offered their salutations, departed to bathe.
And at the waning of the night, he arrived together with the rays of the sun. || 69 ||
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Examination of Delusion," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpattiprakaraṇa*, within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Investigation into Delusion," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The fifth day.
The forty-second canto.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
But for that one who is dull-witted, ignorant, and entrenched in what is not the expansive state,
this world— which is like the essence of a diamond— is as if it were real, though it is actually unreal.
The reality of the world is explained even in ignorance, as in the case of a dream;
however, at the conclusion here, the narrative remains incomplete, ending with the granting of a boon.

Having described in detail the falsity of the world from the perspective of the wise, he states—in the words "But he who"—its absolute, firm reality from the perspective of the ignorant, in order to reinforce that [falsity]:
"rūḍhaḥ" means firmly established; "na vajrasya sāraḥ" means that which has a core or firmness like that of a diamond. Such is [the world].
That which exists in the ultimate sense does exist; for the meaning is that in the world, only that which performs a causal function is recognized as being real. || 1 ||
Just as a ghost causes suffering to a child until his death, so does this world—which though unreal, appears real—cause suffering to the deluded mind. (2)
Where has the existence of a non-existent thing—characterized by its capacity for causal efficiency—ever been observed with respect to an ignorant person? To this, he says: "Just as... (verse 2).
Just as a mirage of water causes delusion for deer, so too does this unreal world appear real to one of deluded mind. (3)

Just as the heat of the sun upon the desert land is but a mirage, which, though appearing as real water to the deer, is the cause of their delusion, so too is it for those with the eyes of the ignorant. || 3 ||
Just as the death of a living being in a dream appears to be real and performs a causal function despite being unreal, so too does the world appear to those of deluded intellect.
It performs purposeful actions such as grieving and weeping. || 4 ||
Just as for one who lacks analytical discernment, there is only the cognition of a bracelet in gold, whether it be fine gold or base metal, and not even the slightest thought of "gold" itself. (5)
"In one ignorant of gold" means in one who has not mastered it and is unacquainted with the true nature of gold. || 5 ||

Likewise, for the ignorant person, there exists only this visible perception— which is as radiant as the ancient abodes, mountains, and lords of serpents— but no other, which is the perception of ultimate reality.
Houses are *agārāṇi*, homes are *gṛhāḥ*, mountains are *nagāḥ*, and trees are *vṫkṣāḥ*; likewise, the lords of serpents are *nāgendrāḥ*, elephants are *gajāḥ*, and snakes are *sarpāḥ*.
One who perceives the ultimate reality (*paramārthadṛk*) possesses the vision of the one, true Brahman that pervades all these luminous things. || 6 ||

Just as in the sky, strings of pearls, peacock feathers, locks of hair, and circular halos appear— though unreal, they attain the status of reality— so too does the world appear to those of perverted vision.
*muktālī* is a string of pearls; *piccha* refers to feathers. || 7 ||
Know this entire universe to be of long duration and joined with the sense of "I" and so forth;
hear now how other men within it are likewise real, just like those in a dream. (8)
Other people who appear distinct from oneself are like dream-people, comparable to other persons seen in a dream.

To the question, "In that case, how is it that they are accepted in the scriptures as being real and capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), such as the scriptural injunctions regarding officiating at sacrifices or receiving gifts? he replies: "Listen to how they are real. (8)
There exists the all-pervading, peaceful, pure, and solid ultimate reality; it is the vast supreme space, whose form is pure consciousness beyond the reach of thought.
It is all-pervading and the substratum of all; it is the solid mass of the ultimate reality, the unsurpassed truth.
For there is a scriptural passage stating, "Truth has indeed been attained by them; this is their truth," and so forth. (9)
That is all-pervading, possessed of all powers, everything itself, and the self of all;
wherever and in whatever manner it arises, in that very place and in that very manner it truly abides.
He describes its form as variegated by *māyā*: "It is all-pervading" (*tatsarvagat*).
By means of *māyā*, wherever and in whatever manner it manifests as suitable for a particular purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), there it exists in that very way. || 10 ||
Therefore, those inhabitants of the city whom the observer perceives in that dream-city are indeed men;
in an instant, they become men for him.

Likewise, although there is a distinction in that [the object] manifests in the waking state as fit for scriptural purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) whereas it does not in the dream state, there is no distinction in its nature as "existent" (*sad-rūpa*). With this intention, he says: "By that... (verse 11).
That which is the conscious nature of the seer resides within the space of the dream;
for it is conceived as appearing like the mind within the space of the dream to human beings. (12)

The meaning is that the "expansion of the dream-appearance" refers to the opening of an extremely subtle channel; situated within that is the semblance of the mind, which revolves within the vast space superposed during the dream state, evolving in accordance with the mental impressions (*vāsanā*). || 12 ||
Due to the unity of the nature of the knower, one perceives [the world] as if it were human;
thus, by the power of consciousness within the Self, both [the Self and the world] attain reality.

He states that in both sleep and waking, the cause for the superimposition (adhyāsa) of mutual identity and relation—consisting in the cognition of "man-ness" and so forth upon the Self, as well as the cognition of reality—is indeed the identification with the knower; thus he says: "The state of being a knower," etc.
The state of being a knower (*veditṛtva*) is the nature of the knower, which is true, self-luminous, and immediate consciousness (*caitanya*); [the term refers to] oneness with that.

The meaning is: because of that, there is the superimposition of identity (tattādātmyādhyāsa), and by virtue of that, there is the superimposition of relation (saṃsargādhyāsa). Thus, the reality of both—whether the states of dream and waking, or the superimposed attributes thereof—is attained and becomes manifest. || 13 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, if even in a dream the dream-people were not real,
tell me, what fault would there be in one whose body consists of mere illusion?

Thus, it has been stated that objects perceived in both dreams and the waking state possess bodies composed of both the real and the unreal—the former being characterized as Māyā and its substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), and the latter as truth. Regarding this, Rāma asks: "Let the dream have a body consisting merely of unreal Māyā; what is the use of introducing a portion of reality?"

He raises an objection with the words "In a dream": if waking persons were not real by virtue of the reality of their substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), then the defect would be the non-correspondence of worldly transactions and the lack of authority for the scriptures on action (*karma-śāstra*); therefore, let them be so [real]. If [it is argued that they are real] in one whose body consists of mere illusion conjoined with the real (*satyāsaṃvalitamāyāmātraśarīrin*)—[the phrase "conjoined with the real" (*satyāḥ saṃvalita*)...]

[The reading: Even in a dream, imagined dream-people would likewise not be real; what fault is there in that? For the Blessed Vyāsa has stated that a dream is "mere illusion" (māyāmātra) because its true nature is not fully manifested. Thus, the point is: how can one's own world be the same as a dream? || 14 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In a dream, the inhabitants of a city do not exist as real entities in truth. Hear from me the proof in this matter: it is perception itself, and nothing else. 15.

It can only be said that dream objects are not real in substance, like Brahman; it cannot be said that they are not real even by virtue of the existence of their substrate, because that would contradict the evidence of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). With this intention, Vasiṣṭha said: "In a dream... and so on, [and] "not otherwise."

This was stated for the purpose of disregarding other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not for the purpose of negating them. The intention is that perception is simply not possible for that which is absolutely non-existent, such as the son of a barren woman, because it is never observed in such cases. || 15 ||
At the beginning of creation, the Self-born (Brahmā) appears as one whose nature consists of experiences resembling a dream;
the entire universe is merely a fragment of his volition, and thus it is indeed like a dream.

Furthermore, if the dream were absolutely non-existent, it would be difficult to avoid the same conclusion for the waking world, since that too is of the nature of a dream belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha; with this intention, he says: "At the beginning of creation," etc. (verse 16).
Thus this entire universe is a dream; therein, you are real to me.
Just as you are, so too are all others—the best of dreams for men—within that dream.

And thus, having established the dream-like nature of the world as well as its previously mentioned reality, he says: "In this way. Therein, that which occurs in the dream is real for me, because it is impossible for you to deny your own reality. Just as you are, so too are others real from your perspective and from my perspective. The same applies to others as well.
The meaning is that the reality of dreams is established for human beings according to their respective individual experiences. || 17 ||
If those inhabitants of the city were not real in the dream,
then here too, in that same form, there is not even the slightest bit of reality for me.
He states again more clearly the very same point with the words beginning "In a dream," etc.
Those who exist on the site of a city—that is, on the ground of its dwellings—are called *nagaravāstavyāḥ*; or alternatively, they are called *nagaravāstavyāḥ* because they reside in the city.
This is according to the rule: "The suffix *tavyat* is used after the root *vas* [to dwell] in the sense of the agent, and [the root] is replaced by *ṇi*. || 18 ||

Just as my very self is truth for you, may all that belongs to me become truth; such is the mutual agreement for the sake of establishing [reality] within this worldly existence, which is like the perception of a dream. (19)
In this vast dream that is saṃsāra, "I am real to you," and "you too are real to me"—this is the sequence for everything within dreams. (20)
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, my conviction is that when the dreamer is awake, the city seen in that dream remains exactly as it was, because its nature is real."

If this is so, then Rāma raises the objection that even when the dreamer has awakened, the dream-phenomenon should persist just like the waking-phenomenon—this is expressed by the words beginning with "svapne. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Such is my understanding, resulting from your words. (21)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: It is exactly so; it remains just as it is because of its reality, like a city in a dream, appearing as clear as the sky even while the dreamer is awake.
Vasiṣṭha dismisses this by conceding the point: "It is so. The meaning is that its form is as clear as space; it is indeed real, having the nature of pure Being as its substratum. || 22 ||
Let this be; for now, understand that which you consider to be like waking is in fact only a dream within, not filling out space, time, and so forth. (23)
"In that case, just like waking objects, there would also be a correspondence of conventional usage for dreams within another dream.
Perceiving Rāma’s intention, [the teacher replied: "Even regarding many waking entities, there is a lack of correspondence caused by their non-persistence across different places and times."

With the intention that no distinction can be established on the grounds that there is a correspondence regarding the persistence of a few categories— such as earth, space, names, and universals— even in dreams, [the author] displays boldness by saying,
"Let this be," or alternatively: "If dream-objects were real, they would persist even in the waking state."
Observing Rāma’s apprehension, Vasiṣṭha said: "This...

If you consider the dream-state to be unreal because it does not persist through the space, time, and other conditions of the waking state, then that which you consider to be the waking state is likewise equal [to the dream], insofar as it too is internally filled with the space, time, and other conditions of the dream. Thus, the two are the same.
The meaning is that it is merely a dream. || 23 ||
Thus all this appears; it is not real, nor is it established in reality. It delights [the mind] even though it is false, like sexual union with a woman in a dream. (24)
Thus, although it is real by virtue of its existence as an objective basis (*adhiṣṭhāna-sattā*), it is not so in itself because it does not fill all places, times, and so forth;
therefore, the falsity (*mithyātva*) of both is equal. He says "evam" (thus): it "colors" (*rañjayati*) through attachment to itself and deludes.
"Everything exists everywhere, likewise both inside and outside the body."
In whatever manner one knows consciousness, in that very same way one perceives it as one's own self.

However, because consciousness fulfills all places, times, and so forth, it possesses reality everywhere, as well as the capacity to manifest as all things through the power of *māyā*; thus he says, "everywhere. It is she herself, by her own self. 25.
Just as whatever substance exists within a treasury is obtained by the one who sees it,
so too everything that exists within the space of consciousness is indeed perceived by this [consciousness] as its object.
In the treasury, that is, the storehouse of wealth; "substance" means wealth. By this [means] by the space of consciousness (cidvyoman). || 26 ||
Immediately thereafter, the goddess Jñapti spoke these words to Vidūratha, having made him beautiful with the sprouts of discernment through the sprinkling of the nectar of awakening. (27)
Having thus consoled Rāma, he took up the subject at hand and said: "Immediately thereafter... (27).
"O King, this very matter has been described by me for the sake of illustration;
may it be well with you, we shall now depart, having seen these perspectives through the lens of examples" (28).
This is the truth previously stated. "For the sake of sport" means for the sake of delighting in sport. "May there be well-being" means may there be the accomplishment of desired goals.

Regarding the falsity of the world that has been described, the observation of examples was seen within the pavilion—namely, the conceptualization of your own universe—as a mere sport; this is the sense of the remaining words. || 28 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When Sarasvatī had thus spoken with words of sweet syllables, the wise king Vidūratha spoke these words. (29)
The wise one, knowing the intended meaning of the words "May it be well with you," [spoke]. || 29 ||
Vidūratha said:
"O Goddess, even for me, an appearance before you would not be in vain when I am a petitioner;
how much more so, then, for one such as you who bestows great fruit?"
The intention is: "Even for me, who am merely a human being capable of giving only small gifts. || 30 ||
"O Goddess, having cast off this body, I shall go from here to another world, just as one goes from one dream to another. (31)
My own [nature] is as it was before. I shall come; I will arrive without delay. || 31 ||
Behold me quickly, O Mother, for I have come to you as one who has sought refuge;
O Giver of Boons, disregard shown toward a devotee does not befit the great.
Behold with a compassionate gaze; command and grant me my requested instruction and the subsequent task.
"May this minister and this maiden come with me to whatever place I go;
have mercy on me, for she is but a child. (33)
He states the object of his prayer with the word "yam": a *kumārī* is an unmarried girl. || 33 ||
Śrī Sarasvatī said:
"Come, O Lord of the mandala of your former birth; fearlessly enjoy this kingdom, which is beautiful with the delights of appropriate wealth."
Know this: we have never, at any time, seen even a single instance of our turning away a petitioner who came with a desire. (34)

"Rule the kingdom beautifully with the playful splendors of wealth appropriate for your fortune and devotion; the implication is that we have never once shown you rejection or refusal—that is to say, it has not been seen by anyone. || 34 ||

Thus ends the forty-second canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Reality of the Dream-Man," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Determination of the Reality of the Dream-Man," in the Utthāna-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-third canto.
Śrī Sarasvatī said:
"O King, you must now meet your death in this excellent battle."
The entire kingdom that was to be obtained in the past has now become manifest before you. || 1 ||
The granting of desired boons, the setting ablaze of the city, and the actions of the city-dwellers as they were being consumed by fire are described. || 1 ||

The Goddess, clearly explaining that which he desired to know—even the future matter—and in order to grant the remainder of the boon, said: "In this... (verse 1). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Everything shall become manifest before your very eyes."
The maiden, the minister, and you must go together to the former city; you shall reach that body which has become a corpse.
And the connection is that you must obtain that former body which has become a corpse. || 2 ||
The two of us shall go back as we came, while you, in the form of the wind, must go to that place where the maiden and the minister are. (3)
Having died, you must return to that former place in the form of wind, as the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha).
The gait of a horse is one thing, while that of a donkey or a camel is another;
the gait of an elephant with temples dripping with rut is yet quite different. (4)

With the intention that this movement of the *ātivāhika* body—like a movement of the imagination—is possible over a vast distance even within the space enclosed inside a pavilion, and does not depend on a previously established spatial extension as in the case of the movement of horses and other animals, he says: "It is indeed different. (4)
While this conversation was thus proceeding between the two sweet-spoken lovers,
a man entered in a state of agitation and, standing upright, spoke.
Standing upright, having ascended to a high place such as the top of a palace, a man who observed the events outside the city at night entered the king's presence and spoke. || 5 ||
O King, that great enemy force, raining down arrows, discuses, swords, maces, and iron clubs, has arrived like a surging, vast single ocean. (6)
"O God" is an address to the King. || 6 ||
Resembling the rocks of the Kulācalas mountains tossed by the winds at the end of an aeon,
he joyfully unleashed a rain of maces, spears, and bhushundis.
The enemy force was contented, energetic, and jubilant. || 7 ||
In the city that resembled a mountain, a fire broke out, pervading the horizons;
burning with crackling sounds and explosive bursts, it was toppling the excellent city.
With its lofty palace spires and abundance of grass, wood, and other materials, it was like a mountain, resembling a peak. || 8 ||
In the sky, great mountains of smoke, resembling jars of clouds at the end of an eon,
began to rise up by force like Garuḍas.
They are equal to the masses—that is, the collections—of the clouds at the dissolution of the world-systems (kalpa) and the clouds of destruction (saṃvarta). || 9 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
While the man was speaking thus with agitation,
a great clamor arose outside, filling the quarters with its harsh sound.
"Saṃbhrānta" means with agitation and fear. "Paruṣa" refers to a clamor consisting of harsh and cruel speech. "Āśā" means the directions. || 10 ||
Of bows drawn forcibly to the ear and raining showers of arrows, and of powerful, highly intoxicated elephants trumpeting loudly; 11.
He describes the clamor itself by distinguishing it according to its various relations, beginning with the words "by force" (balāt), etc. || 11 ||
With the crackling sounds of the fires burning brightly,
and with the great tumultuous cries of the citizens whose wives had been consumed by the flames.
The connection with the subsequent portion is that he was "proclaimed by great tumultuous cries" [the meaning being that this is understood from the second half of the twelfth verse]. || 12 ||
The clanging sound of the fragments of fire as they leap across was described by their roar; and the crackling sound of the blazing flames was produced by their flickering motion.
It is further related that, accompanied by the crackling sounds of flames, the cry of "Tāṭ! arose from the people;
then, at the great hour of night, the two queens, the minister, and King Vidūratha beheld from the window the great city resounding with a loud clamor.
From the window, that is, from the lattice-window of the palace. || 14 ||
It was filled by the supreme force, surging with the speed of a single vast ocean agitated by the fire of universal dissolution,
and possessing waves of clouds that were like formidable weapons.
With fierce weapons, like those possessed by both clouds and waves.
It was being consumed by great tongues of flame that filled the sky, blazing like Mount Meru as it melts under the fire at the end of an aeon.
By the flames and crests of the great conflagrations; if the reading is *jālaiḥ*, it is clear. || 16 ||
[The place was filled] with the fierce, tumultuous clamor of the powerful, threatening roars of great clouds that could be grasped by the fist,
and with the harsh, guttural chatter of bandits.

"Plundering" means seizing by the fist and robbing others; in foreign territories, for the purpose of terrifying the enemy, they [the robbers] are "terrible" through loud shouts resembling the roar of great clouds, and through threats that are formidable, powerful, robust, and full-bodied—[all] uttered by those bandits and thieves. (17)
The sky was covered by smoke-colored clouds resembling the Puṣkarāvarta clouds,
and it was filled without interval by masses of flames with golden tips that seemed to soar upward.
The Puṣkarāvarta clouds are the clouds of universal dissolution; "without interval" means without any space between them. || 18 ||
The sky was made turbulent by fierce stars resembling fragments of falling meteors,
while the multitude of houses in various regions blazed like mountains of fire.
There, the blazing mountain-fires were like fierce, portentous, and blood-red stars— fragments of glowing firebrands—
flaming as they shifted their positions through the turning of the flames.
It caused the cities and their armies to fall, with hollows like clouds of glowing embers;
it was filled with the fierce roars of masses of people being consumed by harsh cries of lamentation.
The meaning is that it was characterized by hollows in the clouds— like pits of glowing embers— through which the remnants of the army formerly fell and entered the city;
and it was marked by the fierce roaring of enemies who had scorched the multitudes of people with harsh cries.
Wherein || 20 ||
The sky was rendered almost solid by sparks from fire and iron arrows, while heaps of burnt cities lay scattered amidst a multitude of weapons and masses of stones.
Where the sky was rendered completely devoid of space, being most densely packed with sparks from firebrands and iron arrows;

where, amidst weapons and masses of stones, people were rolling and falling; and where, by the word *pura*, the city-dwellers are meant—those very inhabitants who, while running about, had burnt the city, and whose hands were thus raised high in the form of *utkaras*.
Or where there are enemies. || 21 ||
Where fierce and noble warriors were crushed by the collision of trumpeting elephants,
and where great wealth was strewn upon the roads as it was seized from fleeing thieves.
Men and women wailed piteously as they fell upon heaps of glowing coals;
the burning wood crackled with loud *caṭa-caṭa* sounds as it crumbled and tumbled down.
In that battle, where the most formidable and heroic warriors were crushed and pulverized by the collisions of elephants, [he was honored] by the severing of the heads of thieves. (22–23)
The surface of the sky was filled with hundreds of suns from the mass of vast whirling firebrands,
and the entire surface of the earth was strewn with glowing embers.
Brandished firebrands are flaming torches; they are strewn about by the flames. || 24 ||
The burning fire crackled through the wood, and the bamboo flutes blazed;
all the soldiers cried out and wept as their bodies were consumed by the flames.
Where there were bamboo sticks, burnt by fire and wood, resounding with the sound "krem," and joined with blazing flames. || 25 ||
The royal glory had become nothing but dust, leaving the sacrificial fire unsatisfied;
it was like a great eater of fire, exerting itself to swallow everything.
Just as only dust remains when royal fortune has been seized and consumed by fire— where the aged, the grown,
and the satiated fire, characterized by flames, a great eater, and a voracious consumer, prevails.
By chance, he entered a house where the fire was crackling with harsh sounds, a place where the fire—
craving fuel consumed by its flames— was devouring food for infinite living beings.

Where houses resound with the harsh noise of thieves—incited by chance and suddenly brought about by fate—who seize all one's possessions and strike at night while people sleep; and where there is fire produced by the friction of hard wood; and where there is food fit for the consumption of infinite living beings.
Where some have a longing for mere leftover fuel when heaps of grain have been consumed by fire.
Then King Vidūratha heard there the cries of the warriors whose wives had been burned, as they looked on and rushed forward.
The mention of "taking a wife" is an illustration for [the giving away of] all one's possessions. || 28 ||

Alas! The travelers on the path of the sun’s heat, amidst the dry grasses and the rustling of leaves, see the embers rising high from the trees in their homes due to the fierce wind, crackling with a harsh *khara-khara* sound.

The word division is *aṅga* and *āra*. Someone addresses another, saying: "O friend (*aṅga*), [look at] these green mangoes (*āmān*) which, by means of their pollen-net (*nīrajālena*)—that is, by their excellence of flavor—are the obstructors (*paripanthinaḥ*) of the path of the sun's heat, [acting as] barriers against its scorching; they stand upright (*ūrdhvasthān*), established in their loftiness."

A fierce wind, or rather a calamitous gale, came rushing toward us with a harsh, rattling roar, in order to uproot the trees that bear the characteristics of our home and those that have grown within our dwelling. "Hā!"—an expression of grief. (29)
Alas! The wives of the elephants, scorched by the cold of the frost, are submerged within their bodies like the eloquent expressions of wisdom sunk within the minds of the great.
Formerly cooled by frost, now scorched and heated, the wives of the elephants have merged and remained hidden within the bodies of the deceased;
though their gross and other bodies were consumed by the fire of knowledge on the side of the well-spoken words,
they remain cooler even than frost due to the allaying of the threefold afflictions.
Alas, father! These arrows have struck the grass of the young woman’s braid;
they blaze like heaps of dry leaves fanned by the wind of heroes. (31)
"Arrows" refers to various weapons, fires, or their flames; "kavaryaḥ" refers to hair, [used here] for grass characterized by it;
these "blaze," meaning they shine. || 31 ||
Long as a river in its whirlpools and bearing exceedingly high waves, this smoke-Yamunā flows; behold, it rushes forth like the celestial Gaṅgā.
Long with its whirlpools, eddies, and river-like branching currents,
she is like the celestial Gaṅgā or the Mandākinī.
Behold! The river of smoke, rising upward from the wood of the burning embers, blinds the inhabitants of celestial chariots; it is filled with bubbles of sparks of fire.
That [river] in which pieces of firewood are carried along and flow; that in which sparks of fire are the very bubbles.
Her mother, father, brother, son-in-law,
and infant grandson have been consumed by fire in this house, burnt along with the fuel of their wickedness.
"Stanapāḥ" means those who drink from the breast, "stanadhayāḥ" means those who suckle; it refers to a daughter, or it may be an address to a daughter.
She too has been as if burnt by fire—even though that fire, characterized by separation from him, is not actually present and lacks fuel—simply because of its nature. || 34 ||
"Hā! Hā! Hā! Come quickly to this house of coals;
from here you shall fall like Mount Sumeru at the time of universal dissolution. (35)
Come quickly, go out! This house of yours, blazing like glowing coals, is beginning to collapse from its very foundation as it shifts from its place. || 35 ||
Alas! These arrows, stones, spears, lances, darts, and swords—these weapons—are entering [the enemy] like moths into a mass of clouds at twilight. (36)
The mass of twilight clouds has the characteristics of the lattice of a window.
Alas! The streams of firebrands enter the blazing submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*) in the sky at the end of time;
[in some other manuscripts, it is read as *raṇāt* (from battle), but this reading follows the root text and is thus more appropriate].
We have gathered [them], like [pearls] from the ocean. || 37 ||
In the month of Nabhasya, when the city, out of fear, desired to fly up into the sky, floods of water—torrents of liquid (the reading *arṇapūrāḥ* is also found)—[surged forth]. || 37 ||
Great clouds are smoking, and flames erupt from the peaks;
even the lakes dry up like the hearts of those filled with passion.
Upon the peaks—the uppermost parts—of millions of palaces possessing turrets; as well as the ponds and other water-filled reservoirs, and the gardens. (38)
As if out of anger at being used as hitching posts, these rows of trees are felled by the elephants with loud *kaṭakaṭa* crackling sounds and shrieks.
An *ālāna* is a tethering post; [the anger] is prompted by the fact that [the elephant] belongs to that same species. || 39 ||
With their trunks, flowers, fruits, and branches once flourishing, the household trees have lost their splendor;
like householders whose entire possessions have been consumed by fire, they have fallen into a state of wretchedness.
Deprived of their parents, these children, sinking into a mass of darkness on the streets, alas, are struck down by falling walls upon their limbs. (41)

"Searching"—meaning seeking out—the rows of darkness as they sink into their dwelling; this is the sense. The form *majjantaḥ* is derived from the root *masj* in the sense of "purifying," with the suffix *śatṛ* (present participle) and the Vedic changes of *k* to *g* and *n*. The word *aṅga* is used as an address. [They search] in streets strewn with arrows, by means of the falling of walls—that is, the collapsing of partitions. || 41 ||
At the front of the battle, the female elephants, terrified by the wind-driven [fire],
let out a bitter cry as they bore heaps of falling embers.

From that which was driven away and blown up by the wind, from which embers were falling—such being its nature; from that *agārabhāri* roof (so called because it has the habit of protecting the householder’s dwelling from rain, heat, and so forth), the female elephants, trembling with a harsh cry (*kaṭukūjitam*), became terrified. [The form *trasyan* is derived from the root *tras* in the *laṅ* tense.]
Or [the form *vibhāśate* is derived] from the root *bhrāś-bhlāś* with the suffix *śyan*; the absence of the augment *aṭ* is Vedic. || 42 ||
Alas, what a tragedy! A stone from a mechanical device has fallen upon his shoulder—already pierced by a firmly fixed flaming torch—like a thunderbolt upon a man. (43)
Alas! Cows, horses, buffaloes, elephants, camels, donkeys, jackals, and rams have begun a terrible battle, as it were, obstructing the path in their agitation.
The ellipsis is: let them see, as it were, a battle that blocks the path of those passing by, commenced with rams and sheep. || 44 ||
With their garments making the sound "paṭa-paṭa" and surrounded by swarms of bees drawn by the mass of water-lilies,
the women go along wailing like a land-lotus thicket.
He describes the women emerging after putting on wet garments out of fear of being scorched by the flames of the fire:
"They appear as if constructed from land-lotuses, whose stalks, feet, and faces are encircled by the characteristics [of their features]. (45)
Behold, the flickering flames lick the creeper-like tresses of the women,
making them resemble *aśoka* flowers like female serpents with their trunks.

*Karabhāḥ* are young camels. *Pannagyaḥ* are female serpents who move in such a way that they fall down (*pannam*), or alternatively, those female serpents who, by chance, happened to be clinging to overhanging tree branches at that time. || 46 ||
Alas, alas! Upon the eyelashes of the fawn-eyed maiden, which are marked like wings, the flames of fire find rest as if upon evil paths.
Upon the eyelashes, which resemble the wings of a bee according to their characteristics, the fire—belonging to that [fire]—is the flame, the crest of Kārśānavī. 47.
Even while being consumed by fire, a man does not depart without his wife;
alas, how difficult it is for living beings to sever the snares of affection! 48.
Even while being consumed by fire himself. || 48 ||
The elephant, having violently uprooted trees with their glowing coals and having scorched the lotuses,
plunged in anger into the Puṣkarada lake.
By him, with impetuous force and speed, the tethering post— mixed with glowing embers— was torn up and broken; therefore,
at the time of its being dragged out, the elephant, whose trunk-tip (*puṣkara*) was scorched and burnt, fled from the people, reached a lotus-lake (*puṣkarada*), and submerged there.
This is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) based on paronomasia (śleṣa), as if [the ocean] desired to recover its burnt lotus. || 49 ||
The smoke, having reached the region of the clouds, with flickering streaks of lightning within, rains down a shower of blazing embers like a multitude of iron arrows. (50)

Having reached the station of the clouds—the locus in the sky that carries out the function of rain—he possesses lightning-streaks characterized by flickering flames of fire within him; he is imagined as raining down, all around, a mass of blazing embers and iron arrows (nārāca) corresponding to his own nature. || 50 ||
O King, with smoke flickering and sparks of fire, and possessing the circular motion of whirlpools,
it stood in the sky like an ocean filled with jewels and adorned with a floral crest.
Addressing the king as "O Lord," this is the speech of someone: smoke stands in the sky like an ocean, possessing *āpīḍas*—that is, possessing waves of crests. || 51 ||
The white garment shines with the brilliance of the crest of flames,
like a casket smeared with saffron bestowed by Death himself at a festival.

The sky is yellowish-white and its garment is yellow. A casket, smeared and colored with saffron, has been given; by implication, it is understood that this was given to the women of the quarters. 52.
"Alas! How truly terrible is this, occurring so devoid of all propriety;
for even the wives of kings are being held captive by the enemy heroes with weapons raised. (53)
Conduct consists of virtuous behavior; by that [vice], it is abandoned and cast out. || 53 ||
With garlands of loose flowers serving as the boundary walls of their paths,
their breasts and chests were strewn with locks of hair half-burnt.

O King, she distinguishes the women alone until the end of creation with the words beginning with "lole" (restless). They are characterized by garlands and flowers—restless makers of the rampart (*prākāra*) which is the scattering (*prakiraṇa*) [of beauty] along the path. || 54 ||
Their hips and the regions of their loins were visible through their swaying garments, and the circles of the earth were encircled by their falling ruby bracelets. || 55 ||
Those by whom the circles of the earth were covered—either strewn with falling rubies or encircled by bracelets inlaid with rubies. || 55 ||
Pure pearls were scattered from the lattices of broken pearl necklaces,
and golden lusters shone from the sides of their breasts, whether visible or hidden.
The roar of battle was drowned out by the harsh cries of female ospreys;
their sides were pierced by the continuous flow of blood, and they lost consciousness.
By those women, the roar of battle was weakened and overwhelmed by their harsh and painful wails,
which were like the cries of female ospreys; their flanks and bellies were as if torn apart, pierced, and tormented by the continuous, unceasing flow of tears emerging from their lamentations.
Of these [women], for that very reason they are "devoid of consciousness," meaning they are empty of the consciousness regarding what ought to be done. || 57 ||
Their garments were knotted together, soaked by blood as if it were mud and tears as if they were water;
they were being led away by force by men who had placed their own arms under the armpits of those women.
Fearing flight, they tied their garments together with one another. || 58 ||

Their soldiers were made to weep all around by those who, perceiving the calamities [of their situation], cried out, "Who indeed might be our protector in this? like a row of blue lotuses shedding raindrops.
By their wistful glances, they caused their own side's soldiers to weep all around out of compassion—those women who were themselves prone to weeping. || 59 ||
With the bases of their thighs, which were as tender as lotus stalks and perfectly pure,
visible against the clear expanse of the sky, they resembled lotuses in the firmament.
In the clear expanses of the sky, visible within the folds of their garments, they resemble celestial lotuses due to the association with the word *ambara* (sky). (60)
With their garlands, garments, ornaments, and body-pastes no longer swaying, and with the creepers of their long, curly locks disarrayed and choked with tears,
they were churned incessantly by the Mandara mountain of bliss.
They were like royal fortunes risen from the ocean of desire. || 61 ||

Those [women] whose long, trembling tresses are like moving creepers; from whom, being churned by Mount Mandara in the form of sensual pleasure—that is, the joy derived from sense-objects—the royal fortunes, which are the very embodiments of the kings' prosperity, or rather the glories fashioned from those kings who are like the moon, emerge. 61.
Thus ends the forty-third canto, titled "The Description of Houses Burnt by Fire," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 43.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the House Burnt by Fire and Other Matters," in the Utthāna-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the meantime, the king’s queen, intoxicated by her youth, [spoke].
He entered that house, just as Lakṣmī enters the hollow of a lotus.
Having observed the queen terrified and having heard of the assault upon the inner apartments, the king’s departure for battle and the true nature of his divine play (līlā) are described. || 1 ||
In that [city], youth was as if reeling with intoxication; the king’s palace was presided over by the wisdom of such playful charm. (1)
With her garlands and garments disheveled, her strings of pearls scattered and in disarray,
she was pursued by her female companions and maidservants, overwhelmed with fear.
With a moon-like face and limbs of pure white, her breasts trembling with her breath,
and teeth like stars, she stood there like the sky incarnate.
She whose face is like the moon, indeed the moon itself; she whose limbs are pure, fair, and translucent. (3)
Then one of her companions addressed that king,
as an apsaras addresses the lord of the gods when he is intent on the battle of the elements.
"O King, together with us, the queen has fled from within the inner apartments and come for refuge to Your Majesty, like a creeper shaken by the wind seeking shelter in a tree. (5)
The queen is the principal consort who has undergone the consecration ceremony. || 5 ||
O King, those wives of yours have been carried off by powerful men with raised weapons,
like the trees and creepers on the shores of great oceans swept away by masses of waves.
Other wives are for enjoyment. || 6 ||
All the masters of the inner apartments were crushed by the arrogant enemies,
who fell upon them unexpectedly like winds upon choice trees.
Pounded means thoroughly ground into powder. || 7 ||
Our city has been seized by enemies who approached unsuspected from afar,
just as lotuses are carried away at night by waters during the rains amidst loud splashing sounds.

"By far, from afar. According to the rule *dūrāntikārthebhyo dvitīyā ca*, there is an option for the second case (*dvitīyā*), and because of the word "also" (*ca*), the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is also employed. "Brought" means "seized."
Our city was assailed by fires raining smoke, roaring loudly with their fierce, licking tongues, and by vast numbers of the enemy's warriors. (9)

[The demons] were raining down and scattering smoke; they were loud and roaring. In the reading *dhūmavarmabhiḥ*, the meaning is clear. In the reading *unmādaiḥ*, it refers to those whose intoxication (*māda*)—meaning either excessive joy or derangement—is preeminent.
Their fierce weapons, both swords and flames, moved like licking tongues. || 9 ||
The playful queens, along with their retinues, were forcibly seized by their hair and led away while crying out like female ospreys captured by fishermen.
By their retinues, who were enemy soldiers; by female ospreys, deer, and birds; and by fishermen and hunters.
Thus, as for this branch of ours that has come forth, flourishing with its spreading tendrils, only the Lord possesses the power to lift it up and purify it. 11.
"Āpad" means calamity; "tām" refers to that [calamity]; "alam" means excessively; "uddhartum" means to rescue; "nivārayitum" means to ward off. || 11 ||
Having heard this and looked upon the two goddesses, he said: "I am departing for battle;
may this wife of mine, who is a bee at your lotus-feet, be forgiven."
Having heard the words "This is the king," and having looked at the two queens, [he] spoke—this is the ellipsis. "O queens, I am going—I depart—for battle; please forgive me.
The offense lies in his departure from the interior without permission. The intention is that, being like a bee at your lotus-feet, he should be protected by you both.
Having spoken thus, the king, his eyes reddened with anger,
went forth like a lion from a mountain cave after tearing through a forest with a rutting elephant.
Then Līlā beheld Līlā, whose form was identical to her own, appearing like a beautiful reflection come forth from a mirror. (14)
Līlā is the play of the Awakened One. || 14 ||
Prabuddhalīlā said:
"O Goddess, tell me, what is this? Tell me, why am I standing here? I who was that person before—how have I become this person standing here? (15)

The sense is: "This [present state] having become that" is the ellipsis. How can she who was "I" be this? How can she who was in her first youth remain exactly as she was? The meaning is that it is impossible for her to be something other than herself, and yet it is impossible for her past state to persist. || 15 ||
The ministers and others, the citizens, and the warriors with their forces and vehicles—
all of them remained there exactly as they were before.
Furthermore, he states that even in the case of ministers and others, the cognition of difference and the recognition [of identity] are contradictory: "Ministers and so forth... (verse 16).
In that case as well, O Goddess, how do all these exist here—both outside and inside, like reflections in a mirror—are they conscious? (17)
Are they conscious, or are they sentient? 17.
The Goddess said:
Just as a cognition arises within, so it is experienced in an instant;
consciousness assumes the state of being an object of thought, just as the mind assumes the state of being an object of the mind.

Because the powers of consciousness (*citiśakti*) are inconceivable, their manifestation occurs in some instances as exactly equal when awakened by identical karma; thus, the Goddess provides the resolution by resorting to the doctrine of "creation through vision" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*), beginning with the word "as follows" (*yathā*).

She explains that the state of being an object of cognition (*cetyārthatā*)—that is, the taking on of the form of an object through superimposition—is just as it is for the mind (*citta*) or the internal organ (*manas*) in dreams and the like.
The meaning is: the state of having the form of objects experienced while awake by the mind. || 18 ||
Whatever form the world takes, that very form arises from that [source] in that very instant;
there is no distance of space or time, nor any diversity born of material objects.

Whatever kind of object, of whatever form, exists within that world-form consisting of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), exactly that same kind arises in the mind and in consciousness (*cit*). The meaning is this: the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), conjoined with *māyā* and awakened by the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the experiencer, is capable of bringing about even what is impossible to construct. And thus:

With the intention of showing that the contradiction regarding the smallness or vastness of place and time has also been resolved, he says "no. The meaning is: if [the world] were born from material objects, then that which is contrary to their nature would not be possible; however, it is not so. || 19 ||
The external and the internal appear [within consciousness]; here, the object of a dream serves as the illustration.
For that which is within—the city of dreams and mental constructs—is but the manifestation of consciousness. (20)
Because it is superimposed upon consciousness, the world—which is internal—appears as if it were external, existing outside. || 20 ||
Therefore, by virtue of its very name "External," this [city] remains clearly manifest through constant practice;
for it was maintained by you as whatever state of being you intended while in that city at that time.

Through constant practice and long-term cultivation, it becomes clear and manifest, as if existing as a reality; whatever kind of disposition or latent impression (vāsanā) one possesses, being of that very nature, one dies. (21)
A being of such a nature, having arrived at that very place for that very purpose,
is indeed distinct from these other beings, even though they too are of a similar kind.

"Samupāgataḥ" means he has arrived or attained. Although there is a similarity of form because their karmic impressions (*karmavāsanā*) have been awakened in the same way, these living beings of the ministers and others are not those very same individuals; rather, they are different. Thus he says: "They are indeed others. Even though they are recognized as being the same through familiarity—having been experienced again and again—they are nonetheless different such [beings]. || 22 ||
Indeed, for this [consciousness], all that is experienced as the form of all objects is non-contradictory and is of the very nature of reality, like an army in a dream or a mental construction. (23)
These [objects] are indeed real by virtue of the king's consciousness-existence (*citsattā*). This alone is the distinction between waking objects and dream objects:

that they are non-contradictory and common to all persons. He says "non-contradictory" to show that truth is not established by this much alone; for even in cases such as the moon being a mere span in size or in magical illusions (*indrajāla*), there is non-contradiction.
The meaning is that it is non-contradictory because it is seen to apply to all objects. || 23 ||
Tell me, then, what kind of reality does that [dream] possess?
Or else, because it perishes at a later time, it is a non-entity. (24)
If it is argued that the dream is unreal because it is sublated at a later time, then this is equally true for the waking state as well;
for there is no difference regarding a real entity between destruction and sublation. With this intention, he says, "Or else," referring to that dream.
And since all this is exactly like that, what further need is there for the doctrine of non-existence?
In a dream, the waking state is unreal; in the waking state, the dream is composed of unreality. (25)

The meaning is that [objects] are more prominent in the objects of the waking state. He states—“In a dream”—that the non-existence of one at the time of the other is likewise indistinguishable. || 25 ||
Death is unreal in relation to birth, and birth is likewise unreal in relation to death; this is because of their perishable nature and because of our direct experience, O Rāghava. (26)
He says "death" (mṛti) to show that even in the case of destruction, the mutual non-existence at each other's time is equal, just as it is in the case of sublation (bādha).

In destruction, because the parts have fallen apart, the substance would fall apart and perish; in sublation, however, because of the force of experience, the experience itself would fall apart. Thus, despite the difference in cause, there is no distinction in the falling apart—this is the meaning.
Thus, this world, being neither existent nor non-existent, appears as mere illusion,
O sinless one, whether in the attainment of the end of a great kalpa or now in this present age.
Having established reality (*satyatā*) previously and unreality (*asatyatā*) here, he states that both are equally characterized by indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*) by saying "Thus" (*evam*).

And thus, he declares that Brahman, whose nature is Being (*sadrūpa*), is established as undifferentiated at the time of creation and at the time of dissolution, by saying "At the end of the great kalpa" (*mahākalpānta*). Even at the occurrence of the end of the great kalpa, even until now...
Immediately thereafter, even through the distinctions of past and future ages, that which never exists at any time does not exist in its own right;

rather, it is Brahman alone that exists as the substratum for the conceptualization of that [unreal world]. Therefore, that [Brahman] alone is the world, and not the world appearing as something other than Brahman—this is the meaning. || 27 ||
That which never exists is none other than Brahman; that is the world.
Within it, these delusions called "creations" shine forth. (28)
Like tufts of hair in the sky, they do not truly shine;
just as waves exist in the ocean, so do these creations in the Supreme.

Although it should have been stated simply that "they do not shine at all," the inclusion of the particle *iva* (as if) is for the purpose of illuminating the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the absence of manifestation as well—just like its presence—as being something distinct from Brahman. || 29 ||
Arising again and again, they dissolve like dust in a great wind;
therefore, I perceive falsity within myself, which is a mere appearance consisting of delusion.
It is entirely false [to conceive] of the self as being divided in this way into "you" and "I."
What reliance can there be on the mass of water in a mirage, or on the ashes of creation?
There are no other delusions there; that alone is the supreme state.

In this phenomenal world, which is like ashes from the fire of creation and resembles the ashes of a burnt cloth—surely, even if the objects are sublated, duality might still exist because the nature of the erroneous cognition itself is not sublated? To this, he says: "And the errors...
[referring to] cognitions devoid of objects, both among themselves and with respect to Brahman.
The meaning is that, due to the absence of any differentiator, there is the state of being Brahman alone. || 31 ||
In dense darkness, there is the appearance of a yakṣa, yet it is only darkness and not a yakṣa;
therefore, birth and death are delusion, and this entire world is pervaded by that very delusion.

The appearance of yakṣas is the child's delusion regarding yakṣas; "vyāmoha" means ignorance, and its state is "vyāmohatva. That very power of concealment and projection belonging to it has spread out in this form of the world.
All that remains at the end of that great kalpa is peace;
therefore, this visible world is neither real nor ever unreal. (33)

The meaning is that the "great kalpa" is the dissolution characterized by the sublation of everything through the knowledge of Brahman; it is "accompanied by that" in the sense that the object of sublation (the phenomenal world) is included therein. He states, beginning with "in the state of peace," that the very existence of Brahman as the substratum precludes all positions regarding the existence, non-existence, and so forth of the visible world: "in the state of the cessation of all."
That which remains is Brahman; therefore, the connection [of the text] is "from Brahman, truth is not," and so forth. || 33 ||

Alternatively, these two are indeed Brahman itself, because it exists therein—just as space exists within atoms, and as substance and so forth exist even within the binary atomic compound (aṇuka). // 34 //

But it is certainly not of the nature of both real and unreal; the meaning is that it is impossible for a single thing to possess two contradictory natures. Among those three contradictory alternatives, since it is possible [only] without contradiction in the case of Brahman, he says "Brahman" to indicate that this alternative is the best.
He states that the state of being mere conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātratva*) is possible everywhere in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), beginning with the phrase "in space" (*ākāśe*).
This applies even to the internal portion of the most minute [entity], such as a subtle atom (*aṇuka*), including its substances, qualities, and so forth. || 34 ||
Wherever a living atom (jīva) is, there it perceives this entire universe as its own body,
just as fire perceives heat as its own nature arising from its inherent sequence of being.
He provides an illustration for the superimposition of the non-self upon the self through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*): "Fire," etc.

Previously, the practitioner, though not fire itself, perceives this very world as such through his own contemplation consisting of the meditation, "I am indeed fire"; likewise, the Self, which is pure consciousness, perceives that which has become its own self.
Just as motes of dust move about in a house at sunrise. || 36 ||
Thus, these atoms of the cosmic egg exist in the supreme space,
just as vibration exists in the wind, fragrance in the air, and emptiness in the sky.
Just as vibration and fragrance reside in the wind, so too does the void reside in emptiness. || 37 ||

Just as the universe remains in the Supreme, liberated from the grasping of a solid mass, so too are existence and non-existence, acceptance and rejection, the gross and the subtle, and the moving and the unmoving. (38)
Lumping together (piṇḍagraha) is grossness. Existence and non-existence are manifestation and disappearance. Grasping (graha) is appropriation;
relinquishing (utsarga) is abandonment. This is an illustration of action in general. || 38 ||
Such are the portions of Brahman, devoid of constituent parts;
they must now be understood by you for the sake of comprehending that which possesses form. (39)
The "parts" (*bhāgāḥ*) are those whose divisions are imagined. The form "bhavata" (be thou) is used in the masculine because it is Vasiṣṭha speaking to Rāma.

And these parts are to be understood as being, for that manifest universe, non-different from its such-like Self—like partless [entities]—for the purpose of realizing the formlessness of that which possesses form. The word "like" (*iva*) implies that even this partlessness is merely a semblance of partlessness, just like the state of having parts.
The purpose is to illuminate falsity. || 39 ||
Non-different from His own self, this universe is as if without parts; it exists exactly as it is, arisen through the sequence of its own inherent nature.

Thus, by means of the sequence of one's own contemplation (*nijabhāvanākrama*) through partlessness, that which has manifested in its ultimate form will not be empty—that is, devoid—of the actual objects denoted by the word "universe" (*viśva*). The point is that since the word "universe" culminates in the sense of fullness, and fullness is incompatible with emptiness. || 40 ||
Empty of the meanings of all words, it abides as non-different from Brahman;
it is neither real nor unreal, like the delusion of a snake in a rope. (41)
The reason for this is: "it is not other. Then, as for that universe which appears with parts, what is it there?

He says: "Due to false experience, the real is unreal; the supreme cause is examined as real; because of its consciousness-nature, it is the state of being a living soul (jīvatva)—enough of this. (42)
Regarding this, he states the reason: "It is false" (*mithyā*). For that which is experienced through erroneous cognition does not become real;

nor does the subverting cognition, which consists in the investigation of the true nature of reality, deny its own reality such that it would itself be unreal—this is the sense. Because of its being consciousness (*cittvāt*), that is, because its essential nature is concealed by *māyā* yet remains consciousness. || 42 ||
Then, through such experience, one clearly attains the state of being a living soul;
whether it be true or false, this world shines forth within the void.

From experience—that is, from the firm impression of long-standing perception—the individual's desire for enjoyment in saṃsāra arises; it is the very coloring of objects that serves as the cause, not whether they are real or unreal. Thus he says: "It is real.
(43) The individual soul indeed colors itself through its own desires and experiences.
Indeed, some [mental impressions] are experienced immediately due to previous experiences. (44)

Having stated the introductory remarks, he provides the resolution to the question at hand with the words beginning "anubhūyante" (they are experienced): the grammatical connection is that certain unprecedented experiences, both similar and dissimilar to previous experiences, are experienced by virtue of those previous experiences. || 44 ||
Some [verses] have never been experienced before; likewise, some are even (sama) and others uneven (asama).
At certain times and places, those very same [verses] appear, while in other instances they are even-uneven (ardhasama). 45.

When there arises the impression (vāsanā) of all those [objects], they appear as such due to the non-apprehension of their difference; when there arises the impression of half [of them], they appear as being even [in number]. (45)
In the space of the individual soul (jīvākāśa), there shine experiences that are unreal yet appear real;
they possess its lineage, its conduct, its birth, and its activities. (46)
He states that this is the first of those two types with the words beginning "tatkulā" (belonging to that family). || 46 ||
These very same people become ministers and citizens when there is presence of mind;
they alone are truly capable within themselves when they are consistent with the place, the time, and what is beneficial. (47)

He states that "those [are... (te ca) to show that, from the perspective of their ultimate substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there is in the highest sense (*paramārthataḥ*) no prior difference, whereas from the perspective of superimposition (*adhyasta-dṛṣṭyā*), they result in being equal. [The verse says: "In the Self, which is the ultimate nature, they alone are sufficient [to be] real; however, from the perspective of what is desired in their respective places and times, they are equal. (47)
Such is the established position regarding the intuition (pratibhā) whose nature is the self of all:
just as an intuition consisting of pure being arises within the sky that is the self of the King. (48)

He states that the abiding of consciousness is exactly thus everywhere: "omnipresent" (*sarvagā*). Now, it might be objected: it is heard in scripture that the Lord (*īśvara*) is the creator of objects according to his intuition (*pratibhā*), whereas for the individual soul (*jīva*), the arising of intuition follows only the object.
Otherwise, there would result the undesirable consequence of the commonality of truth even for objects of mere imagination (*mānorathika*); so how [is this consistent]?

Anticipating the objection that the accomplishment of objects occurs merely through the king's intuition, and that this possesses the fitness for common worldly transactions shared with other living beings, he says: "Just as... Just as a certain intuition consisting of Being (*sanmayī*), which has all things as its common object, arises within the self of the king, so too does [the intuition] precede it, existing prior to that [accomplishment].

By the power of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) that causes common enjoyment, an intuition (pratibhā) consisting of true volition (satya-saṃkalpa) indeed arises within the Lord (īśvara), who is denoted by the word "Being" (sat) and is of the nature of the unmanifest space (avyākṛtākāśa). Thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply; this is the intended meaning. || 48 ||
Likewise, that [image] arises foremost within the very sky of my intuition—possessing your character, your conduct, your lineage, and consisting of your very form. (49)
Thus this play appears, born from the reflection of intuitive insight;
within the all-pervasive mirror of consciousness, intuitive insight reflects itself.
It shines forth in the manner thus described. He states that this very method applies everywhere with the words "sarvage" (in all-pervading). || 50 ||
In whatever manner it exists within, in that very manner it arises there continuously;
the internal manifestation of the space of the living soul (jīvākāśa) manifests by itself externally as a reflection in the mirror of consciousness (cidādarśa). Thus does this [world] stand. // 51 //

The internal faculties, being manifestations of the Lord who is the inner controller, project [objects] outwardly; thus, the intention is that their status as external objects is established by their being perceived in common by all. || 51 ||
This sky, this heaven, this earth,
and even the king— all this is merely I, manifest as I am; O dear one, know that the belly of the bilva-fruit of the space of consciousness contains all.
Therefore, remain here as you are, peaceful and free from impurity.

The sky is space; within it is the world; within that is the earth; and within that are you, I, and the king—all this is merely manifest as the very nature of pure consciousness (cinmātra). I am indeed the form of immediate awareness (pratyagrūpa). In this same way, other knowers of reality [perceive] the interior of the bilva fruit characterized by the sky of consciousness, which is nothing but its own existence.
The wise know it to be the seed-womb; O Angulīlā, you too should understand it thus. Therefore, remain as you are, established in your own nature, peaceful and undisturbed. 52.

Thus ends the forty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the World and Brahma in the Night-Battle of the Fire-Consumer," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* within the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*.
This concludes the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the World as Brahman."
The forty-fifth canto. Śrī Sarasvatī said:
"This Vidūratha, your husband, having cast off his body on the field of battle..."
Having reached that very inner apartment, he will become such a self.
The attainment of the lotus by the second Līlā is here called the boon;
and the living beings obtain the fruit according to their own volition. || 1 ||
Such a self is the self of King Padmabhūpa. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard these words of the Goddess, Līlā, who had previously resided in that city,
stood before her with palms joined in reverence and spoke these words.
Bowing low, humble with devotion, she stood before him with her hands joined in reverence. || 2 ||
The second Līlā said: "The goddess Bhagavatī Jñapti has been constantly worshipped by me;
that goddess grants me a vision of herself during the nights."
O Goddess of gods, O Mother, you are exactly as she is;
therefore, out of compassion for me, a wretched man, grant me a boon, O fair-faced one. (4)
You appear exactly as such; therefore, the intention is that you are indeed that very same one. || 4 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed thus, Jñapti then recalled her state of devotion and,
being pleased, spoke these words to Līlā, who had formerly resided in that city.
Devotion consists of contemplation, reflection, and worship. || 5 ||
The Illustrious Goddess said: "O child, I am well-pleased with you for your lifelong, undiminished, and singular devotion; accept the boon you desire."
Taddeśalīlā said: "Wherever my husband remains after casting off his body from the battlefield, may I become his wife there in this very same body. (7)
"He stands" and "he will stand": [the future tense] is treated like the present when there is proximity to the present time. (Pāṇini 3.3.131)
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"So be it; you have worshipped me for a long time without obstacle, O daughter, with single-minded devotion and abundant offerings of flowers and incense."
"Without obstacle" expresses the completeness of the ritual action; "with undivided devotion" means with exclusive devotion. (8)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then,
when that local sport had blossomed due to the arrival of her husband,
Pūrvilīlā, her heart agitated by doubt, spoke to the Goddess.
When she had blossomed with joy,

her mind became agitated and wavering due to a doubt as to what distinction there could be between her husband’s attainment of the world of the manes through his gross body and her own act of abandoning her body. || 9 ||
(241) Pūrvalīlā said:
Those who possess true desires, whose resolutions are thus [fulfilled], and who are of the nature of Brahman—
For those like you, everything they desire is swiftly accomplished.
Therein, first he states the seed of doubt: "Those who... (verse 10).
O Sovereign Lady, tell me why I was not led by that very body to that mountain village in this other world? (11)
Therefore, by the power of the desire for truth. || 11 ||
The Goddess said:
"O lady of excellent complexion, I do nothing for anyone;
it is the individual soul itself that quickly accomplishes its own desired ends."

He has no desire for himself because he is one whose desires are fulfilled; rather, that [desire] is established solely by the arrangement of the karma of living beings. With this intention, the *Jñapti* provides the resolution, beginning with the words "not at all," and so forth. || 12 ||
I am the beneficial proclamation, the presiding deity of pure consciousness;
within each individual exists the power of consciousness, which is the very nature of the life-force (jīva-śakti).

I proclaim through the granting of boons that which is beneficial, desired by living beings, and auspicious for the future; and in the production of fruits for living beings, I am the very nature of the individual soul-power (*jīva-śakti*), whose essence is consciousness (*cidātman*) as delimited by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of each being's prior desires and karma.
There exists the power of consciousness (cicchakti) conjoined with Māyā, which serves as the seed for those respective effects. || 13 ||
Whatever power arises in a living being, in whatever manner, it always manifests as the bestower of its corresponding fruit for that very being in that very same way. (14)

Therefore, she says "of the individual soul" (jīvasya) to show that she herself bestows the fruit in accordance with that very [desire]: it "shines," meaning it manifests as the object of desire caused by the performance of ritual action. || 14 ||
As you worshipped me, your vital energy (jīva-śakti) arose;
at that time, you thought, "If I were here, I would be liberated," and so it has been for a long time.

The word "I" (*asmi*) is an indeclinable that is synonymous with the term *ahaṃ* (I) and functions as a verbal derivative. The individual power (*jīva-śakti*), whose nature is consciousness, is delimited by a desire containing within it the subtle state of future karma and its fruits, expressed as: "May I be liberated."
In various ways you have been fully awakened by me;
through that method, O lady of excellent complexion, you have been led to a state of stainless being.
The stainless state characterized by abiding in the pure self, from which the veil of ignorance has been dispelled through awakening. || 16 ||
Awakened by this very meditation for a long time, you then attained that very goal through the power of your own consciousness at all times. || 17 ||

"You have been long engaged in this meditation, 'May I be liberated,' and you have been awakened by the reasoning previously shown; that very object which was thus meditated upon [is now realized]. (17)
Whatever effort one's own mind undertakes for a long time, in whatever manner it arises,
its fruit is granted at the proper time in that very same way.
Human effort is an exertion delimited by its own particular locus. || 18 ||

Having become either austerity or even a deity, one's own consciousness itself bestows the fruit in another form, or else it gives [the fruit] at its own will, like the falling of fruit from the sky. 19.
The meaning is that it is false, like the falling of fruits from the sky. || 19 ||
Nothing other than one's own self-awareness ever yields any fruit at any time; therefore, act quickly as you wish.
Whatever kind of fruit you desire, perform the corresponding action accordingly.

Indeed, the inner self, which is the very nature of consciousness and is all-pervading, attains that very thing which it perceives and strives for; from that, prosperity arises. Therefore, reflect upon whether it be beautiful or even repulsive.
Having understood that which is purifying, abide within it.
