The state of consciousness (*cidbhāva*) is the existence of consciousness (*citsattā*). Now, as for the word "nanu," it is used here in the sense of certainty. Consider this: at that prior time, whether it was a pleasant action prescribed or an unpleasant one prohibited, whatever karma one perceives and exerts effort toward, in a subsequent time, its very fruit in the form of prosperity (*śrī*) comes—that is, it arises.
Reflect upon this. And by means of such reflection, having realized that state which is purifying, abide within it.
Thus ends the forty-fifth canto, titled "The Existence of Satyakāma and Satyasaṅkalpa," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Existence of Satyakāma and Satyasaṅkalpa," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-sixth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
While they were thus conversing within that inner chamber of the house,
What did Vidūratha do after departing from his home in anger?
The departure of Vidūratha for battle with the mobilization of his army, his entry onto the battlefield, and the commencement of the fight are described. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Vidūratha emerged from his palace,
surrounded by a great retinue like the moon amidst a multitude of stars.
By the multitude of bears and by the host of constellations. || 2 ||
With all his limbs armored and adorned with clinging necklaces and ornaments, he went forth like the Lord of the Gods amidst great shouts of "Victory! Victory! (3).
With all his limbs fully equipped with armor, weapons, and the like; he whose necklaces and ornaments were fastened and settled in their respective appropriate places. || 3 ||
Giving orders to the host of warriors, listening to the arrangement of the mandala,
and surveying the groups of heroes, the king ascended his chariot.

He was issuing instructions and commands regarding various appropriate tasks, such as the arrangement of the military formation of the circle (maṇḍala) as described by his ministers, or the administrative organization of the countryside.
With a form like that of a peaked roof, adorned with pearls and rubies,
and overspread by five banners, it was like a supreme celestial chariot.
That which has a form equal in shape to a peak (*kūṭa*), such as the summit of Mount Meru; a celestial chariot (*dyuvimāna*) is a chariot well-known in heaven. || 5 ||
(242) With golden shoots gleaming, fixed within the circular frame of its felloe,
and with the beautiful pole of its shaft resounding with the tinkling of pearl nets; (6)
Where golden spikes, shining gold-crests driven into and fixed within the wheels and the walls, were present;
[it had] a Vikrama-pole with a long front portion.
With well-proportioned, auspicious, trembling, and slender horses,
which moved with the speed of flight as if carrying away the gods.
"With excellent horses born of the highest breed, flowing like the celestial winds in the atmosphere"—this is a hyperbolic exaggeration (atiśayokti). || 7 ||
With strides that suddenly surpassed the wind in speed,
they seemed to be dragging their hindquarters along while drinking in the very sky.
By means of the movements of their forebodies, they seemed to be pushing and carrying along their hindquarters; [here] there is a Vedic substitution of verbal suffixes (vikaraṇa-vyatyaya). 8.
It was yoked to eight horses that seemed filled with moonlight from the radiance of their chowries, filling the quarters with their neighing.
"With the lusters of their yak-tail whisks, they were as if joined with full moons"—this is a metaphor (*utprekṣā*) applied everywhere. || 9 ||
Then there arose the sound of kettledrums, as unrestrained as the roar of clouds driven by elephants,
made terrible by its resonance echoing off mountain walls.

The roar of the elephants, those great serpents, was intense and overwhelming with its thundering; it was harsh and terrifying to the timid, amplified by the echoes from the walls and ramparts of the mountains.
It was pervaded by the tumultuous clamor released by the intoxicated soldiers,
by the jingling of clusters of small bells, and by the clashing sounds produced by the impact of weapons.
By the clashing of weapons and the sound of their collision;
by the rattling of bows and the whistling songs of arrows;
and by the jangling of masses of armor crushed against one another’s limbs. || 11–12 ||
With the crackling sounds of blazing fires, with the cries of those in agony, with the mutual challenges of warriors, and with the tumultuous weeping of the bards; || 13 ||

By the bards’ incitements to heroic valor, by the insults [of the enemy], by the lamentations of the cowards distressed by wounds from not having fought, and by the cries of those [cowards] who were agitated— || 13 ||
A terrifying sound, filling the hollows of the ten directions like a forest thicket, arose; it was as solid as stone throughout the entire cavity of the universe and could be grasped with the hand.
By filling himself [with light], he has made the entire cavity of the universe solid like a stone and rendered it without intervals;
because of this very density, it is as if graspable by the hand—this is the poetic fancy (utprekṣā). 14.
Then it flew up toward the sky, as if intent on soaring into the heavens, while its dust-like form thickly obstructed the path of the sun and covered the surface of the earth.

Because it desired to become a thick obstruction on the path of the sun, it is called *rodhaka* (an obstructer); [this is derived from] the root *kam* with the suffix *kvip*. Through its appearance resembling dust, it rose up as if the very surface of the earth had become intent on flying into the sky—an *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
Because that great city had, as it were, entered a state of dwelling in a womb, it became [desolate]. 15.65cd–66ab.
Ignorance reached its full density through youth, just as darkness does.
By the quality of passion (rajas), their natural state of delusion—meaning innate ignorance—attains density and compactness, as if through youth characterized by an excess of passion. || 16 ||
Multitudes of lamps departed somewhere like stars with the coming of day,
while the restless throngs of nocturnal spirits arrived with their strength.
They attained and reached strength and vigor. || 17 ||
The two Līlās and that young girl beheld that great battle with eyes bestowed by the Goddess, as if their own hearts were bursting.

Those two who possessed great vision and divine sight were granted by the command of the Goddess. That maiden, the daughter of Vidūratha, is connected [to the title] through the grammatical transformation of the compound *devīdattamahādṛk* (she whose great vision was given by the Goddess). || 18 ||
Then their weapons, emitting loud clanging sounds as they were raised, were extinguished like forest fires by the surging waters of a single vast ocean. || 19 ||

Then, immediately after Vidūratha’s departure, the clattering sounds of the weapons and arrows of the Saindhavas—who were plundering the city—subsided, just as the flames of the submarine fire (*vāḍava-vahni*) are extinguished by the surging masses of water at the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*). [This is because *la* and *ḍa* are not distinguished here. 19.
Gradually withdrawing his army, he was perceived as another force;
like Meru with its wings outspread entering a single ocean, he entered [the enemy host]. 20.

As Vidūratha drew back his army, the difference in strength between the forces of the Saindhavas and his own own troops could not be discerned. Without even realizing it, he entered the enemy host like Mount Meru entering the single ocean of universal destruction (Sāṃvarta); this is the implied meaning. || 20 ||
Then there arose a clear, crackling sound of the bowstring,
and successions of clouds composed of rays of light moved about.
The twanging of the bowstrings was like the sound of virtues; and the successions of enemies moved about, accompanied by clouds formed from the rays of their own weapons. || 21 ||
Taking to the sky, birds of various weapons flew forth;
the lusters of the arms, having violently taken away lives, became exceedingly dark.
Having seized the lives of others, they were therefore dark and soiled as if by sin; they rushed forth and spread out. || 22 ||
The conflagrations produced by the clashing of weapons blazed like the fire of a brand;
the heroic clouds rumbled as they rained down torrents of arrow-showers. || 23 ||
Weapons as cruel as saws entered the limbs of the heroes,
and the fragments crushed by those weapons fell through the sky with a *paṭapaṭa* sound.
Crushed by the force of the blows, sword-strokes themselves fell and rose again in the sky with a crackling sound.
Darkness was quickly pacified by the lamps of the fire of weapons;
all the armies became as if covered in the hair of new iron arrows.
In that procession of Yama, rows of headless trunks (*kabandha*) rose up like dancers; the female *piśāca* demons sang loudly of the intensity of the battle.

During the Yamayātrā—that is, during the festival of the procession for the propitiation of Yama—the actors [performed], as did the girls—young women who were like ornaments to the festive battle—[who were] maidens. || 26 ||

The great rivers formed by the stones hurled from catapults were carried by the force of the elephants' trumpeting, which produced a clashing sound like the striking of tusks, as they flowed across the surface of the sky.
They have gone upward. || 27 ||
The corpses shrieked like withered forest leaves cast down by a windless storm;
rivers of blood flowed forth from the mountain of battle, raining down death.
They fell like dried forest leaves scattered and blown away by a violent wind;
from that mountain, which was characterized by battle and drenched by the rain of death—the dying of living beings—they fell.
The dust was stilled by the blood, the darkness by the fires of weapons, the sounds by the singular concentration on battle, and the fears by the certainty of death. (29)
The word "they were stilled" is to be connected everywhere; "sounds" refers to the expansions of speech. || 29 ||
There occurred a battle that was purely devoid of vulgar noise and free from confusion; it resembled a cloudless sky, with the waves of swords creating its shimmering ripples.
It is free from incorrect words (apaśabda) and devoid of sound; it resembles a rain-cloud untroubled by wind and other disturbances.
Here, the waves are flashes of lightning, and by them it is rendered beautiful with its mane-like fringes. || 30 ||
With a torrent of arrows whizzing with a *khada-khada* sound, with *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons falling amidst a *ṭaka-ṭaki* clamor,
and great missiles clashing with a *jhaṇa-jhaṇa* din;
That battle was as difficult to cross as the ocean filled with timi and timingila fish.
"Timitimi" is an imitation of the sound of weapons other than swords; such was the battle, difficult to cross, for those who were timid—this is the ellipsis. || 31 ||

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Departure of Vidūratha," within the *Līlopākhyāna* (The Narrative of Līlā) of the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* (Book on Origination) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. || 46 ||
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Departure of Vidūratha," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
While this terrible encounter of battle was thus proceeding,
The two Līlās spoke this again to the Blessed Lady Jñapti.
The cause of Sindhudvīpa’s victory over his enemies, the sequence of the battle at sunrise, and the duel between the two kings with mantras as weapons are here proclaimed. (1)

By the word "again" (punaḥ), he shows that since the meaning of the forthcoming question and answer has already been established by the previously stated arguments, this section—being almost a mere repetition—has as its sole purpose the clarification of what has already been said. || 1 ||
Līlādvaya said: "O Goddess, why does our husband suddenly defeat us in battle?
Tell us, for you are pleased with us as well, even while this elephant is fleeing. (2)
In that battle where elephants were fleeing and rushing about, our lord Vidūratha— Śrī and Sarasvatī said:
"For a long time he has been propitiated by this enemy of King Vidūratha."
"O daughter, I have not been sent by King Vidūratha for the sake of victory. (3)
"She was propitiated with the desire for victory"—this is the ellipsis. || 3 ||
Therefore, it is that very Vidūratha who both conquers and is conquered;
for consciousness, which is the internalized cognition, belongs to whomever, whenever, and in whatever manner.
The remainder is that consciousness—the awareness of "I"—is internalized within all living beings and internalized within their minds. || 4 ||
I swiftly accomplish that very thing for him which he impels me to do;
in whatever way one impels me, I abide as the fruit thereof for him.

It impels—that is, it makes ready for the bestowal of its fruit—by the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire and action. Furthermore, its own manifestation as those various fruits is merely a transformation (*vivarta*); thus, he says "He who... (verse 5) to clarify the meaning already stated.
"Intrinsic nature does not admit of change, just as heat belongs to fire;
by this [realization], I have cultivated the thought: 'I shall indeed be liberated.'"
By this Vidūratha. || 6 ||
Therefore, O child, she who is the embodiment of eloquence shall be liberated;
for he has an enemy of his own, a lord of the earth named Sindhurāja.
The term "bāla" (child) is an address to one whose play is unawakened; for the play of the awakened has already been established [in the preceding verses]. || 7 ||
"I shall be victorious in battle"—by this [thought] I was worshipped;
therefore, Vidūratha, having attained that body together with his wife, [attained his goal]. || 8 ||

"Jaya" [is so called] because it causes victory or afflicts enemies; thus, through the resolve "May I be victorious," there is either a non-differentiation in the connection (abhedānvaya), as in the case of "he cooks" (*pacati*) being equivalent to "he exists" (*bhavati*), between the general sense of "I may be" and the specific action expressed by "I am victorious. || 8 ||
In time, O child, he shall be liberated by you and her;
his own enemy will be the lord of the earth named Sindhurāja.
Together with you and this wife of yours. || 9 ||
"Having slain him upon the surface of the earth, the victor shall rule the kingdom.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"While the goddess was speaking thus, the two armies were engaged in combat."
The sun ascended the mountain of sunrise as if to behold a marvel;
the masses of darkness fled like armies in the form of enemies.

The masses of darkness belonging to Vidūratha, appearing in the form of enemies, manifested at night like his own armies, creating throngs of living beings such as Rākṣasas and Piśācas; this is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā). At twilight, they were like stars—this is the comparison for them. || 11 ||
Other multitudes of living beings were created like stars at twilight;
gradually, the mountainous lands emerged from the dark sky [the reading "from the cave-like sky" appears in the printed edition]. 12.
The world shone as if lifted from the ocean of collyrium;
the rays of the sun fell like beautiful streams of molten gold. (13)
It has been cast out; it has been brought back. || 13 ||
Then, amidst those foremost heroes among mountains, the sky and the surface of the battlefield appeared as if streaked with blood. 14.
The surface of the battlefield was like the sky with its whirling serpents, yet it was like the sky with the rays of the sun through his arms. || 14 ||
With its arms it had whirled serpents; with its splendors it was strewn with gold;
with its earrings it possessed a mass of scattered jewels; and with its heads it revealed lotuses.

The meaning is that both [the sky and the earth] appeared as if strewn with gold by the radiance of both; thus, in what follows, the description of both should be understood through such poetic conceits (utprekṣā). With earrings flying up and falling down, it was like a lake strewn with heaps of gems by its jewels, and with heads, it was like a lake where lotuses were seen. || 15 ||
It was dense with swords as its weapons, filled with arrows like a swarm of locusts,
rich with a blood-red, unsteady twilight, and abounding with corpses as its perfected beings (siddhas).
It was as if densely packed and thick with rhinoceroses of various species; it was as if rich in a steady twilight due to the red luster and crimson glow [of blood]. Thus it was everywhere. 16.
With golden sprouts gleaming, fixed into the circular wall [of the chariot],
and with the beautiful pole of its swift-stepping [steeds] resounding with the tinkling of pearl nets; (6)
Where golden spikes, shining like golden sprouts, were driven into and fixed within the wheels and the walls;
[it had] a Vikrama-bumper with a long front portion.
With well-proportioned, auspicious, trembling, and slender horses,
which moved with the speed of a swift flight like the gods themselves.
"With excellent horses born of the highest breed, flowing like the celestial winds in the atmosphere"—this is a hyperbolic expression (atiśayokti). || 7 ||
With strides that suddenly surpassed the wind in speed,
they seemed to be dragging their hindquarters along while drinking in the very sky.
By means of the movements of their forebodies, they seemed to be pushing and carrying along their hindquarters; [here] there is a Vedic substitution of verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa-vyatyaya*). 8.
It was bound together by eight horses that filled the quarters with their neighing, appearing as if they were full moons complete with the radiance of chowries.
"With the lusters of their yak-tail whisks, they were as if joined with full moons"—this is a metaphor (*utprekṣā*) applied everywhere. || 9 ||
Then there arose the sound of kettledrums, unrestrained like the roar of clouds from a wild elephant, intensified by the mountain walls and made harsh by their echoes.

The roar of the elephants and serpents, possessing those characteristics, was intensified by the sound of the clouds; it was harsh with the echoes from the walls and ramparts of the mountains, terrifying to the timid. (10)
It was filled with the clamorous shouts released by the intoxicated soldiers,
along with the tinkling of clusters of small bells produced by the clashing of weapons.
With the clashing of weapons and the sound of their impact, with the dense thudding of those struck together;
with the *caṭacaṭa* sounds of bows and the whistling songs of arrows;
and with the *jhaṇajjhaṇa* clanging of the mass of armor crushed against one another’s limbs. || 11–12 ||
With the crackling sounds of blazing fires, with the cries of those in distress, with the mutual challenges of warriors, and with the tumultuous weeping of bards; || 13 ||
By the bards' incitements to heroic valor, by insults, and by the wailing of cowards distressed by wounds and suffering from not having fought; || 13 ||
The terrifying sound, which filled the hollows of the ten directions like a thicket and solidified the entire interior of the universe into stone, became as if graspable by the hand.
By filling himself [with light], he has made the entire cavity of the universe solid and continuous like a stone;
because of this very density, it is as if graspable by the hand—this is the poetic fancy (utprekṣā). 14.
Then it flew up toward the sky, as if intent on soaring into the heavens, while its dust-like form thickly obstructed the path of the sun and covered the surface of the earth.

Because it intensely desired (*kāmayate*) to be a thick obstruction (*rodha*) against the path of the sun, it is called *rodhaka*; [this is derived from] the root *kam* with the suffix *kvip*. Through its appearance resembling dust, it rose up as if the very surface of the earth were intent on flying into the sky—an *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
Because that great city had entered, as it were, into a state of dwelling in a womb, it became so [enveloped].
Ignorance reached a state of density, as if through the onset of youth.
By that dust; "delusion" is innate ignorance, as if by youth characterized by an excess of passion (*rajas*); "the darkness of *tamas*" reaches density, that is, thickness. || 16 ||
Multitudes of lamps departed somewhere like stars with the day;
the restless hordes of nocturnal spirits arrived with their strength.
They attained and reached strength and vigor. || 17 ||
The two Lilas and that young maiden beheld that great battle,
as if with their hearts bursting, having been granted the great vision by the Goddess.

Those two [princes] were ones to whom great vision—the divine sight—had been granted by the command of the Goddess. That maiden, the daughter of Vidūratha, is connected [to the previous phrase] through the transformation of the compound as "the one to whom great vision was granted by the Goddess" (*devīdattamahādṛk*). || 18 ||
Then their weapons, emitting loud clanging sounds as they were raised, were extinguished like forest fires by the surging waters of a single vast ocean. || 19 ||

Then, immediately after Vidūratha’s departure, the clattering sounds of the weapons and arrows of the Saindhavas—who were plundering the city—subsided, just as the flames of the submarine fire (*vāḍava-vahni*) are extinguished by the surging masses of water at the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*). [This is because *la* and *ḍa* are not distinguished here. 19.
Gradually withdrawing his army, he was recognized as a different force;
it entered [the enemy] like Mount Meru, with its wings outspread, entering a single ocean.

As Vidūratha drew back the army of the Saindhavas and his own forces, the distinction and relative strength between them could no longer be discerned. Without even realizing it, he entered the enemy host like Mount Meru entering the single ocean at the time of universal dissolution; this is the implied meaning. 20.
Then there arose a clear, crackling sound of the qualities (or strings),
and clouds composed of rays of light moved one after another in succession.
The twang of the bowstring was the sound of their virtues; those successions of enemies, by whom clouds were fashioned from the rays of their own weapons, moved about. || 21 ||
Taking to the sky, various birds in the form of weapons flew forth;
the lusters of the arms, having violently seized life, became intensely dark.
Having taken away the life-force and seized the breaths of others, they were therefore dark and soiled as if by sin; they rushed forth and spread out. || 22 ||
The flames arising from the clashing of weapons blazed like the fire of a brand;
the heroic clouds rumbled as they rained down torrents of arrow-showers. || 23 ||
Weapons as cruel as saws entered the limbs of the heroes,
and the fragments crushed by those weapons fell through the sky with a *paṭapaṭa* sound.
Crushed by the force of the blows, the sword-strokes themselves fell and rose again in the sky with a crackling sound. Darkness was quickly pacified by the lamps of the fire of weapons,
and the entire army became bristling with new arrows like hair.
In that procession of Yama, rows of headless trunks rose up like dancers;
the female Piśācas, acting as war-maidens, sang aloud of the intensity of the battle.

"In the procession of Yama" means during the festival of the pilgrimage for the propitiation of Yama; "actors" refers to young girls—daughters who serve as ornaments for the festive battle—who are suited to that [occasion]. || 26 ||
The great rivers formed by the stones hurled from catapults were carried through the sky by the force of elephants trumpeting with their tusks locked together.
They have gone upward. || 27 ||
The corpses fell like withered forest leaves cast down by a windless gale;
rivers of blood flowed forth from the mountain of battle, raining down death.
They fell like dried forest leaves scattered and driven by a violent wind;
from that mountain, which was characterized by battle and drenched by the rain of death—the dying of living beings—[the arrows] fell.
The dust was stilled by the blood, the darkness by the fires of weapons,
the sounds by the single-minded focus on battle, and the fears by the certainty of death.
The word "they were pacified" (*praśemuḥ*) is to be connected everywhere [with the following]. "Words" (*śabdāḥ*) refers to the expansions of speech. || 29 ||
There occurred a battle that was purely devoid of foul language and free from confusion;
it resembled a cloudless sky and was marked by the shimmering waves of sword-blades.

It is free from vulgar words and devoid of noise; it resembles a rain-cloud whose downpour is undisturbed by wind and other elements; here, the waves are flashes of lightning, and by them it is rendered variegated.
A shower of arrows whizzing with the sound of *khada-khada*,
*bhuśuṇḍī* weapons falling with the sound of *ṭaka-ṭaki*,
and great missiles clashing with the sound of *jhaṇa-jhaṇa*.
That battle was as difficult to cross as the ocean filled with timingila and timi fish.

"Timitimi" is an imitation of the sound made by weapons other than swords; in that manner, the battle—meaning the war—was difficult to cross for cowards. (The word "of cowards" is to be supplied. || 31 ||

Thus ends the forty-sixth sarga, titled "The Departure of Vidūratha," within the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* in the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition. || 46 ||
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Departure of Vidūratha," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
While this terrible encounter of battle was thus proceeding,
The two Līlās spoke this again to the blessed Jñapti.
The cause of Sindhudvīpa’s victory over his enemies, the sequence of the battle at sunrise, and the duel between the two kings with mantras as weapons are here proclaimed. (1)

By the word "again" (punaḥ), he shows that since the meaning of the questions and answers about to be stated has already been established by the previously mentioned arguments, they are for the most part redundant; their purpose is merely to clarify the matter already stated. || 1 ||
Līlādvaya said: "O Goddess, why does our husband suddenly conquer us in battle?
Tell us, even though you are pleased with him, while this elephant is thus put to flight."
In that battle where elephants were fleeing and charging, our lord Vidūratha—
Śrī-Sarasvatī said:
"This enemy of King Vidūratha has long been propitiated by him."
"O daughter, I have not been sent by King Vidūratha for the sake of victory. (3)
She was propitiated with the desire for victory; this is the ellipsis. || 3 ||
Therefore, it is that very [consciousness] which both conquers and is conquered; Vidūratha is [conquered] by it.
This internal cognition, which is pure awareness, [acts] upon me whenever and however it may.
The remainder is that consciousness, the act of cognizing, which is "I," is internalized within all living beings and internalized within their minds. || 4 ||
I quickly accomplish that very thing for him which he impels me to do;
in whatever manner one impels me, I abide as the fruit thereof for him.

It impels—that is, it makes ready for the bestowal of its fruit—by the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire and action. Furthermore, its own manifestation as those various fruits is merely a transformation (*vivarta*); thus, he says "He who... (verse 5) to clarify the meaning already stated.
"Intrinsic nature does not admit of change, just as heat belongs to fire; this is my conviction. By means of this [realization], I shall indeed become liberated. (6)
By this Vidūratha. || 6 ||
Therefore, O child, she who is of the nature of inspired eloquence will be liberated;
his own enemy is the lord of the earth named Sindhurāja. || 7 ||
The term "bāla" (child) is an address for one whose play is unawakened; for the play of the awakened has already been established [as distinct]. || 7 ||
"I shall be victorious in battle"—because she was honored with these words, Vidūratha, having obtained that body together with his wife, [attained his goal]. (8)

"Jayāmī" means "I afflict or torment my enemies through victory," by means of the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) "May I be [victorious]. Alternatively, there is a non-differentiation relation (*abhedānvaya*) between the general "I may be" (*syām*) and the specific action "I afflict" (*jayāmī*), just as in the case of "he cooks" (*pacati*) being equivalent to "he exists" (*bhavati*). || 8 ||
O girl, in due time he shall be liberated by you and her;
his own enemy is the lord of the earth named Sindhurāja.
Together with you and this wife of yours. || 9 ||
"Having slain him upon the surface of the earth, the victor shall rule the kingdom.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"While the goddess was speaking thus, the two armies were engaged in combat."
The sun ascended the mountain of sunrise as if to behold a marvel;
the masses of darkness fled like armies in the form of enemies.

The masses of darkness belonging to Vidūratha, who was like an enemy, manifested themselves at night like armies—his own troops—as they brought forth throngs of living beings such as Rākṣasas and Piśācas; this is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā). At twilight, they were like stars;
this is the simile for them. || 11 ||
Other multitudes of living beings were created like stars at twilight;
gradually, the mountainous lands emerged from the dark sky [the reading in the printed edition is *vilākāśādri*]. (12)
The world shone as if lifted from the ocean of collyrium;
the rays of the sun fell like beautiful streams of molten gold.
It has been cast out and brought back. || 13 ||
Then the sky and the field of battle appeared like streaks of blood upon the mountain-like, preeminent heroes in that fray. 14.
The surface of the battlefield was [covered] by the arms of heroes, like the sky with its revolving serpents, or as if by the rays of the sun through his arms. || 14 ||
With its arms it had whirled serpents; with its splendors it was strewn with gold;
with its earrings it possessed a mass of scattered jewels; and with its heads it bore visible lotuses.
The meaning is that both [the ground and the sky] appeared as if strewn with gold by their respective splendors.

In this way, the description of both should be understood through poetic fancy (utprekṣā) in what follows as well. With earrings flying up and falling down, it was like a lake strewn with heaps of gems; and with heads, it was like a lake where lotuses have been seen. || 15 ||
It was dense with swords as its weapons, filled with arrows like a swarm of locusts,
rich with a steady twilight of blood-red luster, and abounding with corpses as its perfected beings (siddhas).

It was as if densely packed and filled with no gaps by rhinoceroses of various species; it was as if rich with a constant twilight due to the red luster and crimson splendor [of the blood]. Thus it is everywhere. 16.
It was densely crowded with necklaces mixed with sloughed-off snake skins and with girdles;
it was adorned with shimmering creepers and banners, and great archways were constructed from thighs. (17)
With shields and armor. || 17 ||

With hands and feet it was as if covered in sprouts; with arrows it resembled a forest of reeds (śaravaṇa); dark with the grass-blades of the rays of weapons, it was filled with ketaka flowers in the form of an abundance of missiles. || 18 ||

It was strewn with garlands of weapons, as terrifying as one possessed by madness, and took on the appearance of a grove of blossoming aśoka trees due to the fires produced by the clashing of arms. (19)
With the leaders of the Siddhas fleeing amidst loud, tumultuous shouts of "Udaghuṃ," it took on the appearance of a golden city, its weapons glittering like the rising sun.
With loud, tumultuous sounds like those of the ocean—the elision of the syllable *dhi* in the word *udadhi* being a Vedic archaism—it had the form of the golden city famous as Tripura. || 20 ||
The sky resounded with the clashing of spears, swords, javelins, discuses, pikes, and mallets;
it was filled with heaps of corpses being swept away by the force of flowing rivers of blood.
It was crowded with *bhuśuṇḍīs*, spears, lances, swords, tridents, and stones; it was filled with the falling of headless trunks (*kabandhas*) covered by the blows of pikes and weapons.
In the empty battlefield, amidst the tumultuous clamor raised by the Vetālas performing the Kāla-tāṇḍava dance, the two radiant chariots of Padma and Sindhu moved forward.

Having thus described the duel between Sindhu and Vidūratha on the surface of the battlefield, he describes their combat by means of their chariots and other equipment, beginning with the word "śūnye" (in the void). The sense is that it was "void" because the surrounding warriors had been destroyed through mutual combat. || 23 ||
They appeared like the sun and moon, the two signs of the sky in the heavens;
they were crowded with weapons such as discuses, spears, bhushundis, double-edged swords, and lances.
The two signs of the sky, serving as its characteristics; in the heavens, that is, in the celestial realm. || 24 ||
Surrounded by thousands upon thousands of heroes,
they moved about at will in wide-circling maneuvers accompanied by loud shouts.
With a whistling sound, they crushed many who were both dead and alive with their great discus;
then, sporting like intoxicated elephants, they crossed two rivers of blood.
Crossing over two streams of blood produced by one another, they swam on. || 26 ||
The two rivers were filled with hair like moss, possessing wheels as their whirlpools and the moon as their water;
they had agitated elephants cast down by the shock of being struck by the moving wheels.
The two rivers of blood were such that their wheels were indeed *cakras* (wheels) and *cakravākas* (ruddy geese), and they possessed moons reflected in the water.
Resounding with the jingling of gems and pearls and the rattling of the chariot-poles,
and filled with the flapping sound of the edges of banners struck by the wind.
Those two [chariots] possessed the sounds or clamors of the chariot-poles (*kūbara*) which were rattling—characterized by the sound *jhaṇat*—as they were engaged in battle. || 28 ||
They were followed by many great heroes and numerous timid soldiers,
who were discharging streams of spears, arrows, and even from bows.

Followed by many such great heroes who were accompanied by soldiers that struck fear into others, [the two] vomited— meaning, discharged— streams of arrows, spears, and other weapons belonging to their bows; [they were] casting forth spears, javelins, and discuses that glittered in the battle.
There, having turned for a moment within the circle on the ground, those two—Bhūmi and Kuṇḍala—[remained].
Having turned for a moment in circular maneuvers of their chariots—which served as ornaments on the battlefield like earrings—[they fought]. || 30 ||
Both faced each other with their weapons raised, as they emitted the sound of palms striking together while discharging volleys of showers of iron arrows.

In that battle (*āyodhana*), which is a weapon-fight (*āyudhi*), both of them engaged with one another by exchanging their respective actions. The word *vyati-* is used for the purpose of indicating the exchange of actions (*karmavyatihāra*). The reflexive voice (*ātmanepada*) is employed according to the rule *kartari karmavyatihāre*. He demonstrates this reciprocal action with the verse beginning with *nārāca*—namely, "the iron arrow itself... [and so forth].
The showers of water-streams were scattered; thus, "scatters" (*vikṣepāḥ*) refers to spears, darts, and the like, which are themselves hailstones (*karakāḥ*, *varṣopalāḥ*).

Regarding the sound produced by the endurance of their falling, as in the case of the ocean and the clouds, one [the cloud] repeatedly rained down like a cloud in turn, while the other [the ocean] endured like the ocean. And in that instance, only the sound occurred.
The mention of "in the resonance" (dhvanau) is intended to indicate that there is no other result, such as injury and so forth. || 31 ||
Roaring at one another like two intoxicated oceanic clouds, as those two lions among men struck each other with arrows, [the earth trembled]. (32)
Some took the form of stones and clubs, spreading across the sky;
some had the appearance of swords, while others had the faces of mallets.
He describes the variety of those three arrows with the words beginning "pāṣāṇa" (stone) and so forth; the phrase "became widespread in the sky" is to be connected with each instance. || 33 ||
Some had faces like sharp discs, some had faces like axes;
some had faces like spears, some had faces like tridents and rocks; some had faces like tridents, while others were as massive as great boulders. (34)
The repetition of the word "some... some" (kecitkecit) is intended to express distributive iteration (vīpsā). || 34 ||
Then the feathered arrows fell like masses of rocks cast down by the winds of universal dissolution;
at that moment, the two of them became locked in combat.
With the agitation of the ocean swelling at the time of universal dissolution. || 35 ||

The feathered arrows of those two, Sindhurāja and Vidūratha— who had expanded and increased for the sake of their mutual destruction like two oceans surging toward a cataclysm— became equal, as is implied, through the agitation of their mutual encounter. || 35 ||
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Meeting of Vidūratha and Sindhu," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Meeting of Vidūratha and Sindhu," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
(p. 245) 147 The Forty-Eighth Chapter.
48 Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reached the city, the king beheld Sindhuruddhatakandhara standing before him;
he became expanded with a fury like that of the midday sun at its peak.
In this [work], the battle between Sindhurāja and Padmarāja is described in detail— a battle that deludes the entire world through mantras and weapons capable of producing manifold illusions.
It brings to an end the midday heat and binds by means of similarity; thus, it is "madhyāhnatapanānta.
This means "by that which is similar to it. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the root *bandh* in the sense of the object (*karman*). || 1 ||
He strung his bow, causing the quarters of the sky to resound for a long time,
like the blast of the winds at the end of an aeon striking the slope of Mount Meru.
He struck it; he drew it back. || 2 ||
The powerful king released a continuous stream of arrows fixed in his quiver for the night, like the rays of the sun at the time of universal dissolution.

By the word "night" (rajanī), the lotuses situated therein that have closed their buds are indicated; the "arrows with feathered shafts" (śilīmukha) fixed upon them are both arrows and bees, and these constitute the series [of comparisons]. || 3 ||
A single arrow departs from his bowstring,
yet as it travels through the sky, it becomes a thousand, and as it falls, it becomes a hundred thousand.
When he goes forth, then he is truly alone. || 4 ||
The ocean likewise possessed such power and agility;
thus, by the boon of Viṣṇu, the Giver of Boons, both of them attained the skill of archers.

To the question, "Whence did they derive such skill in combat?", he says: "By a boon. It is understood that this was obtained from Viṣṇu, who had been propitiated by their asceticism. *Dhānuṣkatā* means proficiency in archery and skill in fighting with the bow. || 5 ||
Those arrows named Musalās, shaped like pestles and roaring loudly, covered the sky like the thunderbolts at the end of a kalpa.
Loudly resonant, they possess great sounds. || 6 ||
Rows of golden arrows shone resoundingly in the sky,
like crying stars falling, distressed by the winds of the cosmic dissolution.
The iron arrows (*nārāca*), colored with gold, were whizzing and making a sound as they flew. || 7 ||
From Vidūratha, showers of arrows issued forth incessantly,
like floods of water from the ocean or rays of light from the sun.
Like flowers shaken from a great tree by a fierce wind,
or like rows of sparks struck from a heated iron ball.
Like torrents from a rain-cloud, like spray from a waterfall, or like radiant sparks from the great conflagration of that city's fire. (10)

"Varṣamuk" means one who releases rain; therefore, they were like showers from that "Varṣamuk. Of that city, Vidurathanagara. [This was] due to the previously mentioned great conflagration of fire. 10.
Hearing the crackling sound of those two bows snapping,
the two armies became as silent as a calm ocean, rendered mute by the spectacle.
The two forces are the two armies. || 11 ||
In that battle, floods of arrows flowed through the sky like the currents of the Gaṅgā,
rushing toward the ocean with a gurgling roar and great speed.
Of King Sindhu and of the ocean; those whose speeds (raṃhas) are possessed of gurgling roars. || 12 ||
From the cloud that was his bow, there issued forth incessant showers of whetted iron arrows,
accompanied by the "śava-śava" sound of falling corpses.
Seeing Bāṇa approaching with a flood of the Mandākinī river to fill the ocean, Līlā, a resident of that city, watched him from a window.
Fearing for her husband's victory because of that multitude of arrows, she, whose lotus-face blossomed with joy, spoke these words: (15)
"Victory, O Goddess! Our Lord is victorious; look!
Moreover, even Mount Meru would be reduced to powder by this shower of arrows. (16)
While she was speaking thus, the two goddesses—distraught by the sound of their intense affection, intent on gazing [at her], and inwardly laughing at her human nature—[remained there]. (17)
"Human" means the notion that the human body is the self; that is to say, one who is unawakened. || 17 ||
The submarine fire of the ocean drank up that surging sea of flesh,
just as Agastya, with the heat of his arrow, swallowed the Mandākinī.

By means of Agastya—who had become Agastya himself—acting as the instrument through the heat of his arrows, he drank [the ocean]; that is to say, he withdrew it. Having cut that great cloud of arrows into fragments with a shower of shafts, and having reduced it to fine dust, he cast it into the ocean of the sky.
"Having made it into fine dust" means having reduced it to powder. || 19 ||
Just as the movement of an extinguished lamp is not perceived,
so too the movement of that multitude of arrows was not discerned.
Having severed that dense shower of arrows, which was like a thick cloud of bodies,
he spread it out in the sky, filled with hundreds of corpses, out of passion for the field of battle.
It is the bearer of the waters characterized by the body; its origin is accompanied by hundreds of corpses. || 21 ||
Vidūratha also swiftly shattered him with his finest arrows,
just as the wind at the end of an aeon scatters a common, intoxicated cloud.
Thus, with their showers of arrows rendered futile by mere counter-strikes, the two lords of the earth continued to strike each other without hesitation.

They spent the time— meaning they passed a period of one *prahara*— by means of striking and receiving blows with arrows, without hesitation, and by taking aim; or rather, the lengthening of the vowel is an archaic (Vedic) usage, and it means they spent the time by performing counter-strikes against each other's blows.
Then Sindhudvīpa, out of friendship with the Gandharvas, discharged the Mohanāstra; by means of that weapon, all the worlds were rendered senseless, except for Vidūratha.
It was obtained through the Gandharva’s friendship and the power of his affection. "Except for Vidūratha"—that is, excluding Vidūratha alone—the other members of the retinue fell into a swoon.
This is because, according to the rule *pṛthag-vinā-nānābhis tṛtīyā-nyatarasyām*, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*) when these words are employed.
The ablative case is used according to the view that the fifth [case ending] also continues [to apply]. 24.
With their weapons and garments cast aside, mute, and with dejected faces and eyes, the warriors became like the dead, or as if they were figures fixed in a painting. || 25 ||
He describes the very nature of delusion: "vyasta... (verse 25).
As long as delusion led Vidūratha toward indolence,
King Vidūratha then took up the weapon of awakening.
Another person. || 26 ||
Then the subjects, having regained consciousness like a bed of lotuses at dawn,
saw the ocean become as enraged toward the Rākṣasa as the sun is toward the demon Rāhu.
In the distant region, in the Rākṣasa known as Mandeha, he became red with anger like the sun; such is the meaning. || 27 ||
He took up the terrifying Naga-weapon, which causes distress through the binding of nooses;
by it, the sky became filled with serpents resembling mountains. (28)
By the "bhogins," that is, the serpents. || 28 ||
The earth was adorned with serpents like a lake with lotus stalks;
all the mountains became as if covered by blankets of black serpents.
In that regard, he describes the variety—namely, that the earth was covered with white serpents while the mountains were black—with the word "sarpaiḥ" (by serpents). || 29 ||
All these objects indeed became distressed by the heat of the poison; the earth, along with the expanse of its mountains and forests, fell into a state of helplessness.
A state of exhaustion as if by the heat of poison; a state of languor, helplessness, and agitation. || 30 ||
Winds, filled with glowing embers and signaling the onset of poison and calamity,
blew harshly, hot, and laden with frost, while the dust blazed like fire.

Rough and hot mists, as well as snows and cold things that were smooth and cool, blew forth with winds possessing those same characteristics, such that the dust from the fires was strewn about like glowing embers sifted from ashes.
Then Vidūratha, an expert in great weapons, took up the Suparṇa weapon;
by that Garuḍa-weapon, Suparṇas rose up like mountains.
They rose up and went forth; those who were of the nature of Suparṇas were the Sauparṇas. || 32 ||
They have made all directions golden, fulfilling every hope;
they possess the cataclysmic winds produced by the violent onset of their wing-mountains.
With the fury of their flight, their wings—which resembled mountains—generated winds like those at the time of universal destruction. || 33 ||
The circles of hissing serpents were drawn in by the force of the wind from their nostrils,
filling the reaches of the ocean with a great, deep *ghur-ghura* roar.
The trunk is the nose; by the speed of its wind, that is, by the force of the breath. || 34 ||
Like Agastya [drinking] the ocean, that cloud-like Suparṇa swallowed the mass of serpents that filled the earth,
hissing distressfully with a *śala-śala* sound.

That cloud, characterized by beautiful wings, drank—that is, swallowed—that flood characterized by serpents. [The form] *apāt* is derived from the root *pā* (to drink) in the *luṅ* tense; the elision of *sic* is according to the rule *gāti-sthā-*. The adjectives should be applied in common to both the flood and the rain-cloud. || 35 ||
The circle of the earth shone, now freed from its serpent-cloak,
like the hollow of the earth after a long time, or like the ocean when its mass of water has vanished.
Because it was seized and extracted by the Boar after a long time, it emerged from the ocean and thus became "devoid of the mass of water" (nirvārirāśi);
it was like a cavity in the earth, a hollow space within the ground. || 36 ||
Then that army of Garuḍas went somewhere out of sight,
like a mass of lamps by the wind, or like a circle of clouds in autumn by the rain.
Like a mass of mountains with their wings spread out in fear of the thunderbolt,
it stood before him like a world seen in a dream, or like a city of one's own imagination.
Like a multitude of mountains such as Maināka joined by a flood of wings, so too was that city and its surrounding expanse created by mere thought.
Then Sindhu released the weapon of darkness (*tamo'stra*), which produces blinding gloom;
by that, the darkness became as black as the interior of the subterranean realm (*bhūbila*), resembling the belly of the netherworld (*pātāla*).
(In the reading *bhūbile jaṭharopamaḥ*, the meaning is: "resembling that which is like the belly—the middle—of the subterranean realm.")
Kṛṣṇa grew, resembling the belly of the earth. || 39 ||
The belly is the middle. || 39 ||
Spread across the cavity of the earth, it became like a single vast ocean;
the armies became like fish, and the stars became like jewels.

"In the gap," that is, in the intermediate space between the two worlds, heaven and earth. He says "like fish" in order to establish the similarity with a single ocean; this also connects with the phrase "like jewels. || 40 ||
It was like an ocean of ink-paste set in motion by darkness,
as if produced by the winds of the kalpa arising from the mass of the mountain of collyrium.
By the onset of darkness, through its manifestation—the suffix *kta* being used in the sense of existence—the world became like an ocean of ink-paste; this is the ellipsis.

It was pervaded—as if by the winds of cosmic dissolution (*kalpānila*)—by the rising dusts that served as the material cause (*upādāna*), like the masses of the mountain of collyrium (*añjanagiri*). This is the ellipsis. || 41 ||
All the subjects were as if fallen into a blind well;
all worldly affairs fell into confusion, like at the end of an eon.
"Towards every direction" (*diśaṃ prati pratidiśam*). The absence of compound formation is a Vedic (archaic) usage. 42.
Then Vidūratha, the best among those who know mantras, having fashioned the Mārtaṇḍa lamp— a weapon within the pavilion of the universe— set that mantra in motion.
"Mantra" means counsel; "amantra" means one who is independent of such secret deliberation, meaning he acted toward the world without depending on it.
Then, like the pure Agastya drinking the ocean with his rays when the sun has risen, the stainless Kṛṣṇa drank up the mass of clouds like the autumn season. (44)
The stainless quarters of the sky, freed from the garment of darkness,
shone like beautiful women with lovely breasts standing before the king.
With a garment of the sky characterized by darkness; "payodharas" refers both to clouds and to breasts. || 45 ||
All the forest ranges within became manifest, like the intellects of the virtuous when they are freed from the mass of soot that is greed. 46.
Then Sindhu, overwhelmed with anger, instantly discharged the most terrifying Rākṣasa weapon, which, impelled by mantras, took the form of arrows.
Fierce forest-rākṣasas rose up from all directions, harsh and terrifying,
like great oceans agitated by the trumpeting of the elephants of the underworld.
The elephants of the quarters, dwelling in the netherworld, emerged in exultation. || 48 ||
The fires, with their smoke-colored matted locks of hair turned upward, Kapila in hue, crackling with loud *caṭa-caṭa* sounds,
and possessing fierce, licking tongues, were like fires fed with moist fuel.

Those whose fuel is moist are like smoky fires; in the case of fire, the seven tongues well-known in the Śruti are Kālī, Karālī, Manojavā, Sulohitā, Sudhūmravarṇā, Sphuliṅginī, and Viśvarucī—the goddess who flickers. 49.
Moving in whirls through the sky with terrifying whistling and clanging sounds,
they were like great fires with blazing brands, flickering amidst thick smoke.
The function of whirlpools is rotation; they are accompanied by that. || 50 ||
With their faces, mud-like bodies, and eyes overrun by the sprouts of fangs as venom,
they appeared like the banks of a foul pond where hair grows like moss.
Their faces were overrun by lotus-stalk sprouts characterized by fangs and by lotus-fibers;
their eyes and other senses were soiled with mud; their bodies were marked by lotus seeds and mire;
and the moss upon them was nothing but their own body hair.
Swallowing [their prey], rushing forward, and roaring like those who have been provoked, they were like water-laden clouds with masses of lightning amidst their matted locks. 52.
Devouring people and the stars on the wings of the clouds, they appear as if created and sent forth for the very purpose of swallowing the world;
here the causative suffix (ṇic) is used in its primary sense from a root whose causal function has ceased.
In the meantime, Vidūratha, the lord of Līlā,
bestowed the Nārāyaṇa weapon, which wards off wicked beings.
In that battle, he took up [the weapon] to discharge it. || 53 ||
As this king of mantras was being uttered,
the kings of weapons belonging to the Rākṣasas were extinguished, like darkness at the rising of the sun.
The three worlds became rid of the hosts of Rākṣasas;
it shone forth stainless, like the sky in autumn when the clouds have departed. || 55 ||
Then Sindhur released the fiery weapon (*āgneyāstra*), which set the sky ablaze;
by it, the quarters of the horizon blazed as if ignited by the fire of cosmic dissolution (*kalpāgni*).
The quarters are the directions. || 56 ||
All the directions became shrouded by the weight of smoke and clouds,
as if the sky were agitated by the darkness of the netherworld spreading upward.
They were overwhelmed—that is, thrown into confusion—by the darkness pervading the sky and connected to the netherworld (pātāla). || 57 ||
The mountains became like blazing gold,
appearing as if they were dense forests of blossoming campaka trees.
The sky, mountains, and forest thickets assumed the appearance of being matted with masses of flames;
they were as if garlands smeared with saffron at the festival of Death.
With their masses of flames forming tangled locks, they were like garlands smeared with saffron and sprinkled during the festival of Death’s playful drenching.
And that single-mindedly apprehensive multitude was set ablaze by that [fire] which touched the sky,
as if by the ocean agitated by the speed of a thousand-formed [being].

The populace, alarmed by the single sound of the ocean as it surged with thousands of forms of ships moving with great speed, was set ablaze, imagining that the world was nothing but a unity of fire, as if by the submarine fire itself having arrived.
Having conquered his enemy,
Vidūratha, honoring him as he would strike again, discharged the Vāruṇa weapon.

This refers to the specific weapon about to be described. Having conquered the Āgneya weapon, he discharged the Vāruṇa weapon after worshipping it; the word "again" (punar) is used in the sense of "also," meaning that he struck the enemy Sindhu just as he had [previously]. || 61 ||
Floods of water came from all sides like floods of darkness— from below, from above, and from every direction— appearing like mountains in liquid form.
Like portions in the sky of arrows, like clouds bearing their courses, like great oceans situated on high, and like the rocks of the principal mountain ranges; || 63 ||
In the sky of arrows—that is, within the space of the arrow’s trajectory—his portions were like fragments; having maintained their motion, they were fixed in flight.
High up, they were like the massive rocks of the principal mountain ranges tumbling down from the upper regions. 63.
They were like masses of *tamāla* trees flying up, like nights joined together,
or like heaps of collyrium rising from the slopes of the Lokāloka mountain.
They were like masses of soot from the darkness on the slopes of Mount Lokāloka. || 64 ||
Like the vast expanses of the subterranean caves of Rasātala desiring to behold the sky,
their forms were augmented by the force of a great, deep, and rumbling roar.
The phrase "as if desiring to see the sky above" is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā). In the reading "sūrmayaḥ," the meaning is simply that they were like a *sūrmi*—that is, a statue or an image. || 65 ||
The stream of water, pervading the world, quickly swallowed up that intoxicated stream of fire at twilight, just as the night swallows the dark.
Having drunk that continuous stream of fire,
the beauty of the waters filled the earth, like sleep manifesting itself upon a body entwined with matted locks.
Others, running about, created such delusions by means of weapons;
they saw before them various illusory forms and experienced them as well. (68)

The *dhāvana* weapons purify the impurities created by the *pūrva* weapons; others, being different from those, are their opposites. Regarding the term *astra*, the status of being a pronominal (*sarvanāman*) is optional according to the rule *vibhāṣā jasi*.
He demonstrates that even though these weapon-delusions are unreal, they possess causal efficacy (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), saying "mutually" (*mithaḥ*).
People experience [the results] even by way of fruits such as the destruction of enemies; this is the implied meaning. || 68 ||

Then, the excellent protectors of the wheels of the ocean, who were like the weight of its causeway, were swept away by the water as if they were blades of grass; and his chariot also became submerged.
The *cakrarakṣas* are those who protect their own army's wheel; the *hetibhāravaras* are the foremost warriors among those who carry weapons (*hetis*). || 69 ||
In the meantime, Sindhura remembered the drying weapon;
that divine protection against calamity was granted to him in the form of an arrow.
He gave him the drying weapon in the form of an arrow; the meaning is that he fixed it upon his bow. || 70 ||
By that very sun, the water-based illusion was quelled;
those who had died remained dead, and the earth became parched.

By mentioning a part of a name, the whole name is implied; thus, "Yāmā" refers to the night consisting of three watches (*triyāmā*). By the radiant one, the sun, the regions of the earth were dried up. || 71 ||
Then, like the wrath of a fool, a heat that tormented all creatures spread forth,
harsh as the expanse of a forest strewn with withered leaves.
The heat is from the intense sun; it is harsh due to the forest expanses strewn with withered leaves and parched foliage. || 72 ||
The luster of their limbs, beautiful like the flow of refined gold, was like a cosmetic unguent applied to the bodies of the wives of the best of kings as it spread across the quarters of the sky.
It was like a cosmetic paste for the quarters of the sky, serving as a bodily unguent. || 73 ||
Because of that, those who were opposed to him fell into a swoon born of heat,
like tender sprouts scorched by a summer forest fire.
Then, in the height of the battle, Vidūratha, having bent his drawn bow with a loud twang,
took up the Parjanya weapon.
The twanging of its bowstring was a *kreṅkāra*; by that [sound], his glory was pervaded.
Rows of clouds rose up like accumulated nights,
sluggish with water as if startled by the flight from the tamāla groves.
Like the flight of a tamāla grove soaring into the sky, they rose up—meaning they ascended—with impetuosity and agitation. 76.
Dwarfed by the flood of water, they moved about with unrestrained roaring;
yet through their majesty, they served as earrings for the entire circle of the quarters, which had become sluggish.

Due to their bending under the flood of water, they were short and not tall; by their vastness and lateral expansion, the entire circles of the directions became, as it were, like earrings—contracted and with their movements hindered within their natural breadth. || 77 ||
(248) Winds blew, swirling with rain-showers, piercing through the mass of clouds, noble with their burden of scattered spray and mist. (78)
Scattered with droplets of water and laden with frost, the noble winds blew, bringing an excellence of coolness that was pleasant to the touch. || 78 ||
Lightnings flashed in the sky like the gliding of excellent golden serpents,
resembling the flickering side-glances of celestial women.

Those [glances] have as their comparison the well-known act of escaping—of going outside—from the calamity characterized by the previously mentioned torment caused by golden serpents, such as on a mountain; they are divine (*daivyaḥ*), meaning pertaining to the gods; by implication, it is understood that they are the side-long glances of celestial women. (79)
The quarters of the sky, whose mountain caves resounded with the swelling echoes of their roars,
trembled, filled with the gurgling sounds of elephants, lions, and bears that had been set in motion.
In these [mountains], the mountain caves are dense and thickened by the echoes— repeated sounds— of the tall, flourishing canes;
they are resonant and gurgling with the thundering responses of elephants and other beasts that have set out toward [the enemy] in their fury.
Torrential rains fell in streams like great clubs,
as harsh with their painful clattering as the very glances of Death.
They were harsh with the sounds of painful groans, the clattering of falling stones, and the sounds of the piercing of vital organs and veins.
First, hot vapor, resembling fire, rose up from the earth;
it appeared as if it had assumed the guise of a mass of clouds from the netherworld for the purpose of battle.
It is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that he was as if one who had assumed—that is, taken up—the *vibhrama*, the playful display of heroism, for the sake of a battle involving masses of clouds. || 82 ||
Then, in the mere twinkling of an eye, the mirages subsided,
just as the latent tendencies of saṃsāra are dissolved by the overflowing essence of supreme awakening.
By the word "mirage" (mṛgatṛṣṇikā), its causes—the sunbeams—are indicated. The awakening to the Supreme Self is its direct realization;
it is characterized by a flood of the essence of unsurpassed bliss. 83.
The entire circle of the earth became marked with mud and impassable;
the ocean was filled with full torrents of water like the river Sindhu itself.
He is immovable and incapable of being moved; he is Sindhu, the king, filled like the ocean. || 84 ||
He discharged the Vāyavya weapon, which filled the hollow of the sky and was as terrifying as the roaring Bhairava intoxicated by the dance at the end of a kalpa.
The winds blew in all directions, their limbs pained by the falling of thunderbolts and carrying fragments of shattered rocks,
signaling the time of universal dissolution for the warriors.
The winds have rendered the peaks sharp-edged and have produced a sense of keenness.

The winds blowing through the quarters of the sky seemed as if they possessed *ṭaṅkas*— specific weapons for splitting stone— due to the sounds of striking against rocks and other surfaces; these sounds were as sharp as the battle cries of warriors facing their opponents, and they caused the limbs of living beings to ache as if struck by a falling thunderbolt.
They blew into their mouths. || 86 ||
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of Weapons," in the section on "Manifestation" within the *Mokṣopāya* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the work of the Sage. 48.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of Weapons," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Winds blew, swirling with frost and scattering the sprouts of the forest.
The winds blew, shaking the masses of trees and scattering the dust from the playful flower-garlands. || 1 ||

The mountain-weapon (*parvatāstra*), the thunderbolt-weapon (*vajrāstra*), and the Brahma-weapon (*brahmāstra*) are described here; furthermore, the piśāca-weapon is detailed at length along with the deeds of the piśācas. (1)
Those by whom the very dust [of the earth] has been made into crest-ornaments through the playful sport of the virtuous ones personified. || 1 ||
Like birds, they whirled through the multitude of trees, fierce in their falling and rising;
they shattered fragments of watchtowers and pierced through walls like clouds.
By whom the multitudes of trees were whirled about like birds, wandering and being struck down and pulverized. || 2 ||
Then, by that exceedingly terrifying wind, Vidūratha’s chariot was carried away like a withered leaf by a river. || 3 ||
Being carried away, being swept along. || 3 ||
Then Vidūratha, a great knower of weapons, cast aside the mountain-weapon (pārvatāstra),
which was as if striving to seize even the sky with its thick rain-clouds.
As if striving to seize and swallow even the sky with its thick waters— the water of the clouds—
by that blow from the mountain-weapon,
the pervasive vital breath (the wind) was brought to stillness, as if by the cessation of consciousness. || 5 ||

Through the awakening to reality, the illusion (māyā) that constitutes the cause was pacified; consequently, the Virāṭ, who is the vital breath (prāṇasamīraṇa) and the effect of that [illusion], subsided like the wind that is the Sūtrātman. || 5 ||
The rows of trees situated in the sky fell to the earth like tens of millions of crows amidst the vast heap of the corpses of various people.
The whistling, clattering, roaring, and shrieking sounds of the cities, villages, forests, and creepers in all directions subsided, like the ravings of those who have been utterly destroyed.

The sounds of sighing, hissing, and *ḍātkāra* noises; the rattling sounds of rolling, terrifying *bhāṃkāra* sounds, belching, and fierce roars—these were like the incoherent, meaningless utterances of cities, villages, forests, shrubs, and creepers. || 7 ||
Sindhu saw mountains falling from the sky like winged insects,
such as Maināka and others, resembling winged rivers scattered here and there.
Sindhu is the king; Sindhu is the ocean, [as it holds] the Maināka and other mountains as they leap up within it. || 8 ||
Then the hosts of Vajras discharged the blazing Vajra-weapon and moved about,
like fires consuming the darkness of the great mountains with their fiery heat.
Fuel is called "fire-burning" because it is burned by fires.
Thus hurled at the mountains, they shattered their peaks with the blows of their beaks,
causing the heads to fall like fruits blown down by a violent wind.
With millions of tips—that is, with beaks characterized by such features—and by means of pecking, tearing, and cutting, [they shattered] the heads, that is, the peaks, of the mountains. || 10 ||
Then Vidūratha surpassed the Brahmāstra for the sake of neutralizing the Vajrāstra;
thereupon, both the Brahmāstra and the Vajrāstra were simultaneously extinguished. || 11 ||
*Atyagāt*: having surpassed other weapons, he went forth—that is, he reached—the state of being able to employ them; *samam*: simultaneously. || 11 ||
Then Sindhu discharged the Piśāca weapon, which was dark as the color of a young woman;
by it, rows of Piśācas, inspiring extreme terror, surged forth. (12)
The dark [complexion] is like the darkness of night. 12.
Then, as if out of fear of the twilight, the day turned to blackness;
the world was filled with demons like masses of darkness. (13)

The particle *iva* is connected to both [parts] through repetition. Thus, "as if at twilight" (*saṃdhyāyām iva*) is a simile (*upamā*), while "as if out of fear" (*bhītyeva*) is a poetic fancy (*hetūtprekṣā*). They went; they arrived. || 13 ||
Resembling pillars of ash, they moved with the grace of palm trees;
though appearing to be of immense size, they were not at all graspable by the fist.
"A pillar made of ash" means a burnt pillar;
this is an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound) used in the Vedic style (*chāndasa*). "Graspable by the fist" means reachable by the hand. || 14 ||
Some had their hair standing on end and were emaciated in body, while others were even bearded;
they had dark complexions and soiled limbs, appearing like common folk despite being sky-dwellers.
Like poor people who are rustic and village-dwellers, they are sky-rangers, moving through the atmosphere. || 15 ||
Terrified, with bewildered vision, acting recklessly and wavering;
wretched, struck by the thunderbolt of the sword, cruel, and like common folk in their misery. (16)
They were seen by fools, the ignorant, and those of impure conduct; those who held whatever [objects] such as bones and skulls in their hands;
and even more cruel and harsh than the *vajrāsi*—the combination (*samāhāra*) of both the thunderbolt (*vajra*) and the sword (*asi*).
Regarding the neuter gender of the compound, the augment *num* is applied according to the rule *iko'ci vibhaktau*. 16.
Moving through trees, mud, and the interiors of roads, they enter empty houses;
flickering like restless ghosts with blackened limbs, they dart about as if unsteady. (17)
Licking the corners of their mouths, they are as flickering as lightning, appearing and disappearing by their very nature. || 17 ||
Then, being intoxicated, they seized the remaining force of the enemy that had survived the slaughter; the soldiers there were broken, their weapons shattered, and their minds agitated.
His soldiers were the soldiers of Vidūratha. || 18 ||
Having cast aside their weapons, armor, and life-breaths, their movements faltering, they caused great agitation with their eyes, limbs, faces, and feet. (19)
Burdened by transformations, their movements were like those possessed by spirits. || 19 ||
Having cast off their loincloths, with their lower garments submerged,
they voided excrement and urine while maintaining a steady, commenced dance.
He shows those very [women] with the word "abandoned" (tyakta): those whose upper and lower garments were submerged—that is, drawn up and tucked away. || 20 ||
As soon as the king of the Piśācas attacked King Vidūratha,
the wise monarch recognized that it was an illusion.
A row or line of piśācas. || 21 ||
That lord of the earth knew the illusion that creates battles with piśācas;
by means of it, he deployed that army of piśācas against the enemy's host. || 22 ||
By bringing under her own control the piśācas dispatched by others, she causes the engagement of enemy armies in battle. || 22 ||
Then his own soldiers became healthy, while the enemy warriors turned into Piśācas;
and in his wrath, he quickly gave her another weapon, the Rūpikā-astra.
He was an ally of that army of Piśācas. The Rūpikas are a variety of Pūtanās. This one is Vidūratha.
From the earth and from the sky, the Rūpikās rose up with their hair standing erect;
they had sunken-in, terrifying eyes, and their hips and breasts were swaying.
Women whose youth had blossomed, some old, some with stout limbs, and others decrepit;
those whose hips were either naturally shapely or formless— meaning their hips were difficult to discern— and those with ill-formed navels.
With their vulvas blossoming. || 25 ||
With human blood in their hands and heads, their limbs were as ruddy as twilight clouds;
their mouths were agitated by dripping streams of flesh and blood from half-chewed morsels. || 26 ||
By the word "blood" (raktapada), skull-cups filled with it are indicated. Their faces were disfigured by their corners of the mouth (sṛkka) and lips from which blood was trickling. || 26 ||
With various movements of their limbs, they were most excellent at bending and stretching one another;
their bodies, arms, thighs, hips, sides, and hands were like those of stone serpents.
Whose various movements of the limbs and gestures of the members [are such that they are] most excellent—

capable— in bowing down, that is, in causing those who do not bend or even those who are rigid to bend; who are as hard as stone and as crooked as serpents, yet possess curved brows and other such features.
They held the corpses of infants made of women, with entrails pulled out as ropes from their hands;
they had faces like dogs, crows, and owls, with sunken mouths, jaws, and bellies. || 28 ||
This woman among men was adorned with garlands of men, [and] with the corpses of children by which she was thus made. || 28 ||
They seized those Piśācas as if they were weak infants;
thus, that army of female Piśācas became a single mass.

They took them as their husbands, they accepted them; like children who have committed evil deeds. This is an illustration based on the similarity in the aspect of being objects of enjoyment. || 29 ||
With faces, limbs, and eyes upturned from their deep immersion in dancing,
they were pressing against one another and rushing toward one another.
He describes that state of having attained oneness with the words beginning "nirmagna" (plunged): it is completely immersed in the possession of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of play. || 30 ||
With great tongues protruding and displaying various contortions of the face,
it was rich with throngs of śarabhas, while the limbs of corpses were being dragged away from one another.
It was rich with the weight of arrows and pools of blood; it was one by which severed limbs were being carried away for the sake of mutual pleasure.
Sinking and emerging in the blood-water, with his body quivering on his heart, he had a protruding belly, long arms, and pendulous ears, lips, and nose. || 32 ||

It was emerging from the liquor; repeatedly sinking and rising. The absence of reduplication in the *ṇamul* suffix used in the sense of frequency is a Vedic (Chāndasa) usage. It was "ghṛt," meaning its body was radiant with the flowing blood. || 32 ||
They practiced tossing one another about in the great mud of blood and flesh,
amidst the tumultuous, resonant clamor of the milk-ocean churned by Mount Mandara.
He practiced and repeated various embraces and writhings; it was filled with a tumultuous clamor and a resonant din, like that of the milk-ocean being churned and stirred by Mount Mandara. || 33 ||
Just as he had previously performed the movement of that illusion, so too did he quickly perform it in return for him, having understood it with agility. (34)
The movement of the illusion was sent back by that Vidūratha; by him, [the movement] of that Sindhu, that movement of the illusion was performed. || 34 ||
Then he gave the Vetāla-weapon, by which hosts of corpses arose—
headless Vetālas and those with heads, swaying like reeds.

"Then, for the sake of assisting him"—meaning he gave it; "veśena" means by means of the intense possession (*āveśa*) of Paramardana; "vallitāḥ" means moved or set in motion. [The roots] *val* and *vall* are used in the senses of covering and moving. || 35 ||
Then that army became as terrifying as Piśācas, Vetālas, Rūpikas, and fierce headless trunks (kabandhas),
capable of swallowing the very earth.
Then the other king also, having employed that illusion against his preceptor,
discharged the Rākṣasa weapon, which was intent on seizing the three worlds.
The other was Vidūratha; [he entered] the ocean as if into a teacher through the prior practice [of his father], just as one enters a preceptor. || 37 ||
Rākṣasas as massive as mountains emerged from all sides;
having taken possession of his body, they issued forth like hells emerging from the netherworld (pātāla). || 38 ||

Then there arose a formidable force that struck terror into both gods and asuras—a host resounding with the great roars of shouting rākṣasas and filled with dancing headless trunks to the sound of musical instruments. (39)
Abounding in snacks of fat and meat, it was made beautiful by blood and spirits;
it was splendid with the frantic dance of intoxicated kūṣmāṇḍa spirits, vetālas, and yakṣas.
Of those who are intoxicated and drunk. || 40 ||
Sprinkled by waves of blood tossed up and agitated by the feet of Kūśmāṇḍa as he performs his frantic dance,
it possesses the splendor of the tips of the masses of twilight clouds.
A bridge was established by the spirits over the stream of blood.
*Daṇḍapāda* is a specific type of foot-strike well-known from the *Nāṭyaśāstra*. "With the earth sprinkled" means with the elements moistened. "A bridge was provided" means a bridge was constructed.
This connects with the preceding statement that "strength arose. || 41 ||

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Battle with the Three Astras," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, according to the tradition of the Rishis. || 49 ||
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Battle with the Three Asuras," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
Fifty-fifth Sarga.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
While that terrible confusion of battle was then unfolding,
For the sake of destroying the entire army of enemies, and for the sole purpose of pacifying one's own forces.
Herein is described the battle between the two Vaiṣṇava missiles, the disarming of both combatants, and the death of Vidūratha, who had been brought home. || 1 ||
One is uncommon; it is for the pacification of one's own strength and army—that is, for the pacification of the afflictions caused by *rakṣas* and *piśāca* spirits.
The mindful Ananta, possessing great nobility and supreme fortitude, remembered the glorious Vaiṣṇava weapon, the lord of weapons, which was like Śaṅkara himself.

Within, he is the ocean that serves as the ultimate limit for those possessing timely intuition; being exceedingly noble, he possesses both superior fortitude and supreme gentleness; and like Śaṅkara, he is a destroyer like Kālarudra. || 2 ||
Then, that arrow which had been consecrated with the Vaiṣṇava weapon was released by him; from the tip of its blade, sparks of fire issued forth into the sky.
From the edge of the fruit, from the region of the thorn. || 3 ||
The rows of their expanding discs made the horizons appear as if filled with hundreds of suns;
the approaching maces made the sky seem as if it were filled with hundreds of bamboo poles.

He elaborates on the meaning of the word "etcetera" mentioned in the phrase "firebrands etc. with the verse beginning "rows," and so forth. In these three verses, the "rows" themselves are the subjects qualified by the adjectives. By the word *vaṃśa*, bamboo shoots shaped like clubs (*gadā*) are understood. || 4 ||
The sky was turned into a forest of grass by the hundred-edged vajras; the sky was turned into a thicket of trees by the lotus-adorned paṭṭiśa spears. || 5 ||

There were rows of *paṭṭiśa* spears, adorned with lotuses and possessing many branches shaped like the buds of lotus petals; the meaning is that the sky was almost entirely covered by those [spears] which had cut down and severed the trees. According to the rule *lvādibhyaḥ*, the suffix *niṣṭhā* takes the dental *n*. (5)
The sky was turned into a canopy of flowers by their sharp-edged arrows;
the sky was turned into a mass of leaves by their dark-hued swords.
Then the second king also, for the sake of pacifying the Vaiṣṇava weapon,
discharged the very same Vaiṣṇava weapon, which fulfills the destruction of the enemy.
The second king was Vidūratha; he was one who fulfilled—that is to say, completed—the destruction of the enemy and established his own prowess. || 7 ||
Then, from that [lake] as well, rivers issued forth, their waters consisting of arrows, spears, clubs, darts, battle-axes, and other weapons, having destroyed the weapons of [the enemy's] missiles.
Those [missiles] by which the previously discharged weapons were struck down and shattered. || 8 ||
A battle of those rivers of missiles and weapons took place in the sky,
