causing the destruction of the space between heaven and earth and shattering the great lords of the principal mountain ranges.
The spears were felled by arrows, and the sharp-edged spears (paṭṭiśa) were hacked down by swords; the maces were shattered, and the javelins were struck down by clubs and spikes. (10)

He describes the battle in detail with the rivers of weapons and missiles, beginning with the word "śara" (arrow): where *paṭṭiśas* were crushed—that is, pulverized—by spears (*śūla*) and other weapons falling from or emerging from arrows;
[the separate mention of] *asi* and *khaḍga* is intended to indicate a distinction between their sub-varieties; [and where there were] *musala*s...

*Pratānana* means expansion (*pratāna*), derived from the root with the suffix *aṅ* because it belongs to the *bhidādi* group. In that [place], the powers (*śakti*) were cut down—that is, shattered—by that [expansion] and by the *prāsas* and other weapons. || 10 ||
The churning of the ocean of arrows was like Mount Mandara with its mallets; it was joined by the faces of maces, appearing like irresistible weapons.

In the churning of the ocean characterized by arrows, they were intoxicated—meaning they were capable—and where the mallets themselves were the Mandara mountains; from the mouths of the maces—that is, with the word *tasi* used in all cases—their tips were joined together, resembling faces; those whose weapons were irresistible.

Those women were their opponents in combat, resembling them and equal to them in stature and prowess; they were *asinyah*, meaning those who possessed various types of swords (*khaḍga*). [In this compound,] the short vowel [of the suffix] *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule *go-striyo-r-upasarjanasya*. || 11 ||
The circle of moon-like spears whirled about, pacifying both misfortune and prosperity;
the advancing darts were as fierce as the rising God of Death himself.
*Ṛṣṭam*. [The word] *ṛṣ* means "to injure"; the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). It refers to the injury of one's own respective army.

[The compound describes a place] where moon-discs in the form of spears (*kuntāḥ*) whirl about for the sake of pacifying that most inauspicious *ariṣṭa* characterized by such injury. [He is] agitated—that is, enraged—by the onrushes of javelins (*prāsāḥ*). Thus... [ata].
Thus, within him, Kṛtānta—Yama himself—arose, intent upon the destruction of the people he had begun to destroy.
[The weapon] with its upward-pointing shaft encircled by a wheel, which causes the destruction of all weapons;
it caused the cosmic egg of Viriñca to burst asunder with sound and shattered the principal mountain ranges with its blow. (13)
As the two fought with weapons and missiles that were severed by torrents [of counter-magic],
it was as if the thunderbolt had struck the indestructible mountain by means of a stream of rut-fluid.

Where, due to my having warded off Viśvāmitra’s weapon— as if by the mutual neutralization of two Nārāyaṇa weapons engaged in combat— the mountains there are "avijarāḥ," meaning incapable of being worn down even by the thunderbolts associated with those weapons.
The compound with an incapable [first] member is Vedic. || 14 ||
It was filled with hundreds of stone spears that hissed as they were struck by the fear of pikes,
and it contained a formidable circle of long-handled javelins subdued by the *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons.
Where there were spikes like stakes, things suspected due to their purpose, mere whistling sounds, tridents, and hundreds of stones. 15.
With one hand holding an axe and the other a trident, he was adorned with a single axe and a single trident;
he bore a severed head as a garland and was the destroyer of enemy elephants. 16.

Where each weapon was rendered blunt— struck down by one resembling the supreme, most excellent trident of Rudra, who is preeminent over others and capable of destroying all; [where] those very weapons, even as they were being carried and discharged, were utterly severed.

Where there are the curved and unevenly moving blades of broken weapons, and where the movements proceed; [the word *cāraṇāni* is derived from the root *car* with the suffix *yaṅ* in the sense of constant crookedness in motion, followed by the suffix *ac*, then the elision of *yaṅ* before *ac*, the substitution of *u* for the following *a*, and a Vedic lengthening. 16.
It blocked the path of the triple-streamed Ganges with the crackling explosions of bursting [weapons],
forming a vast canopy of smoke from the mass of pulverized missiles and weapons.
The compound *hetyastra* is a collective [dvandva] of *heti*s (missiles) and *astra*s (weapons); its feminine gender is Vedic (*chāndasa*). || 17 ||
From the clashing of their mutual weapons, flashes of lightning gleamed from the whirling masses [of missiles];
the cosmic egg of Brahmā shattered with a roar, and the principal mountain ranges were cast into the fire.
Where lightning flashes like a shimmering net being cast by a whirlwind. || 18 ||
As the two fought with a torrent of weapons severed by their own streams [of power],
the means for Kāla was simply the warding off of his weapons by the one of immovable mind.

The two half-verses have been explained as a repetition. For Vidūratha, whose mind was unshakable and who had become as motionless as a mountain in battle, this state of remaining [alive] by merely warding off my weapons is a means for the mere delay of time. || 19 ||
"To see how much strength he possesses," Vidūratha, standing effortlessly upon the ocean,
discharged the fiery weapon (āgneya-astra) with a sound like a thunderbolt.
But while he stood upon the ocean with a sense of contemptuous ease, thinking, "How much strength does this man have before me? || 20 ||
He set the chariot ablaze like a sapless thicket of dry grass;
meanwhile, in that interval, the interior of the sky was devoid of any openings for weapons.
*Kakṣa* means a clump of grass; *arasa* means dried. || 21 ||
Like a cloud in the rainy season or like a river in the monsoon, he [the demon] engaged in a most dreadful battle with the weapons of the two kings for a moment. || 22 ||

The king who was the armor was like the rainy season, and the other king, like a river swollen by clouds, rained down and carried away arrows. When the two kings had first employed their weapons, those two were the Nārāyaṇa weapons.
When they had reached a state of mutual exhaustion, like two powerful warriors,
in that interval, Agni reduced the chariot to ashes.
That fire is associated with the *āgneya* weapon. || 23 ||
Having burned the forest, he reached the Sindhu river like a lion emerging from a cave;
the Sindhu king, approaching him, neutralized the fire-weapon with the Varuṇa weapon.
Having burned the forest, he was like a lion emerging from a forest cave. || 24 ||
Abandoning his chariot and reaching the ground, he brandished his sword;
in the mere twinkling of an eye, [he struck] the hooves of the enemy's chariot-horses.
He became one who possessed a skin that was cracked open. || 25 ||
With agility, he cut [the opponent's limbs] with his sword as if they were lotus stalks;
Vidūratha, too, being deprived of his chariot, drew his sword and struck out.
Equipped with equal weapons and equal zeal, the two of them moved in circular maneuvers;
as they struck one another, their swords became like saws.

They attained the state of saws—that is, they became capable of tearing apart things as hard as leather and the like—just like saws. 27. As he was chewing up the subjects with the strength of his very row of teeth, Vidūratha took up a spear and hurled it, casting aside his sword. 28.
In the army, there were two hundred thousand. || 28 ||
Resounding with a gurgling roar like the waters of the Indus, like a great portentous thunderbolt,
it came down unceasingly and fell upon his chest.
Like the water of the Sindhu ocean, there was a gurgling roar—a portentous omen indicating the great dissolution;
that power resided upon the chest of this Sindhu.
Just as an unwilling woman might strike her unpleasant husband, yet he did not meet his death by that blow of the hand. || 30 ||
The elephant discharged a mere mass of blood like water;
seeing him broken, Taddeśalīlā was as delighted as the night is by the moon dispelling the darkness.
The elephant, like a serpent, shed its ichor just as water flows from it. || 31 ||
With an expansive and dense joy, she spoke of their former pastime:
"O Goddess, behold! This husband of ours has been slain by Nṛsiṃha. (32)
"Our lord Nṛsiṃha has slain the Daitya Sindhu, Hiraṇyakaśipu"—this is an example of *vyastarūpaka* (distributive metaphor).

|| 32 || With the tips of his claws, which were like millions of spears, the Daitya Sindhu, whose neck was uplifted, [was struck] like the water sprayed from the trunk of a great elephant standing on the bank of a lake. || 33 ||
As he was crushed, his vital fluid flowed out with a splashing sound;
"Alas, what misery! He has been brought to the chariot and is now intent on mounting the elephant. (34)

From the crushed and mangled chest, blood issues forth like water splashed from the trunk of a lordly elephant standing in the middle of a lake; this is how it connects with the preceding verse. || 34 ||
"O Goddess, behold this golden peak of Mount Meru, like the Puṣkarāvarta cloud; it has been pulverized by his mallet. (35)
Mairava is the peak belonging to Meru. Puṣkarāvartaka is the king of clouds. This is the chariot of this Sindhu.
"By the falling of the son of Pṛthā, this city has become like one made of gold;
here is my husband, brought back, ready to mount his chariot. (36)

By the falling of Pārtha Arjuna’s arrows, see that chariot whirling like a golden city whose protective armor has fallen away; the meaning is that it was spinning like such a city. Since the birth of Pārtha and others occurred even within that very universe (Brahmāṇḍa), this comparison is not unfamiliar. 36.
Alas! Like Indra [beating] Vajra or the ocean [beating] its club, my husband has swiftly rushed toward the ruler of the Sindhus, who wields a mace as his weapon. (151.37)
"Looked" means for the purpose of striking; [this refers to] having deceived the Saindhava. || 37 ||
Having deceived him with his gracefulness and swiftly mounting the chariot, alas, what a tragedy! This Sindhu has, by his speed, [overtaken] the chariot of the noble son. (38)
Like one mounted upon a lion’s mane, or like a tree shaken upward by a flood,
Vidūratha, showering a rain of arrows, tormented him after they had sported together.
Marked by a banner like a floating bird,
and green with moss and the like like a pool, she afflicted her own husband, King Vidūratha— the noble son mounted upon the chariot— who stood there like a tree rising high above [the water].
The connection. || 39 ||
His banner severed, his chariot shattered, his horses slain, his charioteer cut down;
his bow and armor broken, all his limbs pierced, he was utterly overwhelmed.
Having pierced with arrows as hard as thunderbolts the broad-headed one, whose chest is as firm as a slab of stone, he casts him down upon the earth. (41)
Having pierced the head—which is as firm as a stone slab in the matter of bursting, meaning it is impossible to burst, and which is moreover thick and massive—[he struck]. || 41 ||
Then, having regained consciousness with great difficulty upon reaching another chariot brought to him,
behold how the shoulder of your master was severed by a sword as he was mounting it.
Behold the shoulder region of my husband, whose shoulder was severed by the Sindhu river as he was mounting his chariot with great difficulty.
It sheds a flood of blood like the radiance of a mountain of rubies;
alas, alas! Woe is me, for by this ocean with its sword-blade current— || 43 ||
For this very reason, she sheds blood that is crimson and abundant, like the radiance issuing from the lord of the split ruby mountain—radiance which, though increasing, possesses a reddish glow.
The word "look" (*paśya*) is also carried over here [from the previous verse]. || 43 ||
"My husband has been severed from my thighs like a tree by a saw!
Alas, alas! I am struck down; I am consumed; I am dead; I am utterly ruined! (44)
The distinction is that "slain" (hatā) refers to one who has been made the object of the act of killing, while "dead" (mṛtā) refers to one who partakes in the result, namely death. || 44 ||
"Both my knees have been severed like two lotus stalks by my husband," she said,
and upon seeing that, she was overcome with fear for her husband's state.
She is one who "sits" (sīdati)—that is, languishes—due to the distress caused by that fear, which arises from her intense affection (bhāva) for her husband.
[The form is derived] from the root *sad* with the suffix *ḍa*, followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. || 45 ||
Like a creeper severed by an axe, she fell to the ground in a swoon; Vidūratha too, his knees giving way, collapsed even as he was striking the enemy.
He fell beneath the chariot like a tree severed at its roots;
even as he was falling, he was carried away by the chariot driven by the charioteer.

"He fell" means he was on the verge of falling. While he was still falling, or even as he was about to fall, the charioteer steadied him with the chariot itself and carried him away toward his home; this is the implied meaning. As it is said: "There are these two persons in the world who pierce the solar orb: the wandering mendicant absorbed in yoga, and one who is slain facing the enemy in battle."

From the *Smṛti*: "In battle, dying facing the enemy, those who pierce the solar orb attain the world of Brahmā. Since this statement regarding the attainment of the world of Brahmā by one who is dispassionate suggests the possibility of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*)—as in the words: "When the dissolution occurs, all those whose selves are perfected enter the supreme state at the end of the highest [Brahmā]"—it follows that this applies to one who is not yet dispassionate.
According to the Vedic scripture, "They do not return to this whirlpool of rebirth," there is no possibility of returning again in another *kalpa*,

nor can the enjoyment of the remainder of their *prārabdha* karma be accomplished through the previous lotus-body; therefore, it is solely by the power of Sarasvatī’s boon granted in accordance with her resolve that [the status of] the Sūta is established.
It should be understood that their inclination was toward the destruction of the king's fame and welfare, as well as his expulsion. || 47 ||
Whenever he struck him, the haughty Sindhu delivered a blow to his throat;
thus, with his throat half-severed, he was pursued by the Sindhu.

When he had been driven away, he then delivered a blow—a stroke of his sword. He qualifies the action with the word "exultant" (uddhata) to indicate that striking an opponent who is being driven off and is not facing him is a deed censured by heroes. || 48 ||
He entered the palace by chariot, just as the sun’s ray enters a lotus; yet,
despite Sarasvatī’s power, he was unable to enter that house,
just as a drunken gnat cannot enter the interior of a great flame.
That ocean was unable to enter the lotus-abode. || 49 ||
With his body, garments, and armor smeared by splashes of warm blood flowing from the wound in his throat, which had been cut open by a sword,
he abandoned her within the house as she stood near the Blessed Lady.
The charioteer, having entered, went to the surface of the bed of the deceased; the enemy was gone.

The charioteer, having brought Vidūratha— who was such that his clothes and other garments were sprinkled and drenched by streams and jets of blood flowing from the wound of the throat severed by the sword—
into the house, [placed him] near the goddess Sarasvatī within the dwelling.

He cast [his body] upon the surface of the funeral bed, which was covered with a soft mat suitable for a peaceful death, directly in front [of him]. In this context, the accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe dvitīyā*), according to the rule "abhitaḥ-paritaḥ-samayā-nikaṣā-hā-pratiyoge 'pi. The enemy—the foe as well as the ocean—having departed because of his inability to enter the house, has turned back; such is the meaning. || 50 ||

Thus ends the fiftieth sarga, titled "The Description of the Death of Vidūratha," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. || 50 ||
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of Vidūratha’s Death," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
Fifty-first Sarga.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"The king has been slain, the king has been slain by a rival king in battle."
When these words were uttered, the kingdom became overwhelmed with fear. || 1 ||
Now, following the account of the king's death, the preeminent ruler of the kingdom is described;
furthermore, the restoration of peace to the country once he was established in Sindh is related in detail. (1)
King Vidūratha, in battle—that is, in combat—with the rival king Sindhu. || 1 ||
A multitude of carts was fleeing, heavily laden with vessels and household goods;
it was filled with wailing and distressed wives, making the city difficult for its inhabitants to escape.
With people fleeing while crying out for help, with groups of women seized on the roads, and with a great terror gripping everyone as they were preoccupied with plundering one another. || 3 ||
Resounding with the clamor of the frantic dancing of the armies of enemy nations,
it was filled with the fallen bodies of heroes— both elephants and horses— left without their riders.
With the joyous exuberance of the dance of victory, it resounded loudly and noisily against the people within the enemy kingdom and the host of rivers. || 4 ||
With the inner coffer-rooms resounding with the clatter of doors being shattered and flying open, and filled with fierce warriors clad in countless plundered silken garments. || 5 ||

Resonating with a gurgling sound caused by the destruction of the treasury at its end— where the sound seemed to fly out into the external sky as the doors were split open— a place where fierce soldiers, clad in silk, overcame the guards of the treasury.
The courtyard of Rājagṛha was filled with fresh entrails torn out by knives,
and it teemed with a multitude of Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas resting within the royal harem.
Where the women of Rājagṛha were found dead, their bodies marked by fresh entrails torn out by thieves with knives and daggers. || 6 ||

The common folk were intent on eating the food and rice that had been carried away from their homes; meanwhile, the young children wept as they were struck by the feet of the multitude of heroes adorned with golden necklaces.
Where commoners and ordinary people are intent upon eating foods fit for the meals of kings. || 7 ||
The women of the inner apartments were overtaken by unprecedented youth;
the paths were bristling with priceless jewels fallen from the hands of thieves.
Where the paths were made white by jewels set like protruding teeth. || 8 ||
The circle of vassal kings was preoccupied with the crowding of horses, elephants, and chariots;

the chief ministers were intent on the instructions regarding the preparations for the consecration. (Note: Although the reading "abhiṣekodyamādeśaparaṃ" is found in other manuscripts, this present reading is preferred.)
Because it is well-coordinated and because it is approved by the author of the commentary, this alone has been accepted by us. || 9 ||
*Saṃghaṭṭa* means a collision; it is a gathering after having been drawn together. In that [gathering], the circle of neighboring vassals was distracted.
They were intent upon the command—the ordering—of the undertaking for the coronation of the son of Sindhu. 9.
He appointed a master architect to begin the construction of the royal capital,
where the king’s favorites would descend through windows and chasms.

There, the beloveds of the King of Sindhu descend and enter through windows and openings fashioned by master craftsmen— the lords of architects and best of artisans— in order to behold the unprecedented beauty of the city. 10.
It was filled with the roar of hundreds of shouts of victory from the kings of the Sindhu region,
and it maintained its stability through the ocean-like multitude of his own innumerable royal hosts.

In that [kingdom], there was an abundance of extraordinary power belonging to the King of Sindhu and his son, who had been consecrated after being ushered in amidst the loud proclamation of hundreds of shouts of victory; and therein, the established order— the boundaries of the kingdom— was maintained by the King of Sindhu himself, with his own royal hosts bearing it upon their heads.
The royal favorites were fleeing, having been overtaken by the invasion of another village,
while plundering of cities and villages was occurring within the various districts.
Where the former king’s favorites, though hidden away in other villages, were recognized by their enemies and consequently fled even from there.
The coming and going on the road was blocked by the plundering of infinite thieves and wealth;
it was like the sunlight of a day obscured by mist due to the absence of a person of great majesty.
Where the coming and going of people traveling on the roads was blocked by infinite thieves for the sake of plunder;
where, due to that destitution, even the days possessed a chill like snowfall, despite the heat of the sun, because of the great-souled Vidūratha.
With the wailing of deceased kinsmen, the sounds of funeral drums,
and the noise of horses, elephants, and chariots, it possessed a dense resonance that could be grasped as a single mass.
The phrase "capable of being grasped like a solid mass" is a poetic conceit (autprekṣika), referring to that place where the sounds are dense. || 14 ||
"Sindhudeva is victorious, the sovereign lord of the earth under a single umbrella!"— thus,
immediately thereafter, the kettledrums were sounded in every city at that time.
Thus making the proclamation, the people began to beat the kettledrums (bherīs)—the word *bherīḥ* being a Vedic archaism for *bherīḥ* due to a transposition of vowels—this is the sense. || 15 ||
Then Sindhuruddhura, with his neck held high,
entered the capital like another Manu entering the world at the end of a Yuga to create progeny.
Then, immediately after the consecration of his son to the kingdom, Sindhu entered his own capital city. || 16 ||
Then, from the ten directions, the tribute-offerings set out to enter the city of Sindhurāja,
like rivers full of jewels flowing toward the ocean in the forms of elephants and horses.
In an instant, the ministers established markers, signs, and instructions for every direction toward the mandala.
The *nibandhanas* are the boundaries; the *cihnas* are the marks, such as seals and the like, which are the names inscribed upon the *sindhus*. 18.
In a very short time, this restriction regarding life, death, and honor arose in every region and in every city, just as follows.
Then, in the twinkling of an eye, the calamities and disturbances of the land subsided, like the movements of objects when the winds of a portentous storm have been stilled.
Just as when the wind has subsided, the revolutions and whirlings of objects such as grass, leaves, dust, and so forth, which were produced by the wind, likewise come to rest. || 20 ||
The region, encompassing the ten directions, quickly attained a state of tranquility,
like the Ocean of Milk whose turbulent whirlpools had suddenly subsided once Mount Mandara was withdrawn.
The winds, agitated by the swirling of droplets of water, blew about, tossing the masses of hair and the swarms of bees upon the lotus-faces of the women from Sindh.
as if [dispelling] all inauspicious qualities in an instant from every side. || 22 ||

The breezes from the Sindhu region, causing the clusters of hair on the lotus-faces of the women to flutter like swarms of bees, become agitated and move slowly as if intoxicated by the swirling of those sweat-drops which are as abundant as honey.

Possessing auspicious qualities such as coolness and fragrance, those winds blew from all directions, agitating—and by the non-distinction between the letters *ḍa* and *la*, as if churning up—all inauspicious qualities such as heat and foul odor;
they blew as if striking down [the miseries]. || 22 ||
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Kingdom of Siṃdu," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Kingdom of Sindhu," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
254) Chapter Fifty-Two: The Fifty-Second.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In the meantime, O Rāma, Līlā spoke to Sarasvatī,
seeing her husband standing before her, stupefied and with nothing but his breath remaining.
In this [work], the death of the king, the illusory nature of that worldly existence (saṃsāra),
and likewise the essential nature of the city’s play as being merely mental impression (vāsanā) are described.
"Stupefied" means rendered unconscious. || 1 ||
"O Mother, this husband of mine has set out here to cast off his body in this battle, which is such a great undertaking and a source of agitation for the kingdom.
Jñapti said:
"In a battle of such a form, a great undertaking, and a turmoil for the realm..."

Even though [the kingdom] was prosperous and firmly established, and even though it was occupied with various grand undertakings, nothing at all was truly accomplished— neither in the realm nor upon the earth.

"Whether accomplished, arisen, or even—by the force of the word 'even' (api)—persisting, or in some place, anywhere; 'kvacana' is an indivisible indeclinable; the meaning is: not accomplished, not persisting, and not destroyed.
Within that pavilion—that very small pavilion previously seen—[he saw] the corpse of a lotus. || 3 ||
Thus this world, being of the nature of a dream, does not abide anywhere at all;
[it appeared] in the space near the corpse within that pavilion.
O sinless one, this kingdom of Bhū appears here within the inner apartments of your husband’s residence; it is this very realm that now constitutes its interior.

The grammatical connection is as follows: that Brahmāṇḍa of Vidūratha, which remained within the inner apartments of the lotus-palace and whose belly was filled with kingdoms—this very Padma-Brahmāṇḍa is situated inside the house of the brahmin Vasiṣṭha. || 5 ||
Within the house of the Brahmin Vasiṣṭha, situated in a village on the Vindhya mountain,
the world exists within the house of the corpse inside the house of the Brahmin Vasiṣṭha.
He confirms what has already been stated by means of a reversal [of the order], beginning with "Vasiṣṭha. || 6 ||
This world-house exists within the belly of the world-house of the corpse;
thus, this great undertaking is a delusion consisting of the three worlds. (7)
Joined with you, me, her, and him, the earth together with the oceans shall be contained within the hollow of the sky, inside the body of this mountain-village.
By this second sport; by this husband of yours. (8)
One's own self alone shines; that which is void does not shine at all anywhere.
Know that to be the supreme state, devoid of destruction and origination.
The notion that [the elements] have arisen one after another with intervals is also merely a conceptual construction. In reality, consciousness exists only in the Self and not in space;

this is stated with the intention that [consciousness appears as such] due to the superimposition of the triad including space and the other elements—hence he says, "one's own Self alone. With the intention that when the object is false, even the form conjoined with it does not exist in consciousness, he says, "it does not shine at all. And thus:
He states that only objectless pure consciousness remains, and that alone is the primary object of knowledge: "That" (verse 9).
It is self-luminous, manifest, tranquil, and supremely free from affliction;
indeed, it exists within the pavilion-house of one's own nature, arisen within the Self.

"Self-luminous" means self-manifesting; that very [reality] appears within the interior of the pavilion-house as its own self, arisen through its own nature as pure consciousness (cinmātra), and not as some other entity—this is the meaning. "Kila" indicates what is well-known among the wise. || 10 ||
Thus, even within those two pavilions, though they appear solid due to their construction, there exists only empty space in their interior; there is no delusion of a world.

With the intention that if even within the elemental space (bhūtākāśa) contained inside the pavilion there is no world, what need is there to mention the pure space of consciousness (śuddhacidākāśa), he says: "Thus" (evam). || 11 ||
For in the absence of a deluded perceiver, what kind of delusion could there be in the illusion?
Since the existence of delusion does not exist at all, that which exists is the unborn state.

Now, if the cognition of a large object within a small space is an error because it cannot be contained therein, then why should the cognition of the exceedingly vast Brahman within the spaces of a pavilion, the heart, and so forth— not also be an error, since it likewise cannot be contained there? Thus [the objection is raised].
He says "not so" because it would contradict that which is relied upon for livelihood, due to the suspicion [of error], stating: "Of the wandering observer... (verse 12).
Error is the appearance of the non-existent; how can there be the state of a seer and the seen for that?
Since the sequence of seer and seen is absent, it is indeed non-dual and innate.
[Objection: "In that case, let error itself perceive error, and nothing else. To this he replies: "Error...

For the object of sight (*dṛśya*) is indeed the locus of the fruit of the seer's activity (*draṣṭṛ-vyāpāra*). And it is not possible for anything to act upon itself, because there is a contradiction between being the agent and the object in a single entity. Furthermore, in the absence of a seer, there can be neither existence nor manifestation for the object of sight.
The sense is that [the non-dual reality] is established. This absence of the sequence of seer and seen is a defect for duality alone;
however, with the intention that it is rather an ornament for innate non-duality, he says: "draṣṭṛ... (seer...). 13 ||
Know that supreme state to be devoid of destruction and origination;
it is self-luminous, manifest, peaceful, primordial, and free from affliction. (14)
It is said that within the pavilion-house, people dwell there according to their own established order, within the Self that has arisen from their respective natures, as if in their own home.

With the intention that even the non-penetration of a larger [space] into a much smaller one is a defect only of the visible object and not of the consciousness that is the substrate of all, he says "kila" and so forth.
They move about— that is, they wander— according to the arrangement of spatial extension suitable for their respective activities.
The word "kila" is used here in the sense of wonder. || 15 ||
Neither the world nor any creation whatsoever is experienced there [or "anywhere," according to another reading]. Therefore, I exist as the unborn space, which is indeed the world. (16)
The meaning is that this is experienced by those who know reality (*tattvajña*).

Therefore, by means of the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) consisting of experience, it is ascertained that the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), which is the witness of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), exists in the form of the world from the perspective of one who knows only a single thing. This is the meaning. || 16 ||
All consciousness of self is empty, like the network of mountains such as Meru;
this is not anything composed of walls, just as a great city in a dream.
Thus, he establishes that certainty through inference as well—by the word "all":
this entire visible world, characterized by the network of mountains such as Meru and so forth, is nothing but the knowledge of the very nature of the void-self; it is not composed of walls.

It possesses the gross nature exactly as it was perceived [externally], because it is experienced within a small space that is otherwise unfit for its immersion; the meaning is that it is like a great city seen in a dream inside the body. || 17 ||
Even in a region the size of a span, the wise know that there are hundreds of thousands of worlds of their own, composed of networks of mountains yet possessing the essence of diamond.

He demonstrates the pervasion established by universal experience in dreams with the words "In the region" (*deśe*). According to the scripture, "Dream enters the throat," the apertures (*khāni*) located within the span of one *prādeśa* from the throat to the end of the heart are nothing other than the self-consciousness (*ātma-caitanya*) delimited by those specific regions. The plural number is used figuratively due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). They consist of networks of mountains.
The wise see all this in a dream.
Even within a single atom, numerous worlds come into being in great abundance through their arrangement, like the leaves of a plantain tree. (19)
Likewise, he demonstrates the possibility in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) by means of the application (*upanaya*): "The worlds," [as stated in verse 19].
The three worlds exist within the atomic point of consciousness like a city in a dream;
within that [city] as well are atomic points of consciousness, and within each of those too is a world.
He confirms what has been established by the conclusion with the words "the three worlds" (trijagat) || 20 ||
O auspicious one, in that world where this King Śava lies upon the lotus,
this Līlā, your co-wife, has arrived long ago.

Having addressed that which was asked, and desiring to explain the true nature of the pastimes therein, she begins the narrative at hand with the words "Of them," and so forth; it is more ancient than the departure of the previous kings. (21)
The very moment this Līlā fell into a swoon before you, she stood at the side of her husband Padma’s corpse.
Līlā said: O Goddess, how did she formerly become embodied there,
and how did she come to abide in the state of being his co-wife?
That state which has a rival wife—that is, that state together with its rival wife. || 23 ||
Tell me in brief: what form do those who dwell in her excellent house see, and what do they say? Tell this to me.
Tell me briefly, in summary, what kind of form those inhabitants—people dwelling upon that site characterized by the excellent abode of that lotus—behold, or what they say. || 24 ||
The illustrious Goddess said:
Listen; I shall tell you everything in brief, exactly as you have asked—the account of my own pastimes, O Līlā, which brings an end to [suffering] and destroys the misfortune of the visible world.
He provides the "end" (anta), meaning the final resolution, regarding the very account of his own self, which was part of his divine play (līlā).
He is "one by whom the visible states"—such as death and the departure to the next world—are capable of being properly seen.
This husband of Padmā still perceives this vast delusion within that very same abode which consists of the entire universe. (26)

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: this delusion consisting of the world, which is being perceived in the form of this city and so forth—this very delusion your husband Padma, having become Vidūratha, beholds in that very same dwelling which is the support for the corpse. || 26 ||
This battle is a battle of delusion; this person is a non-person, being merely a delusion. In this world, death exists only through delusion, and thus this [world] is of the nature of error.

This battle which you have seen is merely a battle of delusion, like a battle in a dream. This playful activity behind you is also nothing but delusion. And this person who appears as a "man" is in truth the non-man—the Self that is devoid of transformations such as birth and so forth. This is saṃsāra. || 27 ||
By this very process of delusion, his beloved Līlā remains;
both you and she, O beautiful woman of noble limbs, are merely a dream.
O beautiful woman, just as this [world] is a mere dream for you both, so too is this husband of yours, and I myself am likewise. (29)
This world-appearance is such that it is here called the "visible" (dṛśya);
yet, when this very thing is fully understood, it relinquishes the meaning of the word "visible."
The meaning of the word "visible" abandons—that is, relinquishes—its status as the object of the act of seeing. || 30 ||
In this way, she is thus, and she is thus; so too is this king, and I have attained truth within myself through the all-pervasiveness of the Self. (31)
This is the nature of saṃsāra; it is thus merely of the form of delusion, [arising] from the self's state of being all-pervasive and complete. || 31 ||
"Thus we are here, provoked by one another"—
so it is because of the state of being established as a mass of great consciousness, which consists of all things.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: just as these kings and others arose through a false conceptualization of the state of existence of the Great Mass of Consciousness (*mahāciddhana*), being impelled and driven by a relationship of mutual benefactor and beneficiary, so too has this queen come into being. 32.
Thus this queen remained there, charming with her playful smile,
her face agitated by amorous play, and radiant with fresh youth.
Sweet with her graceful conduct, speaking with sweet and noble speech, resembling the song of the cuckoo, she was languid with passion and love. (34)
She was gentle and skillful; sweet and pleasing in her conduct; and her voice was like that of the cuckoo, resembling its very sound. || 34 ||
Her eyes were like the petals of a blue lotus, her breasts were round and full;
she was lovely, her limbs were golden-hued, and her lips were like the ripe bimba fruit. (35)
Since she is a portion of your husband’s mind, which consists of your own volition,
she remains here with a form identical to yours within the wondrous play of consciousness.
The mental faculty, the activity of the mind, and its latent impressions (vāsanā) have arisen—this is the implied sense. || 36 ||
Indeed, immediately upon the death of your husband,
this very person was seen before you by him, whose self had become your own mental resolve.
When the mind itself experiences a material (ādhibhautika) state, that which is perceived is composed of pure existence (sanmaya);
therefore, it is a conceptualization of the subtle body (ātivāhika). || 38 ||
If this [experience] consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), how then was it experienced by him as real? To this he says: "When...

In reality, the conception of the *ātivāhika* (subtle body) is merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*). "The object of thought" (*cetya*) means the visible world. Therein, when the mind (*cetas*)—that is, the consciousness (*citta*)—experiences a material, empirical state through the firmness of habitual impressions (*abhyāsa-dṛḍha-vāsanā*), [it perceives it as real].
The meaning is that, from this experience, the object of cognition (cetya) then becomes nothing other than the supreme reality consisting of pure existence (sanmaya). || 38 ||
When the mind perceives a material (ādhibhautika) state as not being composed of reality,
then the resolve for the subtle body (ātivāhika) arises as truth.

But when, through the practice of discriminative knowledge, one perceives that the elemental state is not composed of reality but is unreal, then, by means of that firm and true latent impression (vāsanā), there arises within the phenomenal world a mental resolve toward the subtle body (ātivāhika) and a determinative realization of its illusory nature. || 39 ||
Furthermore, in this delusion consisting of rebirth following the perception of death, he has indeed been perceived by him, and he has likewise gone by you. (40)
Through you, who possess a form that is the very essence of divine play arising from latent impressions, he has indeed attained union.
"Thus he has seen you, and you have seen him;
for you too have become [one with] the Self, because the conscious Self is all-pervading. (41)

The meaning is that even by you, this [universe] was perceived as consisting solely of your own latent impressions (*vāsanā*); thus, it has transformed into the three cosmic eggs previously shown. This is because, being all-pervasive and following after all latent impressions, it is capable of manifesting in every possible form. || 41 ||
Since Brahman is all-pervading, in whatever manner, wherever, and whenever it has arisen, it immediately becomes so there; one perceives it through the very power of dream. || 42 ||

He explains that very point clearly with the words "Brahman," etc. By the power of dream (*svapna-śaktyā*), that is, by the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śaktyā*). In the reading *svasva-śaktyā*, it means by the power of their respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 42 ||

Because [the Lord] possesses all powers everywhere, whatever power may be inferred in a particular instance, it exists there and manifests accordingly, due to the cause of intense momentum (*tīvrasaṃvega*).

In whatever manner and by whatever form the enjoyer might lead [the object] forth—that is, manifest it—by the power of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), that is due to the cause of intense spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of firm attachment. || 43 ||
At the very moment they remained in a state of delusion due to death, this was understood by the couple in their hearts through the power of a mental appearance.

The delusion of death is a fainting fit conducive to one's own dying; when they both remained characterized by that for a moment, at that very time all this which is about to be described was understood by them through their own imagination and experienced.
Or rather, it is an appearance arising from the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); it is by virtue of that [that they saw it]. || 44 ||
"These two are our fathers, and these indeed are our mothers; this is the country, this is the wealth, and such was our former occupation. (45)
The ellipsis implies: "In the past, such karma was performed. || 45 ||
"We two have been married in this very way and have thus attained oneness;
even that public assembly has reached the state of truth right there. (46)
That [cognition], although consisting of conceptual construction, attains the status of reality and the capacity for causal efficiency through the power of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of the enjoyer.
"In this very matter, there is the direct example of the experience of a dream.
O Līlā, as I was contemplating in this way, I was then worshipped by Līlā.
He provides the answer to what was previously asked—namely, "how was [it] obtained"—with the words "ityevam" (in this manner).
She is one whose disposition (*bhāva*) or intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) is of the nature that will be described in this way. || 47 ||
"I shall not become a widow"—this very boon was granted by me as well; for this reason, indeed, this young girl died here even before [the husband]. (48)
For this reason, she had already died previously. (48)
I am the one whose nature is consciousness among you who are portions of consciousness;
as the family deity, I am always to be worshipped, and I perform this of my own accord. (49)
Regarding the question of what the cause is for both her and me in the propitiation of You and in Your grace, he says: "Of you two" (bhavatoḥ).

The consciousness of Hiraṇyagarbha, which possesses the quality of consciousness, consists of the collective consciousness (*samasthi-cetanā*) of all individual conscious entities (*vyaṣṭi-cetanā*). || 49 ||
Then Jīvaka, assuming the form of the vital wind (prāṇa), entered her body through her mind as it moved; he remained with his physical body cast off at the tip of her mouth.

Having provided the answer to the part of the question regarding how [the Self] was obtained in the past, he now states the answer to the part concerning how it became embodied, beginning with the words "Then" (*atha*).
Then, as it was about to depart from the body, the Jīva— the individual soul,
which is minute because it consists merely of the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) measured by the size of a thumb— became joined with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and with fire (*tejas*).

The meaning is that he assumed the form of the vital air (prāṇa), because according to the scripture, "He leads the world as he has willed it," the departure [of the self] is dependent upon the vital air;
and because of the scriptural statement, "Speech indeed merges into the vital air," all the organs merge into the vital air.
Thus, he became the vital air, which possesses the nature of wind (māruta). This is because the scripture states, "He leads the world as he has willed it."

Based on the Śruti and the Smṛti beginning with "Whatever state he remembers," it is by means of the mind— which is characterized primarily by the volition toward the object to be attained— that the tip of his heart flashes forth as he becomes restless and eager for the attainment of that particular object; by that flash, this Self departs, either through the eye or [another aperture].

The ellipsis to be supplied is: "having abandoned his body through the path of the channels (nāḍīmārga), according to the sequence stated in the Śruti as 'either from the head or from other parts of the body'. || 50 ||
Then, at the end of the fainting spell caused by death, he was seen by this very living self (jīvātman) within the space cultivated in the intellect right here in this house.

Thereafter, by this individual soul (jīvātman), within this very house— in the ether of Brahman (brahmākāśa) or the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), or in the intellect (buddhi)— the matter to be described, consisting of the departure for another body and the attainment of the maiden, was visualized, intended, and perceived. || 51 ||
This deer-eyed woman, endowed with the splendor of a moon-like face, haughty with pride yet longing for her lover’s dalliance,
stands within the circle of the assembly, her face turned forward with impetuous eagerness through the memory of their former union.
Or like a lotus pond, whose natural splendor is obscured at the end of a dream, as if awakened. || 52 ||

Then, by the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), through the recollection of her former body— as if at the end of a dream or in the midst of a dream (here the word *vaśāt* or *vāśāt* should be understood in the sense of "as if")— this Līlā, like a lotus plant impelled by the rays of the sun, having its buds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) blossomed,
was herself charming and fit for the enjoyment of her beloved; and she herself [perceived] the beloved as enchanting.

One whose desire (*kāma*) is to enjoy—that is, to experience—her husband; [the *tumun* suffix] *tum* is elided after the words *kāma* and *manas* according to the rule *tuṃ kāmamanasor api*. Being such that her face possesses a sudden impulse (*sarabhasa*) accompanied by the speed of loveliness and beauty, she entered the sphere of the lotus-universe (*padmabrahmāṇḍamaṇḍala*) and became united with her husband; this is the meaning. || 52 ||

Thus ends the fifty-second sarga, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Body Immediately Following Death," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Appearance of the Body Immediately Following Death," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The fifty-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, having obtained the boon, [he addressed] the lord of the earth with this very body.
She proceeds through the path of the sky toward the celestial realm in order to reach her husband. || 1 ||
In this work, the path of Līlā’s journey and her attainment of her husband are described,
as well as the inability of those perfected through the yoga of ignorance to travel upon the path of the sky.

By this very body composed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) previously described; "the world" (*viṣṭapa*) refers to the worlds to be described hereafter—the singular number is used because it denotes a class. || 1 ||
Having reflected thus, she whose banner was the makara leaped up with joy; light of form, she flew into the sky like a female bird. (2)

Having reflected in the manner described above, and having assumed the state of a body through that recollection, she leaped up with joy, as much as possible, out of her eagerness to reach her husband; she was of delicate form and light-bodied. || 2 ||
There she found the maiden, sent by Jñapti herself for her welfare,
appearing as if she had emerged from the great mirror of her own resolve.
The maiden, his own daughter. || 3 ||
The maiden said:
"I am the daughter of Jñapti, my friend; welcome to you, O beautiful one!
I have been standing here on the path of the sky, waiting for you alone. (4)
"O friend of consciousness"—this is an address to the Mother. || 4 ||
p. 257) 161 Līlā said:
"O Goddess with eyes like lotus petals, lead me to the presence of my husband."
For the sight of the great is never in vain.

Having ascertained her mastery of the path from her previous arrival, Līlā said: "O Goddess. [She explained: "O Goddess, you who have attained a divine body; for my husband, who is your father. [Līlā asked: 'Surely, since you yourself desire a husband, what need have I to go to my father's presence? To this she replied: 'By the great ones... And thus, for the sake of my beloved, that which was spoken by me—
The meaning is "accomplish. || 5 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "Come, let us go right there," having said this, the young maiden stood before her in the sky, intent on showing the way.
Then, following after him, she reached the hollow of the sky,
which was as stainless as the tip of a row of rays or a line of auspicious marks.

The hollow (koṭara) is that which has become the aperture of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). Just as the palm (tala), which is the tip of the multitude of hands (karamālā) belonging to living beings, contains the lines (lekhikā) created by the Ordainer (vidhātṛ) which serve as the marks of future auspicious and inauspicious fortune, so too [is this hollow]. || 7 ||
Then, having crossed the path of the clouds, she went into the midst of the wind-spheres;
she passed from the path of the sun and traversed the path of the stars.
She has arrived; she has departed. || 8 ||
By means of his lightness, having leaped over the worlds of Vāyu, Indra, the Suras, and the Siddhas,
he reached the shell of the cosmic egg belonging to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
The meaning is that he has transcended even the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa. || 9 ||
Just as the coldness of snow within an unbroken jar manifests on the outside,
so too did she, perfected by her own resolve, emerge from the cosmic egg into the external world.
Just as the coldness of water within a jar might emerge and escape even through a vessel that is unbroken and without holes. || 10 ||
Having a body consisting of nothing but one's own mind, born from the nature of one's own volitions, one indeed experiences such a delusion within oneself alone. (11)
And he reminds [us] that this going is merely a mental construction, saying: "one's own mind" (svacitta). || 11 ||
Having ascended to and reached the station of Brahmā and the shell of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa-kharpara),
he then [reaches] the coverings of water and the rest situated beyond the cosmic egg.
The half-verse is a restatement. 12.
Having leaped forward, he reached the interior of the great sky of consciousness,
whose farthest limits were unseen even by Garuḍa as he flew with extreme speed from all sides for hundreds of millions of kalpas.

The "consciousness-ether" (cidgagana) is the space of consciousness permeated by māyā; the syntactical connection is that its far-reaching limits are not seen even by Garuḍa as he flies with extreme speed in every direction. || 13 ||
Therein exist hundreds of thousands of Brahmā-eggs, innumerable and vast;
they are unseen by one another, like fruits in a great forest. (14)
There, having pierced through one [of them] that stood before him, provided with an extensive covering, he entered within like a worm into a jujube fruit.
"Having pierced," meaning "as if having made perforated," is a figurative expression (autprekṣika), because it does not depend upon actual physical holes. || 15 ||
Again, having transcended the radiant worlds of Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and others,
he reached that glorious orb of the earth from below the path of the stars.
Beneath that lotus, from the sky of the path of the stars, was the circle of the earth. || 16 ||
Having reached that mandala, entered that city and that pavilion,
she stood near the corpse of Puṣpagupta.
In the meantime, that beautiful-faced woman did not see the maiden; she had vanished somewhere like an illusion once recognized.
Beholding the face of her husband in the form of a corpse, she realized by herself, through the power of intuition, that this was indeed the truth. (19)
[This is established] through one's own intuition, through [one's own] power, and through one's own reasoning. || 19 ||
This is that husband of mine, slain in battle by the Sindhu king;
having attained these worlds of heroes, he lies for a moment as he pleases.
"By the grace of the Goddess, I, being fortunate, have thus arrived here in this very body; there is no one whatsoever equal to me. (21)
"She has obtained a husband"—this is the ellipsis. || 21 ||
Having reflected thus, she took the beautiful chowrie in her hand and fanned him,
just as the sky fans the circle of the earth with the moon.
Prabuddhalīlā said: O Goddess, what will those servants, those female slaves, and that awakened king say—by what speech and with what understanding, O eloquent one? (23)

He asks again, including the remainder of the previous question: "Those servants... With what intention will they speak, and how is that possible? For if the king has forgotten his former history, there would be the doubt, "Who is this, and whose is she? And even if he remembers, her acceptance is not established because it would be censured by cultured people.
This is the state of being. Tell that story.
The Goddess said: That king and those servants— all of them— became one with each other through their immersion in the unity of the space of consciousness and by our power.

Indeed, if there were a universal perception that "this is something unprecedented," the aforementioned fault would arise; therefore, the Goddess provides a resolution with the words beginning "That king... and so forth, [stating] that she herself, possessing true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*), will not come to be due to the power of those such as ourselves. All these—the king and the others—being in complete agreement with one another, spoke thus to each other.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that they perceive in the manner about to be described. The reasons for their unanimity (*aikamatya*) are "the space of consciousness" (*cidākāśa*) and so forth.

This occurs through the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) or penetration (*āveśa*) of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicidākāśa*), which—due to its oneness—is concordant with unanimity, having entered within as it were reflected, like a reflection, in each other's respective intellects (*buddhi*).

The meaning is as follows: [the world is] the Great Consciousness (mahācit), the consciousness of Brahman, because it is a manifestation (*pratibhāsa*) thereof; because it is an illusory transformation (*vivarta*) of that [consciousness] in accordance with the impelling unseen merit/demerit (*bhoktṛ-adṛṣṭa*); because it is the Great Ordainer (*mahā-niyati*), being the will of the Lord (*īśvara-saṃkalpa*) that "this must be manifested in this very way"; and because it rests upon that [will], being dependent upon it. || 24 ||
Because they are manifestations of the Great Consciousness and because of the certainty of the Great Niyati,
they see one another as mutually reflected within each other.
"This is my co-born wife; this is my co-born friend;
this is my co-born queen; this is my co-born servant. (26)
Only you, I, and she shall know this marvel exactly as it happened, without omission; no one else at all shall know it.
And that is the playful conduct of Vidūratha; the meaning is that the other [person] will not know it. || 27 ||
Prabuddhalīlā said:
"Why did this Līlā, who speaks so charmingly, not go to her husband with this very body? She has obtained [this state] through a boon. (28)
The connection [of the verse] is as follows: "Having been described as one who has obtained her husband, why did this Līlā not go with this very same gross body by the power of your boon? || 28 ||
p. 258) 162 The Illustrious Goddess said:
Those of unawakened intellect [desire] the worlds of the Siddhas, which arise through the power of merit.
They are not capable of reaching it with their own bodies, just as shadows cannot reach the sunlight.
Those of unawakened intellect are devoid of the realization of the Self, which is not gross. || 29 ||
And at the beginning of creation, destiny was established by the enlightened ones, such that truth never mingles with falsehood in any way whatsoever. (30)
The law of necessity (*niyati*), which is the boundary of conduct, has been established by the awakened ones, such as Īśvara and Hiraṇyagarbha, whose resolutions are true.

Regarding this, there is an illustration—namely, "just as. And so says the Bhāṣya: "For when something is superimposed upon another, that [substratum] is not connected even in the slightest degree with the quality or defect produced by that [superimposition]. (30)
As long as a child possesses the conceptualization of a ghost, how and by what means could there be the arising of that [realization] for one whose mind is free from ghosts? (31)
Now, one might ask: "By your grace, he has attained the certainty that the Self is not gross; why then did this not happen sooner? To this, he says with the verse beginning "yāvat":
"As long as the feverish heat of non-discrimination (aviveka) exists within the self, how can the coolness of the moon of discrimination (viveka) sufficiently arise? (32)
"How could one who internally possesses the conviction, 'I am the body composed of earth and other elements; I have no excellent movement in the sky,' ever possess a different conviction? (33)
Therefore, by means of the discernment of knowledge, merit, and supreme excellence,
they go to the higher world with this body of merit.
By this [body] which resembles yours. || 34 ||
Just as a dry leaf is quickly consumed by embers— [the reading "patadevāśu" is found in some versions]—
so too this body of mine, once reached, immediately falls apart. (35)

To the question of how the gross sense of "I" ceases upon attaining the *ātivāhika* (subtle) body, he says: "Like a dry [stick]," etc. Just as a dry stick falling into glowing embers—that is, into blazing fire—is consumed, this very illustration applies here: this gross body, having attained the *ātivāhika* body which consists solely of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of egoity, simply dissolves away.
This alone occurs through the manifestation of boons and curses:
that memory arises such that one thinks, "Just as I have intended, so have I been remembered. (36)

Both boons and curses are obtained by living beings only in accordance with their prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and karma, acting as the factors that awaken them; this he states by way of the illustration of memory: "Only this much," etc.
Just as even regarding what was practiced in the past, because the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are not immediately awakened, one must reflect for a long time on that which is fit for reflection.

The meaning is that it is just like when, after someone has reminded one of the subject matter of a section (anuvāka) by citing a specific opening phrase (pratīka), the recollection arises: "Just as I was reminded by you, so too has he been remembered. || 36 ||
How can that cognition of a snake regarding a rope perform the function of a snake? For how can there be causal efficacy for that which does not exist even in its own [substratum]? (37)

Now, one might object: "How can the gross body, which performs purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), be sublated by the realization of reality? Anticipating this doubt, he says "He who... to show that from the perspective of reality (*tattvadṛśā*), there is no such thing as purposeful action at all—at least not within the Self, which is one's own true nature. || 37 ||
But that which is falsely experienced as "this person is dead" is merely the manifestation of a previously cultivated habituation. (38)

If the body is indeed non-existent, then how is it that there is the universal experience, "This body is dead"? To this, he says: "But that which... The meaning is: as for the delusion—the false perception of a false object—this experience unfolds from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of previously accumulated and strengthened habitual practice. || 38 ||
Within the web of the world experienced by oneself, the delusions of memory are easily understood;
such a practice as the creation and so forth is certainly not imagined by another. (39)

It was not properly fashioned by another—such as Hiraṇyagarbha or Īśvara—who bestows boons, curses, and so forth, but rather created entirely independently of our latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and other such factors. || 39 ||
The cycles of transmigration experienced within are [the result] of external networks of elements,
even for those who have not realized the nature of what is to be known.
Like the lunar orb to men who are far away. || 40 ||

Now, raising the objection: "If cyclic existence consists of internal latent impressions (*vāsanā*), how can there be a cognition of its externality?", he resolves it with an illustration: "Internally," etc. Even for the ignorant who do not perceive the true reality, transmigrations exist only internally and not externally; for the second lunar disc, though superimposed and appearing at a distance, [is nonetheless internal].
The meaning is that, just as [the object] is internal because it is conceived through internal delusion, so too is that [the dream-object] internal. || 40 ||

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The World-Cycle Known by the Knower of All that is to be Known," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* within the *Mokṣopāya* of the venerable *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Seers.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Known Object of Knowledge Regarding Saṃsāra," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
Fifty-fourth canto.
Śrī Devī said:
Therefore, those who are knowers of what is to be known, or those who have taken refuge in the supreme Dharma—
They attain those worlds of the *ātivāhika* beings here, and no others.

The fixed order of all things, as well as the sequence of death here, the experience of enjoyment resulting from the conduct of one's karma and qualities, and the measure of lifespan are described. (1)
He concludes by restating the answer to the question at hand with the words "Therefore," and so forth.
Those who know reality are the knowers of the object to be known. The supreme [state] arises from the practice of yoga. || 1 ||
How can this state of a physical body, consisting of false delusion, attain stability in the Truth? How can shadows exist in the sunlight? (2)

One might ask: "In the worlds of Brahmā and others that are *ativāhika* (conveying), why should there not be the emergence of a superior body here as well, due to long-standing practice? To this he replies: "ādhibhautika... [and so on]. In such scriptural passages as, "The fire-nature of fire has departed; the three forms alone are the truth; the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed the truth, and of them, this [Self] is the Truth," the gross is shown to be subsumed within the subtle.

The meaning is that, because it has been stated [in the Upanishads] through the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) and so forth that [the subtle body] is superimposed, it is "real" in relation to the gross body; this occurs when the state of the *ātivāhika* (conveying) body is attained due to the excellence of merit. || 2 ||
Līlā, who knows all that is to be known and has taken refuge in the supreme Dharma, went to the city prepared for her husband solely for that purpose. || 3 ||
If it is asked, "In that case, how does the manifestation of a physical body (ādhibhautika-dehatva) occur for Līlā after she has attained the lotus? he says:
"Līlā... The indeclinable "no," which carries the sense of the negative particle *na*, is connected to both sides according to the maxim of the "lamp on the threshold" (*dehalī-dīpaka*).
[She is] supreme, born of yoga. || 3 ||
Prabuddhalīlā said:
"O Mother, let her depart in this manner; behold my husband."
Since he has set out to give up his life, what remains to be done here now?
Having accepted what the Queen had said, yet considering the uncertainty of life indicated by the sight of the king’s death to be untenable, Līlā spoke, beginning with "evam" (so be it):
"Let that which was described as 'she has departed' be so—that is, let it be acceptable according to the manner you have stated. [As for] the husband..."

"Behold directly how he has set out to give up his life! In this matter, what indeed should be done now? What is the justification here?"—this is the sense. The intention of the question is not "What should be done by me now," for that would be inconsistent with the other questions and because no instruction regarding the duty to be performed is given in the reply. || 4 ||
How has the necessity of entities arisen regarding their existence and non-existence? And how, moreover, has the lack of necessity, as indicated by death, birth, and so forth, come to be? (5)

Regarding entities such as the body and so forth, how did destiny first come into being amidst states such as life and happiness, and states such as suffering and misfortune; and furthermore, how has even non-destiny (indeterminacy) subsequently come into being? || 5 ||
How is there the establishment of intrinsic nature? How does existence reside in categories of things? How is there heat in fire and so forth? How is there stability in earth and so forth? (6)

[Objection: Let there be no necessity; let there simply be non-restriction. To this, he says: "How so? The nature [of things] is such that water is cold and fire is hot, and so forth. The necessity consists in the existence and positive character belonging to objects such as jars and the like.
How is there coldness in snow and such things? What is existence in time, space, and so forth? How can there be the perception of existence and non-existence, or of the gross and the subtle? (7)

How can there be perceptions by the seer of such rules as: the apprehension of an existent thing like real silver; the rejection of a non-existent thing like shell-silver; the grossness of earth and so forth; and the subtlety of the mind, the senses, and so forth? (7)
How is it that things such as grass, shrubs, and humans do not attain ultimate height, even though their own cause for height remains present, despite the presence of undesirable factors? (8)

"Excessive height" refers to extreme vertical length, like that of a *śāla* or *tāla* tree. The meaning is: even when the cause for its own height is present, since there is no fixed rule regarding what is desired or undesired, why should there not be a total lack of confidence in all things?
The Goddess said:
When the great dissolution has occurred and all objects have set,
only the eternal Brahman remains, as the infinite space that has reached ultimate peace.

If the world possessed the nature of a single reality, then such a fixed necessity would prevail everywhere; or if it were purely unreal, having as its sole nature mere illusion, then there would be absolute lack of necessity.
However, because its unmanifested nature (*avyakta-prakṛti*) is a mixture of the real and the unreal, it possesses the nature of both the real and the unreal.

Desiring to establish that [the world] remains fixed solely through the arrangement of the transformations (*vivarta*) of consciousness (*cit*) in accordance with the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the enjoyer (*bhojaka*), the Goddess states the sequence of the transformations of pure consciousness for that purpose, beginning with the words "mahāpralaya... (verse 9).
By virtue of its nature as consciousness, it perceives itself as "I am a spark of light," just as you do in a dream, perceiving such things as traveling through the sky.
By the term "particles of light" (tejaḥkaṇa), the subtle elements are meant, which are luminous because they are pervaded by pure consciousness (śuddhacid). It perceives and experiences. || 10 ||
This spark of light attains grossness within itself by itself;
this very thing is known as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which is unreal yet appears as real.

This Self, which has become a particle of radiance, attains grossness within the coverings of water and so forth—which are imagined as non-self, being distinct from the Self—and acquires it through such imagination; the meaning is that this very grossness is what is perceived here as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 11 ||
Therein, he knows that inner Brahman, thinking, "I am this Brahman.
Then he creates a kingdom of the mind; thus, his own self becomes this very world.

Within that Brahmāṇḍa, that Brahman known as Hiraṇyagarbha exists together with the fourfold [empirical world]— as stated in the previously cited Smṛti— and through its inward-turned aspect, He knows "I am Brahman"; yet,
through that very aspect which is defiled by external latent impressions, He manifests in the form of a creative resolve (saṃkalpa) for creation according to the karma of living beings.
And he forms a mental kingdom; this very mental kingdom is one whose volition is true—the meaning is that this world is such a mental kingdom. || 12 ||
In that first creation, whatever cognitions were manifested in whatever manner and wherever, they remain there even today, exactly as they were, unshakable. (13)
Those functions of consciousness which consist of volitional thoughts—whether they take the form of specific rules or lack such rules—have manifested as they were;
even now, they remain exactly so, unmoving and unaltered. (13)
In whatever manner the mind manifests, in that very manner it becomes the self-consciousness;
by its own nature, without restriction, it may become this or that, for here there is nothing whatsoever [other than it].

[Objection: But since the mind consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of various forms, when such a volition (*saṃkalpa*) arises, how can there be a corresponding illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of the self’s consciousness (*ātmacaitanya*)? To this he says: "That which... and "by itself.
This is because the consciousness of the self has the inherent nature of conforming to its own pure limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Therefore, nothing whatsoever arises with an unregulated nature.
This is the meaning. || 14 ||
Moreover, it is not logical that there should be a state of nothingness for that which possesses all forms;
for how indeed could gold remain after having abandoned all its configurations? (15)

With the intention that the necessity [of the world] is established even by the manifestation of the universe—which exists in an eternal and fixed form within Brahman variegated by *māyā*—he says, "And not... The remainder of the sense is: "the state of being nothingness," which is the emptiness of all things, is not tenable even at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*). For if that were the case, the status of [Brahman] as the cause would be contradicted; this is expressed through the figure of *arthāntaranyāsa*.

He demonstrates this with the words "having abandoned" (*tyaktvā*). How could gold remain after abandoning all its configurations, such as being a bracelet (*kaṭaka*), an armlet (*rucaka*), or a lump (*piṇḍa*)? The meaning is that since all configurations are included within it, it is impossible for anything [of those configurations] to be abandoned. || 15 ||
Just as at the beginning of creation, consciousness itself shone within itself,
so too does it remain even now by its own existence, appearing as snow, fire, and so forth.
The meaning is that just as coldness, heat, and so forth, having been manifested through their own nature, remain even today determined by that very nature. || 16 ||
Therefore, it is not logical for that which exists to abandon its own being;
since consciousness remains, this necessity does not perish. (17)

Furthermore, if Brahman, variegated by *māyā*, were to abandon its own substratum-existence (*svādhiṣṭhāna-sattā*), then the constraints contained within that *māyā* would become non-existent. Showing that this is simply impossible, he concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). [This refers to] the existent Brahman variegated by *māyā*. It does not perish; it cannot be denied.
...up to [verse] 17.
Just as something that has been imagined appears there as if it were made of earth, even though it is of the nature of space,
it is not possible for it to move from its state at the beginning of creation until this very day.
With the intention that the very stability of the earth and other elements serves as the illustration for the non-subversion of necessity, he says: "That which... (verse 18).
Whatever way consciousness manifests, for one who knows the antidote— [or for one whose mind is the antidote, in both cases]—
it does not deviate from that state by itself, due to the cultivation of feeling. (19)
Because the reversal of the certainty of life is seen through the certainty of death, he says: "He leads away those who know the antidote. [1] 19.
That which is experienced here in this world was unproduced from the very beginning;
it is the manifestation of the sky of consciousness, like the sexual union with a woman in a dream. (20)

And all this has been stated from the perspective of the illusory view; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the world itself does not exist—so where is there any room for the imposition of necessity?
With this intention, he says: "The world... (verse 20).
"This manifestation stands as nothing but the unreal, yet appearing as real;
such is the perfection of its own nature—thus are the experiences of beings. (21)

Thus, "certainty" (*iti-niścaya*) itself is the perfection of one's own nature (*svabhāva-saṃpatti*), which is the attainment of one's true form. The meaning is that "beings" (*bhūta*) and "experiences" (*anubhūti*) are cognitions of things as they truly exist. Alternatively, according to the manner previously described, "certainty" (*iti-niyati*) is the perfection of one's own nature, while "beings" and "experiences" refer to the experiences of objective entities such as birth, death, and so forth.

That continuous stream of the manifestation of consciousness which was established at the beginning of creation remains even today unshaken by anything else; this is called *niyati* (the principle of necessity).

With the intention that this very meaning is established even upon a careful consideration of the meaning of the word *niyati*, he says: "At the beginning of creation," etc. By another [factor], namely an opposing one. *Acalitā* means unaltered or not inverted. In the reading *āvalitā*, it means joined or united with another distinct entity; for example, birth and life are necessarily joined with death.

Independently; that is to say, just as coldness and heat meet precisely through their state of opposition, so too do action and its factors meet through the relationship of the goal and the means. || 22 ||
The consciousness-space that has grasped the perception of space has attained the state of space;
the consciousness-sky that has grasped the perception of time has attained the state of time.
He demonstrates the stated meaning by providing an illustration—beginning with the word "gṛhītā" (grasped).

That consciousness-space (*cidvyoman*) by which the perception of space (*vyomasaṃvitti*) was grasped—that is, accepted at the beginning of creation and manifested in the form of space—is described as such. The same applies to what follows.
The space of consciousness, which perceives the apprehension of water, exists like water;
for just as in a dream a person perceives the appearance of water within himself.
He states that the conceptualization of the object of vision within the self that is the seer is well-established in one's own very self, saying: "In a dream... (24).
The consciousness of dream-appearance shines forth and exists exactly as it is; through the skill of the wonder of consciousness, it gathers together this [world] which is unreal.

Even in such a state, it remains exactly as it is, never deviating from its own nature. Why is this? Because the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*) possesses the skill characterized by the nature of non-attachment (*asaṅgasvabhāvatā*). Alternatively, the "wonder of consciousness" refers to *māyā*; because of its skill, that which is unreal is gathered together—that is, it is conceptualized as being real. || 25 ||
Consciousness itself internally perceives even the non-existent states of being a bedstead, water, earth, fire, or air,
just as it does in dreams, mental constructs, and meditations.
Listen to the sequence of experiencing the fruits of karma immediately after death, which brings about the welfare of the deceased and pacifies all doubts. (27)

Having thus established the other types of necessity (niyati), he now undertakes the description of the sequence of experiencing the fruits of karma in order to state that even the necessity of life is determined by one's actions and by the distinction between the ages (yugas), being fashioned by the will of the Lord as delimited by specific times; therefore, death does not constitute its destruction. Thus he says: "After death... and so forth.

The expression "after death" is used to indicate that as long as one is obstructed by the fruits of *prārabdha* karma until death, the karmas accumulated in that body are not capable of initiating their own results; however, once death occurs, the obstruction being removed, they begin to initiate their respective results according to their fitness. This is what is heard here.

For the sake of pacifying all your doubts, this [account], which is renowned in the world through your own mouth, is beneficial even at the time of death for others as well, because it generates a sense of faith. (27)
