In the primary creation (rūḍhādisarga), there is a fixed destiny (niyati) of one, two, three, or four hundred years for the lifespan of men in the eastern and other directions; hear from me that destiny.

The fixed limit of the lifespan of men, numbering four hundred years in the Kṛta age, three hundred in Tretā, two hundred in Dvāpara, and one hundred in the Kali age—this which was established at the beginning of creation—is the general rule; the meaning is that one should now hear the intermediate rules regarding its possible decrease or increase. || 28 ||
The purity or impurity of place, time, action, and substance regarding one's own deeds, as well as their deficiency or excess, are the causes of the lifespan of human beings. (29)

The meaning is that when the actions which serve as the cause for longevity become deficient due to impurity of place and so forth, there is a diminution of the fruit; conversely, through excellence of purity, there is an abundance of the fruit. || 29 ||
In this world, when the dharma of one's own karma declines, the lifespan of human beings declines;
when it increases, it attains increase; and when it is equal, it becomes equal. (30)

Thus, he states that even the non-performance of prescribed duties is a cause for the exhaustion of one's lifespan—beginning with the words "svakarma" (one's own duty). "Equal" means having the same number as is determined for each respective age. || 30 ||

Through actions that bring about death in childhood, a child dies; through those that bring about death in youth, a youth dies; and through those that bring about death in old age, an elder meets his end. (31)
He states that the performance of prohibited acts, like the non-performance of prescribed duties, is also a cause for the exhaustion of one's lifespan: "O child," etc. (Verse 31).
He who abides in his own duty as it has been undertaken according to the scriptures becomes a glorious vessel for a lifespan that accords with the scriptures. (32)
Thus, according to their karma, living beings experience here the final stage;
for one who has reached the end, there arise agonizing pains that cut through the vital organs. (33)

For a person who has reached the end of life— that is, for one who has attained the finality of his lifespan— there occur such "visible" (*dṛś*) pains from the severing of the vital points (*marmaccheda*), which are seen and directly experienced;
this occurs at the time when the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are withdrawn from all the channels of the body into the heart.
It is well known in the Purāṇas that the suffering experienced is equal to the pain of being stung by a thousand scorpions.
Prabuddhalīlā said: O moon-faced one, tell me briefly about death:
what is the pleasure of dying, or what is its pain, and what happens after one has died? (34)

The underlying intent of the question is as follows: has the suffering of death been described as being the same for all, or is there some happiness after death for certain individuals; and is the destination after death equal for everyone, or is it superior for yogins?
The illustrious Goddess said: At the end of the body, there are three kinds of persons who are about to die:
the fool, the practitioner of concentration (dhāraṇā), and likewise the person possessed of skillful means (yukti). || 35 ||
In order to provide an answer precisely according to the intent of the question, he classifies persons as "threefold.

One who practices *dhāraṇā*—the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and mind (*manas*) for a fixed period at the navel, heart, throat, between the eyebrows, and ending at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*)—is one who possesses skill (*yuktimān*). This refers to one capable of exiting at will or entering the bodies of others.
Furthermore, the yogi is one who has practiced skill in the specific exiting and entering through the channels that constitute the path for attaining his desired world. || 35 ||
Having practiced the dhāraṇās and being devoted to them, one who practices dhāraṇā and is likewise endowed with skill departs at ease after casting off the body.
In this regard, one who is devoted to *dhāraṇā* (concentration) is middling; by practicing the method (*yukti*) in due order, he proceeds happily.
However, the distinction is that one who is joined with the method (*yukti-yukta*), remaining in that very state, proceeds happily. This is the meaning. || 36 ||
He who has not attained the practice of *dhāraṇā* and is not possessed of the proper method is a fool; at the time of his own death, he meets with suffering, his mind being rendered helpless. (37)
Observing the fool, he describes his suffering with the verse beginning "dhāraṇā" (37).

One whose mind is intent on sense objects, contemplating the helplessness brought about by the onset of latent impressions, reaches a state of extreme wretchedness, like a lotus that has been torn asunder. (38)

Having attained helplessness and a lack of self-mastery of the mind through the onset of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), for this very reason, his inclination is toward sense objects and not toward the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). || 38 ||
One whose mind is not refined by the scriptures and who is devoted to wicked people experiences an internal burning upon death, like one who has fallen into fire. (39)
In that regard as well, he describes the excessive suffering of one who fails to perform what is enjoined: "Not by instruction... (39).
When this undiscriminating self undergoes a hoarse throat and deformity arising from its complexion and appearance, it then becomes dejected in mind. (40)
He states the indicative signs that characterize such a time of suffering with the words: "When... (verse 40).
It was utter darkness, devoid of light, where stars appeared even by day; the expanse of the quarters was filled with clouds, and the sky was dark as a thick rain-cloud.

The ellipsis "it becomes as if" applies to all [the following descriptions]. It is such that one has reached a supreme blindness where even by day the stars have risen; likewise, it is such that there is no light, being devoid of radiance, and for this very reason the sky is thickly darkened and turned black; and it is such that the expanse of the quarters of the horizon is filled with clouds. || 41 ||
His vision whirling, he was pierced by agonizing pain in his vital organs;
the earth became for him like the sky, and the expanse of the sky became like the earth.
"Vicchuritaḥ" means pervaded. || 42 ||
The circle of the quarters having revolved, he was as if being carried away upon the ocean, and with his mind on the verge of deep sleep, he was as if being led through the sky. (43)
The circle of the quarters, whose wheel of directions was whirling, was turned upside down by him. || 43 ||
As if fallen into a blind well, as if joined within a solid rock,
his own complexion becoming dull, he felt as if cut away in his very heart.

He was fallen, having reached [that state]; he was joined, having been ushered [into it]. Though desiring to speak of his own suffering, his syllables and letters were rendered unable to be uttered as he became paralyzed by a blockage of speech. Within his inner disposition, in his heart, he felt as if cut down, as if severed. || 44 ||
He seemed as if he were falling from the path of the sky like the [demon] Tṛṇāvarta when struck down,
or as if he had swiftly mounted a chariot and was about to tumble from the peak of the Himalayas.
"Tṛṇāvarta" refers to a whirlwind that turns grass; he was as if cast into it. "Hima" means a slab of ice; he was facing toward its melting, that is, its dissolution. (45)
As if explaining the cycle of existence, as if touching his kinsmen,
he stood like a wind-machine with its whirling propeller.

By the word "saṃsāra," its suffering is indicated. Explaining that [suffering] as if illustrating it for others by means of his own self, he speaks of it as being like a stone-throwing machine. || 46 ||
He was whirled about as if by a whirlwind, or dragged along as if by a rope;
he seemed to be spinning in a whirlpool of water, like one placed upon a mechanical weapon. || 47 ||
In the delusion of the wheel of transmigration, he is as if dragged and pulled by the rope of the tongue. || 47 ||
Like a blade of grass being swept away by the wind of a rain-cloud, or like one who has climbed up only to fall back into the ocean with a flood of water; (48)
It flows along with the Parjanya wind, as if falling into the ocean together with a flood of water. || 48 ||
As if falling into the infinite sky, into a chasm, or into a whirlpool, he remains experiencing a state of being turned upside down by the clouds and the earth. (49)
Experiencing what resembles the overturning of the earth, like the ocean falling incessantly—this is a metaphorical simile (*utprekṣikopamā*).
As if falling incessantly and as if leaping up on all sides,
his entire multitude of sense-organs became agitated by hearing the whistling sound.
*Sūtkāra* is the sound of sighing. || 50 ||
Gradually, all his sensory cognitions turn dark,
just as the quarters of the sky grow dim when the sun has set. (51)

Regarding the cessation of the eyes and other senses at the onset of his fainting, he says "gradually" (kramāt). For that dying person, all perceptions of the senses [attain] a darkening, which is to say, a state of turbidity. || 51 ||
He no longer knew what was before or behind him, as his memory had reached a state of exhaustion;
it was like vision lost in the eight directions at the end of the western twilight.
Tānava means emaciation. || 52 ||
Due to delusion, his mind loses its capacity for discernment;
through that lack of discrimination, he sinks into the great abyss of ignorance.
When he assumes delusion, then the vital air (pavana) does not take hold;
and when it does not take hold of the vital breaths (prāṇa), then he fully succumbs to delusion.
"Āmoha" means a slight fainting. "Pavanaḥ" refers to the vital breath (prāṇa); it does not take [it], that is, it does not seize it. The meaning is that it does not stiffen the limbs.
When even the vital breaths he has bowed down to are not taken up by him and cannot be moved, then [he experiences] "moha," which is a deep fainting. || 54 ||
Through the delusions of perception and ignorance, which mutually nourish one another, a living being attains the state of a stone; this has been established since the beginning of creation. (55)
Delusion (*moha*) is the lack of awareness of one's own true nature; perceptions are the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of objects;
and errors are appearances that manifest otherwise than they are. By these [factors], [the soul] attains "stoniness"—that is, insentience like a stone—beginning from the first creation.
Thus everything is fixed [in this state] (some manuscripts read: "everything remains thus").
The meaning is that it remains. || 55 ||
Prabuddhalīlā said:
For what purpose does this body undergo pain, delusion, fainting, wandering, disease, and unconsciousness, even though it possesses all eight limbs? (56)
The head, hands, feet, private parts, navel, and heart are the eight limbs; he who possesses these is likewise [eight-limbed]. || 56 ||
The Goddess said: "If such action was thus ordained at the beginning of creation by the consciousness of vibration, then why is there such suffering at this time after so much time has passed? (57)

By the Lord himself, whose primary nature is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) and who consists of the consciousness of vibration (*spanda-saṃvit*), an action characterized by volition (*saṃkalpa*) of the form to be described hereafter has been ordained: "At this time— whether in childhood, youth, or old age— and for such a duration, may such suffering be experienced by my own self, the individual soul (*jīva*) who is non-different from me."
The subsequent [inference] is by means of positive concomitance (anvaya). || 57 ||
Thinking "may this be mine," one enters into that which arises from its own nature like a thicket;
one perceives what is produced by the expansion of the mind, for there is no other cause here.

The meaning is that suffering—which arises solely from the nature of one's own volition (*svasaṃkalpa-svabhāva-ja*) and is produced by the expansion of the mind, like trees and shrubs imagined by the mind—the individual self (*jīva*), having entered into the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) itself, perceives and experiences it. || 58 ||
When, under the influence of pain, the channels within the body seize the vital air through their own contractions and expansions, it then abandons its natural state.

Having addressed the question, he says "yadā" (when) and so forth as a reply. Because the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) are filled with the essence of heated bile and other humors, they grasp the essence of the food and drink consumed in an irregular manner through their contraction and expansion according to that [disturbance]. At that time—
The vital air (māruta), which is the internal wind (samānavāyu), abandons—that is, relinquishes—its own state of equalizing the food, drink, and so forth that have been consumed.
When the winds have entered and do not exit, having gone they do not re-enter; when they abide within the channels (vināḍī), then through their vibration memory arises. (60)

When the winds have entered the openings of the channels and do not exit, or having exited, do not re-enter, then, upon the cessation of the activity of the channels, because they are no longer "channels" [in that state], there is no vibration of the eyes and other senses; thus, only memory remains, and not sensory cognition—this is the meaning. || 60 ||
When the wind does not enter at all and the breath does not exit due to the failure of the body's channels, then one is said to be dead. (61)

And he states that this deficiency of the channels is the cause of death through the obstruction of the movement of the vital breaths: "The wind does not enter at all. The *apāna* wind indeed enters with the body; when the *prāṇa* wind does not exit through the mouth and nostrils, then, because of the departure of the subtle body (*liṅga*), one is necessarily said to be dead.
This is the meaning. || 61 ||
The consciousness that has been previously determined— "I must meet my destruction by such-and-such time"— reaches its end when impelled by that very [determination] toward death.

Even in that case, he states that destiny alone—consisting of the prior mental resolve of consciousness—is the cause: "It is to be approached. [The subject] is one who possesses prior consciousness, meaning she has a previous resolve; she is impelled by that, meaning she is driven by such a destiny. || 62 ||
The seed-potency of consciousness born of creative ideation—such as "I shall become such-and-such in this way"—never undergoes destruction. (63)
[Objection: "But surely, upon the destruction of that *niyati* (the principle of necessity), the cosmic order would collapse. To this he replies with the word "consciousness" (*saṃvit*).

The seed-potency of *māyā*—which possesses the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of consciousness whose will is true—never perishes at any time; for its cessation occurs only together with [the liberation from] *mukti* and *kāla*. This is the intended meaning. || 63 ||
The very nature of consciousness is the act of cognizing, which is inseparable from it;
therefore, death and birth are not distinct from the consciousness that is one's own nature.

Even when considering the nature of the consciousness of the individual soul (jīva) which is conditioned by ignorance, the intention is that until liberation there is simply no cessation of birth, death, and so forth; with this in mind, he says: "of consciousness" (saṃvidaḥ). "Non-distinct" (avyatirekavān) means possessing non-separation—that is, the absence of disjunction. || 64 ||
In some places it is gentle yet veiled, and in others like water in a river;
thus this consciousness is sometimes gentle and sometimes characterized by the nature of a living being.

He describes the stream of consciousness of the transmigrating soul with the words "In some places" (kvacit). Just as the water in a river is in some places obstructed and turbid, while in other places it is gentle, steady, and clear, so too this consciousness is in some places gentle, but in others it is turbid with the passions of the individual soul, such as attachment and aversion; this is the meaning. || 65 ||
Just as the nodes of a long creeper appear at intervals along its length, so too do births and deaths occur within the continuum of conscious existence.
The joints of the dūrvā creeper are its knots. || 66 ||
The conscious person is never born and never dies;
it is only through delusion, like a dream or a confusion, that one perceives this [world]. (67)

And all this is from the perspective of ignorance (*avidyā*). But from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it says: "The wise one is neither born nor dies," according to such scriptural passages (*śruti*); this is the meaning. || 67 ||
The person (puruṣa) is mere consciousness; when and how could he ever perish? For if he were distinct from consciousness, what else could the person be? (68)
He establishes his immortality through reasoning as well, beginning with the words "The Person" (*puruṣa*).

On the position that the Person is indeed distinct from consciousness, what else could the Person be? Is it the body, or the vital breath (*prāṇa*), or the sense organs (*indriya*), or the mind (*manas*), or the intellect (*buddhi*), or the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and the thinking faculty (*citta*), or perhaps the presiding deities (*devatā*) of those respective [faculties]?

Moreover, [the alternative of] ignorance [is untenable]. The meaning is that, since in all these positions the entire range of worldly activity—which is insentient and dependent upon the manifestation of human effort—cannot be sustained, the position remains established by process of elimination that the Puruṣa is nothing but pure consciousness. || 68 ||
Tell me, who has ever died until this day? To whom does consciousness belong, what is it, and how does it die?
While millions of bodies perish, consciousness remains imperishable.

With the intention that the death of a conscious being cannot be established because a death occurring without a witness is unproven, he says: "Who has seen it today? The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "In this beginningless saṃsāra, up to the present limit—that is, until today—who has seen a conscious being die? Furthermore, what is that death? Is it destruction, or is it the attainment of another body?

Even in the first case, how can there be the destruction of the conscious being? Is it by itself or from another? Not the first, because there is no contradiction within itself; the meaning is that for that which is unattached (*asaṅga*), such [destruction] is impossible through another. Regarding the second, he says: "They die" (verse 69).
If that [mind] were to die while one [person] alone was dead, then the mind would not die;
for upon the death of one here, there would be the death of all beings.

He also precludes the death of the conscious self by means of an undesirable consequence: "it would have died. Since there is no evidence for a plurality of conscious selves in each body, and because of scriptural texts such as "The one God is hidden in all beings," when that particular conscious self dies, [the world]—which has its existence and manifestation dependent upon it—[would perish].
The collective and individual mind would surely have perished. For what purpose is the word *vai* used with an interrogative intonation (*kākvā*)?

It means "would it not have perished? And if that [mind] were dead, since the existence of the world is impossible without its material cause (*nirupādāna*), there would be the fault of the death of all things upon the death of one.
The meaning is: "How could it not have been? || 70 ||
Whatever variety of latent impressions (vāsanā) the individual soul (jīva) experiences by itself,
it is precisely for that [variety] that the two names "birth" and "death" are conventionally assigned.
If that is so, what then are life and death as they are perceived? To this he says: "Vāsanā" [is the cause]. Life is the living being (jīva). || 71 ||
Thus, no one dies and no one is born;
the living soul merely wallows in the pits of the whirlpool of latent impressions (vāsanā).
He concludes what has been established with the word "evam" (thus). || 72 ||
And because the object of perception is absolutely impossible, that latent impression (vāsanā) is destroyed only when it has been firmly known through the inquiry that "it does not exist at all. (73)
The meaning is that the knower, whose nature is the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), perishes indeed when it becomes even more firmly established in conceit (abhimāna). || 73 ||

Having correctly perceived through spiritual practices the continuous flow of the world as neither arisen nor ceased, the living soul is indeed free from unarisen latent impressions regarding the fear of existence.
"One becomes liberated"—this is a real entity in this world. (74)
The qualified soul, having attained the means such as detachment from the fear of worldly existence,

perceives through the right vision of reality— by practicing hearing and other methods under a guru— that the continuous manifestation of the world, which has arisen through delusion, is in fact unarisen from the perspective of ultimate truth.

The meaning is that by the eradication of the root, one who is entirely free from the latent impressions of duality becomes liberated; thus, it is the very nature of the liberated self that is the true reality here, and nothing else. || 74 ||
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Reflection on Death," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 54.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Reflection on Death," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
(263) Chapter Fifty-Five:
Prabuddhalīlā said:
O Goddess of the Gods, tell me how a living being dies and how it is born again, for the further increase of my understanding. (1)
Herein is described the diversity of the soul's course through saṃsāra,
as well as the Lord’s state from the initial creation onwards, which conforms to that karma.
The meaning is: "Tell it again in detail," which has already been stated. Its fruit is the increase of awakening through the excellence of dispassion. || 1 ||
The Goddess said:
When the flow of the channels is disturbed and a person experiences a state of deranged wind,
then his consciousness indeed seems to become extinguished.

The "disturbance" (*visaṃsthiti*) of the vital breaths refers to their state of being contrary to their natural motion; that is to say, their cessation. It is as if they become tranquil due to the dissolution of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which manifests them. The meaning is based on the Vedic scripture: "Having arisen from these elements, one perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death. || 2 ||
For pure consciousness is eternal; it neither arises nor ceases.
It abides in the stationary and the moving, in space, in the mountain, in fire, and in the wind.

In reality, however, it does not subside anywhere; thus he says, "pure. The sense is that this is based on the Vedic scripture: "O, this Self is indeed indestructible, for its nature is non-perishable. || 3 ||
When the movement [of the body] ceases solely due to the obstruction of the vital breath (vāyu), then this body, known as "insentient" (jaḍa), is said to be dead. || 4 ||
And thus, he states that death is a property of the body alone and not a property of the self: "merely," etc. (verse 4).
When that body has become a corpse and the vital air has returned to the state of mere wind,
consciousness, freed from latent impressions, abides in the reality of its own self.

In the bodily wind (*vāta*), [the breath] attains the state of *anila*, which is its own nature as the great wind (*mahāvāyu*). But the *prāṇa*, together with its radiance (*tejas*), dissolves into the *prājña-ātman* alone. He says "consciousness" (*cetana*) to show that upon the dissolution of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the individual soul (*jīva*) also remains in the state of the Supreme Self (*paramātman-bhāva*) along with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*). And so says the Śruti: "Now, when he is departing..."
"Speech merges into the mind; the mind into the breath; the breath into heat; and the heat into the supreme deity."
The name "jīva" is given to that subtle atom (aṇu) which possesses latent impressions (vāsanā);
it resides in that very place, as well as in the chamber of the corpse and in the sky.
Now, if he remains established in the reality of his own Self, then he would be liberated and would be Brahman itself, not a *jīva*; to this, he says:

"Of that [Self] when delimited by those [limitations], the name 'jīva' is used. The meaning is that in reality there is no such thing as a *jīva* other than Brahman. For this very reason, by the power of its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), even while remaining in its own place...

With the intention that the superimposition of going to the next world and so forth does not imply that actual going exists, he recalls the analogy of the space within a pavilion: "He rests right there. (6)
Therefore, it is designated by the term "preta" by those engaged in worldly discourse;
it consists of consciousness mixed with latent impressions (vāsanā), abiding like a fragrant breeze.

Therefore, [it ceases] precisely upon the death of the body. Now, one might ask: "How can there be the persistence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in that which is unattached? To this he says: "consciousness" (*cetana*). The meaning is as follows: just as fragrance resides only in the extremely subtle pollen of a flower, yet the wind remains mixed with that fragrance through the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of an identity with it, so it is here. || 7 ||
When one remains within another state of vision, having abandoned this visible world,
then that [vision] is like a dream or a mental construction, lacking any objective form.

The meaning is this: when that living being (jīva), having abandoned this previous visible body and so forth, abides in another perception consisting of a different body and so on, then— just as in a dream— he himself assumes various forms such as the journey produced by his own latent impressions (vāsanā), the next world, and the objects of enjoyment therein.
In that very place, remaining mindful as before,
at the very moment the death-faintness ends, he beholds another body.
He begins to explain that very superimposition (adhyāsa) in sequence, starting with the words "tasminneva" (on that very [Self]).
"As before" means as in a previous birth. || 9 ||
Within the self, there exists nothing other than the pot and the void;
the sky and the earth together with the moon, the fly-whisk, and the day [or the moon and the fly-whisk].

Now, one might object: "Even if the construction of another body were possible in that extremely small place of death, how can there be the possibility of encompassing a distant journey or the vastness of the next world? To this he says: "In the Self" (ātmani).
[It is like] the dense, expansive, and solitary void, or the two—the sky and the surface of the earth.
Whether it be the sky, the hare-marked moon, the day, or even hundreds of thousands of millions of cosmic eggs, let them all enter within simultaneously;
nevertheless, the manifestation of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) other than the Self is indeed possible within the Self.
This is because the Self is infinite and because Māyā possesses the power to bring about the impossible.

Thus, by reflecting on the nature of the self (*ātman*), it is stated that the entire universe can be contained within even a small space; the sense is that this does not depend merely upon the dimensions of that space. Alternatively, if such things as paths and the next world exist in that space, why are they not perceived by others? To this, he says: "In the self" (*ātmani*).

In the case of a dead man, both the sky and the earth, along with the moon, the day, and the entire world, exist within his own self as if nourished in a jar by the clouds; yet to the sight of another, there is only the empty space of the house, and thus there is no possibility of perceiving those other things.
The meaning is "attachment to seeing. || 10 ||
There are six kinds of pretas; hear this classification of them:
those who have committed ordinary sins, those who have committed middling sins, and those who have committed gross sins. || 11 ||
In order to explain the different types of destinies, he classifies the pretas [with the words] "they become" (bhavanti). || 11 ||
There are common qualities, middle qualities (the term *madhyama* is used here as a Vedic archaism for *chanda-bhaṅga*), and those possessing supreme qualities;
of these, some possess one, while others possess two or even all three.
Among these, the distinction (*bheda*) of any one is its particularity (*viśeṣa*). What is that? For some there are two distinctions;
for example, being a sinner of ordinary degree for a certain time, and thereafter a sinner of middling or extreme degree.
According to the method stated, for some there may even be all three distinctions, either in sequential or reverse order. || 12 ||
Someone who has committed a great sin experiences for a year a state of fainting memory;
utterly deluded within, he is like one whose heart is made of stone. (13)
Therein, he first states the destiny of the third [type]: "Someone" (kaścit). "A year" (vatsaram) means for just one full year.
Then, after a long time, that perfectly awakened one experienced for a long duration the inexhaustible suffering of hell, which had arisen from the womb of latent tendencies.
Having experienced hundreds of wombs and passed from one misery to another,
one occasionally finds rest amidst the delusion of this dream-like saṃsāra.

"Having eaten," it is said. And thus says the Śruti: "Now, those here whose conduct is foul, they quickly attain a foul womb—either the womb of a dog, or the womb of a pig, or the womb of a Caṇḍāla. "Peace" (śama) means the cessation of the fruits of great sins. || 15 ||
Alternatively, at the end of the delusion of death, they experience that very state— agitated by hundreds of dull sufferings—
which exists within the heart and, in an instant, becomes situated in trees and other such things.
[The reading is: "te" || 16 ||
"In an instant"—and this is from another perspective. (16)
Having experienced sufferings in hell that correspond to their own latent impressions (vāsanā),
they are thereafter born from wombs on the earth after a long time.
Now, he who is of middling evil, immediately after the delusion of death, experiences for some time a state of stupor accompanied by a belly made of stone. (18)
He states the course of the second [type] with the words "atha" (now). "Śilājaṭhara" means like the interior of a stone; "jāḍya" means a swoon. || 18 ||
Then, having awakened after some time or even at that very moment,
he will enter the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) after experiencing births in the wombs of animals and other such states in succession.
"At that very moment" is a statement from the perspective of another. || 19 ||
Only a certain person who has committed an ordinary sin experiences [the result] after death,
assuming an unimpaired body in accordance with his own latent impressions (vāsanā).

He states the destiny of the first [type of person] with the words "the deceased. "The body" refers to the human body and so forth, according to the Vedic scripture (Śruti) stating, "By both [the breath and the body], one goes to the world of men. || 20 ||
He perceives it as such, like a dream or a mental construction;
and at that very moment, his memory arises in this way: || 21 ||
It intends and experiences; thus, in the manner previously described. || 21 ||
But those who possess supreme and great merit, immediately after death and delusion,
experience heaven and the city of the Vidyādharas through mindfulness.
He states the destiny of the sixth type: "But those who... By *smṛti* means by the awakening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of merit. || 22 ||
Then, having experienced the fruit of their own karma elsewhere— which corresponds to their other actions—
they are born in the world of men, which is prosperous and the abode of virtuous people.

Thereafter, immediately following the experience of great merit and enjoyment, whatever other slight merit or demerit has been accumulated, its corresponding and suitable fruit [is experienced] elsewhere, in the regions such as Ilāvṛta, Kimpuruṣa, and so forth. (23)
And those who possess middling qualities, immediately after death and delusion, being enveloped by ether and wind, proceed to the sprout of a medicinal herb.

He states the destination of the fifth [type]: "And those who... This means that they go with the bodies of Kinnaras, Kiṃpuruṣas, Yakṣas, and so forth, to forests such as Nandana and Caitraratha, which are preeminent for their medicinal herbs and sprouts (oṣadhipallava).
There, having enjoyed beautiful fruits and having entered the hearts of men...
They preside over the seminal fluids within the womb, according to the sequence of births.
Having enjoyed the beautiful fruit of their own karma, at the end they enter into rice, barley, and so forth on earth by way of wind, rain, and other elements;

having become food, they enter the hearts of men—such as Brahmins and others—and through the emission of semen, they take up residence in the wombs of women. Now, those here whose conduct has been pleasant...
"For it is near that they would attain a pleasant womb—either the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, or the womb of a Kṣatriya, or the womb of a Vaiśya," so says the Śruti. || 25 ||
In accordance with their own latent predispositions, these hungry ghosts experience this state internally,
both sequentially and non-sequentially, at the end of their fainting spell.
Considering that by this [explanation] the course of the fourth [type of person] has also been stated almost entirely, he concludes with the words: "one's own latent impressions."
At first, they perceive, "We have died"; subsequently, through the offering of funeral cakes and other rites for their kinsmen, they come to realize, "We have been reborn. (27)

Now, he specifically shows the sequence of their ascent starting from death with the verse beginning "In the beginning" (ādau) and so forth. The phrase "they are understood to have arisen—that is, to have attained a completed body"—is to be supplied everywhere [in the subsequent verses] according to that sequence, namely, the sequence of rites performed during the ten days of cremation. || 27 ||
Then [he thinks]: "These are the servants of Yama, equipped with the nooses of Time;
being led away by them, I shall go in due course to the city of Yama. (28)
"Supplied with provisions by these servants of Yama through the performance of śrāddha rites and libations in due order, I shall go to the city of Yama within a year. (28)
The meritorious person repeatedly enjoys beautiful gardens and celestial palaces, which are divine and acquired through their own past actions. (29)
He is meritorious, possessed of supreme merit. || 29 ||
The sinner realizes that he has encountered masses of snow, thorns, chasms, and forests of sword-leaves—all of which have arisen from his own evil deeds. (30)
"This path before me is pleasant to traverse, with its cool grassy meadows, lush shade, and ponds," [thinking thus] is the intermediate [type of traveler]. (31)
"Saumya-sampātā" means it is suitable to travel on foot with ease; "saraṇiḥ" means a path.
It is understood that the "madhyamaḥ" is the meritorious one. || 31 ||
"This is the city of Yama; here I am, this lord of beings.
Here, the examination of one's karma has been performed"—thus he experiences. (32)

"Here I am, having reached the city of Yama. That Yama is world-renowned; he is the one standing before me. Here, in this assembly hall of Yama, the examination of my karma has been conducted by Citragupta and others. (32)
Thus, the vast fragment of saṃsāra approaches each [individual] separately, shining with the conduct of all things exactly as they exist without exception. (33)
And this process of superimposition is distinct for each individual, like a dream; thus he says: "iti" (thus).
It is radiant with all those objects, their respective behaviors, and their specific causal efficiencies—all of which exist as they are perceived, as if real, without exception. || 33 ||

Like space, it is utterly void; though possessing the nature of emptiness yet endowed with awakening, it is nothing at all, even while appearing radiant through the vastness of space, time, and action.
He says, "Like space," to show that upon observing the vision of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*), there is nothing whatsoever apart from the Self.

The meaning is that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), though appearing through the extension of space, time, and so forth, abides in the utterly void and formless [Self] as being *na kiṃcana*—nothing at all—but rather the Self alone, devoid of all superimpositions. || 34 ||
Thus, having been instructed in this way regarding the enjoyment of the fruits of my own actions, I shall go quickly from here either to auspicious heaven or indeed to hell. (35)

I have been directed and commanded by Yama to this place, in this direction, for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of one's own karma; that is, from here, from the assembly hall of Yama. || 35 ||
"Whether this heaven was enjoyed by me or this hell was experienced, these various wombs have been traversed; may I be born again in the cycle of worldly existence. (36)

That heaven which was pointed out by Yama has been experienced by me; those animal births and others pointed out by Yama have been experienced by me directly here before my eyes. Now, in this cycle of existence within the human world, I am being born again; I manifest once more. || 36 ||
"This rice plant was born as me; gradually I have become the fruit.
Thus, through the awakening of future insight, he will come to understand.
He states that sequence as follows: "This... Śāli is the sprout of rice. Having become a fruit through the sequence of the stalk, leaf, bud, and cluster, I remain. Now, one might ask:
is this state of being rice and so forth established by experience for him, just like the enjoyment of heaven, hell, and various wombs? He says, "No."

—Thus, "ityudarka" means that in the future human body (audarke), which occurs at a later time, he will become awakened through the enlightenment produced by the Śruti, Purāṇas, and so forth; this is the meaning. || 37 ||
Thus, with his faculties completely dormant, he attains the state of a seed within the man;
that seed, having fallen into the womb, becomes an embryo in the mother. (38)
To the question, "Why does it not then experience the state of rice and so forth? he says: "with its organs dormant.
Because of the absence of a body, its external and internal organs are completely merged [in latency]. The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of indicating this specific distinction.
In this very manner, having entered the human father's body by way of the food consumed, it attains the state of seed, that is, the condition of semen.
That embryo is born in the world according to its past karma;
whether it is destined for excellence or not, the infant appears with a graceful form. (39)
He elaborates on this very point according to past karma: "The fortunate one" (bhavya).
A *bhavya* is one endowed with happiness, good fortune, health, and virtuous conduct; the opposite of that is an *abhavya*. || 39 ||
Then she experiences youth, radiant as the moon and inclined toward passion;
thereafter, O lotus-faced one, she encounters old age, like a fallen thunderbolt from the cold-rayed moon.
It is moon-like, possessing the nature of waxing and waning like the moon, fickle, and beautiful. || 40 ||
From that too, there comes sickness and death, followed again by the fainting of death;
and once more, like a dream, one returns to the assumption of a body through the material elements (piṇḍas).
By means of the funeral rice-balls (piṇḍas) offered by his kinsmen for the sake of the deceased. || 41 ||
He goes again to the world of Yama and once more undergoes the cycle of wandering;
he experiences this repeatedly as various other wombs arise.
Thus, possessing the nature of space itself, he repeatedly experiences the intensely radiant state of coming and going until liberation, even while remaining in space alone.

Thus, the manner described is "ājavamjavībhāva," which means transformation or constant flux. This is derived from the root *ju* (meaning "to go") with the prefix *āṅ*, followed by the suffix *ac* (in the sense of a nominal action), and then the suffix *cvi*.

As for the reduplication and the shortening of the vowel, they should be understood as occurring either by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), or because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* class, or due to its Vedic character. || 43 ||
Prabuddhalīlā said: O Goddess, please tell me again out of your grace, for the increase of my understanding, how this delusion proceeds at the time of the original creation. (44)

[Objection: "Granted that this process of superimposition may occur with respect to the individual soul (jīva), which is the referent of the term *tvaṃ*, since error is possible there; but how can there be a process of superimposing the world upon the Lord (īśvara), the referent of the term *tat*, since error is impossible in His case? To provide knowledge for the purification of that [Lord], Līlā asks: "At the beginning of creation... (verse 44).

The Goddess said: The mountains are the solid mass of ultimate reality; the trees are the solid mass of ultimate reality; the earth is the solid mass of ultimate reality; the sky is the solid mass of ultimate reality. (45)

The superimposition of the world upon the Lord is not due to His delusion; rather, it is the manifestation (*vivarta*) of that which is by its own nature a dense mass of ultimate reality, appearing through its own inherent *māyā* as a form superimposed [upon it]. The appearance of the superimposed object occurs through the Lord’s own unobscured consciousness, and this is not a delusion (*bhrama*), but rather the appearance of the unreal as if it were real. This is always the case for the Lord.

Intending to show that there is no fault whatsoever— on the grounds that even though all objects appear due to omniscience, they do not appear as real in the world because such appearance is sublated by the cognition of the non-deviation from one's own true nature— the Goddess speaks the verse beginning with "paramārthaghanam" (dense with ultimate reality) in order to establish the superimposition upon that [first] term. || 45 ||
Since that Lord of Consciousness, whose nature is the self of all, arises in whatever manner, He becomes exactly so in each respective place, being the pure Self that is the supreme ether.
It arises and evolves; it exists thus from our perspective, not from its own perspective. 46.
At the beginning of creation, by the principle of the person in a dream, the primordial Lord of Creatures appeared clearly;
even now, existence remains just as it was then.

That very Lord, having become the first Prajāpati— the collective self of all individual souls (jīva-samaṣṭi)— according to the analogy of the person who fashions a dream, shines forth through the illusory manifestation (vivarta) of the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ as the essence of his creative resolve (sṛjya-saṃkalpa); likewise, even today, existence remains established by the persistence of such a state of being through that same creative resolve.
This first vibration is indeed the archetype (bimba) of all things;
that which is reflected from it remains established even today.

Even on the view that this existence of the world is distinct from the existence of the world [as conceived] in the purely volitional [state], he states that it is nonetheless false because it is equivalent to a reflection—beginning with the words "First" (prathamam). This vibration, which consists of the manifestation of the purely volitional, is an illusory transformation (*vivarta*). || 48 ||
The air that resides within those cavities of the bodies causes the movement of the limbs; therefore, one is said to "live. (49)
Regarding that, he states the cause for the division into the stationary and the moving with two verses beginning with "yannāma" (49).
From the very beginning of creation, this state has existed thus among moving beings;
therefore, even though they possess consciousness, these trees and such are motionless.
Motionless and devoid of activity. || 50 ||
This very sky of consciousness (cidākāśa) manifests as a portion arising from sentience; it alone becomes consciousness, while that which remains is not consciousness at all.
Thus, he states the reason even for the conceptualization of the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious: "The space of consciousness" (*cidākāśa*).

This very space of consciousness, which is the Lord (*īśvara*) himself, by means of being delimited by the thread-like adjunct of the intellect (*buddhi*)—or rather, through reflection—produces, as it were, a manifested portion (*udita-aṃśa*); that very portion is the division into individual souls (*jīva*) characterized by adjuncts (*aupādhika*). It is that same portion.
Consciousness is indeed sentience; however, the remainder is superimposed, and that sentience does not belong to it—it is rather insentient alone. This is the meaning. || 51 ||
If the city of Nara has been reached, it leads the eye-socket to consciousness; yet that life-force, which is the vision of the eye, does not truly live from the perspective of creation. 52.

He describes how that [Consciousness] enters into gross objects solely through the door of the intellect (*buddhi*), and how it becomes fit for external worldly activity by attaining the eyes and other senses— this he states with the word "nara" (man). That space of Consciousness which has entered into the intellect assumes, due to that intellect as its instrumental cause, a second form consisting of the human body and so forth, which serves as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and constitutes a "city."

Having reached and entered the city, it leads the intellect—which is seated within—the eye-socket and other sensory spheres, to the external objects; thus, through the medium of the functions of visual and other perceptions, it cognizes those external objects. Now, one might object: is it not the case that the eye and other senses themselves, by virtue of being directly superimposed upon consciousness (cit), possess the nature of consciousness and are therefore the individual soul (jīva)?

Having presided over the body, let it engage in worldly activity; what is the use of postulating a "jīva" (individual soul) conditioned by the intellect (*buddhi*)? He says "no"—it is not so. The eye—the collection of sense organs indicated by the word "eye"—is not itself consciousness (*cit*), the sentient being that has become the jīva. Why? Because from the very beginning (*sargataḥ*), nothing at all lives except through the mere superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of consciousness. Such being the case:
The intended meaning is that [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of even jars and the like being endowed with life. || 52 ||
Likewise, space becomes space, and earth attains its state as earth, just as water does; whatever the body conceives of freely, it experiences that very thing in that manner. (53)

Regarding the restriction that consciousness alone (*buddhi*) serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the individual soul (*jīva*) and nothing else, the author clarifies the underlying intention—that the cause is precisely the volition of Consciousness (*cit-saṃkalpa*), which ordains the powers of all things—by stating: "By the power of sustaining everything, it remains; and water [remains] by its nature as water. This means that just as water exists by virtue of its inherent capacity to be water, so too does the intellect remain as the adjunct of the soul through the power of the Supreme Consciousness to sustain all things. Thus, the specific determination of the capacities of all entities is established solely by the creative will of the Absolute.
The meaning is that it remains possessed of the power of nourishing everything; it perceives and wills. || 53 ||
Thus, contemplating with his entire body that the moving is moving by its nature as the moving, and the stationary is stationary by its nature as the stationary, he remains as the Self of all. (54)
While contemplating, intending, and being that very thing, he at that very moment became thus—[the reading "vivṛttaḥ" (turned away) is also found]—and remained so. || 54 ||
Therefore, that which is called "moving" possesses the nature of its own cognition;
by that [cognition] it is perceived, and consequently, it remains exactly as it was even until now. (55)
He says "therefore" and so forth in two verses [to show] that what was accomplished through cultivation continues even today.
Furthermore, that which was awakened under the name of "trees" and established as immobile—such as stones, trees, grass, and so forth—is even today still perceived as insentient. (56)

But there is no such thing as insentience existing separately, nor is there any sentience; at the beginning of creation, there is no distinction whatsoever, due to the nature of universal existence alone.

Thus, refuting the entire collection of differences superimposed upon the referents of the words *tattva* and *padārtha*, he says "But not... and so forth. "Cetana" means the insentient [world] qualified by consciousness (*cit*). Here, within this collection of categories, "creation" (*sarga*) means origination; from the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), stability and destruction are also included.
There is no difference among them, because that which is non-existent cannot serve as the locus of difference. Let it be, then, that [difference resides] in the persisting real entity (*sad-vastu*).
He says "no" [to this], stating: "in the case of the universal of existence (sattāsāmānyaka)" || 57 ||
The internal cognitions residing within trees and stones are indeed produced by the intellect and other faculties; such is the established position regarding them. (58)

Now, one might object: "If everything is indeed of the single essence of consciousness (*cidekarasa*), then how is it that everyone experiences within that very [consciousness] distinctions of name and form characterized by insentience (*jaḍatva*), which are its opposite?

Anticipating this doubt, the secret [of the matter] is as follows: it is solely due to the power of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) produced by the intellect (*buddhi*), which is superimposed through ignorance (*avidyā*) upon the inner, immediate consciousness (*pratyakṣasaṃvit*) of each individual.
First, he demonstrates this with respect to immobile things—beginning with "of trees. [This refers to] stones and mountains;

these are the forms of insentient matter, differentiated by name and form. The meaning is that the ultimate reality (paramārthasthiti) is that these things, such as trees and so forth, are merely fashioned and imagined by the intellect and other faculties, and do not exist in reality. || 58 ||

Because that intellect exists in such a state within the immobile and other beings, its meanings are established through other designations and conventions, even though they are not different from it. (59)
He states again clearly what has already been said: "vidaḥ" (of the knower). "Vidaḥ" means of direct consciousness (*pratyakṣa-vitti*).

The plural number is used because of the distinctions created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Since that [consciousness] exists in a fixed form among the cognitions of stationary beings and so forth—such as "I am a stationary being"—it is designated as "other than those who move."
Likewise, the objects of "abiding" and "conceit," being the referents [of words], exist through other linguistic conventions such as "trees," "mountains," and so forth. (59)
Whatever internal cognitions exist within worms, insects, and moths, those very things constitute their intellect and so forth, though they are designated by various names.
Thus, he reveals the secret even regarding moving beings with the words "worms, insects," and so forth.

The meaning is that those very self-consciousnesses (svasaṃvidas) arise as the objects of cognition and the like—namely, as the meanings of words—which are distinct from [the consciousness] itself. || 60 ||
Just as the people of the northern ocean know nothing at all of those situated on the southern ocean, except through their own individual experience. (61)
He provides an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) that supports both the meaning already stated and the forthcoming conceptualization of insentience (*jāḍya*), beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*).
The term "the people on the shore of the northern ocean" refers to a multitude of persons (*janasamūha*). || 61 ||
When all beings, both stationary and moving, are absorbed in the experience of their own perceptions and are solely intent upon their own conventions regarding one another, [then this occurs]. (62)

Just as in this illustration, so too all things, both stationary and moving, are merged and culminate in an experience witnessed by their own direct perception; they do not know anything imagined by another's intellect—this is the meaning. For this very reason, he says "mutually" (*parasparam*), indicating that in collective worldly interaction, they depend upon mutual convention (*saṃketa*). || 62 ||
Just as there is perception of frogs situated both inside and outside a rock, and likewise among those frogs dwelling within one another, which is unreal and insentient; so it is here. (63)

For this very reason, even the conceptualization of non-existence, insentience, air, space, and so forth within Brahman, which is of the nature of existence and consciousness, is logically consistent;
this too he demonstrates by means of an illustration with the words "just as" (yathā). || 63 ||
The mind, which is all-pervading and that which was perceived by the sky of consciousness at the beginning of creation, is this very wind that remains established here even today.

Just as in this illustration, so too at the time of dissolution, the collective mind (*samaṣṭicitta*) of the world—which is of the nature of all things, omnipresent, and merged within *māyā*—exists in its subtle state; and whatever was perceived by the space of consciousness (*cidvyoman*), which is the inner self of all, in whatever manner at the beginning of creation, that very thing remains even today in that same manner. That indeed is...
He elaborates [on this] with the words "the wind is the impeller," and so forth. Impelling means vibration. || 64 ||
That which is conceived as the void is space; therein is the wind, whose nature is vibration. Such conceptualizations regarding creation arise like [superimpositions] upon objects.

*Sauṣirya* is simply *suṣira*, meaning a cavity or aperture. The meaning is that within that [cavity] resides the wind (*māruta*), whose nature is vibration and which consists of the power of all action. Thus, by means of the wind characterized as described above, there is the movement (*īhā*)—that is, the motions—of all things; just as dry grass, leaves, and other such objects are set in motion by the wind. || 65 ||
But the mind, in the ultimate sense, abides within all things, both stationary and moving; it is only the movements [of the body] that come to be and cease through the winds.

Therefore, although there is in reality an equality of consciousness (*citta*) in both the stationary and the moving, he says "But the mind... to show that there is a distinction between them due to the presence or absence of agitation caused by the vital air (*vāyu*): "In the moving they exist; in the stationary they do not. (66)
Thus, in this world consisting of illusion, all objects are fragments of consciousness; just as they were at the beginning of creation and so forth, even now they remain exactly as they were.

Regarding this rule as well, he states that prior destiny alone is the cause, saying "evam" (thus): at the beginning of creation, i.e., in the primal creation, these "parts"—like rays—have thus manifested within consciousness, whether as active or inactive, and remain exactly so even today. || 67 ||
Just as the manifestation of the intrinsic nature of all diverse objects is unreal yet appears as real, so too has this been explained to you. (68)
He concludes the explanation of the realization of reality, which was introduced as a topic arising from the preceding inquiry, with the words "yathā" (just as). || 68 ||
"Look, King Vidūratha has likely set;
he enters the heart of your husband Padma, who is like a garlanded corpse. (69)

The word *prāyaḥ* indicates a conjecture (*vitarka*). Having set [the sun], that is, having died, he goes—that is, he proceeds—desiring to enter the lotus-bud situated within the heart of the lotus which has become a corpse covered by a garland of flowers. || 69 ||
Prabuddhalīlā said:
"O Queen of the Gods, by which path does this corpse go to the pavilion?
O most excellent one, let us both go quickly so that we may see him."
While we two are still looking at him, let us go quickly; we shall depart. || 70 ||
The Goddess said:
Abiding within the latent impressions of humanity, he who is composed of consciousness proceeds by resorting to the path, thinking, "I am this [person], and I am going far to another world. (71)
The latent impression (*vāsanā*) of being human is the latent impression of the "I" within the lotus-body; the sense is that otherwise, its attainment would be impossible.
(71) By this very path alone, as long as it is accepted, there is no severance of mutual desire, for it is bound by the ties of friendship. (72)
Sauhārda is affection; by that, the bond is formed—the cause of connection. || 72 ||
p. 267) 166 Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, when [the assembly] had become weary from the discourse that had been conducted,
When the supreme vision had spread and the sun of awakening had risen within the noble mind of the king’s excellent daughter,
Vidūratha became one whose mental dullness had dissolved.

When the noble and pure mind of Līlā, the daughter of the best of kings— whose nature was the vision of the supreme reality and the highest insight— had been relieved of fatigue by this discourse concerning her own true essence (svatattva),
and when the sun, characterized by awakening, had risen and spread its light, dispelling all torment; then...
The meaning is that Vidūratha, being insentient due to his mind having dissolved into the wise Self for a specific reason, became devoid of mental continuity and fainted unto death. || 73 ||

Thus ends the fifty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the State of Death in Saṃsāra," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa*, within the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 55.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the States of Saṃsāra and Death," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The fifty-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the meantime, the king’s pupils rolled back in their sockets.
With his dry, white lips remaining, he was left with nothing but a single body and life-breath. || 1 ||
In this [chapter], the departure of that king’s life, his journey to the city of Yama, the pursuit of those two [messengers], and the arrival at the city of the ancestors are described. (1)
When all the organs had fainted, he became such that only the subtle vital breath (prāṇa) remained as his single body within the physical frame. || 1 ||
Having the luster and color of withered leaves, his complexion was pale and wasted; he resembled the humming of bees, his face contorted by the gasping sound of his labored breath. || 2 ||
The humming of the bee was echoed by the sound of her sighing, which possessed a similar resonance; thus, the humming was made resonant by the whistling of her breath.
His mind has fallen into the blind well of the great swoon of death,
while the functions of all his senses, such as the eyes, remain hidden within.
One whose mental disposition (āśaya) has sunk as if fallen into a great blind well characterized by the stupor of death.
Like a figure depicted in a painting, he was visible only in form and devoid of consciousness;
with all his limbs motionless, he was as if carved out of stone.
He describes its subsequent state with the word "variegated" (citra): like an image carved upon a stone slab. || 4 ||
What is the use of saying more here? With only a small portion of his body remaining, his life-force abandoned him, like a bird dwelling in the sky leaving a tree about to fall.

By means of a slender portion—that is, by resorting to only a small part for the purpose of departing—the vital breath abandoned that royal body, just as [a bird] leaves its own tree which serves as its dwelling place. || 5 ||
With their divine vision, those two young women saw him situated in the sky—
life itself, consisting of vital breath, like a trace of fragrance in the wind.

Those two fools beheld that life-force situated in the sky; it was consciousness, consisting of breath and conditioned by the function of the sense of smell, abiding in the wind like a subtle fragrance or a trace of scent.
That consciousness of life, having merged with the wind in the sky,
began to travel far through the ether, following its latent tendencies.
By means of the wind, that is, the subtle vital breath (ātivāhika-prāṇa). || 7 ||
Then he followed that very pair of women who were the consciousness of the living being,
like a pair of bees clinging to a trace of fragrance carried by the wind.
Then, when the fainting caused by death had subsided in just a moment,
he became conscious in the sky through a breeze carrying a trace of the fragrance of awareness.
Consciousness is the consciousness of the individual soul; it perceived [itself] as if in a dream, by means of a body composed of latent impressions.
He saw the messengers of Yama leading away his body,
and he perceived his own body as having been born from the offering of funeral cakes and other gifts.

He perceived his body—the physical frame consisting of the subtle impressions—as if it were a gross body that had been brought back to life by the funeral rites of the ancestors, specifically through the offering of rice-balls by his kinsmen. || 10 ||
On the way, he reached the city of Vaivasvata, which stood at a very great distance, shining with the fruits of karma and surrounded by living beings.

He reached the city of Vaivasvata, the capital of Yama, known as Karmaphalollāsa—so called because it causes the fruits of the actions of living beings to blossom and manifest—situated on the southern path at an exceedingly great distance, reachable only after a year's journey. || 11 ||
Then Yama, having reached the city of Vaivasvata, commanded:
"There are never any inauspicious deeds whatsoever belonging to this man."
"He commanded" means he gave orders; it is understood from the context that he did so after reflecting upon the deeds. "Aśubhrāṇi" means dark or black; that is to say, sinful. || 12 ||
This man is a constant performer of pure and auspicious deeds;
he has been further strengthened by the boon of you, Sarasvatī.
Of those who are pure, untainted by defects such as greed and the like. || 13 ||
"In Kusumāmbara, his former body exists as a corpse;
let him go there and enter it—let him be abandoned [of this life] with such a thought. (14)
Thus, with minds following the manner I have described, let him be abandoned by the soldiers;
it is understood from the context that this occurs either when Līlāsarasvatī has vanished within or when she remains outside awaiting his arrival. || 14 ||
Then, abandoned in the path of the sky, it fell like a stone released from a machine;
thereafter, the triad consisting of Jīva-kalā, Līlā, and Jñapti remained in the ether.
Released from the catapult, he was cast into the path of the sky like a stone hurled by a machine. || 15 ||
The streak of life, however, flew upward; she did not see those two in their embodied forms as they followed her alone, leaping across the expanse of the sky.
The two beautiful women, Jīvalikhā and Rūpiṇī, did not perceive those two [Jñapti and Līlā] as being the King;
however, from the word "tu" (but), it is understood that they [the two women] did perceive her. || 16 ||
Having quickly passed beyond other worlds and emerged from the house of the universe,
he reached a second world and arrived at its terrestrial sphere.
Having emerged from that world-house, the cosmic egg, and having reached a second world-egg;
Those two, whose forms were composed of volition, united with the thread of life and reached the pavilion of the Līlā inner apartments in the city of Padmarāja.
In an instant, they both entered at their ease, like two streaks of wind entering a lotus,
as the rays of the sun enter a lotus, or as a fragrant breeze enters [a flower]. (19)

In the expression "ambuja" and "ambhoja," although there is a difference in the mere sound of the words for the act of entering, because of the difference between the two agents of entry—the wind-current and the solar radiance—this is a "garland simile" (mālopamā) due to the difference in the objects of comparison. || 19 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, how did he reach that house near the corpse?
And how was the path recognized by him, whose body was dead?

Rāma, being doubtful about the knowledge of the path for the soul of the king—since the showing of the way had previously been mentioned for the daughter of Vidūratha-līlājīva but not for the king's soul—asks: "O Brahmin! (20)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, why indeed does that man not reach his own house, since all of that remains within his heart as a corpse situated inside his own latent impressions (vāsanā)?

With the intention that even while the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the previous body have not yet departed, once they are exhausted through the experience (*bhoga*) arising from the manifestation of another birth in the interim by means of powerful *prārabdha* karma, it is possible for the path as previously attained to manifest again due to the resurgence of those former impressions; thus Vasiṣṭha said:
All that pertained to his path and so forth was present within the heart—that is, it manifested clearly within the heart—of that soul who was of such a nature. || 21 ||
Who indeed does not see that this world, numbering nothing more than mere delusion, resides within the belly of a living atom like a banyan tree from a single seed? 22.
It exists within the interior of the subtle internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva), in the form of manifested latent impressions (vāsanā).

Just as one sees a banyan tree—which, though like the living soul itself, exists within the seed—arising by its own nature in the form of a sprout upon obtaining the causal complex of earth, water, and so forth, and experiences it as if within one's own interior; even so [is this]. || 22 ||
Just as one whose body is alive perceives the sprout within the seed in the heart,
so too does the atom of consciousness perceive the entire collection of the three worlds as its own inherent nature.
Explaining the example that was stated, he expresses that very point clearly with the word "yathā" (just as).

Regarding the phrase "the collection of the three worlds": the sense is that it is the secret of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that the entire universe is manifest to the Witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), mediated by either knowledge or ignorance. || 23 ||
Just as a person standing in one place constantly and incessantly perceives with their mind a treasure situated in a far-off land, so too [is the soul]. (24)

He always beholds his own treasure— the wealth buried underground— by means of the mind, the ellipsis being that he does so by continuously cultivating it through meditation (*bhāvanā*). And thus, even by the power of the accumulation of meditation, [it becomes manifest], just like the direct perception of a beloved woman experienced by one who is separated from her.
The meaning is that the proof of its perception [is thereby established]. || 24 ||

In this way, even though the individual soul (jīva) is burdened by hundreds of births and enveloped in delusion, it perceives its desired object residing within its own latent impressions (vāsanā). 25.

Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, what kind of form does a living being attain who is devoid of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and the like, and for whom no funeral cake is offered? (26)

Rāma raises a doubt regarding the universality of what was previously stated— that one perceives the body born of oneself through the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) by kinsmen— by saying, "O Blessed One": "For one to whom no cake is offered,
since the cause for that latent impression (*vāsanā*) is absent, how can that soul, being devoid of such an impression, possess a form and be embodied?"
The meaning is that it is accomplished. || 26 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "Whether the funeral cake (piṇḍa) is given by me or the thought 'the cake has been given by me'—if such a latent impression (vāsanā) is firmly rooted in the heart, the person [who died] partakes of the fruit of that cake. (27)

The fruit of that *piṇḍa* is the perfection of the body, which is what one partakes of. The ritual procedure for offering the *piṇḍa* and so forth, while essentially teaching the duty toward kinsmen, is nevertheless well known to yield a fruit pertaining to both [the giver and the deceased] because it accords with the fruits of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the dead; this is the intended meaning. || 27 ||
Whatever the mind may be, the living being becomes that;
such is the experience among those with bodies and those without bodies, and it is never otherwise. (28)

The meaning is that the direct scriptural statements such as, "The mind alone is indeed saṃsāra, and one should purify it with effort; for whatever the mind is like, one becomes that—this is an eternal secret," as well as the experiences of the wise, are well-known among embodied yogis. Alternatively, [the term] refers to living beings who possess bodies (*sadeha*) and those who are bodiless (*videha*), that is, those who have died.
The meaning is that this rule is never otherwise in any case whatsoever. || 28 ||
Through the consciousness "I am a sapinda," even one who is not a sapinda possesses the state of being a sapinda;
through the consciousness "I am not a sapinda," even one who is a sapinda does not possess the state of being a sapinda. || 29 ||
For the reality of these objects consists precisely in their being so conceived; and such conception indeed arises from the objects themselves as its causes. (30)

However, this much is the distinction made by the author of the treatise: with the intention that when the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) have been offered by the kinsmen, the latent impression (vāsanā) for offering the cake to the deceased necessarily arises, he says: "and [the] mental cultivation" (bhāvanā). || 30 ||
Just as poison becomes like nectar for a living being through habitual conditioning, so too does an unreal object attain the status of reality through intense mental cultivation. 31.

Even the poison of snakes and the like becomes nectar for one who worships Garuḍa through the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) "I am Garuḍa"—that is to say, it is digested. Likewise, even though the piercing by thorns and the like, or the delusion of being bitten by a snake, are unreal, they attain reality through such contemplation; that is, they acquire the capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), such as death. || 31 ||
One never dispels anything for anyone by means of a cause;
be certain that there is not even the slightest cultivation [of such a thing]. // 32 //

For if the cause were real, the effect would indeed be real; however, since mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is not a real entity, an effect produced without a real cause does not exist at all. Thus, the meaning is that one should become certain that pure Brahman alone exists in reality.
Nowhere has an effect ever been seen or heard of without a cause until the great dissolution; indeed, nothing exists apart from its own arising.

To the objection, "Why should the effect not arise even in the absence of a cause?", he replies with the words "by the cause" (*kāraṇena*). The meaning is that the dependence of the existence of every effect upon the existence of its cause is established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Then, [the opponent asks], "In that case, is the existence of Brahman also dependent on a cause? To which he replies, "But it is itself," meaning "it is self-existent."

The meaning is this: apart from that Brahman which is a single arising and eternally self-luminous, there is no other [reality], because it is only for that which possesses non-eternal existence that dependence upon a cause is required. || 33 ||
Consciousness alone is the latent impression (vāsanā), and that very same thing assumes the status of an object, as in a dream;
it enters into the relationship of cause and effect, and having come forth, it remains as such.

Thus, the established conclusion—that pure consciousness alone appears through delusion in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the world of latent impressions, and so forth—is stated as follows: "Consciousness alone... (verse 34).
Śrī Rāma said:
"If a deceased person who, being possessed by latent impressions (vāsanā), thinks 'I have no dharma,' should have abundant dharma performed and dedicated to him by a friend— "

Regarding what was previously stated— that the fruit of the commencement of a new body for the deceased follows precisely from the latent impression (vāsanā) of the deceased, based on the consciousness "I am a sapinda"— Rāma asks about "Dharma" [verse 35], for the purpose of raising an objection that will be formulated later.
167. In that case, would that dharma here be destroyed, or rather not?
Is meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) more powerful when it has a true object or even one that is untrue? (36)

The meaning is: having perished, would it be fruitless due to conflict with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of a *preta*, or, on the other hand, would it not be fruitless because of the predominance of the latent impressions of a friend? In that regard, because the latent impression of a friend consists of *dharma* and *sattva*, it has a real object; whereas the latent impression of a *preta* has an unreal object. Among these, when there is predominance of a latent impression, does it reside in the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*)?

Is it the motivating factor, or is it the truthfulness of the meaning? In the first case, there is the fault of abandoning what has already been established (*kṛtahāna*). In the second case, however, the meaning would have to be true, which results in a contradiction with what was stated previously. Thus, the intention is that this is like a rope that binds one from both ends. || 36 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Through the perfection of place, time, action, and materials, a creative conception arises;
wherever that conception has fully emerged, he shall be the superior victor over the two.

Vasiṣṭha resolves the matter with a hidden intention: the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of a friend that conforms to the scriptures is powerful because it follows the authority of the scriptures through practice performed at the place and time prescribed by the scriptures; however, the latent impression of a ghost is weak because it is purely worldly. Thus, he maintains that it is the scripture itself, and not the objective reality of the object, that is the determinant of strength.
"Ten," it is said. In whatever object, which is the form of the fruit, that [aspiration] has arisen, that object alone becomes victorious; this is the meaning.

If the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the giver of merit has proceeded toward that [object], then by means of that [impression], the mind of the deceased is gradually filled; otherwise, the consciousness of the deceased remains impure through its own [unwholesome] thought. (38)

He says "of the giver of Dharma" (dharmadātuḥ) to explain that, either within the inner consciousness of the deceased through the power of the treatise on the gift of Dharma, or at that very moment, the impression (*vāsanā*) arises: "I am one who possesses such Dharma. Furthermore, it must necessarily be stated that the deceased obtains the fruit solely by the power of the treatise; for [the word] "of him" (*tasya*)—referring to that heretic—is not found in some versions.

It is recited [in the commentary]: "With the intention that those whose intellects are defiled by unwholesome latent impressions—such as hatred toward the Vedas and nihilism—do not obtain the fruit even when their friends bestow dharma upon them, he says: 'If not.
The sense is that if the strength [of the gift] were caused by the reality of the object, then that [nihilist] would also incur the fruit of dharma. || 38 ||
Thus, through mutual victory, the one of superior vigor triumphs here;
therefore, with auspicious effort, one should practice what is virtuous.

For this very reason, having previously established the predominance of human effort, I stated that one should always practice what is auspicious; with this intention, he says: "In this way," etc. (39).
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, if latent impressions (vāsanā) arise by means of place, time, and so forth, then at the beginning of creation in a Great Kalpa, from where do place, time, and the rest come?

If it is admitted that the arising of dharmas and their latent impressions (vāsanās) occurs through the conjunction of auxiliary causes such as place and time, then— given the Vedic scripture stating, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second"— the production of the world consisting of those [dharmas] would be impossible, because at the initial creation there is an absence of auxiliary factors such as place and time, and thus the arising of latent impressions is untenable.

And if that were so, there would be a contradiction with subsequent scriptural passages such as, "It thought: May I be many, may I procreate. With this intention, Rāma raises an objection, beginning with the word "deśa" (space). || 40 ||
This arises from its cause together with those auxiliary factors;
in the absence of the auxiliary causes, how could there be a latent impression (vāsanā)? 41.
Then, whence could there be latent impressions? For it is only when a cause exists that this effect, consisting of latent impressions and so forth, arises. || 41 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
