"It is even so, O mighty-armed one whose nature is truth;
at no time whatsoever, at the beginning of creation following the great dissolution, do space and time exist."
This very point has been established by you against me: there is neither cessation nor origination;

this is that Brahman which is without prior and without posterior, neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long; and as for the instruction "not this, not this," that which is unseen and ungraspable, wherein one sees nothing else, hears nothing else—and so on, according to hundreds of such scriptural passages.
Because the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is seen precisely there, and because this very point is what is sought to be made known with great effort,

even the creation-śrutis such as "He desired" (*so 'kāmayata*) serve to establish the non-reality of the duality that appears therein, thereby leading to the realization of the Self devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*), which is the fruit of the inquiry commenced.

With the intention that [the text] refers specifically to the act of grasping (*ādāna*) and not to the beginning of creation (*sṛṣṭyādi*), Vasiṣṭha, expressing his approval, said "It is so" (*evam etat*) and so forth. [The phrase] "in the Self which is the Supreme Reality" (*satyātman paramārthasatye ātmani*) refers to the state prior to creation, which is the nature of the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). Regarding the form *satyātman*, the case-ending *ṅi* is elided according to the Vedic rule *supāṃ suluk*.
By the rule "ṅisaṃbuddhyoḥ," there is a prohibition of the elision of the *n*. || 42 ||
In the absence of auxiliary causes, this perceptual cognition does not exist;
it has not arisen, nor does anything whatsoever manifest. (43)
Precisely because the visible object is impossible, whatever is seen here is indeed Brahman itself, abiding in this way as its own pure consciousness, free from all affliction. (44)
We shall indeed explain this to you with hundreds of arguments later on;
for that purpose, this effort is being made now—listen to the present narrative.
Thus they beheld the temple, with its beautiful interior, strewn with offerings of flowers, as cool and refreshing as the spring season. (46)
Thus, having arrived at Padmanagara according to the manner previously described, Jñapti and Līlā beheld the Lotus Mansion. || 46 ||
Endowed with a capital city where all agitation of conduct has been stilled, he remained there, equal [to all], adorned with garlands of Mandāra and Kunda flowers and other ornaments.

In that royal capital, where the bustle of kingly affairs had been stilled, the two [brothers] saw— in that house, together with those people— the corpse covered with garlands of *mandāra* and *kunda* flowers; this is drawn forward from what follows hereafter.
It was draped with garlands and wreaths of mandāra and kunda flowers, its vast shrouds covering it like garments;
at the head of the bier lay the preeminent auspicious vessel, the full water-pot (pūrṇakumbha), and other such auspicious items.
The house had its doors, windows, and bolts firmly secured;
the light of the lamps was fading, leaving the pure walls darkened;
and it was made resonant by the breath from the mouths of those sleeping in one part of the dwelling. (49)
He describes that very house again with the words beginning "anivṛtta" and so forth: where the hard bolts and firm crossbars of the large doors and windows have not been withdrawn nor opened;
and which is dark and soiled by the light of the lamps, which is becoming extinguished—that is, turning dim.
In reality, he is one whose walls are stainless. || 49 ||
It is as lovely as the splendor of the full moon rising in its entirety;
it surpasses the opulence of Indra’s palace with its beauty;
and it possesses a charming radiance within the bud of Brahmā’s lotus.
It was as if silent and gentle, stainless and lovely as the moon.

It is lovely because it is illuminated by the rising of the full moon together with its digits from the outside; yet, within, it possesses a beautiful splendor like the inner womb of the lotus-bud at the navel of the Lord— the abode of Viriñca—
and it remains silent, as if mute and slow, like the moon, which is lovely.
The meaning is that they beheld a most beautiful house. || 50 ||

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Disposition of the Deceased Immediately Following Death on the Bed," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Condition of the Departed Soul Immediately Following Death and Sleep," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Fifty-Seventh Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then they both saw Līlā there, lying on one side of a corpse-bed,
dead and having arrived first before Vidūratha.
In another play, the falsity of the body of Līlā is declared, as well as the emergence of the *ātivāhika* (subtle) body for yogins. || 1 ||
Earlier, they both witnessed the pastimes of Vidūratha, who had died previously, within the sphere of their own perceptions. || 1 ||
She possessed their former dress, their former conduct, their former bodies, and their former latent impressions;
she resembled their previous forms, and was beautiful in every aspect of her form and limbs.

The reason for her former appearance and so forth is stated as follows: "Her own latent impressions" (*svavāsanām*—this is the reading)—[she who possessed] the vibration of limbs in her former form, who was formerly enclosed by garments, and who was formerly covered by a multitude of ornaments, remained there in that state alone. (3)
The meaning is that only her being situated there in the lotus-palace was unprecedented; everything else was exactly as it had been before. || 3 ||
Holding a chowrie, she gracefully fanned the lord of the earth,
adorning the surface of the earth as the rising moon adorns the heavens.
She was standing in silence, her face like a moon resting upon her left hand,
and she appeared like a forest glade in full bloom with the flower-like rays of light from her ornaments.
With the rays and beams of her ornaments, she stood like a forest glade in full bloom with its leafy creepers and flowers. || 5 ||
Beholding her with glances that rained down *mālatī* and blue lotuses in all directions,
she seemed to create from her own loveliness a moon after every moon risen in the sky.
"Indumindum" is a distributive repetition (vīpsā). "As if creating all the moons from her own beauty" is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
"Nabhoditam" is an archaic sandhi; or it may mean "she who creates again that which was 'ditam'—cut or shattered—in the 'nabhasi'—the sky. 6.
Like the Fortune of Viṣṇu who had come to him as the protector of men,
she was like the splendor of spring arisen from a profusion of flowers.
With her gaze fixed upon the face of her husband, she performed her desired gestures;
yet with her countenance somewhat faded, she was like a night whose moon has grown dim.
That woman was seen by those two, but they were not noticed by her;
because they were of truthful resolve, she did not manifest herself to them in that way at that time.
Thus, due to her power of true resolve, she was neither impelled nor manifested. || 9 ||
Śrī Rāma said: It has been described how, in that region, having established her body for the sake of her former pastimes, she departed through meditation accompanied by Jñapti.
Rāma asks out of doubt— beginning with "tasmin" (in that)— as to why, setting aside the necessary prior search for his own lost body, the vision of Vidūratha’s pastimes was described first. || 10 ||
O Lord, tell me now: why was Līlā’s body not described there? What became of it, and where did it go? Tell me this. (11)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Where was that body of sport, and from where could it possess reality?
It was merely an illusion, like the perception of water in a desert.

Because it is sublated by the arising of the consciousness of the *ātivāhika* state and by the realization of reality (*tattvāvabodha*), the vision of his own body during the divine play (*līlā*) was not described. However, for those ignorant ones whose vision is not so sublated, the death, cremation, and so forth of that body in the subsequent creation will be described from their perspective; thus, the author has withheld what was to be said.
In order to bring about the realization of reality, Vasiṣṭha, elaborating upon its very falsity, said:
"Where was it? and so forth. (12)
This entire world is indeed the Self; whence [could there be] the conceptualization of the body and so forth?
That which you perceive as blissful Brahman is itself Consciousness. 13.
Just as this playfulness (līlā) gradually reaches its transformation within Awakening,
so too does that supreme [state] from which his body has fallen away like a mountain of snow. (14)

Just as it has undergone transformation—characterized by full maturation—in whatever sequence, so indeed in that same sequence; [it is] dissolved, meaning sublated, into that supreme Brahman beyond awakening. || 14 ||
(Regarding the subtle body [this verse, marked by a bow-ornament, appears occasionally]:
An error has arisen through time, [thinking], "I am a physical body," just like [the perception of] a snake in a rope. || 1 ||)
Whatever is perceived by means of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), such as earth and so forth, is given the name "the objective" (dṛśya); that indeed is the material realm (ādhibhautika). || 15 ||
Not only has the material nature of one's own body dissolved, but that of all things, such as the earth and so forth, has as well.

With the intention that even for these, their grossness is sublated by the Śruti statement, "The fire-nature of fire has departed; only the three forms remain as the truth," and thus their subtle, transportive (ātivāhika) nature is established as the remainder, he says: "subtle-transportive" (ātivāhika).

That very visible world which was perceived by that vision of reality—through the intellect of the *ātivāhika* state, through the intellect of it being merely the collective subtle mind, and through that [higher] perception—is what was previously designated as "earth" and so forth due to delusion;
that alone is the *ādhibhautika*. 15.
In its actual form, however, the material world consisting of earth and so forth, as well as the self, is neither established by word nor by object; it lacks a real essence, like the horn of a hare.
Therefore, he says "vāstavena" (in reality) to show that there is nothing whatsoever that is actually material. || 16 ||
If a man has the thought in a dream, "I am a deer," would he go searching for a deer once his own state as a deer has ceased? (17)
And thus, since there is no possibility of searching for that which has been sublated, he says: "Of the person" (puṃsaḥ) || 17 ||
Untruth quickly arises, and likewise truth dissolves;
just as for one who is deluded, the error of a snake in a rope vanishes once the delusion has passed. 18.

Just as for one who is wandering, that which is unreal alone arises and dissolves, so too, when the delusion has passed, does it arise? This is to be construed with an interrogative intonation (kāku). || 18 ||
For anyone who is entirely unawakened and born of the mind, this [world] is merely false, having attained the status of falsehood without any seed. (19)
Thus, it follows that the material (ādhibhautika) phenomenal world is imagined by the collective mind of the ignorant; he states this with the words "of the entire...

The word *jāta* signifies a collection. This gross delusion pertaining to this particular cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) arises from among the various mental productions of the infinite, distinct ignorant minds belonging to each individual cosmic egg.
The meaning is that it has arrived at a false conviction and a vain reputation; it is indeed in vain. || 19 ||
Experiencing all that which is called creation as a dream-perception,
he remains for a long time with his self identified with the body, like the revolving of the wheel of the earth.
All that ignorant person, being one whose body is repeatedly subject to coming and going for a long time, experiences it just as a child experiences the whirling of a wheel. || 20 ||
Śrī Rāma said: For the yogin who is traveling toward his own abode while preceded by the worlds of Brahmā, what kind of body is this "conveyance-body" (ātivāhika-deha) seen to be? || 21 ||
Now, if the body of a yogi does not possess a material (ādhibhautika) nature, then what kind of body is this that is seen by people when he is standing before them alive,
or when he has departed to his own essential nature as the Self, or when he is dead and has attained the state of a subtle body (ātivāhika)? For a subtle body cannot be perceived by ordinary people.
The meaning of Rāma’s question is: "Is it what remains at the time of liberation? || 21 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The transition from one body to another always occurs without the former body,
for this subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) is as perishable as those in dreams.

The death of yogis is of two kinds: one is the voluntary assumption of various bodies for the sake of experiencing the remaining *prārabdha* karma; the other is *videhakaivalya* (bodiless liberation) upon the exhaustion of all *prārabdha*. Regarding the former, he states that there is no remainder from the previous [body], beginning with the words "from the body" (*dehāt*). Just as in dreams, there is a single subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*)...

The meaning is that, just as the conceptualization of another state such as being human occurs after abandoning the state of being a deer and so forth—without any remainder of the previous body—it is perishable and impermanent. || 22 ||
Just as a speck of frost in the heat, or a white cloud in the autumnal sky, though visible, attains invisibility—so too does the body of a yogi. (23)
He states with an illustration that "he" does not exist even in the second [state], beginning with "yathā" (just as).
Thus, the meaning is that while that [ego-sense] is gradually wasting away like an autumnal cloud or the like, there remains for a short time a delusion of its persistence. || 23 ||
Or else, suddenly, the body of the yogi is no longer perceived, like a bird that has swiftly flown up into the sky before the eyes of other yogis. (24)

It is not an absolute rule that what is waning must necessarily be seen by others, for in some cases destruction occurs immediately through the very intention of destruction; thus he says "suddenly" (drāk). The meaning is that it is not even perceived by other yogis, much less by ordinary people. And so, even during the state of being alive—

The meaning is that the people's vision of His body occurs solely by the power of His own true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*)—thinking, "Let these see Me in this way"—and not by virtue of the body being material (*ādhibhautika*). || 24 ||
Due solely to the delusion of their own latent impressions (vāsanā), some people at certain times and in certain places perceive even those yogis walking before them as being dead. (25)

Alternatively, with the intention that there is no contradiction whatsoever— since even though yogis experience their own bodies as being of a subtle (ativāhika) nature through their own vision, the possibility remains for them to conceive of that body as material and subject to death due to the latent impressions (vāsanā) of ignorant people, which are conjoined with the unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa) that cause its enjoyment— he says:

"By their own latent impressions" (svavāsanā) means that some superior persons see him as dead in one place, while others see the yogi as living in another. For this very reason, there is no contradiction in the fact that Śuka, though already liberated from the body (videhamukta), was seen again in the assembly of Parīkṣit and performed such acts as the instruction in the *Bhāgavata*.
The object of enlightenment. || 25 ||

But for them, the notion that the body is the self is mere delusion; it subsides through the realization of truth, just as the perception of a snake in a rope ceases upon realizing the rope's true nature. (26)

Furthermore, since for yogis the body and so forth are sublated at the very moment knowledge arises, the body does not exist even during the state of living from their perspective; thus he says: "It is mere illusion" (verse 26).
What is the body? Whose is its existence? Whose is its destruction? How and from where?
That which existed remains exactly as it was; only ignorance has departed. (27)
That which exists from the perspective of ultimate reality is precisely what has become manifest through knowledge.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Lord, does the physical body itself attain the state of being subtle (ātivāhika), or is it something else? Tell me this, so that I may be carried across [the ocean of existence], O Master. (28)

Now, if the body of yogins is indeed subject to dissolution, then—since that which is dissolved cannot undergo further transformation—another subtle body (*ativāhika-śarīra*) must arise for the sake of experiencing the *prārabdha* karma; and if that were so, because it would constitute a new birth, the state of being liberated while living (*jīvanmukti*) would be untenable, as it is said: "He is not born again."
Thinking that such [a view] contradicts the scriptures and so forth, Rāma asks: "Is it the state of being *ātivāhika*?
Does the very same physical (*ādhibhautika*) body of the yogin attain the state of being *ātivāhika*, or does a different *ātivāhika* body arise?
In the first case, a transformation of that which has been sublated is contrary to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In the second case, however, [there is the problem of] knowledge...

The meaning is that, because it is untenable in either case—since [the soul] would lose its status as having liberation as its fruit—one is carried away in a continuous flow of doubt, as if being swept along, and does not attain stability. || 28 ||
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
O best of men, though this has been told to you many times, why do you not grasp it?
There exists only the subtle body (*ātivāhika*); here, the material body (*ādhibhautika*) does not exist at all. (29)
This is not a transformation; rather, it is simply the persistence of the subtle substrate once the gross has been sublated.

Since the scripture on "trivṛtkaraṇa" (the tripartition) teaches the superimposition of the gross upon Brahman as conditioned by the subtle body, and since it states that "these three forms alone are real"—thereby indicating the persistence of the subtle through the sublation of the gross—there is no room for the aforementioned objection.
He provides the resolution by reminding of what was stated previously, beginning with the words "bahuśaḥ" (repeatedly), etc. || 29 ||
Even as he practices that very [wisdom], when the notion of being associated with the material world (sādhibhautika) subsides, then his former [spiritual] state returns to him. || 30 ||
The former is the prior one; that itself is the state of being *ativāhika*. || 30 ||
Then, that vain grasping at weightiness and hardness will subside—just as [the perception of a ghost] vanishes for a waking person through healthy awakening—like that of a man in a dream. (31)

Now, one might ask: "Without another transformation, how can the heaviness, hardness, and so forth of the body cease? To this he says: "At that time. The meaning is that those [qualities] are indeed sublated, just like the heaviness, hardness, and so forth of a city seen in a dream. || 31 ||
From that, the meditative attainment of lightness arises for the yogi, just as one recognizes a dream within a dream regarding the body. || 32 ||
Just as the body becomes light through the recognition of a dream within a dream,
so too, through awakening, this body becomes capable of leaping like something gross.
One who possesses *pluti* is fit for such things as traveling through space. || 33 ||
For those whose selves have been transformed through the mental constructs of many days,
even when this corpse-like body is burned, they attain their abiding state right there.

If even for the ignorant, whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are exceedingly firm and gross, there is the attainment of a prior subtle body despite the destruction of the gross body— characterized by its disappearance into its cause through cremation and so forth, which results in it becoming a corpse— then what need is there to mention the case of the wise who are free from latent impressions, wherein that [subtle body] is sublated by the uprooting of its very foundation?

He states, by way of a *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument, that the attainment of natural subtlety occurs—using two verses beginning with "aneka"—[referring to] *āsthiti*, which is characterized by firm self-conceit. 34.
Likewise, the experience of a subtle body is necessarily bound to occur;
due to the excellence of awakening, this happens even for yogins while they are still alive. (35)
When memory has arisen there, the "I" consisting of volition is sufficient; whatever kind of body that [previous] one was, this one becomes exactly like it upon awakening. (36)

In that state, when the memory arises in a dream, "I am indeed of the nature of volition alone, not of a gross nature," such a memory is established by the experience of meditators in dreams, but not of common folk—
[a memory] such as [the one] capable of wandering through space at will. (36)
Thus this delusion alone appears, like the form of a snake in a rope.
When it has perished, what is lost? When it has arisen, what is produced? (37)

"Is it not the case that knowledge which subverts the body—dear to all people—is indeed a misfortune? To this he replies: "It is an illusion. [The opponent asks: "What has been lost? The sense is: for no one grieves when the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is sublated. || 37 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Lord, if those who reside there subsequently witness the divine play, do they perceive it through the power of their own true resolve? Or is it otherwise? (38)

Thus, once the incidental matter has been resolved, Rāma asks regarding the subject of the present narrative itself—beginning with the words "immediately thereafter" (*anantaram*). Following the union in the Lotus-Palace during both the previous pastime and the fresh pastime, those people residing in the Lotus-Palace [beheld] that pastime; for, due to its nature as a subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*), it was otherwise impossible to see.

The meaning is that if people see her because of her power of true resolve (satyasaṃkalpatā) thinking, "May these people see me," then do they recognize her, wondering, "Is this the very same person standing right here? or do they think with astonishment, as Jyeṣṭhaśarman and others did, "Is this some unprecedented deity who has arrived? || 38 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "In this way, O Queen, they will understand: 'This woman stands here in sorrow; she is some other friend who has come from somewhere to her.'"

In that regard, Vasiṣṭha spoke, relying on the very first alternative, beginning with "Thus" (*evam*). To the question, "Then do they perceive the second sport (*līlā*)?", he replied: "As companions" (*vayasya*); thus [ends verse 39].
What doubt could there be in this regard? For these are indeed animals, lacking discrimination;
they act exactly as they have seen. Whence could there be any deliberation for them? (40)

One might object: "Since this second pastime was unprecedented, how could they not have had doubts such as, 'Who is she? From where has she come? Is she a woman of good character or a harlot? Is she real or unreal? To this, he says: *saṃdeha* (doubt). [The answer is:
according to what was seen (*yathādṛṣṭam*), that is, strictly in accordance with the objects previously perceived."
They act; that is to say, they engage in worldly affairs. || 40 ||
Just as a rolling clod of earth quickly bypasses a tree, so too do the ignorant and the beasts [bypass] the city and other [realms] while remaining in a state of ignorance. 41.

If it is asked what the cause is for the non-arising of their investigation (*vicāra*), the answer is that the cause is attachment to the gross, the solidity and firmness of its essence, and its subtlety, as well as emptiness; indicating this by means of an example, he says:
"Just as," [and in some places "by force" (*balena*)]. By a child.
A clod of earth or a lump of dry dust thrown to strike down a tree, having avoided the tree as it rolls and strikes itself, does not enter within like an arrow,
nor does it adhere like a lump of mud, nor does it merely cause a slight wound like a stone, or [simply] fall away by itself.

Furthermore, although it remains capable of withstanding injury, it quickly—that is, very swiftly—departs and falls apart; likewise, those people who lack knowledge are "ignorant" (*ajñāna*). In reality, being such, they are like goats, hence "goat-animals" (*ajāpaśavaḥ*); the meaning is that due to their flimsiness, they are incapable of internal penetration or reflection. Now, as for one who [perceives] another...
According to the Śruti: "He who worships a deity [thinking], 'That one is another and I am another,' does not know, like a beast.

For those [beings], the non-arising of inquiry is caused not only by ignorance alone, but also by their respective bodies (*purāṇi*), and—by the force of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)—by desire, karma, latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and so forth; at that time, they act exactly in accordance with those [causes], just like beasts.

The meaning is that the non-arising of such an inquiry is indeed appropriate because [the Lord] exists. Regarding the reading *ajñapaśavaḥ*, it should be explained as: "they themselves are ignorant, and they are the cattle of the ignorant gods. || 41 ||
Just as one does not know where the body of a dream goes upon awakening,
because it is entirely unreal, so too is this physical body here.

However, for those who investigate, because their [notions] are sublated by the gradual arising of the awakening to reality (*tattva*), the very perception of them as material (*ādhibhautika*) does not exist; much less, therefore, can there be any possibility of doubt or the like. With this intention, he concludes with the words "yathā" (just as). [The word] "bodhāt" means from awakening. || 42 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, where does the mountain of a dream go upon awakening?
Cut asunder this doubt of mine, as the wind disperses an autumnal cloud. (43)

In connection with the discussion of the analogy, Rāma asks— "O Blessed One"— because the absolute sublation of the objects of a dream is impossible without the sublation of their root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*); therefore, there must be a persistence of that [object] in some concealed state, and he asks where that is.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In a dream-delusion or in a mental construction, objects such as mountains and the like merge within consciousness, just as vibrations merge within the wind.

Vasiṣṭha provides the resolution that the concealment of the phenomenal world of dreams and mental desires occurs in that very [waking state], because it is the effect of the consciousness of the individual soul (jīva) as conditioned by ignorance, which is nourished by the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the waking state; thus he says: "In a dream... (verse 44).
Just as the moving air enters fully into the motionless wind,
being non-different from it, so too the object of the dream— the impurity of consciousness— enters into the Self, being non-different from it.

"Non-different in essence" means devoid of any other real nature. The meaning is that the impurity of consciousness—namely, ignorance itself, which is like a stain and an obscuring agent—enters its own material cause. || 45 ||

Through the manifestation of objects such as those in dreams, consciousness alone shines forth abundantly; yet, when not so manifesting, it attains oneness with that very object, being of its same nature.

And thus, it follows that consciousness itself, when unknown, sometimes manifests in the form of dream-objects due to the power of karma; this is what he states with the words "In a dream... (verse 46).
Duality between consciousness and the objects of a dream is never found, just as there is no duality between liquidity and water, or between motion and the wind. (47)
But in the state of discernment (*viveka*), there is no such thing as an object of dream that exists apart from consciousness; thus he says: "Consciousness" (verse 47).
Whatever lack of awakening might exist therein is that unsurpassed ignorance;
this is said to be transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti), which has arisen with the nature of false knowledge.
In that regard, he says "He who... (verse 48) to explain that what appears there as something other is in fact nothing but ignorance (*avidyā*) itself, and that this alone is *saṃsāra*.
"Indeed, in the absence of auxiliary causes, what kind of duality could consciousness possibly have regarding the objects of a dream? In a dream, such duality is purposeless. (Verse 49)

He states that dream objects are non-existent also because they are not produced by auxiliary causes such as the staff, the wheel, and so forth, which are well-known in the world—thus: "sahakārī" (verse 49).
Just as a dream, so is this waking state; there is no doubt about this.
In a dream an unreal city appears, and at the beginning of creation the unreal world appears. (50)

[Objection: "In that case, does it not follow that the waking world, which possesses auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*), must be real? [Reply: He says "as... [to answer] "no. Regarding the phrase "at the beginning of creation": although auxiliary causes and so forth exist now, nevertheless, at the initial creation there was nothing apart from the consciousness of Hiraṇyagarbha as conditioned by ignorance (*ajñāna*); thus, the meaning is that it is exactly like a dream. || 50 ||
And it is not possible for the object arising from a dream to be real;
consciousness possesses eternal reality, while the objects of dreams lack reality. (51)

He says that if the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) were real, it would follow that it possesses consciousness (*cit*), just like cognition itself (*saṃvit*), which would result in a contradiction regarding its being an object of consciousness:
"By cognition... [the meaning is] that it is possible for the object to become or to be conceived as such.

Furthermore, he says that objects are not real because they do not invariably coincide with the existence of cognition, whereas cognition does not deviate from its own existence: "Of cognition... (51).
Just as a dream-mountain becomes space instantly or gradually,
so too does the physical world become space upon awakening.

He states that [the world] is not real even because it is sublated by the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna): "Immediately" (*jhaṭityeva*). The meaning is that space becomes empty; not even an atom remains. "In awakening" (*bodhe*) means in waking or in the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). This occurs either through the gradual process of practicing awakening or suddenly through the grace of the Lord and others. *Kham* (space).
The meaning is that it is empty because it does not arise. || 52 ||
Those standing nearby wonder whether he has flown away or died, for they, being struck by their own nature, do not perceive the wise one who has become the *ātivāhika* body.
How then is it that people perceive Śuka flying up to the solar orb, or see the dead bodies of Dadhīci and others? To this he says: "Uḍḍīna" (having flown up).
"Jña" means one who knows reality. "Ātivāhikībhūtam" means having become the subtle body, with the physical body sublated. "Sveṣāṃ svabhāvaḥ" means their own inherent nature.
By that adventitious ignorance, people are indeed struck and for the most part destroyed;
thus, they perceive only a body imagined by their own respective ignorance, and not that body of the Knower—this is the meaning. || 53 ||
These creations are indeed false views, views born of delusion;
they are the error of seeing mere illusion, empty like the experiences of a dream. (54)
He concludes by means of two verses, strengthening the stated point through inference:

these views of duality are indeed false views, because they are views born of delusion. For instance, it is well known that the perception of a magician’s illusion is merely an error; they are devoid of objective reality.
And the meanings experienced in dreams are well-known; such is the sense. || 54 ||
These experiences of dreams, appearing as the clear manifestation of creation, are all seen through the delusion of error and its opposite at the moment of awakening at the end of death;
they all appear while one is situated within the subtle body (*ativāhika-śarīra*).
They are falsely proclaimed through the process of following a mirage.

For a person who perceives various delusions of difference— seeing successive delusions of difference— the extremely firm latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of difference arise; thus, at the moment of death,

in the cognition produced in the instant preceding the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there appears a manifestation of objects conducive to future experience, and all [these impressions] [are present].

These appearances of a manifest creation, which belong to the subtle body (*ativāhika-śarīra*) and reside solely in the mind, are like the experience of a dream; yet, through delusion, they appear as if falsely arisen externally—like the flow or current of a mirage (*mṛga-nadī*). The meaning is that they do not, in reality, exist outside of the mind. || 55 ||

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Examination of the Meaning of Dreams," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa*, within the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the work of the Sage.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Examination of the Nature of Dreams," in the Utpttiprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
Fifty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the meantime, Jñapti [again] addressed the jīva Vaidūratha.
By means of his resolve, he quickly restrained the vibration of his mind.
In this [chapter], time, the destruction of the body in the sport of the place of meditative absorption, the playful conversation with the King, and his life are described. (1)

Having thus resolved Rāma’s questions and being about to describe the remainder of the narrative at hand, Vasiṣṭha prepares the stage for the subject matter to be discussed at the end of this canto with the verse beginning "In this... He provides an illustration to show that even for that which is formless, cessation is possible through mere volition (saṃkalpa), stating: "Of the mind... (1).
Līlā said: "Tell me, O Goddess, how much time has passed while I was absorbed in samādhi in this palace, and while the king remained as a corpse?"
In this creation of lotuses. || 2 ||
Jñapti said: "One month has passed here; these two maidservants of yours have remained vigilant in the sleeping chamber for the sake of guarding you while you slept. (3)
In this creation, here in this chamber, these two maidservants stand for the protection of your body;
they are now sleeping. The absence of the suffix *iṭ* is a Vedic archaism. || 3 ||
Listen, O lady of excellent complexion, to what has happened here to your body;
your frame, having been moistened by your tears for a fortnight, has become parched.

Previously, the subtle (ativāhika) nature of Līlā’s own body—which was imagined through her own ignorance, established by her own experience, and though sublated by the knowledge of reality, still appears for the sake of experiencing the remainder of her prārabdha karma—was described. Being moist with sweat and being heated by the digestive fire kindled by the suppression of the breath, it attained the state of vapor—that is, the state of wet smoke. || 4 ||
Lifeless, fallen upon the ground like a withered leaf,
the corpse has become as cold as ice, resembling a piece of wood or a wall.
Then, having gradually become withered and lifeless, it became a corpse. || 5 ||
Then the ministers, having arrived and determined for themselves by the sight of her moisture that she was indeed dead,
carried her out of the house once again.
Furthermore, because she was seen to be on the verge of dissolving due to the appearance of moisture, he concluded that she was dead. || 6 ||
What is the use of saying more here? Having carried him away on a pyre made of sandalwood logs, they quickly reduced him to ashes along with the clarified butter after placing him upon it.
Then, crying out loudly, "The queen is dead! your entire retinue performed the funeral rites with great agitation.
The absence of any physical disorder in the king's body, however, is to be understood as resulting from his own conscious resolve and the power of his unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Now, seeing you arrived here in personified form,
it will be a great marvel that you have come from the other world.
It will be a wonderful marvel for the people; this is the implied sense. || 9 ||
But you, O daughter, by virtue of your power of true resolve, appear with that very body in its natural whiteness; it is a marvel regarding you.
He says, "But you," indicating that even the sight of your divine body will be a supreme marvel.

By that subtle (ātivāhika), bright, and exceedingly pure [body], which is impossible for humans to see, you are seen; thus it follows that their minds will be directed toward that vision of you there. || 10 ||
O child, that very latent impression which you had toward the body has now arisen as your form; therefore, it resembles what you were before.

Now, one might object: since a divine body lacks the form of the previous body, recognition of it would be impossible; therefore, that [previous] form must necessarily be present there. To this he states the reason: "That" (yat).
That is, whatever kind of latent impression—that is, a latent impression of a particular form—[exists]. || 11 ||
Indeed, everyone perceives everything according to their own latent predispositions;
the non-contradictory example here is the vision of a child by a vetāla.
O beautiful Siddha lady, you have become possessed of a subtle body (ātivāhika-deha);
indeed, that former body of yours has been forgotten, for it was devoid of latent impressions (vāsanā).

Now, one might ask: "If that body were merely a mental impression (*vāsanā*), why was that very same body not obtained by me, just as it was by the king? To this he replies: "The *ātivāhika* [body]," and so on. Siddhā is one who is perfectly established in the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). If she had completely forgotten [her previous state], then the formation of that specific form in the *ātivāhika* body would not have been possible; therefore, he says "unabandoned by latent impressions" (*anapavāsanā*).
The intention is that its latent impressions have not been completely eradicated. || 13 ||
For the wise man who has attained the vision of the subtle body (ativāhika), the perception of the material world (ādhibhautika) subsides,
even while it is being perceived, like an autumn cloud in the sky.

To the question, "In that case, why did he not also possess a physical (ādhibhautika) nature there?", he says: "Rūḍha" (established). Even though he was perceived by others as being physical. || 14 ||
Every embodied being becomes established in a subtle, transportable state, resembling a cloud without water and like a flower devoid of fragrance. || 15 ||
When the consciousness of the subtle body has taken root through the latent impression of the True,
the physical body falls into oblivion, just as the embryo is forgotten once it has reached youth.

However, since there is not even the conception of a subtle body (*ativāhikadeha*) when latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are completely severed, the phrase "of one possessing good impressions" (*sadvāsanasya*) was stated to indicate this. The "body" (*deha*) here refers to the material body (*ādhibhautika*). || 16 ||
"Thirty-one days ago today we arrived here in the sky;
now, at dawn, these two maidservants have been stupefied by me with sleep. (17)
Therefore come, O Līlā; by means of our creative will, let us both manifest ourselves to Līlā so that worldly activity may proceed. (18)
By the play of his volition, that is, by the manifestation of his true resolve. || 18 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
As soon as the thought arose, "Let us two behold this sport," the two of them then became visible there through the consciousness of the Goddess.
When the Goddess thought, "Let these two, Vidūratha and Līlā, behold [this]," Jñapti and Līlā became visible as radiant and shining objects of perception. || 19 ||
Then Vidūrathalīlā, her eyes agitated,
gazed upon that house, which was radiant with a mass of splendor.
It was as if carved out from the lunar orb, or as if washed with molten gold;
it possessed walls of liquid light, cool as a flame.
Because of the power of the blazing, molten, and cool flame, it stood as if carved out from the lunar orb;
because its walls were pervaded by the liquid radiance of that body's splendor, the meaning is that it stood as if smeared with liquid gold.
Having observed the house before her, she beheld those playful commands.
Rising up in agitation, she fell at their feet.
In this context, "agitation" (saṃbhrama) refers to an intensity of joy. || 22 ||
"O Goddesses who grant life, may you be victorious! I have arrived here first, clearing the path for you both. (23)
"For my victory and for the excellence of my welfare; that is to say, like a female attendant who clears the path. || 23 ||
When she had spoken thus, those proud women, intoxicated by their youth,
sat down upon the seats like [creepers] upon the peaks of Mount Meru.
Jñapti said:
"Daughter, tell me how you first came to this place;
what has happened to you, what did you see on the road, or where [were you]?"
Speak from the very beginning. Where on what path, or what wondrous event, was that seen by you? This is the meaning. || 25 ||
Vidūratha’s wife Līlā said:
"O Goddess, in that place I then fell into a swoon;
I was like a digit of the second moon struck by the flames at the end of an aeon."
In that chamber of Vidūratha’s house, as a second guest, I fell into a swoon like a digit of the moon, belonging to him, when struck by the flames at the end of an aeon. || 26 ||
I did not intend anything, whether even or uneven;
therefore, I closed my eyes with their tremulous lashes. (27)

With eyes closed in a swoon, nothing was perceived or known. Regarding the phrase "nothing was perceived," since it is impossible to speak of that which has not been experienced, it means that although it was not known through the functioning of the senses (*sākṣibhāvena*), ignorance was not perceived; rather, it was indeed perceived [as the reading *cetitam eva* suggests], so there is no occasion for the suspicion that the nature of consciousness (*cidātman*) has been lost. || 27 ||
Then, O Supreme Goddess, at the end of my swoon from death, I saw that I had quickly risen and was floating within the belly of the sky.

As long as I have arisen through superimposition in the form of a body resembling my previous bodies imagined by latent impressions (vāsanā), so long have I been floating and leaping within the belly of the sky of consciousness, the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa). || 28 ||
Then, having mounted a chariot of wind in the elemental ether,
I was brought by him to this abode like a streak of fragrance.
Anila means breath (prāṇa) or a mass of wind; [he mounted] a chariot of that form, by means of that wind-chariot. || 29 ||
"O Queen, I see the dwelling adorned by the leader;
it is illuminated by a radiant lamp, secluded, and furnished with a costly couch. (30)
I shall look upon this husband while this Vidūratha lies with his limbs covered by flowers, like honey in a grove of blossoms. (31)
The meaning is: "I shall look upon them while they remain thus, awaiting [me]. Madhu is the spring season. || 31 ||
'Now, he is thoroughly exhausted by the fatigue of the fury of battle; let him sleep.
Thinking thus, O Goddess of the Gods, I did not ward off this sleep of his."
With the thought, "This man, exhausted by the fatigue of battle, is sleeping," I did not then disturb his sleep. || 32 ||
"Immediately upon arriving at this region, these two goddesses were described by me exactly as they were experienced, O you who bestow grace upon me. (33)
"O two goddesses, I have related to you exactly as it was experienced by me: that you both arrived at this place, my home.
Jñapti said:
"O you who walk with the grace of a swan, O Līlā of lovely eyes!"
"Let us raise this king from the surface of his funeral bier."
Having spoken thus, she released her life-breath as a lotus releases its fragrance;
taking the form of a wind-blown creeper, it went near her nose.
Having spoken thus, the *jñapti* released the king’s life-force (*jīva*), which had been restrained by his prior resolve.
Although that life-force was invisible like the wind, it took the form of a creeper because it was made to blossom by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion and other afflictions. (35)
He entered within the cavity of the nose like the wind into the hollow of a bamboo,
concealing hundreds of his own latent impressions (vāsanās) within, as the ocean hides its jewels.
He says that very thing: "causing hundreds of his own latent impressions (vāsanās) to disappear within. || 36 ||
His face, which contained the inner soul, attained its natural luster,
like a lotus when the obstruction to the rain has ceased and it is well-watered.
Of that lotus: when there is an obstruction to rain, the lotus withers, as if it were well-watered by water. || 37 ||
Gradually, all his limbs shone with vitality,
like the clusters of creepers on a mountain during the flowering season.
In the spring season, when flowers are in bloom. || 38 ||
Then he shone like the lord of stars on a full-moon night, his digits complete, illuminating the world profusely with the rays from the moon of his face. (39)
He caused his limbs to throb— limbs that were tender and full of passion,
radiant with a golden luster like the sprouts of the springtime tree.
He caused to quiver; that is, he caused to move. The absence of both the substitution of *ā* (for *i*) and the *guṇa* change in the root *cisphur* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). || 40 ||
He opened his eyes, which possessed pure and trembling pupils;
they were captivating with their beautiful expanse, like the moon and sun illuminating the world.
The two eyes, captivating and enchanting, possessed of auspicious fullness and endowed with the physical form characteristic of good fortune—
He, the Soul of all worlds, manifested them as the Sun and Moon, which became His own eyes within the Virāj, the universe itself. (41)
He rose up with his body radiant, like the Vindhya mountain increasing in height;
then, with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, he asked, "Who stands there? (42)
Then he said to the two Līlās standing before him, "Let it be commanded.
He beheld the two Līlās standing there, bowing low before him.
"Let the two Līlās be commanded—that is, ordered—by the Great King," he said. || 43 ||
Equal in conduct, equal in appearance, equal in form, and equal in stability; equal in speech, equal in effort, equal in joy, and equal in prosperity. || 44 ||
Looking about, he asked, "Who are you? Who is she? And from where has she come?
To him, Līlā said, "O Lord, listen to what I am saying. (45)
Līlā said, referring to her former pastimes: || 45 ||
O Lord, I am your Līlā, your former wife;
like the inseparable union of word and meaning, I remain joined to you in close embrace. (46)
Just as speech is conjoined with its object by way of being its signifier, so it is in that case. || 46 ||
This second Līlā, this auspicious woman who is like a reflection, has been effortlessly acquired by me for your sake. (47)
"For your sake" means for the purpose of your enjoyment. || 47 ||
Seated at the head of this [throne], protect her on the great golden seat;
O Lord, she is Sarasvatī, the auspicious mother of the three worlds. (48)
"O Lord of the Earth, by means of our accumulated merit, she has appeared here in person;
by her, these two have been brought from the other world to this one. (49)
"We two have come from the other world, from within the cosmic egg. || 49 ||
Having heard this, the lotus-eyed king rose up,
wearing hanging garlands and garments, and fell at the feet of Jñapti.
O Sarasvatī, salutations to you, O Goddess who bestows the welfare of all;
O granter of boons, grant me wisdom, long life, and wealth. (51)
Intelligence (medhā) is the faculty of intellect (buddhi) endowed with the capacity to retain the ultimate meaning of what has been heard. || 51 ||
To him who had spoken thus, the goddess Jñapti touched him with her hand.
Sarasvatī said:
"May you, together with your wife, become enriched by all desired objects, O son! (52)
Be enriched—most fully endowed—with the desired objects of this world, such as long life, wealth, and so forth;
and be joined with the state of being, manifested through the growth of reality, which is the abiding in one's own true nature as the ultimate self. 52.
May all calamities, all misdeeds, and all wrong views come to rest for you, and may infinite happiness arise perfectly;
may people always be joyful and may they flourish.
And may fortunes always sport, remaining firmly established in the kingdom. || 53 ||
May those with evil deeds and wicked intentions go to destruction and ruin;

may infinite and innumerable joys of worldly prosperity come to you. Likewise, may the people—the multitudes of subjects—in your kingdom be ever joyful, and may riches and fortunes always abide with you.
In the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), the *loṭ* [suffix] is used, as in "may they shine" (*vilasantu*). || 53 ||

Thus ends the fifty-eighth canto, titled "The Life of Padma," within the "Legend of Līlā" of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, a work of the Seers (*ārṣa*).
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Life of Padma," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
p. 276) Chapter Fifty-nine (59).
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
Sarasvatī, having said "So be it," vanished on the spot;
at dawn, all the people awoke together with the lotuses.

Due to the king’s restoration to life and his exultation, the festival within his city and inner apartments is described; as well as the kingdom of those liberated while living and their long-lasting liberation. || 1 ||
Having said, "O Sarasvatī, let that which was previously requested by the king be so," she vanished right there in the royal palace. || 1 ||
And he embraced Līlā, and Līlā in turn embraced her beloved;
again and again, out of great joy, they were as if dead and then revived once more.
And Līlā, out of great joy, embraced him again and again as he had died before and been revived once more. || 2 ||
Then the royal palace became languid with intoxication and love; its people were intoxicated with joy, and it resounded with the noise of musical instruments and songs.
At that time, the royal palace was such that the populace there was intoxicated with joy and their minds were beyond control;
it resounded with the deep, humming drone of auspicious victory cries and the proclamation of sacred days,
its courtyards filled with people who were contented and well-nourished, and crowded by the assembly of courtiers.

The "king's people" (rājaloka) are the king's servants; they are called rājaloka because they look toward the king, and they include both the citizens and the rural folk. The courtyard was surrounded by them. || 4 ||
It bore thousands of showers of flowers released by perfected Vidyādharas,
while mṛdaṅgas, murajas, kāhalās, conchs, and dundubhis resounded.
The word *kāhalāśabdaḥ* refers to the sound of a specific musical instrument known by the name *kārṇāla*. || 5 ||
It was intense with the trumpeting of elephants whose massive trunks were tossed upward,
and its courtyards resounded with the cries of women performing vigorous, high-stepping dances.
In which [place] the sound of the threefold arts (song, dance, and instrumental music) resounded, as the courtyards were filled with groups of women engaged in exuberant dances. || 6 ||
It was rugged with the gifts brought by people falling and crowding together,
and it was as beautiful as the world itself, consisting of a multitude of flower garlands.
It was beautiful and radiant with the throngs of various people moving about in the world, who were adorned with flower-crests and abundant festive ornaments. || 7 ||
The sky was filled with large lotuses in the form of the red hands of the dancing ministers, vassals, and citizens, who had scattered their silken garments.
Because it was covered on all sides by ministers, vassals, and citizens who had scattered flowers, parched grain, and pearls, it appeared as if made of silken garments; and in the sky,
with the red hands of dancing girls performing the *tāṇḍava* dance, it became filled with large lotuses, abounding in long-stemmed blossoms.
The intention is that it stands like a lake. || 8 ||
From me [came] the rolling of the three-necked one’s earrings, swinging playfully as he turned;
and the mud of the Puṣpaka chariot, splashing up from the impact of his falling feet.
Where earrings were swayed by the playful movements and graceful turns of the necks of intoxicated and joyful women. || 9 ||
The courtyard of that palace was a canopy formed by the outspread silk garments and autumn clouds,
while the faces of beautiful women dancing there were like a hundred thousand moons.
Where there were canopies made of fine silken cloths resembling the expanse of autumn clouds, and where courtyards of such houses existed in which hundreds of thousands of moons danced.
"The queen and her husband have been brought back from the other world"—thus did people in other lands sing in completed verses. (11)

"That queen was brought from the other world by the second Līlā"—this is understood by implication; "and her husband alone was brought [by the first]"—thus they sang in verses composed of hundreds of narrative threads. (11)
Having heard the brief account thus related, Padma, the lord of the earth,
performed his ablutions with waters brought from the four oceans.
Having heard the account of his own death and so forth, related briefly and in summary. || 12 ||
Then the brahmins, ministers, and kings consecrated him,
who had attained his rise and possessed infinite energy, just as the immortals consecrated Indra.
Just as for one who has returned from a long journey abroad, so too for one who has returned from the other world, the consecration of the feet is for the sake of auspiciousness.
In the case of Indra (Amarendra), it refers to him whose endless efforts (*īhā*) were directed toward the recovery of his own kingdom;
therefore, he is one by whom the dawn of his own sovereignty was regained after the fall of Nahuṣa. 13.
Līlā, Līlā’s husband, and the king— those of great intellect who were liberated while living—
delighted in recounting their past adventures as if they were amorous dalliances.

If it is asked, "Why could there not be a *sarūpaikaśeṣa* (retention of one of two identical forms) here in the case of *līlā līlā*?"—understand that it would be like the analytical sentence for the *ekaśeṣa* [compound] *rāmaśca rāmaśca rāmau*. For it is not the case that there is no analytical sentence (*vigraha*) for the operation of *ekaśeṣa*; rather, when two words have already been fully established through grammatical derivation independently of one another, there subsequently arises the intention to express them together, which is the occasion for that [operation].

Because it is free from contradiction. Since the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) rule finds its scope precisely when there is an intention to express two nominal stem meanings together even before the derivation of case endings, there is no possibility for its application once the two words have reached their final form. || 14 ||
By the grace of Sarasvatī and through his own personal effort,
that king Padma attained the highest welfare for the three worlds.

Now, observing the doubt residing in Rāma's heart— that if the King obtained that restoration to life and his kingdom through the grace of Sarasvatī, then it was obtained solely by destiny and not through his own human effort— he offers a conclusion while dispelling that doubt with the words "By Sarasvatī."

"By his own human effort" means that his grace was produced solely by his own human exertion, such as the propitiation of Sarasvatī, and was not accidental. According to the manner described [in the verse], he obtained the most excellent of blessings in the three worlds:
renewed life, sovereignty, and knowledge. || 15 ||
Having awakened through the knowledge of realization, that blameless king, endowed with the two-fold play,
ruled his kingdom there for eighty thousand years.

Having become perfectly awakened through the knowledge taught by Jñapti—that king, having realized the true nature of the self, ruled the kingdom for eighty-eight thousand years. The accusative case is used here according to the rule *kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge* ("in the case of time and distance, when there is continuous connection"). 16.
Having ruled the kingdom for eighty thousand years as those who were liberated while living,
they— whose consciousness was perfected— attained the state of liberation beyond the body (videhamukti).
Those who have attained perfected consciousness have their awakening firmly established in the enemy [of ignorance]. || 17 ||
171 That which is bright with its emergence, clever yet charming, appropriate, beneficial to oneself, and refined;
Having protected their own kingdom for a long time— which brought satisfaction to all people— the virtuous couple were liberated.

That kingdom which is radiant through the constant prosperity of its subjects; which is faultless; which is charming and delightful to the wise because it follows the scriptures; which is worthy of the family lineage;
which is beneficial as it is the cause of one's own enjoyment, fame, and merit; and which is elegant through the pleasing of the people.

And it was fourfold. Therefore, having protected their own kingdom—which brought satisfaction to all people—for a long time, that virtuous couple, at the end of the enjoyment of the fruits of their *prārabdha* karma, were liberated and attained disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*), like two lotuses in play. Now, one might object: "Previously, the state of being liberated while living (*jīvanmukti*) was stated for three [of them]; how is it that here the liberation of only the two is concluded?"
This is because the second *līlā*, consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of King Cedi, is intended to be included within the former *līlā*, as it is essentially a reflection of it. || 18 ||
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Extinction of the Lotus," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki according to the ancient seers. 59.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Extinction of the Lotus," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Sixtieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This has been told to you, O Rāma, for the sake of removing the defect of the perceived world.
Abandon this sinless narrative of Līlā’s play, which causes the density of the world to increase.
First, the purpose of narrating the divine play (līlā) is described here in detail;
furthermore, the cause for the equality and inequality of time and other factors is explained herein. (1)

For the cessation of the defects of the visible world; and thus, if the cleansing of the mind of the visible world has been accomplished through the realization that "the visible does not exist," then the supreme bliss of Nirvāṇa is attained.
This is the sense: the very purpose of this work is the fulfillment of that which was promised at its outset. [The text continues: "solidity..."
Truthfulness. || 1 ||
The reality of the visible world is indeed quiescent; therefore, its pacification is not required.
For there is the labor of cleansing what exists, but never for that which does not exist.
[Objection: But how can there be the cessation of the visible world merely by abandoning the notion of its reality? To this he says: "It is already peaceful.

The meaning is that as long as the cognition of reality persists, there is effort involved in the negation (*apavāda*) such as "it is not so" through cleansing; however, once the falsity has been determined by means of reasoning, that effort no longer exists. || 2 ||
Having perceived that the object of sight, which is of the nature of the knowable, has become one with knowledge in the form of space, the knower remains like the sky. (3)

Thus, in the manner described, [the universe] has become one through negation, having attained the state of being an indivisible single essence. If this world, which is devoid of earth and other elements, has been established by the self-existent one—who is pure consciousness and a knower of reality—then it is established within his own self. (4)

Now, one might object: "How can there be a state of identity with consciousness for the insentient visible world? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] explains that at the beginning of creation, by the Self-existent One (Svayambhū) himself, who is of the nature of pure consciousness alone, the manifestation of the visible world was imagined within his own self, just as the hardness of a clod of earth [is imagined] in the hand.
With the intention that [the case] is established just as there is no contradiction between liquidity and oneness, he says: "devoid of earth and so forth. (4)
Just as she strives, so indeed is she established;
once released into the river of creative knowledge, she flows on until she is restrained by effort.
In that case, one might ask: why does the dissolution of the visible world not occur without effort, just as the hardness of a water-jar [dissolves] when placed in fire?
To this he replies: "Consciousness" (saṃvit). That which knows creation is the "knower of creation," the self-existent consciousness (*svayaṃbhū-caitanya*).

In the river characterized by that [consciousness], there exists the individual consciousness (*jīva-saṃvit*), which is but a part of it; and just as [the individual consciousness] functions through a certain flow of activity—*yathā-yādṛśa-pravṛtti-pravāheṇa*—[so too does the dissolution depend on that].

Just as one exerts effort toward the state of performing a particular action and attaining its fruit, so too, having been projected with that very state of performing the action and attaining the fruit, it remains established exactly according to its own effort; and as long as it is not obstructed by an effort toward the cessation of its contrary, it does not cease.
This is the meaning. || 5 ||
This world is understood as the manifestation of the space of consciousness;
it exists within the very self, the pure sky of consciousness, even down to the finest atomic particle.

One might object: "How can this world, created by Brahmā, be contradicted by the effort of an individual soul? Indeed, that which is established by the command of a great king cannot be overturned by the effort of an ordinary person.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the clear sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*)," and so forth. Although [the world] exists within the very clarity of the space of consciousness...

It is understood that this world is a mere illusory appearance of the space of consciousness within the Self that is Brahman; thus, the world is created by Brahman. Nevertheless, it does not appear as such to the unconditioned state of Brahman, but rather—

The meaning is as follows: with respect to the individual soul (jīva), which is extremely limited by means of adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth—being as minute as an atom—it is for the sake of experiencing the fruits of karma produced by its own effort that [the world] is superimposed upon Brahman. Thus, the cleansing of the visible world through the knowledge produced by that effort is indeed possible. || 6 ||
Thus, regarding this vain delusion, tell me: what is its existence, or what is its latent impression (vāsanā)? What is its locus, what is its necessity, and what is said to be its inevitability? (7)

This being the case, with the intention that there is no possibility of the appearance of objects even through the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the necessity of beings (*sattvaniyati*) and so forth, he says:
"All this remains exactly as it is seen, thus unbroken;
this is but an infinite illusion (*māyā*), yet no such illusion exists at all. (8)

All this exists as it is perceived within the perspective of illusion (māyā-dṛṣṭi), yet it does not exist within the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha-dṛṣṭi). For this creation, being an effect of illusion, is indeed illusion itself; and the meaning is that illusion is not a real entity. || 8 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Oh, what a supreme vision has been shown by you, O Blessed One!
It is like the cooling moonlight for those whose dry grass has been consumed by a forest fire.

The meaning is that this view is like a digit of the moon for the regrowth of green sprouts for those scorched by the heat of saṃsāra, just as the regrowth of green shoots occurs when the burning of dry grass and heaps of straw consumed by a forest fire has been extinguished. || 9 ||
Ah! After a very long time, that which was to be known has today been known by me—unimpaired, as it is, what it is, of what nature it is, from whence it comes, and when it arises.

By means of five verses, the aspects appropriate for the awakening to reality—namely, the method, the essential nature, the illustration, the means of valid cognition, and the time—are proclaimed in sequence;
or rather, [the reality] is to be known by means of such illustrations or by those who are qualified [to understand them]. (10)
O best of the twice-born, as I contemplate this, I feel as if I am becoming tranquil and as if I am attaining liberation;
for this wondrous narrative is an exposition upon the perspectives of the scriptures. (11)
Conceptualizing the reality of the world and investigating it, I feel as if I am becoming tranquil through the cessation of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Through the attainment of the nature of eternal liberation, I feel as if I am extinguished. The scriptures and the Vedas [serve] regarding the views and knowledges revealed therein; the commentary serves as a means of expansion. || 11 ||
172. O Blessed One, Knower of All, resolve this doubt for me!
I am not yet satiated by drinking the nectar of your words with the vessels of my ears. (12)
This which is about to be stated. || 12 ||
Indeed, for the Lord who sports through yoga, that time which exists within the three creations is sometimes a single day and night,
and sometimes merely a month.

The time that has passed in the three previously mentioned creations—the Vāsiṣṭha, the Pādma, and the Vaidūrattha—is stated to consist of eight days and nights in a certain mountain village; however, in the Pādma creation it is merely a month, while in the Vaidūrattha it consists of many years—such is the distinction between the Brahmāṇḍas. || 13 ||
In some cases it lasts for many years; for someone else, is it perhaps very brief? For one it may be exceedingly long, while for another it remains but a moment. (14)
In a single universe, the year of humans is but a fleeting day for the gods;

yet for some small creature, that very same period is exceedingly long; and for the Self-born Creator (Svayambhū), it is but a moment. Thus, how can a single time exist in such contradictory forms according to differences of place, world, and so forth? This is because the existence of objects possesses a single uniform nature.
The intention is: "How is there a discrepancy in experience? The syntactical connection is: "Tell me this doubt."
O Blessed One, please speak to me according to the truth out of your grace;
for what is heard but once does not remain still, like water on a clod of earth. (15)

"Is it not true that just as there is no length of space, so too there is no length of time? Since the answer to this has already been stated almost entirely previously, why do you ask again? To this he says: "At once," etc. "Loṣṭe" means in a clod of dry earth; "jalaṃ" means a drop of water. || 15 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O sinless one, whatever is perceived by whomsoever, in whatever manner, and whenever it is,
that very thing is experienced by them in that very way at that very time.
If cognition were to conform to the existence of an external object, then this contradiction would indeed arise;

however, since the existence of the object is indeterminate (anirvacanīya) and conforms to cognition, there is no fault of temporal discrepancy due to the difference in the objects perceived by each observer.
With this intention, he provides the answer: "By whatever [means]... (verse 16).
Amṛta becomes poison through the constant perception of it as poison;
an enemy becomes a friend through the perception of him as a friend. (17)
He illustrates this very point with the passage beginning "immortality" (*amṛtatvam*) and so forth. "Immortality" means being the cause of life, like nectar (*amṛta*).

[This occurs] from the knowledge of nectar—that is, from the knowledge that it is the means for sustaining life. For instance, insects that are the objects of such firm conviction live by means of poison itself. How then [is this possible]?

If it is argued that death is observed in one who has consumed poison through negligence with the thought that it was edible food, [the answer is: like worms, for them there is an absence of a firm consciousness regarding the poison as being a cause of life due to long-term habituation, and because there exists a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the certainty that the poison is a cause of death. || 17 ||
Just as the inherent nature of these categories has been meditated upon,
that very nature, through long-term practice, comes under the sway of necessity.

He clarifies this very point with the words "tadeva hi" (for that indeed). Thus, the meaning is that *niyati* (necessity) is the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in objects, which follows the long-practiced perception [of those objects] up to the point of mastery over necessity. || 18 ||
In whatever manner this consciousness, whose sole essence is like a mirror,
reflects, in that very manner it immediately becomes so, because its own nature is the sole cause.

Furthermore, the nature of consciousness is its luminous manifestation (*sphuraṇa*), whereas its taking on the form of specific objects depends upon the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the perceiver. Thus, within a single act of consciousness,
the attribution of a mere moment (*nimeṣa*) by one person and the attribution of an eon (*kalpa*) or more by another— according to their respective impressions— is not contradictory.
Thus he says with three verses beginning with "kacanaika": || 19 ||
If one attains the consciousness of a multitude of kalpas within a single moment, then that kalpa becomes a mere moment; of this there is no doubt.
If one perceives an eon as a mere blink of an eye, then even that eon quickly becomes a blink; for consciousness is of such a nature.
For one who suffers, a night is like an eon; for one who is happy, even an eon is but a moment.
In a dream, a moment may become an eon, and an eon may become a moment.
He states that this manner of proceeding is well-known even in the world: "Of one who is suffering," etc. (22).
Just as one experiences in a dream: "Having died and been born again, I have become a youth established in my prime, and I have traveled a hundred yojanas. (23)
Thus, a dream is experienced by some; this is the ellipsis. || 23 ||
Hariścandra experienced twelve years as a single night,
while Lavaṇa enjoyed a lifespan of one hundred years in a single night.
He illustrates this very point with the example "Hariścandra. This is well known from the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* and other sources as King Lavaṇa; and he will explain this further below. || 24 ||
That which is a single muhūrta for Prajāpati Manu is the lifespan of the sage;
that which is the lifespan of Viriñca is indeed a single day for the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu).
That which is the life-span of Manu is but a single moment for the sage Prajāpati, who is habituated to self-contemplation;
the word "sage" (muni) is to be connected with the subsequent [verses] as well. || 25 ||
O Rāma, for one whose mind is worn away by meditation, there are neither days nor nights; it is as if Viṣṇu’s life were but a single day for Śiva.
But in the non-conceptual samādhi, there is no distinction between day and night; thus he says: "In meditation... (verse 26).
For the yogin, neither objects nor the world are real within the Self;
sweet things turn bitter when contemplated with a sense of bitterness. (27)

The category of sense-objects is sweet and pleasant; [he perceives it as] pungent, that is, unpleasant, by means of its pungent nature, which is the latent impression of dispassion (vairāgya). || 27 ||
That which is bitter attains sweetness when contemplated as sweet;
an enemy becomes a friend through the perception of friendship, and a friend becomes an enemy through the perception of enmity. (28)

That which was previously bitter and unpleasant becomes most dear through the sweetness arising from the restraint of the senses, mind, and vital breaths, and through the clarity of one's own bliss. When practiced with the perception of enemies, teachers, scriptures, and so forth as friends, and with the perception of them as the most trustworthy authorities, they become a friend and the supreme authority. Thus, that which was formerly...
A fool who considers his companions in sensual enjoyment and his own kinsmen as enemies—thinking them to be obstructors of the goals of human life—becomes exactly so. || 28 ||
O mighty-armed one, the world appears according to one's own perception;
likewise, those objects that have not been practiced, such as the recitation of scriptures and the chanting of mantras, [do not appear]. (29)
He shows that the same principle applies to recitation, meditation, protection, and so forth, with the words: "When not practiced," etc. (29).
Through the repeated practice of those perceptions, one certainly attains equanimity;
for the earth appears to whirl due to the perception of those traveling by boat who are afflicted by dizziness. (30)
"Equally" means sameness; its state is "sameness-ness," which is non-differentiation, self-dependence, or—in other words—attainment. It becomes so; that is to say, it evolves or moves. || 30 ||
Even for those afflicted by the delusion of non-feeling, this does not change:
the empty becomes crowded through feeling, just as in the visions of a dreamer. (31)
But for those standing on the shore—those who are empty of the delusions and afflictions of sensation—it does not turn back when viewed with right vision. || 31 ||
Due to sensation, yellow, blue, or even white is experienced;
like a calamity, a festival causes distress through delusion. (32)
"It is experienced that the sky is being deluded. For instance, even during their own festivals, children are sometimes seen weeping. || 32 ||
Indeed, even on a wall, the conduct of one who does not investigate is seen to be like that in empty space;
for an unreal yakṣa [projected by] the deluded can even snatch away their lives. (33)
He states that even the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) of objects that are unreal is well-known in the world, beginning with the words "asadyakṣa" and so forth. || 33 ||
A woman seen in a dream bestows pleasure as if she were awake;
whatever appears in such a manner becomes established exactly in that way. (34)
The sky is indeed non-existent within the conscious self, and the conscious self is indeed like the sky;
it is spread out like the dance of a hundred-cubit shadow of a cloud.

"Asadeva" means "it does not exist at all. If one asks, "In that case, what is it that is not false? he says: "And just like the sky. Since the effect is nothing but the cause, the meaning is that it is simply the unmanifested space (*avyākṛtākāśa*).
And thus, that very sky [is superimposed] upon its own substrate, the conscious Self (*cidātman*), just as a false actor is imagined through the shadow of a cloud upon a hundred-cubit [tall] tree.
The meaning is that the world, being extended—that is, spread out—through its manifold variety, is like a dance characterized by specific dramatic gestures (abhinaya). || 35 ||
Know that the movement of the mind in the sky is the world; it is not a real entity.
The perception of movement is the form of the demon of false knowledge.
With the intention that its unreality follows from its being an effect of both the collective and individual totality of all minds, he says: "In the sky.
That which has a form consisting of mind alone is comparable to the perception of the movement of a ghost imagined by a child through false cognition. || 36 ||
This is merely illusion, unobstructed and without a foundation;
it stands as a radiant manifestation, like the vision of a dream. (37)
Because it lacks substantial form, it does not itself obstruct anything else;
it is devoid of any other obstructing object that is not based on a wall; and this world appears clearly and radiantly.
Those who know reality understand this to be a dream-vision arisen for the first time even while a man is not asleep.
The subsequent [connection] is with another. || 37 ||
The wise know that for one who is not asleep, this [state] is like something unprecedented arising, just as a senseless pillar perceives a wooden statue. (38)

Though devoid of consciousness and empty of its own activity conducive to self-manifestation, it becomes conscious within itself and projects a statue in the form of an image. Whatever it is itself, whatever kind [of creation],
and whatever nature of creation it conceives at the time of emanation— it beholds that very thing as the Great Pillar of Ultimate Reality.
The meaning is that the conscious self, which is the substrate of all, having become such [a form], perceives such a creation at the time of emanation. || 38 ||
The Great Pillar of Ultimate Reality perceives the creation as being just like that man who appeared by my side in a dream, agitated by great warriors. (39)

In my dream, a man agitated and disturbed by great warriors—even though he is awakened—is like one in deep sleep, having as his very nature mere ignorance and not being a real entity; the creation of Brahmā is likewise just such, as is the connection with the subsequent [verse]. || 39 ||
Such is the heaven of Brahmā; it is indeed the Buddha himself, like deep sleep, like the sap at the end of winter that pervades the grass, shrubs, and creepers. (40)
