At the end of the cold season, at the time when the leaves of trees and other plants are falling, the spring juice—accompanied by grass, shrubs, and creepers—is present in the earth as its material cause; the meaning is that it exists there exactly as it will later manifest in the spring in the form of sprouts, flowers, and so forth. || 40 ||
The springtime remains upon the earth, and likewise, creation resides in the supreme state;
just as fluidity exists within gold, yet remains unmanifest.
Thus situated in the supreme creation, from the self within atom to atom, the arrangement of the limbs is non-different from the self of the possessor of the limbs. 42.

The meaning is that from the category of the self—that is, from the aggregate of living beings—as a cause, there exists and will exist in the Supreme that creation which is to be experienced by them. The arrangement, the specific configuration, of the limbs—the constituent parts—is non-different from the whole, the Self; because it is not distinct [from it], meaning it does not possess a separate existence. || 42 ||
Just as a single man in a dream might engage in battle against another man, so too does the world exist for the bodiless one (Ananga) and for Brahman, who is his own self.

Likewise, the meaning is "from Brahman, which is non-different from its own self, as the world," that is, by way of non-distinction (*avyatireka*). The term "of the unreal" (*anaṅgasya*) is stated to exclude [the possibility of] having an equal ontological status (*samasattākatva*). For instance, when one man fights with another man in a dream, at that time, although [the other man] has the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*) for the dreamer, he has the nature of non-existence (*asad-rūpa*) for someone else.

In this same way, this world, which resides in the space of *māyā*, is one's own self; though it appears real from the perspective of *māyā*, it is in fact unreal from the perspective of the other, pure vision—this is the meaning. || 43 ||
Such is this world, which exists within the sky of one's own self, possessing the nature of both being and non-being;
at the beginning of creation following the end of a great aeon, this world is of the very nature of consciousness. [The reading "vapuḥ" (body) is also found.]
He states that it is of the nature of that alone (*tanmātra*) by way of elimination, since at the times of the beginning and the end there is only the existence of Brahman alone:
"At the end of the great kalpa... (44).
Mutual causality does not exist subsequently as something real;

for if, within this liberated Brahman, another [world] born of memory were to arise, then even in that creation born of the cognition of memory, the state of being pure consciousness remains established. (45)
The state of being a cause consists in the conceptualization of mutual causality when there is a differentiation of effects.

Furthermore, because the world is constructed by memory—which is produced by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of meditation consisting of the conceit of identity (*ahaṃbhāva*) with Hiraṇyagarbha, who has transformed into the form of the entire universe—the world is not distinct from the pure Being (*sanmātra*) that serves as its substratum; thus he says:
"In the liberated" (mukte). || 45 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
How was the lineage of Vidūratha manifested equally to all those eminent ministers of the city at that time? (46)

With the intention of asking whether, just as for beings residing within different cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*), so too for those residing in a single city, there might not be a superimposition of sequential variety even in the waking state—due to the diversity of their individual latent impressions (*vāsanā*), karma, and so forth, just as in a dream—Rāma asks: "Of the citizens" (*paurāṇām*). "Equally" (*samam*) means in an identical manner.
How could it appear as such? What is the cause therein? This is the meaning. || 46 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
All primary perceptions follow from the consciousness of the principal [Self],
just as ordinary gusts of wind follow from a massive whirlwind.

With the intention that the very cause for the conformity of the consciousnesses of other living beings to the consciousness of the primary living being is the restriction established by the will of the Creator, Vasiṣṭha said, beginning with the words "Of the consciousness... [and so forth]. They are common and few. 47.
O Protector of Subjects, those ministers dwelling among the people have been brought together in such a manner through mutual agreement. (48)
And with the intention that the meeting of the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) which brings about a fruit corresponding to that [action] is the cause therein, he says:

"paraspara... and so on. Likewise, that which is "tathārūpa" (of such a form) is the collection of *adṛṣṭas* which fashions (*rūpayati*) or accomplishes [the result] in a uniform manner (*aikarūpyeṇa*);
by means of that, the protector of the subjects (*prajāpāla*), as well as the subjects (*prajāḥ*), the residents (*vāstavyāḥ*), the city-dwellers (*puravāsinaḥ*), and the ministers (*mantriṇaḥ*).
They are manifested through mutual conformity. || 48 ||
"This king of ours was born from such a family;
he is indeed well-known among the residents in the city of Vaidūrathe. (49)
Expanding upon the variety of appearances in the mirror, he states their falsity with the words "of such a form" (*evam-rūpāt*).

Things existing in the city of Vaiḍūrya—namely, the inhabitants (*vāstavyāḥ*) residing on the ground of the houses (*veśma-bhūmiṣu*) and the people who know them and enjoy them—are as if reflected in the mirror. (49)

Furthermore, when the nature of something is already manifest, it is not reasonable to search for a cause elsewhere than its own nature, just as one does not seek the cause of the radiance of a great gem elsewhere than from its own nature. (50)

If it is asked, "What is the cause for the manifestation of superimposed objects in the shining forth of consciousness, which is itself indifferent?"—we reply that consideration of a cause is not appropriate here, because this shining forth is adventitious; therefore, such inquiry is appropriate only regarding other adventitious objects.
Just as, for example, there is no dependence on any other cause for the diffusion of light from an indifferent cintāmaṇi gem, but rather—
He says "in the act of shining" (kacane) to show that, just like that [the sun], there is a dependence on the variety of the mental desires of those who contemplate when producing various objects.
"I alone shall be king in this manner according to family custom"—
such was the intuition that arose from the jewel for Vidūratha and his kinsmen.
He states that even the arising of the variety of volitions favorable to that [creation] occurs precisely according to the manner already described—beginning with the words "I am.

[This occurs] from the living-consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*) of Vidūratha, the knower, acting as the efficient cause; thus, he is like a *cintāmaṇi* jewel. He shows that even the jewel of consciousness produces objects exactly according to one's desires, beginning with the words "from the gem. [This is] intuition (*pratibhā*).
Manoratha || 51 ||
However many beings there may be, in whatever creation, at whatever time—
because the element of consciousness is omnipresent, they have all entered into a state of mutual reflection [the reading "sargagatvāt" is also found]. (52)

He says—“as many as... (verse 52)—to explain how, through the process of attributing identical objects to the various individual consciousnesses (*jīvacaitanya*), it is as if the mirrors have come to possess reflections of one another within themselves.
That consciousness which, possessing intense momentum, becomes unshakable therein,
attains supreme stability and remains uniform in form until liberation.

Now, one might object: "If this is so, since the emergence of a reflection is unavoidable when there is an original object (*bimba*), how can there be the attainment of liberation characterized by the absence of objects? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Possessing intense momentum" (*tīvravegavatī*). In that context, among those individual consciousnesses (*jīvasaṃvit*), that very consciousness of the individual which is a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of Brahman is what possesses intense momentum.

Being unshaken by the defects of sense-objects, it remains of a single form until liberation; that alone, being supreme and most excellent, attains stability in the state of Brahman, which is characterized as liberation, and nothing else—this is the meaning. || 53 ||
By following after one another through the powerful play of consciousness, the various natures naturally reflect within the mirror of consciousness. 54.

Thus, regarding the reflection of the individual consciousness (jīvaciti) in the form of either the world or Brahman, he says "powerful" (balavat): it is precisely those manifestations of consciousness in various forms—characterized by intensity and force—that serve as the regulator, owing to the very nature of necessity (niyati). || 54 ||
There, through great effort, they conquer the true cognitions and make them their own,
just as rivers flowing toward the ocean appropriate the tributary streams.

An objection is raised: "If this is so, since the tendency toward the world has been practiced for a long time, and because a powerful impulse arises toward that very [world], there can be no hope for liberation.

Anticipating this, he says: "Therein" (*tatra*). Because it is observed that an effortless impulse is more powerful than an effortful one, the impulse in the form of Brahman, accomplished through extreme effort, alone prevails.
Furthermore, because it is observed that among cognitions whose objects are both real and unreal,

those whose objects are real possess greater strength, it is the very cognitions whose form is Brahman— the reality— that bring this [individual self] under their own control, making it dependent upon themselves.
Just as small rivers that flow into the great ocean, once merged with it, cause their own course to become subject to the ocean's will.
The meaning is "in that same way. || 55 ||
Those who are equal therein strive by virtue of their conscious nature only so long as one prevails here and the second sinks away. (56)

Granted that victory occurs when the momentum toward the form of Brahman is intense; however, one might raise the objection that when, due to being of dull or middling capacity, the mind lacks stability and the emergence of the form of Brahman and the emergence of external forms occur intermittently, then because of their equality there can be no hope for victory over either side. Anticipating this, he says:
Regarding the word "ye" (those who): those qualified persons who are equal and possess equal momentum in the two aforementioned forms do not remain as they are;

rather, they strive until, between these two mentioned forms, one—the form of Brahman—becomes established, prevails, and reaches the pinnacle of excellence, while the second, the external form, sinks away.

They exert effort characterized by the repetition of hearing and so forth; thus, for them as well, through the sequence of practice, there arises an intense momentum, whereby the mastery of the other [breaths] is achieved—this is the meaning. || 56 ||
Thus, throughout thousands of creations— as beings are born, perish, and exist in great numbers— even down to every single atom— (57)

Having thus established the refutation of the incidental consequence that liberation would be impossible, he addresses the subject at hand— the uniform and diverse manifoldness pertaining to every individual soul— beginning with the words "jāyamāneṣu" (among those being born) and so forth.
Due to the superimposition of limitation caused by adjuncts (*upādhi*), even for the multitude of souls, which are as minute as atoms, it is in the manner described above...

Throughout thousands of creations—whether equal or unequal—arising, persisting, and perishing through delusion, in the ultimate sense (paramārthatas), nothing whatsoever has been obtained by anyone, whether by one who is running about with a fragment of life or by one who remains indifferent;
for that which is not a real entity (avastu) is incapable of both obtaining and not obtaining. This is the meaning. || 57 ||
Nothing is pervaded by anything—[the reading "pervaded by anything" (kenacid vyāptam) occurs in some versions]—nor does anything abide in anything.
This is the peaceful space of consciousness; therefore, everything is without a foundation.
This dream appears as if one were sleepless and devoid of sight; yet its awakening is inevitable, and though it was personally experienced, it is composed of unreality. (59)

Devoid of [wrong] views and empty of the vision of [false] discrimination, he is one for whom awakening—the direct realization of the substratum—is inevitable; yet, even though it has been experienced before, it is as if non-existent, resembling something unreal. || 59 ||
Just as a single tree, established in its own state, consists of the essence of leaves, flowers, and fruits,
so too the all-pervading Lord is truly one, consisting of the essence of infinite and universal powers.
Having stated that the phenomenal world has no existence apart from pure vision, he says "on the page" (patra) even from the perspective of the vision colored by māyā. || 60 ||
The unborn state, whose nature is illusory—consisting of the knower, the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and so forth—is never forgotten by anyone at any time. (61)

He says "mātra" (only) to show that although [the world] appears as diverse through the perspective of the living soul until enlightenment, it remains as one alone within pure consciousness, because of the absence of ignorance—which is the cause of forgetfulness—once awakening has occurred. || 61 ||
The reality of the arising and setting of emptiness is both darkness and light; though possessing the form of space and time, it is eternally one, beginningless, and pure.
Devoid of beginning, end, or middle, it abides as clear water.
It is like a single entity enriched by the surging waves of gentleness. || 62 ||

With the intention that even though there is multiplicity resulting from its role as the manifester of illusion (*māyā*), there is no contradiction to the persistence of the pure [Self] in its truly singular nature, he concludes with the verse beginning "śūnya": "It illumines darkness by way of being the witness; thus, although it is of the nature of space and time, it is eternally pure in the ultimate sense."

In that wherein both the arising and the passing away of all modifications are empty, such a reality of the Self remains as one alone, devoid of beginning, middle, and end; just as water— whether clear and stainless,
or rich in gentleness and abounding in the rippling of waves— is one and the same because it possesses the single uniform nature of water.
The meaning is "in that same way. || 62 ||
She, whose nature is the world beginning with "I" and "you," shines as the single manifestation of pure consciousness.
Just as one's own emptiness exists within the expanse of space,
so too [the world] arises from the conceptualization and mental construction of duality and unity.

The manifestation of Brahman, whose sole nature is pure consciousness, is its very essence; yet, due to the cause that is the mind— which consists of conceptualizations and mental constructions regarding duality and unity— and due to the word "and" (ca), which implies the influence of ignorance, desire, karma, and latent impressions (vāsanā) rooted therein, [it appears as] "I," "mine," and so forth.

It shines forth as having the nature of the superimposed world; the meaning is that it is just as one's own emptiness alone appears within a sheath characterized as space in the form of a floor, filth, pearls, hair-whorls, bowls, and so forth. || 63 ||

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Purpose of Līlā," in the section on Origination within the Means to Liberation of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki according to the tradition of the Sages. || 60 ||
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Purpose," in the section on Origination within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The sixty-first canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"The delusion that 'I am the world' occurs without any cause other than the Supreme."
O Brahmin, please explain to me properly once more how it arises.

For the sake of establishing the purpose [of the treatise] and for the sake of detachment from cyclic existence (saṃsṛti), its lack of essence and its non-existence are described through various types of reasoning. (1)

Just as the delusion of "I" arises regarding the body and so forth— which are not the self— even in the absence of a cause for the sense of "I," and just as the delusion of a "world" arises within the interior of an atom or a moment— even in the absence of a cause for the world's configuration characterized by vastness and duration— so too does it arise through such a process of conceptualization and such a manner of reasoning.

The meaning is "please speak. Now, one might object: since this was already stated previously in the passage beginning with "this body is of the nature of consciousness at the beginning of creation at the end of the great aeon," why is it asked again? To this he replies: "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*).
[Speak] in such a way that it is refined by those logical arguments (*upapatti*) by which one may ascend to direct experience; that is, [speak] so as to be adorned with such arguments.
The meaning is "he said. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Since all perceptions are understood as being essentially equal within consciousness,
therefore everything is in every way, at all times, and in its entirety, the unborn Self of all.

In this regard, Śrī Vasiṣṭha first spoke—beginning with the words "All these"—to establish that the primary logical proof for all delusions is their very state of being first manifested within consciousness. For this knower, in every way and in all modes, all delusions are always within consciousness; they are internalized within the very nature of consciousness itself.

It is never perceived as anything whatsoever external to It; therefore, everything has everything as its essence, and that is indeed equanimity (*samatā*). For when everything has everything as its essence, no inequality remains. Since transformations such as birth and so forth are not possible in the absence of that [inequality], the world-illusion exists only as the unborn Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in reality.
The meaning is that what was stated—that [the world arises] even without a cause—is logically established. || 2 ||
For all perceptions of word and meaning are indeed Brahman alone; they are not separate from it.
Among these, there exists no form whatsoever that consists of the subtle essence of all objects and words.

[Objection: But how can the identity of everything with everything be established merely by the fact that it is cognized within another consciousness? [Reply: If you say "because of the manifestation of identity with a single mind," we say no; for since there is an experience of difference in consciousness itself—due to the experience of difference between distinct objects such as "the cognition of a jar" and "the cognition of a cloth"—consciousness must be diverse. Anticipating this objection, he says: "For all... (sarvā hi).

There is no difference in consciousness (*cit*), because all perceptions of words and their meanings are Brahman alone. Indeed, there is no substratum of consciousness (*cid-dhātu*) apart from Brahman. For it is only through the coloring (*uparāga*) of objective diversity that difference is perceived in consciousness; yet when objects are abstracted away, that [consciousness] is not distinct from the nature of pure consciousness (*cid-rūpa*). The meaning is that it does not differ. Now, one might object:

To the question, "Might there not be a distinction [between cognitions] due to their appearing as objects, just like the objects themselves? he replies with the words "sarvārtha... (regarding all objects).

Those things which are sought after are "objects" (*artha*), meaning the entities that serve as sense-objects, such as words and their referents. The "parts" (*kalā*) of those—namely, the forms consisting of broad bases, bellies, and so forth—are not found in these perceptions (*dṛś*). This is because they reside in consciousness (*cit*).
Because there is no possibility of existence for an insentient form [independently], the sense is that the form which is experienced belongs only to the mental modification (*vṛtti*).
Just as the state of being a bracelet does not exist apart from gold, nor the state of being a wave apart from water,
so too the world does not exist apart from the Lord.

Thus, once the distinction between consciousnesses has been refuted, the distinction between insentient objects can also be refuted, since they lack existence and manifestation apart from that [consciousness].
He states this with an illustration: "The state of being a bracelet," etc. (Verse 4).
This very [Brahman] is the form of the world, but the form of the world does not exist in the Lord;
just as gold alone is the bracelet and so forth, but the state of being a bracelet does not exist in the gold.

Nevertheless, how is it possible to say that [consciousness] has arisen without a cause? Since consciousness itself is the cause, just like gold, he says: "This very [consciousness]... For if the world were different from that [consciousness], it could have that [consciousness] as its cause; but if there were absolute non-difference, consciousness would not possess causality. What then?

He says "no" to the idea that Brahman is indeed of the form of the world, stating: "But the form of the world... The intention is that an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) does not exist as something separate [from its substrate]. And thus, with the intention that even bracelets, earrings, and so forth are merely illusory manifestations of Brahman whose nature is gold, he says: "Gold alone... (5).
Just as the form of a whole consists of many parts, so too the partless consciousness is that which consists of all things. 6.
One might object that there is a contradiction in a single entity having a manifold nature; however,

since in the world it is not contradicted for a single whole to have an identity of equal ontological status with its many parts— even those possessing equal ontological status— then what need be said regarding [an identity] with many parts that are merely imagined, as opposed to real?

With the intention that identity with Brahman is not contradictory, he says "just as" (yathā). Furthermore, with the intention that there is no contradiction because, in the state of oneness, everything attains the nature of being the self of all and thus multiplicity ceases, he says "and consisting of all" (sarvātmakam) || 6 ||
That which is perceived as the totality of the sense-data at the same time, O Supreme One, appears internally as this world, as well as as "I. (7)
What then? To explain how the world and the "I" appear as a manifoldness established by universal experience, he says: "That which...

It is that very ignorance—the non-cognition of one's own nature as Brahman alone—which dwells within all living beings within the Supreme Brahman at the same time, that appears as the manifoldness of the world and the "I."
The meaning is that it shines. || 7 ||
Just as the arrangement of various inscriptions exists within the interior of a stone,
so too do the world and the "I" exist densely within the mass of consciousness, non-different from it. (8)

Just as lines or streaks appear within the interior of a crystal stone, and just as the arrangement of reflections of a multitude of forest lines is not contradictory even though there is no actual division [in the crystal], so it is here as well; thus he says: "of the multitudes of lines. (8)
Just as waves abide within water that is surging with internal motion,
so too do creations exist within the Supreme, devoid of the words and meanings of "creation."
The supreme does not abide in the creation, nor does the creation abide in the supreme;
their existence is like that of a part and the whole, yet they are without parts.

One might object: "Just as waves that have subsided remain within the great ocean as its constituent parts (*avayava*), or as a whole (*avayavin*) resides in its parts through inherence (*samavāya*), why should the world not abide in Brahman in the same way? To this he says: "No.
In reality, even between a part and a whole, a mutual relationship of substratum and superstratum is not logically tenable; thus he says: "Existence" (*sattā*).

To explain: does the whole (avayavin) residing in its parts exist in each part in its entirety, or does it reside by means of its parts? In the first case, there would follow the consequence of a plurality of wholes for every single part; that is, since the entire cow would exist even in the region of the ear and so forth, it would follow that the functional effects such as milking could be performed [on that single ear].

Furthermore, even when the parts are separated, it would follow that the whole is not destroyed, just as a universal (jāti) is not. In the second case [that the whole exists in its entirety within each part], there would be an infinite regress;
and if there were an infinity of parts, it would follow that Mount Meru and a mustard seed would have equal dimensions. Likewise, regarding the parts themselves in relation to the whole:
would they reside in one part of it or in its entirety? In the first case, there is an infinite regress. In the second case...

Since another part cannot be included [within a part] and since it is impossible for a non-dual entity to possess parts, it follows that all substances would necessarily be partless; thus, the meaning is that the existence of both those—the part and the whole—is ultimately established as being itself without parts. || 10 ||
By means of its own self-awareness as the nature of consciousness, one's own pure consciousness is manifested;
it is one's very own form and heart, just as vibration is produced by the wind. (11)

Desiring to demonstrate that the world is non-different from Consciousness even by means of the process of establishing "creation-in-vision" (dṛṣṭasṛṣṭi), [the author] first states that Consciousness, though devoid of action, manifests itself otherwise through reflection within ignorance: "By the nature of Consciousness," etc.; that is, by Brahman, whose nature is ultimate Consciousness.

First, by means of self-awareness— which is like a mirror reflecting the eyes when they are turned back by ignorance— one perceives and conceptualizes one's own very heart, which is the secret essence of the phenomenal world consisting of pure consciousness, yet remains shrouded in nescience. The word "eva" (only) [is used for emphasis].
This is for the purpose of indicating the forgetting of one's own prior, ultimate nature. || 11 ||
At that moment, this atom of sound, assuming the form of the wonder of consciousness,
perceives within itself as if it were its own mind, like a mental volition by the intellect.
At that very moment, he explains that the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*), which was dissolved in the cause, manifests in the form of space:

"At that time," etc. The "atom of sound" (*śabdāṇu*) is the subtle element of sound. The "wonder of consciousness" (*ciccamatkāra*) is Brahman, which assumes that form through its conjunction with *māyā*—the possessor of all powers—and is perceived as the void of consciousness (*cidrūpa*).
The meaning is that this itself is the arising of space. || 12 ||
That very [consciousness] itself knows its own state as the nature of wind,
possessing an internal flavor of touch, like the vibration of the air.

That very Brahman, having become space, experiences and perceives within itself the state of air— which contains touch and taste and possesses the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the subtle element of touch manifested within it—
just as a still wind experiences the state of vibration at the proper time. || 13 ||
That very [consciousness] itself attains the state of manifestation, consisting of its own inherent existence,
just as light within a sheath attains the state of being manifest through even a small fragment of its radiance.

That very Brahman, having attained the nature of wind, assumed the state of light—that is, the state of fire. It was such that it contained within its womb, in the form of a minute spark of light, the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra). || 14 ||
Thus, it itself attains the state of water, consisting of its own essential being,
like water reaching the state of fluidity while containing within it a particle of its own internal taste.
That which has become fire is indeed Brahman; a minute particle of its taste is the subtle element of flavor (rasa-tanmātra). || 15 ||
Then he perceives the Earth, which consists of the essence of his own mind, as being composed of the subtle element of smell residing within; it is like the quality of stability itself.
That manifestation of one's own consciousness which perceives even a hundred-thousandth part of a moment as being of equal duration— that is the succession of the flood of creations.

[Objection: "But surely, since the world appears instantaneously at the very moment the eyes are opened, this process of superimposition (*āropa*) is not perceived there; how, then, can the theory of 'creation upon perception' (*dṛṣṭasṛṣṭi*) be established? To this, he says: "simultaneous" (*tulyakāla*). Such is this wonder (*camatkāra*) of Consciousness (*cit*), that [the two] are simultaneous—meaning they are as difficult to discern as if they were weighed on a balance scale (*tulā*). [This refers to the portion of the closing of the eyes.]

Even that manifestation of the world in the form of the universe, which is perceived as but a hundred-thousandth part [of consciousness], constitutes a succession of floods of creations spanning millions of kalpas. Thus, within the radiance of consciousness,
there is the superimposition of a hundred-thousandth part of a moment— though such moments are indivisible by time— or rather, the superimposition of millions of kalpas.
The meaning is that since the illusory does not contradict reality in fact, the conceptualization of a sequence is logically tenable. || 17 ||
Pure, manifesting at once from the beginning, invisible yet perceptible, free from disease,
and liberated from rising and setting, Brahman remains unestablished.

For that which is impure, insentient, limited by space and time, defective, having a beginning and an end, and terminated in time is delimited by time; but Brahman is not like that, as he says: "Pure.
It is eternally enlightened (*sakṛtprabhātam*), meaning it is not enlightened again and again after being interrupted, but is eternally self-luminous.
That within which creations and dissolutions—visible and intermediate—are contained; that which is unestablished and without support;
that which is awakened and eternally liberated, yet remains equal even in association with creation;
and that which, when unawakened, is the very self of the form of creation, yet is always free from it. 19.
Now, if that which is within is the middle of the visible, then it would not be a liberation of a single form, being either with creation or with dissolution;
to this he says: "Awakened, it is existent. "Existent" (sat) means ultimate reality.
"Equal" (sama) means devoid of inequality. "Emission" (visarga), though in the ultimate sense empty of creation, [is so described]. 19.
In whatever manner and by whatever means the Consciousness-Brahman is perceived by itself within itself,
in that very manner it becomes all things, possessing the power of all its limbs.

In whatever manner it is perceived by perceivers, in that very manner that Brahman, distinguished by those respective modes, comes to exist within the self and assumes those various forms through *māyā*; this is the meaning. The particle "nu" is used in the sense of "indeed.
For [Brahman] possesses power in all its limbs; that is to say, it possesses the power of *māyā* which conforms to all things. || 20 ||
That [the Self] is real because it is the play of consciousness and consists of eternal experience;
that [the world] is unreal because it has emerged from the mind as the sixth sense, having departed from all [true] designations.

The world as well, when viewed from the perspective of the play of the scriptural consciousness (*śāstrīyacit*), is none other than Brahman, which is the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*). Conversely, Brahman too, when viewed from the perspective generated by the six senses—the eyes and so forth directed outward with the mind as the sixth—is nothing but the unreal world; thus he says, "That is the Truth" (*tatsatyam*). To the question, "How can that which is real be unreal?", he replies, "It is called 'all' (*sarvākhyā*)."

The meaning is that since [the Absolute] has thoroughly attained (nitarāṃ gatam) all designations—that is, all names—for that which is beyond the range of speech cannot truly possess a form within the range of speech. In the reading *sarvārthātigatam*, the meaning is that since it has thoroughly transcended (atitarāṃ gatam) and pervaded all objects, it has assumed that very nature. || 21 ||
Just as this movement exists in the wind, so does creation abide in the Supreme;
even though it is like the unreal, it is a mental construction, and though it is real, it is as if unreal.

Just as in the case of wind, its movement—though appearing real before it actually begins—is as good as unreal; yet at the time of movement, because the existence of the wind is understood, it is as if real despite being merely stable within that reality. In the same way, although creation is as good as unreal within the fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), it appears as if real due to the existence of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). And even though the substratum is real...
Because its nature is that of unreal illusion, the meaning is "as if unreal. || 22 ||
Just as light within fire, though appearing as something different, is not other than it,
so too the splendor of the universe within the consciousness of Brahman consists of both the real and the unreal.
And so, he says "anyarūpa" (in another form) to show that the universe possesses the nature of both real and unreal according to the difference in perspective.
"Ālokatā" means luminosity. The meaning is that it is unreal when perceived in another form, and it remains real when perceived in its own true form. || 23 ||
Just as a figurine is not carved out of mud or wood,
and just as colors exist within a mass of ink, so do the creations abide in the Supreme.

The first two [illustrations] are the examples of the self as the material cause of the dreaming and waking states, while the third is the example of Brahman as the material cause of the creation of the universe. || 24 ||
In the desert of the reality of Brahman, which is non-dual, there shines the mirage of the three worlds; though the Self is unreal, it appears as if real. (25)
By means of the Brahman consisting of consciousness, the Self is perceived as the very essence of creation;
yet, due to its non-duality, it is not perceived [as distinct], just as a tree within a seed is not perceived.

Through delusion, it is perceived by that which consists of consciousness—the individual soul characterized as a reflection of consciousness; however, from the perspective of reality, it is not so conceived, because of its non-difference from the Supreme Brahman.
Just as sweetness belongs to milk, pungency to black pepper, liquidity to water, and motion to the wind. (27)
Just as another [object] existing elsewhere does not exist there [in its own place], so too the creation, which is of the nature of pure consciousness, exists within that Self;
it is the Supreme Self itself assuming the form of the individual self. 28.

Being non-different, he remains; being different, he does not exist—this is the meaning of "non-existent. He is "melted" (nirgala), meaning he has merely dissolved away, being of the nature of consciousness alone, bearing a form in which only the Supreme Self remains.
That which exists as the world is indeed the golden jewel of Brahman;
since it is without cause, it is not distinct from Him.
He concludes the established proof of its being uncaused with the words "shining" (kacanam).
The meaning is: because it is not distinct from that Brahman, therefore it is without cause. || 29 ||
Latent impressions (vāsanā) consist of the perception of the mind, the self, and so forth; they arise from that which is perceived.
They do not arise from the absence of perception, but rather from effort through human exertion.
If it is causeless, then it is simply unarisen; how, then, can there be the experience of that sensation? To this he says: "vāsanā.

Vāsanā is the latent impression of the mind, the individual soul (jīva), and so forth; that which experiences is sensation (*vedana*), and that by which it is experienced is the instrument—namely, the mind (*manas*). Therefore, [the sensation] has arisen from that. What, then, is the means for its non-arising? To this he says: "it does not arise."

"Because there is no sensation and because the mind is destroyed. And why is that? To this he says: "From effort alone. The meaning is: from human exertion characterized by firm practice of the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga). || 30 ||
Nothing whatsoever ever sets nor does it rise anywhere at any time;
everything is the peaceful, unborn Brahman, a mass of consciousness as solid as a block of stone.
To demonstrate what that yoga of knowledge is like, he says: "It does not set. (31)

Toward every atom, floods of creations arise from the consciousness through thousands of delusions; since there are [delusions] within each and every one of those atoms, what need is there to mention how many latent impressions (vāsanās) exist here? 32.

Since the mind exists, even within the interior of an atom, the succession of creations is difficult to resist; thus he says: "With respect to each atom. Here, *aṇvantah* means the dwelling place (*āvasati*) or the latent impression (*āvāsanā*) of the flood of creation. The suffix *yuc* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) from the causative root. What kind of existence could there be through such a total immersion, or how could it be? It is not possible in any way whatsoever; therefore, the meaning is that it is entirely false. || 32 ||
Just as the powers such as waves and the like exist within water, both concealed and unconcealed,
so too do the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the rest abide within the individual soul (jīva).

He states that the subsistence in the form of an indefinable power of illusion (māyā-śakti) is the same even in the case of the analogies such as waves and so forth, with the words "Just as" (yathā). || 33 ||
If a living being develops even the slightest lack of interest toward enjoyments, then by that alone he has attained the highest state; such is the sacred tradition. (34)

With the intention that dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the cause for such an effort of a person, he cites a Vedic scripture: "If born... and so forth. Likewise, there is another [scripture]: "He who, thinking [of objects], desires desires, is born again and again through those very desires;
but for one whose desire is fulfilled and whose self is perfected, all desires dissolve away right here. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.5) || 34 ||
From whatever one becomes detached, from that one is liberated;
therefore, being free from the consciousness of "I," how could one attain the consciousness of birth? (35)

He also cites a Smṛti passage: "yataḥ" (from which). The remainder of the Smṛti should be understood as: "Because of turning away from everything, he does not experience even the slightest suffering. Therefore, through the firmness of knowledge and dispassion, not perceiving—that is, not seeing—the body and so forth as "I," who would undergo the consciousness of birth, the delusion of being born and dying?
He attains nothing at all; such is the meaning. || 35 ||
Those who know the consciousness that is both supreme and inferior, unborn, formless, nameless, and consisting of the moving and the unmoving as its foundation— they are victorious.
That very knowledge demonstrates the scope of the indivisible unity of the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam*— namely, consciousness (*citi*)— as follows:
"consciousness" refers to the supreme consciousness consisting of the nature of the Lord (*Īśvara*), and the non-supreme consciousness consisting of the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*),
which is beyond names and forms.

But those who [meditate on] the other [form], which is devoid of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the conceptualization of the world as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and which is devoid of identity with those lower, inferior adjuncts characterized by the bodies of moving and non-moving beings— [the compound *acarācarādharamayīm*] should be understood as "consisting of that which is lower than the moving and the non-moving"; the placement of the negative particle (*nañ*) before the suffix *mayaṭ* in this Vedic usage,
instead of saying *na-mayaṭ-anta-samāsa*, is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).

And thus, those who—by means of the Guru, the scriptures, and their own direct experience—know the indivisible Consciousness (cit), which is the purified referent of the term "that" (tat), unborn and devoid of transformations such as birth and so forth, they conquer saṃsāra; this is the meaning.
[They conquer it] by knowing that [Consciousness] which consists of those lower bodies composed of moving and non-moving beings, being essentially identical with them.
Or those who know her as Jīvabhūtā, Anāmikā, and Amarūpikā. || 36 ||
In others, consciousness is self-manifest and non-dual, like the swirling eddy within water; as that [consciousness],
I sustain these worlds.
Neither existent nor non-existent are things that consist of another's self. || 37 ||
The mind, consisting of the "I" and consisting of the meditation on the Lotus-born (Brahmā), expands the universe through the differentiation of its own volitions;
yet, when turned inward, it experiences the infinite.
In the process of [measuring] even a ten-millionth part of a blink of an eye, it is the end of an eon.

Showing that the conceptualization of the cycle of existence within oneself occurs under the influence of both egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and volition (*saṃkalpa*), whether in the individual state (*vyaṣṭi*) or the collective state (*samaṣṭi*), he concludes with the words "consisting of 'I'" (*ahaṃmayī*). He states the distinction between the collective state and the individual state with the words "turned inward" (*antarmukhā eva*).

The meaning is that he is not outward-looking like us and others. He experiences his own lifespan until the end of the *yuga*—that is, the end of seventy-two thousand divine *yugas*—within that "ordinance" (*vidhi*), which is time (*kāla*) as a ten-millionth part of a single blink (*nimeṣa*) of the infinite Viṣṇu. "Oh, what a power of illusion! (*aho māyā*)!
The state of being. || 38 ||

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the World," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* within the venerable *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Seers.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of the World," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
p. 284) 175 The sixty-second canto. 62 Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Even when calculating a millionth part of an atom or a blink of an eye,
thousands of world-ages appear as if they were real.
The fact that the universe is mere illusion was stated at the outset;
now it is elaborated, as well as the power of Great Necessity (mahāniyati-śakti), for the sake of attaining liberation while living (jīvanmukti) and other such goals. || 1 ||

The syntactical connection is as follows: when one conceives of a millionth part of an atom, there are thousands of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa) termed "the world" therein; and when one conceives of a millionth part of a moment (nimeṣa), there are thousands of kalpas therein; these appear as if they were truly real, just like the currently perceived cosmic egg, to an extreme degree. || 1 ||
Within those too, and likewise within each infinitesimal atom, this very same infinite delusion appears as "this" and "that. (2)
He states, "In those too," [meaning] that since such a conceptualization is possible for each of them individually, this is merely an error because their nature is not fixed. || 2 ||
These [streams] flow away, subsided, having reached the ultimate limit of creation;
they are like water flowing within, manifesting with swirling eddies.

These present, future, and past successions of creations— whose internal revolutions and transformations are clearly manifest as the turning of whirlpools— carry, sustain, and flow forth these apparent existences, just as water flows in liquid form. (3)
In this great desert, the splendor of creation exists only as a false self,
like a river whose rows of flowers have been shed by its banks, trees, and creepers.
In that place, the river-like mirage was fashioned such that its rows of flowers were released and showered down by the trees and creepers on the banks.
Like a dream, a city of Indra’s magic, or a mountain in a story,
the ground of the experience of creation appears as something unreal, like a mere mental construction.
Śrī Rāma said: O best among the wise, when, through such thorough inquiry, there arises the realization of the supreme non-conceptual Self as the oneness of the single Self; (6)

Rāma raises the doubt that once all delusion has been destroyed by the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the continued existence of the body for the wise would be impossible—beginning with the verse "ekātma" (the one Self). From such correct inquiry as described above, when the one, non-dual Self—which is Brahman—is realized as being one with that [Brahman], through non-difference from it, in the supreme, unsurpassed, and non-conceptual self-knowledge; [then... 6.
For what purpose do the bodies of even those who know the ultimate reality remain here?
They are overcome by destiny alone; and what indeed is this "destiny" in this context?

Like Bali and others, they have been completely overcome by destiny (*daiva*). In this regard, concerning the knower of reality (*tattvajña*), what could destiny possibly be? For the Śruti declares: "Neither the gods nor misfortune have power over him; he becomes their very self.
Since it is stated that destiny is powerless against the knower of reality, the meaning is: what could be conceived as even more powerful than that? || 7 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Here exists the divine destiny, the power of consciousness whose form is vibration;
it is the sole reality of that which must inevitably come to pass, persisting throughout all kalpas.

With the intention that even the maintenance of the body by the wise is established through the very same great cosmic necessity (*mahāniyati*)— characterized by the volition of Īśvara conjoined with the power of the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings— just as all worldly transactions are regulated, Vasiṣṭha gives the reply beginning with "It exists" (*asti*), etc. *Spanda* refers to the activity by which the established transactions of the entire world are maintained.
As if material, it is manifest. || 8 ||
For at the original creation, destiny determines the inexhaustible variety of existents;
it results in the supreme principle that "this must always be thus."

He explains when and what its form was by saying, "at the beginning of creation. By this [statement], he shows that the Supreme Brahman itself—whose nature consists of the functions of volition, which are imperishable and unimpeded—becomes established as such through its own resolve, thinking, "This fire and the rest must always exist with such natures as heat and upward flaming. || 9 ||
She is called Mahāsattvā, she is known as Mahāciti;
she is renowned as Mahāśakti, and she abides as Mahādṛṣṭi. || 10 ||

Because she is the cause of the stability, manifestation, capacity, discernment, emanation, birth, purposeful activity, and so forth of all worlds, she is successively renowned by names such as Mahāsattā and others. || 10 ||

She is declared to be "Great Action" (Mahākriyā), remembered as "Great Origin" (Mahodbhavā), matured as "Great Vibration" (Mahāspandā), and proclaimed as the unity with the Great Self (Mahātmaikatā). || 11 ||
"Thus the worlds are like blades of grass"— regarding them as Daityas, as Suras, as Nāgas, and as mountains, he has maintained this conviction until the end of the kalpa.

The ellipsis is that she turns the worlds around like blades of grass by means of this visible method. "Daityas" refers to those of a cruel nature and so forth; "surās" (gods) refers to those of a gentle nature and so forth—such is the form of the established order (*āsthiti*) or arrangement (*vyavasthā*) created by her until the end of the kalpa. || 12 ||
Sometimes the deviation from the existence of Brahman is inferred;
it appears as a manifold within the treasury of space, for otherwise the stability of the cosmic order would not exist. (13)

He states that "kadācit" (at some time) because, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), just as the existence of Brahman (*brahmasattā*) is unerring in conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*), so too is this [the law of necessity]. For while the deviation of the existence of Brahman or the painting of a picture in the hollow of space might be inferred even if they are utterly impossible, it is not possible to infer that the state of necessity has become otherwise.
"It is possible" is an exaggeration (atiśayokti). || 13 ||

For the sake of awakening those whose self is unknown, that very reality which is Brahman and the Self is designated as Viriñci and other Buddhas; this is called the "law of necessity" (niyati) and this "emanation" (sarga). || 14 ||

And this has been stated from the perspective of conventional discourse; however, from the perspective of one who knows reality, the referents of the words "Brahmā," "niyati" (destiny), and "sarga" (creation) do not differ. With this intention, he says: "Viriñcyādi...
[by] the Buddhas, those who know reality. || 14 ||
Remaining after filling all of Brahma, he who is immovable appears as if moving;
this creation, without beginning, middle, or end, stands like a tree in the sky. 15.
[Objection: Surely Brahman is immovable, while creation is moving; how can there be identity between these two? To this, he says: "Immovable.
Pervading Brahman—which has no beginning, middle, or end—creation remains as if it were pervading [it], from the perspective of the ignorant.

By Brahman abiding within itself, according to the analogy of lines carved on the interior of a stone, the law of necessity and creation are perceived, just as the empty sky is perceived by one who lacks awakening.
One might ask: "How was this necessity (niyati) understood by Hiraṇyagarbha, such that he created exactly in accordance with it?
To this, he says:
"Like the reflection of a multitude of forest lines within a crystal stone. [This occurs] within the Self, which is variegated by Māyā.

While Brahmā, the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha), remained within the Absolute (Brahman) like a man fast asleep and unaware, it was Niyati alone who perceived the future creation as a void, like the mental construction of a dream within oneself. || 16 ||

Just as the limbs and so forth of an embodied being are seen within the body due to its nature as consciousness, so too is the world, beginning with Niyati, seen as the limbs of Brahmā in his form as the Lotus-born.
Likewise, it is observed that the creation arising from necessity (niyati) and so forth possesses limbs; the ellipsis implies that these are seen to be its own constituent parts. || 17 ||
This is declared to be destiny (daiva), which pervades everything throughout all time;
having completely transcended the nature of objective entities, it abides as pure consciousness (cit). || 18 ||
The pure consciousness, unassailed by delusion, is the consciousness of the Lord’s volition; thus it exists in the form of the world-order.
"The object must vibrate, or there must be the state of being an enjoyer; 'by this it must be thus, by that it must be thus'—this is the intellect of destiny. (19)
This very [consciousness] is the vibration of the Puruṣa, as well as everything from grass and shrubs onwards;
this alone is all beings and so forth, or rather, the world, time, and their functions.
By this human existence and by its human agency, the world is perceived as far as it extends; for indeed, these two exist in a state of single identity.

He states the mutual assistance between the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings and Necessity (*niyati*) with the words "by this": *pauruṣī* refers to the state connected to the person’s unseen merit/demerit; it is characterized by the certainty of the fruit and indicates its persistence (*sthiti*). *Sattā* means the existence of Necessity.
To the question of how long this arrangement lasts, he says: *bhuvanam*. *Bhuvanam*...

The meaning is: "as long as the three worlds exist. To the question of how this is so at the time of dissolution (pralaya), he says: "These two existences," meaning that at that time, these two existences remain solely as a single essence. || 21 ||
Both effects, which consist of existence, are accomplished through human effort alone;
thus, by this [statement], destiny and human effort are shown to be of such a nature.

He says "by man" (nareṇa) to show that both [fate and human effort] follow from human exertion, and that their persistence is likewise eternal. When a task is to be accomplished, both destiny and human effort are thus carried out by the unseen merit of living beings (prāṇyadṛṣṭa). By this sequence, such a destiny remains established; this is the sense. || 22 ||
"O Rāma, you must ask me for the determination of fate and human effort;
it is the established law that you must carry out the human effort I have prescribed. (23)

What more need be said? That you possess the status of a disciple, that you are an inquirer, and that you are one who practices the meaning taught by me, is all determined by destiny (niyati). Thus he says: "That which is to be asked" (*praṣṭavya*). Now, an objection may be raised: according to the rule of Kātyāyana, "In the case of roots such as *duh* [milk], the secondary object (*gauṇa-karman*) is used; in the case of *nī*, *hṛ*, *kṛṣ*, and *vah*, the primary object (*pradhāna-karman*)"; therefore, since the root *pracch* (to ask) belongs to the class where the secondary object is unexpressed (*akathita*), it would follow that the secondary object is intended here.

If it is asked: "Since the primary object (*mukhya-karman*) is not expressed by the suffix *-tavya*, there ought to be an accusative case ending in the form *daivapauruṣanirṇayam*; how then can there be the use of the nominative?"—this is true. However, [the author] intends to convey two types of necessity (*niyati*) through a single expression (*tantra*), by repeating the sense: "You must ask me," and "In that regard, you must ask specifically about the determination of fate and human effort. Thus, for the purpose of making known these two kinds of necessity, he uses a single expression.
This is because it is possible to intend to express both actions by means of the suffix -tavya. || 23 ||
"Destiny will feed me"—thinking thus, one who is devoted to destiny remains inactive and silent; this is the certainty of necessity.

Even when someone, relying solely on destiny and refraining from human effort, remains established in the vow of the python (ājagara-vrata), that too occurs only through the certainty of necessity (niyati) awakened by prior karma conducive to that state; thus he says: "He will feed me. (24)

There would be no cognition, no actions, no transformations and so forth, and no form; rather, they remain fixed in the conviction that "it must simply persist in this manner until the end of the kalpa. (25)

Furthermore, if the Puruṣa were exclusively inactive even previously, then intellect, the action impelled by it, the modifications of the elements and elemental derivatives impelled by that [action], and the structural forms of transformations such as cows—none of these would exist.
Thus says the Śruti: "If he did not do this, it would indeed perish. In this way...

The meaning is that, because worldly convention must persist until the end of the aeon (kalpa) based precisely on the root of human activity, all things exist in such a manner solely by the power of necessity (niyati). || 25 ||
This state of affairs—that such a thing must necessarily happen in this way—cannot be transgressed even by the intellects of Rudra and others. (26)
And he says that this destiny is difficult to overcome even for the lords (īśvara), stating: "necessarily" (avaśyam). || 26 ||
A wise person, relying on this, should not abandon human effort;
for destiny is indeed governed by the very form of human exertion. (27)
The word "this" refers to the aforementioned certainty; this is the ellipsis. || 27 ||
For destiny is indeed non-human, while that same [destiny] when directed toward creation is human;
it is fruitless when taking a non-human form, but fruitful when consisting of human effort.

Now, he states that the meanings of the words *niyati* (destiny) and *pauruṣa* (human effort) are indeed one and the same, and that the difference in conventional usage arises solely from a difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), by saying:

"That which is non-human" (*apauruṣam*). That which is non-human—that is, not intended as consisting of human exertion—but rather [intended] merely as the volition of the Lord (*īśvara*), is called *niyati*. That very same thing, when proceeding toward creation in the form of that [volition], is called *pauruṣa*.

That which is endowed with the fruit of creation is called *pauruṣa* (human effort). For *niyati* (destiny), being *apauruṣa*—that is, not transformed into the form of human exertion—is fruitless; whereas that which consists of *pauruṣa* is fruitful. Thus, the meaning is that the attainment of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) comes from *pauruṣa* alone. || 28 ||
For one who remains inactive due to being rendered mute by destiny and devoid of personal effort, where can the movement of the vital breath go? (29)
If it is argued that even for one who follows the lifestyle of a python (*ajagara*), which is devoid of human effort, the attainment of results such as satisfaction is observed, to this he replies:

"Satisfaction will be accomplished by destiny. Thus, having attained a state of muteness—meaning a state devoid of the exertion of speech and other actions—one remains inactive due to the absence of human agency, remaining just as one would be while devoid of actions such as swallowing. He does not [attain satisfaction through his own effort].
He is satisfied. Even though he is hungry, the fact that he lives for some time is also solely due to human effort conducive to the movement of the vital breath; thus he says: "prāṇa... (verse 29).
Furthermore, if a virtuous person remains even after bringing about the cessation of the activity of the vital breaths and granting rest to them, why is he not called liberated? (30)

If he remains engaged in the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇanirodha*), which grants cessation and provides rest for the mind within non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpasamādhi*), then from that effort, if he is a virtuous knower of reality, he becomes liberated and attains liberation characterized by the state of the fruit of all human endeavor; that too—
Since the fruit belongs only to human effort such as the restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇa), what is meant by "non-human fruit"? The meaning is: nothing at all. || 30 ||
The identity with the Supreme Spirit is the highest good; liberation is the absolute state of non-agency.
Between these two, the side of the Great-Souled Ones is powerful, for it is indeed free from suffering. (31)

Therefore, the identity with the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*)—that is, exclusive devotion to the person taught in the scriptures—is "the good" (*śreyas*) by way of being a means (*sādhana*), because it is the cause of the ultimate good. Liberation, characterized by the absolute cessation of all karma, is "the good" by way of being the fruit (*phala*). Between these two—the good as the means and the good as the end—the position of the great-souled knowers (*jñānins*) is the stronger.
The meaning is that their destiny is indeed free from suffering, as they are capable of destroying ignorance along with its effects. || 31 ||
If destiny—which is the manifestation of the existence of Brahman—is transformed within that [consciousness], then surely the supreme goal known as the "Supremely Pure" has been attained. (32)

And this very state of being free from suffering is the radiance and manifestation of the reality of Brahman (brahmasattā). If that [state] is transformed through effort and made stable, then that indeed is the station called "supremely pure" (paramaśuddha);

it is that which is known as "the ultimate limit" (kāṣṭhā) and "the supreme goal" (parā gatiḥ), as established by the Śruti. Therefore, the meaning is that even that supreme goal has already been attained. || 32 ||
p. 286) 176 By means of these great manifestations of necessity and the rest, Brahman alone, the omnipresent Self, vibrates forth.
Like grass, creepers, trees, shrubs, and thickets, it exists as if it were a living being within the water, situated inside the earth.

By these aforementioned great and unimpeded manifestations, Brahman itself vibrates— meaning it flashes forth— just as the essence of water existing within the earth manifests as liquidity through various distinctions such as grass, kuśa, and kāśa, and through the states of creepers, trees, shrubs, and thickets. || 33 ||

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Definition of the Meaning of the Word 'Fate' (Daiva)," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Definition of the Meaning of the Word 'Fate' (Daiva)," in the Utthāna-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixty-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This reality of Brahman is in every way, at all times, and from every side, possessed of all powers and all forms.
The Lord of All, the All-pervading, indeed the All itself. || 1 ||
Just as Brahman vibrates everywhere and in every form, so too is it demonstrated here through the play of the power of Māyā. || 1 ||
It has been stated that Brahman alone manifests through the play of necessity (*niyati*) and so forth; to explain for what reason this is so, he says: "That which is this...

Since this reality of Brahman, variegated by *māyā*, is in every way—regarding all things, at all times, and from all places—possessed of all powers and capable of all states, it is for that very reason of every form.

He is the Lord of All (*sarveśvara*) because, through omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), He is capable of governing everything. The qualifiers "all-pervading" (*sarvaga*) and "everything itself" (*sarvam eva*) are intended to exclude, respectively, remoteness and neutrality. Thus, the meaning is: for this reason. || 1 ||

This very Self, due to its omnipotence, manifests consciousness in some instances, tranquility in others, inert power in some, and effulgence in others; in yet other instances, it manifests nothing at all. || 2 ||

To the question of why there is no remoteness or neutrality [in this regard], he says: "But this is the Self. Then, to the objection that it would manifest everything everywhere, he says: "In some places. Because of its entry into the state of the individual soul (*jīva*) within the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in some cases, it manifests the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*); [it manifests] peace in a *sāttvika* adjunct, and [delusion] in a *tāmasa* adjunct.
The inert power (*jaḍaśakti*), within the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *rajas*, manifests as the surging forth of passion, greed, activity, and so on;

because it is an effect of the *guṇas*, it is somewhat mixed and thus particularly difficult to describe. However, during deep sleep and cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), it reveals nothing at all. || 2 ||
In whatever place, at whatever time, and in whatever manner he meditates upon something, in that very place, at that very time, and in that very manner, he perceives that very thing. || 3 ||
And in that regard, he states that his very nature of having true resolve is the cause: "Where... (verse 3).
For that which arises from the All-Powerful in whatever manner, it is exactly so.

He states that the diversity of existence is precisely in accordance with the manifestation of powers, saying "of all-powerful" (*sarvaśakteḥ*). The repetition "yā yā" is an elliptical distributive expression (*vīpsā*). || 4 ||
Then there exists a power of manifold forms; by its very nature, these powers are this Self. || 5 ||

He says—“these” (imā)—to show that this conceptualization of the distinction between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) exists only from the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahāra-dṛś*), and not from the standpoint of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). || 5 ||
Thus, this web of conceptual constructions has been imagined by the wise for the sake of worldly convention; in reality, no distinction exists within the Self.

Just as there is no real duality between the waves, ripples, and water in the ocean, or between bracelets, armlets, and earrings and gold, so too the cognition of part and whole is conceptual; it is not real.

The passage beginning with "Just as... and ending with "...is not real" is intended to demonstrate three examples regarding the point that no difference exists within the Self. "Conceptualized consciousness" refers to duality—that is, division—constructed by the intellect of the one who explains.
For whatever is conceptualized is exactly as it is; it arises neither from the external nor from the internal.

For indeed, whatever—such as a rope—is perceived or cognized in the form of something else, such as a snake, that exists as a mere illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) in that very way, and not in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*). Why? Because this snake and so forth do not arise externally from the rope, nor do they arise from within it.
Because it is the self of all, it perceives some particular thing as having a uniform appearance in certain instances.

The meaning is that the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), which has a uniform appearance (*samābhāsa*) and consists of a common manifestation, being awakened by the impelling unseen merit (*bhojakādṛṣṭa*), perceives only this or that through delusion in certain instances, neither everywhere nor its own true nature. || 9 ||

This entire expanse is Brahman alone, consisting of all forms; however, by those possessed of false knowledge, the relationship between power and the possessor of power, as well as the nature of parts and the whole, are imagined rather than being ultimately real.

In the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), however, this entire universe, consisting of all forms, is nothing but Brahman, which is pervasive and expanded. One might ask: "Is Brahman, in the ultimate sense, characterized by power (*śakti*) and possessed of the world as its limbs? To this he replies:
"By those possessing false knowledge" (verse 10).
Whether it be real or unreal, whatever consciousness conceives and becomes attached to, that very thing it perceives; thus, all that appears as consciousness is indeed Brahman alone. 11.
And thus, consciousness (cit) as conditioned by false knowledge— whether it be real in accordance with the scriptures or unreal contrary to the scriptures—

becomes intent upon whatever it conceives as a duty to be performed, and exerts itself toward that object. And by means of such intentness, having performed that very act, whether prescribed or prohibited, in accordance with it...

Even at the time of experiencing the fruits [of karma], it perceives those very things; thus, from the initial volition of creation until the end of the experience of the *puruṣa*, it is Brahman-consciousness alone—which takes the form of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the creation of elements, elemental bodies, objects of enjoyment, and so forth—that shines and manifests, and nothing else. || 11 ||
Thus ends the sixty-third canto, titled "The Transformation of the Mind," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 63.
The nature of consciousness is the mind; its state of changelessness is the purpose of creation.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Modification of the Mind," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*. 63.
(p. 287) 176 The Sixty-fourth Chapter.
64 Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This God who is omnipresent, the Supreme Self, the Great Lord, is pure, whose essential nature is the bliss of self-experience, and who is devoid of beginning, end, or middle. || 1 ||
The manifestation of the object of enjoyment has been described through the diversity of its powers;
here, the process by which the enjoyer attains the state of being a living soul (jīva) is set forth. || 1 ||
From this supreme bliss, whose nature is pure consciousness alone, the individual soul (jīva) is first born; from the soul, the mind (citta) arises, and from the mind, the world.

According to the Śruti, "Having entered by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms," prior to the creation of the world characterized by the manifestation of names and forms,

the individual soul (jīva) comes into being through the production of the collective totality of the subtle bodies (liṅga-samaṣṭi) which serve as its limiting adjuncts; it is that very [soul] which, by virtue of the predominance of its adjuncts, [is so designated].
It is called "mind" (citta). || 2 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
In this Brahman, which is expanded as Brahman and is the authority of one's own direct experience, how does the individual soul attain existence within that which is devoid of duality? (3)

Rāma raises the objection regarding the impossibility of the existence of the limited and dualistic individual soul (*jīva*) within Brahman, which is indivisible, non-dual, and self-luminous—beginning with the words "svānubhūti" (one's own experience). [He asks: How can there be the existence of a small, living soul within Brahman, which, by virtue of being Brahman, is expanded and has attained an increase characterized by unsurpassed and unlimited pervasiveness?
The meaning is: how can it attain a separate existence that contradicts its previously established state of being Brahman? || 3 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The unreal appearance is the pure Self; here exists Brahman, expanded, the vast body of the Bhairava of Consciousness, imperishable and named Bliss. (4)

Desiring to explain by making a distinction— that from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛśā*), there is no possibility of the existence of the individual soul (*jīva*) in Brahman which is Truth and free from ignorance (*niravidya*), whereas its existence is not contradictory when accompanied by ignorance (*sāvidya*)— he first states its common nature, beginning with the word "asat. "Asat" means that wherein the appearances (*ābhāsāḥ*) of dualistic cognitions (*dvaita-pratyayāḥ*) are non-existent.

The phrase "expanded" (*prabṛṃhitam*) is further explained by the expression "the vast body of Cid-bhairava. His body, or essential nature (*vapuḥ-svarūpam*), is *bhairava* because it is terrifying to those who have not attained the realization of the Self (*anātmayogin*). As the elders have said:
"This so-called 'untouchable yoga' is difficult for all yogins to perceive; indeed, yogins are afraid of this [state] which is itself fearless."
"Those who perceive danger. Thus [ends the verse]. 4.
That which is equal, fully complete, pure, and unmarked— though it cannot be described even by those who know it— that is the tranquil, supreme state.
He shows the first [point] with the words "of that" (tasya) || 5 ||
That very being which is of the nature of consciousness, as if rising from that [ground] toward tranquility, vibrates by its own nature; that is designated by the term "jīva."

He shows the second [point] with the words "of that very [Self]" (*tasyaiva*). From the beginningless until liberation (*ā mokṣam*), because the seed of manifestation exists, there is a form that appears as if arising; the vibration (*spandana*) of that [form], which consists of the maintenance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) characterized by the power of movement due to its nature as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), occurs therein—within the supreme mirror of the space of consciousness (*cidvyoman*)—as these experiences consisting of pure awareness.
Innumerable successions of the world-web are reflected therein. || 7 ||
Regarding that very point, he says "therein" (tatra) to indicate the exposition of all names and forms. || 7 ||
O Rāghava, know that to be the individual soul (jīva) which is a slight vibration of Brahman, like [the movement] of an ocean without wind, or like that of a lamp in a windless place.

Regarding the statement that the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*) is simply the state of *prāṇa*—predominantly characterized by the power of action conducive to the conceptualization of the world’s diversity—belonging to consciousness (*cit*), he provides an illustration with the words: "of Brahman" (verse 8).
O dear one, when tranquility has departed, that natural radiance of the sky of consciousness which consists of a slight self-awareness is the individual soul (jīva).

When there is the superimposition of movement dependent on the vital breath upon the pure Brahman, and when its tranquility—that is, its actionlessness—is removed or concealed, that which consists of even a slight perception [arises]. (9)
Just as there is motion in the wind, heat in fire,
or coldness in frost, so too is the nature of the self (jīvatva).
And he says that this state of being a living soul (jīvatva) is, as it were, innate to the soul until liberation—“just as,” etc. (10).
That which, by the very nature of the reality of the Self consisting of consciousness, is itself a slight semblance of self-awareness, is known as the *jīva*. 11.

Non-existence is the non-contemplation of one's own [nature], which is ignorance; by virtue of that, there is a slight perception, which is like a partial determination of the nature of consciousness. || 11 ||
Through intense awareness, that very [consciousness] gradually attains the state of "I-ness," just as a spark of fire, due to an abundance of its own fuel, attains its own capacity for illumination.
He describes its state as Rudra, whose nature is ego (ahaṃkāra), with the words "That very... and so forth.

By means of intense consciousness—that is, through the firmness of latent impressions—it attains the state of "I-ness," which is the state of ego. Just as a spark of fire, when there is an abundance of fuel such as clarified butter or oil that serves to kindle it, [blazes up]. || 12 ||
Just as the blueness of the sky manifests along the path of its own stars,
so too does the conception of "I-ness" arise within this living being, though it is empty.
The eye of the observer, characterized by the pupil as its *tārakā*, is extended into the sky—that region which is beyond its range and object;
for as far as the eye is able to go, it does not perceive any blueness.
However, from the point where it reaches its limit and becomes obstructed, that region of its path remains devoid of blueness.

Likewise, a dark-blue luster flashes forth; this means that even for this living being (jīva), who is devoid of egoity, there arises within its own self—a domain that is not its object—the cultivation of the sense of "I-ness" (ahambhāva). || 13 ||
The individual soul assumes egoism, kindled by the fluctuations of volition;
through its own density, it becomes like the sky assuming the quality of blackness.

Indeed, the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva)— which is delimited by space and time and takes on various forms— is ignited by its own latent impressions from prior volitions; it is awakened, superimposed upon itself, and made manifest as a dense mass, like a smooth sapphire stone, through its own compactness.
It vibrates by its own power of volition, like the movement of the wind.

He is the one who effects the spatial and temporal delimitation of the Self, bringing about its limitation in terms of space and time; by the power of his own volition, he assumes the form of a body and so forth. (15)
Having turned toward volitional thought (*saṃkalpa*), it abides under the name of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*);
it is known by such names as mind (*citta*), individual soul (*jīva*), intellect (*manas*), illusion (*māyā*), and primordial nature (*prakṛti*). (16)

He states that the distinctions such as the mind (citta) and so forth are rooted in the superimposition of the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva-adhyāsa), beginning with the words "the mind" (cittam): "That ego (ahaṃkāra) is Rudra; the mind (citta) is Viṣṇu; the individual soul (jīva) is Brahmā. Of these very [entities], in their respective order, they have the names of action: mind (manas), Māyā, and Prakṛti. (16)

The mind, consisting of that volition, performs the conceptualization of the subtle elements (tanmātras) of the gross elements; proceeding from that, it indeed departs, and through volition and the like, it attains dissolution into the five elements.

Therein, that mind consisting of volition— Brahmā, performing the conceptualization of the subtle elements (tanmātras) from volition— truly departs and falls away from its prior conscious state and attains the fivefold dissolution into insentience. || 17 ||
The mind, taking the form of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), becomes a spark of fire, like a delicate star in the sky where the world has not yet been born. (18)
By means of the fivefold process (*pañcīkaraṇa*), he describes the state of the light that constitutes the nature of the golden egg (*haimāṇḍa*) with the words "tanmātra" and so on.
It is called a "particle" (*kaṇa*) because it is minute from the perspective of the vision of Brahman. It is "delicate" (*pelavā*), meaning its manifestation is indistinct. || 18 ||
The mind assumes the state of a spark of fire through the conceptualization of the subtle elements (tanmātras),
