just as a seed gradually attains the state of a sprout from its own internal movement.
He states clearly what has already been said: "the state of being a spark of light. || 19 ||
This spark of light, known as the cosmic egg, through its own conceptualization, attains the state of an egg; within it, Brahman vibrates like water attaining the state of a solid mass.

In this regard, he states the distinction: for one who has been refined by the meditation on the Virāj-self in a previous kalpa, there arises the state of being the gross collective Virāj; whereas for another, due to the latent impression of identifying with the individual gross body, there arises that [individual] state.

By the words "asau" and so forth: [the author] specifies [the Self] with the intention that its knowledge of the Self is established by tradition (smṛti), namely, that "its fourfold [nature] is co-existent," which refers to the conceptualization of the state of "I" belonging to the section concerning meditation prior to conceptual construction. The meaning is:
"He whose [face] is four-faced. "Āpiṇḍatām" means the state of solidification, such as the thickening of water into ice and the like. || 20 ||
Someone, through the rapid conceptualization of the body and so forth, attains the state of being a body;
that delusion, appearing as both that and not-that, is like a city inhabited by Gandharvas.

A certain person who is not a lay follower (anupāsaka), yet is a performer of meritorious deeds, by virtue of the fashioning of a divine body and so forth in the manner about to be described, very quickly attains the state of a deity or similar being. In that body, which is not of that nature and is not the self, he falls into the delusion characterized by the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva). He dwells there, protected by Gandharvas or other gods.
He goes to the city of Amarāvatī and so forth. || 21 ||
By his own volition, someone attains the state of an immobile being, another even that of a mobile being, and yet another assumes the form of a sky-walker and so forth.
But some evildoer [attains] the state of an immobile being; others become sky-faring birds, or Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and so forth—the word "and so forth" (ādipada) including aquatic creatures. || 22 ||
At the beginning of creation, the primordial body is born; the individual soul (jīva) arises from volition (or "from creative ideation," according to the variant reading *bhāvana*).
Having gradually attained the station of Brahmā (Vairiñca), it brings forth the universe.

The meaning is that the Self, as the first-born Viriñci-jīva, having the collective subtle body as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), creates the world within the cosmic egg by means of his own volition. || 23 ||
This one, whose nature consists of the transformation of the self, perceives as already born that very thing which he conceives in an instant, solely by virtue of its own inherent nature. (24)

With the intention that his state of having true resolve (satyasaṃkalpatā) is caused by the meditation on the Self as consisting of the former true resolve, he qualifies [the Self] as "the Self whose nature is the realization of the Self" (ātmabhūkalpanātman). || 24 ||
The state of Brahman, the cause of all, has emerged from the very nature of consciousness;
subsequently, having fashioned karma, it remains as the cause within the cycle of worldly existence.

He states that for the world, which possesses the dual characteristics of manifestation and motion, the conscious self (*cidātman*) is the cause of manifestation first, whereas action is the subsequent cause regarding motion, modification, and so forth—beginning with the words "from the nature of consciousness" (*citsvabhāvāt*).
The first word, *kāraṇa*, has its primary emphasis on the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*). || 25 ||
The mind flashes forth from its own nature like foam from water;
it is subsequently bound by karmas, just as bubbles are bound by ropes. (26)

He clarifies what has already been stated from its very root with the words "the mind" (cittam). Just as a mass of foam (ḍiṇḍīram) is bound and obstructed by ropes used to moor a boat and so forth, but not the water itself; likewise, it is the mind alone that is bound by the karmas that tether it to the body, and not the conscious Self (cidātman)—this is the intended meaning. || 26 ||
Volition is the seed of conceptualization; indeed, that very self becomes the individual soul (jīvaka).
Then, rising from a state of non-action, it subsequently projects karma intensely and in succession.

Since even in the world one observes the construction of objects such as jars through action preceded by volition (*saṃkalpa*), he says "volition" with the intention of establishing the aforementioned sequence. "From non-action" means from the proximity of the inactive Self. || 27 ||
First, the living soul sustains its own life by embracing the sprout;
afterwards, it attains diversity through the sequence of leaves, sprouts, and fruits.

With the intention that even by subsequent actions, that which already exists in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) within the living being—like a sprout within a seed—is merely manifested and not something previously non-existent, he says: "having embraced the sprout" (*kroḍīkṛtāṅkuram*). Just as the living being residing in the seed has previously embraced—that is, held within itself in a subtle state—the sprout.

Just as such a thing maintains its own life and subsequently attains diversity through the sequence of sprout, leaf, stalk, branch, twig, flower, and fruit, so too does the life-force of Hiraṇyagarbha; this is the meaning. || 28 ||
Other living beings who have assumed this very same form enter into a state of dependence upon the elements within the world already produced. (29)

The individual souls (*vyaṣṭi-jīva*) likewise attain the very same form—the shape of the body and so forth—which exists within their own respective lords in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). However, this much is the distinction:
they [attain it] in the world already produced by the volition (*saṃkalpa*) of the Hiraṇyagarbha-jīva, [and] in Brahmā.
They undergo the acquisition of a body, which is a state caused by living beings and based upon the physical forms of parents and others. || 29 ||
Then, by means of their own karmas which have become the cause of birth and death, beings go upwards or downwards; and karma is said to be the vibration of consciousness (citspanda).
He explains the word *karma*: "The vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*) is so called. (30)
The vibration of consciousness becomes action; that very mind becomes destiny, and it becomes here the auspicious, the inauspicious, and so forth.
Therefore, the worlds and the universes come into being first [from that].
Having become [one with it], may he today [shed] his own bodily flowers like those from a tree. || 31 ||

Explaining the very meaning of the word *karma*, he concludes the description of the creation of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, which was depicted in the two preceding chapters, with the words: "The vibration of consciousness.
Just as the branches and other parts of a tree, as well as its flowers, having existed previously, come into being again; so too...
From the primordial cause, Brahman, who is like space, and from karma— characterized by the vibration of consciousness and marked by good and evil—
as the instrumental cause, arise the worlds, the collection of living beings who are the enjoyers, and the realms that serve as their support and objects of enjoyment.
The meaning is that they come into being again and again. || 31 ||

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Sprout from the Seed of Origination," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 64.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Sprout from the Seed of Origination," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparyaprakāśa*.
(289) The sixty-fifth canto. 65.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For this very reason, the mind first arose;
consisting of thought and expansive in nature, it attained its state while remaining established in that [source] alone. || 1 ||
Having now investigated the reality of the mind, the objects of experience, and the subject who experiences, that which remains as pure consciousness alone is demonstrated. (1)

In this regard, first, in order to state that all conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) do not exceed consciousness (*cit*), he declares their identity with that alone—since the causes of the origin and persistence of the mind (*manas*), which is their root, possess no existence apart from it—with the words "from the Supreme" (*parasmāt*). || 1 ||
Therefore, this creation— appearing as both existent and non-existent— is perceived by Him as a wave of the power of existence and non-existence, like a previous scent [recollected] by His will.

He states the dependence of the appearance of duality upon the mind with the words "bhāvābhāva" (existence and non-existence). The phrase "whose oscillation is like a swing" refers to the mental fluctuation that swings between two objects—existence and non-existence—in the form "this is thus" and "it is not thus"; this is to be construed with the preceding [sentence].
By that mind, a scent previously experienced is remembered according to one's will.
In the same way, even that which is not near is perceived through a mental wish.
No distinction whatsoever exists, consisting of the conceptualization of duality or unity,
between Brahman, the individual soul, the mind, māyā, the agent, the action, and the perception of the world.
And so, he says "not anything" (na kaścit) to show that the distinction imagined by the mind disappears upon the departure of the mind. || 3 ||
Through the surging waves of consciousness, which extend across the boundless expanse of the near and the far,
this Self alone manifests as the single ocean of consciousness.

He shows the nature of the Self that remains when distinctions have vanished with the words "pāra" etc.: by the surging, that is, the undivided expansions, of the water characterized by consciousness. || 4 ||
Due to its lack of reality and instability, that which appears as real is like a dream; likewise, the mind and the world consist of both the existent and the non-existent. (5)
Now, one might object: "If both the mind and the world are sublated, how can there be a remainder of the real?

Anticipating this, and with the intention of showing that because the world consists of both real and unreal elements—being a composite of the stable and the unstable—the sublation of the unstable portion logically results in the remainder of the stable, he says: "Unreal," as in the case of a dream.

The meaning is that, just as in the case [of the dreamer], even when the parts of the unstable objects are sublated, there is the observation of the persistence of the stable seer of those [objects]. || 5 ||
The delusion of the world of consciousness has not arisen as something existent, nor as something non-existent; rather, it has emerged like a magical illusion from the conjunctions of the intellect.

Now, having raised the objection that even for that which is absolutely non-existent (*atyantāsataḥ*) no sublation (*bādha*) is observed, he states their indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*), which makes them susceptible to sublation, with the words "not real" (*na sat*). Now, [one might ask]: if they are false (*mithyātve*), how can there be a single uniform form (*ekākāratā*) among many? To this he says: "Now" (*atha*). The word "now" (*atha*) has the sense of "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). Nevertheless...
The meaning is that it arises like the delusion of a single form among the collections of social cognitions, which are agitated by the illusion of a magical display (indrajāla). || 6 ||
This long-lasting dream called saṃsāra persists through the power of the mind;
yet, through right vision, it is as futile as the perception of a person in a wooden post.
To the question, "Whence then does its long duration there arise?", he says: "dīrgha" (long). This is due to the power of the mind—that is, by the force of attachment produced by the mind. || 7 ||
Through the vision of selflessness, the mind does not grieve over its own nature,
just as a fool does not grieve over a fear imagined through the construction of a ghost.

Now, why does the Self not grieve for its own mental state—which is the cause of falling away from the condition of its own full bliss and the root of all suffering? To this, he says: "Because of the perception of the non-Self" (*anātmālokanāt*). "Non-perception of the Self" (*anātmālokanam*) means ignorance regarding the Self; it is the perception of things that are not the Self.
And because of that perception of the sign, even though the Self has attained the state of being the mind,

it grieves over the misfortunes produced by the state of being the mind; just as a child, when a fear of a Vetāla is correctly imagined and firmly established, does not grieve for the cause— the imagination of the Vetāla— because his mind is so deeply attached to it.
The meaning is "in that same way. || 8 ||

From the inexpressible essential nature, whose self transcends all directions, the mind arises through its orientation toward objects of cognition; from that mind comes the conceptualization of being a living soul (jīva).

And thus, he states with the words beginning "of the inexpressible" that the very nature of consciousness being oriented toward an object of cognition (*cetyonmukhatva*) is the root of the succession of misfortunes: || 9 ||
From the state of being a living soul arises the sense of "I," and from the sense of "I" arises the nature of the mind;
from the nature of the mind arises the state of the senses and so forth, and from that come the delusions of the body and other such things.
Due to delusion regarding the body and so forth, heaven and hell, as well as liberation and bondage, arise from the mutual growth of the body and karma, like a seed and its sprout. (11)
Due to delusion regarding the body and so forth, there arises the conceit of "I" and "mine."
Just as duality does not exist between consciousness and the self, nor between consciousness and the individual soul,
so too there is no distinction between the individual soul and the mind; just as there is no distinction between the individual soul and the mind—
In the same way, there is no difference between the body and its actions.

With the intention that this entire succession of misfortunes is rooted in the delusion of the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, and is therefore sublated when that delusion is sublated by the realization of their identity, he refutes duality: "Duality" refers to the distinction between the conscious self (cidātman) and Brahman—the individual soul; the duality is the difference between these two. || 12 ||
Karma alone is the body, and the body itself is the mind; that very thing is the "I," which is the living soul (jīva) here.
That living soul is indeed the consciousness of the Lord (īśvara), and that is the Self (ātman).
"All is Śiva"—this is what is expressed by the single word. || 13 ||
Having condensed the secret of the investigation of all the scriptures into a single statement, he has clearly declared: "Karma alone... (13).

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Investigation of the Living Being," within the "Story of Līlā" in the "Section on Origination" of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 65.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "An Inquiry into the Living Being," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixty-sixth canto.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
In this way, O Rāma, a single supreme reality attains manifoldness to an extreme degree;
it appears as if manifold, just like hundreds of lamps arising from a single lamp.
Here, it is elaborated that duality is merely a manifestation of the mind alone;
through the attainment of the desired [truth] and awakening, there occurs the destruction of the ignorant mind. || 1 ||
"In this way," meaning according to the sequence described starting with "the mind is oriented toward the object" (*cetyonmukhatayā*). Regarding that, he provides an illustration:

"multiplicity" (*nānātva*). Multiplicity has arisen—that is, a hundred lamps have appeared. Or rather, not only has multiplicity arisen for the object of consciousness (*cetya*), but by the aforementioned direction, it has also arisen for consciousness (*cit*) itself, according to each particular limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

It has become as if manifold. Regarding this, he provides the illustration stated in the Śruti: "Just as the one fire, having entered the world, becomes the counterpart of every form," saying: "From a lamp... (1).
If one perceives the self as it truly is— in its form of non-existence—
and investigates within, finding it devoid of any experience, one does not grieve.

Just as bondage occurs through the conceptualization of these [states] such as the mind as being "lifeless" (ajīvatva), so too does liberation occur through investigation and the awakening to reality which are themselves dependent upon the mind. With this hidden intention, he says: "as it truly is" (yathābhūtam). If one investigates at the outset, then the experience of that [investigation] is free from the insistence on duality; for that very reason, it is "as it truly is."

It exists as it is, yet its form is non-existent; the mention of "form" (rūpa) is an elliptical indication for "name" (nāman) as well, meaning it is empty of both name and form. When one perceives the Self in such a manner, then one does not grieve, according to the Vedic scripture: "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow. This is the meaning. || 2 ||
When that [duality] has ceased, the person realizes this world is merely mind and is thus peaceful;
for indeed, to one whose feet are encased in shoes, the earth is as if covered with leather. (3)
Now, one might ask: even if the mind is pacified through inquiry, how can there be the cessation of all duality?

To this he says: "It is mind-only" (*cittamātram*). "Man" (*naraḥ*) refers to the individual soul (*jīvaḥ*). The meaning is that since the existence of duality is not being perceived by him, when the mind ceases, the cessation of duality is established. || 3 ||
Just as nothing exists apart from the mere leaf of the plantain tree,
so too nothing exists apart from mere delusion within the world.
With the intention of showing that the cessation of the world—which is derived from the substrate of mental delusion—is established because it lacks any nature apart from that [delusion], he says:
"from the mere leaf. The mention of the "leaf," however, is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for the bark, the stem, and the root as well. The rest is clear.
The word "own-nature" (svarūpa) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the verb]. || 4 ||
It is born, it attains childhood, then youth and old age; through delusion, the mind indeed dances, wandering toward death, heaven, and hell. (5)
He elaborates on what has already been stated: "It is born," etc. (5).
Just as the potency of wine manifests in the frothing of various bubbles distinct from itself, so too does the power of the mind manifest in the cycle of worldly existence.
Just as when bubbles arise in the sky, they produce the illusion of many thousands of bubble-forms, so too does the mind experience the arising of bubbles in the form of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).

Just as one with eyes clouded by impurities perceives duality in the moon and other such objects, so too does consciousness, when overcome by the fraction of sentience, perceive it within the Supreme Self.

The eye, turbid and clouded by impurity and darkness, sees what is defiled; likewise, the conscious mind—its "kalā" being the power that generates delusion—is assailed and rendered subservient by that [impurity], such is the consciousness of the living being.
Just as a drunkard, deluded by the power of intoxication, perceives trees [as dancing],
so does consciousness perceive the worlds of saṃsāra when its awareness is agitated.
*Kṣība* means intoxicated by liquor. || 8 ||
Just as children, due to the delusion of a toy, perceive the world as revolving like the wheel of a potter, know that the visible world likewise arises from the mind alone.
"By play," meaning through wandering or revolving, "like the wheel of a potter, that is, a potter. (9)
When consciousness perceives duality, then the delusion of dualism and unity arises;
when it does not perceive duality, then there is the cessation of both dualism and unity. || 10 ||
He states that the existence of duality, which is perceived solely in dependence upon the mind, ceases when the mind ceases: "When... (verse 10).
Whatever is conceived does not exist apart from consciousness;
through the cessation of the thought that "nothing exists," the consciousness of the conscious self comes to rest. (11)
He says "that which" (yad) to show that even at the time of its perception, it does not exist separately from consciousness. Its other form is inert (jaḍa).
Then, from where comes the peace of the mind? To this he says "something" (kiñcit): when objects are denied, the mind subsides by itself, like a fire without fuel; such is the meaning. || 11 ||

When one remains motionless, having attained oneness with the mass of consciousness (cidghana), whether remaining still or even engaging in worldly activity, then one is said to be perfectly tranquil.
He then states when one becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta): "By the mass of consciousness" (cidghanena). "Becoming tranquil" means absorbed in samādhi.
The subtle consciousness perceives the object of perception, while the dense consciousness does not perceive its own limbs;
one who is slightly intoxicated experiences agitation, whereas one who is deeply intoxicated becomes tranquil.

If it is argued that when the consciousness of one with little knowledge merges into the single mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), there would necessarily be omniscience rather than the cessation characterized by objectlessness, he says in response: "tanvī" (slender), etc. "Aṅga" is a term of address. "Ghanakṣībaḥ" means utterly intoxicated. "Śāmyati" means he becomes free from activity. The underlying point is this: the consciousness does not possess objective content [in that state].
It is not caused by mere consciousness alone, but rather by the distraction of the mind due to ignorance (*avidyā*).

And that [distraction] indeed vanishes when the distraction of ignorance has departed, through the unification with the mass of consciousness manifested by the firmness of knowledge and meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
As for the omniscience of the Lord (*Īśvara*) and others, that too is merely illusory (*māyikī*) and not real; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. || 13 ||

For that which has ascended to the supreme state as the singular, dense mass of consciousness, there occurs a description through synonymous terms such as "selflessness," "emptiness," and "the object of knowledge. (14)

Intending this very point, he says: "the single plunge into the mass of consciousness" (*cidghanaika*). This refers to that state in which there is a single plunge into the mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), characterized by having no other object and being uninterrupted. Precisely for this reason, it is said that one is "established in that supreme state," which expresses the direct realization of non-conceptual absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*). The selflessness (*nairātmya*) of such a mind—
It is designated by such synonyms as "emptiness of its own nature," "an object of cognition that is empty," and "absence of an objective referent. || 14 ||
Thus one perceives the delusion that "I am consciousness," whereby the state of being an object of thought is attained;
one thinks, "I am born, I live, I see, I transmigrate"—all of which is composed of unreality.

Even the conceptualization of consciousness as having the form of the process of inert transmigration—which consists of the cognizer and the cognized—is caused by the mind alone; therefore, with the intention that its cessation results in the disappearance of that [transmigration], he says: "Consciousness" (cid). || 15 ||
But apart from its own nature, there is no consciousness belonging to the mind;
for what indeed could be cognized within it, except through vibration, as in the case of the wind? (16)

To the objection that "consciousness is the activity of the mind; while it may cease through the practice of concentration and knowledge, the mind itself does not cease," he says: "by its own nature. Just as fire remains even when its heat ceases, the mind remains even when its activity ceases; for [the mind] is not contained within that [activity].
He states that another nature is experienced by someone else: "internally," etc. (verse 16).
Thus, the state of being an object of cognition (*cetyatva*) is indeed possible for whatever is cognized by consciousness;
they know that appearance, which is like the delusion of a snake in a rope, to be the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*).

With the intention that, when consciousness has thus departed, there is no manifestation of either the subject (*cit*) or the object (*cetya*), and that which is not manifest cannot be established due to the absence of any other means of proof, he says "the state of being an object" (*cetyatvam*). If it is asked what the appearance of the object was like prior to that, he replies with "like a rope" (*rajjv-*) [verse 17].
In this disease called saṃsāra,
which is to be treated by pure consciousness alone and consists merely of the movement of the mind, there is no cause for any agitation whatsoever.

And thus, since saṃsāra—which consists of the vibration of the mind—is like the movement of a snake [seen] in a rope, it can be cured by mere awakening; so he says: "Consciousness" (saṃvit). "Exertion" (saṃrambha) means fatigue; "anything" (kiṃcana) means some small thing. || 18 ||
If you remain having renounced everything and transcended all latent impressions (vāsanā), then at this very moment you are liberated from that; of this there is no doubt.
One whose latent impressions have departed is empty of the mind consisting of those impressions. || 19 ||
Just as the appearance of a snake in a rope perishes simply through inspection, so too does transmigratory existence perish through the manifestation of pure consciousness alone. (20)
The manifestation (*vivarta*) of pure consciousness, having turned back toward itself through inward orientation, is the vision of its own true nature by means of that [turning].
If one remains having truly renounced that which is the object of desire, then, my dear, liberation is already attained; what is difficult in this? (21)

And since the transformation of consciousness (*saṃvit-parāvṛtti*) has restraint of the senses as its cause, and therein the abandonment of longing for sense-objects is the cause, he says— with this intention— "where there is longing" (verse 21).
Even great-souled men here give up their very lives like a blade of grass;
how then can there be any meanness in relinquishing merely that which one desires?
He encourages the renunciation of sense objects with the words "even" (api). || 22 ||
Abandoning with an unrestrained mind whatever is the object of desire, O friend, remain—grasping with your organs of action what is obtained and renouncing what is lost. 23.
It is unrestrained and unattached. To the question of how one lives therein, he says: "having obtained. This means not grieving when losing what has been lost. || 23 ||
Just as a bilva fruit in the palm of one's hand, or as a mountain standing before one, so too is the non-duality of the Supreme Self clearly manifest to him.

The meaning is that for that knower of reality (tattvavid) whose characteristics have been described, his state of being unborn—his nature as Brahman, which is devoid of transformations such as birth—is "alam," that is, extremely evident, not hidden from direct perception. || 24 ||
The Self alone shines as the world, just as at the end of an aeon the immeasurable ocean appears as its waves;
for when known, that very Self grants the attainment of liberation.
Without even your knowledge, it is for the sake of long-term bondage to the mind. || 25 ||

He summarizes the three points already stated in brief: "The Self alone... The Self alone, appearing in the guise of the world, shines forth for those of ignorant vision; just as the ocean at the end of an aeon appears through its various waves, so it is. That very same [Self], when known—that is, when manifested by knowledge—[shines in its true nature].

It bestows the perfection characterized by liberation, which is the goal of human endeavor. However, if it is not understood, it first becomes for the mind a cause for all [worldly] objects, for the state of mental existence, and for long-term bondage through its application; this is the remainder [of the meaning]. || 25 ||

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Supreme Yoga of Saṃsāra," in the *Līlopākhyāna* (The Narrative of Līlā) within the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* (Book of Origin) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Supreme Yoga of Saṃsāra," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixty-seventh canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"Who could this individual soul (jīva) be, who is unsuitable for the mind [and yet] belongs to the Supreme Self?"
How did he arise in this world, or who indeed is he? Tell me again.

The nature of that living being (jīva) who is called the "enjoyer" is now described here; following this, the origin of his instruments and so forth will be explained primarily from the perspective of individual manifestation (vyaṣṭi).

Desiring to clearly understand the individual soul (*jīva*)—which was previously described with emphasis on its collective aspect (*samaṣṭi*)—Śrī Rāma asks again: "But as for the mind... Having created the mind, due to the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of identity with it upon himself, who is that relative of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) who possesses the nature of the mind? Which part [is it]?

Is it an effect (*kārya*) or is it that very [Brahman] itself? If it is that very [Brahman], then how has it arisen in this [form]? Is it through transformation (*pariṇāma*) or through illusory manifestation (*vivarta*)? In the first case, there would be impermanence; in the second, there would be sublation (*bādhyatā*). If it has not arisen, then the existence of an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) is unestablished, because of the scriptural statement that Brahman is beyond hunger and so forth. If it is something other [than Brahman], then who indeed is it?

The meaning is that he speaks again in order to resolve the doubt that, when one considers the alternatives—whether [the effect] is of the same class as its cause or of a different class—not a single position is tenable. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Brahman, the Lord of all, is eternally inlaid with all powers;
by whichever power it manifests, it perceives that very same power as attained.

Brahman, endowed with inconceivable and infinite power, variegated by the power of *māyā*, though in reality manifested as non-different from itself, yet through its own *māyā* having as it were attained duality,
superimposes adventitious modifications and sports in the guise of infinite individual souls (*jīvas*) and in the state of the omniscient Lord (*Īśvara*).

With the intention that there is no fault whatsoever in [the Lord] being capable, Vasiṣṭha begins his resolution with the verse beginning "samasta-": "The Lord of all, who is capable of everything. (2)
That which the Self, the soul of all, knows itself to be as the eternal form of consciousness is designated by the word "jīva"; it is that very same [consciousness] which performs volition.
She who has existed for a long time since beginningless time, whose nature is consciousness, and whose form is consciousness endowed with mental formations. || 3 ||
From its own nature, the causal duality arises as the prior volition of consciousness itself;
subsequently, it assumes various causal forms for the sake of birth, death, and persistence.

He states that the inherent duality within the self is the primary cause for the subsequent engagement in saṃsāra, whereas the individual consciousness (jīvacaitanya) permeated by the impressions (vāsanā) of successive prior volitions (saṃkalpa) is merely the cause of later diversity: "By its own nature" (svabhāvāt). || 4 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O best of sages, this being the case, what is called "destiny" (daiva)? What is called "action" (karma), and what is said to be the cause? || 5 ||

Thinking that by this much alone the answer to the remainder of the question has already been effectively given, Rāma—desiring to know the causes of birth and so forth for the individual soul (jīva) as they truly are, namely destiny, karma, and other causal factors—asks, beginning with "Thus" (evam).
The ellipsis is: "Since the nature of the jīva stands thus, and being established in the intellect, I ask. (5)
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
Indeed, it is pure consciousness alone that exists here, whose very nature consists of both vibration and non-vibration.
Like the wind in the sky, it is full of radiance through its vibration, otherwise it is quiescent.
Its nature is vibration, being dominated by *rajas* and conditioned by *māyā*. Its nature is non-vibration when pure.
The ellipsis implies that it becomes "joyful" (*sollāsa*), meaning it is oriented toward creation. Otherwise, in the absence of vibration, it remains merely quiescent; such is the meaning. || 6 ||
When the mind is cultivated as pure consciousness, it is called "vibration" by the wise; when that same mind is cultivated as the state of being an object, it is known as "non-vibration. (7)

Therein, he explains the first [point] with the words "cittvam" (the state of being consciousness): the very state of being consciousness (*cittva*) which is one's own and natural, when it is made to appear as the object-aspect of thought (*citta*) through one's own ignorance (*svāvidyā*), conceptualized, and existing in that form, is called "vibration" (*spanda*). He explains the second [point] with the words "dṛśyatva" (the state of being the visible). || 7 ||
From vibration (spanda), the creation of consciousness flashes forth; from the absence of vibration, the eternal Brahman remains.
The soul, the cause, karma, and so forth, are known as designations for the vibration of consciousness.

Having established that the nature of consciousness (cit) consists of both manifestation and non-manifestation precisely through vibration (spanda) and non-vibration, it follows that vibration alone is designated by such names as the individual soul (jīva), cause, karma, and destiny; thus he says: "From vibration" (spandāt).
The word *cit* is a separate term. In this context, with the intention of referring to the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa), it is called the "individual soul" (jīva).

The intended meaning is that the distinction is as follows: when one intends to express the vibration characterized by the manifestation of effects contained within itself, it is "cause" (kāraṇa); when one intends to express the vibration of the body and so forth, it is "action" (karma); and when it is in a subtle state, long-enduring, and ready to initiate its fruit, it is "fate" (daiva). Thus is the difference. || 8 ||
This very vibration of consciousness, which consists of experience, is indeed what is called the individual soul (jīva), the cause, and karma; for this is the seed of transmigratory existence.
And because their existence consists precisely in being objects of experience, they possess the capacity for their own effects; thus he says: "That which... and so forth.
Due to the power of the manifestation of consciousness as doubled, the body is presented;
through volition, the vibration of consciousness assumes the state of manifold objects within creations.
He provides the answer to the question asked—“How did it arise in this [body]?”—with the words “having performed duality” (*kṛtadvitvā*) and so forth.

In accordance with its respective karma, at the time prior to death, it attains—that is, reaches—a body such as that of a god, human, or animal which has presented itself to the intellect, as well as the state of various objects of enjoyment that follow its previous volitions. || 10 ||
The vibration of consciousness (citspanda), having reached various states of causal conditions, is liberated after a long time;
some after a thousand births, and some after a single birth.

Having long been subject to that state which consists of thousands of various wombs—the causes and reasons for birth—a certain person of dull scriptural inclination is finally liberated through the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*).
However, one who has attained the qualification for knowledge is liberated in a single lifetime. || 11 ||
Through its own nature and by uniting with consciousness, it gradually attains duality and becomes the cause of bondage in heaven, liberation, or hell.

Regarding what was stated—that it has attained various forms—he explains that manner with the words "from its own nature" (*svabhāvāt*). The manifestation of consciousness (*cit*) occurs in the form of whatever limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) it is connected to. Just as light appears blue when in a blue cloth, red when in a red cloth, and yellow when in a yellow one; it is solely by virtue of such a nature [that this occurs].
The meaning is that, having attained non-duality— oneness— with the causes of the body’s birth (the essences of food), and through them with the bodies of the father and so forth,

it gradually undergoes transformation into the form of semen, blood, and so on, and slowly attains, reaches, the state of a body which is the cause of heaven, liberation, hell, slaughter, bondage, and the like.

In the reading "apagacchati," the meaning is that it departs or issues forth from the body of the father in the form of semen and so on, in order to attain the state of a physical body which is the cause for heaven and other realms. || 12 ||
Just as gold exists in various forms such as bracelets and the like,
so too does multiplicity— born of the modifications of states— reside within the insentient body, which is essentially no different from wood or a clod of earth.

And thus, through the merging of adjuncts (*upādhi*), when there is unity, the distinction between the father and the son's *jīvas* is not perceived; however, when the adjuncts are separated, their distinction is recognized. Therefore, he says "as in the case of gold" to show that the mutual difference among *jīvas* is a property of the adjunct alone, and not of consciousness (*caitanya*). This also applies to the adjuncts themselves.

Because [the elements] are modifications of the primary elements (*bhūta*), and because each subsequent element is a modification of each preceding one, there is no room for real difference since they are merely the undivided space of the ether (*akhaṇḍākāśa*).
With this intention, the illustration of the gold bracelet is presented. [The states of] birth and so forth...
The six modifications of being; from these arises manifoldness, which is differentiation. || 13 ||
This delusion of the mind perceives even that which is unborn as having a non-existent form;
afflicted by this delusion, one thinks, "I am born, I am standing, I am dead," just like [the deluded person] in the city.
Thus, even though difference is false, he states that the perception of differences such as birth and so forth is merely a delusion of the mind:
"Even though unborn," etc. (14).
The mind perceives only that which is unreal in the form of "I" and "mine";
because it has not seen the ultimate reality, it remains subservient to its desires.

With the intention that the root of all notions of duality—the conceptualization of "I" and "mine"—is the ignorance of the nature of the perfect Self, and that the latent impressions of the desire for enjoyment are the root of even that [ignorance] in succession, he says: "I... (verse 15).
Just as the king, the lord of Mathurā, experienced agitation toward the outcaste, so indeed does this state of the world flash forth within the mind. (16)
Regarding the point already stated, he says "In Mathurā... (verse 16) to provide an illustration for the meaning of the story of Lavaṇa that is about to be told.
O Rāma, this entire world manifests as such through the expansion of the delusion of mind-only, like the rippling of water. 17.
Prior to Śiva, the primordial cause, consciousness arises as it inclines toward the perception of objects, just like the slight movement of water from a tranquil ocean. (18)
Having already stated the method of superimposition, he now makes it understood again through individual examples, beginning with "Śivāditya" and so forth. || 18 ||

Through its vibration, it attains the state of the living-wheel (jīvacakra), assuming the form of mental waves; within the ocean of Brahman, which is the water of consciousness, it produces the bubbles of creation.
From throbbing, that is, from vibration; "the state of being the wheel of life" means the state of revolving in the form of the individual soul (jīva). || 19 ||
O gentle one, this yawning of the lion is natural for one who is composed;
it is like the manifestation of consciousness within Brahman, appearing as its own object of perception.
O gentle one, he is called a "Lion" because by his mere self-awareness he destroys the bond of *māyā*;

thus, that very manifestation of *māyā*—the bending of the limbs—of such a Brahman who possesses inconceivable power like a lion, which exists as the reflection of consciousness residing within its own Self, is what stands as the individual soul (*jīva*). That indeed is it.
The meaning is that the object of thought exists as if it were the form of an external object, yet it does not exist separately [from consciousness]. || 20 ||
Through the consciousness of the intellect (citsaṃvitti), it is called the individual soul (jīva); through volition (saṃkalpa), it becomes the mind (manas).
From that [intellect], it subsequently receives such designations as the intellect (buddhi), the thinking faculty (citta), the ego (ahaṃkāra), and illusion (māyā).

By what limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then, do the various distinctions of terms such as *jīva*, *manas*, *buddhi*, *citta*, and *ahaṃkāra* arise? He states these: "by the consciousness of the intellect" (*citsaṃvittyā*). Through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) by the consciousness of the intellect—which is of the nature of the reflection of consciousness—it is the *buddhi*; through recollection (*smaraṇa*), it is the *citta*; through ego-inflation (*abhimāna*), it is the *ahaṃkāra*; and because it is the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*), it is *māyā*. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [other states are included].
This is a summary of the designations stated in such scriptural passages as: "Breathing, it becomes breath by name; speaking, speech; seeing, the eye," and so forth. || 21 ||
First, the mind, through the conceptualization of those subtle elements (*tanmātra*), spreads out this world—which is unreal yet appears real—just like a city of Gandharvas. (22)

In that context, he states that for one whose primary faculty is volition (*saṃkalpa*), there is the power to conceive the world preceded by the conceptualization of the subtle elements such as sound, etc., in the verse beginning with "tanmātra" (22).
Just as in emptiness there is the perception of a pearl necklace and so forth due to the expansion of vision,
and just as there is delusion in a dream, so too is the cycle of existence of the mind.

And he says that what is imagined by the mind is indeed false, just like an object of mere wishful thinking—using the words "yathā" (just as). This refers to the expansion or spreading out of vision (*dṛś*) within the void (*śūnya*), which is space (*ākāśa*). || 23 ||
Pure in essence, as if eternally satisfied, peaceful and established in equanimity,
he does not see, yet he seems to see this delusion called the mind, which is like a dream.
But the witness of that is indeed eternally pure; thus he says: "Pure.
Because of the absence of hunger and other such states, it is as if eternally satisfied. || 24 ||
Transmigration is said to be the waking state; they know the ego-sense to be the dream state;
the mind would be the state of deep sleep; and pure consciousness is called the fourth state (turya). || 25 ||

The outward movement of that very [consciousness] through the doors of the senses is the waking state (*jāgrat*). The movement from the heart up to the throat of that which is permeated by the internal sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) is the dream state (*svapna*). Abiding in the heart with only the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the seeds of memory remaining is deep sleep (*suṣupti*); the transcendence of that is the fourth state (*turyatā*), as he says: "the movement... (verse 25).
In that which is absolutely pure and pure existence alone, there is the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), free from transformation and disease; established in that, one does not grieve again.

Thus, he says "atyant... [verse 26]: the very state of that purified inner reality (pratyaktattva), having been merged into the Self of Brahman, remaining as it is in a manner that is free from all affliction—that indeed is the state beyond the fourth (turyātītatva).
In that [Brahman] all this arises, and in that very same [Brahman] it is dissolved;
yet this world does not exist there, nor does that [Brahman] exist in this world—just as a string of pearls appears in a vision.

In order to prevent the suspicion that the referent of the word *tat* (*that*) has not been purified, he demonstrates its purification according to the direction shown by the scripture, "He should meditate on it as peaceful, [thinking] 'That art thou, water, and food'" (*tajjalān iti śānta upāsīta*), with the words "in that" (*tasmin*). And the remainder of the phrase is "this is not that" (*na cedam tat*).
The first negation is of the identity (*tādātmya*) of the world in Brahman; the second, however, is of their relation (*saṃsarga*). || 27 ||
Just as space is the cause for the growth of trees because it does not obstruct them, so too the ocean of consciousness, though not an agent, is the agent for the existence of the world. (28)
If [Brahman] is devoid of any connection with the world, then how can it be stated in the Śruti to be the cause of the world? To this he replies:

"Because of non-obstructiveness. This refers to "samunnati," meaning increase or growth. The sense is that the designation of "agency" is used figuratively merely because [Brahman] does not prevent the creation produced by Māyā. || 28 ||

Just as a mirror made of metal becomes the cause of a reflection due to its proximity, so too does this [consciousness], though consisting of pure spirit, become the cause for the perception of objects.
Iron is the transformation of iron, such as a mirror. || 29 ||

Just as a fruit comes into being through the process of the seed, sprout, leaf, and so forth, so too does the mind arise from pure consciousness (cinmātra) through the process of the intellect (citta), the individual soul (jīva), and the rest. || 30 ||

If so, why then does everything not arise simultaneously? To this he says: "The seed. The reasoning here is [the principle of] succession; the meaning is that it is due to the persistence of beginningless necessity (*niyati*). || 30 ||
Just as a drop of water, being its own seed and fruit, may become a seed again,
so too consciousness does not remain established in itself when it has abandoned the object of thought, the mind, and so forth.

[Objection: "But why does Consciousness (cit), which remains established in its own nature even during the dissolution (pralaya) when everything has vanished, not remain in that state forever? To this, he says:

"Just as... Just as a drop of rainwater, joined with a soul possessing residual karma (anuśayin), enters into trees, crops, and so forth, and becomes a seed once again rather than remaining indifferent, so too [is Consciousness].

Even consciousness (cit), when permeated by the latent impressions of the individual soul (jīva-vāsanā), necessarily becomes once again the nature of the creation consisting of the object of thought (cetya) and the mind (citta) and so forth; the meaning is that it does not remain established in its own state without having abandoned that [condition]. || 31 ||
Just as there is no difference between the seed and the tree within the seed— whether in its state of non-awareness or awareness—
so too there is no difference between the world and Brahman, nor between their respective consciousnesses.

One might object: "If it is the case that the power to produce a tree does not depart from a seed—whether that tree exists in a subtle state within it or whether it is not cognized—or even if it is cognized, so too there would be no distinction between the world and Brahman when they have attained the nature of the mind, regardless of whether they are truly cognized or not; thus, enlightenment would be futile. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even though... (yadyapi).

Although such a diversity of powers for producing trees is observed, it does not exist at all between the world and Brahman, which are of the nature of consciousness; for by the mere understanding of the seed and the tree,
their true, indivisible form is not revealed, whereas by the awakening of Brahman, it is— like the beauty of a form by means of a lamp.
"That it is manifested"—this much difference or distinction exists; thus, by repetition, it should be connected with what follows. || 32 ||

Nevertheless, when awakening occurs, that which consists of pure consciousness and is of an indivisible nature is manifested—just as the beauty of form is revealed by a lamp—as it has the nature of the light of pure awareness. (33)
Just as whatever is dug out from the earth becomes that very thing [in the air], so too whatever science is investigated becomes supreme. (34)

If it is asked, "From where does such power belong to consciousness?", the intention is that it is because [consciousness], being produced by inquiry, penetrates reality; with this in mind, he says: "Whatever... *Avidyā* refers to ignorance and its products, such as cloth and the like.
*Para* refers to the mere existence of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). || 34 ||
Just as the state of being a post is perceived within a crystal despite there being no such perception,
so too does the world appear as if manifold within the pure interior of Brahman, though it is not manifold.

Just as the arrangement of forests and so forth within a crystal, its state as a pillar, and its immutability occur through the non-perception of that [crystal], so too—in the remainder of the verse—it is implied that although there is no plurality in the pure interior of Brahman, the world appears as if plural. || 35 ||
The entire world-reality is Brahman, a single undivided mass,
existing like a fruit, leaf, creeper, shrub, pedestal, and seed.

The meaning is that Brahman exists in the form of the world, like a mass of solid crystal; its pedestal or support consists of the forest fruits, leaves, creepers, and so forth reflected within it, and the seed situated inside it—Brahman stands as the world in this very manner. || 36 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Oh, how wondrous is this world, which, though unreal, appears as if real!
Oh, how vast! Oh, how stable! Oh, how manifest! Oh, how subtle!

Having heard this description of the nature of the individual soul (jīva), mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), consciousness (citta), and ego (ahaṃkāra)— extending up to the conceptualization of the subtle elements (tanmātra)— as well as the incidental teaching on the world’s being mere illusion (māyāmātratva), he was struck with wonder; and through his trust in the words of his teacher, he expressed his assent to the world’s illusory nature by way of reiteration, [and then spoke] regarding those subtle elements...
Desiring to know the sequence of the arising of the gross body, which consists of the collective and individual states of the sense organs, he asks with the words beginning "Aho! (Verse 37).
In Brahman, that which consists of appearance and has as its sphere the qualities of those subtle elements flashes forth like a drop of dew; thus it is heard in the scriptures. (38)
O Lord, tell me how he goes to the state of non-existence, how he becomes a self-born being, and how this occurs from the perspective of that which is established by its own nature.
The state of the gross body, both as the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*),

arises from the reality of the self-substance established in its true nature; just as the Self becomes the universal Vaiśvānara, consisting of the universe, through the gross forms of the individual and the collective.
"Tell me"—this is the meaning. || 39 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
[That which is] of an absolutely impossible nature, non-different from its own inherent nature—
That which had never been experienced before appeared right before him as if it were his own direct experience.
Just as the phrase "one whose limbs are blossomed with joy" clearly arises in the heart of a child,
so too does the state of being a living soul arise within the Supreme Brahman.

To describe the back [of the body], he first demonstrates, with an illustration, the manifestation of the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*), which is an utterly improbable and inexpressible expansion of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) resulting in grossness, by means of two verses beginning with "atyanta... (extremely...).

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: just as a Vetāla, whose characteristic of being alive is an utterly impossible form, who is in reality devoid of blooming limbs yet appears to have blooming limbs, clearly arises in the heart of a child; so too does [the Self] arise. || 40 ||
Consisting of the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge, she is pure and truly real, yet established as if unreal;
though appearing divided, she is not divided from Brahman, whose nature is that of expansion.

Since there can be no mental reflection (*manana*) without prior experience, and since experience is dependent upon the means of knowledge (*māna*) and its object (*meyya*), he states that the cause for the manifestation of the mind is the arising of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the means of knowledge and their objects—thus, "the means of knowledge... (verse 42).
Just as the individual soul, whose life consists of conceptualization, quickly becomes Brahman, so too the mind quickly becomes the individual soul through the experience of thinking. 43.

From the sensation of thinking, and from the arising of the latent impressions of thinking, the individual soul becomes the mind; for the meaning of the scriptural text is that "the mind is so called because it thinks" (manvānaḥ). || 43 ||
The mind, perceiving itself as mere thought, quickly beholds its own true nature;
like a fleeting fragment of wind, it instantly flashes within the void.

The meaning is that he perceives his own mind— that which consists of thought having as its sole object the subtle elements— as having manifested in the form of those very subtle elements, like its own essential nature. This essence of the subtle elements, which is without blinking (ever-awake), whose form is uninterrupted vision, which resembles a particle of wind, and which is exceedingly subtle, flashes forth within the void, in the space of consciousness.

While that which is self-luminous shines forth, through its manifestation, there arises the cosmic egg— the very nature of consciousness, produced during the period of creation by means of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), lovely, shining like the sun due to its golden nature,
yet appearing like a drop of dew when viewed from the perspective of the undivided Consciousness.
It is understood that he perceives within himself the form of bodies such as those of human beings and so forth. || 44 ||
The eighth [state], consisting of pure consciousness and measured by time, experiences within itself that which is as subtle as a drop of dew and yet beautiful. (45)

The individual soul perceives the consciousness that consists of the experience and enjoyment of the meaning of the word "I," as well as the consciousness that is the reality of the word's meaning, along with its corresponding object. (46)
In that state, first, due to the non-appearance of the distinction between word and meaning, there is a vague superimposition of the "I-sense" (ahaṃtādhyāsa);

thereafter, he describes the recollection of the reality of transmigratory existence with the words "I am. He does not experience that consciousness in such a way as to specifically perceive it in its true nature as "Who am I? or in terms of the forms of humans and so forth. That is the aforementioned consciousness.

First, then, it becomes meaningful—that is, accompanied by reflection on the goals of human life—and through the recollection of thousands of previous births, one perceives within the womb both the reality of the world (the referent of the word *jagat*) and pure consciousness (*saṃvit*); this is the meaning. || 46 ||
Then, through such a sensation, he momentarily experiences the perception of the meaning of the word "taste" as a partial experience of the future object named "tongue. (47)

He explains the conceptualization of the sense organs for that [state] in sequence, beginning with the words "tādṛkṣa" (of such a kind) and so forth. The meaning in all cases is: "due to the clear experience of the 'I-sense' within the physical body, which is of such a kind. The word *jihvā* refers to the organ of taste;
the remainder of the sense is that it is characterized by the name of its object, *rasa* (taste). "In one part" means in a location such as the opening of the mouth. || 47 ||
Having attained such a sensation, it becomes oriented toward the meanings of the words "light" (tejas) and "sound" (śabda);
thus, there occurs an illumination within a portion of that which is to become the eye.

Then, from the sensation of that [smell], and from the sensation of seeing that [form], he remains; as long as he remains [in that state], the state of being an object of sight and so forth persists. (49)

"The vision of that [is] the vision of the nose. In this manner, for as long as he remains in any state such as that of the ear and so forth, for that long he eats—that is, he consumes—the visible objects such as sound; the meaning is that his habitual nature (śīlatā) is established in this way. || 49 ||
In this manner, that individual soul, by chance as it were,
gradually perceives for itself the state of being a specific configuration, once it has been brought into manifestation.
He states his conceit regarding that aggregate: "Distinguished," etc. That which was previously cultivated, fashioned by latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

(50) He [the yogin], through the act of hearing, attains the status of being a single part of the nature of sound for that configuration, even though it is non-existent as such, yet exists [as a mental construct]. (51)

Regarding his enjoyment of sound and other objects through the ears and other senses, he describes the superimposition of identity with those respective organs by means of the passage beginning with "sa tasya" (he, of that...). [This refers to] the non-existent appearing as existent— that is, as having attained existence— and how,
for the sake of the purpose characterized by the act of hearing, one brings sounds into being, that is, causes them to be perceived.
The nature of sound is the auditory faculty; it acquires, that is, obtains, the characteristic of being a specific part of the body. || 51 ||

It perceives its status as a portion of the nature of touch through the meaning of the word "skin," and it perceives its status as a portion of the nature of taste through its state as the tongue. || 52 ||
One perceives the portion that constitutes the nature of form as the shape of the object of the eye; one perceives the portion that constitutes the nature of odor as the nose. || 53 ||
In this way, through these [subtle elements] consisting of being, he perceives within the body that cavity called the future sense-organ, which is capable of manifesting existence.

Thus, that which is capable of manifesting the existence of external objects through the nature of the senses—both those already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned—is called "the sense" (indriya) because it will become a sign (liṅga) of Indra, the Supreme Self. 54.
In this manner, for the individual soul and for Rāghava and others of the present day, there arises the subtle body (*ativāhika-deha*), which consists of mere appearance. (55)
Of the individual soul (jīva), both in its form as a totality (samaṣṭi) and in its present form as a particular (vyaṣṭi). || 55 ||
The supreme existence of this [consciousness] is ineffable, as if it were of a transportive nature;
though it moves, it does not move, due to such a realization of its true self-nature.

He shows that the state of possessing a diverse subtle body (ativāhika-deha) arises solely from the ignorance of Brahman, and its disappearance results from knowledge—thus he says, "anākhyā" (the inexpressible). The word "iyam" (this) is to be understood as a separate term. || 56 ||

When the mother, the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and so forth, are realized as Brahman itself through direct experience, then what occasion is there for discourses on the subtle body (ativāhika)? That very [Brahman] is it.

With the intention that even the conceptualization of superimposition and negation (*adhyāropāpavāda*) by way of the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) and so forth pertains only to the perspective of conventional usage for the sake of instructing others regarding the Self, and not to the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), he says: "Mātra" (only). || 57 ||
The subtle body (*ātivāhika*) is distinct from the supreme self because it is perceived as something other;
Brahman is perceived through the realization of one's own nature as Brahman, for that consciousness is not born of anything else.
If the object is indeed exactly as it is perceived, then what is the distinction [between this and other perceptions]? To this he says: "That is consciousness" (sā saṃvittiḥ).
The meaning is that this consciousness, called the realization of Brahmanhood, is not born of anything else, nor is it an error. || 58 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Since there is neither possibility nor perception [of duality], due to the oneness of Brahman and the Self, what is liberation and what is inquiry? Enough with these conceptualizations of difference!

If this is so, then since ignorance is impossible within Brahman, which is of the single essence of consciousness, and in its absence there would be no basis for the conceptualization of the distinction between individual souls (jīvas), the oneness of Brahman and the Self would be self-evident;
consequently, how could there be any possibility of a fruit of liberation distinct from that [oneness], or of the inquiry and other means for attaining it? How [could these exist]?
Rāma raises the doubt that its activity [is impossible], stating: "Because of impossibility" (asaṃbhavāt). || 59 ||
p. 295) 180 Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, this very conclusion of yours shines forth as the answer to your question.
For a garland of out-of-season flowers does not shine, even if it is beautiful. || 60 ||

"Is this question asked after having realized the truth, or without having realized it? If the former, then since inquiry would be purposeless, we grant your point; if the latter, there is no occasion for such a question. With this intention, Vasiṣṭha replies with the words "At the time of the final conclusion," and so forth. [He says this because] it is not appropriate [to ask], as it would cause fear through the suspicion of sudden calamity.
The state of being. || 60 ||

Just as a garland out of season, though meaningful, is useless when it is not the time for enjoyment, so too everything that is undertaken at the wrong time is in vain; indeed, everything is beautiful when done at the proper time.

He clarifies the point already stated by way of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) through a simile as well: "sārthaiva" and so forth. Just as a flower garland that is "vilasitā"—meaning beautiful—though it is meaningful only for immediate enjoyment, becomes meaningless because it is a cause of calamitous misfortune and thus fails to produce joy in people; in the very same way, [a thing] when it has reached a state of incomplete ripening...
The meaning is that even the statement "a *mit* [measure] measures (*minoti*), that is, it validates an object," is purposeless when applied to a living being produced at an improper time. || 61 ||
It is observed that Time is the giver of prohibitions and permissions;
for indeed, all purposes attain their fruit through Time. (62)
To explain why that is so, he says: "pratibandha...

[The Lord is] the giver of the obstruction of the sprouting of rice and other crops during times such as winter, as well as the permission for the sprouting of barley and other crops, and their favorable conditions—this being established through both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
It is seen in the world; however, the word "na tu" (but not) is used here in the sense of "not necessarily. || 62 ||
In this very way, that individual soul, having become the dream-self,
perceives within itself over time the exalted state of being a grandfather.

Having thus dispelled Rāma’s doubt by means of a reprimand, and following that which was said up to the point— "the supreme Brahman, which is inexpressible, is as it were his subtle body" (with the reading *vastunaḥ*)— he describes the conceptualization of him as the Grandfather (*pitāmaha*) as being superposed upon the aggregate of subtle bodies.

"Even so. The dream-self is the collective self of the dream state. It has become manifest through the ripening of meditation, having attained the state of the object of worship as its fruit. "In time" means by means of time appropriate for that state. || 63 ||
Through the awareness and realization of the utterance of "Oṃ," one perceives clearly;
whatever mental kingdom one creates, one quickly becomes identical with that.
By means of the utterance of the *praṇava* and the realization of its meaning, he demonstrates his status as the creator of the entire phenomenal world: "With the utterance of 'Oṃ'... (64).
All this, though non-existent in this way within the Self that is as vast as space,
expands like the sky in the form of lofty mountains within the sky of the world.

And thus, it follows that this world—which is a collective mental construction (*samaṣṭi-manorājya*)—is indeed non-existent, just like an individual mental construction (*vyaṣṭi-manorājya*). He states this with the words "this is thus": everything imagined in the sky is like the surface or the impurity [of the sky].
Likewise, even the lofty form and elevated shape of mountains such as Meru are nothing but the sky itself. Why?

Furthermore, there is another minor point: since the world unfolds through the sequential superimposition [of elements] such as air and so forth upon the void alone, it follows that this [void] possesses an identity of nature with the surface-dirtiness and other such qualities of the world. This is the meaning. || 65 ||
Nothing is born here, and nothing perishes here;
the world unfolds as Brahma in the form of a city of Gandharvas.

And thus, intending that the exposition of creation is solely for the purpose of making known the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca) and not for demonstrating a real creation, he reveals the purport of such scriptural passages as "neither destruction nor origination" with the words: "Not here. || 66 ||
Just as the existence of living beings such as lotuses consists of both the existent and the non-existent, so too is the existence of all beings, from crawling insects up to the gods.

To show that even the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) exists only within the range of the world, he demonstrates that the world possesses the same ontological status as the soul with the words "yathaiva" (just as). From the perspective of logical reasoning, it consists of both the existent and the non-existent and cannot withstand critical inquiry. "Below, including the crawling creatures" means down to the subhuman level; "above, including the Asuras" means extending up to and including the gods. || 67 ||
This agitation of consciousness, though thus arisen, is unreal;
it ceases through the perfect realization of consciousness, from Brahma down to a worm. (68)

But from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), he says: "consciousness" (saṃvit). Even though one has emerged from the experience of consciousness—which is well-known to exist from Brahma down to a worm—that [duality] is non-existent. Why? Because its destruction, meaning its sublation, occurs through perfect realization (samyaksaṃvedana). || 68 ||
Just as one becomes Brahmā, so too does one become a worm;
for the worm possesses trivial karma due to being submerged in the surging flood of the multitude of elements.

He provides the justification for the previously stated portion, "from Brahmā down to a worm," with the words "yathā" (just as). To the question, "In that case, how can a worm possess such insignificant karma?", he replies with "kīṭas tu" (but the worm...). This means that due to the surging of the multitude of elements within the mind, there is an excess of material impurity. || 69 ||
Whatever life one lives as consisting of consciousness oriented toward the source of thought—
that alone is true manliness, and within that, action is the very essence.

The meaning is that life follows the limiting adjuncts (upādhi), human effort follows that [life], and action results in its fruit; furthermore, that very action is itself nothing other than human effort. || 70 ||
Whether arising from the merit of Brahmā or the sin of a worm,
that which consists of pure consciousness (cit-tanmātrātmikā)—
which was previously described in the fifty-sixth verse as "the ineffable supreme existence" (anākhyeyaṃ parā sattā) in the root text— is here referred to as "the ineffable" (anākhyeyam).

The term "the supreme Brahman" continues [from the previous verse]; in that regard, it should be investigated by those who discern existence and non-existence: delusion would be merely a matter of observation, and its destruction [would follow]. || 71 ||

In this regard, although there is a distinction in the causes of diversity— where the state of Brahmahood is the ultimate fruit of the excellence of the essence of well-performed form, and the state of an insect is the ultimate fruit of the excellence of the essence of ill-performed form— [both] are impelled by the unknown pure consciousness alone.
He states that "the delusion of duality is caused solely by ignorance, and its removal [is likewise caused by knowledge]; this is equal in both cases" with the words beginning "of Brahman. || 71 ||
Since the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge are nothing other than pure consciousness alone,
therefore the meaning of doctrines concerning duality and unity is like the horns of a hare or the flowers of a lotus in the sky.
[Objection: "Is it not the case that as long as the knower perceives the object of knowledge through the means of knowledge, there is duality, and upon its cessation, there is unity?
Thus, would it not be the case that the very nature of reality (vastu) is actually one of successive duality and unity? To this, he says: "The knower..."—there is no duality.

The measure (māna), the object of measurement (prameya), and the duality between the measure and its object would also entail an infinite regress, since that very duality would require another measure. Therefore, if these were mere consciousness (cinmātra), there would be no other means to establish either duality or unity; thus, the purpose of the doctrine of duality and unity [is undermined].
The meaning is that it is like the horn of a hare or a lotus in the sky. || 72 ||
The bliss of Brahman, which is essentially the firmness of existence, is falsely conceptualized,
just as the self itself is [falsely conceived] by the silkworm as being essentially the firmness of its cocoon-threads.
If there is no duality, then how is this world and its various entities—characterized by a solidity so firm that they cannot be pierced even by millions of spades—perceived? To this he replies:
"consisting of the solidity of entities. It is the Self alone that consists of the nature of Brahman-bliss.
Duality, which consists of the firmness of states such as the world of bondage and so forth, is experienced through delusion;
the meaning is that it is just like the experience of confinement by a silk-worm through the firmness of its own cocoon.
Whatever is perceived by the mind, which is Brahman, and however it is visualized, that is seen exactly so by those who know reality; such is the certainty regarding intrinsic nature. (74)

If bondage were merely imagined by the self, then for each individual there would be only the imagination of what is desired and not the imagination of what is undesired; anticipating this doubt, he says: "By the mind. By Brahman, who is the self of the collective totality of all minds, whatever object is perceived as something to be created according to the karma of the enjoyer—[that is how it appears].
Whatever purpose for which a thing has been manifested is seen in that very same way by other living beings who are likewise knowers of it.
Why is this? Because this determination of inherent nature (svabhāva) and necessity (niyati) is firmly established; such is the meaning. || 74 ||
Just as whatever entity has arisen cannot exist without that [nature], whether for a moment or for an eon—this is the certainty regarding intrinsic nature. (75)

The sprout of a banyan tree arises only from a banyan seed, not from a *kuṭaja* seed; a bubble lasts for only a few moments, whereas the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) lasts for a great aeon (*mahākalpa*). Thus, due to the power of the necessity inherent in cause and effect, there is no possibility of imagining things according to one's own whims. To this he says: "Just as... (verse 75).
This has arisen as false, and it grows as false;
it tastes as false, and likewise it dissolves as false. (76)

One should not be deluded into thinking that this world is real simply because of the apparent independence of ourselves and others, or because of the observed regularities of destiny (niyati), power (śakti), time (kāla), and so forth; thus he says: "It is false" (alīkam). The word *alīka* signifies "false" (*mithyā*). It "tastes sweet" (*svadate*), meaning it is pleasing to experiencers at the time of enjoyment. || 76 ||

Brahman, which is pure, all-pervading, infinite, and non-dual, is perceived— as if impure, as if non-existent, as if manifold, and as if not all-pervading— due to the power of the awakening to suffering. || 77 ||

He shows, by means of prose, the collection of topics that were explained at length through the three chapters in verse, beginning with the words "pure" (*śuddham*) and so forth. [The world] is difficult to comprehend due to delusion (*bhrānti*), and because of its power... 77.
Just as the distinction that "the water is one thing and the wave another" is merely imagined through the false conceptualization of a child, so too is this distinction unreal.

Therefore, whatever distinction appears here is imagined solely by those who do not know reality, like a snake in a rope; such is the case with the powers of difference and non-difference, which are themselves neither enemies nor friends.
It would arise in Brahman alone. || 78 ||

Just as the unreal distinction that "the water is one thing and the wave another" is imagined through the false conceptualization of the ignorant and foolish, so too the distinction of the world is imagined as merely unreal. Since, in the case of the water, the perception of the wave's distinction as a transformation (*pariṇāma*) does not clearly manifest its nature as an illusory appearance (*vivarta*), he states another illustration: "in a rope..."

"Like a serpent," etc. The remainder [of the sense] is that there is a state of both difference and non-difference between the two powers. The meaning of the particle *eva* (only) is that this applies only to the enemy and the friend—those who are respectively opposed and non-opposed—and never to those whose very nature is to remain as such [without change]. || 78 ||

Thus, by that very Self which is non-dual, duality is spread out as it were—just as waves are imagined through water, or a bracelet is imagined through gold; therefore, by that very Self, the Self itself is perceived as if it were something other than itself.
By that inward-facing Self, which has become Brahman, [the world] is spread out and expanded. || 79 ||
From this, ideation was born; that very ideation, attaining expansion, became the mind (*manas*).
By means of that, the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) was imagined. This [mind] is initially of the nature of non-conceptual direct perception;
through the cultivation of the meaning of the word "I," that mind quickly becomes the "I. (80)
*Kalanā* is the manifestation of the world as non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). It attains expansion, which is the state of being conceptual (*savikalpa*). He explains this in the same way:
"This [manifestation], whose nature is non-conceptual perception, first becomes that mind and then 'I'";
this is due to the cultivation of the meaning of the word "I" and the arising of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding the objects of both [mind and ego]. (80)
Then, memory is connected by means of the mind and the ego;

by those three, the subtle elements (tanmātra) experienced therein are conceptualized. Within those subtle elements, whatever arrangement of the world—originating from Brahman as its material cause—is seen to be constructed by the individual soul (jīva), whose nature is the intellect (citta), it occurs spontaneously, like the "crow and the palm fruit" (kākatālīya).
"Anusaṃhitā" means produced according to experience. By that memory, the experienced objects are remembered according to their experience.

"Kalpitāni" means created. By the individual soul (*jīva*), from the material cause characterized as Brahman, this vast arrangement of the world extending through the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) has been fashioned. In an alternative reading, it says "possessing hands, feet, and so forth."
This is clear. || 81 ||
Thus, whatever the mind conceptualizes, that very thing it perceives.
