Whether it be existent or non-existent, whatever the mind—clinging to it—conceptualizes, it perceives that very thing as if it were immediately attained, appearing as if it were real. (82)

He states that "the sequence of creation described is likewise well-known even in the world in dreams" with the words *yadeva* (whatever...). The phrase "he sees through his own delusion" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Now, one might ask: since a dream-object is merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*) and unreal, how can it serve as an illustration for that which is real (*sat*) in the empirical world (*vyāvahārika*)? To this he replies with *sad-vā* (or it is real). The mind (*citta*), that is, the intellect (*manas*), is deeply attached [to it].

The meaning is that whatever one imagines, having long been accumulated through the cultivation of that [mental impression], one necessarily sees it; appearing as if it were a real truth through perception, it has arrived and is attained, and immediately thereafter it will go forth—that is, it will be obtained for the sake of practical utility. || 82 ||

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Instruction on Truth," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* (Section on Origination) of the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Instruction on Truth," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In this very context, they cite this ancient history.
The Rākṣasī spoke this entire web of great questions, which encompasses everything. || 1 ||
Here, the Rākṣasī named Karkaṭī is described in detail;
her fierce ascetic penance was performed with the intent to destroy the entire multitude of living beings. (1)

In order to strengthen the meaning described both in detail and in brief, the author wishes to relate at length the dialogue between the Rākṣasī and the minister of the Kirāta king by means of the historical narrative known as the *Karkaṭy-upākhyāna*; he introduces it with the words: "Right here... [The matter] has been turned over for thorough investigation through reflection.
In which the entire world is pervaded. || 1 ||
On the northern side of the Himalayas, there is a fierce Rākṣasī named Karkaṭī, who is like a carved statue upon a mountain of collyrium mud.
She was fashioned from the soot-like mud of the mountain like a statue of a woman (śālabhañjikā), identical in color, yet fierce in her actions. || 2 ||
And another [woman], known by the name Viṣūcikā, was likewise oppressed by injustice;
with her body withered, she had become emaciated like the Vindhya forest.
He shows two other names for it: *viṣūcikā*. || 3 ||
With eyes like a fire of great power, filling half the space between heaven and earth,
wearing blue garments and black in hue, she was like the night embodied.
Blazing like fire, she fills the interval—the gap between the two worlds, heaven and earth—thus expressing her extreme vastness. || 4 ||
Clothed in a garment of mist, with a head-cloth of thick clouds,
she shines with the orb of hanging clouds, her upward-reaching hair being the ever-rising darkness.

She is covered by mists as if by a lower garment; she whose upper garment is the thick clouds like a head-cloth; she who is radiant with a hanging mass of clouds like a dangling [ornament]; she whose hair rises upward like perpetual darkness. || 5 ||
Her eyes are like steady streaks of lightning, her knees resemble *tāla* trees, the tips of her nails are like *vaidūrya* cornucopias, and she smiles with the radiance of ashes and frost.
Her nails are the color of lapis lazuli and have the shape of the tips of winnowing baskets. || 6 ||
Adorned with garlands and wreaths of flowers formed from the mass of fleshless human bodies, she shone,
resplendent with a necklace of corpses beautifully draped across all her limbs.
Her earrings were black skeletons trembling from the possession of vetālas;
her circle of long, sharp, and terrifyingly fierce arms was eager to seize the sun.

She whose skull-earrings, dark as Time, tremble and quiver due to her immersion in and intense devotion to dancing with the *vetālas* (vampires). Her long-tipped [tongue] seems eager and longing for the seizing of the Sun; because of her massive body, it is difficult for her to obtain food for herself.
The fire within his belly remained as insatiable as the ocean's shoreline.
Of his own food, that is to say, of the boiled rice (odana) suitable for his own kind; that is, of his sustenance. || 9 ||
That large-bellied woman never attained satiety;
like the tongue of the submarine fire, she once reflected thus: (10)
If I were to swallow all the people dwelling in Jambūdvīpa incessantly with my breath, like the ocean swallows a mass of water.
With every exhalation and inhalation. || 11 ||
Like a mirage quenched by a cloud, my hunger is thus appeased;
for that method by which one lives in times of distress is indeed not contrary to righteousness. (12)
Just as a mirage subsides when the cloud obstructs its own cause, the heat of the sun, so too is that method by which one survives in times of adversity considered uncontradicted and approved. 12.
Who can oppress all people equally when they are protected by mantras, medicines, asceticism, charity, worship of the gods, and other such means, and are free from affliction? (13)
With the intention that the attempt to swallow all people simultaneously is indeed contradictory because it is impossible, he says: "The mantra," etc.
"Simultaneously" means at once. || 13 ||
I perform supreme austerity with an entirely unwearied mind;
for by means of most fierce austerity, even that which is difficult to attain is obtained.
To the question, "In that case, how is the fulfillment of the desire to subdue all people achieved? he says: "By austerity" (tapaḥ). || 14 ||
Having reflected thus, she, with the desire to destroy the multitude of all living beings,
then remembered a mountain difficult for creatures to access, for the sake of performing penance.
To the Himalaya mountain. || 15 ||
And she, whose eyes were steady flashes of lightning and whose body was composed of hands, feet, and other limbs, ascended that peak like a dark circle of clouds.
The word "body" (deha) refers to its own essential nature (svarūpa). || 16 ||
Having gone there and bathed, she established herself to perform penance;
she remained standing on one foot, her eyes fixed upon the moon and the sun.
Her two eyes were radiant and motionless, like the moon and the sun. || 17 ||
Day after day, fortnights, months,
and seasons passed for her as she remained motionless in the cold and heat, as if she had been carved from a mountain.
The phrase "as if fashioned from stone" is a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) arising from her endurance of the hardships of asceticism. || 18 ||
She became like a mass of clouds, her form paralyzed;
with her black hair standing erect, she seemed as if risen up to seize the sky.
"Resembling clouds because of their blackness. "To bring" means to take food; that is to say, to swallow. || 19 ||
Beholding her, whose skin was weathered by the wind,
whose body was clad in rags, and who bore a mass of darkness in the form of hair standing erect, shaken by the blowing breeze;
The unborn Brahmā arrived, bringing a flood of stars as his pearl necklace.
She was one whose body— already emaciated and with limbs loosened and shattered by winds that were cold, hot, dusty, and harsh— was draped in skin alone as her garment,
like a bark-cloth (valkala); such was the form of the hosts (gaṇas), meaning they were of that very appearance.

Beholding that [earth] which bore pearls in the form of clusters of stars— that is, the mass of darkness characterized by hair standing on end, shaken and stirred by the whistling winds— Aja, Brahmā, desired to grant her a boon.
"Samupājagāma" (he arrived) is a concise statement of what is about to be described. || 20 ||

Thus ends the sixty-eighth canto, titled "The Description of the Rākṣasī," in the *Līlopākhyāna* of the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rākṣasī," in the Utthāna-prakaraṇa of the Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa.
The sixty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, after a thousand years, the Grandfather (Brahmā) arrived there.
For even poison and fire become cool for one performing severe austerity for the sake of spiritual perfection. || 1 ||
Having granted here to Karkaṭī the boon desired by the Element (Dhātṛ), as well as the mantra for the protection of the virtuous, his departure to his own world is proclaimed. || 1 ||

From where [does this arise]? He says "dāruṇam" (terrible) regarding that [element], even though she is ill-behaved, for even in her, the element of grace is most difficult to obtain. The ellipsis is "it surely leads to success. For when asceticism is perfected, even fire mixed with poison becomes cool; the sense is that there is nothing unattainable through asceticism. || 1 ||
Having mentally bowed to him, that virtuous woman remained just as she was, filled with the thought: "What boon will suffice to alleviate my hunger? (2)
O Lord, I shall now request this one boon from you:
may I become both non-metallic and metallic, a needle for the living.

In this context, *smaraṇe* is a particle (*nipāta*) with this form, and not the prefix *āṅ*. *Anāyasī* means "not made of iron" (i.e., non-metallic). *Jīvasūcikā* means "a needle joined with life. || 3 ||
By his utterance, having become a two-fold needle, I shall enter the hearts of all living beings through their targets, like a fragrant scent.
By the utterance of this Brahman, together with the boon, it was like the fragrance drawn by the sense of smell from a *surabhi* flower.
"According to my desire, I shall devour the entire world in due order to destroy my hunger; for the destruction of hunger is the supreme happiness. (5)
By this sequence, by this means. || 5 ||
As she was reflecting thus, the dweller of the lotus (Viṣṇu) spoke to her;
seeing her so different from before, he addressed her with a voice resembling the roar of thundering clouds.
Because she desired the injury of the world—contrary to the dharma of ascetics such as peace, self-restraint, compassion, and so forth—she was another [form].
Brahmā said:
"O daughter Karkaṭikā, you who wear a garland of clouds upon the mountain-like race of Rākṣasas!"
Arise! I am pleased with you; accept the boon you desire.
Praise is for the purpose of illuminating future welfare. (7)

Karkaṭī said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, if you grant me a boon, O Creator, may I become a needle for living beings, both one that is not made of iron and one that is made of iron."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having said to her, "So be it," the Grandfather spoke again:
"You shall become the needle-bearing Viṣūcikā, accompanied by afflictions."
With subtle illusion you shall bring harm to all the worlds;
those who are gluttonous, engaged in evil undertakings, foolish, and of unstable character—[you shall afflict them].

"Subtle" means difficult for people to perceive. "Bad eaters" refers to those who consume forbidden food, uncooked food, food out of season, or who overeat. "Those of evil undertakings" are those who initiate actions detrimental to others. "Those of unstable conduct" are those who abide by paths not sanctioned by the scriptures. || 10 ||

Those wicked ones dwelling in an evil land— you shall inflict injury upon them by entering their hearts and afflicting them with the spleen, the lotus-organ, and other ailments, thereby depriving them of their life-breaths.
Through the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) by way of the gateway of the breath, having entered from the *apāna* up to the heart,

there is pain and pressure caused by the affliction and squeezing of the heart-lotus, the spleen— that is, the mass of flesh situated near it— and, by the word "etcetera," the bladder, the head of the vessels, and so forth. || 11 ||
"You shall become the disease known as *viṣūcikā*, consisting of a streak of wind;
you will afflict people both virtuous and devoid of virtue. (12)
That which is endowed with qualities is devoted to the scriptures and the conduct of the virtuous; that which is other than this is devoid of qualities.
This mantra is being uttered by me for the purpose of providing treatment endowed with [therapeutic] qualities.
Brahmā said:
On the northern side of the Himālaya mountain, there is a rākṣasī named Karkaṭī.
Medical treatment is the counteraction of disease; it is for that purpose. || 13 ||
Known by the name Viṣūcikā, she is an oppressor even by her name alone.
Her mantra is:
Oṃ hrīṃ hrāṃ rīṃ rāṃ, obeisance to the power of Viṣṇu; Oṃ, obeisance, O Blessed One.

"Oṃ, [drive away] this power of Viṣṇu! Oṃ hara hara, nayana ya, paca paca, matha matha, eradicate it, cast it far away, svāhā! Go to the Himavat mountains! Live! Saḥ saḥ saḥ! You have entered the lunar orb, svāhā!
Having thus placed this great mantra upon the palm of his left hand, the practitioner—
Joined with that hand, he should wipe away the appearance of the patient.

Unrighteousness, which transgresses the path of justice, is its subduer. For the power of Viṣṇu is twofold: the first is Māyā, under whose control all other powers reside; the second, however, is dependent on that [first], is restricted to each individual object, and is divided into categories such as *sāttvika* and so forth. Among these, it is the portions of the *tāmasī* power of destruction that constitute unrighteousness.

Diseases are specific powers that produce the fruits of the evil karma of living beings. Therefore, for their cessation, the primordial power of *māyā* is addressed, saluted, and entreated by means of the five secret seed-syllables (*bīja*), beginning with the *praṇava-māyā*. "Oṃ" is in the dative case, because it is joined with the word "namas. [The mantra is: "Salutation to her whose nature is the Supreme Brahman."

This is the meaning. *Bhaga* means majesty or the power of universal control; in you, the primordial Viṣṇu-śakti who possesses that [majesty], [I pray] you [to withdraw] this second [power], this Viṣṇu-śakti consisting of disease, which is a portion of yourself. [Withdraw her] into the causal form denoted by the syllable *Oṃ*. The word *bhṛśam* is used in the sense of intensity according to the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*.

The doubling of the word [indicates repetition]. *Naya*: lead [her] to her own place; cause her to reach it. *Paca*: soften her immediately, as if by cooking. *Matha*: churn her, like curds. *Utsādaya*: remove her from this place to another. By these or other such means, place her at a distance. *Svāhā* is for the purpose of indicating her worthiness of worship through the offering of oblations and so forth. Having thus prayed to her with such powers...

The power of the disease, which is dependent on that [demon], is entreated, saying, "Go back to your own abode, Himavat. Then he says to the patient: "He is overwhelmed by past evil karma; he is overcome by disease; he is being dragged away by death—[yet] you, by means of nectar capable of reviving the dead through the power of the mantra..."

[In some versions, it reads: "Because of the power of the mantra, he is restored from death to life. You have gone to—that is, you have reached—the full orb of the moon through my visualization (*bhāvanā*). This indicates that, just as an oblation is cast into a blazing fire with the utterance of *svāhā*, the patient must be mentally projected into the full lunar orb through visualization. Thus.
Having written this mantra, the practitioner of mantra should place it on the palm and inside of his left hand. || 14 ||
One should contemplate her as having fled toward the snowy mountains—Karkaṭī, with harsh cries, crushed by the mallet of the mantra. (15)
That cholera, having fled and run away. || 15 ||

One should meditate on the patient as being situated within the heart of the moon, which is the elixir, endowed with freedom from old age and death, and liberated from all mental afflictions and delusions. (16)
With a concentrated mind, he was joined with the elixir of immortality within the heart. || 16 ||
For the practitioner, having become pure, having sipped water for ritual purification, and being well-composed, destroys all cholera by means of this sequence. (17)
Since the sequence of meaning (arthakrama) is more authoritative than the sequence of recitation (pāṭhakrama), the acts of purification, sipping water, and so forth must be performed first.
Well-composed, with an undistracted mind. || 17 ||
Thus the Lord of the Three Worlds, dwelling in the sky, has received the perfected mantra from the sky-dwelling Siddhas.
Having gone forth and returned, being praised by Śakra, he of radiant glory entered his own imperishable city.

Brahmā, the lord of the three worlds, was accompanied by *siddhas* traveling through the sky who had mastered unimpeded mantras; being thus honored by Śakra, who had approached him for the accomplishment of another task, he possessed inexhaustible *māyās*—
powers of illusion established through the fulfillment of his true resolve— which were impossible for others to thwart.

Having gone to his own city, Satyaloka, which is of such a nature that it consists of the world-forms of fathers, mothers, brothers, perfumes, garlands, and so forth—created by the volitions of others—and which is an illusion of various objects of enjoyment; || 18 ||

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Discourse on the Mantra for Cholera," in the *Sūcī-upākhyāna* (The Story of the Needle) within the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 69.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Discourse on the Viṣūcikā Mantra," in the Utthāna-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The seventieth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, that great black rākṣasī, who resembled the peak of a mountain, [spoke].
She was as if preparing to attain thinness upon the very petals of clouds made of collyrium.
First, the gradual attenuation [of the body] and then the movement in the form of two needles;
the entry of the needle into the bodies of living beings is thus described. (1)
*Tanu* means subtle; its state is *tānava*. || 1 ||
Then she took on a form resembling a cloud, and from that, a form like a tree;
then she became the size of a man, and thereafter she was only the size of a hand.
He elaborates on that very point with the words beginning "babhūva" (she became): "viṭaparūpiṇī" means having the size of a tree branch. || 2 ||
Then she became the size of a span, then the form of a finger;
then she became equal to a bean or a śamī seed, and then she indeed became a needle.
Māṣaśamī is a bean-pod; sūcī is a thick needle. || 3 ||
Then she, beautiful with the filaments of lotuses and possessing a pointed form, attained the state of being indicated by silk, becoming as minute as a mountain of one's imagination.

An extremely fine needle is suitable for sewing silk; this gradual refinement of the gross body belongs only to that [body] fashioned by its own volition. However, he will later state that what is fashioned by supreme knowledge (parā-vidyā) simply dissolves right there. || 4 ||
The slender, black needle, made of fine iron,
shone as it moved through the city of the eightfold body, traveling through the sky and dwelling in the void.
Having become a subtle modification consisting of iron, she shone as a black needle that was yet not made of iron— a needle for the living soul—
arising from the aggregate of the great elements, the organs of action, the organs of knowledge, the vital breaths, the internal organ, ignorance, desire, and karma.
With the eightfold city-ornament. || 5 ||
This needle is indeed visible, yet its "otherness" does not exist;
within the multitude of the delusions of consciousness, it appears like a tiny needle.
And this "needling" of hers is merely imagined through a delusion regarding the visible world, not real;

for even by a thousand boons or curses, it is impossible for a thing to change its nature. With this intention, he says: "Needle..."—the meaning is that she too is but one delusion within the multitude, the collection, of the delusions of consciousness. || 6 ||
Smooth like a jewel-needle, joined with the contemplation of the mind;
beautiful as a streak of luster from a cat's-eye gem within the radiance of the sun.

She is perceived like a beautiful needle of jewels or like a streak of luster from lapis lazuli, due to the penetration of a continuous stream of sunbeams. The meaning is that the distinction in this simile lies in the phrase "joined with the mind's reflection" (manomanana-saṃyutā). || 7 ||
Like a streak of collyrium-cloud paste carried by the wind,
the pupil of light was seen through the clear vision of his subtle eye-cavity.
Regarding the lack of contact with the sun's rays, he says: "like collyrium" (*kajjala*). A cloud (*ambhoda*) consists of collyrium;

a creeper-like extension (*latā-pratāna*) is a small portion of that mass (*saṃkalpa*) which has the form of such a cloud. Brought and conveyed by the wind, it appears like the pure light seen through the eyes—the two distinct eyes—within a subtle aperture.
She whose pupils are the black circles [of the eyes]. (8)
With a face pleasant to behold and a tail and crest that were smooth and fine,
she then entered into the supreme vow of silence for the sake of attaining vast tranquility.
With his subtle tail-tip— the minute extremity of the tail resembling an atom—

as a sign in the form of a needle, which was most desired and acceptable due to its granting of boons, he then observed silence for the sake of pacifying the bulkiness of his former body so that it might become well-proportioned with a pleasant countenance.

"She has surely gone to the supreme [state] through the ascetic vow belonging to a sage"—this is the poetic fancy (utprekṣā). The intention is that her ascetic vow, having resulted only in the pacification of her own excessive [passion], was as if in vain. || 9 ||
Seen from afar like a lamp, she has attained the state of being mere space;
even from a distance, she proclaims the void with her beautiful mouth.
"What kind of thing is it, and how did she attain that form of a needle? To this he replied: "From afar," and so forth.
Because she was seen from a great distance, with her eyes blazing, she was perceived like a single lamp due to the lack of perception of any intermediate stages;
because the body of the needle was not seen, she attained its state as a mere subtle element (*tanmātra*), reaching a state of equality with space. Within the body—

The poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is that she seems to be vomiting or spitting out the sky with her mouth—which is pleasing due to its attainment of excellence and serene because of the attainment of a boon—after the space contained within it has reached a state of extreme subtlety by remaining outside. 10.
Visible with her eyes slightly contracted, she was as delicate as the wick of a long lamp;
she was as beautiful as a young girl who had just bathed and emerged from the water.
Furthermore, he describes what that [vision] is like there with the words beginning "kuñcita" (contracted): it is long, extending far;

it is delicate and subtle like the rays of a lamp. For this very reason, it is to be beheld by the eyes of the observer—eyes contracted for the sake of one-pointed concentration. It is as if by one who has just bathed.
Exalted among fools and children, she is like the hair of a fool, playful and fond of sporting. 11.
Like a silken thread or lotus fiber that has flown upward out of curiosity for external movement,
the beautiful woman is intent upon the external aperture like the Brahma-nāḍī.

The *brahmanāḍī*, the *suṣumnā*, having flown up—having emerged upward from the lotus-stalk—and having gone out through the external aperture, the *brahmarandhra*, it is directed upward toward the solar orb. || 12 ||
That power of the senses, though situated externally by means of the individual soul (jīva), remains unperceived, like the continuum of consciousness of the Bauddhas and Tārkikas. || 13 ||

That [power] whose capacities of the senses, such as the eye and so forth, are fixed and established in their respective locations; which exists externally in the form of a needle-like projection by means of the *jīva* alone, that is, the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*), just as the stream of the *ālayavijñāna* according to the Buddhists, though its domain is restricted to itself alone, remains unperceived by others; or as...
Just as the stream of continuous cognition belonging to logicians remains unobserved because they do not admit the existence of a witness (sākṣin), so too [this state] remains unobserved by others.

It is established as being continuous and followed by the invisible life-needle (jīvasūcī), which is empty, having the meaning of the perfected, possessing openings, consisting of the blue, and sounding.

Because the objects established by the proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādins) are absolutely imperceptible, there arises the poetic fancy that [the goddess] is their progenitor, possessing transformation.
When the sky, which is a void, possesses a blueness—that [blueness] consists of her or is of her nature. She is "aravā," meaning soundless.

Although the suffix *mayaṭ* would normally require the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, its absence here is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). Alternatively, it may be a *karmadhāraya* compound with the masculine form applied.
Having thus described the iron needle, he states that the life-needle (jīvasūcī) follows it by means of being invisible:
"by the invisible one" (adṛśyayā). || 14 ||
It possesses the nature of both differentiation and non-differentiation, its essence being nothing but latent impressions (vāsanā);
it is as subtle as the wick of a dying lamp, sharp, and imperceptible.

The *kalās* are the reflections of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) within their respective functions, belonging to that which possesses the nature of such manifestation. They are like the needle characterized by the rays of a lamp that is exhausted and in a state of extinction; for just as such a needle, though imperceptible to the eye, is sharp because it burns when touched, so too are these *kalās*. || 15 ||
Having gone to that very place indicated for the sake of food, she found it no longer useful;
she reflected, "Alas! This was merely the manifestation of my own foolishness. (16)

Now, he mocks the fruit of her asceticism—characterized by the state of being a needle—because it serves no desired purpose, beginning with the words "For the sake of a morsel": "That [needle], being merely for the sake of a morsel, is of no use to a needle that has no belly. (16)
She reflected with intensity, perceiving that the needle’s form was not insignificant; for her, as she beheld it, the mind’s desire alone remained, while everything else appeared meaningless.

Without even investigating, that person of deluded intellect persists in asserting his own authority; for one whose mind is fixed on what is harmful, reflection upon the preceding and following context does not arise. (18)
It was resorted to and desired by a being who possesses a mind set on what is harmful and a mind that perceives the meaningless as meaningful. || 18 ||

Through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), an object—possessing its own capacity for purposeful action and enriched by its intended aspects—undergoes transformation, just as a mirror does through the breath [of a person]. (19)

To the question, "Why does it not manifest in a mind that is fit for investigation? he says: "svārtha... (regarding one's own purpose). The object of the mind is one who is wealthy—that is, deeply attached—to a desired part or object.
Through intense cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there arises from his formidable and unavoidable capacity a firm effort toward the desired object, which constitutes its own causal efficacy (*svārthakriyā*).
Through the coloring by that passion, it undergoes a change—a reversal of its prior purity; that is to say, it becomes turbid, just as a mirror does through breath. || 19 ||
For this ogress, who has attained the state of a needle and is casting off her bulky body,
even this great death remains exceedingly pleasant.
Furthermore, because of her firm attachment to her own interest, even great suffering has become like happiness for her; thus he says: "The needle... (verse 20).
Oh, how strange is the destiny of those who are excessively attached to a single object!
Even her own body was cast away like a blade of grass by the Rākṣasī according to her own will. (21)
For other perceptions perish through the overpowering scent of a single object;
indeed, by the mere smell of a Rākṣasī’s prey, even the destruction of the body is not avoided. (22)
Even destruction brings happiness to the ignorant man who is excessively attached to a single object;
even when she became a bodiless needle, the Rākṣasī was truly contented.
Another was Lagnā—

[the reading *lagnāśā* means "one whose desire (*āśā*) is fixed (*lagnā*) upon devouring living beings"]— that Jīvaviṣūcikā; she is of the nature of space, formless, and has the functions of space as her body.

Having described the principle as an incidental digression, he follows the main subject and describes the nature of the disease called *jīvasūcī* with the verse beginning "anyā" and so forth. Its subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) has the nature of being as subtle as space, like the sky, and it abides in the ether. || 24 ||
She has the luster of a stream of light, consists of the threads of vital breath,
takes the form of fundamental consciousness, and is as beautiful as the silken garments of the moon and sun.
The primordial consciousness is the Kuṇḍalinī power, whose form is that [consciousness]; she is beautiful like the tiny rays of light from the moon and sun serving as her garments.
Distinct indeed, like the edge of a sword, yet subtler than an atom; she is a mere fraction (kalā) whose form consists of creative ideation, like a trail of fragrance from a flower.

The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: the sinful mental disposition of that *karkaṭī* (the crab-plant), which is therefore cruel like the edge of a sword, exists in the form of a "life-needle" (*jīvasūcī*) quite distinct from the iron needle;
it is like a streak of fragrance from a flower, existing in the manner of an atom—that is, extremely subtle.
Having entered within the bodies of living beings, she remains manifest in the form of the accomplishment—that is, the performance—of the arts of violence and other such acts. || 26 ||
For that mental disposition of his was inherently evil and remained so;
it was devoted solely to the ultimate goal of bringing the lives of others under its control. (27)

He states that very point clearly with the words "pareṣām" and so forth: following the vital breaths of other living beings by means of their life-force, they are intent upon—that is, devoted to—the supreme goal, which is the fulfillment of their own desires. || 27 ||
Thus her body was formed; for it consisted of two needles—slender like the moonlight through mist, and as delicate as a thread of cotton.
He concludes the description of the two bodies with the word "evam" (thus). || 28 ||
Having entered the hearts of men with those two slender forms,
that cruel woman then wandered through the ten directions, piercing them.
Now he describes her life story in brief: "By means of two bodies," [verse 29].
Everyone becomes light or heavy by the power of their own volition;
the karkaṭī creeper, having cast off its formidable body, has assumed the state of a needle.
He says "all" to show that this very point is the illustration for the power of *saṃkalpa* (volition) to bring about even the impossible.
Even a trivial object becomes desirable to those of little strength;
through ascetic penance, a Rākṣasī attained the state of a needle-bodied Piśācī. (31)
For those of little being and base minds, such a state of being a *piśācī*—whose circumference is like that of a needle—is [the result]. (31)
Even for those of meritorious bodies, the bond of birth does not cease;
thus, this Rākṣasī acquired the state of a needle-bodied Piśācī through her ascetic penance.

[Objection: Surely she has been purified by austerity and has attained a meritorious body; how then is it appropriate for her, being such as she is, to request a body of needles—a cause of suffering to others? To this he says: "Even" (api). "Bond of birth" (jātibandha) refers to the bondage of latent impressions (vāsanā) that follows one's species. || 32 ||
While she was engaged in wandering to the ends of the earth,
her gross body dissolved right there by great winds, like an autumn cloud.
That gross body, common to all and fashioned by ignorance, like a crab's shell, was dissolved and shattered by great winds. || 33 ||
183. When someone’s limbs have become powerless, whether they are emaciated or corpulent,
the needle-like wind enters within and causes extreme dysentery (*viṣūcikā*).

Now he describes the course of *viṣūcī* in detail, beginning with the words "of someone" (*kasyacit*). [It occurs] in one whose limbs have been rendered helpless by a previous disease; in one who is emaciated (*kṣīṇa*) with thin limbs; or in one who is corpulent (*vipula*) with stout limbs.
An excessive onset of *viṣūcikā*, which is like an iron needle piercing deep into the wind-channels (*vātalīna*), arises as the disease. || 34 ||
Even for someone who is healthy, free from bodily affliction, and possessed of great intelligence,
once they have entered into the state of being indicated as a living soul, an internal cholera-like malady arises.
The internal cholera is the form of evil intellect. || 35 ||
Thus, that [thirst], residing in the heart of one with a wicked mind, is satisfied in some cases;
in other cases, it is cut away by means of merit, mantras, medicinal herbs, and the practice of austerities. (36)
In some case or other, regarding a certain person; it is cut off, that is, it is warded off. || 36 ||
For many years she remained solely devoted to wandering, traveling through both the sky and upon the surface of the earth by means of her two bodies. (37)
On the ground she is concealed by dust; in the hand, she is concealed by the fingers;
in the sky, she is concealed by light; and on a garment, she is concealed by thread. || 38 ||
He states the specific locations for its concealment with the words beginning "rajaḥ" (dust), etc. || 38 ||
Within the river of sinews situated inside, it is unfortunate, pale with dust, dug up by the rivers of dry lines, and overgrown with the withered grass of fine wrinkles. (39)

He speaks of those [inauspicious signs] even within the body, beginning with the words "antaḥstha" (situated inside). In a vulva or the organ of generation (*upasthendriya*) defiled by faults such as sexual misconduct; in one whose limbs are greyish-white with dust, such as the dust of ash and the like; in a dry riverbed characterized by dry and rough lines on the hands, feet, and so forth; and in that which is subtle...
The lines of hair and so forth are its characteristics; it is like withered grass. || 39 ||
Devoid of wealth, lacking luster, empty, yet causing one to breathe with relief; greened by the wind from flies and entirely devoid of *śrīvṛkṣa* trees.

*Artha* means that which is desired; here, it refers to the mark of good fortune (*saubhāgya-lakṣaṇa*) when it is absent from a limb. *Gata-cchāya* means having lost its luster. *Śūnyā* means empty of internal essence. *Ucchvāsa* is the upward breath of those who are afflicted.
Even outside the body, [the area] is filled with flies and harsh, foul-smelling winds.
In a place covered with green grass and the like, or one devoid of trees that bring prosperity, such as the *bilva*, mango, and other such trees. || 40 ||
In that which is entwined with thick knots of bone, perpetually trembling and intensely quivering;
in that mist of non-self which produces the delusion of a clean white cloth where there is no purity. (41)

[The place] is entwined with large knots of bones from animals, humans, and so forth; it is intensely throbbing and intensely quivering due to the constant shaking caused by whirlwinds and the like. Those very [beings] who are established in the Self are "clear"—that is, pure—and like mist, they remove the suffering of others. [It is a place] where there are no "clear mists" belonging to oneself.
In which [place] there was the movement of such ill-mannered people whose garments were unclean.
Where flies, crows, and pigeons rest upon scars, stumps, and limbs;
where the trees have branches of trembling fingers amidst winds that carry the scent of dryness and rising sap.

Where honey-bees and cuckoos and crows rest in succession upon scars, hollows, stumps, and trees with broken tops; where the wind, harsh due to excessive cold, has arisen and become manifest, whistling and sounding; and for that very reason, its branches—its fingers—are trembling and wavering.
In the world that is like a garland or a streak of clouds, within the hollows of the wounds on one's own fingers,
amidst the droplets of dew from movement, and upon the mountain of anthills formed by footprints— 43.
Where there is a continuous succession of garland-like streaks of clouds and layers of mist;
where people dwell in places resembling pits with wounds on their own split fingers;
where trembling droplets of frost—drops of dew—are found; and where there are anthills in places marked by the footprints of men.
And in the case of "Vāmalūra" and "parvata," there is singular number due to collective composition. 43.
In one place, there was the swift shimmering of water-mist upon a surface as rough as a scorpion's tail;
in another, terrified lice and bedbugs fled like travelers at the sight of a spreading swarm of insects.
In a desert land where the shimmering mirage of water quickly flashes,

in a forest that is exceedingly harsh and most rigid with tigers, bears, and others— predators whose primary weapons are their claws— and with pythons and the like, there are those who dwell here and there, scattering and fleeing even from those who are themselves afraid.
Where travelers and wayfarers were terrified by lice and treated with contempt. || 44 ||

In a place where foul-smelling, withered betel rolls were gnawed by hideous creatures, amidst stagnant pools of putrid water, in the midst of a path strewn with parched earth, and within the reach of a cold wind blowing from a torrent of clouds; (45)

In such a putrid pond— a pit of foul-smelling water where withered leaves, resembling betel-quids, have been bitten by hideous and emaciated piśācas and other spirits; and which is situated amidst channels and ditches carved out in the middle,
within the range of a cold wind blowing along those paths.
At a place of rest for travelers. || 45 ||
Moving everywhere as she traverses [the world], she holds with her thumb and wing-like fingers those whose mouths, nails, and nostrils are filled with the blood of swarms of men devoured by gadflies.

By means of the web of fingers acting as a thumb-enclosure— that is, by the thumb surrounded by the other fingers— he assumed the state of one whose nails alone serve as mouths for those base men, monkeys, and others, whose corners of the mouth were filled with the blood of multitudes of men residing within the bellies of lice that had been swallowed and chewed.
The remainder of the sentence is: "She became one who moves—having the nature of going—to every part of the body, to regions such as the earth, and to the previously mentioned locations. (46)
Traveling toward the city of variegated cloth, adorned with various patterns, she became utterly exhausted by her coming and going after traveling there for an exceedingly long time. (47)

Likewise, she was accustomed to traveling through cities and towns adorned with various kinds of paintings depicting arrays of elephants, horses, and other such forms; there, it is implied, she became exhausted by her constant coming and going and wandering about. (47)
In town after town, she carries alone the burden of the scattered collection of sūtras;
in the scorched forest of her own body, she moves about like a bullock.

Furthermore, by her very nature as a needle, she has the habit of supporting all things— whether they be cotton threads and the like scattered in cities, non-cities, and villages, or cast upon the streets; and whether they be glass beads and such items strung upon them, or vessels and ornaments.

Because it is incapable of being removed by others due to its subtlety. Furthermore, when the forest of the body of living beings is scorched by fever and other afflictions, this needle behaves like a bull;
just as a spirited bull turns back while tearing up anthills and the like with its horns, so too does this needle possess that same disposition. || 48 ||
Hidden for the sake of rest, slightly slipped from the hand, and threaded upon a strand, the weary mouth-drawing [of the shuttle] dissolves somewhere. (49)

Having been held by someone for a long time to sew, and having become weary and exhausted from pulling the threads protruding from her face during the sewing, she slips slightly from his hand and hides herself somewhere in secret, concealing herself to rest.
Even though it was hard, the piercing did not succeed when conjoined with [her] karma;
for fire, however sharp, does not abandon its own nature if it is to be made [into something else]. (50)
Anticipating the objection, "Why did she not perform the piercing for the one who was doing the sewing?", he says: "piercing.

Although she was hard and cruel, because she was attached—out of curiosity—to the needle due to its very nature as a needle during the sewing work appropriate to her, she did not perform the piercing. Why? Because that needle [was bound] by its own-ness, its own inherent nature.

If one abandons, relinquishes, and does not manifest the sewing [of the wound], then—due to its being of a similar nature—one's own sharp and cruel disposition should not be made manifest externally; for it cannot be manifested outwardly, as it is no different from being one's own. This is the meaning. || 50 ||
With her needle-like mind entangled by the needle of [worldly] thought,
she wandered about like a heavy stone cast into the quarters of the sky, her limbs withered and pale.

That iron needle, by means of the mind-needle and the life-force-needle—being heavy like a stone, she remained as if upon a ship in the midst of a withered old woman; and like a bird, she wandered and roamed through the quarters of the sky. Or, "aṅga" may be taken as a vocative address. 51.
It spread out to the ends of the quarters along with the existence of the internal organ,
like a streak of husk by the power of the wind in the form of worldly existence.
It takes on the form of worldly existence (saṃsṛti) because it manifests—that is, makes evident—the wandering of cyclic existence; [it is] by that [form]. || 52 ||
With her mouth, she seemed as if moving through the fine threads of a subtle sūtra woven by another;
and by the effort of another’s loom, she was as if suddenly brought to life, endowed with a heart.

Moving about as if devouring the subtle threads woven and interlaced by others, she is indeed possessed of a heart—meaning her mind is at ease—solely through the effort of filling her belly directed by others; this is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) imagining her to be "born" [with such a disposition].
Her heart was fully opened by the very essence of her lover's passion;
she remained motionless, as if pinned by the end of a fine thread that had fallen incessantly [into it]. 54.

With the intention that this poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is indeed appropriate, he says "parā" (the other). For, even before [the piercing], her own mind—already tormented by the hardship of penance—was well-expanded and uplifted solely by the desire to fill her belly through the slaughter of others, driven by the very essence of the act of filling another; therefore, she falls incessantly into her mouth. [This occurs] at the end of the fine thread.
The meaning is that the simile of being "as if paralyzed" or "as if obstructed" when one's own desired object is nearly attained is entirely appropriate. || 54 ||
Even when long depleted by intense [efforts], non-discernment (nirvicāraṇā) is filled;
here the illustration is a tattered cloth that is filled in an instant by a needle. || 55 ||

Now, he states that the practice of austerity by the foolish has resulted merely in filling the bellies of rags with needles as threads, rather than filling their own bellies; this is a world-renowned general statement and illustration based on a metaphorical meaning—expressed thus: "Even by sharp [needles]," and so forth.

A family that has long been diminished and afflicted by the emaciation of poverty is filled and nourished even by those who are sharp and cruel; there is no deliberation required in this matter, for the illustration here is the visibly seen example of a tattered cloth filled with a needle. || 55 ||
The heart was pierced by the needle, ready for the emergence of the threads of the sūtra;
and for the sake of filling the other [the body], there was quickly the splendor of the sun of poetic art.
To the question "Why was her own belly not filled by the needle?", he says: "By the needle.

Because, through austerity, she acquired a heart so perfectly smooth that it was fit for the passage of the thread—that is, the tip of the fiber—both in its exit and its entry; likewise, she possessed the radiance of splendor and intelligence.
Because she possesses the fortune of awakening to the ultimate reality (*tattva*), her poetry—like the solar radiance of the sun-gem (*arkaruk*)—is of a luminous nature;

yet, it is quickly pervaded solely for the sake of fulfilling others, as if by the sewing of cloth and such, and not acquired for her own enjoyment. This is the meaning. [The word *āśu* is derived] from the root *aśū* (to pervade) with the prefix *ā*, according to the *auṇādika* suffixes.
The suffix *up* [is applied]. || 56 ||
Suddenly, by that [feeling] which had arisen, whose fullness was exhausted, she became possessed of form;
and in her heart, O Rākṣasī, she was tormented by the needle-like effect of her own action.
For this very reason, he says "akasmāt" (suddenly) to indicate that she felt remorse. *Pūra* means the belly, as it is filled (*pūryate*).
By that act of austerity (*tapaḥ-karman*), which had suddenly grown—that is, manifested—as a needle-like state, she became embodied by that needle; she was that very needle. || 57 ||
Like a stream in full flood, she herself brings about piercing;
even by her own innate nature, she is employed for the purpose of piercing. (58)
If she were remorseful, would she then have desisted from piercing his vital organs? No; he says "piercing" (vedham).

Nevertheless, by her own innate nature as a Rākṣasa—which is like the force of a river's current—and even by her natural disposition toward piercing with a needle, she [remained] intent upon piercing him alone.
When it has been practiced according to its own nature, first initiated and subsequently employed in daily practice, it certainly effects penetration (vedha). || 58 ||
It transmits the thread through the cloths by means of fourfold piercing,
just as the long thread of latent tendencies (vāsanā) transmits consciousness through bodies.

Therefore, he states— with an illustration— the point previously mentioned, that it also performs its function by means of its nature as a mere needle, using the words "it causes to move": just as, at the time of death, a long thread in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) directed toward objects such as children and wife arises, and [the consciousness] enters into bodies such as those of women in accordance with those various impressions.
The meaning is that just as one transfers the living consciousness, so too does one transfer the thread among the garments. || 59 ||
Like arrows being discharged by a shifting archer as they fly toward their mark,
wicked people pierce the vital spots while keeping their faces hidden from view.

For this very reason, when those [patterns] were being transferred onto the cloths by weavers through piercing, it is implied that they seemed as if they were running away, having hidden their faces behind the cloth at the moment of contact with the eye during its fall.
He confirms that "this was indeed poorly done by her" through an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth), beginning with the words "adarśita... (not shown...).
The meaning is that wicked people such as slanderers and thieves are well known to pierce the vital secrets of others without even showing their own faces. || 60 ||
With her face fixed upon the blade of cloth around his neck, she gazes at him with piercing eyes,
thinking, "How shall I pierce this?"— this is the desire of those who are sharp.

Sometimes, having threaded [the needle] through the string of an upper garment caught upon her neck, she gazes at the faces of women with her "piercer's eye"—that is, her own eye characterized by its [needle-like] aperture. He asks her with what intention she does so, saying: "How? (61).
And she entered at the same time into both the silken and the linen garments;
for what person, indeed, would be so dull-witted as to disregard the difference between quality and defect? (62)

[The intellect] has entered with equal engagement into *kauśeya*—a silk cloth possessing qualities such as softness and smoothness—and into *kṣauma*, the bark-fiber of the *kṣumā* plant, which possesses defects such as hardness and roughness. A fool is one who is ignorant; he "considers" means he reflects upon what is devoid of quality, that is, what is a defect. || 62 ||
Holding the stretched-out thread pressed between her thumb and fingers,
she gazes as if vomiting forth the inner entrails from beginning to end.

At the time of sewing, the emergence of the thread from the eye of the needle is poetically imagined as the vomiting out of the thread-intestine located within the belly of the needle, which has been pressed by the thumb of the sewer—this is expressed by the word "sā" (she/it).
It is "not finding room" (amāntam), meaning it does not find a place to remain inside due to the lack of space. || 63 ||

Though sharp, she is devoid of heartlessness; though flavorless, she is full of flavor; though merely indicated, she enters into the objects of experience as one who attains aesthetic relish (rasa). 64.

Threaded upon a string and sharp, that needle—though it enters into objects both flavorful and flavorless—is, due to its lack of heart and the emptiness of its inner core, ignorant of distinctions; for this very reason, lacking the relish of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), it enters by its very nature as a mere needle. 64.

(185) Not laughing, with her face fixed [in concentration], though her intellect was extremely sharp; though well-pierced [by insight], she was heartless; and though a princess, she was ill-fated. (65)
"Alas, what a miserable plight this is, that she suffers punishment for no fault! Thus he says: "She does not bellow" (*agardatī*). [The roots] *nard* and *gard* mean "to sound.

Though she does not utter sounds such as harsh speech, being pierced in the mouth by a thread, her intellect (*dhī*) is itself heated—meaning it is full of torment—even though it is capable of tormenting others; she is thoroughly pierced.
The meaning is that although she has a vulva, she is heartless and lacks the cavity of a womb; thus, just as even a princess may become unfortunate and ill-fated, so too has she become. || 65 ||
Without inflicting harm upon others, the sharp [sensation] seeks death;
obstructed by pain, the needle hangs suspended in the noose of karma. (66)

"It is indeed fitting that she has such a miserable state," he says with the word "vinā" (without). Since she desires—seeks—slaughter, that is death, even without causing harm to others, she is therefore bound by her own intellect due to the suffering resulting from that sin;
thus, being confined within the thread, she hangs by the very noose of her own karma—this is the poetic fancy (utprekṣā). || 66 ||
Why does even the dark-fleshed friend of the night lie far away, cast off by his hand?
Indeed, who would not take pleasure in a friend who resembles one's own nature? (67)

Having fallen by fate from the hand of Sīva, she— [the word "in the lap" (aṅke) implies that lying without support is impossible, thus it must be understood as such]— was in the lap or on the side of another person, in a distant place where the touch of a hand was impossible, along with hairs that were darkish, meaning of a contemptible dark color and hanging downwards.

Maitrī alone sleeps, as it were, among them due to her very nature as a friend. To the question of why she finds pleasure in such union with them, he says: "because it is similar to her own nature. || 67 ||
Mixed with the mental fluctuations of the ignorant among common folk, who indeed would wish to abandon the company of those who are equal to oneself? (68)
For this very reason, he says "mixed" [in verse 68], meaning that even association with the mental states of fools is pleasing to her.
When the blacksmith’s wealth ceases to exist, she departs into invisibility;
stirred by the blasts from the bellows, she is intent on flying up from the earth into the sky. (69)

Now, since it is equal to other iron needles, might it—by virtue of its friendship with them—ever happen by chance to reach a blacksmith along with them? To this he says: "She becomes... When the blacksmiths have obtained wealth (or reached their workshop), she is placed in the fire for the purpose of heating; she is then moved about by the blasts from the bellows made of their skins.
The meaning is that Satī, having abandoned them, went into concealment; being thus hidden, she rose up from the sky with her face turned upward, intent on flight. || 69 ||
Moving within the heart-lotus situated in the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, the most terrible power of suffering has arisen like the power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti). || 70 ||
He describes her movement within the bodies of living beings by means of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, starting with the words "the vital breath" (*prāṇa*).

The power of action (*karma-śakti*), which bestows suffering, is itself the power of the individual soul (*jīva-śakti*); it is said to be "with life" (*sajīvā*), as if it has arisen or become manifest. || 70 ||
By way of being the opposite of samāna, it moves together with samāna;
by way of being the opposite of udāna, it moves together with udāna. || 71 ||
Established in the vyāna [vital air], she generates disease; she circulates the essence through all the limbs.
In the heart and throat, she causes piercing pain and wind, and brings about discoloration and madness. (72)
"In the spear-wind" means having entered the wind whose nature is the disease of colic; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 72 ||

For the most part, she delights solely in piercing the bed formed by the fingers of a child’s hand within the hollow of a woolly scent-moth, while the goat stands nearby with its foreleg resting there.

Generally, at the time of sewing blankets and such, she would sometimes sleep in the hollow of her hand— which belonged to the sheep-herders of the woolen fleece— merely to catch a trace of its scent; at other times, however, she was the sole playful woman, full of primary curiosity, regarding the piercing of her own bed in the form of the fingers and limbs of children.
The word "was" (āsīt) is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 73 ||
Having entered her feet, she is amazed at the acquisition of the drinking of blood;
she who is satisfied by eating clusters of flowers is exceedingly pleased with these meager offerings. (74)
At the time of weaving garlands of flower clusters, she who eats clusters is satisfied and satiated by those who eat little, by those whose food is meager. || 74 ||
She has lain for a long time with her face turned downward, situated within a mire;
for who would abandon a dwelling once it has been obtained according to their desire? (75)
The "mud-encasement" (kardamakośa) refers to the encasement of the root-support (mūlādhāra) which is fouled by impurities and mire. || 75 ||
Through acts of piercing, he reveals his soul to be overcome by cruelty;
even for the base, a quarrel is more pleasant than a festival.

She considers herself defiled and corrupted by "piercings" (*upavedhana*), that is, by acts of piercing that extend even to the taking of another’s life. To the question of how she could be motivated to kill another when there is no personal interest at stake, he says:
"even from a festival. This refers to those for whom, even in the absence of the capacity to cause suffering to others, [there is a desire] to do so with others.
The sense is: "Even quarrel becomes a source of pleasure for them; what then need be said about the killing of others?"
The miser considers himself fortunate at gaining even half a cowrie shell;
for the wondrous delusion of egoism is indeed difficult for living beings to sever.
He explains that her engagement in the supreme slaughter [of the enemy] is justified by her greed for tasting even the smallest drops of blood, saying:
"kapardaka... (like a cowrie). Or, he says that its justification arises from her pride in sporting in the injury of others, which is characteristic of the race of Rākṣasas, saying:
"duruccheda... (difficult to eradicate). || 77 ||
Deluded by the acquisition of a mere pair of needles, humans fear death; how strange that such folly does not arise regarding one's own true self-interest! 78.

She, being pierced by the two needles of her own actions—namely, the "living needle" (*jīvasūcī*) and the "iron needle" (*lohasūcī*)—performs this with a deluded and bewildered self; thus she apprehends and speculates upon the death of all men.
This occurs among the foolish, where it is inevitable—or according to another reading, "among the foolish, it is in vain."
Ignorance does not arise regarding its own object; that is wonderful, meaning it is a marvel. || 78 ||
"Through the separation of the threads of the cloth, my supreme essence quickly becomes this [body]; thus thinking, she becomes inwardly pure. (79)

Now, because my supreme skill in cutting—formerly practiced through the piercing of the threads of cloth during the time of sewing—is quickly accomplished, her mind becomes exceedingly pure and serene within through the recollection of her own proficiency;
that is to say, she rejoices. || 79 ||
Just as a stone placed [in water] takes up impurity without being rubbed with clay, so too does disease arise for her due to the absence of any offense against others. (80)

Just as a needle well-known in the world, when left silently without being rubbed on a whetstone—[the phrase "by sewing" and so forth being understood from the context]—takes up and acquires dirt and impurity; likewise, even for her, disease and suffering arise due to the absence of any transgression. This is the meaning. || 80 ||
Subtle, invisible, and a giver [of pain], she causes forgetfulness in an instant;
cruel and piercing with sharpness, she is like the needle of destiny.
Invisible, she is the giver and the destroyer; she is like a divine or portentous movement. 81.
She was satisfied by the mere piercing of a thread, thinking "another has been killed";
yet she feels joy when that very same person destroys a wicked man. 82.
By the mere skill of piercing the threads of his upper garment that covered his vital points. || 82 ||

He sinks in mud, he travels through the sky, he dwells among the winds of the atmosphere, and he sleeps upon the dust of the earth as if on the ground; he rests in the forest, on a silken cloth, in a house, or within the inner apartments; and he lies upon his hand, his lotus-like ear, or on a soft fragment of wool as he pleases.
In the case of holes, wood, or clay, that [cognition] measures them within the heart by the very power of the substance's own nature. || 83 ||
He summarizes the conduct described at length by way of a brief conclusion with the verse beginning "In the mud": he sinks into the mud of ponds and the like;

he goes to the sky, the atmosphere; and together with the winds of the firmament, he wanders upon the horizons of the quarters. The particle *iva* (as if) is displaced in its grammatical order. In the inner apartments of the palace, or on a silken rug—a spread of fine cloth upon a couch—he [wanders] as if upon the ground in the forest.

He sleeps even upon dust; likewise, he sleeps at will upon the hands of men—marked by the ear—or within the lotus of the ear, or upon heaps of fragments of wool from sheep. He fits even into the smallest aperture, such as the holes in wood, clay, walls, and the like.

The meaning is that it resides within the hearts of living beings just as a magician or a yogi, through the power of substances such as gems and mantras, wanders everywhere at will; it is exactly like that. || 83 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the performance of the evening rites.
Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe;
it returned to the abode of Śyāma along with the rays of the sun. (84)
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Needle Transaction," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Activity of the Needle," in the Utapatti-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa.
The sixth day.
The seventy-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, after a long time, that rākṣasī named Karkaṭī did not attain satisfaction from all the human flesh [she had consumed]. (1)
Here, the remorse of Karkaṭī, who has become like a needle, is described;
as she remembers her former body, there is an extensive lamentation. (1)
"Even upon tasting the flesh of all kinds of men"—this is the ellipsis; [it refers to] the attainment of satisfaction, that is, the sense of having had enough. || 1 ||
It is said that she was satisfied by a single drop of blood on the very first day;
yet how can the needle of craving, so difficult to bear, ever find its end within?
They were satisfied, their hunger gone. || 2 ||
She reflected: "Alas, what misery! What has come upon me?
I am minute and my power is destroyed, yet even a morsel does not fit within me."
"With its power destroyed" means its capacity for devouring is blunted. "It does not fit"—the word "in the belly" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 3 ||
"O evil-minded one, where have those broad limbs of mine gone?
As vast as dark clouds, they have withered like leaves in the forest. (4)
Those are the previous ones; the limbs are the hands, feet, and so forth. || 4 ||
Indeed, even a morsel of savory meat, seasoned with fat, does not find room within this unfortunate woman, even in the slightest degree.
In this [state], when she has reached this condition: "perfumed with fat" means fragrant. Regarding the word *āsani*, it refers to that which enters into the mouth (*āsya*);

the suffix *śatṛ* is used here. According to the rule *paddan-*, because the inclusion of the term "et cetera" (*prabhṛti*) in the sūtra serves to indicate a class or type, the substitution of *āsanna* occurs. || 5 ||
I am sinking into the midst of mud, I fall upon the surface of the earth;
I am seized by the multitudes of people's feet, and I am defiled by impurity.
The sinking into the mire and so forth were previously described in the section on creation; [this occurs] by means of semen, the final constituent element.
Alas! I am ruined, I am without a protector, without consolation, and without refuge;
I sink from sorrow to sorrow, and from calamity to calamity as well. (7)
"Without consolation" means devoid of the comfort provided by friends, kinsmen, and others; "from distress" means from a life-threatening crisis. (7)
I have no friend, nor do I have a maidservant; I have no mother, nor do I have a father;
I have no kinsman, nor do I have servants; I have no brother, nor do I have a son.
To the question "Why is that so?", he says: "No. (8)
I have no body, no place, and no refuge whatsoever;
I do not dwell in one spot, but wander like a leaf in the forest.
It is the common support and that which is to be lived upon. || 9 ||
I stand at the forefront of calamities; I am settled in a most dreadful state.
I even desire non-existence, yet even that does not come to pass for me.
Death is non-existence. || 10 ||
With a deluded mind, I have abandoned my own body,
like a fool who, through a mistaken perception, lets the wish-fulfilling gem fall from his hand.
For the mind that falls into delusion first presents a calamity; afterwards, it expands into the form of a widespread misfortune. || 12 ||

And he says that this suffering is indeed produced by a mind possessed by delusion: "āpataddhi... etc. The mind, acting as the agent, first encounters delusion (*moha*) and thereby brings about a thousandfold suffering; thus, *āpad* refers to that state of corrupted intellect (*durbuddhi*).
The nominative case is used here by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). 12.
I am stationed among the smokes, and I am tossed about upon the path;
I am sent among the blades of grass—alas, my succession of sorrows!

Furthermore, at times I am threaded onto strings by certain people and, tied up, I remain suspended above the smoke. At other times, fallen upon the road, I am tossed about and trampled by donkeys, camels, and the like.
At other times, being placed among reeds such as *nalikā* and other grasses, I am sent inside and thrust within them. (13)
Constantly sending forth errands for others and always moving about on others' business,
I have fallen into extreme wretchedness and have become utterly dependent upon others.
I am deluded by this trivial thing, yet she too is of a piercing nature;
alas! for me, the unfortunate one, even misfortune is ill-fated.

She has delusion and longing for trivial objects of internal relish, such as passion and the like; yet even that delusion consists of piercing, having piercing alone as its fruit and not the fruit of tasting—this is because she possesses a tongueless mouth.
"The great Vetāla has arisen today while I was performing a rite for my peace;
thus, for me who had set out with pure intent, total ruin has come to pass. (16)

He says that this popular proverb, "the rising of a Vetāla during the rite for pacifying a Vetāla," has come true in his own case, by the words "he has arisen" (utthitaḥ), [referring to him] through his pure asceticism (avadātena tapasā). || 16 ||
Why was such a magnificent body abandoned by me, so dull-witted? Or rather, an inauspicious thought arises in such a way that it must inevitably lead to destruction.
For what reason was that former great body abandoned? Or rather, in whatever manner it must perish once the intellect (*buddhi*) exists; for such destruction is inevitable. || 17 ||
Who indeed will lift me up— me who am submerged within, as subtle as the body of an insect,
and covered by heaps of dust? [The reading "hāritāṃ pāṃsurāśibhiḥ" is more consistent with the commentary.]

"The Creator of the Universe did not worship Gaṇeśa when creating the needle; therefore, a man does not find a lost needle that has gone beyond the thread. Following this popular proverb, he says, "Me.
On the way, by chance, who will lift me up when I am submerged in the dust? Because of my invisibility, no one—
The meaning is that someone will rescue her; "hāritām" means caused to be lost. However, if the reading is "āvṛtām," the sense is clear.
In the awakened consciousness of those with detached minds, where do the ruined desires manifest?
They are like the blades of grass on a village path to those dwelling upon a mountain peak.

"Even though those of unrefined vision are unable to lift you up, nevertheless, yogis with discerning minds and subtle insight will rescue you. Anticipating this thought, he says: "Discerning... The words "those like me, whose hopes are destroyed" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 19 ||
While I remain in the ocean of ignorance, how could my spiritual rise ever occur?
For one who is blind and serves only the glow of a firefly, how can the light of the sun ever dawn? 20.
To the objection, "Surely you yourself must rescue your own self," he replies with the words "sthitāyāḥ" (of that which is situated). It illuminates;
thus it is "prakāśa. Its state is "prākāśya," which is the perception of the object. || 20 ||
Therefore, I do not know for how long I shall have to wallow in the pits of the earth’s chasms with my hopes destroyed, while calamities swirl around me.
One should roll about in such a way that one is surrounded by calamities—[the word *āpadā* here ends in the suffix *ṭā*]—in whatever action that may be. || 21 ||
When shall I become like a daughter of the great mountain Añjana, assuming the form of a pillar and remaining steadfast amidst the desolation of heaven and earth? (22)
In the event of failure, [the fault lies] in the slaughter of living beings and in the stubborn persistence in lifting the burden. || 22 ||
Her arms were like a mass of clouds, her eyes were fixed upon the lightning,
she was clothed in a garment of misty nets, and her hair reached high into the sky.
She whose eyes have taken the place of lightning-flashes;
she whose garment is measured by her towering tresses. (23)
With her peacock-feathered crest dancing at the sight of clouds resembling a pot-bellied one,
she is dark-complexioned with long, dangling breasts that seem to melt from the wind blowing over her body.
She by whom the peacocks were made to dance at the sight—that is, the observation—of clouds possessing the characteristic of a protruding belly;
she whose breasts were running—that is, trembling—due to the wind of her body, namely her breath. 24.
She veiled the solar disc with a mass of laughing ashes,
assuming a singular form intent upon devouring the Destroyer himself.

She who obstructs— that is, has the nature of covering— the solar orb, which is shrouded by masses of forest dust and showers of ash along with her laughter and the playful display of her loud, boisterous laughter; she who is like Death (Kṛtānta),
having undertaken and begun the very act of devouring all living beings— such was that one.
"Ākṛti" means one who possesses a terrifying form. || 25 ||
Resembling fire and a mortar, wearing a garland of suns,
she sports from mountain to mountain, placing her feet upon each peak.

Her two eyes, blazing like fire, were submerged as if in a mortar. According to the opinion of Bhāguri, the word *dṛśā* is grammatically correct by the rule *āpaṃ caiva halantānām*. The phrase "When shall I become [thus]?
is to be supplied everywhere. 26.
When will my great belly become as radiant as a deep pit for my teacher? When will my row of claws become as thick as a cloud at the end of the rainy season? 27.
"Nakharāḥ" means nails; "āvalī" means a row or series of them. || 27 ||
When shall I have a smile that causes the great Rākṣasas to flee? And when, intoxicated with joy, shall I dance in the vast forests to the music of my own buttocks?

A smile that causes the hearts of great and haughty demons to tremble; an *īṣaddhasita* (a slight laugh). "With the buttocks as musical instruments" means by playing upon the buttocks. "In the forest" (*araṇyānyām*) means in a great wilderness. [The suffix] *ṅīṣ* with the augment *ānuk* is applied according to the rule beginning with *indravaruṇa*. || 28 ||
When shall I incessantly fill my bloated belly with great jars of fat and liquor, and with heaps of dead flesh and bones? (29)
When shall I, having drunk the blood of the great world and become intoxicated, be joyful, haughty, and sealed by sleep? (30)
By me alone, in the fire of my penance, that foremost and radiant body was reduced to ashes,
just as gold accepts the state of being turned into ash.

Because it culminates in the fruit of suffering, his former radiant body was reduced to ashes in the fire of asceticism—which is worthy of contempt; this is the implied meaning. It is comparable to how gold might accept being turned into ashes or into the state of iron-dust, which destroys its own nature as gold. || 31 ||
Where is this body, resembling Mount Kālāñjana and filling the horizons?
And where is this state of being a eunuch, as fragile as a blade of grass and like the hoof-print of a cricket? 32.
The *prācikā* is a species of long-legged spider; its "hoof" (*khura*) refers to the tip of its foot, and it is equal to that. || 32 ||
The ignorant man quickly abandons even gold bracelets once he has obtained them;
likewise, out of greed, I have cast away my radiant body as soon as it was revealed by me.
Even upon finding a golden armlet covered in mud, one might discard it without reflection, mistaking it for mere earth. || 33 ||
"Alas, Mahodara, you who resemble a cave of mist on the Vindhya mountains!
Why do you not bring this to an end today, like a lion among elephants? (34)

Now, having addressed each of his limbs beginning with the belly, he laments, saying "Alas" and so forth: "O Mahodara, you who possess a resemblance to the caves of the Vindhya mountains shrouded in mist— alas, by this lion-like manifestation of yourself, you have brought an end to the elephant-like sorrows of separation from you."
Why do you not bring about my destruction? || 34 ||
Alas! Why do these two arms, their tips shattered by the moon-like nails, not strike the moon today with the intent of devouring it as a sacrificial cake? (35)

With their mountain peaks shattered by an excessive weight, how could those [tigers] not strike down the moon—which resembles the hare-bearer (the moon) and stands like a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) because it is fit for the enjoyment of the gods—using claws like those of the hare-bearer? This is an exaggeration (atiśayokti) regarding their extreme length. || 35 ||
Alas, O chest, as beautiful as the slopes of the king of mountains, now bereft of its jeweled necklace!
That dwelling-place of lions and other beasts, the forest of body-hair, has likewise been taken away today. (36)
O beautiful chest, even in the absence of necklaces of glass beads, you are as naturally magnificent as the slope of a great mountain;

for by you, just as lions and other beasts are supported, the forest of hair— wherein lies a swarm of lice (*yauka*) that has the habit of devouring lions, or which is like a lion-eater— has been maintained exactly as it was before.
The meaning is that it was not worn in such a manner today. || 36 ||
Alas, O eyes, which are ignited by the dry fuel of the dust of the black night;
why do you not adorn the quarters with a garland of flames from your gaze? 37.

Because it is colored by, or attached to, the "black night"—that is, the darkness consisting of the dust of the black fortnight—it is called *kṛṣṇarajanī-raja-andhakāra*. [The Lord acts] upon the shaking—that is, the kindling—of that dry fuel which has the form of such darkness. [The root] *ejṛ* means "to shine" (or "to move"), with the suffix *lyu*.
O my eyes, why do you not direct your vision (*dṛk*) toward the quarters of space by means of that flame-garland (*vakṣaṇā*)?
Of the two who adorn [it]. || 37 ||
"Alas, O bundle of aggregates! You are destroyed; you are forbidden from the surface of the earth.
You have been crushed by Time; you have been cast down upon the surface of a rock. (38)
"Prohibited" means avoided; that is to say, completely renounced. || 38 ||
Alas, O moon of a face, why do you not today [shine] upon me with your rays, you who are as charming as the lunar orb when the forest fire at the end of an aeon has been extinguished? (39)
Like the lunar orb, scorched and extinguished by the forest fire at the end of an aeon, it was captivating due to its dark hue.
Alas, alas! Where have those two large hands of mine gone today?
I have become like a great needle, struck by the hoof of a fly.
Shaken and moved even by the hooves and the tips of the feet of flies; the meaning is that she was exceedingly small. || 40 ||
Alas! [I grieve for you.
O you who are beautiful with excellent caves and fine *kanda* roots abounding in fierce *karañja* trees;
O you whose pure orb is like the broad hips of the most excellent Vindhya mountain! 41.
It was beautiful like a pit or a hollow that possessed a "kanda"—a bulbous root—meaning a very thick root of a tree. || 41 ||
Where is this form that fills the sky, and where is its body as thin as a needle? Where is its hollow interior as vast as the space between heaven and earth, and where is this needle-pointed mouth?
Where is its mouthful, heavy with a great burden of flesh, and where is its meal consisting of a single drop of water?
"Alas! This subtle drama, which brings about the destruction of my own self, has been composed by me alone. (42)
A mouthful or food that is abundant and vast due to many loads of meat. || 42 ||

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Lamentation of Kaṅka and Sūcikā," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* (Section on Origination) of the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Lamentation of the Needle," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having thus reflected, that Sūcī, whose speech was now manifest, spoke to Akampana.
Furthermore, for the sake of regaining that body, I shall quickly become an ascetic woman. || 1 ||

Furthermore, the fierce penance performed by Sūcī on the Himālaya mountains is described here, as well as the resolution reached by Śakra, who was filled with wonder, upon hearing the words of Nārada. (1)

Devoted to grief, Sūcī remained silent with no words forthcoming; having reflected upon her own body and so forth, as well as the manner about to be described—in such a way that she was entirely motionless and unwavering according to the previously mentioned method—she spoke of that very method, beginning with the word "again" (punar). || 1 ||
Having reflected thus, he withdrew the power of killing people that resided in his mind and went to that very peak of the Himalayas, where he remained established in asceticism.
He went for the sake of asceticism; he remained as he had previously remained. || 2 ||
She, whose nature consists of the vital breaths, entered that slain mind by means of the life-forces and perceived within herself the state of being indicated by that mind.

He explains how it moved with the words "he saw indeed. First, he saw his own state as a needle, imagined by the mind within himself. To the question of how movement is possible when the self is devoid of the power of action, even while seeing itself as a needle, he says: "the vital breath," etc. That which is the living-needle, consisting of the vital air (*prāṇa-vāta*), is that [which moves].
