Having entered the mind—which is indicated by the vital breaths that serve as its own limiting adjuncts—the meaning is that she entered the iron needle imagined by the mind. Alternatively, in the reading *hatamānavām*, the sense is that she entered that iron needle by which human beings (*mānavāḥ*) have been struck down. || 3 ||
Then, perceiving within himself that very mind-made state of being a sage,
he, whose body was composed of the vital breath, went to the peak of the Himalayas.
Then, within the living needle itself, it perceives the mental state of being an iron needle.

Thus, due to the mutual superimposition of identity between the iron and the living needle, this female crab—possessing a body non-different from the vital breath (prāṇavāta)—attains the power of action and went to the peak of the Himalayas. In the manner to be described, [she attained] the body of a vulture.
The meaning is "having entered. || 4 ||
There, in that place where a fierce forest fire raged, which was deserted by all living beings, harsh with the luster of massive boulders, and grey with dust; (5)

"Great" means vast; it refers to a massive stone slab made of sapphire, which is preeminent in its qualities. Its luster (ābhā) is like that very [sapphire]. Or, it may mean "rough with rays" (ābhābhiḥ), that is, with beams of light. || 5 ||
He stood upon a vast, grassless plain like one risen up,
like a blade of grass that had suddenly sprung up and then withered away.
It has arisen right there, as if it were a sprout.

Having resorted to her own consciousness as her single foot with the other half [of herself], she whose excellent thighs were thus supported began to perform austerities for that most subtle single-footed state.

By her, the barren earth was supported by a mere fraction— a half of a single foot that is as subtle as the tip of a needle; therefore, although it is impossible for a biped to exist as a "single-footed" being by abandoning one foot,
she [remains] within two imagined parts through her own consciousness and her own conceptualization.
Asceticism consists in standing on one foot, having abandoned half of the [usual] time for sitting, and taking the form of remaining in that one-footed posture. || 7 ||
With the soles of her delicate feet, she pressed down upon this earth crowded with dust; having restrained the entire triple world with effort, she stood with her face turned upward.

"Vasudhāreṇusaṃkaṭī" means one who, with the sharp-tipped surface of the sole of the foot, crushes even the dust of the earth as she treads upon it. From the word *saṃkaṭa*, the suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense of "one who performs that action," followed by the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the object. Due to the status of the original form (*sthānivadbhāva*) of the *aṅga*, there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening of the penultimate vowel. [She treads] upon the three-footed [mark].
Having withdrawn the gaze from the entire range of objects, so that it extends only to the three parts characterized by the front and both sides; || 8 ||
187. With their blackness, ferocity, sharpness, pervasive reach, gaping mouths, and wind-devouring breaths,
they laboriously set foot upon the ground crowded with dust, atoms, and stones.

Now, one might ask: "If her vision is directed upward and she is shielded from all sides, how is the stability of her feet established amidst the dense mass of dust particles and pebbles? To this, he says: "By virtue of being black.
Stability is established precisely because of her firmness; and her firmness is due to her being black, that is, by virtue of her being made of black iron.

The meaning is that [the power] is established through its ferocity, sharpness, and sharp-pointedness; by pervading all limbs with its mouth; by devouring the wind through swallowings; and by the effort characterized by its obstruction. || 9 ||
In the forest, she imitated the elephant that was agitated by the prospect of approaching the treasure,
which had risen up for the sake of a distant view and stood with its trunk curled over its tail, swaying in the wind.
That needle, agitated by hunger in the forest— therefore for those travelers in the forest, who approach closely because they fall [into danger] together—
the sight of them from afar is the "light" (āloka); for that purpose, she had raised her upper part, having lifted up her head with her tail.

On the tip of a blade of grass or a leaf at the threshing floor, she remained motionless even by the wind to avoid confusing travelers; thus, by implication, she imitated—that is, mocked—the *tṛṇajalūkā* (the "grass-leech"). In the reading *dūrālokāya*, it means for the sake of being seen from afar, so that her arrival (*āyam*) might be long (*āyatam*), that is, extended.
The meaning is "having arisen. || 10 ||
The ray of the sun, emerging from the aperture of her mouth,
became her companion— shining like a needle— and remained as her sole protector at her back.
Because even the sunlight passing through the eye of a needle has the shape of a needle, he imagines it to be her companion—this is expressed in the two verses beginning with "mukha... (verse 11).
People show affection even toward a lowly kinsman as if he were a living being; likewise, a needle, though made of iron, maintains the conduct of a female friend through its inherent purity.
A second ascetic woman, her own clear reflection, became her companion;
thus she was like a soiled needle left behind by her.
He imagines even the shadow of the needle to be her companion, saying "she became" (babhūva). It was just like the rays of light.
He states the distinction as follows: "as if by the needle. By that needle, that shadow-needle was made to follow behind, as if acting as a rear-guard. || 13 ||
Having emerged well through that needle with beautiful eyes slightly narrowed,
the virtuous one was subsequently embraced by her friend out of fear, as they were alone in their mutual conduct.
Regarding those three needles, he imagines that through their mutual interlocking at the base of their heads, they have acted with mutual conformity due to their mutual support—
expressed by the word "sūcyā" (by the needle). Subsequently, by means of the friend's protection, which was like a ray of the sun acting as a gateway, [she entered] well...

Having emerged, with eyes like beautiful banners (*supātākṣyā*), she performed a steady gazing (*dīdhītiṣupāta*) with knitting eyebrows (*kūṇitair-grathanaiḥ*) along with the needle of her shadow (*chāyāsūcyā*). The plurality [of the action] arises from counting it together with the knitting at the base of the shadow-needle.
Thus, strength—that is, firmness—was exerted in mutual conduct (*anyonyācārake*), meaning in the assistance of stability provided to one another.
The remainder [of the verse] is as follows: "sma kila. Thus, the meaning is that this practice is indeed virtuous. || 14 ||
When Sūcī cast her gaze upon them, even the trees, creepers, and other plants attained a state of mental composure;
seeing Sūcī, the great ascetic, who among them would not feel a longing for her? (15)

Thus, while Sūcī was performing her ascetic penance, even the trees, creepers, and other things within the range of her vision attained *mati*—that is, they acquired right understanding (*sadbuddhi*). In the reading "rati," the meaning is clear. || 15 ||
With their feet firmly planted, they caused the wind to consume this rising mental activity of theirs by means of the "bhaṃ" sounds emitted from their mouths.

This is a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*): the trees, creepers, and other plants seemed to feed the wind—which was scented by their own flowers and fruits—with this [speech] that had arisen like the steady movement of her own mind fixed upon the subject of asceticism.
The reason for imagining such feeding on her part is expressed by the phrase "with the *bhāṃ* sounds issuing from her mouth"; it was accompanied by sound.
The sense is that food is well known among commoners. || 16 ||
The future flowers of the gods, which were to be born long ago,
filled her mouth with their pollen.
He imagines that the needle-holes have been plugged by the trees and creepers through fate with the pollen of flowers—expressed by the word "prasūtāni" (those produced).

This refers to those which were previously produced, those yet to be produced, and those other than for the gods (*gīrvāṇa*); the meaning is "not intended for the deities. All those floral pollens belong to her.
The meaning is that they are to be given to the needle, or perhaps [something else]. || 17 ||
Then the dust, driven by the wind sent forth by Mahendra like a morsel of food,
was swallowed by her as it entered her mouth under the pretext of becoming a cloud.

By chance, through an opening in the wind-foundation (*vātavudhna*), there was an entry of the dust-particles; because of the obstacle created by Mahendra, those who had entered were unable to exit, and thus their various movements... [he does not imagine this] with the two verses beginning with "tataḥ."
Under the pretext of being cloudless, though her mouth remained open with its surface exposed,
she did not swallow those particles of dust due to her firm resolve;
for even the light achieve their purpose through internal strength.
The purpose (prayojana) is the task characterized by the warding off of obstacles to ascetic practice. || 19 ||
The wind did not drink even the pollen of flowers resting upon its surface; it experienced a wonder exceeding that of uprooting Mount Sumeru.
Though its surface was covered with mud, though it was filled with great waters, though it was shaken by mighty winds, and though it was scorched by forest fires; || 21 ||
He states that she was not disturbed even by other brahmins with the verse beginning "bhāśira" (21).
Though shattered by the falling of hailstones, though whirled about by the flickering of lightning, though agitated by the clouds, and though disturbed by their thunderous roars; || 22 ||
Even for thousands of years, that ascetic woman, her firm resolve fixed upon her mind,
did not waver even slightly, like one who is fast asleep on the tips of her feet.

Just as a flower [is not affected] by the fainting caused by poison and the like at the very moment of its piercing; "pādārtha" means the size of the tip of a needle, that is to say, even an atom's measure.
The word "tu" (but/also) has the sense of "api" (even/also). || 23 ||
When her outward movement had ceased and she had entered the fire at the proper place and time,
she contemplated her own self as truly conscious.

He states that as she was performing penance, through the destruction of her sins, knowledge arose in her mind after a long time preceded by inquiry, beginning with the words "nivṛttāyāḥ" (of her who had desisted). Contemplating that Truth which is pure consciousness, her very Self became the world of knowledge, consisting of the realization of its direct perception.
The meaning is that it arose. || 24 ||
The light of knowledge arose, which perceives both the higher and the lower;
it became pure, exceedingly radiant, all-pervading, and the supreme purifier.
Once her evil deeds were exhausted through asceticism, she herself became one who had known what was to be known by that very intellect; she was like a needle that indicated her own happiness. (26)
Thus, for thousands of years, she performed severe austerity,
looking upward and causing distress to the seven worlds and their seven great inhabitants.
For seven thousand years, she performed a penance that caused great torment to the fourteen great worlds, beginning with Bhūr; she was *unmukhī*, meaning with her face turned upward. || 27 ||
Indeed, by her asceticism, which was as terrible as the fire at the end of an aeon, that great mountain became ablaze;
because of it, the entire world seemed to burn.
Then Vāsava asked Nārada, "Whose ascetic power has thus overwhelmed the world? and he related that matter to him.
That is the needle-penance (sūcītapas). || 29 ||
For seven thousand years, this long-suffering woman held a needle;
she possesses a body of great wisdom, and by her, this world is set ablaze.
The nāgas hiss, the mountains tremble, and the celestial beings, the oceans, and the clouds fall;
the quarters of the sky, together with the sun, go to desiccation and become soiled.
O Lord of the Gods, it was as if the needle had reached its exhaustion through ascetic penance.
The oceans and the clouds go to desiccation. || 31 ||
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Power of the Needle-like Penance," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Power of Sūcī’s Austerity," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having heard the entire account of Karkaṭī’s bitter experience, Vāsava [said]:
His curiosity aroused once again, he questioned Nārada.
In this [chapter], the expansion of experience is described again by means of the "needle of the living soul" (jīvasūcī);
thereafter follows the search for the wind everywhere, impelled by Śakra.
Having heard the account of Karkaṭī’s harsh and unpleasant ascetic practice, he became filled with curiosity upon hearing the manner in which she sustained her life by means of a needle. || 1 ||
Śakra said: O Sage, having acquired that state of being a Piśāca with the needle-like body through ascetic penance, what riches were enjoyed by that Karkaṭī and Himamarkaṭī?

Like a needle, it is round; like a piśāca spirit, its state as a living soul is invisible; like a female monkey, it is fickle due to trivial enjoyments, having attained a dull intellect as if from contact with frost, just like a karkaṭī fruit. || 2 ||
Śrī Nārada said: O Śakra, when Jīvasūcī had become a Piśāca,
her support was a slender iron needle.
The support is the basis of equal reliance. || 3 ||
Having abandoned that focal point, she— seated upon a chariot of wind in the sky—
entered the body by way of the path of the vital breath.
Once, having abandoned her support on that iron needle, she mounted a chariot of that same form—the wind moving through the sky, the air that travels in the firmament. || 4 ||
Like a bird hidden within the hollows of all those whose souls are defiled— of their entrails, sinews, fat, flesh, and blood— it dwells inside.

By means of that "life-needle" (jīvasūcī), which has a defiled nature, having entered through the opening of mantras, tantras, and so forth belonging to sinners, it means that it remains hidden within the body for a long time, staying concealed inside. || 5 ||
In whichever channel the wind of space enters,
there a piercing pain is produced, as intense as that caused by a large banyan tree.

In the *nāḍī*, that is, in the vessel; the external air which is the locus of disease measures [it], becoming equal to it. That [air] flows in such a manner. There, in that *nāḍī*, there is *śūla*, a pain known as *śūla*.
Just as, for example, a Śaiva *śūla* was placed at the tip of the vessels of the large Nyagrodha tree belonging to the venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
In the same way, that [attachment] is fixed. || 6 ||
With those very bodies and senses, they likewise consumed many other human flesh meals as well as their accustomed foods.
Through the bodies and sense organs of those living beings, foods appropriate for those beings were consumed.
She was asleep, her face slightly turned away by the young girl who was charmingly innocent, while the decorative leaf-patterns drawn upon her cheeks were fixed upon the surface of her lover’s chest.
By that lovely young girl— whose garlands and abundant wreaths were crushed and twisted by the embrace of her lover,
meaning she had attained that state— and whose cheeks bore imprinted leaf-patterns (patra) transferred, sewn, or created upon the surface of her lover’s chest; and thus:
The meaning is that even the suffering of an innocent child has indeed been experienced [by her]. || 8 ||
She wandered through the forest paths, free from sorrow, where flocks of birds flew about and rows of lotuses— twice as abundant as the blossoms on the clusters of wish-fulfilling trees— abounded.

By means of the female bird who had entered the body of the male bird, [he wandered] through the forest avenues—that is, through rows of lotuses possessing a fragrance twice as intense as that of the finest flowers of the *kalpavṛkṣa* trees—[and] through the series of lotuses pervading the quarters. || 9 ||
In the forests of the immortals and the *aila* spirits, he sported with the bee-like playfulness of the dark night, drinking the liquor of drops of nectar from the yellow, fragrant *mandāra* flowers.
The words "having entered the *alī* [line]" are to be understood as the ellipsis. || 10 ||
The greedy old woman swallowed the chewed limbs of corpses,
just as a swift mare in battle devours the limbs of heroes with the edge of her sword.
By the vulture—having entered the body of a vulture—the limbs of corpses were made to fall into pits that had been dug;
[this was done] by the edge of a sword (*khaḍgapṛṣṭhyā*), that is, by the blade of a sword. If the reading is *khaḍgayaṣṭyā* (by a sword-staff), the meaning is clear. || 11 ||
Like streaks of wind in all directions, they flew up and down through the channels of the sheaths of all limbs, as if through the pathways of the sky filled with masses of glass.
In the pathways of the sky, blue as a mass of glass.
Just as the vibrations of the vital breaths manifest within the heart of the Virāj-Ātman, so too does she flash forth within every individual body as its dwelling place.
Just as the vibrations of the collective vital breath (prāṇavāta) manifest spontaneously, so too has this [text] been manifested. 13.
Likewise, the powers of consciousness shine within the bodies of all living beings,
just as the light of a lamp illuminates its own house through its flame.
Now, by what manifestation was she engaged in worldly activity within each house-like body?

To this he says—[the reading is "tam āha"]—"sarvaprāṇi... and so forth. Just as the vital breaths (*prāṇavāta*) vibrate within the bodies of all living beings, so too do the powers of consciousness (*cicchakti*) shine forth. The plural number is used due to the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The meaning is that, by virtue of being illumined by the radiance of such power of consciousness—just as a housewife is illumined by the light of a lamp—he conducted his affairs as if in his own home. || 14 ||
It was spread within the bloods as if by the power of fluidity in waters;
it surged within the bellies as if by the motion of whirlpools in oceans.

He tasted the fragrance within his own limbs, as if the nectar of power had been drunk internally by Śauri while he slept upon his pure coils of serpent-fat, as it were, upon the remaining parts of his body.
By the yellow power, by the drinking power. || 16 ||
The heart-essences of trees, shrubs, medicinal herbs, and so forth—enjoyed by the beauty of the wind, unrefined, and rendered into food through destruction; (p. 309) 17.

Those which invigorate the heart and produce strength, health, and so forth are called *hṛdaujāni*, such as extracts of the *rasana* plant and others. By means of the splendor of the wind—that is, in the form of air—they are non-white, meaning they possess colors other than white. || 17 ||
Then, thinking "May I become a needle made of life," she was joined with the stationary;
thus she became an ascetic woman, a needle, conscious, purifying, and white.
It is she herself who, through her own resolve and steadfastness in asceticism, has become this most purifying female ascetic; thus he says:
"By her, who was invisible here, moving with the fierce speed of the wind, flowing like a needle of iron in the form of the wind, and obstructing the quarters of the sky. (19)
By means of an iron needle, moving and traveling with the speed of the wind due to its nature as air. || 19 ||
Drinking, eating, sporting, giving, causing to give, and taking—dancing, singing, and dwelling—all these have been performed by infinite embodied living beings. (20)
Invisible, bodiless, with a body of mind and wind,
and having the form of space— there is nothing that was not accomplished by her.
Keeping in mind the ultimate nature of the life-needle (jīvasūcī), he says: "by the invisible one.
The sense is that the entire universe was created by her, who possesses the collective and individual minds, vital airs, and bodies. || 21 ||
By this [mind], which has been moved from its natural state by the taste of the flavor of power and intoxication,
it has reared up like a female elephant that has taken hold of the tethering post of Time.

If she possesses such power, why were all beings not destroyed by her while she was in the form of a needle? To this he replies: "By her power... Even though she possessed that power, she remained intoxicated solely by the relish of tasting the blood and other fluids of a few living creatures; thus, she relied upon the tethering post—the very time characterized by the destiny of the life-span of those beings.
The meaning is that he leaped about—that is, wandered—only within small spaces, like a female elephant. || 22 ||
In the rivers, whose currents cause distress with their force, the intoxicated [elephant] acted like a sea-monster, his body shaken by the many surging waves.
When the rivers seen in the form of bodies— meaning the rivers perceived directly— are present, it is the impairment of living beings' bodies that causes their distress.
Unable to swallow the fat and flesh within her heart, she surely wept like one whose mind is distressed by the loss of wealth, a relative, or an aged kinsman.

In the heart—that is, in one's own mind—it is like the weeping of the wealthy, the elderly, and the sick due to their intellect [or lack thereof], such as when one is unable to eat because of wealth. || 24 ||
The goat, camel, deer, elephant, horse, lion, tiger, and others performed a dance, while on their limbs bracelets and armlets moved about like a female dancer long upon the stage. 25.

Just as a dancer’s limbs are made to dance by bracelets, armlets, and so forth, so too have even camels, buffaloes, and other animals been made to dance by her while she was pressing upon them; such is the meaning. || 25 ||
And by means of that single, weak line of fragrance produced within her, she perceived the oneness of the winds both outside and inside. || 26 ||
[She is] outside in the masses of wind; inside, in the vital breaths. "By the weak one" means by that which is subject to the movement of the winds.
(26) Destroyed by mantras, medicinal herbs, asceticism, charity, worship of the gods, and so forth;
she is afflicted externally like the high waves of mountains and rivers. (27)
"Outside," that is, in the vicinity nearby; "fled," meaning she has run away. || 27 ||
Like the light of a lamp whose course is unknown, it quickly dissolves through its movement;
like [a drop] on an iron needle, O Mother, it finds rest there.
By means of his power of movement, he possesses the ability to become invisible; he merges into an iron needle. Nirvṛti is the bliss of rest. || 28 ||
Everyone seeks a basis in accordance with their own latent tendencies;
the very nature of the ogress was made her basis by means of the needle. (29)
Even after wandering through all directions, a dull-witted person returns in times of distress to his own home, just as a living needle returns to its iron needle-case.
Striving thus as she dwelt throughout the ten directions,
she attained mental satisfaction, but never physical.
For properties exist here only when there is a substratum, not when it is absent;
indeed, that [property] which belongs to one who possesses a body is satisfied by that [body]. (32)
Then, upon remembering her former body,
she became distressed at heart, longing for the happiness of a full belly.
She was desirous of that happiness of satisfaction which arises from a full belly. || 33 ||
Then, reflecting thus, "I shall perform extensive austerity for the sake of my former body," he determined a place for penance along with his own self.
Like a female bird entering its nest, she entered the heart of that youth, who was like a vulture soaring in the sky, through the path of the vital breath (prāṇa-māruta).
This refers to the vulture that moves through the sky. That was the "living needle. By what path did it enter? He says:
"By the vital breath" (*prāṇa*). "Space" (*kha*) refers to the opening of the nest. "Crawling in a hole" (*bileśayā*) means lying within the hollow of the nest. || 35 ||
A certain vulture, having resorted to this very state of being indicated by its own nature, and being intensely impelled by the needle, set his mind upon acting. (36)

Relying on the state of being indicated by a needle within itself—that is, the condition of being signaled by a needle located inside it—a certain vulture previously mentioned set its mind upon performing the action desired by the needle that had entered it. (36)
Taking the needle, that vulture went to the mountain he had envisioned; driven by the point of the needle within him like a cloud by the wind, he departed. (37)
A needle means an iron needle. When the time for cessation has arrived at the end of the Piśācī who has entered within the needle... || 37 ||
There, in that desolate great forest, he established her in a state free from all mental constructs, just as a yogi establishes his consciousness in the ground of being.
Volition is a modification of the intellect. || 38 ||
By that very same foot-tip, the goddess was instantly and firmly established by the vulture upon the mountain peak, as if she were being set down there.
The meaning is that the iron needle, having been placed upon the mountain peak by the vulture, became as firmly established as a statue of a deity. || 39 ||
With one foot placed upon a small particle of dust resting on the peak of a mountain, he stood with his neck upraised like a peacock atop a mountain summit.

A mere speck of dust is the house; for the atom situated therein, [the world] is on its head by means of a single, most subtle atom—the foot or the tip. It is like fire with its crest; however, in the reading "udgrīvaṃ śikhīva," it is like a peacock with its neck upraised. || 40 ||
The reading "ujjihvaṃ śikhīva" is superior, as it conforms to the commentary which explains it as "like a cresting fire" (śikhī agniriva).
Seeing the life-needle that had been raised and fixed by the vulture, Jīvasūcikā began to emerge from the body of the bird in order to go outside.
With her consciousness turned upward, the needle emerged from the body of the bird,
like a trail of fragrance rising from the wind toward the tip of the nostril.
She whose consciousness—her intellect—is turned outward and eager for departure. || 42 ||
The vulture went to his own place, like a porter who has laid down his burden;
he became free from inner agitation, as if his disease had been cured. || 43 ||
Like a person whose disease has been cured, he is undisturbed and established in his own nature. || 43 ||
Therefore, she has prepared a firm and well-suited support for her penance with that needle;
indeed, the proper application of resources shines forth.
Therefore, for the reason that will be stated: "sūcī" means an iron needle; by that "jīvasūcī" (the needle of the living soul). || 44 ||
"For indeed, actions of that which is formless cannot be accomplished without a support.
Thinking thus, she remained engaged in asceticism, relying solely upon a physical support.
Like a whirlwind encircling a streak of fragrance, Jīvasūcī enveloped the iron needle Piśācī on all sides, as one might wrap a *śiṃśapā* tree.
She encircled [it], having pervaded it. || 46 ||
From that time forward, O Śakra, this long-suffering needle remained in the vast forest for many groups of years.
O you who are skilled in what must be done, exert yourself for the sake of her boon;
for that penance of hers, accumulated over a long time, is indeed sufficient to burn away the world.
For the sake of an excellent boon, [it is] for the purpose of deceiving with a worthless boon. || 48 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having heard this from Nārada, Śakra, while observing Sūcī,
then dispatched Māruta to the ten quarters of the horizon.
Then, with his mind intent on meeting the Maruts, he went to see her;
having ascended the path of the sky, he proceeded with great haste.

The Maruts went toward the quarters to behold that consciousness characterized by divine vision; the meaning is that they deliberated upon going to the quarters with their divine sight. "Having ascended the path of the sky, he moved upon the earth"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 50 ||
That consciousness of his, being all-pervasive,
suddenly beheld it in just half a moment, like a supreme flame, without any obstacle.

"Swift" means possessing haste. "By half," that is, by a single portion, she is "all-pervading," being intent on surveying all directions, like the supreme and most excellent radiance, the light of Brahman (*brahmajyotis*). "Without obstacle" means without impediment. || 51 ||
Then [he saw] the vast land fixed upon the earth as far as the seven oceans,
with the Lokāloka mountain as its girdle, resembling a jewel.

He elaborates on what was already stated—that he saw everything—beginning with the words "of the earth" (bhūmeḥ) and so forth. "Vipulasthalīm" means a vast expanse of golden land devoid of living beings. Here, the sequence of the continents and oceans should be understood either according to the previously mentioned order or according to the order specific to this context, as it occurs within the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 52 ||
The circle of Puṣkara-dvīpa, surrounded by the ocean of sweet water and containing the groups of quarters with their caves, lies within that circle of mountain ranges.
By the word "koṭara," the regions situated at the junctions of mountains are meant. || 53 ||
The surrounding ocean of wine, inhabited by aquatic creatures, forms a ring;
its center is the Gomedadvīpa region, which contains a multitude of territories.
It was inhabited and resorted to by those creatures that move in water; by this, it is understood that the living beings there possessed the capacity to move both in water and on land. || 54 ||
It has moats consisting of oceans of sugarcane juice and water, is peaceful, and is situated amidst a multitude of mountains;
it is the sacred seat (pīṭha) of the excellence of Krauñcadvīpa, tranquil and possessing a succession of mountains.
It is peaceful and free from affliction. || 55 ||
The circle of the Milk Ocean with its central Nāyaka,
and the circle of the island named Śveta, together with the distinct divisions of the elements (or beings). || 56 ||

That [world] has the Ocean of Milk itself as its bracelet inlaid with pearls; it is joined by Viṣṇu, the leader of the three worlds, who resides in its center; and its divisions are the distinctions between its intermediate sections. 56.
Beyond that is the city and palace situated within a girdle of clarified butter (ghṛtoda),
which is encompassed by the boundary of Kuśadvīpa and contains the hollows of great mountains.
The belly of Śākadvīpa was filled with oceans of curds reaching up to its waist,
while its interior regions were filled with the objects of the semi-vowels (antastha).
He whose front belly is covered by a garment that is both dark (sānta) and adorned with a border (sāvadhi), [perceived] by the tongue.
[He saw] Jambūdvīpa, surrounded by the ocean of salt water, containing within it the various regions and the great Mount Meru, crowded with the principal mountain ranges.
By the word "region" (viṣaya), the people residing therein are indicated. || 59 ||
At the very beginning, there is the sensation of wind falling from the masses of wind;
by this sequence, at the end, it likewise spreads forth directly through that same [wind].

The consciousness of the vital breath (vāyu), previously described, has fallen—that is, it has descended. By means of this sequence of the descent of one's own consciousness, the vital breath has issued forth or descended. || 60 ||
Vāyu, having clearly surveyed and gazed upon Jambūdvīpa,
reached that peak of the Himavat where the ascetic woman Sūcī resided.
The wind reached that vast forest where the ascetic woman remained like a needle, due to the karmic actions of living beings and their movements. || 61 ||
Upon the great and formidable summit of the peak,
he reached that vast forest region which was like a second expanse of space, devoid of the activities of living beings.
Because of its proximity to the sun, it was devoid of any growth of grass and was spread out as if consisting entirely of dust, like the structure of worldly existence.

"Because of its proximity"—by this, the extreme height of the peak is understood. "Consisting of dust" (rajomayīm) means abounding in particles, as well as being a transformation of the quality of rajas (the active quality). In this way, the other adjectives as well should be understood as being common to both the great forest (araṇyānī) and the structure of saṃsāra. || 63 ||
It had attained the state of an ocean to be filled by the rivers of a mirage;
it possessed the appearance of a river of mirages resembling the rainbow of Indra.
It was immeasurable, infinite, and boundless, watched over even by the world-protectors;
it consisted solely of a swirling mass of dust carried along by the movement of the wind.

A forest (araṇyānī) characterized by such attributes as: one in which the boundaries, intermediate regions, and divisions are immeasurable—meaning they are not determined by limit—and infinite; and one whose two sides have earrings formed by the very layers of dust flowing through the movement of the wind in the form of a whirlwind. By these and other such qualifiers, [the forest is described].
She is figuratively described as the playful mistress of the sky. || 65 ||
Smeared with the saffron of the sun’s rays and anointed with the sandalwood paste of the moon’s light,
she was like a wanton woman of the sky, quenching her thirst with the hissing sound of the wind.
The whistling sound, which manifests the pleasure of embracing her beloved, causes her—who is characterized by that habit—to drink it, that is, to hear it.

189) Having wandered all around the surface of the earth— which rests upon a single portion of the seven islands and oceans that have been completely covered— the wind has become worn out by its long journey.

Having reached that formidable mountain region which seemed as if clinging to the edge of the sky, he— possessing a massive body that filled the infinite reaches of the quarters— rested there, appearing like a great bee.

That wind, possessing a vast body that fills and pervades the infinite quarters of space, having moved all around the pedestal characterized by the earth— the support for that portion [of the body] which is properly covered and pervaded above by the seven islands together with their oceans as its seal and mark— [remains there].

Worn out and exhausted by the long journey, having reached that formidable mountain plateau which seemed as if it were clinging to the body of the sky—whose form resembles a bee—he rested; that is to say, he attained repose. || 67 ||

Thus ends the seventy-third canto, titled "The Description of the Needle-like Austerities," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (sage-authored) tradition.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Needle-Penance," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: There, upon that ground in that great forest, of that mountain with its upward-pointing peaks...
He beheld the middle needle standing upright like a crest of flame. || 1 ||
Having seen that female ascetic Sūcī, the departure of Vāyu to the presence of Śakra, the prayer of Dhātṛ for the sake of a boon, and the knowledge of Sūcī are described. (1)

In that land which was a great forest (*mahāvanī*)—that is, a vast wilderness (*araṇyānī*) as previously described—the word *mahāvanī* takes its short vowel according to the rule *go-striyo-r-upasarjanasya*. It was like the central peak of a mountain horn. || 1 ||
She was performing penance on one leg, withering away from the heat of her own head;
constantly fasting, the skin of her belly had become shriveled and solidified.

In the reading "sa tataḥ," the connection is with the preceding phrase "sa tato dadarśa" (he then saw). [He saw her] as if her abdominal skin were shriveled into a single mass; for it is impossible for the skin of the abdomen to be pierced by a needle. || 2 ||
Having grasped the sunlight and the breeze as if with her mouth once blossomed wide, she now lets them go;
thus she does not cease from filling my heart.

[He offered] the heat and the winds. In the rule *temayāvekavacanasya*, because of the governing heading *apādādau* ("not at the beginning of a quarter-verse"), the substitution of *me* for *mayā* at the beginning of a quarter-verse is Vedic (*chāndasa*). || 3 ||
She was withered by the rays of the fierce sun and worn out by the forest winds;
yet she did not move from her place, as if bathed by the beams of the moon.
Previously, with her head covered and resting upon a single mote of dust,
she spoke of having achieved her purpose, offering no place for another.

By not allowing even a particle of dust—another member of the same class as itself—to enter upon the tip of its needle, it seems to declare, through that very mark, that its purpose has been fulfilled; thus it appears to be providing inferential proof. || 5 ||
Having given away the very forests as wealth, she was like one whose topknot has been grown for a long time,
with the coil of her matted locks of vital breaths established upon her head.

Having given her own wealth— the substance consisting of her trees, shrubs, deer, and other creatures— to other forests by means of the aforementioned forest-dweller (*araṇyānī*), she produced a crest (*śikhā*) that stood like a topknot (*cūḍā*), born through long austerity in the form of a needle; and from that, through the ripening of yoga, she established the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) upon her head.

The line of the matted locks is described as if it were a fold or a winding. Because of its fineness at the commencement of her asceticism, there is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) identifying it with the crest of a forest thicket. However, it should be understood that because the splendor of her penance has become dense and massed over time, there is a poetic fancy identifying it as the winding of her matted locks. The first word "iva" [indicates this].
It is an indicator of poetic fancy (utprekṣā); the other two, however, have the meaning of a fancied object of comparison (autprekṣikopamāna).
Beholding that needle, Pavana, his mind overwhelmed with wonder,
bowed down and gazed upon it for a long time, as if he had arrived in a state of extreme fear.
The word "having prostrated" (praṇamya) is used to indicate that those who know Brahman are to be revered even by the gods; "bhītabhītaḥ" means as if extremely terrified. || 7 ||
Overwhelmed by her mass of splendor, he was unable to ask, "O great ascetic Sūcī, for what purpose are you performing this penance? (8)
Thus, the construction [of the sentence] is: "he was not able to ask. || 8 ||
"O, how wonderful is the great penance of the Blessed One Mahāsūcī!"—meditating thus alone, Māruta went into the sky. || 9 ||
Having leaped across the path of the clouds, having passed beyond the layers of wind, having placed the hosts of perfected beings beneath him, and having reached the path of the sun; || 10 ||
Having ascended from the celestial palaces, he reached the interior of Indra’s city;
there, Purandara embraced him who possessed the merit of beholding the needle.
From the celestial palaces and from the worlds of the preeminent constellations of the Vaimānika gods, merit was rendered pure by the sight of the needle. || 11 ||
And when questioned, he said to Indra, the lord of the hosts of Sahadevas who dwells in that abode, "I have seen everything."
Vāyu said:
In Jambūdvīpa there is a lord of mountains named Himavat, exceedingly lofty,
whose son-in-law is the Blessed One, the wearer of the crescent moon himself.
To the north of that, on the back of Mahāśṛṅga, there stands a most beautiful ascetic woman named Sūcī, who performs severe penance.
She is of supreme form and possesses great splendor.
Enough has been said here by way of illustration; for the sake of pacifying hunger and other ailments such as wind, she filled her own abdominal cavity and thereby warded them off. (15)
"Having made into a mass" means having achieved the state of a solid lump of iron; because the formation of a compound was not intended, the suffix *lyap* is not used. 15.

Today, her mouth— which was previously closed for the sake of subtle objects that were peaceful— has been opened by a particle of passion (rajoṇu) and covered [with saliva] to ward off the cold wind of hunger.

By her, for the sake of warding off cold winds, hunger, and thirst, the mouth—its contraction stilled, its narrowing prevented, and its aperture made minute—was opened; yet it remained covered and closed over by a particle of dust. || 16 ||
O God, by means of his intense asceticism, he abandoned his lunar form and assumed a fiery form, thereby becoming difficult to approach.
The expression "tuhinākara" (the moon) is a designation emphasizing its essential nature.

The sense is that iron, assuming the form of fire because the rocks have been melted by the heat of the fire and thus attained the state of being a mass of glowing iron, takes on the appearance of fire while abandoning its state as the moon (tuhinākara) under oath. Thus, the Himavat has become difficult to approach.
This is the remainder. However, if the reading is "ago gṛhṇan," it is clear. || 17 ||
Therefore, arise quickly; let us all go to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Know that this very great asceticism was undertaken for the sake of obtaining boons, yet it has resulted in misfortune.
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "it was neglected for the sake of what is harmful. || 18 ||
Thus impelled by Vāyu, Śakra, together with the hosts of gods,
went to the world of Brahmā and petitioned that omnipresent Lord.
"I shall go to the peak of the Himalayas to give you a needle," Brahmā promised; having said this, Śakra returned to heaven.
After this much time, she became exceedingly purifying,
scorching the abodes of the immortals with the heat of her own ascetic penance.
By this much, [a period] measuring seven thousand years. || 21 ||
By means of her own clear shadow, which was like a ray of the sun situated within the cavity of the mouth,
she— standing amidst the unfolding [lotuses] and directed toward the end— was beheld.

Intending to describe that very penance until the end of creation, he says "mukha... and so forth: while the revolving penance was expanding, she remained standing there; the needle itself, impelled by its own shadow alone, reached its conclusion—the limit of time known through her resolve, as ordained.

[The reading is: "She was observed. For what reason? By means of a gaze characterized by the rays of the sun—that is, by the light—situated within the opening of the mouth which had been opened and extended. || 22 ||
Mount Meru has been surpassed in stability by the needle in the form of the silk garment;
even as it grows, it does not sink, being thus released on the first and last days.
If that is so, why is its appearance [of the sun] during the two twilights and at night abandoned? To this he says:

"Kauśeya... etc. By means of a needle whose form is as minute as a silk thread (*kauśeya-tantu*) and which is light, Mount Meru—having been surpassed by its quality of stability—is suggested through a rhetorical question (*kāku*) as not even sinking into the ocean out of shame.

Thus, with this intention, as if to see it, having increased its length by expanding during the first and last parts of the day, it is "freed" from seeing it—that is to say, it has ceased [from that activity]. || 23 ||
At midday, as if out of fear of the heat, she entered within the wind;
at other times, seeing her from afar, she gazed upon her with reverence.

To the question, "Why then was she hidden at the base at midday?", he replies with the verse beginning "At midday. It is understood that [she] was released by one entering the "needle's belly"—the internal space or opening for the needle-like vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—out of "gravity," meaning out of respect for her. || 24 ||
She gazes upon him; from the caustic liquid, he sinks into her body.
In times of distress, a person indeed forgets respect and hospitality.

That is the shadow; that is the needle. From "caustic" (kṣārāt) means from the sharp; from "heat" (tāpāt) means from the sun's glare. How then is there the abandonment of heaviness at midday? To this he says: "in a narrow space" (saṃkaṭe). || 25 ||
The needle of shadow, the needle of asceticism, and the self as the third—this triangle, purified by austerity, has been made equal to Vārāṇasī. || 26 ||

And that which is the iron needle (*lohasūcī*)—together with that third [element], the triangle consisting of the space between their mutual interlacing was made equal to Vārāṇasī, which is situated in the interval of the interlacing of Varaṇā and Gaṅgā; this is the meaning. || 26 ||
By that triangular path, which had a moat of three colors, even the winds and the dust particles that went there attained supreme liberation. || 27 ||
Being dry, she is formless; being dark and white, she possesses the characteristics of a moat with a stream of three-colored needles.
She possesses liberation as her purpose—the liberation of those people with whom she is in contact—or she possesses sanctity characterized by freedom from defects.

Having understood the supreme cause from the beginning, and having personally reflected upon the consciousness that is devoid of thought, [the Self] arises according to its own internal mental construction as the One—
For here, O Raghava, there is no other supreme teacher than you.

She became one who had directly realized and personally experienced Brahman, the supreme cause; she did so by herself investigating the conscious awareness that is the inner self (pratyagātman). To the question, "Who then was her teacher? he says:
"Her own. This refers to the mental contemplation—the investigation through reasoning—of her own [self].

The realization of one's own self, the following of that [realization], and the adherence to that alone is the primary Guru; the meaning is that any other Guru is not primary. Although the Śruti says, "A man who has a teacher knows," nevertheless, it is also stated: "But it is seen by those of subtle vision with a sharp and subtle intellect."
The sense is that, in accordance with another scriptural passage, [the Lord] follows the very intelligence of the disciple. || 28 ||
Thus ends the seventy-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the Ripening of the Penance of Sūcī," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Seers.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ripening of Sūcī’s Austerities," in the Utapatti-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa.
The seventy-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, after a thousand years, the Grandfather (Brahmā) arrived there.
"O daughter, choose a boon," he proclaimed from the expanse of the sky.
Even though the Creator was pleased, the needle remained silent due to its awakening;
nevertheless, it is celebrated for the manifestation of a body by virtue of the boon from the Maker.
Then, after awakening, [it occurred] after a thousand years. || 1 ||
Because she lacked the organs of action, Sūcī possessed only the subtle constituents of the living soul;
she said nothing at all to him, but merely reflected within herself.

Because of the absence of the organs of action, there is also the absence of the organ of speech; and the absence of the organs of action in her [the subtle body] is due to its needle-like nature and because it is sublated by awakening. || 2 ||
I am fulfilled and my doubts have vanished; what need have I for a boon?
I am at peace, I am extinguished, and I abide in solitary bliss. (3)
He clearly states the very manner of his reflection with the words beginning "pūrṇa" (verse 3).
Everything that was to be known has been known; the web of doubt has been stilled; one's own discernment has blossomed—what further need is there for anything else? (4)
Everything is known, because through the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all. || 4 ||
Just as I am situated here, so indeed shall I remain;
having abandoned the very notion of truth and untruth, what need have I for anything else? (5)
Truth is of the nature of the ultimate reality (paramārtha). Having abandoned that very essence of truth, what is the use of anything else—that is to say, nothing at all—is the meaning. || 5 ||
For so long a time I have been joined with lack of discernment,
like a young girl possessed by a vetāla arisen from her own imagination.
Now, having become tranquil through my own inquiry, what purpose could there be for me in objects acquired, whether desired or undesired? (7)
This is non-discrimination. By "kalitaiḥ" is meant "attained. || 7 ||
Thus, the Blessed One remained there, observing that needle which was fixed in its resolve, devoid of the organs of action, and standing in silence, while he himself maintained his self-restraint.
Accompanied by *niyati*—the divine will that determines the necessity of the fruits of actions—that Grandfather [Brahmā] was present. || 8 ||
Then Brahmā, his mind serene, spoke again to her who was free from passion:
"O daughter, choose a boon; remain upon the surface of the earth for some time."
In the view that *kiṃcit* is a grammatical refinement (*pada-saṃskāra*) of the word, it is neuter as a general term.
"After enjoying worldly pleasures, you shall thereafter go to the supreme state;
such is the certainty of destiny, whose nature is irreversible. (10)

O most excellent one, may this resolve of yours become fruitful through this penance, for the previously mentioned destiny— which is of an immutable nature and impossible even for those like us to avert—
remains fixed. O Rākṣasī of the snowy forest, become fat once again upon the mountain!
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "by this ripened asceticism"; "pīnā" means having a fully developed body. || 11 ||
"By that body in the form of a cloud with which you were previously separated, O daughter, just as a seed attains the state of a tree through its growth into a great tree. (12)

Just as the generic nature of a tree, which is latent within the seed, is not separated from the individual tree when it has grown large, so too you shall attain union with that very body with which you were separated—this is the connection with the subsequent verse. || 12 ||
And you shall attain yoga once more, existing within the body in the form of a seed;
by the sprinkling of that very essence, you will abide like a sprout upon a creeper.
Anticipating the objection, "How can that which has perished arise again?", he says: "Existing internally in the form of a seed.
The sense is that she is not destroyed; rather, she is merely dissolved in the state of a seed, like [a thread] within a needle. || 13 ||
Because you have known all that is to be known, you shall not cause any affliction in the world;
pure within and vibrant, like a circle of autumn clouds.
He says "bādhām" [verse 14] regarding what use I have for that body when it is the cause of harm to the world.
If, at some time, you who are devoted to unwearied meditation should sportively manifest an external form, you will be one whose very nature is the meditation upon the Self of all. 15.

If at any time you should emerge from non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpasamādhi*) with an external form, then you will, by logical necessity, bring about the sublation of the elements; such is the connection with what follows. || 15 ||
She is the embodiment of the support for meditation and concentration, which consist of worldly activity;
she is playful through the movement of the body, which has the nature of wind.
Is there truth in meditation, dhāraṇās, and so forth? He says "no": "In conventional usage" (vyavahāra).
With the intention that even such conventional activities as *spanda* and the like are not real, he says: "The body is like the nature of the wind" (vātasvabhāvavaddeha). || 16 ||
Then, O daughter, being opposed [to me] and obstructing the movement of your own karma, you will by right cause an affliction of the elements for the sake of ceasing hunger. (17)
One's own karma consists of actions such as violence that are unscriptural and characteristic of a *rākṣasa*; the [practice] is that which obstructs such movement. || 17 ||

You shall become one who acts with justice in the world, subduing injustice; while still embodied, through your state of liberation-in-life, you shall be the sole protector of your own discernment. (18)
Having spoken thus, the god departed from the expanse of the sky.
"Let that needle be mine"—what contradiction is there in this? Or rather, my passion lies in warding off the meaning of the words of the Lotus-born (Brahmā).
she became, for a moment, entirely composed of her own body. || 19 ||

The god Brahmā departed. That needle thought: "Let what was spoken by Brahmā indeed be mine; what does it matter whether there is opposition or not? Having reflected thus—"Is there passion in me for the purpose of warding off the boon that is the meaning of the lotus-born one’s words?
And for what reason [should I do so]?"—she became, within her inner mind, slightly composed of her own body, assuming the form of her former self.
It came to pass. || 19 ||
In the blink of an eye, it first became a span, then a cubit, then a fathom, then a branch, and then a mass of clouds; with its own emerging limbs as tendrils, it shone forth.
Through the sequence of the sprouts of the seed-particle of the wish-fulfilling tree. || 20 ||
He describes the manifestation of the gross body through the very process of mental conceptualization with the word "prādeśa.

*Prādeśa* means a body of the measure of a *prādeśa*. By the rule *pramāṇe laḥ*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *dvayasac*. The same applies hereafter. *Viṭapa* means the measure of the tip of a tree branch; from that, it expands. *Abhramālā* (a mass of clouds) is its measure. Thus...
Gradually, in the blink of an eye, that needle shone forth as the creeper of its own emerging parts, following the sequence of sprouts from the seed of the wish-fulfilling tree of her own volition.
Then, the sense organs, having emerged from the body with their powers unimpaired,
were perfectly present on all sides like flowers in a forest of the wish-fulfilling trees of volition.
The floods of seeds became entirely extinguished.

The limbs, the members, the organs, the seats of the senses, and the senses themselves had emerged; though previously latent, existing as a mass of seeds, they then became fully manifest and sufficient. Thus, because they are rooted in the imagination of the mind, the meaning is that they are indeed illusory. || 21 ||

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Acquisition of a Needle-Body," in the *Sūcī-upākhyāna* (The Narrative of the Needle) within the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* (Book on Origination) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Acquisition of the Needle-Body," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then that female Rākṣasa Sūcī became Karkaṭī once again.
The subtle itself has attained grossness, like a streak of clouds in the rainy season.
Having regained her body and remaining absorbed in meditative concentration, she arose from her hunger after six months;
then, at the word of Vāyu, Karkaṭī went to the region of the Kirātas.
Then, immediately after the manifestation of all the limbs. || 1 ||
Having attained her own true nature as space, she became somewhat joyful;
through that awakening, she cast off that state of being a great Rākṣasa like a discarded garment.

Having reached his own self-nature, the space of Brahman, and having reconnected with it through its awakening—that is, through direct realization—and because of its long-standing growth, he abandoned his state as the great Rākṣasa. || 2 ||
Right there, she remained meditating, established in the posture of the bound lotus (*baddhapadmāsana*); having grasped pure consciousness, she stood firm like a mountain peak. (3)
Having firmly grasped and taken refuge in the pure, non-conceptual consciousness as her very self by means of a continuous stream of mental states,
she then attained awakening through meditation after six months,
like a peahen at the sound of a great rain-cloud during the monsoon.
By the roar of the great cloud, there is awakening from meditative absorption; on the side of the peahen, it is the arousal of passion.
Her external consciousness awakened and she became intent on hunger;
for as long as the nature of this body has not ceased, it persists throughout the life of the body.
"As long as this body exists, as long as it remains, its nature of hunger and so forth does not cease. (5) Then, she reflected with thought:
"The life-force of another must be consumed by me, and that cannot be done without a [just] means. (6)
By means of thought—that is, by the mind which has thinking as its cause. || 6 ||
I consider this death of embodied beings to be better than that morsel of food which is censured by the noble or not acquired through righteous means. (7)
That which is censured and condemned by the noble, the venerable, and the great; || 7 ||
If I must abandon this body, let it be without anything acquired unjustly;
for wealth enjoyed through injustice is indeed like poison.

If I were to abandon my body without even a morsel of food acquired through righteous means, then there would be nothing more unjust or improper than that. However, wealth acquired through unrighteous means acts like poison when consumed;
it amounts to a multitude of calamities. || 8 ||
What would it matter to me if that which was obtained through the course of worldly events were consumed by him?
For me, there is no concern whatsoever regarding either life or death.

The "worldly order" (lokakrama) is the sequence approved by the world; that which has not been obtained by means of it—by death, that is, by dying—is the cause, whether desired or undesired, which acts as the motivator. || 9 ||
For I was indeed nothing but mind, adorned by the delusion of the body and so forth;
that [mind] has been stilled through self-awakening—whence, then, can there be the perception of a body or the like? (10)
The perceptions of body and non-body, and the delusions of life and death.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Remaining thus in silence, she heard a voice from the sky,
spoken by the Wind-god who was pleased by her abandonment of her demonic form.
Because of his renunciation of the identification with that body which was the very form of a Rākṣasa, he was gratified by the Wind-god.
"Go, Karkaṭī; awaken the deluded through knowledge. For it is the very nature of the great ones here to rescue the deluded. (12)
He demonstrates that speech with the words beginning "Go," etc. [to] the deluded who do not know the Self; [and to] the great ones who know reality. This is the reason. || 12 ||
Even when being awakened by you, he who does not attain awakening was born only for his own destruction; it is right that he should become your prey.
That person is a fool. A "bite" (grāsa) is a mouthful that is proper, meaning it does not deviate from what is right. || 13 ||
Having heard this, she said softly, "I have been favored by you," and she rose from the mountain peak and gradually descended.
Having heard these words, she spoke slowly, as if feeling ashamed to speak in such a manner because you, Vāyu, who perceive the ultimate truth, have shown no favor. 14.
Having quickly crossed over the ridges and descended from the slopes of the valleys,
he entered the settlement of Kirātas situated at the foot of the mountain.

The *adhityakā* is the upper portion of a mountain; the *upatyakā* is the land near the foot of a mountain, situated at its slopes. [He dwelt] on the foothills (*pāda*) of the Himavat mountain, that is, upon the surrounding mountains. 15.
[The world] provides food, water, cattle, multitudes of people, wealth, grass, herbs, and meat;
it is an infinite source of roots, drinks, food, and animals such as deer, insects, and birds—[in the reading "mūlapānānna," the word "anna" would be redundant;
in an alternative reading, "mūlapāḥ" refers to trees; "adantāḥ" means those without teeth].
These are specific types of living beings; the reading is "ending with Ananta and Mūlapāda. || 16 ||
The compound *annādīnām* is a *dvandva* within a *bahuvrīhi*. The same applies to *mūlādīnām*. *Śaṣpāṇi* means young grass; *āmiṣāṇi* means meats. || 16 ||
Resembling a moving and rolling mountain of collyrium,
that night-stalker followed him to that auspicious region where the foot of the Himālaya mountain was set.
At night, on a path through ground of thick, blinding darkness. || 17 ||

The connection is as follows: the night-stalker woman, who resembled a mountain—rolling with its moving collyrium (kajjala) applied to it—having set out and proceeded, went to that excellent place situated at the foot of the Snowy Mountain (Himagiri). || 17 ||
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Subduer of Unrighteousness," in the section on the Means to Liberation within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the work of the Sage.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Subduer of Unrighteousness," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the meantime, there in that region inhabited by Kirātas, [the following occurred].
The night became as dark as a mass of charcoal that can only be grasped with the hand.
Thereafter, the darkness is described, followed by the meeting of the king and his minister;
then, for the purpose of testing Karkaṭī, her desire to ask questions is recounted here in detail. (1)
A mass of darkness is *tamaḥpiṇḍa*. That which can be seized with the hand is *hastahārya*. The night (*yāminī*) is that in which there is a mass of darkness that can be seized with the hand. || 1 ||
The interior of the sky was covered by a cloth of blue clouds, devoid of the moon;
it resembled a dense grove of *tāla* trees, thick with rising soot.

That night, Karkaṭī’s friend describes it through the intermediate form of a *bhūta-rākṣasī*, beginning with "nīlamegha" and so forth: "The interior of the sky from which the moon has fled out of fear of being plundered of its nectar;
which, as if massing together the groves of *tamāla* trees, makes them appear as a single solid block (*tamālavanasaṃpiṇḍā*); which is thick (*māṃsalā*)."
She is nourished; she whose collyrium for the eyes darkens everything as it flies upward. (2)
Like a young woman in a city crowded with houses and courtyards, she is sluggish due to the blinding darkness within the hollows of the villages caused by the density of creepers.

In the mountain villages, due to the density of creepers, even the light of the stars cannot spread; thus, as if primarily blinded, she is like an old woman, slow and with faltering steps. Yet in the city, crowded and congested by the courtyards of houses, she moves about like one in the bloom of youth, guided by lamps.
At the four corners, a mass of darkness has eclipsed the lamp;
the light of the lamp, emerging from its curved openings, is rendered lusterless. (4)

In the outer courtyards, the lamps were bent and made crooked by the wind; for this very reason, they seemed to be "massing the darkness" (tamaḥpiṇḍī). They shone beautifully, illuminated by the faint glimmers of lamp-light emerging from the apertures of the curved, arched windows. In the compound *ādīpikārocibhiḥ*, the prefix *ā* is used in the sense of "slightly."
The absence of the long vowel [due to the elision of the *ḍh*] is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). || 4 ||
Like a dancing female imp beside a ripe karkaṭī fruit,
she stood as motionless as a wooden post, like a drunken vetāla or a skeleton.

Like a beautiful, good companion, she was like a friend; having undertaken a vow of wooden silence, as it were, due to the absence of any restraint when intoxicated Vetālas engaged in carrying away skeletons and other remains. || 5 ||
She dispels the thick mist of the multitude of creatures who have become like those in deep sleep;
she possesses droplets of frost shimmering from the touch of a gentle, slow-moving breeze.
It was enchanting, adorned with dense fogs and herds of animals such as deer sleeping in deep slumber. || 6 ||
In the lakes, with their gates wide open, it was rippled by crows, frogs, and waves; in the inner apartments, it resounded with the voices of sporting men and women.

From this point onward, setting aside the form of the Rākṣasīs, he describes [the city] in its own true nature with the words beginning "In the lakes" (saraḥsu). It is filled and pervaded by crows and frogs at the entrances of hollows and large banyan trees; it is that in which the faces of women and men resound during dalliance and play. || 7 ||
In the forests, she blazes with a world-consuming fire, radiant with tangled flames;
in the fields, she appears under the guise of ripening crops at the back after being sprinkled with water.

Blazing with a mass of matted locks like the fire at the end of an aeon, which is a flame for the world, she is radiant; yet in her, the thorns of the *śalalī* plant meet their end—through the moistening of water in the case of the *śalyaka* (porcupine), and through being uprooted by ripeness in the case of the *kedāra* (field). || 8 ||
The circle of stars was clearly distinguished by the shimmering movements visible in the vault of the sky,
while in the forests, the trees shed their flowers and fruits due to the blowing winds.
In which [city] the circles of stars—the clusters of constellations—are as if born like eyes that are imperishable, and as if distinguished and separated from their flickering. || 9 ||
Within its ravines, it resounded with the cries of crows disturbed by owls; on its borders, it was harsh with the lamentations of villagers overrun by thieves.
Having heard the cry of the owl from within the chasms and the hollows of trees—this is the ellipsis. || 10 ||
In the forests, the birds were silent; in the cities, the citizens slept;
in the woods, the winds blew forth; and in their nests, the birds remained motionless.
Like a forest, it was almost silent, with very little sound. || 11 ||
In the caves she abounds with lions asleep; in the groves she has hares at her own feet; in the sky she possesses clusters of frost; and in the forest she moves in silence.
Having the luster of the interior of a collyrium-cloud, resembling the belly of a mountain of glass, dense like a mass of mud, and thick with the blindness that can be cut by a sword. 13.
Like the interior of a lump of mud—that is, a clod of earth—it is dense and compact. || 13 ||
Turbulent like a mountain of soot agitated by the winds of universal dissolution,
it was thick with the belly of mountains and the great mire of the single vast ocean.
Agitated, shattered, or shaken; it was as thick as the belly of a mountain or like the great mire of a single vast ocean.
Dense with hollows of glowing coals, beautiful in the state of deep sleep,
thick with the slumber of ignorance, it possesses the luster of the wings on the back of a bumblebee.
Like the hollow of a burning charcoal log, the dark cloud; like the state of deep sleep, Sundarī is profound ignorance; like the sleep of nescience, the dense cloud is fundamental ignorance;
and she whose splendor is like the backs and the wings of bees.
The connection [of the sentence] is with the opening phrase: "the night became dark. || 15 ||
On that terrible night, in the midst of the Kirāta people,
the king was then at that moment together with his minister.
The wise-souled Vikrama departed from the city where the citizens were asleep,
proceeding with heroic conduct into a perilous forest.
By conduct appropriate for a hero, intended for the purpose of slaying thieves and the like. || 17 ||
In the forest, that cucumber saw those two— the king and the minister— wandering about,
their fortitude lost as they gazed upward at the sight of the vetāla.
Those two, who had maintained both their fortitude and their weapons, were looking up at the sight of the Vetāla, the village deity situated outside the village. 18.
Then she thought: "Ah, I have indeed found my prey!
These two are fools, ignorant of the Self; their bodies are truly a burden. (19)
That is the crab. || 19 ||
A fool lives for the sake of suffering, leading to ruin both in this world and the next;
he must be restrained with effort, for one does not nurture a calamity.
In this world and in the next world, the fool is one who does not know the self. 20.
For the fool who does not perceive his own self, death is life;
for through death there is his exaltation, because it is the cause of the non-attainment of sin. (21)
Death itself is life; that is to say, it is better than life. He demonstrates this very point through reasoning:
"By death... (verse 21).
And at the beginning of creation, a rule was established by the Lotus-born One:
"Let the self-controlled man be food for the violent ones, who are themselves deluded in spirit. (22)
Therefore, these two, having become my food, must be eaten by me this very day;
for one who is unfortunate disregards a faultless gain when it has come to hand. (23)
He is indeed incapable and unfortunate. || 23 ||
Perhaps these two might become virtuous and noble-minded;
for such destruction of Ravi does not please my own nature.
They are endowed with the quality characterized by self-knowledge. || 24 ||
Therefore, I shall thoroughly examine these two; if they are endowed with such qualities, I will not eat them, for I would never harm those possessed of virtue.
Then that [is the case]. || 25 ||
By one who desires unartificial happiness, fame, and long life, those endowed with virtuous qualities should be honored by granting everything they desire. (26)
By the giving of all things that are desired and cherished. || 26 ||
I would rather perish with this body than ever enjoy that which is fraught with the qualities of worldly existence;
for the virtuous bring more joy to the heart than even life itself. (27)
Because one bows with the body, not with the self, since [the self] is indestructible. || 27 ||
One should protect a virtuous person even by the gift of one's own life;
through the medicine of association with the virtuous, even death attains the state of friendship.
By means of a subjugating herb. || 28 ||
If even I, a Rākṣasī, protect this man who is endowed with virtues, then who else would not hold him in their heart like a pure necklace? (29)
Him who possesses those qualities. || 29 ||
Those embodied beings who dwell here endowed with noble virtues are moons upon the surface of the earth; through their association, they cool [the world] intensely.
On the surface of the earth, the *indavas* are the moons. || 30 ||
Death is the neglect of the virtuous, while life is the refuge of the virtuous;
from a life devoted to the virtuous comes the fruit of heaven, liberation, and so forth. (31)
The fruit is accomplished; this is the remainder [of the sentence]. || 31 ||
Therefore, I shall examine these two lotus-eyed ones through some playful inquiry: "Of what mother's knowledge are these two the possessors? (32)
I have examined; I shall examine. || 32 ||
Having first deliberated upon the application of even a slight degree of merit or demerit, and subsequently [ascertained] whether one is superior by virtue of one's own qualities,
one should then inflict punishment according to the force of the circumstances.
[He gave] to Daḍhya that which was appropriate for his logic, by means of the production of clouds. || 33 ||

First, having investigated whether this person possesses qualities or is devoid of them— even by means of a mere trace of quality— and having subsequently examined whether he is superior to oneself or otherwise, if he should be found lacking in qualities, then immediately thereafter, according to the perspective of the scriptures and by way of logical justification, one should impose upon the one deserving of punishment a penalty consistent with that logic.
The meaning is that one should perform [the rite] oneself when there is a dense abundance of qualities, but one should not do so when such excellence is already present. || 33 ||

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Reflection on the Rākṣasī," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Reflection on the Rākṣasī," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then that Rākṣasī, the blossoming creeper of the forest of the Rākṣasa race, [spoke].
It roared deeply, like a streak of clouds in the darkness.

The king’s vision of the crab, despite being unafraid even at the terrifying words [of the minister], and the commencement of the questioning by the queen, who had been conciliated by the minister’s speech, are now narrated. || 1 ||
She stands like a cluster of blossoms upon this forest characterized by the lineage of Rākṣasas, owing to its sweetness like the nectar of the fragrance of awakening. || 1 ||
At the end of his roar, he spoke these words, harsh with the sound of "huṃ," like the crash of thunderbolts produced immediately after a peal of thunder.
Though terrifying by its sound through the utterance of "huṃ," it is not harsh or cruel in its meaning.
O you two, the moon and the sun, who traverse the path of the sky in this terrible forest; you are like insects dwelling within the hollows of the stone seat of the darkness of Mahāmāyā!
The moon and the sun are the illuminators of the path of the sky, which is characterized by a formidable wilderness;

yet they are but insects within the hollow of that [sky], which is characterized by the darkness of great illusion (*mahāmāyā*) and serves as the foundational seat (*pīṭha*) for all beings. By this, his own self-knowledge is indicated. (3)
Who are you two, possessed of great intelligence or perhaps of evil intellect, who have come together and fallen into the range of my grasp, destined for death in an instant? (4)

When self-knowledge exists, they possess great intelligence and worshipful intelligence because their intellect is fruitful; in its absence, they possess base intelligence because their intellect is futile. They are thus suited for that which is called "death," a contemptible form of passing away. (4)
The king said:
"O Bhūtaka, who might you be? And where do you dwell in this body? Show yourself! Who would fear these words of yours, which sound like the humming of bees?"
Show your tiny little body! Who would be afraid of these words of yours, which are like the humming of a female bee? The meaning is: no one at all. || 5 ||
Those who seek wealth indeed fall upon their object with all the speed of a lion;
therefore, abandon your agitation and rashness, and demonstrate your own capability.
*Saṃrambham* means anger; *ārambham* means a terrifying exertion. || 6 ||
"Tell me, O observer of noble vows, what do you seek from me? I shall grant it to you.
Why do you frighten us with such agitation and harsh words? Are you afraid? (7)

The address "O you of excellent vows" is used to indicate that the self-knowledge pointed out by you has been understood by me. What is the use of terrifying us with the words "wrath" and "fear"? Or do you yourself fear? 7.
"Quickly, by means of the syllables 'ā' and 'kā', appear before me through your illusory power!
For those who procrastinate, nothing is accomplished except for their own ruin. (8)
By means of *māyā*, which possesses the power to imagine bodies visible to others; [this refers to] those who are procrastinating and slow to act. (8)
When the king had spoken thus, she reflected, "A delightful thing has been said," and for the sake of revealing her lack of fortitude to those two, she both shrieked and laughed.
Then the two of them beheld her, filling the quarters of the sky with sound,
her form revealed by a mass of radiance arising from her boisterous laughter.
Her own form is illuminated by the masses of light radiating from the teeth of her loud laughter. || 10 ||
Like a mountain slope ground by the friction of the thunderbolt at the end of an eon,
she illuminated the sky with the circle of lightning that was her own eyes and with cranes that were her bracelets.

It was as if ground and crushed by the friction of lightning and the impact of thunderbolts; its sky was illuminated by the lightning of her own eyes and by the cranes of the marks upon her conch-like bracelets.
Her dark neck was as thick as a mass of roaring clouds, appearing like the flickering flames of the submarine fire within the single ocean of darkness.
Of the single ocean characterized by darkness. || 12 ||
Again, she sportively manifested herself, making the night-stalkers cry out "Hā hā! in their agitation as their teeth clashed, turning heaven and earth into pillars of soot.
She had hair standing on end, a body covered in veins, tawny eyes, and was composed of darkness;
she brought about misfortune and fear even to the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas. (14)
She by whom the night-stalkers—thieves, tigers, jackals, and the like—were struck down and killed amidst cries of "Alas! Alas! due to the fury and fear arising from her clashing and grinding teeth;
she who, with the soot [from her eyes], causes the two worlds, heaven and earth, to become motionless as if paralyzed. 13–14.
Terrifying with the whistling sound of the breath-wind entering the cavities of her body,
she bore upon her head a pestle, a mortar, a firebrand, a plowshare, and a winnowing basket.
She whose crest is adorned with winnowing baskets that have become broken winnowing baskets. || 15 ||
Like the peak of a cat’s-eye gem quivering at the end of an aeon, she was like the Night of Doom (Kālarātri) arisen, making the Lord of the Universe (Viśveśa) burst into laughter. || 16 ||

"At the end of the aeon" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. She is like Kālarātri, the messenger of Śiva, who, by her laughs, strikes—that is, destroys—the lords of the Dānavas of the entire universe. 16.
She was like an autumnal forest with clouds that had taken bodily form,
or like a fleshy night endowed with a great mass of clouds.
By the configuration of her body, she appeared like a mound of mud rising up,
as if her slender form had resorted to darkness to combat the light of the moon and sun.
