The "mud-seat" is the seat of the earth; [it was seized] by Tamas, that is, Rāhu. || 18 ||
Her two dark breasts, resembling a pair of large, beautiful, and hanging sapphire clouds, bore a multitude of necklaces beginning with mortar-shaped pendants.
It resembles a pair of hanging clouds that are as dark blue as a great, brilliant sapphire. 19.
He possessed a massive body equal in size to a pillar of red-hot wood,
with a form like a tree, quivering with veins, and having arms like swaying creepers.

Marked with auspicious signs, symmetrical, and of the same complexion; she was no ordinary woman, possessing great and slender vine-like arms that shone brightly, resembling tree trunks, motionless, and marked with visible veins. || 20 ||
Beholding her, the two great heroes remained just as undisturbed as before;
for there is nothing that can cause delusion to one whose mind is secluded.
Of one who is secluded and possesses the discernment between truth and falsehood. || 21 ||
The minister said:
"O great Rākṣasī, what is this agitation of yours?
For even those of small stature may be excessively hurried when it comes to a minor task."
Desiring to pacify her with gentle words, thinking that if she were so great, such intense agitation was not appropriate for a minor matter, the minister said: "O Great Rākṣasī!
O Great Rākṣasī, regarding the accomplishment of your own desired aim, why this agitation—this anger—which is directed toward one who is a Great Soul and whose nature is unsurpassed?"

The meaning is: "For what purpose? The sense is that there is no need for anger, rashness, or the like regarding a task characterized by the acquisition of food, which can be obtained through mere words. Alternatively, with the intention of saying, "If you are insignificant, then we do not fear your agitation," he says: "For those who are insignificant... (22).
Abandon this agitation; this undertaking does not befit you.
For wise men, seeking to accomplish their own goals, engage only within their proper domain.

Resorting once again to the primary method, he says, "Abandon," employing conciliation (*sāman*). The implication is that wise people do not resort to force when a matter can be accomplished through conciliation. || 23 ||
O frail one, thousands like you are like mosquitoes;
by the gale of our fortitude, they are scattered like blades of grass and leaves. (24)
Furthermore, relying on the second alternative, he states the futility of exerting force with the words "of those like you.

By the word *vātyā*—meaning a whirlwind characterized by fortitude—the term is derived from the root *vāta* (wind) with the suffix *ya* in the sense of a collection (belonging to the *pāśādi* group), followed by the feminine suffix *ṅīp* by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), and the elision of *y* according to the rule *halastaddhitasya*; thus, *vātyā* here stands in the instrumental case. [The objects] were arrayed...
They have been rejected. || 24 ||
Having abandoned the gateway of agitation, the wise person accomplishes their own goal through a mind that is pure in its equanimity and through skillful worldly conduct. 25.
If so, how is one's own purpose accomplished therein? To this he says: "With zeal," etc. [This is] by means of that which is practical—that is, appropriate for the conduct of the wise. || 25 ||
Whether the task succeeds or fails through one's own worldly activity, what occasion is there for the delusion that it is solely "great destiny"? (26)

Even when there is doubt regarding the accomplishment of the task, the means of conciliation (*sāma*), established by beginningless destiny, must not be abandoned; how much less so when its success is certain?
With this intention, he says: "By himself," etc. This refers to the delusion—that is, the agitation appropriate to one who is deluded.
"Tell us what is desired by you, and for what purpose you come as a petitioner;
for among us, no seeker has ever gone before us with his purpose unfulfilled, even in a dream. (27)
How, then, is success achieved through conciliation? To this he says: "Speak. (27)
Having been addressed thus by him, that rākṣasī then reflected:
"Aha! How pure is the conduct and the character of these two lions among men! (28)
Vigor, fortitude, and the strength of intellect. || 28 ||
I do not consider these two to be ordinary; this is a wondrous marvel, for by the very glance of her curved speech, she expresses her inner certainty.
By means of a sidelong glance, by the mere sight of her face, and through signs such as her graciousness, she declares—that is, indicates—the ascertainment of the internal reality. || 29 ||
Through the doors of their speech, wit, and insight, the intentions of the wise become one with each other, just as the waters of rivers merge through their various windings.
By means of turnings and associations. || 30 ||
"By these two, my state has for the most part been fully understood;
and by me, these two are not to be destroyed, for they are themselves indestructible. (31)

I believe these two must be knowers of the Self; for without the knowledge of the Self, the mind—having its notions of existence and non-existence wiped away—becomes free from fear at the time of death.

Since the certainties of existence and non-existence, as well as the notions of life and death, are wiped away by the certainty of falsehood, there is nothing other than such self-knowledge [to effect this]. || 32 ||
Therefore, I ask these two about a certain doubt that has arisen;
for those who do not question when they have encountered a wise person are the lowest of men. (33)
Having reflected thus, and then creating an opportunity for inquiry,
she restrained her laughter— which sounded like the roar of untimely clouds at the end of an aeon— and spoke.
Laughing and jesting; having restrained and suppressed them. || 34 ||
"Who are you two, O steadfast men? Tell me, O sinless ones;
for friendship arises at the mere sight of those with pure hearts. (35)
The minister said:
"This is the king of the Kirātas, and I have attained the position of his minister;
we are prepared to subdue people like you by means of a night-raid."
Indeed, we two are prepared and exerting ourselves for the suppression of violent people such as yourself. || 36 ||
Day and night, the duty of a king is the suppression of wicked beings;
however, those who abandon their own duty are fuel for the fire of destruction.
The Rākṣasī said:
"O King, you are a man of evil counsel; a king should not be one of evil counsel.
A king should have a minister of good character, and a king of good counsel shall prevail. (38)

Introducing the question that is about to be asked, he says: "O King," etc. You are one whose minister is wicked; the word "esteemed" (saṃbhāvita) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. || 38 ||
At the outset, the king must be joined with discernment by a wise minister;
for as is the king, so are the subjects, and through that [discernment] he attains nobility. (39)
Nobility and excellence. || 39 ||
Among all the networks of virtues, knowledge of the inner self (adhyātma-jñāna) is supreme.
One who knows that is a king; and one who knows that is a minister who truly understands counsel.
"Entire" (*samasta*)—thus they have said: "That action which does not lead to bondage is knowledge (*vidyā*), while that which leads to liberation is [also] knowledge;
other action leads to exhaustion, while other knowledge is merely skill in the arts. [The practitioner is] one who knows the mantras and knows the secret of deliberation.
Sovereignty and impartial vision—these arise from the science of kingship (*rājavidyā*).
He who does not know this very [science] is neither a minister nor a ruler. (41)
Because sovereignty depends upon equanimity (samadṛṣṭitva), it is metaphorically attributed to it— just as one says "clarified butter is life"—

and thus it is called *rājavidyā* (the royal science) because it is the king of sciences, namely, the science of the Self (*ātmavidyā*). By means of that [science], the wise [behave] alike toward even a dog and an outcaste dog-cooker.
"Because of the Blessed One's statement: 'They are those who see with equanimity. || 41 ||
If you two are virtuous experts in that matter, then you shall attain the highest good; if not, I shall devour you both as a source of calamity for my own nature.

Since it was previously stated that "as is the king, so are the subjects," when the king is foolish, the subjects likewise cannot avoid it; therefore, I devour—that is, I consume—the misfortunes resulting from that [folly]. || 42 ||
By a single means you two shall emerge from my side, if you examine with your intellect the essence of the cage of my questions. (43)
They are objects of affection for their parents, like two young children. || 43 ||
"O King, answer these questions, or else [consult] your minister; I am intensely seeking a purpose there, so fulfill my aim.
For who is there in the world who, having promised a purpose, does not grant it?"
He who is not joined with the fault that causes total destruction. || 44 ||

O King, explain these questions and matters that have been asked; or else, O minister, you may speak. In this regard, I am intensely desirous and full of entreaty. Grant my heart's desire; I shall give what has been promised.
Who is there like him who, failing to give the object promised, is not joined with the fault that causes total ruin? The meaning is: there is no such person at all. || 44 ||
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Rākṣasī," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rākṣasī," in the Utthāna-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa.
The seventy-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, that Rākṣasī began to answer the questions.
When the king said, "Let it be told," [the sage replied: "Listen to these, O Raghava."
In this creation, Karkaṭī posed seventy-two questions in sequence to those who know the selfless, who are equal to Vajra in their realization of the self, and who have reached the heart of truth.
When the king said, "Let it be told," and gave his permission, he began to speak. || 1 ||
The Rākṣasī said:
Within a single atom—which, though one, contains manifold numbers—hundreds of thousands of universes dissolve like bubbles within an ocean. (2)

The intention behind the questions and their answers will become clear in the subsequent creation; therefore, no excessive elaboration is made here, as [the distinctions] are difficult to perceive due to the multiplicity arising from the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and because the atom is indivisible, like the ocean.
Is space non-space? Is nothingness indeed something? Who have I become, and who are you who stands as "I"? (3)

It is neither space nor empty. That which is renowned in the world is nothing at all; that which is renowned by the knower of reality is something entirely different. Who is it that, while walking, does not walk? Who is it that, even while standing, remains standing? Who is it who, though conscious, is like a stone? And who is it that performs wonders in the sky?
They stood still, making no movement; like a stone, they were devoid of any support for consciousness. || 4 ||
And who is it that abandons the state of being fire? What fire is there that does not burn?
O King, how can fire arise from what is not fire, and why would it do so incessantly?
Who is it that, though devoid of moon, sun, fire, and stars, is indestructible and illuminating? And from what source does this light proceed, which cannot be grasped by the eye? (6)
Being imperishable, it is illuminating. || 6 ||
What kind of supreme light could there be for creepers, thickets, sprouts, and the like, as well as for those born blind and others who lack eyes? (7)
Of those who are without sense organs, whose faculties have not yet manifested. || 7 ||
Who is the progenitor of space and the other elements? Who is the giver of their inherent nature?
Who is the treasury of the jewels of the universe? And whose treasury is this world-jewel? (8)
The giver of intrinsic nature, the bestower of existence. || 8 ||
Which atom is both darkness and light? Which atom both exists and does not exist? Which atom is both far away and near? And which atom is indeed a great mountain? (9)
What is a kalpa? It is but a moment. What is a moment? It is also a kalpa. What is perceptible that lacks reality? What is conscious that is unconscious? (10)
Although appearing directly before the eyes, it is of the nature of non-existence to one of deluded vision.
What is wind and what is non-wind? What is sound and what is indeed soundless? What is everything and yet nothing? Who am I, and what might that be which is not "I"? || 11 ||
Even after attaining that which is obtainable through hundreds of efforts over many lifetimes, nothing at all is truly gained;
rather, everything remains unattained.

Although it was obtained even previously in many births simply by virtue of being one's own self, because it is veiled by ignorance, it is as if unobtained; therefore, it is to be attained through hundreds of efforts. All is complete. 12.
By what high-souled person has his own self been utterly abandoned through a healthy life?
By what minute thing is Mount Meru contained within, while the three worlds are made out of a blade of grass? 13.
"By whom has one's very self been stolen away and rendered as good as destroyed? And why is the threefold world treated like a blade of grass?"—this is a separate question. (13)
By some [being] as small as an atom, a hundred yojanas were filled;
yet who, being merely an atom, can be contained even within hundreds of yojanas? (14)
By whose mere glance is the world led astray like a child? Within the belly of which atom (aṇu) indeed reside the multitudes of mountains? (15)

In the forms *praṇāḍyate*, *praṇartyate*, and *anarḍāṭi*, the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur because they are excluded from the list of roots taught with an initial *ṇ*. *Ghaṭāḥ* means "multitudes. 15.
Who is that atom which, without abandoning its atomic nature, possesses the form of the massive Mount Meru;
and who is that atom which, being the essence of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, becomes a towering mountain peak? (16)
A heap of moral conduct is like a mountain. || 16 ||
What atom is the lamp that bestows illumination upon light and darkness?
Within the belly of which atom do all atoms of experience reside? (17)
The atoms of experience are fragments of cognition delimited by mental modifications. || 17 ||
What atom, though exceedingly tasteless, constantly provides flavor? By what atom, when it abandons everything, is everything supported? (18)
"Niḥsvādu" means devoid of sweet and other such tastes; "āśrita" means accepted, so to speak. || 18 ||
By which atom, incapable of concealing itself, has the universe been concealed?
At the dissolution of the universe, what atom—even though existing—remains alive? (19)
Although the world is concealed by dissolution, it becomes real once again through the existence of even a single atom; thus it lives on at the time of creation. || 19 ||
What is an atom that has no parts? Who is he who possesses a thousand arms and eyes? What is a moment, a great aeon, and hundreds of millions of aeons? (20)
In the subtle atom (aṇu) all worlds abide, as a tree exists within its seed;
for seeds, though unmanifest and yet to sprout, contain within them everything down to their most minute parts.

In what do the worlds abide during the dissolution, even though they have not yet arisen? And at the time of creation, in what do all those seeds—whose limit is the succession of seeds within the unmanifest, partless, and undivided—remain forever unarisen, even though they are clearly manifested as the world itself at the time of creation? (21)
Whose blink is a kalpa, as if residing within a seed?
Who is the agent who acts even without relying on the status of being a causal agent for a purpose? (22)

If such is the case, in what does even the dissolution (pralaya) reside? Its purpose is the setting in motion of the respective causal factors; therein, agency consists in being the instigator of the activity of those factors. What [agent] could be called a "doer" without relying on this, since [the Self] is actionless? Or rather, the agency of purpose is the accomplishment of the fruit of the action. || 22 ||
In order to perceive the object of sight, the seer brings his own self into the state of being seen;
for who, indeed, seeing the object, can see their own self if they lack eyes? 23.
For the perfection of the visible world and for the accomplishment of objects of enjoyment, he perceives the visible through external vision. || 23 ||
And when the visible world has been dissolved within, who—perceiving the indivisible Self—is not seeing the visible world before them, since that visible world no longer exists? (24)
Beholding in such a way that the visible world is dissolved within through knowledge. || 24 ||
Who illuminates the self, the seer, and the seen, as if they were objects to be seen? And by whom are these three—like bracelets and other ornaments—manifested from gold alone? (25)

Who illumines the seer (the self), the act of seeing (the mental modification), and the object of sight—which is as if directly perceived like the eye—when they are scattered and dispersed? That is to say, when these three—the seer, the act of seeing, and the object of sight—are manifested by the power of distraction. || 25 ||
Why does nothing exist separately, like waves and so forth from the great ocean?
By whose will does anything exist separately, like a ripple from the great ocean? (26)
From that one, non-existent yet existent, which is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, duality also arises— not as something separate— from it, just as waves arise from the great ocean.
From that which is non-existent, from that which is not gross, from that which is like the non-existent, and from that which is existent. || 27 ||

Who, moving through the three times, holds within himself— like a seed contained within— a self, vision, and the visible world, both existent and non-existent, and the three worlds whose sequence has passed away? (28)
Having placed within itself both that which exists in a manifest state and that which exists in a concealed state of non-existence, it remains existing throughout the three times;
the meaning is that it is always thus. || 28 ||
The vast multitude of the world—past, present, and future—is eternally contained within Him, like a tree existing within its seed. (29)
The ellipsis is "of whom does it eternally exist within"? || 29 ||
Just as a seed quickly becomes a tree and a tree likewise [becomes] a seed, what is it that arises without having abandoned its own singular form, even though it has not yet arisen? (30)

He states the distinction between the illustration and the illustrated by means of two examples, beginning with "itself as one": that is to say, it remains entirely unmodified. The ellipsis to be supplied is "it arises in the form of the transformations of the world. || 30 ||
O King, compared to whom the great Meru is but a spider’s thread, in whose belly could there be millions of Merus and Mandaras? (31)
The meaning is that, in comparison with which—relying upon its firmness—the great Mount Meru is exceedingly more solid than even a lotus fiber.

Alternatively, the meaning is that by comparison with which, through mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), even a lotus fiber is as firm as the great Mount Meru. Within the interior (*udara*) of such an entity... || 31 ||
By whom has this universe, which is nothing but manifold consciousness, been spread out?
What is its essence, such that you sport, strike, and protect with such exceeding vigor?
Is it through some philosophical view that you exist, or are you always so?
Surely Bhava, whose face has eyes free from impurity, [acts] for his own peace.
By whom has this universe— which consists of manifold layers of consciousness— been extended and manifested through creation? And who are you, whose essential nature is such that, being thus,
you move with preeminence in all worldly affairs, conducting yourself, protecting the subjects, and slaying those deserving of death?
And thus, the meaning is: what is the cause for all the processes such as creation and so forth? Whose is the vision?

"Whose-vision" (kiṃdarśana) refers to that; by means of that, you, being of the nature of pure vision, do not become something other than that. Or rather, you surely always remain of that very nature for the sake of our own peace regarding that reality.
"Speak for the sake of liberation from your own death"—this is the conclusion. || 32 ||
Let this great doubt of mine, which is a foul smearing upon the mist-like face of the glory of my mind, now dissolve;
for before whom does doubt not vanish, root and all?
This [position] does not accord with the words of any wise person whatsoever. || 33 ||

May this doubt of mine—which has been described by its characteristics, which is the face of the glory of consciousness (*cittaśrī*), that is, the mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of one’s own Self, and which is like a coating of impurity characterized by mist obscuring the moon—dissolve along with its root, together with the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*). It does not at all attain the status of a "learned man's statement" (*paṇḍitokti*), nor even the fitness for the title of "learned. || 33 ||
O you of excellent intellect, if you do not thus instruct me in due order— [according to some readings: "without doubt"]— so that my doubts are thoroughly pacified and rendered most slight,
then I shall become fuel for the ancient fire of the Rākṣasas.
"You two shall go instantly and without obstacle in a mere moment. || 34 ||

If you do not dispel or remove such a slight doubt of mine, then you shall become fuel for the fire in the belly of your own bodies, born of the race of Rākṣasas—in other words, you shall be devoured. Then you will depart instantly, in a moment, without obstacle. [This is said] regarding those who lack self-knowledge and whose nature consists solely in identifying the body as the self.
The meaning is that the state of being a destroyer of obstacles is difficult to ward off; this is the intention behind the reading "bhāvanām. || 34 ||
Afterwards, I shall instantly devour that entire circle of your subjects, who possess large bellies, from every side;
thus may it be for you, O good king— so I think.
For fools, excessive passion leads only to their destruction. || 35 ||

He says "afterwards" (*paścāt*) to show that this misfortune has not arisen for you two alone, but has also befallen the entire realm. "With a large belly" (*urujaṭhara*) means having a vast abdomen. I believe that by thus providing answers to the questions asked, [the king] will become a true sovereign (*surāja*) through his protection of all subjects along with himself. This is the great delight of fools who lack self-knowledge (*anātmajña*).
The excessive craving for enjoyments caused by the status of kingship leads only to destruction;
the sense is that even if one does not consume [the kingdom], at the end of the reign, hell is inevitable. || 35 ||
Having spoken thus with a voice as resonant and manifest as the thundering of vast and deep clouds, that night-stalker—
Even in silence, he of exceedingly formidable appearance then became like a circle of clouds, pure as autumn, within the inner apartments.

Having spoken thus with a voice as clear as the resonance of vast and deep thunderclouds, she—though her outward form was exceedingly formidable—remained silent, pure within like a circle of clouds in an autumn sky; such is the meaning. || 36 ||
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Question of the Rākṣasī," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the holy *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Question of the Rākṣasī," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Eightieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In the great forest, during the dead of night, by a daughter of a great Rākṣasa...
When this great question had been thus asked, the great mantra-master gave his reply.
In this [work], the practitioner first undertakes the sets of questions in their proper sequence, and also out of order as appropriate, through subtle logical demonstrations. (1)
The speech characterized by the vow that is about to be declared. || 1 ||
The minister said:
"Listen, O one who resembles a rain-cloud; I shall resolve this question of yours, just as a lion tears apart a rutting lordly elephant in due order. (2)
I split apart the question and the multitude of questions; I tear them asunder with logical demonstrations. || 2 ||
"O lotus-eyed lady, this Supreme Self has been described by you through these very words, which are worthy of awakening one who knows how to inquire. (3)
To loosen all questions, he first reveals the very heart of every question:
Because it is inexpressible, because it is ungraspable, and because it abides as the sixth sense, the mind;
thus the Self is pure consciousness alone, an atom subtler even than space. (4)

He reveals the intention behind the use of the word *aṇu* (atom/minuscule) in the subject of the first question—"Of what [is it the size] like that of an atom or an ocean?"—with the words "because it is inexpressible" (*anākhyatvāt*). Thus, it is well-known in such scriptural passages as: "The path is subtle (*aṇu*), far-reaching, and ancient."
The state of being. || 4 ||
Within the supreme,
indivisible Consciousness, this world exists as if it were both real and unreal, vibrating like the potentiality of a tree within its seed.
By the phrase "lakhs of internal cosmic eggs," he shows the portion that was asked about—namely, the term *cidaṇoḥ* (of the atom of consciousness).
By this, the question, "In what do the worlds reside within the atom, like a tree in its seed? is also answered. || 5 ||
Because it is the experience of some existent reality by its very nature, and because it is all-pervasive,
entities have indeed attained their existence previously through being of that same nature.
Having indicated this by the statement "whether real or even unreal," he provides the answer to the question "What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of existence?
with the words "existence is something [real]":
because the existence of all things depends upon the existence of experience, that [experiential] existence...

The meaning is that because an infinite regress would result if [existence] were dependent on something else, all entities attain their existence solely through experience, whose own being is self-established. || 6 ||
Space is [called] external emptiness, yet it is non-space because of its nature as consciousness;
because it is beyond the senses, it is nothing at all, and that very same thing is the atom and the infinite.

He reveals the underlying intent of the question, "Is it space or non-space? by saying, "It is space. He provides the answer to the question, "Is it nothing, or is it something? by saying, "Because it is beyond the senses. The meaning is that it is not something whatsoever that can be grasped by the senses. || 7 ||
Because it is the self of all, nothing at all is experienced by it as something other than itself. That manifestation of the single atom of consciousness occurs as a multiplicity;
it is like the state of being a bracelet [which exists] even when gold is not [perceived as such], or even when it is perceived as such—so says a certain [author].
Just as bracelets and other ornaments [are made] from gold, so too are [all things] in the Supreme. || 8 ||

But if the meaning of the question is that when nothing whatsoever exists within one's own being, then he says: "Because it consists of all things. Since one's very self consists of all things, when everything has been experienced and swallowed by means of one's own self directly realized, that very thing [which was thought to exist] is nothing at all; for nothing remains of it as a distinct self—this is the intended meaning.
This is the meaning. He states the intention behind the opening question, "of the one [which has] many numbers," with the words "of the conscious atom" (*cidaṇoḥ*).
The meaning is that for the single conscious atom alone, the appearance of multiplicity spoken of by you is merely phenomenal (*prātītikī*), not real (*vāstavī*).
With this, he says "just as [the ornaments] of gold," intending that the question regarding bracelets and so forth being [identical to] gold itself is also essentially answered.
This is the subtle, supreme ether, unperceived even due to its subtlety;
it stands transcending the six senses, including the mind, even while existing as the self of all.

Regarding the repeated use of the word "aṇu" in questions such as "Which one would be the atom (aṇu) of darkness or light?", he states that the intended meaning is exactly as previously explained: "This is the aṇu. (9)
Because it is the self of all, this [Self] never becomes empty;
he who says "that which exists does not exist" is known as a speaker and a thinker [of falsehood]. (10)

Regarding the question, "Does that which is atomic both exist and not exist?", he refutes it by stating "because it is the self of all," etc., on the grounds that the portion [of the answer] saying "it does not exist" is indeed contradicted. He explains how it is contradicted with the words "that which exists":
for the reason that the person who speaks and thinks "that exists" and "that does not exist" is none other than the Self itself.
It is remembered as being well-known in the form of the speaker, the mantra, and so forth;
thus, since it is impossible for its own self to be denied, its non-existence is simply not tenable—this is the meaning. || 10 ||
By no reasoning whatsoever is the non-existence of that which exists here logical;
it is perceived as the self of all, protected by its own self, like camphor. || 11 ||

He says that this is also not tenable because it contradicts its being both existent and non-existent—using the phrase "by any means whatsoever. Raising the objection, "If it truly exists, then why is it not seen? he replies: even if it is not seen in its extracted form, it is nevertheless seen in its nature as pure Being (sadrūpa) which pervades all things; just as camphor, though hidden by its covering, is perceived through its own essence of fragrance.

Thus he says: "the Self of all. The meaning is that by one's own self, which is concealed—that is, hidden—in its form as the immediate [witness], the Self of all, the eternally existent Self that pervades everything, is seen. || 11 ||
That very atom of pure consciousness alone is everything that exists here within the mind;
yet, because its nature transcends the senses, it remains as nothing at all, established in stainless purity.

He provides the answer to the question, "What is everything, and yet nothing at all?"—namely, "the atom of pure consciousness" (*cinmātrāṇu*). Now, one might ask: how can that which is unlimited (*aparicchinna*) possess the form of everything limited (*paricchinnasarvarūpa*)? To this he says, "something" (*kiṃcit*).
Because of the cognition of manifoldness through the functions of the mind and the senses, [it appears] as "something" by way of the very form limited by the mind.

The meaning is "everything. For this very reason, with the intention that there is nothing whatsoever in its natural form as it is unconditioned by the mind, senses, and so forth, he says "nothing" (na kiṃcit), implying that you have spoken thus. || 12 ||
And that very [Self] is both one and many, because it is the self-experience of all sentient beings;
it alone sustains this world, for it is indeed the sheath of the world. 13.
With this intention, he says "sa evaikaḥ" (He alone is one), referring to your opening statement that "one [is] many in number.
He provides the answer to the question, "Within whom is there always equality? and to the question, "Who would be the treasury of the jewels of the world? with the words "sa eva" (He alone). || 13 ||
These waves, which are the three worlds, surge within the great ocean of the mind;
therein, wisdoms shine like reflections in water, appearing as circles due to its fluidity.
To the question, "Why is there nothing whatsoever separate [from it], like waves and so forth from the great ocean? he provides the answer with the words "These...

In that which undergoes transformation like the great ocean through the nature of the mind (*cittātman*), these *prajñās* are merely of the form of mental constructs (*vikalpa*). By this, the question of by whose will they exist separately is also fully resolved. (14)
Because it cannot be apprehended by the mind, the senses, and so forth, it is subtle and has the nature of emptiness;
yet, because it is apprehended through self-awareness, it is non-empty even though its form is like space.

He states the intended meaning of the teaching that "from the one, which is both non-existent and existent, and which is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, [the world arises]"—namely, that it possesses the nature of both the void and the non-void—in the verse beginning with "cittendriyāt" (from the mind and senses). || 15 ||
Through the realization of non-duality, I have become you yourself, and you have become me;
yet, having been born with the vast body of awakening, neither you nor I exist as separate entities.
He provides the answer to the question, "Who have you become? with the words, "I am He. Because of the realization of non-duality (*advaita*), I have become that very Self;
being that Self, you are indeed my own Self, and you have become He. I alone am He.

This too pertains to the conventional usage of identifying oneself with the state of "I-ness" and "you-ness"; however, from the perspective of the non-conventional vision, that Self is not [subject to such distinctions].
The meaning is that neither you nor I have been born, but rather the great body of awakening itself has arisen or manifested. || 16 ||
By swallowing up everything consisting of "thou-ness" and "I-ness" through awakening, there is neither "thou," nor "I," nor "all"; yet all becomes the Self by itself.
He states clearly the very meaning already mentioned: "tvanteti" (verse 17).

Though this subtle atom has traveled across a multitude of yojanas, it neither goes nor does it come; for through its own consciousness, the state of being a multitude of yojanas resides within that very atom.
To the question, "Who is it that neither goes nor does not go?", he provides the answer: "Going...

[verse 18]. Although pervading a multitude of *yojanas* like space, even while occupying such a multitude of *yojanas*, one goes by means of consciousness through mental construction (*kalpanā*), as in a dream.
Though it has gone, it does not go; and though it has arrived, it has not come, because it dwells within the interior of the space-receptacle of its own existence, transcending both space and time.
To the question "Who remains standing even while standing?", he gives the answer in the same manner: "He does not go. || 19 ||
Where indeed can he go when his destination is situated within his own body? Is a son residing in the hollow of his mother's breasts seen anywhere else by her? (20)

Having stated both [points], he establishes them by means of an illustration, beginning with "the object to be gone to" (gamyam): "The object to be gone to" (gamyam) is another location that is to be reached by the act of going. || 20 ||
For him whose great domain is accessible and remains inexhaustible as long as existence endures, who indeed dwells within the creator of all—how and where could he go? (21)
Just as when a jar is moved to another location,
there is no corresponding coming or going of the space within it, so it is not with the self.

He clearly states another illustration with the word "yathā" (just as). The meaning is that just as there is no going or coming when the mouth is closed—that is, when it is shut like a curved [tube]. || 22 ||

When consciousness (cittatā) and insentience (sthāṇutā) both exist within the internal self as having experience as their essence, then that [self] consists of both the conscious and the insentient. (23)

If the meaning of the question "Is even a stone conscious? is that it possesses both contradictory natures—being of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) and being of the nature of insentience (*jaḍa-rūpa*)—then he says: "The state of being consciousness" (*cittatā*).

This means that when, due to the superimposition of identity with the Self upon the body and so forth which are indeed insentient, the insentient thing acquires the state of being consciousness—that is, the nature of luminosity (*prakāśa-svabhāvatā*) or the state of being a pillar (*sthaṇutā*).

And when both insentience and experience exist as having their own experience as witness, then, due to the absence of reflective awareness (avimarśa), that [subject] indeed becomes a duality consisting of both the insentient and the conscious; such is the meaning. || 23 ||
O Rākṣasī, when consciousness, stone, existence, the single self, and the singular form of consciousness are one, then that very consciousness is like a stone.

But when the meaning of the question is "Who is this conscious being that is as solid in form as a stone?", then he says "When... (verse 24), stating that "he" is indeed the ultimate nature of the Self, which is a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*).
In the supreme ether, which is without beginning or end, by the Supreme Self who is pure consciousness alone,
this manifold painting of the three worlds was created by that which is itself uncreated.

He provides the answer to the objection that "someone has created various things in the sky" with the words: "In the supreme sky. Because it is illusory, that which is uncreated is treated as if created. || 25 ||

Through the cognition of that [fire], the existence of fire is established; thus, not abandoning its fiery form, that purifier of all substances, though omnipresent, indeed burns the world. (26) [The reading *sa sarvadravyapāvakaḥ* is correct.]
"Does he abandon his nature as fire, and what fire is there that does not burn? To this, he gives the answer: "By means of the consciousness of That.

Since the existence of fire is nothing other than the existence of the Self, and since that [Self] is all-pervading, even though He is omnipresent, He does not burn; indeed, He does not burn at all. The letter *a* is a particle used in the sense of negation, according to the rule "amā-nonāḥ in negation. It is not by this much alone that He...
It should not be thought that [the Self] is omnipresent; for the meaning is that it is the illuminator of all substances, like fire. || 26 ||
From that stainless sky, which possesses a blazing and radiant form,
that fire is born, whose singular essence is a blazing consciousness.
He provides the answer to the question, "From what is fire born? with the verse beginning "prajvalat" (blazing). || 27 ||

That which illuminates the light of the sun and other luminaries through perception and so forth— being of the nature of the self-luminous soul— it is not destroyed even by the clouds at the end of a great aeon.
To the question, "Who is the indestructible illuminator even though devoid of moon, sun, fire, and stars? he provides the answer:
"Because of self-awareness" (saṃvedanāt). || 28 ||
Unattainable by the eyes, consisting of pure experience, the lamp illuminating the chamber of the heart, the bestower of existence to all, it is remembered as the infinite, supreme light. (29)
He provides the answer to the question, "Why does that light proceed from that which is not obtainable by the eye? with the words: "Not obtainable by the eye. (29)
Our light proceeds from that which transcends the senses, with the mind as the sixth;
by means of it, the wondrous splendor of objects is perceived even within.
He demonstrates its self-luminosity with the words, "it proceeds.

Our perception—the manifestation of the ego and so forth—proceeds from the Self, which transcends the six organs including the mind. It is just as when one situated in dense darkness asks, "Where are you? [and the other replies].

When asked, "Am I here?", he says, "I am. For this reason, in the interval—meaning, in the presence of light, lamps, and so forth—the wonder of the visible, the immediate manifestation (*aparokṣa-prathā*) of objects such as one's own body and senses, is observed;
that is to say, it is well-established through universal experience. || 30 ||
It nourishes creepers, shrubs, sprouts, and so forth, as well as those that lack sense organs; its form is upward growth and sensation, and it is luminous and of the nature of experience. (31)

He provides the answer to the question beginning with "the creeper and the shrub" by saying "the creeper": the nourisher is the cause of growth through its own proximity; and that Witness whose form is the very perception of that result, namely the upward growth (utsedha).
Time, space, action, and existence exist within that world-consciousness;
yet, because of its nature as the Self, it is nothing other than the master, the agent, the father, and the enjoyer. (32)

He provides the answer to the question "Who is the creator of space and the rest? with the words "Time, space, etc. From the perspective of conventional usage, this is so; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, he says: "Because of its nature as the Self. || 32 ||
Not abandoning its atomic nature, that atom is the casket for the jewels of the universe;
within the absolute alone, the world consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge does not exist.

He states the answer again to the question, "What could be the treasury of the jewels of the world?"—namely, "minuteness" (aṇutva). A *samudgaka* is a casket. To the question, "Whose treasury is the world? [Is it] of the jewel? he gives the answer with the half-verse beginning with "mātra" (measure).
He alone shines clearly everywhere throughout the entire world;
when this world-ocean exists, he is the supreme jewel within that ocean. (34)
Because it is difficult to comprehend, it is darkness; because it is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), it is the perceiver of light.
It exists because its nature is awareness (*saṃvitti*); likewise, because it transcends the senses, it is not [an object of] existence.

He provides the answer to the question, "What could be a subtle atom that is both darkness and light? with the words, "Because it is difficult to comprehend. He provides the answer to the question, "What exists as both existing and not existing? with the words, "That exists. (35)
It is distant because it cannot be grasped by the senses; yet, being of the nature of consciousness, it does not go far away.
Because it perceives everything, it is indeed the mountain, even while remaining as subtle as an atom.

He provides the answer to the question, "What is minute? Is it far away or not far away? with the words, "That [Self] is far away. He provides the answer to the question, "What is minute yet a great mountain? with the words, "Because of being perceived by all. The meaning is as you have stated: because, even without the operation of the senses, everyone perceives it directly as "I, I," just like a mountain standing before one's eyes. || 36 ||
This world that appears here is merely the perception of that [consciousness];
mountains and such things have no reality, and thus even Mount Meru is but an atom.
Regarding that, he states the intended meaning of the portion "being indeed minute" as follows: "tatsaṃvedana... (verse 37).
For that which appears as a blink is called a "blink" (nimeṣa);
indeed, that which appears as a world-age is expressed by the word "kalpa. || 38 ||
He provides the answer to the question "What is a kalpa in relation to a mere blink of an eye? with nine verses beginning with "nimeṣa... (verse 38).
Indeed, the play of the activities of an eon appears as a mere blink of an eye;
even a great city situated many millions of yojanas away appears as if within the mind itself. (39)

He establishes the meaning already stated with the word "kalpeti" (it imagines). The sense is that the play of the activities of a kalpa appears as if occurring within a mere moment; that is, the manifestation of the activities of a kalpa shines forth. He provides an illustration for the appearance of something vast within a small space with the word "bahu" (much). || 39 ||
Indeed, the arising of an eon occurs within the hollow of a single blink of an eye,
just as the construction of a great city appears within a spotless mirror.

To prevent the doubt that this is impossible, he states another illustration: "In a moment," etc. "In a mirror, millions of yojanas—the blink of an eye, the Kalpa-age mountains, and so forth—are contained within a mere atom; where such is the case, how can there be duality or unity? (41)

The meaning is this: where even in an extremely subtle atom there exist contradictions regarding its own reality—such as moments being eons, mountains filling [the space], and millions of *yojanas*—and these enter [into that atom] by taking recourse in falsity (*mithyātva*), then duality and unity likewise enter into it precisely through their falsity. || 41 ||
For the thought "I did this in the past" arises in the mind;
yet in an instant it becomes true and then false—the dream-delusion serves as the illustration. (42)
The real is the empirical, and the unreal is the apparent. || 42 ||
For time is indeed very long in suffering, but always much shorter in happiness;
thus, the night of Hariścandra is said to have lasted twelve years.
To illustrate the point already stated, he cites popular experience and a narrative—beginning with the word "duḥkhe" (in suffering). "Uditā" means manifested or arisen.

The certainty that arises within, whose nature is truth and which is indeed truth itself— just as the state of being a bracelet and so forth exists in gold— that very certainty shines in consciousness.
He says—“ascertainment”—to show that the manifestation of consciousness (citi) follows only the fluctuations of the mind (cittavṛtti), and not the actual state of things (vastuvṛtta). || 44 ||
There is no twinkling of an eye, nor is there a kalpa; there is no nearness, nor is there distance.
It is only the reflection of the atomic consciousness that thus stands as various other things, as if they were distinct entities.
What, then, is the actual state of affairs? He says: "No" (na). || 45 ||
Between light and darkness, between the distant and the near, between a moment and an eon, and even between two bodies that are one consciousness—there is not the slightest difference at all. (46)

In the same way, he states that even among other contradictory things, there is no difference precisely because of the non-difference from the consciousness that is their substrate: "prakāśa... (verse 46).
Because it is the essence of the senses, it is direct perception; because it transcends them, it is beyond direct perception.
Though it arises as the object of sight, this mind is in truth the seer itself, whose nature is existence.

He provides the answer to the question, "Is perception of an unreal nature? with the word "perception" (*pratyakṣam*). It is so called because it is the essence of the external and internal organs (*akṣa*), as it brings about the manifestation of their respective objects in immediate presence.
Therefore, that which transcends it is beyond its scope. Alternatively:
He states that this [knowledge] is also perceptual because it arises through the superimposition of what is visible and accessible to means of valid cognition such as perception;
thus, the meaning is "it is perceptual. || 47 ||
As long as there is the perception of a bracelet, so long does the state of being gold not exist;
and as long as there is the occurrence of visibility, so long does that subtle essence not exist.
If that very [Self] were of the nature of the visible, then from what source could there be the abandonability of the visible? To this he says: "As long as...

That "portion" (kalā) is the reality whose sole essence is consciousness. Thus, since it does not constitute the supreme human goal in the form of the visible, its abandonability follows; this is the intended meaning. || 48 ||
Just as when the state of being a bracelet is unmanifest and unseen, only the pervasive nature of gold remains;
so too, only Brahman—pure, stainless, and absolute—is perceived.

For this very reason, with the intention that when there is no conceptualization of the object as having the nature of the visible, or when that which is conceptually constructed is not seen, it is the goal of human life because it is of the nature of Brahman, he says: "In the state of being a bracelet," etc. The division of the words is: *akṛte* (when unmade) and *adṛṣṭe* (when unseen). || 49 ||
Because it is everything, its nature is existent; because it is difficult to perceive, its nature is non-existent.
Because it is of the nature of consciousness, it is sentient; because there is no possibility of an object of cognition, it is insentient.

He states the intention behind the portion of the question, "of the nature of non-existence," with the words "because it is everything. It is of the nature of existence because it manifests as the existent form permeated by all things; and it is of the nature of non-existence because it is difficult to perceive in its isolated form.
The intention is that such usage is seen in the Śruti: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; from that, the existent was born."

Furthermore, he provides the answer to the question "What is conscious and what is unconscious" with the word "conscious. The meaning is that you have stated that the non-conscious (acit) is the unconscious (acetana). || 50 ||

195. In this world, which consists solely of the wonder of consciousness and is of the nature of the self-luminous manifestation of consciousness— resembling a tree moved by the wind— how can there be any differentiation between consciousness and its object?

He establishes the non-existence of the object of consciousness (*cetya*) with the words beginning "the wonder of consciousness" (*ciccamatkāra*): in that which is the self of the manifestation of consciousness (*citpratibhātmā*), whose nature is the manifestation of consciousness, which is unstable like a tree shaken by the wind, and which is utterly non-existent like a tree made of air;
[this occurs] in the conceptualization of the object of consciousness (*cetyakalana*), that is, in the construction of the state of being an object resting upon consciousness. || 51 ||
Just as a mirage is the appearance of thick heat, so too is the world the appearance of consciousness, though non-dual and substantial. 52.

He provides an illustration regarding the mere flash of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*) with the word "yathā" (just as): [it is like] heat (*tāpa*), meaning sunlight (*ātapa*); [like] thick (*pīna*), meaning abundant (*pracura*). || 52 ||

That which is free from disease, fashioned by the rays of the sun in an exceedingly subtle manner—what thought can there be regarding existence or non-existence therein, as if at the beginning of a kalpa? (53)

Just as the creation of gold and other substances by the rays of the sun—regarding which it will be explained later—is characterized by both existence and non-existence, like the world in the form of the Brahma-kalpa and so forth, the non-existence of that which serves as a mere metaphor for what is unreal is perfectly clear.

And in this way, what indeed is the cognition of the distinction between consciousness (cit) and the object of consciousness (cetya)? The meaning is that it is devoid of any objective referent. || 53 ||
Just as gold shines in the sky when marked by particles of dust through illusion, so does this world appear; for where is there any real differentiation between consciousness and its objects? (54)
Just as through illusion (māyā) and ignorance (avidyā), gold shines and appears in the sky, which is marked by particles of dust and touched by a mere fragment of a sunbeam. || 54 ||

Just as in a dream, a city of Gandharvas, or a city of one's imagination, there is no perception of walls— being neither existent nor non-existent— know the world to be likewise a long-lasting delusion.
And so, for one who perceives things as they truly are, [the mind] emerges through the space of consciousness, purified by the practice of cultivating such reasoning. (56)
"Let it be so that the world is established through delusion; what follows from that? To this he replies: "And thus...

And thus, for those whose minds have become pure through the repeated practice characterized by the constant contemplation of these aforementioned arguments establishing falsity, there arises the vision of things as they truly are.

The meaning is that for a person who has perceived the ultimate Brahman, once ignorance is destroyed, the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) no longer emerges from the space of consciousness (cidākāśa); thus it is established that there is no return. Alternatively, according to the vision of reality refined by logic, the meaning is that creation itself never occurred. || 56 ||

There is no difference between a wall and space apart from the perception of what is seen; so too, from the conceptualization of Brahman down to the individual soul (jīva), whatever has been established is indeed merely established [as such]. 57.

Alternatively, he says "no" [in verse 57], meaning that although [the Self] appears as if divided solely due to the distinctions in the perceptions that differentiate the forms of objects, it is not so in reality, because the experience of the living being (jīva) is established from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
Due to their appearance, they are devoid of reality within the space of consciousness;
for they shine forth, being unmanifestable, like rays from a mass of light.
If there is no difference [between them], then how do the perceptions of distinctions such as walls and so forth arise? To this he says: "Because of appearance" (*pratibhāsāt*).

The meaning is that those perceptions occur in such a way as to be devoid of reality (*sattva-śūnya*). He says "unmanifestable" (*anirbhāvya*) because, if they were absolutely non-existent, their appearance would be impossible, like a sky-flower. This is from the perspective of logical reasoning (*yauktika-dṛśā*).
The meaning is that they are inexpressible. || 58 ||

Because of its union with its own wonder, the manifestation of the appearance of multiplicity is indeed the supreme intuition (pratibhā), which is the self of all, like a seed that is the essence of the tree.
Having thus provided the answer to the question "What is sentient and what is insentient? along with its supporting arguments and incidental discussion, [the author],
in order to dispel the King's doubt regarding his ignorance, sets aside the answers to the remaining questions for the King’s sake and provides the response to two or three of them individually.

He provides the answer to the question— "Why is duality, which was introduced as a consequence of describing the falsity of duality, not separate [from that falsity]?"— with the words "pṛthaktā" (separateness).

This refers to the self-luminous nature (*svacamatkāra*) of the internal light of the Self, which is the manifestation of the mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) conditioned by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of separateness.

The meaning is that, although duality appears due to its connection with that [consciousness] which is characterized by the power of manifesting distinctness, it is nonetheless non-distinct. He states the reason for this: "consisting of all" (*sarvātmikā*). "Manifestation" (*pratibhā*) refers to the self-luminous light of consciousness (*ātmaprakāśa*).
Just as the seed contains the tree within it, whether manifold or non-manifold, yet appears as a single vision;
so too is Brahman, the infinite universe, peaceful like the expanse of space.

Explaining the analogy "like the seed that is the self of the tree," he provides the answer to the question, "Who, having placed within [itself] like a seed within [the fruit], exists as the one who traverses the three times?"— namely, "the seed. The seed, which is of a single vision (*ekadṛk*) and a single form (*ekarūpa*), is both manifold (*nānā*), meaning distinct, and non-manifold (*anānā*), meaning non-distinct, in its state of being the tree existing within.
Having assumed the form of a tree situated within, even Brahmā exists as the innumerable worlds; such is the meaning.
Just as the tree existing within a seed remains in a state of non-duality with space,
so too does consciousness remain in a state of being the witness of the world existing within Brahman.

He clarifies the intended meaning of the statement "like the hollow of space" with the words "of the seed," etc. The two genitives are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Just as the existence of the tree within the seed—due to its extreme subtlety—is non-dual with space and equal to the ether, so too is the existence of the world within Brahman [non-dual] because of the Self being the witness; that is, [the world exists] in its witness.

Because it is not perceived as separate, its existence is solely in the form of consciousness; thus, due to the absence of any differentiator of consciousness, its similarity to the expanse of space is the intended meaning. || 61 ||
All is peaceful, unborn, one, without beginning or middle; here there is no manifestation of parts whatsoever in any way.
With a mind tranquil and free from dualities, [one perceives] the one as many, pure—
It exists as the unborn, single expansion, whose nature is beyond manifestation.

Indicating that by this much alone the answer to all questions has been effectively stated, he concludes by demonstrating the ultimate reality of non-dual pure consciousness, which is the supreme intended object of all inquiries,
with the word "Peaceful" (śāntam). It is realized only by those whose minds are tranquil and free from dualities.

It is purified by the removal of illusion (*māyā*), its effects, and impurity; thus it is the singular state of mind, free from dualities and tranquil. It is manifold yet devoid even of the quality called oneness. Because it is the greatest of the great, it alone expands everywhere without restraint; thus it is the "single expansion. In ultimate reality, it exists as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) in the form of radiance.
This is the meaning. By the two words "aja" (unborn), there is the exclusion of the modifications such as birth and so forth, as well as those things possessing them. || 62 ||
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Shattering of Karala's Doubts," in the section on the Means to Liberation within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the work of the Sage. 80.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Dispelling of Doubts," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
p. 324) 196 The eighty-first canto, 81.
The Rākṣasī said:
"Oh, how purifying is the speech on the ultimate truth uttered by your minister!
Let this lotus-eyed king speak now. (1)

Here, the King, the knower of distinctions, while providing answers in sequence to the remaining questions, occasionally expresses logical arguments even regarding those that have already been stated. (1)

Although the king’s own knowledge of reality was already recognized through the mere sight of the marvel in the minister’s words, the Rākṣasī, desiring to hear more as she anticipated an even greater marvel in what the king would say, spoke: "Aho! (Verse 1).
The King said:
They say that the absence of the perception of the world is the supreme perception, which is the renunciation of all mental constructs and the grasping of that [Reality] with the mind. (2)

And the King, perceiving his intention, demonstrates Brahman— the primary object of the essential meaning of all questions— through the great charm of an expression that appears to be a contradiction, by means of the four verses beginning with "jāgata-". The absence of the worldly cognition, which is characterized by the perception of the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], is characterized by pure awareness.
The meaning is that his vision is characterized by the fourth state (*turya*), which is the nature of the self-luminous substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) itself, consisting solely of cessation.
And since that [vision] occurs through the grasping of that [substratum] in the form of exclusive devotion to it, he shows that grasping by means of its definition: "all... (verse 2).

That through whose contraction and expansion the dissolution and creation of the universe occur, which is the ultimate goal of the Vedānta scriptures, and which is beyond the reach of words—[to that I bow]. (3)
By whose illusory contraction and expansion [the world arises]; the remainder of the sentence being "that which is beyond the reach of words. (3)
Situated between the two extremes, yet consisting of those two extremes in its center,
his play, which is of the nature of consciousness, is this entire world of moving and non-moving beings.

The meaning is that it is inexpressible (*anirvacanīya*), situated in the interval between the two extremes of existence and non-existence, manifestation and non-manifestation. For this very reason, although it is swallowed by the extreme of non-existence at both the beginning and the end, in the middle it consists of both extremes—being "in some places" and "not in some places"—due to spatial limitation. Likewise, although it is swallowed by non-manifestation at the beginning and the end, in the middle...

It appears in various forms according to the capacity of each respective sense organ, yet in its true essence it does not appear as such; thus, in the interim, it consists of these two poles. Therefore, because it is a modification of the mind belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha—which is of the nature of a junction between existence and non-existence, and a junction between consciousness and insentience—this world is a mere play (līlā); this is the meaning. || 4 ||
O auspicious lady, that which, despite being the soul of all, is never divided even as a single mass—
that you describe as the eternal Brahman, pure existence alone.
The state of being a single mass is the state of being an indivisible reality; this is what is spoken of and what is inquired about. || 5 ||
This subtle atom (aṇu) is the wind born of sensation; its own delusion is seen by the seer [the reading "bhrāntidṛgadṛśyata" is correct].
Therefore, nothing such as wind and so forth exists; there is only pure consciousness.

Among the remaining points mentioned in the counsel, he first answers the question: "What is wind, and what is non-wind?"—[this is the explanation of the resultant meaning of the phrase beginning with "In its own self"]: He who, being of such a nature that his perception of wind constitutes an error or a misconception, saw the wind.
But from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is indeed air alone; thus he says: "Therefore... (6).
Because sound is perceived through cognition, there is the appearance of error regarding sound;
therefore, one has gone very far from the perception of the word and the meaning of the word here.
One should understand that the answer to the question, "What is sound, and what is non-sound? is exactly the same; thus he says: "Sound... (verse 7).
He is the subtle atom, he is everything, and yet he is nothing; he is "I," he is not "I," and he is indeed that very reality.
For this Self, whose nature is all-powerful, his own intuition alone is the cause here.

He provides the answer to the question "Who is everything and what is nothing? with the words: "He is the subtle atom" (*so’ṇuḥ*). He resolves the question "Who am I, and what might I not be? with the words: "He is I" (*so’ham*). Upon the extraction of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), "He is I" [remains], but in that form, "I am not. Alternatively, "He is I" refers to the indication by means of both the ego-sense and the essence (*tattā*); however, when there is no indication by those two, [it is simply "He"].

The meaning is: "Neither I nor he. Thus, regarding the diversity of the real and the unreal, he states the cause: the meaning is that the power of manifestation (*pratibhāśakti*) is the cause for the manifestation of the real form. || 8 ||
The self is attained with hundreds of efforts, yet once it is attained, nothing at all [remains to be gained];
and even that which is attained here is either the supreme or nothing at all.

To answer the two questions—"Is anything not obtained that can be attained through hundreds of efforts? and "Does nothing become obtained [in this state]?"—he says: "The Self. He establishes the point that "nothing is obtained" when this [Self] is obtained by saying: "Obtained.
Because this very thing is of the nature of the Self, it is already obtained even beforehand; therefore, effort is not fruitful in its regard. Consequently...
The meaning is that you asked in such a manner with the intention that there is nothing whatsoever—the supreme, the most excellent, or otherwise—that is the fruit of effort. || 9 ||
The creeper of worldly existence continues to flourish for a long time during the springs of birth as long as awakening has not arisen to act as its root-destroyer.

Then, dispelling the doubt that the effort toward knowledge is entirely useless, he states the intended meaning of the phrase "but not everything is obtained" with the word "tāvat": thus, as long as the destruction of the ignorance that is the root of saṃsāra has not occurred, even though the reality of the Self has been attained, it is not attained in its entirety—that is, in its full form. However, through awakening...
The meaning is that since the full [attainment] is obtained, there is no futility in the effort. || 10 ||
By this subtle form, which as it were attains visibility,
this [world] has been carried away while remaining in its own state, just as the ocean is by heat.
"By what high [gain] has one's own self been lost for the sake of a healthy life? To this he gives the answer: "By the subtle," and so forth.

The ellipsis is "having attained the state of form (*rūpatvam*), that is, the state of possessing shape. "By heat" means by the heat of the desert land. This refers to the actual nature of the self. || 11 ||

By means of this subtle consciousness, Mount Meru and the three worlds are regarded as a blade of grass; having vomited forth that which was situated within and without, it is seen as being composed of māyā.
He provides the answer to the question, "By what subtle thing is Meru contained within, and the three worlds reduced to a blade of grass?"—namely, "by this.

The meaning is that Meru is contained within, and the three worlds are made like a blade of grass. If it is contained within, then how is it perceived outside? To this he says, "having vomited forth," meaning as if having vomited it out from within.
That is to say, having conceptualized it as if it were external. || 12 ||
Whatever exists within the atom of consciousness is seen externally;
for this, the example is the embracing of a desired woman in one's mental constructs (saṃkalpa) by a person possessed by passion. (13)

The meaning is that, according to the experience of those possessed by passion, they perceive even an internal woman created by imagination and her embrace as if they were external, because they serve as the seeds for external impressions (saṃskāra). || 13 ||
Just as at the initial creation, consciousness possessing all powers perceives everything through its own arisen nature, so too does a mountain instantly perceive everything within its own volition.

Regarding the cause for such a fixed rule, he says: "In the initial creation" (*ādisarge*). The meaning is that the very *niyati* (destiny or necessity) active at the beginning of creation is the cause. Just as from the first joint of a sugarcane or a bamboo, a specific emergence of branches, leaves, sprouts, and so forth occurs, and exactly the same occurs from the second and subsequent joints, so it is by its own nature (*svataḥ*).

Likewise, there is a restriction in the original creative resolve; even though it was a mountain [then], in the present resolve, the restriction arises from itself—this is the implied meaning. || 14 ||
Whatever appears internally to one who is noble, he perceives it exactly as it is; the mind in this case is like a clear mirror. (15)
Of one who is well-born and whose mind has become manifest. || 16 ||
Even by this pure consciousness, which is as subtle as an atom,
the entire universe is completely filled on every side.
He provides the answer to the question, "How was a distance of a hundred yojanas filled by something as small as a single atom? with the words *paramāṇutayā* ("by way of being an atom").

The meaning is: by being an atom spatially (*deśataḥ*), by being pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) substantially (*vastutaḥ*), and by being most subtle temporally (*kālataḥ*)—that is, by that which serves as the very limit even for the conceptualization of the three kinds of delimitation. *Viṣvak* means everywhere (*sarvataḥ*). || 16 ||
Though minute, it does not fit even within hundreds of yojanas;
because it is all-pervading, beginningless, and formless, it is without shape.
To the question, "How is it that he who is but an atom (aṇu) appears [to occupy space], even within hundreds of yojanas?", he provides the answer: "He is indeed an atom. (17)
Just as a child is deceived by a rogue man using a sword [the reading "khiṅgena" is also found], through the movements of beautiful eyebrows, glances from the eyes, and various gestures. (18)

The foolish and deluded man is deceived by women through their playful gestures, the beauty of their forms, the movements of their eyebrows, their glances from the eyes, and their various actions; having been enticed, he is brought under their control and led away. 18.

By means of the pure light of consciousness, the world—including its mountains and grass—is incessantly made to dance; likewise, it always performs the dramatic representation through its own manifestation. (19)

Just as in this illustration, so too by the light of consciousness (cidāloka), having manifested the dramatic performance—that is, the expressive gestures—the world is eternally enacted; such is the meaning. || 19 ||

Just as by means of that very subtle cloth, because it is of infinite form, one covers Meru and the other mountains after having placed consciousness outside while it is within; so too, having placed that [consciousness] outside while it is within... [the reading *saṃvid antarbhavad bāhye* is correct]. || 20 ||
To the question, "In whose belly, it is said, do the multitudes of mountains exist? he replies with the word "tena" (by that).
The meaning is: just as a cloth, having made the various forms within itself—such as Mount Meru and so forth—appear as if they were external, envelops them; in that same manner.
Because its nature is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, it is greater than Mount Meru;
yet, being of the nature of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, it is subtle, supreme, and most minute.
To the question, "How can an atom, without abandoning its atomicity, take on a form even more massive than Mount Meru? he provides the following answer: "Space and time... (Verse 21).
A comparison between that which has the nature of pure consciousness-space and an atom is not at all fitting, just like a comparison between Mount Meru and a mustard seed.
The intention expressed by the minister regarding the use of the term "atom" (*aṇu*) with respect to the self in response to the counter-question was as follows:

"Because it is inexpressible and because it is inaccessible due to its abiding in the mind as the sixth sense-organ, the self is pure consciousness alone; thus, the atom is subtler even than space. And [this was stated] by Karkaṭī as well.

Having determined that this was indeed intended and accepted, the king, in order to demonstrate his own discernment, refutes it with the words "pure" (*śuddha*). It is not unperceived merely on account of its subtlety;
rather, by resorting to a similarity with an atom—the ultimate limit of excellence in perception—it is designated as an "atom" (*anu*) through figurative usage (*gauṇī*).
The sense is that it is possible. || 22 ||

Having fashioned the state of atomicity within the Supreme Self by means of the power of illusion (māyā), there arises a diversity here, just as bracelets are formed from gold; yet in this, there is equality.

If it is asked how there can be such designations in scriptural passages as "smaller than the small, greater than the great; this atomic Self is to be known by the mind," the answer is that because the Self possesses all powers, it manifests through *māyā* both greatness and atomicity; thus, in this context, the word "atomic" (*aṇu*) is used in its primary sense. It is not [used figuratively] here.

He says that it is the "sign of equality" (*samatānimitta*), namely: "by illusion" (*māyā*). By means of illusion, [it is] adorned with peacock feathers; that is to say, by the variegated (*śabala*). Just as there would be no equality here between gold and its own produced form, such as a bracelet, because of the grammatical rule stating that *nānā* has the senses of "many" and "without," and because the negative particle *nañ* is prescribed in its own sense [as *nānā*].

The word "nānā" has the sense of negation. For it is precisely in this way that such scriptural passages as, "The individual soul (jīva) is to be known as a part of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair divided a hundredfold," and your own statement that "the self is the hundredth part of the tip of a hair," are rendered consistent; this is the intended meaning. || 23 ||
By this lamp, which is of the nature of experience, illumination is made manifest;
for otherwise, there would be the destruction of its own existence. (24)
He provides the answer to the question, "What is the lamp of light and darkness?"—namely, "The manifest" (prakaṭa).

The meaning is: if there were another illumination occurring without this lamp of the Self, then indeed there would be the destruction of its own existence—that is, its non-appearance; prior to that [illumination], it would simply not exist. || 24 ||
If the entire world, including the sun and so forth, were a single inert entity, then what would the nature of light be, where would it exist, or what would it be? (25)
Furthermore, he states that if this were so, the entire world would be blind: "That which... (verse 25).
That state of being pure consciousness consisting of pure existence, which is established by itself within its own self—that very same thing is seen as a subtle light situated externally. (26)
Since light, darkness, and so forth are imagined within its own interior by the atomic consciousness (cidaṇu), its manifestation is dependent upon that [consciousness];
thus he says: "Pure," etc. This very thing [is] by that, by this atomic [consciousness]. || 26 ||
The splendors of the sun, the moon, and fire are not distinct from the mass of darkness;
the only difference lies in their color, being white or black.
[Objection: But surely, since illumination is accomplished by the sun, the moon, and so forth, what is the use of a conscious atom (cid-aṇu) there?

To this he says: "The lights... [meaning] from the mass of darkness, which is their own cause, ignorance. "To this extent" means that there is no difference in the aspect of insentience; this is the intended meaning.
Just as there would be no distinction between soot and mist, or between a cloud and mist, such is the state of light and darkness: there is no difference between them.

The meaning is that when there is a mist the color of collyrium, it is designated as "cloud"; thus, whatever distinction exists between a cloud and mist, the same applies to light and darkness. Therefore, the established position is that there is no inherent distinction between the two. || 28 ||
It is said that when the sun of consciousness shines upon these two inert things so that they may be perceived,
they attain a state of identity with the existence [of consciousness] itself.
He states that there is no difference between those two even on account of their having existence and manifestation dependent upon consciousness: "Of the two insentient things," etc. (29).
The one Sun alone shines tirelessly day and night,
both within and without, even inside stones and other such things, never setting nor rising.
But since consciousness never faces the possibility of non-manifestation, he says: "It shines" (tapatīti). || 30 ||
By him, the soul of celebrated self, this triple world shines as a hut with a hard interior, richly filled with various vessels of perception. (31)
Rich with various kinds of perceptions, enjoyments, vessels, and their means of attainment, it is like a hut with a hard, hollow interior.
By this [fire], which destroys the body of darkness, even the quality of darkness is tormented;
through its illuminating radiance, all darkness is made manifest.

Now, one might object: "If darkness is illuminated by the Self, then its very nature as darkness would perish; for it is impossible to make that which is non-manifest by nature manifest without destroying it. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The state of being darkness... By means of this light—namely, consciousness (caitanya)—which is devoid of the manifestation of its own objective essence (svatattva).

By not destroying the body of *tamas* which is its own essential nature, *tamas* is heated—that is, it is agitated for the sake of becoming an effect; consequently, the meaning is that *tamas*, having become the entire world, is manifested. || 32 ||
Just as the existence of light and darkness is made manifest when the lotus and the water-lily are revealed by the shining sun, so too is the existence of consciousness made manifest. || 33 ||

With the intention that this [consciousness] does not cause the cessation of those [objects], because it is the cause for manifesting their existence, he says: "Just as the sun, by bringing about day and night, displays form;
so too consciousness, having made both existent and non-existent, displays form. (34)
Being and non-being are light and darkness, characterized by manifestation and disappearance. (34)
Within the atom of consciousness reside all atoms of experience, just as within a sweet-tasting fruit reside the splendors of its flowers, leaves, and fruits. (35)
He provides the answer to the question, "In whose interior do all experiential atoms reside? with the words "of the atom of consciousness" (*cidaṇoḥ*).
As for the phrase "just as": the intention is that honey is produced by bees through their gathering of the juices of leaves, fruits, and so forth; or alternatively, [it refers to] the sweet juice.
Or [it is] the beauty of spring, or the sap of trees and so forth existing at that time. || 35 ||
