All these atoms of experience arise from the minute atom of consciousness,
like various successions of sugar-candy pieces from the essence of the springtime.
He explains that very point clearly with the words "rising" (*udyanti*): "Successions of forest tracts" (*khaṇḍaparamparā*) refers to the sequences of the beauty of forest groves. || 36 ||
The supreme atom, though utterly devoid of flavor due to its extreme subtlety, by virtue of being the sole generator of all existing flavors, becomes flavorful of its own accord. (37)
He provides the answer to the question, "What is that subtle essence which, though utterly tasteless, is tasted incessantly?"—namely, "The Supreme Self.
"Whatever flavor exists in its entirety within water, that does not exist by itself apart from it, just as a reflection does not exist apart from a mirror. (38)
It can also be said that he "tastes" because the manifestation of flavor within all water has him as its cause;
thus he says, "Whichever... This refers to that flavor. (38)
By one who has abandoned everything established [in duality] through the supreme atom of pure consciousness (cinmātra),
the world is abandoned through non-perception, while through perception, everything is embraced.
He provides the answer to the question, "By what does one who abandons everything, while being subtle, remain supported by everything?"—namely, "by abandoning.
This means by non-perception (*asaṃvitti*), that is, by non-manifestation (*asphuraṇa*). || 39 ||
"The entire world was covered by that which was incapable of protecting itself;

having extended its own atomicity (or, according to another reading, the atomicity of consciousness) to the highest degree like a canopy—who, being an atom incapable of covering itself, could have covered the world? To this, he provides the answer:
"By means of incapacity": in concealment, having delimited [the object] within the secret place. || 40 ||

One whose form is like the sky of the Supreme Self is unable to protect oneself for even a moment, or by even the slightest degree, just as an elephant cannot protect itself in a grove of durva grass.
He clearly states the intention of what was said: "In the protection of the self," [verse 41].
Nevertheless, having pervaded the universe and been known, he protects it in an instant;
like a child, he makes the world his playground—oh, how profound is his illusory power! 42.

The "Jagat" is the multitude of living beings included within the world; being known—that is, having attained its own Self—it protects or preserves them, just as a child, when known and awakened, protects a grain of corn, whereas it does not do so while asleep.
Now, one might ask: how can such a self-luminous and full Self experience the forgetfulness of its own nature like a child? To this, he says:
Through its inclination toward pure consciousness alone, this world, though existing, lives;
it is like a variegated forest grove that comes to life through the awakening of the essence of spring.
To the question, "In the dissolution of the world, what exists that truly lives even though it has perished?", he provides the answer:

"By the support of pure consciousness" (*cinmātrānunayena*). Although the world has perished—here the elision of the *m* is Vedic—the meaning is that it has dissolved through dissolution (*pralaya*). It lives by the support (*avalambana*) of pure consciousness; for even in dissolution, it exists solely through the presence of consciousness.
The meaning is that it remains as a residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of the world; by means of the cause, which is the awakening of the sprouts and so forth during the spring season. || 43 ||
In this way, the entire world arises from the mind itself, just as a forest grove appears variegated through the joy of the honey-scented spring breeze. (44)
If the world lives by the very existence of Brahman alone during both dissolution and creation, then what is the distinction during creation such that it manifests?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "the existence of the mind" (*cittasattā*). The sense is that during dissolution, the existence of the mind does not exist separately; this is the distinction. || 44 ||
Know for certain that this world is truly composed of consciousness alone;
know that the cluster of sprouts is nothing other than the very essence of the spring.
Because it is the essence of all composite parts, this very atom possesses a thousand rays and eyes; it is eternal and arises without parts.
And thus, he says "It is true" [in verses 45 and 46] to show that there is no real difference between consciousness and the world.
For the awareness of a fraction of a moment appears to the atomic consciousness,
since a flood of thousands of kalpas [is experienced] in a dream, like old age and childhood.

To the question, "What is the atom that has no parts, yet possesses a thousand hands and eyes? he gives the answer: "All," and so forth. The meaning is: because [He] is the essence and the very self of all composite entities—that is, the fourfold collection of beings. To the question, "What is a moment (nimeṣa), a great aeon (mahākalpa), and hundreds of millions of aeons? he gives the answer: "A moment," and so forth. And this...
This has already been demonstrated by the narrative of Līlā. || 47 ||
Then, even that atom of a moment expands for hundreds of millions of kalpas through the play of universal existence; it is but a single intuition that unfolds.
Just as the conviction arises, "I have eaten," even when one has not yet eaten, so too does the determination of conceptualization arise within a mere moment. (49)

Those possessed by latent impressions (vāsanā)— or, according to another reading, those established in latent impressions— are seen to have the conviction "I have eaten" even without having eaten, just as one perceives one's own death in a dream. (50)
The worlds are established within the supreme atom, the conscious self;
indeed, all worldly appearances proceed from that alone. (51)
He provides the answer to the question, "In what do the worlds abide, as seeds in a tree?"—namely, "The worlds... (verse 51).
Whatever exists in something arises from that very thing; it is that [itself].
Modifications and the like are observed in that which possesses form, but not in the stainless sky.
Whatever exists here arises from that very source, just as a statue arises from a pillar; and that [effect] is indeed identical to that [cause]. || 52 ||
In consciousness (citi), the beings that exist at present, as well as those that will come to be in the future, reside like trees within a seed. (53)

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "The seeds end in the partless" (bījāni niṣkalāntāni) as follows: "In consciousness" (citi). The meaning is that past beings, those existing now, and those yet to come in the future—all beings—always abide in consciousness. || 53 ||

By means of these two— time and consciousness— the subtle Self, like a grain of rice within its husk, has resorted to its own bodily limbs, which are as vast as an eon yet as fleeting as a blink of an eye.
He states the purport of the verse, "A kalpa [is contained] within a single blink of an eye, like a seed," as follows: "nimeṣeti.
Two grains of food—meaning a grain of rice and its constituent parts—are encircled and enveloped on all sides by the husk, just as a rice-grain is by its bran.
This subtle atom (aṇu) and these two—the kalpa and the nimeṣa—resort to a mere portion of their own self.

The meaning is that [the Lord] is the one who has taken recourse [to this world], according to the words of the Blessed One: "Pervading all this, I stand supporting the universe with a single portion. || 54 ||
Remaining like one who is indifferent, not touched even in the slightest degree by the states of being an enjoyer or a doer—such is one's own Self throughout the entire world. (55)
He provides the answer to the question, "Who is an agent if they do not even resort to being an author of purposeful action?
with the verse beginning "as if indifferent," and so forth. || 55 ||
For when the existence of the world arises from the supreme atom of pure consciousness, the states of being the enjoyer and the agent reside solely within that atom. (56)
It remains alone, entirely without any connection to activity or experience.
Nothing whatsoever is ever created by anyone at any time, nor does anything ever perish; this is the shattering of the perceived world from the human perspective.

To the question "Why is there no connection with action or enjoyment there?", he says: "The world," etc. The meaning is that the object of action is ultimately non-existent. Then, for what purpose is the refutation of the unreal visible world performed in the Vedāntas? To this he says: "From the human state," etc.
The meaning is that [this occurs] by virtue of the human condition and through the power of conventional and rational vision, not by the power of the vision of ultimate reality. || 57 ||
O night-walker, know that all this, appearing as a uniform manifestation within the treasury of space, is designated by the term "world" and is beginningless.

What, then, is the vision of ultimate reality? He shows it with the word "all": the world, as such, is merely a verbal designation, expressed by sound alone. The sense is that this is based on the Vedic scripture stating, "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name. (58)

The atomic consciousness, for the sake of establishing the appearance of the visible world, assumes as an external form that internal wonder of consciousness which is perfectly established within itself. (59)
"To bring the object of sight to completion, the seer leads his own self into the state of being seen;
for who, while seeing the object, can see their own self without eyes? To this question, he gives the answer:
"The atom of consciousness" (*cidaṇu*). [He sees] the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkṛti*), which is the power of Māyā pervaded by consciousness, as an external form.
By way of external conceptual proliferation. || 59 ||
This [reality] exists externally and internally within sound, but not as a material object;
it exists throughout the three worlds for the sake of instructing sentient beings because its nature is consciousness.

Now, one might object: since Brahman is understood through the Śruti as "without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior," being devoid of the distinction between inner and outer, how can it be said that "it bears the internal wonder of consciousness in an external form"? To this, he says: "This [world]," etc. That which is external and that which is internal—this [is what exists] within the three worlds.

It is intended for the instruction of sentient beings—that is, those living beings who possess the requisite capacity—only in words, not in the actual reality; the meaning is that [reality] consists solely of the nature of consciousness. || 60 ||
The seer, proceeding toward the unperceived state, perceives the various selves as if they were falling within the range of the eye's vision—appearing as if real, though they exist as if unreal. (61)
Having explained the purport of the passage ending with "leading [the self] to the state of being seen," he states the meaning of the remainder of the question as follows:

"The seer. Although the Self is eternally immediate, because it is veiled by ignorance, it always manifests through the limitation of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa); through identification with that [organ], it is the "seer."
Because it is veiled by the limitation of external objects, the unperceived state—

having become as if directed toward an object visible to the eye— goes outward through the channel of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) that has emerged via the eyes; thus, while being the very nature of the Self, it stands as if it were the unreal form of a jar or similar object.

He perceives by his own self-consciousness alone and illuminates [objects] through that, not with the eyes, because the eyes serve merely as a gateway; thus, the meaning is that he is said to be "eyeless. || 61 ||
And the seer does not attain visibility, for he is unreal and non-substantial;
since nothing whatsoever exists within the Self, how could another reach that state? 62.

He establishes this point—that what exists appears as if non-existent—with the words "And not... He asks why it does not go [elsewhere] and answers with "In itself," the sense being that it is impossible for that which exists to become of the nature of non-existence. || 62 ||
Vision itself is the eye, and that [vision] is her own body which terminates in latent impressions (vāsanā);
having made herself visible through external form, she has arisen as the seer.
Thus, he states that the state of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtā*) is also false because it is dependent upon a false object of sight: "The seer alone...
The eyes, the two organs of sight, are merely gateways; rather, the seer is the immediate self-consciousness (*aparokṣātmacaitanya*) itself within the eyes, according to the Vedic scripture:
"The eye of the eye. And that seer, from its manifestation until its subsequent disappearance, [remains constant].
The meaning is that, having brought the visible world to an end by means of the cessation of latent impressions (vāsanā), she herself arose as its seer and thus imagined herself [as such]. || 63 ||
The existence of the object of sight can never occur without the state of being a seer,
just as there is no son without a father, nor unity without duality.
And thus, since both conceptualizations are mutually dependent, they are both false; so he says with the words beginning "not without," etc. (64).
The seer alone becomes the object of sight; there is no such thing as the state of being a seer without that [object].
It is like a son without a father, or like the state of being enjoyed without one who enjoys. 65.

In the manifestation of the seer and the seen, the mind certainly possesses the capacity due to its nature as consciousness, just as pure gold has the capacity for the making of bracelets and other ornaments. (66)
The object of perception lacks the capacity to create its own perceiver because it is insentient, just as a golden bracelet has no power to produce gold. (67)
The manifestation of what is unseen through volition makes that which is non-existent appear as existent;
it is without cause and has delusion as its basis, just as gold appears in the form of a bracelet through error. (68)
Because consciousness (cit) is endowed with the capacity to perceive and illuminate the object of perception, it therefore brings about the manifestation of the visible world;
this has ignorance as its cause, being rooted solely in nescience (ajñāna). || 68 ||

For just as the nature of gold does not manifest when there is the appearance of a bracelet, even though the gold is present, so too the [true] form [of consciousness] does not shine forth while the state of subject and object persists. (69)

If the seer himself becomes the object of sight, then why is this object not clearly perceived as being merely the seer? To this he replies: "As the state of being a bracelet... Just as the nature of gold does not shine forth clearly while the state of being a bracelet exists—because it is only imagined in the deluded mind due to its non-manifestation when [the gold] is present—so too, if the seer were to exist in the form of the object of sight...
The meaning is that the body of the seer does not shine forth. || 69 ||
The seer, existing as the object of sight, depends upon the state of being a seer,
just as gold maintains its nature as gold when there is the cognition of it as a bracelet.

If it is asked, "In that case, why could it not be that [the object] exists independently of the perceiver when the perceiver does not manifest?"—[the author] says "draṣṭrā" (by the perceiver), with the intention that this is not so because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of [the object] no longer being dependent upon that [perceiver]. [It is like] gold-ness which is already established beforehand. || 70 ||

For when there is a single manifestation, there is no existence of both the seer and the seen; when the cognition of the Supreme Being (puṃ-pratyaya) shines forth, where could the cognition of a bound soul (paśu-pratyaya) arise? 71.

If it is argued that—just as in the appearance of a bracelet, the nature of gold does not manifest while the gold itself exists—it is improper [to say the same here], because in the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "this bracelet is gold," both [the bracelet and the gold] appear as existing, so too it must be in the cognition "I am the seer"—to this he replies: "In one... (*ekasmin*).

Just as when there is doubt regarding a distant object as to whether it is a man or an animal, the state of being an animal does not appear within the scope of the cognition of "man," nor does the state of being a man appear within the portion of the cognition of "animal"; likewise,
even in the case of a cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it is impossible for both portions to be the object of a single cognition.
This is the meaning. || 71 ||
While perceiving the visible object, one does not perceive one's own self as the seer;
for when the seer falls into the state of being an object of sight, its existence remains as if non-existent.
For by being turned outward one perceives the object of sight, and by being turned inward one perceives the seer;

yet, with the intention that a twofold orientation of consciousness cannot occur simultaneously, he says: "the object of sight. "Existence" means the existence of the seer. "As if non-existent" means as if it were non-existent. || 72 ||
For the seer from whom the visible has fallen away through awakening, only pure existence shines forth;
just as in an unperceived bracelet, there is for one's own gold the state of being "not-a-bracelet."

"And who, seeing the visible world dissolved within [himself], beholding the undivided Self, does not see the visible object before him because it has ceased to exist as a visible object?"—to this question he gives the answer: "From awakening" (bodhāt). This refers to one who, having fixed their gaze upon the investigation of gold as the sole reality, disregards [the appearance] because it has not been re-integrated [into that realization]. (73)
When the object of sight exists, there is indeed a seer; the object of sight appears within the seer.
Without these two, neither one exists, nor does even a single entity exist apart from them.

Since the seeing of the seer is unavoidable even when the seen is not perceived, how can the absolute non-perception of the seen be established? To this, he says: "It is seen. The words "while the seer exists" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
For the person from whom the seen has fallen away through awakening, not even one of these two—the seer and the seen—remains.
The meaning is that, just as shade disappears when the umbrella is removed, the seer also disappears upon the disappearance of the object of sight; thus, only pure vision remains. || 74 ||
Having understood everything exactly as it is through the self consisting of pure consciousness,
there remains only something indescribable by words, utterly transparent.
By this single atom of pure consciousness, the self, the seer, and the seen have all been illuminated, as if by a lamp. (76)
To the question, "Who illuminates the self, the seer, and the seen, as if they were objects? he provides the answer:

"The self," and so forth. By this [self], which is the ultimate atom of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-paramāṇu*), the seer and all else—comprising the triad known as the knower (*mātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*māna*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—is illuminated and made manifest; thus the wise one [perceives].
"He swallows" is the syntactical connection with what follows. || 76 ||

The wise one swallows this triad known as the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, just as one regards the state of being a bracelet or other ornaments as unreal when it is actually gold. (77)

He answers the question—"By what are the three [the body, organs, and objects] scattered like bracelets and so forth from gold?"—implicitly by means of the very example mentioned previously (reading "prāktanokti"): "Gold... (verse 77).
Just as there is not even the slightest thing separate from water, earth, and so forth,
so indeed there is nothing whatsoever separate from this intrinsic nature of phenomena.

He provides the answer to the question "Why is nothing separate? with the word "yathā" (as follows): "Whatever is material, because its nature is the experience of all and it consists of the form of universal experience, for when the principle of experiencing oneness has become established, there is indeed the oneness of all in it. (79)
He demonstrates non-separateness even through reasoning: "Omnipresent," etc. (79).
By his will, there is no separation [between him and his desires], just as there is none between a wave and the great ocean;
for through the fulfillment of his every wish, there is indeed a single identity with all that is conceived.
He refutes the notion that [the world] exists separately by the will of anyone with the word "asya" (of this). The word "kila" indicates the reason.
The meaning is: because there is non-separateness—that is, oneness—between the attainment of a fruit corresponding to one's will and the object brought about by that will. || 80 ||
The Supreme Self alone exists, unconditioned by space, time, and the like;
because He is the self of all, He is the Self of all by virtue of His own inherent experience of everything. (81)

He provides the answer to the question—"How can there be duality from that single, non-existent Reality which is not limited by space, time, and so forth, yet is existent and non-different [from itself]?"—in two verses beginning with "dikkāla": "Because He is the Self of all, He is the Self of everything;
that of which nothing exists separately is the 'Self of All. By His own nature, however, He is pure experience itself, not insentient. (81)
Because it is essentially conscious, and because of the lack of realization through [dualistic] vision,
neither duality nor unity exists here in this Great Self, who is the form of all.

To explain the meaning of "of the non-existent" and "of the existent," he says: "This is existent. Because for sentient beings whose own existence is beyond doubt, this is their very Self; therefore, regarding this Self, duality and unity—pertaining to the nature of worldly existence—are not found during perception, that is, during the observation by the eyes and other senses. Thus, it is said in the Śruti that [the Self] is not "non-existent."
The meaning is: "with the intention that [they] do not exist in reality. || 82 ||
If there were some second [entity], then the oneness of the one would exist;
for duality and unity are established in relation to each other, like sunlight and shadow. (83)

[Objection: Surely duality must be false because it is dependent in nature, whereas oneness is indeed real because it is independent of a second; so why is it said that it does not exist? To this, he says: "If," for where there is no second, how can there be oneness of the one?
When unity is not established, duality itself does not exist. || 84 ||

With the intention that even the form of number conceived for the purpose of excluding a second is itself dependent on a second and is thus exactly like duality (dvitva), he says: "Where... (verse 84).
This being the case, that which exists as such must indeed exist as that very thing;
therefore, its form is not distinct from it, just as fluidity is not distinct from water. (85)
He explains this aspect—that duality also does not exist as something separate from [the Absolute], just as waves do not exist apart from the great ocean—in the words:

"But such being the case" (*evaṃ sthite tu*). This means: while reality remains thus devoid of both duality and unity, that which appears as if possessing such duality and unity, and as if abiding in duality and unity, is merely a manifestation.
Therefore, the meaning is that this form of non-dual unity is not distinct from it, just as fluidity is not distinct from water. || 85 ||
The world, appearing as various undertakings and [destructions], exists within Brahman in a state of equilibrium and undisturbed form, like a tree within a seed. (86)

"Who, moving through the three periods of time, remains having placed within himself—like a seed containing its interior—the self, the seer, the seen, and the triple world, both existent and non-existent? To this, he gives the answer: "Nānā... (in diversity). In the case of the seed, this refers to the equilibrium of earth, water, and so forth; in the case of Brahman, it refers to the undisturbed state of the equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
Of that which has not fallen away from its previous state. || 86 ||
Duality, moreover, is not separate from that [Reality], just as the state of being a bracelet is not separate from gold;
for duality is indeed the lack of perfect awakening, and it does not consist of true existence.
For one who has correctly awakened and understood, the realization of duality consists solely of knowledge; and that knowledge is Being itself, not composed of the existent.
Just as liquidity belongs to water, motion to the wind, and emptiness to space, so indeed there is no separate duality apart from the Lord. 88.
For the perception of duality and non-duality leads only to suffering for one whose nature is action;
however, those who are skillful know that the non-perception of these two is the supreme state.
It is for the sake of the accomplishment of worldly activity for one whose nature is action, and not for the sake of cessation. || 89 ||
The knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and so forth, as well as the seer, the act of seeing, and the seen—this entire world exists within the atom of consciousness. (90)

He provides the answer to the question regarding "the past, the present, and the future" with the word "mātra" (only). Whatever constitutes the world—past, future, and so forth—is, according to the scriptures, merely the triad of the knower (*mātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*māna*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*); by the inclusion of the word "and so forth," the resulting cognition (*pramiti*) is also included. This much is common to both the scriptural and the worldly perspectives;

however, from the perspective of the seer and so on, there is only this triad (*tripuṭī*), and nothing more than that. All of that exists within the atom of the consciousness that is its witness (*sākṣiciti*).
The meaning is "it remains. || 90 ||
This atom of the world is eternally moved by this atom of Mount Sumeru, just as its own body is moved by the wind, whether it be already formed or yet to be formed. (91)

By this atom-like Sumeru wind in the form of the Self, this world-atom—characterized as the universe—has been repeatedly made to vibrate within its own limb; the meaning is that it has been created and then withdrawn when uncreated. || 91 ||
"Aha! Is this a terrible illusion, or perhaps the supreme power of magicians, that within the space of a single atom there exists the entire succession of the three worlds? (92)
He establishes the portion [of the verse] beginning with "bṛhadbhrama" (the great delusion) as follows: "Aho!

This consciousness of the Self (*ātmaciti*) is *māyā* because it is variegated by *māyā*; or rather, it is the supreme (*parā*) among the *māyins*, those who delude people. For this reason, the succession of the three worlds exists within a single atom.
The meaning is that it is indeed a vast delusion, like a mountain perceived on the surface of a mirror, which does not exist at all. || 92 ||
Now, this very state of being like an illusion, which is eternally established, is the existence of the world as nothing more than the subtle atom of pure consciousness alone. (93)

But if, by such scriptural passages as "One only, without a second," even *māyā* is non-existent, then the world is merely an atom of consciousness (*cidaṇu*) and there is no other reality; with the intention that the perception of the world is therefore a vast delusion, he says: "Now" (*atha*).
"Now" (*atha*) indicates an alternative position. "Non-existence" (*asaṃbhava*) refers to the state of being a possessor of *māyā* (*māyitva*), which is impossible [under this view].
The meaning is: even in the view that this very nature of the self remains always exactly as it is within that [body]. || 93 ||
Although containing within itself the entire web of the world, this atom does not abandon its state of equality;
it remains as if a seed containing a vast tree within its belly were situated inside a vessel.
To answer the question, "Of what eternal one is [the world] within, like a tree within a seed?", he says: "Antargata... (contained within).

This is for the purpose of establishing that even within the Brahman-consciousness contained within the atoms and so forth—just as a seed is within the interior of a vessel—it is endowed with the power to produce the entire universe. || 94 ||
Just as the expansion of a tree, complete with its fruits and sprouts, exists within a seed,
so too the entire universe exists within the interior of the atom of consciousness when viewed with the supreme vision.

He describes the portion beginning with "Like a tree within a seed" with two verses: "Within the seed... and so forth, by means of the supreme [power], refined by yoga, and that which belongs to Brahmā. || 95 ||
Just as a tree remains while its own branches, fruits, and flowers fall into the hollow of its seed, so too does the world expand from the atom of consciousness.
Duality and non-duality are established like a tree within its seed-vessel;
he who perceives the world within the supreme atom of consciousness—he truly sees.

To answer the question, "Who is it that rises even before sunrise, yet does not abandon its own singular nature?", the author refutes the superimposed phenomenal world of gross and subtle forms with the three and a half verses beginning with "saṃsthitam" (established), in order to establish the portion: "who does not abandon its own singular nature. || 97 ||
Neither duality nor non-duality, neither seed nor sprout;
neither gross nor subtle, neither unborn nor already born. 98.
This [world] neither exists nor does it not exist; it is neither gentle nor agitated.
Within the atom of consciousness, there is nothing at all—not even space or air—within the three worlds.
Neither the world nor the non-world exists; there exists only the supreme, auspicious Consciousness.
Since it is the self of all, wherever and whenever it arises, it does so in that very manner.
He establishes the point as to who arises even before rising with the verse beginning "sarvātmikā" (consisting of all):
that consciousness (*cit*) arises—that is, manifests in the form of the appearance of creation—in accordance with its prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 100 ||

Even though he has not yet risen [as the sun], this supreme Self— the single atom that is the one essence— arises spontaneously through the unfolding of self-awareness, manifesting as the totality of all selves within the void.
The meaning is that, though expanded— that is, increased— by the manifestation of creation through its own self-awareness in the form of its own self,

even while so expanded, it remains as the single Self within the sky of its own nature which is devoid of phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), existing precisely as the totality of all selves. || 101 ||
Just as a tree arises on the earth from its own seed and subsequently perishes,
so too does the supreme reality arise as the world through its own manifestation and likewise perish through the dissolution of the world.

Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Like a tree. Just as a tree, while producing seeds, arises without abandoning its own nature as a tree and without losing its status as its own seed, and subsequently reaches the earth—that is, attains it—so too does the Supreme Reality arise in the form of the world, and through its own arising, it assumes the state of the world.
And he "goes to," meaning he attains, the conceptualization of birth, death, and so forth. || 102 ||
The tree, by virtue of being the seed itself, does not quickly abandon its state of equilibrium;
remaining motionless, the subtle atom (aṇuka) is intent upon both relinquishing and not relinquishing.

However, this is the distinction: the tree is one by whom the state of being a seed has been relinquished, yet remains subject to transformation even as a tree; for we observe a disparity in its modifications due to its dual nature. The individual soul (ātmāṇuka), on the other hand, is intent on both relinquishment and non-relinquishment; yet, because it is unattached and non-dual, it is ultimately intent on the relinquishment of everything.

And because its true nature pervades all things, while remaining intent on the non-abandonment of all, it always abides as one devoid of movement and free from modification; such is the meaning. || 103 ||
The great Mount Meru is merely a spider’s thread when compared to an atom;
indeed, the thread would enter the field of vision, whereas the state of being a supreme atom remains invisible to the eye.
Regarding the statement, "O King, the great Mount Meru [is small] in comparison to the lotus fiber," he provides the answer: "The lotus fiber...

The ellipsis is to be supplied as "because of its grossness in comparison to the atom. He states the reasoning for this: "It is visible. This is a designation where the abstract quality (bhāva) is primary. It would enter into or depart from the range of vision. || 104 ||
The great Meru mountain is indeed like a spider's thread within the atom that is the Self;
likewise, millions of Merus and other mountains exist densely packed within that very Self.

Establishing what was stated in the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) upon the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), he provides the answer to the question, "In whose belly are there millions of Meru and Mandara mountains? with the words "the lotus fiber" (*bisatantu*).
Even a lotus fiber is a Meru mountain in comparison to that very Self, Brahman, who is subtler than even an atom.
Within their own hearts, those who are dense with consciousness—whose nature is the ultimate reality—remain as firm as millions of Mount Merus and Mandaras.
By that single, great atom,
the visible universe— composed of manifold elaborations— is pervaded, extended, fashioned, produced, and created, just as the sky [pervades all].
Emptiness has indeed been attained clearly and on all sides. || 106 ||

The answer is fourfold: "created" (viracita), "generated" (janita), "made" (kṛta), and [the fourth]. It is "spread out" (tata) by means of the unevolved elements; it is "created" (viracita) as the cosmic egg and the worlds through the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa); therein, it is "generated" (janita) according to the distinctions of gods, humans, asuras, and animals;
and it is "made" (kṛta) for their enjoyment through the various distinctions of their respective objects—this is the meaning. Just as by space...

The meaning is this: just as a city of Gandharvas and other such visible phenomena, though constructed with a manifold variety of diversities, are found on all sides to be transparently empty and to have the nature of space alone—so too is this world. By this, [it is shown that] even your exultation, "What essence is there?", as well as your protecting and killing, since these too are included within the universe, possess that same essence.
Thus, by implication, it is indeed in a state of meditative concentration. || 106 ||
One's own form, which is more beautiful when not abandoned by duality, becomes like deep sleep through the absence of awakening.
Having attained unity, liberated from staying, going, and coming, the subtle body of the world thus stands as the mass of ultimate reality. || 107 ||
He provides the answer to the question, "By seeing what do you not exist, or rather, do you surely always exist?
with the words "by duality" (*dvaitena*).
When, through the realization of the true nature of the Self as it actually is, [the world] consists merely of insentient ignorance inseparable from consciousness, it is like deep sleep (*suṣupta*).

Thus, even at its own time, for the sake of establishing existence, manifestation, and worldly transaction (*sattā-sphūrti-vyavahāra*), it remains through duality— which has not abandoned (*anujjhita*) the foundational reality of its own most beautiful form, which is the essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānandaikarasa*)— by means of persistence, coming, and going.

When [the world] has attained oneness—freed from existence, activity, and their cessation—then that wretched, insignificant world is thus merely a mass of ultimate reality; it exists solely as the singular nature of Brahman.
The meaning is: "I am never of the nature of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), but rather I exist as the single form of non-dual Brahman. || 107 ||
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Essential Compendium of the Supreme Reality," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Summary of the Ultimate Reality," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vasiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus heard from the mouth of the king, Karkaṭī, the forest-monkey-woman, [spoke].
Having realized the ultimate state, he abandoned his own envy and fickleness.
By this [chapter], the bestowing of mantras by her while devouring is described;
and by her, who has emerged from meditative absorption, the offering of the victim and the food [is described]. (1)

Having realized that the state of Brahman is indeed the end—the destruction of which consists in the cutting off of its very root—he abandoned his own envy and fickleness, which were appropriate to his birth. || 1 ||
Having attained inner coolness and reached a state of rest free from distress, she was like a peahen in the rainy season or like a night-blooming lily under the moonlight.
Free from calamity, free from the torment of external views. || 2 ||
Thus, by the king's word, Ānandā conceived intensely within her womb, just as a female crane in the sky conceives at the roar of a rain-cloud. || 3 ||
Like a pregnant crane within the womb of a cloud in the sky by means of its cry. || 3 ||
The Rākṣasī said:
"Oh, how pure this intellect of yours shines!
It is illuminated by the sun of awakening whose essence has not yet set. (4)
Śemuṣī means intelligence (buddhi). || 4 ||
Cool, of equal flavor, and pure like moonlight from the lunar orb, this [speech] has issued from your heart upon hearing even a mere fragment of discernment. (5)
The construction is to be applied everywhere as follows: "She shines like moonlight proceeding from the lunar orb.

Having heard this drop of the nectar of discernment issued forth from your heart—that is, from your intellect—by way of speech, I [think]: "These people like you, who possess discernment, are worthy of worship by the world and are fit to be served."
"I think [this is] by those desiring liberation"—thus it connects with what follows. || 5 ||
I consider those like you, who are discerning and honored by the world, worthy of service;
through association with the virtuous, I have blossomed like a night-lotus at the sight of the moon.
Fragrance arises from association with flowers, and auspiciousness from association with the virtuous; indeed, it is like the blossoming of lotuses through contact with the sun. (7)
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "just from contact with flowers. || 7 ||
Only through association with the great does suffering no longer afflict one;
for who, indeed, can be overcome by darkness when holding a lamp in his hand? (8)
Suffering, once overcome by discernment, does not afflict again. || 8 ||
Since you two, who are like suns upon the earth, have arrived here in this forest, you are worthy of worship; therefore, let your auspicious desire be told quickly.
They are to be honored by the granting of desired objects and to be gratified; "īhitam" means what is wished for. || 9 ||
The king said:
"O Mañjarī of the forest of the race of Rākṣasas! (This is an address to the Rākṣasī).
It causes extreme affliction to the people and is a constant thorn in their hearts.
Since the entire populace was afflicted by a severe cholera-like plague within the district,
I indeed departed for my nocturnal wanderings.
The people, that is, the multitude of folk, being afflicted by a severe cholera-like plague, were consequently tormented and consumed with feverish heat. || 11 ||
When the piercing pain and other ailments in the hearts of men do not subside through medicines,
then I emerge by means of the meaning of the mantras spoken by those such as you.
The meaning of the mantra spoken by those like you is "artha," which signifies desire; for that reason [it is so called]. || 12 ||
And my exertion for the sake of restraining a person like you, who strikes down the simple-minded world, has indeed attained complete success. (13)

The meaning is that prosperity comes to the knower of reality because there can be no failure of his desires, according to the scripture previously cited which states, "whatever world [he desires]... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.20). || 13 ||
O auspicious lady, you must accept these words alone:
henceforth, your life must not be harmed by anyone. (14)
Then, not believing that he had obtained the mantra, he chooses something else, saying, "It is only this much. || 14 ||
The Rākṣasī said:
"Certainly, O Lord, from this day forward I shall act thus without fail;
indeed, in truth, nothing at all shall be harmed by me now. (15)
The king said:

"If this is so, O lotus-eyed one, who subsists solely on the bodies of others, what would happen to you while remaining here for the sake of maintaining your body? (Note: The reading *bhṛtyai*—for the sake of your servants—is also found.)
In my desired [aim]. || 16 ||
Of her who is established in the vow of non-violence, which is my own desire. || 16 ||
"O King, after six months on this mountain, she has awakened from her meditative absorption;
due to the mental resolve for food, this desire for food has arisen in me today. (17)
Now, having gone to the summit, she remains there at her pleasure, motionless in meditation like a living statue.
Like a *śālabhañjikā*, a doll made of wood or other materials. || 18 ||
"Having bound the concentration on the nectar (āmṛtī-dhāraṇā), I maintain this little body;
furthermore, it is my intention that I shall relinquish it at will when the time comes. (19)
"Amṛtīm" means having the nature of the contemplation of the immortal self. || 19 ||
"O King, from this moment until the abandonment of my body, the lives of others must not be harmed by me; therefore, listen to these words of mine. (20)
There is a mountain named Himavat, pure as the rays of the autumn moon,
which touches both the eastern and western oceans at the heart of the northern quarter.
In the heart, the center of the northern region, the northern quarter, by which the eastern and western oceans have been touched and plunged into.
There, at the forefront, I dwell in a cave-house with golden peaks;
I am a Rākṣasī named Karkaṭī, like a dark cloud-streak made of iron.
"O Lord, desiring to bring about the destruction of the people, Brahmā was acquired by me through ascetic penance; [I resolved] that I would become a life-taking cholera in the form of a needle. (23)
"Acquired and brought under one's own control"—this is the expression of desire; [the reading "icchābhilāṣa" occurs in some manuscripts]. || 23 ||
Therefore, having obtained that boon, for many groups of years I have existed as cholera,
tormenting living beings with afflictions of life.
"By Brahmā, for the sake of a restrictive rule, I was then established with this great mantra: 'You must not harm those who possess virtues. Therefore, I remain dependent upon that."

The phrase "given" is to be understood as being for the purpose of restriction and for the purpose of establishing a boundary; therefore, she is dependent on that, meaning she is subject to the mantra. || 25 ||
Therefore, let this [illusion] be grasped by him; by that, all the piercing pain in his heart will come to rest in this world—what then need be said regarding the delusion caused by me?
Everything other than what was done by me—indeed, everything. || 26 ||
For I was indeed intent upon violence when I previously caused harm; because of that, the hearts of people and my own channels have fallen into distress. (27)
"Spread out" means extended, that is to say, long-continued. For the heart has been wounded and dried up by the sucking of blood;
for that reason, there is in people a stupor, a state of distress, and a loss of vitality due to the depletion of blood. || 27 ||
Those great people who, having slaughtered [beings], renounced their blood and flesh—even those born from their veins of distress are likewise [cursed]. (28)

He says "having harmed" (hiṃsitvā) to show that even while they were alive, their descendants likewise became utterly devoid of affection; therefore, the meaning is that violence is a great evil. || 28 ||
"O King, this very mantra for cholera has now been accomplished by you;
for there is nothing whatsoever in this world that is difficult for those possessed of courage to achieve. (29)
He indicates by way of a statement of fact that [the goal] will be accomplished and attained. || 29 ||
Therefore, O King, quickly take up that mantra which was proclaimed by Brahmā for the complete pacification of pains in the sheaths of the vital channels.
"Come closer to the river, O protector of the earth; let us go there.
Once you have sipped water for purification and are self-restrained, I shall bestow my daughter upon you. (31)
"O Sumatā, being well-pleased, I give [this]. || 31 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, during that night, the ministers and the king of the Rākṣasīs went to the bank of the river, having developed mutual affection for one another.
Then, having understood the Rakshasi’s friendship through positive and negative concomitance,
those two residents of the hermitage remained there after performing their ritual sipping of water.

By means of the logical mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the examination of existence through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [the teacher] became a resident disciple at the end [of his studies]; thus is the sense to be supplied.
Then, having been instructed by Brahmā, he bestowed upon those two, in due order, out of affection, a mantra for cholera that grants success through recitation (*japa*). (34)
This mantra was previously taught by Brahmā. || 34 ||
Then, having developed mutual affection and dismissed her, when that night-stalker woman prepared to depart, the king spoke these words: || 35 ||
Sauhārda is the state of being a friend. || 35 ||
The king said:
"O you of great body, you are our guru and our companion is well-pleased;
O beautiful one, we both earnestly invite you for a meal."

"O you of great body"—this is an address to the Rākṣasī. "Guru," "vayasyā," and "sakhī" [are other terms of address]. She is addressed as "Sundarī" (the beautiful one) because of the beauty of her heart. || 36 ||
And you ought not, out of affection, to render our request in vain;
for the friendship of virtuous people increases simply by seeing one another. (37)
Having assumed a charming form endowed with modest beauty,
come to our house, O blessed lady, and stay there at your ease.
"Small" means of little dimension; "endowed with good fortune" means possessed of beauty, ornaments, and so forth; "form" refers to the body. || 38 ||
The Rākṣasī said:
"Are you able to give food to one who has assumed the form of a charming woman?
By what means will you satisfy me, who bear the appearance of a Rākṣasa? (39)
Food consists of edibles, drinks, and so forth, suitable for human beings. || 39 ||
It is for the satisfaction of the Rakshasas alone, not for the food of ordinary people;
this innate nature, established from before, does not cease until the end of the body. (40)
The king said: "O blameless one, remain in my house for some days in the form of my wife, adorned with golden garlands, for as long as you desire."
"In my house, I shall give as much as you desire"—this is how it connects with what follows. || 41 ||
Then, having brought from various districts hundreds of thousands of wicked thieves deserving of execution, I gave them excellent food for you. (42)
Those deserving of execution, those worthy of being put to death. || 42 ||
Having abandoned his lovely form and assumed the body of a Rākṣasa,
he took those hundreds of men who were to be slain and gathered them together.
"Lead me to a peak of the Himalayas; there, enjoy yourself as you please.
For the consumption of great quantities of food in solitude truly brings happiness. (44)
Satisfied, take a little sleep and then become absorbed once more in meditative concentration;
having emerged from that concentration, return again at another time. (45)
You will not desire other people to be killed, for this violence is not their dharma;
yet, through one's own duty and great compassion, even such violence is equal [to non-violence]. (46)
And you shall certainly meet me again when you have become detached from meditative absorption;
for even among the wicked, a firmly rooted friendship does not perish.
"Free from desire" means one who has emerged [from meditative absorption]. "Well-rooted" means fully grown. || 47 ||
The Rākṣasī said: "O King, you have spoken rightly; O friend, I shall indeed do this.
Who would not welcome the words of one who acts out of friendship? (48)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the rākṣasī there became a beautiful woman,
wearing necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and garlands of woven flowers.
A *suvilāsinī* is a beautiful woman; *paṭṭa* refers to silk (*kauśeya*) or a silken girdle (*kāñcīpaṭṭa*). || 49 ||
Having said, "O King, come, let us go," the king and the minister set out to proceed ahead; she followed them through the night.
He followed after; he went behind. || 50 ||
Then, having reached the king’s palace, they spent that night together in a beautiful house, conversing with one another with great respect.
In a single house, in one hall, they spent the night. || 51 ||
At dawn, she remained within the inner apartments amidst the playful activities of the women;
meanwhile, the Rākṣasī and the minister-king each attended to their own duties.
Those two whose respective appropriate activities consist of protecting the people and performing the duty of not killing [those deserving death]. 52.
Then, within six days, the king had gathered [wealth] from enemy cities as well as from his own circle of territories.
"The king gave" is the syntactical connection with what follows. || 53 ||
He then gave those three thousand condemned men to her;
at that time of night, she became that very fierce Kṛṣṇa-rākṣasī.
He took those thousands of victims upon his circle of arms,
as a row of clouds holds masses of rain-showers within its hollows.
The ellipsis implies that they were hanging down from the hollows. || 55 ||
Having taken leave of the king, she returned to that very peak of the Himalayas,
like a poor woman who has found gold, or like the fierce-bodied Umā among the planets.
Among the planets, Pūtanas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and others, she possesses a formidable body; that is to say, she is the most excellent by virtue of her massive form. || 56 ||
Having eaten her fill there and slept happily for three days,
she who possessed a mind fixed in meditative absorption (samādhi) became once again fully restored and awakened.
She whose intellect is transformed into meditative concentration. || 57 ||
After five or four years, she fully awakens;
from that point, she enters the maṇḍala by means of that vessel for the royal assembly.
Then, after awakening; by that reason of the former king’s words; when the king desired to perform a reception—a meeting filled with affection—that circle of Kirātas proceeds [to him]. 58.
There, having spent some time in conversations filled with confidence, she took those victims and returned to her own abode. (59)
With words full of confidence and imbued with trust, she [spoke of] her own abode, her own place— the peak of the Himavat. Even now,
that woman of the Rākṣasas remains on that very mountain in the forest, in the state of one liberated while living, with her mind focused one-pointedly in unwavering meditation.
When that king had attained peace, having abandoned all desires, she remained for a long time in that kingdom, enjoying her own portions through the friendship of the local rulers.

That Rākṣasī woman, Karkaṭī, even today remains on that very mountain in the forest, liberated while living (jīvanmukta) in the manner previously described; her mind (āśaya) being such that it occasionally engages in worldly activity during the state of emergence (vyutthāna), and at other times is entirely absorbed in knowledge during meditative absorption (samādhi). Among those Kirātas...

When the king, having abandoned all desires through his own mind and self, had attained supreme peace characterized by disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya), the meaning is that [the state of worldly existence] remained for a long time, enjoying its own portions— the objects of enjoyment— as before, through the friendships of the rulers born in his lineage who governed that kingdom. || 60 ||
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Benevolence of the Rākṣasīs," in the section on Origination within the *Mokṣopāya* of the holy *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Ṛṣis. 82.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Benevolence of the Rākṣasīs," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"In that Kirāta region, those who are the rulers of the earth..."
With each and every one of them, supreme friendliness arises toward him. || 1 ||
It is described here that the Goddess, having not emerged from her meditative absorption for a long time, became established in the region of Kairāta within this cave. || 1 ||
He elaborates on the statement that she relishes her own morsels through her friendship with the rulers of those kingdoms:
"There, the Rākṣasī, perfected in yoga, wards off all great portents, even the fears of Piśācas and the like, as well as diseases. (2)
He qualifies [the power] with the words "perfected through yoga" (yogasaṃsiddha) in order to establish its capacity for pacifying portents and other such calamities. || 2 ||
After many groups of years, she ceased from her meditation;
having arrived there, she [saw] all those creatures she had intended to kill, who were well-accumulated [there].
"He eats those who are to be slain"—this is the ellipsis. || 3 ||
Even today, those who are to be executed there are led away by the king for that purpose; for who indeed would not be resolute in honoring a friend? (4)
Those who are not intent [on liberation] are not engaged [in the practice]. || 4 ||
While she remained seated in meditation within that circle of Kirātas,
a long time passed without her returning, as the people waited for the pacification of their afflictions.

She is called Maṅgaletaranāmikā because she possesses a name other than auspicious—one by which she is known as "she who, together with the people, splits open the heads of those condemned to death" for the sake of pacifying the aforementioned defects such as portents.
Alternatively, she is Maṅgaletaranāmikā because her other name is Maṅgalā. She is in the hollow of the sky, that is, within the interior of a palace reaching to the heavens. || 5 ||
That goddess named Kandarā, whose name is other than auspicious,
was established in person within the hollow of the sky-city.
From that time onwards, whichever ruler of the earth was there, he himself would install the goddess Bhagavatī in the cave. || 7 ||
He establishes [the image] at the proper time; the meaning is that when the previous image has gone, he causes another image to be made. || 7 ||
That lowest of kings who provides neither caves nor dwellings for his subjects—
his multitudes of afflictions strike down his people with great effort.
Regarding the question "For what purpose does he establish [it]?", he states the reason by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "He who... (verse 8).
By worshipping that, a person obtains all its fruit;
by not worshipping it, one goes toward misfortune swollen by the power of one's own latent impressions (vāsanā).

He states [the same] by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) as well, beginning with "that" (*tat*). "That" refers to the fruit consisting of the pacification of calamities, diseases, and so forth.

To the question, "Why is there a necessary occurrence of such arising and so on?", he replies: "by one's own latent impressions" (*svavāsanā*). By the power of their respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it swells forth—that is, it manifests. || 9 ||
That goddess is worshipped with the offering of people condemned to death;
that image, remaining even today, bestows fruits when depicted in a painting.
That image remains even today; furthermore, even when situated in a painting, being depicted in a picture, it bestows fruit. || 10 ||
Victorious is she here in this abode of the Kirātas— she who brings all soft blessings and has swallowed up all the great people destined for slaughter.
The goddess Cirā is possessed of supreme awakening. || 11 ||
She is the deity who has persisted for a long time, bringing about auspiciousness, prosperity, and the abundance of tender young grass, grain, and so forth for all people. 11.
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Worship of Karkoṭaka and Kandarā," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Worship of the Cave," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"I have thus related to you this entire, irreproachable narrative."
Of Karkaṭī and Himarākṣasī, in due order and according to the rules. || 1 ||
The illustration known as "the crab" (*karkaṭī*), the conceptualization of its purpose for instruction, and its utility in stating an example are described here in detail. || 1 ||
By the word "hima," Himavat is expressed, according to the rule that a name may be taken by means of a part of the name. || 1 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord, tell me exactly how that black demoness, who had arisen in a cave of the Himavat mountains, became known by the name Karkaṭī.
Rāma asks what the cause is for her being black in color and for the absence of karkaṭīs: "Himavat... (verse 2).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
There are many lineages of Rākṣasas by their very nature;
they are white, black, green, and brilliant.
Regarding that, he states the cause for the first [type]: "The families," etc. (verse 3).
Because of her resemblance to a crab (karkaṭa) creature, the Rākṣasa was named Karkaṭa;
born from him, that Kṛṣṇā became a female crab (karkaṭī) with the form of a crab.

He states the cause for the second [type]: "Karkaṭa," etc. Karkaṭa means a crab; it is so called because that creature itself, by virtue of its similarity, possesses a large belly and long hands and feet, and thus has the form of a crab. || 4 ||
This has been told by me to you through the recollection of the question regarding the female crab, in the context of spiritual discourse during the description of the universal form.

While the investigation into the nature of the universe as a manifold form was underway, this narrative was told by way of recollecting the questions posed by Karkaṭī in the context of the discourse on the spiritual self. || 5 ||
Why does this world—which clearly proceeds from that supreme cause, the state without beginning or end—appear to me as if it were unaccomplished, when in truth it is fully accomplished? (6)
He applies the aforementioned narrative to the present context with the words: "It was accomplished. (6)
Just as waves in water, though they are distinct from one another, remain within it;
so too do other creations, even while existing, remain established within the Supreme.
"Plāvinyah" means possessing overflowing [waters]. By the word "api" (also), there is an inclusion of the past and the future. || 7 ||
Just as fire, even while not burning within pieces of wood, performs a purposeful function such as removing the cold for monkeys and others; || 8 ||

If present things also possess equality with the past and future, then how is it that they alone possess causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*)? To address this distinction, he says: "Not burning," and so forth. Regarding the reading *prajvalan* (burning), it means burning in the mind of monkeys and others, but not in reality. || 8 ||
Without ever abandoning its equanimity or its state of perpetual emergence,
Brahman likewise creates this manifold world as if it were an agent.
Being truly like a creator, it produces the manifold world. || 9 ||
Has this creation already come to pass even though it is yet to come? O, it is like the consciousness of a wooden statue that has arisen in vain within the wood itself. 10.
"Bho" is an address to Rāma; "śālabhañjikā-saṃvit-pratibhā-buddhiḥ" refers to the intellect that perceives the consciousness of a carved statue. || 10 ||

Just as within a seed the fruit and so forth, though non-different from it, appear as if different; so too, within consciousness, the object of cognition, though non-different from it, appears as if different. (11)
The sequence beginning with the fruit and ending with the sprout is called "beginning with the fruit" (phalādi) when stated in reverse order. || 11 ||

Because their single existence is indivisible, there is no distinction whatsoever between the fruit and the seed, nor between consciousness and its object, just as there is none between a wave and the water in a substance. (12)
There is no difference [between the states], because there is no interruption of the existence of a single substance that persists from the seed up to the fruit. || 12 ||
Without inquiry, how could a distinction between these two be possible?
For whatever has arisen from any cause whatsoever perishes through inquiry. (13)
O scion of Raghu, let this delusion depart just as it has come;
once awakened, you will understand it—simply cast it aside.

Just as it has come by being without cause, so let it go; let it depart. What, then, is my duty in this regard? To this he says: "enām" (this). This delusion—being awakened, you shall know that Brahman. || 14 ||
Once the knot of delusion has been severed by hearing my words, you will then fully understand for yourself the reality behind the distinctions between cognition, words, and their objects. (15)
If I were to abandon my delusion, then how could I perceive the distinction between the cognition of the word and the cognition of the meaning upon hearing what you have said?

To this, he replies with the verse beginning "bhrānti" (delusion). Although you may not perceive the distinction, nevertheless, you will yourself come to know the reality that lies beyond the scope of those respective [cognitions]. This is the meaning. || 15 ||
This calamity, beginning with the loss of consciousness, and both that prosperity and its opposite—by merely hearing my words, these shall undoubtedly come to rest. (16)

Nevertheless, how is the accomplishment of the cessation of misfortune established? To this he says: "from the mind" (*cittāt*). That is the mind; that is the "misfortune-glory" born of the mind, as well as the other, which is ignorance (*avidyā*), the cause of the mind. || 16 ||
Everything has arisen from Brahman, and everything likewise returns to Brahman;
being fully awakened by my words, you shall understand this perfectly, O blameless one.

With the intention that even the description of the origin and so forth of the world has as its sole purpose the realization of the reality that is free from phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), he says: "Of Brahman. The entire world, through dissolution, goes to—that is, attains—Brahman; it is *alam*, meaning full. || 17 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Therefore, O Brahman, this [usage] "from that" (tasmāt) is the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the sense of distinction (*vyatireka*).
But surely, one might ask: "Do you not know that everything is non-different from the Lord of Gods? (18)

If difference is indeed non-existent, then regarding your statement that "everything has arisen from Brahman," as well as in such scriptural passages as "From this very Self, space was produced," why is this ablative case (*pañcamī*) used in the word "from this" (*tasmāt*), which conveys a sense of distinction (*vyatireka*)? [The answer is: Know that everything is non-different from the Lord of Gods.

What [is the objection]? The underlying intention of the doubt is that if there were no distinction between the defined (lakṣya) and the non-defined (alakṣya), nor the existence of their counter-correlates and so forth, then because words would not function, the linguistic practice of communicating the defined through its definition would be impossible, and thus instruction itself would be unestablished. || 18 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In the scriptures, a word arises for the purpose of instruction, whether born from a verbal root or derived from a meaning;
it possesses the characteristics of contrast, exclusion, number, and gender.

With the intention that no fault whatsoever arises—since instruction is possible through the conceptualization of temporary difference, or by resorting to differences established by the empirical perspective (*vyāvahārika-dṛṣṭi*), just as the linguistic usage characterized by "original" (*bimba*) and "reflection" (*pratibimba*) proceeds from the flow of words—Vasiṣṭha offers this rebuttal beginning with "For the sake of instruction" (*upadeśāya*). [The term] *jāta* means "imagined" (*kalpita*). Alternatively:
The implication is that the word, arising from meanings established in common worldly usage and depending upon conventional distinctions, will continue to spread. || 19 ||
This distinction is indeed perceived through conventional usage, but it is not real;
it is like a ghost imagined by a child for the sake of some purpose. (20)
He states that even in the world, the establishment of purposeful worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) through the imagined (*kalpita*) is well-known, saying: "Difference" (verse 20).
In that state where even duality and unity do not exist, as things abide in their true nature—how could such a subversion of one's resolve occur therein? (21)

The meaning is: even in that state where duality and unity do not exist—such as in the states of dreams or a city of Gandharvas—there still exists such conventional usage as defining characteristics and so forth; therefore, for those whose will is true, how could there be any subversion of their resolve regarding conventional usages such as instruction? || 21 ||

For the relationship of cause and effect, as well as the characteristic of owner and owned, the relation of cause and that which possesses the cause, and the sequence of part and whole [are all established by this]. (22)

And regarding the worldly activity beginning with your instruction, he says—with the words "kāryakāraṇa" and so forth—that the distinction between cause and effect and so on has been imagined by me alone through my own volition. || 22 ||
Distinction and non-distinction, transformation and so forth, are but delusions;
likewise, the play of existence and so on, knowledge and ignorance, and pleasure and pain [are the same]. (23)
Such a limited construction based on false conceptualization exists for the sake of awakening the ignorant; however, there is no actual division in reality.
Measured and conceptualized. || 24 ||
This dispute arises from lack of awakening; once [reality] is known, duality does not exist. When it is known, all mental constructions are stilled, and only silence remains. (25)
And this conventional usage applies only during the state of ignorance of the one being instructed, not during the state of awakening;
thus, there is no loss of non-duality (advaita). He says: "Because of the lack of awakening. Mauna means silence, or the absence of words. || 25 ||
"In time, having attained awakening, you will understand this established conclusion: that everything is one, without beginning or end, indivisible, and undivided. (26)
For those who have not awakened dispute by means of the manifestations of their own conceptual constructions;
this debate arises from instruction, but once [reality] is known, duality does not exist. (27)

Unawakened persons, who do not know the reality, [engage] through those arguments manifested by their own conceptual constructions; for this entire discourse exists only prior to the instruction on the truth of Vedānta, since duality does not exist once that truth is known—this is the meaning.
(27) Without duality, the cognition of the signified and the signifier is not established.
Furthermore, duality cannot possibly bring about even the state of silence. || 28 ||

"Let there be no duality; even so, how is it that dispute is impossible? To this he says: "In what is expressed," etc. "Then let there be duality"; to this he says: "And not," etc. The word *vā* (or) is used for emphasis; thus the meaning is that it brings about silence itself. || 28 ||
O scion of the Raghus, having fixed your intellect upon the ultimate meaning of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), disregard the differences in words and listen to that which I tell you. (29)
To this, he replies with the words "mahāvākya" (great sentence): in the defining statement beginning with "from which," one should not understand the meaning of the ablative case and so forth;

rather, disregarding the difference in phrasing conveyed by the ablative and other cases, that cognition arising from the defining statement should be directed toward the indivisible meaning of the great sentence itself.

The meaning is: "Having established that [teaching] which culminates through the process of deriving the indicated meaning expressed by the final word, listen to this which I am about to say. || 29 ||
From whatever cause it may arise, the mind—like a city of the Gandharvas—spreads forth this mere illusion called the world as its own unfolding. (30)
That whose height or manifestation arises from some indefinable cause whatsoever. || 30 ||
O sinless one, listen as I tell you this illustration for the perception of reality, showing how the mind expands this illusion of the world. (31)

He introduces the narrative that is about to be told as an illustration for the meaning already stated with the word "yathā" (just as): "That by which the subject of the illustration is perceived through one's own vision is 'dṛṣṭivedana'. (31)
O Rāma, having heard this and becoming personally convinced that all this is merely illusion, you will cast away latent impressions far behind you.
The three worlds are nothing more than a creation of mental ideation;
having abandoned everything, you, with a tranquil soul, shall dwell in your very own self.
Intent on grasping the meaning of my words, you shall exert effort in treating the mental disease by means of even a small portion of the medicine of discernment.
This being so, it is the mind alone that unfolds here as the form of the world;
the body and so forth do not exist, like oil within sand. (35)
Thus, it stands according to the manner of the narrative that is about to be told.
The mind itself, when defiled by the afflictions such as passion and the like, is indeed saṃsāra; when it is liberated from those very same [afflictions], it is called the end of existence. (36)
The end of existence—that is, of saṃsāra—is its destruction. || 36 ||
The mind is that which must be perfected, guarded, investigated, and acted upon like a noble person; it must be brought forth, engaged in worldly affairs, directed, and held with reverence. (37)

He says, "It is the mind," meaning that it is the mind alone that expands in the form of all things—whether worldly or scriptural, such as goals to be accomplished or duties to be observed—and nothing else. Among those things already established, the goal (*sādhya*) is what is not yet established; among those previously established, it is what is to be maintained (*pālanīya*).
When various unestablished means (*sādhana*) present themselves, one should investigate their relative weight and ease through diligent effort.
Having prepared the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), one should subsequently deliberate upon the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

In that regard, one should act like a noble person regarding that which is to be achieved through means approved by the learned alone. That which is already established in another land and is fit to be brought to one's own home is "imported" (*āhārya*). That which is already present in one's own home and is suitable for purposes such as buying and selling is [the other category].

That which is to be transacted; among those, horses, chariots, and so forth are to be driven, while ornaments and the like are to be worn. The word "with respect" (ādarāt) is to be connected with every instance. All this is nothing but the mind; for it is the intention that nothing such as an object to be accomplished is established for one who is without mind. || 37 ||
The mind within sustains the sky of the three worlds;
it expands in due time like the swelling of the ego. (38)
The mind, which is like the sky or space—the very basis for the conceptualization of the three worlds—bears all that is visible within itself.

That same mind, as time passes while the body, vital breath, senses, and so forth are active, expands like a flood of egoism, manifesting as the flow of "I-ness" with the thought, "I alone am active. This is the meaning. || 38 ||
That which is this conscious aspect of the mind is the seed-nature of all objects; and that which is its insentient aspect, my dear, is this world—a mere delusion. (39)

Regarding this, he explains the distinction: that which is called "this" is, through the predominance of the conscious aspect (*cidaṃśa*), non-inert *ahaṃtā* (the sense of "I-ness") which serves as the seed of all conceptual constructions and is synonymous with the state of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtā*); however, through the predominance of the non-conscious aspect (*ajaḍāṃśa*), it takes the form of the error of the object (*dṛśyabhrānti*).
Thus he says: "This which... (verse 39).
This earth and the other elements did not exist at all during the initial creation;
like one seeing a formless dream, he does not see them as they truly are.
He establishes the stated point by recalling the previously mentioned order of creation: "Even though it does not exist," etc.
"Aja" refers to Brahmā. || 40 ||

Through the long-lasting perception of creation and so forth, through the perception of inert things such as mountains, and through the subtle perception of the knower of the subtle—the body is thus empty and not real. (41)

How does one see it? To this he says: "Beginning with creation" (*sargādi*). One sees the gross body of Virāj, consisting of mountains and so forth, through the consciousness of the Witness (*sākṣi-saṃvit*) which is common to millions of cycles of creation, maintenance, and dissolution by means of a long-lasting perception;
and [one sees] the subtle [body] through the inert consciousness (*jaḍa-saṃvit*)—which takes the form of the inert sense of "I-ness"—and through the Vaiśvānara-consciousness.

The meaning is that the knower of the subtle perceives the body of Hiraṇyagarbha—which consists of the aggregate of the *liṅga*—as well as the consciousness of "I-ness" regarding it, and thus sees all three bodies as being nothing but emptiness (*śūnya*). || 41 ||
Pervaded by its all-pervading self, the mind—whose body is its own object of cognition—is spread out, gentle, and stainless, like water permeated by the light of the sun. 42.

He establishes that this conscious portion of the mind is the seed of all objects with the words "by the all-pervading" (*sarvageṇa*). Thus, the meaning is that it is the seed [of all] precisely by virtue of being pervaded by consciousness (*cidvyāpti*). || 42 ||
Due to a lack of awakening, the foolish mind falsely perceives the world as a demon;
once awakened, it beholds its own supreme form, free from all affliction.

It is said that by the power of the pervasion of consciousness alone, when the mind does not investigate, there is the perception of the world; when it investigates, there is the vision of the Self—thus he says, "the child-mind" (cittabāla). || 43 ||
Listen, I shall explain to you how the Self comes to be perceived as giving rise to the delusion of duality and unity, through the accounts of the stories that are about to be told. 44.

And thus, it follows that the pure Self itself, by way of becoming the mind, has as it were attained the state of being an object; in order to suggest this possibility, he introduces the story about to be told with the words "Just as... (44).
For that which is spoken with heart-touching analogies, by means of sweet speech endowed with appropriate meanings,
spreads throughout the listener's heart, my dear friend.
He pervades [all things], just as oil pervades water; thus, one should dispel doubt. || 45 ||
He states how the certainty that the world is mind-only is established through the analogy of the legend of Aindava:

"That which... By means of a "heart-pleasing" [narrative], that is, one that delights the mind; having warded off or dispelled doubt—the form *lyap* being Vedic—it pervades the heart of the listener. || 45 ||
Devoid of comparison, consisting of unpleasant words, difficult to attain, agitated, distressed by the earth, and having its syllables swallowed—
such speech does not enter the heart of the listener, but goes to utter ruin.
Indeed, such speech is like clarified butter being poured as an oblation into ashes.

He establishes the aforementioned point also by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), stating: "devoid of simile" (*tyaktopamānam*). That sentence which is "devoid of simile," meaning it lacks the presentation of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*); and that in which there are "unpleasant words"—that is, words not sanctioned by the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*) or composed of harsh phonemes and the like.

Difficult to attain because its phonemes (*varṇa*) are unmanifest, it is impossible for the ear to grasp with clarity (the reading *varṇāsphuṭatayā* is preferred). Being agitated by the onset of anger and the like, it is "disturbed by the earth," meaning its phonemes have fallen from their proper positions. "Swallowed phonemes" means the syllables have been devoured. It is "constricted, hoarse, and blown."
