This is an illustration of the defects of vowels and phonemes mentioned in the *Mahābhāṣya* and other sources. Thus they say: "Choked, suppressed, overly protracted, hurried, nasalized, blown, tremulous, slurred, nasalized like a deer, half-articulated, struck, and scattered—these are the conditions of the defects of vowels."

Such speech does not enter the heart of the listener nor does it delight it; even when presented with great effort, it goes to ruin or fruitlessness, resulting in the perception of faults such as loquacity. He shows that this is a well-known illustration by saying "like clarified butter" (ājyamiva). || 46 ||
O virtuous one, whatever narratives exist on earth, whatever stories there may be, and whatever object of knowledge is appropriate— whether substantial or trivial—
all these come forth through the presentation of illustrative examples.
He quickly illuminated the world, just as the moon with its white rays does. || 47 ||

He concludes by means of a statement of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) the matter already established through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), stating: "The narrative works" (*ākhyānakāni*).
Great narratives such as those of the *Mahābhārata* and others, which consist of various stories, are called "narrative works. Shorter stories, however, are simply "stories" (*kathāḥ*).
Whatever is appropriate—that is, suitable for pleasing the connoisseurs—whether in the form of poetry, drama, philosophical treatises, and so forth, [is included].
The meaning is that whatever is subtle in both word and sense, and whatever is soft and perceptible by the ear—
all that attains clarity and a state of being clear and pleasing in its meaning through the narration of examples and the perspectives of world-renowned authorities. || 47 ||

Thus ends the eighty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the Sprouting of the Mind," within the "Story of the Needle" in the "Section on Origination" of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the ancient seers.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sprouting of the Mind," in the Utthāna-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa.
p. 336) 203 The eighty-fifth canto.
85 Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O sinless one, O Raghava, everything that was previously told to me by Brahmā,
I shall now relate to you as you ask.
The vision of the ten cosmic eggs by the Creator while desiring to bring about creation, and the statement of their essential nature by a single sun therein, is described here. (1)
He begins to relate the promised narrative of Indu with the words "In former times," and so forth.

O sinless one, that which was previously told to me by Brahmā—that this entire world is merely mind—I shall explain all of that through the story of Indu as told by Brahmā; such is the construction of the verse. || 1 ||
Formerly, indeed, I questioned the Blessed One, the Lotus-born:
"O Brahmā, how do these multitudes of creations come into being?"
To that end, he states the question he himself previously posed: "In the city," etc. (Verse 2).
Having heard that, the Blessed Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds,
spoke these great words to me, accompanied by the narrative concerning Aindava.
Having heard my question and having promised, "I shall speak," [he spoke] that which is vast and of great significance. || 3 ||
Brahmā said: Indeed, this entire world, full of manifestations, flashes forth as nothing but the mind itself, like water appearing through the various and expansive whirlpools of a reservoir.
Possessing prosperity, it has the power to sustain the existence of the world, like whirlpools within a circle.
Listen, my dear, to what occurred long ago in a certain former age (purākalpa), when at the beginning of the day, having fully awakened and desiring to create the world of transmigration (saṃsāra).

"O dear one, listen to what occurred in my former aeon (purākalpa) at the beginning of the day, that is, at the commencement of the kalpa, when I had awakened and desired to create the world of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra)—that which came to pass, hear that. This is the meaning. || 5 ||
Once, at the close of day, having withdrawn the entire creation,
I, alone and one-pointed, spent that night established in my own self.
At the end of the night, having fully awakened and performed the twilight rites according to the rules,
I directed my wide-open eyes toward the sky in order to create living beings.
He performed the twilight ritual—that is, he extended the practice of the sandhyopāsanā. || 7 ||
As long as I beheld the sky, neither pervaded by darkness nor by light,
it was exceedingly vast, empty, and devoid of end.
Although darkness was present, it was not said to be "by means of darknesses" because it did not obstruct the expansion of my own divine vision.
(8) Having resolved upon the thought, "I shall bring forth creation," and becoming absorbed in that, I began to contemplate with a pure and subtle mind. (9)
To examine—that is, to reflect upon—the object to be created. || 9 ||
Then, in that vast expanse of the sky, I beheld with my mind various great undertakings— creations whose maintenance was unrestrained.

In the sky, in the unmanifest ether, he [perceives] the creations—the cosmic eggs—unrestrained and unimpeded by their maintenance, that is, by the established order of protection and so forth performed there by Viṣṇu and the other deities. || 10 ||
Within them, ten lotus-born ones stood, possessing the luster of my own reflection, dwelling within the calyxes of lotuses and mounted upon royal swans.
In those variously situated creations where rows of beings were emerging, amidst pure masses of water that bestow worlds like clouds; || 12 ||

In those masses of water, that is, in the nets of clouds, where rows of beings—meaning the fourfold classes of living creatures—are rising up or being born; [the elision of the *da* is Vedic]. Alternatively, it refers to the clouds which are like a net for waters, being pure and free from defects such as drought. 12.
The great rivers flow on, the oceans roar as they do, the suns scorch with their heat, and the winds flash forth in the sky. (13)
They flash forth intensely; they move about. || 13 ||
The gods sport in heaven, humans sport on earth,
and the Dānavas as well as the serpents are established in the netherworlds.
The *vibudhas* are the gods. || 14 ||
All the seasons, whose natures are impelled by the wheel of time,
adorn the earth on all sides, filling it with fruits according to the season.
Whatever the nature of things may be—such as cold, heat, rain, and so forth—all the seasons, beginning with spring, are likewise of such a nature.
Maturity, the recollections of auspicious and inauspicious conduct toward every direction, and those which yield the fruits of hell or heaven, have arrived everywhere. (16)

The auspicious practices that were ordained and the inauspicious ones that were prohibited, along with the traditional codes and the Smṛti texts that distinguish between them, have everywhere in every direction and among all social classes attained maturity and full development. || 16 ||
All classes of living beings, desiring the fruits of enjoyment and liberation,
strive for their own desired ends at the proper time and in due order.
"In due order" means not transgressing the sequence of activity as it was ordained for each of them in their own creation. || 17 ||
The seven worlds, as well as the continents, oceans, and mountains—
even when reaching the end of the eon— throb with an ever-increasing roar.
The end of the aeon is the dissolution. Even though it is being brought about by time, it vibrates at its own appointed time with a most intense roar. || 18 ||
In some places it has become darkened, in others it remains very firm;
it is present everywhere in the groves, though tinged by a fragment of light.

In some places where the region is not covered, darkness undergoes diminution and decay; in other places, such as mountain caves and the like, it remains. However, in groves, it is pervaded by fragments of light through openings in the sunlight; the meaning is that it has become blended with oiliness (moisture). || 19 ||
Within the blue lotus of the sky,
it was filled with bees wandering about and possessed filaments consisting of clusters of shimmering stars.
By implication, he describes the world as being like a lake: "The sky," etc. (Verse 20).
The dense mist at the end of the eon remained within the groves of Mount Meru,
like the pure cotton-wool of the *śālmalī* tree inside the hollows of its seed-pods. (In the printed edition, the reading is *aṣṭhilā*.)
Like Mount Meru in its height, and like the Himavat among its groves; it is like a stone or a skull-fragment within its hollows.
Resounding with the roar of the ocean against the ridges of the Lokāloka mountain,
she possesses the luster of sapphire fragments amidst the darkness and is adorned with her own jewels.

The Lokāloka mountain itself is her girdle; the roaring oceans themselves are the humming sounds of her ornaments; the masses of darkness themselves are the luster of her sapphires; and she is resplendent with the jewels contained within herself. 22.
With the humming of the *kākalī* notes of the spirits like nectar from the lower lip,
she stands within the expanse of the world like a woman in her inner apartments.
She whose grains—namely the seeds of rice and other crops—are the nectar of the lower lip for living beings because they are to be tasted by them;
she whose cries—the sounds of living beings—are the sweet, indistinct vocal play of a warbling coo; such is she, the Earth, within the expanse of that world.
The meaning is that she remained within her inner apartments like a young woman. || 23 ||
The row of fair-limbed women standing in the middle, illuminated by the courtyard of the night, appears like a garland of lotuses and water-lilies belonging to the Fortune of the Year. (24)

She stands in the midst of, and is thus situated within, the garland fashioned from lotuses and water-lilies— characterized by light and darkness— which was worn around the neck of the Fortune of the Year (the Goddess of the Saṃvatsara);
for this reason, she is the Queen of Night, being pervaded by lightning, stars, and the like, which resemble the pollen of that very garland.

The sky appears, as it were, like a row of limbs— such as the necks, breasts, bellies, folds, and navels— of fair-complexioned women, colored by a series of nightly ointments consisting mostly of turmeric paste;
that is to say, the worlds of beings situated in the various divisions of many hollows are seen separately.
Having become ruddy, they appear like the lusters of pomegranate fruits. || 25 ||

The meaning is that many beings situated within the divisions of the hollows of the worlds— which serve as the seeds from which such worlds, the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍas*), have arisen— appear like radiant, shining pomegranate fruits. || 25 ||
Flowing in three currents, traversing the three paths, she has made her way upward and downward;
appearing like the sacred thread of the universe, she shines with the stainless digit of the moon.
Moving here and there, they wither away and spring up again—cloud-leaves, tossed by the wind, with lightning for flowers upon the creepers of the quarters. (27)

The construction is as follows: those cloud-sprouts, which have lightning itself for their flowers, being agitated by the wind, move hither and thither upon the creepers of the quarters; they wither away and they spring forth. || 27 ||
Adorned with garlands of celestial cities, gardens, and spreading creepers, the path of the ocean, the earth, and the sky shines forth brilliantly. 28.

And he shows that this manifested world is indeed false with the words "gandharva... etc. The meaning is: that path of the ocean, earth, and sky, adorned with a vast canopy, shines like the vine of a garden in a city of the Gandharvas; it is not real. || 28 ||
In other worlds, gods, asuras, humans, and serpents stood amidst the Saṅgha like gnats buzzing around udumbara trees. (29)
In other worlds, within the wombs of the universe. || 29 ||
Time, marked by ages, kalpas, days, nights, moments, lavas, kalās, and kāṣṭhas, flows on,
awaiting the dissolution of all things which remains unperceived.

The meaning is that even time, characterized by the beginning of the Yugas, flows through those intermediate worlds; he is the one who awaits the unforeseen and unexpected destruction of all things. || 30 ||
Having thus perceived this with his own pure and supreme mind, he was filled with great wonder, exclaiming repeatedly, "What is this? How can this be? (31)
He was filled with wonder; the word "I" is to be understood as the subject. || 31 ||
"How is it that with my fleshly eye I see nothing at all, yet with my mind I behold that incomparable net of illusion in the sky? (32)

He expresses that very astonishment along with its cause, asking: "How? The meaning is: "That which I do not see with the eye—consisting of flesh and situated within the eyeball—I see with the mind; how has this come to be? This is my astonishment. || 32 ||
Then, after gazing for a long time from the sky with my mind alone,
I brought the sun from that web of worlds and questioned him.
Having brought it from the sky—that is, from the space of that world—and having placed it before him by means of his power of true resolve (satyasaṃkalpa). || 33 ||
"Come, O Lord of the gods of gods! O Bhāskara of great splendor!
Welcome to you!"—thus was he addressed by me, and then he spoke as well.
First, he was addressed with "Welcome to you," and then he was told the matter about to be explained and questioned. || 34 ||
"Who are you? How did this world and the worlds themselves come to be?
O Blessed One, O sinless one, if you know this, please tell me."

He demonstrates that very point with the word "ka" (who). How did this world of yours come into being? Likewise, how were the other nine worlds produced, and by which creators were they fashioned? This is the meaning. || 35 ||
Thus addressed, he looked at me and then recognized me;
having offered his salutations, he spoke these words in a voice of irreproachable tone: (36)
"He has fully recognized me," the remainder of the sentence being "as this Brahmā of this universe. (36)
Śrī Bhānu said: You are the eternal cause of this visible universe; why have you departed? Do you not know me? Why do you question me, O Lord? (37)
"Constantly" means perpetually. || 37 ||
Now, O omnipresent one, if your play consists in the sequence of my words, then listen as I speak of my own birth, which was unthought of. (38)
There is a curiosity to hear of your divine play; [that which was] unthought of and unimagined by you. || 38 ||

O Lord, that which is extended by the powers (kalās) as "existent" and "non-existent"— powers that bestow delusion through the non-comprehension of existence and non-existence— by means of their incessant manifestations.
O Great-Souled One, here the mind shines forth most brilliantly.

O Great-Souled One, who in the conventional sense is the Lord-Self possessing all powers, yet in the vision of ultimate reality is the Supreme Self— for those [powers] by which the creation of the world proceeds incessantly, and which, due to the lack of realization of the truth as being either "existent" or "non-existent," are habitually productive of delusion, [the world appears] sometimes as existent and sometimes as non-existent, or in some places existent and in others non-existent.

The meaning is: know that it is that very mind which shines forth in such a manner, having spread out and expanded everywhere here through its skill in manifesting the existence of the world as delimited by time and space. || 39 ||
Thus ends the eighty-fifth canto, titled "The Meeting of Brahmā and Āditya," at the commencement of the Legend of Aindava, in the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, the Vālmīkīya Mokṣopāya.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Meeting of Brahmā and Āditya," in the Utapatti-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-sixth canto.
The venerable Bhānu said:
O Mahādeva, on the day before yesterday, during your [meditative] construction, [it was as follows].
Thus [is] the mountain Kailāsa, located at one corner of Jambūdvīpa. || 1 ||
Here, for this Moon who dwells with his wife and performs penance,
the creation of the world is undertaken through the instruction of their eldest brother, Dhātṛ, by means of meditative contemplation.
On a level stretch of ground on the surface, which forms part of Mount Kailāsa situated in a corner of Jambūdvīpa. || 1 ||
That glorious mandala, beautiful with no small measure of happiness, which was fashioned by your sons—those who have produced offspring—under the name Suvarṇajaṭa; || 2 ||

The meaning is that it refers to the region known by the name Suvarṇajaṭa; in that region, by those sons such as Marīci and others who had produced offspring—that is, progeny—a circle (maṇḍala) was established for the purpose of providing a dwelling for people. || 2 ||

There lived a Brāhmaṇa named Indu, whose soul was exceedingly devoted to dharma and who was the best among the knowers of Brahman; he was born into the lineage of Kaśyapa and possessed an extremely tranquil mind.
In that mandala, he is the most excellent knower of Brahman, the best among those who know the Vedas. || 3 ||
At that time, while that great-souled one was constantly dwelling among his own circle of kinsmen, he had a certain wife who was as dear to him as his own life.
No son was born to him, just as there is no grass in a desert;
his wife did not shine, like a flower that blooms without fruit.

Just as the straight, fair, and perfectly pure *śaralatā* creeper is empty [of fruit], so too were that couple distressed; for the sake of a son, they went from there to the mountain to perform austerities.
Empty means empty of fruit; "straightness" refers to a stalk of *kāśa* grass. || 6 ||
Having ascended a portion of Kailāsa like two newly grown trees,
they were in that empty bower of Kailāsa, which was unoccupied by spirits.
The portion above is the upper part; by "beings" (bhūtaiḥ) is meant living creatures (prāṇibhiḥ). || 7 ||
Those two performed severe penance, subsisting on water and remaining perched upon trees;
at the end of each day, they would drink a single handful of water.
Those two whose stability and steadfastness are like the standing of a tree; he explains that very stability of the tree with the word "one" (ekam).
At the end of the day, during the final portion of the day. || 8 ||
Remaining motionless,
they stood there for that length of time, observing the vow of trees and subsisting on the manner of life belonging to trees.
"Vākṣīm" means pertaining to a tree; that is to say, resembling it. || 9 ||
When those two ages, Tretā and Dvāpara, had indeed passed away,
the God who bears the digit of the moon became pleased with them.
The construction is: "only after two yugas had passed. Furthermore, the long penance was for the sake of obtaining a distinguished son. || 10 ||
Like the moon approaching two night-blooming lotuses scorched by the heat of the day,
the moon arrived at that place where those two brahmin husband and wife were.
The summary and the detailed exposition. || 11 ||
Like the Lord of Spring in a region of sal trees,
he [beheld] that couple mounted upon the bull, with Soma as their crest-ornament and the crescent moon upon his head.
Like the spring season when flowers bloom, he beheld Soma accompanied by Umā. || 12 ||
With their faces blooming like two night-lotuses beholding the moon,
they both bowed down to that god, the Lord who is as pure as frost.
*Kumuda* and *kairava* refer to the white water-lily; the very blossoming [of these] is what is shown as the illustration. || 13 ||
He threatened heaven and earth with his roar, which sounded like the rustling of new trees shaken by the wind, as he appeared like the full moon risen in the sky.

By the term "Heaven and Earth" (dyāvāpṛthivī), the people dwelling therein are indicated. The *uḍupa* is the moon. By the sound of the humming bees, cuckoos, and other birds—which, like the faces of mango and other trees whose sprouts are slightly shaken by the breeze from Mount Malaya, surpass with the sweetness of their own voices the very sound of those trees—[the scene is described].
Threatening as it were, and reviling. || 14 ||
Then Śiva, remaining gentle yet majestic and trembling slightly, spoke these words. The Lord said:
"O Brahmin, accept a boon quickly; I am pleased with your desire. (15)
With a gentle, unrestrained, and exquisitely beautiful smile that causes your lips to quiver slightly, accept the boon desired by you. 15.
"Be joyful like a forest of trees overwhelmed by the nectar of the spring season.
The Brahmin said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, may ten sons of great intelligence [be born to me]. (16)
"May I become such that sorrow no longer oppresses me.
Sūrya said:
"So be it," and having spoken thus, the Lord vanished from sight.
They were worthy, endowed with auspicious virtues and conduct; by which [act] they obtained a son. || 17 ||
Then, having created a roar in the sky like an ocean with its great body of waves,
those two, the husband and wife who had obtained boons from Śiva, went home satisfied.
"In the sky" connects with what precedes. Alternatively, "vārinidhi" means a cloud, that in which water is stored;
he whose great body has parts divided as if by waves. 18.
Having gone there, they appeared like two gods, resembling Umā and Maheśvara themselves;
there, in the house of a Brāhmaṇa, she became pregnant with a noble child.
The *gīrvāṇas* are the gods; that couple was like them.

Or rather, because they possessed imagined divine bodies created by *māyā*, Umā and Maheśvara were like the *gīrvāṇas*, just as the sky is like the real, absolute space of Brahman (*brahmākāśa*). || 19 ||
With her full womb, the dark-complexioned woman shone like a streak of cloud filled with water;
then, in due time, she gave birth to sons as tender as the new moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight.
Then those ten youths, like sprouts on the earth,
having received the sacraments of the Brahmins, grew in great splendor.
"Charming" means beautiful.

"Upon whom the Brahminical sacraments"—namely, the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), the initiation (*upanayana*), the Vedic vows (*vedavrata*), the study of the Vedas (*adhyayana*), and so forth—have been performed. || 21 ||
Indeed, in a very short time, like fresh clouds in the rainy season,
they reached the age of seven years and became masters of the sciences of speech.
By the rainy season, that is, by the monsoon. || 22 ||
They shone there with splendor like pure planets in the sky;
then, after a long time, their two parents [passed away]. (23)
Having abandoned their bodies, those two, skilled in knowing the goal, went to their own destination;
thereafter, those ten Brāhmaṇas were left deprived of their mother and father.
Their own goal is disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya), since they are experts in Brahman, which is the supreme state of attainment.
Abandoning their home, they went dejectedly to the peak of Kailāsa;
there, being distressed and separated from their kinsmen, they reflected deeply.
They were weary and suffering. By the power of their fortune, a reflection arose in them that led toward the attainment of future sovereignty like that of Hiraṇyagarbha; thus he says:
"What might be the highest good here? and they spoke this to one another.
"O brothers, what would be appropriate here? What could possibly be free from suffering? (26)
Thinking, "The highest excellence is the supreme bliss," they spoke these words that are about to be related.

It is appropriate to accept this as a means for attaining happiness both in this world and the next. O brothers, what is there that, even if it is not a cause for worldly pleasure, does not result in suffering in the end? (26)
What is greatness? What is sovereignty? What is auspicious, great prosperity?
What is this sovereignty of people? For a feudal lord (*sāmanta*) is indeed a great lord (*maheśvara*).

Having thus reflected in general, they reflect in detail as well—namely: "Is this sovereignty of people superior to that of the lords of houses and villages? For indeed, a *sāmanta* (feudatory), a lord of a province (*maṇḍalādhipati*), is a great sovereign, one possessed of power. || 27 ||
What indeed is the perfection of a vassal? For kings are indeed great lords;
what indeed is the perfection of subordinate rulers? Here, the universal emperor is the great lord. (28)
What indeed? How much indeed? Kings are the lords of regions. || 28 ||
What indeed is that status of Mahendra which perishes in a mere moment before the Lord of Creatures; what could such a thing be considered auspicious in this world? (29)
In that case, Mahendra would be Maheśvara; to this he replies: "What indeed? (29)
Then, while they were speaking thus, the eldest brother, Mahāmati,
spoke these words with a deep voice, like a deer emerging from a herd of deer.

While his brothers were speaking thus, there was an elder brother named Mahāmati, who had attained a supreme birth because his worship of Hiraṇyagarbha in a previous life had been interrupted by obstacles; through this very conversation with his brothers, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of his former worship were awakened within him.

The brother, desiring to instruct his younger brothers on the sequence of meditations he had previously practiced, said: "While they were speaking... [referring to] the deer, the leader of the herd. (30)
"O brothers, since there is no sovereignty among all powers that is indestructible until the end of the kalpa, therefore the state of Brahmā is what pleases me here, and nothing else. (31)
Until the end of the kalpa, until the dissolution of the unmanifest; O brothers, [this is] the state of Brahmā, the condition of Hiraṇyagarbha. || 31 ||
When this had been said, all those excellent sons of the twice-born, who were like the sons of the Moon, honored him there with their words, saying, "Excellent! Excellent! (32).

He says "this" (etad) because, by the power of fortune, a desire for that [path] has arisen even in others. Regarding the reading "tad-uttamāḥ," it means he—the one of great intelligence—is the most excellent, the eldest, and the best among them. || 32 ||
They said this: "O Father, how may we attain the state of Virañci—the lotus-seated one, worshipped by the world—which wipes away all suffering? (33)

For this very reason, he says "they said" (ūcuḥ), asking about the means to that [liberation]. The word *adhikaraṇe* [in the compound] takes the suffix *lyuṭ*, meaning that in which all sufferings—caused by old age, death, comparison with others, and so forth—are wiped away (*upamṛjyante*). "We shall obtain" (*avāpnumaḥ*) means we will quickly attain; the present tense (*laṭ*) is used here because of the intention to express proximity to the present time. || 33 ||
Then that brother spoke again to his brothers of great splendor:
"May you all indeed uphold everything that I have said."

To those who have approached him, intending to instruct them in the worship of the *ahaṃgraha* (the "I-seizing") of Hiraṇyagarbha along with its ancillaries, he prescribes the firmness of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) until death as a constituent part of that practice, saying:
"What I have said... The word "verily" (*vai*) is used to indicate the necessity for firm conviction in that regard. || 34 ||
May this meditation be for you for a long time: "I am the radiant Brahmā, seated upon the lotus throne; by my splendor, I create and I withdraw. (35)
From the indicative mark (liṅga) "I create and I destroy," it is understood that this Saṃvarga-vidyā has been taught.

By the word "iti" (thus), it should be understood that the entire sequence of the manner to be described hereafter has been taught. "For a long time" means until the arising of the state of identity [with the teacher], according to the maxim of the bee and the worm. || 35 ||
When the elder brother had spoken thus, those excellent ones, saying "So be it," remained together with their superior out of devotion, their minds absorbed in meditation.
Having made it firm, having firmly accepted; together with the elder brother, the *jyāyas*;
out of passion (*rasāt*), that is, from an excess of attachment to the fruit. || 36 ||
With their forms depicted in paintings and their minds absorbed in meditation,
they, being respectful, reflected with their internal minds alone.
The work of a painter is *citralekhya*; those whose forms are depicted therein are *tadarpitākārāḥ*.
Then, seated upon a high throne as wide as the calyx of a full-blown lotus, Brahmā declared: "I am the creator of the worlds, the agent, the enjoyer, and the Great Lord. (38)
Therefore, he begins to explain the manner of reflection with the words "Now," and so forth. || 38 ||
These men are the Vedas themselves, possessed of the sequence of sacrificial rites along with their primary and secondary limbs, and joined with the great seers, Sarasvatī, and Gāyatrī. 39.

The great sages who are my officiating priests for me, whose form is sacrifice and who possess the sequence of sacrificial rites—these embodied men are the Vedas themselves, accompanied by their limbs (aṅgas) such as phonetics (śikṣā) and their subsidiary limbs (upāṅgas) such as the Purāṇas, and joined with Sarasvatī and Gāyatrī; the meaning is that they reside within me. || 39 ||
This heaven, adorned with celestial sounds, possesses the prowess of the world-protectors, contains moving circles of perfected beings (siddhas), and is endowed with unrestrained splendor.
This very orb of the earth, adorned with mountains, islands, oceans, and forests, serves as the earring for the ear of the three worlds. 41.
It was like an earring for the woman whose form is the three worlds.
This cave of the netherworld (Pātāla), once inhabited by Daityas and Dānavas,
is now filled with hosts of immortal women— a home within the hollow of the sky.

It was filled to the brim with the Daityas and Dānavas who had been fed, and it was crowded and pervaded by throngs of immortal women, the Apsarases; "house after house" is the intended meaning. || 42 ||
This Indra, the mighty-armed one, the supreme protector who adorns his subjects,
alone guards the city of the three worlds, he who partakes in the purifying sacrifice.

This [quality] resides within me; kings are called "givers of adornment to their subjects" because they bestow upon them an adorned ornament consisting of splendor. For it is by means of kings that subjects shine, and you are the most excellent among them. (43)
Then, having hemmed in the multitude of directions with their blazing garlands of rays,
these suns of abundant radiance shine forth in succession.

Having bound the multitude of directions with nooses characterized by radiant networks of light—so that they cannot escape—they scorch them in order to extract their essence (rasa). These are the twelve suns (*bhānu*), possessing abundant rays (*bhūribhānu*). This occurs sequentially according to the order of the months beginning with Caitra. || 44 ||
These world-protectors, possessing pure conduct and unshakable behavior, protect the world with their noble boundaries, just as cowherds protect a herd of cattle. (45)

By means of those [qualities] which are not vain because they are logical, and which are great—[there is also a reading: "by those which are not vain because they are other than vain, and which are great"] || 45 ||
These creatures emerge and submerge, quiver and fall, day after day like waves upon the waters. (46)

They emerge and manifest; they submerge and become invisible; they quiver and shine resplendent through various forms of prosperity and power; and they fall due to the affliction of poverty and other such misfortunes. (46)
I create this manifold creation, and likewise, with due regard, I withdraw it.
I abide within the Self; as the Lord of the World, I am at peace. (47)
I abide in the self, which is the ultimate reality, my own true nature; therefore, I am at peace, having attained cessation. 47.
This year has passed; this age (yuga) has come to its end.
This is the time for creation, and it is also the time for its own withdrawal.
Stating clearly what has already been said, he concludes with two verses beginning with "This" (ayam): || 48 ||
This very eon has passed; this is the vast night of Brahmā. I abide within myself as the full Self, the Supreme Lord.
Thus, having been uplifted by that meditation, those twice-born sons of Indra stood as if carved out of stone,
with their bodies as firm as ten mountains.
Now, the form "aindavāḥ" lacks a sandhi-conjunction due to the non-obligatory nature of *saṃhitā*. They dwell upon the mountains and are firmly established in their postures.

Having attained the succession of the Lotus Throne (Kamalāsana) and having cast off the entire web of other trivial modes of conduct, they remain constantly and most firmly seated upon the seat of Kuśa grass.
They shone for a long time in the imagining of them as lotuses. || 51 ||

Seated upon auspicious seats, while the lotus-posture was being assumed, those holy men shone forth—having cast off the entire web of other trivial activities and having attained the lineage of the Lotus-Seated One. || 51 ||
Thus ends the eighty-sixth canto, titled "The Stabilization of Aindava," in the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, belonging to the Divine [Tradition]. 86.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Consolation of Aindava," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-seventh canto.
Bhānu said:
"In that lineage of the Grandfather (Brahmā), because of your many contemplations..."
Their minds overcome by those karmas, they remained there with full reverence.
When those who have become one with Brahman through the mind are devoured by flesh-eaters during a dissolution or a creation, their continued existence in that state is thus described.

O Grandfather, those sons of Indu remained in that sequence of worship with their minds entirely occupied by various acts such as the creation, preservation, and dissolution of the world and its multitude of beings— just like you— and they remained there, devoted and deeply attached, until [the time came for] them.
The connection with the following verse is as follows: "the embodied beings, their bodies emaciated, having reached a state of desiccation, have become dissolved. (1)
As long as those bodies of theirs endure, through heat and likewise by the winds,
they eventually reach desiccation over time and fall away like withered leaves.
There, the flesh-eating forest-dwellers devoured those bodies as they lay rolling here and there,
like monkeys eating choice fruits.
They devoured and ate; the flesh-eating beasts and birds were consumers of raw meat. || 3 ||
Then, with external objects stilled and having cultivated their meditation upon the state of Brahman,
they remained until the end of the four ages, when the kalpa came to its destruction.

And since their destruction of the body has occurred, the cessation of the perception of external objects becomes absolute; thus he says, "Then," etc., meaning at the end of the remaining four yugas. || 4 ||
Then, as the eon waned and the multitude of suns blazed forth,
the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds rained down with a loud and harsh roar.
While the winds of the kalpa blew and all beings had perished, they remained situated in that same manner within the single great ocean.
Those sons of Indra likewise remained occupied with the activities of creation and so forth within their own mentally constructed universe.
Then, O Lord, when you had withdrawn that entire state at the end of the night's course and remained established in your own self, they likewise remained established in their respective positions.
While you, intent upon that [duty] and awaiting it, remain within yourself through yogic sleep, there is the passing of the night—the progression, the step, and the transcendence thereof. || 7 ||
Now that you have awakened and desire to create the cycle of worldly existence,
they remain established in their respective high positions exactly as before, by a process that is indeed effortless.
Likewise, O Blessed One, these ten Brahmins of Brahmā—these ten transmigrations—are situated within the void of the mind. (9)
O Lord, among them, I am this Sun, stationed here in the celestial palace on earth, employed in the work of the divisions of time.

Having provided the answer to the question "How did this come to be? by means of this much text, he states the answer to the question "Who are you? with the words beginning "teṣām" (of them). [The meaning is: in the abode characterized by the ether that constitutes the cavity of one among those Brahmāṇḍas belonging to the lunar creation; on earth—so it is said.

It is an illustration of the three worlds; for it is specifically in the world of earth (bhūloka) that knowledge of the divisions of time is of particular utility as a constituent of ritual action. || 10 ||
O Lotus-born One, this creation of the quarters has been described to you;
as for the origin of the Brahmas in the sky, do as you wish.
With the intention that even though these creations exist, there is no contradiction whatsoever in your own creation, he says: "Just as you wish."
This supreme world that has arisen, its garment wrapped in manifold conceptualizations,
is a network of organs that instills delusion.
All of that is merely a delusion within one's own mind.

If it is asked, "Why is there no contradiction? the intention is that [the world] is unreal because it is merely a mental construction; with this in mind, he says "vividha" (various). O Supreme One! This entire collection of worldly objects that has arisen—which is delusive due to the attachment placed [upon it] and which is like a net that binds the external and internal organs—[is all unreal].
The meaning is that for them, the delusion within their own minds—that is, within their own consciousness—is mere error and not a real entity. || 12 ||

Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Ten Worlds," in the *Aindava* section of the *Uttara-khaṇḍa* of the *Devalokamokṣa*, within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki according to the *Ārṣa* tradition.
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Ten Worlds," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
p. 341) Chapter Eighty-Eight. 88.
The venerable Brahmā said:
"O Brahmā, O Brāhmaṇa, you are my radiance," having thus spoken to me, the Brahman, he—the best among the knowers of Brahman—became silent. || 1 ||
In this [system], the accomplishment of creation through non-attachment to the elements is proclaimed;
likewise, for one who has attained firm mastery by means of the mind, there is no turning back by others. (1)
He concludes the story told: "O Brahmā. This is an address to Brahmā as "O Brahmā, best among the knowers of Brahman," made by Bhānu; it is also an address to Vasiṣṭha made by Brahmā.
Those ten Brahmās mentioned previously were indeed Brāhmaṇas and none other; thus that Bhānu was before me, Brahmā.
The meaning is that having spoken thus, he remained silent. || 1 ||
Then, after reflecting for a long time in my mind, I said to him:
"O Bhānu, O Bhānu, tell me quickly: what else shall I create? (2)
The repetition of "bhāno bhāno" is due to reverence. || 2 ||
"O Bhāskara, tell me: if these ten worlds indeed exist there, what purpose would my own creation serve for me?"
What is the meaning? What is the purpose? || 3 ||

O great sage, having been addressed thus by me, Bhānu reflected for a long time with his intellect and spoke these appropriate words in this matter: [Note: The original text provided consists of a single verse (numbered 4). The translation reflects the content of that verse.]
It is appropriate, being worthy of my question.
Bhānu said:
"O Lord, what purpose is there for you, who are free from effort and free from desire, in creation?
O Lord of the Universe, this creation of yours is merely for diversion."
O Lord, from you alone, who are free from desire, creation comes into being—
just as reflections of the sun appear in water, though they are devoid of intellect.
Like a reflection consisting of the sun, water, and the sun itself, [it arises] from the intellect devoid of the mind. || 6 ||
When you are free from desire regarding both the abandonment and the attachment to the configuration of the body, O Blessed One, your state neither longs for nor rejects anything.
He confirms the state of desirelessness regarding creation by means of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic—starting with the phrase "the body" (*śarīra*).

Whether it be the abandonment of attachment to the arrangement of parts that constitute the body, or the coloring [of it] through the appropriation of ego-identification (*ahaṃ-abhimāna*), your disposition remains free from desire. || 7 ||
O Lord, O Protector of Beings, you create this world merely for sport,
repeatedly withdrawing it again and again, just as the sun withdraws the day.
Just as the sun creates the day, so do you create it.
This world must be sustained by you eternally as something entirely unattached, solely for the sake of diversion, and not out of a desire for exertion.
That which is worthy of being created must be performed; exertion is [proper] when there is a desire for one's own welfare, but not merely out of a wish for that [creation].
O Maheśa (or O Maheccha— where the reading *maheccha* means "O noble-minded one"), if you do not perform the creation of the Supreme Self,
what unprecedented result will you obtain by abandoning your obligatory duties?
What else—something unprecedented and unseen—will you obtain by abandoning your own obligatory duties?
The meaning is: nothing at all. || 10 ||
For a virtuous person should always perform whatever comes to hand without attachment, just as a stainless mirror performs the function of reflecting images. 11.
In that case, is cessation appropriate? No; he says: "as it has been attained. || 11 ||
Just as the wise have no desire for the performance of action, so too they have no desire for the renunciation of action. || 12 ||
The meaning is that, just as there is no cause for bringing about what has not been attained, so too there is no cause for abandoning what has been attained. || 12 ||
Therefore, with that intellect which is like deep sleep and free from desire,
perform your duties as they arise, remaining in a state like one awakened from deep sleep.

From the perspective of ultimate reality, because there is no activity, it is like deep sleep; yet from the perspective of empirical cognition, because there is activity, it is the waking state, while the dream state corresponds to the interval between them.
O Lord of the World, O Lord of the Gods, you find satisfaction through the creations of the sons of the Moon;
therefore, these [beings] shall satisfy you by their very creation.

Furthermore, if you find satisfaction through these creations of the lunar dynasty (Aindavas) as if by witnessing the increase of prosperity for your own sons, grandsons, and others, then these Aindavas will satisfy you—who are by nature inclined toward such satisfaction—even before their creation; this is the meaning. || 14 ||
These worlds are led by the eyes of the mind; they are not seen by the eye of another.
Who indeed can know that "this world was created by the eye"? (15)
"Let it be so; yet, why is my own creation not thereby rendered superfluous? To this he replies: "By the eye of the mind.
You behold the creation of another with the eye that is the mind, but you do not behold it with the physical eye.
Who, however, as its creator, does not necessarily perceive his own creation with the physical eye itself, thinking, "This was created by me"?
Therefore, this creation is worthy of being seen by your own eyes; its purpose has not been realized by anyone else—this is the meaning. || 15 ||
O Supreme Lord, he by whom the creation was fashioned with the mind alone beholds it indeed with the eye of flesh; no other does so.
In that case, it must be the creation of Aindava alone that is to be seen by me with my eye; regarding this, he says: "By which indeed... (verse 16).
And no one is able to destroy these ten cycles of existence, born from the ten dustless [virtues], which have long endured due to the firmness of the mind. (17)
"If this is so, then this creation of the moon (the lunar dynasty) is visible only to my mind and is indeed adverse to me;

therefore, it should be destroyed by me. To this, he says: "And not these... No one is able to destroy these ten worlds, their ten causes, or the ten born of Nīraja (Brahmā), who is born from the lotus. || 17 ||
That which is performed by the organs of action can indeed be restrained; however, no one is capable of restraining that which has been determined by the mind. (18)
The meanings of "to obstruct" (roddhum) and "to cause to obstruct" (rodhayitum) are both "to destroy. || 18 ||
O Brahmin, whatever firm resolve has taken root in the mind of a living being cannot be overturned by anything other than that very resolve itself. (19)
The state of having established roots, that is, having taken firm root. || 19 ||
That which has been practiced for a long time with a firm resolve by the mind suffers no destruction even through a curse, nor when the body has perished.
"In that case, he must be cast out by me through a curse"; to this, he replied: "For a long time. || 20 ||
Just as a seat of clay that has taken root in the mind becomes that very form for a person in this world and nothing else; so it is with the Self.
Therefore, I consider any other means for awakening him here to be as utterly fruitless as pouring water upon a mountain torrent. || 21 ||

The bound seat has become firm. For this very reason, he says "by awakening that [seat]," meaning that for the ignorant, the means to prevent further wandering in saṃsāra is precisely that awakening, and not something else such as boons or curses.
It is like the watering of a multitude of mountain torrents—the masses of stone fragments—with the desire for the emergence of sprouts.
I consider it to be entirely fruitless. || 21 ||
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of Aindava’s Resolve," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the scripture of the Sage.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of Aindava’s Resolution," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-ninth canto.
Bhānu said:
"For the mind is the creator of the worlds; for the mind is the supreme person."
In this world, it is that which is performed by the mind that is truly performed; it is not that which is performed by the body.
The immovability of the mind when its seat is firmly established by supreme virtues is illustrated here by the story of Indra’s mental state regarding Ahalyā. (1)
The mind itself, having attained the state of the universal aggregate (samaṣṭi), is the Supreme Person, Hiraṇyagarbha. || 1 ||
Having been ordinary Brahmins, it is said that through the cultivation of the mind, the sons of Indu attained the state of Brahmā; behold the power of the mind! (2)
For when the subtle body is meditated upon by the mind, it attains the state of a physical body;
yet one who is not joined with the notion of being a body is not afflicted by the attributes of the body.
The analysis is: "it is improper [to say] by way of the cultivation of a body. The reading "mukta" (liberated) is clear.
[This refers to being unaffected] by the attributes of the body, such as birth, death, and so forth. || 3 ||
For one whose vision is directed outward inevitably experiences pleasure, pain, and so forth;
but by being inward-turned, the yogi does not perceive what is pleasant or unpleasant within the body.
He is one who possesses an external view—that is, a view of self and what belongs to the self—regarding the body and so forth. || 4 ||
Therefore, this world with its manifold delusions has the mind as its cause;
the story of Indra together with Ahalyā serves here as an illustration.
He concludes what was stated in order to speak the story that is about to be told: "caused by the mind" (manaḥkāraṇaka). || 5 ||
Śrī Brahmā said: O Blessed One, O Sun, who is this Kāhalyā, and who here is Indra, the dispeller of darkness, the hearing of whose account brings about a purifying vision?
"Udanta" means news; it refers to the occurrence [of an event] upon hearing it. || 6 ||
Bhānu said: "O Lord, it is heard that in ancient times there was a sovereign of the Magadhas known as Indradyumna, who was like a second Indra."
Another [type] is well-known from other Purāṇas, such as Indradyumna. || 7 ||
He had a lotus-eyed wife named Ahalyā, who was like a reflection of the moon's orb, just as Rohiṇī is to the Moon.
In that very city, there was a certain eminent young Brahmin named Indra, a *ṣiḍga* who was the crest-jewel among the assembly of *ṣiḍgas*.
*Ṣiḍga* means a libertine (*viṭa*). Even when the reading is *ṣiḍga*, the meaning is the same. A wise man is one who is skilled in the arts of a libertine. || 9 ||
Once, during the course of a conversation, it was heard by the queen, Ahalyā, that Ahalyā had previously been the beloved of Indra.
Ahalyā was the wife of Gautama. || 10 ||
Upon hearing this, Ahalyā became enamored of Indra;
she then grew anxious, wondering, "Why does he not come to me, Ahalyā, even though he is attached to me? (11)
Longing and filled with yearning, they wondered: "That Indra, being so closely attached [to us], why does he not come? Why does he not approach us? (11)
Upon beds of lotus stalks and plantain leaves,
that young woman suffered intensely, like a creeper cut down in the forests.
She felt weary of all those royal splendors,
like a fish scorched by the summer heat tossing about on parched ground.

Like a fish tossing about on parched ground scorched by the summer heat, [she was distressed]. The elision of the *ya* in *sūryatiṣyāgastyamatsyānām* occurs according to the rule "of the penultimate [vowel] in *sūrya*, *tiṣya*, *agastya*, and *matsya*. (Pāṇini 6.4.149) || 13 ||
"Here is Indra! Here is Indra!"—with such idle chatter she spoke, and even her sense of shame was abandoned by her as she fell into a state of utter helplessness.
Likewise, shame was also abandoned by her as she followed after him. || 14 ||
Then, her friend, distressed with deep affection, said to her:
"My dear, I shall bring Indra here without hindrance. (15)
Immediately thereafter, having seen her in such a state, her distressed companion spoke thus:
"O dear friend, I shall bring Indra before you so that there may be no obstacle. (15)
Hearing the words, "I shall bring what you desire," her eyes blossomed with joy,
and she fell at the feet of her friend like one lotus falling upon another.
Just as a withered lotus falls at the base of another lotus, so it is in this case. || 16 ||
Then, when the day had passed and the arrival of night drew near,
that female companion went to that young brahmin named Indra.
Having awakened him as was appropriate, that woman then quickly brought Indra to the vicinity of Ahalyā during the night.
Then, adorned with many garlands and ointments, she took her pleasure with that Siddha Indra in a certain secret chamber.
Then that young woman was won over by him with his charming necklace and armlets, just as a creeper is overcome by the juice of honey through its passion for it. (20)
She was won over—that is, brought under her control—by Rati through amorous play suited for dalliance, and by Madhu, that is, by Spring. || 20 ||
Then, being devoted to him and perceiving the entire world as consisting of him alone,
she did not hold her husband— who was endowed with every excellence— in high regard.
Then, after some time, that lion among kings discovered her passion for Indra— that moonlight from the sky of her face.
It is the cause of illumination, like moonlight from the sky of her face. || 22 ||
As long as she meditates upon Indra, her face shines forth like a full moon or like a night-lotus in full bloom. (23)
He states that very point clearly: "Indram" || 23 ||
And even Indra, his entire sensory apparatus agitated by attachment to her, could not remain anywhere for even a moment when separated from her—oh, how strange! (24)
Then, the king heard the painful account of their conduct, which was characterized by excessive density of affection and lack of restraint.
Of those two whose activities were unobstructed and unrestrained by an excessive, very thick, and continuous affection; that from which there arose a bitter and unbearable pain. || 25 ||
Having observed this mutual attachment between them,
the king then issued a decree against both by means of many punishments.
The teaching is an affliction. || 26 ||
Both of them, having abandoned [their bodies] in a body of water during the winter, were content and laughed there; they did not fall into despair.

He demonstrates that very point in detail with the words beginning "tāvat" (so much so): when there is no suffering and there is the attainment of happiness even regarding an object that is worldly, unreal, or contemptible— then, when the mind is established in the Supreme Self,
any possibility of attachment to it is cast far away, and the attainment of unsurpassed bliss is self-evident.

Hinting at the secret of the intended meaning (*tātparya-rahasya*), he elaborates upon the two fruits resulting from the steadiness of their minds, beginning with the words "They praised," and so forth. || 27 ||
Then the king asked, "Are you two weary? But not from evil intent? They, having been rescued from the body of water, replied to the protector of the earth: || 28 ||
Remembering here our mutually blameless facial splendor, we do not recognize ourselves, our mutual passion having taken root. (29)
"Ātmānam" means one's own body; "rūḍhabhāvam" is an adverbial modifier of the action. || 29 ||
And because we are free from doubt regarding the teachings, we are gladdened by that;
O protector of the earth, we do not become deluded even if our own limbs were to be cut off. (30)

Since our association— that is, the connection of our minds— is free from apprehension, being devoid of any suspicion of division, for that reason we are delighted by the afflictions found in the teachings composed by you, and we do not become deluded. || 30 ||
Then, having been cast into the frying pan, the two of them remained undaunted;
with joyful hearts and delighted by their mutual recollection [of their former lives], they spoke to one another. (31)
Thus, they spoke in the very manner previously described. || 31 ||
Tethered to the feet of the elephant, they remained there without any sign of distress;
thus, delighted by their mutual recollection, they spoke to the king.
Though struck with whips and yet undaunted, those two spoke exactly as they had been instructed by the king’s repeated commands from another source.
Being questioned, Uddhṛtau spoke again and again on that very same matter;
Indra said to the protector of the earth, "This world is dear to me. (34)
No piercing pains or sufferings afflict me in the slightest;
and for her, O King of the World, everything is indeed composed of my very self. (35)
The construction is as follows: neither the sufferings nor even the causes of suffering that torment the body cause him the slightest affliction at all. || 35 ||
Therefore, no suffering whatsoever exists apart from another's teaching;
O King, "I" am mind alone, for the mind is traditionally known as the person (puruṣa). (36)
"From another teaching or even from another affliction, [no fear] exists for us"—this is the ellipsis. || 36 ||
This body is indeed nothing but mere conceptual proliferation (prapañca), for it is clearly seen [to vanish] suddenly by means of a mass of staffs applied simultaneously. (37)
The meaning is that *prapañca* (the manifold world) is an imagined expansion of the mind alone. [An objection: "In that case, I shall shatter the mind itself with blows.
To this he replies: "simultaneously" (*samakāla*). The word *sama* here means "one" (*eka*). || 37 ||
It is not possible to break the mind of this hero even in the slightest degree.
O Great King, who indeed are they, what are they like, and whose powers are they? (38)
A hero is one who is steadfast in his desired goal. || 38 ||
By those [words] even minds that possess firm conviction are shattered;
whether the body attains growth or goes to ruin, [let it be so]. (39)

The certainty that culminates in the attainment of the state of that which is seen and being experienced is "certainty regarding what is seen" (*dṛṣṭaniścaya*); even those minds possessing such certainty fall into a state of dissolution and disintegration. || 39 ||

The mind, having fallen upon the contemplated object, remains as before; when it has long been permeated by a desired object and maintains that state, the mind is said to be "steadied" (or, according to another reading, "gone there"). 40.
Possessing an obsession that has taken hold. || 40 ||

O King, the existence and non-existence residing within the body are not able to cause affliction, O Lord of the Earth, for that which has been intensely contemplated by the mind with great force. (41)
He beholds only that which is immovable, not the movement of the body, nor any actions whatsoever, O King, including even boons or curses. (42)
Immovable and steady. || 42 ||
Men are indeed able to move the mind when it is possessed of intense momentum, for [they can do so] from what is desired by one endowed with intense momentum. (43)
With intense force and firm adherence, [one seeks] to move away from the desired and wished-for object. || 43 ||
Just as deer are unable to move a great mountain, this dark-eyed woman is firmly established within the treasury of my mind. 44.
In the lofty temple of the gods, just as the divine goddess [is worshipped],
I experience no sorrow because of my beloved, who protects my life.
O King, like a mountain scorched by the heat of summer that is embraced by a garland of clouds, wherever and in whatever manner I stand or move about, [that is my state]. 46.
In that regard, I experience nothing other than union with my beloved;
with my mind named Ahalyā’s lover, I have become a mind called Indra.
"I experience nothing else, even for the slightest moment, other than union with the beloved and the attainment of desired objects.
Thus, the mind itself is firmly bound by two forms; it is impossible, even through hundreds of efforts, to lead it from one nature to another. With this intention, he says: 'Ahalyā'. (47)
O King, this [mind] of the wise man comes to be closely attached to nothing other than its own essential nature when it is intent upon a single task. (48)
It is one-pointed, being intent upon a single task; it is supreme, as it is directed toward no other object. 48.
It cannot be shaken even by the power of excellent boons or curses, like Mount Meru;
for the body undergoes a change as if it were something other [than itself] due to boons and curses.
Indeed, O King, the mind remains steadfast because it is intent on victory. (49)
It remains intent on conquering all distractions. || 49 ||
And these, O King, are not minds, nor are they causes; they are merely fragments of bodies that have arisen in vain.
For the mind is the cause within these little bodies, just as water is the cause for the sap of all the creepers in every forest grove.
[Objection: Is it not the case that the body itself is the cause of the mind? Why then is the mind not afflicted when the body is afflicted? To this he says: "These...

These visible fragments characterized as the bodies of living beings are but partial constructs (*kalpanaikadeśāḥ*) and are not the causes of the minds; rather, the meaning is that the mind (*cetaḥ*, *manaḥ*) alone is the cause within these little bodies. || 50 ||
Know that the mind is the primary body here; by it, the great-souled one has fashioned the multitude of bodies in this world.
Wherever that primary body presides, [there the other bodies follow].
That alone bears fruit abundantly for this person, and nothing else. || 51 ||

The "first" refers to the primary locus of experience for the self. It "presides over" [the body], meaning it manifests through the conceit of "I-ness. By means of that presiding, it brings forth the various forms of the body and so forth; this is the meaning. || 51 ||

O fortunate one, know that the mind is indeed the primary sprout of man; from it the bodies have spread forth like the shoots of a tree. When the sprout is destroyed, the beauty of the shoots does not arise again.
The sprout does not reach destruction even when its petals fall away. || 52 ||
Establishing the very point already stated by means of an illustration, he says: "The primary sprout," etc. (verse 52).
When the body is wounded, the mind quickly creates a multitude of various bodies, one after another, like in the land of dreams;
but when the mind is wounded, it indeed does nothing at all.
Therefore, protect this body, which is the jewel of the mind. || 53 ||

For this very reason, it is well known that even upon the destruction of the body, the body arises again and again; however, upon the destruction of the mind, there is only liberation (*kaivalya*) and no further rebirth. Thus he says: "The body... Therefore, preserve the jewel characterized as the mind—the *cintāmaṇi* which is the cause of all objects—by means of concentration on the supreme human goal.
"Protect [me]; do not destroy [me] by falling under the sway of trivial anger and the like"—this is the meaning. || 53 ||
O King, in every direction I see only deer-eyed women like my beloved; because of this, I am constantly delighted. As for the fruit that brings suffering to the subjects of your city—
Then, for a moment or even for a very long time, I did not see anything at all.

Summarizing the meaning already stated and concluding by reiterating it, he describes the futility of the effort to punish with the words "In every direction" (*diśi diśi*). Among your city, its constituent elements, or the subjects such as servants, whatever infliction of suffering there may be—such as blows from sharp weapons—and whatever resulting misery arises from that; [all this is futile].
The meaning is that I do not see this or that particular thing for even a moment, or perhaps for a very long time. || 54 ||
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Affection of the Artificial Indra for Ahalyā," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the holy *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Seer (*ārṣa*).
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Artificial Passion of Indra and Ahalyā," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Ninetieth Chapter.
Bhānu said:
Then, having been addressed in this manner by Indra, that lotus-eyed king—
He spoke to the sage named Bharata, who was standing by his side.
Although their physical bodies perished due to the curse of the sage Bharata, it is proclaimed that the mental absorption consisting of [the Lord] was not lost for them. || 1 ||
He whose eyes are like a *rājīva* lotus. || 1 ||
The king said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharma, I behold in the face of this most wicked soul, who has carried off my wife, an extreme and expansive audacity."
In the mouth of this Indra; "sphāram" means abundant. || 2 ||
O great sage, quickly bestow upon him a curse corresponding to his sin;
for the sin incurred by killing one who should not be killed is indeed the same as that incurred by abandoning one who should be killed.
The meaning is that it is well known in the treatises on Dharma (dharmaśāstra) that the same sin results from abandoning one who deserves execution as it does from failing to execute him. || 3 ||
Thus addressed by the king’s son, Bharata, the best of sages,
quickly and properly reflected upon the sin of that evil-minded man.
"Go to your destruction, O evil-minded one, along with this woman of wicked deeds who has overcome you through her betrayal of her husband"— thus he uttered this curse.
Together with this Ahalyā; destruction means death. || 5 ||
Then those two, Rāma and Bharata, replied with these words:
"You two are of evil mind, by whom this difficult penance has been destroyed."
They spoke these words to King Bharata.
By this bestowal of a curse, nothing happens to either of us;
for when the body is destroyed, nothing of ours perishes, as we exist in our own internal forms.
Nothing whatsoever perishes for us two; the reason for this is: "because they are our own internal forms. (7)
Indeed, one's own inner self can never be destroyed by anything;
know this from us, for it is subtle, composed of consciousness, and difficult to perceive. (8)
"To destroy" means to cause destruction; the elision of the suffix *ṇi* [after the root *naś*] before the suffix *seṭ* is a Vedic usage, as well as being difficult for others to perceive. || 8 ||
Śrī Bhānu said:
With their minds bound by intense affection,
they both fell to the earth due to the curse, like two leaves fallen from a tree.
"Fallen" means, that is to say, dead. || 9 ||
Then, having fallen into misfortune and entered the womb of deer,
both of them, remaining attached to one another, were again born as birds.
"Bound" means attached, fettered by calamity—that is, by a firm passion for sense objects. || 10 ||
Then, O Lord, in our creation, there were born a brahmin couple who conceived a mutual bond, were devoted to austerity, and possessed great merit.
Then, after a succession of many births, in our creation—that is, in our own universe. || 11 ||
O Lord, that curse of theirs proved effective indeed in assailing their bodies alone, but not in restraining their minds.
The curse bestowed by Bharata upon Bhārata was capable of destroying their bodies alone when they intruded [upon one another], but not their control over the mind; such is the meaning. || 12 ||
For even now, by that very same cause consisting of the formative forces of delusion (*moha-saṃskāra*), wherever they are born, there you two become husband and wife. (13)
Beholding that beautiful affection of theirs, permeated with the essence of unfeigned love,
even the trees were permeated with the essence of love.
They become agitated by the gestures of love. || 14 ||
"Even the trees become agitated by amorous gestures, how much more so others?"—this is hyperbole (atiśayokti). || 14 ||
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Artificial Indra’s Attachment to Ahalyā," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. || 90 ||
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Artificial Passion of Indra for Ahalyā," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*. 90.
The ninety-first canto.
Bhānu said: "O venerable sage, my mind is thus at the wrong time; therefore, I speak this."
It was unseizable and indestructible, even by difficult-to-withstand curses.
In this [work], having taken Bhānu as the Manu, the creation of the Creator is described;
the nature of the universe as a mere manifestation of mind is shown, just like the lunar creation.
For that reason, it was said that the curse of Bhārata was not capable of restraining the mind. || 1 ||
Therefore, O Brahmin, the destruction of the lineages of Aindavas through the process of creation is not appropriate; this is inconsistent with the nature of that Great-Souled One.
For this reason, it is not fitting for you to effect the destruction of the lineages of the sons of Indu;
it is not possible, nor is it appropriate or suitable for you, O Great-Souled One—this is the meaning. || 2 ||
What is there in this world, or indeed in all the various worlds, that could lead even you, O Lord of lords, the Great-Souled One, to such wretchedness? (3)
Then, observing his despondency that "in that case, my creation would be in vain," [the Lord] said: "What is that? (verse 3).
For the mind is the creator of the worlds; the mind is indeed remembered as the person (puruṣa).
Whatever is accomplished by the resolve of the mind cannot be achieved by means of wealth, medicines, or punishments.
The reflection of a living being cannot be destroyed, just like that of a gem;
therefore, let these remain here amidst their radiant displays of creative activity.
These belong to Indra. || 5 ||
Having created the subjects here, remain; for the space of the intellect is indeed infinite.
There is the space of the mind, the space of consciousness, and the space is the third.

Where, then, is there room for my attachment? To this he replies with the word "thou" (tvam). The sense is that it is within this space of one's own mind (svacittākāśa), according to the Vedic scripture: "The mind is indeed infinite. First, there is the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), and then the space of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsākāśa). || 6 ||
These three alone are infinite, illuminated by the sky of consciousness;
O Lord of the World, create one, two, three, or even many worlds.

Illuminated by the sky-like consciousness (cidākāśa) that stands as the witness, there is space even for infinite millions of universes within the sky of the mind; how much more so for just one? With this intention, he says:
"One" (verse 7).
"Abide in yourself by your own will; what has been taken from you by the sons of Indu?
Brahmā said:
Thus was it spoken by Bhānu regarding the web of the world of the sons of Indu.
O Great Sage, this was spoken by me after long reflection;
O Bhānu, what you have said is indeed appropriate, for the sky is truly vast.
The garment is as previously described; it is also the fourfold space.
The mind is expansive, and the space of consciousness is vast;
therefore, I perform my eternal activity by creating whatever manifestation is intended.

In this regard, with the intention that the status of being the substratum of creation belongs primarily to these two alone, he says: "and the mind. The space of consciousness (cidākāśa) is delimited by the mind. This is because the elemental space (bhūtākāśa) is included among the objects of creation, whereas the space of Brahman (brahmākāśa), due to its non-attachment, cannot be the substratum of creation. || 10 ||
O Bhāskara, I quickly conceive many hosts of beings;
therefore, O Blessed One, become my first Manu immediately.
Therefore, in that creation, Svāyambhuva was the first Manu.
"Create the world as you desire, being thus urged by me.
Then that radiant one of great splendor [accepted] these words of mine.
Being equally impelled and commanded. || 12 ||
Having divided himself into two parts, O best of those who practice austerity,
he became the sun in this present body with his former self.
"O best among those who radiate heat" is an address to Vasiṣṭha; this refers to the present creation of Indra (the Aindava-sarga). 13.
In that creation, having assumed a second body in an instant, he, through his state of being the "I-maker," spread out a series of days by traveling through the path of the sky.
He created that entire creation, each part according to my desire.
O Sage, all this has been told to you: the true nature, the agency over all things, and the power of the great-souled Vasiṣṭha’s mind. (16)
He summarizes: "This" refers to the mind of the Great Soul. || 16 ||
Whatever indeed appears as a manifestation to this mind, that very thing attains clarity, stability, and fruition. (17)
[It possesses] both fruitfulness and the quality of being the cause for the engagement in worldly enjoyments. || 17 ||
Having been ordinary Brahmins, it is said that by the power of their realization, the sons of Indu attained the state of Brahmahood; behold the potency of the mind! (18)
Just as those who were the lives of the moon attained the state of Brahman due to their nature as consciousness,
so too have we attained the state of Brahman from our state of consciousness because of our being the mind.
He states that even his own state as Hiraṇyagarbha was merely a matter of mental conception, like that of Aindava, by saying "just as":
having attained the state of mind (cittatva) from the state of consciousness (cidbhāva), and from the state of mind, the state of Brahman—that is, the state of Hiraṇyagarbha. || 19 ||
For the mind is of the nature of appearance, and that which is its appearing is this very body and so forth; it shines within itself, and there is no other perception of a body.
That very thing is one's own inner self; it is the mind alone. The perception of the body—the cognition of the body—is nothing other than the mind. || 20 ||
The mind is the self’s own wondrous manifestation, and it produces that [manifestation] spontaneously from itself,
according to its actual occurrence, within its own very self, like the internal heat of pepper and such.

It becomes such that its conceptualizations (*kalpanā*) are wonders (*camatkāra*) within itself, within its own being. He explains the nature of this self-wondering by saying: "And that performs that. If so, why does it not conceive of the minds of all beings as equal? To this he replies: "according to their actual occurrence" (*yathāvatsambhavam*).
The meaning is: "in whatever manner, to whatever extent, and at whatever time it arises, according to the latent impressions (vāsanā) of one's desires and actions, it remains exactly so.

Just as black pepper transforms within the body through its pungency, the neem tree through its bitterness, and grapes through their sweetness—each being determined by its own specific latent impression—it is the same in this case. || 21 ||
This very thing, appearing as if it were the mind, is called the *ātivāhika* (subtle body); they describe that same thing, which is a dense delusion, by the name "body. 22.

For this very reason, people designate [the self] according to the specific names of various bodies—such as "I am a god" or "I am a human"—rather than as having a single uniform form; thus he says, "This very [self]. He explains that it is the subtle body, called *ātivāhika*, which appears like the mind, that is perceived through the dense delusion—that is, the error of grossness—under the respective names of those various bodies.
They cite [the following]: || 22 ||
This mind, whose latent impressions have become attenuated, is called by the name "jīva"; know that the jīva, in which the wonder of the body has subsided, is gradually the Supreme.

If the mind is the body, then how was it previously stated that "this alone is the living being" (jīva)? To this, he says: "It is said. The meaning is: "The living being is that which has attenuated latent impressions (vāsanā), whereas the body is said to be dense delusion"; thus, by way of this distinction, one should know the Supreme Brahman as the wondrous state in which the three bodies have been stilled. || 23 ||
"I do not exist, nor does anything else exist here; this mind alone remains, like the consciousness of Vasiṣṭha and Indu, which has attained the appearance of reality though it is unreal.
(24) And thus he says that, just as a cloth is not distinct from its threads, there is no such thing as a body separate from anyone: "I do not exist," and so forth.
O mind, just as Brahmā was like the moon, so too am I situated here;
and this which has been done by him is indeed myself, appearing solely as the nature of volition.
He says, "That which was created by him is also merely a mental construction of my own; I alone am that as well," with the words "tatkṛtam" (created by him). || 25 ||
Someone might say: "I am Brahman, abiding here as a mere play of the mind;
know that the body and so forth are simply its own nature, for they are utterly void within the space of the Self. (26)

The meaning is that the very nature of the Supreme Self, being more void than all phenomenal expansion, appears as if distinct from the space of the Self in the form of the body and so forth. || 26 ||

Through the contemplation that "I am of the single nature of the ultimate reality, pure consciousness," the living being (jīva) becomes the mind once more and thus falsely perceives itself as having a bodily form.
The particle *mudhā* is used in the sense of the negative particle *na*. || 27 ||
This entire world, appearing like the cycle of existence of the son of Indu, shines as the body of consciousness;
it is a long dream born of its own power, whose nature is fully awakened awareness.

The Supreme Self alone, whose body is consciousness, shines as the self of all, like the world-cycle of the moon; the meaning is that just as a dream born of one's own power of ignorance, though long, appears as a fully realized waking state, so it is here.

The entire world arises from the mind alone, appearing first as the manifestation of those [mental] constituents, taking on forms such as the illusion of two moons, firmly established like the moon in the sky. (29)

The meaning is that since the world arises preceded by the superimposition of the sound-tanmātra, which consists of extremely subtle latent impressions (vāsanā), it is therefore conceivable that it is established just like the mental space of the moon (Aindava). || 29 ||
It does not have the nature of being or non-being, nor is it both being and non-being;
through perception it has the form of being, yet it is unreal because of its contradiction [with that very perception]. (30)

If everything were established solely from the indifferent mind, then how is it that [the self] appears as non-indifferent through the conceit of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) regarding the body and so forth? To this, he says: "It is not real" (*na sat*).
That form of "I," which is of the nature of attachment and experienced as having a non-indifferent character, is not real in any respect.

Because it is not observed in the effects of consciousness (*cittakārya*), it is not non-existent either; for that which is non-existent is never perceived. Therefore, existence and non-existence are precisely that [consciousness]: existence is indeed existent because its nature is exclusively being, and non-existence is indeed non-existent because its nature is exclusively non-being. However, the form of the "I" (*ahaṃrūpa*) is not restricted to a single nature; for by the reason of being perceived in some instances, it appears as if existent, yet in other instances...

Because it is not perceived due to its contradiction with that [reality], it is unreal and of a non-existent nature; thus, the meaning of "illusory" (māyika) is that it appears as a contradictory nature. || 30 ||
Know that the mind, which has a vast form consisting of volition, is both inert and non-inert;
it is non-inert because its nature is Brahman, and inert because it is subject to the state of being the perceived object.
Thus, he states that the mind is illusory even because its nature is contradictory, being both insentient and sentient: "insentient and sentient" (jaḍājaḍam) || 31 ||
That which consists of the reality of perceived experience does not persist in its true being;
just as the state of being a bracelet exists within gold, so too is it established within Brahman.
