When does that [mind] have the nature of the visible, and when does it have the nature of Brahman? To this he says: "The visible," etc.

That mind, at the time of experiencing the visible, appears as if it were the visible; yet in its true being—the experience of Brahman—it is not playful, meaning it does not have the habit of manifesting separately. Thus, it is Brahman alone, just as the state of being a bracelet is nothing other than gold.

The meaning is that, from the perspective of seeing the effect as distinct [from its cause], it appears as if the gold were separate; however, from the perspective of seeing the gold itself, it remains exactly as it was. || 32 ||
Because Brahman is everything, everything— whether insentient or consisting of consciousness,
from ourselves down to a stone— is neither purely insentient nor purely sentient.
With the intention that the world likewise possesses only a nature consisting of illusion (māyika) because it consists of the contradictory natures of the insentient and the sentient, he says:

"Because of its being everything" (sarvatvāt). The meaning is that from ourselves down to stones, and from Brahmā down to stationary objects, although these possess contradictory natures according to the perspective of logic (yauktika-dṛśā), they do not possess the attributes of insentience and sentience according to the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha-dṛśā). || 33 ||
Since wood and other such things lack consciousness, perception of them is impossible;
for perception arises only from a connection with something similar [to the perceiver]. (34)
The distinction between the insentient and the sentient would have to be established either prior to perception or subsequent to perception.

In the first case, since perception itself is impossible, existence is not established at all; far less, then, can there be any consideration of sentience or insentience. With this intention, he says:
"Of wood and so forth. [This refers to] two similar things.

The perception [of objects] is well known to arise from the relationship of identity between the cognizer and the cognitive principle (cid-dhātu) by means of their respective functions; however, in the doctrine that [the world] is of a purely insentient nature, there is no consciousness of the object, and thus perception is impossible—this is the meaning. || 34 ||
Know that because [the Self] is perceived as non-inert, all this indeed [is perceived];
for perception occurs between two similar entities due to a relationship of homogeneity. (35)
Regarding the second [verse], he says: "In what is perceived" (*upalabdhe*). The word division is: "Know it to be non-inert" (*ajaḍaṃ viddhi*).
Since [the object] is included within the perception of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) when it is perceived, its nature as a single, non-inert entity remains as a residue;
for perception arises precisely from the relationship characterized by the identity of the previously mentioned consciousness (*cit*). And thus, in the case of what is not perceived...
And once [the object] is perceived, it is impossible for there to be a duality between the insentient and the sentient; such is the meaning. || 35 ||
The splendor of the meanings of words such as "insentient" and "sentient" does not exist in that indescribable state, just as foliage and creepers do not exist in the great desert.
He states what results from the fact that both [alternatives] are untenable: "insentient," etc. (verse 36).
That which is the cognition of the object by consciousness is declared to be the nature of the mind (manas).
Here, the conscious portion is the non-inert part, while the state of being an object of cognition is indeed the inertness in this context.

The state of being mind (*manastā*) is simply the mental construction of the forms of the cognized within consciousness; therein lies the conceptualization of the inert and the non-inert, and the discernment of that very [duality] is "mindlessness" (*nirmanaskatā*).
With this intention, he says, beginning with "of consciousness" (*citaḥ*), etc. (verse 37).
In this context, the conscious portion is the element of awareness, while the insentient is seen as the object of cognition;
thus, the individual soul (jīva), perceiving the delusion of the world, falls into a state of agitation.

Regarding this, he says—"Thus [is] the individual soul"—to show that through the forgetting of the conscious self-nature, the delusion of the insentient self, the individual soul, and the world has arisen. || 38 ||
p. 347) 208 This very state, which resides in the mind, is pure, yet it is made twofold.
Therefore, she alone is the entire world, and she alone is that which is perceived as duality. (39)
Pure being, which is the very nature of consciousness (*cit-svabhāva*), is divided into two as "mind" and "the world.

Therefore, the meaning is that everything perceived through the single cognition of consciousness is that very consciousness itself; even that which is perceived through dualistic cognition is that same consciousness. || 39 ||
Having perceived its own self as something else, and its own body as an object of perception,
consciousness— though partless— appears as if it were a single part, wandering as if afflicted by delusion.
It is without parts and without division; it has the appearance of a single part, being equal to its own internal divisions. || 40 ||
There is no delusion, nor is there any one who experiences delusion; such is the certainty here.
Consciousness remains established in this way, resembling the full ocean. (41)
There is no person at all who is subject to delusion. || 41 ||
Everything would be insentience for her as well; yet you know that she possesses consciousness and the nature of a cognizer.
The conscious portion is a part of pure awareness, whereas the emergence of egoity is what constitutes insentience.
Even the insentient form of this consciousness must be consciousness itself; for you perceive sentience even within that insentience.
The meaning is that if it were of a purely non-conscious nature, manifestation would be impossible, and if there were no manifestation, even insentience could not be established.
He shows that just as there is awareness in the insentient, so too there is an insentient portion in the conscious—thus: "I-ness" (ahantā). || 42 ||

In the supreme reality that transcends egoism and the like, not even the slightest [distinction] exists, because that [reality] has consciousness as its essence, just as waves and so forth are not separate from water. (43)
If it is asked how the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) is insentient, he says: "Because it is excluded from Brahman"—namely, the phrase "the ego-sense and so forth.
[Brahman] has consciousness as its essence, consisting of the single flavor of pure awareness. || 43 ||
Know that the object of cognition, which appears as the notion of "I," has arisen like water within a mirage; it certainly does not exist at all.
For this very reason, he states that it is also non-existent: "By the notion of 'I'... (verse 44).

Know that the state of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) is the end, while the state of the Self (ātmapada) is free from all affliction. The wise know that "I-ness" and the like are identical to it, just as coldness is identical to snow.
Know that the state of the inner Self is the ultimate reality of the Self, which is the limit of the sublation of all duality; it is the non-state of "I-ness" (ahantā), meaning it is without support.

People perceive and see this very consciousness-nature as having the form of "I-ness" and so forth, solidified by latent impressions (vāsanā); the meaning is that it is just as people perceive coldness itself as ice due to its solidification. || 45 ||
In the mind alone is insentience perceived, like one's own death in a dream;
yet, by being the self of all and exercising all powers, it never attains a state of mere passivity.
Exercising all powers and manifesting them, consciousness does not attain equanimity without the firmness of knowledge. || 46 ||
The mind unfolds as all forms, appearing as objects and so forth;
this body of consciousness is not a manifold self, yet it possesses a form as clear as space.
The subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) is manifold in nature and characterized by consciousness. || 47 ||

By one who is existent and who abandons the identification with the body and so forth—which are of the nature of appearances—the mind, which is itself of the nature of appearance, must indeed be investigated by the mind itself. (48)
How can this be understood? He states the means for that: "dehādi" (the body, etc.).

The meaning is that the qualified seeker, having abandoned the sense of selfhood—which is merely the appearance of the three bodies beginning with the gross body—must investigate the mind itself, which is of the nature of an appearance (*prātibhāsika*), by means of the mind alone. || 48 ||
When the copper of the mind has been purified and attained the state of the ultimate gold, there is unartificial bliss; what is the use of fragments of stone that are bodies? 49.

What becomes of the mind when that purification characterized by inquiry has been performed? To this he says: "The mind... (citteti). The remainder of the sense is that unartificial, eternal, and unsurpassed bliss is attained. [Objection: In that case, let the body and so forth also be purified; why then is the human goal not obtained from those as well? To this he says: "What... (kimiti). The meaning is that their purification would be in vain. || 49 ||
That which exists is purified; that is awakening. And what are one's own feet?
If the ignorance regarding the body and so forth were real, then attachment toward it would be appropriate. (50)

Furthermore, he states that because the body and so forth do not exist, they are not fit for purification—beginning with the words "That which... (yad iti). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "the realization of that [non-existence] is fruitful. The meaning is: what trees imagined in the sky have ever been seen being purified? Thus, regarding this ignorance, it is proper and fitting to maintain a firm resolve (*graha*) toward purification—that is, to apply oneself to its removal. || 50 ||
But those ignorant ones who, being attached to the unreal, teach here that the body is the self—they are merely rams among men. (51)
For this very reason, although words such as "self" (*ātman*) are applied to the body in common usage, they do not denote the body in the Śruti,

because it is impossible for the Śruti to have an unreal object as its referent. As for those such as the Cārvākas and the vulgar who are immersed in the unreal and possess a firm conviction that the body is the self— they maintain that words such as "self" do indeed denote the body.

They believe that those who teach even the slightest authoritative reality are ignorant men, mere rams, or nothing more than human cattle. The meaning is this: words whose true referents are realities such as the Self lack the power to convey the knowledge of that truth to those who possess a perverted understanding, because they have learned the meanings of such words through their application to unreal things like the body. || 51 ||
Just as one contemplates this within one's own mind, so it becomes in an instant;
the illustrations here are the certainties regarding the moon, Ahalyā, and the artificial Indra, and so forth. 52.
If it is asked, "How then has the formless mind come to possess a material body?", he says "Just as this" with the intention that it is through cultivation alone. || 52 ||
Whatever manifests in whatever manner within the mind that is the nature of supreme intuition, that very thing arises as the body for the self;
this body exists, yet "I" am not— it is such the true nature.
Having understood that consciousness is one, remain free from desire.

Stating the very same point clearly, he concludes with the words "yadyat" (whatever): this body does not exist, nor does the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) well-known as "I" exist. Therefore, having realized one's own nature as consciousness which is of a single essence, remain—meaning, stay—just as you would be without desire. || 53 ||
"This is the body, and this indeed is that"— by such a nature,
one thinks "this is the body," and thus all of this comes to destruction;
like a child who falls into fear through the power of imagining a yakṣa or similar spirits.
By some means, he has indeed entered into a body devoid of sense organs. || 54 ||
This body, whether human or otherwise, is directly perceived; this phenomenal world is the object of enjoyment for this body.
By its very nature, through the power of its own conceptualization, this self becomes the body itself and regards all this as its object of enjoyment.
Consequently, because of that identification, it undergoes destruction following the destruction of the body—just as this child [does] by some means.

The meaning is as follows: even while remaining within the body of a yakṣa, one becomes "seized by a yakṣa" and "residing in the body of a yakṣa" through the power of mental construction—such as its terrifying appearance or its devouring nature—just as it occurs in dreams and the like. || 54 ||
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Sequence of the Descent of the Living Soul," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Sequence of the Descent of the Living Being," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
p. 348) Chapter Ninety-Two: The One Hundred and Ninth.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus to me, O scion of Raghu, that Blessed One, the lotus-born creator and lord of beings, was questioned again by me as he paused from his speech.
Here, the unfailing power of the mind is drawn in and established firmly; once stabilized, through human effort, it becomes capable of being directed as desired. (1)
Having challenged his previous statement by pointing out its logical inconsistency, I questioned him once again. || 1 ||
O Blessed One, you yourself declared that the powers of curses, mantras, and the like are unfailing; how then have those very same powers been rendered futile once again?
He demonstrates the very manner of this objection with the words "by you yourself": therefore, your statement is contradicted by your own statement;
for it is said that among living beings, even the mind, intellect, and senses are all seen to be utterly deluded by a curse—that is, by the power of a mantra. (3)

Thus, he states that there is also a contradiction with worldly perception, saying "by a curse. Accordingly, Nahuṣa, having attained the state of a python due to a curse, proceeded to devour Bhīma—who was born of his own lineage—out of mental delusion. In the same way, although Saudāsa was righteous, he became a Rākṣasa due to a curse.

The engagement in acts such as the killing of a Brahmin arises from the delusion of the intellect; likewise, the destruction of the visual faculty occurred to Dhṛtarāṣṭra due to the curse of the Gandharva king. The meaning is that this is observed in other instances as well. || 3 ||
Just as wind and its movement, just as oil and sesame seeds, are inseparable, so too are the mind and the body; that [mind] is indeed that [body].

With the intention that there is likewise a contradiction regarding the effect (*kāryavirodha*), he says "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth. The third occurrence of the word "just as" (*yathā*) is for the purpose of including other examples such as fire and heat. This is because no distinction can be established between cause and effect.
And thus, when the mind is not affected by blessings, curses, and the like, it follows that the body—which is non-different from it—is likewise not affected.
The intention beginning with "it might be" (syāt) is as follows. || 4 ||
Now, if there is no body here at all, but it exists solely through the mind, then it is experienced in vain—like a dream, a mirage, or a double moon. (5)

Now, one might raise the objection that since the mind possesses an existence subordinate to that of the body, the mind is not subject to the influence of curses and the like even when the body is; this is the counter-argument proposed by way of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*). This is introduced with the words "atha" (now/if). || 5 ||
In this case, the destruction of both occurs simultaneously upon the destruction of one;
indeed, upon the dissolution of the mind, the decay of the body necessarily follows.

Regarding that, he states another fault: "In the destruction of one," etc. When one is destroyed, the destruction of both necessarily follows. Just as the dissolution of the body is observed upon the destruction of the mind, so too the dissolution of the mind is possible upon the destruction of the body; thus, the body does not possess an existence subordinate to the mind, but rather—

The meaning is as follows: on the contrary, since it is not an object of perception while being inaccessible to the eyes and other senses, like [the objects] in dreams and so forth, the mind possesses a lower degree of reality than the body; thus, just as a snake ceases to exist when the rope [upon which it was imagined] is destroyed, it is possible for the mind to persist only upon the destruction of the body. 6.
O Lord, how is it that the mind is not overcome by defects such as curses and the like?
Or how is it overcome? Tell me, O Supreme Lord. (7)
Brahmā said: There is nothing within the treasury of the world that cannot be attained by people through pure human effort accompanied by auspicious deeds.

In that regard, first, in order to resolve the contradiction, he recalls the fact that even for boons and curses, human effort (pauruṣa) supported by karma is more powerful— the very basis upon which they depend— thereby establishing that the statement regarding the inherent strength of boons and curses must necessarily be accepted as a general rule (autsargika), in accordance with the observation of numerous instances.
Not that [is it]. || 8 ||
From Brahmā down to the stationary beings, at all times and of every species,
all embodied souls in this world possess two bodies.

Since it is observed in the world that only the gross [body] is subject to injury and not the subtle one, [the author], in accordance with common worldly perception, shows that the two bodies have distinct natures by stating "from Brahmā... and so forth. || 9 ||
The one body, however, is the mental body; it acts swiftly and is always mobile. The other body, composed of flesh, is incapable of anything.
In this regard, the body composed of flesh is connected to everyone;
it is assailed by all curses as well as by the accumulation of spells and the like. (11)
"Vidyās" refers to spells for malevolent purposes such as *abhicāra* (sorcery) and the like; by the word "and the like," weapons, poisons, and so forth are included.
"By their collections" means by their multitudes. || 11 ||
For he is almost mute, indeed powerless, wretched, and perishing in an instant; as fickle as a drop of water on a lotus leaf, his state is dependent on destiny and the like.
By the word "daiva" and so forth, the inclusion of the king, father, and others is intended. (12)
This second body, called the mind, belongs here to those who possess a body; though it is dependent [upon the elements], it is not subject to the elements within the three worlds. (13)
Dependent means under one's own control; non-dependent means not under one's own control. || 13 ||
If one stands firm, relying upon his own manliness and maintaining eternal fortitude, he becomes invulnerable to sufferings; thus, he remains irreproachable. (14)

Therein, he establishes self-dependence by stating the reason: "pauruṣam" (human effort). It is "agamyaḥ," meaning unassailable; it is "aninditaḥ," meaning untainted, by those causes of suffering. || 14 ||
In whatever manner the mind-body of embodied beings exerts itself, in that very manner it becomes, reaping exclusively the fruit of its own resolve. (15)
He says "just as" (yathā) [in verse 15] to show that for this person, not only is there non-affliction by suffering, but even the accumulation of happiness increases.
No human effort regarding the body of flesh bears fruit;
however, every action of the mental body is entirely fruitful.
But this sequence does not apply to the gross body; thus he says: "accompanied by its fruit" (saphala). || 16 ||
The mind that constantly contemplates the sacred remains ever mindful;
therein, curses and the like are fruitless, like arrows shot at a stone. 17.

With the intention that the mind is indeed defiled by the defects of sense-objects and not by the defects of anything else, he says: "It is pure. Thus, the sense is that there is no occasion for the suspicion of contradiction with worldly perception. || 17 ||
Whether the body falls into water, fire, or mud,
whatever the mind intends, that very thing it attains at that very moment.
He also removes the contradiction with the effect—[stating] "let it fall" (patatu)—in verse 18.
O Sage, every superior person, when crushing all worldly states of being, bestows the fruit [of his purpose] without obstacle; for the mind, indeed, is the master of the mind.
Even when all states such as the body and so forth are destroyed, every human effort that is perfected bestows its fruit without obstacle. That which it bestows is the mind itself;
it bestows the fruit of the mind, because even human exertion is a manifestation of the mind—this is the meaning. || 19 ||
Having inwardly transformed his mind into one consisting of his beloved through the power of his manly resolve,
that artificial Indra did not experience even the slightest pang of suffering.

With the intention of suggesting that if one does not perceive suffering even when there is a defect in the object due to firmness of mind, then what need be said regarding a pure object, he recalls the legend of Indra and others with the words "by human effort" (pauruṣeṇa). || 20 ||
Having made his mind free from passion and devoid of fever through human effort, Māṇḍavya conquered the afflictions even while remaining upon the tip of a stake. (21)
The story of Māṇḍavya is well known from the Mahābhārata and other sources. || 21 ||
Even while remaining in a blind well, the sage Dīrghatapas attained the station of the gods through mental accumulations of sacrifice.

Dīrghatapas, also desiring to perform a sacrifice, went out to procure the sacrificial requisites; by chance, he fell into a blind well, and when the time for the sacrifice was about to pass, he offered it mentally. Indra, being pleased by this, lifted him out of the well and led him to his own abode; thus it is well known in the Mahābhārata and other texts. 22.
Even by men who are sons of the Moon (Soma), through human resolve and meditation, the state of Brahman was attained; that [attainment] is not subverted even by me.
There were others as well, wise and vigilant gods and great seers, who did not abandon the contemplation of their own Self from their minds even for a moment. (24)
Contemplation, worship, or knowledge. || 24 ||
Mental anxieties, physical ailments, curses, and likewise evil glances do not shatter his mind, just as blows from lotuses cannot damage a stone.

Evil-sighted beings such as *rākṣasas*, *piśācas*, and the like do not shatter—that is, they do not overcome—their mind, which is one-pointedly focused on the object of meditation. Nor do they inflict blows, even with lotuses. || 25 ||
And as for those who have been broken by curses and other such arrows of mental anguish, I consider their minds to be devoid of manliness, incapable of exercising self-discernment. (26)

Those such as Saudāsa, Nahuṣa, Viśvāmitra, and others—the word "etcetera" including desire, anger, pride, and so forth—their minds are "devoid of manliness," meaning their manliness is not firm; that is to say, I consider them incapable of self-discrimination in spiritual practice and incompetent regarding knowledge. || 26 ||
Never at any time in saṃsāra has anyone, even in a dream or in what is seen, been rendered barren by the webs of defects with even the slightest heedful mind. (27)

But when the mind is made firm through discernment and human effort, there is no loss of one's desired goal; thus he says: "Never," even while the visible world remains manifest in the waking state. || 27 ||
Therefore, with his own mind and through his own human effort,
a person here should unite his very self with the path of purification.
O Sage, whatever appears to him becomes sufficient as it truly is; in an instant, his mind becomes bloated like a child’s ghost.

The meaning is that even that which has only slightly appeared in the mind becomes firmly established after a long time; it becomes full, as it truly is, like reality itself, and fit for enjoyment. || 29 ||
Immediately upon its manifestation, the appearance abandons its prior state,
just as a pot abandons its condition as a lump of clay immediately after the potter's work.

[Objection: "But surely, because the firmness of the manifestation of his former state as a human being and so forth remained, why did his persistence as a lunar deity (aindava) and so forth not also occur? To this he says: "Of the manifestation... The sense is that the former latent impression (vāsanā) is sublated by a subsequent, more firmly established latent impression. || 30 ||
O Sage, the mind attains the state of appearing as an object in an instant,
just as water, whose nature is mere movement, assumes the form of towering waves.

To the question of how meditation—which has been exhausted by the destruction of prior latent impressions (vāsanā)—can possess the capacity for another effect, he replies: "By intuition" (*pratibhāsa*). There is a delay in its own function only until the destruction of opposing factors; thereafter, however, because it is immediately free from obstacles, it attains the state of being the object of meditation within the scope of the meditative intuition.
The meaning is that since it is indeed attained, there is no diminution. || 31 ||
Merely through mental construction, one with impure faculties perceives night even in the solar disc, just as one perceives duality in the lunar disc.
[Objection: Even so, how can there be the conception of a creation that is contrary to them at the time of dissolution?

To this, he says: "by mere recollection" (*anusaṃdhānamātreṇa*). In their creation, nothing belonging to your creation—whether favorable or unfavorable—is required; for in that case, only their own recollection is necessary. Thus, even at the time of dissolution, [there is no contradiction].
The meaning is that there is a contradiction with that. "One with impure eyes" refers to one whose vision is obstructed by a finger. || 32 ||
Whatever this mind perceives, that very thing quickly comes to fruition;
it experiences that [result] along with joy and sorrow, and therefore it is that [mind] itself which is that [result].

He states that its being an enjoyer, just like its being a creator, belongs to the mind alone—using the words "yat" (that which). The meaning is: that very thing which is the agent is itself the enjoyer. || 33 ||
Even upon seeing a hundred flames of fire in the moon at every step of his inspired eloquence, the mind experiences burning; and being burnt, it suffers intense anguish. (34)

He demonstrates the stated point by means of an illustration—namely, "inspiration" (pratibhā). Inspiration is a synthesis [of memory and perception] arising from latent impressions (saṃskāra) awakened by the impelling unseen force (bhojakādṛṣṭa); it follows immediately upon and conforms to that [awakening]. Thus, the meaning is that this is well known among those separated from their beloveds. || 34 ||
Indeed, for a mind that follows the flow of inspired eloquence, even bitter words are an elixir;
having seen and drunk them, it attains supreme satisfaction, leaps, and dances. (35)

In "kṣāre" [it refers to] alkaline substances such as salt-earth (ūṣa) and the like; if the reading is "kṣīre," it means in water. "Rasāyana" refers to the various distinctions of tastes, beginning with the sweet.
The intention is that it is observed, for instance, that camels, goats, and others eat even the leaves of the arka and nimba plants after they have been made sweet. || 35 ||
At every step of his inspired eloquence, he perceives even the sky as a vast forest;
having seen it, he cuts it down and then repeatedly plants it anew.
In this way, O dear one, the mind quickly perceives that very same magical illusion which it itself imagines;
having truly understood that the world is neither non-existent nor existent, it surely [ceases its delusion].
Abandon this mangled vision, which is characterized by manifold distinctions.
He concludes what has been said with the word "ittham" (thus): "Abandon, that is, give up, the severed—that is, limited—vision. || 37 ||
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Mind," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Mind," in the Utthāna-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus was this previously spoken by the Blessed One to me, and that very same thing has been told to you today.
In this context, the mind was born from Brahmā; from that arose the Taijasa Creator.
From that came delusion (moha), from which egoism (ahaṃkāra) arose, and from that the universe is said to have emerged. || 1 ||

Desiring to elaborate upon the sequence of creation previously described as beginning with the mind (*manas*), he concludes the dialogue with Brahmā: "Thus," [referring to] by the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, from that Brahman which is ineffable, the entirely ineffable arises everywhere;
having itself attained a state of density, it becomes the mind. || 2 ||

From the unmanifest name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which is indeterminate because it cannot be described; from that which is "unnameable" because of its subtlety and thus unfit for association with names—there arises the entire manifold form (*prapañca-rūpa*) consisting of movement, illuminated by non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*). At that time, it [arises] by itself alone.
Having attained density through the emergence of the power of *manas*, which consists of the nature of conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*) and discursive thought (*vikalpanā*). || 2 ||

Preceded by the conceptualization of those subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the mind (*manas*), there arises a structural arrangement; from that, the person (*puruṣa*) consisting of fire (*taijasa*) is produced.
He gave the name "Brahman" to this very self. || 3 ||

The subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are the subtle forms of matter; preceded by the conceptualization of those [elements], they assume a configuration like a dream-body, having the form of a person consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Thereupon, the Person (*puruṣa*), who is the Self (*ātman*), conditioned by that configuration as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), is the Taijasa, because his limiting adjunct is the collective totality of the subtle body (*liṅga-samaṣṭi*) in which light (*tejas*) predominates. This very one is Brahmā Parameṣṭhin. (3)
Therefore, O Rāma, know that this Parameṣṭhin is the very essence of the mind.
He states that his capacity for the volition of creating the world arises precisely from his being of the nature of mind: "By him," [it is said]. || 4 ||
The Blessed Lord Brahmā has the form of the principle of mind (samanas); because he consists of volition (saṃkalpa), whatever he wills, that very thing he perceives. || 5 ||

Then, by that [Brahman], this ignorance—which consists of the conceit of a self in what is not-self—was conceptualized; by that Brahman, this world, composed of mountains, grass, and oceans, was gradually conceptualized.

[Objection: Let it be that the world arises from His volition; but from where does the identification (abhimāna) of the individual souls (jīvas) with it arise? To this he says: "Then by Him... Here, *avidyā* refers to the effect-avidyā, which consists of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) characterized by misapprehension. Thus, in this manner. || 6 ||
Thus, through this sequence, this creation originating from the principle of Brahman appears as if it had come from some other source. || 7 ||

Although it has come from the reality of Brahman, which is of the nature of pure consciousness, it is nevertheless perceived by the logicians as having come from something else—namely, from an insentient source such as primordial matter (pradhāna) or atoms (paramāṇu). || 7 ||
Therefore, O Rāma, the origin of all things existing within the belly of the three worlds is from Brahman, just as waves arise from the ocean.

The theory that atoms are the cause is not tenable, because it involves the conceptual burden of postulating multiple material causes for each single effect. Furthermore, the theory that primordial matter (*pradhāna*) is the cause is not tenable, because the diverse arrangement of the insentient world cannot be established without an agent, and because agency is impossible for that which is unattached and indifferent. [Therefore, it must be] of consciousness...

The theory of the transformation of consciousness is not tenable, because it is impossible for that which is insentient in nature to undergo transformation. Furthermore, since emptiness is never observed to function as a cause anywhere, the theory of its causality is also untenable. And since there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for any of these alternative theories, it is certain that this creation did not originate from anything else.

With the intention that, on account of the authority of the sacred scriptures (śruti) and for the sake of parsimony (lāghava), the theory of the world as an illusory manifestation (vivarta) of Brahman—possessing the power of indeterminable māyā—is the only one remaining, he concludes with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). || 8 ||

Thus, while the world has not yet arisen, that [power] of Brahman which consists of the form of consciousness, having been projected upon the ego (ahaṃkāra), causes Brahman to attain the state of being Brahman. || 9 ||
The manner of origination is thus according to this method. He states that very point with the words beginning "in the unarisen" (*anutpanne*).

Precisely because the world is a phenomenal manifestation (*vivarta*) and is therefore ultimately unarisen, one should conceive of Brahman as having entered into the aggregate adjunct of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra-samaṣṭy-upādhi*); thus, it attains the state of Brahman, that is, the status of Parameṣṭhin. || 9 ||
As for those other powers of consciousness, they are conceived as being non-different from the omnipotent one. || 10 ||
Others are the powers of consciousness (cicchakti) or manifestations of consciousness (cidābhāsa) conditioned by the individual ego (vyaṣṭyahaṃkāra). || 10 ||
When the world has been expanded by him in the form of the Grandfather (Brahmā), they shine forth within the mind. || 11 ||
The meaning is that they first manifest through the form of the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) by means of the mind in its state as a collective consciousness;
these are called the thousands of transmigrating individual souls (jīvas). || 12 ||

Having risen from the sky into the atmosphere, enveloped by the subtle elements (tanmātras), those fourteen kinds of beings who abide within the space and wind and exist in the midst of the aggregate of living things— having entered that very stationary body through the gateway of the vital power (prāṇaśakti)— [they remain].
Even mobile beings go to the state of being seeds. || 13 ||
For they have indeed arisen from the very thought-sky; enveloped in the sky of illusion by the subtle elements (tanmātra) which serve as the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) for the gross elements (bhūta),
they exist within the various divisions of the mass of wind— such as the distinctions of *āvaha*, *udvaha*, and so forth— which resides in the space of the atmosphere.

Among those fourteen kinds of worlds, whatever species of beings exists therein, the living beings who abide within it through the practice of such latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and karma enter— by means of the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) of that very same species— a body, whether stationary or moving, in the form of semen, blood, and so forth.
They become seeds. || 13 ||

Thereafter, they are born in the world from a womb; thereafter, by the principle of the "crow and the palm fruit" (coincidence), they become partakers of the fruits of karma corresponding to the stream of latent impressions that has arisen.
Then, their bodies bound by the ropes of karma entwined with latent impressions (vāsanā), they wander about and repeatedly spring upward. || 15 ||

Then, being bound by the cords of meritorious and non-meritorious karma— which are interwoven with the latent impressions (vāsanās) of good and evil— those whose bodies are thus constituted as subtle bodies (liṅgaśarīras) fly up to the highest worlds or fall into the hells. || 15 ||
These classes of beings are indeed desire itself. || 16 ||
And since desire alone is the seed of both karma and its latent impressions (vāsanā), living beings consist of that very essence; thus he says:
"These are indeed [born of] will. And so says the Śruti: "This person consists of desire alone. (16)
Some, driven by the whirlwind of karma, fall like forest leaves into the depths of thousands of people; wandering about, they roll in the hollows of mountains.

He elaborates in four verses, beginning with "kāścit," upon the very succession of births for those following desire, which culminates in liberation: "Certain classes of beings, their progeny, birth, and people; people, births, and thousands of them—those whose end is the limit of the awakening to reality, being such as they are, fall into saṃsāra. Certain species of living beings, their offspring, birth, and men;
men, births, and thousands of them—the limit of which is the boundary of the realization of truth—being of such a nature, they fall into the cycle of existence.
The meaning is that they are liberated from that; the phrase "like the leaves of a forest" and so forth connects with what precedes and follows. || 17 ||
Some immeasurable beings, deluded by the ignorance regarding the knowledge of the existence of consciousness,
have been born here for a long time, even for many hundreds of kalpas.

But some, deluded by ignorance regarding the existence of consciousness, are such that their births—being immeasurable and thus beyond determination by calculation and the like—are long-standing; indeed, they continue to exist here in this saṃsāra for even many hundreds of kalpas. || 18 ||
Some, having passed through only a few delightful intermediate existences, dwell in this world devoted to virtuous deeds. (19)

The remainder of the verse implies that those women, who have passed through several past lives that were not pleasing but are now devoted to auspicious deeds, will experience [the fruits of their merit] in only a few more births. || 19 ||
Some, having realized full consciousness, have gone to the supreme state,
like drops of ocean water driven by the wind that vanish into the midst of the sea.
But some were already liberated even before this; thus he says, "some. Like drops of seawater stirred up by the wind entering the midst of the ocean, they enter the ocean of milk. || 20 ||
The birth of all living beings here proceeds from the station of Brahmā;
thus, worldly existence is characterized by the fragile nature of manifestation and disappearance.
He concludes what has been stated with the words beginning "origination" (utpatti), etc. || 21 ||
It sustains the fever of distress caused by the imbalance of the poison of latent tendencies;
it brings about endless calamities, misfortunes, and the performance of improper deeds.
Wandering through various directions, countries, times, and even within mountains and caves— the word "within" (anta) indicating the worlds to be reached after death—
this unchaste woman has fashioned herself with supreme variety and established herself without agitation. (23)
Wandering through various directions, various lands, various times, and various mountain caves,
she moves about like one experiencing the fruits of karma; by her, bewildering delusions were produced through various excellent diversions, yet in the ultimate sense, she is non-existent.
This withered vine of the world’s wilderness has been cut down by the axe of perfect vision;
like a vine, it has its body and mind agitated.
It does not grow again, O Rāmabhadra.

Having thus elaborated upon the creeper of saṃsāra, he states the means for its eradication with the words "This... This world-characterized, dried-up creeper of delusion is that whose very body or nature is the mind, which is agitated and full of mental distractions.
"Perfectly clear vision" is the direct realization of reality; by means of the axe characterized by that [vision], [ignorance] is cut—that is, severed.
"Like a creeper" is a negative example (vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta). The sense is that it does not grow again because the root-ignorance has been eradicated. || 24 ||
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Vision of Origination," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition. 93.
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Vision of Origination," in the Utthāna-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Of objects—superior, inferior, and middling—scattered here and there...
O Rāghava, listen; I shall explain this classification of origins. 1.
In this world, the species of living beings are described as divided into twelve types;
due to the diversity of their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and qualities (*guṇa*), they attain liberation either slowly or quickly. (1)

Having observed through signs Rāma’s desire for specific knowledge regarding the previously mentioned distinction between the long-term and short-term liberation of living beings, Vasiṣṭha spoke in detail to explain that [distinction], beginning with the words "The superior... and so forth;
[he did so] by means of the classification of objects as superior, inferior, and middling, according to the distinctions of *sāttvika*, *tāmasa*, and *rājasa*.

The meaning is: there exists this division, which is about to be described, of those births of the limiting adjuncts of the individual soul (jīvopādhi) in various worlds that were previously mentioned; listen as I shall explain it. || 1 ||
That which has arisen for the very first time in this very life is called "firstness" (idaṃprathamatā); it arises from the cultivation of virtue. || 2 ||

Among the distinctions to be described— namely: (1) *idaṃprathamatā* (the state of being first), (2) *guṇapīvarī* (abundant in qualities), (3) *sasattvā* (possessing *sattva*), (4) *adhamasattvā* (possessing inferior *sattva*), (5) *atyantatāmasī* (extremely characterized by *tamas*), (6) *rājasī* (characterized by *rajas*), (7) *rājasasāttvikī* (having *rajas* and *sattva*), (8) *rājasarājasī* (having *rajas* and [excessive] *rajas*), (9) *rājasatāmasī* (having *rajas* and *tamas*), (10) *rājasātyantatāmasī* (having *rajas* and extreme *tamas*), (11) *tāmasī* (characterized by *tamas*), (12) *tāmasasattvā* (having *tamas* and *sattva*), (13) *tamorājasī* (having *tamas* and *rajas*), and (14) *atyantatāmasī* (extremely characterized by *tamas*)— [this refers to the first].
Since the last two divisions—the fifth and the ninth—are included within others, twelve divisions remain;

of these, he shows the first: "one arisen for the very first time. This refers to a soul (*jīva*) who, in his final birth during a previous *kalpa*, possessed the full attainment of all the qualities of the means to liberation, such as tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), and so forth.
The meaning is this: for one whose knowledge has not arisen— either due to the non-attainment of hearing [the teachings] or due to powerful obstacles—
who, in this very life and at its very first beginning, has become endowed with all virtues such as tranquility (*śama*) and is thus fit for knowledge,
that class of living beings is called "first-born" (*ādijāti*).
For that [realization] arises from the practice of virtue in previous kalpas; the meaning is that one becomes a partaker of liberation in that very life. || 2 ||
And that [consciousness] is the support for auspicious worlds and is connected with the performance of auspicious deeds;
yet it is also the agent of the diverse latent impressions of saṃsāra. (3)

If that very [wisdom] is conjoined with former dullness of dispassion (*vairāgya*), with the performance of worship, ritual acts, and so forth born from the desire for auspicious worlds, and for this very reason functions within the experience of enjoyment due to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the diverse *saṃsāra*—then it brings about liberation after the exhaustion of those latent impressions through only five or ten births; this is the remainder [of the statement]. For this reason:
The meaning is that she is called "plump with virtues" because that peace is augmented by both sets of qualities, beginning with passion (rāga) and so forth. || 3 ||
Having been told that liberation occurs after only a few more existences, she, who was robust with virtues,
gave an inference regarding what was to be done and what was not to be done, based solely on the necessity of bestowing such a fruit.
He states the third [verse]: "tādṛk" (such). The word "tādṛk" is to be repeated [as *tādṛk-tādṛk*].

That [intellect] which, by means of certain primary signs characterized by the bestowal of such and such fruits of pleasure and pain, causes one to infer the merit and demerit—what was done and what was not done—in the previous kalpa, she too [is the intellect].
It follows by implication that through a gradual accumulation of merit over births numbering up to a hundred, one becomes a partaker of liberation. || 4 ||
Therefore, O Rāma, she is called "possessing consciousness" by those of perfected self;
yet, if she functions through the latent impressions of the manifold world-process, [she is called "unconscious"].
He states the fourth [verse]: "Now," etc. || 5 ||
Extremely turbid for thousands of births, it becomes a partaker of knowledge;
such is that which provides the inference of dharma and adharma through the granting of their respective fruits.
"Exceedingly turbid," meaning possessed of the impurity of the evil latent impressions (*durvāsanā*) accumulated through many misdeeds in previous kalpas;
"of such a kind," and so forth, as before. (6)
Therefore, he is rightly called by the virtuous "the lowest of beings";
for immediately after that very [state], there follows a multitude of births beyond counting and infinite.

He states the fifth [verse]: "That very same... It means that she, possessing those very characteristics, being averse to the science of the self (*adhyātma-śāstra*), has her liberation doubted in this *kalpa*—that is, her liberation is only somehow possible. || 7 ||
If that which is characterized by doubt regarding liberation is called "utterly dark" (*atyantatāmasī*), then birth in this present life is indeed the cause of such a state. (8)

He defines the sixth [type]: "anadyatana" (non-recent). That which is a *jāti* (birth/species) preceded by births not belonging to the current day—that is, following the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from previous kalpas—and for this very reason, performing such conduct, occurring within two or three intervening existences, specifically within two or three births of this current kalpa, and being of a middling nature such as that of a human and so forth—this is [the sixth].

The meaning is that birth which results in such effects—leading to the attainment of heaven, hell, and so forth corresponding to those actions—and which is characterized by doubt and delusion, is of the nature of *rajas*. (8)
O Rāma, best of the Rājās, that birth of a person which occurs within two or three intermediate existences is middling; such a birth in this world is characterized by passion (rājasī).
Even one whose birth is not yet distant is called so by those of perfected intellect;
for she is considered fit for liberation by seekers of release through the mere death of that [body]. (10)

He defines the seventh [type of seeker] with the words "not remote" (*aviprakṛṣṭa*). When she, through the attainment of dispassion and other qualities induced by the experience of the suffering inherent in *rajas*, becomes one for whom knowledge arises without delay, then, by the mere death occurring at that time, she is declared by those seeking liberation to be fit for emancipation. She herself—
The meaning is that I have declared her to be of a rajasic-sattvic nature through an inference based on the mark of such actions. || 10 ||
By inferring from such effects, she is said to be rajasic-sattvic;
if she is so, then through other minor births she becomes a partaker of liberation.
He defines the eighth [type of devotion] with the words "saiva cet" (if that very same [devotion]).
If that same [devotion] is characterized by births among those other than humans— namely, among the highly exalted Gandharvas and so forth— in successive order,
then such [devotion] is called by the knowers of truth "rājasarājasī."
If she is a seeker of liberation for a long time, she alone becomes a partaker of liberation after hundreds of births.
He defines the ninth [type] with the words: "That very [devotion], through hundreds of births... (verse 12).
That undertaking described by you as being of such a nature is characterized by passion and ignorance;
it is the very same [path] that results in liberation only with uncertainty, even after thousands of births.

The tenth [type of action] is characterized as follows: it possesses undertakings such as those of the Rājasa and Tāmasa types, including ritual actions (*karma*), meditative practices (*upāsana*), and sacrifices (*yajña*). This is indicated by the words "that very same" (*saiva*). || 13 ||
That birth of men from Brahmā, which follows thousands of previous lives and is characterized by such undertakings as those described, is of a predominantly rajasic and tamasic nature. (14)
He speaks of the eleventh [day] with the words "mukta" and so on. The "origination of Brahmā" refers to the manifestation of Hiraṇyagarbha and others at the beginning of the kalpa. || 14 ||
For that [birth] has been described by the great seers as leading to liberation after a long time;
however, if one is destined for liberation through that very birth, then it is so called. (15)
"Long-term liberation" (ciramokṣā) means liberation in another kalpa. He states the [second] type of intelligence: "by that very birth.

By "that birth" is meant the first birth in a *tāmasa* state. The point is that it is well known that Prahlāda, Karkaṭī, and others attained knowledge through an excellence of *sattva*, even though they were born in a *tāmasa* state such as among dānavas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and so forth. || 15 ||

If one who possesses such undertakings is declared by those who know [the truth] to be "tāmasa-sattva" (of a tamasic nature yet possessing sattva), and if she becomes a partaker of liberation after only a few births, then that is so stated. (16)
The *rājasa-tāmasī* [nature] was previously described; now, based on the sequence of its effects, he states the thirteenth [type] with the words "by existences" (*bhavaiḥ*). || 16 ||
"Consisting of the nature of Tamas and Rajas" means [endowed] with such qualities augmented by thousands of previous births and even hundreds of future births. (17)
The meaning is: characterized by fruits that abound in passion (rajas) and ignorance (tamas), yet are augmented by virtue (guṇa). || 17 ||

Therefore, those who are fit for liberation are declared by the knowers of truth to be *tāmasa-tāmasī*; whereas those previously endowed with hundreds of thousands of births, even if they possess hundreds of thousands of births prior [to this], are not so. (18)
He states the procedure for the fourteenth day: "First," etc. (18).
That which has liberation as its uncertain goal is called "extremely tamasic.
All these classes of beings come from Brahman. (19)

In order to strengthen the possibility of the non-difference of all things from Brahman by way of their origin from Brahman through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), he speaks by means of various examples: "All these... (19).
Like waves slightly stirred from the ocean,
all the multitudes of individual souls (jīvas) have indeed emerged from Brahman.
Just as rays [emanate] from a lamp through the expansion of its own radiance,
all the series of elements have arisen from Brahman.
Like sparks from a blazing fire produced by its own rays, all these multitudes of individual souls have arisen from that Brahman— [the reading being "dṛśyadṛśya" (the seen and the unseen)]. 22.
The particles are sparks. || 22 ||
All those who possess the form of Mandāra blossoms, like rays of light from the lunar orb, have emerged as the perceptible visions of Brahmā. (23)
Just as various trees arise and the perceptions of those trees arise in their respective forms, so too have all the series of individual souls (jīva-paṅkti) emerged from Brahman.
The splendor of the branches is the beauty of the boughs. || 24 ||
O Rāma, all the multitudes of individual souls have arisen from Brahman, just as bracelets, armlets, and earrings arise from gold. (25)
O Rāma, just as drops of water emerge from a stainless cascade, so too do all the conceptualizations of the succession of beings arise from the Unborn alone.

Having thus demonstrated the fitness for non-difference through the conceptualization of the relationship between part and whole, he shows their actual non-difference by demonstrating the falsity of limiting adjuncts (upādhi): "Of the unborn alone," etc. (Verse 26).
Just as the spaces within a jar, a bowl, or a hole are all [merely] of the nature of space, so too all the conceptual constructions of the world arise from the state of Brahman. (27)

In order to demonstrate, through the reasoning of "non-difference from that," the falsity of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) by means of an illustrative example, he states that the world is an effect of Brahman, beginning with the words "all indeed... (verse 27).
O Rāma, just as droplets, whirlpools, and waves arise from water, so indeed do all perceptions of the visible world arise from Brahman. 28.
Just as the waves of a mirage are not distinct in nature from the light of the sun,
so all objects of perception are not distinct in form from the perceiver.
Just as the moonlight is the radiance of the cool-rayed one, or as self-luminosity is the light of fire, so indeed are these various species of living beings. (30)
One's own light is like its radiance. He concludes with the words "In this way," and so forth. || 30 ||
For it is from that very source they emerge and into that same source they enter:
some births are of long duration, occurring at the end of thousands of lifetimes; others are established as forms belonging to only a few past births. (31)

"Coming together" means they manifest; "entering" means they attain oneness through the dissolution of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). The phrase beginning with "certain [rays]" is a restatement of what was previously mentioned. || 31 ||
Thus, in the various worlds, diverse forms exist according to the will of that Blessed One, functioning within the realm of worldly convention.
Forms and cognitions come and go, fall down and likewise spring up, like dust motes rising from the feet.

From that Blessed One, the Lord Brahman, whose very self is Īśvara, the various previously mentioned classes of living beings— whose splendor consists of the very forms that serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for His manifest glory— fall away and wander from one existence to another,
like clusters of sparks arising from a fire.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth canto, titled "The Narration that Everything is Produced from Brahman," in the section on the Means to Liberation within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage. 94.
Thus ends the ninety-fourth sarga, titled "The Exposition that Everything is Produced from Brahman," in the Utpatti-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The agent and the action are non-different, both arising simultaneously from the supreme state.
They became manifest of their own accord, like the fragrance of a tree's flowers.
In order to awaken the masses of unenlightened people,
it is not from the standpoint of ultimate reality that the simultaneous arising of action and its agent is here asserted by implication.

By means of the statement that all species of living beings manifest from Brahman alone at the beginning of a kalpa, it is shown that Brahman itself has entered into limiting adjuncts (upādhis) in the form of individual souls (jīvas). And thus, since the state of being a soul is adventitious, prior karma cannot be said to be its cause; for that [karma] depends upon a prior agent.

If, for that purpose, one were to accept the beginninglessness of the individual soul (jīva), then the previously mentioned state of being a soul as a mere adjunct (aupādhika) of Brahman could not be established; thus, seeing that a fault would result in either case, [the author], with a hidden intention, proceeds to resolve this by resorting to a distinction in perspectives through the method of elimination (pariśeṣa) during the stage of rational inquiry.
He demonstrates their simultaneous origination with the word "abhisrav" (flowing forth together).

Because they are conceived as being identical with one another, they are non-different; therefore, at the beginning of creation, they both simultaneously and equally emerged from the Supreme Brahman by their own inherent nature alone. And thus:
The word of the Blessed One: "The Lord creates neither agency nor actions for the world, nor the connection with the fruits of action; rather, it is inherent nature that operates. (1)
When all mental constructs have ceased, individual souls shine forth within the stainless Brahman,
like the appearance of blueness in the vast, expansive sky to one whose eyes lack discernment.

Regarding the manifestation of that [state] and the primary chapter on that [subject], he provides an analogous example, stating that the very nature of living beings is the cause, with the words "all... (sarva...). || 2 ||
O Raghava, wherever the conduct of unawakened people is observed, there the doctrines stating that "living beings are born from Brahmā" remain established. (3)

For this very reason, he states that this doctrine of creation pertains only to the level of conventional discourse accepted by those who do not see its refutation, and not to the state of ultimate reality: "By one who is unawakened... (verse 3).
O Rāghava, it is not fitting for those who follow the conduct of the fully awakened ones to speak thus: that this world was born from Brahman, or that it was not born.

There is neither cessation nor origination, neither one bound nor a practitioner, neither one seeking liberation nor indeed liberation—such is the ultimate reality. That very Brahman is without prior, without posterior, and without interior... [it is] not possible to speak of the origination and so forth of the world, of individual souls, or of karmas, nor of their negation.
Thus he said: "Fully awakened," etc. (verse 4).
O Raghava, as long as even a single conceptualization has not been brought to manifestation,
the splendor of the teaching for the one to be taught does not shine in the world.
In that case, what is the purpose of a scripture that teaches the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
Therefore, having provisionally accepted the views of those who perceive duality, it is taught: "This is Brahman" or "These are indeed the individual souls (*jīva*). Such is the sequence of words.
The meaning is: "having accepted [the means] for as long as the time of conventional usage lasts. *Vai* signifies certainty (*niścaye*). *Vā* signifies doubt (*saṃśaye*).

The word *iti* signifies manner (*prakāre*). The meaning is: having accepted, with certainty, whatever measure of proof (*yāvat-pramāṇa*) there may be for the sake of purification, and with doubt, in whatever manner, until the determination of the object of knowledge (*yāvat-prameya-nirṇaya*). || 6 ||
Thus it is seen that the world arises from Brahman through non-attachment; born from That, it is That itself, yet it is perceived as distinct from its cause due to the difficulty of comprehension.
He says, "Thus it is seen," because even in the world, such a statement is well known in many instances. If duality is thus accepted, how then is it refuted?
To that he says, "Because of being unattached. [This means] because of being unattached to the second, which is Brahman.
* * * before their birth, the causes * * * many multitudes of living beings, resembling Mount Meru and Mount Mandara,
having arisen again and again, dissolve back into that very supreme state.
But because they arise and dissolve right there within that very substrate throughout the three periods of time, they are perceived [as such]. || 8 ||
Then these [beings], being born by the thousands, flash forth limitlessly,
like birds upon trees of various crooked branches and hollows.
The streams of living beings will emerge like new sprouts in the springtime,
and they will dissolve back into that very same source like sweet juices in the summer heat.
They remain incessantly throughout time, as do many others;
the multitudes of living beings are born and dissolve within that Supreme One.
O Rāghava, the individual soul and its karma, which are inseparable from the fragrance of a flower and so forth,
having emerged from the Supreme Lord, slowly re-enter into Him alone.
He brings forth the intention of the deluded with the words "the flower and its fragrance. With the words "they are non-different," he provides a specific illustration: "the flower and its fragrance.
It is observed in this world that these—Daityas, serpents, humans, and gods—are [all alike].
Non-existents arise through existents and flash forth again and again. || 13 ||
He says "the seen" (*dṛṣṭam*) to show that there is also conformity with what is observed regarding simultaneous origination (*sahotpatti*). The meaning is:

in reality, even non-existent things arise through entities whose limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consist merely of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); they flash forth and move at that very moment, because simultaneous origination and identity are directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*). || 13 ||
O virtuous one, no cause whatsoever is observed for their dwelling [in this state] other than the forgetting of the self; nothing else is seen that bestows the fruit of another birth. 14.

And thus, regarding its production, there are neither actions nor any other cause, because those [actions] are preceded by an agent; therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it is said that ignorance alone, as previously mentioned, is the cause—this is expressed by the word "cause" (*hetu*). This is the underlying intention (*abhisaṃdhi*): first of all, it is impossible to assert that the agent is beginningless, for if agency were inherent (*svābhāvika*), [it would follow that the world is eternal].
For if it were of an eternal nature, like the heat of fire, it could not be removed even by a thousand means, which would result in the impossibility of liberation.

If it were adventitious (*aupādhika*), that limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) must be either ignorance (*avidyā*) itself or something else. In the first case, in effect, it falls within the category of the Siddhāntin’s own position. Furthermore, regarding ignorance in the self...

Does the capacity to produce agency belong to ignorance (*avidyā*) intrinsically or through dependence on something else? It cannot be intrinsic, for otherwise agency would result even during deep sleep, fainting, or cosmic dissolution—even for the Self (or, according to another reading, for the non-Self). If it is through dependence on something else, then that upon which ignorance depends must be specified.

That very thing which brings about agency must itself be the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), not ignorance (*avidyā*); for it is not the case that a limiting adjunct can have another limiting adjunct. Regarding the second alternative as well, that adjunct would either be an effect of ignorance or independent. If it were independent and beginningless, then it would bring about agency even during deep sleep and cosmic dissolution. If it were beginningless, then the nature of the agent conditioned by it would likewise [be beginningless].
Thus, there is no proof of a diverse plurality of agents. Even in the view that the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*), this same fault remains;

for although the Self is eternal, its connection with the agent-adjunct varies from kalpa to kalpa and from day to day, and consequently, the form of the conditioned agent dependent upon that adjunct arises simultaneously with the action.

Furthermore, the position that [the self] consists in an identity with the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) possessing karmic power, and that the very cause for this is the forgetting of the Self, remains as the only logically tenable view. The scriptural passage, "Having arisen from these elements, one perishes after them," is also favorable to this point. || 14 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Whatever has been determined by those free from passion, who possess authoritative vision, regarding a non-contradictory reality—that is called a scripture (śāstra). || 15 ||

In this context, wishing to demonstrate the logical inconsistency [of the opponent's position], Rāma sets forth the definition of scripture (*śāstra-lakṣaṇa*) in order to establish the necessary background, stating: "by those who are non-contradictory... By those of authoritative vision and those free from passion—those for whom the Veda is the authority regarding the supramundane Dharma and Brahman, and whose insight originates from it.

Whatever has been determined and codified by Manu and others regarding matters consisting of dharma and adharma— by means of the collection of logical principles established in the systems of Jaimini and others, which do not contradict their own root source,
the Śruti— and which is found in the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Kalpasūtras, Itihāsas, and so forth, that is called "Śāstra. And thus:
The intention is that the Vedas, as well as the Smṛtis and other texts rooted in them, are the means of valid cognition regarding supersensuous matters. || 15 ||

Those who are endowed with the qualities of great beings, who are steadfast and possess an even vision, and who are possessed of an indefinable nature—they are declared to be the virtuous ones. || 16 ||
Thus, in order to state that even right conduct (*sadācāra*) is a form of pride, he describes the characteristics of the virtuous: "Possessed of great being" (*mahāsattva*), etc.

They are endowed with the quality of *sattva* that is exceedingly pure; they are steadfast (*dhīra*), unshakable by sense objects and by states of suffering; they possess an equal vision (*samadṛṣṭi*), being free from attachment and aversion.

"Inexpressible" means incapable of being described by words; they are endowed with that portion of the direct realization of Brahman which is unsurpassed bliss. The meaning is that those "virtuous ones" are truly good people. || 16 ||
For the two-fold view of the ignorant serves for the accomplishment of all actions;
likewise, the scripture always follows the conduct of the virtuous.

The conduct of the virtuous whose characteristics have been described, as well as the two—the scriptures and the Śruti-Smṛti—constitute the pair of eyes for the learned who are like children, being ignorant of the ultimate reality; that is to say, they serve to perceive the truth of Dharma and Brahman. || 17 ||
He who does not follow the scripture for the sake of proper conduct among the virtuous is cast out by all, and he sinks into suffering. (18)

The word "sādhuḥ" refers to that worldly transaction which is conducive to heaven and liberation; "for that purpose" means for that objective, the scripture [is composed], and "all the learned" (śiṣṭāḥ) is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 18 ||
In this world and in the Veda, O Lord, it is always heard thus:
that both action and the agent are joined together here in a continuous succession.
In this world, among authoritative people, and in the Veda, it is heard thus; therefore, "Śruti" is a conventional expression for a well-established report.

The word "exists" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Having uttered the report itself, he states the intended meaning by means of the words beginning with "yathā" (just as), etc., showing it through a sequence—that is, non-simultaneously—which amounts to saying "by way of the relation of cause and effect. (19)
The agent is produced by action, and the action is brought forth by the agent;
this principle, such as that of the seed and the sprout, is indeed declared in both the world and the Veda. (20)
He states that very point clearly with the words "by action": it is brought forth, that is, it is produced. || 20 ||
A living being is born from karma, just as a new sprout arises from a seed;
karma is produced from the living being, just as a seed is produced from a sprout. (21)
By whatever latent impression a living being is led into the cage of worldly existence,
a fruit corresponding to that very impression is experienced.

He states that even past latent impressions (*vāsanā*), like karma, are the cause of the agent—by means of the word "yayā" (by which). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "it is experienced by that living being. || 22 ||
This being the case, how indeed can you say that the birth of beings from the state of Brahman occurs without karma, which is the seed of birth? (23)
Having thus established the context, he refutes the position that the agent and the action arise simultaneously, stating: "This being the case.
For if the position of simultaneous arising were true, it would follow that an action arises even without a prior [cause], which is untenable.
[As it is said: "One who performs good deeds becomes good; one who performs evil deeds becomes evil; indeed, one becomes pure through a pure deed."
The meaning is that [this view] contradicts such scriptural, traditional, and authoritative declarations as: "A being becomes sinful through sinful action" and so forth. || 23 ||
By this argument, O Blessed One, you have refuted the notion that birth and action are invariably concomitant throughout the world. (24)

The meaning is that by this position of simultaneous origination, the mutual relationship of cause and effect between these two— the living being and karma— which has arisen in the world, is established through valid cognition, is characterized by positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), and is inseparable, becomes obscured. || 24 ||

In this world, two things have been wiped away: the notion that Brahman is not the cause, O Brahman, and the notion that fruits exist for those who perform actions toward Brahman and other such results. (25)

Since actions have no cause— because they are non-dual and devoid of any cause external to themselves— there exists within Brahman, which is variegated by *māyā*, a fruit in the form of a creation consisting of the locus of experience from the ether down to the gross body; and within that fruit, in the cases of Brahmā and others who possess gross and subtle adjuncts such as Hiraṇyagarbha, there exists a fruit in the form of a creation of the totality of conditions for experience.
The meaning is that you have cleared away the two types of discourse well-known in the world. || 25 ||
When confusion has arisen in the world and actions no longer yield their fruits, and the law of the fish prevails, only destruction remains.

He states another defect as well: "When [the world] has become... When actions have ceased to yield their fruits and have become fruitless, there is an absence of fear of hell and other such realms; thus, while the "law of the fishes" (mātsyanyāya)—characterized by the killing and devouring of the weak by the powerful—prevails like that of fish, [this state arises]. || 26 ||
"O Blessed One, tell me truly: what does that [action] actually produce? O best among those who know what is to be known, sever this vast doubt of mine. (27)
Therefore, O Brahmin, tell me truly and according to the facts: does an action performed necessarily come to fruition as its result, or not? Cut through this doubt.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
"Well asked, O Rāghava! You have questioned me on this auspicious matter.
Listen, for I shall speak to you so that there may arise in you a profound awakening of knowledge. (28)
Thus challenged, Vasiṣṭha praises the challenge as authoritative and promises its resolution, saying: "Excellent! (28).
This mental manifestation arises from the nature of the perception of parts;
it is the seed of those actions, and its very fruit exists herein.
He prepares the introductory framework to demonstrate how there is no fault whatsoever even in the position that [the three] arise simultaneously, stating:

"It is mental" (*mānasa*). For according to the Vedic scripture, "What one contemplates with the mind, that one speaks with speech; that one performs with action," that which pertains to the mind—in the form of the discernment of parts (*kalā-kalanarūpa*) and as the synthesis of skillful activity—[is what constitutes the initial impulse].
"Unfolding" (samunmeṣa) means expansion; this is well known as the seed of actions. How is this known?
Because its fruit, consisting of the accomplishment of action, exists only later for this [unfolding], and not for mere bodily movement preceded by mental intention—this is the meaning. || 29 ||
For as soon as the reality of the mind arose from the state of Brahman,
at that very moment the karma of living beings became established as the individual soul (jīva) in the form of a body.

To demonstrate what was stated—that "the fruit belongs to this very [mind]"—he provides an illustration with the words "yadaiva" (at the very moment). At the time of the primal creation (*ādisarga*), at the very moment when the principle characterized as the mind (*manas*) emerged from the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*), at that same moment, the karma of living beings—the individual and collective souls (*jīvas*) manifested through those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—also arose. And the soul (*jīva*)...
He exists with the identification "I am the body" by virtue of having a body that follows from past latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Thus says the Śruti:
"He made that mind, thinking, 'May I have a self'; he moved about worshipping.
Indeed, both the state of being embodied—denoted by the term *ātmanvī*—and the activity characterized by wandering are entirely dependent upon the birth of the mind.

[The author] shows [this by citing]: "Whatever they become, then they become"—so says another Vedic scripture (*śruti*). Thus, the intention is that I have presented the theory of simultaneous origination (with the Self) in order to demonstrate that the mind alone is the agent, and not the Self. || 30 ||
Just as there is no distinction here between two different flowers and their receptacle,
so too there is no distinction between action and the mind, for they are inseparable.

Thus, the intent in demonstrating that even from the statement regarding the non-difference of agent and object (*kartṛ-karma-abheda*), the action belongs solely to the nature of the mind and not to the nature of the self—due to the contradiction with its immutable (*kauṭasthya*) essence—is expressed by the example beginning with "kusuma" (flower). Here, "āśaya" refers to the fragrance residing within. || 31 ||
In this world, the vibration of action is called "karma" by the wise;
since that [vibration] first occurs in the mind and the body, karma is indeed the mind alone.

Now, it may be objected: by the word "karma," is sacrifice and the like meant, or the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by them? In that case, the former is a property of the body, while the latter inheres in the enjoyer (the self); how then can these two be properties of the mind? To this he replies: "Action" (*kriyā*).
For action itself, through its latent impression (*saṃskāra*), resides in the mind, and manifests as the nature of an unseen result.

It takes on the form of the body, heaven, hell, and so forth. Thus, the very mind was the prior substratum even for that body of action; for the scripture states, "He becomes endowed with consciousness; he passes over into consciousness itself," since it is taught that the departure from the previous body occurs only when the mind has attained the conceit of assuming the form of the future body.
Furthermore, as was previously established, it is precisely the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) that, through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), is imagined as having the state of a gross body;
therefore, the mind (citta) is indeed the mental organ (manas), and because its nature is action, it is "action" (karman)—this is the meaning. || 32 ||
There is no mountain, no sky, no ocean, and no world where there is no fruit for the deeds one has performed oneself. (33)

And thus, with the intention that the fault of the fruitlessness of action (karmanaiṣphalyadoṣa) mentioned by you is also avoided—since it is established that the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), which is the work of the mind, is the fruit of action—he says: "Not that... The word *phala* is used here with the abstract sense as its primary meaning; that is to say, "the state of being a fruit" (*phalatva*). || 33 ||
Whether it be an action performed in this life or one from the past that manifests, this supreme human effort is never without fruit. (34)

That action which is performed with vigilance, executed with all its constituent parts, and shines forth with splendor—this is indeed human effort (*pauruṣa-prayatna*), and it never, at any time, becomes fruitless; this is the meaning.
The underlying intention is this: the mind alone arises from ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because it possesses the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) and because it is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the conscious self (*cidātman*), it is both the agent and the enjoyer. For that mind, my dear, consists of food (*annamaya*);

it made that mind for itself; it made three for itself: mind, speech, and breath—according to such scriptural texts as these, and according to the reasoning previously stated. Although it arises and dissolves at every kalpa and every day, nevertheless...
