Manifesting every day at night in the darkness and then vanishing, she was like the shadow of a wall; or like the reflection of a face that appears when a mirror is brought near and disappears when the mirror is removed.

Because of the validity of uncontradicted recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the form "this is that very same thing," and because of the identity of the self with its limiting adjuncts (*upahita-ātmaikya*), it does not differ [from itself] and thus remains beginningless (*anādi*). For what is called "destruction" is neither the attainment of emptiness nor the existence of the non-existent (*asataḥ sattvam*),
such that there would be a difference from destruction during daily deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

Furthermore, because we rely on the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), even though we accept the simultaneous production of the previously existing past agent and action— in their nature as the seed of ignorance— and the phenomenal world consisting of space and so forth as their fruit,

there is no contingency of the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāna*) or the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*); thus, there is neither a subversion of the authority of the scriptures nor [any other such fault].
There is no risk of falling into the "law of the fishes" (the strong preying on the weak), nor is there any need to refute the rule of the invariable concomitance between birth and karma;

for since it is accepted that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the mind itself in its latent state as well as its manifest state, the statement that the sole cause [of bondage] is the forgetting of the Self (*ātman*) is likewise not contradictory— this is the truth.
Just as soot vanishes of its own accord when the darkness is destroyed,
so too the mind perishes when the activity of vibration ceases.
He states what the result of accepting the position that [the mind] arises simultaneously [with the body] and is identical to it is: "blackness," etc.

Thus, the sense is that for one who desires the destruction of either karma or the mind, the fruit is the practice of either Haṭhayoga—characterized by the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of movement—or Rājayoga; this is the result. || 35 ||
Upon the destruction of karma, there is the destruction of the mind; indeed, the destruction of the mind is the state of non-action.
This occurs for one who is liberated, but never for one who is not liberated.

The statement "of the liberated one" is made with the intention that when ignorance is destroyed by the direct realization born of yoga, there occurs the absolute destruction of both [the self and its attributes], and not otherwise. || 36 ||
Just as fire and heat are always conjoined, so too are the mind and its activity;
in the absence of either one of these two, both simply dissolve away. (37)
Of the two that are "conjoined," meaning connected by way of identity (tādātmya). || 37 ||
213. Know that the mind, having always attained the play of vibration, is indeed of the single nature of vibration; it is karma.
O Rāma, it is said that when karma and the mind have both reached the state of the activity of phenomena (dharmakarma), they are indeed mutually dependent upon one another.
Demonstrating the logical proof for the principle that "with the destruction of one, there is the destruction of the other," he concludes with the words: "The mind.

For the mind, having entered into the play of vibration (*spanda*), undergoes transformation into the forms of merit and demerit—dharma and adharma—consisting of virtue and vice, by means of performing prescribed and prohibited acts. Now, as for action (*karman*)...

The mind becomes a manifestation consisting of fluctuations corresponding to the experience of those fruits; therefore, having mutually attained the status of "dharma" and "karma" as their respective causes, they are conventionally designated by the terms *dharma* and *karma* in the world—this is the meaning. || 38 ||

Thus ends the ninety-fifth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Identity of Karma and the Person," in the Holy Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, belonging to the Divine, the Great, the Ultimate [Uttara-kāṇḍa]. || 95 ||
Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Identity of Karma and the Person," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "The mind is indeed nothing but ideation; ideation is characterized by vibration."
Everyone pursues the fruit, which is the form manifested by that action. || 1 ||
Due to the diversity of mental karma, there are various forms here;
the different designations are explained for the sake of clarifying the reality of this [mind] so that it may be purified. (1)
He first shows, in brief, the meaning of the creation (*sarga*) which serves to elaborate upon the meaning already stated—beginning with the word "mind" (*manaḥ*).
It is the mere conceptualization (*vikalpa*) called "vibhāvanā," which is the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of objects previously experienced.
That cultivation, being characterized by movement (*spandadharmiṇī*), becomes the performance of enjoined and prohibited actions; it is from that very action [that the world arises].

Because of its subtlety, having entered a state of invisibility, every living being pursues—that is, follows after—that very fruit which consists of future births and the like, and whose form has been previously cultivated. The meaning is that the mind alone successively assumes both states. || 1 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, you ought to describe in detail to me— the dull-witted one, though appearing in a non-dull form— the form of the mind that has ascended to the level of volition.
The question is clear. || 2 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: They know that form which is fashioned by the power of volition belonging to the infinite, omnipotent, and great-souled Reality of the Self— that they call the mind.

The meaning is that "mind" (manas) refers to that form which was fashioned—that is, first brought into existence—by the Power of Will (saṃkalpa-śakti) of the All-Powerful One, who is variegated by Māyā and possesses all powers. || 3 ||
That which moves among men, flickering between existence and non-existence, and having turned toward conceptualization—that they know to be the form of the mind. (4)
He states that this is well-known even in the contemporary dealings of men—namely, "the state" (bhāva).

In the doubt, "Is it a post or a person?", the state which is unstable, oscillating, and moving—that is, shifting between the two alternatives of existence and non-existence—is what is meant. This refers to the tendency toward conceptualization (*kalana*) being preceded by the recollection of both alternatives. || 4 ||
"I am not the nature of the manifestation of the Vedas; I am the one who acts"—this is the firm conviction.
Therefore, the wise know that form of the mind to be the exclusive ideation of that [Self].

He says that the mind is that by which there arises the notion "I do not know" regarding the Self—which, though always manifest due to its nature as consciousness—and the notion of agency in one who is actually non-agent; this occurs because the mind is constantly changing and is invariably being produced. (Verse 5)
In this world, the mind devoid of the power of action consisting of conceptualization is not possible, just as a possessor of qualities cannot exist without those qualities.
Fearing that this definition might not extend to the mind when it is motionless, he says:
"by that which consists of conceptual construction," and so forth. (Verse 6)
Just as the existence of fire and heat is not possible if they were distinct,
so too it is with action and the mind, and likewise with the self and the mind.
Of the self and the mind, that is, of the individual soul and the mind. || 7 ||
By its own nature as the mind, characterized by the fruit of action, having volition as its sole body, and possessing manifold expansions; (8)
By means of the property-bearer (dharmin) which possesses the result and is endowed with the probandum (sādhyavat). || 8 ||
This universe, consisting of many selves, composed of illusion, and without cause, is devoid of structural arrangement and agitated by latent impressions and mental constructions.
Whatever latent impression (vāsanā) has been deposited by whom, where, and in what manner, that very thing yields its fruit there for that person in that same way. (10)

This clarifies the phrase "agitated by the mental construction of latent impressions" (*vāsanākalpanākalanākulām*) with the words "by whom [and] in what manner" (*yā yena*). The meaning is: "wherein [something] appears as if real, just as those staying here [on earth] imagine themselves to be in Satyaloka by means of lunar rays. This is clear in the reading *lateva* ("like a creeper"). || 10 ||
Karma is said to be the seed and the movement of the mind; its various activities are like the branches of a tree that bear manifold fruits. (11)

The meaning is that it is stated in the scriptures—and is experienced as a result—that for this tree of latent impressions (vāsanā), action is the seed, the movement of the mind is the trunk, and the body is the branches. || 11 ||
Whatever the mind intends to connect with, all these functions of the organs of action accomplish it; therefore, the mind is traditionally called "action" (karma).
Now, one might object: "Action is the function of the organs of action; how could that belong to the mind? To this, he says: "The mind," [verse 12].
Mind, intellect, ego, consciousness, action, as well as imagination, worldly existence, latent impressions, ignorance, effort, and memory itself. (13)

Showing that there is no fault in the statement "the mind alone assumes the state of all the senses," he states its various names: "O Brahman, 'sense-organ' (indriya), 'primordial nature' (prakṛti), 'illusion' (māyā), and 'action' (kriyā)—these and other diverse verbal designations are the causes of the delusion of saṃsāra. (14)
These are not the only ones; rather, there are others as well. [The word] "brahman" means "in Brahman. The elision of the locative case-ending is Vedic (chāndasa).

The prohibition of the elision of the final *n* is by the rule *na ṅisaṃbuddhyoḥ*. The delusion of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-bhrama*)—that is, the various distinctions that serve as the grounds for activity as will be described, which are imagined within transmigratory existence—is itself the cause of these [powers]. || 14 ||

By a chance occurrence, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow, synonyms have been applied to the consciousness (citi) which has abandoned its expansive form of vision and does not follow after objects of thought (cetya). || 15 ||

"By chance" (kākatālīyam) means accidental; by means of that [chance], the vast and undivided form of vision—which, though seemingly abandoned, is not actually experienced as such because its own nature has been forgotten—is the very essence of consciousness (cidekarasākāra).

Of that consciousness which does not follow after objects of thought (citetyānupātinī), but is instead oriented toward external conceptualization (bāhyakalponmukhā); [of that consciousness, it is said]. 15.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, these are the synonymous functions of supreme consciousness.
How have these various objects, being merely conceptualized, attained established existence? || 16 ||

Desiring to know specifically the synonymous application of the names already mentioned—such as *manas*, *buddhi*, and so forth—based on the distinction of their etymological grounds (*nimitta*) as the activity of consciousness directed toward objects, and through both their etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) senses, Rāma asks: "Of the supreme [intellect]... Those [names] whose diverse etymological meanings are being conceived...
Such are the truths. || 16 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Once, having as it were departed from its state of being manifold and conceptual, that which exists as the mind remained then indeed in the form of pure manifestation.

Thus questioned, Vasiṣṭha, desiring to explain all fifteen names in sequence, first explains the name "Mind" (manas) with the words "As if gone": when the supreme consciousness, as if having become defiled by ignorance, at some point becomes manifest in the form of unfolding (unmeṣa), it exists in the nature of conceptualization (vikalpa) such as "this is thus" or "this is not thus."
The meaning is that at that very moment she becomes manifold, existing in the form of the mind; thus she is called "Tannāgikā. || 17 ||
When she remains established, having ascertained the continuity of cultivation, then this intellect is said to be capable of grasping the full extent [of reality]. (18)

But when, having attained a specific cultivation either following the first conceptualization or subsequent to it, one remains firmly established after determining the pursuit of one particular alternative, then this is called "cognition-consciousness" (*saṃvid-buddhi*).
Its meaning is that it is capable of grasping the delimitation (*pariccheda*) such as "this object is exactly of such a measure."
When one imagines existence for oneself through false pride, it is called the bondage of worldly existence by means of the conceit of egoism. (19)

But when, through the conceit of identifying with the unreal body and so forth, it itself imagines and considers its own existence, then—by reason of that conceit of egoism—it is called "egoism" (ahaṃkāra); the meaning is that this very [power] is the binder to worldly existence because it is the seed of all misfortunes. || 19 ||
When, like a child, she is fragile and abandons this to come to that, completely relinquishing all deliberation, then she is called the mind (citta). || 20 ||

But when, having abandoned one object, one remembers another object while setting aside deliberation—the linking together of what precedes and what follows—then that consciousness is called "mind" (citta); this is the meaning. || 20 ||
When, because its sole nature is vibration, the agent's [consciousness] rushes toward the fruit of that vibration while proclaiming it to be empty, then that is declared to be "action" (karman).
That very consciousness, because its sole essential property is vibration (spanda), though in reality empty and non-existent, proclaims—that is, makes manifest—vibration;

being of such a nature, it seems to rush forth in order to accomplish the fruit of vibration, namely the conjunction with another location of the body and its various parts, and at that time it is called "action" (karman). This is the meaning. || 21 ||
By way of a chance occurrence, having abandoned the certainty of a single, solid [reality],
whatever desired state one imagines, by that very means is there "imagination" (kalpanā) here.

The meaning is that when one abandons the certainty of that single, solid, and essential nature which is devoid of any internal space or interval, and having forgotten its own state of fullness, imagines a limited state as something sought after or desired. || 22 ||
When one internally determines, "This has been seen before," whether it was previously perceived or not, that is designated as memory (smṛti). (23)
Smṛti is perfect recollection. || 23 ||
When the potencies of objects, as if already consumed, abide in the sky [of consciousness] with all other worldly activities subsided, then it is called *vāsanā*.

The meaning is that when the words, their meanings, and their powers— having been experienced, as if swallowed, and become latent— dwell in their own nature within the void-like sky in an extremely subtle state, and all other activities have subsided, then they are called "latent impressions" (vāsanā). || 24 ||
The stainless reality of the Self exists, marked by the second vision;
for when that which was previously non-existent has arisen, it is then called "knowledge" (vidyā). || 25 ||
"Aṅkitājātā" is a single compound word. "Aṅka" refers to the stain of ignorance (avidyā); the state of being characterized by that is "aṅkitā.

That second vision—the appearance of the phenomenal world (prapañca)—is born under its influence. When one realizes that this [appearance] does not exist even in the three periods of time, then it is called "Vidyā" (Knowledge); such is the meaning. || 25 ||
It throbs for the sake of its own destruction and causes that state to be forgotten;
through a web of false conceptualizations, that impurity is imagined. (26)
Regarding the reading "vismṛti-mala eva ca," he explains those two names together with the words "sphurati" (it manifests).

The destruction of the Self is its absolute non-appearance. The meaning is that because it causes [the Self] to be forgotten, it is called "vismṛti" (forgetfulness). Alternatively, it means that it causes various things to be remembered—that is, it distracts—by means of a web of false conceptual constructions.

Thus, the sense is that *mala* (impurity) is characterized primarily by the power of obscuration (*āvaraṇa-śakti*), while forgetfulness (*vismṛti*) is characterized primarily by the power of projection (*vikṣepa*).

However, according to the reading "effort (*prayatna*) and memory (*smṛti*) alone," *mala* is so called because it "strives" (*yatate*)—meaning it vibrates and moves toward the destruction and non-perception of the Self—and it is so called "memory" (*smṛti*) because it causes various things to be remembered; thus it is the "impure" (*malina*) impurity.
"It is the very nature of that consciousness which is conceptually designated by a name"—this must be explained with care. || 26 ||
Having heard, touched, seen, tasted, smelled, and reflected, this [faculty] gladdens Indra; therefore it is remembered as an *indriya*. (27)

The meaning is this: when this consciousness, having become the mind (*manobhūtā*), gladdens Indra— the Lord of the body and its organs (the Supreme Lord, according to the reading *parameśvaram āmodayati*)— who has assumed the state of the individual soul (*jīvabhāvāpanna*), by means of activities such as hearing and so forth, and delights him with enjoyments, then it is called an "organ" (*indriya*).
For such is the grammatical rule of Pāṇini: "That which is enjoyed by Indra is called *indriya*. (27)
Since all the network of visible phenomena is unmanifest within the Supreme Self, it is called "prakṛti" (nature) in the world because of its being the fundamental source of all entities. || 28 ||
Because it was created by a creator whose self is non-different from the material cause, due to being the subject under discussion. || 28 ||
It swiftly leads to existence what was non-existent, or directly leads to non-existence what was existent;
because this conceptualization of existence and non-existence occurs, it is called "māyā. (29)
This is clear. || 29 ||
In the world, that which has entered into the state of cause and effect through the functions of seeing, hearing, touching, tasting, and smelling is called "action" (kriyā). // 30 //
The state of cause and effect, consisting of the nature of cyclic existence and its seed.
These are the synonymous designations for that which follows the cognizer and the cognized, which has fallen into a state of defilement, and whose nature is characterized by manifest form. (31)
He concludes the explanation of the name with the words "of consciousness" (citer). || 31 ||
Having attained the state of pure consciousness and returned to her natural abode,
[these impressions] have reached full maturity through hundreds of her own volitions.
The subject at hand is the state of saṃsāra. "By their own"—meaning by their very own hundreds of mental constructs such as volitions (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth.
These are synonymous terms. "Establishment" refers to conventional usage based on etymological derivation (*yogarūḍhi*). || 32 ||

The calculation of numerical divisions, which follows the web of dullness due to being marked by the stain of what is to be willed, is like consciousness itself when it is agitated by its own deficiency.

Regarding the question of how there can be any calculation of numerical divisions such as mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and so forth for that which is one Consciousness (*cit*), he says: "by being made conscious" (*cetanīya*).
Consciousness is that which is capable of self-experience as "I am ignorant"—that stain of ignorance—or that which has been acquired from objects that are themselves conscious (*cetanīya*).

Because of its proximity to that [intellect], the stain of the latent impression of duality, as if distressed by the deficiency of its own full nature within the embrace of that [intellect], follows after the web of insentience consisting of the body and so forth; such is the meaning of "yataḥ" (since). || 33 ||
214. In the world it is called the *jīva*, and it is also spoken of as the *manas*;
it is called the *citta*, and likewise it is called the *buddhi*.
Having already stated the calculation of the divisions, he explains it again with greater detail through the two verses beginning with "jīva" (34).
The wise describe this defiled one, fallen from the Supreme Self, as a collection of synonyms muddled by various conceptual constructions. (35)
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brahman, O knower of reality, is the mind inert or is it indeed conscious?
Thus, O knower of truth, a single certainty does not arise within me. (36)

Having stated, "It is called the *jīva*," Rāma, being in doubt because [the term] implies sentience according to other philosophical systems while its insentience is well-known in the world, asks: "Is it the mind? (verse 36).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, the mind is indeed neither inert nor has it attained the state of consciousness; rather, that vision which is neither dull nor insentient is called "mind. (37)

Because it consists of a combination of both consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), the mind (*manas*) does not have the form of either one exclusively; yet, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), considering it as "mind," these are indeed merely names derived from its functions. This is because, in the Śruti, among the names of the Self (*ātman*) conditioned by its functions, the term "mind" is specifically enumerated. Therefore, at that time, the non-inert vision is indeed consciousness itself (*cideva*).
The meaning is that in the state of saṃsāra, that which is withered, experiencing the impurity of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi), is called "mind" (manas). 37.
That turbid form which appears as both existent and non-existent in the interim, known as the cause of the world—this indeed is called the "citta. 38.
He states that it possesses a distinction from both the existent and the non-existent, just as it possesses a distinction from the conscious and the unconscious—by saying "in the middle.
"Pratibhūtam" means for every individual living being. In the reading "pratibhātam," the meaning is clear. || 38 ||
Without a permanent, uniform, and certain state of abiding, that which exists is called "mind"; from that, this world has arisen. (39)
Alternatively, he says that the very existence of the self when unknown is the mind, by means of the word "eternally" (śāśvatena), which serves as the reason. || 39 ||

That which is a mental construction in the form of a swing between the two views of the insentient and the sentient, arising from the consciousness whose nature is withered—this is called the mind (manas). (40)
Clarifying what was stated previously, he describes its nature as being mobile with the word "jaḍa" (insentient). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "that which is the form of consciousness. || 40 ||
O Rāma, that which is insentient yet stained, possessing an interior marred by blemish, is called the mind; it is neither inert nor composed of pure consciousness.

The meaning is this: the conscious principle (cit) is motionless, yet possesses a state of movement due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and is impure externally; however, because its inner witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) is free from obscuration, that form which is internally devoid of stain is called the mind (manas). || 41 ||
For him, these various names have been fully assigned:
ego, mind, intellect, the individual soul (jīva), and others as well.
Just as an actor assumes various roles with great skill as he moves about, even so the mind assumes many names as it proceeds to different activities. (43)
A *śailūṣa* is a specific class of actor. He "goes exceedingly to various forms," meaning he assumes them one after another. "Another action" refers to a difference in activity. || 43 ||
Due to the influence of various mental dispositions, there arise diverse and distorted designations;
just as a person goes according to the power of his karma, so too does the mind go. 44.

Just as a man receives various distinct designations— such as "cook" due to his office of cooking, "reciter" due to his office of reciting, or "village headman" due to his lordship over a village— and thus undergoes diverse and modified names that manifest those respective activities, so too does the mind undergo them through the power of karma.
The meaning is "he goes. || 44 ||
O Raghava, these designations of the mind which have been described by me are the very same ones that have been explained otherwise by proponents through hundreds of conceptual constructions.
Otherwise, [one would proceed] with hundreds of conceptual constructions and hundreds of reasonings advanced by one's own imagination. || 45 ||
Having superimposed upon the intellect (buddhi) what is regarded as its own nature, various systems of nomenclature for the mind, intellect, senses, and so forth have been fashioned by the mind.

The meaning is that their own conceptualizations (*bhāvanā*) and arguments (*tarka*), having superimposed upon the mind the notions they favor— such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and atomicity (*aṇutva*)— have created, by means of the mind according to their own will, various systems of names and distinctions of designations for the mind, intellect, and so forth. || 46 ||
For the mind of one [proponent] is inert, while that of another living being is distinct;
likewise, the ego-sense belongs to one, and the intellect to another disputant. (47)
He demonstrates the various modes of their conceptualization by means of the passage beginning with "For the mind," and so forth. || 47 ||
O descendant of Raghu, the views concerning ego, mind, and intellect, as well as the conceptualizations of creation, have been described by me as being of a single nature.
Because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is of a single nature, those conceptualizations of its creation—

which have as their cause the production of distinct functions such as volition (*saṃkalpa*), and which are views of distinctions under the names of ego (*ahaṃkāra*), mind (*manas*), and intellect (*buddhi*)— have been described by me. (48)
They have been conceptualized otherwise by the Naiyāyikas and others like them;
they have been conceptualized differently by the Sāṃkhyas, and yet differently even by the Cārvākas. (49)
Those who follow the *Gautamīya-tantra* have imagined those [categories] in such a manner through their own intellectual constructs;

for instance, they conceive that the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is a specific substance, all-pervading, and the individual self (*jīvātman*), while the mind (*manas*) is atomic and the cause of its direct perception,
and that cognition (*buddhi*) is a quality of that [self] which lasts for three moments— but the meaning is that it is not so in reality.
The Sāṃkhyas, however, conceive of these differently:

namely, that *buddhi* is directly the effect of *prakṛti*, which consists of the three *guṇas*—it is the principle of *mahat*; whereas *ahaṃkāra* is a distinct principle that is its effect; and *manas*, on the other hand, is included within the group of eleven sense organs and thus falls among the sixteen transformations (*vikāras*).

According to the Cārvākas, however, consciousness is a quality [of the body], cognition belongs only to the effect [the body], the body itself is the ego and the self, and the synthesis of its prior and subsequent states is the mind. (49)
By the Jaiminīyas, the Ārhatas, the Baudhas, and likewise the Vaiśeṣikas;
by others as well, such as those various [schools] beginning with the Pāñcarātra. || 50 ||

According to the Jaiminīyas, however, some hold that the mind (*manas*) is an all-pervading substance, while others consider it to be non-eternal. Furthermore, they maintain that cognition (*buddhi*) is the conscious aspect of the self (*ātman*), which is essentially of the nature of the dull-cum-conscious ego (*ahaṃkāra*). According to the Ārhatas, however, the ego is precisely the *jīvāstikāya* (the category of living beings), which is conscious in nature and possesses a medium dimension; its desire for objects [constitutes its activity].

The mind (*manas*), the manifestation of objects (*arthaprathā*), and the intellect (*buddhi*) are as follows: according to the Buddhists, the stream of consciousness known as the *ālayavijñāna*—which is momentary—is itself the self (*ātman*) and the ego (*ahaṃkāra*). The active cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*) constitute the intellect (*buddhi*), which takes the form of external objects as its transformation; moreover, the past immediately preceding cognition is the mind (*manas*). However, according to the Vaiśeṣikas...

Like the Naiyāyikas, [they hold that] there are the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and the mind (*manas*); however, the intellect (*buddhi*) is fivefold, being divided into the categories of memory, perception, inference, reasoning, and error, as well as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). According to other Pāñcarātras, from the Supreme Self known as Vāsudeva, the individual soul (*jīva*) known as Saṃkarṣaṇa arises.

Thus, from that [Śiva] arises the ego (ahaṃkāra), then the mind called Pradyumna, and then the intellect called Aniruddha. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the various different conceptualizations of the Yogins, Māheśvaras, Nākulās, and others are included. || 50 ||
And all of them must reach that ultimate state, just as travelers from various places and times arrive at a single city. (51)

He says "by all" (sarvaiḥ) to indicate that for everyone, according to their respective intellects, the very determination of the reality of the Supreme Self will gradually bear fruit. By the word "variegated" (vicitram), it is suggested that that state is capable of remaining in the form of various fruits corresponding to those respective intellects. || 51 ||
Due to ignorance of the ultimate truth and because of their perverted understanding,
these seekers who desire to ascend merely engage in disputes through conceptual constructions.
If only one [reality] is attained, then for what purpose do they dispute? To this he says: "Due to ignorance" (ajñānāt). || 52 ||
Proponents praise their own paths with diverse perspectives,
just as travelers arising in various places and times praise their own respective routes.
These [doctrines] arise in various places and times,
produced in locations and periods suited to people who are predominantly of *rājasa*, *tāmasa*, or partially impure *sāttvika* natures. Thus,
the idea is that since those following such times and conditions have a natural inclination toward their own respective positions, it is appropriate to praise each of them accordingly.
O Rāghava, those whose minds are intent on ritual action have falsely declared their own various logical arguments regarding objects projected by their own conceptual constructions. (54)
If so, one might ask: "Should even those seeking liberation (mumukṣus) adopt the arguments stated by them? To this he says: "By them" (tair).

For the sake of those whose minds are occupied solely with ritual action (karma), and whose hearts long for the mental desire for the means to that [action] out of a wish for its fruit—[for them], there are their own respective arguments, fashioned from their own imaginations and full of various diversities.
The meaning is that they have been spoken falsely; they are not in accordance with the Upaniṣads, which stand at the pinnacle of authoritative sources. || 54 ||
Just as a person performing actions such as bathing, giving,
and receiving attains the diversity of being their agent, so too does this mind.
Due to the influence of various effects, the agency [of the mind] is designated by different names; it is called "mind" (manas), "living being" (jīva), "latent impressions" (vāsanā), and "karma. (56)
With the intention that, by process of elimination, only the arguments stated by himself are authoritative, he states them once more, beginning with "vicitra... (verse 56).
All this is nothing but mind, as is experienced by everyone;
for a person devoid of mind does not see the world, even while looking at it. (57)
He corroborates his own stated arguments with worldly experience, beginning with the words "the mind alone," etc. (verse 57).
Having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled what is pleasant or unpleasant, one who possesses a mind indeed experiences internal joy or dejection. (58)
The mind is the cause of objects, just as light is for forms;
for one whose mind is bound is indeed bound, while one whose mind is liberated is indeed liberated.

Of forms—that is, of the manifestations of form. Alternatively, the intention may be that the forms perceived in the five-fold compounded earth and other elements belong only to the portion consisting of light. Or, "one whose consciousness is liberated" means one whose consciousness is free from latent impressions (vāsanā), or one who possesses the certainty: "I am liberated. || 59 ||
Know that to be the supreme insentient among the insentient by which the mind is said to be produced;
for the mind is indeed insentient, since it does not perceive that which is conscious.

For this very reason, he says "that," [meaning] that for the disputants, even in the case of the mind, the experience of insentience and the experience of sentience are both logically established according to their respective latent impressions (vāsanā). || 60 ||
When this mind, which is neither conscious nor inert,
arose, then the world— with its manifold pleasures, pains, and egoism— emerged.
For when the mind is of a single form, saṃsāra dissolves;
it is through delusion that the world is presented by them as a turbid cause.

When there exists the single-formed, non-dual nature of Brahman, that which is turbid—like muddy water—and near it that which is similarly turbid, namely the impure form of the intellect (*cid-rūpa*), is the cause of *saṃsāra*; the meaning is that it is caused by those minds of such a kind existing as a collective totality (*samaṣṭi*). || 62 ||
O Rāma, the non-inert mind is not the cause of saṃsāra;
and that which is inert, possessing the nature of a stone, is likewise not the cause of saṃsāra.
He reveals the secret of the intended meaning of the statement "upāvilam" with the two verses beginning with "ajaḍam. || 63 ||
Therefore, O Rāghava, in this world there is neither consciousness nor insentience;
the mind is the cause of all objects, just as the faculty of sight is the cause for the manifestation of forms. (64)

The meaning is that just as for the various distinctions of form such as blue, yellow, and so forth, the cause is not merely the light denoted by the term "illumination," nor is it earth and the other elements, but rather light rendered impure through the process of triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa), so it is in this case as well. || 64 ||
If there were anything other than the mind, what would that world be for one who is mindless?
The entire aggregate of all created beings dissolves [into it]. (65)
He states that the world is mind-only because the existence of the world cannot be established in the absence of the mind:
"The entire world dissolves into the whole mass of living beings; therefore, it is mind-only"—this is the meaning.
Through the influence of various karmas, the mind assumes various designations.
Time becomes manifold through its various seasons, just as a single entity attains diversity.
If indeed non-attention, egoism, the senses, and activity agitate the body, then let there be other factors such as the individual soul (jīva) and so forth.
Without mental attention (*amanaskāra*), that is, without the application of the mind; then, in that case, they are distinct from the mind for others. (67)

However, those distinctions among the philosophical systems (darśanas) that have been proclaimed in the mind through reasoning—whether by proponents or indeed by critics—occur here and there in various places. 68.
If that is so, how is it that the aforementioned disputants stated that there are others? To this he says: "In the philosophical systems" (*darśaneṣu*).

By the "disputants" (*vādibhiḥ*), meaning those who engage in debate; the "differences" (*bhedāḥ*) stated here and there in certain philosophical systems—that is, in their own treatises—are "exceptions" (*apavādāḥ*), meaning they were spoken by those with fallacious reasoning (*kutarkaiḥ*), and not by authoritative figures such as Vyāsa and others. || 68 ||
For they, O Rāma, do not perceive [this], nor are they distinguished anywhere;
for all powers reside in the Divine, since He is omnipresent.

He states the causes for the arising of their fallacious reasoning (kutarka) with the words "te hi" (for they...). They are never, at any time, distinguished from—that is, they are not instructed by—the knowers of reality such as Vyāsa and others. Thus, there is ignorance, a lack of traditional instruction, and the innate powers of fallacious reasoning belonging to the mind of the deity [the individual soul]. In that regard:
The meaning is "causes. || 69 ||
Indeed, as soon as even a slight consciousness of pure faith arises,
the power that was like an insentient thing then attains diversity.

In that case, since reasoning is not firmly established, there would always be mere doubt for them; how then could there be the variety of determining one specific, settled position? To this he says: "When indeed... The meaning is that the variety arises from the rigidity of faith in the reasoning imagined by each individual. || 70 ||
Just as thread is produced from a spider through its consciousness,
so too does primordial nature (prakṛti) arise from the eternally awakened Puruṣa, who is Brahman.

Anticipating the objection, "In that case, why is the very dullness of your own faith not the cause [of your position] even in your own view? [the author replies]: "This is not something imagined by my own intellect; rather, it is as a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web], as herbs arise upon the earth, and as hair and body-hair grow from an existing person."
With the intention that this position is established by such scriptural passages as, "Thus the universe arises here from the Imperishable," he says:
By the power of ignorance, the mental impressions (citta-bhāvanās) have attained stability.
For those synonymous terms for consciousness are indeed distinct; they are not [identical] here for the disputants. (72)

But for the proponents [of other systems], there is no regard for the sacred revelation (śruti); rather, under the influence of ignorance (avidyā), [the world] has become solidified through its own inherent nature.

For that very reason, he says "ignorance" (avidyā), meaning that the distinctions of name and form have been falsely imagined by them through the mind alone within consciousness (citi) which has assumed the state of the intellect (citta). || 72 ||
Indeed, this impure consciousness (cit), having attained manifestation as the living soul (jīva), the mind (manas), the intellect (buddhi), and the ego (ahaṃkṛti),
is called in the world the sentient being (cetana), the mind (citta), and the living soul (jīva).
Indeed, there is no dispute regarding this group of designations. || 73 ||
Clarifying what has already been stated, he concludes with the verse beginning "The living being" (jīva). || 73 ||

Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Investigation into the Designation of Mind," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, according to the tradition of the Rishis.
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "An Inquiry into the Designation of the Mind," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-seventh canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, this internal display has been created by the mind alone."
For it is understood from the meaning of the sentence that that very thing is karma. || 1 ||
In this [work], the configuration of the mind is examined in all its aspects;
the space of the mind, the space of consciousness, and the elemental space are also treated in detail. (1)

Thus, having been enlightened in many ways regarding the nature of the agent, the object, and the mind, as well as their various designations, Rāma expresses his own understanding in order to confirm it with his teacher’s wisdom,
saying: "O Brahmin!"— referring to this elaborate display whose meaning has already been shown by your words.

The drum of the universe has been emitted—that is, manifested—from the very presence of the mind; therefore, the intended meaning is understood and realized by me that this world itself is the activity of the mind. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: By the mind alone, colored by firm conviction,
the body was accepted as a radiant covering, just as a bright covering is assumed by the fierce heat of the wind.
Again: || 2 ||

Vasiṣṭha himself, in order to express his approval that Rāma had understood the essential meaning exactly as it is, spoke again both concisely and in detail, beginning with the words "dṛḍha" (firm) and so forth. He stated that the obscuration of luminosity— that is, the cause for its non-manifestation— is like the water of a mirage.
The dullness born of ignorance, which is the cause of the non-manifestation of the luminous Self, has been accepted; that is to say, it has been admitted.
In this world, the mind—having attained a single form within the Self that is Brahman—is established in some places as humanity and arises in others as divinity. (3)

He has attained—that is, reached—the single, primary form which constitutes the structure of the world. He elaborates upon this very point with the words beginning "In some places," and so forth. || 3 ||
In some places it shone forth as a Daitya, in some it arose as a Yakṣa;
in some it attained the state of a Gandharva, and in some it took the form of a Kinnara.
I believe that it is the mind itself that expands through its vast form, appearing in the guise of various modes of conduct, regions of space, cities, and towns. (5)
By means of an extended and expansive form, that is, through the variety of its configurations. || 5 ||
This being the case, the flood of bodies is comparable to grass, wood, and creepers;
what purpose is there in investigating them? It is the mind alone that we must investigate.

The meaning is that, just as for those who desire to know the true nature of the elements such as earth, individual items like grass and wood are not worthy of investigation, so it is in this case. || 6 ||
Therefore, this entire world, which is expansive and agitated, is pervaded by that [consciousness];
I believe that apart from it, only the Supreme Self remains.
Thus, once the nature of the agent and the object has been understood, he says "I consider" (verse 7) in order to demonstrate the Self as the substrate of those two through their purification.
The Self transcends all states, is all-pervading, and is the refuge of all;
by its grace, the mind runs and leaps about within saṃsāra.
He states that the movements of the mind and so forth occur by its power alone and not by themselves: "by its grace" (tatprasādena). || 8 ||
I consider the mind to be the agent; it is the cause within bodies.
It is that which is born and dies, for such qualities do not belong to the Self.
He states the method of purification with the words "the mind" (manaḥ). By the phrase "of such a kind," even the intermediate modifications of mental states are indicated. || 9 ||
I believe that through inquiry alone, the mind itself will reach dissolution; and by the mere dissolution of the mind, thereafter the highest good shall come to pass. (10)
Liberation is better. || 10 ||
When that which is called the mind is completely exhausted, the living being who has cast off all agitation regarding karma is said to be liberated; he is not born again under any name.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, you have described the three types of births for human beings;
the primary cause of these is the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent.

Granted that the world may thus arise from the mind, the mind itself cannot originate from Brahman, whose nature is that of immutable pure consciousness (*kūṭastha-cinmātra*). For its creation is heard in scripture to be preceded by intelligence, as in: "He created the mind, thinking, 'May I be possessed of a self. And [this is so] because of the origin of the mind...

Rāma raises an objection with the two verses beginning "O Blessed One," stating that prior intelligence cannot exist because no determination is observed in the absence of cognition. Regarding the phrase "of three kinds": although twelve types have been mentioned, the statement that they are "of three kinds" is made with the intention of including them within the threefold classification characterized as *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*.
Of men, that is, of living beings. || 12 ||
How then did the mind, which is the painter of the world, arise from that reality called pure consciousness—which is devoid of intellect—and attain expansion? (13)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, there are indeed three spaces that exist, vast within;
the space of the mind (cittākāśa), the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), and the elemental space (bhūtākāśa) as the third.

Desiring to resolve even this doubt by relying on the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) with the intention of explaining the distinctions between the views that will be presented hereafter, Vasiṣṭha demonstrates the conceptualization of the three spaces necessary for that purpose, beginning with the words "For the spaces...
(ākāśā hi). [They are] "vitata-antarāḥ," meaning those whose interiors are expanded or whose bellies are vast. 14.
For these [principles] are common to all and are established everywhere;
however, they have attained their essential existence through the power of the pure mind. || 15 ||
The phrase "common to all their own effects" means they are established and follow along in every one of their own effects; this is the reason for that [non-difference].
And there is no loss of non-duality (advaita) in this way, because a difference in existence (*sattā*) is not admitted—this is the intention with which he says: "pure," etc.
That which abides both outside and inside, which makes known existence and non-existence, and which pervades all beings—that is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). || 16 ||
Anticipating the objection that if these three possess a single existence within the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), what excellence does it have,
the author demonstrates this by defining the space of consciousness as variegated by *māyā* with the words "sabāhya" (with the external).
This refers to internal [states] such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, as well as external objects.
The witness is that which cognizes existence and non-existence, as well as their arrival and departure.
He who is the benefactor of all beings, the most excellent, whose nature is the measurement of time, and by whom all this is pervaded—he is called the space of consciousness (cittākāśa). || 17 ||

He characterizes the space of the mind (cittākāśa) with the word "all" (sarva). It is beneficial (hita) because it is the cause of all worldly activities for all beings; it is supreme (śreṣṭha) because it is the controller of all effects and causes; and it is "extended" (ātataṃ), meaning it has been expanded by one's own conceptualization. || 17 ||

He whose body is indeed uninterrupted throughout the expanse of the ten directions, who is the elemental self (bhūtātman), is that space which is the substratum of the wind, the clouds, and so forth. 18.
He defines the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*) with the word "ten": the clouds, the years, or the sun which is the soul of the year.
(18) The two spaces—the physical space and the space of the mind—both arise from the power of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*).
For consciousness is the cause of the entire multitude of effects, just as the day [is the cause] of all that occurs within it. (19)
In that regard, he demonstrates that in the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), the cause is merely the proximity of the conscious element (cidaṃśa) by means of the analogy "just as the day. || 19 ||
The mind is that very thing which is the impure consciousness characterized by the doubt, "Am I insentient? Am I not insentient? Know that by it the ether and other elements are brought into being.
However, because the insentient portion undergoes transformation into the form of the mind and so forth, it serves as the primary material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to the mind;
yet, since both consciousness and insentience are experienced within the mind, it is only that which is conjoined [with consciousness] that attains the state of being the mind. Thus he says:
"I am insentient" (verse 20).
The conceptualization of the three spaces has the unawakened self as its object;
it is imagined for the sake of instruction, but not with the awakened state as its object.
Furthermore, this conceptualization of creation by the mind and so forth is intended for the instruction of the ignorant and is not real;

from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), nothing whatsoever has arisen or perished in pure consciousness (*śuddhacit*). With this intention, he says "unawakened," etc., [in verse 21], leaving no room for any objection.
The Supreme Brahman alone is everything, filling all things;
it is eternally the object of awakened consciousness, devoid of parts and the act of dividing.

The ignorant person alone is instructed by means of various distinctions between duality and non-duality embedded within the composition of sentences; the awakened one is never instructed in this way.
As long as you have not awakened from this state like Rāma,
for that long alone shall I instruct you for the sake of your awakening.
Space, mind, the space of consciousness, and so forth, have been produced from the stainless expanse of consciousness, just as mirages arise from a forest fire in the desert.
From the forest fire, from the scorching of the desert land, or from the heat comparable to a wildfire. || 25 ||
Having attained the state of the mind, it accumulates a defiled form;
with its nature agitated, it weaves the illusory nets of the three worlds.
With the intention that the mind is not the effect of pure consciousness even because impurity is observed in its effects, he says:
"It accumulates" (cinoti). || 26 ||
Indeed, this state of being mind— which is essentially consciousness yet appears as defiled— is perceived by those devoid of awakening;
it is not so for those possessed of awakening, just as the appearance of silver in mother-of-pearl is not seen by the wise.
In this world, bondage arises through ignorance, while liberation comes through the power of awakening. || 27 ||

Because it is perceivable only by the ignorant, the mind is also an effect of ignorance; for this very reason, bondage exists only from the perspective of one who does not know reality, whereas from the perspective of one who knows reality, the Self is eternally liberated. Thus he says: "The state of being the mind... (verse 27).
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Consciousness-Sky," in the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Majesty of the Consciousness-Sky," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Whatever mind arises from any source whatsoever, it is indeed nothing at all.
O sinless one, one should always strive diligently to apply oneself to the liberation of the self.
In order to awaken one to the meaning already explained, the discourse on the mind (citta) is here set forth;
for through the investigation into the true nature of the mind, the destruction of the mind occurs in detail. (1)

The origin of the mind from the Self—which is eternally liberated—has been explained in detail in order to establish the conclusion that the notion of bondage is produced by the delusion of the mind due to ignorance; this is just as the description of the etiology and unwholesome diet is given in order to determine the true nature of a disease. Now, however, that the true nature of the mind has been determined:

With the intention that one must certainly exert effort in the treatment itself, and that there is no further need for repeated consideration of the causes, he says: "from whatever [source]"; one should apply it, that is, one should settle it within oneself.
When the mind is joined with the Supreme, it becomes pure and free from latent impressions;
thereafter, O Rāghava, being void of conceptual construction, it attains the state of the Self.
He states the fruit of samādhi: "It is joined" (saṃyojitam) || 2 ||
This entire world, consisting of both the stable and the moving, is dependent upon the mind;
O Rāma, it is clear that even bondage and liberation are subject to the mind.
Now, one might ask: "How can the cessation of all dualistic bondage, both external and internal, occur through the mere cessation of the mind?
To this, he says: "The world is dependent upon the mind" (verse 3).
In this regard, listen with great care, O Rāma, to the unsurpassed narrative of the mind (Cittākhyāna) which was told by Brahmā in ancient times as it is being recounted by me.
He introduces the illustrative narrative that establishes the stated point with the words: "In this regard" (atra). || 4 ||
There is a vast forest named Rāmāṭavī, empty, desolate, and extremely terrifying,
in which even a hundred yojanas appears as a mere atom.

The intended meaning of words such as "forest" (aṭavī) and so forth, he himself will explain in the following chapter. "Empty" (śūnyā) means devoid of animals, birds, and the like, and unreal (mithyābhūtā). "Unpeaceful" (aśāntā) means abounding in distraction. Alternatively, it may mean that its horizons (diganta) are empty and unpeaceful. "A mere speck" (kaṇamātrakaṃ) means like an atom (aṇumātra). || 5 ||
In that [city], there stood a certain man with a thousand hands and eyes,
terrifying, of vast form, and with a deeply agitated mind.
Taking up many iron clubs with his thousand arms, he strikes his own back and flees by his own power. (7)
Of one's own self; by one's very self. || 7 ||
Striking himself with his own self by means of firm blows,
he, with a terrified soul, flees even for hundreds of yojanas.
Crying out as he fled, having gone far away here and there,
he was exhausted, helpless in appearance, with his feet and limbs shattered.
Helpless indeed, he quickly fell into a great blind well,
terrifying with the darkness of the black night, within the deep cavity of the sky.
Blind, he is devoid of the vision of discernment, like Kṛṣṇarāti in the terrible darkness.
Then, after a long time, he emerged from the blind well;
striking again with blows, he caused himself to flee by his own hand.
From the very cause that is oneself. || 11 ||
Having gone even further, he entered a thicket of Karañja trees covered in thorns,
like a moth entering a flame.
The forest thicket is dense with *karañja* thorny creepers, providing little shade and abounding in suffering;
furthermore, it is pervaded by other thorns. || 12 ||
Therefore, having emerged from that thicket of karañja trees as if in an instant,
he again flees from himself, striking himself with blows.
Having gone even further, he entered, as if smiling, the lovely grove of plantain trees, cool as the rays of the moon.
Hasana was as if delighted. || 14 ||
Emerging from that grove of plantains in an instant,
he himself, striking with blows, flees before himself (or: before his own self).
Having gone even further, that blind man quickly entered that very same blind well,
his limbs and form shattered.
Having emerged from the blind well, he entered a grove of plantain trees;
from the plantain grove, he went to a chasm filled with thickets of *karañja* forest trees.
Like a deep abyss or pit. || 17 ||
Entering from a grove of *karañja* trees into a well, and from the well into a thicket of plantain trees, he struck down [his enemies] while remaining established within his own self. || 18 ||
The pit is the blind well mentioned previously; the interior of the Rambhā grove is the middle of a plantain forest. || 18 ||
Having observed his conduct of such a nature for a long time, I forcibly restrained him on the road and blocked him for a moment. (19)
Having observed with the eye of discernment, and having grasped by means of the power of yoga. || 19 ||
He was asked: "Who are you? What is this? For what purpose do you do it?
What is your name, and what is your desire here? Why do you wander about in vain? (20)
For what purpose is this—such as striking oneself or falling into a well? It is for that which is desired and longed for. || 20 ||
O descendant of Raghu, being thus questioned by me, he replied:
"I am nothing at all, O sage, nor do I perform any action whatsoever. (21)
"I have been defeated by you; alas, you are my enemy!
I have been seen by you, and I am ruined—for both sorrow and for joy. (22)
Having spoken thus, looking at his own distressed limbs and feeling dissatisfied,
he wept with a loud cry, wretched like a cloud raining upon a forest.
One who is dissatisfied with enjoyments is insatiable. || 23 ||
In a mere moment, having ceased his weeping there,
he looked at his own limbs and laughed and roared.
Then, at the conclusion of his loud laughter, that man gradually cast off his own limbs from all sides before me.
First his most dreadful head fell,
then his arms, followed by his chest, and after that his belly.

The head consists of volition (*saṃkalpa*); because it is the root of all misfortune, it is most terrible. The arms are the tendencies toward conceptualization (*vikalpa-āśaya*). The chest is attachment to sense objects (*viṣayābhiniveśa*), and the belly is thirst (*tṛṣṇā*)—these are to be understood according to their respective fitness.
Then, in an instant, that person [perceived] those limbs in their proper order.
Having abandoned [the body], he is about to depart somewhere by the power of destiny.

By the phrase "to go anywhere" (kvāpi gantum), it is stated that there is a reduction to a state devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvarūpāpatti) for that which has been sublated, because no other place to go remains, due to the power of knowledge to necessarily sublate ignorance and its effects. || 27 ||
Then, in another secluded place, I saw yet another man;
he too was striking himself all over with blows. (28)
To demonstrate that this same process applies to the minds of others just as it does to one's own mind, he says, beginning with "He saw," and so forth. || 28 ||
With his thick-set arms, he flees all by himself;
he falls into a well, and having risen from the well, he runs toward it.
Again he falls into the pit; again, afflicted, he flees;
again he enters the abyss, and for a moment the cool forest.
In a pit or a blind well; a chasm or a hollow in a forest of *karañja* trees; a cool grove or a grove of plantain trees. (30) "Alas! Again and again he is satisfied, yet again he strikes out himself.
Having observed for a long time such a general disposition of his own conduct, he looked on with wonder. (31)
Having firmly restrained him, I questioned him in that very manner;
and he, having wept and then laughed, spoke to me today in that same sequence.
Having reached a state of disintegration through his limbs, he became invisible according to his power; then, having reflected upon the force of destiny, he prepared to depart.
"Alakṣyatām" means "the state of being invisible. || 33 ||
Again, in a secluded place, I saw another man who, while striking [himself] in exactly that same manner, fled of his own accord. || 34 ||
Fleeing, I fell into a great, blind, and dark well;
there I dwelt for a very long time, awaiting him.
It blinds, thus it is "andha"; in a blind well, that is, a well shrouded in darkness. || 35 ||
When that rogue had not emerged from the well even after a very long time, I then rose up to depart and saw the man once again. (36)
As he was falling in such a manner and with such a form, I quickly seized him just as he was, and spoke to him once again.
Just so, O lotus-petal-eyed one, he did not understand that; that fool knows nothing at all, perceiving me alone. (38)
"O lotus-petal-eyed one"—this is an address to Rāma; it connects with the subsequent clause: "he became solely intent on his own duty. (38)
Having said, "O sinful, wicked brahmin," he departed intent on his own business.
Then, while I was wandering in that great forest in such a manner, (39)

The expression "O, you sinner! and so forth is intended to indicate that he was not only himself ignorant of discrimination, but moreover intent on disregarding those who possess discrimination. || 39 ||
Many such men who cause harm have been seen;
some, when questioned by me, come to rest like the agitation of a dream.
Having been questioned by me and being enlightened, they attained tranquility—that cessation characterized by the destruction of the previously mentioned nature. || 44 ||
Some do not welcome what I have said, like a corpse-like body;
others, having fallen into the blind wells, have risen from them once again. (41)
They do not rejoice in them, they remain indifferent toward them, and they loathe them. || 41 ||
Some did not emerge from the thicket of plantain trees even after a long time; others disappeared within the vast grove of *karañja* bushes.
They have not departed; rather, it means that having attained knowledge right there, they were liberated. || 42 ||
"O descendant of Raghu, that vast great forest was such that no one devoted to the Dharma found a place of rest anywhere."
Those devoted to dharma are those intent upon dharma performed for the sake of specific desires. || 43 ||
Even today that [intellect] exists within which these persons are thus situated;
and she was seen by you, O Rāma, as one engaged in worldly activity here.
Yet, O Rāghava, because of the immaturity of your realization of the true nature of the intellect, you do not remember her.

By you, as its cause, that great forest was seen as possessing all worldly transactions—that is, as being full of all conventional dealings—[yet it is actually] the reality of the intellect, the essence of intelligence, which is discernment. [This was so] because of your childhood, that is, your lack of maturity. || 44 ||

That terrifying and dreadful forest, its body crowded with various thorns and destructive even to the dense thickets of worldly existence, having arrived in this world, [afflicts] those who have not attained liberation or supreme awakening.

She was enjoyed in the *rāsa* dance like a garden (*vāṭikā*) consisting of clusters of flowering shrubs— meaning a garden where the shrubs are primarily flowers (the commentary explains that "flower-grove" and so forth has this same underlying meaning). || 45 ||

He summarizes: "He" (sa). In this world, where the reality of Dharma and Brahman is perceived through the eye of discrimination, even having attained—that is, reached—bliss (*nirvṛti*), which is the happiness of the perfection of the means, in such a birth as one who is qualified [for liberation].
By those who, due to the power of misfortune, have not attained the realization of the Supreme Self, [this world] is resorted to through attachment to sense-objects;
it is served like a garden grove of flowers—this is the illustration for its superficial attractiveness. (45)
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Mind," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 98.
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Citta," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
Ninety-ninth Sarga.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, what is that great forest? When and how was it seen by me?
And who are those men there, and what is it that they have exerted themselves to do? || 1 ||
The intended meaning of the aforementioned exposition on consciousness, presented both in sequential and non-sequential order,
is here described by means of Rāma’s inquiry.

For what purpose, or for what reason, have you become so intent on striking your own bodies with iron bars and entering into wells, karanja thickets, forests, and the like? In the reading "intent upon being made to do that by someone else" (*kiṃ-tat-kartṛ-kṛtodyamāḥ*), since it is impossible for one to engage in what is undesirable to oneself spontaneously, that agency must be attributed to another; [the question is] by which such agent would one be made to act toward such an undesirable end?
The meaning is that they have become those who have exerted effort toward striking themselves and so forth, by means of the cause that is the one who forcibly enjoins them.
As for the analysis of the compound: "What is that [cause], and who is its agent? What is that which the agent does? They are those who have exerted effort by means of that. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O mighty-armed Raghunātha, listen; I shall tell you everything.
That great forest is not far away, O Rāma, nor indeed are those men.
In reality, Brahman alone—through the conceptualization of the manifold variety of false states such as heaven and hell—is the forest of saṃsāra;
those who conceive it are merely the minds themselves. Thus, he says "O Raghunātha," etc., to show that those people were not described by me as being located at a distance. || 2 ||
Know, O Rāma, that this path of saṃsāra— deep, with its boundless hollows, empty yet rich in transformations— is a vast wilderness.

The meaning is this: know that this well-known path of saṃsāra is empty because it lacks reality from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārthadṛśā), yet from the perspective of delusion (bhrāntidṛśā) it is rich in transformations because it appears to exist; thus, it is that aforementioned great wilderness. || 3 ||
When this [reality] is attained through the light of inquiry by means of a single object alone—
being complete and not conjoined with anything else— it is at that very moment as if it were absolute.
When is she empty, and by what means is she attained? To this he says: "By the light of discernment" (*vicārāloka*).
When she is filled by one non-dual reality alone and is not joined with anything else, then she becomes purely empty (*kevalā śūnyā*).
The word "as it were" (*iva*) indicates that terms such as "purely empty" and so forth apply to her only figuratively.
This is for the purpose of illuminating that it is impossible to define [terms] such as "emptiness" (śūnyatva) when their counter-correlate (pratiyogin) cannot be defined.
And the meaning is that this [emptiness] is obtained through such a light of discrimination (viveka), characterized by the purification of the referents of the terms *tattvam* and *padārtha*. || 4 ||
In that regard, know those large-bodied men who wander about to be the very minds fallen utterly into suffering. (5)
O Mahāmati, I am the observer of these [objects] with discernment; by means of discernment, O sinless one, they were seen by me as something entirely other.
In this context, *viveka* means discernment (*vicāra*).
For by me those very minds are awakened through discernment,
just as lotuses are constantly awakened by the well-shining sun.
O great-minded one, having attained awakening through me and by my grace, how many minds have reached the supreme state of tranquility? (8)

"By my awakening"—that is, by the knowledge of reality—"through my grace," which is the grace of discernment, "and through tranquility," which is the destruction of mental constructs, they have attained the supreme liberation. || 8 ||
Some do not welcome me because they are deluded regarding solitude;
due to their contempt for me, they fall headlong into wells.
Mindfulness, discernment, and equanimity. || 9 ||
O descendant of Raghu, those dark wells and impenetrable hells have now become for them groves of plantain trees. (10)
You ought to know those minds that find their sole delight in heaven—those which have entered into the depths of a blind well and never emerged again. 11.
O Raghava, those minds were possessed of great sins,
for they had not emerged from their dwelling in the plantain grove.
O Rāghava, those minds endowed with the accumulation of merit have entered the forest of Karañja trees, yet they have not emerged from it.
O descendant of Raghu, among those human beings, some minds were fully awakened and there they were liberated from bondage.

"Born and matured in the human state"—that is, within the human condition—means "fully awakened"; this is intended to show that the primary qualification for knowledge exists in the human body because of the possibility of attaining specific qualities such as detachment (*vairāgya*). || 14 ||
Indeed, some minds, assuming many forms, enter from one womb into another; they remain there, and they fall down and spring up again.
They fall into the hells; they soar up into the heavens. 15.
They know that dense thicket of karañja trees to be the passion for a wife;
human existence, crowded with the thorns of suffering and filled with various desires, is likewise so perceived. (16)
Human existence is like the taste of a wife, filled with affection for one's family; for this very reason, it is crowded with the thorns of suffering and characterized by manifold cravings. (16)
But those minds which have entered the dense thicket of the Karañja tree, having been born again in the human state, remain full of aesthetic relish (rasika) for that very same thing.
Or [those] who are attached to aesthetic flavors, being intent on tasting the flavor of sense objects. || 17 ||
O best of the Raghus, know that this grove of plantains, cool as the rays of the moon and bringing delight to the mind, is heaven itself.
Some maintain their bodies— whether already established or newly arisen— through merit consisting of austerity characterized by self-restraint.
By means of that which is meritorious and prescribed by the scriptures— this qualification being for the purpose of excluding what is not prescribed by the scriptures—

and by means of worship characterized primarily by *dhāraṇā*, which consists of binding the mind to the object of meditation, they sustain those bodies such as those of the planets, the Seven Sages, and the Pole Star; these, compared to others, [are so described].
Having arisen through the excellence of splendor, enjoyments, and so forth, as well as through the realization of reality, they became prosperous;
"saṃsthitāni" means that they remained for a long time. || 19 ||
By those ignorant men who have disregarded my intellect and consciousness, their own discernment has been disregarded by their minds that know not the Self. || 20 ||
The meaning is that he was disregarded and neglected by their intellects or minds; that is to say, he was neither resolved upon nor remembered.
(20) "I am ruined, I have been seen by you! You are my enemy!"—what was thus spoken was indeed a lamentation uttered by a faltering mind. (21)
"Galatā" means dissolving through the realization of reality; "paridevitam" means lamentation. || 21 ||
O Raghava, that great wailing which was wept by the man so swiftly and profusely was actually the lamentation of the mind as it renounced the snare of worldly enjoyments.
For one who has attained partial discernment but has not yet reached the stainless state,
intense anguish arises as they renounce worldly enjoyments.
With compassion, he beheld their weeping limbs and thought in his heart: "Alas! Having abandoned these, why should I depart? (24)
Regarding the statement, "Beholding his own limbs, he laughed and roared," the author explains its intended meaning with the words beginning "rudatā" (weeping).
"Avabodhinā" means by one possessing slight discrimination. "Kāruṇyena" means by affection for women, sons, and so forth. || 24 ||
For one who has attained partial discernment but has not yet reached the stainless state,
anguish indeed increases as the mind abandons the limbs of the body.
The factors [of attachment] are affection, greed, and so forth. || 25 ||
But when a man laughs with joy from the awakening of his own realization, having attained discernment, that laughter is one of contentment, O Rāma, with a tranquil mind.
That was satisfied and gladdened; the suffix *kta* is used in the neuter sense of the state [of being] from the root *tuṣ*. || 26 ||
For one who has attained solitude and abandoned abiding in saṃsāra, as the mind relinquishes form, bliss indeed increases. (27)
He clarifies that very point: "Pariprāpta" (fully attained), etc. || 27 ||
Those limbs which were seen by a man while laughing in derision were seen by his mind as the very grounds for his own deception.
The words of deception are the causes for one's own self-deception. || 28 ||
"Alas! For so long we have been deceived by things fashioned by false conceptualization.
Thus, with a sense of derision, he looked at his own limbs with his mind. (29)
"Deceived and cheated by imagined objects fashioned by false conceptualization"—this is said in derision. (29)
For the mind that has attained discernment and rests in the expansive state looks back from afar with a smile at its former vessel of wretchedness.
The basis, support, and entire range of objects for prior dejection; "from afar" means by way of not coming into contact with the unattached Self. || 30 ||
When he was firmly restrained and questioned by me with great effort, it was shown that discrimination forcibly seizes the mind. (31)
This is that Puruṣa mentioned previously; he takes up, that is, he sustains. || 31 ||
When his limbs were shattered and vanished before his eyes, it was demonstrated that the hope for objects ceases without that mind. (32)

The term *arthāśā* means hope accompanied by wealth. The meaning is that it has been shown that even the thirst for sense objects (*viṣayatṛṣṇā*) is suppressed along with the mental afflictions and their corresponding objects. || 32 ||
That which has been described as the state of having a thousand eyes and hands for a person is indeed shown to be the infinite form of the mind. (33)
Just as a man strikes himself with a torrent of blows,
so does his own mind strike itself with the blows of its own evil imaginings.
That mind flees from the blows of its own latent impressions, just as a man flees from himself while striking his own body.
It strikes its own mind by itself and of its own will;
it flees away by itself as well—behold the manifestation of ignorance! (36)
Svāntam means the mind (manas). || 36 ||
For all minds indeed, scorched by their own latent impressions, flee of their own accord when they are fit to go to that state. (37)

They were heated and agitated; yet they were fit to go to and realize that state of Brahmā, being suitable by their very nature. Alternatively, they were "yoked," meaning they were even restrained through yoga. || 37 ||
This suffering itself stretches out the mind;
yet, once it has become utterly exhausted by itself, it flees from that very [suffering].
He explains the term "tormented" as follows: "That which is this... (38).
Through the webs of volitions and latent impressions, the mind binds itself, just as a silkworm binds itself with webs made of saliva. (39)
The silkworm is well known for its own saliva—the liquid from its mouth—and its transformations thereof, which serve as the ground for the production of silk. (39)
Just as he encounters misfortune, so too does he play restlessly,
failing to perceive his own future suffering, like a child with its own wicked pranks.
Just as the monkey who pulled out the wedge suffered pain because he did not see the bull’s testicles caught in the crack of the wood, so too does this mind suffer. (41)

He cites a worldly verse regarding the point already stated: "Not seeing," etc. It is said that once, in a forest, while carpenters were splitting a large log in half and had inserted a wedge in the middle, a certain monkey happened to sit upon that log; [he felt] the pressure of his own testicles lodged within the cleft of the wood.

The meaning is that, like one who, failing to see what is about to happen, tears out a supporting wedge through his own recklessness and thereby incurs the suffering of death and so forth by means of the pincers of his testicles, so it is here. || 41 ||
Through long-term protection as well as through long-term cultivation,
having attained insignificance by means of practice, one does not grieve again.

If, even when restrained, it flees due to distractions, then how is the desired goal accomplished? To this he says: "For a long time" (*cireti*). The desired goal is not achieved by restraint alone once, but rather through its long-term maintenance and through long-term cultivation of the nature of the non-attached Self; this is the meaning. [He speaks of] "insignificance," meaning that which is sublated by knowledge. || 42 ||
Through mental negligence, sufferings increase like mountain peaks;
yet by the power of that same [mind when disciplined], they perish just as frost vanishes before the sun. (43)
And thus, it follows that the mind alone, through negligence or discernment, is the cause of bondage or liberation; so he says:
"For as long as one lives, the mind indeed delights in blameless conduct born from the meaning of the scriptures, and remains equal toward passion and the like through silence, like a sage."
Afterwards, having attained that unborn state which purifies even the purifiers, which is cool, and by remaining in which, a person no longer grieves even in the midst of great calamities.

The word "ca" (and) is used here in the sense of "yadi" (if). If the mind— being equal and of one flavor with blameless mental impressions (*vāsanā*) born from the meaning of the scriptures— wanders like a sage throughout its life in silence and restraint amidst objects such as passion and the like, then, through the subsequent awakening to reality, it becomes the supreme purifier of purifiers, the unborn.

Having attained that state of Brahman—which is devoid of transformations such as birth and is therefore cool, untouched by the threefold affliction, pure, and full—a person who is liberated while living and established therein does not grieve again, even in great calamities such as the dissolution of the universe. This is the meaning of such scriptural passages as, "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow. (44)
