Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Mind," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* (Section on Origination) of the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (Sage) tradition. 99.
Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Mind," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The One Hundredth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This mind has emerged from the supreme state of Brahman.
It is both non-identical with it and identical with it, like a wave from the ocean. || 1 ||
Here, the omnipotence of Brahman is described through the power of the mind;
the conceptualization of bondage, liberation, and so forth within non-duality arises solely from ignorance.

Regarding what was stated—that the conceptualization of bondage and liberation is dependent solely upon the mind—the author provides the logical justification for this with the verse beginning with "cittam" (the mind).

The phrase "not consisting of that" (*atanmayam*) refers to the modification (*vikāra*) of ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is not Brahman. "Consisting of that" (*tanmayam*) refers to the illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of the pure Brahman.
The meaning is: just as a wave is a modification of water and yet an illusory manifestation of its existence (*sattā*), so it is in this case. || 1 ||
O Rāma, for those who are awakened, the mind here is indeed Brahman alone and nothing else;
for those who perceive the commonality of water, a wave is not something other than the ocean.
The generality of water is the existence of water. || 2 ||
For those who have not awakened to the Delightful One (Rāmā), the mind is the cause of wandering in saṃsāra;
it is like one who fails to see the commonality of water and does not perceive the non-difference between the water and its waves.
For those whose vision is unawakened, a distinction based on the relationship between the signified and the signifier is merely postulated for the sake of awakening them. (4)

For this very reason, it was stated previously that even the conceptualization of scriptural conventions—such as the terms "teacher" and "taught," or "word" and "meaning"—is based solely on the perspective of the ignorant, and not on the vision of reality; thus he says: "The unawakened...
(4) "The Supreme Brahman is all-powerful, eternal, ever-full, and immutable."
There is nothing that does not exist within that expansive Self.

With the intention that even the state of being the cause of the entire world belongs to Brahman only when it is unknown and not when it is known, he establishes its possession of all powers with the words beginning "possessing all powers" (sarvaśakti) and so forth. || 5 ||
For the Blessed One is all-powerful; whatever pleases him, the omnipresent Lord makes that very power manifest in its full extent.
It reveals; it makes manifest in the form of an effect. || 6 ||
O Rāma, the power of consciousness (cicchakti) is perceived within bodies,
the power of motion (spandaśakti) within the winds, and likewise the power of inertia (jaḍaśakti) within stones.
In bodies, that is, among the fourfold collection of living beings. || 7 ||
Likewise, the power of fluidity resides in waters, the power of fire in fire,
the power of emptiness in space, and the power of existence in the persistence of being.
The power of emptiness, because it is non-obstructive, is the power of receptivity for everything; the power of existence is the fitness for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). (8)
Indeed, the all-pervading power of Brahman is seen extending through the ten directions:
the power of destruction in things that perish, and the power of grief in those who grieve.
The power of destruction is the power of concealment within the cause;
it is the power of grief, or the power of despondency, which has the capacity to produce a body born of sorrow.
The power of bliss is in the Joyful state, and likewise the power of vigor is in the Fierce;
the power of emanation is in the Emanations, and the state of all-pervading power at the end of the aeon.
At the end of the aeon, during the primordial dissolution (*prākṛtapralaya*), there is the state of possessing all powers within primordial nature (*prakṛti*), because it is the seed of all effects.
In the reading *sarvaśaktitā*, it refers to the power of withdrawal (*saṃhāraśaktitā*). || 10 ||
218. Just as a tree exists within the seed of a tree, possessing fruit, flowers, creepers, leaves, branches, twigs, and roots, so too does this [universe] abide within Brahman.
He states that very point: "The fruit," etc. (verse 11).
By the power of appearance alone, the mind— designated as either the "living being" or "other"— is seen within Brahman as something intermediate between mental clarity and dullness.

With the intention that Brahman alone, though unknown, is the seed of the world—since the first effect, the mind, is seen to possess a dual nature of both consciousness and inertia—he says: "Appearance," etc. Here, "appearance" refers to the witness of ignorance;
it exists solely by virtue of that [ignorance], not by virtue of the Pure [Brahman] alone. (12)
The various trees, creepers, shrubs, clusters, sprouts, and rice-paddies are nothing but non-conceptual pure consciousness; their diversity is merely an unknown mental construction.

Since this visible manifold of trees, shrubs, and so forth is a transformation (*vivarta*) of consciousness when it is not known, he says "nānā" (not manifold) to indicate that pure consciousness alone is the reality. The meaning is that this conceptualization occurs regarding the reality that is not yet fully realized. || 13 ||
O Raghava, behold today this very reality of the self as Brahman—the world itself;
it is the Self, all-pervading by name, whose great form is eternally manifest. (14)

The meaning is: perceive that the world, the principle of ego (ahaṃtattva), and the principle of the individual soul appearing as "I" are none other than Brahman, whose nature is immediate consciousness. || 14 ||
That power which sustains the mental channel is called the mind;
it is like the illusion of feathers in the sky, or the perception of a whirlpool in water. (15)

He states with the words beginning "That which" (yad) that it is Brahman alone—preceded by its respective powers—that is spoken of through delusion by such terms as "mind" (manas) and so forth, and nothing else. || 15 ||
The mind is merely a fragment of appearance within the Self as the living soul;
this very form of the mind that has arisen is essentially of the nature of mentation.
Therefore, O subduer of enemies, this is the power of Brahman; it is Brahman itself.
The distinction of "this," "that," and "I" arises merely from appearance.

The meaning is that this threefold division of the visible world— appearing as "this" through its presence before one, as "that" through its remoteness, and as "I" through identity with the self— is born of appearance and is merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*), not real. (17)
And nothing other than the mind is the supreme cause of delusion for Brahman;
whatever exists, whether being or non-being, is contained within this very mind. (18)

[Objection: But surely desire, the impressions of karma (*karmavāsanā*), and so forth are also heard in scripture to be the causes of the manifold world of duality (*dvaitaprapañca*); how then can it be said that the power of Brahman alone is their cause? To this, he says: "Of the mind.

When there is delusion—namely, the error of duality and so forth—of the mind, which is the individual soul (*jīva*), and of Brahman, whatever else there may be, such as desire and so on, [all] have the Supreme Cause as their source.

Whatever is designated as "the world" in common parlance—all that, consisting of both existence and non-existence through its manifestation and disappearance within the mind alone—they know to be none other than that aforementioned Brahman-hood, the very power of expansion (*bṛṃhaṇa-śakti*) of the omnipotent Brahman; this is the connection with the subsequent verse. || 18 ||
They know that power, which is designated as "all-pervading" (vyā), belonging to the All-Powerful One, to be the state of Brahman;
for it is the very essence of the existence of the mind, just as this [power] resides within the mind. (19)
Now, one might ask: how can the mental faculties—the powers of desire and so forth—reside in Brahman such that they would be its powers?

To this, he says: "The mind. Just as the mind, whose essence is existence and which is of the nature of Brahman, appears to reside in the mind through the superimposition of association; or just as the powers of the seasons, such as spring and the like, [reside] in trees and other things.
In the same way, the mental states (manodharmas) also abide in Brahman while living; this is the meaning. || 19 ||
Just as the powers of the seasons exist within the life-force of a living being, so do they abide in Brahman;
for the earth, though pervaded by the flowers of all seasons, manifests them through the various distinctions of place and time.

If all the powers of Brahman reside here within every living being, then why are they not all intermingled in all beings? To this he replies: "Pervasive" (vyāpta). Just as the earth, though possessing the power to produce flowers of all seasons, yields flowers and the like only in specific locations according to the distinct regulations of seed-potency and other factors, so too [is the case with the powers of Brahman].
The meaning is that even Brahmā, the creator of the world, does not establish the powers of the mind through confusion, but rather with systematic order. || 20 ||
Just as the Creator of the World places flowers [in various spots], so does He place minds;
for from Him, powers emerge here and there at various times. || 21 ||
They come forth, manifesting in the form of established fruits; the meaning is that they appear like the potentialities of rice from the surface of the earth.
Due to the diversity of place, time, and other factors, rice grows here on the surface of the earth;
yet one does not perceive it by means of that very same appearance through which it was previously born.

Having provisionally accepted this worldly diversity—which consists of distinctions such as the exclusion of counter-correlates (*pratiyogi-vyavaccheda*), number, form, and so forth—the non-confusion [of categories] has been demonstrated; yet, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), this diversity is not [ultimately real], because that which is merely an appearance cannot function as a causal agent, and because no other distinct causal agents can be established apart from appearance itself. Thus, it is merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*).

He says—through the verse beginning with "na jātam" (not born)—that one should understand that those who are born from Brahman, which is conceptualized by the word "mind" (*manas*), are indeed Brahman itself, [according to the teaching]: "One sees nothing as something born, nor as nothing at all, by means of anything. (22)
Those things such as the exclusion of counter-correlates, number, and form, which are conceptualized by means of mental words—know them to be born from Brahman and to be Brahman itself. (23)
In whatever manner an appearance arises for this mind, in that very same way it comes to be; indeed, the sons of Indu are the illustration in this matter. (24)
Just as movement occurs in the great ocean, which is itself unagitated and pure,
so does this individual soul (jīva) exist within the Supreme Self (paramātman), being the cause of saṃsāra.
With the intention that the living being alone is the creator of the world and there is no other Brahmā, and that the world imagined by him is far removed from reality, he says: "Himself," etc. (25).
O Rāma, for the knower, everything perceived always revolves as Brahman alone within the Self, like the water of the ocean amidst its surges, waves, and billows.
"Citta" means accumulated, filled, or full; it exists everywhere. || 26 ||
There is no second being; there is but one whose nature consists of the activity of name-and-form.
It is like a conceptualization distinct from the water, occurring upon another ocean with its various waves. (27)
In the Supreme Brahman there is no second existence; rather, there is only one.
That which is born and likewise perishes, that which moves and stands still—all this is Brahman; it is Brahman that manifests through Brahman by means of illusory transformation (vivarta).
It evolves, appearing in an unreal form. || 28 ||
Just as a fierce heat within one's own self appears through a mirage, so too does the manifold [universe] flash forth from the Self by means of the manifold [manifestation]. (29)
By means of a mirage, which has the nature of a river of mirages, it appears variegated, even though it is devoid of name and form. || 29 ||
The instrument, the action, and the agent; birth, death, and persistence—all this is Brahman alone, for there exists no other conceptualization apart from it.
There is no greed, there is no delusion, there is no thirst, and no passion.
How can there be greed, thirst, or delusion for the Self within the Self? Or from where could they arise? (31)
He states that in the absence of a second [object], there is no possibility whatsoever for greed, delusion, and so forth—beginning with "not": *na*. *Rañjanā* means excessive attachment. || 31 ||
This entire world is indeed the Self; the process of mental construction is the Self alone. Just as gold arises in the form of a bracelet, so does this Self arise in the form of the mind.
By way of the mind, through the state of being the mind. || 32 ||
That supreme abode which is unawakened is called the mind and the individual soul (*jīva*).
As long as it remains unrecognized, that very kinsman quickly becomes a stranger. (33)
Unawakened, it is shrouded by ignorance. || 33 ||
By the ignorant self, which is composed of consciousness, emptiness has been manifested through its own volition,
just as the sky is manifested by a living being.
Just as emptiness is manifested by the sky—which, though not empty, is made the object of ignorance by the ignorant—in the same way [emptiness is manifested here]. || 34 ||
In this world, the Self alone shines as the living being (jīva), appearing as if it were not the Self;
like the appearance of two moons due to faulty vision, both the existent and the non-existent have arisen from it.
Like that which is not-self, it is like the object of the notion of "I" through identification with the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth;
and while it is non-existent as an object—that is, in its second form—it is existent in its ultimate singular form. || 35 ||

Since these two—the perception of the meaning of delusion and the perception of the meaning of words—are utterly impossible, and because the Self alone is real, where is the bound self, and where is it liberated? (36)
Regarding delusion and its object, which are the causes of confusion:
because these two—the perceptions of the meanings of the words "bondage" and "liberation"—are absolutely impossible [in reality]. (36)
For one for whom bondage is eternally non-existent, the conceit "I am bound" is a false imagination;
for him, liberation is likewise imaginary and not real in truth.

The meaning is that since permanence is not possible, there is "non-occurrence" (asaṃbhava) of bondage for him. Thus, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha-dṛṣṭi), even bondage and liberation, though conceptual, are insubstantial. As the Śruti states: "There is no cessation and no origination; no one is bound and no one is a seeker; no one desires liberation and no one is liberated—this is the ultimate truth. || 37 ||
Śrī Rāma said: Whatever resolution the mind arrives at, that very thing comes to pass and not otherwise.
Therefore, O Lord, how can there be no bondage that is merely conceptual? (38)

Since it has already been established at length that bondage is conceptual and indeterminable from the perspective of reasoning, Rāma—unable to endure the statement that even conceptual bondage does not exist—asks: "The mind... (verse 38).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This conception of bondage for fools is false and merely imaginary;
likewise, their other conception of liberation has arisen as nothing but a falsehood. (39)

This rational perspective is conceived as a gateway to the vision of ultimate reality (paramārtha-dṛṣṭi) for the purpose of dismantling the firmness of worldly views; therefore, it does not rest therein, but rather in the scriptural vision of [the world's] insubstantiality. With this intention, Vasiṣṭha replies with the words beginning "mithyā" (it is false).

Just as a conceptual dream-conception is false and trivial when viewed by the waking eye, so too is the "indefinability" (anirvacanīyatā) not the actual reality of the thing, but rather the inability to define it through logical reasoning. And since that [indefinability] is a characteristic of foolish persons and not the intrinsic nature of the object, it is said "of the fools" (mūrkhāṇām) to indicate this. || 39 ||
Thus, from the very state of ignorance, there arises the perception of bondage and liberation due to non-remembrance;
but in reality, O Mahāmati, there is neither bondage nor liberation.

Thus, according to the manner previously stated, insubstantial ignorance is itself the cause of ignorance; from that alone arise the perceptions of bondage and liberation. This is because it would contradict the Smṛti: "The unreal has no being, nor does the real have non-being; the truth regarding both of these has been perceived by the seers of reality."
The meaning is that it is because there can be no resting in an indeterminable state that lies between existence and non-existence. || 40 ||
The unreality of conceptual construction is [known] to one whose intellect is fully awakened;
O wise one, it is like the snake in a rope to one whose intellect has awakened to reality. (41)

Non-substantiality (avastutva) means worthlessness (tucchatva). That previously mentioned indeterminability (anirvacanīyatva), however, is intended for the investigator who possesses an unawakened intellect—that is, one who is not wise—not for the wise man. || 41 ||
No delusion whatsoever regarding bondage, liberation, and so forth exists for the wise man;
for it is only the ignorant person, O Rāghava, who possesses such delusions as bondage and liberation.
He states that very point more clearly: "Bondage," etc. (42).
First is the mind, then the views of bondage and liberation, and afterwards the construction of conceptual proliferation known as the world;
for this state of affairs has reached its established form.
O fortunate one, this narrative is like that told by children. || 43 ||

Introducing the story of the boy (Bālaka) regarding the matter already stated, he concludes with the verse beginning "In the beginning": "O fortunate one," etc. This state of bondage has attained firm establishment, like a story about to be told which was narrated by a nurse to a child. || 43 ||

Thus ends the one hundredth canto, titled "The Description of the Arising of the Mind Preceded by the Treatment of the Mind," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arising of the Mind," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and first canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O best of sages, what is this sequence called the 'Narrative of the Child'?"
Tell me this cause for the description of the mind in due order.

In this very context, the sequence of the story of the boy is described as an illustration for the cycle of hundreds of conceptual constructions that arise from a volition devoid of any objective reality.

Desiring to hear the story of the boy (Bālaka), which was previously introduced to indicate that for the mind— which consists of resolve (saṃkalpa) and conceptualization (vikalpa)— resolve is the root, and that by its cessation, through the cutting off of the root, conceptualizations do not arise, thereby accomplishing establishment in the state beyond conceptualization (nirvikalpa-pada), Rāma asks: "What is said?"

Thus, relying on the view that [the word] undergoes grammatical refinement (*padasaṃskāra*), the neuter gender is used for these two words in the sense of a general category (*sāmānya*). The meaning is: "In what manner is the sequence characterized by the narrative of the young crow observed in the world? Tell it in this sequence. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, a certain child of simple intellect asked his nurse: "O nurse, tell me some entertaining story. (2)
One of deluded intellect is devoid of the discrimination between what is appropriate and what is inappropriate. || 2 ||
O Great-minded One, for the amusement of that child, the nurse tells him a narrative with clear and sweet syllables. (3)
In a certain place, where there was no city at all, there lived three noble and auspicious princes who were righteous and exultant in their valor.
The mention of the "preeminent royal capital" implies that there is no city whatsoever [comparable to it]. || 4 ||
In that vast empty city, like water-drops and stars in the sky, two were not born, and likewise one did not even remain in the womb. (5)
The phrase "in which the cities and branch-towns were empty" is an epithet [of that place].
The stars consist of water because they are portions of the moon. || 5 ||
Then, for the sake of obtaining the highest gain, they may sometimes assemble together;
yet their kinsmen have dejected faces and minds overwhelmed by grief. (6)

At one time, having lost their kinsmen through fate, with the deaths of their relatives and their faces distressed by famine and other hardships, they departed from their own community of citizens—either by coming together or through mutual consensus—in order to seek another excellent city; this is the sense of the remainder. || 6 ||
Having emerged from that empty city with their faces cast down,
they appeared like Mercury, Venus, and Saturn joined together as if emerging from the sky.
"Saṃśliṣṭāḥ" means joined together. || 7 ||
With limbs as delicate as the śirīṣa flower, scorched by the sun from behind as they traveled on the road during the day, they were like tender shoots withered by the heat of summer.
They have reached a state of witheredness; this is the ellipsis. || 8 ||
With their lotus-feet scorched by the heated sands of the path,
they lamented, "O father!", like deer strayed from the herd.
With their feet pierced by the tips of darbha grass and the joints of their limbs exhausted by the heat,
they had traversed a long distance with bodies grey with dust.
On the way, they reached three trees that were dense with clusters of blossoms, garlanded with fruits and shoots, and served as a refuge for flocks of beasts and birds.
Among these three trees, two have not grown even slightly;
as for the third, the self-climbing tree, its very seed does not exist.
"In the three trees" is a locative case used for specification (*nirdhāraṇe*). "Easy to climb" means capable of being ascended with ease. || 12 ||
Exhausted and weary, they rested there beneath a single tree,
like Śakra, Anila, and Yama at the foot of the Pārijāta tree in heaven.
Having eaten fruits that were like nectar and having drunk their juice,
they fashioned garlands from clusters of blossoms, rested for a long while, and then departed.
With clusters [of flowers], that is, with the blossoms of specific creepers. || 14 ||
Having gone even further, when midday had arrived,
they reached a triad of rivers resounding with the rippling noise of waves.
There, one river was completely dried up, and not even a trace of water remained in the other two; their sight was like that of those with blind eyes. (16)
In the expression "of the two blind ones" (*saritoḥ*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*). "Vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) means seeing.

The meaning is that it is utterly non-existent for the two blind ones, as if by the two blind eyes themselves. Because the capacity of being an instrument (*karaṇatā-śakti*) alone is intended to be expressed in the form of a general relation (*sambandha-sāmānya*), the genitive is used [in the word] "blind" (*andhasya*).
Or rather, the gaze does not exist within the eyeballs of the eyes, just as water does not exist within the currents of two rivers. || 16 ||
In that [lake] which was utterly parched, they bathed with great reverence, like Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, afflicted by the heat, bathing in the Gaṅgā. || 17 ||
One should apply this by separating the phrases as follows: "like people afflicted by heat" and "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara [are] as if in the Gaṅgā."
Having engaged for a long time in water-sports and having drunk water resembling milk, those princes themselves departed with delighted minds. (18)
With their minds filled with joy upon reaching the city they had desired. || 18 ||
Then, at the end of the day, as the sun was hanging low,
they reached the city that was to be newly built, which resembled a mountain.
Resembling a naga, as tall as a mountain. || 19 ||
The lake of the blue sky was filled with the lotus-ponds of banners,
and the circle of citizens sang along with the sounds of their distant laughter.
It was pervaded by banners above and by lotus ponds below; there were beautiful, empty reservoirs that resembled the dark blue sky, and there were melodic modulations of vocal intonations.
There they beheld three beautiful,
excellent mansions made of jewels and gold, like the peaks of a great mountain.
In that place, there were two uncreated dwellings; one of them was indeed without walls.
Those three men entered that beautiful, wallless mansion.
There, among those three, they entered the house without walls. || 22 ||
Having entered and quickly sat down, those fair-faced women,
while sporting there, came upon three vessels fashioned from refined gold.
There, two of them turned into shards and one was reduced to powder;
those long-witted ones took that pot in the form of powder. (24)
The state of being a skull-cup, that is, the condition of a severed head. || 24 ||
With those ninety-nine droṇas of that [grain] and one droṇa of the cooked food,
a hundred droṇas were consumed there by those who eat much, leaving nothing remaining.

There, in that vessel, one hundred droṇas minus one—that is, ninety-nine droṇas—of *andhas*, meaning rice in its raw state as unhusked grain (*taṇḍula*), had been cooked (*randhita*); the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the action itself. || 25 ||
Three Brahmins were invited by those princes;
however, two were bodiless, and for one, there was no mouth at all.
O son, a hundred *droṇas* of food were eaten there by the blind man with his mouth;
and what remained after the brahmins had eaten was consumed by the princes.
By these three, the princes attained supreme peace.
For those three princes who were to be born in that city are now dwelling happily today, O son, engaged in the pursuit of hunting. (28)
They attained peace and satisfaction, sporting as they engaged in the activities of the hunt. || 28 ||
This delightful narrative has been told by me to you, O sinless one.
Keep it in your heart, O wise one; you shall become an adept. (29)
One who is *vidagdha* is a wise man (*paṇḍita*). || 29 ||
"O Rāma, this auspicious narrative called 'The Child' was told by the nurse;
and the child attained satisfaction through this auspicious story. (30)
O lotus-eyed Rāma, this story of the boy has been told by me to you concerning the narrative known as the Citta-ākhyāna.

The meaning is: with reference to that discourse on the world-cognition being mere conceptual construction which proceeded immediately after the explanation of the mind, [this verse serves] as an illustration thereof. || 31 ||
This construction of saṃsāra has reached its present state through fierce volitions firmly imagined, like a story told to children.

"Stability" means firmness. Thus, it consists of the nature of mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). By the word "the story told to a child," the cognition produced in the child by that [story] is understood through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*). || 32 ||
O sinless one, this net of conceptual construction, whose very nature is appearance, unfolds itself in the form of the notions of bondage, liberation, and so forth. (33)

He explains that very point clearly with the words "vikalpa" (conceptual construction) and so forth. In the analysis of the compound *vikalpajālikā*—meaning "that in which the conceptual constructions themselves are the nets"—the suffix *ṭāp* produced from the compound does not trigger the application of the rule *pratyayasthātkātpūrvasya* because it follows a *sup* (nominal ending). || 33 ||
Nothing other than mere volition exists here;
by the power of volition, something may appear as something, or as nothing at all, or indeed as anything whatsoever.
With the intention that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) lack existence apart from their being the effects of volitional imagination (*saṃkalpa*), he says:

"merely through volitional imagination" (*saṃkalpamātrāt*). For whatever appears in the form of a conceptual construction, all of that appears by the power of volitional imagination; and that which appears as a conceptual construction is either nothing at all or it becomes something [real]. It follows the cognition of words (*śabdajñānānupātī*).
The meaning is that this is because Patañjali has likewise defined its characteristic as "conceptual construction is empty of a real object" (vastuśūnya). || 34 ||
The heavens, the earth, the wind, the ether, the mountains, the rivers, and the directions—all this is fashioned by mental conception; thus, it is like a dream to the Self.
He elaborates on this very point specifically: "The sky," etc. "Kṣamā" means the earth. || 35 ||
Just as three princes may become rivers in a city, so indeed is the existence of this world according to the construction of one's own conceptualization. (36)
Merely as a mental construction, the flickering ocean, consisting of nothing but water, vibrates everywhere within itself by its own power, like waves in water. (37)
The ocean is restless. || 37 ||
This world, which first arose from the Supreme Self as mere volition,
has expanded through its various activities, just as a day expands through its daily functions.
By activities: by the activities of the sun and by the activities of people. || 38 ||
The entire world is merely the weaving of the web of mental constructs; know that mental construct alone is the object of experience in its playful manifestation.
Abandon even that mere mental construct and become free from conceptualization.
Relying upon this, O Rāma, attain certainty and peace.

And thus, demonstrating that one abides in the nature of the non-conceptual (nirvikalpa) merely through the renunciation of mental constructs (saṃkalpa), he concludes with the verse beginning "saṃkalpa-".
The "play of the mind" refers to the fluctuations such as attachment (rāga) and their objects; [the word "samāhāra"] denotes the collection of these.
He states that the very cause for the renunciation of mental constructs is the firm conviction in the non-conceptual Self, by saying "having resorted to" (āśritya). || 39 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Boy," in the Section on Origination (*utpattiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the Holy Scripture (*ārṣa*). 101.
Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Young Boy," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"By the power of his own volition, the fool falls into delusion, but not the wise man."
Indeed, like a child, one is deluded by the notion of exhaustion regarding that which is inexhaustible.
Herein is described the means for the destruction of the conceptualization of egoism:
the discernment of the group of non-self entities and the eternality of the supreme Self. (1)

"Deluded" means ignorant. "In the imperishable Supreme Self"—that which perishes is "perishable," meaning a perishable self; [the ignorant person acts] from the volition of that [perishable self]. "Child" means a young boy. "Is deluded" means he is afraid. || 1 ||
Śrī Rāma said:

O best of the knowers of Brahman, who was this [world] conceived by whom, and how did its destruction come about, since that which is always truly non-existent has been grasped as the Great Delusion? (2)

When the cause was stated as "due to the volition of destruction," Rāma, desiring to know specifically the agent and the object of that volition, asks: "What is this?"— that is, what is this imagined destruction, and by whom was it imagined,
such that this Self (Ātman) took on, through an unreal cause, the great delusion of the wandering of saṃsāra?

The meaning is this: does the eternal self conceive of itself as a perishable self, or is it the perishable self itself that conceives? Not the first, because it is impossible for it to conceive something that contradicts its own essential nature. Nor the second, because it would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Furthermore, even that perishable self thus conceived—is it insentient (*jaḍa*) or...?

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because it would result in the loss of the identity between consciousness and the self. Nor is the second, because consciousness cannot be an object of volition. || 2 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This destruction called "egoism," brought about by an unreal collection of elements, has been falsely imagined here just as a vampire is imagined by a child. (3)

According to the Vedic scripture, "Whatever they become, that they then become," [the self] is composed of the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) of its former states as a collection of beings such as lions and tigers;
it is a perishable self consisting of the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) with lions, tigers, and so forth, which is itself a confluence of consciousness (*cit*) and unconscious matter (*acit*).
The Supreme Self, conditioned by ignorance, assumes the names of various individual egos; it is perishable and subject to decay. (3)
When the single supreme reality alone exists as everything,
whence comes this thing called "I," and how indeed has it arisen?
One might ask: why should the ego not have the very nature of the Self, and from where would its falsity arise? To this he says: "In the one," etc.; that is, in the all-pervading Whole. || 4 ||
In reality, there is no ego-sense in the non-dual Supreme Self;
it arises from imperfect vision, like [the mirage of] a river on a path in the intense heat of the sun.
The river of the path is the mirage-river. || 5 ||
The great undertaking of the mind-jewel is perceived as saṃsāra;
resting upon itself by means of itself, it vibrates within like water [upon water].

The great undertaking—the creation of the multitude of effects—of the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) characterized by the mind; if one asks, "Is there then independence belonging to the mind alone? he says, "having resorted to the Self" (ātmānamāśritya). [In the phrase] "by water," the word "water" (ambhaḥ) is to be supplied. || 6 ||
Therefore, O Rāma, abandon false vision, which is without support;
take refuge instead in right vision, which has its support in truth and is blissful.
Incorrect vision is error; it is without support and has non-existent objects. Correct vision has a support and has real objects. || 7 ||
With an intellect characterized by discernment and free from the agitation of delusion, investigate now the truth; completely abandon what is false.
Regarding that, he states what the means is there: "By wisdom" (dhiyā) || 8 ||
Having said that you are bound when you are actually unbound, why do you grieve in vain?
How, by what means, and by whom can the infinite reality of the Self be bound?
In this entire reality of Brahman, which is the undivided Great Self, there is no conceptualization of diversity or non-diversity; what is bound, and what is liberated? (10)

The conceptualization of diversity and non-diversity is the delusion of difference and non-difference; the meaning is that when this entire [phenomenal world] has been sublated within the reality of Brahman, only that alone remains. || 10 ||
Even though free from affliction, it appears as if afflicted; moreover, it suffers when a limb is severed.
Yet, no suffering arising from the modifications of difference or non-difference exists within the Self.

Since there is no occasion even for the suffering caused by the cutting or piercing of the body in one who perceives the Self as incapable of being cut or pierced—let alone for any other [suffering]—with this intention he says: "He is unafflicted" (anārta). [The Self] appears thus even when the body is afflicted. 11.
When the body is destroyed, wounded, or wasted away, no injury has come upon the Self;
for when a bellows is burnt, the air within the bellows is not destroyed.
The wind that fills the bellows is called "bhastrāpūra. || 12 ||
Let the body fall or let it rise; what loss has befallen us? When a flower is destroyed, who is ruined? The fragrance takes refuge in the sky. || 13 ||
*Prakṣate* means "is destroyed. *Āmodaḥ* is fragrance. || 13 ||
Let the glories of cold and heat, representing pleasure and pain, fall upon the lotus of my body;
what injury can possibly befall us who are soaring through the sky? (14)

"Uḍḍayanam" means that in which one flies; it is formed with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). Thus, "of those bees (*alīnām*)" refers to those whose flight is in the sky. In the reading "uḍupanālīnām," it means "of those situated in the sky."

The "uḍupa" refers to the moon, Venus, Jupiter, and other such excellent stars; it denotes the characteristics of those [lotuses]—namely, the *nalī* lotuses—and, due to the non-distinction between the letters *ra* and *la*, it also refers to the female consorts of the moon (*uḍupa*), as well as all the stars beginning with Aśvinī. || 14 ||
Let the body fall, or rise up, or go to the ends of space;
what loss can that cause to me, whose nature is entirely distinct from it? (15)
Just as there is between the cloud and the wind, and just as there is between the bee and the lotus,
so too, O Raghava, is the relationship between your body and your own self.

Even if a connection were admitted, there would be no possibility of suffering resulting from it for the untainted Self; with this intention, he says "Just as..."— for the mind and the body belong to Rāma alone, whereas the wind and the clouds belong to the entire world.
The primordial power, which is consciousness, is the inner self and never perishes.

Since the entire world, beginning with the body, is nothing but mind, it is not appropriate to grieve over the destruction of the body and so forth even when the mind exists; how much less so when [the world] is merely the Self? With this intention, he says: "The mind.
The word "body" (śarīra) here denotes its essential nature (svarūpa). The reason for this is: "The primordial power," because the mind is the world.

The primordial causal power is indeed of the nature of consciousness (cidātman), and it stands even above the mind; therefore, the delusion that it can be destroyed is in every way untenable—this is the meaning. || 17 ||
O one of great wisdom, that Self which neither perishes nor departs never perishes at any time; why then do you grieve in vain? (18)
Since the delusion of self-destruction and the like is the very root of all sorrow and other afflictions, he speaks again and again to ward it off:

"Just as the wind goes to the infinite space when the cloud has dispersed, and just as the bee goes to the infinite space when the lotus has withered, so does the Self go to the infinite space upon the dissolution of the body. (19)
For one wandering in this saṃsāra, even the mind does not perish;
yet, without the fire of knowledge, what need is there to speak of the destruction of the self for a living being? (20)

The relationship between the body and the self, which are subject to destruction and non-destruction respectively, is the same as the analogy of the jujube fruit in a bowl and the sequence of the pot and space. || 21 ||

In reality, the soul's residence in another body does not exist at all. Even if it were admitted, there would be no consequence of its destruction upon the destruction of the body; with this intention, he says: "He who... Order is the rule (nyāya); persistence is also the rule.
That [order] is exactly of such a kind. || 21 ||
Just as a jujube fruit falls into one's hand when its husk bursts open,
so does the Self emerge into the sky when the body moves away.
He applies the analogy of the jujube fruit in a pit (*kuṇḍabadaranyāya*) to the present case with the words "the jujube fruit":
the Self is the individual soul (*jīva*), and the sky is the space of latent impressions (*vāsanākāśa*). When [the body] moves, [the soul] perishes. Thus says the Śruti:
"Indeed, it is when deprived of the soul that this [body] dies; the soul does not die. (22)
Just as the space within a jar moves when the jar moves, yet remains in the sky when the jar is gone, so too does this embodied soul remain free from affliction when the body has perished. (23)
He establishes the second [point] with the words "in the jar": non-jarhood is destruction. || 23 ||
For the mental body of living beings is concealed by space and time, repeatedly shrouded by the cloth of death; O rogue, why this lamentation?
Death is dying; by its very nature, one is repeatedly covered by a shroud. What lamentation is improper toward this deceitful and fraudulent mind? This is the meaning. || 24 ||
O mighty-armed one, when concealed by place and time, even a deluded man fears death; yet here, no one perceives it at all.

What, then, is death? To that he says: "In a place" (deśe). The meaning is that death is merely the self's disappearance from the sight of others at the time of the final breath in a place such as a house; the ellipsis is "no one here perceives the destruction of the self. || 25 ||
Therefore, O Rāma, abandon this latent impression (vāsanā) which persists as the false notion "I am," just as the lord of birds abandons his egg when he longs to travel through the sky.
A bird with fully grown wings is no longer a fledgling. [The world] is like a loosened eggshell that serves as its own boundary.
For this mental power is the basis of the desirable and the undesirable; by this very power, through vain delusion, there arises a conceptualization like a dream. (27)
It is bound by attachment and aversion toward the desirable and the undesirable, and it causes the bondage of clinging. || 27 ||
This ignorance is of evil end; it increases for the sake of suffering.
Through its lack of discernment, it expands this world consisting of non-existence.
It is ignorance because it is the manifestation of ignorance. 28.
This deluded [intellect], by its very nature, perceives its own form as if it were empty, like something soiled with frost. (29)
"Stained by frost" means made greyish-white. Thus he says, "of its own nature," because perception is the very essence of the mind. || 29 ||
This expansive, imagined world, which was previously non-existent and now appears as if arisen from a sluggish beginning, has been projected by this [avidyā] like a long dream.
Its very nature has attained the state of agency as mere mental cultivation (bhāvanā) alone; it is the turbid world-appearance within the eye, like the reflection of the sun’s rays in the sky. (31)

Now, since all mental operations are directly perceived, one might ask: why is the state of being the creator of the world not experienced by everyone? To this, he says: "Through creative contemplation" (*bhāvanā*). Its nature is such that agency resides solely in the mere creative contemplation of the form of the world, and not in the creation of anything beyond that.
Because it is not established that false objects are produced apart from perception, that very thing is known as the "world. The meaning is:

just as a turbid eye, impaired by cataracts and the like, acts merely through the manifestation (*vibhāvanā*) of forms such as tufts of hair or nets of flies in the sky, along with the radiance of the disks of the sun, moon, and so forth; it is the same in that case. Manifestation (*vibhāvana*)...
The intended meaning is that it is indeed direct perception itself. || 31 ||
O Rāma, lead her to the realization of her own true nature through inquiry, just as the sun, the lord of the day, [melts] a slab of snow. (32)

For this very reason, since the dissolution of that which is established merely through the contemplation of non-investigated duality is accomplished solely by knowledge born of investigation, he says "dissolution" (layam) to indicate that investigation must be performed. Just as the lord of the day, the sun, through its heating— that is, from its own radiance— effects the dissolution, meaning the destruction, of the nature of the cold stone.
It leads [the soul] in the same way. || 32 ||
Just as the desired goal of the sun, who seeks the absence of cold, is accomplished by its own rising,
so too is the object sought by one who desires the dissolution of the mind achieved through inquiry.
The desired destruction of the mind has been sought. || 33 ||
For ignorance, unawakened and spreading through the difficult terrain of misfortune,
causes Śambara to rain down gold as a manifestation of various magical illusions.
Fearing that even when one mind has perished, there might still be the possibility of rebirth through the bondage of the mind and its causes due to ignorance (*avidyā*), he says:

"Ignorance" (*avidyā*). For indeed, because the cloud-bank of ignorance—belonging to those who are unawakened and have not realized the true nature of the Self (*ātmatattva*)—exists, at that very moment, like the demon Śambara, it manifests as unreal gold in the form of various illusory displays (*indrajāla*).
The meaning is that she does not rain down because she is then not fully awakened, owing to her lack of manifest form. || 34 ||
The mind alone is fully capable of performing this act of its own destruction;
for the mind dances the drama known as "the slaying of the self. (35)

And thus, when the mind itself has been dancing for a long time in the form of the world, it brings about its own destruction through a transformation consisting of knowledge; this is the established conclusion. He states this by saying: "the act of its own destruction.
Having observed the drama called "the slaughter of the self"—that is, its own annihilation—as a composition written by itself.
He dances. || 35 ||
The mind perceives itself solely for its own destruction;
for the one of evil intellect does not realize that destruction is at hand. (36)
By his own mere volition, he swiftly accomplishes this for those who perceive their own destruction; no affliction is required here. (37)

For the discerning ones who perceive their own destruction and seek the means for the dissolution of the mind, this method for the dissolution of the mind accomplishes it swiftly by the mind itself through mere volition. || 37 ||
Having abandoned the portion of its own volitions and conceptualizations, the mind— when endowed with discernment— casts off its expansive form and effects the realization of the Self.

The mind, refined and purified by discernment, having abandoned its former portion of volitions and conceptual constructions, undergoes a transformation into the expansive form of Brahman— vast and all-pervading— which consists of the realization of the Self and takes the nature of the mental modification that is the direct perception of one's own essence. || 38 ||
The destruction of the mind is a great attainment; indeed, it is the dawning of the great transcendence.
Therefore, apply yourself to the destruction of the mind, and not to the impetuous flow of the mind.

Great attainment (*mahodaya*) is the acquisition of the supreme human goal; great eradication (*mahoccheda*) is the eradication of all suffering; and "in speed" (*jave*) refers to external activity. || 39 ||
In this forest, where dense thickets of trees are pleasure and pain and the great serpent is the treacherous God of Death,
the Lord alone is the master of all this which is devoid of discernment.
O fortunate one, the mind is the sole cause of great calamity. || 40 ||

Showing the onset of misfortune that results from neglecting what has already been taught, he concludes with the words "avirala-": "In this entire, inexhaustible [cycle] characterized by saṃsāra, wherein there are dense, thick groves of trees consisting of pleasure and pain, and wherein Death— the great serpent— is formidable."
In the forest of sword-leaves, it is this very mind, devoid of discernment, that is the master and the cause of insufferable suffering; such is the meaning. || 40 ||
When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites,
and the assembly, having offered their salutations, departed to bathe.
At the waning of the night, he arrived together with the rays of the sun. || 41 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Giving of Instruction," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. 102.
Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Instruction," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The mind has arisen from the Supreme, like a wave from the ocean.
Having attained expansion, it spreads this world here and there. || 1 ||
Whatever course of conduct leads to the uselessness of the undiscriminating mind, all of that is here elaborated for the sake of discrimination by those seeking liberation. (1)
He shows that the arising of the mind from another is indeed for the sake of what is not beneficial—namely, "from another" (parasmāt) || 1 ||
It quickly makes the short long, and brings the long to a state of being dwarfed; it likewise reduces another part to its own state, and similarly brings its own state to that of another. (2)

He demonstrates the mind’s capacity for conceptualizing things that contradict their actual nature with the passage beginning with "short" (*hrasvam*). By imagining that a finger or similar object held near the eye can cover the vastly extended solar disc, it makes the [finger] appear long; and [conversely], it makes the long [object] appear short.

The solar orb and so forth [attain] dwarfishness and shortness. Thus, he says "svatām" (its own state) to show that it is the mind alone that performs even the conceptualization of an exchange of essential natures between the self and the non-self. || 2 ||
Even that which is merely the size of a span, by the very power of meditating upon it as a real object, quickly becomes— as if spontaneously accomplished— resplendent like the king of mountains.
As if she were herself endowed with her own physical form through meditative cultivation and mental construction. || 3 ||
The mind, having gained a foothold and surged forth from the supreme state,
creates and dissolves the cycles of worldly existence in a mere moment.

To the question, "From where does it derive such power?", he says: "Having attained its foundation" (labdhapratiṣṭham). The meaning is that it has acquired its existence by being augmented with diverse powers through the reality of Brahman (brahmasattā). || 4 ||
Whatever is seen here—this world, both stationary and moving, all of it enriched with every variety—has come forth from the mind. (5)
Agitated by the powers of place, time, action, and substance,
the mind passes from one state to another due to its fickleness, like an actor.
From one state to another state—that is, from the form of one object to the form of another object—and the various types of transitory emotions (saṃcāribhāva) well-known in the *Nāṭyaśāstra*. || 6 ||
It quickly leads to existence that which was non-existent, or it fully brings to existence that which already exists;
and having been so conditioned, it takes up exactly such pleasures and pains as those. (7)
When the mind, being fickle by nature, takes hold of whatever it has acquired,
then the aggregate of the hands, feet, and other limbs exerts itself accordingly. (221.8)

When the flickering mind, having attained an object presented by karma that is to be experienced, takes hold of it— whether as favorable or unfavorable— by whatever mode of conceptualization, then the aggregate of hands, feet, and so forth proceeds accordingly toward either grasping or abandoning; such is the nature of the mind.
This means that [the Lord] possesses absolute sovereignty over all worldly transactions. || 8 ||
Then that very same action, whether its fruit is concentrated in the mind or not, yields its result in an instant, just as a creeper watered at the right time yields its corresponding fruit.
That activity which brings about objects of enjoyment is [perceived] by the mind as pleasure and pain, whether they be fruit or non-fruit, being concentrated and imagined. || 9 ||
Just as a child in a house makes a series of variegated toys out of mud,
so too, O Rāma, does the mind create the world through its conceptual constructions.
From a lump of moist clay from the mud. || 10 ||
Therefore, regarding these fragments of the mud of the playthings of all people, what indeed is this that is imagined as being established among the objects in the world? (11)

He says that in this world, which is a mere mental construction, not even a single form can be real— thus, "The mind. For this reason, whatever form is conceived as established and true among all objects— which are but a trace of mud consisting of the human bodies and so forth that serve as the playground of the mind for all people— what indeed is that?
The meaning is that it would be nothing at all. || 11 ||
Just as time, acting as the seasonal agent, causes the various forms of a tree to change,
so too does the mind cause these very objects to appear as if they were otherwise.

The "season-maker" (*ṛtukara*) is that which effects the divisions of spring and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of forms" (*rūpāṇām*), although there is a prohibition [against such a compound] by the rule *pūraṇaguṇa* (Pāṇini 2.2.11), a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is nonetheless formed either because it is Vedic (*cchāndasa*), or because in that context only a *kṛt*-derivative or a nominal stem (*anyaya*) is understood through its association with the preceding and following terms. || 12 ||
In a daydream, in a dream, and in the fabrications of one's imagination, even a multitude of leagues becomes as small as a cow’s footprint within the playful activities of the mind. (13)
He demonstrates that the power of the mind to bring about the impossible is indeed well-known, by means of the verse beginning with "In a mental wish" (manorathe).
The meaning is that even a multitude, a collection, of *yojanas* is as insignificant as the hoofprint of a cow. || 13 ||
The mind makes an eon appear as a moment and brings a moment to the state of an eon;
therefore, the wise know that the sequence of space and time is dependent upon it.
Therefore, the meaning is that all wise people know that the entire sequence of space and time is dependent upon that [mind] and subordinate to the mind. || 14 ||

Due to the intensity or mildness of their spiritual urgency, due to the distinction between many or few [practitioners], and due to delay over a long period—yet not because of incapacity versus capacity. (15)

[Objection: If the mind is indeed capable of creating everything, then why is it that we currently lack the power for universal creation? To this, he replies with the word "intense" (*tīvra*). Intensity occurs when the quality of *rajas* predominates, whereas dullness occurs when *tamas* predominates; thus, there is a difference in the degree of momentum (*saṃvega*). Furthermore, through the accumulation of food, there is increase [in capacity], and through its depletion, there is decrease.

The distinction [between the powers] arises from the delay caused by various acts such as instruction that are conducive to the creation of specific objects, and from the resulting incapacity for creation;
thus, one must supply the ellipsis and connect the thought: "we are not able to negate the mind's actual power to create all things.
15. Delusion, agitation, misfortune, and the movement between space and time...
These arise from the mind, just as sprouts emerge from a tree. || 16 ||
For this very reason, he states that even the occurrence of delusion and so forth arises [from this], beginning with the words "vyāmoha... (verse 16).
Just as the ocean is nothing but water, and fire is nothing but heat,
so too this worldly existence with its manifold agitation is nothing but the mind.
Because the effect is not different from its cause, he says that everything is indeed mind-only: "It is only water.
The word "vā" is for the purpose of completing the meter. || 17 ||
Whatever has come into the range of cognition— accompanied by agent, object, and instrument,
and enriched with the seer, the seeing, and the seen— all that is indeed only the mind.

The object of thought (*cetya*) consists of the entities whose nature is the experiencer, the experienced, and the act of experiencing (the word *bhoktṛ* is not read in some versions). Thus, the meaning is that even the ninefold cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is nothing but the mind itself. || 18 ||

The mind itself is perceived as having arrived at its own various manifestations— worlds, universes, and forest depths— just as the shining form [of a person] is perceived through armlets, crowns, and bracelets.
Just as people abandon gold by perceiving it as mere brass, [so too should one abandon worldly things]. 19.

Showing the means by which it is discerned that "everything is indeed mind," he concludes with the word "mind": just as gold is [discerned] by those who examine the essence of gold through armlets, crowns, ornaments, bracelets, and so forth.

Just as pure gold can be identified in reality only by one whose mind is fixed upon the gold alone, examining it while setting aside its various imagined forms such as bracelets and the like— which shine with diverse appearances—
it cannot be so identified by one whose intellect is deluded by the variety of arrangements such as armlets; likewise, it is for the discerning person in this world.

The meaning is that the worlds contained within that [mind], as well as all things such as the forests and groves contained therein, are perceived as being nothing other than the mind itself—having arrived of its own accord through its own various manifestations and diversities—as "mind-only" (cittamātra), and not as any entity distinct from the mind; this is the reality (tattva) that is clearly discerned. || 19 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Mind," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* (Section on Origination) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (sage-authored) tradition.
Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Mind," in the Utapatti-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In this regard, listen as I relate to you this most excellent account.
The splendor of this worldly illusion exists here entirely dependent upon the mind.
Here, at the beginning of the narrative concerning Lavaṇa, the setting of the king’s assembly hall is described;
therein, the presence of magicians and the resulting state of wonder are recounted. (1)
Vṛttānta means a narrative or account. || 1 ||
On this surface of the earth, there is a great and prosperous kingdom named Uttarāpāṇḍava, filled with various forests. (2)
Where ascetics rest in dense, deep, and unbroken forests,
and where the groves and cities possess vine-swinging arbors inhabited by Vidyādharīs.
The ascetics have taken rest in his forests, which are dense and uninterrupted, and for that very reason profound. By this, the absence of disturbances such as tigers and thieves is indicated. (3)
The mountain is tawny with masses of lotus filaments stirred by the wind;
it is adorned with forest garlands and crest-ornaments consisting of shimmering clusters of flowers. || 4 ||
Its jungles were bordered by thickets of *karañja* flower-clusters;
villages were hidden by date palms, and the sky resounded with the humming of bees.
"Bordering jungles" refers to forests situated at the outskirts of villages; those are places where villages are screened or hidden by date-palm trees. (5)
Tawny with rows of *ekapiṅga* rocks and fields of ripening rice, it is adorned by wild forests resounding with the unrestrained cries of peacocks. (6)
The *ekapiṅga* stones are a specific kind of gemstone of an excellent reddish-brown color; the fields of ripened rice, resembling rows of those stones, are likewise reddish-brown (*piṅgala*). || 6 ||
Its golden forests resounded with the frantic cries of cranes,
and it was adorned with earrings of mountain villages dark as tamāla and pāṭalī trees.
The banks of the river were crimsoned by *pāribhadra* trees in full bloom, while a cacophony was produced by the warbling of flocks of various birds.
The *pāribhadra* trees are in bloom without sleep, and the *nimba* trees are reddened by them.
The god of love was captivated by the young maidens in the rice fields who were singing sweetly;
the clouds of flowers were shaken down by the wind moving through the swaying blossoms and fruits.
Where clouds in the form of flowers were shaken by the wind blowing to cause the falling of blossoms whose stalks had become loosened.
With siddhas, cāraṇas, and bards emerging from his palace,
he was created as if having been brought forth from heaven itself, fashioned from pure loveliness.

The meaning is that his celestial beauty—adorned by perfected beings (*siddhas*), celestial musicians (*cāraṇas*), and bards, and having emerged from the chambers of Mount Meru—was as if fashioned by bringing the splendor of heaven down to earth. || 10 ||
It was a pavilion formed by groves of plantain trees and singing kinnaras and gandharvas; it was white with flowering gardens, stirred by the sound of gentle breezes.
With gentle breezes, abounding in flowers, and situated in excellent groves, there is a region named Uttarāpāṇḍava; such is its connection with what precedes. (11)
There dwelt a king named Lavaṇa, supremely righteous,
born of the lineage of Hariścandra, like a sun upon the earth.
He descended to the earth like the sun. || 12 ||
There the mountain peaks, their circular shoulders white with the flowers of fame serving as crest-ornaments, shine resplendent like tossed pearl necklaces. (13)
By ornaments characterized by flowers, that is, by floral head-ornaments or by their pollen. || 13 ||
Having completely severed the entire circle of his enemies with fragments of his sword,
he causes fever to seize the world of his foes merely by being remembered.

The world of enemies—that is, his circle of servants—was such that the principal groups of adversaries were completely cut down by his swords, so as to be reduced to mere fragments; he was one whose enemies were thus utterly destroyed. || 14 ||
Whose conduct—characterized by noble undertakings and the protection of the noble world—people will long remember, just as they do that of Hari. (15)
The conduct of a protector consists in the preservation and protection of the noble world and of righteous people. || 15 ||
Upon the peaks of the king of mountains, in the celestial abodes of the gods, the songs of his virtues are sung by the Apsarases with the thrill of bristling hair.
The songs of his virtues, sung by the celestial beauties and long heard by the world-protectors,
are echoed by the swans of Brahmā through their own constant practice.

The compositions consisting of songs of praise for his virtues, sung by the celestial nymphs who are beautiful as the heavens, are echoed by the swans of Brahmā; that is to say, they are imitated by their resonant sounds. || 17 ||
O Rāma, even in dreams, no action characterized by the fault of wretchedness has ever been seen or heard of in one whose noble genius is so extraordinary.
"Common" means shared with other kings. || 18 ||
He who does not know crookedness, by whom audacity has never been seen, and by whom nobility is maintained like a rosary of beads by Brahmā; (19)
Crookedness is dishonesty; audacity is lack of discipline; if the reading is *gṛdhnutā*, it refers to the longing for another's property. || 19 ||
When the lord of the day had reached the eighth part of the sky,
he once sat upon his throne in the assembly hall.
"An eighth part" means an eighth portion; that is to say, two muhūrtas. || 20 ||
While the king sat there comfortably like the moon in the sky,
the armies of the vassal lords entered with great haste.
Then, while the beloved women were singing and the kings were seated comfortably,
the delightful sound of the lute and the flute captivated the mind.
Among kings and neighboring vassals. || 22 ||
While the king rested— his hand graced by beautiful fly-whisks, full of graceful charm— the circle of ministers, resembling the preceptors of the gods and asuras, was also at ease.
While the playful women were fanning [him] playfully, Jupiter and Venus—the teachers of the gods and asuras—were like him. (23)
When the royal affairs had been presented and entered into by the ministers, and when the reports of the country were recounted by the skillful and eloquent counselors; || 24 ||
While the meritorious Itihāsa was being recited from the book, and while the bards stood bowed before him chanting auspicious hymns; (25)
A certain magician entered that assembly with arrogance, like a rain-cloud entering the earth with a downpour that excites agitation. || 26 ||

He was full of pride, endowed with the pomp of dress, ornaments, and titles appropriate for a magician; he was one in whom the fury of lightning flashes and the like had been aroused by the approaching rain.
Having approached the feet of the protector of the earth, whose shoulders were as noble as a mountain peak, he bowed down to him, just as a tree laden with fruit bows toward a lovely mountain.
He whose noble neck and throat are like a mountain peak, the crest of a crown, and a summit;
and who is like a fruit-bearing tree laden with the weight of its fruit. || 27 ||

He entered before the king— whose form was like that of a tree possessing deep shade, lofty shoulders, laden with fruit, and radiant with flowers— just as a monkey might enter before the top of a tree.
The monkey is an appropriate illustration for one who performs improper and wicked deeds. || 28 ||
Fickle and greedy for riches, he spoke with his neck outstretched to the king—who was like a lotus—as a bee speaks to a lotus, the wind being the fragrance and pleasure of wealth. (29)
O Lord, while remaining seated upon your throne, behold for a moment this single, wondrous display of harshness here on earth, like the moon in the sky gazing down upon the world.
A harsh mockery, a false and curious sport. || 30 ||
Having said this, he whirled his peacock-feather whisk, which caused confusion and served as the seed for various arrangements, like the Māyā of the Supreme Self.
A *picchikā* is a bundle of peacock feathers. || 31 ||
The protector of the earth beheld her, resplendent with a cloud of radiant dust,
just as Śakra, seated in his celestial chariot, beholds the vine of his own bow.
With masses of radiant particles of various beautiful colors.
At that moment, a vassal of Sindh entered the assembly hall,
just as a cloud enters the path of the sky filled with a multitude of stars. (222.33)
The horse-keeper was a feudatory of Saindhava. || 33 ||
And that gentle horse, possessed of supreme speed, followed him just as Uccaiḥśravas follows the gratified Śakra when he is intent upon the world of the gods.
Taking that horse, he spoke to the king, just as the Ocean of Milk, possessing Uccaiḥśravas, spoke to the Lord of the Maruts. || 35 ||
He is the horse-herder. || 35 ||
O Lord of the Earth, this jewel among horses is like Uccaiḥśravas;
by its habit of soaring with speed, it is as if the Wind-god himself were incarnate.
"Behold the jewel among horses"—this is the ellipsis. "Speed," and so forth, connects with what follows. (36)
"O Lord, this horse has been sent to you by our master;
for the auspicious splendor of an object truly shines when offered to the great. (37)
Because of the offering to the great; that is, because of giving to those who are worthy—[in some places, "to the great" is read erroneously as "to the great worthy ones"]. || 37 ||
When he had spoken thus, the magician replied, like a cātaka bird crying out to a rain-cloud once the thundering has subsided. (38)
He spoke to the king. || 38 ||
O Lord, mount this excellent horse and wander the world, just as the sun traverses the earth which possesses no small splendor bestowed by its own radiance. (39)
That [city] in which there was abundant splendor, fortune, and beauty produced by its own majesty, heroism, and heat. || 39 ||
The king looked at the horse and spoke to him,
like a peacock with outspread tail feathers responding to a cloud thundering with a roar.
Thus addressed by him, the king said: "He who makes the head well up (suṣṭhu ut) is a *sūtkara*, one who produces a particular sound. || 40 ||
Then the king, whose form was like a painting, gazed at the horse with an unblinking gaze, appearing as if he were fixed in a work of art.

"Rendered by the hand of a painter, fixed in a painting, motionless, and resembling that [original]—this and the like are restatements of matters established through the common consensus of the assembly. As for what is observed through the King’s own perception, the King himself will explain it later."
Having gazed for a moment, he remained seated upon his throne with his eyes closed;
unperturbed by the sight, he was like the ocean with its fish and mountains when the sun has set.

Just as the ocean—called *karava* because it roars (*karoti*) with its sound when agitated by the sight of Agastya intent upon drinking it—remained motionless, paralyzed by fear along with the mountains and fish within it; so too [is he]. However, in the reading where "the mountains and fish of the agitated ocean" (*ākṣubdhasamudrādimīnakaiḥ*) is taken as a compound:
It should be explained as: "Whose sound is it, like the roar of water, that has been silenced? (42)
For two muhūrtas he remained as if absorbed in meditation within himself,
like a sage free from passion, agitated yet established in supreme bliss.
"Agitated" means internally stirred up by external perception; that is to say, devoid of external perception. || 43 ||
"He was not awakened by anyone, for he is powerful, having been conquered by his own majesty;
moreover, with his intellect, he is contemplating some further thought. (44)
By whom the powerful and mighty [enemies] were conquered through his own majesty; this is an adjective containing a reason (hetugarbha). 44.
There, only the white chowries remained motionless;
for the female chowrie-bearers were like nights in which the rays of the moon have been frozen still.
Those members of the assembly, filled with wonder, stood motionless,
like lotuses whose filaments and petals have become rigid from being submerged in mud.
Those made of clay are fashioned from mud. || 46 ||
The clamor of the people in the assembly hall gradually subsided,
like the thundering of clouds in the sky at the end of the rainy season.
This [world] belongs to the ocean; it is "of the ocean. || 47 ||
Immersed in an ocean of doubt, the excellent ministers fell into anxiety,
just as the immortals did when the wielder of the mace (Balarāma) was distressed like the king of the asuras.
In that battle, which is a conflict together with the asuras. || 48 ||
While the king stood with eyes motionless, that multitude remained paralyzed with wonder, dejected by fear and delusion.
It bears the splendor of a forest of lotuses in bud. || 49 ||
By that assembly of people—that is, by the multitude of persons—with wide-spread and extensive astonishment, which was rendered dejected and crooked—meaning, deprived of all enthusiasm. || 49 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Delusion of the King," in the *Indrajālopākhyāna* (The Narrative of the Magic Show) within the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* (Section on Origination) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki;
and thus ends the [chapter] titled "The Delusion of the King" in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The one hundred and fourth canto, titled "Nāma."
The one hundred and fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, after two muhūrtas, the lord of the earth regained consciousness.
Like a supreme lotus released from the waters of the rainy season. || 1 ||

The commencement of the inquiry by the members of the assembly regarding the king—who was free from delusion and possessed a healthy heart—is undertaken for the sake of investigating the cause of that [apparent] delusion. (1)
In the rainy season, by means of the rainwater belonging to the monsoon.
Awakened from his seat, he— adorned with armlets and crest-jewels— caused the earth to tremble,
like a mountain whose peaks encompass the entire expanse of a forest during an earthquake.
He caused his own body to tremble; this is understood from the sense of the passage. || 2 ||
Then he awoke, trembling upon his seat,
like Mount Śaṅkara when the elephant of the netherworld is agitated.
When the world-supporting elephant of the quarters, the subterranean beast, was agitated and shaken, Mount Kailāsa, the mountain of Śaṅkara,
held up that king as he was falling with its arms,
just as the principal mountain ranges hold up Mount Meru when it is tossed about at the time of universal dissolution.
The principal mountain ranges, such as Mandara and others, are the supporting mountains. || 4 ||
Supported by those walking before him, the king, his mind deeply agitated, bore the splendor of the moon disturbed by waves as it enters a forest. || 5 ||

By means of the secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*), "indoḥ" refers to the ocean swollen by the rising of the moon; "vanamāḥ" are the glories (*śriyaḥ*) or beauties that measure (*minvanti*), that is, compare themselves to, the forest-water [of that ocean]. Thus, she bore the splendor of the glories. The reading "vapuṣā śriyaḥ" is clear. || 5 ||
What place is this? Whose assembly is this? the king pondered slowly, like a bee trapped within the heart of a lotus sinking beneath the water. (6)
He uttered an indistinct sound.
Then the assembly spoke respectfully to the god, "What is this?",
like a lotus plant with humming bees upon it seeing the sun eclipsed by Rāhu.

By the word *sabhā*, people are meant. Here, the lotus-pond’s speaking toward the sun is a metaphorical conceit (*autprekṣika*); the qualifying phrase "with humming bees" serves as the basis for establishing that conceit. (7)
Then the ministers who were his attendants questioned him,
just as the gods questioned Mārkaṇḍeya when he was terrified by the onset of the dissolution of the world.
O Lord, while you are situated thus, we are utterly distressed;
for delusions, though causeless, shatter even that which is indivisible—the mind.
The delusions—meaning the cognitions of error—shatter and agitate the mind with fear, despondency, and so forth, even without an external cause; this is the meaning. || 9 ||
In which conceptual constructions—like sensual enjoyments that are pleasant at first sight but bitter in their ultimate consequence—is your mind agitated? (10)
For what reason was your mind agitated by passion and other such defilements toward enjoyments, as is the case with ordinary worldlings?
The meaning is that it was utterly deluded. || 10 ||
Why does your mind, which has become pure and cooled by constant discourse on noble conduct, sink into these agitations? (11)
It is cooling through the cultivation of discourses and discussions on discernment; [it is likewise so] amidst agitations and fears. || 11 ||
The mind, which has empty objects and is mangled and shattered amidst worldly activities, takes on delusion; it does not manifest the expansion of greatness.

What kind of mind, then, is fit for delusion? To this they say: "having a trivial object" (*tucchālambana*). Since its objective support is a trivial thing, therefore, when the object is torn asunder, it is as if torn asunder; when it is shattered, it is as if shattered; thus it takes on delusion amidst worldly activities—this is the meaning. [Such a mind] is manifested by greatness (*mahattva*) and refined by discernment (*viveka*).
For whatever state of mind has arisen in him through constant practice, that very state follows him even when he is intoxicated by the pride of his body. (13)

Intoxicated by bodily conceit—that is, by the identification with the body—in those states where discrimination has not been touched, this mind runs only toward whatever mental modification (vṛtti) has arisen regarding objects such as wife and children. || 13 ||
For even your mind, O wise one—though it has a substantial object, is steadfast, awakened, and possessed of virtue—appears strangely as if it were severed. (14)
But they say that your mind is not like that—“not base,” [they say]. || 14 ||
For the mind that has not practiced discernment follows the influence of place and time; it falls under the power of mantras and medicinal herbs, but not one whose conduct is noble.
How could there be any tearing or withering for one who possesses constant discernment?
Like a whirlwind, it shakes the expansive mind, yet leaves the Mountain of the Wise unshaken.
Spread out and expanded by discernment; the mountain of the wise, Meru. || 16 ||
Thus, the splendor of the king, who had swallowed his newborn son,
adorned his face just as fullness adorns the moon at the end of the month.
At the end of the month, on the full moon day, he was swallowed up by the multitude of his kinsmen who had been born [to him], and comforted by their favorable words. || 17 ||
With his eyes opened, the king with his gentle face shone like the month of Mādhava when the winter season has passed and a profusion of blossoming flowers appears.
Himartu is the cold season; Mādhava is spring. || 18 ||
Then, with his face devoid of memory due to extreme agitation, wonder,
and distress, he appeared like the moon in the sky when its death is imminent upon seeing Rāhu.

Then, perceiving the moon—whose death was imminent and whose setting was near—to be like a magician’s Rāhu, he became distressed by extreme agitation, fear, and wonder; his face was marked by recollection, deep reflection, and the reassembling of all preceding and subsequent events. Thus he was.
He shone, for death was near, ready to swallow him. || 19 ||
