Beholding the sorcery, he then spoke as if laughing, like Takṣaka in the form of a serpent upon seeing a predatory beast. (20)
The tawny mongoose; Takṣaka, the king of the Nāgas, disguised in the form of a serpent, concealed by the appearance of a small snake. || 20 ||
O fool, what has been done by you with this mass of matted locks, that the ocean, which was motionless and serene, has suddenly returned to its placidity? (21)
O fool, O you who act without reflection! By the word "net," his own mind—resembling a net made of illusion and snares like that of Jaṭālu—is figuratively expressed. (21)
How wondrous are the hundreds of powers inherent in the objects of the Divine! For by these very powers, even my mind, though possessed of great strength, has been cast into delusion.
The word "variegated" (citram) is syntactically connected with the word "placed" (niveśitam). || 22 ||
Where are we, who have understood the state of the world’s inevitable end;
and where are these widespread, inherent calamities that bring delusion to the mind? (23)

Acting out his very bewilderment, he says: "Where? Those who know the "word of the final conclusion" (kṛtāntapada)—that is, the secret of the established doctrine—are the perceivers of the "turns of the world," meaning all worldly conventions well-known to the people.
The "calamities" (āpadaḥ) are those currently under discussion, which have been experienced at this present time. || 23 ||
Even the mind of the wise, though it has practiced great knowledge, may at times remain within the body and momentarily succumb to delusion. (24)
Even the mind that has practiced great wisdom may at times remain within the body; though it exists [in its true state], it still assumes the delusion of dreams and magical illusions. (24)
"O members of the assembly, listen to this wondrous account of what was displayed here for a moment by my magician. (25)
The magic of Śambara is "śāmbarī"; one who possesses that is a "śāmbarika," by him [it was performed]. || 25 ||
I have observed many shifting states of affairs within this world;
for a moment, I was like the lotus-born Brahmā when his creation was destroyed by Śakra.

The analysis of the compound is: *adhvasta-śakra-sṛṣṭiḥ* (one by whom Śakra’s creation was destroyed). It is said that in ancient times, Bali, having encountered Śakra who was without allies, seized him and desired to carry him off; however, Śakra, having created his own army through illusion, bewildered Bali with an illusory bond. Then, Bali, being propitiated by hymns of praise for the sake of releasing himself from that bond—

The meaning is as follows: Brahmā, having arrived there, proceeded to destroy Śakra’s creation; yet, at the request of Śakra, he did not destroy Śakra’s creation and beheld that marvel of his Māyā for only a moment. || 26 ||
Having spoken thus, while the members of the assembly looked up with wide-eyed curiosity, the king, as if smiling,
began to describe the wondrous event.
p. 376) 223 The King said:
In this world, which is crowded with various objects,
This region, abounding in wealth, exists upon this earth which is crowded with lakes, rivers, cities, and mountains, and where the great peaks and oceans mingle. || 28 ||
By way of an introduction to what is about to be said, he first restates the existence of his own country, which is included within the earth well-known to all people, with the word "here" (iha).
Although the term "mountains" (parvata) would already include the great peaks (kulaśikharin), they are mentioned again for emphasis.

It is for the sake of establishing preeminence according to the logic of the "Brahmin-wanderer" (brāhmaṇaparivrājaka). It is called *saṃkara* because it is mixed (*saṃkīryate*). The suffix *śa* is applied to the root *kṛ* in the sense of the object by virtue of the rule *kṛñaḥ śa ca*, due to the diversity of usage (*bāhulaka*). However, if the reading is *saṃkaṭāyām*, the meaning is "in that which is difficult to traverse. Thus [ends] the section from the holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, in the *Deva-mokṣopadeśa*.
The one hundred and fifth canto, titled "The Awakening of the King," within the narrative of Indrajāla. || 105 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Enlightenment of the King," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and sixth canto.
The King said:
"This land, indeed, is endowed with various forests and rivers."
He was like a younger brother born of the same womb as this entire circle of the earth. || 1 ||
In this [chapter], the marriage of one who was carried away by a horse to the forest and led to a hamlet (pakkaṇa) by a Caṇḍāla maiden according to an agreement is described. (1)
The word *saha* has the sense of "identical" (*samāna*). Thus, "uterine brother" (*sahodara*) means one who is as if born from the same womb. || 1 ||
And here I am, the king, conducting myself according to the wishes of the citizens, seated in the midst of this assembly like Indra in heaven. (2)
Meanwhile, this certain conjurer has arrived from afar;
like Maya himself, he has risen up from the subterranean realm as a master of illusion.
The particle *yāvat* is used here in the sense of manifestation (*prākāśye*), and not as a suffix of the *vatup* type; the meaning is "he has come before one's very eyes" (*pratyakṣam*). || 3 ||
By this, the peacock-feather whisk, intensified by its splendor, was whirled here today like a streak of Indra’s bow by the clouds driven by the winds at the end of an eon.
*bhramitā* [is derived from] *bhrami* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*); there is shortening of the vowel for roots marked with *mit*. (Pāṇini 6.4.92)
Beholding this restless mare standing before me, I,
alone and with a bewildered mind, mounted her back.
"Alone" means without a companion. || 5 ||
Then, as Puṣkarāvartaka [stirs] the ocean agitated at the time of dissolution,
I likewise mounted my horse and set out after him as he was moving.

The syntactical connection is as follows: "Just as the king of clouds, Puṣkarāvartaka, moved while mounted upon a mountain that was agitated by the dissolution of the world and shaken by the force of portents, so too have I moved. (6)
I set out alone for the hunt with extreme speed,
like the wave of the ocean at the end of an aeon rushing toward the desolate waste.
"Urvarām" means land rich in all kinds of crops. "Nirbharteḥ" means of one who possesses abundance; that is to say, of one who has increased [in power].
"Kallolaḥ" means a large wave. || 7 ||
By that horse, flickering like the wind, I was carried far away,
just as an ignorant person is led astray by a deluded mind rendered insensible through the practice of yoga.

The reading *mugdhaḥ svamanasā* is clear. Regarding the reading *mugdhasya manasā*, it means "by the mind of one who is deluded"—that is, by one rendered dull through the habitual enjoyment of objects that are charming only at first sight.
This is an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound) used in accordance with Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). || 8 ||
It was a mind devoid of anything, as utterly empty as the heart of a woman;
it was as terrifying as the abode of the world when consumed by the fire of universal dissolution.
For the ascetic who possesses nothing, the universe—the abode of the world—is like the mind: empty and devoid of objects; whether full or light, it is the same. || 9 ||
Having reached this vast, boundless forest, which is devoid of salt, frost, trees, and water, my mounts are exhausted. (10)
An alkaline mist with an unbearable cold. || 10 ||
It was like a second sky, like a second ocean,
like a fifth sea that had completely dried up, a hollow void.
Beyond the ocean of sweet water lies the eighth sea, resembling the moat previously described as encircling the earth;
it is situated within Jambūdvīpa on all four sides, corresponding to the fifth ocean among the four seas well-known there.
His mind was as expansive as that of a wise man, yet as impetuous with wrath as that of a fool;
it was untouched by the company of people and had not seen the sprouts of grass.

To the wise man who knows reality, it is like the mind expanded in the form of Brahman—vast and indivisible; but to the fool, it is like anger (the word *ruṣā* here is in the feminine accusative), meaning as difficult to traverse and treacherous as wrath—or, according to another reading, as "an object" (*viṣayam*). || 12 ||
Having reached this forest, my mind has fallen into despondency,
like a woman who, having encountered poverty, finds herself without food, fruit, or kinsmen.

"Having fallen into poverty," meaning having reached it and remaining there; the word "like a woman" (*lalanā*) is to be understood as "remaining like a woman. Alternatively, the connection is with the distant word "by me who am sinking" (*sīdatā mayā*). || 13 ||
With my face submerged in the mirage-water of the shimmering desert sands,
that day passed for me in exhaustion until the setting of the sun.
Wherein the quarters of the sky were drenched and inundated by the waters of the mirage before one's eyes. || 14 ||
That forest was traversed by me with great difficulty and exhaustion,
like the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is traversed by one seeking solitude, appearing empty at its core.
Having passed through this by means of it, I have gradually reached the Jangala forest,
like the sun whose horses are exhausted reaching the peak of the sunset mountain with the illusion of a vacant sky.

By means of this horse—that is, by traveling through space due to the delusion of emptiness—the connection with the subsequent phrase "where they flash forth" is established for the verb "he reached. || 16 ||
In those regions abounding with Jambu and Kadamba trees, where birds warble sweetly in the groves like kinsmen to travelers, (17)
Wherein rows of young grass-tips appear sparse upon the ground,
like the stirrings of joy within the heart of a crooked man who possesses only meager wealth.
By the wealth of hardship—that is, by wealth acquired through unrighteousness—of the crooked person, that is, the deceitful man. || 18 ||
For that [pleasure] derived from former forest-dwelling brings some small measure of happiness;
indeed, among living beings, illness is better than death, which is absolute suffering. (19)
There, I reached the ground of Jambīrakhaṇḍa,
just as Mārkaṇḍeya did upon the Lord of Mountains after wandering through the single ocean.
The king of mountains, the best of trees, the banyan tree presided over by Viṣṇu.
There, scorched by the heat, I took hold of a creeper entwined with the mountain's slopes, like a dark blue mass of clouds clinging to a mountain tormented by the sun.
"Seized" means grasped for the purpose of abandoning the horse. || 21 ||
While I was hanging down from this [branch], that horse galloped away, just as the accumulation of evil deeds departs from a man who has taken hold of the Gaṅgā. || 22 ||
Exhausted from traveling a long distance for a long time, I rested there like the sun upon the slope of the western mountain at the foot of a wish-fulfilling tree.
Just as the sun has settled in the courtyard of the western mountain as if to rest, together with the entire burden of worldly activities of saṃsāra.

The syntactical connection is with the remote [verb]: "As long as the sun, together with all the worldly activities of saṃsāra, remained stationed in the courtyard of the sky at the edge of the mountain of sunrise—marked by the setting mountain—I remained hidden within that cluster of trees."
When the entire interior of the world was gradually seized by darkness, and the nocturnal activities had fully commenced in the forest; (25)
I remained hidden within that soft tree-stump with its small hollows, my face long concealed, like a bird in its own nest.
Just like a bird whose beak has been hidden for a long time, concealed within the hollow of its own wing.
For one whose discrimination has been bitten by poison, who is like a wretched man, whose memory is failing, who is as if sold into slavery, and who is submerged in a blind well; (27)
By the word "poison" (viṣa), the poison-bearer is indicated; by the word "Kīnāśa," one under the sway of death is indicated through figurative usage (lakṣaṇā). || 27 ||
There, a night equal to an eon passed for me, submerged in delusion,
like that of the sage Mārkaṇḍeya as he was being carried away by the single vast ocean.
I did not bathe, nor did I perform worship, nor did I eat at that time; for me, who stood at the forefront of calamities, that night passed away in vain. (29)
Or that night belongs to those people who have fallen into calamities and are beset by misfortune. || 29 ||
For him who was sleepless, lacking fortitude, and trembling along with the sprouts,
that night passed away together with its wicked and excessive length.
Along with its sprouts, it was quivering and trembling; together with its wicked, difficult-to-cross, and extreme length. || 30 ||
Then, as streaks of darkness appeared along with the stars, the moon,
and the night-lotuses, a state of complete dejection was produced upon my face as if it were upon me.
Then, the connection with the third [verse] is as follows: he saw [the sun] having reached the eastern direction, appearing as if reddened by the drinking of honey (madhu).

While the streaks of darkness were being brought to a state of fading and lack of clarity along with the stars, the moon, and the night-lotuses (*kairava*), their comparison is "as if upon me" (*mayīva*); for the comparison for the stars, the moon, and the night-lotuses is the face (*ānana*).

By this, it is understood through the sense of the meaning that the moon’s taking away [the light] is the cause for the eyes of the night-lilies, and that the pupils of those [eyes] serve as the standard of comparison for the stars. || 31 ||
And as the shrieks of the vetālas subsided in that forest of swift-moving beasts,
there arose the clicking sounds and whistling sighs of rows of teeth suffering from the pain of the cold.

In the midst of roars and lion-like shouts; in the swift-moving wilderness, that is, the vast forest—here "asaha" is to be read as a compound with "jaṅgale" (meaning in the unbearable forest). It is a description of the region: [it is] as if mocking me with the clattering sounds of teeth grinding and the whistling of sighs from living beings afflicted by the unbearable cold.
He saw me, submerged in distress, as if laughing;
I appeared like the eastern quarter reddened by the drinking of honey-wine. || 33 ||
In an instant, like an ignorant man [attaining] knowledge, or a poor man [finding] gold,
I beheld the sun in the sky, intent on mounting its elephant.
In the east is the directional elephant named Airāvata; mounting it means ascending therefrom, and "toward that" means facing upward.
Rising up, I tore apart the bedding and the cloth,
like one fond of the twilight dance who strips away the elephant hide with his hands.
The bedding and the garment were beaten and shaken. || 35 ||
I set out to roam through that vast wilderness,
which was like the world-hut at the end of an eon when its multitudes of living beings have been consumed by fire.
Kāla is Kālarudra; kalpa is the dissolution (pralaya). || 36 ||
Nothing real is seen there in that withered wilderness,
just as not even a trace of virtue is found in the body of a fool.
Noble-born and pleasing to the heart. || 37 ||
Free from all doubt, though restless in their wandering through the countryside, they roam about without restraint, uttering cries of "cī-cī" and "kū-cī. (38)
The ellipsis to be supplied is that they roam there in such a manner as to manifest their fickle innate restlessness through wandering fruitlessly in the forest groves alone. || 38 ||
Then, when the lord of the day had reached the eighth part of the sky, and the creepers, having shed their last traces of dew, appeared as if they had just bathed; (39)
Dewdrops are particles of frost-water. || 39 ||
As I was wandering about, I saw a girl carrying a vessel of boiled rice;
she was like the Mādhavī creeper held by a Dānava who had seized a precious jar of nectar.
The girl was another; she was like Mādhavī, Hari himself wearing a female disguise. || 40 ||
With eyes like shimmering stars, dark-complexioned and clad in white garments, I approached her there as the moon approaches the night.
She whose eyes consist of shimmering stars. || 41 ||
"O child, give me this rice quickly in my great distress;
through the removal of the suffering of the wretched, one's fortunes attain expansion. (42)

When [the danger] is powerful, reaching even to the point of loss of life. And thus says the Smṛti: "He who, having fallen into a situation where his life is at its end, eats food from whatever source it may come, is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.

The sense is that there is permission for all kinds of food when life is at stake, as seen in Bādarāyaṇa’s Sūtra: "There is permission for all food when life is at its end, because that is observed [in scripture]. 42
This great hunger within me has grown strong, O child,
like a black serpent giving birth while dwelling in the hollow of an old tree.

"Prasūtā" means one who has given birth; she is so designated to illustrate that hunger performs what is improper, for it is said that such a woman would even devour her own eggs. Thus they say: "For the sake of this wretched belly, who would not do what is unseemly? (43)
Even through such entreaty, nothing at all was given to me by her,
just as wealth is not given by Lakṣmī to a wrongdoer despite diligent supplication.
By means of a prayer joined with effort—that is, by an effortful prayer. || 44 ||
Only after a long time did it fall from piece to piece by me, who followed it most closely, as it stood before me like a shadow.
It falls from one forest thicket to another and follows after it; for this very reason, it has become like a shadow. || 45 ||
She said to him, "Know me to be a Caṇḍālī adorned with necklaces and armlets,
as cruel as a Rākṣasī, devouring men, horses, and elephants. (46)
By this mention of necklaces, armlets, and so forth—which indicates a noble birth—it is illuminated that my food is not to be eaten. || 46 ||
O King, you shall not obtain food from me merely by honoring me,
just as one cannot obtain beautiful nobility from a rustic person of ignoble intent.
Because of his lack of noble birth and his desire for what was not conducive to perfection; from the vulgar, that is, from the village folk;
[he received] kindness as if it were affection. || 47 ||
When she had spoken thus, as Khelā walked along, pausing at every step, and immersed herself in the groves with graceful, playful bends of her body, she said: (48)

By her who was sinking—that is, dissolving herself—through her playful gestures (*līlābhiḥ*), such as side-long glances that indicate her intended purpose, she became bowed down, that is, humble. || 48 ||
"I give you this food if you will become my husband; for people do not benefit others with wealth unless they share a bond of affection. (49)
The world of ordinary beings is common [to all]. || 49 ||
"In this field, my father, a Pulkasa, drives my oxen like a hungry Vetāla in a cremation ground, grey with dust. (50)
He drives the tamed oxen; that is to say, he ploughs. || 50 ||
This food belongs to him while he remains in the position of a master;
for beloved persons are to be honored even at the cost of one's own life. (51)
It is given while you remain in the position of husband. || 51 ||
Then she was addressed by me: "O lady of virtuous vows, I shall be your wife; for in times of distress, who takes account of caste-duties or family traditions? (52)
Then she offered half of that rice to me,
just as in ancient times Māghavī offered half of her nectar to Indra when he was in great distress.
The Mādhavī creeper gave to Indra half of her nectar as if out of distress—that is to say, out of great regard for him due to the pain of hunger. || 53 ||
I drank the juice of jambu fruits and ate the cooked rice from the village;
there, with my mind overcome by delusion, I rested. (54)
Having filled me there like the sun, that dark rainy season has passed away,
as if taking hold with its hand of my life-breath standing outside.
Having filled [it] and having concealed [it]. || 55 ||
He approached his father, who was of hideous appearance, of evil intent, and inspiring fear, with a massive form like the Avīci hell of torment.
Avīci is a particular type of hell. || 56 ||
By her, who was attached to me, her own purpose was communicated to him,
just as a bee clinging to a flower communicates its intent to the elephant through its humming sound.
"He was announced to the Mātaṅga, the Cāṇḍāla"—the word "in the ear" is to be supplied. For this very reason, there is a simile: [he was like] a female bee clinging to another bee (alī). || 57 ||
"O father, let this man be my husband; may it please you.
Having said "So be it" to her, when the end of the day had arrived, [he acted accordingly].
Kṛtānta released the two bound ones like his own servants;
and as the quarters were turned tawny by frost-clouds and covered in rising dust,
we departed from that place of Vetāla-binding at the close of day.
From that forest, which was filled with tawny and brownish-red creatures, and which was a dwelling place for *piśācas* due to its binding of *vetālas*.
In an instant, at twilight, they reached the settlement from the Dīrghajaṅgala forest;
like Vetālas emerging from one cemetery, they arrived at another great cemetery.
There were monkeys, cocks, and crows lying in their mangled and dismembered portions;
swarms of flies hovered over the parts of the earth drenched with blood.
Even when cut, they remain distinct through the act of cutting. || 61 ||
Where birds alighted upon the network of moist entrails spread out for drying,
and where the cries of birds echoed from fragments of citron trees situated in the garden groves.
In the pleasure gardens and domestic groves. || 62 ||
The porch was filled with clumps of heavy, drying fat, while birds fluttered about;
blood-stained hides spread out before their eyes dripped drops of gore.
The *alinda* is the outer vestibule of the door. || 63 ||
Where flies buzzed over lumps of raw flesh held in the hands of children,
and where infants shrieked, threatened by a decrepit Caṇḍāla.
By decrepit, aged, and eminent Caṇḍālas who were presiding over [the place]. || 64 ||
Having entered that terrifying settlement strewn with severed heads and entrails, we were like the attendants of Kṛtānta entering a world that had become like a dead corpse at the end of a kalpa.
Where living beings, that is, creatures, have died; at the time of dissolution, during the kalpa. || 65 ||
There, in my new father-in-law’s house, I sat upon a seat made of many plantain leaves, which had been prepared with great haste.
Upon a small seat or stool that had been provided—that is, spread out—with agitation and great reverence. || 66 ||
But my mother-in-law, who was squint-eyed, with her eyes full of drops of blood, said, "This is my son-in-law," and she welcomed that [which was rightly welcomed]. (67)
Then, having rested upon a seat of antelope skin, he consumed the food of the Caṇḍālas like a multitude of accumulated evil deeds.
Those words of affection, though they were not even very pleasant, were heard as seeds of endless suffering and were truly unfortunate. (69)
Then, on a certain day when the sky was cloudless and the stars were visible,
[he performed the rites] with various displays of water and offerings of garments and wealth.
And by those various endeavors and preparations for the accumulation of liquor, meat, and so forth, which are appropriate for the festivals of the Caṇḍālas. || 70 ||
Although that girl was given to me by him, she is a source of fear—dark-skinned like a wicked deed resulting in torment for one of dark complexion. (71)
There, the outcastes, having drunk their fill of flowing, potent liquor, roared impetuously on all sides;
they were wanton, having struck the sharp-sounding drums.
Like great heaps of their own misdeeds. || 72 ||

In this context, "atrasmin vivāhotsave" means in this marriage festival; by the two words "madirā" and "āsava," their intoxication is indicated. "Mahāntaḥ" refers to great [sins] such as the killing of a Brahmin (brahmahatyā) and so forth. || 72 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Marriage of the Caṇḍālī," within the *Indrajālopākhyāna* of the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* in the glorious *Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Seer. 106.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Marriage of the Caṇḍālī," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
p. 379) 225 The one hundred and twenty-fifth canto [or] 107.
The King said:
What is the use of saying more here? From that time forward, with my heart captivated by the festival, I became a well-nourished Pulkasa there.
In this regard, that which is called "living" consists of his own long residence there for sixty years, maintaining a livelihood through activities appropriate for a Caṇḍāla. (1)
His heart was won over—that is, his mind was brought under control—by a marriage accompanied by festivities. || 1 ||
At the conclusion of the seven-night festival, after eight months had passed in succession, she became blooming with flowers; thereafter, she remained pregnant.
She is my wife; she is in flower, that is, in her season. || 2 ||
She gave birth to a daughter who brought her sorrow, like a calamity that brings the pain of misfortune;
that girl grew up quickly, becoming stout like the swelling anxieties of a fool.
After three years, she gave birth again to an inauspicious son,
who was like a calamity and a source of evil intent that binds one with the noose of hope.
Again a daughter, then again a son;
thus, in the forest, I have become an old Pulkasa with a wife.
One who has a wife is a householder.
Many years were spent by me there with her,
like the torments of hell experienced by a slayer of a Brahmin along with his remorse.
Helpless against the afflictions of cold, wind, and heat within the forest,
he has long been tossed about like an old tortoise in a small pond.
With a mind struck by anxiety for wife and family,
and burning with distress, he beheld the quarters of the sky as if they were ablaze, filled with arduous undertakings.
Wearing a tattered garment made of many worn-out pieces of linen,
he carried a load of wood through the forest as if it were his own evil deeds personified.

*Kṣauma* refers to a cloth made from the fibers of the *atasī* plant, which has become worn out and decayed after many years of use. A *ceṇḍaka* is a ring-shaped head-protector made of grass or similar materials, used for carrying heavy loads. || 9 ||
Clad in a foul-smelling loincloth that was tattered, old, and damp,
he spent many years breathing beneath the shade of Dhavalī trees.
A swarm of lice is *yauka*. He whose garment was merely a loincloth that was old, worn out, and foul-smelling.
Having rested—that is, having refreshed himself. Of the *dhavalīka* trees, which are a specific species of tree. || 10 ||
Eager to fill his wife's belly, he was worn out by the icy winds;
like a frog in winter, he had dissolved away within the hollows of the forest.
By Dardura alone. || 11 ||
Driven away by the spreading heat of the surging waves of various quarrels, drops of blood have been released from the eyes under the guise of tears. 12.
As if melted by the spreading heat, they have fled and dissolved. || 12 ||
In the drenched forest, those nights— distressed by the clouds— were spent within the hollows of stone-slab huts by those who feed on the flesh of boars.

When the Rohiṇī constellation has reached its waning at the proper time, and the clouds have assumed the dark hue of the rainy season, due to the lack of affection among kinsmen and by means of incessant quarrels; || 14 ||

When the rainy season—the cause for the emergence of all seeds—had reached its height of density and intensity through dark-colored clouds, and when the growth [of vegetation] had come to an end; || 14 ||
With my mind rendered wretched by constant apprehension, I have spent my years in another's house, surrounded by children who are noisy with their artistic skills.
The phrase "with children" is to be understood as the ellipsis. And "in another's house" means in the dwelling of a Caṇḍāla. || 15 ||
Due to the threats of fierce outcastes agitated by the quarrels of Caṇḍālīs, his face has reached a state of decay, like the moon with the teeth of Rāhu. 16.
Like the moon by the tusks—that is, the teeth—of Rāhu. || 16 ||
Chewed by his protruding lips,
the strips of panther flesh were like the girdles of hell-beings, purchased with the price of their own suffering.

"Seized by the denizens of hell" means they were sold to the denizens of hell. By this it is understood that even in hell there exists a corresponding commerce for those guilty of buying and selling. "Rasanās" refers to ropes made of entrails. (17)
In the winter season, the fierce waves of the Himalayan caves, along with the long-lasting masses of frost and showers of spray, [prevailed]. 18.
On his naked body, arrows were endured as if they were messengers of death;
by him, deluded by the decrepitude of old age, the roots of withered trees [or, according to another reading, milk-yielding trees] were consumed.
As if by a single person who had performed many good deeds,
numerous cooked meat-pastes were respectfully extracted from earthen bowls in the forest.
By me, who possesses a wicked wife and whose face distorts with many expressions, this was eaten untouched by people, for the sake of destroying my seized splendor. (21)
For the destruction of the fire that has been grasped. || 21 ||
Like one's own merchandise sold elsewhere for a mere trifle,
that butcher repeatedly cut away piece by piece the limbs and body of that living being.

The meat of deer is *mārga*; the meat of sheep is *āvika*. When one has purchased merchandise from others—that is, from other [traders]—it is as if one’s own body-meat were purchased; this is an expression of revulsion. || 22 ||
In the regions of the Vindhya forest, she was sold as iron;
it was as if her own sin, accumulated over thousands of previous births, had increased for its own growth.
"Having placed it in an iron vessel" means having prepared it within an iron container; "sold for the sake of increase" means sold for the purpose of obtaining a higher price. || 23 ||
With a gaze freed from affection for the twilight hour, he beheld with his eyes a spade lying scattered among the grounds of outcaste gardens, amidst what was not even strewn with refuse.
But that which remains after being sold was scattered upon the grounds of Caṇḍāla gardens for the purpose of drying;
it was strewn—that is, covered—with impure filth such as excrement and urine by the wicked.
It had fallen into an utterly wretched state, like one who has fallen into the Raurava hell, and had become the companion of the thickets of the Vindhya mountains.
By me, who remained as if undergoing the state of being nourished, yet at twilight was devoid of affection—
meaning by one who hated the time of twilight because it became an obstacle to the gathering of roots, tubers, meat, and so forth—
by such a gaze, that is, by such an intellect, [I beheld] the kudālaka, a specific kind of spade.

The meaning [of the verse] follows from the two positive concomitances (*anvaya*): that because he was a nourisher, he was seen to possess at that time a gentleness and a friendship appropriate for that moment, and no other [such person] was seen. || 24 ||
Like one who has fallen into the Raurava hell and attained a momentary state of tenderness,
he felt as if he were entering into kinship with the thickets of the Vindhya caves.

Where, in that state of misfortune, they were delivered by destiny through a series of linked circumstances in the form of Pulindas, who—by the force of their blows from clubs, which surpassed the speed of dogs—satisfied [their hunger]. (26) *Note: Regarding the variant reading "laguḍātkāla" (death from the club), it refers to the same event.* Where, in that particular calamity, they were surrendered by fate through "yuktayogaiḥ," meaning through successive connections or a chain of events.
My sons, wife, and others were gratified by me with coarse food, while the harassment of dogs was warded off by me—using the speed of a trained hound—with blows from clubs and lashes of whips. (26)
With wife and children sustained by wretched food fit for village outcasts,
and with nights spent under the dry palm leaves of a forest where the rain falls in torrents.

"Grāmakaḥ" [the reading "grāmakāḥ kugrāmāḥ" is also found]; there, for those who are blind, it refers to such things as kodrava grain, oil-cakes, and so forth, which are appropriate for them. || 27 ||
I have been led away by the forest monkeys together with Raṇitadanta,
while my body, inhabited by the cold, has its pores bristling with hair standing on end.

The tip (*koṭi*) is the point of the needle for piercing pearls; those [lotuses] which rise toward its seal (*mudrā*)—that is, reach a state of equality with it in their upper portion—are called *koṭimudrodyāni*. 28.
During the rainy season, drops of water were held by him like pearls; with his belly emaciated and parched by hunger, he swallowed them as if they were fragments of clouds.
A "vanala" is a cloud because it takes or receives water (*vana*); the drops belonging to that are the *vānala* drops.
A small piece of flesh is like a fragment of a cloud (*jīmūtakhaṇḍa*), a mere portion of a cloud; [it was cut] for that purpose. (29)
In the forest, he engaged in a tumultuous quarrel with his wife,
who gnashed her teeth and squinted with eyes narrowed from the cold.
With his body soiled by the dust of the earth, he acted like a kinsman to the vetālas;
carrying a fishhook, he wandered along the riverbanks for the sake of fish. (31)
The Vetāla’s own people and kinsmen acted in such a manner that their conduct was, as it were, like that of a Vetāla. || 31 ||
In that eon, for the sake of the world's total destruction, he was like Kṛtānta armed with a noose;
having fasted for many days, he drank the blood from the chest of a deer just slaughtered.
Of the chest, that is, the breast, of a deer recently slaughtered and cut down by an arrow. || 32 ||
That blood, warm as it was at that moment, was like the milk from a mother's breast;
yet I, intoxicated, gazed upon those dwelling in the cremation ground, crimson with blood and devourers of filth.
"Koṣṇam" means slightly warm. "Raktena" means with blood; "raktān" means stained [red].
"Mattaḥ" refers to those who eat impurities—those whose habit is to consume offerings at cremation grounds, flesh, and other such unholy things. || 33 ||
The forest-demons fled like those pursued by Caṇḍikā;
snares were spread in the woods for the purpose of binding deer and birds. (34)
"Vidrutāḥ" means fled out of fear; "vyuptāḥ" means spread out. || 34 ||
Like hopes for the sake of increase, the worlds consisting of sons, wives, and kin were created by me through illusory means, like garlands made of a web of threads.
The quarters of the sky were brought to a state of decay by the snares of that one whose life was devoid of merit;
even there, he gave free rein to his mind for the arising of evil deeds. (36)
In that regard, even toward such evil deeds, he gave free rein to his mind. || 36 ||
Hope has been stretched out far, like a surging river in the rainy season;
it has fled far away from my mind, as a female camel flees from a snake. (37)
By means of the intellect (*dhiyā*), which is like a female camel (*karabhī*), [the mind] has gone far away from the presence of the body (*bhakyāḥ*) by means of right understanding (*sadbuddhyā*).
The suffix *-kta* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). For it has already been stated that a female camel draws a snake out of its hole by means of her breath and devours it;
likewise, compassion (*dayā*) has been cast far away from the body, just as a snake sheds its slough.
It was characterized by cruelty, easily provoked to fury, raining down arrows, and making a loud noise. || 38 ||

"In his own body" (*dehe*) means in his own person; "in the bodies of others" (*paraprāṇidehe*) means in the bodies of enemies. "One whose nature it is to rain down" (*varṣituṃ śīlam asya*) refers to arrows, *bāṇas*, and water.
"Resounding" (*ninādi*) means speaking harshly, and "thundering" (*garjanaśīlaṃ*)—these are adjectives common to both the cloud and the cruelty [of the enemy].
Thus, in what follows as well, the adjectives common to the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) should be understood. || 38 ||
At the end of the summer heat, they were accepted [by the people] like dark clouds by the sky;
yet, though blooming, they were wounded, salted, and avoided from afar by the people. (39)
They are alkaline, foul-smelling, and difficult to endure. || 39 ||
Like withered jasmine flowers cast into a chasm, calamities have long been borne by me in the vast lands of hell, within the dark corners of my own time.

In these [streams], the family-limits (*kulakoṇāḥ*)—which are the embankments (*setu*) that demarcate the divisions of the fields—are fixed as the very times determined by the thought, "This much must be enjoyed by me for this long. || 40 ||
While staying in the caves of the Vindhya mountains, I have mercilessly sown handfuls of seeds of evil deeds with showers of delusion as snares. (41)
Those for whom delusion alone is like rain that causes their fruit to increase. || 41 ||
Like Death himself among living beings, he pounced upon the deer;
I rested my head against the wall-like necks of the yak-cows. (42)
She was asleep, devoid of discernment, like Śauri upon his remaining limbs;
her foot and garment were dangling, and she was accompanied by a dark smoke rising with a flicker.

In the case of the mountain caves, the meaning is: those whose foothills have feet (slopes) as restless as birds (vibhiḥ pakṣibhiḥ), and whose form is smoky and radiant with roaring tigers and other beasts accompanied by sound; in the case of the body, the meaning is clear. 43.
My body has long served as a cave for the Vindhya mountains filled with streams of tears; my shoulder, abounding in lice, has been used by me as a pillow for Kṛṣṇa’s body. 44.

The word *kaccha* refers to a marshy region abounding in water; the conduct [of lice] therein is what is meant by the term *kacchaguhā*. By applying the suffix *ky-aṅ* in the sense of "acting like" (*upamānād ācāre*) and then the suffix *kta* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), we derive *kacchaguhāvadācaritam*. The connection of the words is as follows: "In the summer, I endured—that is, I patiently bore—the burden of a swarm (*yauka*) of lice. || 44 ||
In summer, I was endured by moving beings, just as the earth is by a boar;
many times I have been surrounded by forest fires that have scorched the circles of living creatures. (45)

Having followed the course of Time, which consumes the world with the fire at the end of an aeon, my wife gave birth there— like a wicked seizure that brings disease and misfortunes to one who is greedy for its signs— bringing forth both sorrows and joys.
Just as one characterized by greed and addicted to sexual indulgence brings about diseases such as consumption, or just as a malignant planet,
a stubborn obsession, or an evil influence brings about calamities such as enmity and strife, even so my donor has brought forth offspring who have produced both sufferings and pleasures for me.
Then, by me— the only son of the king—
through a fault that was constant and dense, sixty years were passed as if they were sixty eons.
He concludes: "O protector of men! The phrase "by an only son" is stated to indicate extreme impropriety.
47. Loud abuse was uttered, weeping was done excessively in times of calamity, wretched food was eaten, and one dwelt in the sordid hamlets of outcasts.
O members of the assembly, for a long time I have been afflicted there, bound by the shackles of evil latent impressions. 48.

Summarizing all the aforementioned misfortunes, he concludes by saying "ākruṣṭam" (was reviled): "O members of the assembly, [I] was reviled through an outburst of anger and wept in calamities; this refers to another time in comparison with the period you have experienced. (48)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh canto, titled "The Description of Calamity," within the "Story of Indrajāla" in the "Section on Origination" of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (sage-authored) tradition. 107.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Adversity," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
(381) Chapter 226, [Verse] 108.
The King said:
Then, as time passed and my lifespan became worn out by old age,
I was covered with a beard resembling a mass of young grass filled with frost.
While he was living for a long time here in that outcaste settlement, the wretched state of the country due to famine arising from drought is described. (1)
His face was filled with a beard as thick as a mass of young grass. || 1 ||
As the floods of days fall away—driven by the winds of karma, now sapid and now sapless, like clusters of withered leaves. (2)
In those full of flavor yet accompanied by suffering, and in those devoid of flavor yet accompanied by pain, as the floods of days fall and pass away. || 2 ||
Like a torrent of arrows in battle, amidst joys and sorrows without ceasing, and even as quarrels and improper deeds approached and fell upon him; (3)
In battle, that is, in war; in improper acts, those unfit to be performed, such as killing, binding, theft, and so forth. || 3 ||
O twice-born one, when the mind is dull and whirled about like the ocean with its mass of waves, it revolves in the whirlpool of conceptual construction and imagination.
Like a bird, the twice-born one moves through the supportless [space] as he wanders; thus, it is called *dvijaga*. (4)
When the self has mounted the wheel composed of flickering thoughts and is whirling about,
it is carried away like a blade of grass in the ocean of time with its whirlpools.
"Thus, for me—a two-armed donkey who is like a worm in the forest of the Vindhya mountains and whose sole refuge is a mouthful of fodder—this entire lifespan has been exhausted here. (6)
When the multitude of years in the cycle of ages had been exhausted. || 6 ||
When my status as a king was forgotten, like that of a corpse,
and my state as an outcaste became fixed, I was like a mountain with its wings severed.
Like that of a corpse, as if dead. || 7 ||
Like the end of an eon to the cycle of existence, like a forest fire to a grove,
like a wave of the ocean to its shore, and like a thunderbolt to a withered tree.
Then a circle of fierce Caṇḍālas, flying forth at the moment of sudden death,
arrived at the marshy banks of the Vindhya mountains, which were devoid of food, grass, leaves, and water.

When the thick clouds do not rain, there occurs a famine characterized by sudden death and the flight of people to the next world; such a famine makes the marshy regions of the Vindhya mountains— where the circle of outcastes is fierce— devoid of food, grass, leaves, and water.

"Āyayau" means he arrived. The preceding phrases such as "as if [into] saṃsāra" should be understood as successive metaphors for the object and the agent of the action respectively. Alternatively, the meaning is that he went to another region called Vindhyakacchasthala, which was a circle of fierce Caṇḍālas. || 9 ||
When the mass of clouds does not rain and has vanished from wherever it was seen,
and when the wind blows carrying scattered fragments of glowing embers.
Its movement was mixed with extremely fine particles of charcoal, as if purified by being strained through a cloth.
In the forest glades, where the leaves were withered and rustling, and which were enveloped by forest fires— desolate places that seemed as if they had long since abandoned their worldly life.
The comparison "as if they had long since gone forth" is based on [the Buddha's] having matted hair that is tawny in color and so forth. (11)
Suddenly there arose a terrifying fire of unrestrained fury,
which dried up every thicket and reduced all grass and shrubs to mere ashes. (12) [The reading "tṛṇopala" is also found.]
Famine that arises unexpectedly and at an inappropriate time. || 12 ||
With all its limbs grey with dust, with every man famished,
devoid of food, grass, and water, the entire region was like a parched wasteland.
Uddāva is a district in which there is a circle [of land] that has become a superior wilderness. || 13 ||
The region of the earth was like a herd of buffaloes plunging into the mirage-waters of the desert;
the sky was filled with a forest of clouds consisting of masses of spray raised by the wind.
Where the forest-canopy is "without overflow" (aparivāha), for it does not even carry away the mass of spray raised by the wind.
A multitude of men, longing only to hear the sound of water, with all their people perishing from exhaustion and dehydration due to the heat of the sun. (15)
The extension of the sunlight is its expansion. || 15 ||
Its life-force was aroused by the frenzy of devouring leaves;
its circle of teeth rolled about in the intensity of gnawing at its own limbs.

Where life has arisen and departed from those agitated by the effort of devouring leaves; where, in their frantic longing to chew their own limbs, they roll about and strike one another with their circles of teeth.
It swallowed a mass of fierce khadira-wood embers mistaking them for meat,
and it devoured fragments of forest stones, taking them for a pond of soft cakes.
Where even worthless fragments of forest stone were swallowed, mistaking them for cakes made of flour mixed with oil.
A multitude of mothers, sons, and fathers were entangled with one another as living beings;
excellent sarika birds, crying out from within the bellies of vultures, were being swallowed whole.
It is swallowed by the essence, it is swallowed in its entirety. || 18 ||
The surface of the earth was drenched with blood from the mutual mangled limbs [of combatants],
while the elephants were frantic and hungry, enraged by the devouring of their prey.
It was terrifying due to the roaming of individual lions amidst the narrow passages,
and it bore the appearance of wrestlers among the people who were intent on devouring one another.
In the caves, terrifying due to the lions roaming one by one with the fear of being swallowed,
and by people intent on devouring and harming one another, there was the performance of wrestlers, like the conduct of wrestlers.
The wind there was filled with glowing embers that flew up from trees stripped of their leaves;
the ground along the mineral-rich slopes was licked by cats eager for a drink of blood.
The forest wind was filled with the whirling eddies of dense masses of flames,
and the jungle was turned tawny by heaps of fire blazing across every spot.
The thickets were dense with smoke rising from the forest groves of burnt pythons,
while the sky was enveloped by evening clouds amidst flames tossed by the wind.
Where the pythons were scorched by the smoke rising from the burnt thicket, as if by a longing that made the thickets lush and full of blossoms.
The circle of pillars was obscured by flying ashes raised by a wild clamor,
while the cries of distressed children were heard at the tips of the tusks of the trumpeting elephants.
Where there were circles of parasols that were without pillars and without handles.
It was a great corpse with the teeth and skin of a multitude of bewildered men,
its own fingers— both red and not red— seized by the force of the stench of flesh.
Where her own finger, reddened by blood, was swallowed with speed and haste due to its devouring.
With the luster of dense yellow smoke mistaken for blue-leafed creepers, it was filled with the brilliance of firebrands wandering through the sky as they were swallowed by circling vultures. (26)
It was agitated by the fleeing of people who were terrified by their limbs being torn from one another,
while its heart and belly were rent asunder by the crackling sounds of blazing fires.
It was filled with the leaping of terrifying forest fires accompanied by the whistling winds from chasms,
and its trees were covered in glowing embers falling from the hissing of frightened pythons.
Where there is the terrifying leaping of forest fires, sounding like the deep "krāṅkāra" roar of the wind entering a chasm;
and where the trees are such that embers fall and spring up from the hissing of terrified pythons.
Reaching that dry hollow where the ground was instantly split asunder by the thunderbolt,
it took on the likeness of the world consumed by the fire of twelve suns.

Having reached that region on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains, which was previously described as a place where the land suddenly bursts open due to famine, it became like that very [desolate] state; "anukṛti" here means similarity. || 29 ||
The people were driven away by the spreading winds from the forest groves where the trees were entangled with blazing fires—
the [fires] of Agni, Sūrya, and Yama.
The region took on the likeness of a pleasure-house. || 30 ||
By the spreading of such a wind— one whose mass of matted locks consists of clusters of trees ablaze with fire—
the people there were oppressed and afflicted; it was a place that imitated the house of the son of the Sun, Śanaiścara, which serves as his playground for both blazing and scorching.
Equanimity. || 30 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sudden Event," in the Narrative of Indrajāla, within the Section on Origination, in the *Mokṣopāya* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the Holy Scripture of the Sage.
Thus [ends] the [section] on the Illumination of the Essential Meaning of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in the Section on Origination.
The one hundred and eighth canto, titled "Description of the Unseasonable Occurrence."
The one hundred and ninth canto.
The King said:
While that painful reversal of fate was occurring at that time...
In this world, which is like a premature and violent dissolution at the end of an eon, and which inflicts extreme torment. || 1 ||

Having seen the calamity that befell his son after he had gone out with his wife, and having awakened with the desire to enter the funeral pyre, the conversation of the assembly members is related. (1)
In the reversal of prescribed rules and in the adversity of fate. || 1 ||
Some people, having departed together with their wives and friends, went to another land from the sky, like clouds in the autumn season. || 2 ||
With their sons, wives, and chief kinsmen clinging to the limbs of their bodies,
some there were shattered, like trees in a forest that have been cut down.
That is to say, they are like the limbs of the body—so closely attached as to be impossible to abandon. || 3 ||
Some devotees, however, fled from their own dwellings by means of tigers,
like fledglings that have not yet grown wings when driven out of their nests by hawks.

The letter *ca* (and) is placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakrama*) for the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; that is to say, [they were attacked] by tigers and other beasts of prey. Some entered the blazing fire like moths;
others fell into pits like rocks fallen from a mountain. || 5 ||
But I, having abandoned them— my father-in-law and the others— and taking only my wife, who was capable of managing herself, have emerged from this country with great difficulty.
"Suitable" means capable of following after oneself. || 6 ||
Having escaped from the fear of death by deceiving even the fire, the wind, the devourers, and the Takṣakas, I have emerged together with my wife.
"Beast-eaters" refers to tigers and the like; "biters" refers to serpents. || 7 ||
Having reached the edge of that region,
he set down his sons from his shoulders there at the foot of a palmyra tree, like various formidable calamities.
The limit of that region is the border. || 8 ||
I am at last rested, having been weary for a long time, like one who has emerged from Raurava hell,
or like a lotus without water in summer, suffering from the heat of a long, parching forest fire.
The meaning is that I am withering like a lotus flower without water, or else, like a frog or similar creature resting in the root of a lotus plant, I have found my rest there. || 9 ||
Then, while the Caṇḍāla girl rested at the foot of the tree in the cool shade, she fell asleep, embracing her two children.
"My only son, named Pṛcchaka, stands before me;
he is our youngest, exceedingly dear to us, and full of innocence. (11)
With a distressed soul and eyes filled with tears, he said to me:
"O father, give me your flesh quickly, and let me drink your blood this very moment."
Speaking thus again and again, that foolish son of mine reached a life-ending state, crying out once more from hunger.
Although I told him many times, "O son, there is no meat," that evil-minded man continued to say, "Give me meat. (14)
Then, deluded by affection—or as the reading goes, "endowed with it"—and burdened by excessive grief, I said to him: "My son, please eat my cooked flesh. (15)
That too was accepted by him as he spoke again,
"Give [it]," while his livelihood was exhausted and his conduct was characterized by attachment to eating my flesh.

"By one whose activity is exhausted" means by one who has not obtained food; that is to say, by one who is extremely hungry. "By one whose mode of life is embracing" means by one intent on hugging. || 16 ||
Out of affection and compassion for one who removes all suffering, and beholding his distress, I, burdened by extreme grief, [acted]. (17)
In a dvandva compound consisting of the words *sneha*, *kāruṇya*, and *moha*, the suffix *hani* is applied. 17.
Unable to endure that intense calamity, I, with a ruined soul, made a firm internal resolve to die for the sake of my dear friend. (18)
To Atimitra, his kinsman suited for that occasion. || 18 ||
There, having gathered wood, I constructed a funeral pyre;
and the pyre, with its crackling and popping sounds, stood there longing for me. (19)
As if longing for me. || 19 ||
But while I was still casting myself upon that funeral pyre, the king suddenly rose up from this lion-throne with great speed. || 20 ||

The ablative case (*pañcamī*) in "from the throne" (*siṃhāsanāt*) should be understood as denoting the point of departure (*apādāna*), with reference to the action of falling—which is inferred from the movement—as well as its result, namely separation (*vibhāga*), which is currently being undergone. || 20 ||
Then, awakened by the sound of trumpets and shouts of victory, [he thought]:
"Thus has this delusion been produced for me by the sorcerer. (21)
When the lord of kings, Lavaṇa of immense splendor, had spoken thus—"The state of the individual soul is endowed with hundreds of conditions through ignorance alone"—[the sages said: 22.
The magician instantly vanished there in a moment.
Then those members of the assembly, their eyes wide with wonder, said this: ||| 23 ||
"O King, this man is not a conjurer who lacks a desire for wealth;
rather, this is some divine illusion that makes one understand the nature of worldly existence. (24)
But the divine [power], employed by the gods for the sake of bestowing grace upon you, is precisely that which awakens one to the fact that such is the nature of worldly existence.
In that [state], it is perceived that the world is a play of the mind;
for the world of the mind is indeed the play of the omnipotent and infinite [Brahman]. (25)
Of the infinite Viṣṇu, the mind alone is the world. 25.
For the powers of the All-Powerful Creator are indeed manifold and hundredsfold,
since even this discerning mind He bewilders with His illusory power (māyā).
This is the rule. 26.
Where is this lord of the earth, who is well-acquainted with the ways of the world; and where is this vast agitation, which is fit for the mental disposition of an ordinary person? (27)
It is suitable for the mental activity of ordinary persons who possess common [perceptions]. || 27 ||
Nor is this delusive illusion in the mind the mere whim of a magician;
for it is said that magicians constantly strive for the accomplishment of their purpose.
They strive for the attainment of wealth and property, and they exert themselves to display affection and curiosity,
but not for such a delusion as this.
"O sirs, they strive with effort for wealth and do not vanish from sight;
thus we remain agitated, standing at this time of doubt. (29)
Having been told this, and while they remained on the firm ground of certainty— the shore of the ocean of doubt— after those two signs had appeared,
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Rāma, I was indeed present in that assembly at that time."
This was seen by me through direct perception; it was not heard from another.
This narrative has been told; it is not a fabricated story like the *Bālakāṇḍa*, nor was it heard from another source, but rather was witnessed directly. Thus he says: "In the assembly... (30).

Thus, victory to the expansive mind of the Great-Souled One, whose limbs have been nurtured by many skillful means; for when the nature of the "other" has been brought to rest, it triumphs for all time.
You shall attain that supreme, purifying state.
Applying the previously told narrative to the present subject—that the world is a mere play of the mind—the author states its result:

"Thus," etc. In this manner, the mind—which has had its limbs developed through many conceptualizations and constructions, which has long been grown and extended, and which is vast like the body of a tree with its fruits, sprouts, and branches—is victorious.
Having transcended the nature of the self, it exists in its own state of supreme excellence; when,

through the yoga of knowledge consisting of mental inquiry— [here, the reading "yasmān manasi" is required]— the mind has been brought to, or attained, tranquility characterized by the absence of latent impressions (*nirvāsanatā*) within the Supreme Nature (*parasvabhāva*), then you [are that].

"Through the sublation of the limiting adjuncts that cause differentiation, you shall attain the supreme, purifying state of the full Self; therefore, strive for that end by means of the methods to be described"—this is the meaning. || 31 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and ninth canto, titled "The Dispelling of the Cāṇḍāla State," in the *Indrajālopākhyāna* of the *Mokṣopāya*, within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Dispelling of the Status of a Caṇḍāla," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The One Hundred and Tenth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the beginning, from the supreme cause, consciousness (citi) falls into the state of the object of thought (cetya).
Having reached the state of limitation, the creative power (kalā) has become entangled in confusion. || 1 ||
The means for the pacification of the mind is here undertaken to be proclaimed by the son of Brahmā to Rāma, through descriptions of the majesty of the mind. (1)

Since the mind consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the sole means for its complete pacification is the absolute eradication of the impressions regarding objects of knowledge. This is achieved through the scriptures, the teacher, and one's own experience, by first ascertaining that the entire range of perceived phenomena is nothing but a mental delusion, and continuing until the ascent to the seventh stage (*bhūmikā*).

To state that the effort to restrain the mind (*manas*) alone is the means (*upāya*) for maturing wisdom, he speaks—purifying the essential nature of the mind from its very root—beginning with "from the Supreme" (*paramāt*). Ignorance conjoined with consciousness (*cit*) is the supreme cause; it is from that very cause that consciousness falls into the state of the objectifiable (*cetya*), becoming the domain of objects, though not in reality.

Because it is changeless (*avikāratvāt*). By the word "in the beginning" (*ādau*), it is indicated that since the initial falling into the sphere of the object of cognition (*cetyapadapāta*) is caused by ignorance (*ajñāna*), it is established all the more so that the various perceptions of duality (*dvaitadarśana*) rooted therein are likewise caused by it.
From this very falling into the sphere of the object of cognition, conceptualization (*kalanā*)—having reached the state of being a name (*pada*) for the purpose of designating an object—arises.
It has reached a state of turbidity and impurity through the acquisition of objects and the manifold variety of forms;
this is the sense that it is the very first sprout of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 1 ||
O Rāma, amidst these very delusions, whose nature is of such a kind,
one becomes utterly stupefied for a long time, having reached a state of utter emptiness within the dense thicket.

In those states of delusion— consisting of such habitual tendencies and conditions, where the accumulation of wealth has increased amidst the errors of the appearance of objective gains— that very consciousness, having forgotten its own fullness and having fallen into a state of insignificance and the nature of unreal desires, remains in a swoon for a long time, from beginningless time.

One is deluded by the errors of birth, death, and so forth; thus, the very tendency of consciousness toward objects of thought is the seed of the mind that produces misfortune, and it is precisely this that must be restrained—this is the intended meaning. || 2 ||
The mental activity, though itself non-existent and withered, spreads forth suffering excessively through thousands of defects, just as a young girl conjures up ghosts.

Thus, with its mental activity withered by thousands of defects arising from vain latent impressions, that consciousness remains in the state of the mind and spreads forth suffering that is truly non-existent. || 3 ||
For indeed, great suffering, once it exists, brings about non-existence in an instant;
yet the stainless activity of the mind dispels it, just as the sun’s light dispels darkness. (4)

Just as the mental state accompanied by stains spreads forth the suffering of consciousness, so too, upon the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanākṣaya), the stainless state devoid of impressions—being in its very nature the true reality—leads great suffering to non-existence, that is, to emptiness. The meaning is that it is sublated by awakening. || 4 ||
It brings what is distant near, and it may bring what is near far away;
like a child among young birds, the mind leaps about among living beings.
To establish the possibility of what has been stated, he describes the mind’s power to bring about the impossible with the words beginning "nayati" (he leads).
"Abhyāśatām" means proximity. || 5 ||
Fear exists where there is no fear for the ignorant mind possessed of latent impressions;
to a deluded traveler from afar, even a tree stump appears as a demon.
A mind stained by suspicion suspects enmity even in a friend;
a creature whose intellect is possessed by intoxication sees the very ground spinning.
For when the mind is agitated, a thunderbolt is produced from the moon;
nectar, when consumed with the perception of poison, undergoes the effects of poison. (8)
Enveloped by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the mind perceives the construction of a celestial city as if it were real, even while one is truly awake, just as in a dream.
Surapattana is a city of the Gandharvas. || 9 ||
For a living being, the intense latent impression (vāsanā) of the mind has delusion as its sole cause;
therefore, that very impression must be uprooted with effort by cutting it off at the root.
They are to be uprooted; they are to be eradicated from the very root. || 10 ||
The deer-like mind of men, drawn by the snare of latent impressions (vāsanā),
falls into utter helplessness within the thicket of the forest of saṃsāra.
The light of that person shines forth, like the sun in a cloudless sky, by whom the latent impressions of the knowable regarding the individual soul have been severed through inquiry.
Āloka means light. || 12 ||
Therefore, O mind, know this person to be the mind alone, and not the body;
for the body is inert, whereas they know the mind here to be neither inert nor non-inert.

Regarding this, he says that one must constantly practice the meditation: "In this matter, my body is the mind alone and nothing else"— "O dear Rāghava, know that whatever is done by the mind is truly done;
O sinless one, know likewise that whatever is abandoned by the mind is truly abandoned. (14)
The entire world is mind alone; the circle of the universe has the mind as its limit.
The mind is space, the mind is earth, the mind is wind, and the mind is the Great One (mahat). 15.
The limit is the edge of the earth; that is its mandala. || 15 ||
If the mind does not join the object with its own nature,
then even at sunrise, these things would never be illuminated. (16)
One should not join with, nor imagine, that state as being the state of light and so forth; the sense is that this is because those blind by day perceive things in a contrary manner. || 16 ||
The mind takes up delusion, and he who possesses it is called deluded;
when the body has fallen into delusion, it is not called "deluded," for it is a corpse. || 17 ||
Delusion is lack of awakening. || 17 ||
Behold, the mind becomes the eye when seeing; it attains the state of the ear when hearing;
it reaches the condition of the skin through touching; and it attains the state of the nose through smelling.
In those various activities, the mind attains the state of being tasted through the tongue;
in the body, it is the mind alone that follows along like an actor on a stage. (19)
It indeed makes the short long and bestows non-existence upon what exists;
it turns the sweet into bitterness and brings the enemy to the state of a friend. (20)
The sweet [taste] has sweetness as its quality. || 20 ||
Whatever manifestation belongs to this mind as it functions, that alone is perception; for such is the experience here. (21)
Due to the power of a mere appearance, for Hariścandra, whose mind was agitated by a dream, a single night became twelve years long.
By the power of his mental resolve, a yuga passed as a mere moment for Indradyumna, who was dwelling within the city of Vairiñcya.
"Anubhāva" here means experience or power; [it refers to] Indradyumna, whose other name is Revata. || 23 ||
Through a pleasant mental disposition, even the Raurava hell becomes a state of bliss, like the imprisonment of one who is firmly bound but expects to obtain the kingdom in the morning. (24)

Where has the transformation of suffering into happiness been observed? To this he says: "By that which is pleasing," meaning by the recollection of Hari and so forth. Even the Raurava hell-suffering [is transformed]. For one who possesses certainty through valid means of knowledge that "the kingdom must necessarily be attained tomorrow morning," even though he is firmly bound with shackles on his hands and feet and the like—
The meaning is "as if it were a bond. || 24 ||
When the mind is conquered, the entire array of the senses is likewise conquered;
just as a string of pearls is destroyed when the thread is burnt.
By the power of consciousness (cicchakti), which is omnipresent, of pure nature, immutable, eternal, subtle, and acting as the witness; || 26 ||

O Rāma, what else can be said regarding the mind’s capacity for conceiving objects contrary to reality, such that— by its own existence, which is everywhere uniform and consists of pure consciousness characterized by transparency and changelessness— it renders even the body, though mute and devoid of all functions such as speech, identical to the body of Brahman and yet inert through the imagination of identity with it?

Having performed internal reflection through such delusive errors as "desire," "seeking," and "volition," one wanders in vain by projecting external forms—the play of mountains, rivers, sky, oceans, and cities; this constitutes the single syntactical connection for the three verses beginning with "sarvatra. (26)
By means of the reality of the Self, which pervades all existents and is not distinct from the object of consciousness, even that which is mute, inert, and like the body [is transformed]. (27)
The mind wanders aimlessly within, deluded by thoughts and desires, outwardly occupied with the play of mountains, rivers, sky, oceans, and cities. (28)
While awake, a desired object brings one to the state of being cleansed by nectar;
yet that very same object, when undesired, turns even nectar itself into poison.
[The opponent objects: "Surely, the mind that is vigilant through inquiry will not imagine things otherwise than they are;
so what is the use of contemplating a means for its destruction? To this he replies: "Even while awake," and so forth.
Even a mind vigilant through discrimination may still relish objects such as the lips of a woman, which are like the leftovers of something unpalatable.
Under the influence of passion, one regards what is desired as nectar and brings it to a state of sweetness and deliciousness.
However, that which is undesired and uncraved—even if it be nectar—one brings to the state of poison, making it as something to be rejected like poison.
The meaning is that even for those who are dispassionate, there is seen the perception of nectar itself as something to be rejected. || 29 ||
[The mind] is sufficient for the self-revelation of those for whom all states of being have been polished away.
To the question, "In that case, why would it not cause even those who know reality (tattvajña) to wander? he says: "Not polished," etc.
It is the mind of only those by whom "all states of being"—that is, fullness—have not been polished, i.e., directly realized.

It creates a form that possesses its own intended aspect and constitutes a wonder for the self, but not for those who know reality; for the latter, there is an absence of the perception of wonder regarding the mental playings of those whose minds have been sublated by false cognition—this is the intended meaning. || 30 ||

In vibrations, the mind—which is the manifestation of the power of consciousness—attains the state of air; in luminous manifestations, it attains the state of light; and in fluids, it attains the state of fluidity. (31)
He elaborates upon the creation of form itself with the verse beginning "In the vibrations," and so forth. || 31 ||
On earth it attains hardness; in those with nihilistic views, it becomes emptiness;
everywhere the mind, which is the vibration of the power of consciousness, assumes the state of desire.

[He taught] emptiness as non-existence; [he taught] the state of desire—that is, unimpeded and independent conduct—regarding those things perceived as "non-existent" within the views of emptiness. || 32 ||
Behold the power of this mind: it makes the white black, and it brings the black to whiteness, all without regard for place or time. (33)
When the mind is attached elsewhere, even the taste of delicious food that has been chewed by the tongue is not experienced. (34)
That which is seen by the mind is not truly seen; that which is not seen is what is truly unobserved.
Just as a form in darkness, so too is the sense faculty a mere mental construction.

By that mind, even what stands before it has not been looked at or seen. Thus, he says "in darkness" to show that the sense organs, such as the eye, are likewise imagined by that very [mind] within itself;
just as in darkness a blueness or a variety of shadows is produced. 35.
Give me the mind through the senses, and the senses through the mind that is beyond the mind.
The senses are produced from the mind; the mind is not produced from the senses.

Although the mind possesses form by means of the sense organ as its instrument—since it assumes the form perceived by the senses—and the sense organ likewise possesses form by means of the mind, because it perceives objects dependent upon the mind, there is thus a parity between them; nevertheless, the mind is superior (*ut*).
To the question "Why is that?", he says: "The senses... (36).

Those great-souled ones who perceive the absolute identity between the mind and the body—which are otherwise utterly distinct—are wise men who have known that which is to be known; they abide within the mind. (37)
This very mind, having been cast into the category of the Self by the ignorant, is grasped as the Self through the notion of "I.

However, by those who know reality, it is cast into the category of the body and grasped as the inert body-self. For this very reason, they are worthy of veneration as seers of the changeless Self; thus he says, "absolutely," etc., from the perspective of the ignorant.
Of two things that are absolutely distinct. || 37 ||
With her braided hair adorned with flowers and her eyes moving playfully,
the woman, though clinging to limbs that were like wood or a wall, remained devoid of mind.

For this very reason, he says "kusuma... [and so on], explaining that no transformation such as desire is observed in them: even when a woman is clinging to the body of one who is mindless, she is like wood or a wall; the meaning is that she is incapable of producing any transformation. || 38 ||
While his mind was otherwise engaged in the forest, that man, though free from passion, did not even notice his own hand lying on his lap being devoured by a carnivorous beast. (39)

Thus, he says "in the mind" to show that even for them there is no transformation consisting of suffering due to the signs of suffering. By the sage named Vītarāga, [the child] was placed on his lap—meaning spread upon his lap—at the time of meditation. (39)
O Sage, the extraordinary powers of the mind can easily and swiftly transform great sufferings into happiness and happiness into suffering.
The intensifications of cultivation produced by the proficiency of practice in the minds of sages are joined with ease—that is, without effort—and are capable [of sustaining themselves]. || 40 ||
Alas, when the mind is attached elsewhere, even a story being told with effort is cut short like a creeper severed by an axe. (41)
When the mind has ascended to the mountain slope, even a creature who is a householder experiences the suffering of the delusion that it is a cave in a white cloud.
It is experienced; "in a dream" is the ellipsis. || 42 ||
When the mind is delighted in a dream, cities, mountains, and even the earth appear as if constructed within the heart itself, like vast objects seen in the sky. (43)
They are seen as if fashioned within the heart, internalized, and capable of their respective functions. || 43 ||
When the mind is agitated in a dream, it projects a series of mountains and cities within the heart itself,
just as a surging ocean projects a multitude of waves within itself.
When the mind is agitated—that is, when the self is distracted—it expands or spreads out. 44.
Just as waves, surges, and ripples arise within the water of the ocean, so too do the mountains, cities, and rows of palaces appear within the mind inside the body during a dream. (45)
Just as from a sprout there arises the splendor of leaves, creepers, flowers, and fruits,
so too from this mind arise the various states of waking and dreaming.
Just as a golden woman is not distinct from the gold itself,
so too the splendor of the activities of waking and dreaming is not distinct from the mind.
A golden woman is a golden image. || 47 ||
Just as the beauty of the stream, droplets, waves, and foam is perceived in water, so indeed does this manifold variety of diverse manifestations appear to the mind. (48)
"Multiplicity" means manifold variety. || 48 ||

In this world, it is the very movement of one's own mind that arises as the states of waking and dreaming; through the immersion in aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), it assumes various roles just like an actor on a stage. (49)

It takes up the rising emergence that has arisen; "rasa" refers to passion, such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth, through immersion in that [passion]. "Śailūṣa" means an actor. "Bhūmikā" refers to the variety of costumes [and roles]. || 49 ||
Just as the state of being a Caṇḍāla appears in salt by the power of perception, so too this expansive world is merely the mind’s act of thinking. (50)
Whatever is perceived, by that very thing one quickly becomes;
the mind is the creation of its own thinking—do as you wish.
Having assumed the forms of various cities, rivers, and mountains for embodied beings,
this mind— which consists of waking and dreaming— spreads forth that which is actually situated within.
Just as Lavaṇa attained the state of a Daitya from being a god, and the state of a non-serpent from being a serpent, so too the mind attains various states through the power of its own appearances.
Neither because of being a man, an elephant, or a serpent; nor because of being a tree, a mountain, or anything else. (53)
Just as a man quickly attains womanhood from his own volition, or reaches the state of a son from being a father, so too does the mind.
Just as a man who has become a son by virtue of being a father may likewise attain womanhood by virtue of being human, so it is in this case.
Through volition one dies, and through volition one is born again;
the mind, due to long-standing habituation, attains the state of living without a physical form.
Though formless and naturally devoid of shape, it assumes the form of a living being for those who live. || 55 ||
The mind, deluded by its own thinking and expanded by the latent impressions of ignorance,
enters the womb of volition and so forth, [experiencing] pleasure and pain, fear and fearlessness.
"By *manana* (reflection), those who are completely deluded have attained an excess of infatuation; that in which such deluded latent impressions (*vāsanā*) reside is [the womb].
Alternatively, the word may be divided as *ūḍhavāsanam*. It is the *yoni*, the place of birth.
For the Śruti says: 'The mind, by its own action, enters this body. || 56 ||
Pleasure and pain reside in the mind like oil within sesame seeds;
depending on the influence of place and time, they may become intense or slight. (57)
Just as oil from sesame seeds becomes manifest through pressing, so too do pleasure and pain become solidified when the mind is attached to its own thinking. (58)

By means of "overpowering," that is, through the compression of the mechanism [of the mind], pleasure and pain become internalized within the consciousness; because of the non-attachment to mental reflection, the connection [is made] by modifying the verbal expression to "let those which were throbbing go away from here. || 58 ||
O Rāma, it is indeed volition alone that is designated by the names "space" and "time," for it is under its influence that space and time maintain their existence.

[Objection: Is it not well known that the variety of pleasure, pain, and so forth arises precisely from the variety of place, time, action, and object?
