Why, then, is it said [to arise] "from attachment of the mind"? To this, he says: "Place... Because even when place and time are small, if one conceives of them as vast through the mind, there is an experience of vastness; likewise, even with regard to a trivial object, by means of the mind...
The meaning is that it is because an excess of passion is observed in those who hold [the object] in high esteem. || 59 ||
When the mental construction of body and mind has borne fruit, the mind becomes tranquil, exultant, joyful, delighted, and leaping; yet the physical body does not [participate in these states].

In this way, he states that the body as well is dependent solely upon the volitions of the mind—namely, "it becomes tranquil. The implication is that when the volition of the mind has borne fruit, the gross physical body undergoes modifications such as tranquility; it does not do so independently. || 60 ||
With various expansive outbursts fashioned by its own volitions,
the mind frolics within this body like a virtuous woman in the courtyard of the inner apartments.
Therefore,
he who does not restrain the mind from its outward flow toward fickleness seizes the dissolution of that mind, just as an elephant [destroys] its own tethering post.
He shows the means for restraining the mind along with its fruit: "In restlessness," etc. Restlessness is the pursuit of sense objects. (62)
He whose mind does not waver, like an excellent pillar of steel, is a man established in reality; all others are but worms in the mud.

Just as an enemy does not move when paralyzed by the weapon of *stambhana* (paralysis) employed against him, so too is this very [self] the Puruṣa from the perspective of the real entity and the ultimate truth. 63.
O sinless one, he whose mind, having attained steadiness, remains fixed on a single point, has followed after the unsurpassed state through meditation.
By means of meditation as the cause, he has attained and become united with the unsurpassed state; the meaning is that he has indeed become one with Brahman.
Through the restraint of the mind, the delusion of saṃsāra attains peace, just as the great ocean of milk becomes motionless when Mount Mandara has ceased its churning.
The word division is "aspandatām iti. || 65 ||
Whatever mental fluctuations arise through the delusions of conceptualizing enjoyments, those alone are the sources of the sprouts for the poisonous tree of saṃsāra. (66)
These fools, dull-witted and sluggish with pride and delusion, whirl about like trembling blue lotuses in the great, swift current of the mind;
their thoughts are torn asunder and shattered as they turn within the vortex.
In the whirling of the wheel, men fall like deluded bees. || 67 ||

These dull-witted human-bees, intoxicated by the delusion of "mine," circle and revolve around the lotus of the mind— which is like a trembling blue lily being carried away by the current of the turbulent river of saṃsāra—

whirling within the whirlpool of childhood that exists in the force of the water consisting of a torrent of great stupidity, due to the non-differentiation between the letters *la* and *ḍa* in the word *mahājaḍa*.

The meaning is that they fall into a whirlpool resembling a wheel—a circular motion characterized by thoughts that have long been severed by powerful internal reflections and have crumbled along with the body due to their fruitlessness. || 67 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and tenth canto, titled "The Description of the Mind Preceded by the Diagnosis of the Mind," in the section on the Means to Liberation within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the work of the Sage.
Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mind Preceded by the Treatment of the Mind," in the Utthāna-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and eleventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This is the great medicine for the treatment of this great malady of the mind.
Listen to that which depends on oneself; I shall speak it well, sweetly, and with certainty. (1)

The renunciation of the "I-ness" and "mine-ness," which is the abandonment of what is cherished through effort, as well as the means for conquering the mind and one-pointedness of consciousness, are described herein. (1)
"Dependent on oneself" means under one's own control. It is "excellent" because it necessarily accomplishes the goals of human endeavor. || 1 ||
By one's own human effort alone—swiftly, through the form of self-awareness—and by exertion, the vampire of the mind is conquered once it has abandoned its desired object. (2)

Having abandoned the desired object of passion—the external object—consciousness, as a continuous flow of mental modifications taking the form of its own self alone, is mastered through a human effort of that same nature. || 2 ||
He who remains free from affliction while renouncing an object of attachment has truly conquered his mind, just as a tusker destroys a mere clump of grass.
With the intention that the renunciation of what is desired (*iṣṭatyāga*) in the first chapter must be made firm, he says: "Renouncing...
*Abhimatam* means what is desired. *Nirāmayaḥ* means free from the mental diseases such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth. || 3 ||
By the effort of self-reflexive awareness, the infant mind is protected;
it is joined to the real from the unreal, and it is also awakened.

It is protected—that is, it is guarded—by means of the treatment for diseases such as passion and fickleness; the phrase "having withdrawn from what is unreal" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. || 4 ||
O Sage, with a mind made steady through the study of the scriptures and the company of the virtuous, and scorched by the heat of contemplation,
cut through the iron-like mind with the very sword of the mind.
The form of the mind is like iron heated in a fire characterized by anxiety; cut it with the very instrument of the mind itself—iron that is unheated and free from the fever of passion.
Just as a child is effortlessly directed here and there by various objects, so too is the mind within; what, then, is difficult about this? (6)
By means of dispositions such as fondling, terrifying, and other such methods.
One should apply the mind, through its own conscious effort, to a virtuous deed that brings about a future rise of prosperity.

One should direct—that is, unify—the mind, which has entered into or undertaken the true practice characterized by the cultivation of meditative absorption, with the conscious self, the *cidātman*. || 7 ||
Fie on that worm of a man for whom the renunciation of his own cherished desires— which is entirely beneficial and within his own power— has become difficult to perform! (8)

He censures those who are not dispassionate with the words "svāyattam" (dependent on oneself). The abandonment of what one desires and the resulting awareness directed toward that [abandonment] is the function of dispassion (*vairāgya*). || 8 ||
Having meditated upon the forest as something delightful through one's own self-awareness,
the mind is conquered without effort, just as a child is subdued by a wrestler.
Having meditated upon the entire range of sense objects as being delightful in their ultimate nature, which is the form of Brahman. || 9 ||
By human effort, the mind is quickly conquered;
by the state of no-mind and without effort, the station of Brahman is attained. || 10 ||
The foot is placed upon Brahman; that is to say, Brahman is attained. || 10 ||
Fie upon those jackal-like men who are unable to accomplish that which is within their own power, easily achieved, and requires nothing more than the conquest of their own minds. 11.
The conquest and restraint of one's own mind is, for that time, sufficient. || 11 ||
Without the mere pacification of the mind—achieved solely through one's own effort and consisting in the renunciation of what is desired—there is no auspicious destiny. (12)
By means of the object to be accomplished, which consists solely in the slaying of the mind through self-awareness,
let that which is without rival, without beginning or end, and immovable be proclaimed here.

Through the self-awareness that is the direct realization of the reality of one’s own Self, let the bliss of self-sovereignty— which is without rival (being free from enemies such as delusion that oppose the happiness of one's own empire), therefore unwavering, immovable, and without beginning or end—
be declared here in this very body of one liberated while living; let it be realized without doubt.
The meaning is: "Let it be promised. || 13 ||
But apart from the pacification of the mind through the realization of what is desired,
methods such as the teacher’s instruction, the meaning of the scriptures, and mantras are like blades of grass.

The non-perception (*anavabhāsa*) is the non-manifestation of the desired external object. The "communication" (*āvedana*) of the desired bliss of liberation is either the means of reporting it or its verbal expression. The "reasons" (*yuktayaḥ*) are the means of proof.
Here, the intent is not to disparage the teacher’s instruction, but rather to praise the calming of the mind. || 14 ||
When the mind has been severed by the weapon of non-conceptualization and has come to rest, it then attains Brahman—entirely, omnipresent, and peaceful. (15)
The meaning is that it has gone, having been uprooted along with its very foundation. || 15 ||

In this teaching that dispels the calamity of conceptual construction, which is to be accomplished through self-awareness, what possible affliction can there be for a person when their body has become stilled? (16)
In the teaching—that is, the restraint—of that misfortune which consists of mental construction;

in liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), which is peaceful and endowed with the means for peace and so forth; here, in this body, the body of the qualified practitioner; there is affliction, which is suffering. || 16 ||
Surely, disregarding destiny—which is fashioned by the deluded thoughts of the mind—bring your consciousness to the state of non-mind through human effort. 17.
Now, one might ask: "If fate is adverse, how can there be success in one's undertaking? To this, he says: "Surely" (nūnam), etc. || 17 ||
Having long attained that certain great state—this very path—make the mind devoured by consciousness, and become even beyond the mind. 18.

Regarding the means for attaining the state of mindlessness (*acittatā*), he says: "That" (*tām*). Having caused the mind to attain—that is, to reach—that great state, which is the nature of Brahman, at the end, by means of the cognitive function of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra-vṭtti*), one causes the mind to be devoured by Consciousness (*cit*) once it has become manifest as the mind-with-mind (*samanaska*) through the sublation of ignorance (*avidyā*); thus, one becomes that which is beyond even the mind, consisting solely of full Consciousness (*pūrṇa-cinmātra*).
The meaning is "become. || 18 ||
Endowed with the cultivation of existence and joined with the supreme intellect, remain undistracted and sustain yourself; thereafter, restrain the mind that has been seized by external objects.

In that regard, first become engaged in the contemplation of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*); for the sake of its stabilization, become engaged with a mind (*dhi*) that is supremely and most attentively vigilant. Then, hold—meaning, establish—the Self, which is beyond the mind, within the mind that has been swallowed [by it], and nothing else. || 19 ||
Resorting to the supreme human effort and leading the mind to the state of non-mind,
attain that great state where no destruction exists.
O Rāma, the mind— which is like an immovable intellect characterized by the perversion of perception— can be conquered quickly only through manly effort.

Just as in the case of disorientation regarding the directions, the erroneous cognition that perceives the west as the east—though it is fixed and immovable—can be overcome by human effort characterized by discernment and stability, so too can the mind; this is the meaning. || 21 ||

Freedom from agitation is the root of prosperity; from freedom from agitation proceeds the conquest of the mind by a living being, by which the victory over the three worlds becomes as a blade of grass.

Lest one who has long been engaged in restraining the mind should abandon it out of weariness, he speaks to increase that person's enthusiasm, saying: "Freedom from agitation. This is the root of prosperity, such as sovereignty and other forms of wealth;
this is stated for the sake of illustration. The conquest of the mind proceeds—that is to say, it reaches fulfillment. || 22 ||
In that [state] where there is not even the slightest cutting by weapons or the occurrence of calamities, what distress can there be when only one's own nature has been set aside? (23)

In the pleasure of wealth there is the distress of being crushed by weapons in battle; in the pleasure of heaven there is the distress of the portents that precede death and the subsequent fall from it after one has died; but in the pleasure of mental victory, there is none at all—thus he says: "Not by weapons," etc. (23).
How will those lowest of men, who are incapable even of experiencing their own sensations when overcome by them, conduct themselves in the affairs of worldly life? (24)
The mind is that which experiences itself; [the suffix] *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). Its "assault" means its suppression. || 24 ||
"I am a man," "I have died," "I am born," "I live"—such are the false views; they appear as flickering fluctuations of the mind, arising from what is unreal. (25)

Because one does not experience the sufferings of birth, death, and so forth during states such as deep sleep (*samādhi*), and because those experiences occur only through the activity of the mind (*manovṛtti*) during the time of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), [the author] demonstrates that transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) consists merely of mental activity by means of the verse beginning with "pumān" (the person). They have arisen as something entirely unreal. Because it is a *karmadhāraya* compound, the first member [of the compound]...
Like the masculine. || 25 ||
No one here dies, nor is anyone born;
one knows for oneself that one's own mind has died and has reached another, its own world.
He demonstrates its very non-existence with the words: "not anything whatsoever" (na kaścana). || 26 ||
From here the mind goes to the next world, manifesting itself through its own transformation;
since this is its nature until liberation, whence can there be fear of death? (27)
May he wander through this world and the next;
his mind remains [fixed] until liberation, for no other form exists for him. (28)

"Let it wander and roam in this world by means of this world, with the nature of this world; and likewise in the next world, with the nature of the next world"—this is the ellipsis. Nevertheless, the mind alone remains in such and such a manner. The meaning is that no form of this saṃsāra exists apart from the mind. || 28 ||
When a brother, a servant, or another has died, false suffering is inflicted;
it is my conviction that this is one's own mind, whose nature is turned away from its own consciousness. (29)
And thus, he states that grief and the like are also merely attributes of the mind, which is distinct from the consciousness of the Self—by the words "when dead.

"Affliction" (kleśa) means grief. The meaning is that one's own mind itself, which has turned away from its own unchanging pure consciousness and is differentiated as the Self, takes on the form of its own modifications. || 29 ||
230. While the pure, extensive, and wholesome [path] exists, apart from the pacification of the mind,
one has repeatedly investigated [it] across, above, and below.

Concluding by means of the verse beginning with "sati," he establishes through elimination that the destruction of the mind along with its root is the sole means to liberation, and nothing else, within the Supreme Self: "sati" [means] existing as that whose existence is independent of anything else; "pathye" [means] beneficial to all; "śubhre" [means] free from the impurity of *māyā*; "ṛte" [means] as revealed by the *Śruti*, the preeminent among the means of valid knowledge.

Since the state of consciousness within the Supreme Self is the mind (*citta*), and because of its pacification—which is characterized by the remaining of that state alone—there is no other means to liberation apart from the pacification of the mind. The word "yāvat" is used for emphasis; the meaning is that there is simply none other.

This has been determined by the perceivers of reality after investigating it above in the higher worlds, below in the worlds such as Pātāla, and horizontally all around in other continents; this is the connection with what follows. || 30 ||
Indeed, there is no means whatsoever for the pacification of the mind other than when the true, expansive, pure awakening has arisen within the heart. (31)

And when the mind has dissolved, purified by the ripening of meditative absorption (samādhi), the means [to liberation] is precisely the realization of Brahman as the Self, which has become manifest through direct perception; with this intention, he says: "Except for the Truth.
"Except" (ṛte) means in that which is uncontradicted (abādhye). || 31 ||
Through the mere dissolution of the mind, rest arises;
it expands within the space of the heart by means of the support of the wheel of consciousness in pure awareness.

The connection with the subsequent [verse] is as follows: "Kill the mind" by means of the wheel-edge characterized by the final mental modification (*caramavṛtti*), within the heart-space—which is exceedingly vast and consists of the form of the small space (*daharākāśa*)—that is, within the consciousness (*cit*) which is Brahman. || 32 ||
Kill the mind without hesitation; then mental afflictions shall not bind you.
If what is pleasant has been perceived by you as unpleasant through knowledge, [then it will no longer bind you]. (33)
"Anxieties"—mental sufferings—will neither bind you nor will they bind you in the future.
With the intention that one must first achieve the perception of lack of delight by investigating the defects in sense-objects that appear pleasant at first sight, he says: "If... (verse 33).
"It is my view that those very limbs belong to the mind; 'this is I,' 'this is mine'—the mind consists of nothing more than this. (34)
Having stated that the limbs are to be severed by the mind, he speaks of the body: "This is I.

This visible body produced by the father is "I"; and this—house, field, and so forth, which belong to the body—is "mine," meaning it was previously acquired by the father and others. Such is the delusion, and it consists of nothing more than this.
The meaning is that the mind is of this much extent, namely, the size of the body. || 34 ||
By the mere non-contemplation of that [object], it is cut away as if by a sickle;
like a mass of clouds severed in the sky, it is dispersed in autumn. (35)
In this way, the mind is thus consumed by the wind alone through its lack of conceptualization;
wherever there are weapons, fire, or wind, there fear arises.

Just as a mass of clouds is dispersed and blown away by the wind, in that very way the mind is dispersed by the previously mentioned non-conceptualization of "I" and "mine"; this is the meaning. || 36 ||
What fear can there be for one who is composed, gentle, and pure, and free from conceptualization?
That "this is better" or "this is not" remains unimpaired from childhood until death.
"Soft" means not hard; that is to say, easily accomplished. "Established" means well-known. || 37 ||
One should employ the mind in the noble and supreme good, as one would a young son;
those who slay that mind—the lion that is inexhaustible, peerless, and the nourisher of worldly existence—are victorious here, for they bestow the state of Nirvāṇa. (38)
He states what is well-known: "the child" (*bāla*). "Inexhaustible" (*akṣaya*) means incapable of being destroyed. "Not lowly" (*anava*) means not childish.

Those who slay the lion characterized by the mind (*cetas*), they conquer; that is, they exist with supreme excellence. The meaning is that they become bestowers of the state of *nirvāṇa* upon others as well. || 38 ||
Terrors that cause agitation and begin with the crushing of one's intentions are produced like mirages in a desert. (39)
"The mind alone is the great fear; the conquest of the mind alone is the foundation of fearlessness," he says in two verses beginning with "The terrible ones" (39).
Let the winds of the end of the aeon blow, let the oceans become one, and let the twelve suns scorch; for one who is free from the mind, there is no injury. (40)
From the seed of the mind arise pleasure and pain, the auspicious and the inauspicious;
these are the fragments of saṃsāra, the sprouts of the seven worlds. (41)
The forest groves are the *khaṇḍakas*. || 41 ||
Abiding firmly in that state, remain in the sovereign realm of non-conceptualization, which is accomplished solely by the mere absence of thought and bestows all perfections. 42.
Remaining as one who has firmly seized and supported that lion-throne of the supreme state of the Self, abide in the empire of non-conceptualization. || 42 ||
As the mind gradually wanes, it bestows supreme bliss, just as the embers of wood that has been consumed grant satisfaction to one seeking the extinction of those embers. (43)

Now, one might ask: "How can the bliss of the mind's dissolution be accomplished by mere non-mental-conception (*asaṃkalpana*) alone? To this, he provides an illustration with the word "kāṣṭha" (wood): Just as for a person seeking the cessation of embers—who desires the pleasure of the subsiding of heat through the destruction of burning coals—there is the removal of the wood, whereby the embers are extinguished.
The meaning is that just as a burning coal, whose constituent parts have gradually turned to ash, bestows the bliss of the subsiding of heat, so it is in this case. || 43 ||
Even if a hundred thousand Brahma-cells are the object of one's mental desire,
they are clearly seen, distinct and separate, within the space of an atom.

He says "even" (api) to indicate that when the power of volition (*saṃkalpa*) increases, even the conceptualization of hundreds of thousands of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) can be accomplished within the interior of a single atom of consciousness (*cidaṇu*). "Brahma-cottages" refers to the cosmic eggs; if they are "desired," meaning sought after through volitions. (44)

Having conquered the mind by means of the power of contentment alone— [the mind] which creates great calamities through the power of mere volition and accomplishes its goals through the power of mere volition—
Conquer through that which is eternally arisen and free from desire. || 45 ||
That mind by which the objects of existence, such as millions of cosmic eggs, are perfectly accomplished through its own power characterized by mere volition (*saṃkalpa*),

and by which, through that very power of mere volition, great calamities such as birth, death, and hell are likewise created— that [mind] is [stilled] by means of that which is eternally arisen, continuously cultivated, effortless, and free from volition.
Having conquered Vijaya through the power of mere contentment, come and attain supreme excellence. || 45 ||
By that supreme purity, by that state of mental detachment, by that equanimity esteemed even by the knowers of the Self,
and by that internal "I-ness" which has been stilled and measured;
May that which remains be the unborn state. || 46 ||

By means of that "I-ness" (ahaṃtā)—which is approved by the consensus of those who know the Self, which functions without partiality, which is pacified, cast out, immeasurable, and yet like fire—may that very unborn state, devoid of modifications such as birth and remaining as the sole residue within, be your goal; this is expressed in the imperative mood as a benediction. 46.
Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Medical Treatment of the Mind," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of the Mind," in the Utthāna-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa.
(389) Chapter One Hundred and Twelfth (112): The One Hundred and Thirty-Second [Chapter].
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For upon whatever object, by whatever means, and in whatever manner,
the mind endowed with intense spiritual urgency beholds it, that which is desired is seen.

In this regard, the means for the destruction of the mind is held to be the abandonment of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), through the practice of the impression of pure consciousness alone and through firm resolve fixed upon that alone. (1)

In order to explain that for the sake of exhausting latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the intense momentum of the mind toward dualistic objects must be restrained, while that same momentum must be directed toward the form of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), he states the mind's inherent nature of producing results according to its own intense momentum, beginning with the words "In which...
(*yasmin*). [The meaning is: in whichever object, by whichever desired motive, and in whatever manner...
The meaning is that the mind becomes intensely possessed of a powerful impulse toward that object, whereby one perceives each and every desired thing within it. || 1 ||
This intense agitation of the mind arises and perishes;
it is causeless by its very nature, like a series of bubbles on gentle water. (2)
O gentle one, it is born through indifference; it dies and is stilled through the effort of cessation. Therefore, the meaning is that its arising is without cause. || 2 ||
Coolness is like that of frost, and blackness is like that of collyrium; restlessness is the very nature of the mind, possessing forms both intense and non-intense. (3)
He clarifies what was stated as "by way of intrinsic nature" with the words: "coldness," etc. (verse 3).
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, how can the force of this exceedingly restless mind— which has its sole cause in its own momentum— be forcibly restrained from its flickering?
The word "vega" (impetus) is explained as "calatā" (mobility). This is the primary and principal cause of impetus, that is, of intense velocity. || 4 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Nowhere in this world is a mind seen that is devoid of restlessness;
restlessness is the inherent nature of the mind, just as heat is the nature of fire.
For know that this flickering power of vibration, which resides within the essence of consciousness, is the mental power whose nature is the manifestation of the universe.

The nature of consciousness (*cittatva*) is the sentience conjoined with the *māyā* that is the cause of the universe; the power of vibration (*spandaśakti*) residing therein is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). The meaning is that one should know that [power] as mental, having transformed itself into the form of the mind (*manas*). || 6 ||

Just as the very existence of wind cannot be conceived apart from its movement and stillness, so too there is no existence of the mind apart from its flickering vibration. (7) *Note:* *Sattā* means "existence" or "being. *Nohyate* means "is not conceived" or "is not perceived. (7)
That mind which is devoid of restlessness is said to be "dead";
that alone is austerity, the established conclusion of the scriptures, and is called liberation.
Through the mere dissolution of the mind, the cessation of suffering is attained;
through the mere mentalizing of the mind, supreme suffering is attained.
The rakshasa of the mind, having arisen, produces intense suffering;
therefore, with effort, cast it down for the sake of infinite enjoyment and happiness. 10.

It is "for infinite enjoyment" (anantabhogāya), that is, for the bliss of liberation, because it manifests as if being enjoyed in such a way that it is infinite—devoid of the three kinds of limitations. || 10 ||
O Rāma, this very flickering state of his is called ignorance;
destroy it, which is known by the name of latent impression (vāsanā), through inquiry. 11.

It is called *avidyā* because it has the seed-power of the quality of passion (*rajas*). Regarding the term "named by the word *vāsanā*": since this falls under the scope of the prohibition [of the feminine suffix] by the rule *ano bahuvrīheḥ*, the application of the suffix *ṅīp* by the rule *ana upadhālopinaḥ* is only optional. || 11 ||
Through that ignorance, through that latent impression, and through that internal existence of the mind—once these have dissolved by virtue of renunciation, the supreme good is attained. (12)
By virtue of renunciation, through the power of abandoning the pursuit of external objects. || 12 ||
That which lies between existence and non-existence, and between consciousness and insentience— that, O Rāma, is called the mind, appearing as if oscillating between the two.
Having thus established the mind's nature of restlessness through its utility as an object of description,

[the author] says "That which... in order to demonstrate the rejectability of the unreal portion within its dual nature of both real and unreal, and to prevent the consequence of the destruction of its established real nature.

The interval between existence and non-existence is of the nature of a union; for this very reason, when either aspect predominates, it takes on a swaying form and remains in a state of instability. (13)
For, by the power of firm practice, the mind— struck by the contemplation of dullness and kindled by its own nature as dullness— indeed attains the state of dullness.
Why, then, does he speak of resting in one of the two extremes? He says, "By dullness," in two verses. [The word] *iddhayā* means by that which has grown firm. || 14 ||

Through the exclusive pursuit of discernment, the mind, by virtue of its nature as a portion of consciousness, attains oneness with consciousness here in this world by the power of firm practice. (15)
It is understood that [the mind] is kindled by virtue of having consciousness as its essence. || 15 ||
By means of human effort, whatever state the mind is directed toward,
that very state is attained through practice.
By means of effort, whether it be natural or scriptural. || 16 ||
Furthermore, relying on human effort and mastering the mind with the intellect,
take refuge in the sorrowless state and remain steadfast, free from doubt.
O Rāma, if the mind is not withdrawn by the mind itself from its immersion in worldly existence, there is no other means to forcibly uplift it. 18.
The other [is] "tattata. || 18 ||
The mind alone is capable for you in the firm restraint of the mind;
for who other than a king would be capable of restraining a king, O Raghava? (19)
For those seized by the crocodile of craving in the swift current of the ocean of saṃsāra, and being carried away by its whirlpools, one's own mind alone is a boat far removed from danger.
For those being carried away and swept along at a distance, the boat is the crossing. || 20 ||
Having severed with the mind alone the mind— that bond which is the supreme fetter—
he by whom the self has not been liberated shall not be liberated by any other means.
Whatever latent impression (vāsanā) called "mind" arises, having perfumed the interior, the wise person should abandon each and every one of them; thereby, the destruction of ignorance occurs.
That which is called "mind" (manas) is so designated because it contemplates external objects; the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied as before.

One should avoid it—that is, one should cast it out—by means of the contemplation of its falsity. The sense is that just as fire is extinguished when its heat is exhausted, so too ignorance perishes along with the mind when latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are destroyed. || 22 ||
Having abandoned the latent impressions of the flood of enjoyments, abandon the latent impression of duality;
then, having abandoned both existence and non-existence, become free from conceptual construction and happy. (23)

He describes the sequence for the abandonment of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) with the words "the flood of enjoyments" (*bhogaugha*). The meaning is that existence and non-existence are the mind and its objects;
their abandonment occurs through the reversal of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). || 23 ||
The non-cultivation of cultivation is indeed the exhaustion of latent impressions;
this alone is called the dissolution of the mind and the destruction of ignorance. (24)
Fearing that even upon the abandonment of the mind and its objects, the ignorance that is their cause might remain, he says: "non-contemplation" (*abhāvanam*).

That veil of ignorance by which [reality] is not contemplated—that is, is not experienced in its fullness—is abandoned through the contemplation of the direct realization of truth (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*); "be happy" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 24 ||
Whatever is perceived as an object of consciousness, therein non-perception is supreme;
for non-consciousness is nirvāṇa, while suffering arises from consciousness. || 25 ||

Alternatively, whatever is perceived by the witness—whether directly or through the medium of the mind—the non-perception of that very perceptibility in each instance is the supreme, most excellent nirvāṇa of the dissolution of the mind; this is the summary.
Thus he says: "Whatever... (verse 25).
By that very effort of one's own, the non-contemplation of existence is realized by a person in an instant; therefore, one should constantly practice that for the sake of prosperity.
And he says that this non-perception of the object of knowledge arises from human effort—by means of the word "by oneself.
The non-contemplation of an entity is the non-perception of the object of knowledge. One should constantly bring about and practice that through one's own effort.
(26) Those [qualities] such as passion which are desired by the mind...
Having realized here that those various things are insubstantial,
and having abandoned them— thereby rendering the seedless sprout of that [existence]—
do not fall into joy or sorrow, but remain satisfied.

Having restated what was said, he concludes with the words "rāgādayaḥ" (passion and so forth). Those objects in which you take delight in your mind are "rāgas" (passions); by the word "ādi" (and so forth), their means and desired things are included. Having realized those various [objects] to be of the nature of misfortune (*anartha*), those passions and so forth are like sprouts emerging from the mouth of a seed; that [mind] of yours is of such a kind.

The meaning is as follows: having abandoned even the mind—which possesses eight seeds—along with the seeds of the latent impressions of ignorance, and being satiated by the nectar of the experience of the Full Self, the wise man does not undergo joy or sorrow; for it is said in the Śruti: "The steadfast one, realizing this, casts off both joy and sorrow. (27)

Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth canto, titled "The Narration of the Section on Instruction by Mukharava," in the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, belonging to the Divine, the Supreme, and the Ultimate.
Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth canto, titled "The Narration of the Portion of Instruction by Mukharava," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and thirteenth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Indeed, this latent impression (vāsanā) which has arisen is eternally unreal.
Therefore, O Rāghava, it is appropriate to abandon [the notion of self], just like the delusion of seeing two moons. || 1 ||

The realization of reality, which uproots all evil latent impressions through various forms of inquiry, and which is firmly established in the understanding of the falsity of duality, is described here. || 1 ||
Whatever arises from whatever cause, being indeed unreal, it is proper to abandon and refute that very thing on account of that cause. || 1 ||
Ignorance exists, as it were, among those whose wisdom is lost; since its non-existence is accepted only in name, how could it exist among those of perfect wisdom? (2)

Among those whose wisdom has perished and who are devoid of discernment and higher knowledge, that [ignorance] exists as something more firmly established than even ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*). However, among those with correct wisdom, it is accepted as a mere name—like the son of a barren woman—because it does not exist and is not ultimately real. Therefore, how could it [exist]? 2.
Do not be ignorant; be wise and investigate thoroughly, O village-dweller!
There is truly no second moon in the sky; it is perceived in vain through delusion.
Therefore, he says "Do not be... (verse 3), meaning: accomplish the state of knowing reality itself through inquiry.
In this [reality], apart from the ultimate truth (tattva), there exists no entity whatsoever, whether real or unreal,
just as in the vast ocean garlanded with waves there is nothing other than the mass of water.
Reality is the supreme self; existence is a thing, and non-existence is a non-thing. || 4 ||

Apart from your own conceptual construction, do not superimpose these entities— neither existent nor non-existent, neither being nor non-being— upon the Self, which is eternal, unchanging, pervasive, and pure.
In *asite*, which is devoid of bondage to the body and so forth; [the root] *ṣiñ* means "to bind," with the suffix *kta*. || 5 ||
You are not the doer; why then do you have this sense of "mine" regarding these actions?
For when there is only the One, what is done by whom, and how?

Since bondage has its root in the state of being an agent, he says "nāsi" (you are not) [in verse 5], instructing one to first abandon that very state. He explains: "in the One, the non-dual. The sense is that an action accomplished by a single agent alone is nowhere well-known. || 6 ||
Or rather, O wise one, do not become a non-doer; for what is desired is achieved through non-action?
That which is to be accomplished is indeed to be accomplished and is to be undertaken; therefore, O sinless one, remain established in yourself.

Do not be a non-doer who yet possesses the conceit of being a non-doer. When such a conceit is formed regarding an endeavor performed through non-agency, what fruit remains to be accomplished—that which is to be acquired, attained, or achieved through one's own effort? The meaning is: none at all. || 7 ||
O scion of the Raghus, because you are unattached, you are indeed the agent when there is existence;
yet because of that very non-attachment, even as a non-agent, how can there be vibration, as if you were an agent? (8)

Existence (*bhāva*) is identification (*abhimāna*); in the absence of that, because of non-attachment, one is a non-doer (*akartā*). Thus, even while being a non-doer, because of non-attachment even toward that state of non-doership due to the absence of identification, one is also a doer (*kartā*). If it is asked, "In that case, am I a doer like an ignorant person? he says: "Like a doer" (*kartṛvat*). This refers to you who perceive the Self as motionless (*aspanda*).
The meaning is that, unlike an ignorant agent, there is no possibility of agency characterized by the delusion of the Self’s own vibration through the movement of the body.
If it were real, it would be something to be accepted; if it were false, it would simply be something to be abandoned.
Indeed, attachment to action is appropriate only because of one's exclusive attachment to what is to be accepted.
Strengthening [his position] with reasoning—that since the falsity of the fruit of action renders attachment to karma itself untenable—he says:
"It is true," etc. (9).

Where the entire world is a magical illusion, consisting of *māyā* and devoid of substantial reality, what basis can there be for views concerning what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted? How indeed could such perspectives exist? (10)
He shows the conclusion of the counter-argument for one who has presented the reasoning: "Where... etc. The words *yatra* and *tatra* have the sense of *yarhi* and *tarhi*. || 10 ||
O descendant of Raghu, this seed-syllable of saṃsāra is indeed ignorance;
for though it does not exist, it has attained expansion as if it were real.
If it is asked, "Whence this illusion (indrajāla)? he says, "Because of its being rooted in ignorance (āvidyaka)," [in the verse beginning] with "saṃsāra... || 11 ||
This wheel of the undertaking of saṃsāra, which is full of effort yet devoid of essence—this is to be known as the latent impression (vāsanā) of the mind, which bestows delusion. (12)
Like a beautiful bamboo stalk, it is hollow within and pithless at its core;
like a row of river waves, though not yet severed, it is destined to perish.
He describes in detail the very wheel that initiates cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), which is of the nature of ignorance, beginning with the words "beautifully" (*cāru*) and so forth.

The phrase "hollow within" (*antaḥśūnya*) is explained as "having a core devoid of essence" (*niḥsārakoṭarā*). Even though it is severed without the destruction of its root, it is not subject to perishability. (13)
Even when grasped with the hand, it cannot at all be held;
though soft, its tip is exceedingly sharp, like a rising wave from a mountain torrent. (14)
In the case of the "waves of the mountain torrent," it should be understood that she has a sharp point because of her cutting down of the trees on the bank. || 14 ||
It appears as a semblance of a wave, yet it is not employed for any real purpose; it is like a wave that is not a wave, being established solely in its own form. (15)

A "prakara" is a collection of causes capable of producing an effect; that which has an appearance like such a collection is its manifestation (*prathā*). Nevertheless, even though it possesses a real object—that is, a true purposeful activity (*satyārthakriyā*)—in the case of the river, this refers to activities such as bathing and drinking. However, it is "without waves," meaning it is like a dream-river devoid of actual waves.

Like a river of mirage-water, its own form is one that shines merely as a perception; it is "perfected" or "completed" in that very [perception] alone, meaning it does not exist in terms of causal efficiency (arthakriyā). || 15 ||
In some places crooked, in others clear; long, short, stable, or moving—since they arise through his grace, they have attained their distinctness from him. (16)

He elaborates on her very own form with the words "in some places" (*kvacid*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: by the grace of that Goddess whose wheel is being described, all things—having arisen (*udbhavāḥ*), meaning having become manifest (*āvirbhūtāḥ*)—have reached a state of distinction (*vyatirekam*), that is, mutual difference (*parasparabhedam*). || 16 ||
Though empty within, that beautiful essence is seen everywhere;
though not established anywhere here, it is perceived in all places.
Though consisting of consciousness, she is as if inert, subsisting on the movement of another;
not remaining still for even a moment, she gives rise to the suspicion that she is stable. 18.
She subsists on the movement of others and the fickleness of the mind; such is her nature.
Though its pure color is like a flame, its hollow is soiled with soot;
it leaps up by the favor of another, for it is given [its light] by looking toward that [other]. (19)

Though her complexion is pure by virtue of the quality of *sattva*, she has a hollow darkened by soot due to *tamas*. By the grace and presence of another, the Supreme Self, she leaps and moves; yet, through his gaze—that is, through direct realization—she is dissolved (*dīyate*), meaning she is shattered. [The root] *do* is used in the sense of "shattering. (19)
Faded in pure light, she yet shines even in darkness;
like a mirage, her parched appearance sports with various colors. (20)
In the stainless light of one's own self, [ignorance] is withered because it acts as an obscuration. 20.
Crooked, uneven, slender, soft, yet narrow and harsh;
fickle like a woman, greedy, and thirsty—thirst is like a black female serpent.

He describes that very same [suffering] even in the form of craving and so forth—starting with "the crooked" (vakrā). Because it is the cause of distress, it is harsh (karkaśā). Like a wanton woman (lalanā), it is fickle (cañcalā). It is a female serpent (bhoginī) because it is a viper (sarpiṇī). || 21 ||
Like the flame of a lamp itself, it quickly perishes when the oil is exhausted;
like a streak of vermilion powder, it shines brilliantly even without redness. (22)
Even without the oil of passion, she shines with redness like a streak of vermilion powder. || 22 ||
Flickering in its momentary flashes, assuming various forms, and resting upon dull matter, it arises like a crooked lightning bolt, striking terror into the simple-minded. (23)

"Established by a dull expectation," meaning she has secured her position through a lack of intelligence; alternatively, because of the non-distinction between the letters *la* and *da*, it means "established in a cloud" (jala-āśayā), that is, having taken up residence in a rain-cloud. || 23 ||
Having been seized with effort, it burns; having come into being again and again, it dissolves away.
For even when sought, it is not found, being as exceedingly fragile as a flash of lightning. (24)
It burns; that is to say, it culminates in the suffering of torment. In the case of lightning, this is clear. || 24 ||
Though delightful, that which comes unasked brings misfortune;
it is not welcomed as a blessing, like a garland of flowers out of season. (25)
Even a garland of out-of-season flowers brings misfortune because it is an omen of ill omen.
Excessively indulged for the sake of great pleasure, this [desire] brings about delusion;
when reflected upon, it leads only to misfortune, like the perception of a bad dream. (26)
"Speculated" means being repeatedly investigated through logical reasonings. || 26 ||
By the power of her manifestation, she creates these three vast worlds in a mere moment, sustains them, and then devours them.
By her, a single moment was made into a series of years for Lavaṇa,
and a night was fashioned to last twelve years for Hariścandra.
By her grace, for others who are separated from their beloveds yet possess the splendor of their wives, the night shall become as long as a year. (29)
By whose grace time becomes short for the happy and long for the suffering—time, which is characterized solely by its reversal [of states]. (30)
Error is delusion for those men whose character is solely devoted to that [delusion]. || 30 ||
In these activities, its agency exists by its mere presence, just as a lamp [is the agent] of the effects of light; yet that is not so in reality.

He demonstrates his own position—that even ignorance (avidyā) is merely the instrumental cause for the superimposition of the world-appearance upon Brahman by its mere proximity, and not its material cause—by saying "of this" (asyāḥ). || 31 ||

Just as a woman with breasts and buttocks, though appearing in a painting, is not a woman possessing female characteristics, so too this contemplation of form is incapable of accomplishing anything at all. (32)

If it is asked, "Why does she not possess agency?", he says: "Because of her unsuitability," namely, "possessing hips" (*sanitambā*). This means she is a woman subject to feminine characteristics, capable of performing household duties and so forth. The "contemplation of form" (*ākāracintā*) consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of objects previously experienced.
This is ignorance (*avidyā*). || 32 ||

Though it may possess hundreds of thousands of treatises and be radiant in its form, it is devoid of truth—like a kingdom of the mind—and from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is nothing at all. (33)
He states that very point clearly: "It is a kingdom of the mind. || 33 ||
Like a mirage in the forest, it is entirely false and full of ostentation;
it deceives only those deluded deer and not human beings.
Like a mass of foam, it arises and perishes; it is devoid of continuity, inert, flickering in form, and when grasped, it is nothing at all.
It is born and perishes as soon as it arises; it is devoid of interruption and is eternal in its flow; it is insentient, like a mass of mist. (35)
Moving with a terrifying form, grey with the spreading of dust, she forcibly pervades the interior of the world like the whirlwind at the end of an aeon. (36)
Like a column of smoke clinging to the body, causing the distress of burning, it pervades the worlds, having internalized the sequence of aesthetic flavors (rasa). (37)
She by whom the supreme self (paramātman) and water are contained within as her essential flavor (rasa); for this very reason, she moves about, traversing, advancing, and overwhelming the worlds. 37.
Like a very long stream of water produced from a cloud,
this firm rope of unsubstantial saṃsāra is woven from a multitude of grasses.
Firm amidst the insubstantial and fragile worldly existences and the conditioned tendencies of transmigration—therein lies this illustration: (p.
392) 232 Like a garland of water-lilies upon a wave, it is described as being merely a mental construction.
Like a lotus stalk, it is full of many holes, matured in mud, and composed of water. || 39 ||

Described by poets through mere imagination as a garland of waves or a garland of lotuses, she is mature in both sin and mud; she consists of water and she consists of dullness (jaḍa), for there is no distinction between the letters *la* and *ḍa*. 39.
People see her as intent on prosperity, yet she does not truly increase;
like the taste of poison, sweet at first but extremely terrible in the end. (40)
The tasting of poison is like the tasting of poisoned water. || 40 ||
Like the flame of a lamp that has gone out, this [consciousness] is lost; I know not where it goes.
Like a mist seen at close range, though it is perceived, it is nothing at all.
"I do not know. The meaning is that it is impossible to determine the true nature of that which has been sublated, even by thousands of disputants;
"mihikā" refers to a mass of mist, frost, or smoke. || 41 ||
Like a handful of dust scattered away, this atomic state has been observed;
it appears as nothing more than the blueness of the sky, utterly devoid of causal characteristics.
Born like the delusion of seeing two moons, its produced error is like a dream;
just as a stationary post appears to move to one traveling by boat, so too has this [delusion] arisen here.
When the mind is afflicted by this [ignorance], the delusion of the long dream of saṃsāra is constructed by people who are as if agitated for a long time. (44)
The word "iva" (like/as if) indicates falsity. || 44 ||
When one's own mind is afflicted by this [ignorance], various delusions arise and perish, like waves in the ocean. (45)
The meaning is: when [the Self] has been offered up within one's own self by this [practice], that is, when it has been rendered as if non-existent by the veil. || 45 ||
That which is pleasing and true is seen as both existent and non-existent;
that which is unpleasant and untrue is seen as non-existent even while appearing to exist. (46)
He states her power of perversion: "The agreeable" [means] the real Brahman; "the disagreeable" [means] the unreal world. || 46 ||
Mounted upon the chariot of the objects of the senses, this powerful mental construction swiftly assails the mind, just as a snare catches a bird.

Objects are the sense-objects; their form is the chariot, meaning its very configuration. This ignorance, consisting of manifest latent impressions (*vāsanā*), assails the mind—that is, it overcomes it—and having deluded it, binds it. || 47 ||
With eyes overflowing with compassion and breasts dripping with drops of milk, she becomes a mother whose joy is exultant, just like a housewife. (48)
He states that ignorance alone also assumes the form of the mother’s wife and so forth: "Compassion," etc. (48).
The lunar orb, though already exceedingly moist with nectar, quickly turns it into poison, having saturated the three worlds with its own outflow. 49.
Even the lunar orb, which satiates the three worlds with outpourings of nectar-fluids transformed into moonlight and the like, turns into poison. || 49 ||
Even the silent trunks of trees, through this blinding [dust], give rise to a frantic agitation as if for the commencement of a dance by Vetālas shrieking like madmen.
Because it blinds, it is called "blindness" (andhayā); by means of this [state] acting as a cause, even senseless logs— devoid of all activity of the organs of speech and action—
are made to produce, or give rise to, a frantic onset of dancing by mad ravens and vetālas in the forest.
This is the meaning. || 50 ||
And at times such as dawn and so forth, even clods of earth, stones,
and walls are seen by her through the gaze of a serpent or a python, by virtue of her grace.
By means of such delusions as the visions of serpents and pythons. || 51 ||
Just as a single moon appears as two when one sees two moons, or as one's own death occurs in a dream, so too does even a single thing arise as a duality. || 52 ||
Abhyāśatā means proximity. || 52 ||
Just as a desired night seems long at first but attains the state of a moment,
so too does a single moment appear like a year to those separated from their beloveds.
The night was dear to Kāla, the Rudra of destruction, like the night of universal dissolution.
"There is nothing here that this arrogant woman will not do; behold, O Raghava, the power of her who possesses nothing! (54)
Of one who possesses nothing, even in her own being, and is thus destitute. || 54 ||
One should diligently restrain consciousness by means of consciousness itself;
through the damming of the river's current, this river of the mind dries up.

"By *saṃvit* means by the intellect of discrimination (*vivekabuddhi*). [The word] *saṃvidam* means the cognition of objects. He states the fruit of its restraint with the words "like a river": the phrase "as a river by the blocking of its current" is to be supplied. || 55 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
By this utterly insignificant and fragile-bodied false imagination,
which does not even exist, the world has been wondrously made blind.

Thus amazed—astonished by his contemplation of the true nature of ignorance—Rāma describes her and acts out his wonder with the words beginning "By that which is indeed non-existent," and so forth. || 56 ||
By means of formlessness, by being devoid of a beautiful consciousness, and by being as if non-existent yet indestructible—how strange that the world has been rendered blind! 57.
Because it is mentioned separately from the generic form (ākṛti), the word "form" (rūpa) refers to blue and so forth. Like a mirage-river that does not exist, it perishes without ever drying up. 57.
By the light of the owl’s gaze, which flickers within the darkness and perishes as it does so,
the world has been wonderfully blinded.
The glance, the eye of Kauśika, was like that [glance] belonging to the woman who possessed those qualities.
It is strange that the world has been blinded by her who performs only evil deeds, who cannot endure being looked upon, and who is unaware even of her own body. 59.
Because she rests solely upon the power of action, she is exclusively devoted to evil deeds;
because she is devoid of the power of knowledge, she does not even recognize her own body. || 59 ||
The world has been wondrously blinded by her who is of exceedingly base conduct and character, eternally beloved by the vulgar, and who never ceases to set [into the darkness]. (60)
By the lovely and charming Prakriti; by the beloved wife of the ordinary person (pṛthagjana); and by her having set, being unreal, and being obscured by darkness. || 60 ||
Where the world has been rendered blind by this [ignorance], which is always as if dead, agitated by infinite suffering, and devoid of awakening—how strange! (61)
By one who is dead or as good as dead. || 61 ||
The world was wonderfully blinded in no time by that bodiless [darkness], which was the offspring of desire and anger and followed the crooked course of the spreading gloom. 62.
Before long, there was the arising of knowledge and the slaying by an incorporeal voice.

By this insentient [nature], which has as its locus the form of its own self, which is worn out by dullness, and which utters long lamentations of suffering—the world has been wondrously blinded. (63)

In these five verses, through the use of punned adjectives and the figure of speech *samāsokti* (implied metaphor), a certain wretched female night-stalker—a woman who is the abode of delusion, being blind regarding her own true self—is understood as the point of comparison. (63)
By this impassioned activity, which clings to attachment to men and flows forth toward desires for speech, man is wonderfully rendered blind.
With the following three verses, he describes her as a wife who is adverse to the *puruṣa*—beginning with the word "puruṣa": "Of the *puruṣa*" means:
through attachment (*āsakti*), which is non-attachment (*asaṅga*) due to the superimposition of identity; thus, she is "one who is attached to the *puruṣa*.
Through the activity of imagining various and diverse objects, she brings about the enjoyment of the *puruṣa*; thus, she is "one who is devoted to the *puruṣa*."
She who flees from the investigations into her own true nature within the various intentions of speech.
It is a marvel that a man is blinded by a woman who is a mere veil, and who is not even capable of enduring his gaze. (65)
"Īkṣita" means direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). It is called "āvaraṇā" because it covers (*āvṛṇoti*); the suffix *lyu* is applied here according to the rule for the *nandī* group of roots. || 65 ||
A man is wonderfully blinded by that harsh woman who possesses no consciousness at all, yet perishes even while remaining unperished. 66.

O Lord, by what means does this incomparable [samsara] dissolve— this which produces endless and difficult-to-restrain diversions, and which partakes in pleasure and pain oriented toward decline and rise?
The latent impressions are bound within the cave of the mind.

Concluding the description of ignorance (*avidyā*) consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he asks about the means for its eradication with the verse beginning "ananta-": "duṣprasara-vilāsā" refers to the delusions of wicked conduct; "kṣayodayonmukhāni" refers to pleasures and pains such as death and birth, which are prone to rise and fall; "bhājayati" means she brings about or distributes these; and "tacchīlā" means having that as her nature. She is "asamā" (unequalled).
It is uneven; by what means does it dissolve, that is, perish? || 67 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Ignorance," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Ignorance," in the Utthāna-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the *Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The one hundred and fourteenth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
Indeed, dense is the [suffering] of a person, arising from the expansion of ignorance.
O Brahmin, how indeed shall this great blindness be destroyed? || 1 ||
In this context, the means for the destruction of ignorance is said to be the vision of one's own Self;
and the nature of the pure Self is such that, through the absence of volitional thought (*asaṃkalpa*), there is the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). (1)

Having asked about the means for the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he now asks about the means for destroying the veil of ignorance (*avidyā*) which is their root, beginning with the word "ignorance" (verse 1).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as a drop of frost perishes in an instant from the sight of the sun, even so, O Rāghava, does this ignorance vanish through the contemplation of the Self.

Thus questioned, Vasiṣṭha first explains the means for the destruction of ignorance with the words beginning "Just as": "First, it causes the embodied soul, together with its own self, to oscillate within the pits of saṃsāra, which are filled with the dense thorns of suffering. (2–3)

In the mountain precipices characterized by the nature of saṃsāra, it causes the embodied being—who possesses the ego and the conceit of a body—to oscillate, tossing him down further and further. || 3 ||
As long as ignorance has not arisen for him— that which brings about its own destruction—
there remains within himself the desire to perceive the Self, which bestows the total exhaustion of delusion.
O Raghava, for her who perceives that which is beyond [this world], her own destruction comes to pass, just like that of a shadow seeking to experience the sunlight.
The Supreme Self. || 5 ||
When all-pervading awakening is seen, it dissolves by itself,
just as the shadow of desire arising from all hopes vanishes when the twelve suns have risen.
Just as when the multitude of twelve suns has risen in all directions and quarters, so too is the shadow.
In this world, ignorance is merely desire; its destruction is called liberation.
And that, O Rāghava, is accomplished simply by the absence of volitional thought.
Having explained the means for destroying causal ignorance (*kāraṇāvidyā*), he states the means for conquering its effects (*kāryāvidyā*) with the word "icchet" (one should desire).

Regarding "tannāśa" (its destruction): thus says the Śruti: "When all desires that dwell in his heart are liberated, then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7) || 7 ||
Even slightly, when the night of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in the sky of the mind comes to an end, the darkness diminishes due to the great rising of the sun of consciousness. (8)
Vāsanā is the latent impression of desire; kālimā is the veil of ignorance. || 8 ||
Just as the night vanishes somewhere when the sun has risen,
so too does ignorance dissolve somewhere when discernment has arisen.
Through firm latent impressions, the bondage of the mind reaches density,
just as a child's conceptualization of a ghost arises by force at the time of twilight.
The phrase "of the child" implies that he is one who has been thoroughly permeated by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of a *vetāla*. || 10 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brahman, whatever is seen here is ignorance, and that ignorance is destroyed by the contemplation of the Self. Of what nature is that Self said to be?"
The question is clear. || 11 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That reality of consciousness which is free from the pursuit of objects of thought, which is universal and all-pervading, and which is inexpressible— that is the Self, the Supreme Lord.
The pervasion of objects is the entry into all that is objectified; that which is devoid of this is [the state].

Because it is the cause of all objectified things, ignorance (avidyā) is the universal (sāmānya); and by that, [the Self] is abandoned. This means it is the "obscuration without distinction" (*nirviśeṣāvaraṇa*)—[the reading *nirvikṣepāvaraṇa* is also found]. || 12 ||
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, whatever this world is—all that is always the Self alone; O sinless one, ignorance does not exist.

To ward off the doubt that this is impossible, he elaborates upon the sublation (*bādha*) of ignorance along with its effects therein, beginning with the words "From Brahman" (*ābrahma*) and so forth. || 13 ||
Indeed, all this is Brahman—eternal, a mass of consciousness, and unimpaired;
no other mental construction called "mind" exists at all. (14)
Nothing whatsoever is born or dies here in the three worlds;
nor does the existence of the modifications of being exist anywhere. (15)
Only the absolute, appearing as the absolute, the undifferentiated universal and unimpaired,
pure consciousness devoid of any object of thought, exists here.
It is the universal commonality, the form of existence that pervades all things. || 16 ||

233. In that which is eternal, pervasive, pure, consisting of consciousness alone, free from affliction, peaceful, characterized by an even distribution of experience, and whose self has arisen as changeless— (17).

That which, having itself conceptualized what transcends its own nature, runs [after it], and which, though consciousness (citi) and its object (caitya), withers away by itself—that is known as the mind (manas). || 18 ||

In that Self, this consciousness—which is withered and veiled—having itself conceptualized an object of thought (cetya) whose nature is contrary to the essence of consciousness, such as insentience and limitation, and which runs toward it, becomes "withered by distraction" (vikṣepamlānā);
the meaning is that this is known as the mind (manas). || 18 ||
From this all-pervading deity, the Great Soul who possesses all powers,
the power of differentiation has arisen like a wave from water.
From this god Mind. || 19 ||
In that one, vast, and peaceful [reality] where nothing exists,
she attained perfection within the Supreme Self through mere volition alone.
That which is cyclic existence. || 20 ||

Therefore, this accomplishment born of mental resolve perishes by resolve alone; by that very thing through which it was produced, just as a flame of fire is extinguished by the wind. (21) Regarding "by the wind": the sense is based on the Vedic scripture, *From wind comes fire*. (21)
The hope for enjoyment, having attained the form of success achieved through human effort, dissolves away by mere non-mental-construction; that is ignorance. 22.
By the mere absence of volitional thought, accomplished through the human effort of the maturation of profound meditation (nididhyāsana) and established in direct realization. || 22 ||
The mind is bound by the firm conviction that "I am not Brahman"; the mind is liberated by the firm conviction that "everything is Brahman. (23)
And thus, since both bondage and liberation are properties of the mind alone and not properties of the Self, he says: "Not 'I'..."
Volition is the supreme bondage, while the absence of volition is liberation;
having conquered internal volition, do as you wish.
The meaning is that he has completely conquered the notion "I am not Brahman" by means of the knowledge established through the opposing notion "everything is Brahman. || 24 ||
There is no firm lotus pond here in the sky with golden lotuses, bees hovering over vaidūrya stones, and fragrant quarters of the sky. 25.

In this sky, that which does not exist is like a lotus; just as a child constructs a firm mental object for the sake of play through the power of desire (*manoratha*), so too is this twofold ignorance. Thus, like a web of conceptual constructions, though unreal, it appears as real to the foolish person (*bāla*); yet it leads to no happiness.
The connection with the fourth [verse] is that it was firmly grasped and imagined solely for the sake of extreme suffering. The epithets of the lotus (nalinī) are clear. || 25 ||
With her circles of lotus-stalk arms, their stalks erect and their fullness manifest, she seemed to laugh at the orb of the radiant moonbeams. (26)
In this way, the net of conceptual construction, though non-existent, appears as if real;
it is imagined by the mind for the sake of its own playful enjoyment with objects, just as it is imagined by a child.
In the same way, this ignorance here, which binds one to the fetters of existence, is fickle; though it is grasped firmly by the fool, it leads not at all to happiness.
"I am emaciated," "I am extremely miserable," "I am bound," "I possess hands, feet, and so forth"—it is by such worldly conduct, corresponding to these notions, that one is bound. (29)
He elaborates on the different conceptualizations of bondage with the verse beginning "kṛśa" (emaciated). || 29 ||
"I am not suffering, nor do I have a body; for what self could bondage exist?"—by such conduct in accordance with this realization, one is liberated.
"I am neither flesh nor bones; for I am other than the body, the Supreme.
One who possesses such certainty within is said here to be one whose ignorance has been destroyed.
He shows the conceptualization of the means to that liberation: "I am not," etc. (30–31).
Or perhaps it is the splendor of darkness standing above, possessing the luster of the vaidūrya peaks on the summit of the lofty divine mountain, yet difficult to pierce even by the rays of the sun.
He states another illustration for the conceptualization of ignorance and so forth, beginning with the words "prottuṅga" (highly elevated).

According to the view of the author of the *Yogabhāṣya*, it is said that the radiance of a peak composed of *vaidūrya*—a specific kind of blue gem—spreads all around and appears as the blackness of the sky. He also states this according to the view of astronomers, beginning with "athavā" (or else).

Just as the beauty— that is, the dark luster— of the darkness previously described, which is situated near the shell of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and is impossible to dispel due to its distance from the rays of the sun,
is imagined by a person standing on the earth to be the "blackness" of the sky; so too is this [ignorance] imagined through its blazing [power].
The meaning is that it is imagined through one's own conceptual construction. || 32 ||
For just as blackness is imagined in the sky by a person standing on the earth, impelled by his own volition, so too is this [imagined] by nature. (33)
Thus, O Rāghava, this ignorance is merely imagined as the conception of a self in that which is not the self; it belongs to the unawakened person, not to the awakened one.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brahman, this is neither the shadow of the sapphire on Mount Meru nor the radiance of darkness; tell me, what is the cause of this blueness of the sky?"

Because the blue color of the sky would result in the appearance of blueness even in autumn clouds and water-masses due to their proximity to sapphire, because an excess of blueness would be perceived further away,

and because the appearance of redness and other colors could not be avoided due to the light from the peaks of Mount Meru— which are composed of rubies and other gems— there is no decisive evidence [to favor one view over another]; thus, the assumption of a "conjunction" (yogika) is not tenable.
Because the upper and lower hemispheres of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) consist of gold and silver respectively,
it is stated in the Purāṇas that "that egg was made of gold, possessing a splendor equal to a thousand suns";
thus, as one ascends higher and higher, the cosmic egg is heard to possess great luminosity.
Because the space up to the shell of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa-kharpara) is pervaded by the worlds beginning with Satyaloka, which are increasingly more luminous,

and because it is impossible for darkness to exist in the midst of this due to the irresistible penetration of the sun’s rays when there is no obstruction, [darkness exists] in a most remote region inaccessible even to the sun’s rays that travel to the furthest distances.

This is not the case, because it is impossible to conceive that the range of vision for those such as ourselves could extend [that far]; because darkness is not observed to act as an obstruction when stars and other celestial bodies are seen at night; because it would follow that even the shell of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa-kharpara) would be visible; and because it would entail the undesirable consequence of seeing the intervening worlds, such as Satyaloka, and their celestial palaces.
Thinking that even the astronomical hypothesis is logical, Rāma sets aside that position and asks about the true nature of the sky's blueness: "Meru... (verse 35).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Indeed, blueness does not exist as a quality of the void sky;
nor is this [blueness] derived from the light of other jewels, nor is it the radiance of Mount Meru.

Restating the very arguments intended by Rāma, Vasiṣṭha himself demonstrates the impossibility of both positions, beginning with "no": because other gems such as rubies lack such luster, the same applies to the sapphire radiance belonging to Meru (the Mairavī); that too does not exist. || 36 ||
Because the cosmic egg consists of light, like the expansion of fire itself,
and because the far reaches of the egg are luminous, there is no possibility of darkness existing here.
Having rejected the first position, he rejects the second with the words "because it consists of light" (*tejomayatvāt*).

The word *iva* is either meaningless or indicates well-known usage. "Because of its luminosity" means because it is pervaded by light on all sides. "The limit of the egg" refers to the limit of the space contained within the cosmic egg. || 37 ||
O fortunate Agni, only this emptiness (śūnyatā) is perceived in these [elements],
which is unreal and conforms to ignorance, like a companion suited to it. (233.38)

Having thus restated the two opposing views, he states the established conclusion (siddhānta) with the words "kevalam" and so forth: "She who is perceived as a vast, extensive, and like-minded companion or friend of ignorance. || 38 ||
When there is the perfection of the destruction of one's own vision, darkness arises precisely before the eyes;
due to the nature of things, that is perceived as the blackness of the sky. (39)

The meaning is this: when there occurs a deficiency—that is, a remote state of impairment—of the eyes' own vision, their inherent power of seeing, then that object which by its very nature arises as "darkness" or non-perception is perceived as the blackness or blueness of the sky. || 39 ||
Having understood this, just as the blackness seen in the sky does not give rise to the cognition that it is "blackness," so too is the darkness of ignorance. (40)
This is the illustration; "understand it to be so" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 40 ||
For the wise have declared that the absence of mental construction is the suppression of ignorance;
yet it appears as easy as [the growth of] a lotus in the sky. (41)
Having concluded this incidental discussion, he returns to the subject at hand with the words beginning "asaṃkalpa" (absence of volitional thought).
The meaning is that this absence of volitional thought appears easy to accomplish, not difficult. || 41 ||
O holy one, for this worldly delusion that has arisen like the color of the sky, I consider its non-recollection to be better than mere forgetting. (42)
Intending this very point, he says "of the delusion," referring back to what was previously promised. || 42 ||
Just as one perishes through the thought "I am destroyed" out of sorrow, so indeed does a person attain happiness through the thought "I am awakened. (43)
In a dream, one perishes through suffering; yet upon waking, through the resolve "I am awake," there is happiness and the disappearance of the dream-suffering. (43)
Thus, from the resolution of one who is utterly deluded, the mind indeed attains a state of delusion;
but from the noble resolution of awakening, it hastens toward awakening.
For the sake of awakening—that is, for the state of Brahman whose sole essence is consciousness. || 44 ||
For this eternal ignorance arises from a momentary recollection, whereas that which is perishable perishes within through forgetfulness. (45)

"From recollection" means from the conceptualization "I am ignorant. The phrase "eternal" is intended to indicate that, although beginningless due to the presence of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), its beginninglessness is itself imagined at the very moment of its manifestation; thus, there is no contradiction with its being eternally liberated.
"From forgetfulness" means that through the uprooting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of conceptualization, it becomes perishable and eternally destroyed. (45)
She is the nourisher of all states of being and the deluder of all creatures;
she is the bearer when her own self is destroyed, and the destroyer when her own self increases.

In the destruction and non-perception of one's own self, it is "heavy," meaning exceedingly weighty; that is to say, [it is heavy] in the case of the growth of one's own self, which is the attainment of an undivided nature. || 46 ||
Whatever the mind intends to connect, all the functions of the senses accomplish that in an instant, just as ministers carry out the command of a king. (47)
To the question, "Even when the mind is restrained, how could the arousal of latent impressions (vāsanā) by means of the senses not occur? he says: "The mind... (verse 47).
Therefore, he who does not direct the mind toward external objects attains peace through internal conscious effort. (48)
The internal conscious effort is the contemplation of "I am Brahman. || 48 ||
That which did not exist in the beginning does not exist even today;
that which shines here is Brahman—peaceful, one, and beyond reproach. 49.
He demonstrates that very internal mode of conscious effort with the words beginning "yad" (that which), etc. (verse 49).
Therefore, there is nothing else to be contemplated—never, for no one, in any way, or from any source. Remain without constraint in that which is changeless, without beginning or end.

Therefore, there is nothing other than Brahman. By the four interrogative forms (*kiṃvṛtta*), the temporal relations, modes, and causes are excluded. It is "without restriction" (*apayantraṇa*), meaning free from limitation, that is to say, in its fullness. || 50 ||
Relying on supreme human effort and with the highest intelligence,
one should diligently uproot from the mind the desire for enjoyments along with its very roots.
That supreme delusion which arises as the cause of old age and death—that is the manifestation of latent tendencies (vāsanā) flourishing through hundreds of snares of hope. (52)

Supreme delusion is one's own ignorance; that very ignorance is the cause of old age, death, and so forth. Whatever arises in the form of an effect, all that is merely the unfolding of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and is not a real entity—this is the meaning. || 52 ||
"My sons, my wealth, this is I, this is mine"—thus this very latent impression (vāsanā) leaps about like a magical illusion (indrajāla). 53.
In this very empty body, which is as flickering as wind upon water,
the serpent of ego-sense has been placed by means of a singular latent impression (vāsanā).

Just as a serpent is imagined in water by means of a wind-wave, so too is the serpent characterized by the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) imagined within the Self by means of latent impressions (vāsanā). || 54 ||
O Knower of Reality, from the perspective of ultimate truth, such notions as "I," "mine," and "this" are quite enough;
apart from the reality of the Self, nothing whatsoever is ever truly real.
For him who knows reality and is discerning, both "I" and "mine" are sufficient [only] through the vision of the ultimate truth;
the meaning is that they do not exist at all. || 55 ||
Mountains, oceans, the earth, and rows of directions—through the repeated creation of vision, this very ignorance, or something else entirely, revolves in its manifold variety. (56)
