The compound "khaṃ ca adrayaśca dyauśca urvī ca nadīśreṇyaśca" (the sky, mountains, heaven, the broad earth, and rows of rivers) is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound. [This occurs] through a creation simultaneous with the act of seeing. The sense is that, according to the perspective of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), the doctrine of "creation upon seeing" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*) alone is established in the scripture. || 56 ||
It arises through mere ignorance and perishes through mere knowledge; it is to be eliminated within the Pure Being alone, just as the perception of a snake is removed from a rope. (57)
It is to be severed on all sides, possessing a threefold delimitation. || 57 ||
O Rāghava, this ignorance which exists for the ignorant person is like the ocean, the earth, and the rivers;
but for the wise one, there is no such ignorance, for that Brahman remains established in its own majesty.
This is a collective dvandva compound beginning with *khādi*. The feminine gender is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*). This which is ignorance belongs to the ignorant;
for the knower, ignorance does not exist. The meaning is that this "khādi" is Brahman itself. || 58 ||
The two conceptualizations of the rope and the snake are imagined only by the ignorant;
by the wise, however, there is determined only the one, uncreated vision of Brahman.
There are two types of conceptual constructions: the conventional and the apparent. The [ultimate] is uncreated and self-established. 59.
Do not be ignorant; be wise. Abandon the latent tendencies of saṃsāra.
Why do you weep like an ignorant man by perceiving a self in that which is not-self? 60.
O Rāghava, what is this dull and mute body of yours?
For its sake you are helplessly overwhelmed by pleasure and pain. (61)

The delusion of selfhood in the body, which is non-self, is indeed the root cause of all suffering; therefore, he first wards it off with the word "Who" (ka). Because of its insentience, [the body] is mute, being a non-governor of speech and other faculties. || 61 ||
Just as there is no identity between wood and lacquer, or between a jujube fruit and its bowl, even though they are joined together, so it is with the body and the embodied self.
*Jatu* means lac.

By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even though they are joined," it is indicated that for those who are not at all joined and upon whom non-attachment is superimposed, unity is utterly cast away. || 62 ||
Just as when a bellows is burned, the fire does not belong to the air within it, so too, upon the destruction of the body, the self is not destroyed. 63.
He states that because the self is bodiless (*videhatva*), there is not even the possibility of birth, death, and so forth, in the verse beginning with "The bellows" (*bhastrā*). || 63 ||
"O scion of the Raghus, realizing that the delusion 'I am suffering' or 'I am full of happiness' is like a mirage, abandon it and take refuge in the Truth. (64)
Oh, how strange it is that the truth, which is Brahman, has been forgotten by men, while that which is unreal, called ignorance, has surely come to their memory! (65)
O descendant of the Raghu line, do not grant scope for ignorance;
when the mind is obscured by this, there is suffering here in this world that is difficult to cross.
From ignorance, which is the forgetting of the self, comes improper seeking and ill-spoken words; it is difficult to cross and difficult to transcend. 66.
Having churned it with this mind— full of mental cogitation,
productive of misfortune, bestowing suffering, and culminating in the fruit of great delusion— (67)
He elaborates upon how ignorance produces thousands of improbable calamities with the words beginning "mithyaiva" (only falsely).
The connection with the following verse is: "By this [ignorance], even in the orb of the moon, the suffering of burning and desiccation is experienced.
Even though the lunar orb is moist with nectar, one constructs the notion of the Raurava hell within it.
The suffering of burning and desiccation is experienced in hell. || 68 ||
In lakes where the waves of water, the spray of kahlāra flowers, and the ripples abound, the nature of a mirage is perceived. (69)
The word "by this" (anayā) is to be supplied here and also in the following verse. || 69 ||

In dreams and other such states, various experiences that bestow pleasure and pain are undergone, such as the agitation caused by the creation, falling, and rising of celestial cities in the sky. (70)
Even if the latent impressions of saṃsāra do not fill the mind, could the frantic activities of waking and dreaming lead one to calamity here? (71)
One should not fulfill [this], such is the remainder [of the sense]. Then what? One should lead oneself [to that state], such is the remainder. || 71 ||
When false knowledge has increased, the hells of Raurava, Vīci, and Anarthaśāsana are seen within the dream-landscapes of the groves. (72)
There is instruction and torment when false knowledge has increased. || 72 ||
Pierced by this [wisdom], even for a moment, the mind perceives the delusive miseries of the entire ocean of worldly existence, even within a single lotus fiber. (73)
For when the mind is corrupted by this [passion], people remain even in sovereignty who are such that they would not be fit even for the outcaste dog-cookers (śvapāka). (74)
They are not suitable; they are not appropriate. || 74 ||
Therefore, O Rāma, having abandoned the latent impression that binds one to worldly existence and consists of all forms of passion, remain free from passion like a crystal. 75.
All passion is the coloring of all dualistic forms; it consists of that. || 75 ||
While you remain engaged in your duties, let there be no attachment to passions,
just as a crystal takes on various reflections without being stained by them.
In matters, that is, in legal affairs; in passions, that is, in objects of attachment; *rañjanā* means attachment. || 76 ||
If you always act with excellent conduct, having understood the assembly of curious people and being enriched by them, with a noble intellect that has abandoned vulgar behavior—
With whom can you, O city, be compared? || 77 ||

Those by whom Brahman—which is the supreme curiosity because its nature is unsurpassed bliss—has been known are "those who have known the curiosity"; they are the knowers of reality (*tattvavidaḥ*). In their assembly or gathering, through repeated inquiry, [the mind] is kindled by the lamp of the firm conviction of the identity with Brahman (*brahmāhaṃbhāva*), which has become more intense; for this very reason, it is everywhere...

If you always act and conduct yourself with equanimity, excellent conduct, noble intelligence, and a mind free from attachment, then you are one for whom the ordinary activities born of ignorance and the delusions of birth, death, and so forth have departed and vanished; that is to say, your essential nature is eternally liberated. At that time—

By what liberated soul (jīvanmukta) of great power—whether by Brahmā, Hari, or Hara—are you compared? You do not attain comparison with them. The compound *na asti* [with a verbal form] is Vedic (*chāndasa*). It may somehow be construed either as *anupama ātmā iṣyase* in the passive sense with the suffix *kyac*, or as *anupama ivācarasi* with the suffix *kyaṅ*, where the Vedic shortening of the vowel (*itva*) is applied.

The reading "mahān upamīyase" (you are compared to the Great One) is straightforward. Furthermore, according to the statement in the *Chandaḥśikṣā*—"a heavy syllable preceding a conjunct, or even one before a conjunct preceded by a consonant [is light]"—one should not fear a violation of the meter in the phrase "gataprākṛtikaḥ.
Thus ends the [seventy-seventh] chapter in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya*, within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the work of the Sage.
The one hundred and fourteenth canto, titled "Instruction on the Avoidance of the Faults as Previously Described."

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Instruction on Avoiding the Faults as Previously Described," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and fifteenth canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Thus addressed by the venerable and high-souled Vasiṣṭha, [Rāma spoke].
Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, appeared as if he had just awakened.
The wonder of Rāma’s awakening, the persistence of the destruction of that illusion,
and the cause of the removal of the salt are proclaimed here as they were asked.
"Unmīlita" means blossomed; by implication, it is understood as "like a lotus. (1)
With his inner heart blossomed, he attained a pure splendor,
like a lotus that has been refreshed when the darkness has faded through the sight of the sun.
He states that very point clearly with the words "vikāsitā" (expanded): "āśvastaḥ" means satisfied by the attainment of composure. || 2 ||
With his face brightened by a gentle smile born of wonder at this awakening, he spoke these words, which were washed white by the nectar of the radiance from his teeth.
His face was whitened—that is, brightened—by a gentle smile born from the wonder inspired by [his] awakening.
Śrī Rāma said:
Oh, how wonderful! Mountains have been bound by threads produced from lotuses;
all things that do not exist have been brought under control by that which is non-existent.
By that which is non-existent, meaning absolutely non-existent. || 4 ||
This very world, though consisting of mere straw, has attained the state of a vajra within the three realms;
for even through ignorance, that which is non-existent appears as if it were existent. (5)

This very suffering of saṃsāra, which is being perceived here as well known, [is produced] by ignorance acting as its material cause (upādāna) or its limiting adjunct (upādhi)—the word "nāma" is used in the sense of "indeed" (kila). || 5 ||
Out of compassion, please describe once more the nature of this river of worldly illusion within the courtyard of the three worlds, for the sake of my awakening.
"Speak again for the sake of my awakening—for the sake of strengthening my realization—of that Māyā which is the root cause of saṃsāra, like a flowing river. (6)
O Great-souled One, there is another doubt that dwells within my heart:
what calamity did that illustrious Lavaṇa encounter?
"From what? means "from what cause? The word "nāma" is used in the sense of "it is said. (7)
When the body and the embodied soul are either joined together or struck [by one another], who among them is the transmigrating being that alone experiences the fruits of good and evil? (8)
He asks the third question: "Of the two joined together.

Whether they are joined like lacquer and wood, or whether they strike one another like wrestlers or rams—among the body and the embodied soul, which one is the single enjoyer of the fruits of good and evil karma? The meaning is: who is the primary experiencer? || 8 ||
Having thus brought about that unsurpassed calamity for Lavaṇa, where has that one of flickering undertakings gone, and who was this magician? (9)
The fourth question is clear. || 9 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, this body is like wood or a wall; it is nothing at all here, for it is merely imagined by the mind, like the vision of a dream.

Thus questioned, Vasiṣṭha—because of the excellence of his firmness in discernment—first answers the third question, which implicitly answers the first as well, with the words beginning "kāṣṭha" (wood). The meaning is that there is no such thing as a real entity [in the body]. And thus, because it is insentient and non-existent, the body [is not the Self].
The meaning is that there would be the consequence of being the enjoyer of the fruits of karma. || 10 ||
One should know that the mind, which has entered living beings and is adorned by the power of consciousness,
is as restless as a young monkey and causes the agitation of saṃsāra.

What then is the enjoyer? He says: "the mind" (*cetas*). He removes the defect of its insentience by saying: "the power of consciousness" (*cicchakti*); the meaning is that it has attained identity with the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). That which possesses *saṃrambha*—that is, intense attachment (*abhiniveśa*)—to the state of being an enjoyer within saṃsāra. || 11 ||
For the embodied being, subject to the fruits of its actions, assumes various forms of bodies;
it is designated by the names of ego, mind, and life-force. 12.
He states that this very [self] is the individual soul (jīva): "The embodied one," etc. (verse 12).
O Raghava, for one who is unawakened but not yet awakened, these endless experiences of pleasure and pain belong to the body; they do not belong to the Self at all.
The unawakened mind, through its conceptualizations fashioned by various perceptions, follows diverse modes of activity and assumes a manifold form. (14)
"Following various modes of existence" is the statement of the cause for the difference in names. || 14 ||
For as long as the mind is unawakened and remains asleep, it perceives agitation in a dream; once awakened, it never does so again.
And he states that its cause is non-awakening: "perceived as foremost" (agrabuddham). || 15 ||
As long as the individual soul, agitated by the sleep of ignorance, has not been awakened,
so long does it perceive the delusion of the world's inception, which is difficult to penetrate.
In one whose mind is fully awakened, all darkness dissolves, just as the interior of a lotus opens at the light of day. (17)
The "hārda" is that which resides in the heart. || 17 ||
That which is designated by the self-realized as mind, ignorance, mental life, and latent impression, and which is called the "karmic self," is the embodied soul that experiences suffering. (18)
He is an experienced enjoyer of suffering. || 18 ||
The body is insentient and not deserving of suffering; it is the embodied soul who suffers due to a lack of inquiry.
This lack of inquiry arises from dense ignorance, and ignorance is the cause of suffering. (19)
The living being has fallen into the domain of both auspicious and inauspicious phenomena due solely to the fault of lack of discernment, just as a silkworm is enclosed within its own cocoon.
The *kīṭaka* is the insect known as the silkworm (*kauśeyakośakāra*). || 20 ||
Bound by the disease of non-discrimination, the mind, possessing manifold fluctuations,
wanders like a wheel through its various forms of movement.
Bound and fettered by the disease characterized as lack of discernment. || 21 ||
It rises, it cries out, it kills, it eats, it moves, it leaps, and it reviles;
it is the mind alone within this body, never the body itself. (22)
He elaborates upon this very wandering [of the mind] with the words: "It arises," etc. (verse 22).
Just as a householder performs various activities within his home, yet the house itself is insentient, O Rāma, so indeed is the individual soul within the body. (23)
In all pleasures and pains, and in all mental constructions, know that the mind is the agent, the mind is the enjoyer, and the mind is the human being. 24.
The human soul. || 24 ||
In this regard, listen as I relate to you this supreme account of how that Lavaṇa, through a delusion of mind, attained the state of a Caṇḍāla.
He introduces the answer to the second question as that which establishes this [point], saying: "In this regard" (atra). || 25 ||
The mind experiences the fruit of its actions, whether auspicious or indeed inauspicious;
O Raghava, listen now to how you should truly understand this.
O sinless one, in former times, Lavaṇa, born of the lineage of Hariścandra,
while seated in solitude, reflected deeply in his mind for a long time.
"My grandfather was the officiating priest at a very great Vājapeya sacrifice;
born into his lineage, I worship that sacrifice mentally. (28)

It should be understood that when external requisites are unavailable—such as when there is oppression by a king and so forth—or when there is a lack of consent from ministers, priests, and others, one may perform the mental construction of a sacrifice in the form of the Rājasūya. || 28 ||
Having reflected thus in his mind and having prepared the necessary materials with great care,
the lord of the earth entered into the initiation for the Rājasūya sacrifice.
He summoned the officiating priests and honored the virtuous sages;
he invited the gods and kindled the sacrificial fire.
According to the desire of the sacrificer,
more than a full year passed within the garden while he honored the celestial sages and the twice-born.
Having given away all his possessions as a sacrificial fee to the beings, beginning with the twice-born,
the king woke up at the end of the day in his own grove.
"Awaken" means "attain external vision"; the absence of the augment *a* (in *vibudhyata*) is a Vedic archaism. "Sve" means "one's own. || 32 ||
Thus King Lavaṇa attained the Rājasūya sacrifice;
for he was endowed with a satisfied mind and possessed its fruit.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "it ought to be endowed with its fruit. || 33 ||
Therefore, know that the mind is the man who experiences pleasure and pain;
O Rāghava, apply that mind to the truth, which is the means of purification. 34.

Therefore, for that reason, regarding the means for the purification—that is, the cleansing—of the mind through reflection, restraint, and so forth: the mind itself is the agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of the predominance of its power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and it is the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the action (*kriyā*) as well. That very [mind], having transformed into the nature of the fruits of pleasure and pain, is the fruit itself; and the mind alone, through the pervasion of the reflection of consciousness (*cid-ābhāsa*), becomes the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) by virtue of the predominance of the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*).

And "experience" (bhoga)—meaning that the very flow of the states of being agent and enjoyer is the essential nature of the river of Māyā—should be understood as having been indicated by this section, even though it was the subject of the first question.
As for the fourth question, he will resolve it in the subsequent creation. || 34 ||
When the body is whole, the person is fully complete; when it is destroyed, he perishes.
O wise ones, enough with those who hold the conviction, "I am the body. (35)
Having thus consoled Rāma, [the author] summarizes the meaning described in detail to the gods and other members of the assembly, saying:

"In the Full," and so forth. O wise ones, this Person in the form of Manu—*pūrṇe* means in that which is devoid of limitations such as time; *deśa* means the locus or support, because it "gives" (*diśati*) its own nature; in that [locus]...

Established [in the Self], one becomes complete. However, when that which is eternally perishable and limited—the locus of the body and so forth—is destroyed, one who is established in it perishes through the attainment of its nature. Therefore, enough with those for whom there is the certain conviction of a perishable ego-sense such as "I am the body"; the meaning is that there is no purpose [in them]. || 35 ||

When the mind, possessed of lofty discernment, is fully awakened, the sufferings of one whose intellect is purified utterly dissolve; for indeed, when the cluster of lotuses is revealed by the rays of the sun, they wither away.
The darkness of contraction and dullness has been destroyed for a long time. || 36 ||
He summarizes: "Loudly.

When the mind has become fully awakened—possessing lofty discrimination (*viveka*) through the ripening of correct inquiry preceded by the scriptures and the teacher, and having firmly established the distinction between the essential and the non-essential—one realizes: "I am never of the nature of the body and so forth."

However, when there arises the perfect awakening that "I am indeed Brahman, whose sole essence is self-luminous full-bliss," then for such an eligible person who has become one with Brahman— by whom even the mental fluctuations of the intellect have been sublated through the awakened consciousness kindled by discriminative discernment— all sufferings have utterly and completely dissolved along with their roots for a long time.

The meaning is that these never occur at any time. Just as in a cluster of lotuses revealed by the rays of the sun, contraction, budding, coldness, withering from frost, and darkness—the internal and external gloom within the calyx—are long destroyed and vanish; such is the meaning. || 36 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Experiencer of Pleasure and Pain," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the sacred work of the Seer.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth canto, titled "The Instruction on Being the Experiencer of Pleasure and Pain," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The one hundred and sixteenth canto.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord, it is said that Lavaṇa indeed obtained the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice."
What kind of means of valid cognition could there possibly be here in this deceptive net of conceptual constructions?

Because the meaning described in the resolution of the fourth question serves as an illustration, the stages of yoga (yogabhūmi) are therefore introduced here along with their introductory context. || 1 ||

Desiring to know the answer to the fourth question, Rāma asks for the authoritative proof supporting it within the answer to the second question, saying: "The fruit of the Rājasūya. [This refers to] the *Jālaśambara*, which consists of the king Lavaṇa’s fabrication of states such as being a Caṇḍāla, a magical net displayed by a magician.

An undesirable result has been obtained through the performance of the Rājasūya sacrifice. Regarding what is said here "kila"—that is, by way of tradition—what indeed could be the proof for this matter? The word *iva* is intended to indicate the impossibility of such proof. First of all, it is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is impossible for Lavaṇa himself to know, "This is the fruit of my own mental Rājasūya."

The meaning is that because the logical marks (*liṅga*) pervaded by that [object] are themselves unestablished, it cannot be known either by that [mark] or by others; consequently, neither the word rooted in that nor *aitihya* (tradition) can apply there. However, if the reading is "the web of conceptualization in the sky," the construction is: "in the sky"—that is, in the space of the mind—there is a result consisting of a web of conceptualization. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the magician arrived at the assembly hall of Lāvaṇī at that time,
I was dwelling there and witnessed it with my own eyes.

Vasiṣṭha provides the resolution with the verse beginning "yadā" (when), [arguing that] although other people have no access to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that matter, nevertheless, by the power of yoga, it is directly perceived by himself; thus, the renown of others is rooted in that very perception. || 2 ||
Then, when that sorcery had vanished, I was questioned with effort by the members of the assembly and by Lavaṇa, who asked, "What is this? (3)
"Śāmbara" means "possessing the art of Śambara"; [the term refers to] one whose deeds or conduct are of such a nature. He was questioned by the members of the assembly and by Lavaṇa. || 3 ||
Having reflected and seen it there, I have now spoken of it;
listen, O Rāma, as I declare to you the purpose of the Śāmbarika. || 4 ||

"Having seen"—the remainder is "by the power of yoga. Having resolved the incidental question, he promises the resolution of the previous fourth question, saying: "Listen"—[to] the intention (abhiprāya) of the magician. || 4 ||
For those who perform the Rājasūya sacrifice undergo for twelve years the suffering of calamity, consisting of various forms of pain and disease. || 5 ||
Therefore, O Rāma, that divine messenger, appearing in the form of a juggler, was sent by Śakra from the sky for the purpose of causing distress to Lavaṇa.
Having bestowed the supreme station upon that performer of the Rājasūya sacrifice,
he departed by way of the sky, which is frequented by gods and Siddhas.

The phrase "great calamity" (mahāpadam) means a calamity lasting sixty years, which is five times greater than the twelve-year calamity resulting from the physical Rājasūya sacrifice. By this, it is understood that even the fruit of happiness such as sovereignty over heaven (svārājya) resulting from the mental Rājasūya and other rites is five times greater than that resulting from the physical one. || 7 ||

Therefore, O Rāma, this is indeed evident; there is no doubt in this matter. For the mind alone is the agent and the enjoyer of diverse activities. By rubbing and purifying that very mind, and by bringing this jewel of the heart to dissolution through discernment—like a speck of frost dissolving in the heat—you shall attain the supreme good.

Know that the mind alone is ignorance (*avidyā*), which creates the entire display of phenomenal beings. Under the influence of its various magical illusions (*indrajāla*), it brings this world into being. Knowing that there is no difference between the terms *avidyā*, *citta*, *jīva*, and *buddhi*—just as there is none between the words *vṛkṣa* and *taru* (tree)—you should perform mental construction (*vikalpana*) within the mind itself.

O Rāghava, when the solar orb of the mind’s stainlessness has risen, there is nothing that does not become visible, nothing that is not assimilated, nothing that is not relinquished, nothing that does not cease, nothing that is one's own,
and nothing that belongs to another; for everything becomes everything at all times.
The ultimate truth. || 8 ||

Concluding what has been said, he applies it to the present context with the prose passage beginning "Therefore" (*tasmāt*): "Having rubbed [the mind] away by means of *haṭhayoga*, having purified it by means of *rājayoga*, and having brought it to a state of dissolution through non-conceptual absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*), you shall attain the supreme good—liberation—by means of discernment (*viveka*), which is the direct realization of reality. This is the *Vicitraka*.

By means of that which is the very nature of the composition of various paintings, like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*) consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), perform a conceptualization that is free from conceptualization. The remainder of the sentence is: "The removal of darkness will occur. However, it is not the case that upon the dissolution of one's own mind or the destruction of one's own ignorance, there is merely the cessation of the effects of one's own ignorance acquired through one's own unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

One might object that it is not the case that everything is seen, because one's own mind and so forth—which are effects of one’s own unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—cannot be the cause of [the experience of] another’s unseen merit. Anticipating this, [the author] states: "Everything is the effect of everyone’s unseen merit and is to be enjoyed by everyone.
Thus, because of the vision of one’s own Self as being identical with all, everything becomes seen; indeed, everything is assimilated as one's own.

With the intention that there is no room for doubt here—namely, that "everything is abandoned" and "everything is killed"—he says: "That does not exist. To the question "Why is that so?", he replies: "Because nothing belongs to oneself.
For everything belongs to oneself and everything belongs to another, since everyone becomes everything at all times.

The meaning is that this is the state of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). And thus, the *Madhubrāhmaṇa* Śruti is well-known, beginning with: "This earth is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this earth," and so forth; such is the intention. || 8 ||
Likewise, the entire mass of existent things and consciousness attain the state of a single lump, just as a collection of various unbaked clay vessels remains [as one] when placed in water. (9)

Therefore, he concludes with the verse beginning "The mass of entities" (*bhāvarāśi*), stating that through the awakening produced by the maturation of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there remains only the nature of Brahman as a single essence (*ekarasa*) for the mind, its effects— the manifold world (*prapañca*)— and ignorance (*avidyā*).

The mass of existence—the collection of perceptible objects—and likewise the consciousness consisting of various mental modifications directed toward them, as well as every individual soul conditioned by that [consciousness], attain the state of a single lump, which is the single-flavored nature of Brahman. The word *apakva* (unripe) should be understood as a separate term [meaning "not yet digested" or "not yet fully realized"]. || 9 ||
Śrī Rāma said:

"O Great-Souled One, you have stated that when the mind is thus completely dissolved, the end of all happiness and suffering is attained; how then does the non-existence of this mind, which is characterized by a flickering nature, come about?"

Having restated the entire purport of the Guru’s instruction and demonstrating it, Rāma, considering the eradication of the mind to be impossible through the means devised by his own intellect and reasoning, desires to know another means for it and asks in prose: "Thus... (10).

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O moon of the Raghu dynasty, listen to the method for the pacification of the mind, by knowing which you will attain a state of mental composure that stands far beyond your own habitual conduct.

Vasiṣṭha promises to explain that means with the words "O moon of the Raghu dynasty": "The mind's union" (manaḥsandhiḥ)—the stream of mental fluctuations—should be directed toward Brahman, which is "far from their activity," meaning outside the range of the senses, each of which has its own external sphere of operation. (Note: the term *manaḥ* is used here because of the non-distinction between the letters *ra* and *la*).
Through reconnection, you will reach or attain dissolution. || 11 ||
For here, first of all, it has been previously stated that the threefold origin of all beings proceeds from Brahman. 12.
Now, one might object: "How can the destruction of that which has never been known to perish at any time throughout beginningless saṃsāra be even conceivable?

Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states the following previously mentioned [verse] in order to demonstrate the possibility of its destruction by showing, through its nature of transformation (*pariṇāmin*), its similarity to other elements such as the earth, and to establish the fact of its destruction occurring from time to time.
He reminds us of the threefold creation of living beings according to the division of *sāttvika* and so forth, with the words "For here," etc.

The ellipsis is to be supplied as "the previously mentioned [creation] is to be remembered. Although twelve types of living beings were previously stated, nevertheless, because those twelve are included within the threefold division of *sāttvika* and so forth, it is described as "threefold."

Alternatively, they are threefold according to the distinctions of the internal (ādhyātmika), the divine (ādhidaivika), and the elemental (ādhibhautika). It has also been stated previously that in all these three types of creations, the root cause is the mind belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha, and the other minds follow its volitions.

In this regard, through its very first mental construction, that [consciousness], which is of the nature of Brahman, becomes composed of volition (*saṃkalpa*) and thinks, "Let there be a body. Whatever it then conceives, that very thing it perceives; by means of that, this grand display of the worlds is constructed. || 13 ||

In this regard, the dissolution at the end of a kalpa of the mind of Hiraṇyagarbha—which has transformed into the form of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) through the variety of its own volitions—is well known; and since the dissolution of its material effects is observed, it can be inferred that the mind itself possesses the nature of dissolution. Thus it is with the mind as the root cause.

With the intention that, once the nature of dissolution has been determined, that [nature] can be conceived as existing even in the minds of ourselves and others by virtue of having an identical nature, he says: "In this regard, by the very first," and so forth.
"The first" means the primordial. "The embodied one" refers to that which is of the nature of Brahmā, thinking "I am the body in the form of the four-faced one."
The intention is that conceptualization, which has the Creator as its true nature, perceives that very [object] because of its power of true volition (satya-saṃkalpatva). || 13 ||
There, conceptual construction (kalpanā)— which imagines the cycle of transmigration consisting of birth, death, pleasure, pain, delusion, and so forth—
having remained for a long time with many names and forms, dissolves of its own accord like a drop of frost when it encounters sunlight. 14.

He states that even the saṃsāra consisting of birth, death, and so forth for beings such as ourselves is merely His conceptualization— thus he says, "therein. Within the kalpas, which consist of a thousand cycles of four yugas, during His own days, having remained for a long time in a manner that is slow and exceedingly heavy, He exists through the many names of the gods, asuras, and others, who are fashioned by various arrangements suited to each [kalpa].
When Viṣṇu lies upon his serpent-couch, [the individual soul] dissolves into him of its own accord, just as a drop of frost dissolves into its own cause, fire, when it encounters heat. || 14 ||

Arising in accordance with time through the power of volition, it is born again as something else; that too dissolves, and yet it arises once more as that very same thing—thus, wandering on again and again, it subsides of its own accord. || 15 ||

Furthermore, when arising at the time of creation, having manifested from the lotus of the Lord's navel, that previous conception is born again in another form—through another cycle and another creation—and it dissolves again at the end of that cycle, only to arise once more. Thus, she continues to transmigrate until the exhaustion of the *prārabdha* karma pertaining to her office; upon its exhaustion, [she attains liberation].
From the self-established realization of the Self, at the conclusion of two parārdhas, [saṃsāra] subsides of its own accord along with its very root. || 15 ||
In this manner, infinite millions of Brahmās have passed away in this cosmic egg and in others, and there will be others yet to come;
indeed, they are infinite, such that even their number cannot be known. || 16 ||
Thus, the perishable nature of other mental faculties belonging to Hiranyagarbha is also established by valid means of knowledge;

this is stated with the words beginning with "ittham" (thus). It should be understood, according to the method previously explained, that even within this single cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), there exist conceptions of tens of millions of cosmic eggs for every single atom. || 16 ||
236. Thus, while this [state] is occurring in such a manner, listen to how the individual soul (jīva), having come from the Lord (Īśvara), lives and is liberated. || 17 ||
Just as the collective minds are nourished and pacified by the knowledge of meditation achieved through human effort, so too are the individual minds of living beings nourished by the volitions,
latent impressions, desires, and karmas that serve as the seeds of birth and death.

With the intention that the destruction of the mind (*manonāśa*) is not impossible because [the mind] is pacified through the excellence of the practice of the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), he elaborates upon the transmigratory cycle of the living being (*jīva-saṃsṛti*)— from the time of creation up to the conception of liberation—
in both brief and detailed forms, beginning with the words "In this [cycle]... In this...

While that aforementioned collective conception exists within such a Supreme Self, the individual soul—the *vyaṣṭi-jīva*—lives (*jīvate*, *jīvati*). The transposition of the verbal suffix and the root is a Vedic archaism. || 17 ||

The mental power of Brahmā, having arisen and supported itself upon the power of space situated before it, follows the state of the wind residing therein and attains the condition of dense volition. || 18 ||
Desiring to explain the meaning briefly indicated in the aphorism, he first elucidates the portion beginning with "having come from Īśvara":

"The power of the mind. At the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), due to the dissolution of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the power of the mind—which remains for the individual souls (*jīva*) who have merged into the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*) as mere latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—first [emerges] from the undifferentiated.

When the power of space (ākāśa-śakti), whose essence is the subtle element of sound (śabda-tanmātra), manifests, she— having first arisen and being supported by that which stands before her— herself also awakens; then, upon the production of the subtle element of touch (sparśa-tanmātra), whose essence is the power of air (pavana-śakti),
she follows the state of that air and attains a state of dense volition characterized by a slight capacity for movement.

Then, having attained the state of the five subtle elements (tanmātras) that had arrived before her, and having been led to the state of the internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa), she became the subtle Prakṛti consisting of sattva;
through the volition of assuming the forms of ether, air, and fire, she took the form of frost and [became] the rice-plant.
Entering [the body], she becomes the embryo of living beings. || 19 ||

Then, having first attained the state of the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) consisting of form, taste, smell, and so forth, and subsequently reaching the state of the five unevolved gross elements (*pañcabhūtas*), she leads [the individual soul] to the state of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—

namely, the designations of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and thought (*citta*)— thereby becoming the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the living being (*jīva*), which is the seed of worldly experience. Having reached that state, she...
The previously mentioned mental power (*manaḥ-śakti*), having become the subtle and accumulated fivefold-natured gross primordial matter (*pañcīkṛta-sthūla-prakṛti*),

and through the volition of taking on the form of the fivefold-natured ether, air, and fire, sequentially attains the state of frost and the form of water such as mist and rain, and then enters the medicinal herbs and crops such as rice and wheat.

Having become food and been consumed by men, it attains the state of semen and, being infused into the womb of a woman, undergoes the embryonic stage of living beings through the sequence of the embryo, the bubble, and so forth. || 19 ||
From that it is born; from that, the person (puruṣa) comes into being. || 20 ||
Therefore, one is born and produced from that; the meaning is that, at some point due to the preponderance of merit, a person becomes qualified for action and knowledge through that birth.
By that very person, as soon as he is born, the acquisition of learning must be undertaken starting from childhood.
The teachers should be followed. || 21 ||
"By that," and so forth, is explained by the words themselves (nigadavyākhyāta). || 21 ||
Then, in due course, a sense of wonder arises for the person as if within themselves. || 22 ||
Only through you does that very wonder arise—the perfection of the means such as discernment, dispassion, and so forth. || 22 ||

Through the vision of one's own clarity, there arises in the person—the nature of consciousness—a discernment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted regarding the fluctuations of the mind. || 23 ||

Through the vision of one's own clarity, there arises in the person the inquiry that the misfortune of worldly existence must be abandoned from the mental fluctuations, and that the means to liberation must be adopted. || 23 ||
When a person endowed with such discernment, whose ego has been integrated, abides in the foremost birth consisting of pure *sattva*,
the sevenfold [nature] descends in succession for the sake of liberation.
Indeed, this stage of yoga brings about the illumination of the mind. || 24 ||

Having stated in verse the essence of the meaning already expressed in prose, the author concludes by introducing, in such a person, the stage of yoga which serves as the means for the ultimate dissolution of the mind— beginning with the words "tādṛk" (such).
That [stage] consists of pure *sattva* and is characterized by that discrimination (*viveka*) accumulated through other such means.

When that qualified person remains steadfast— possessing the ego-conception (*abhimāna*) which has been consolidated and accepted as "I am such a one of the highest birth, namely the *brāhmaṇa* and other superior castes"— then for the sake of Śiva,
the supreme human goal, there is the manifestation of the mind in its sevenfold nature as will be described.
The stage of yoga (*yogabhūmi*), whose nature is to blaze with that knowledge, descends gradually through the progressive degrees of the mind's cessation;
the meaning is that it manifests through the characteristics to be described hereafter. || 24 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth canto, titled "The Incarnation of the Aspiring Seeker," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* (Section on Origination) of the *Mokṣopāya*, within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Incarnation of the Aspiring Practitioner," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The one hundred and seventeenth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, what are the stages of yoga (*yogabhūmikā*) that bestow the seven perfections (*siddhi*)?"
Tell me this in brief, O best among those who know all principles.

By way of introduction to the distinctions of the stages of knowledge (*jñānabhūmi*), the sevenfold stage of ignorance (*ajñānabhūmikā*) is described; or rather, it is discussed as a relevant digression. (1)

"In brief" means by way of summary. The word "iti" serves to indicate the questions concerning the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and their divisions, as well as other matters relevant to them. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The ground of ignorance consists of seven steps, and the ground of the knower likewise consists of seven steps;
however, there are countless other intermediate stages between these two.

In this context, wishing first to explain the differentiation of the stages of ignorance—which was inquired about by the word "iti" and is useful for awakening to the stages of knowledge—Vasiṣṭha shows them by dividing the stages of knowledge and ignorance, beginning with the verse: "Ignorance... (2).
Because they possess the essence that accomplishes one's own effort and are elevated by the weight of great being,
these [virtues] take root at every step and bear fruit with abundant results.

Human effort characterized by natural inclination and the immersion in aesthetic flavor (rasāveśa) characterized by the firmness of passion for enjoyment are the uncommon causes for being established on the ground of ignorance.
Effort consisting of hearing and so forth, distinguished by the fourfold means prescribed in the scriptures, [is the cause for the ground of knowledge].
And the immersion into the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) characterized by the firmness of the desire for liberation occurs upon the establishment on the ground of knowledge (*jñānabhū*).
However, the acquisition of one's own existence—which depends on the excellence of the reality of Brahman as the substrate—is the common cause in both cases.
Due to these causes, these two stages become firmly rooted at every step within their respective domains.

The respective fruits— characterized by the suffering of existence in saṃsāra and characterized by the attainment of unsurpassed bliss in liberation— bear fruit accordingly. Just as the seven levels of the lower worlds become increasingly full of passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas), abounding in suffering, and ending in hell, whereas the levels of the upper worlds [become increasingly...]

It is understood by implication that those [beings] up to the end of the Satyaloka, who abound in the knowledge of the happiness of sentient beings, likewise possess the fruit of gradual liberation. || 3 ||
In this regard, listen to the sevenfold stage of ignorance;
thereafter, you shall hear of the sevenfold stage of knowledge.
In that regard, it is between those two stages. || 4 ||
Liberation is abiding in one's own true nature; its loss is the experience of "I-ness.
This has been briefly stated as the defining characteristic of knowledge and ignorance of that [reality]. (5)
In that regard, he states the general characteristic of each of the two stages according to their fruit: "By its own nature," etc. (Verse 5).
For those who do not deviate from the essential nature of pure consciousness, which is mere existence,
there is no possibility of ignorance, because of the absence of the arising of attachment and aversion.
Therein, he clarifies the first characteristic: "Pure," etc. (Verse 6).
That the conscious principle sinks into the object of thought due to the loss of its own true nature—
there has never been, nor will there ever be, another delusion greater than this.
He clarifies the second [point] with the words "yad" (that which). || 7 ||
When one object of thought passes away and another arises within the mind, that intermediate state which is free from mental construction is called abiding in one's own true nature.

He prevents the objection that the first [state] is unestablished by saying "from the object" (*arthāt*). The meaning is that the abiding in one's own nature (*svarūpāvasthiti*), which is preceded by the cessation of mental activity (*amananā*) due to the non-contemplation of another object once one has fallen away from the previous object, is well-known. || 8 ||
That state which is like the interior of a stone, wherein all volitions are completely stilled,
yet which is free from the numbness of inert sleep— that is known as abiding in one’s own true nature.
He qualifies [the term] with "the sleep of dullness" (jāḍyanidrā) in order to exclude fainting and deep sleep. || 9 ||
When the portion of egoity is destroyed and stilled, and when duality has attained motionlessness, that which shines forth as non-inert is established as the true nature (svarūpa). || 10 ||

When the internal aspect of the "I" has dissolved into external differentiation, and both have reached a state of motionlessness—that which is non-inert and self-luminous consciousness is the remainder. || 10 ||
In that regard, listen to these stages of ignorance which have been superimposed:
the seed-waking, the waking, and likewise the great-waking. (11)
In that regard, within that inward-facing consciousness (pratyakcit), it is superimposed (āropita)—that is, falsely attributed (adhyasta) due to beginninglessness. || 11 ||
Waking-dream, dream-waking, waking-in-dream, and deep sleep—thus there are seven kinds of delusion, which further arise from one another. (12)
When conjoined, it possesses manifold names; hear now its defining characteristic:
that which is the consciousness of the intellect (citi) in its first state is called "the Nameless" (anākhyam) and is stainless.
He explains what was stated—that there are innumerable other states—by saying, "once again, mutually intertwined. The meaning is: "Listen to the definition of each of these seven kinds of delusion.
He states the definition of the seed-waking state (*bījajāgrat*) with the word "first. Of consciousness...
From the perspective of consciousness variegated by *māyā*, that which first arises at the beginning of creation or at the onset of waking—

consisting of a form conjoined with a reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)— becomes the locus for the future names such as "mind" (*citta*), "living being" (*jīva*), and so forth, as well as for their respective referents, through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of functions such as the maintenance of vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The connection with what follows is as follows: that which exists as the seed of the waking state about to be described is "the waking [state] residing in the seed. || 13 ||

That which exists as the seed-form, serving as the vessel for the meanings of words such as "future," "mind," and "living being," and which is awakened—that is called "waking within the seed-waking" (bījajāgrat). || 14 ||
This is the ninth state of cognition; now hear from me about the cycle of waking existence.
For one newly born, there arises this supreme notion: "I" and "this is mine. (15)

He causes [the disciple] to hear the definition of the waking state with the words "Thou art. The meaning is that the waking state is that conviction held by one who has newly emerged from the seed-waking state—that "this gross body is I" and "this collection of objects to be enjoyed by the body is mine"—[arising] from that which is beyond the beyond. || 15 ||
Thus, that cognition which is established in its own nature arises prior to waking from the state of deep sleep;
it is this "I am he," and "this is mine," which has been awakened by another birth.
This [ignorance] arises immediately after the birth of the waking cognition characterized by such expressions as "this is he," "I am this," and "this is mine.
The elision of the letter *na* is a Vedic (archaic) usage. Alternatively, it arises more firmly through the awakening of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) from preceding births of the same kind;
for this very reason, it is "robust" (*pīvara*), having been accumulated through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). To illustrate:

Even though birth as a Brāhmaṇa and so forth is common [to all], it is observed that due to practice in previous lives, some possess an inclination toward and an exceptional proficiency in the activities appropriate for Brāhmaṇas, while this is not the case for everyone. Thus, an intensified inclination is produced through the strength of firm practice, whether from this life or from a prior one.
The meaning is that the cognition of the waking state is "great waking. || 16 ||
The intense cognition that manifests as a great waking state is called "pīvara";
whether it be unestablished or established, it is in every respect of the nature of that [state]. (17)
He characterizes the waking-dream (jāgratsvapna) with the words "not yet established" (arūḍha). "Not yet established" means weak due to a lack of practice;
"established" means firm through practice, as in the case of salt [dissolving in water]. || 17 ||

That which is a kingdom of the mind for one who is awake is called "waking-dream" (jāgrat-svapna), categorized by such instances as the double moon, silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, and the mirage. (18)
He states that even delusions such as the double moon or silver in a mother-of-pearl shell are merely distinctions between waking and dreaming—namely, "the double moon," etc.
Through repeated practice, having attained the state of waking, the dream may become manifold; one thinks, "This was seen by me for only a short time," and likewise, "It is not real. (19)

He defines dream: "for a short time. A *pratyaya* (cognition) is that which is perceived at the beginning, middle, or end of sleep. The meaning is that the cognition which is subsequently recollected is called a dream. Of that ignorant one; and that [dream] occurs in the heart of the gross body situated within the state of great waking (*mahājāgrat*).
The meaning is that it occurs in the region of the channels (nāḍī) extending from the throat to the heart. || 19 ||
Indeed, that cognition which occurs at the end of sleep regarding an object experienced during the time of sleep is called a dream; its great waking state resides within the heart. (20)
Due to the absence of long-term vision, his great body did not fully blossom;
yet, having become established as a waking state within a dream, he attained the stage of the Great Waking (mahājāgrat).

To establish the definition already stated, he further qualifies the dream itself with the words, "due to the absence of long-term perception. He states the definitions of dreaming and waking as "dreaming as waking" and so forth.
It is "established" (*rūḍha*) either through firm attachment or through the conceptualization of its persistence over a long period; it is thus "accumulated" (*upacita*). Just as...
The twelve-year period of Hariścandra was such that he reached the state of "Great Waking" (mahājāgrat), meaning he attained an equality with the Great Waking state. || 21 ||
Whether the body is wounded or unwounded, that state is indeed considered the dream and waking states;
whereas the state of the living being which remains when the six conditions have been abandoned is called the state of the insentient (jāḍya).

And because that [state] continues for him in the same manner even after the destruction of the body due to destiny, the phrase "when the body is wounded" (*kṣate dehe*) was stated to indicate this. He defines deep sleep (*suṣupti*) with the words "the six states. The previous six states are born of karma (*karmajāḥ*) because they are the grounds for experiencing the fruits of karma; however, deep sleep is [the cessation] of those previously arisen karmas through their experience.

With the intention that, upon the destruction of the subsequent [states] and the non-arising of others—in the interim, when all subtle and gross manifoldness has dissolved like the removal of a parasol, and only the ignorance that is their seed remains, resulting in the state where only the Self as conditioned by that [ignorance] remains—he says:
"That which is the inert state of the individual soul. (22)
The state of deep sleep is said to be a condition rich in the awakening to future suffering.
In that state, [all things] such as grass, clods of earth, and stones [are perceived as identical]. (23)

The impressions (*vāsanā*) and karmas that awaken to and experience future sufferings are called "awakeners of future suffering. One who is enriched and endowed with these is in a state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptī*). For the world, which has dissolved into its cause during deep sleep, existence as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) alone remains, not non-existence.
With the intention that [otherwise] there would be the consequence of their non-reappearance, he says: "These... (verse 23).
O Rāghava, all objects exist as having the dimension of atoms; these seven states have been described by me as belonging to ignorance.
He summarizes: "The seven stages. || 24 ||
Each single branch here has a hundred sub-branches, appearing in various forms of manifestation;
having long flourished as waking and dreaming, it finally returns to the state of pure waking.

He states that infinite varieties arise from the manifestation of each one within the others and from their mutual intermingling—thus he says, "each one... [In this state,] one moves and meets [the other] even while in the waking state itself. || 25 ||
Through the differentiation of various objects, she unfolds and expands;
even within her belly exist the visions of the great waking state. (26)

When this [intellect] has entered the state of waking—that is, during the waking and dreaming states—there are perceptions (*dṛśaḥ*) within the belly (the internal organ) characterized by the great waking state (*mahājāgraddaśā*). Alternatively, there may be a separate division of words: "The perceptions of the witness (*sākṣiṇaḥ*) are the great waking states. || 26 ||
In the midst of these as well, a person, through delusion, would go from one delusion to another;
like a boat caught in a whirlpool within the water, it rushes into confusion.
The world—meaning people, that is, living beings—runs about in delusion, like a boat in a whirlpool of water within a river.
Some cycles of existence remain for a long time in the state of being both dream and waking;
others, moreover, are both dream-waking and waking-dream, as well as other types. || 28 ||
"Long" means for a long time. "In sleep and waking" is a singular used for the class [of states]. || 28 ||
I have spoken of these seven stages as the ground of ignorance,
which is devoid of distinctions within the various transformations of the world;
you shall cross beyond this by means of beautiful investigations.
"When the self has been perceived by itself as stainless awakening. || 29 ||
Concluding the description of the stage of ignorance (*ajñānabhūmikā*), he states the means for transcending it:
"The stage of ignorance" (*ajñānabhūmiḥ*). This means it is devoid of various transformations and internal distinctions of the world; it is contemptible and must necessarily be abandoned.
Thus, through the beautiful investigations of the manner already described and yet to be described, [one attains] awakening within one's own impurity.
When the Self, whose sole essence is the inward-facing [consciousness], is seen, you have "crossed over" from this plane of ignorance;
the meaning is that you have indeed emerged from it. Alternatively, the connection may be: "you yourself cross over. || 29 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth canto, titled "The Description of the Ground of Ignorance," in the section on the Means to Liberation within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the work of the Sage. 117.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Grounds of Ignorance," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and eighteenth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O sinless one, listen to this ground of knowledge consisting of seven stages.
Once this is understood, you shall not sink again into the mire of delusion. || 1 ||
Here, the seven stages of knowledge are properly described according to their own characteristics and the characteristics of those who have ascended them, culminating in liberation. (1)
By that which is known through the sequence of practice and experienced. || 1 ||
Proponents on the stages of yoga speak in many different ways;
however, these very [stages] are surely what I consider to be the bestowers of auspiciousness. (2)

Now, one might object: "In the Yoga Śāstra, the stages of yoga (yogabhūmikā) are well known as being divided into the eight limbs beginning with restraint (yama) and observance (niyama); are these [stages] the same as those? To this he replies: "They say... The proponents referred to are the exponents of Yoga and Sāṃkhya. Those stages of yoga, which they consider to have the attainment of trivial supernatural powers (tucchasiddhi) as their fruit, are what others hold; but for me, these [are different].
They are intended as the very ground of knowledge; for the meaning is that they bestow the auspiciousness characterized by the supreme human goal. || 2 ||
They know that awakening is knowledge, and this consists of seven stages;
liberation, however, is said to be beyond these seven stages.
He defines what that object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is, or what that knowledge (*jñāna*) is, for which these stages (*bhūmi*) are described, by stating:

"It is awakening" (*avabodham*). Brahman, when established through an unbroken mental modification (*vṛtti*) in its own form, is knowledge because it removes ignorance; and that very same [Brahman], once ignorance has been removed, is [the state of] liberation.
The meaning is that it is said to be twofold by way of the metaphorical designation "that which is to be known. || 3 ||
The realization of truth and liberation are indeed synonymous terms.
This living being, through the realization of truth, does not sprout again in this world.
And thus, when the false distinction between the intermediate causal factors— imagined through the prior and posterior states— is removed,
it follows that the two terms "awakening" (avabodha) and "liberation" (mokṣa) are synonyms, as they both reside solely in a single identical object.
With the intention that such a living being (jīva) does not sprout again—by which [rebirth] there would be non-synonymy due to difference—he says:
"the realization of truth" (satyāvabodha). || 4 ||
The first stage of knowledge is declared to be called "Pure Desire";
the second is "Investigation"; and the third is "Subtle Mind," [the reading in the printed edition being "Future Suffering"].
The summary is clear. || 5 ||

The fourth is the attainment of being (sattvāpatti); thereafter is that named non-attachment (asaṃsakti). The sixth is the contemplation of the non-existence of objects (padārthābhāvanī), and the seventh is remembered as the state beyond the fourth (turyagā).
Liberation stands at the end of these; once it is attained, one no longer grieves.
Listen now to this definition of these stages.
He promises to state the definitions of those [categories] already enumerated: "etāsām" (of these), || 7 ||
"Am I truly a fool remaining as I am? I shall examine myself through the scriptures and the company of the virtuous.
Desiring this preceded by dispassion is called *śubhecchā* (the desire for the auspicious) by the wise. (8)

"Having observed, I shall observe. The absence of the *iṭ* augment is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). "By the scriptures" refers to the Vedānta passages investigated by them, as well as by virtuous gurus. The mention of "detachment" (*vairāgya*) is an indicator for the entire set of four qualifications (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*). Thus, it is brought about by the performance of the avoidance of prohibited acts and the practice of desireless sacrifice, charity, and so forth.

The meaning is that the first stage (*bhūmikā*) is precisely the intense longing for the direct realization of the Self— which results from the engagement in hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, which culminates in liberation, and which is accompanied by the attainment of the fourfold means for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-sādhanacatuṣṭaya*). || 8 ||
That engagement in virtuous conduct which is preceded by the study of the scriptures, association with the wise, and the practice of detachment is called *vicāraṇā* (investigation).

In this context, right conduct (*sadācāra*) consists solely of hearing and reflecting accompanied by the observance of the duties of an ascetic, such as service to the guru, subsisting on alms, and ritual purity; for anything else has already been established as a cause merely for the purification of the mind.

The state of non-attachment toward the objects of the senses, which arises here from both investigation (*vicāraṇā*) and the desire for the auspicious (*śubhecchā*), is called *tanumānasā* because of the attenuation (*tanutā*) of [worldly] existence (*bhāva*). (10)
The word "vicāraṇā" (investigation) is placed first because it is more important [than the other terms]. "Bhāva" means cultivation, which is *nididhyāsana* (meditative reflection);

therefore, following the attainment of the fourfold qualification (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) and so forth, through *nididhyāsana* accompanied by *śravaṇa* (hearing) and *manana* (reflection), there arises non-attachment of the mind toward sense objects, such as sound and the rest.

The state of attenuation (*tanutā*), which culminates in non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*) and consists of the nature of conceptual meditative absorption (*savikalpa-samādhi*), is called the stage known as *tanumānasā*. This is because of the etymological derivation: "that in which the mind (*mānasa*) has become attenuated (*tanu*), that is, extremely subtle.
Since the suffix *aṇ* is treated as a secondary member (*upasarjana*), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is not applied. Thus it is stated in the *Yogaśāstra*: [text follows].
"As long as there is the grasping of objects such as sound by means of the instruments of perception such as the ear, that is called dhyāna; beyond that is samādhi. (10)
Through the practice of the three stages, by virtue of detachment from objects in the mind, one's abiding in the pure Self is declared to be the attainment of *sattva*. (11)

When there is the absolute cessation of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding external objects— that is, when there is a total renunciation of the mind due to its stability therein— then, through the dissolution of the "threefold enclosure" (*tripuṭī*), the Self, which is the pure substratum of all and consists of pure existence alone, becomes like milk and water within the purified state, free from *māyā*, its effects, and the three states of consciousness.

The meaning is that the state culminating in direct realization, which consists of non-conceptual samādhi, is the attainment of being (*sattvāpatti*), because the mind has attained its true nature as the very being of the Supreme Self (*paramātmasattva*). For it is in this state that one is called a "knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*). || 11 ||
Through the practice of the four stages, by means of the fruit of non-attachment,
and from the blossoming of the wonder of awakened being, that which is called "non-attachment" is proclaimed.
Non-attachment of the mind toward external and internal forms and their latent impressions, together with its characteristic—

the fruit of the maturation of samādhi— and as its cause, a wonder established and accumulated in the mind characterized by the direct realization of the nature of Brahman-Ātman, which is unsurpassed bliss and eternally immediate.

In which [state] that [realization occurs]. Although for those of the highest capacity, direct realization is well-known even on the second stage due to its being a verbal immediacy (*śābdāparokṣa*), nevertheless,
on the fifth stage there is a preeminent excellence resulting from the absolute eradication of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of duality.

The term "established" (*rūḍha*) is used as a qualifier for "wonder" (*camatkāra*) to indicate that even for practitioners of dull or middling capacity, the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) that arises at the end of the fourth stage becomes more firmly rooted in the fifth stage.
For this very reason, it is said that one who has reached the fifth stage at the conclusion of the fourth stage is a "superior knower of Brahman" (*brahmavidvara*).
Thus it is said: by the etymological derivation "that in which there is no attachment whatsoever to ignorance and its effects," it is named *Asaṃsakti* (Non-attachment). 12.
Through the firm practice of the five stages, by delighting in one's own self and by the non-contemplation of internal and external objects, [the state of liberation is attained]. || 13 ||
With the intention that the two subsequent stages arise from the excellence of the maturation of this very [stage], he says:
"the fivefold stage. He provides an etymological explanation of the name to be mentioned, based on its literal meaning, by saying:
"of those who are internal. || 13 ||

Through long-continued effort applied by another, because of the cultivation of the meaning [of the word], the sixth stage arises, known as the "cultivation of the referent" (padārthābhāvanā). || 14 ||

If so, how is the maintenance of the body accomplished? To this he says: "by means of what is provided by others. And in this stage, one is designated as a "most excellent knower of Brahman" (brahmavidvarīyān). || 14 ||

Due to long-term cultivation on the six stages and because of the non-perception of differentiation, that state of abiding solely in one's own essential nature is to be known as the "Fourth" (turyagā) state. || 15 ||

He speaks of the seventh stage (*bhūmikā*) with the words "in the six stages" (*bhūmiṣaṭke*). This implies that even through the effort of others, no duality is perceived. According to the Śruti, "They consider the fourth to be the auspicious non-dual [state] which is free from the three states beginning with waking," such a state is established by the experience of the wise.

The state in which one goes to the established Brahman and experiences it as the Self in its undivided form is *turyagā*. Having attained that, one is called the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman (*brahmavidvariṣṭha*). And because he goes to that fourth state (*turīya*) among those beginning with the knower of Brahman, it is called *turyagā*. 15.
For this fourth state (turya) exists here among those liberated while living;
beyond that, the object of liberation after death (videhamukti) is the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). || 16 ||

This [state] exists right here in this very body; therefore, since the object of liberation beyond the body (videhamukti) is the Brahman that transcends the fourth state (turyātīta), it is not counted among the stages (bhūmikās)—this is the meaning. || 16 ||
For those highly fortunate ones, O Rāma, who have reached the seventh stage—
those great-souled ones who delight in the Self— have attained the supreme state.
Those liberated while living do not cling to the states of pleasure or pain;
they perform their necessary duties through natural inclination, or perhaps they do nothing at all.
The intention is that they perform some [actions] on the sixth stage, or do not perform them at all on the seventh stage. || 18 ||
Being awakened by those standing nearby, they indeed perform the conduct that has come down through the sequence of all traditional practices, as flawlessly as one who is perfectly enlightened.

By stating "or they do not," he clarifies his own intention while warding off the suspicion that they might be intent on acting according to their own whims, saying: "The *pārśvastha* [and others]. This means that all those established in their respective stages of life (*āśrama*) practice only the conduct that has come down through the traditional sequence of conduct—that is, right conduct (*sadācāra*).
The word "ācaranti" (they practice) implies that both types of restriction are intended here. "Akṣatam" means not defiled by attachment.

In the reading "akṣatāḥ," the meaning is those who are free from the "wound" characterized by attachment to fruits. Thus, the sense is that there is no possibility of acting according to one's own whims. And so they say: "For one who has realized the reality of Brahman..."
"If there were such a thing as acting according to one's own whims, what difference would there be between dogs and those who know the truth, regarding the consumption of impurity?
(19) "Because they delight in the Self, no worldly activities bring them pleasure, just as the sight of forms does not please women who are fast asleep. (20)
He states, with an illustration, that through conduct free from attachment there is no arising of pleasure or pain, saying:

"by being delighted in the Self. Worldly activities and transactions do not bring pleasure to those who are liberated while living; just as those in deep sleep, under the power of profound slumber, are not affected even when beheld for their beauty or supreme physical charm.

The meaning is that forms, lights, and women do not bring happiness in that same way. However, regarding the reading "Just as forms, lights, and women [do not awaken] those who are fast asleep to the activities of the world," it refers to those who are as if asleep because they perceive the worldly affairs as false, like a dream, in accordance with the teaching of the Blessed One: "That which is night for all beings is day for the sage who sees."

Even the riches of Brahmā and others do not bring happiness; the meaning is that just as the sight of one woman's form does not please other women because of the absence of passion for them, so it is in this case. || 20 ||
And these seven stages are the domain of the wise alone;
they are not for animals, immobile beings, and the like, nor for the minds of barbarians and such. (21)
The meaning is: those humans and others whose minds possess the notion that the body is the self, just like the Mlecchas and similar groups. || 21 ||
Even those who are beasts, barbarians, and the like, have attained this state of knowledge;
whether they possess a body or are bodiless, they are liberated—of this there is no doubt.
The animals include Hanumān and others; the barbarians (mlecchas) include Dharmavyādha and others; and by the word "others" (ādi), the asuras such as Prahlāda and Karkaṭī are included. || 22 ||
For *jñapti* is the severing of the knot; when that occurs, there is liberation.
It consists essentially of mere tranquility, like the [cessation of] the cognition of water in a mirage. (23)

That which has as its measure (mātrā) or standard (tulā) the cessation—that is, the sublation—of the cognition of water in a mirage and, by the phrase "and so forth," the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; that is to say, it is equal to that. || 23 ||
But those who have crossed over through delusion, yet have not reached the purifying state,
remain established in these stages, intent upon the attainment of their own true self.

Although they have indeed completely crossed over delusion due to the destruction of the veil of ignorance through the arising of knowledge on the second and subsequent stages, or even on the fourth stage, nevertheless, because of the distractions induced by powerful *prārabdha* karma, their unsurpassed [state]— characterized by the total dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) which is purifying— is not yet fully realized.
The meaning is that they have not attained videhakaivalya, which is characterized by the fullness of bliss. || 24 ||
Some exist throughout all stages; some belong to two, three, or one stage;
some belong to six stages; and some belong to seven or one stage. (25)
In a single birth alone, they gradually attained all the stages; thus, in every case, Sanaka and the others possessed seven stages within one birth and the seventh stage within another birth.
Some have reached three stages, some have reached the final stage;
some have traversed four stages, while others remain in two stages. (26)

"Some occupy four earths"—this is a restatement of what was previously mentioned for the sake of further elaboration. (26) Some are recipients of a portion of the earth; some occupy three and a half earths;
some occupy four and a half earths; and others occupy five and a half earths. (27)
A portion of the ground refers to a quarter of the ground, half of the ground, and so forth. || 27 ||
Discerning men move through the worlds, established in the specific states of vision belonging to the asceticism of the abode of the planets. (28)

Thus, those who move through the stages (*bhūmis*) described in this manner are called "seizers" (*grahas*) because they grasp by means of the vision of the Self as the plenum (*bhūman*). These are known as the "seizers" (*grahas*) and the "over-seizers" (*atigrahas*), consisting of the internal and external organs together with their objects.
Furthermore, the "abode" (*āyatana*) refers to the body which serves as their support, as well as the suffering—divided into internal (*ādhyātmika*) and other categories—caused by that [body].
The meaning is that they remain—meaning they are intent—upon the "possessions" (āveśas), which are characterized by overwhelming force and involve the entry into the self.
For those wise and excellent kings who conquer these ten states, the defeat of the warriors—the hosts of elephants of the quarters—is here regarded as a mere blade of grass. (29)

The conquest of the senses and the mind alone is superior to the conquest of all external enemies; indeed, sovereignty over one's own self is the only truly supreme kingship, and no other. Thus he says: "For they... [referring to] "the auspicious ones," meaning the most excellent kings.

The suffix *ṭac* is not applied here because it is not used after a word ending in *pūjanāt*. Here, before him [the Self], there is [no need for] the hosts of all enemy warriors accompanied by their arrays of elephants with poisoned tusks.
Defeat and even the sovereignty over the seven continents resulting from that [defeat] are treated as mere straw; the meaning is that they become insignificant. || 29 ||
Those great ones who indeed conquer those stages are truly worthy of worship, for they have vanquished the enemy of the senses;
even the Samrāj and Virāj appear as mere blades of grass before them.
Therefore, they attain that which is supreme in the world. || 30 ||
Stating the very same point clearly, he concludes with the words "In these": "He by whom the Rājasūya has been performed;

he who alone is the sovereign of the entire circle of the earth and the ruler of other kings—he is the Emperor (samrāṭ). He should be young, a youth skilled in teaching; most eloquent, most firm, and most powerful. To him belongs this earth."

"May it be full of all wealth"— the meaning is that he is endowed with the human bliss characterized by the Śruti as "that is one human bliss. Beyond that [seventh stage], where even Virāṭ Prajāpati— the body of Brahman and the ultimate limit of divine bliss— is regarded as a mere blade of grass, [is the next state].
The meaning is that they attain the bliss of disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya) right here in this very world. || 30 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Stages of Knowledge," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* (Section on Origination) of the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation), within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 118.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Stages of Knowledge," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and nineteenth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as gold, through the consciousness of being a ring, forgets its nature as gold;
Just as gold does not cry out, "I am gold," so too the Self does not cry out through this sense of "I-ness."
Having cast aside the illusory form, the method for stabilizing the vision of the oneness of pure Being within the stages [of yoga] is here elaborated.

To illustrate how, for that reason, one forgets the innate, self-luminous state of the Supreme Self’s own full bliss and, through the superimposition of the illusory states of the individual soul and the world, encounters various kinds of suffering, grief, and so forth, he provides the following example: "Just as a ring... Just as gold, by its very nature, [remains unchanged] throughout all time and in every respect...

Although gold is, from the perspective of ultimate reality, of a single nature and devoid even in the slightest degree of what is not gold, it nevertheless— through the imagined consciousness of a ring upon itself, mistaking it for a finger-ring, and forgetting its own state as gold and its singular essence as gold—
fails to see this and instead imagines itself to be bronze or other such things due to the conceptualization brought about by contact with external impurities.

"Virauti" means it weeps. Since it is impossible for an insentient object to weep, the expression of sounds such as those from a bell-metal ring is metaphorically attributed to its owner's weeping, or the weeping itself is figuratively described as belonging to that [object].
