Likewise, the meaning is that the Self also weeps by way of the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā). || 1 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, how does the consciousness of a ring arise from gold?
And how does egoism arise from the Self? O Lord, explain this to me exactly as it is.

The word "yathā" (as/how) also carries the sense of "how" and connects with what follows. Thus, explain through proper arguments both the illustration and the subject of the illustration—namely, how the ego-sense belongs to the Self—and describe them clearly;
this is the meaning. || 2 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O virtuous one, the coming and going of that which exists alone can be questioned, not of that which does not exist;
for "I-ness," "you-ness," and the nature of a wave are never truly real.
The meaning is that coming and going, which are birth and destruction, can be perceived by a seer who is self-established;

therefore, it is precisely such things that you should inquire about. This is the underlying idea: among the six modifications of being, the middle four are established as belonging only to what exists, not to what does not exist; likewise, birth and destruction also belong only to what exists.
This must be stated: for that which is non-existent is incapable of performing the action of arising or becoming the locus of the action of perishing.
If the non-existent were to arise or perish, then the two properties of arising and perishing would themselves be non-existent, as they too would be non-existent.
Indeed, they could not then be perceived, because there can be no relationship between the existent and the non-existent. Therefore, it is gold alone [that exists].
Brahmā indeed arises in the form of the wave, the hammer, and so forth. || 3 ||
*Hema*: If gold is to be accepted, then the buyer—being implicitly addressed by the neutral mediator who says, "Take a ring as the price for this gold"—is thereby [bound].

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "That which is given by the seller for the sake of the ring is true. In the reading where *udite* is in the locative case (*saptamyanta*), the connection is: "If [the ring] has been mentioned, then [it is given] for the sake of the buyer by the mediator," and so forth.
The locative case in *hemni* is used according to the rule *nimittāt karmayoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.36); thus, "and you [gave] the ring upon the gold."
If he says, "Take it," then whatever is given by him who possesses waves—that indeed exists; of this there is no doubt. (4)
He states that even the connection with actions such as abandoning or acquiring is observed only for that which exists, not for that which does not exist—thus he says, "Gold.

When the price has been paid, saying "Take it, buy it," that gold which is given by the seller for a high price along with its weight is truly existent. And in the same way, Brahman alone is the object of all worldly transaction.
The meaning is that not even an atom's worth of anything other than that can be determined, even in conventional discourse. || 4 ||
Śrī Rāma said: "If it is so, O Lord, what would that be? And of what nature is the state of being a ring?
By determining the meaning through this very inquiry, I shall know the form of Brahman. (5)

If gold alone is the object of all worldly transactions such as buying and selling, then what would be the nature of the form of a ring and so forth perceived therein—distinct from the nature of gold—and of what kind or of what character would it be that is denoted by words such as "ring" and the like? This is the meaning of the question. || 5 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, if the formless nature of the unreal were to be described as having a form,
then you might as well describe the features and qualities of the son of a barren woman.
With the intention that "that which is pleasing only so long as it is not investigated vanishes when investigated," he gives the reply: "Form" (rūpam).
"The state of being a ring is a vain delusion; this is an illusion whose true nature is existence.
Its form is precisely this: that which is not seen by one who looks closely. (7)

If its nature must necessarily be stated, then with the intention that the nature of *māyā* is its existence for only so long as it is not investigated, he says: "Its nature. The meaning is that when it is "prekṣitā"—that is, examined and seen—it is no longer seen but becomes void; this well-known fact is precisely its nature. || 7 ||
In the water of a mirage, in the double moon, and in such things as the form of a killer;
this alone is their true nature: that when examined, they are not found.
Likewise, he demonstrates that this very same established consensus applies elsewhere in the illusory realm as well, beginning with the words "a mirage" (mṛgatṛṣṇā) and so forth. || 8 ||
He who perceives the form of silver in mother-of-pearl never, at any time or place, obtains even a minute particle of actual silver for a single moment.
Through mere non-investigation, the real appears as if unreal,
just as the nature of silver appears in a mother-of-pearl shell, or water in the mirages of the desert.
The non-existence of that which does not exist becomes manifest when it is investigated;
yet when not investigated, it appears as real, like a body of water in a mirage.
The remainder of the sense is that non-existence, when not being perceived, manifests itself in the form of silver and so forth. || 11 ||
That which is non-existent acts as if it were existent and appears stable; this delusion of mistaking a phantom for real is only for the destruction of the foolish. (12)
[Objection: But where has the capacity to produce an effect and stability ever been observed in that which is non-existent? To this he replies: "Of children" (*bālānām*).
It is agitation induced by delusion, such as fear, weeping, and so forth. || 12 ||

Excluding the single state of being gold, nothing else exists in gold, just as there is no reality to the forms of rings, bracelets, and so forth, apart from the sand in which oil and other substances may rest. (13)

In this world there is neither truth nor falsehood; whatever appears [or shines forth], in that very way it performs a causal function, like the illusory transformation of a yakṣa perceived by children. (14)

The existence of a real entity (*vastusattā*) is not the cause for the determination of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); rather, it is the appearance of the existence of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhānasattā*) even when there is a superimposition (*āropa*).
With this intention, he says: "Not here. The meaning is that there is no fixed rule that only what is real performs causal efficiency, or that only what is false performs causal efficiency. || 14 ||
Whether it be real or even unreal, that which is firmly rooted in the heart performs its respective purposeful action, just as poison can perform the function of nectar.
And he reminds us that this has indeed been stated many times before: "Or rather... (15).

This alone is the supreme knowledge: that this cycle of worldly existence is indeed an illusion, consisting of the cultivation of a sense of "I-ness" toward that which is unreal and without foundation. (16)
Having established the illustration, he states its correspondence with the subject of the illustration as well, beginning with the words "parameṣaiva" (this very same [is] in the supreme).
In gold there is no such thing as being a ring or the like, nor does egoity exist in the Self;
for this reality, which is the absence of egoity, is pure, tranquil, white, and supreme. (17)
The meaning is that a non-existent thing is merely an unreal entity; it is not an ultimate reality. || 17 ||
There is no such thing as eternity, nor is there anything belonging to Viriñci;
there is no such thing as being the cosmic egg, nor is there anything such as being a son or the like. (18)
The unreality of everything other than Brahman is established by the teaching: "Not this, not this. This Self is "not this, not this";

it is this Brahman—without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior. There is no diversity whatsoever here; where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūmā).
With the intention of showing that this is established by thousands of scriptural passages providing such exceptions, he says, beginning with "not eternal-ness" (na sanātanatā):

"Eternal-ness" (sanātanatā) is the connection with all time, and that does not exist in that which transcends time. "Sons" (sutāḥ) refers to the Prajāpatis, the sons of Brahmā; [the phrase] "headed by them" (tadāditā) [refers to the lineage]. || 18 ||

There is no such thing as being another world, nor is there anywhere such a thing as heaven and so forth; there is no state of being Mount Meru, no state of being an asura, no state of being the mind, and no state of being the body. (19)

There is no such thing as the nature of the great elements, nor is there any causality anywhere; there is no reckoning of the three times, nor is there the substantiality of existence or non-existence.
There is no such thing as "thou-ness," "I-ness," "selfhood," "that-ness," "existence," or "non-existence;
there is no conceptualization of difference anywhere, nor is there any being or any attachment. || 21 ||
Bhāva is passion; its effect is coloring (rañjanā). || 21 ||
The entire world is quiescent, without support, eternal, and auspicious; it is free from affliction, without appearance, nameless, and without cause.
The meaning is: you are the entire world, the ultimate reality of the world, peaceful, and consisting of nothing but the pure substratum (adhiṣṭhāna-sat-mātra). || 22 ||
Neither existent nor non-existent, neither middle nor end, neither all nor yet all at all;
ungraspable by mind or speech, it is emptier than the empty and more blissful than bliss. (23)
The existent (*sat*) is like the modification of being called "origination" (*utpatti*); the non-existent (*asat*) is like the modification of being called "destruction" (*nāśa*);

and that which is between the two (*madhyānta*) is like the intermediate modifications of being. Alternatively, "existent" means not destroyed and "non-existent" means not yet established; that which has these two—origination and destruction—as its middle, its ends, and its limits is so described. (23)
p. 406) 239 Śrī Rāma said:
"I have now fully realized that Brahman alone is everything, and all is equal."
Nevertheless, tell me further: how indeed is creation perceived? (24)

Thus, although Brahman—free from conceptual proliferation and of a single flavor as the ultimate reality—has been explained, Rāma, turning away because he is unable to stabilize his mental fluctuations therein and fearing the cultivation of contrary notions, asks:
"It has been understood. [He asks: "In what manner is it perceived? [The answer is: When ignorance is destroyed by knowledge...
The sense is that since the world, which has that [ignorance] as its root, is also sublated, its re-appearance is untenable. || 24 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In the supreme, tranquil [Brahman], that which is called the "Supreme" exists in this manner as "this-ness.
Herein there is no creation, nor does any so-called creation ever exist at any time.
If reality has been realized by you, then the appearance of the world is nothing but the appearance of Brahman.
Like water contained within the waters of the great ocean, [the individual soul] is established in the Supreme Lord;
yet, just as water moves due to its fluidity, the Supreme State is motionless.

In this regard, Vasiṣṭha offers a rebuttal with the words "in the Supreme" (pare), intending that the occasional manifestation and its designation cease to exist precisely because their cause has vanished: "The Supreme Reality remains only in the Supreme, the Peaceful, its own essential nature, and has not deviated from it. Thus, due to the state of the full Self, both creation and its designation [arise] as 'this-ness' (idantā)."

The meaning is that here in Brahman nothing exists [as an object], but it exists solely by its own nature (*svabhāva*). By the use of the word "kadācana" (at any time), the absence of occasionality (*kādācitkatva*) regarding such a state is expressed. As for the question "What is perceived as what?", does it refer to a question about an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) or about a cause (*nimitta*)? In the first case, there is a contradiction (*bādhā*), because name and form have become one with Brahman.
Having stated the illustration regarding the state of abiding in the nature of Brahman, he now describes the distinction that exists beyond that: "Water... (verse 26).
"Light shines as if within its own self, yet that state does not shine at all;
for the essence of lights is shining, whereas they know the state [of Brahman] to be non-shining. (verse 27)
Having stated an illustration for its self-luminosity, he states a distinction regarding that as well, as before: "Light" (bhā).

Light—the radiance of the sun and other luminaries—shines, that is, it blazes. Shining is the act of illumination; it is the essence, the inherent nature, of lights such as the sun. Non-shining is devoid of action. || 27 ||

Just as water within the interior of the ocean manifests [as waves] when excluding what is below and above, so too this world appears as manifold within the Supreme due to its consciousness; yet that Supreme remains non-different from it.
The knower of only a little, by virtue of its own consciousness, becomes as if the object of cognition;
thus it perceives "creation" and will remain established in that state eternally.

Regarding the second [verse], he says: "Slightly" (īṣat). "Of you who know slightly" means of one whose awakening is not yet mature. The clarification of the phrase "it goes as if toward the state of being an object of cognition" is that "creation is simply perceived. And that creation, upon the maturation of knowledge, will be established in the eternal nature of Brahman. || 29 ||
The determination is this: the creation of the ultimate reality is merely a designation;
it does not exist as something diverse, nor is it absolutely non-existent, just as space is not [different from] space itself.

Since, from that perspective, this manifold variety perceived by the ignorant does not exist at all— just as there is no other "sky" within the sky of space, for that would lead to an infinite regress— so too,
because there is no ultimate reality other than the ultimate reality, the term "creation" (sarga) is merely a designation for Brahman itself.
The meaning is: the certainty of the wise. || 30 ||
The emission from the mind is its attainment [of manifestation], and the cessation of that emission from the non-mind is its dissolution;
this occurs within the Supreme, which is supremely tranquil, just as the delusion of being a bracelet exists within gold.
And thus, with the intention that the very absence of the absolute destruction of the mind is the cause for you to behold creation once again, he says: "From the mind," etc. (31).
Only that which is real attains reality upon the arising of the tranquility of the mind;
that which is unreal attains the state of being real through the arising of self-awareness.
Consciousness is the mind; [it arises] upon its emergence. || 32 ||
Know that consciousness is the "I-ness" (ahaṃtā), the agitation arising from the flurry of creation;
know that non-consciousness is the supreme tranquility, yet it is not inert matter.
Now, the delusion of wandering through creation is indeed the mind itself, which is consciousness endowed with the conceit of "I-ness. || 33 ||
To the knower, this manifold creation is not diverse, for it consists of the single, auspicious Self;
it is like an army of clay figures fashioned by craftsmen according to their respective functions and actions.
He explains how even for the wise (*jñānin*), when the manifestation of the mind arises during the state of emergence (*vyutthānadaśā*), there is the appearance of creation:

"The remainder [is as follows]: Just as for artisans, there is the 'masculinity'—that is, the skill of a man—which results in the accomplishment of their work; likewise, an army made of clay, though in reality merely clay, appears as if it were an actual army."

The meaning is "in that same way. Alternatively, the meaning is: "just as an army made of clay, having the form of a man and so forth, appears to perform the actions of a male, such as fighting and other human activities, in that same way [it appears here]. || 34 ||
This is full, without beginning, infinite, and of sinless interior;
in the Full, it remains as the Full itself through the supreme floods of the Full.

In their ultimate view, however, this entire world remains as Brahman alone; here he demonstrates the meaning of the Śruti: "That is full, this is full; from the full, the full arises. Taking away the fullness of the full, the full alone remains"—by the words "this" and so forth.

It is without beginning and without origination; it is infinite and devoid of destruction. For this very reason, its "belly"—that is, its center—is free from the defects of further transformation. Since it is filled by the fullnesses—the all-pervading expansions—of the Perfect Supreme Self alone, it is therefore "Full."
The meaning is that it remains entirely full and does not undergo even the slightest degree of incompleteness. || 35 ||
That which is perceived as this creation is Brahman, abiding within Brahman;
like space resting in space, it is the peaceful Śiva, auspiciously established in the peaceful Śiva. (36)
To further strengthen that very point, he says again: "That which this... The neuter gender is used for the sake of the general category. || 36 ||
Just as in a city of nine yojanas reflected in a mirror,
there is neither distance nor proximity, so too is the sequence of "that" and "not-that" with respect to the Lord.
In the Lord, who is Brahman, there is no sequence—meaning no succession—of either distance or proximity.
(37) The universe has arisen from the non-existent, yet it has also always arisen from the existent;
though appearing as real due to its manifestation, it consists of unreality because it lacks substantial existence. (38)

And this being so, because that which is real appears in the form of the unreal universe, it is the Real alone that has arisen from the perspective of one who sees reality, while from the perspective of one who does not see reality, it has become the unreal.
For, due to the appearance of duality, that which is the manifestation of the Real becomes composed of the unreal when there is the perception of duality; such is the meaning. || 38 ||
In this creation—which has the form of a city in a mirror, which shines like the water of a mirage, and which appears as the delusion of two moons—what indeed is real? (39)
Just as a city appears in the sky due to the scattering of magical powder, so too does saṃsāra appear within consciousness, both substantial and insubstantial. (40)
The "illusion-powder" (māyā-cūrṇa) is medicinal powder consecrated by magicians for the purpose of supreme delusion;
it is the essence, the truth, the non-essence, and the dead. || 40 ||
239) Until ignorance has been forcibly consumed, root and branch, by the fire of investigation— like a withered creeper— [then [rebirth continues]].
It produces many dense thickets of spreading branches—forests of various kinds of pleasure and pain. || 41 ||

As long as the destruction of ignorance along with its latent impressions (vāsanā) has not been accomplished up to the point of ascending to the seventh stage (bhūmikā), the suffering of distraction continues to appear even to those who possess the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna). Therefore,
with the intention that those seeking the bliss of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) must practice the stages, he concludes:
"Up to this point," [it means]. || 41 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Waves of Gold," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki and belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition. 119.
Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Golden Waves," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The One Hundred and Twentieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Like a golden ring or similar object that is falsely described, [the world] is headed toward its destruction.
O Rāghava, hear what kind of greatness belongs to ignorance.
Lavaṇa went once again to the Caṇḍāla hamlet on the Vindhya mountains that he had previously seen;
here, the conversation between the Caṇḍāla woman and her mother-in-law is set forth. (1)

With the intention that the illusory nature (*vivarta*) of the universe described by the illustration of the golden ring is established as an experience for Lavaṇa who has examined it, and that you too should see this after reflection, he says:
"The golden ring... The word *iti* is to be supplied after the word *mithyā*. By mere reflection—
Greatness tending toward exhaustion is a state of wonder. || 1 ||
Having thus witnessed that delusion,
King Lavaṇa set out for that great forest on the second day.
This is that salt previously described; it was shown by a magician. || 2 ||
I remember that forest where I witnessed such suffering;
for perhaps it may be found again within the mirror of my mind from the Vindhya mountains.

The mind itself is the mirror; "tadgatām" [means] that which has entered it. The ablative case in "vindhyāt" is used either with the elision of a gerundive suffix (*lyap*) governing the object or the locus;
the meaning is "having reached the Vindhya" or "having gone to the Vindhya. || 3 ||
Having thus resolved with his ministers, he set out for the Deccan,
reaching the Vindhya mountain as if once again for the conquest of the quarters.
Out of curiosity, he wandered across the entire coastal land of the eastern, southern, and western great oceans, like the sun traversing the path of the sky.
The hot-rayed one is the sun. || 5 ||
Then, in one place, he beheld that formidable forest, which stood before him like a personified thought, resembling the earth of the world beyond.
*Araṇyānī* means a great forest (*mahāraṇya*). The suffix *ānuk* is applied after *araṇya* to denote greatness. (6)
While dwelling there, he saw all those various events, inquired about them, and having understood them, he was filled with wonder.
The meaning is: those various [objects] previously experienced. || 7 ||
He recognized that they were indeed hunters born of the Pulkasa caste;
then, his mind overwhelmed with wonder, he wandered about again in great agitation.
He was agitated and full of curiosity. || 8 ||
Then, having reached the edge of the great forest, which was grey with smoke,
he arrived at that very village where he had previously become a well-nourished Pulkasa.
There he saw various people, those women, those small huts,
various receptacles for the people, and those various riverbanks of the earth.
*Kuṭīrakāḥ* means small huts; [the suffix] *ra* is applied after *kuṭī*, *śamī*, and *śuṇḍā* in the sense of the same meaning (*svārthe*), and the suffix *kan* is added. (10)
And those trees fallen unexpectedly, those trails he had followed,
those very same regions, and his many sons who had been struck down by hunters— [he beheld them all].
During a sudden famine, those who have fallen away and are overcome by misfortune; those followers who travel with them; and those who are alone, deprived of kinsmen. || 11 ||
While other elderly women, their eyes filled with tears and overcome by the agony of distress,
were describing how their kinsmen had perished in the untimely wilderness—
The sorrows among her friends have increased beyond counting.

He describes the events occurring there with the words beginning "In others... Her mother-in-law was elderly. While other elderly female friends were occupied with the sufferings of their own distressed kinsmen, she—describing the sorrows of her own kinsmen who had been scattered in the wilderness during that untimely and calamitous season—spoke this.
The connection with the subsequent clause is: "he weeps in the manner that will be described. || 12 ||
An old woman, her eyes blazing with overflowing tears,
wretched indeed— her body emaciated and her breasts withered, clad in a tattered rag—
like a region scorched by a fierce thunderbolt during a drought.
There, uttering cries of distress, she wept thus: || 13 ||
He further qualifies her with the word "vṛddha": she is one whose eyes are intensely overflowing with tears compared to other elderly women.
[The phrase] "in a region mostly burnt by a fierce thunderbolt characterized by drought (avagraha)" refers to a place where rain has failed. || 13 ||
"Alas, daughter! Your entire body was covered with sons; now, after three days without food, your limbs are worn out, and having struck your armor with a sword, your body is decayed."
How and where were those taints abandoned by you?

He describes the manner of his weeping with the words "Alas, my sons! and so forth: "By you, the King, who remained having entered [the city] like a sword into its own sheath (varman), why were you—dear as life itself—abandoned and left behind? And where were you abandoned? The plural usage "by you" is employed in reference to the sons because they are many. Alternatively:

As before, the meaning is: "How were your own vital breaths (asavaḥ), which are your life-forces, released by you, the King, whose body was worn out and frame decayed? Where were they released? In the reading without the visarga (*asava*), however, it should be construed thus: "How were you, with your body worn out, released, and how were those vital breaths of yours released? || 14 ||
I remember my husband’s garland of *guñjā* berries on the cloud-mountain, which has palm leaves for its support and the red, excellent fruits resting between his teeth.
They possess a smile free from the mudrā of fear. || 15 ||
Now, remembering the rash act committed for the sake of supporting the king’s family, she says:

"Tālī... Having climbed a palm tree on a mountain as lofty as a cloud and taken its fruit, at the moment of descent, because both hands were occupied and thus unable to hold the fruit, [she held it] between her teeth.

Of you, who by nature have the habit of laughing at Hanumān— who, though immortal (free from death) due to his appearance at that very moment as indicated by the *purasthamudrā*, was nevertheless like a ripe fruit that had turned crimson while being bitten by teeth— the falling of a palm leaf [upon you] through fate [was the cause].
Grasping the branch of a palm tree that is close at hand is a rash act. In the reading "talālambanam," the meaning is that I remember the descent to the base (tala), the root, as a rash act. || 15 ||
240. Furthermore,
from within the groves of *kadamba*, *jambīra*, *lavaṅga*, and *guñjā* trees, a *tarakṣu* (hyena) was prowling.
When indeed shall I again behold my son’s terrifying leaps as he prepares for battle? (16)

Within the innermost recesses of a grove of *kadamba* and *jambīra* trees and *lavaṅga* and *guñjā* creepers, as a tiger— a species of beast of prey— roamed while lying in wait, there arose terrifying and fear-inducing leaps caused by the soaring flight of his son’s son, who was dearer than a son: his daughter’s husband.
The journeys for the purpose of slaying him. || 16 ||
Those playful splendors of desire do not exist even in the mouth here;
they reside only on that portion of the chin which is dark as the *tāla* tree.
And of the meat that has gone to another's mouth, even though it was [once] one's own food. || 17 ||

Now, remembering and describing the beauty of the face of his own son who was filled with desire for his daughter, he says: "Not those... At the time of drinking and so forth, [he refers to] that beloved son who is worthy of compassion, whose mouth had at another time gone toward the mouth of his own mistress and obtained a morsel of meat (*āmiṣa*) out of affection; [this refers to him] at the time of chewing that very thing.
The meaning is that those playful charms which shine with beauty upon the dark lower lip— where the beard resembles the *tamāla* tree—
are not found here in this world, O playful woman, even on the full face of Kāma, the god of love. || 17 ||
Her Yamunā river, equal to the Yamunā itself, was led away by her husband Yama along with him;
likewise, her Tamāla vine was stripped of its clusters of flowers.
Like the wind in a choice forest. || 18 ||
Now, anticipating her own death along with her husband and daughter, she says: "O daughter!
The meaning is that my daughter, who was equal in complexion to Yamunā, has surely been carried off by her husband, Yama, by means of his superior strength. || 18 ||
Alas, daughter, you who wear a necklace of *guñjā* berries, whose limbs are graced by full and swelling breasts,
and whose complexion is as flickering as collyrium shimmering in the wind!
On the leafy garment [of the sky], at the teeth of the Badara and Jambu trees. || 19 ||
She whose garments and such for wearing are made of leaves alone; she whose teeth are like jujube seeds (*bādarāṇi*) or like jambu seeds. 19.
Alas, O Prince, whose splendor is like the moon, having abandoned those beautiful women of the inner apartments,
you have found delight in my daughter!
Even that [faith] of yours has not attained a state of firm stability. || 20 ||
O Lord of Men, what trivial thing indeed has not been done by the playful activities of this river of saṃsāra, which mock us with its breaking waves?
He who was united with a Puṣkasī girl. || 21 ||
By such playful acts and the ripening of their karma, they were subjected to appropriate ridicule;

this is an instance of a "dissolved metaphor" (*vyastarūpaka*) using the phrase "by the breaking of beautiful waves. What insignificant or contemptible fruit indeed was not produced? He states that very thing: "O Lord of Kings" (*nṛpeśa*). || 21 ||
She, with eyes like those of a startled deer, and he, with prowess like that of a proud tiger—
both went to their destruction in a single step.
The word "mā" is used in the sense of "together with," as in the expression "mahehā."

The meaning is that just as the great earth, when struck by a single footstep, simultaneously meets with destruction along with its many long-cherished hopes and its wealth of resources due to a reversal of fortune, so it is here. || 22 ||
My husband has died, my own children are no more, I have traveled to a wretched land, I am fallen into misfortune,
I am born of a low birth, and I am in great distress.
O, I am manifest fear; I am the great calamity! || 23 ||

Now, lamenting for herself, she says: "With my lord dead," etc. My own son has quickly perished; I am wretched and impoverished. I am in a great calamity, in a perilous situation. Moreover, O friends, I am indeed fear personified.
The superimposition of non-difference in the statement "I am Mahādeva" is for the purpose of highlighting excellence. || 23 ||
Of pride arising from the insults of the lowly,
of one whose wife is overcome by hunger,
and of grief whose course is unstoppable in its occurrence—
I am wretched, without a refuge, and deprived of many dwellings.

"I am a protectorless woman, created by the Creator as a vessel for many things—such as pride arising from lowly insults, anger, grief that is irresistible in its course toward the maintenance of one's wife and dependents, and the matter of food—indeed, a home for all these. This is the implied meaning. || 24 ||
For one tormented by fate, deprived of kinsmen, deluded, and rooted in the great soil of mental anguish—
whatever his life may be, and whatever his death, it is a great calamity.
That for whose sake one gives up one's own life is the supreme [object]. || 25 ||

Now, censuring another person who is like himself, he says: "By fate," etc. For such a person—who has grown, that is, manifested, upon the ground characterized by great mental anguish (ādhi)—whatever his life may be, whatever his death, and whatever his great calamity; [all these are by fate].
Therefore, that which is devoid of self-life and empty of a soul by its own nature, such as stone and the like, is "uttama," meaning the most excellent or superior.
For one who is abandoned by people and dwells in an evil land,
endless sufferings arise,
crowded with thousands of branches and sap.
Like grass upon a mountain during the rains. || 26 ||
Of such a man who is deprived of his people and kinsmen, and whose livelihood and residence are in a wretched land; [the two] adjectives apply equally to both the man and the mountain. (26)
Having comforted his wife’s elderly nurse— who was speaking thus— with female servants, the king asked that woman:
"What has happened here, and who is she?"
"Who is your daughter, and who is your son? || 27 ||

"Lamenting" means wailing. "The old woman who was his own wife"—that is, the mother-in-law who had become an outcaste Pulkasī among those she had supported—was consoled by the female slaves; this is stated to indicate that she was no longer fit for direct conversation. || 27 ||
Then she, with eyes full of tears, said:
"This village is named Puṣpasaghoṣa."
In this world, my husband was a Puṣkasaka;
he had one daughter who was like the moon.
By the turn of fate, she found her husband, a king equal to Indra, who had come here by the power of destiny—
just as one finds a shattered jar of honey.
Like a single, wretched female crane in the forest. || 29 ||

"By the turn of fate," that is, by the power of fortune; "by the power of destiny," meaning by the force of adverse karma (*duradṛṣṭa*), she obtained a vessel of honey containing an auspicious rite—this is the ellipsis. A female camel, a she-ass, or a female camel (*karabhī*, *gardabhī*, or *uṣṭrī*) found a jar of honey whose lid was shattered and fallen off. || 29 ||
Having enjoyed pleasures with him for a very long time, she gave birth to sons and daughters;
they grew up in this hollow of the forest.
Like a creeping vine clinging to a tree. || 30 ||
The *tumbī* creeper is the *alābu* vine. || 30 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Lamentation of the Caṇḍālī," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* (Section on Origination) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the *Ārṣa* (Sage) tradition.
Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Lamentation of the Caṇḍālī," in the Section on Origination within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*. 120.
The one hundred and twenty-first canto. Caṇḍālī said:
"O lord of men, after some time had passed in this village..."
There occurred a terrifying suffering due to drought, which shattered the human spirit.
Having heard that, when Lavaṇa arrived at his home in astonishment,
the resolution reached through the words of Vasiṣṭha is here recounted, as well as that of Rāma.
The suffering of famine caused by lack of rain; that by which men are broken. (1)
Due to this great suffering, all those people of the village departed and went far away; they have all met their death. || 2 ||
The state of the five elements is death. || 2 ||
Therefore, O Lord, we who are here are empty and partakers of suffering;
O gentle one, we grieve with noble tears that wash away the streams from our eyes. (3)

Because of that death of Bandhu and because of the famine, we—with tears, with tears—[are as if] with a stream of tears flowing as if from a mouthful of water taken; [we are] with a stream of tears. In the reading *sadbāṣpāḥ*, it is an adjective qualifying "we" (*vayam*). || 3 ||
Having heard this from the mouth of the woman, the king was struck with amazement;
looking at the faces of his ministers, he became as if fixed in a painting.
He reflected further upon that unsurpassed wonder;
thus, again and again, he became filled with amazement. (5)
The word "iti" indicates the multiplicity of the modes of questioning. || 5 ||
Having brought about the destruction of their suffering through appropriate gifts and honors, he, filled with compassion, was the one who knows the high and low of the desired worlds.
Of those people of the hamlet (*pakvaṇa*)—[the reading *pakvaṇa* appears everywhere in the printed edition]. || 6 ||
Having stayed there for a long time and reflected upon the courses of destiny, he returned home; saluted by the citizens, he entered his residence.
Of necessity and fate. || 7 ||
In the morning, at that place in the assembly hall, the king asked me, filled with wonder:
"O sage, how can a dream be such as this—a matter of direct perception? (8)
"Seen directly"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 8 ||
Because it was stated according to the actual state of things,
that doubt of his was driven from his heart, like a cloud from the sky by the wind.
That question of his was answered by me, in accordance with reality and according to the true nature of things, and thus resolved—from heaven and from the intermediate space. 9.
Thus, O Raghava, this great ignorance, which causes delusion, quickly brings the non-existent into the state of existence, and thoroughly reduces the existent to non-existence. (10)
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brāhmaṇa, how can you speak thus? How has a dream attained the state of reality? This matter is like a grand delusion; it does not fade from my mind."

"Reality" (*satyatvam*) means the fitness for experience during the waking state. In the reading "this object is like a grand delusion," the phrase "it does not slip from my throat"—which is a point of doubt—must be supplied as the response. However, in the reading "O Blessed One, this is that very doubt," the meaning is clear. || 11 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
All this indeed occurs within ignorance, O Rāghava,
just as the appearance of cloth is seen in jars, or as in dreams, delusions, and the like.
He establishes the very possibility [of this] with the words beginning "In jars," etc. (verse 12).
The distant appears as if near, like a mountain within a mirror;
the long seems to become swift, just as the night becomes excellent [at dawn]. 13.
It was like a night spent in a most excellent and peaceful sleep. || 13 ||
And it comes to pass that it is impossible, just like one's own death in a dream;
though non-existent, it appears as if existent, like the movement through the sky in dreams.
That which is well-established moves excessively during a delusion, like the turning of the earth; that which is immovable comes to appear as moving, like a mind agitated by intoxication. (15)
"Susthita" means steady. "Bhrame" means in wandering. By the word "citta," that which is perceived by it is indicated. || 15 ||

Whatever the mind, enveloped by latent impressions (vāsanā), intensely contemplates, that it immediately experiences in that very way; there is nothing that exists [for it] nor anything that does not exist.
The very moment the false knowledge consisting of egoism and the like has arisen,
at that very moment the beginningless, middleless, and endless nature of delusion is said to have emerged.
Infinite extent and incalculability. || 17 ||
By the power of appearance alone, everything revolves:
a moment attains the state of an eon, and an eon becomes a moment. (18)
A creature with a perverted mind perceives itself as a sheep;
yet, by the power of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that sheep assumes the state of a lion. (19)
One's own self as a sheep or a ram. || 19 ||
Unevenness, delusion, ignorance, infatuation, egoism, and so forth are all equal,
because they are the causes for the full attainment of the fruits of mental perversion.
Like the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit, worldly activities of great undertaking coincide with one another spontaneously through the power of mental impressions (*vāsanā*). (21)

And thus, with the intention that even though there is no difference in their being imagined, the worldly convention of "truth" and "falsity" proceeds solely on the basis of correspondence and non-correspondence, and not through an investigation into ultimate reality, he says:
"like the 'crow-and-palm' [coincidence]. || 21 ||
Whatever occurred previously in the salt-mining village of a certain king has appeared to his mind, whether it be true or false. (22)
He then states the manner in which there is a correspondence regarding the conduct of Lavaṇa with the words "vṛttam" (the event).

The meaning is that whatever had previously occurred in the hamlet—such as the marriage of a Cāṇḍālī and so forth—that appeared in Lavaṇa’s mind as his own thought; thus, it is a delusion of correspondence. || 22 ||
Just as the mind forgets even an extensive mental action once performed, so too it certainly remembers what was done as if it had not been done. 23.
With the intention that even the recollection of what was never experienced is not a defect— just like the forgetting of what was experienced— he says, "he forgets.
Although in Lavaṇa’s case there was only an experience during the delusion and no actual memory,
nevertheless, even the internal distinction between experience, memory, and so forth, does not [constitute a flaw], because it is merely a mental construction (kalpanāmātra).
This was stated in this manner in order to indicate that [the work] is capable of withstanding critical inquiry. || 23 ||
Likewise, even an ordinary person perceives in a dream that he has not eaten when he has eaten, or that he has traveled to another country. (24)
In the village of Puṣkasa near the Vindhya mountains, such was his legal proceeding;
it appeared to him just like a story from the past in a dream. (25)

With the intention that even the temporal sequence of appearance and correspondence is not established because it is a mere conceptual construction, he says [the following] in two verses beginning with "vindhya": "of that salt" (tasya lavaṇasya). || 25 ||
Or rather, that very same dream-delusion which was quickly witnessed by Lavaṇa has now entered the consciousness of the Puṣkasa of the Vindhya mountains.
The aesthetic charm (*lāvaṇī*) ascended to the intuition (*pratibhā*) of the Puṣkasa of Vindhya;
and the consciousness (*saṃvit*) of the Puṣkasa of Vindhya ascended to the heart of the king. (27)

With the intention that the postulation of a distinction in manifestation (*pratibhā*) is likewise unnecessary—since it is possible for that which has arisen in one place to appear in both—he says: "Lāvaṇī. This is *lāvaṇī*, belonging to salt (*lavaṇa*). The word division is: "ubhayatra ārūḍhā" (ascended in both). || 27 ||
Just as the mental impression known as speech occurs similarly for many people,
so too do time, place, and action occur even in a dream.
He provides an illustration for the correspondence between the appearance and its object with the word "yathā" (just as). Just as the speech of many poets,

which expresses the meaning of a poetic work fashioned from mental imagination, sometimes becomes similar— meaning there is a correspondence both in words and in meaning— even so it is in the case of a dream consisting of the delusion of a *lavaṇapulkasa*.
The meaning is that it comes into being. || 28 ||
Its existence is established through its appearance within the course of worldly transaction;
for the existence of all things does not exist apart from cognition. (29)
If so, is that course of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) absolutely non-existent? No; he says: "worldly transaction" (*vyavahāra*).
He states that the existence of all things is due solely to the existence of the consciousness (*cit*) which is their substrate, and not independently: "existence" (*sattā*) || 29 ||
It appears as both consciousness and its opposite, like a wave in the union of waters;
it exists as the past, present, and future, just as a tree resides within a seed.

The word "vā" is used in the sense of "iva" (like). The meaning is that the very existence of consciousness, when it extends through the manifold of the past, present, and future, appears as if distinct from consciousness itself—just as a wave appears [distinct] in water, or a tree [appears distinct] in a seed. || 30 ||
Its existence and non-existence are established as being neither existent nor non-existent;
for it is truly existent through consciousness, and non-existent through the absence of consciousness.

Regarding that existence which is other than [mere] cognition: its being an existent arises from the perception of it as an existent by the faculty of sight, whereas its being composed of non-existence arises from the lack of such perception. Thus, the meaning is that its existence and non-existence are dependent upon erroneous cognition. || 31 ||
Ignorance does not exist as anything at all, just as oil and the like do not exist in sand;
for what state other than being gold could there be for a bracelet apart from its nature as gold? (32)

With the intention that the object of delusion, being nothing but ignorance (*avidyā*), results in non-existence itself, he says "no" (*na*). The meaning is: could it be a real entity (*pada*)? No, it cannot. || 32 ||
A connection between ignorance and the reality of the self is not tenable;
for a connection is clearly observed, through one's own experience, only between things that are similar. (33)
To the question, "Why would an object not exist there due to its connection with another object? he replies: "By ignorance" (avidyayā). || 33 ||
The connection between a bird and wood and so forth, which arises from the conjunction of the similar and the dissimilar, does not result in mutual experience; it is merely a single vibration.

The connection between lac and wood, which arises from the combination of earthiness and fluidity, is not fit to serve as an example for the relationship between two dissimilar things; for that [connection] is merely the vibration, the play, of that single ignorance alone—this is the meaning. || 34 ||

Everything consists of the ultimate reality; just as, by that [consciousness], stones and other such things are perceived equally through cognition due to the power of their connection [with it]. (35)

If, however, [the objects] were admitted to consist solely of consciousness (*cinmaya*), then a connection with consciousness would be possible through their being equal; thus he says: "This [world] consists of the supreme. Just as, in whatever manner they consist of the supreme reality, by that reason they are equal to consciousness; therefore, by virtue of that connection, they are perceived—that is, they are manifested—by consciousness. This is the meaning. || 35 ||
When all things existing in the world consist of pure consciousness and pure being,
then they shine forth in mutual relation through the stability of one's own self-experience.
He states the defect even in that position with the words "when" (yadā).
At that time, because they abide in one's own experience, they shine by the very power of self-luminosity, and not by the power of a connection with another consciousness.
The meaning is that, in the case of a lamp’s own manifestation, there is no dependence on a connection with another lamp. || 36 ||
A continuous connection between dissimilar things is not possible;
nor is mutual experience possible without a reciprocal connection. (37)
Having already stated the two alternatives, he explains them again clearly with two verses, beginning with "na saṃbhavati" (it is not possible). || 37 ||

When a similar object [the reading *sadaṃśe* is also found] attains oneness with it in an instant, consciousness projects a single form; this occurs precisely because of that oneness, and not otherwise. (38)

In the second alternative, because there is an absence of even an atom-sized differentiating non-conscious element (*acid-aṃśa*), the result is simply the self-luminosity of the partless Brahman; with this intention, it was said: "Having attained oneness in an instant, [one becomes] pure. (38)

241. Consciousness arises as the union of the conscious and the object of consciousness; consciousness arises from the two forms of the seer and the seen. (The reading *ciccetyacititārūpadṛśyayodeti cetanaḥ* is in accordance with the commentary.)
"Inert matter, when joined with inert matter, becomes a solid mass of inert matter;
yet, because of their distinct characteristics, the identity of consciousness and inert matter can never occur anywhere. (39)

The experience of the arising of the triad—the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing—within the consciousness of the deluded, by way of the visible [object], cannot be established by assuming a relationship of non-difference between consciousness and the insentient;
with this intention, he says: "Consciousness... (verse 39).
The two aspects of consciousness (cit) and the insentient (ajaḍa) are distinct; they never meet anywhere.
Because it is of the nature of consciousness, the apprehension of consciousness occurs through the apprehension of consciousness alone, which constitutes true perception.

Nor can it be established by resorting to a relationship of difference; thus he says, "consciousness and the insentient. Nor can it be established even by adopting the position that there is a relationship between consciousness and those things consisting of consciousness; thus he says, "because they consist of consciousness."

The meaning is that even if a perception of consciousness were possible through similarity, since there is no differentiator (bhedaka), the knowability [of consciousness] is not established; therefore, the division into the seen and the seeing is untenable. || 40 ||
For these [objects] such as wood and stone are not of the nature of consciousness;
indeed, one object is experienced by being transformed by another object. (41)

[Objection: "But surely, even though there is equality in being insentient (*jaḍatva*), just as wood, stone, and clay have a connection by virtue of being components of a single house, or as there is a connection between the tongue and taste despite their commonality in being watery (*āpyatva*), so too, even though they are equal in being consciousness (*cittva*), let there be a connection between the seer (*dṛk*) and the seen (*dṛśya*). To this, he says: "Wood, etc."—the insentient objects such as wood and the like.
The meaning is that [the self] is experienced as undergoing transformation into the form of objects such as a house, and not as consciousness (cit). || 41 ||
Know that the tasting of flavors occurs by the tongue alone, arising from a homogeneous and pure source;
understand that this connection is a state of identity, for it does not exist between two dissimilar things. (42)

The connection is as follows: the experience of taste, which consists of a mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) of the gustatory faculty, is perceived as undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmin*), arising clearly and stainlessly from the tongue and the taste-objects, which are of the same class (*sajātīya*).
For a relation indeed consists in the unification of two things that are slightly non-different, and that [unification] is difficult to establish in either of the two positions; thus he says:
And unity. || 42 ||

Therefore, because of that [consciousness], the insentient stone and so forth are not considered insentient; rather, it is determined by consciousness that consciousness itself takes the form of the stone, the wall, and so on. (43)

The phrase "of the insentient and the sentient" connects with what precedes. He states what results from this: "By that," etc. Thus, being limited [by ignorance], it has attained a state of oneness and produces the delusion of the seer, the seen, and so forth;
for everything—including wood, stones, and the rest—is in reality composed of the Supreme Reality. (43–44)
But from the perspective of ultimate truth, she has attained a state of oneness. || 44 ||
Through that very nature, its connection [the reading *tatsambandham* is correct] is perceived as an object of sight;
everything, rich in all modes, appears as if infinite through effort. (45)

If that is so, how is it observed that wood, stone, and the like—which are in essence the ultimate consciousness (*paramārthacidātman*)—have a connection with the state of being a house? To this he says: "by means of that nature" (*tadātmanā*). The meaning is that their connection is observed only through an imagined form (*kalpitarūpa*), and not through their actual conscious nature (*vāstavacidrūpa*). For this reason, [the world] is infinite...
Brahman alone, enriched with all modes of existence, shines as if it were everything; for that reason, the universe is pure Being—this is the connection with what follows. || 45 ||
O best among the knowers of reality, know that this entire universe is indeed nothing but pure Being;
for one who is established in the non-abandonment of existence, the universe [appears] through hundreds of thousands of delusions.
The relinquishing of non-existence and the non-grasping of falsity—that alone is the wonder of consciousness. || 46 ||
The wonder of consciousness is filled [with all], yet nothing at all is filled;
for men, the cities of their own volitions do not move against one another. (47)
Thus, it is established that there is no obstruction of space or time within the creations;
for it is only when there is a perception of duality that the state of being a creation arises, along with the emergence of delusions such as "I-ness" and so forth.
Just as there is the delusion of bracelets and the like when gold is set aside, so too the delusion of bracelets and the like exists within the gold; from place to place, and from birth to birth.

The delusion regarding bracelets and the like within gold is indeed false; for it [the bracelet] derives its location from the very location of the gold, and its birth and existence from the very birth and existence of the gold—this is the implied meaning. || 49 ||
When seeing and the seen are abandoned, ignorance does not exist separately at all;
it is like pure gold, which remains one despite the great diversity of bracelets and other ornaments.
Just as gold remains one and the same when the perception of distinctions such as bracelets and other ornaments is abandoned, so it is in this case;
such is the meaning. || 50 ||
Because this creation is one with consciousness, it is entirely non-existent; like a variegated army made of clay, it is merely clay, just as an object fashioned from clay is nothing but clay.

Because the manifestation of awakening is one, it brings the universe—which is existent—into non-existence, that is, it leads it to the state of non-being; or else, it brings the universe—which is non-existent—into existence, that is, it leads it to the state of being identical with the existent. || 51 ||
Water is one, though appearing as waves and the like; wood is one, though appearing as carved figures;
clay alone is one, though appearing as jars and the like; Brahman is one, while the three worlds are but an illusion.
Within the relationship between the seen and the seer, that which is the true nature of the seer—devoid of the seer, the act of seeing, and the seen—is indeed this supreme reality. (53)

Just as the nature of clay is extracted when threaded through jars and other objects, so too the pure consciousness that is the witness (*sākṣin*)—which is threaded through the triad of the seer, the seen, and the seeing—is revealed by the removal of that triad; this is shown in the verse beginning with "In the relationship" (*saṃbandhe*).
That which was previously shown as the Supreme Brahman is indeed this very extracted nature of the inner self (*pratyak*); thus, the meaning of the sentence is indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*).
That which is to be seen has been shown. || 53 ||
When the mind has moved from one object to another, that form of consciousness which exists in the interval—awake, conscious, and reflective—become ever absorbed in that. 54.
When was the emptiness of the threefold enclosure (tripuṭī-śūnyatā) established for him? To this he says: "From space" (deśāt), which has been explained previously.
That which is your eternal form—neither waking, nor dreaming, nor deep sleep; neither insentient nor inert—be always absorbed in that.
"Insentient" means devoid of mental activity; "composed of that" means having that as its sole essence. || 55 ||
Indeed, that heart of yours is like a stone, for it has abandoned all but its single quality of dullness; therefore, whether unagitated or agitated, always become one with That.
The heart of stone is solid, meaning it is a single mass of consciousness; one who is unagitated is established in samādhi, while one who is agitated is engaged in worldly activity.
For anyone here, nothing whatsoever arises nor does anything perish;
whether unagitated or agitated, remain at ease as you please.
Now, one might ask: how can one who is agitated abide in that state of identity with the Self? To this he says: "of someone" (kasyacit).
The intention is that even during the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), one should follow only the vision of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). || 57 ||
The person does not desire nor does he hate anything whatsoever in the body anywhere;
remain established in yourself, free from anxiety, and do not fall into the functions of the body.
Having stated it generally, he speaks specifically: "No. Here, "puruṣa" refers to the Self (ātman). || 58 ||
Just as one intent on the affairs of a village that is yet to be reached does not dwell upon those affairs,
so too, having attained the nature of reality, do not dwell within the fluctuations of the mind.

Just as the mind’s natural non-attachment toward future objects of worldly discourse is self-evident, so too must it be cultivated toward the present through the vision of their falsity; with this intention, he says: "The future... (verse 59).
Just as a person from another land, just as a piece of wood, just as a stone—so too, behold the mind as being no-mind by its very nature. (60)

The meaning is: just as a man situated in a distant land is as good as non-existent even though he exists, and just as wood and stone, though present nearby, are incapable of attachment, pride, and so forth due to their lack of consciousness—so too should one view the mind. For, when one discerns through the Self—that is, by means of the nature of the Self—it is simply the absence of mind (acittatā).
The meaning is that it is established by the experience of the wise; the elision of the suffix *tal* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). || 60 ||
Just as there is no water in a stone, and just as there is no fire in water, so too the mind does not exist within its own self; how then could it exist in the Supreme Self? (61)
He states that very point clearly with the words "just as" (yathā). || 61 ||
Thinking that whatever is done anywhere by one who does not perceive anything at all has not been done, one should transcend the mind.
Since the mind is not a real entity, the effects of the mind are even more non-existent; thus he says: "That which is being perceived... and so forth.
Why does one not follow the example of a border-dwelling barbarian who conforms to a mind that is ultimately not his own? (63)
Intending to show that the following of an impure mind by the pure self is to be abandoned because it is improper, he says:

"extreme," etc. "Paryantāḥ" refers to border regions and those who dwell there. This is based on the Vedic scripture: "Therefore, one should not go to birth, nor should one go to the end; lest I should follow after evil and death."
The sense is that following the practices of the Mlecchas is prohibited. || 63 ||
Disregarding from afar that mind which is like a wild beast, remain established in yourself, free from anxiety; you have been rendered as inert as mud. 64.
Like an image or the like fashioned and constructed from mud or clay. || 64 ||
"My mind truly does not exist; it knows today as if I were dead.
Having become thus resolute, remain as motionless as a stone statue. (65)
"It does not exist at all" is the primary interpretation; "it perceives today that which was real and dead as being [present]" is the secondary interpretation. || 65 ||
In the state of discernment, our mind does not exist; you are therefore devoid of it in reality.
Why then are you tormented by that which is useless and brings only misfortune?
In observation—namely, in the observation of the self and the observation of the mind. || 66 ||
For those of feeble intellect who have been rendered senseless by the non-existent yakṣa of the mind and brought under its power, a cry has arisen from the moon. 67.
The thunderbolt is the fire of lightning. || 67 ||
Having cast the mind far away, remain firm as you truly are;
be liberated from mental constructs and endowed with the supreme method.
By means of reasoning, reflection, meditative cultivation, and concentration. || 68 ||
Fie upon those who follow after the unreal, whose minds take on the form of what is untrue—those for whom time has been spent solely in the futile task of attempting to kill the sky! 69.
This is for the purpose of censuring the deluded, removing their distress, and encouraging those who are qualified. || 69 ||
With a mind completely dissolved, O one of great majesty, become one who has reached the further shore of existence; become one whose self is stainless.
Though investigated for a very long time, [the goal] was not found.
Within the self that is free from impurity, there exists a certain mental self.
Being of great power and skilled in the awakening to reality, first become one whose mind is utterly dissolved;

then, being of stainless self through the awakening to reality, go beyond the ocean of worldly existence. To reinforce the stated meaning, Vasiṣṭha speaks of his own experience purified by inquiry, beginning with the words "suciram" (for a very long time): "By me, even for a very long time..."

Thus, although it was investigated for the sake of attaining the true nature of the mind, not even the slightest stain consisting of the mind was found within the stainless Self; therefore, become firm in the conviction that [such a stain] simply does not exist—this is the meaning of my words. || 70 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Non-existence of the Mind," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* (Section on Origination) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Non-existence of the Mind," in the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the *Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The One Hundred and Twenty-Second Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
At the very moment of birth, by a person whose intellect has only just begun to unfold, it is thus [perceived]:
One should be intent upon the company of the virtuous. || 1 ||
Here, at the outset, the sequence of the arising of the stages of knowledge for the person is described;
following that is the awakening [of Rāma] through the removal of his grief, delusion, and so forth. (1)
Therein, wishing to explain the sequence of the stages of knowledge (*jñānabhūmikā*) in prose, he states the first section concerning the means for attaining it:
"First" means by one whose intellect has slightly blossomed through desireless actions (*niṣkāmakarma*) performed either in this life or in another birth—that is, by one with a purified mind. || 1 ||
This torrent of the river of ignorance, falling in an unceasing flow, cannot be crossed except through contact with the scriptures and virtuous people. || 2 ||

Through association with the virtuous (satsaṅga), the connection with the spiritual scriptures (adhyātmaśāstra) is accomplished, accompanied by the attainment of the fourfold means (sādhanacatuṣṭaya).
With the intention that this itself is the first stage (bhūmikā), he says "uninterrupted" and so forth. || 2 ||
From that isolation, there arises in the person an inquiry into what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted. || 3 ||
Then he reaches the stage of discernment called "the desire for the auspicious" (śubhecchā). [The reading "he has descended" (avatīrṇo bhavati) is also found. || 4 ||
Then, by virtue of seclusion, there is investigation. || 5 ||
By means of that victory, he shows the entry into the second stage with the words "Then," and so forth. || 5 ||

For one who abandons improper latent impressions (*asamyag-vāsanā*) through right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), the mind attains attenuation due to the cessation of the perception of worldly existence (*saṃsāra-bhāvanā*);
from that victory, there is entry into the third stage (*bhūmikā*). Thus he says, beginning with "through right knowledge" (*samyag-jñānena*), etc. (verse 6).
By that, he has descended to the stage of discernment called "thinness of mind. || 7 ||
At the very moment that right knowledge arises for the yogin, at that very moment there is the attainment of pure being (sattva). || 8 ||
He states the manner of entering the fourth stage: "As soon as... (verse 8).

When, by virtue of that [knowledge], his latent impressions (vāsanā) have become attenuated, at that very moment he is said to be "unattached," meaning he is no longer bound by the fruit of action. || 9 ||
He states the entry into the fifth [stage] with the words "by virtue of that" (*tadvaśāt*). He explains that name [of the stage] with the words "by means of the fruit of karma.
Then, by virtue of the attenuation of those [defilements], one practices the attenuation of cultivation regarding the unreal. (10)

He describes the descent into the sixth stage with the word "atha" (now). When external objects are unreal, through the thinning of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) by remaining constantly inward-turned— [the reading is *sadaivāntarmukhatayā*]—
and through the accumulation of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the identity of Brahman, the external object gradually...
The meaning is "forgetting. || 10 ||
As long as one, even while not acting and not engaging in worldly affairs,
remains situated within one's own self— [the reading is *svātmanyavakṣīṇa*]—
one does not perceive external objects, despite acting upon them, because of the power of practice and the exhaustion of the mind (*manastva*).

He does not serve with an objective referent, nor does he covet, because his latent impressions are attenuated; being merely deluded, like one who has just awakened from sleep, he performs what is to be done. || 11 ||

Regarding how long that practice lasts, he says: "as long as... [meaning] even while not acting, though established in samādhi; even while engaged in worldly activity, though emerged from it; and even while performing external acts such as bathing and eating, one does not see. For this very reason, one does not serve with attachment to an object, nor does one covet it, nor does one remember it. One is like a fool, a child, a madman, or one who has just awakened from sleep.
One should perform such acts as bathing and eating according to the will of another. || 11 ||
With his mind thus refined, he ascends to the meditative cultivation of the stages of yoga. || 12 ||

With his mind refined through practice and his consciousness made one with the essence of the most subtle Brahman, he—by means of that [practice] characterized as described above—ascends to the stage of yoga known as *bhāvanā*, which is called the "non-contemplation of objects"; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Having practiced for several years with the mind thus dissolved within, even while continuing to perform all external activities, one abandons objective conceptualization (*bhāvanā*), becomes the Fourth Self (*turyātman*), and is then called "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*).
He describes the sequence of entering the seventh stage as follows: "with the mind thus dissolved within. Thus.

With his mind dissolved within the Brahman internally in the manner described, even when occasionally performing external activities such as bathing and eating merely through the will of another or for the sake of duty, he abandons that mental preoccupation in every respect. He himself becomes the Fourth State (turyātman). This pertains to the mind up until the sixth stage (bhūmikā).

The sense is that while there is a slight persistence of effort when stability in the form of Brahman is attained, on the seventh stage (*bhūmikā*), however, because that [effort] has ceased entirely, there is a natural establishment; this is the distinction. He alone is called "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*). || 13 ||
He does not rejoice in what has been attained, nor does he grieve for what has not been attained; he simply follows what has come to him, free from all anxiety. (14)

Although those who have attained direct realization even on the previous stages are indeed *jīvanmuktas*, nevertheless, because they may occasionally experience the touch of pleasant or unpleasant things brought about by powerful *prārabdha* karma, they do not possess the primary bliss of *jīvanmukti*; however, this is the case in the seventh stage.

With the intention that the *prārabdha-karma* (commenced karma), being overwhelmed by the exceedingly intense excellence of merit born from the maturation of yoga, remains merely as an appearance in the activities of life and is no longer capable of producing joy, sorrow, and the like, he states its definition in a verse: "He does not rejoice," etc. (14).
O Raghava, you too have understood everything that is to be known regarding the inner nature of all things;
indeed, your latent impressions (vāsanā) have become attenuated in respect to all worldly activities.

But because your mind is extremely pure, you have realized the reality of the inner self (pratyagātmatattva) through your own inquiry while still on the second stage; with this intention, he says: "By you. || 15 ||
Whether your activity transcends the body or you remain within the body, do not give way to grief or joy; you are the Self, free from all affliction.
His functioning always transcends the body, yet he remains eternally established in samādhi; though abiding in the body, he engages in worldly affairs for the sake of sustaining the world.
In you, the Self—white, pure, all-pervading, and eternally risen—whence, O Rāma, can there be pain and pleasure? Whence can there be death and birth? (17)
On that site, which is self-luminous, clear, and stainless. || 17 ||
Why do you, who have no kinsman, grieve for the sorrows of kinsmen?
For when this self stands alone and without a second, what indeed are kinsmen to it? 18.

Even when grief caused by death, birth, and so forth has been overcome through self-knowledge, how is the grief born from association with kinsmen to be conquered? To this he says: "He who has no kinsman" (verse 18).
Only a collection of atoms is seen in the body;
because it undergoes change through differences of place and time, the self neither arises nor perishes. (19)

Is it the body of kinsmen that deserves grief, or the self? He says "not the first" with the words "is seen": [the body] having been reduced to mere ashes. Since it is a collection of atoms and is insentient, it does not deserve grief; this is the meaning. He says "not the second" with the words "deśa... (verse 19).
Since you are imperishable, why do you grieve, thinking "I shall perish"?
For what kind of destruction could there be for the Self, which is pure and the abode of immortality? (20)
Just as when a jar is reduced to shards, the space within the jar is not destroyed, so too, even when this body perishes, [the Self] does not perish. (21)
The self does not perish; this is the remainder [of the statement]. || 21 ||
Just as the heat does not perish when the river of a mirage has dried up, so too the Self does not perish when the body is destroyed. 22.
Why does this desire arise within you? It is a meaningless delusion. Being non-dual, what second object could the Self possibly desire? 23.
O Raghava, whatever is audible, tangible, visible, tastable, or olfactory—there is nothing in the world that exists apart from the Self. (24)
All these powers, being omnipotent, reside entirely within that Self; they abide in the manifest, pervasive [Self] just as emptiness abides in space. || 25 ||
[Objection: "But surely, like the powers of the delusion of a mirage in the heat of the sun, the powers of the world would then exist separately.
To this he replies: "The powers... (verse 25).
O Rāghava, this world, which is called the ornament of the three realms, has arisen from the mind;
it is produced here by birth through a threefold process, causing delusion.
If it is asked, "In that case, what is the seed for the sprouting of the world which is absolutely non-existent?", he replies that it is the mind itself, as was stated previously:
"When the pacification of the mind—known as the destruction of latent impressions—is accomplished, this illusion, known as the destruction of karma, utterly perishes. (27)

For this very reason, he says "the mind" (manaḥ) to show that its destruction follows from the destruction of the citta; for [the term] denotes the abode of the destruction of the powers of action, such as the capacity for activity. || 27 ||
O Rāghava, exert yourself to sever this latent impression (*vāsanā*), which is the rope for the mechanical contrivance mounted upon this formidable water-wheel of *saṃsāra*. (28)

At the water-wheel (*āraghaṭṭa*); that is to say, at the peg in the middle of the lower stone of the grinding machine. It is "mounted," meaning it is fastened to the edge of a horizontal beam. For this very reason, the rope has the quality of carrying the upper grinding stone of the machine. To illustrate: the earth is like the lower stone of the machine, and Mount Meru is like its peg.
The meaning is that the world is perceived as a wheel of light, like a machine of upward-facing stones, held fast by latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
This ignorance is the giver of great delusion;
but when fully understood, it is called the Infinite, the bestower of happiness and the giver of Brahman. (29)
Having come here to this worldly existence as a sport after enjoying the state of Brahmā, one again remembers Brahmā alone and dissolves into Brahmā itself. (30)

The syntactical connection is as follows: having experienced saṃsāra, by means of the knowledge of Brahman—which has become his own sport—and having recollected Brahman alone, he dissolves into Brahman itself. || 30 ||
O Rāghava, from Śiva— who is formless, immeasurable, and free from affliction—
all beings have arisen, just as manifestations arise from light.
Just as a multitude of lines [appears] on a leaf, as a network of ripples in water, as bracelets and the like in gold, and as heat and so forth in fire; || 32 ||
The multitude of lines is the network of veins. || 32 ||
Thus, these three worlds exist in the form of that very creative contemplation;
they are situated within it alone, born from it alone, and are indeed identical to it.
Or [it resides] in Brahman, which consists of meditative cultivation and is delimited by latent impressions (vāsanā). || 33 ||
That very Self of all beings is called Brahman;
when He is known, the entire world is known, for He is the Knower in the three worlds. (34)

He says, "In that [Self], by the knowledge of one, all is known," and "That is the Knower. The intention is based on such scriptural passages as, "There is no other seer than this," and so forth. || 34 ||

For the sake of conventional usage in the treatises, names such as "Consciousness" (cit), "Brahman," and "Self" (ātman) have been devised for this [Reality] of vast form by those of perfected minds. (35)
When there is contact between the objects and the senses, that which is free from joy and resentment is indeed this pure experience; it is this very self, the imperishable consciousness.

Even when there is a fortuitous conjunction of the sense organs with pleasant and unpleasant objects, because of the certain conviction that these are illusory, one is free from joy and resentment; this very experience, characterized as described above, is the well-known Self—that is, the state of being liberated while living—and not the nature of transmigratory existence experienced by the deluded. This is the meaning. || 36 ||
This world, which is clearer than even space, is reflected as if separate within that Self of Consciousness, solely by virtue of its own inherent manifestation.
To substantiate what was stated—that [the Self] is "devoid of joy and resentment"—he says, beginning with "In that, this...

Within its own expanse, within its own interior, the world appears as if separate, as if it were something else, like a reflection. Since it is impossible for the pure witness to distinguish between the pleasant and unpleasant aspects of that [world], for the sake of such distinction, one must look into the interval beyond both of them.

The meaning is that the internal organ, the intellect (buddhi), reflects [objects], and it is that very intellect which undergoes those states such as greed and delusion through the conceptualizations of the pleasant and the unpleasant; the Self (ātman), however, does not do so. || 37 ||
For greed, delusion, and the like cast them down by means of what is unreal, distinct from that [Buddha];
and they [the virtues] likewise cast him down by means of that very same [unreal], distinct from those [defilements]. (38)

And that world, along with the intellect and the greed, delusion, and so forth produced by it, are reflected in that conscious Self (cidātman) as if they were non-existent through their mutual distinction; thus, in the ultimate sense, they are of the very nature of that Self. For the meaning is this: just as mountains, forests, rivers, and so on, which are seen within a mirror, do not exist apart from the mirror itself.
O Rāma, for you who are indeed bodiless and whose form is non-conceptual consciousness, from where has this delusion arisen—delusion that stems from shame, fear, and despair? (39)

And thus, he states with the words "of one who is indeed bodiless," etc., that fear, despondency, and so forth are appropriate only for the deluded who possess the notion of the body as the self, but not for you.

O you who are bodiless, why are you overcome by these unreal constructs such as shame and the like, which arise from the body? Why do you, like a fool of poor intellect, succumb to such mental fluctuations? (40)

When the body undergoes fragmentation, there is no destruction even for one who lacks right vision; how much less so for one of sound understanding, whose nature is the indivisible consciousness? (41)
Even if it falls upon the path of darkness, the mind does not have its coming and going obstructed;
that which is called "mind" should be known as the Person (Puruṣa), and not the body. 42.

To demonstrate that even for one who lacks right vision there is no destruction [of the mind], he explains the nature of the conscious self (*cit-tman*) as distinct from the body, beginning with the words "it would fall": "That mind which, due to its independence of movement, would fall everywhere— even upon the path of the sun, though it is without support— [is not obstructed]."
The meaning is that the mind itself—characterized by such movements as going and coming—is to be understood as the "Person" (puruṣa), the transmigrating self, and not the body. || 42 ||
