Whether the body exists or not, O Rāma, it is the person alone who remains throughout the three worlds—whether conscious or unconscious; when the body is destroyed, he is not destroyed.
All these various sufferings that you perceive belong to the body; they do not belong to the ungraspable Self, which is consciousness.

Now, in order to demonstrate that the Self is not subject to saṃsāra, [the author] states—beginning with the words "Those which"—that even the mind is situated within the confines of the body, and thus the experience of pleasure and pain belongs to the body alone. || 44 ||
Since it has transcended the path of the mind and remains as if empty, how indeed can consciousness be grasped by either sufferings or pleasures? (45)
It is grasped; it is pervaded. || 45 ||
Having emerged from the cage of his destroyed body, he returned to his own true self,
which was his habitual latent impression (vāsanā), just as a bee returns to the sky from a lotus.
Now, one might ask: when the body has perished, where does the individual soul (*jīva*) go? To this he replies: "to its own abode, the Self" (*svāspadātmānam*).

This *jīva*, having abandoned the identification with the destroyed cage of the body, first goes to its own abode—the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is its own foundation. [As it is said: "The mind into breath, the breath into fire, the fire..."

The meaning of the scriptural statement "in the highest deity" is that, through the dissolution of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the mind and vital breath, one attains identity with the Lord who is the original prototype (bimba).
To the question "In that case, why is one not liberated?", he replies: "abhyastām" (to that which has been practiced).
The sense is that one is not liberated because knowledge that uproots the latent impressions of duality has not arisen. || 46 ||
If the reality of the self does not exist, then what indeed would be lost when this cage of a body perishes, O Rāma? Why do you grieve? (47)

If it is objected: "If the individual soul (jīva) is a reflection, then, since it cannot have an existence apart from its limiting adjunct (upādhi), it must be non-existent, and its destruction would follow upon the destruction of that adjunct," [the author replies: "Let it be so; nevertheless, you are not the individual soul. Therefore, whether that soul be non-existent or destroyed, grief on your part is not appropriate. Thus he says:
"Not non-existent" refers to that well-known reality of the Self in the form of the individual soul (jīva). || 47 ||
Meditate upon the Truth; do not allow yourself to experience delusion.
For you, whose nature is stainless, there is no desire whatsoever for a self that is free from longing.

In reality, however, the reflection is nothing other than the original object (*bimba*); for it is apprehended as a reflection only through the conceptualization of distinctions such as its entry into limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just like the original object itself. Furthermore, if the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) were an effect produced by an insentient adjunct, it would follow that it is itself insentient, which would result in the impossibility of the manifestation and experience of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Therefore, you are the individual soul (*jīva*), yet by the relinquishing of those adjuncts, you are truly Brahman alone.
Cultivate and realize delusion—the unreal and perishable state consisting of the body and so forth—which has been attained through error;
contemplate it as the light of the sun, for you are free from desire precisely because you are satisfied by the nature of the perfect Brahman.

In the conscious self (cidātman), which is the witness, impartial, pure, and free from conceptual construction, the worlds are reflected without desire, just as [images] are reflected in a mirror. (49)
To the question, "In that case, how is the accomplishment of creation and so forth possible for Him without desire?", he says: "Being the witness" (sākṣibhūte) || 49 ||
Within the Consciousness-Self—which is the witness, impartial, pure, and free from conceptual construction—the worlds appear of their own accord, like rays within a genuine gem. (50)
Just as there is a connection between a mirror and its reflection even against one's will, so too here the distinction and non-distinction between the Self and the world are established. (51)
Just as the activity of the world arises by the mere proximity of the sun,
so too this world is brought forth by the mere existence of Consciousness.
O Rāma, thus the grasping of this world-existence has ceased;
it has become like space even within your own minds.

"Piṇḍagraha" means having a formal, embodied form. "In this way" refers to the manner of instruction as previously described. "Of you" is a statement addressed to the listeners other than Rāma. || 53 ||
Just as light is the inherent nature of a lamp by its mere existence, so too is this worldly condition the inherent nature of the reality of consciousness (cittattva). 54.
Āloka means light. || 54 ||
In the beginning, the mind arose from the reality of the Supreme Self;
by it, this entire world was spread out through the nets of its own conceptual constructions.
Though empty, it is made empty by that [mind], just as space is made empty by space itself.
The state of being blue is that which possesses a most exquisitely radiant designation.
Concluding by summarizing the meaning of the detailed exposition,

he says "previously," and so forth: just as the sky, though empty and non-existent, manifests through the experience of all people a blueness that resembles a great vessel made of polished sapphire turned upside down.
The expression "the sky appears dark-blue" is a most beautiful verbal usage because it is suitable for figures such as simile (upamā) and poetic fancy (utprekṣā);
that which is thus "extended" or spread out is such a discourse, and by means of that, this world is [perceived] even by the mind—this is the meaning. || 55 ||
When the mind has dissolved through the destruction of volitional constructions,
the mists of delusion regarding saṃsāra vanish;
it shines forth with clarity, like the sky when autumn has arrived.
Pure consciousness alone is one, unborn, beginningless, endless, and internal.

For this very reason, he says "saṃkalpa... [and so on], because when the cause (nimitta) is removed, that which is caused by it (naimittika) is also removed, resulting in the establishment of the remaining pure self alone. "Mihikā" refers to frost. Just as one's own sky becomes clear when autumn has arrived, so too does the pure consciousness (cinmātra) remain within the nature of the innermost Self (pratyagātman). || 56 ||
At the very outset, the mind, whose nature is action, arises from volition; having approached the primordial nature of the Lotus-born,
it vainly expands this world of manifold names.
Like an innocent child imagining the body of a vetāla. || 57 ||

He shows that, just as in the conceptualization of the individual cycle of transmigration (*vyaṣṭi-bhrama-kalpanā*), so too in the conceptualization of the collective creation (*samaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi-kalpanā*), manifestation and disappearance are dependent solely upon the mind— by stating, "consisting of action" (*karmātmakam*).
The mind consists of the collective totality of the actions of all living beings and is primarily characterized by the power of collective activity (*samaṣṭi-kriyā-śakti*).

First, it arises—that is, it manifests. Then, from that reflection of consciousness, having approached and assumed the various primordial natures (prakṛtis) such as Brahmā and others which constitute the bodies of the Creator, it vainly—that is, pointlessly—extends or creates the world under various names by means of its volition; this is the meaning. || 57 ||
Unreal, yet appearing as real before one's eyes, it manifests again and then dissolves again;
the mind itself is consciousness, its body flashing forth from within that consciousness.
Just as there is a series of circles of water in the great ocean. || 58 ||

Therefore, the entire visible world—conceived through the distinctions of individual and collective forms—is merely the mind (*manas*); and since the mind is an effect of unreal ignorance (*ajñāna*), it is itself unreal. Thus, by way of the power of the existence and manifestation of the substrate and witness (*sākṣin*), which are real, there occurs the appearance and arising of that which is unreal. In this manner, [Brahman] is the illusory material cause (*vivartopādāna*) of the birth and so forth of the universe.

With the intention of establishing that the *tāṭasthya-lakṣaṇa* (indirect definition) of Brahman—by which Brahman itself, as the single essence of non-dual existence, consciousness, and bliss (*niṣprapañca-saccidānanda-ekarasa*), and as the full (*pūrṇa*), is indicated as the ultimate reality—is the intended purport of all scriptural texts concerning creation, he says: "consisting of the unreal" (*asanmaya*). Here, "the unreal" (*asat*) refers to ignorance (*ajñāna*), and "consisting of that" means being composed of it.

The mind, which has come about as a transformation of that [consciousness], itself perceives before it—as if it were real—the body of the world shimmering through its own expansion within the consciousness of its own substrate (the Witness-consciousness). The meaning is: just as in a full great ocean there is a series of unbounded circles of water established by the mere existence of that [ocean] itself.

Therefore, since everything that is merely perceived consists of words and is unreal, it is established that Brahman alone—the inner Self, which is of one essence, full, and unchanging—exists eternally. || 58 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second canto, titled "The Determination of Essential Nature," within the section on the Means to Liberation, spoken by the Divine Messenger, in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.

Thus [ends the work] by the venerable Rāmacandra Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Sarvajña Sarasvatī, who was himself the disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Sarvajña Sarasvatī.

The Exposition of Essential Nature in the Section on Origination, composed by the monk named Śrīmad Ānandabodhendrasarasvatī, disciple of the venerable feet of Śrīmad Gaṅgādharendra Sarasvatī, in the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second canto.
This chapter on Origination is completed.
